So when people turn away from this, soon deceived by the darkness of their own intention, they institute worship from themselves, magnificent indeed in appearance, but which has nothing beyond outward splendour that could move a person's mind with any sense of religion. For even if something remains that agrees with God's institutions, it is nevertheless adulterated by pretence and falsehood, while we, intent only on externals, depart the further from God the more stubbornly we cling to those things which he neither needs nor can be worshipped or honoured by. That such was the religion of the Jews in former times, the sermons of the Prophets teach, through whom God condemns and rejects even those sacred rites which he himself had handed down to their fathers, since they were empty of that faith which alone purifies the heart of man and commends us to God. The use of this place for us, therefore, is that, leaving human traditions far behind, we should worship God in spirit and truth, through faith in that only-begotten Son, Jesus Christ, by whose merits he has rightly been propitiated toward us. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXCVII.
units.tr: HOMILY 197.

units.la: Et aduocata turba dixit eis: Audite & intelligite. Non quod ingreditur in os polluit hominem, sed quod egreditur ex ore, hoc polluit hominem. Tunc accedentes discipuli eius dixerunt ei: Nosti Pharisaeos audito sermone isto offensos fuisse? Ipse vero respondens, dixit: Omnis plantatio, quam non plantauit Pater illius meus coelestis, eradicabitur. Sinite eos: duces sunt caeci caecorum. Porro si caecus caeco praeierit, ambo in foueam cadent.
units.tr: And when the crowd had been called together, he said to them: "Hear and understand. It is not what goes into the mouth that defiles a man, but what comes out of the mouth, that defiles a man." Then his disciples came and said to him: "Do you know that the Pharisees were offended when they heard this saying?" But he answered and said: "Every plant that my heavenly Father has not planted will be uprooted. Leave them alone; they are blind guides of the blind. And if a blind man leads a blind man, both will fall into a pit."

units.la: Postquam Dominus noster IESVS CHRISTVS grauiter respondit Scribis & Pharisaeis, qui discipulos eius accusabant, quod contra Seniorum traditionem non lotis prius manibus ad cibum sumendum accederent, & ea occasione docuit, hominum traditiones non inutiles modo, verum etiam noxias & perniciosas esse, eo quod corda a Deo auocent: nunc illis dimissis ad populum conuertitur, & ne discipulorum suorum facto, & corrupto de his Pharisaeorum iudicio sim, plices offendantur, illud excusat, & in quo nam hominis pollutio simul atq; purificatio consistat, docet: & hoc ipsum postea suis discipulis priuatim amplius explicat. Si causam quaeras, cur disputationem hanc a Scribis & Pharisaeis, qui doctrina & sanctitatis praecipuam exstimationem fusti uebant, ad rude vulgus transferat, haec est: Quod illi hypocritae erant, & in suis superstitionibus indurauerant, ut nullam admitterent institutionem, cum suas traditiones Verbo Dei praeferrent: in populo autem multi erant ex electorum numero & doctrina sana appetentes, de quibus dixerat: messem esse copiosam, & quorum ipsum miserebatur. Est ergo hoc memorabile exemplum, quo primum docemur, quam exosi sint Deo hypocritae, cum eos institutione indignos iudicet ipse, qui pro sua bonitate vult omnes homines saluos fieri, et in veritatis cognitione venire. Deinde simplicium & imperitorum cofolationi serviit, ne dubitet, si Deo cura esse, qui etiam ad tempus errare finit, tandem eos colligit, ac in viam reducit. Et confirmatur in praesenti gratulatio illa siue Ἀξιολογία Christi, qua gratias agit Patri, qui regni sui mysteria absconderit a sapientibus & intelligentibus: & re-uelarit ea infantibus. Debent etiam hinc exemplum petere doctores, quo discant, ita argui debere hypocritas impostores, vt interim simplices atq; rudes nequaquam negligant. Sunt autem loci huius partes duae: In priori cum populi turba publice, in altera cum discipulis suis agit priuatim.
units.tr: After our Lord Jesus Christ had sharply answered the Scribes and Pharisees, who accused his disciples of eating with unwashed hands, contrary to the tradition of the elders, he took the occasion to teach that human traditions are not only useless but also harmful and pernicious, because they turn hearts away from God. Now, having dismissed them, he turns to the people. Lest his disciples' conduct, and the Pharisees' corrupt judgment of it, cause offence to the simple, he excuses them and teaches where the defilement and the purification of a man consist. He later explains this more fully to his disciples in private. If you ask why he transfers this dispute from the Scribes and Pharisees, who claimed the highest reputation for learning and holiness, to the rude crowd, the answer is this: those men were hypocrites, hardened in their superstitions so that they admitted no instruction, since they preferred their own traditions to the Word of God. Among the people, however, were many from the number of the elect who longed for sound teaching, of whom he had said that the harvest was plentiful and for whom he himself had compassion. This is therefore a memorable example, by which we are first taught how odious hypocrites are to God, since he himself, who by his goodness wills all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth, judges them unworthy of instruction. Secondly, it serves to comfort the simple and the untaught, so that they need not doubt that God cares for them, even though he allows them to err for a time; in the end he gathers them and brings them back to the way. And in the present passage that joyful acclamation of Christ [Ἀξιολογία] is confirmed, by which he gives thanks to the Father, who has hidden the mysteries of his kingdom from the wise and understanding and has revealed them to infants. Teachers too should take an example from this, so that they learn that hypocritical impostors must be rebuked in such a way that they do not neglect the simple and unlearned in the meantime. This passage has two parts: in the first, Christ deals publicly with the crowd; in the second, he deals privately with his disciples.

units.la: Priorem Matthaeus sic narrat: Et adducata turba dixit eis: Audite & intelligite, Non quod ingreditur in os, &c. Confutat autem exemplo suo Christus superbos fidei dominatores, qui doctrinae mysteria vulgo exponi debere negant, & de his quaerentes simpliciter credere iubent ea, quae Ecclesia credit, nec tamen docent, quae illa fides sit, quae nos veras Ecclesiae filios facit. Idem tunc Scribas & Pharisaeos populo inculcauisse, ex eo apparet, quod apud Ioannem seruus suis aliquid in Christi honore dicentibus responderunt: Num & vos seducti estis? Num quis ex principibus credidit in eum, aut ex Pharisaeis? Sed turba haec quae non nouit Legem, execrabilis est.
units.tr: Matthew narrates the first part thus: "And when the crowd had been called together he said to them: Hear and understand, It is not what goes into the mouth, etc." By his example Christ refutes those proud lords of faith who deny that the mysteries of doctrine ought to be explained to the people, and who, when questioned, bid them simply believe what the Church believes, yet do not teach what that faith is which makes us true sons of the Church. That Christ had likewise rebuked the Scribes and Pharisees before the people is clear from John, where the Pharisees answer the servants who spoke something in honour of Christ: "Have you too been deceived? Has any of the rulers believed in him, or any of the Pharisees? But this crowd, which does not know the Law, is accursed."

units.la: At nos relictis illis, Christum videamus, & hunc nobis quoque putemus dicere, Audite & intelligite. Duo requirit. Primum, vt Verbum audiamus. Quia enim ex auditu est fides, hanc non assequuntur vnquam, qui illud audire dedignantur. Hos certe Dauid serpentibus aures ad vocem incantatoris obturantibus confert, vt offendat eos non Dei, sed veteris serpentis, id est, diaboli filios esse. Et vt deplorata est eius contumacia, qui patris sui vocem ne audire quidem vult: ita in regno Dei nihil de illis sperari potest, quibus Patris caelestis vox sordet. At non satis est audiuisse, nisi quod audis intelligas. Ad hoc opus est, vt quae dicuntur fidam demissa per aurem (vt Poeta ait) corde recondas, & assiduameditatione rumines, & tibi ipsi applicare discas. Hoc Dauid docet, quando beatum pronunciat, qui Domini legem dies noctesque meditatur. Ex eo deinceps obedientia fidei nascitur, quae totum hominem Deo vindicat, & quam Apostolus Euangelicae praedicationis finem atque scopum esse scribit; nimirum quoad vitam nostram in hoc seculo. At hodie praedicatur quidem Verbum Dei, at qui ex illo proficiant pauci sunt: quia multi illud impie fastidiunt, vt ne audiant quidem, multi aliis affectibus & studijs occupati non attendunt, de quibus supra Cap. 13. prolixe dictum est.
units.tr: But let us, leaving those men aside, look to Christ, and let us suppose that he says to us too: "Hear and understand." He requires two things. First, that we hear the Word. For since faith comes by hearing, those who disdain to hear it never attain it. David certainly compares such people to serpents that stop their ears at the voice of the charmer, to show that they are sons not of God but of the old serpent, that is, of the devil. And just as the obstinacy of him who will not even hear his father's voice is desperate, so nothing can be hoped for in the kingdom of God from those for whom the voice of the heavenly Father is worthless. But it is not enough to have heard, unless you understand what you hear. To this end it is necessary that you lay up in your heart what is said, letting it sink in through the ear (as the poet says), and that you chew it over by constant meditation and learn to apply it to yourself. David teaches this when he pronounces blessed the man who meditates on the Law of the Lord day and night. From this there then arises the obedience of faith, which claims the whole man for God, and which the Apostle writes is the end and aim of the evangelical preaching, namely, as far as our life in this world is concerned. Yet today the Word of God is indeed preached, but few profit from it, because many impiously despise it so that they do not even listen, and many, occupied with other passions and pursuits, do not pay attention; of these things we spoke at length above, in chapter 13.

units.la: Quid vero illud est, quod audiri & intelligi debet? Non quod ingreditur in os polluit hominem, sed quod egreditur ex ore, hoc polluit hominem. Ab eo, quod Pharisaei in discipulos reprehendebant, in generalem doctrinam digreditur. Illis nefas videbatur illotis manibus cibū sumere, & in crebris ablutionibus purificatione hominis internam, qua ad salutem opus est, consistere credebat, & hoc ipsum vulgo facile persuaderi poterat, cum Patrum traditionibus haec superstitio niteretur, & homines natura ad ceremonias procliues sint. Itaque periculum erat, ne in suspicionem veniret, quasi cum prophano contemptu Patrum religionem, & quaecunque ab his pie instituta, & iam longo tempore religiose obseruata erant, ipse reijceret, & discipulos suos idem facere doceret. Docet ergo per se non esse peccatum, si quis manibus non prius ablutis ad mensam accedat. Id vero generali argumento probat: Quia nihil, quod per os ingreditur, hominem polluat, sed pollutione per ea fieri, quae ex ore egrediuntur. Et apud Marcu Epiphonema graue addit, quo huius dicti meditationem diligentem amplius commendat: Si quis habet aures ad audiendum, audiat. Sumitur autem argumentum ab origine siue initio peccati, & ab eiusdem effectu. Nam primo sic vult dicere: Peccatum non extra hominem nascitur, neque aliunde in hunc ingreditur, sed intra hominem, in corde nimirum, initium habet, & inde sese per os, manus, pedes & omnes hominum actiones diffundens hominem totum polluit. At cibi qualescunque sint, extra hominem sunt, & siue lotis prius manibus siue illotis edantur, aliunde in illum ingrediuntur: Ergo illotis manibus edere, per se peccatum non est. Ad maioris confirmationem facit, quod Paulus nos Legem peccati in membris nostris gestare dicit: & quod Iacobus scribit: Nemo cum tentatur, dicat se a Deo tentari (nam Deus malis tentari non potest, nec quenquam tentat.) Sed vnusquisque tentatur, dum a propria cupiditate abstrahitur & inescatur: deinde cupiditas postquam concepit, parit peccatum, &c. Deinde ab effectu quoq; peccati argumentatur: Omne peccatum polluit hominem, vt Deo displiceat, qui sanctus est: At manibus illotis cibum sumere, non polluit hominem, neque a Deo alienum facit: Ergo manibus non lotis edere, non est peccatum. Sufficit hoc Christi dictum confutandis omnibus com mentis sive decretis, quae posteris temporibus de ciborum delectu & ieiunijs ad certos dies astri-ctis homines superstitiosi in Ecclesiam introduxerunt. Et ad illud respexisse videtur Paulus, quando traditiones huiusmodi doctrinas daemoniorum vocavit. Etenim revera diaboli opus est peccatum facere ex eo, quod Deus licitum esse voluit, aut e contra licitum dicere, quod ille prohibuit. Daniel item de paruo illo cornu in quarta bestia, id est, in Monarchia Romana enato, quo Antichristum denotari veteres intellexerunt, vaticinans, inter alia ei tribuit, quod sibi arrogaret potestatem mutandi leges & tempora. Quia vero de hac re pofiea Dominus prolixius loquetur, in praesenti ista paucis monuisse sufficiat.
units.tr: But what is it that must be heard and understood? "It is not what goes into the mouth that defiles a man, but what comes out of the mouth, that defiles a man." From what the Pharisees rebuked in the disciples, he passes to a general doctrine. They thought it a sin to eat with unwashed hands, and believed that the inner purification of a man, which is necessary for salvation, consisted in frequent washings; and this could easily be persuaded to the people, since this superstition was supported by the traditions of the Fathers, and men are by nature inclined to ceremonies. Therefore there was a danger that he would come under suspicion of despising with profane contempt the religion of the Fathers, and of rejecting whatever had been piously instituted by them and had long been religiously observed, and of teaching his disciples to do the same. He therefore teaches that in itself it is no sin to come to the table without first washing the hands. He proves this by a general argument: nothing that enters through the mouth defiles a man, but defilement comes from what proceeds out of the mouth. And in Mark he adds a weighty exclamation, by which he further commends careful meditation on this saying: "If anyone has ears to hear, let him hear." The argument is drawn from the origin or beginning of sin and from its effect. For first he wishes to say this: sin is not born outside a man, nor does it enter him from elsewhere, but it has its beginning within the man, namely in the heart, and from there, spreading through the mouth, the hands, the feet and all human actions, it defiles the whole man. But foods, of whatever kind, are outside a man, and whether they are eaten with hands washed first or unwashed, they enter him from outside. Therefore to eat with unwashed hands is not in itself a sin. In support of this greater point it is relevant that Paul says we carry the law of sin in our members, and that James writes: "Let no one, when he is tempted, say that he is tempted by God (for God cannot be tempted by evil, nor does he tempt anyone). But each one is tempted when he is drawn away and enticed by his own desire; then desire, after it has conceived, gives birth to sin," and so on. Then he argues from the effect of sin also: every sin defiles a man so that he displeases God, who is holy; but to eat with unwashed hands does not defile a man, nor make him alien to God; therefore to eat with unwashed hands is not a sin. This saying of Christ is enough to refute all the commands or decrees which, in later times, superstitious men introduced into the Church concerning the choice of foods and fasts on fixed days. Paul also seems to have had this in view when he called such traditions doctrines of demons. Indeed it is truly the work of the devil to make a sin of what God wished to be lawful, or conversely to call lawful what he has forbidden. Daniel too, prophesying about the little horn that grew in the fourth beast, that is, in the Roman monarchy, by which the ancients understood Antichrist, attributes to it, among other things, that it claims for itself the power of changing laws and times. But since the Lord will speak more fully on this matter afterwards, it is enough to have given this brief warning here.

units.la: Transeamus nunc ad alteram huius loci partem, quasi duum de Pharisaeis & horum doctrina sive traditionibus iudicium discipulis apertius exponit. Occasionem ei praebuerunt discipuli, qui priuatim illi dicunt: Nosti Pharisaeos audito isto sermone offensos fuisse? In eo autem officium faciunt, quod illum de ijs admonent, quibus alios offendi sciebant, ut indignius de ipso loquerentur. Decet enim hoc discipulos, ut suis praeceptoris honori studeant, & hoc ipsum filij parentibus, et sub diti suis magistratibus debent. At si Christum & totam hanc actionem spectes, nihil hic fecerat aut dixerat, quo aliquis merito deberet offendi. Itaque sua culpa offenduntur, & fuit hoc scandalum non datum, sed acceptum, ut in Scholis loquuntur. Nam etsi hominum traditiones damnauisset, quod simpliciorib. durum videri poterat, non tamen hoc insolens debebat videri Scribis & Pharisaeis, cum suam illam sententiam Isaiae testimonio confirmasset. Fortasis autem non fallantur, qui ipsos etiam discipulos dicto illo offensos fuisse suspicantur, ut quisciebat, Deum iam olim sanguinis esu interdixisse, & postea in Lege discrimen fecisse inter animalia munda & immunda, &c. Non potuerunt ergo homines illiterati & rudes in Legis doctrina intelligere, quo sensu diceretur, Nihil, quod in os ingreditur, edentes polluere, cu Deus ipse in omni genere animalium tam terrestrium, quam aquatilium & volatilium quaedam immunda dixerit. Quod vero Scribas & Pharisaeos, longe alia erant, quibus offensi sunt: nimirum quod ipsorum hypocrisim arguisset, quod impietatis & transgressionis praeceptorum Dei conuictos publice damnasset, quod cum Seniorum traditionibus cultum ipsorum euertisset, qui ipsis hucusque quaestuosus admodum fuerat. At hac ipsa offensione se tales omnino esse produnt, quales esse Christus dixerat, hypocritas nimirum, quorum superstitiones Deo probari non possint. Etenim qui germani Dei cultores sunt, is veritatis doctrina non offenduntur, sed ei cedunt, & se melius edoceri gaudent. Fit autem idem hodie etiam omnibus, qui puriorem Euangelij doctrinam cauillantur, & exijs scandali occasionem arripiunt, quae secundum illius normam fiunt. Ita enim se scripturarum & mysteriorum regni Dei ignorantes, adhaec correptione dignos esse docent. Discipulorum autem error eti tolerabilis fit & venia dignus, apparet tamen illos nimirum pusillanimes & aequo meticulosiores fuisse, quam do Pharisaeorum sermonibus tam facile offenduntur, quorum improbitas ipsis iam pridem perspecta esse debebat.
units.tr: Let us now turn to the other part of this passage, in which he explains more openly to his disciples his judgement of the Pharisees and their teaching or traditions. The disciples gave him the occasion, when they privately said to him: "Do you know that the Pharisees were offended when they heard this saying?" In this they were doing their duty, in warning him about those whom they knew to have been offended, so that he would speak of them with more care. For this is fitting for disciples, who ought to be eager for their teacher's honour, just as sons should be for their parents and subjects for their magistrates. But if you look at Christ and at the whole action, he had done or said nothing for which anyone could rightly be offended. So they were offended through their own fault, and this was not a scandal given but one taken, as the schools put it. For although he had condemned human traditions, which might seem harsh to the simple, this should not have seemed strange to the Scribes and Pharisees, since he had confirmed that very judgement by the testimony of Isaiah. Those are perhaps not wrong who suspect that the disciples themselves were offended by that saying, since they knew that God had long ago forbidden the eating of blood, and afterwards in the Law had made a distinction between clean and unclean animals, and so on. Uneducated and unskilled men could not understand in what sense it was said, "Eating nothing that enters the mouth defiles," since God himself had called some animals of every kind, land, water and air, unclean. But as for the Scribes and Pharisees, they were offended by something quite different: namely, that he had exposed their hypocrisy, that he had publicly condemned them as convicted of impiety and of breaking the commandments of God, and that he had overthrown their worship by the traditions of the elders, which until then had been very profitable to them. Yet by this very offence they showed themselves to be exactly what Christ had said they were, hypocrites, whose superstitions cannot be approved by God. For those who are true worshippers of God are not offended by the teaching of truth, but yield to it and rejoice to be better taught. The same thing happens today to all who carp at the purer doctrine of the gospel and seize on an occasion of offence from those things that are done according to its rule. For by this they show that they are ignorant of the Scriptures and of the mysteries of the kingdom of God, and that they are worthy of rebuke. The disciples' error, though it is tolerable and deserves pardon, nevertheless shows that they were rather timid and too anxious, since they were so easily offended by the words of the Pharisees, whose wickedness ought to have been plainly known to them long before.

units.la: In veritatis vero apparet, quae in hoc mundo veritatis fors sit. Offenduntur ea hypocritae et irritantur, eo quod sua luce lucem eis abstergit, & existimationi derogat, qua illi nihil antiquius habent. Adhaec germanis etiam Christi discipulis & Euangelij professoribus interdum obscura, & saepe acerbior esse videtur. Est hoc hodie vtrunq; nimium frequens, ut electi errent in ijs, quae ipsis notissima esse debebant: & insuper de suis doctoribus inique iudicent, quando aduersarios illorum libertate & acrimonia offensos esse audiunt. Tunc enim ipsi etiam illos reprehendere incipiunt, quasi multa dicant, quae praestaret non attingere. Multi etiam eo vsq; progrediuntur, ut illos omnium turbarum atq; calamitatum, quibus orbis terrarum infestatur, authores esse clament. Sed non debent ista aliquem mouere. Quid enim mirum, si Verbi Dei libertate offendatur mundus, qui, ipso Christo teste, Spiritum veritatis non potest accipere? Et cur a nobis requiritur, ut nos et nostram doctrinam omnibus approbemus, quando hoc ne Filius Dei quidem praestare potuit? Audiamus potius hunc discipulis respondentem, in qua responsione duo potissimum agit.
units.tr: Yet in truth it appears what sort of lot the truth has in this world. Hypocrites are offended and provoked by it, because its light wipes away their darkness and detracts from the reputation that they hold dearest of all. Moreover, to true disciples of Christ and professors of the gospel it sometimes seems obscure and often too harsh. Today both of these happens far too often: the elect go astray in things that ought to have been best known to them, and they also judge their teachers unfairly, when they hear that their opponents have been offended by their frankness and sharpness. For then they begin to rebuke them too, as if they said many things that it would have been better not to touch. Many even go so far as to cry out that these men are the authors of all the disturbances and calamities with which the world is afflicted. But such things ought not to move anyone. For what wonder is it if the world is offended by the freedom of the Word of God, the world which, as Christ himself testifies, cannot receive the Spirit of truth? And why is it demanded of us that we and our doctrine should be approved by everyone, when even the Son of God could not achieve this? Let us rather listen to him answering his disciples, in which answer he chiefly does two things.

units.la: Primo docet diserte & grauiter, quod modo diximus: nimirum non aliquam istorum rationem haberi debere, ut eorum offensa quisquam moueatur. Omnis plantatio (inquit) quam non plantauit Pater ille meus caelestis, eradicabitur. Plantationem a Patre caelesti plantatam dicit reprobos, qui
units.tr: First, he teaches plainly and gravely what we have just said: namely, that no account should be taken of such men, so that anyone should be moved by their offence. "Every plant," he says, "which my heavenly Father has not planted, will be uprooted." He calls the reprobate a plant planted by the heavenly Father, those who

units.la: Dan.7. Pharisaeidoctrina Christi offenduntur. Gen.9. Leuit.11. Deut.14. Veritatis fors in mundo. Ioan.14. Pharisaeorum offensa nemo offendatur. qui neque fidei normam ab illo traditam, neque ab eo praescriptum vitae genus sequuntur. Etenim Pater ille caelestis suos in IESV CHRISTO elegit, priusquam mundus hic conderetur & eosdem suo tempore vocat & illi per fidem inserit, vt suo spiritu plantati & Verbi riuis rigati in-ipso adolescant, & fructus ferant, quibus ipse glorificetur. Et hi sunt arbores illae, de quibus in Psalmis canitur: Qui Lege Domini delectatur, & hanc meditatur dies noctes, erit veluti arbor iuxta fluenta aquarum, quae fructum suum dabit in tempore suo, & folii eius non marcescit. Item, Iustus vt palma germinabit, tanquam cedrus in Libano succrescet cum augmento: plantati in domo Iehouae, in atrijs Dei nostri florebunt: Etiam in senectute germinabunt, pingues & virides erunt. E contra vero Satan quoque suos plantat, homines reprobos & a veri Dei cognitione atque fide alienos, quos alibi Christus zizaniis confert, quae hostis ille bono semini interserit, vt in agro Domini, id est, in Ecclesia ad tempus locum habeant, & succrescant, & ijdem non durant, sed sunt laurus illa frondosa, quae ramos quidem diffundit, sed quia radices non egit in Christo, subito marcescit & extirpatur funditus, vt ne locus quidem eius possit inueniri. Argumentum Christi quod hinc petit, eiusmodi est: Qui vere fideles & germani filij Dei sunt, ij non moueri debent reproborum & hypocritarum iudicijs, sermonibus, exemplis & successibus. Ratio, quia quae non ex Deo sunt, caduca & fluxa sunt: qualescunque ergo isti videantur, & vtcunque sese ostentent sanctita-tis fuco ac splendore, eradicabuntur: Atqui tales omnino sunt Pharisaei & Scribae: Ergo non moueamini eorum offensa & caeco iudicio, quo meam doctrinam atque discipulos temere damnant. Ad minoris confirmationem facit, quod ex historijs constat, Deum nuspiam instituisse Scribarum ordinem, qui tunc erat: multo minus Pharisaeos & Sadducaeos, sed hos ex Schola illa Graeca siue Ethnica originem duxisse, quam Iason summus sacerdos a Seleuco constitutus, contra Legem Dei Ierosolymae instituit, & Pharisaeos quidem Stoicorum, Sadducaeos autem Epicuraeorum germina siue plantas fuisse. Itaque, etsi ad tempus floruerint, & penes Pharisaeos summa esset tam in Repub. quam Ecclesia authoritas, tamen eradicati sunt.
units.tr: (Dan. 7.) The Pharisees are offended by the doctrine of Christ. (Gen. 9. Lev. 11. Deut. 14.) The lot of truth in the world. (John 14.) Let no one be moved by the offence of the Pharisees. neither follow the rule of faith handed down by him nor the way of life prescribed by him. For that heavenly Father chose his own in Jesus Christ before this world was founded, and in his time calls them and grafts them into him by faith, so that, planted by his Spirit and watered by the streams of the Word, they may grow up in him and bear fruit by which he is glorified. These are the trees of which the Psalms sing: "He who delights in the Law of the Lord, and meditates on it day and night, will be like a tree planted by streams of water, which will give its fruit in its season, and its leaf will not wither." Again: "The righteous will flourish like the palm tree, and grow like a cedar in Lebanon; those planted in the house of the Lord will flourish in the courts of our God. They will still bear fruit in old age; they will be full of sap and green." On the other hand, Satan also plants his own, men who are reprobate and alien to the knowledge and faith of the true God, whom Christ elsewhere compares to the tares which that enemy sowed among the good seed, so that they may have a place and grow in the field of the Lord, that is, in the Church, for a time. Yet these do not last, but are like that leafy laurel which spreads its branches, but because it has not taken root in Christ, withers suddenly and is torn up root and branch, so that not even its place can be found. The argument Christ draws from this is of this kind: those who are truly faithful and genuine children of God ought not to be moved by the judgements, words, examples or successes of the reprobate and hypocrites. The reason is that what is not of God is frail and transitory; however such men may appear, and however they display themselves with the gloss and brilliance of holiness, they will be uprooted. But the Pharisees and Scribes are altogether such men. Therefore do not be moved by their offence and their blind judgement, by which they rashly condemn my doctrine and my disciples. To confirm this lesser point, it is also to the purpose that it is clear from histories that God nowhere instituted the order of the Scribes which then existed, much less the Pharisees and Sadducees; rather, these had their origin in that Greek or heathen school which Jason, the high priest appointed by Seleucus, established at Jerusalem against the Law of God, and the Pharisees were offshoots or plants of the Stoics, the Sadducees of the Epicureans. So, although for a time they flourished, and supreme authority in both state and Church lay with the Pharisees, nevertheless they were uprooted.

units.la: Debet hoc Christi argumentum ad nostra quoque tempora transferri. Etenim nouissimo saeculo multa in Ecclesia plantauit Satan contra Dei verbum, & inter alia Sacerdotes siue Sacrificos introduxit, & postea monachorum ordines diuersos, vestitu & ritibus atque moribus distinctos, qui diu in Ecclesia dominati sunt, & adhuc multis in locis dominantur. Offenduntur hi vehementer Euangelij doctrina, & indignissime factum existimant, si per hanc libertas Christiana in cibis & coniugio reducatur, si feriae ab hominibus instituta aboleantur, si imagines & altaria ex templis auferantur, Purgatorij ignis Alchymia cum suis impostuMis detegatur, sacra pro defunctis tollantur, & a Christianis principibus in ordinem redigatur Pseudoclerus ille, qui saeculis aliquot sub emendito Apostolicae successionis praetextu regnum sibi vsurpauit terrenum, & sub castitatis aut caelibatus velo libidinibus vagis omnes prope familias polluerunt, religionem deniq; omnem sibi quaestum fecerunt. Sed neminem illorum querelae aut murmura moueant. Nec enim sunt a Patre caelesti plantati, sed ab eo, qui viuentibus adhuc Apostolis Corinthiorum Ecclesiam in Cephias, Paulinos & Apollonianos scidit, de quibus, quid Paulus scripserit, satis notum est. Eradicabuntur ergo, & vt aut principum atq; regum quorundam fauore adhuc iuuentur, non tamen euadent, quo minus aeternus Dei Filius, qui Antichristum iam annis aliquot spiritu oris sui ingulauit, eundem cum omnibus suis membris aboleat.
units.tr: This argument of Christ ought to be applied to our own times as well. For in the last age Satan planted many things in the Church against the Word of God, and among other things he introduced priests or sacrificers, and afterwards various orders of monks, distinguished by dress, rites and customs, which for a long time have dominated the Church and still dominate in many places. These men are violently offended by the doctrine of the gospel, and they think it most unworthy if through it Christian liberty in foods and marriage is restored, if holidays instituted by men are abolished, if images and altars are removed from the churches, if the fire of purgatory, that alchemy with its impostures, is exposed, if masses for the dead are abolished, and if that false clergy, which for some centuries under the pretext of apostolic succession has usurped an earthly kingdom, and under the veil of chastity or celibacy has polluted almost every household with wandering lusts, and finally has made a profit out of all religion, is brought into order by Christian princes. But let not the complaints or murmurings of any of them move us. For they were not planted by the heavenly Father, but by him who, while the apostles were still living, split the Church of the Corinthians into Cephas, Paulines and Apollonians, and what Paul wrote about them is well enough known. They will therefore be uprooted, and although they are still aided by the favour of certain princes and kings, they will not escape, so that the eternal Son of God, who for some years now has slain Antichrist with the breath of his mouth, will not destroy him together with all his members.

units.la: Faciamus ergo, quod altera sua responsionis parte Dominus iubet. Omittite (inquit) eos, id est, discedite ab eis, ne quid cum illorum doctrina aut vita siue morum exemplo commune habeatis. Et huius mandati rationem adducit: Sunt duces caeci caecorum. Duces vocat, eo quod tales dici & haberi vellent tam in Repub. quam in religione, & in primis ad Pharisaeos pertinet quod Paulus scribit: Confidis te ducem esse caecorum, lucem eorum, qui sunt in tenebris, eruditorem insipientium, magistrum infantium, &c. At quemadmodum in religione ignari erant Veritatis, & ne prima quidem rudimenta tenebant (sicuti Nicodemi exemplo probatur) ita in Republica etiā turbulenti erant, & seditiones quotidie mouebant, & sui similes faciebant discipulos. Sed si caecus caeco praierit (inquit Dominus) quid aliud fiat, quam quod ambo cadant in foueam? Impleum hoc in Iudaeis quoad praesens seculum, & ea quae ad salutem aeternam faciunt. Etenim infeli-
units.tr: Let us therefore do what the Lord commands in the second part of his reply: "Leave them alone" (he says), that is, depart from them, so that you have nothing in common with their teaching, or with their way of life and example of conduct. He also gives the reason for this command: "They are blind guides of the blind." He calls them guides because they wished to be, and to be thought, such both in the commonwealth and in religion. This applies above all to the Pharisees, as Paul writes: "You are confident that you are a guide to the blind, a light to those who are in darkness, a teacher of the foolish, a master of infants," etc. But just as they were ignorant of the truth in religion and did not even hold its first rudiments (as the example of Nicodemus proves), so in the commonwealth they were also turbulent, stirring up sedition every day and making disciples like themselves. "But if a blind man leads a blind man" (says the Lord), "what else happens than that both fall into a pit?" This has been fulfilled in the Jews as regards the present age, and in those things which pertain to eternal salvation. For the unhappy

units.la: Falsi doctores omittendi. ci Iudaeorum genti persuaserunt, non posse saluam manere ipsorum Rempub. nisi Christo extincto. Si fi-namus eum (inquit Caiaphas) omnes credent ei, venientq; Romani, & delebunt tum locum nostrum tum gentem. Persuaserunt item populo, ut eundem Pilato traderent, illi praeferrent latronem Barrabam, & seditiosis clamoribus illum ad crucem deposcerent. At ita scipsos & gentem totam in exitij foveam adduxerunt. Haec enim causa fuit praecipua, qua Deus ad iustam iram accensus, Romanos eis immisit, qui terra tota miserabiliter vastata, urbe eversa & templo destructo, multis item millibus horribiliter caesis, infelices reliquias in totu orbem disperserunt, & durat iam annis amplius mille quingentis illorum calamitas, ut cum Aenea dicere possint: Quae regio in terris nostri non plena laboris? Quoad animas vero miseri adhuc Rabbinorum suorum traditionibus atq; commentis excaecati ad inferos properant, & cum suis ducibus in damnationis sempiternae barathrum precipitantur.
units.tr: False teachers are to be avoided. They persuaded the Jewish nation that their commonwealth could not remain safe unless Christ were put to death. "If we let him alone," said Caiaphas, "all will believe in him, and the Romans will come and destroy both our place and our nation." They likewise persuaded the people to hand him over to Pilate, to prefer the robber Barabbas to him, and with seditious shouts to demand him for the cross. In this way they led themselves and the whole nation into the pit of destruction. For this was the chief cause by which God, kindled to just anger, sent the Romans against them. These, having miserably laid waste the whole land, overthrown the city and destroyed the temple, and having likewise slaughtered many thousands horribly, scattered the unhappy remnants throughout the whole world. Their calamity has now lasted more than fifteen hundred years, so that they can say with Aeneas: "What region on earth is not full of our suffering?" As for their souls, however, they are still wretched, blinded by the traditions and inventions of their Rabbis, and they hasten to hell and are cast down with their guides into the abyss of everlasting damnation.

units.la: Vtinam vero in Iudaeis solis haec Christi sententia locum habuisset, & non ad Christianos quoque suum rigore extendisset. Enimvero postquam in Ecclesia locus datus fuit philosophiae veteri Ethnicorum, & in Scholis pro Christo & huius Apostolis atq; Prophetis audita sunt Platonis, Aristotelis, Auerrois & similium nomina, perinde ut olim inter Iudaeos factum fuit, Christiani homines in sectas scissi sunt, & horribiles tenebrae omnium mentes occuparunt, ut pleriq; neq; scipsos, neq; Deum & eius bonitatem, neq; Christi meritum agnoverint, & per infinitas ambages a caecis magistris circumducti, cum ipsdem in foueas & Labyrinthos superstitionum inciderint. Quid vero mali dent in Repub. duces illi caeci, quos fere summi pontifices in regum aulas submittere solent, Jues nimirum a latere legatos. seculorum aliquot exempla docent, & hodie ipsdem praecipui turbarum, seditionum & bellorum tam civilium, quam exterorum authores sunt. Ab illis ergo sibi caveant, qui in pace cupiunt vivere. De hoc autem diligentius cogitent, qui se coram Deo excusatos dicunt, si simpliciter credant suis doctoribus, et eorum vestigia sequantur: hos enim Deo rationem reddituros esse, si quos seducunt. Nam etsi maior sit horum culpa, qui alios in errore abducunt, attamen Christianorum hominum est, non cuius spiritui credere, sed probare spiritus, num ex Deo sint. Oves meae (ait Christus) vocem meam audiunt, & sequuntur me: Alienum autem nequaquam sequentur, sed fugient ab eo, quia non norunt vocem alienorum. Et Paulus olim scribebat: Omnia probate, quod bonum fuerit tenete. Nec est, quod de difficultate aliqua hic quaeritemur. Nam qui principijs Christianae fidei & religionis, quae in Decalogo, Symbolo Apostolico & Oratione Dominica habentur, insistunt, & ad illa, ceu Lydium lapidem, doctrinas examinant, mox videbunt, num illis consentiant, aut ab eis discrepent. Deinde discant ex hoc loco suum scelus agnoscere tyranni, qui sua fidei commisso populo seductores aut caecos duces praeficiunt, & ut hos ille sequatur, violenter cogunt. Quid enim hi aliud faciunt, quam quo dinuitos ad exitium trahunt, & in miserorum corpora ferro & igne saeviunt, ut eorum eadem animas quoq; male perdant. Ferent illi graue iudicium, quando suorum sanguinem & animas Deus ex manibus ipsorum requiret. Agnoscant ergo felicitatem suam omnes, quibus fidos veritatis doctores dat Deus, & simul pios principes excitat, qui Ecclesiae nutritij & verae fidei propugnatores sunt. Itaq; quicunq; sub talibus viuunt, sese his & Deo Patri gratos praebeant, & reliquis caecis ducibus vere bonum illum pastorem sequantur, aeternum Dei Filium, IESVM CHRISTVM, qui solus est via, veritas & vita. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: Would indeed that this saying of Christ had held good for the Jews alone, and had not extended its rigour to Christians as well. For since room was given in the Church to the old philosophy of the heathen, and in the schools the names of Plato, Aristotle, Averroes and the like were heard in place of Christ and his apostles and prophets, just as formerly happened among the Jews, Christian men have been split into sects, and dreadful darkness has occupied the minds of all. So most have recognised neither themselves, nor God and his goodness, nor the merit of Christ, and, led about through endless windings by blind masters, have fallen with them into the pits and labyrinths of superstition. The examples of several centuries teach what harm those blind guides do in the commonwealth, whom the supreme pontiffs are wont to send into royal courts almost as legates a latere; and today these same men are the chief authors of disturbances, seditions and wars, both civil and foreign. Let those who wish to live in peace beware of them. Let those think more carefully about this who say they are excused before God if they simply believe their teachers and follow their footsteps: for they will render account to God for those whom they lead astray. For although the guilt of those who lead others into error is greater, yet it is the duty of Christian people not to believe every spirit, but to test the spirits, whether they are from God. "My sheep," says Christ, "hear my voice, and follow me; but a stranger they will by no means follow, but will flee from him, because they do not know the voice of strangers." And Paul once wrote: "Test all things; hold fast what is good." Nor is there any difficulty here about which we need complain. For those who abide by the principles of the Christian faith and religion, which are contained in the Decalogue, the Apostles' Creed and the Lord's Prayer, and who test doctrines by these as by a touchstone, will soon see whether they agree with them or differ from them. Then let tyrants learn from this passage to recognise their crime, who set over the people entrusted to them by their faith seducers or blind guides, and violently compel them to follow these. For what else do such men do than drag those held captive to destruction, and rage with sword and fire against the bodies of the wretched, so that they also lose their souls? They will bear a heavy judgement when God requires the blood and souls of their subjects at their hands. Let all, therefore, to whom God gives faithful teachers of the truth, and at the same time raises up pious princes who are the nurses of the Church and defenders of the true faith, acknowledge their happiness. And so whoever live under such rulers should show themselves pleasing to these and to God the Father, and, leaving the other blind guides, truly follow that good Shepherd, the eternal Son of God, JESUS CHRIST, who alone is the way, the truth and the life. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXCVIII.
units.tr: HOMILY CXCVIII.

units.la: Respondens autem Petrus dixit ei: Edissere nobis parabolam istam. IESVS autem dixit: Adhuc & vos sine intelligentia estis? Nondum intelligitis, quicquid ingreditur in os, in ventrem cedere, & in latrinam eijci? Quae autem proficiscuntur ex ore, ex ipso corde egrediuntur, & illa polluunt hominem. Nam ex corde egrediuntur cogitationes malae, caedes, adulteria, fornicationes, furta, falsa testimonia, obtrectationes. Haec sunt, quae polluunt hominem: illotis autem manibus vesci, non polluit hominem.
units.tr: Peter answered and said to him, "Explain this parable to us." Jesus said, "Are you also still without understanding? Do you not yet understand that whatever goes into the mouth passes into the belly and is cast out into the latrine? But the things that come out of the mouth proceed from the heart itself, and these defile a person. For evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false testimonies and slanders come out of the heart. These are what defile a person; but to eat with unwashed hands does not defile a person."

units.la: DEus in Lege frequenter vrget & repetit dictum hoc: Sancti estote, quia ego sanctus sum Dominus Deus vester. Consentit huic, quod Paulus Apostolus scribit: Sectemini sanctitatem, fine qua nemo videbit Deum. At hic diligenti studio opus est, vt teneamus, quae illa sint quae hominem polluunt, & vicissim in quo sanctificatio nostra consistat. Nam vt olim pleriq; Iudaeorum quod verum Legis sensum ignorarent, jefe esu & contactu inquinari arbitrabantur, & contra vero purificationem in externis sacris, sanguinis aspersione & crebris ablutionibus quaerebant: Ita hodie multi, qui reliquis sanctiores haberi volunt, diligenter cavent, ne quid humanis traditionibus vetitum comedant, ne contra suae sectae regulam coniugium contrahant, aut vestem mutent, interim crebris psalmodijs, fuffitibus, aqua benedicta aspersionibus & preculis abfq; sensu demum muratis vacent. Est ergo hodie etiam non minus quam olim necessaria Christi doctrina, qui nuper in genere docuit, quibus polluantur homines, in praefenti vero hoc ipsum diligentius explicat, & rem omnem luculentissime comprehendit.
units.tr: God in the Law often urges and repeats this saying: "Be holy, for I the Lord your God am holy." What the Apostle Paul writes agrees with this: "Follow after holiness, without which no one will see God." Here, however, we need careful study, so that we hold what those things are that defile a person, and in turn where our sanctification consists. For just as many of the Jews once, because they did not know the true sense of the Law, thought that they were defiled by food and by contact, and on the contrary sought purification in external rites, by sprinkling with blood and frequent washings, so today many who want to be thought holier than others take great care not to eat anything forbidden by human traditions, not to marry outside the rule of their sect, or to change their clothing; meanwhile they occupy themselves with frequent psalmodies, fumigations, sprinklings with holy water and prayers devoid of sense, and finally with mumbling. Therefore the teaching of Christ is today no less necessary than it was before. He recently taught in general terms what defiles people, and now he explains this very thing more carefully and sets out the whole matter most clearly.

units.la: Rursus autem occasio huius explicationis praemittitur, quam discipuli praebuerunt. Dixerat Dominus, nihil quod per os ingreditur, hominem polluere, &c. Id non intelligunt discipuli, et parabolam fine proverbio obscurius dictum appellant, & apertius exponi cupiunt: Quod vt fiat, omnium nomine Petrus rogat. Apparet hic ingenij humani tarditas atque ignorantia, & quam vere Apostolus dixerit, hominem animalem non percipere ea quae sunt Spiritus Dei. Etenim nihil erat in hoc dicto, quod obscurum videri deberet ijs, qui sciebant hic de esu agi, & controversia esse de eo. Num polluatur, qui manibus illotis ad mensam accumbit? Attamen haerent discipuli, nec quid sibi velit Christus, intelligunt. Idem Dauidi accidisse legimus quoad parabolam, qua adulteri cum recens commissum illi exprobrabat Nathan. Et huius generis multa frequenter fiunt, eo quod fere vel opinionibus ante conceptis, praeoccupati sumus, vel affectu aliquo prauo impedimur, qui nos non finit cogitare de ijs, quae quam maxime ad nos pertinent. Quapropter non satis est, si verbum Dei ex Scripturis populo recitetur, sed insuper interpretatione opus est, qua, quae obscuriora videri possunt, explicentur, & omnia pro ratione praesentis loci & temporis auditoribus applicentur, vt eorum institutioni & consolationi seruiant. Ita olim Prophetae Legis interpretes fuerunt, & hunc morem docendi in Ecclesia proprio exemplo Christus confirmauit, sicut supra Capite quinto vidimus. Apostolus item doctorem eiusmodi requirit, qui Verbum Domini recte secare, id est, auditorum captui & institutioni accommodare norit.
units.tr: Again, the occasion for this explanation is introduced beforehand, and the disciples supplied it. The Lord had said that nothing that enters through the mouth defiles a person, and so on. The disciples did not understand this, and they call the parable a saying too obscure without a proverb, and they wish it to be explained more plainly. To bring this about, Peter asks on behalf of all. Here appears the slowness and ignorance of the human mind, and how truly the Apostle said that the natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God. For there was nothing in this saying that ought to have seemed obscure to those who knew that the matter concerned food and that there was a dispute about it. Does a man who sits down to table with unwashed hands become defiled? Yet the disciples hesitate and do not understand what Christ means. We read that the same thing happened to David in the case of the parable by which Nathan rebuked him for the adultery he had recently committed. Many things of this kind happen often, because we are almost always preoccupied either with opinions formed beforehand, or hindered by some perverse affection, which does not allow us to think about those things which pertain most of all to us. Therefore it is not enough that the Word of God is read to the people from the Scriptures; interpretation is also needed, by which those things that may seem more obscure are explained, and everything is applied to the hearers according to the circumstances of the present place and time, so that it may serve their instruction and comfort. Thus the prophets were interpreters of the Law of old, and Christ himself confirmed this manner of teaching in the Church by his own example, as we saw above in chapter five. The Apostle likewise requires a teacher of this kind, one who knows how to handle the Word of the Lord rightly, that is, how to adapt it to the understanding and instruction of his hearers.

units.la: Debet etiam Petrus obseruari, qui vt alibi alijs feruentior fuit, ita hic quoq; hominis ingenui & Veritatis auidi exemplum nobis exhibet. Nec enim pudet ipsum sua ignorantia, quam hac potius fatetur, quam Veritatem diutius ignorare. Non ergo eorum similis est, qui ne quid nescire videantur, interpretationes ex suo sensu fingunt, & semel conceptas mordicus tenent, atq; alijs etiam obtrudere conantur. Est hoc hominum genus Ecclesiae pernitiosissimum. Itaq; Petrum imitentur, qui serio Veritatis cognoscenda studio flagrant, & vt hic ipsum Christumconuenit, & ab eo edoceri cupit, ita nos quoq; hunc vnum audiamus, qui nobis a Deo Patre sapientia factus est, neq; ipse sua eos frustratur, qui ex ipso discere volunt, quae cognitu sunt necessaria.
units.tr: Peter also should be noted, who, though elsewhere more fervent than the others, here too sets before us the example of a frank man, eager for the truth. For he is not ashamed of his ignorance, which he confesses here rather than remain longer ignorant of the truth. Therefore he is not like those who, so as not to seem to know nothing, invent interpretations from their own sense, cling stubbornly to what they have once conceived, and try to force it on others as well. This kind of people is most destructive to the Church. Let them therefore imitate Peter, who burns with a serious desire to know the truth, and, as he here comes to Christ himself and wishes to be taught by him, so let us also hear this one, who has been made wisdom for us by God the Father, nor does he himself disappoint those who want to learn from him what is necessary to know.

units.la: Exemplum huius in praesenti habemus. Etenim facilem se praebet Dominus, & absq; mora respondet Petro, ita tamen, vt discipulorum ignorantiam corripiat, dicens: Adhuc & vos sine intelligentia estis? Quasi diceret: Vos ne, quos ego tanto tempore mecum habui, familiariter instituti, arcanorum omnium, quae a Patre accepi, conscios feci, vt aliquando orbis totius doctores fitis, adhuc ignari & rudes estis eorum quae scire oportebat? Simili increpatione alibi quoq; erga eos vsus est, quando eos propter prohibitum fermentum Pharisaeorum folicitos inter se disceptare animaduertit. Quid (inquit) disceptatis, quod panes non habetis? Nondum animum aduertitis, nec intelligitis? adhuc callo obductum habetis cor vestrum? Quibus exemplis docemur, non excusari per ignorantiam eos, qui Verbum Dei diu audiuerunt, interim vero oblatis discendi ac proficiendi occasionibus non vtuntur. Sunt hi ex eorum numero, qui quod habent non habere dicuntur, & ideo illud amittunt. Vult enim Deus nos in Veritate proficere, & in omnem occasionem intentos esse. Fuit ergo reprehensione dignissima securitas illa & oscitantia, qua hic discipuli peccarunt, & qua hodie vulgo peccatur. Quales vero censeri debent, qui non modo ofeitantes & securi nimis sunt, sed
units.tr: We have an example of this in the present passage. For the Lord shows himself approachable and answers Peter without delay, yet in such a way that he rebukes the ignorance of the disciples, saying: "Are you also still without understanding?" As if he said: "Do you, whom I have had with me for so long, familiarly instructed, and to whom I have made known all the secrets that I received from the Father, so that you may one day be teachers of the whole world, are you still ignorant and unskilled in those things which you ought to know?" He used a similar rebuke elsewhere too, when he noticed that they were anxiously disputing among themselves about the leaven of the Pharisees. "Why," he said, "do you dispute because you have no bread? Do you not yet perceive or understand? Do you still have your heart hardened? " By these examples we are taught that those who have long heard the Word of God, but meanwhile do not use the opportunities offered for learning and advancing, are not excused by ignorance. They belong to the number of those who are said not to have what they have, and so they lose it. For God wills us to make progress in the truth and to be alert to every opportunity. That carelessness and dullness with which the disciples here sinned, and with which people commonly sin today, was therefore most worthy of rebuke. But what sort of people must be judged to be those who are not only dull and overly careless, but

units.la: Occasio huius doctrinae.
units.tr: The occasion of this teaching.
1 Cor. 2.
2 Tim. 2.

units.la: Petri ingenium et studium.
units.tr: Peter's temperament and zeal.

units.la: Christus discipulorum ignorantiam corripit.
units.tr: Christ rebukes the ignorance of the disciples.

units.la: Marc. 8.
units.tr: Mark 8.

units.la: Matth. 16. insuper institutionem oderunt, & admonitiones quoq; reijciunt? quales olim Prophetarū tempore fuerunt, qui Dei serui dicebant: Ne rideatis, ne contemplemini nobis plana, loquimini nobis blanda, &c. Audiuntur eiusmodi voces hodie passim. Sed sentient illi olim magno suo malo, quid sit ad Dei Verbū aures obturare, quando inter tentationes grauissimas fame illa multabuntur, quam contemptoribus suis ille minatur. Vide Amos 8. cap. Porrò Dominū nostrū IESVM CHRI-STVM audiamus, qui dictum illud suum repetit, cuius partes duæ sunt, vtramq; aut non modo interpretatur, sed rationibus quoq; & argumentis solidissimis confirmat.
units.tr: Matt. 16. moreover hate instruction and also reject admonitions? Such were the people in the time of the prophets, who said to the servants of God: "Do not prophesy to us, do not gaze at us with plain things, speak to us smooth things," and so on. Voices of this kind are heard everywhere today. But those people will one day feel to their great harm what it means to stop one's ears to the Word of God, when among the most severe temptations they will be punished with that famine with which he threatens those who despise him. See Amos chapter 8. Further, let us listen to our Lord Jesus Christ, who repeats that saying of his, of which there are two parts, and he not only explains both of them but also confirms them with most solid reasons and arguments.

units.la: Priori Scribas ac Pharisaos amplius cofutat, & in genere docet, homine nullo cibo (nimirum cū gratiarū actione & temperanter sumpto, vt nuper monuimus) pollui aut inquinari. Id probat ratione, quam apud Marcū luculentius expressit, dicens: Nam quod extrinsecus in hominem ingreditur, nō introit in cor ipsius, sed in secessum exit, & ita eijcitur ac expurgatur. Docet ergo hic locus, purificationē hominis nō in externis cosistere, sed in eo, vt cor nobis purū & mundū sit. Etenim si ea sola polluere possunt, quæ in cor penetrant, vicissim ijs etiam solus homo purificatur, quæ ad cor vsq; pertingunt. Idē olim per Mosem Deus in Lege monuit. Nam etsi præter Circumcisionem vera purificationis symbolū, multos alios ritus purgationis tradidisset, tamē postremo hoc vrget, vt corda sua circucidant. Et Prophetas idē sensisse, ex Ieremia apparet, qui dicebat: Circumcidimini Domino, & auferte præputia cordis vestri, &c. Nec obscura est huius præcepti ratio. Quia enim cor omnium hominis cogitationū, consiliorū, studiorū atq; actionū fons est, nihil ex illo purum emanare poterit, nisi probè repurgetur. Ideo supra etiā dixit Dominus: Beati mundo corde, quoniam ipsi Deū videbunt. Dauid quoq; hoc rectè intelligēs precabatur: Cor mundū crea in me, Deus, & spiritu rectū innoua in visceribus meis. Et idē precari debet quotquot vere purificari cupiunt.
units.tr: In the first part he refutes the Scribes and Pharisees more fully, and teaches in general that no person is defiled or polluted by any food (namely when it is taken with thanksgiving and in moderation, as we recently advised). He proves this by a reason which he expressed more clearly in Mark, saying: "For what goes into a man from outside does not enter into his heart, but passes into the drain and is thus cast out and cleansed away." This passage therefore teaches that the purification of a person does not consist in external things, but in our having a pure and clean heart. For if only those things can defile which penetrate into the heart, so in turn a person is purified only by those things which reach as far as the heart. God once taught the same thing through Moses in the Law. For although, besides circumcision, which is the true sign of purification, he had given many other rites of cleansing, yet at last he urges this, that they circumcise their hearts. And that the prophets thought the same is clear from Jeremiah, who said: "Circumcise yourselves to the Lord, and take away the foreskins of your hearts," etc. Nor is the reason for this precept obscure. For since the heart is the source of all human thoughts, counsels, pursuits and actions, nothing pure can flow out of it unless it has first been thoroughly cleansed. Therefore the Lord also said above: "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God." David too, understanding this rightly, prayed: "Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within my inward parts." And everyone who truly desires to be purified ought to pray the same.

units.la: Quod si quæras, qua ratione, aut quo medio cor purgetur? nihil est eorū, quæ extrinsecus homini adhibentur, aut etiam in eum ingrediuntur, quod in cor ipsius penetret: & proinde nihil illorū hoc purificare potest. Solius Spiritus Dei hoc opus est, qui vera Christi cognitione & fide corda illuminat, qua deinde purificantur. Docet hoc Petrus, quando in celebri illa Ierosolymitana Synodo de gentium vocatione disseres, inter alia ait: Deus qui nouit corda, reddidit eis testimonium, dato ipsis Spiritu sancto, sicut & nobis: nihilq; discreuit inter nos & illos, fide purificatis cordibus illorum. Fides ergo medium illud est, quo purificamur, quia per hac Christus apprehenditur; cuius sanguis nos emundat ab omni peccato. Nam vt nostram immunditiē in se receptam expiauit, ita vicissim in ipsum credentibus suam sanctimoniā communicat. Ideo iam morte aditurus de discipulis & omnibus horū prædicationi creditur s Patri dicebat: Ego pro eis sanctifico meipsum, vt sint & ipsi sanctificati per veritatē. Idem in se credentes ex Verbi sui semine regenerat in Dei filios; adeoq; nouos homines facit, in quibus ipse viuit & agit suo Spiritu. Quo Paulus respicies, de seipso scribebat: Viuo nō amplius ego, sed viuit in me Christus: & vitam quam nunc viuo in carne, in fide viuo Filij Dei, qui dilexit me, & tradidit semetipsum pro me. Quia ergo credentibus nō modo iustitia & sanctitas Christi imputatur propter fidē, sed cunde intra se viuente habent, atq; eius Spiritu animantur, fieri nō potest, quin cordibus ipsorū atq; coscientijs per fidē illā purificatis, etiā ipsi vere mundi atq; puri sint, & ijsdē omnia quoq; pura atq; licita sint, neq; vllis externis actionibus siue cibis polluantur. Nam quicquid faciūt (sicuti Apostolus monet) sermone aut factō, illud omne in nomine IESV & ex animo syncero faciūt, tanquam Domino, gratias agentes Deo & Patri per eum. Ideo ijsdem cibi omnes sanctificati sunt, adeo vt quoad suam conscientiā, ex ijs etiā vesci possint, quæ idolis immolata sunt, si non scandalum aliunde offeratur, vt aliorum ratio habenda sit, quii-psorum libertate offendi poterant. Vide 1.Cor.10.
units.tr: Now if you ask by what method or means the heart is cleansed: nothing that is applied to a man from outside, or even enters into him, can penetrate to the heart itself, and so nothing of that kind can purify it. This work belongs to the Spirit of God alone, who enlightens hearts with the true knowledge and faith of Christ, and by that faith they are then purified. Peter teaches this when, in his famous discussion of the calling of the Gentiles at the Synod of Jerusalem, he says among other things: "God, who knows the hearts, bore witness to them by giving them the Holy Spirit, just as to us, and made no distinction between us and them, their hearts being purified by faith." Faith, therefore, is the means by which we are purified, because through it Christ is apprehended, and his blood cleanses us from all sin. For just as he atoned for our uncleanness by taking it upon himself, so in turn he imparts his holiness to those who believe in him. Hence, about to go to his death, he said to the Father concerning his disciples and all who believe through their preaching: "For them I sanctify myself, that they also may be sanctified in the truth." He also regenerates those who believe in him, from the seed of his Word, into sons of God, and so makes them new men, in whom he himself lives and acts by his Spirit. Looking to this, Paul wrote of himself: "I no longer live, but Christ lives in me; and the life I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself up for me." Since to believers not only the righteousness and holiness of Christ are imputed on account of faith, but they also have him living within them and are animated by his Spirit, it cannot be otherwise than that, their hearts and consciences being purified by that faith, they themselves are truly clean and pure, and all things are pure and lawful to them, and they are not defiled by any external actions or foods. For whatever they do, in word or deed (as the Apostle admonishes), they do in the name of Jesus and from a sincere heart, as to the Lord, giving thanks to God the Father through him. Therefore all foods are sanctified to them, so that, as far as their conscience is concerned, they may eat even what has been sacrificed to idols, provided no offence is given elsewhere, so that account is taken of others who might be offended by their liberty. See 1.Cor.10.

units.la: Rursus ergo hic validissimè cofutantur superstitiosæ de ciborū deleētu & ieiunijs papisticis traditiones. Nam vt idē Apostolus ait, esca nos nō comendat Deo: neq; si vescamur, abundantiores sumus: neq; si nō vescamur, egetiores reddimur. Et regnū Dei nō est esca & potus, sed iustitia & pax, & gaudiū in Spiritu sancto. Ne quis ergo aliū iudicet ob cibū & potum, neue audiamus temerarios illos, quiChristianis audet dicere, Ne attigeris, ne gustaris, neq; cotrectaueris. Sūt enim hæ peregrinæ doctrinæ, imò dæmoniorū doctrinæ sunt, vt nuper diximus. Bonū aut est gratia con stabiliri cor, nō cibis, quibus (vt rursum Apostoli verbis vtamur) non sunt adiuti, qui in ipsis versati sunt. fati sunt. Quod si qui obijciant, Ecclesia has leges statuisse, non quod cibos aliquos per se immun-dos & illicitos putarit, sed disciplinae ergo, ut licentiam quorundam frenaret, & carni lasciuienti libidinis fomenta aut irritamenta subduceret. Ideo Christianorum esse, Ecclesiae statutis obedire. Ad ista primo respondemus, nos no agnoscere aliam Ecclesiam, quam eam, cui in Psalmis dicitur: Audi filia & vide, & inclina aurem tuam, obliuiscere populi tui, &c. quae (inquâ) leges no dat, sed a sponso suo IESV CHRISTO accipit: utpote ex veris ouibus constans, quae solius pastoris fui voce audiunt & sequuntur. No possumus ergo ea sequi aut colere, in qua voces alienae sonat, & a Christi voce dissonates. Deinde si disciplinae ergo haec decreuit Ecclesia, cur ipsi magna parte diuini cultus in ieiuniis illis pharisaicis constituunt? cur in eis meritu salutis statuut? cur istis decretis cosci entias obstringunt, cur propter eum homines Christianos iudicat? cur haereseos condemnant? cur grauius animaduertunt in eos, qui vetito die carnis fructu degustarunt, ouae aut lactarium aliquod opus comederunt, quam in adulteros, vsurarios, periuros, homicidas deniq.? Imo si carnis licentiam coercere, & libidinis aestuantis feruore restinguere volunt, cur per ipsos licet vino nimio inebriari, & ferculis lautissimis atq; aromatu calidissimorum exquisito apparatu feruentibus tuc stomachum farcire, & viscera omnia accendere, quando ieiunijs quam maxime vacare videri volunt? Ad ista respondeat, et sua illa decreta Verbi Dei authoritate tueatur, aut Ecclesiae molesti esse desinat.
units.tr: Again, therefore, the superstitious traditions of the Papists about the choice of foods and fasts are here most powerfully refuted. For, as the same Apostle says, food does not commend us to God; if we eat we are not the better, and if we do not eat we are not the poorer. "The kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit." Let no one, therefore, judge another on account of food and drink, nor let us listen to those rash men who dare to say to Christians: "Do not touch, do not taste, do not handle." For these are strange doctrines, indeed doctrines of demons, as we said recently. It is good for the heart to be established by grace, not by foods, by which (to use the Apostle's words again) those who have been occupied with them were not helped. But if anyone objects that the Church has laid down these laws, not because she thought certain foods unclean in themselves, but for the sake of discipline, to restrain the licence of some and to withdraw from the lascivious flesh the fuel and incitements of lust, and that therefore it is the duty of Christians to obey the Church's statutes, we answer first that we do not acknowledge any Church other than the one of which it is said in the Psalms: "Hear, O daughter, and see, and incline your ear; forget your people," and so on. That Church does not give laws, but receives them from her bridegroom Jesus Christ, being made up of true sheep, which hear and follow the voice of their one shepherd alone. We cannot, therefore, follow or honour a church in which other voices sound and which is out of tune with the voice of Christ. Next, if the Church decreed these things for the sake of discipline, why do they themselves place a large part of divine worship in those Pharisaic fasts? Why do they set up merit of salvation in them? Why do they bind consciences with these decrees, judge Christians on account of them, and condemn people as heretics for them? Why do they punish more severely those who have tasted meat on a forbidden day, or eaten some dairy food, than adulterers, usurers, perjurers and, finally, murderers? Indeed, if they really wish to restrain the licence of the flesh and quench the heat of seething lust, why do they allow men to be drunk with much wine, and to stuff their stomachs and inflame all their insides with the most lavish dishes and the most exquisitely prepared, very hot spices, at the very times when they most want to seem devoted to fasting? Let them answer these points, and defend their decrees by the authority of the Word of God, or else stop troubling the Church.

units.la: Caeterum no satis esse debet Christianis hominibus, libertate suam tenere contra superstitiosos fidei & conscientiae dominatores, nisi simul caueant, ne libertas in licentiam carnis degeneret, sed vt solicite ab ijs abstineat, quibus homo totus polluitur ac prophanatur. Idcirco altera parte de his quoq; Christus admonet, dicens: Quae aut proficiscuntur ex ore, ex ipso corde egrediuntur, & illa polluunt hominem. Et mox quae illa sint, docet: Nam ex corde egrediuntur cogitationes malae, caedes, adulteria, fornicatio, &c. Vbi dicat quis, qua ratione homo ijs pollui possit, quae ab eo exeunt? Nam si egrediuntur, vtiq; ab illis homo purgatur. Sed extra dicuntur ex corde vitia, non quod locum in corde deinceps nullum habeant, sed quod tanquam ex perennis fonte, ex vitiosis & illicitis affectibus cordis promanant, & sic de eius impuritate indicium praebent. Vt enim ex cordis abundantia os loquitur, sic eiusdem impuritas in reliquis etiam membris, tanquam peccati organis sese exerit: quod ne fiat, Apostolus quoq; prohibet.
units.tr: Moreover, it should not be enough for Christians to maintain their liberty against superstitious lords of faith and conscience, unless at the same time they take care that liberty does not degenerate into licence of the flesh, but that they carefully abstain from those things by which the whole man is polluted and profaned. Christ therefore admonishes on this point too, saying: "What proceeds out of the mouth comes from the heart itself, and these things defile a man." Soon after he explains what those things are: "For out of the heart come evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications," and so on. Here someone may ask by what reasoning a man can be defiled by what comes out of him. For if these things come out, surely the man is cleansed of them. But vices are said to come out of the heart not because they have no further place in the heart, but because they flow forth as from a perennial fountain, from the vicious and unlawful affections of the heart, and so they give evidence of its impurity. For just as the mouth speaks out of the abundance of the heart, so its impurity also shows itself in the other members, as instruments of sin; and the Apostle forbids this too.

units.la: Interim docet Catalogus iste, a quibus abstinere debeant, qui prophani & immundi haberi nolunt. Primus locus malis cogitationibus tribuitur, a quibus nemo immunis est. Quia enim in peccato concipimur & nascimur, natura peccatores sumus, & Deo teste, figmenta cordis nostri praua suntab ineunte aetate. Hic ergo caveant sibi Christiani homines, ne cogitationibus indulgendo cupiditati praua fomenta subministret, quae peccatu concipiat & pariat, ut alibi ex Iacobi epistola dictu est. Semper ergo meminerimus Dauidici illius: Auerte oculos, ne videant vanitate. Deinde caedes nominat, sub quibus omne sanguinis innocentis effusione intelligit, qua non homine modo, sed terram ipsam prophanari, Deus per Mosem docet. Quid, quod dicit preces abominatur, si manus sanguine madentes ad ipsum extendamus? Tertio adulteria & fornicationes ponit, quae omnes libidinis vetitae species comprehendunt. Merito aut hic recensentur, quando (vt Paulus scribit) qui fornicantur, in proprium corpus peccant, & templu Spiritus Sancti polluunt, & simul extrema contumelia eorum personas afficiunt, quibus ad libidine sua abutuntur. Quarto furtorum memi-nit, ad quae rapinae etiam, vsurae & omnes ex alieno ditescendi rationes iniustae referri debet. Quinto falsa testimonia numerantur, quibus proximo iniuria fit sub iuris praetextu, & ideo falsum testem Deo exosum esse, Solomon dicit. His subtexit obtrectationes & calumnias, quibus nihil iniquius, nihil turpius & illiberalius esse, philosophi quoq; intellexerunt. Apud Marcu species plures addutur, auaritiae nimirum aut omnis generis cupiditates immodicae, scelera manifesta qualia cunq;, doli & fraudes, proteruia vel nequitia, oculus malus siue inuidia, quae aliorum felicitate non finit rectis oculis intueri: superbia ite, qua peccati principiu Sirachides dicit: & amentia, quae Dei immemores facit, & mentes a seria coelestiu meditatione auocat. Et his infert: Omnia haec scele ra intus exeunt, & polluunt hominem. In praesenti autem causa, de qua agitur, catalogum hunc applicans ait: Haec sunt, quae polluunt hominem: illotis autem manibus vesci, non polluit hominem.
units.tr: Meanwhile this catalogue teaches what those who do not wish to be considered profane and unclean ought to abstain from. The first place is given to evil thoughts, from which no one is free. For since we are conceived and born in sin, we are sinners by nature, and, as God testifies, the imaginations of our heart are evil from youth. Christians must therefore take care not to indulge their thoughts, lest they supply evil fuel to desire, which sin conceives and brings forth, as was said elsewhere from the Epistle of James. Let us always remember that word of David: "Turn away my eyes, lest they behold vanity." Next he names murders, by which he understands every shedding of innocent blood, by which, as God teaches through Moses, not only man but the land itself is profaned. What of the fact that he says prayers are abominable if we stretch out hands dripping with blood? Third, he lists adulteries and fornications, which comprehend every kind of forbidden lust. These are rightly listed here, since (as Paul writes) those who fornicate sin against their own body and defile the temple of the Holy Spirit, and at the same time inflict the extreme insult on the persons whom they abuse for their lust. Fourth, he mentions thefts, to which robberies, usury and all unjust ways of getting rich at another's expense must also be referred. Fifth, false witnesses are counted, by whom injury is done to a neighbour under the pretext of law; and Solomon says that a false witness is hateful to God. To these he adds slanders and calumnies, than which philosophers too have recognised nothing more unjust, nothing more base and illiberal. In Mark more kinds are added: avarice, or every sort of immoderate desire, manifest crimes of whatever kind, deceits and frauds, wantonness or wickedness, an evil eye or envy, which does not allow a man to look on another's happiness with a sound eye; pride too, which the son of Sirach calls the beginning of sin; and folly, which makes men forget God and turns their minds away from serious meditation on heavenly things. And he adds: "All these evils come out from within and defile a man." But in the present case, to which he applies this catalogue, he says: "These are the things that defile a man; but to eat with unwashed hands does not defile a man."

units.la: Habetur hoc loco euidens & irrefragabile vitiositatis nostrae & corruptae natura testimonium, cui remediū aliunde accedere oportet. Nisi enim regeneretur homo, ex sui cordis thesauro nō alia depromere poterit, quam quæ hic enumeratur. Regeneramur autem (vt paulo ante diximus) per fidē in Christū, quæ huic nos inserit, qui solus est medicus & seruator, qui natura corrupta instaurat. Interim discāt de his omnibus diligentius cogitare, qui sibipsis inter peccata delitias faciunt, et illa mirifice extenuant. At cum cogitationes malæ hominē polluāt, quid de cupiditatibus, de dictis obscenis, minacibus, impudicis aut scandali plenis, de factis item iniquis et illicitis dicemus? Qui his vacāt, ij impuri & immundi sunt, & ideo eos a regno Dei excludit Scriptura, atq; ferūt eos, quod in Apocalypsi dicitur: Foris canes & venefici & fornicatores, & homicidæ & idololatræ, & quisquis amat & comittit mendacium. Ideo ne ista in nobis dominentur, nosipsos abnegare, carnem mortificare, & homine nouum induere iubemur. Ne ergo leniter de illis iudicemus. Qui vero hos sepollutos sentiunt, resipiscant, & ad ESVM CHRISTVM conuersi, hunc vera & constanti fide apprehendant, qui se pro nobis sanctificauit, vt nos in ipso iustitia Dei efficeremur. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: There is in this passage a clear and irrefutable testimony to our vicious and corrupt nature, and a remedy for it must come from elsewhere. For unless a man is regenerated, he can bring forth from the treasure of his heart nothing other than what is listed here. We are regenerated (as we said a little earlier) through faith in Christ, which joins us to him, he who alone is the physician and saviour, who restores corrupt nature. Meanwhile, let those who make pleasures for themselves among their sins, and wonderfully minimise them, learn to think about all of these more carefully. But since evil thoughts defile a man, what shall we say about lusts, about obscene, threatening, impure or scandalous words, and likewise about wicked and unlawful deeds? Those who indulge in these are impure and unclean, and therefore Scripture excludes them from the kingdom of God, and it describes them as the Apocalypse says: "Outside are dogs and sorcerers and fornicators, and murderers and idolaters, and whoever loves and practises lying." Therefore we are commanded to deny ourselves, mortify the flesh, and put on the new man, so that these things may not rule in us. Let us not, then, judge these things lightly. But those who feel these defilements should repent, turn to JESUS CHRIST, and lay hold of him with a true and steadfast faith, who sanctified himself for us, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXCIX.
units.tr: HOMILY CXCIX.

units.la: Egressus illinc Iesus, recessit in partes Tyri & Sidonis. Et ecce mulier Chananæa a finibus illis egressa, clamauit dicēs: Miserere mei Domine, fili Dauid: filia mea male a dæmonio vexatur. Ille vero non respondit ei quicquā. Tunc accedentes discipuli eius rogarūt eū, dicētes: Dimitte eam: nā clamat post nos. Ipse vero respondens dixit: Non sum missus nisi ad oues perditas domus Israel. Illa autē venit & adorauit eum, dicēs: Domine succurre mihi. Ipse vero respondens dixit: Non est bonū accipere panem liberorum, & obijcere catellis. Ipsa autē dixit: Etiā Domine: etenim catelli vescuntur micis, quæ cadunt e mensa dominorū suorū. Tunc respondēs Iesus dixit eis: O mulier, magna est fides tua, fiat tibi vt vis. Et sanata fuit filia eius ab eo mométo.
units.tr: Jesus went out from there and withdrew into the regions of Tyre and Sidon. And behold, a Canaanite woman came out from those borders and cried out, saying: "Have mercy on me, O Lord, thou son of David; my daughter is grievously vexed by a devil." But he answered her not a word. Then his disciples came and begged him, saying: "Send her away, for she cries after us." But he answered and said: "I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel." Then she came and worshipped him, saying: "Lord, help me."
