But he answered and said: "It is not good to take the children's bread and throw it to the dogs." And she said: "Yes, Lord, for even the dogs eat the crumbs which fall from their masters' table." Then Jesus answered and said to her: "O woman, great is your faith; be it done for you as you desire." And her daughter was healed from that very hour.

units.la: Onia Iudæus in æternæ salutis negotio potissimum nocuit, quod patrum traditionibus adictí, se per externas ceremonias iustificari & seruari posse, & proinde sibi alio Seruatore nequaquam opus esse arbitrabantur, nuper Dominus noster IESVS CHRISTVS grauiter docuit, externis Deum colinō posse, salute vero omnem in cordis puritate consistere, quæ nobis per solam fidem in ipsum contingit. Quia vero illi doctrina ista offensi sunt, nimirum quod sui priuati commodi & honoris ergo traditiones maiorum suorum Verbo Dei præferrent, nunc relictis illis, infines Tyri ac Sidonis secedit, & hac secessione docet, quid omnes maneat, qui vt mundo placeant, & existimationi aut quæstui suo cōsulant, in tenebris errare malunt, quam in luce ambulare, & Deo in fide pura seruire. Transfertur ab illis regnū Dei ad alios; quod Iudæis euenturum, Prophetæ omnes olim prædixerant, & ipse Dominus nunc hoc suo facto testatur. Debemus autē hoc exemplum nobis applicare, quibus ab humanarum traditionum iugo liberatis sese per Euangelium hodie offert. Quia enim sui semper similis est, similiter ab omnibus discedet, qui vt mundo placere possint, ad superstitiones redeunt. At ne quis Iudæorū incredulitate Christo aliquid derogauisse putet, sequitur modo, quid de illo factum sit, cum in partes Tyri & Sidonis venisset.
units.tr: The Jews chiefly suffered harm in the business of eternal salvation because, bound to the traditions of the fathers, they believed that they could be justified and saved through outward ceremonies, and therefore thought they had no need of any other Saviour. Our Lord Jesus Christ lately taught them earnestly that God can be worshipped with outward things, but that salvation consists wholly in purity of heart, which comes to us through faith alone in him. Since they were offended by this teaching, namely because for the sake of their private gain and honour they preferred the traditions of their ancestors to the Word of God, he now leaves them and withdraws to the borders of Tyre and Sidon, and by this withdrawal he teaches what awaits all who, wishing to please the world and to look after their reputation or profit, prefer to wander in darkness rather than walk in the light and serve God in pure faith. The kingdom of God is transferred from them to others; all the prophets long ago foretold that this would happen to the Jews, and the Lord himself now confirms it by this deed. We ought to apply this example to ourselves, who, freed from the yoke of human traditions, are today offered salvation through the Gospel. For as he is always like himself, so he will likewise depart from all who return to superstitions in order to please the world. But lest anyone think that Christ lost anything through the unbelief of the Jews, the account goes on to tell what happened to him when he came into the regions of Tyre and Sidon.

units.la: Quo loco Marcus annotauit illum in domum quandā ingressum, noluisse vt quis suum in illas partes aduentū resciscerēt: nimirum quod nondum venisset tempus illud præfinitum, quo gentes publice ad regni Dei societatē vocari debebant. Veruntamen latere diutius nō potuit. Est enim Sol iustitiæ & Lux mundi. Vt ergo Sol exoriens luce sua seipsum prodit, quā nec nubes quidē omnino occultare possunt: ita Christus quocunque venit, per Euangelium suum electis innotescit, neq; aliquid obstare potest, quo minus illius salutifica virtute aliqui fruantur. Exemplum huius rei in præsenti mulier Chananæa exhibet, cuius fides admiratione digna Iudæorum cōtumaciæ opponitur, vt hoc ceu præludio adumbraretur, quanto cum feruore gentes Christum a Iudæis reiectum effent amplesur xura. Quia vero exemplum hoc imitari oportet omnes, qui illo Seruatore vti volunt, proderit si gulas huius historiae partes considerare: Quae nimirum fuerit, & quid fecerit? Qualem se initio erga eam Christus praebuerit? Quam inuicta fidei constantia vicissim illa ipsum quodammodo supera- rit? Quam denique laudem atq; fructum ex sua fide retulerit?
units.tr: At this point Mark notes that he entered a certain house and did not want anyone to learn of his coming into those regions, because the appointed time had not yet come when the Gentiles were to be publicly called into the fellowship of the kingdom of God. Yet he could not remain hidden for long, for he is the Sun of righteousness and the Light of the world. Just as the rising sun reveals itself by its light, which not even clouds can wholly hide, so Christ, wherever he comes, makes himself known to his elect through his Gospel, and nothing can stand in the way so that some should not enjoy his saving power. The Canaanite woman in the present passage provides an example of this, whose admirable faith is set against the obstinacy of the Jews, so that this might be foreshadowed, as in a prelude, with how great an eagerness the Gentiles would embrace Christ after he had been rejected by the Jews. Since all who wish to make use of that Saviour must imitate this example, it will be profitable to consider the separate parts of this story: who she was and what she did; how Christ at first behaved toward her; with what unconquered constancy of faith she in turn somehow overcame him; and finally what praise and fruit she gained from her faith.

units.la: Quoad mulierem, gente Chananaea fuit, ex eorum reliquijs, quos olim excindere iussit Dominus. Marcus Syrophoenissam dicit, quod in ea Phoenicia parte habitaret, quae proxime Syriam attin gebat. Addit, Graecam fuisse, quod tunc commune nomen erat omnium, qui non pertinebant ad cen- sum populi Dei. Et ista omnia commemorantur, vt eo illustrior fit eius fides. Habuit autem filio- lam, quae a daemonio obsessa misere vexabatur. Itaq; cum Christum venisse reciuisset, de cuius mi- raculis prius multa audiverat, illum conuenit, clamans: Miserere mei Domine, Fili Dauid, filia mea male a daemonio vexatur.
units.tr: As to the woman, she was of the Canaanite people, one of the remnants of those whom the Lord once commanded to be destroyed. Mark calls her a Syrophoenician, because she lived in that part of Phoenicia which bordered on Syria. He adds that she was a Greek, which at that time was the common name for all who did not belong to the census of the people of God. All these things are recorded so that her faith may shine the more brightly. She had a little daughter, who was wretchedly tormented, being possessed by a devil. So when she heard that Christ had come, of whose miracles she had previously heard much, she went to him, crying out: "Have mercy on me, O Lord, Son of David; my daughter is grievously vexed by a devil."

units.la: Praebet ergo primo charitatis maternae exemplum. Quia enim dicit, Miserere mei: nō obscure exprimit animi dolore, quo perinde afficiebatur, ac si ipsa a daemone isto torqueretur. Debent hoc parentes ex se natis liberis secundū Legē naturae, quae στοργας sive affectiones istas omnium cordibus insculpsit, adeo vt nulla gens tam barbara, tam immanis aut seuua fuerit, quae non detestata sit Ne- rones, Medeas, Thyestas, tanquā naturae monstra. Et Paulus ex communi sensu argumentū petijt, quando eū, qui suis nō prospicit, fidē abnegauisse, & infideli deteriore esse scribit. Praecipua aut pa- rentibus cura haec esse debet, vt suos liberos a daemonijs liberari curet. Habet hac locū in nobis pro- pter peccatū, in quo omnes concipimur & nascimur: quae causa est, vt figmenta cordis humani prava sint ab ineunte aetate. Quia vero Christus semel illud promissum est, cuius virtute & merito Serpen- tis veteris, id est, diaboli caput conculcatur, nenobis dominari posset, illi cōsecrari debet paruuli: quod ipse diserte monet, quando discipulis dicebat: Sinite pueruulos ad me venire, &c. Idolim fiebat per Circumcisionem, qua infaederis cū Deo societatem recipiebantur. In cuius locum cum Baptismus successerit, hodie baptizari debet, vt Ecclesiae ciues siue membra fiant. Accedat deinde cū aetate institutio in Lege Dei & vera fide: de quo Deus diligenter & graviter admonet per Mosem. Et quia hanc fere non libenter admittunt pueri, eò quod, teste Solomone, stultitia in corde ipsorū col- ligata sit, eam ferula expelli oportet. Iubet hoc Apostolus, quando parentibus praecipit, vt liberos suos enutriant in eruditione ac monitis Domini. At quia ista fere negliguntur hodie, non mirum est, si plerique ab ipsa pueritia mali daemonis ipsos miserē exagitantus indicia praebent.
units.tr: First, then, she gives an example of maternal love. For when she says, "Have mercy on me," she clearly expresses the pain of her mind, by which she was affected just as if she herself were being tormented by that demon. Parents owe this to their children born of them, according to the law of nature, which has engraved these affections, which the Greeks call storgai, on the hearts of all, so that no nation has been so barbarous, so savage or cruel that it has not detested Neros, Medeas and Thyestes as monsters of nature. Paul too drew an argument from common feeling when he wrote that anyone who does not provide for his own has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever. Yet the chief care of parents ought to be that they see to it that their children are freed from demons. This has a place in us because of sin, in which we are all conceived and born; this is why the imaginations of the human heart are evil from earliest youth. But since Christ has been promised once for all, by whose power and merit the head of the old serpent, that is, of the devil, is trampled, so that he cannot rule over us, little children ought to be consecrated to him. He himself clearly urges this when he said to the disciples: "Suffer the little children to come to me," and so on. In former times this was done through circumcision, by which people were received into the fellowship of the covenant with God. Since baptism has succeeded in its place, today children ought to be baptized, so that they may become citizens or members of the Church. Then, as they grow in age, instruction in the Law of God and in true faith should be added, about which God warns diligently and seriously through Moses. And since children scarcely ever receive this willingly, because, as Solomon testifies, foolishness is bound up in their heart, it must be driven out with the rod. The Apostle commands this when he instructs parents to bring up their children in the discipline and admonition of the Lord. But since these things are nearly always neglected today, it is no wonder that many, from their very childhood, show signs that the evil demon is cruelly tormenting them.

units.la: At non minus fidei quoq; verae exemplū in hac Chananaea proponitur. Huius specimina sunt: Primum, quod neq; ad Deos gentiū confugit, neq; ad artes siue media illicita conuertitur, qualia sunt, Exorcismi & adiurationes daemoniorum, quos nusquam praecepit Deus, saepe aut vetuit, sed apud Christum ope petit, de cuius virtute (vt paulo ante diximus) multa audierat, & quae procul dubio ex operibus pro Deo vero & aeterno agnoscebat. Deinde, quod eundē vocat Filiū Dauidis, id est pro missum humani generis Seruatore: quem ex Dauidis prosapia expectari, nō poterat ignorare. De nīq;, quod nullū suum meritū allegat, aut pollicetur, sed eius misericordiā gratuitā implorat, simpli citer clamans: Miserere mei, &c. Ijsdē officijs siue operibus fide sua publice testantur, quicunque ea gloriari solet. In omni necessitate ad vnū verū Deum cōfugiant per IESVM CHRISTVM quē ille nobis Mediatorē dedit. Huc agnoscat verū illum Dauidis Filiū esse: cui dictū est: Sede a dextēris mihi, donec ponā inimicos tuos scabellū pedum tuorū. Per hunc solum enim venitur ad Patrē, & idē gloriā suā dat nemini. In eius aut cōspectu humiliati, nō aliquod nostrū meritum al- legemus (quod reuera nullū est, cum ex nobismipsis ne ad cogitandū quidē idonei simus, neq; aliquid habeamus, quod non acceperimus) sed in misericordia illius omnem salutis ipsem collocemus, &c.
units.tr: Yet an example of true faith is set before us no less in this Canaanite woman. Its marks are these. First, she did not flee to the gods of the Gentiles, nor did she turn to arts or illicit means, such as exorcisms and adjurations of demons, which God nowhere commanded and often forbade, but she sought help from Christ, of whose power (as we said a little before) she had heard much, and whom without doubt she recognized from his works as the true and eternal God. Next, she calls him the Son of David, that is, the promised Saviour of the human race, whom she could not fail to know was to be expected from the line of David. Moreover, she claims no merit of her own and offers none, but implores his free mercy, simply crying out: "Have mercy on me," and so on. Those who are accustomed to boast of such works or deeds openly bear witness to their faith in the same way. In every necessity let them flee to the one true God through Jesus Christ, whom he has given us as Mediator. Let them acknowledge that he is the true Son of David, to whom it was said: "Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet." For through him alone do we come to the Father, and he does not give his glory to anyone else. Humbled in his sight, let us not allege any merit of ours (which truly is nothing, since we are not even fit to think anything of ourselves, nor do we have anything that we have not received), but let us place the whole hope of our salvation in his mercy, and so on.

units.la: Porro videamus, quale se mulieri isti Christus praebuerit. Non respondit ei quicquā. Fuit hoc plane nouū & insolens. Etenim alibi omnes qui laborat & onerati sunt, sitientes ite & efurietes omnes ad se vocat. Et hucusq; nemine reiecerat. Quid quod Samaritidē ipse innitat, & tu ea collo quendi occasione vænatur? Ista vero surda aure negligit, et ne respōsō quidē dignatur. Deinde in tercedentibus pro illa discipulis, negat se eius causa veniisse. Non sum missus (inquit) nisi ad oues perditas domus Israel. Nimirū quod promissiones et pacta salutis ad solos Iudaeos olim pertinue- runt (vt Paulus scribit) neq; in hoc venerat, vt ipse gentibus praedicaret, sed vt Circumcisionis effet Apostolus. Adhac occurrere voluit errori, quæ circa invocationē & intercessione Diuorū exoritur esse præuidebat: ne quis ex hoc loco eius defendendi occasione captaret: quod hodie nonnulli nimis ridicule faciunt. Etenim exemplu hoc cū eo, quod ipsi faciunt, minimè conuenit. Chananæa enim non aliquē ex mortuis invocat, sed discipulorū in terris viuentiū intercessione vtitur: illi cœlites iam olim vita defunctos copellant. Deinde nihil impetrant pro illa intercedentes Apostoli: vt neq; Maria virgo, quādo pro nuptijs Chananaicis, vino defitutus, intercessit. Deniq; nullo exemplo confirmari potest invocatio aut intercessio Diuorū: quādo omnes quotquot iā in cœlis beati viuūt, vnū Deū invocarunt per vnū Mediatore IESVM CHRISTVM, quē suū quoq; Aduocatum dicit dilectus ille discipulus, cui Virgo Mater ab illo iā morituro comendata est. Sed omissis his, quæ alterius loci sunt, ad Christum reuertamur, qui cum Chananæa propius accedēs & ad eius pedes prostrata (hoc enim etiā adoradi verbo significatur) denuò precaretur, Domine succurre mihi: ipse durius et nō abscq; cōuiciji specie illā reiicit, dicēs: Nō est bonū vel honestū, accipere panē liberorum, et obijcere catellis. Et apud Marcū præmittit, Sine primū saturari liberos. Quasi diceret: Turem inhonestā, iniustā, inquā petis. Filij Dei, quibus panis ille viuificus & saluberrimus debetur, cuius ego promus atq; dispensator sum, imò qui ego ipse sum, sunt Iudæi, qui ex semine Abrahami descendunt. Gentes aliæ omnes canes sunt, & indigni qui in Dei familia censeantur. Quin ergo facessis hinc, ne filijs obstrepas, quorum tam multi adhuc fame ringuntur?
units.tr: Let us next consider what sort of person Christ showed himself to be toward this woman. He answered her nothing at all. This was plainly new and unusual. For elsewhere he calls to himself all who labour and are burdened, bidding everyone who thirsts and hungers to come. And until now he had rejected no one. Why is it that he here ignores the Samaritan woman, and you hunt for an occasion for quarrelling in these words? That woman, however, he neglects with a deaf ear, and does not even deign to answer her. Then, when the disciples interceded for her, he says that he did not come for her sake. "I was not sent," he says, "except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel." Surely because the promises and covenants of salvation belonged of old to the Jews alone (as Paul writes), and he had not come in order that he himself should preach to the Gentiles, but that he might be an apostle of the circumcision. Moreover, he wished to meet an error which he foresaw would arise concerning the invocation and intercession of the saints: lest anyone should seize on this passage as a pretext for defending it, which some today do very absurdly. For this example does not agree at all with what they themselves do. The Canaanite woman does not invoke anyone who is dead, but uses the intercession of the disciples who are living on earth; they call upon the heavenly ones who have long since departed this life. Next, the apostles who interceded for her obtained nothing for her, just as the Virgin Mary, when she interceded for the Canaanite wedding, when the wine had run out, obtained nothing either. Finally, the invocation or intercession of the saints cannot be confirmed by any example, since all who now live blessed in heaven have invoked the one God through the one Mediator, Jesus Christ, whom that beloved disciple, to whom the Virgin Mother was commended by him as he was about to die, also calls our Advocate. But setting aside these matters, which belong to another place, let us return to Christ, who, when the Canaanite woman drew nearer and, prostrate at his feet (for this too is signified by the word "worship"), prayed again, "Lord, help me," rejected her more harshly, and not without the appearance of insult, saying: "It is not good or proper to take the children's bread and throw it to the little dogs." And in Mark he prefaces it with, "Let the children first be satisfied." As if he were to say: You seek a dishonourable, unjust thing, I say. The children of God, for whom that life-giving and most wholesome bread is owed, whose steward and dispenser I am, indeed whom I myself am, are the Jews, who descend from the seed of Abraham. All other nations are dogs, and unworthy to be counted in the family of God. Why then do you not get away from here, and stop disturbing the children, so many of whom are still perishing with hunger?

units.la: Vbi nō temere quærat aliquis, cur tā difficile & austerū sese præbuerit matri afflictæ, cuius pietas erga filiolā miserā, & egregia in ipsum fides merebatur (si carnis iudicium audias) vt mitius exciperetur, ne suæ gentis hominibus ludibriū fieret. At nō fecit hoc Dominus, quod suæ bonitatis aut promissionū immemor fuerit, aut affectui alicui indulserit. Sed quia fide istius publicè comendare, & toti posteritati in exemplū proponere volebat, necesse fuit eā manifestari, & in hac quasi lucta sive certamine omnibus conspicuā fieri. Deinde ipsi Chananæa proderat, vt fidem suam exerceret, & in Christi amore atq; salutis filiæ desiderio magis accederetur. Præterea eo illustrius fuit beneficiū, quod post tot tamq; graues rationes in contrariā partē adductas, illi contulit: vt eius posteā nō posset vnquā obliuisci. Et hæ causæ sunt, propter quas etiā hodie Dominus sese nobis difficiliore præbet, & interdū intra cōscientias nostras nos duris tentationū grauissimarū certaminibus exercet, priusquam opem optatam ferat. Alioqui suijpsius semper similis est, & inexhaustus est bonitatis eius thesaurus sive fons. Difficilior autem videri vult aliquando, vt & nobis consulat priuatim, & nostro exemplo plures alios instituat atq; consoletur.
units.tr: Here one may not rashly ask why he showed himself so difficult and severe to the afflicted mother, whose devotion toward her poor little daughter and remarkable faith in himself deserved (if you listen to the judgement of the flesh) to be received more gently, lest she be made a laughing-stock to the men of her own nation. But the Lord did not do this because he was forgetful of his goodness or of his promises, or because he indulged any feeling. Rather, since he wished to commend her faith publicly and to set it before the whole of posterity as an example, it was necessary that it be made manifest and be made visible to all in this, as it were, wrestling or contest. Furthermore, it benefited the Canaanite woman herself, so that she might exercise her faith, and be kindled more strongly with love for Christ and with desire for her daughter's salvation. Moreover, the kindness was all the more illustrious because he conferred it upon her after so many and such weighty reasons had been brought against her, so that she could never afterwards forget it. These are the causes for which the Lord even today shows himself more difficult to us, and sometimes, within our consciences, exercises us in the harsh contests of the gravest temptations before he brings the help we desire. Otherwise he is always like himself, and the treasury or fountain of his goodness is inexhaustible. He wishes, however, to seem more difficult at times, both so that he may look after us in private and so that by our example he may instruct and console many others.

units.la: Itaq; in lucta ista Chananæa imitemur. Hæc Christo tacēte nō tacet, sed precādo pergit, adeò vt discipulis mysterium nō intelligentibus molestia exhibeat. Deinde cum horū intercessione reici videret, nō propterea desperat, neq; eo exemplo terretur, sed preces ardentius & supplici gestu repetit. Postremo durius & ignominiosius copellata, nō exardescit in iram, vt vicissim conuitietur, aut de contumelia sibi factā impotentius queratur, vel vocibus desperantibus omnia copleat: Sed artificiosa concessione argumentū Christi in ipsum retorquet, dicens: Etiā Domine. Quasi diceret: Iam habeo quod volo, & ex tuo ore conuictu teneo. Fateor quod dicis, catella sum, & si quid hac vilius est. At tua catella sum, neq; alterius domini esse volo. Liceat ergo mihi per te quod aliis catellis conceditur. Repūt hi sub mensa dominorū suorū, vt micas & offa, quæ ex illa decidūt, colligat. Atqui tanta est tuæ bonitatis vbertas, tā lautus est tuæ mensæ, ad quā tuū populū inuitas, apparatus, vt mihi satis factū putē, si micis modicis frui possim, &c. Hæc & quæcunq; alia in hanc sententiā dici possunt, breui hoc dicto continentur, quo nō solū fidei suæ constantiā mulier ista declarat, sed eius exemplo docet insuper Spiritus sanctus, quàm ingeniosos & industrios faciat fides, vt ijs etiā pro nobis vti doceat, quæ Deus ipse contra nos allegare videtur. Et placet hæc industria Deo, qui a nobis vinci vult, vt (quod olim in Iacobo adumbratū fuit) veri Israelitæ, id est, principes aut victores Dei efficiamur. Imitemur ergo hanc Chananæā, & si quando Deus nostri oblitus esse et preces nostras surdis auribus præterire videtur, nō tamen animū despondeamus, sed instauratis fidei viribus illū vrgeamus, nec vereamur clamare: Quoūsq; obliuisceris nostri Domine? num perpetuò? quoūsq; faciem tuam a nobis abscondis? Excitare, excitare, & induere robur ô brachium Dominiz Excitare vt olim priscis temporibus. Annon tu ille ipse es, qui contudit hostis nostri ferociam draconem conculcauit? Annon benignitas tua & veritas durant in aeternum? Cur ergo nunc mu-tatus videaris? Ita si quando aliorum quoq;, imo publicas Ecclesiae preces, quae pro nobis fiunt, Deus aspernari videtur, id quoq; non terreat nos, sed ipsi in eius conspectum penetremus, & preces saepe fastiditas & reiectas repetamus. Quod si conscientia propria nobis objiciat: Non aequum neq; bonum est, ut exaudiaris. Canis es, porcus es, asinus es contumax, quis perdita es, & habe-nus tuas cupiditates secutus a Dei viis declinauisti. An nescis Sanctum canibus, & margaritas porcis proiici non debere: ne hoc quidem nos a statione deiciat, sed meminerimus, nos quales cum-que simus, Dei tamen canes, porcos, asinos esse, et hunc non hijce modo animalibus, verumetiam bestijs immanibus de suo victu proscicere, vulpibus sua lustra, coruorum pullis suam escam praeparare. Deniq; pia concessione fateamur nos eos esse, quos nos esse mens propria dictitat, petamus autem, ut pro suis tamen nos agnoscat Deus, & si filiorum nomine nos appellare dignetur, saltem (ut filius ille prodigus dicebat) nos mercenariorum loco habeat, aut catellos suos esse sinat, qui micis gratiae suae recreari possimus. Haec si constanti & invicta fiducia vrgeamus apud Deum, non su-strabimur spe nostra.
units.tr: Therefore in this wrestling let us imitate the Canaanite woman. When Christ is silent, she is not silent, but persists in praying, so much so that she causes trouble to the disciples, who do not understand the mystery. Then, when she sees herself rejected through their intercession, she does not on that account despair, nor is she terrified by that example, but repeats her prayers more ardently and with a suppliant gesture. Last of all, though addressed more harshly and insultingly, she does not flare up into anger so as in turn to revile him, or to complain too intemperately about the insult done to her, nor does she fill everything with despairing cries. Instead, by a skilful concession she turns Christ's argument back against himself, saying: "Yes, Lord." As if she said: Now I have what I want, and I hold it from your own mouth. I admit what you say, I am a little dog, and even something lower than that. But I am your little dog, and I do not wish to be the dog of another master. Let me therefore have through you what is granted to other little dogs. They creep under the table of their masters to gather the crumbs and scraps that fall from it. And yet the abundance of your goodness is so great, and the feast of your table, to which you invite your people, so splendid, that I shall think I have been satisfied enough if I may enjoy small crumbs, and so on. These and whatever else can be said to this effect are contained in this brief saying, in which this woman declares not only the constancy of her faith, but the Holy Spirit also teaches, by her example, how ingenious and diligent faith makes us, so that it teaches us to use even those things for ourselves which God himself seems to bring against us. And this diligence pleases God, who wishes to be conquered by us, so that (as was once foreshadowed in Jacob) we may become true Israelites, that is, princes or victors with God. Let us therefore imitate this Canaanite woman, and if at any time God seems to have forgotten us and to pass by our prayers with deaf ears, let us not lose heart, but with our strength of faith renewed let us press on, and not be afraid to cry out: "How long will you forget us, Lord? Will it be for ever? How long will you hide your face from us? Awake, awake, and put on strength, O arm of the Lord! Awake as in former times. Are you not he who crushed the fierceness of our enemy and trampled the dragon? Do your kindness and truth not endure for ever? Why then do you now seem to have changed?" So too, if at any time God seems to spurn even the prayers made by others for us, indeed the public prayers of the Church that are offered for us, let this not terrify us either, but let us press into his sight and repeat prayers that have often been despised and rejected. But if our own conscience objects to us: "It is neither fair nor good that you should be heard; you are a dog, a pig, a stubborn ass, you are lost, and having followed your own desires you have turned aside from the ways of God"; do you not know that what is holy must not be thrown to dogs, nor pearls to pigs? Even this should not cast us down from our post. Let us remember that, whatever we are, we are nevertheless dogs, pigs and asses of God, and that he is accustomed to cast the scraps of his food not only to such animals, but even to savage beasts; to foxes he gives their dens, and for the young of ravens he prepares their food. Finally, let us confess, with a devout concession, that we are what our own mind keeps saying we are, but let us ask that God nevertheless acknowledge us as his own, and if he deigns to call us by the name of sons, at least (as that prodigal son said) let him count us among his hired servants, or allow us to be his little dogs, who may be refreshed by the crumbs of his grace. If we press these things upon God with a steadfast and unconquered confidence, we shall not be disappointed in our hope.

units.la: Et huc facit huius historiae Catastrophe consolationis plena. Nam Christus Dominus quasi vi- tus respondet: O mulier, magna est fides tua, fiat tibi ut vis. Primo fidem mulieris commendat a magnitudine. Et sane magnam & haud vulgare esse oportuit fidem, quae toties repulsa non de-fecit, tot aerumnibus prostrata non succubuit, & inter tentationes gravissimas victrix fuit. Deinde liberaliter ei largitur quod petebat. Fiat tibi (inquit) ut vis. Plus ergo pollicetur, quam illa ver-bis eloqui potuerit. Fit hoc frequenter electis, ut quando ipsi dignis verbis non possunt exprimere animi sui desideria, Spiritus Sanctus pro illis postulet suspiriis inenarrabilibus, & Deus benigne ea etiam largiatur, quae ipsi nesciebant sibi necessaria esse. Apud Marcum addit: Propter istum sermonem abi, exijt daemonium ex filia tua. De sermone eo loquitur, quem fides constans & invi-cta extorserat. Huic ergo totu istud ascribi debet. Nec defuit effectus verbis Christi. Nam sana ta fuit filia eius ab eo momento. Sunt ergo verba Christi non otiosa aut inania, sed cum effectu coniuncta. Est enim ipse Verbum illud omnipotens, cuius virtute omnia creata sunt. Nec, obfuit hic loci distantia, quo minus ipse corpore absens filiam Chananaeae huius domi suae laborantem sanaret. Similis fuit servi Centurionis Capernaitici restitutio, de qua alibi dictum est. Simili etiam ratione & virtute aulici illius filium a morbo liberauit, cuius historiam Ioannes descripsit: Neminem ergo moueant absurda de omnipraesentia corporis Christi disputationes, quibus hodie Ecclesiam turbant ambitiosi rixatores, qui cum Maiestatis Christi vindices acerrimi haberi velint, talem fingunt, qui nisi corpore praesens adsit, & in fauces nostras se corporaliter ingerat, nos seruare & alere non possit. Nos cum agnoscamus, qui dilexit nos, & semetipsum pro nobis tradidit, peracto autem in terris nostrae redemptionis negotio, corpus suum in caelos subuexit, & illic ad dextram Patris sedet, accepta omni potestate in caelo & in terra, inde etiam nos tuetur, regit, seruat & alit ad vitam aeternam. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeter-num, Amen.
units.tr: And the conclusion of this story is full of consolation. For Christ the Lord answers, as it were, with the words: "O woman, great is your faith; let it be done for you as you desire." First he commends the woman's faith for its greatness. And indeed the faith must have been great and no ordinary faith, which was not wearied by being rebuffed so often, was not overcome by so many troubles, and triumphed over the most severe temptations. Then he generously grants her what she asked: "Let it be done for you," he says, "as you desire." So he promises more than she could have expressed in words. This often happens with the elect: when they cannot express the desires of their heart in fitting words, the Holy Spirit asks for them with unutterable groanings, and God graciously grants even those things which they did not know were necessary for them. Mark adds: "Because of that saying, go; the demon has gone out of your daughter." He is speaking of the saying which a constant and invincible faith had wrung out. This, therefore, must be ascribed entirely to it. Nor was the effect lacking to Christ's words, for her daughter was healed from that moment. Christ's words, then, are not idle or empty, but joined with effect; for he himself is that almighty Word by whose power all things were created. Nor did the distance of the place prevent him, though absent in body, from healing the Canaanite woman's daughter who was suffering at her home. Similar was the restoration of the servant of the Capernaum centurion, of which we have spoken elsewhere. In a similar way and by a similar power he freed the official's son from disease, whose story John has described. Let no one, therefore, be disturbed by the absurd disputes about the omnipresence of Christ's body, with which the ambitious wranglers now trouble the Church. Though they wish to be regarded as the most fierce defenders of Christ's majesty, they imagine a Christ who, unless he is present in body and bodily thrusts himself into our mouths, cannot preserve and nourish us. We, however, acknowledge him who loved us and gave himself up for us; and, when the work of our redemption on earth was finished, he lifted his body up into the heavens, and there sits at the right hand of the Father, having received all power in heaven and on earth. From there he also watches over us, rules, preserves and nourishes us to eternal life. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CC.
units.tr: HOMILY CC.

units.la: Et digressus illinc IESVS venit iuxta mare Galilaeae, & cum ascen-disset in montem, sedit illic. Tunc adijt illum turba multa, habens secum claudos, caecos, mutos, mancos, & alios multos: & abiece-runt eos ad pedes IESV, & sanauit eos: adeo ut turba mirata sit, cum videret mutos loquentes, mancos sanos, claudos ambulantes, caecos videntes: & glorificauerunt Deum Israelis.
units.tr: And Jesus departed from there and came near the Sea of Galilee, and went up into a mountain and sat there. And great crowds came to him, having with them the lame, the blind, the dumb, the maimed, and many others. And they laid them at Jesus' feet, and he healed them, so that the crowd marvelled when they saw the dumb speaking, the maimed made whole, the lame walking and the blind seeing. And they glorified the God of Israel.

units.la: Dominus et Seruator noster Iesus Christus nuper propter Scribarum et Pharisaeorum incredulitate et contumacia a Iudaeis secessit in fines Tyri et Sidonis: vbi insigne illud inuicta et incopa-rabilis fidei exemplum in muliere Chananaea est editum: Obsedit aut hac secessione sua, quid Iudaeos moueat
units.tr: Our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ lately withdrew from the Jews into the regions of Tyre and Sidon, because of the unbelief and obstinacy of the scribes and Pharisees. There he set forth that remarkable example of unconquered and incomparable faith in the Canaanite woman. It should be noted, however, what this withdrawal of his was meant to stir up in the Jews.

units.la: Nimirum vt ab ingratis & poenitere nescijs regnum Dei ad gentes transferatur. Quia vero non dum venerat tempus illud fatale, quo gentes promisicue per Euangelium vocari debebant, narratur hoc loco, vt post non longa moram Christus a Tyrijs & Sidonijs in Galilaeam redierit, & illic de nuo se Iudaeis per doctrinam & miracula multa & salutaria manifestarit: Vt ite maiori quam antea populi concursu & applausu exceptus sit. Quo loco primum eius bonitas commendatur, qui illic, vbi etiam contemnitur & reijcitur, non cessat benefacere: deinde diuinae virtutis & omnipotentiae specimen praebet, qua suos vocare potest illic, vbi hostes eius dominantur, adeoque omnes suas congregare et seruare inter medios lupos. In populi autem concursu dissicimus, quid eos facere oporteat, quos ille inuisit, et qui illo ad salutem frui cupiunt. Sed praestat singulas huius loci partes inspicere,
units.tr: Clearly, it was so that the kingdom of God would be transferred to the Gentiles from an ungrateful people who did not know how to repent. But since that fated time had not yet come, when the Gentiles were to be called indiscriminately through the Gospel, this passage relates that, after a short delay, Christ returned from the Tyrians and Sidonians to Galilee, and there again revealed himself to the Jews through his teaching and many saving miracles, so that he was received with a greater crowd and applause of the people than before. Here, first, his goodness is commended, for he does not cease to do good where he is despised and rejected. Next, he gives a proof of divine power and omnipotence, by which he can call his own where his enemies rule, and so gather and keep all his people in the midst of wolves. In the crowd of people, we shall see what those ought to do whom he has visited and who desire to enjoy him for salvation. But it is better to look at the individual parts of this passage one by one.

units.la: Prima Christum proponit qui a finibus Tyri & Sidonis digressus in Galilaeam redijt, non vt latere, sed vt se rursus propitium & beneficum Iudaeis sisteret: ideo in montem ascendit, notum videlicet omnibus et quo saepius se solitus erat recipere: & illic consedit, quasi expectaturus omnes, qui ipsius ope aut consilio vellent vti. Est hic obseruanda eius bonitas. Antea dissecerat ab ingratis & contumacibus: Nunc sponte redit, & patre imitatur, qui et filijs proteruientibus iratus, ab illis se alio conferat, aut eos iubeat e suo conspectu facescere, mox tamen eosdem reuocat ad se, aut ipse ad eos reuertitur, amica omnia pollicens si resipiscant. Ita olim saepius Deus cum Iudaeis egit, quorum sacra quoque reiecit, & ne posthac in templi sui atrijs comparerant, vetuit: mox tamen eosdem iterum inuitauit, & promissionibus amicis ad se pellexit. Sed & tota die se manus suas expandisse ait ad populum desertorem. Et quod in praesenti de Christo narratur, hoc illum frequenter fecisse legimus: quod item Laodicensibus dicit, se ad ostium stare & pulsare, hoc ipsum quotidie in temporalibus, quae corpori seruiunt, & in spiritualibus, quae animarum, vel potius hominis totius salutem concernunt. Quoties enim fit, vt frugibus, valetudine & corporis viribus abutamur. At licet illa tunc a nobis auferat: tamen denuo largitur, si quo modo ad resipiscentiam nos perducat. Idem fit quoad Euangelium, quod interdum contemnitur & reijcitur cum salute, qua nobis suae mortis merito Dei Filius acquisiuit. Veruntamen huius luce denuo offert miseris Dominus, et ad se inuitat omnes, qui laborant, aut sitiunt et esuriunt iustitia, & saepe ipse nos diutius expectat, nec mora & cunctatione nostra offenditur. Frequenter etiam Ecclesias illic instaurat, vbi prius hospitium ipsi negatum fuit: neque illi difficile est ouile suum inter medios lupos constituere, qui in illud crudeliter saeuiunt. Hanc facilitatem eius nos agnoscere decet, & Iudaeorum populum, de quo in praesenti agitur, imitari.
units.tr: First, it presents Christ, who, having departed from the regions of Tyre and Sidon, returned to Galilee, not to hide himself, but to show himself again as gracious and beneficent to the Jews. Therefore he went up into the mountain, a place known to all and to which he was accustomed to retire fairly often, and there he sat down, as if about to wait for all who wished to make use of his help or counsel. His goodness is to be observed here. He had previously withdrawn from the ungrateful and obstinate; now he returns of his own accord, imitating a father who, though angry at unruly sons, either withdraws from them or bids them leave his sight, yet soon calls them back to himself, or himself returns to them, promising all friendly things if they repent. So God often dealt with the Jews of old. He rejected their sacrifices too, and forbade them to appear again in the courts of his temple. Yet soon he invited them again and drew them to himself with friendly promises. He also said that he had stretched out his hands all day long to a rebellious people. And as is related now of Christ, we read that he often did this. Likewise, what he says to the Laodiceans, that he stands at the door and knocks, he does every day, both in temporal matters, which serve the body, and in spiritual matters, which concern the salvation of souls, or rather of the whole man. For how often do we abuse crops, health and bodily strength! Yet although he takes these from us at times, he gives them again, if in any way he may lead us to repentance. The same happens with the Gospel, which is sometimes despised and rejected together with the salvation that the Son of God has gained for us by the merit of his death. Yet the Lord offers again his light to wretched men and invites all who labour, or thirst and hunger for righteousness. Often he waits for us a long time, and is not offended by our delay and hesitation. He also frequently restores churches in places where hospitality was previously refused him. Nor is it difficult for him to establish his fold in the midst of wolves that rage cruelly against it. We ought to acknowledge this readiness of his and to imitate the people of the Jews of whom the present passage speaks.

units.la: Venit ad illum (inquit Matthaeus) turba multa, habens secum claudos, &c. Multa hic concurrunt magni studij & feruoris argumenta. Primo enim multi venerunt, vnde apparet illum ex pectatum venisse, & fama aduentus sui mox fuisse diuulgatam. Deinde venerunt domi relictis rebus omnibus, ex quo constat, illos Christum omnibus alijs, quae habebant, antepositisse. Veniunt autem ad eum, qui ab illis nuper abierat, & quem sciebant principibus suis inuisum & exosum esse. Adhaec non soli veniunt, sed adducunt variis morbis affectos & debilitatos, qui vehendi, aut gestandi erant, quod absque magna molestia, labore & sumptu fieri non poterat. Et hos omnes abiecerunt ad pedes IESV: quod etiam magnae contentionis indicium est, certum deniq; fidei argumentum, qua persuasi sufficere credebant, si illos possent in Christi conspectum adducere: Accedit his, quod totum triduum cum illo manserunt, vt postea ex eius verbis patebit: ex quo colligi potest, affectum hunc non temere conceptum aut momentaneum fuisse.
units.tr: "A great crowd came to him" (says Matthew), "having with them the lame," and so on. Many signs of great eagerness and zeal come together here. First, many came, whence it appears that he was expected, and that the news of his arrival was soon spread abroad. Next, they came leaving behind all their affairs at home, from which it is clear that they put Christ before all the other things they had. Moreover, they came to him who had lately departed from them, and whom they knew to be hated and detested by their rulers. Besides, they did not come alone, but brought with them those afflicted and weakened by various diseases, who had to be carried or borne, which could not be done without great trouble, labour and expense. And they all laid them at Jesus' feet. This too is a sign of great earnestness, and surely a clear proof of faith, by which they were persuaded that it was enough, if they could bring them into Christ's sight. To this is added that they stayed with him for three whole days, as will afterwards be clear from his words. From this it may be gathered that this feeling was not conceived rashly or was merely momentary.

units.la: Docemur autem hoc exemplo, quid eos deceat, quos Christus propitius inuisit. Accurrant ad eum, auidi et toto corde ampleCTantur, et nullis vel commodis priuatis sese retineri, vel minus abstinere sinant, quo minus id faciant. Qui amat patrem & matrem supra me (inquit ille) non est me dignus, qui amat filium et filiam supra me, non est me dignus. Imo si quis venit ad me, nec odit patrem suum ac matrem, & uxorem & liberos, & fratres & sorores, amplius autem etiam animam suam, non potest meus esse discipulus. Et nota est parabola eorum, qui quod villa aut boues emissent, aut circa nouas nuptas essent occupati, noluerunt ad nuptias coelestes accedere. Etenim Sodomae instar est mundus hic quem cum omnibus quae in eo sunt, relinquere oportet, si Christi & salutis in illo participes fieri volumus. Cur autem tyrannorum minis, aut egestatis & exilij metu nos auocari sinamus ab eo, qui Regum corda in manu sua tenet, neque suis aliquid deferri finit, adhaec patria et ciuitatem permanentem nunc in cælis parauit omnibus, qui ipsum sequuntur. Deinde nō ipsi modò ad Christū festinemus, verumetiā alios excitemus, vt se nobis socios & comites coiungant. Vaticinantur hoc de credentibus Propheta, quoniā dicit: Et proficiscentur populi multi, dicentes: Adeste, & ascendemus ad montē Domini, ad domū Dei Iacob, & docebit nos de vijs suis, &c. In primis aut eos adducamus nobisçu, qui ex nostris animo male affecti sunt, & quos peccati seruitus debilitauit, vt in Dei vijs ambulare nō possint. Et hos simul atq; nosipsos ad pedes Christi abijciamus, sic, vt omnia illius voluntati permittamus, qui quid de nobis debeat statuere, melius quàm nos ipsi intelligit. Deniq; quando assecuti sumus illū, cū eo in fine vsq; perseueremus, & stationē nostrā teneamus constanter, donec ipse de nobis aliquid aliud statuerit. Neq; vnquā excidat illud dictū: Nemo qui manu sua admota aratro, respexerit ad ea quæ a tergo sunt, aptus est regno Dei. Qui autē perseuerauerit vsq; in finem, saluus erit: Luc.19. Matth.24. Videamus nunc, quid Christus fecerit. Id vno verbo docet Euangelista, dicēs: Et sanauit eos. Satisfecit ergo desiderio & expectationi ad se venientiū, sicuti promisit, dicens: Venite ad me omnes, qui laboratis & onerati estis, & ego refocillabo vos. Item: Eum qui venit ad me, non eijcio foras. Sanauit autem eos, vt populus totus admiraretur. Admirationis causa fuit, quòd miraculose sanauit, nullis adhibitis medijs externis, sed vel verbo solo, vel contactu, & virtute, quæ (vt alibi dicitur) ex ipso exibat: deinde quòd perfectè illos curauit, vt nulla morbi vestigia remanerēt. Videbat enim populus mutos loqui, mancos sanos esse, claudos ambulare, cæcos videre: & hæc quidem subitò fiebant, cùm in morborū curatione, quæ remedijs fit, res paulatim & succesiuè (vt aiunt) procedat, vt non statim vires restaurentur. Visus vero horū hic nobis esse debet, vt ipsum agnoscamus medicū nostrū tā corporis quàm animæ, quale cap.9. supra se professus est, & ad illū solū accurramus. Medici est velle inualidos mederi, & id ipsum posse. At de Christi voluntate nō possumus dubitare, cùm eius causa sponte in mundū venerit, & omnes male habētes ad se vocet, adhæc facilem semper se omnibus præbuerit, qui opem eius requisiuerunt. Apparet hoc in præsenti, quādo promisit cuē omnes sanauit, qui adducebātur, & cùm toto triduo ipsum fatigarint, adeò nō offensus est populi importunitate, vt ne in via deficerēt præ inedia, prius gratuito epulo exceptos & saturatos dimiserit. Posse vero illū omnibus subuenire, certo argumento colligitur ex eo, quod eius virtuti & mandato omnes morbi cedunt, imò mors quoq;, quos morborū vi superauit, ad eius iussū restituere cogitur. Neq; aliquid illius potentiæ obstare potest, quādo nullis medijs externis ipsi opus est, et si medijs vti velit, quoduis obuium illi sufficit, vt pote nudus cōtactus, puluis, sputū, & alia similia: cuius rei exemplū in præsenti ædi tum esse Marcus scribit in homine surdo & difficulter loquente, quē curauit, cū digitos suos in eius auriculas misisset, & suo sputo linguā tetigisset. Simile de quoda, qui ab vtero matris cæcus fuerat, Ioannes narrat. Quis ergo de Christi virtute dubitet, quādo quæ in illo contemptissima sunt, ad quiduis perficiendum posse sufficere? qui deniq; morte sua vitam nobis conferre potuit? Quapropter hic medicus ante omnes alios solus confutandus erit in animæ morbis, qui per corporis infirmitates adbrantur. Etenim primū hominē Deus ad suā imaginē bonū & perfectū creauerat, qui diuina & cœlestia sapiebat, videbat, audiebat, loquebatur & faciebat. At ille veteris serpētis, diaboli cōsilio obediēs in Dei Creatoris sui Lege peccauit, & a dignitate sua excidit, & talis omnino factus est, quales isti describuntur: cæcus, claudus, mutus, mancus & mutilus. Aperti quidē dicitur fuisse Adamo oculi, sed nihil aliud vidit, quàm se nudū & miserū esse, qua aut ratione nuditatē suā velaret, & cū Deo in gratiā rediret, videre nō potuit. Perizoma quidē fecit, sed quo ne suos quidē oculos, nedū Dei fallere potuit. Et qui sua sponte ad Dei præceptū obsurduerat, nūc voce quidē eius audit, sed horribiliter tonante ac fulminante, vt ea ferre nequaquā possit. Ergo in pedes quidē se coijcit, sed claudos, quibus Dei iudiciū nō poterit effugere. A Deo aut citatus, vt ad eius tribunal causam dicat, loquitur quidē, sed vt surdastri & μογιλάλοι solet, & quæ causam ipsius nō defendunt, sed aggrauant, dum hanc in mulierē, imò in ipsum Deū transferre studet. Itaq; ad mortem damnatur infelix, & propter ipsum terra maledictioni subijcitur, sub cuius seruitio adhuc tota machina mundi ingemiscit, redemptionem suam expectans. At in hac imagine sua, id est, corrupta & depravata conditione sive statu Adam liberos suos genuit, & ita Legem peccati in omnem posteritatem propagauit, quæ (sicut Paulus & Dauid proprijs exemplis docent) in electis quoq; locum habet, qui prius quàm regeneratur & innouatur, tales omnino sunt, quales ante diximus: Caeci nimirum, qui non percipiunt quae sunt Spiritus Dei. Intellectus et rationis caecitate voluntas prava sequitur, ut figmeta cordis humani prava sint ab ineunte aetate, & caro Spiritui perpetuo reluctetur. Nec vires sunt aliquae, quibus illius proteruia frangamus, quàdo ex nobisipsis ne ad cogitandum quidem idoneifumus. Manci ergo sumus, et opera bona ex nobisipsis facere non possumus: claudi sumus, qui per semitas iustitiae et veritatis, etiam si nobis moestrentur, recto pede noncedimus: muti deniq; ut errores et delicta nostra neq; excusare, neq; culpa deprecari possimus, sed quo magis hoc conamur, eò magis nostra infantia prodimus. At his vitiis omnibus unus IESVS CHRISTVS medetur, qui lux mundi est omne hominem illuminans: ideo solus aures cordis nostri referat, ut Dei Verbu recte & cum fructu audiamus: manus viribus nouis instruit, ut faciamus, quae Deo probatur: pedes dirigit, ut in viis praeceptorum vita ambulet: lingua moderatur, ut Deum laudare, honesta ac pia loqui possit, adhaec Spiritu adoptionis cordibus nostris inserit, in quo clamamus, Abba Pater, et qui ideo lamentationis Spiritus dicitur, quod nos Deum recte inuocare et ea petere docet, quae nobis utilia et salutaria sunt. Deniq; vires omnes hominis ita instaurat Christus, ut in illo possimus omnia: Ad huc ergo solu coeddamus, reliquis procul agyrtis et impostoribus, qui dunos alio vocant, et vita pollicetur, toxica miscet, & inani labore et sumptu miseros fatigant.
units.tr: We are taught by this example what becomes those whom Christ has graciously visited. Let them run to him, eager and with their whole heart embracing him, and let them not allow themselves to be held back by any private advantages, nor fail to do so because of any lesser reluctance. "He who loves father or mother more than me," he says, "is not worthy of me; he who loves son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me. Indeed, if anyone comes to me and does not hate his father and mother, his wife and children, his brothers and sisters, and even his own soul, he cannot be my disciple." The parable is also well known of those who, because they had bought a farm or oxen, or were busy with a newly married wife, were unwilling to come to the heavenly wedding. For this world is like Sodom, and it must be left behind together with all that is in it, if we wish to become partakers of Christ and of salvation in him. Why then should we allow ourselves to be called away from him, by the threats of tyrants or by the fear of poverty and exile, when he holds the hearts of kings in his hand, allows nothing to be taken from his own, and has prepared in heaven a lasting homeland and city for all who follow him? Next, let us not only hurry to Christ ourselves, but also stir up others, so that they may join us as companions and fellow travellers. The prophet prophesies this of believers, since he says: "Many peoples shall go and say, Come, and let us go up to the mountain of the Lord, to the house of the God of Jacob, and he will teach us his ways," etc. Above all, let us bring with us those among our own people who are ill-disposed in mind, and whom the bondage of sin has weakened, so that they cannot walk in the ways of God. Let us cast these and ourselves together at the feet of Christ, so that we commit everything to his will, for he understands better than we do what he ought to decide concerning us. Finally, when we have obtained him, let us persevere with him to the end, and hold our position constantly, until he himself decides something else about us. Let that saying never fall from our minds: "No one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back to what is behind is fit for the kingdom of God. But he who perseveres to the end will be saved" (Luc. 19; Matth. 24). Let us now see what Christ did. The Evangelist teaches this in one word, saying: "And he healed them." So he satisfied the desire and expectation of those who came to him, as he had promised, saying: "Come to me, all you who labour and are heavy laden, and I will refresh you." Likewise: "Him who comes to me I will not cast out." Moreover, he healed them so that the whole people might marvel. The cause of the wonder was that he healed miraculously, using no external means, but by a word alone or by touch, and by power which (as is said elsewhere) went out from him; and further, that he cured them perfectly, so that no traces of the disease remained. For the people saw the dumb speaking, the maimed made whole, the lame walking, the blind seeing; and these things happened suddenly, whereas in the cure of diseases that is effected by remedies, the matter proceeds gradually and successively (as they say), so that strength is not restored at once. Yet the sight of these things ought to be for us a sign that we acknowledge him as our physician, of body and of soul alike, as he professed himself to be above in chapter 9, and that we run to him alone. It is the physician's part to wish to heal the weak, and to be able to do so. Now we cannot doubt Christ's willingness, since he came into the world of his own accord for this very cause, and calls all who are ill to himself; moreover, he has always shown himself easy to approach by all who sought his help. This appears in the present case, when he promised and healed all who were brought to him; and although they had wearied him for three whole days, he was so little offended by the people's importunity that, lest they should faint on the way from hunger, he first received them to a free feast and dismissed them satisfied. That he is able to help all is clearly gathered from the fact that all diseases yield to his power and command, and even death itself, which has overcome those whom diseases have struck, is compelled to restore them at his bidding. Nor can anything stand in the way of his power, since he needs no external means; and if he wishes to use means, anything at hand suffices for him, such as bare touch, dust, spittle, and other similar things. An example of this, which Mark writes was given in the same case, is the deaf man who spoke with difficulty, whom he healed when he had put his fingers into the man's ears and touched his tongue with his spittle. John relates something similar about a man who had been blind from his mother's womb. Who then could doubt Christ's power, when those things which are most despised in him are able to suffice for effecting anything whatever? Indeed, by his death he was able to confer life upon us. Therefore this physician must be acknowledged alone, before all others, as the one who cures the diseases of the soul, which are made manifest through the infirmities of the body. For God had created the first man good and perfect, in his own image, one who understood, saw, heard, spoke and did things divine and heavenly. But he, obeying the counsel of the old serpent, the devil, sinned against the Law of God his Creator, fell from his dignity, and became altogether such as those described here: blind, lame, dumb, maimed and crippled. It is true that Adam's eyes are said to have been opened, yet he saw nothing but that he was naked and wretched; and by what means he might cover his nakedness and return into favour with God, he could not see. He did indeed make a loincloth, yet with it he could not deceive even his own eyes, much less God's. He who had of his own accord grown deaf to God's command now hears his voice, but thundering and lightning terribly, so that he can by no means bear it. So he throws himself at God's feet, but lame feet, by which he cannot escape God's judgment. Summoned by God to plead his cause before his tribunal, he does speak, but like a stammerer and one who is dumb [μογιλάλοι], and what he says does not defend his cause but aggravates it, while he strives to transfer the blame to the woman, and indeed to God himself. And so the unhappy man is condemned to death, and because of him the earth is made subject to the curse, under whose servitude the whole frame of the world still groans, waiting for its redemption. But in this image of his, that is, in his corrupt and depraved condition or state, Adam begot his children, and so propagated the law of sin to all posterity; and this law (as Paul and David teach by their own examples) also has its place among the elect, who, before they are regenerated and renewed, are altogether such as we said before: blind indeed, for they do not perceive the things of the Spirit of God. Through the blindness of the understanding and reason the perverse will follows, so that "the imaginations of the human heart are evil from youth," and the flesh constantly resists the Spirit. Nor are there any strengths by which we might break its obstinacy, since of ourselves we are not even fit to think. We are therefore maimed, and cannot do good works of ourselves. We are lame, who, though the paths of righteousness and truth are shown to us, do not advance with a straight foot. Finally, we are dumb, so that we can neither excuse our errors and sins nor plead guilty to them; but the more we try to do so, the more we betray our childishness. Yet Jesus Christ alone heals all these defects, he who is "the light of the world, enlightening every man." Therefore he alone opens the ears of our heart, so that we may hear the Word of God rightly and with profit; he equips the hands with new strength, so that we may do what is pleasing to God; he directs the feet, so that we may walk in the ways of his commandments; he governs the tongue, so that it may praise God and speak what is honest and pious. Moreover, he implants in our hearts the Spirit of adoption, in whom we cry, "Abba, Father"; and he is called the spirit of lamentation for this reason, that he teaches us to call upon God rightly and to ask for those things which are useful and salutary for us. Finally, Christ so restores all the strength of man that in him we can do all things. Let us therefore cleave to him alone, leaving far behind the other charlatans and impostors, who call us elsewhere while promising life, mix poisons, and wear out the wretched with vain labour and expense.

units.la: Porro videamus postremo quid isti his visis fecerint. Admirati quidem sunt (ut diximus) cum viderent mutos loquentes, mancos sanos, claudos ambulantes, caecos videntes: nec aut in otiosa admiratione (ut stupidi & attoniti solet) subsistunt, sed (ut Marcus annotauit) primò veritati testimonium ferunt, & illum omnia bene & recte facere fatetur: deinde glorificat Deum Israelis. Loge ergo alia illis mens fuit, quàm Pharisaeis, qui illum in nomine & virtute Beelzebub daemonia eijcere, & miracula facere calumniabantur. Et nominatim Deum Israelis glorificat, qui etiam Sanctus Israelis apud Prophetas dicitur, quod Israelitas sese foedere obstrinxerat, & inter illos cultus fui fedè coli tuerat, Lege ite & iudicia sua illis comendarat: deniq; quod promissum humani generis Seruatore ex Iudaeis in carne nasciturum erat pollicitus. Vnde in Psalmis canitur: Notus in Iuda Deus, magnum nomen eius in Israele: In Salem est tabernaculum eius, & mansio eius in Zione: Nuntiat Verbum suum Iacobo, & decreta sua atq; iudicia sua Israeli. Hunc (inquam) Deum non alienum glorificarunt, & ex miraculis ipsius, quae Messias facturus esse Prophetae praedixerat, in fide confirmati, Deo huic gratias egerunt, qui misericordiae & veritatis suae recordatus erga domum Israelis (ut Dauid cecinit), diu expectatum Redemptorem miserit. Imitemur nos horum exemplum, quando hodie eadem videmus fieri, & multi per Euangelij praedicationem reflituuntur, ut diuina & caelestia videat, audiant, loquantur, & in viis Dei ambulent, qui prius in tenebris caeci oberrabant, & infelicia erat peccati mancipia, & ad proprium interitum ruebant. Admiremur bonitatem Dei, & eius Filium IESVM CHRISTVM, qui hanc gratiam nobis meruit, praedicemus, & eundem constanti fide ampleftamur. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Next let us see, finally, what those men did after these things were seen. They were indeed amazed (as we have said) when they saw the dumb speaking, the maimed made whole, the lame walking, the blind seeing; nor do they stay in idle wonder, as stupid and astonished men are wont to do, but (as Mark noted) first they bear witness to the truth, and confess that he does all things well and rightly; then they glorify the God of Israel. Their mind, therefore, was far different from that of the Pharisees, who slandered him as casting out demons and performing miracles in the name and power of Beelzebub. And they glorify by name the God of Israel, who is also called in the Prophets the Holy One of Israel, because he had bound himself by covenant to the Israelites, had faithfully been worshipped among them, had entrusted to them his law and judgments, and finally had promised that the Saviour of the human race would be born in the flesh of the Jews. Hence it is sung in the Psalms: "God is known in Judah, his name is great in Israel. In Salem is his tabernacle, and his dwelling in Zion. He declares his word to Jacob, and his statutes and judgments to Israel." This God (I say) they did not glorify as a stranger, and, confirmed in faith by the miracles of him whom the Prophets had foretold the Messiah would perform, they gave thanks to this God, who, mindful of his mercy and truth towards the house of Israel (as David sang), sent the long-awaited Redeemer. Let us imitate their example, since today we see the same things happening, and many, through the preaching of the Gospel, are restored, so that they see, hear and speak divine and heavenly things and walk in the ways of God, who before were blindly wandering in darkness, and were unhappy slaves of sin, and were rushing to their own destruction. Let us admire the goodness of God and praise his Son Jesus Christ, who merited this grace for us, and let us embrace him with steadfast faith. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCI.
units.tr: HOMILY CCI.

units.la: IESVS autem aduocatis discipulis suis, dixit: Miserictordia commoueor erga turbam, quia iam triduum permanent apud me, & non habent quo vescantur: & dimittere eos ieiunos nolo, ne deficiant in via. Tunc dicunt ei discipuli eius: Vnde nobis in deserto tot panes, vt saturemus turbam tantam? Dicit igitur eis Iesus: Quot panes habetis? Illi autem dixerunt, Septem, & paucos piscciculos. Tunc iussit turbam discumbere humi. Et acceptis septem illis panibus ac piscibus, cum gratias egisset, fregit, deditq; discipulis suis: discipuli vero turbae. Comederuntq; omnes, & saturati sunt: & sustulerunt quod superfuerat fragmentorum septem sportas plenas. Erant autem qui comederant, quatuor mille viri, absq; mulieribus & paruulis. Et dimissa turba ineecndit in nauigium, venitq; in fines Magdala.
units.tr: Then Jesus called his disciples to him and said: "I have compassion on the crowd, because they have now been with me for three days and have nothing to eat. I am unwilling to send them away hungry, lest they faint on the way." The disciples said to him: "Where in the desert could we get so many loaves to satisfy such a great crowd?" Jesus said to them: "How many loaves do you have?" They answered: "Seven, and a few small fish." Then he ordered the crowd to sit down on the ground. He took the seven loaves and the fish, gave thanks, broke them, and gave them to his disciples, and the disciples gave them to the crowd. They all ate and were satisfied, and they took up the broken pieces left over, seven baskets full. Those who had eaten numbered four thousand men, besides women and children. After sending the crowd away, he got into the boat and came to the region of Magdala.

units.la: IESVS. Matth. 15.
units.tr: JESUS. Matt. 15.

units.la: MEmorabile & obseruatu dignißimū est Pauli Apostoli dictum: Pietas ad omnia vtilis est, vt quæ promissionē habeat præsentis vitæ & futuræ. Nam consentit huic quod Dominus noster IESVS CHRISTVS dixit: Quærite primò regnū Dei & iustitiā eius,& cætera omnia vobis adijcientur. Etsi vero hæc multis exemplis confirmata sint olim, subinde tamen exerit sese innata vitiofitas, quasit, vt præsentibus intenti nos a Deo negligi putemus, & ab inopia & fame nobis metuamus, si non abundanter suppetant, quæ caro expetit, aut sibi necessaria esse arbitratur. Et obrepit tentatio ista plerunq;, si quando propter Christum & Euangelii eius defacultatibus no stris periclitamur, aut saltē ad tempus deposita rei domestica cura audiendis sacris cōcionibus aut publicis precibus vacare iubemur. Ideo Dominus nuper nos insigni miraculo confirmauit, quando quinq; millia virorum quinq; panibus hordeaceis et duobus piscibus ad satietatem vsq; cibauit. At quia hoc ne apud discipulos quidem domesticos tantum profecerat, quantū necesse erat, nunc alterū subijcit, priori prorsus simile, nisi quod in circumstantijs aliquod est discrimen, quoad numerū panum & conuiuarum, et quoad reliquias siue fragmenta, quæ superfuerunt. In priori enim quinq; panibus & duobus piscibus quinq; millia virorum satiata, & ex reliquijs cophini 12.repleti sunt. In præsenti panes plures, septem nimirum, numerantur, conuiuæ autem pauciores, & fragmentorum quoq; minus superfuit. Ita vero fieri voluit Dominus, vt doceret virtutem suam nullis circumstantijs alligatā esse, sed prout ipsi placuerit, posse se suos in copia & inopia alere. Id quod frequenter videmus accidere, vt annonæ pretiū tolerabilius fiat, quando granaria fere exhausta sunt: et rursus caritas rerum & penuria crescat, post colleētas fruges et impleta horrea omnia. Deinde in hoc miraculo clarius elucet Christi erga suos seētatores studium, & humani ingenij tarditas in percipiendis regni Dei mysterijs. Præcipuum autem totius historiæ vsus est, quòd docemur, nunquam de futurum Deum ijs, qui reliētis huius seculi rebus Filium eius sequuntur, & æternæ vitæ mysteria terrenis præferunt. Præstat autem primò Occasionem miraculi videre: Deinde quàm tardos & crassos sese præbuerint discipuli, qui pra alijs in fide debebant excellere. Præterea, vt Christus, horum incredulitate non passus fit fraudi esse populo, qui ipsum fide ardenti & constanti sequebatur.
units.tr: Memorable and most worthy of observation is the saying of the Apostle Paul: "Godliness is profitable for all things, since it holds the promise of the life that now is and of that which is to come." This agrees with what our Lord JESUS CHRIST said: Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these other things will be added to you. Although these things were confirmed long ago by many examples, our innate vice still breaks out from time to time, so that, intent on present things, we think that God neglects us, and we fear poverty and hunger if the things the flesh craves, or thinks necessary to itself, are not abundantly at hand. This temptation often creeps in when we are put in danger for Christ and his Gospel with the loss of our possessions, or when we are ordered to lay aside our household cares, at least for a time, to attend to the hearing of sacred sermons or public prayers. For this reason the Lord recently confirmed us by a remarkable miracle, when he fed five thousand men with five barley loaves and two fish until they were satisfied. But since this had not profited even his household disciples as much as was necessary, he now sets before us another, quite similar to the first, except that there is some difference in the circumstances, both in the number of loaves and guests, and in the scraps or fragments that were left over. In the first, five thousand men were satisfied with five loaves and two fish, and twelve baskets were filled with the leftovers. In this one, there are more loaves, namely seven, but fewer guests, and less of the fragments was left over. The Lord wished it to happen this way so that he might teach that his power is bound to no circumstances, but that he can, as he pleases, feed his people in plenty and in want. We often see this happen: the price of grain becomes more bearable when the granaries are nearly empty, and again the scarcity of goods and want grow after the harvest is gathered and all the barns are full. Furthermore, in this miracle the care of Christ for his followers and the slowness of the human mind in grasping the mysteries of the kingdom of God shine out more clearly. The principal use of the whole story is that we are taught that God never fails those who, leaving the things of this age, follow his Son and prefer the mysteries of eternal life to earthly things. Now, first, we should consider the occasion of the miracle; then how slow and dull the disciples showed themselves to be, who ought to have excelled the others in faith; and besides, how Christ did not allow their unbelief to harm the people who followed him with a burning and steadfast faith.

units.la: Occasionem ipse Dominus exponit, quæ eum mouet, vt miraculū hoc ederet. Cùm enim videret, populum doctrinæ & sanationibus inualidorū intentū famem perpeti, aduocatus ad se discipu-lis suis domesticis, ait: Misericordia commoueor erga turba, quia iam triduū permanent apud me, & nō habēt quo vescātur, et dimittere eos ieiunos nolo, ne desiciat in via. Status cōsilij siue insti-ti Christi est, Quòd nolit populū ieiunū et famelicū dimittere. Id vero consiliū illi misericordia sug-gessit, qua esurientes prosequebatur. Et ne hæc commiseratio superuacanea & inanis putetur, ratio-nes adducit, quæ ipsum moueant & impellant. Prima est, quòd iam totum triduū cum ipso perseue-rent. Est hoc magni studij & feruoris indicium in populo, quorū pleriq; a longinquo et remotis locis venerant, vt ex multitudine cōijcere licet. Altera ratio est, Quod nō habeat quo vescatur. Nā hoc triduo absumpserat, quicquid secū domo attulerat: et credibile est, multos in hoc subito et tumultua-rio concursu, vt fieri solet, vacuos venille. Additur tertia ratio, Ne deficiat in via. Quod de illis præcipuè dicitur, quibus etiā pecuniæ deerat, quibus in vicis et oppidis vicinis cibaria sibi emeret.
units.tr: The Lord himself sets out the occasion that moved him to work this miracle. For when he saw that the people, intent on his teaching and on the healing of the sick, were suffering hunger, he called his household disciples to himself and said: "I have compassion on the crowd, because they have now been with me for three days and have nothing to eat, and I am unwilling to send them away hungry, lest they faint on the way." The settled plan or purpose of Christ is that he is unwilling to send the people away fasting and hungry. This purpose was prompted by the mercy with which he cared for the hungry. And lest this compassion be thought superfluous and empty, he adduces the reasons that move and impel him. The first is that they have now remained with him for the whole three days. This is a sign of great zeal and fervour in the people, many of whom had come from far away and remote places, as we may gather from the size of the crowd. The second reason is that they have nothing to eat. For during these three days they had used up whatever they had brought with them from home, and it is credible that many came in this sudden and tumultuous gathering, as usually happens, with empty hands. A third reason is added: lest they faint on the way. This is said chiefly of those who lacked money, with which they might buy food for themselves in the neighbouring villages and towns.

units.la: Habemus in hoc sermone exemplū paternæ curæ & prouidentiæ Christi erga suos, plenū dul- cissimæ consolationis. Toto hoc triduo multa in illos beneficia contulerat, adhæc multū laboris et molestiæ sustinuerat, dum omnium, qui ad ipsum promiscuè afferebantur, morbis medetur. At non cessat, quasi iām omni officio defunctus sit, sed vt fidus et indulgens pater curas suas longius exten-dit, vt quid eis porrò opus sit cogitet, & in futurū quoq; egentibus prospiciat. Scit enim illos nō ha-bere quod edant. Scit quid de illis, qui insuper pecunijs destituebantur, in via futurū sit, si incæna-tos dimittat. Ideo miseretur illorū, deq; illis pascedis cōsiliū init, et hoc discipulis suis priuatus com-municat, nō quod ab ipsis iuuari posset, sed vt simul horū diffidentiæ medeatur. Et hoc facit nō re-quisitus a quoquā, neq; alicuius merito prouocatº. Seruiat hæc cōsolationi in omni necessitate. No-uit Deus omnes nos, et victu et amictu nos indigere intelligit. Qui ergo volatilibº cœli et pullis cor norū, bestijs ite illa largitur, procul dubio suos cultores nō negliget. Et generale est quod hic de istis dicit, Nolo illos ieiunos dimittere, ne in via deficiat. Nā similiter in huiº vitæ via, quæ laborū et periculorū plena est, nō ulla ut deficiamus, quoad opera nostra vti voluerit. Nō finit Domin° (vt Solomo ait) vt anima iusti fame laboret. Et Dauid huic suggess: Leūculi, id est, homines raptores & violenti, penuria & fame laborabunt, qui autem Dominum inquirunt, nullo bono destituentur. Eius enim voluntas cum effectu coniuncta est, & sufficit ad remouendas omnes remoras aut obstacula, quae nobis mundus aut eius princeps obicit. De illo enim verissime canitur: Deus noster in caelo est, omnia quae vult perficit. Ipsi ergo securi & quiete fidamus: & si quid durius nos premit, in ipsum reiiciamus sarcinam nostram: & ipse faciet. Vide quae in hanc sententiam a Davide dicuntur Psalmo 55.37. & 23. Licet autem nobis in hac Christi erga populum indulgentia videre, quis spiritus personatos ipsius vicarios agitet, qui miseros & famelicos humanis traditionibus circumducunt, & egenos cogunt, relictis uxoribus ac liberis per terras et maria peregrinari, ubi frequenter non facultatum modo inutilem iacturam faciunt, sed domi uxorum pudicitiam, ipsi foris vitam propriam in discrimen adducunt, &c.
units.tr: In this passage we have an example of Christ's fatherly care and providence for his own, full of the sweetest consolation. Throughout these three days he had conferred many benefits on them, and besides had endured much labour and trouble while he healed all who were brought to him indiscriminately with their diseases. Yet he does not stop, as if he had already done all his duty, but, like a faithful and indulgent father, he extends his cares further, considering what they will need besides, and provides for them who are in want even for the future. For he knows that they have nothing to eat. He knows what will become of those who, besides, lack money, on the way, if he sends them away unfed. Therefore he takes pity on them and resolves to feed them, and he tells this plan privately to his disciples, not because they could help him, but so that he might at the same time cure their distrust. He does this without being asked by anyone, and without being provoked by anyone's merit. Let this consolation serve us in every need. God knows all of us, and understands that we need both food and clothing. Therefore he who gives such things to the birds of the heaven and the young ravens will undoubtedly not neglect his worshippers. And what he says here about these people is a general truth: "I am unwilling to send them away fasting, lest they faint on the way." For likewise, on the way of this life, which is full of labours and dangers, no one shall faint, as far as our works are such as he wishes us to use. The Lord, as Solomon says, does not allow the soul of the righteous to suffer hunger. And David, drawing on this, says: "The young lions, that is, men who are plunderers and violent, shall suffer want and hunger, but those who seek the Lord shall lack no good thing." For his will is joined with effect, and it is sufficient to remove all the hindrances and obstacles that the world or its prince throws in our way. Of him it is most truly sung: "Our God is in heaven; he does whatever he pleases." Therefore let us trust in him securely and quietly, and if anything weighs on us more heavily, let us cast our burden upon him, and he will act. See what David says to this effect in Psalms 55, 37 and 23. We may see, from this indulgence of Christ towards the people, what spirit drives those who play at being his vicars, who lead the wretched and hungry about by human traditions, and compel the needy, leaving their wives and children, to wander through lands and seas, where they often not only suffer the useless loss of their goods, but also, while at home bring their wives' chastity into danger, and abroad their own lives, etc.

units.la: Quia vero Christus in suis actionibus exemplum nobis praebuit, ut hunc commiserationis affectus indulgentiae imitemur, necesse est. Vult enim nos sui similes esse, maxime quoad dilectionem. Dicit enim: Mandatum novum do vobis: ut alij alios diligatis, sicuti dilexi vos, ut & diligatis alij alios: Ex hoc cognoscent omnes, quod discipuli mei sitis, si charitatem habueritis alij in alios. At charitatis proprium est misereri aliorum & egentium molestijs & curis tangi, sicuti Samaritani exemplo alibi docet: cui in praesenti proprium coniungit. Et omnes immites ac immisericordes mendacij arguit Apostolus, scribens: Qui habuerit facultates mundi, & viderit fratrem suum egentem, & clauserit viscera sua coram eo, quomodo charitas Dei manet in ipso? Nec satis est, si in praesenti aliorum labores & miseriae nobis cordi sint: sed in futuru quoq; omnibus prospiciamus, quoad eius fieri poterit: quod Christus hic fecisse audimus. Nam non modo beneficijs maximis cumulatos dimittit, sed nec in via prae inedia deficiant, prospicit. Pertinet haec cura ad omnis ordinis & loci homines, & in primis eos, quibus aliorum salus publice credita est. Aduersus futuras conscientiae tentationes audito resque suos praemuniat Verbi administri, ne forte ignitis diaboli telis succumbant. Norut quotidianis exemplis edocti magistratus omnes eos perire & ad egestatem redigi, qui communi nostri seculi viam secuti intemperantia & luxui sese dedunt, comessantur, ludunt, & in omne petulantia atq; libidines effunduntur. Frano igitur proteruos illos coerceat, & sumptuarijs legibus intemperantia modum praescribat. Sicut ijdem vulgus monopolijs grauari, vsuris voracibus exedi & a faeneratoribus deglubi. Hos ergo in ordine redigant, ne aliquando publicorum motuum & calamitatum auctores sint. Deniq; diligenter annonae ratione siue curam habeant, qui ad Rempub. gubernacula sedent (sicuti olim in Aegypto Iosephus fecit) ne famis tempore aliqui rerum nouarum occasiones possint aripere. Priuatim vero ad parentes haec cura maxime pertinet.
