Etenim hunc sensum bestijs et volucribus natura infeuit, ut suos pullos aut catulos fideliter alat, imo p eis periclitetur, donec sibi ipsis illi possunt prospicere. Et ut alibi monuimus, apud prophanas gentes pessime audiuerunt ἄσοργοι illi, qui liberorum suorum cura nulla tanguntur. Quid ergo de illis iudices, qui dies noctesq; comessantur et suas facultates inter pocula, alea, scorta et scurras prodigunt, esurientibus interim uxoribus & ex se progenitis liberis? Sunt hi infideli deteriores (ut Apostolus ait) & fidem abnegarunt, et proinde indigni quos terra ferat, nedum ut Ecclesiae Christianae membra censeantur. 1. Tim. 5.
units.tr: Since Christ has given us an example in his own actions, it is necessary that we imitate this affection of compassionate kindness. For he wills us to be like himself, above all in love. For he says: "A new commandment I give you, that you love one another, as I have loved you, that you also love one another. By this all will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another" [John 13:34–35]. But it is the proper mark of love to be concerned for others and to be moved by the troubles and needs of the poor, as he teaches elsewhere by the example of the Samaritan, and here he adds it as a mark of its own kind. The Apostle also convicts all who are hard-hearted and merciless of lying, writing: "Whoever has the goods of this world and sees his brother in need, and closes his heart against him, how does the love of God abide in him?" [1 John 3:17]. Nor is it enough if the labours and miseries of others are dear to us in the present; we must also look ahead for them in the future, as far as it can be done, which we hear Christ did here. For he not only dismisses those who have been loaded with the greatest benefits, but also takes care that they do not faint from hunger on the way. This care belongs to people of every rank and place, and above all to those to whom the salvation of others has been publicly entrusted. The ministers of the Word should fortify their people against the future temptations of conscience, so that they do not perhaps succumb to the fiery darts of the devil. The magistrates, taught by daily examples, know that all those perish and are reduced to poverty who, following the common way of our age, give themselves over to intemperance and luxury, feast, gamble, and pour themselves out into every kind of wantonness and lust. Let them therefore curb those wanton people with a bridle, and let them prescribe a limit to intemperance by sumptuary laws. Likewise let them restrain the common people, who are burdened by monopolies, eaten away by ravenous usury and flayed by moneylenders. Let them bring these men into order, lest at some time they become the authors of public upheavals and calamities. Finally, let those who sit at the helm of the commonwealth take diligent care of the grain supply (as Joseph once did in Egypt), so that in a time of famine some men cannot seize the chance for revolution. Privately, this care belongs chiefly to parents. For nature has implanted this feeling even in beasts and birds, so that they faithfully feed their young chicks or puppies, and even risk themselves for them until the young can provide for themselves. And as we have noted elsewhere, among the heathen nations those "without natural affection" [ἄσοργοι] who are moved by no concern for their own children have had a very bad name. What, then, will you judge of those who feast day and night and squander their means on drinking, dice, prostitutes and buffoons, while their wives go hungry and the children they have begotten are starved? These are worse than unbelievers (as the Apostle says), and have denied the faith, and are therefore unworthy of the earth that bears them, let alone of being counted members of the Christian Church. 1 Tim. 5.

units.la: Sed tempus est, ut Apostolos videamus. Hi paternae bonitati & prouidentiae Christi suas rationes opponunt, et quantum in ipsis est, illa impediunt. Unde nobis (inquiunt) in deserto tot panes, ut saturemus turbam tantam? Haud dubie sibi ipsis videntur egregie sapere, sed stultitia et infantiam sua turpiter produnt. Primo perinde loquuntur, ac si ipsos oporteat conuiuium populo tam multo et numeroso adornare. Unde NOBIS tot panes inquiunt? Atqui hoc non requisierat ab illis Dominus, sed ut amicis (quales alibi vocat) suu consilii ipsis manifestauerat: de cuius executione non debebant dubitare, cum maiora & difficiliora opera ab ipso fieri multoties vidissent, & in omnium ore adhuc esset miraculu non ita pridem editum, quo maiorem hominum multitudinem paucioribus panibus cibauerat. Potius ergo dicere debebant: Quod non vis ieiunos dimittere aut incoenatos, id vero iure probamus, et facile tibi fuerit illis coena parare, cum tibi omnia obediant: & ut id facias, precamur. Sic leprosum illum dixisse legimus: Domine si vis, potes me mundare.
units.tr: But it is time to look at the Apostles. They set their own reasoning against the fatherly goodness and providence of Christ, and, as far as lies in them, they hinder it. "Where," they say, "are we to get so many loaves in the desert, to satisfy such a great crowd?" Undoubtedly they seem to themselves to be wonderfully wise, but they shamefully betray their folly and infancy. First, they speak as if it were their business to furnish a feast for so large and numerous a people. "Where," they say, "are WE to get so many loaves?" Yet the Lord did not ask this of them, but had made known his plan to them as friends (as he elsewhere calls them), and they ought not to have doubted its execution, since they had often seen greater and more difficult works done by him, and the miracle not long before performed, by which he had fed a larger crowd of people with fewer loaves, was still on everyone's lips. They ought rather to have said: "What you do not want, that we dismiss the hungry or unfed, that we rightly approve, and it will be easy for you to prepare a meal for them, since all things obey you; and we pray that you do it." Thus we read that the leper said: "Lord, if you will, you can make me clean."

units.la: Deinde loci incomoditate allegant: Unde nobis IN DESERTO tot panes? Quasi diceret Vbi nihil nascitur, quod demeti possit et colligi: Vbi ita nihil venale inuenitur. Quasi vero Dominus, vbi versaretur, versaretur, nesciret. Tertiò multitudinis quoq; & turbæ numerosæ meminerunt, ad quam pascendam multò pluribus panibus opus fit, quàm ipsi habere possint. Ad eundem ergo lapidem offendunt cum Mose, qui olim similiter Domino obloquebatur: Unde mihi caro, ut dem vniuerso populo huic Num.11.
units.tr: Then they allege the inconvenience of the place: "Where in the DESERT are we to get so many loaves?" As if to say: where nothing grows that can be gathered and collected; where nothing for sale is found at all. As if the Lord, wherever he was, would not know, indeed, would not know where he was. Thirdly, they also mention the multitude and the large crowd, for whose feeding far more loaves are needed than they themselves could have. So they stumble over the same stone as Moses, who once likewise grumbled against the Lord: "Where am I to get meat to give to all this people?" Num. 11.

units.la: Apparet in his exemplis carnis ingenium, quæ sibijpsi fidei remoras obijcit, quando cumpri- mis Verbo Dei credendum erat. Fit hoc in re domestica frequenter, quando liberos plures dat Do minus, & numerosæ familiæ alendæ sunt, annui reditus autem, aut proventus siue quæstus, qui ex opificio nostro potes{ } colligi, sumptibus tantis non sufficere videntur. Tunc similes voces audiuntur: Unde mihi opes & pecuniæ in hoc rerum statu, tam afflictis nostri sæ-culi rebus, quibus meos alam? Solus sum, neminem habeo qui me iuuet, &c. Quòd si quæstionibus istis indulgere lubet, mox demissa fide desperationi locus datur, vel ad furta, rapinas, imposturas omnis generis & media illicita conuertimur. Atqui non postulat hoc Deus, ut ex tuo illos omnes alas. Tuo quidè labore, tua industria vtitur. Interim ex sua benedictione domus tua dependet, & melius nouit ille, quàm tu, quàm multi tibi sint liberi, quàm tenues facultates, quàm difficilia tempora. Quin ergo illi res tuas commendas, &c. Idem soleت in Republica & Ecclesia fieri, si quando persecutio feruet, & in fide constantes esse iubemur. Mox audiuntur qui ogganniant: Unde nobis vires suppetent? Vnde auxilia aut præsidia sperabimus, quæ hostium potentia & conatibus reprimendis sufficiant? Soli sumus, amicum aut socium habemus neminem, qui sua authoritate aut potentia nos subleuet, &c. At cogitandum erat, non nostrum, sed Dei negotium agi, qui causæ suæ non deerit, & facile di scutiet bullas istas, quas humana ratio, vel ipse etiam Satan, obtendit.
units.tr: The nature of the flesh shows itself in these examples, which throws obstacles in the way of its own faith, when above all the Word of God ought to be believed. This happens often in domestic affairs, when the Lord gives more children and a large family must be fed, while the yearly income, or the profit that can be gathered from our trade, seems not enough for such expenses. Then similar words are heard: "Where am I to get wealth and money in this state of affairs, with the troubles of our age so harsh, to feed my own? I am alone, I have no one to help me," and so on. But if we are pleased to indulge these questionings, soon faith is weakened, and room is given to despair, and we turn to theft, robbery, deceits of every kind, and unlawful means. Yet God does not demand that you feed all of them from your own resources. He uses your labour and your diligence. Meanwhile your household depends on his blessing, and he knows better than you how many children you have, how slender your means are, how difficult the times are. Why not therefore commit your affairs to him, and so on? The same thing is wont to happen in the commonwealth and the Church, when persecution rages and we are commanded to be steadfast in the faith. Soon there are those who grumble: "Where shall strength come from for us? Where shall we hope for help or protection sufficient to repress the power and attempts of our enemies? We are alone; we have no friend or ally who may raise us up by his authority or power," and so on. But we ought to consider that it is not our business but God's that is being carried on, and he will not fail his cause, and will easily scatter those bubbles which human reason, or even Satan himself, puts forward.

units.la: Porrò ad Christum redeamus, qui nihil offensus discipulorum rationibus, ad miraculum accin gitur. Primò autem, quia illi de panibus quæstionem mouerunt, amicè quàm multos habeant panes, quærit: & est hoc nouum bonitatis argumentum, quòd tam benignè cum illis agit, qui seuerius corripi merebantur. Sed & ad miraculi certitudinem faciebat, quòd certò constaret de panum numero. Deinde hoc cognito mox iubet populum discumbere humi: ut illos omnes in spem et expectationem conuiuij excitaret, et facilius conuiuæ numerari possent. Humi autem discumbere iubet, ut humilitatis & modestiæ admoneat, quæ in primis opus est iis, qui Christi conuiuæ esse volunt. Tertiò sumit illos ipsos panes & pisces, idque omnibus videntibus, quòd præter hos nulla alia cibaria præsto essent. Quartò gratias agit pro more, ut victum & omnia necessaria à Deo nobis dari doceat, & gratiarum actione sanctificari, ut nobis sint salutaria. Meminerimus autem nos Deo illas etiam pro modico debere, quod nobis non sufficere videtur: quia ne hoc quidem nobis debet ille, sed gratuitum donum est quicquid de manu eius accipimus. Quintò frangit, quo opus erat, ut possent in multos distribui, & ut inter manus frangentis multiplicarentur. Sextò dat discipulis, hi populo appo-nunt. Vbi obseruari debet, quòd horum ministerio vtitur, ut proprio testimonio conuincantur, qui impossibile putauerant tam paucis panibus tantam turbam hominum satiare. Fit hoc sæpe nobis, ut per nos conficiat Dominus, quod fieri non posse existimabamus. Tunc vero eius bonitatem a-gnoscere, & illi obsequium nostrum fideliter præstare debemus. Septimò, omnes comedunt, nec mo-do comedunt, sed saturantur. Non fuit ergo præstigium, qualia in antatores multa facere solent. Octauo ex septem panibus supersunt septem sportæ plena fragmentorum: quod per se miraculum est, quo admonemur, Dominum suorum laboribus & studijs ita benedicere, ut in futurum quoq; prospiciat, & ut supersit quod alijs largiantur, secundum illud Psalmi: Dispersit, dedit pauperi-bus, iustitia eius manet in æternum. Nono amplificationis ergo annotatur numerus conuiuarum, qui fuerunt quatuor mille viri, præter mulieres & paruulos.
units.tr: Let us return, however, to Christ, who, not at all offended by the reasoning of the disciples, proceeds to the miracle. First, because they raised the question about the loaves, he kindly asks how many loaves they have; and this is a new proof of his goodness, that he deals so gently with those who deserved to be rebuked more severely. But it also served to make the miracle certain, since it was clearly established how many loaves there were. Then, this being known, he at once orders the people to recline on the ground, so that he might rouse them all to hope and expectation of a feast, and so that the guests could be counted more easily. He orders them to recline on the ground to remind them of humility and modesty, which is especially necessary for those who wish to be guests of Christ. Thirdly, he takes those very loaves and fishes, and does so with everyone looking on, because there were no other provisions at hand besides these. Fourthly, he gives thanks, as was customary, to teach that food and all necessities are given to us by God, and to be sanctified by thanksgiving so that they may be wholesome for us. We should remember, however, that we owe thanks to God even for what seems to us little and insufficient, since he owes us not even this, but whatever we receive from his hand is a free gift. Fifthly, he breaks the loaves, as was necessary, so that they could be distributed among many, and so that they might be multiplied in the hands of the one breaking them. Sixthly, he gives them to the disciples, and these set them before the people. Here it should be observed that he uses their ministry, so that those who thought it impossible to satisfy so great a crowd with so few loaves might be convicted by their own testimony. This often happens to us: the Lord accomplishes through us what we thought could not be done. Then indeed we ought to acknowledge his goodness and faithfully render our obedience to him. Seventhly, all eat, and not only eat but are satisfied. It was therefore no sleight of hand, such as jugglers commonly perform. Eighthly, from the seven loaves there remain seven baskets full of fragments: which is a miracle in itself, by which we are admonished that the Lord so blesses the labours and efforts of his people that he also provides for the future, and that there remains something to give to others, according to that verse of the Psalm: "He has scattered abroad, he has given to the poor; his righteousness endures for ever." Ninthly, to add emphasis, the number of the guests is noted: they were four thousand men, besides women and little children.

units.la: Vsus vero miraculi idem est, quem in priori Cap.14. annotauimus: Vt nimirum videamus, ni-hil defore Dominum serio sequentibus. Est ergo sigillum promissionū, quas initiò recitauimus, & quæ multæ in Veteri & Nouo testamento occurrunt: & quæ quotidianis exemplis confirmantur, vt alibi dictum est. Neq; hic aliquis obijciat, interdum aliter fieri, & Christi cultores sæpe cum egestate & fame conflictari, exules incertis sedibus iactari. Sunt enim promissiones Christi cum cruce coniunctæ: quam partim nostra securitate & aliis deliciis meremur, partim quòd illa no-stram petulantiā coerceri, & insuper nos ad desiderium cœlestium bonorum, ad patientiam item & constantiam exerceri oportet. Quæ etiam causa est, quòd non semper initiò statim votis nostris satisfacit quemadmodum his quoq; non primo aut secundo, sed tertio demum die epulum illud gratuitum exhibuit. Nec nos hunc Dei morem mirari conuenit. Solent delicatuli, qui stomacho laborant, & quibus pra abundantia appetitus languet, hunc acetarijs & condimentis exquisitis acuere, & ijsdem fere optimum condimentum est fames. Ideo Artaxerxes Mnemon, cum in fuga essent impedimenta eius directa, et siccis ficis atq; hordeaceo pane esuriens vesceretur, exclamabat: Pape, qualis voluptatis baltenus inexpertus fui? Et Ptolomaeus Ægypti Rex, cum illi famelico in casa pauperis rustici cibarium panis daretur, Nil visum, ait, illo pane iucundius. Et miramur, o fratres, Deum hoc condimento nos, qui caelestia fastidimus, excitare ad eorum desiderium? Agnoscamus ergo in eo quoq; bonitatem eius, qui inter aduersa, etsi opem interdum differat, non tamen obliuiscitur Veritatis sua, & ita nobis adest, vt cum Paulo possimus dicere: In omnibus premimur, at non coarctamur: haesitamus, at non prorsus haeremus: persecutionem patimur, at non in ea deserimur: deiicimur, at non perimus. 2. Cor. 4.
units.tr: The use of the miracle is the same as I noted in the earlier chapter 14: namely, that we may see the Lord will lack nothing to those who sincerely follow him. It is therefore the seal of the promises which we recited at the beginning, and which occur often in the Old and New Testaments, and which are confirmed by daily examples, as has been said elsewhere. Nor should anyone object here that sometimes things turn out otherwise, and that the worshippers of Christ are often struggling with want and hunger, and exiles are tossed about with no certain home. For the promises of Christ are joined with the cross, which we deserve partly through our own carelessness and other pleasures, and partly because it is right that these be restrained, and that we be trained, besides, in longing for heavenly goods and in patience and constancy. This is also the reason why he does not always satisfy our prayers immediately at the start; as he did not give that free feast to these people on the first or second day, but only on the third day. Nor is it fitting for us to wonder at this manner of God. Delicate people who suffer from a weak stomach, and whose appetite is dulled by excess, are accustomed to sharpen it with relishes and exquisite seasonings, and hunger is almost the best seasoning for these same people. So Artaxerxes Mnemon, when his baggage had been sent ahead during his flight, and he was eating dried figs and barley bread while hungry, cried out: "Pape, how much pleasure have I until now gone without!" And Ptolemy, King of Egypt, when a hungry man was given a piece of bread in the hut of a poor farmer, said: "I have seen nothing more pleasant than that bread." And shall we, brothers, wonder that God rouses us, who scorn heavenly things, to desire them by this seasoning? Let us therefore recognize in this also his goodness, who among adversities, though he sometimes delays help, nevertheless does not forget his truth, and so is present to us, so that with Paul we can say: We are pressed on every side, yet not crushed; we are perplexed, yet not in despair; we are persecuted, yet not forsaken; we are cast down, yet not destroyed. 2. Cor. 4.

units.la: Sequitur Epilogus praesentis historiae, quo dicitur, Christum dimissa turba populi navigium ingressum esse, & venisse in fines Magdala, unde oriunda fuit Maria, quae Magdalena vocatur, & cuius frequens est mentio apud Euangelistas. Duo narrantur: primum, quod non solum initio amice excepit ad se venientes, deinde amice tractauit sanando aegrotos & cibando esurientes, verumetiam dimisit amice: quod vera ac syncera humanitatis argumentum est. In eo enim a multis peccatur, qui amici officia praestant initio, sed mox pertaesi eorum, quos exceperunt, eosdem odio suis & non sine animi abalienati significatione repellunt. At non sic Dominus: & quod in praesenti fecit, hoc ipsum ab eo obseruatum fuit, quando iam ex hoc mundo discessurus erat. Nam mortem aditurus, discipulis pollicebatur, se nolle ipsos orphanos relinquere, & addebat: Pacem relinquo vobis, pacem illam meam do vobis. Et cum caelos ascenderet, postremum quod in terris fecit, hoc erat, quod manibus ad discipulos sublatis benedixit eis, & se ipsis adesse velle promisit vsque in consummationem saeculi. Hinc ergo consolationem petamus in tentationibus: Nec enim iratus a nobis abijt Christus, sed quamvis corporis praesentiam abstulerit, gratia tamen & merito suo, ac Spiritus virtute nobis adest. Alterum est, quod in fines Magdala abijt, non vt otiaretur ignauus, sed vt eius etiam loci hominibus beneficeret. Nam vniuersalis Seruator est, & proinde plurimus innotescere debuit: quae causa est (vt alibi diximus) quod nunquam diutius haesit in vno loco, sed peregrinationibus assiduis vacauit, vt quam plurimos seruaret. Itaq; ei fidamus securi, nec dubitemus de eius gratia, quam nobis offert per Euangelium. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: There follows the epilogue of the present story, in which it is said that Christ, having dismissed the crowd, got into a boat and came into the region of Magdala, whence came Mary, who is called Magdalene, and who is often mentioned among the Evangelists. Two things are related: first, that he not only received kindly those who came to him at the start, but then treated them kindly, healing the sick and feeding the hungry, and moreover dismissed them kindly; which is a proof of true and sincere humanity. For many go wrong in this respect: they perform the duties of friendship at the start, but soon, weary of those whom they have received, they repel the same people with hatred, and not without a sign of an alienated mind. But the Lord is not like this; and what he does in the present case, he was also seen to do when he was about to depart from this world. For, about to die, he promised his disciples that he did not wish to leave them orphans, and he added: "I leave you peace, my peace I give to you." And when he was ascending to heaven, the last thing he did on earth was this, that with his hands lifted up to the disciples he blessed them, and promised that he would be with them even to the end of the age. Let us therefore seek consolation from this in temptations: for Christ did not depart from us in anger, but although he has taken away the presence of his body, yet by his grace and merit, and by the power of the Spirit, he is with us. The second point is that he departed into the region of Magdala not to be idle and lazy, but so that he might also do good to the people of that place. For he is the universal Saviour, and therefore he had to be known to very many; this is the reason (as we have said elsewhere) why he never remained longer in one place, but devoted himself to constant journeys, so that he might save as many as possible. Therefore let us trust in him securely, and let us not doubt his grace, which he offers to us through the Gospel. To him belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPUT XVI.
units.tr: CAPUT XVI.

units.la: HOMILIA CCII.
units.tr: HOMILIA CCII.

units.la: ET cum accessissent Pharisaei & Sadducaei, tentantes rogarunt eum, vt signum e coelo ipsis ostenderet. Ipse vero respondens dixit eis: Quando serum est diei, dicitis: Serenitas rubet enim coelum. Et mane: Hodie tempestas erit, rubet enim coelum triste. Hypocritae, faciem quidem coeli nostis discernere, signa vero temporum non potestis? Natio mala & adultera signum requirit, sed signum non dabitur ei nisi signum illud Ionae Prophetae. Et relictis ipsis abijt.
units.tr: And when the Pharisees and Sadducees came and, to test him, asked him to show them a sign from heaven, he answered and said to them: When it is evening, you say, "It will be fair, for the sky is red." And in the morning, "Today there will be a storm, for the sky is red and lowering." Hypocrites, you know how to discern the face of the sky, but you cannot discern the signs of the times? An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign, but no sign will be given to it except the sign of the prophet Jonah. And leaving them, he went away.

units.la: ICVTI Dei Filius IESVS CHRISTVS vbiq; locorum habet electos suos, qui in ipsum credendo Veritati testimonium ferunt, et quotidie maiores faciunt in pietate progressus: ita Satan quoq; sua organa habet, impios nimirum & reprobae mentis homines, qui excitat ad contradicendum Veritati, & qui si semel caeperint (vt Apostolus scribit) quotidie in peius proficiunt. Na quo efficacius confortantur, eo contumaciores fiunt, et conuictis pugnam. pugnam instaurant. Exemplo sunt Pharisæi, quorū frequentes & continuas cum Christo pugnas Matthæus narrat: quas ideo nos sæpè & diligenter nobis in mentem vocare oportet, vt discamus, nunquam desore nobis aduersarios, qui se Euangelio oppomant, nec tamen nos ideo animo frangi, sed stationem nostram fortiter tueri debere, nec dubitare, eò illustriore exurgere Veritatis lucem, quo pertinacius eam mundus infelix obscurare conatur. Et huc referri debet historia, quam modò recitauimus, in qua eandem pugnam, quam supra cum Christo Pharisæi habuerunt, instaurant: & voluit hanc quoq; describi Spiritus Sanctus, quia de multis nos admonet, quæ omnibus sæculis cognitu perquam necessaria sunt.
units.tr: Just as the Son of God, Jesus Christ, has his chosen ones in every place, who bear witness to the Truth by believing in him and make greater progress in godliness every day, so Satan also has his instruments, namely the impious and men of reprobate mind, whom he stirs up to contradict the Truth. Once they have begun (as the Apostle writes) they advance for the worse every day. For the more they are strengthened, the more stubborn they become, and once they are convicted they renew the fight. The Pharisees are an example, whose frequent and continual conflicts with Christ Matthew relates. We ought often and carefully to call these to mind, so that we may learn that we shall never lack adversaries who set themselves against the Gospel, and that we must not on that account be broken in spirit, but must bravely defend our position, and not doubt that the light of the Truth rises all the brighter the more stubbornly the unhappy world tries to obscure it. The story we have just recited should also be referred to this point, in which the Pharisees renew the same struggle they had earlier with Christ. The Holy Spirit wanted this also to be recorded, because it warns us about many things that are exceedingly necessary to know in every age.

units.la: Primò nominantur Christi Domini aduersarij, Pharisæi nimirum & Sadducæi. Fuerunt hi diuersæ religionis, imò si verù dici debeat, Sadducæi ab omni religione alieni censeri possunt, cum religionis principia, animarum immortalitatem, corporum resurrectionem, adhæc spiritus tam bonos quam malos negauerint. Veruntamen quæ erat eius sæculi calamitas, inter Iudæos in pretio erant, haud dubiè, quòd Romanis præsidibus probaretur hæc illorum opinio, quæ ad Epicuræos proxime accedebat, quorum secta apud gentes erat celeberrima. Et ideo videntur illos sibi adiunxisse Pharisæi, vt facilius Christum in invidiam aut suspicionem traherent, vt qui ne illis quidem probaretur, qui ab ipsis prorsus dissentiebant. Quæ etiam causa fuit, quòd alibi Herodianos sibi sociarunt, quando quæstionem de censu Cæsari persoluendo mouerunt. Matth.22.
units.tr: First, the adversaries of Christ the Lord are named: the Pharisees and the Sadducees. These belonged to different religious parties; indeed, if the truth must be told, the Sadducees could be regarded as altogether alien to religion, since they denied the principles of religion: the immortality of souls, the resurrection of bodies, and, in addition, both good and evil spirits. Nevertheless, whatever the misfortune of that age, they were held in esteem among the Jews, no doubt because their opinion, which came very close to that of the Epicureans, whose sect was most famous among the Gentiles, was approved by the Roman governors. For this reason the Pharisees seem to have joined them to themselves, so that they might more easily bring Christ into odium or suspicion, since he would not be approved even by those who wholly dissented from them. This was also the reason why, elsewhere, they joined the Herodians to themselves when they raised the question of paying the tax to Caesar. Matt. 22.

units.la: Et est hoc obseruatu dignum, quòd etsi in mundo sectæ sunt & opiniones de religione multùm inter se diuersæ & contrariæ, omnes tamen illæ aduersus Christum consentire possunt. Etenim dum rat adhuc ista mundi facies, quòd alij in eo sunt iustitiarij hypocritæ, & hi inter se in plurimas su perstitiones scinduntur: alij Epicuræi, religionis omnis contemptores: & licet hi inter se pugnent acerrimè, neutri tamen Christum ferre possunt, eò quòd hic sua luce vtrofq; arguit. Idem fieri solet etiam apud alios, quorum eadem est in superstitionibus aut prophano Dei contemptu sententia. Sic Pilatum & Herodem conuenisse legimus, vt alius alij gratificaretur aduersus Christum, qui Luc.23. hucusq; inimicitias inter se exercuerant. Arguit hoc mundi corruptissimū ingenium, qui (vt Ioannes ait) totus in malo iacet: simul verò admonet, ne ex impiorum dissensionibus spem nobis faciamus (reuera enim hæ si ad Christi causam veniatur, amoris redintegratio sunt) sed vni Christo si damus, & in hoc vnum simus, eoq; arctiori dilectionis vinculo coalescamus cum iis, qui idem nobiscum in Christo sentiunt & loquuntur. Peccatur in eo multum hodie ab illis, qui propter leniculas causas ab iis sese separant, quos pro fratribus in Christo debeant agnoscere: Et est hoc exquisitum Satanæ stratagema, qui cum Ecclesiam credentium consensione crescere & augeri sciat, dissensionum & simultatum semina spargit, ex quibus lites acerbissimæ & nocentissimæ nascuntur. In primis ergo vtile ac necessarium est, à priuatis litibus renuntiare, quando communis Christi causa agitur.
units.tr: It is also worth noting that, although in the world there are sects and opinions about religion that differ and conflict greatly with one another, yet all of them can agree against Christ. For while this face of the world still lasts, some are self-righteous hypocrites, and these are split among themselves into very many superstitions; others are Epicureans, despisers of all religion. And although these fight among themselves most fiercely, neither can bear Christ, because he convicts both of them by his light. The same thing usually happens among others whose opinion is the same in superstitions or in profane contempt of God. Thus we read that Pilate and Herod came together, so that one might gratify the other against Christ, though until then they had carried on enmity between themselves (Luke 23). This reveals the most corrupt nature of the world, which (as John says) lies wholly in evil. At the same time it warns us not to build any hope on the dissensions of the impious (for in truth, if they come to the cause of Christ, these are a restoration of their friendship), but to give ourselves to Christ alone, and to be united in this one thing, and to cling together with a closer bond of love to those who think and speak the same as we do in Christ. Today many sin greatly in this respect, separating themselves for trifling reasons from those whom they ought to acknowledge as brothers in Christ. This is an exquisite stratagem of Satan, who, knowing that the Church of believers grows and increases by agreement, scatters the seeds of dissension and enmity, from which the most bitter and most harmful quarrels arise. Therefore it is above all useful and necessary to renounce private quarrels when the common cause of Christ is at stake.

units.la: Quid verò isti fecerunt? Marcus illos cum Christo disceptauisse aut disputasse scribit: nimirum de vocatione eius & quis ipsi docendi potestatem fecerit. Nam de eo alibi quoque eos quæsiuisse constat. In præsenti autem mouit eos, quòd doctrinam eius miraculorum multitudine indies propagari videbant. Nec dubium est, in omnium ore fuisse, quæ nuper in frequenti concursu populi facta fuerunt, quando inualidos multos curauit, & quatuor millia virorum cum magna turba mulierum & paruulorū gratuito epulo excepit. Hoc enim illud erat, quòd Iudæos vulgo in primis quæsiuisse constat ex Ioan. Cap.6. Quia ergo hæc omnes admirabatur & prædicabant, consilia sua maturanda esse putarunt aduersarij, vt miracula eius (quod prius etiā conatifuerant) in dubium vocarent, & ea ratione existimationem illius labefactarent. Ideo disceptatione mota, vt signum aliquod e cælo ipsis ostenderet, postulauerunt. Id verò tentandi eius causa factū est, vt commodam & optatam calumniandi occasionem inuenirent, qua illum ludibrio populi exponerent.
units.tr: But what did those men do? Mark writes that they disputed or argued with Christ, namely about his calling and by whose authority he taught. For it is established that they asked about this elsewhere too. At present, however, what troubled them was that they saw his teaching spreading daily by the multitude of his miracles. Nor is there any doubt that what had recently been done in the crowded gathering of the people was on everyone's lips, when he healed many who were sick and fed four thousand men, with a great crowd of women and children, at a free feast. For this is what the Jews are known to have sought above all, as John 6 shows. Because they all admired these things and proclaimed them, the adversaries thought that their plans must be hastened, so that they might call his miracles into doubt (which they had already tried before) and by this means undermine his reputation. Therefore, with the dispute stirred up, they demanded that he show them some sign from heaven. This was done for the purpose of testing him, so that they might find a convenient and desired occasion for slandering him, by which they could expose him to the mockery of the people.

units.la: Exprimitur hoc exemplo vafrum & arrogans hypocritarum ingenium. Simulant veritatis studium, quam tamen nolunt audire, multò minus agnita credere, etiamsi propria mentis testimonio conuincantur. Deinde audaciter signū petunt non necessarium. Nam nihil docebat Christus nonum & insolens, & iampridem sua omnia Mosis & Prophetarum authoritate probauerat. Et Ioan.3. si ex signis indicari oportuisset de eius doctrina, innumera iam ante viderant, & quotidie fiebant quæ illis poterant fidem facere. Adhæc confidenter præscribunt, vt signum e cælo ipsis ostendat, quasi in illum ius habeant & imperium. Præterea sibi ostendi volunt peculiare quid, quasi quæ in populi conspectu hucusque fecerat, nihil ad ipsos pertinerent. Imò illa omnia in dubium vocant, quæ tamen neq; negare, neq; improbare poterunt, & totius populi consensu probabantur. Tales hodie multi passim audiuntur. Profitentur se veritatis studiosos esse: at cùm nihil doceatur, quàm quod cum principiis Christianæ religionis conuenit, cum Decalogo nimirum, & symbolo & Oratione Dominica, non tamen credunt. Interim Pharisaica impudentia signa postulant, qualia olim Apostoli & Martyres fecerunt. At quid illis opus est, cùm non aliud doceatur, quàm quod illi olim tradiderunt? Cur nouitatis insimulant doctrinam, quam illi nō miraculis modò, sed sanguine pro prio obsignarunt? Deniq; vt Pharisæi signa, quæ quotidie secundum Scripturas fiebant, nō obser- uabant, petebant autem noua & scripturis contraria. Sic hodie isti faciunt, & proinde eodē Spiritu agitantur, quo Pharisæi: neq; eorum clamoribus aliquis debet moueri.
units.tr: This example reveals the crafty and arrogant nature of hypocrites. They pretend a zeal for the truth, which yet they are unwilling to hear, much less to believe once it is recognized, even when they are convicted by the testimony of their own minds. Then they boldly demand a sign that is not necessary. For Christ taught nothing new or strange, and he had long since proved all his teaching by the authority of Moses and the Prophets. And if (John 3) his teaching had to be shown by signs, they had already seen countless ones before, and things were happening every day that could have given them faith. Besides, they confidently prescribe that he show them a sign from heaven, as if they had a right and authority over him. Moreover, they want something peculiar shown to them, as if the things he had done until then in the sight of the people were of no concern to them. Indeed, they call into doubt all those things which they could neither deny nor disapprove, and which were approved by the consent of the whole people. Many such people are heard everywhere today. They profess to be zealous for the truth, yet when nothing is taught but what agrees with the principles of the Christian religion, namely the Decalogue, the Creed and the Lord's Prayer, they still do not believe. Meanwhile, with Pharisaic shamelessness, they demand signs of the kind that the Apostles and Martyrs once performed. But what need have they of these, since nothing else is taught than what those men handed down? Why do they accuse of novelty a doctrine which they sealed not only with miracles but with their own blood? Finally, the Pharisees did not observe the signs that were daily performed according to the Scriptures, but they sought new ones contrary to the Scriptures. So today these men act, and they are driven by the same spirit as the Pharisees; no one should be moved by their outcries.

units.la: Porrò videamus alteram huius loci partem, qua, quid Christus fecerit aut dixerit, narratur. Marcus ipsum Spiritu suo alte ingemuisse dicit. Vehemens animi affectus notatur, quo perturbatus fuit: nimirum quod eos in pertinacia sua inuictos videret. Qui enim nostræ salutis ergo in mundum venit, non potest non perturbari, si quos videt contumaciter & scientes volentes sibi ipsis exitiū accersere. Et debent huius meminisse, qui hodie vel incredulitate vel peccandi licentia Filium Dei, aut Spiritum Sanctum, per quem ab illo obsignati sunt (vt Apostolus scribit) in diem redemptionis tristitia afficiunt. Cæterum responsionis partes sunt duæ.
units.tr: Next let us look at the other part of this passage, in which what Christ did or said is related. Mark says that he groaned deeply in his spirit. A strong emotion of mind is noted, by which he was troubled, namely because he saw them invincible in their obstinacy. For he who came into the world for our salvation cannot but be troubled when he sees some stubbornly and knowingly bringing destruction upon themselves. Those who today, by unbelief or by licence in sinning, grieve the Son of God or the Holy Spirit, by whom they have been sealed (as the Apostle writes) unto the day of redemption, ought to remember this. Moreover, there are two parts to the answer.

units.la: Prima malitiosam ipsorum ignorantiam arguit, docens, eos signum postulare minimè necessarium. Quando serum est diei, dicitis: Serenitas: rubet enim cælum, &c. Sensus verborum est: Hypocritæ estis nefarij, qui veritatis studium simulatis, sed id malitiosè & fraudulenter facitis. Si enim illa vobis cordi esset, facile in eius notitiam peruenire posset is. Nā non adeo stupidi estis & amentes, quin ex signis naturalibus, seu prognosticis, tempestatibus, & harū vices quantumuis varias & instabiles possitis præuidere. Atqui habetis signa temporum æque clara & perspicua. Cur ergo illa non obseruatis & discernitis? Vocat autem temporum signa ea, ex quibus apparebat nouissimum tempus iam esse, quo Messiam venturū esse, Deus olim per Prophetas prædixerat: quale erat, quòd sceptrū a Iuda prius auferri debuit: quod certum annorum numerum ab instaurata vrbe decurrere oportuit, & Dauidis domum ad pristinam egestatē redigi, vt non amplius regali splendore illustris, sed aridus Isai truncus, & terra arida sine siticulosa posset censeri: quòd ite prædictum erat: Tunc aperientur oculi cæcorum, & aures surdorum reserabuntur: tunc exiliet claudus tanquam cervus, & iubilabit lingua muti. Atqui hæc omnia (inquit) iam pridem impleta sunt, & quotidie implentur. Sceptrum a Iuda ablatū est, & Romano imperio subditi, Cæsari censum exoluitis: euoluti sunt anni illi fatales, de quibus Daniel vaticinatus est: Dauidis posteri non regno modò exciderunt, sed vix vitam sustinere ac tueri possunt: sanationes miraculosas quotidie cernitis. Et potuerunt hæc obseruare dudum Zacharias, Simeon, & hodie multi ex vulgo obseruant, & regnum Dei appropinquasse sentiunt: quod ipsum Ioannes perspicuè testatus est, & ego quotidie vobis inculco. Ergo malitiosi & scelerati estis hypocritæ, qui in re manifesta perinde vt in dubia ac incerta signum e cælo requiritis, &c.
units.tr: The first answer exposes their malicious ignorance, teaching that they demand a sign that is in no way necessary. "When it is evening, you say, 'Fair weather,' for the sky is red," and so on. The sense of the words is this: you are wicked hypocrites, who pretend to care for the truth, but you do this maliciously and deceitfully. For if that truth were dear to you, you could easily come to know it. You are not so stupid and foolish that you cannot foresee the weather from natural signs or forecasts, however varied and unsettled their changes are. Yet you have signs of the times that are just as clear and plain. Why then do you not observe and distinguish them? He calls signs of the times those things from which it was already evident that the last age had come, the age in which God had long before foretold through the prophets that the Messiah would come. Such were these: the sceptre must first be taken from Judah; a fixed number of years must run from the restoration of the city; and the house of David must be reduced to its former poverty, so that it could no longer be thought illustrious with royal splendour, but like the dry stump of Jesse and a parched and thirsty land. It had also been foretold: "Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf unstopped; then the lame shall leap like a deer, and the tongue of the dumb shall sing for joy." Yet, he says, all these things have long since been fulfilled and are being fulfilled every day. The sceptre has been taken from Judah; subject to the Roman empire, you pay tribute to Caesar; those fated years of which Daniel prophesied have run out; the descendants of David have not only lost their kingdom but can scarcely sustain and preserve their lives; and you see miraculous healings every day. Zechariah and Simeon could have observed these things long ago, and today many among the common people observe them and perceive that the kingdom of God has drawn near. John has plainly testified to this very thing, and I impress it on you every day. Therefore you are wicked and wretched hypocrites, who in a matter that is plain, just as in one that is doubtful and uncertain, demand a sign from heaven, and so on.

units.la: Perstringitur autem his verbis communis hominum peruersitas, qua fit, vt in ijs quæ corpori seruiunt, pleriq; folertes, perspicaces, industrij & laboriosi sint, nec facilè aliquid negligant, quod ex re ipsorum esse videtur, in diuinis autem, & ad æternam salutem necessarijs voluntarij cæcutiunt. Possunt tempora sementis, arationis & messis obseruare agricolæ: ijdem norunt astrorum quorundam ortus & occasus, & secundum Lunæ incrementa opera sua distribuunt. In obseruandis ventorum & tempestatum prognosticis mirifica est nautarum & piscatorum industria, vt iam nihil dicam de ijs, qui in hoc plus quàm barbaro vitæ genere astrorum & cœlestium orbium motus ita obseruarunt, vt nemo philosophus vnquam illos certius cognouerit. Quanta vero est venatorum, aucupum & piscatorum sagacitas, contra quam neq; sua lustra feras, neq; maris & fluuiorum profunditas pisces, neq; aues volatus tueri poterit, quin illis præda fiant. Similis est hominum auarorum, numulariorum & monopolarum folertia, quorum artes vsurarias si quis enumerare velit, dicendi finem vix inveniet. Interim plerique, in illis quae ad regnum Dei faciunt, ignari, caeci, & hebetes sunt, & de obscuritate Scripturarum atque Verbi Dei quiritantur in iis quoque articulis, qui pueris recte institutis notissimi sunt. Est ergo illorum etiam hominum ignorantia simulata & voluntaria, ac eandem cum Pharisaeis reprehensionem meretur.
units.tr: By these words is censured the common perversity of human beings, by which it happens that in matters serving the body many people are shrewd, perceptive, diligent and hard-working, and do not easily neglect anything that seems to concern their own affairs, but in divine matters, and those necessary for eternal salvation, they willingly grow blind. Farmers can observe the times of sowing, ploughing and harvest; the same men know the risings and settings of certain stars and arrange their work according to the waxing of the moon. Sailors and fishermen show remarkable diligence in observing forecasts of winds and storms; I say nothing of those who, in this more than barbarous way of life, have observed the motions of the stars and heavenly spheres so closely that no philosopher has ever known them more accurately. And how great is the cunning of hunters, fowlers and fishermen, against whom neither the lairs of wild beasts, nor the depths of sea and rivers, nor the flight of birds can protect their prey from becoming their catch. Similar is the cleverness of greedy men, moneylenders and monopolists, whose usurious arts, if anyone wished to list them, he would hardly find an end to his speaking. Meanwhile most people, in those things which pertain to the kingdom of God, are ignorant, blind and dull, and complain of the obscurity of the Scriptures and of the Word of God even in those articles which are best known to children rightly taught. This ignorance of such people, then, is feigned and voluntary, and deserves the same rebuke as the Pharisees.

units.la: Docet praeterea Dominus, non officitanter negligi debere signa temporum, quae in Scripturis commendantur. Etenim ut primum Filii Dei in carnem adventum signa praecesserunt, ex quibus illius tempus agnosci potuit: ita ab ipso & Apostolis eius multa praedicta sunt, quae finem mundi sint praecessura, in quo ille in gloria Patris veniet ad iudicandum vivos & mortuos. Et haec quidem omnia quotidie cernimus. Surgunt pseudoprophetae & pseudochristi, qui schismata et differentiones in religione graves & acres pariunt. Sedet in templo Dei Antichristus, prae se ferens se esse Deum. In terris monstratur non uno loco corporaliter IESVS CHRISTVS, Deus & homo. Audiuntur dogmata illa daemoniorum, quibus coniugium & libertas ciborum quorumvis prohibetur. Regnat plus quam Simoniaca factorum omnium nundinatio. Inter homines fides rara, & extincta charitate regnat iniquitas. Surgunt ergo passim horrendi motus, rumoribus bellorum omnia perstrepunt, & multis in locis bella tam externa quam intestina feruent. Comites horum sunt fames & pestis, quae crebris vicibus quasi continuantur. Accedunt his prodigia & signa graviora irae Dei in caelis, terra & aquis, denique caelorum vires commouentur, maria terras inundant, terra sylvis & lignis destituitur, fertilitas eius fere exhausta est, ut multis in locis colonos suos vix alat; adhaec mutato ordine naturae non ea sunt vices temporum & partium anni, quae olim fuerunt hyemes pluviis frequentibus agros alluunt, & tempore suo illos emori ac quiescere non sinunt: ver novum nimbis & pruinis horret, aestas frigida & humidior aequo fruges ad maturitatem non potest excoquere: quo fit ut autumni proventus sit tenuior, & eundem praeter solitum approperans hyemes abrumpat. Ipsa ergo mundi machina laborare, & ruinam minitari videtur. Debebamus ergo dum ista fiunt, capita attollere, & redemptionem nostram vigili mente & forti fide expectare. At paucos ista mouent, sed ut in diebus Noe & Lothi, fatalis securitas apud omnis loci & omnis homines regnat, dormitant pastores tum politici tum ecclesiastici, speculatores caecutiunt & conniuent, editur, bibitur, luditur, saltatur, & in medijs periculis plerique, sibi ipsis omnia laeta pollicentur, nec quisquam doceri, moneri aut corrigi vult. Haec (inquam) postremi aduentus Christi & finis mundi verissima prognostica sunt. Quid ergo aliud speremus, quam quod Dominus dicit: Dies ille ut laqueus superueniet, & inuadet in omnes, qui habitant in superficie totius terrae. In horum ergo meditatione frequentes simus o fratres, & excussofatali veterno, qui multorum mentes occupat, vigilemus, & praeparemur ad excipiendum sponsum nostrum IESVM CHRISTVM ut cum illo possimus ad nuptias caelestes ingredi.
units.tr: The Lord further teaches that the signs of the times which are commended in the Scriptures must not be negligently disregarded. For just as the signs preceded the coming of the Son of God in the flesh, by which his time could be recognised, so he himself and his apostles have foretold many things that are to precede the end of the world, at which he will come in the glory of the Father to judge the living and the dead. And indeed we see all these things every day. False prophets and false Christs arise, who produce grave and bitter schisms and dissensions in religion. Antichrist sits in the temple of God, claiming to be God himself. In various places on earth Jesus Christ, God and man, is bodily displayed. Those doctrines of demons are heard, by which marriage and the freedom to eat any foods are forbidden. A trade in all things more than Simoniacal holds sway. Faith is rare among men, charity is extinguished, and iniquity reigns. Thus dreadful upheavals arise everywhere; all things resound with rumours of wars, and in many places wars, both foreign and civil, rage. Famine and pestilence accompany these, and follow in such frequent succession that they seem almost continuous. In addition there are prodigies and more serious signs of the wrath of God in the heavens, on the earth and in the waters. Finally the powers of the heavens are shaken, the seas flood the lands, the earth is stripped of forests and timber, and its fertility is nearly exhausted, so that in many places it can scarcely feed its inhabitants. Moreover, with the order of nature changed, the seasons and divisions of the year are no longer what they once were: winters no longer wash the fields with frequent rains and do not allow them to die and rest at their proper time; the new spring shivers with storms and frosts; a cold and damper summer than is right cannot ripen the crops; as a result the autumn yield is meagre, and the winter, hastening earlier than usual, cuts it short. The very machinery of the world therefore seems to labour and to threaten ruin. While these things are happening, we ought to lift up our heads and await our redemption with a watchful mind and a strong faith. But few are moved by these things. Rather, as in the days of Noah and Lot, a deadly complacency reigns in every place and among all people. The ministers, both civil and ecclesiastical, are asleep; the watchmen grow blind and close their eyes; people eat, drink, play and dance, and in the midst of dangers many promise themselves every happy outcome, and no one wishes to be taught, warned or corrected. These things (I say) are the most true forecasts of the last coming of Christ and the end of the world. What then can we hope for, except what the Lord says: "That day will come upon them like a snare, and will fall on all who dwell on the face of the whole earth." Let us therefore, brothers, be frequent in meditating on these things; let us shake off the deadly drowsiness that occupies the minds of many, keep watch, and prepare ourselves to receive our bridegroom Jesus Christ, so that with him we may enter the heavenly marriage.

units.la: Caeterum alteram quoq; responsionis Domini partem audiamus, qua Pharisaeos & Saddu-caeos cum tota secta satorum suorum colluvie gravius adhuc corripit et comminatione acerrima terret, dicens: Natio mala & adultera signum requirit, sed signum non dabitur ei, nisi signum illud Ionae Prophetae. Cur nationem malam & adulteram dicat, supra Cap. 12. expositum est. Repetit autem crimen, cum ait: Natio mala signum petit. Quasi diceret: Magnae malitiae & impudentis audaciae argumentum est, quod ista fecerunt. Fiunt quotidie signa, & ea quidem, quae olim praedicta, & proinde certa & infallibilia sunt. At illi his non contenti, noua petunt pro suo arbitrio, quae si darentur neque certa essent, neque ipsis utilia. Sed non dabitur ei signum, quale nimirum ipsi petunt, nisi signum Ionae Prophetae. Simpliciter negat quod petunt (signum videlicet e caelo) ut offendat, indignos esse, ut ipsorum petitioni annuat, aut aliquid faciat in ipsorum gratiam. Interim signum polliceretur, quod merebantur: nimirum signum illud Ionae: cuius supra quoq; meminit. In praesenti autem simpliciter Ionam adducit, ut totam eius historiam ipsis in mentem reuocet, quae Christi & eorum, quae cum Iudaeis gesta sunt, typum euidente & proprijssimum continet. Nam primo Ionas typum a nautis suis, quibus se totum crediderat, in mare eicitur, & quantum in eis est, neci datur: Ita Christus a Iudaeis suis, quibus peculiariter promissus, ex quibus natus erat, & quibus se totum impenderat, occisus est. Ut Ionas mortis periculum volens subijt, ut nautas & vectores alios seruaret: ita Christum mori oportuit, ut non totus populus periret. Ut Ionas in mare, ceu in mortem ... fauces eiestus tempestatem sedauit : Ita Christus mortis sua merito iram Dei placauit & pacem nobis peperit certam ac stabilem. Vt Ionas post tertium diem ex balaenae faucibus terra redditus est: Ita Christus tertio die rediuiuus & discipulis suis restitutus est. Vt Ionas tunc Niniuitis prae dicauit, & resipiscentibus salutem attulit: Ita Christus resuscitatus per Apostolos praedicauit Iudaeis, ex quibus plurimi seruati sunt, qui animis suis compuncti resipuerunt. Denique vt Niniuitae postea relapsi inscelera, perierunt, sicuti ex Nahumi prophetia apparet. Ita Iudaei, quotquot a Christi resurrectione Euangelij doctrinam spreuerunt, & insceleribus incurabili malitia perseuerarunt, a Deo reiecti & funditus excisi sunt. Reuera ergo Ionas illis signi loco fuit, quo conuicti sunt, vt nulla ipsis reliqua manserit excusatio, quando Christum reiecerunt, Iona tanto praestantiorem, quanto Dei Filius aeternus & Sanctus sanctorum omnisq; labis expers, homine mortali & peccatore praestat.
units.tr: Let us now hear the other part of the Lord's answer, in which he rebukes the Pharisees and Sadducees, together with the whole brood of their sect, more severely still, and terrifies them with the sharpest threat, saying: "An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign, but no sign shall be given to it, except the sign of the prophet Jonah." Why he calls the nation evil and adulterous has been explained above, in chapter 12. But he repeats the charge when he says: "An evil generation seeks a sign." As if he said: this is a proof of great malice and shameless audacity, that they have done these things. Signs happen every day, and indeed those which were foretold long ago, and so are certain and infallible. But they, not content with these, demand new ones at their own pleasure; if these were given, they would be neither certain nor useful to them. "But no sign shall be given to it," namely the kind they themselves ask for, "except the sign of the prophet Jonah." He simply refuses what they ask (a sign from heaven, namely) in order to offend them, showing that they are unworthy that he should grant their request or do anything for their sake. Meanwhile he promises the sign they deserved, namely that sign of Jonah, which he also mentioned above. Here, however, he brings forward Jonah simply in order to recall to their minds his whole history, which contains a clear and most fitting type of Christ and of what happened with the Jews. For first, Jonah, as a type, is thrown into the sea by his sailors, to whom he had entrusted himself entirely, and as far as they were concerned he was given over to death. So Christ was killed by his Jews, to whom he was especially promised, from whom he was born, and for whom he had devoted himself entirely. As Jonah willingly underwent the danger of death so that he might save the sailors and other passengers, so Christ had to die so that the whole people would not perish. As Jonah, cast into the sea as into death, calmed the tempest by being thrown into the jaws [of the whale]..., so Christ, by the merit of his death, appeased the wrath of God and brought us a certain and stable peace. As Jonah was restored to the land after the third day from the jaws of the whale, so Christ, rising again on the third day, was restored to his disciples. As Jonah then preached to the Ninevites and brought salvation to those who repented, so Christ, raised up, preached through the apostles to the Jews, of whom many were saved, and who, pricked in their hearts, repented. Finally, as the Ninevites afterwards relapsed into their wickedness and perished, as is clear from the prophecy of Nahum, so the Jews, as many as from Christ's resurrection have rejected the doctrine of the gospel and persisted in their wickedness with incurable malice, have been cast off by God and utterly cut down. Truly, then, Jonah was for them the sign by which they were convicted, so that no excuse remained for them when they rejected Christ, who is as much greater than Jonah as the eternal Son of God, the Holy One of the saints and free from all stain, is greater than a mortal man and sinner.

units.la: Additur, quod ipsis relictis abierit. Et hic disceptationis insidiosae, quam Pharifaei cum socijs suis Sadducaeis contra Christum instituerunt, finis fuit: & suo discessu testatus est, indignos esse, quibus sese porro per Verbum aut signa manifestaret. Manet idem fatum omnes, qui simili contumacia illum & Euangelium eius auersantur. Persuadent hi sibi ipsis, posthac se quietos & beatos fore, si illo liberentur, cuius doctrina mundo exosa est, & eidem exosos reddit & periculis obiicit eos, qui illam sectantur. Nec dubium est, vehementer sibi ipsis placuisse Pharifaeos, quod Christus suo discessu ab ipsis se victu esse fateri videretur. Sed magno illis constitit haec victoria. Nam si ille discedat, aufert simul Dei regnum, quod est iustitia & pax, & gaudium in Spiritu Sancto: in huius autem locum succedunt peccatum, ira Dei, conscientiae inquietudo, dolor, & maledictio, quae desperationem parit & interitum. Et haec quidem omnia Iudaeos adobruerunt, & adhuc hodie miseris & infelicibus incumbunt. Terreat ergo nos illorum exemplum, qui in postrema mundi senectu versamur, & sese nobis benigne offerentem Dei Filium gratis animis excipiamus, & constanti fide retineamus, precemur item ex corde, vt nobis perpetuo adesse, & nos Spiritu suo confirmare ac regere dignetur. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: It is added that he left them and went away. And with this departure the insidious dispute which the Pharisees, together with their allies the Sadducees, had begun against Christ came to an end; and by leaving he showed that they were unworthy to be further revealed to by his Word or by signs. The same fate remains for all who, with like obstinacy, turn away from him and from his Gospel. They persuade themselves that they will be at rest and blessed hereafter if they are freed from him, whose teaching is hateful to the world, and which makes hateful, and exposes to dangers, those who follow it. And there is no doubt that the Pharisees were greatly pleased with themselves, because Christ seemed by his departure to confess that he had been defeated by them. But this victory cost them dearly. For if he departs, he takes with him the kingdom of God, which is righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit; in its place come sin, the wrath of God, unrest of conscience, sorrow, and the curse, which brings despair and destruction. And all these things have overwhelmed the Jews, and to this day they weigh upon the wretched and unhappy. Let the example of them therefore terrify us, who live in the old age of the world, and let us gladly receive the Son of God, who offers himself kindly to us, and hold him fast with a steadfast faith. Let us also pray from the heart that he may deign to be always present with us and to strengthen and guide us by his Spirit. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCIII.
units.tr: Homily 203.

units.la: Et cum venissent discipuli eius in vlteriorem ripam, obliti fuerant sumere panes. IESVS autem dixit eis: Videte & cauete a fermento Pharisaeorum & Sadducaeorum. Ipsi vero disceptabant inter se dicentes: Panes non sumpsimus. Id autem cum nosset IESVS dixit eis: Quid disceptatis inter vos, exigua fide praediti, quod panes non sum psistis? Nondum intelligitis neq; meministis quinq; illos panes homi num quinquies mille, & quot cophinos acceperitis? neq; septē illos panes quater mille hominum, & quot sportas acceperitis? Quomodo non intelligitis, me non dixisse vobis de pane, vt caueretis a fermento Pharisaeorum & Sadducaeorū? Tunc intellexerunt, eum non dixisse, vt cauerent a fermento panis, sed a doctrina Pharisaeorum & Sadducaeorum.
units.tr: When his disciples had come to the other side, they had forgotten to take bread. Jesus said to them, "Take heed and beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and the Sadducees." But they reasoned among themselves, saying, "It is because we have taken no bread." When Jesus knew this, he said to them, "Why do you reason among yourselves, O you of little faith, because you have no bread? Do you not yet understand or remember the five loaves for the five thousand, and how many baskets you took up? Nor the seven loaves for the four thousand, and how many baskets you took up? How is it you do not understand that I did not speak to you about bread? Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees." Then they understood that he had not told them to beware of the leaven of bread, but of the teaching of the Pharisees and Sadducees.

units.la: Quoniam Pharisaei non solum humanis traditionibus et falsa doctrina populum seducebant, verumetiam aperti veritatis hostes erant, & nuper cum Sadducaeis coniuratione fasta Dominum nostrum IESVM CHRISTVM, aggressi sunt, & ab eo signum de caelo postularunt, vt eius miracula & doctrinam calumniari & in dubium vocare possent: ipse non modo acriter illos corripuit, sed insuper illis relictis nauigio discessit. Quo exemplo docet, eos qui ipsius discipuli esse volunt, omnem cum hypocritis & falsis doctoribus consuetudinem deuitare debere, vt nihil cum eorum doctrina & consortio commune habeant. At quia sciebat, discipulos adhuc tardiores esse, & id per se non intelligere, nunc eis nouam & seriam admonitione adhibet, in qua primum illius fides & bonitas, deinde discipulorum, adeoq; omnium hominum tarditas elucet, quam ita ille corripit. ripit, ut simul doceat, quid nos facere & cauere oporteat, si in vera pietate & regno Dei proficere velimus.
units.tr: Because the Pharisees not only led the people astray with human traditions and false doctrine, but were also open enemies of the truth, and recently, in league with the Sadducees, attacked our Lord Jesus Christ and demanded from him a sign from heaven, so that they might slander his miracles and teaching and call them into doubt. He not only rebuked them sharply but, leaving them behind, departed by boat. By this example he teaches that those who want to be his disciples must avoid all association with hypocrites and false teachers, so that they have nothing in common with their doctrine and company. But because he knew that the disciples were still slow and did not understand this on their own, he now gives them a new and serious warning, in which first his own faith and goodness, then the slowness of the disciples and indeed of all men, is made plain, and which he rebukes in this way. so that at the same time he teaches what we ought to do and beware of, if we wish to make progress in true piety and in the kingdom of God.

units.la: Praemittit autem Euangelista pro suo more tractationis istius occasionem, quae fuit, quod cum Christus subito ex illis locis discederet, discipuli in ipsum potius quam in alia intenti, ne ab ipso auellerentur, obliti sunt panes aut commeatum secum deferre, adeo, ut (sicuti Marcus anno tauit) unum modo panem haberent, cum in ulteriorem ripam peruenissent. Tantus in illis fuit Christi amor, tantum cum illo perseuerandi studium, qui alioqui naeuis & vitiis non vulgaribus laborabant, ut in illa festinatione de aliis, quae per se necessaria erant, non cogitarent, aut quod exi- stimarent, illic loci, quo ille tendebat, victum sive alimenta facile inueniri posse. Estq; zelus hic immortali laude dignus, & hoc ab omnibus postulatur, ut reliquis aliis rebus omnibus Christum sequamur, qui solus verba vitae aeternae habet, & nobis ad omnia sufficit.
units.tr: The Evangelist, after his usual manner, sets out the occasion of this discussion: when Christ suddenly left that region, the disciples, intent on him rather than on other things, and not wanting to be separated from him, forgot to bring bread or provisions with them. So much so that (as Mark notes) when they reached the other side they had only one loaf. Such was their love for Christ, and such their eagerness to persevere with him, though they were otherwise burdened with no ordinary faults and failings, that in their haste they gave no thought to other things that were necessary in themselves, or they supposed that food and provisions could easily be found in the place to which he was going. This zeal deserves immortal praise, and this is what is required of all of us: that, forsaking all other things, we follow Christ, who alone has the words of eternal life and is sufficient for us in all things.

units.la: At simul adumbratur illorum exemplo, quid fere electis accidat: ut nimirum, dum feruore maximo Christum sequuntur, ea negligant, quae ad huius saeculi & praesentis vitae commoditatem faciunt: quae causa est, ut interdum necessariis egeant, & in angustiis non ante praeuisas addu- cantur. Exempla huius rei quotidie cernimus. Et ex his tunc multi arripiunt calumniandi occa- sionem, qui in illis reprehendendis suam prudentiam & eloquentiam mirifice ostentant, & mor- daci aceto eos perfundunt, qui commiseratione digni erant. Itaq; si quid huius fit, in mentem nobis veniat, filios huius saeculi prudentiores esse quam filios lucis, & proinde non miru esse, si aliquando isti offendan in ijs, quae ad hoc saeculum pertinent. Praeterea meminerimus, Deum nostra proui- dentia aut industria nequaquam opus habere, & suos vbiq; etiam sine externis subsidiis seruare posse: & frequenter ipsorum incogitantia bene uti ad nominis sui illustrationem. Ita paulo ante factum fuit, quando populi egestas miraculo in septem panibus edito occasionem praebuit. Simile quid in causa grauioris argumenti nunc quoq; factum est.
units.tr: Yet at the same time their example shows what usually happens to the elect: that, while with the greatest fervour they follow Christ, they neglect those things which serve the comfort of this age and the present life. This is why they sometimes lack necessities and are brought into difficulties that they did not foresee. We see examples of this every day. And from these lapses many seize the chance to find fault, displaying their own cleverness and eloquence in rebuking them, and they pour bitter vinegar on those who deserved pity. So if anything of this kind happens, let us bear in mind that the sons of this age are more prudent than the sons of light, and therefore it is no wonder if at times these men stumble in matters that pertain to this age. Moreover, let us remember that God has no need of our foresight or industry, and that he can preserve his own everywhere, even without outward aids, and that he often makes good use of their thoughtlessness to illustrate his name. So it happened a little before, when the people's want gave occasion for the miracle of the seven loaves. Something similar has now happened in a matter of greater weight.

units.la: Nam Christus Dominus, quem haec discipulorum incuria non latebat, ansam arripit illos admonendi de eo, quod ad aeterna vitae alimentum pertinebat. Ait enim: Videte & cauete a fermento Pharisaeorum & Sadducaeorum. Et hoc de doctrina horum illum dixisse, postea Matthaeus dicet. Non autem nouum est, quod doctrina fermento confertur. Supra certe Cap.decimo tertio Euan gelium suum fermento simile esse ait. Etenim ut fermentum, primo intuitu res leuicula videtur, maiorem vero sive conspersionem totam, si huic commisceatur, acore suo penetrat, & illi saporem suum confert, ut panes gustui suauiores, & concoctu faciliores sint, & melius nutriant. Ita Euan gelium iudicio mundi leuiculum & contemptibile quid videtur, at idem intra cordis recessus per fidem admissum, hominem totum sua virtute penetrat, & innatam nobis vitiositati medetur, ut ex illius femine renati illud unum redoleamus, & Deo accepti simus, qui paulo ante filij irae eramus, & exitio digni. E contra falsae etiam doctrinae fermenti parabola probe conuenit. Videtur haec quoq; no magni momenti res, ex qua periculu aliquod timeri debeat: & solent huius authores eam mirificis rationibus commendare, ut facilius fucum faciant simplicioribus. Sed semel admissa, & recepta ut cancer serpit, hominem totum occupat, mentem extollit contra Deum, ut huius Verbo reliquo, nouas leges in eius regno condere, eidem nouos cultus obtrudere, & omnia pro suo arbitrio instituere ausit. Ita vero acidi & insipidi Deo fiunt homines, qui, ut hypocrisim odit, ita superbis resistit. Et hoc quidem de omni falsa doctrina verissime dicitur.
units.tr: For Christ the Lord, who was not unaware of this carelessness of the disciples, seizes the opportunity to admonish them about what pertains to the food of eternal life. For he says, "Take heed and beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees." Matthew later states that he was speaking of their teaching. Nor is it new for doctrine to be likened to leaven. Indeed, in chapter 13 above he says that his Gospel is like leaven. For just as leaven at first sight seems a trifling thing, yet once it is mixed into the whole mass of dough it penetrates it with its sharpness and gives its flavour to it, so that the bread is more pleasing to the taste, easier to digest, and more nourishing; so the Gospel, in the judgement of the world, seems a slight and contemptible thing, yet when it is admitted by faith into the recesses of the heart, it penetrates the whole man by its power and heals the vice that is innate in us, so that, born again from its seed, we savour of that one thing, and we who a little before were children of wrath and deserving of destruction are made acceptable to God. On the contrary, the parable of leaven fits false doctrine too. This also seems a matter of no great importance, from which some danger ought to be feared; and its authors are accustomed to commend it with striking arguments, so that they may more easily deceive the simpler sort. But once admitted and received, like a cancer it creeps on and takes hold of the whole man, lifts up the mind against God, so that it forsakes his Word, presumes to establish new laws in his kingdom, to impose new forms of worship upon it, and to order everything at its own discretion. So men become sour and insipid to God, who, as he hates hypocrisy, so he resists the proud. And this is most truly said of every false doctrine.

units.la: In primis autem de Pharisaeorum & Sadducaeorum traditionibus & placitis, quae in praesenti coniungit Christus, cum sectae hae (ut nuper diximus) multum inter se diuersae, & earundem doctrina plane alia alij contraria fuerit. Pharisaei enim operum iustitia, & totius vitae sanctimonia a suis exigebant, illius studium mirifice ostentabant, & in eo no solum vulgi applausum, sed aeternae etiam salutis meritu quaerebant. E contra Epicurei, cum animarum immortalitate, corporum resurrectione, spiritus ite tam bonos quam malos negarent, iustitiae vero vsum nullum aliu esse crederent, quam qui praesenti vitae feruit, religione prorsus omnem ex hominum cordibus eximebant. Apud Marcum Sadducaeorum loco Herodes nominatur, qui ab eis hoc vno differebat, quod animas a corporibus digressas viuere non negaret, earum aut transmigrationem in aliena corpora & hominis πυλιγγενεσιαν statuebat, ut Cap.14. est dictum. At Christus Pharisaeos cum Sadducaus coniungit in admonitione ista, non ex priuato affectu, quod ipsi coniunctis viribus ipsum aggredi essent, sed quod ytriusque sectae doctrina saluti ex aequo officiat, & vt demonstret, quid in negotio regni Dei vitari debeat. Vt videlicet neque hypocriticam & confidentem operum nostrorum & propriae iustitiae fiduciam statuamus, neque Epicureas persuasiones admittamus, quae omnem futurae vitae spem ex animis hominum adimunt. Vt enim illa nos a Christo abducit, vt iustitiae Dei, quam hic nobis in illo offert, non possimus participes fieri: ita haec omnem religionis sensum reflinguunt, vt cum Nabali dicant multi, non est Deus. Deus Iacob non videt, non audit, non intelligit, neque curat quid in terris geratur. Itaque haec Christi admonitio non minus nobis hodie seruit, quam olim domesticis Christi discipulis. Nec enim haec diuersae & inter se distinctae sectae inter homines audiuntur modo, sed eo usque progressa est impietas, vt plerique simul Pharisaei & Sadducaei sint. Nam ita viuunt, vt illos neque Deum neque Satanam, neque coelum neque inferos credere appareat: interim ijdem pro suorum operum iustitia & pro superstitiosis cultibus contra Christum & Euangelium eius ferro & igne pugnant. Et in templis quidem pharisaicum fermentum omnem, quae adhuc reliqua est, fidei doctrinam adulterat, in colloquijs autem & conuersatione cum alijs audiuntur Epicureae illae voces, Scilicet hic labor est superis, haec cura quietos solicitat. Et illae, quas Petrus vulgo regnaturas praedixit nouissimis temporibus. Vbi est pollicitatio aduentus eius? &c. Edamus, bibamus, cras enim moriemur. 1. Pet. 3. 1. Cor. 15.
units.tr: Above all, Christ in the present passage joins the traditions and opinions of the Pharisees and Sadducees, although these sects (as we said recently) were very different from one another, and their doctrines were quite contrary to each other. For the Pharisees demanded of their followers the righteousness of works and sanctity of life throughout, and they displayed a remarkable zeal for it, seeking in it not only the applause of the crowd but also the merit of eternal salvation. On the other hand, the Epicureans denied the immortality of souls, the resurrection of bodies, and both good and evil spirits, and believed that there was no use of righteousness other than what serves the present life; they removed religion entirely from men's hearts. In Mark, Herod is named in place of the Sadducees, who differed from them only in this, that he did not deny that souls separated from bodies live, but held that they transmigrate into other bodies, and a [παλιγγενεσία] palingenesia of man, as was said in chapter 14. But Christ joins the Pharisees with the Sadducees in this admonition not out of private feeling, as if they had attacked him with combined forces, but because the doctrine of each sect equally hinders salvation, and to show what must be avoided in the matter of the kingdom of God. Namely, that we should not place a hypocritical and self-confident trust in our works and our own righteousness, nor admit Epicurean persuasions, which take away from men's minds all hope of the life to come. For just as the former draws us away from Christ, so that we cannot share in the righteousness of God which he offers us in himself, so the latter wipes out every sense of religion, so that many say with Nabal, "There is no God." "The God of Jacob does not see, does not hear, does not understand, nor cares what happens on earth." Therefore this admonition of Christ is no less useful to us today than it was once to his household disciples. For these divided and mutually distinct sects are not heard of only among men; impiety has advanced so far that many are at once Pharisees and Sadducees. For they live in such a way that it appears they believe neither in God nor in Satan, neither in heaven nor in hell; meanwhile these same men, for the righteousness of their works and for superstitious worship, fight with sword and fire against Christ and his Gospel. And in the temples the leaven of the Pharisees corrupts whatever remnant of the doctrine of faith is left, while in conversations and dealings with others those Epicurean voices are heard: "Surely this labour is for the gods above; this care troubles the quiet." And those words which Peter foretold would be spoken by the common people in the last times: "Where is the promise of his coming?" etc. "Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die." 1 Pet. 3; 1 Cor. 15.

units.la: Quia ergo haec nocentissimae pestes sunt, magno ferio de illis praemonet Dominus. Videte (inquit) & cauete. Duo iubet. Primum, vt qui discipuli eius esse, & ipsius merito partae salutis potiri volunt, diligenter videant, obseruent & examinet quid doceatur, & singula expendant. Monent hoc ipsum Apostoli, ne quouis vento doctrinae nos circumferri sinamus. Et nota est Ioannis admonitio: Dilecti, ne cuius spiritui credite, sed probate spiritus num ex Deo sint. Pauli item, Omnia explorate: quod bonum fuerit, retinete. Et hoc est, quod in praesenti Christus dicit VIDETE. Deinde addit, CAVETE. Non ergo simpliciter doctrinas explorare debent pij, sed in eum finem id faciant, vt falsa dogmata & quae a Veritate abducunt, caueant atque deuitent, abstque omni persona rum respectu, ne videlicet fides nostra ab vllius hominis authoritate, sed ex Dei solius ore pendeat. Enimuero Christus dum Pharisaeos nominat, de ijs loquitur, qui tunc primatu in Ecclesia tenebant, in Mosis cathedra sedebant, & penes ipsos suprema erat doctrina & pietatis existimatio. Sadducaei vero ad Reip. gubernacula sedebant cum Pharisaeis, & (vt nuper dictum est) Romanis rerum dominis tunc praealijs probabantur. Et his Herodem tetrarcha coniungit, qui vita & nencis imperium in omnes habebat, & eo in Ioannem Baptistam crudeliter vsus fuerat. Attamen vt omnium istorum doctrinam siue opiniones fugiant fui discipuli, Christus iubet. Et consentit huic admonitioni, quod alibi dicit: Oues meae vocem meam audiunt, & sequuntur me: Alienum autem nequaquam sequentur, sed fugiunt ab eo: quia non norunt vocem alienorum. Quisquis ergo ille furit, qui vocem alienam affert, siue Pontifex, siue Rex, siue doctus, siue indoctus, aut quocunque titulo superbus, non meretur audiri. Etenim Dei domus est Ecclesia, solius ergo Patrisfamilias vox in illa sonare debet. Animae item negotium hic agitur, in quam nemini ius est, praeter Christumqui illas sanguinis sui pretio redemit. Itaque nullius hominis authoritate excusari possunt, qui alienam doctrinam Dei Verbo anteponunt: Sed de illis dicitur, Si caecus caeco dux fuerit, ambo cadunt in foueam. Matthaei decimoquinto.
units.tr: Since these are most pernicious plagues, the Lord warns about them with great earnestness. "See," he says, "and beware." He commands two things. First, that those who wish to be his disciples and to possess the salvation won for them by his merit should carefully see, observe and examine what is taught, and weigh each thing. The Apostles likewise warn this, that we should not allow ourselves to be carried about by every wind of doctrine. The admonition of John is well known: "Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits whether they are from God." Likewise Paul: "Test all things; hold fast what is good." This is what Christ means now by SEE. Then he adds BEWARE.
