Therefore the godly ought not merely to test doctrines, but to do so to this end, that they may guard against and avoid false dogmas and whatever leads away from the Truth, and this without any regard for persons, so that our faith may depend not on the authority of any man, but on the mouth of God alone. Indeed, when Christ names the Pharisees, he speaks of those who then held the primacy in the Church, sat in Moses' seat, and in whose hands lay the supreme teaching and the reputation for piety. The Sadducees, however, sat at the helm of the state along with the Pharisees, and (as was said recently) were then approved by the Romans, the masters of affairs. With these he joins Herod the tetrarch, who had power of life and death over all and had cruelly used that power against John the Baptist. Nevertheless, Christ bids his disciples to flee the teaching or opinions of all these men. He agrees with this warning when he says elsewhere: "My sheep hear my voice and follow me; but they will by no means follow a stranger, but flee from him, because they do not know the voice of strangers." Therefore whoever he is who brings forward a strange voice, whether pontiff, king, learned or unlearned, or proud by whatever title, does not deserve to be heard. For the Church is the house of God, so only the voice of the Father of the household ought to sound in it. Likewise, the matter at hand concerns the soul, over which no one has right except Christ, who redeemed it at the price of his blood. Hence those who prefer the teaching of another to the Word of God cannot be excused by the authority of any man. But of them it is said: "If the blind lead the blind, both will fall into the pit." Matthew 15.

units.la: Quia vero singuli priuatim sibi cauere debent a falsa doctrina & praues opinionibus, quanto magis haec cura ad eos pertinet, qui Ecclesiae aut Reipublicae praefecti sunt ne quid suae fidei comissis obtrudi sinant, quod fermentum Pharisaicum vel Sadducaicum redoleat. Solent interdum impostores additionibus nouis puriorem doctrinam corrumpere, nouis ceremonijs item cultus externi simplicitatem adulterare, & mellitis verbis inuentiones suas comendare: Ita multi doctrinam de fidei iustificatione dubiam faciunt, dum hominis vires & opera nimium extollunt: Alij imaginum vsum aliquem in templis esse volunt, vt doctrinae & institutioni laicorum seruiant: altaria papistica & luminaria instaurant, vestes sacras reducunt & ritus superuacaneos atque inutiles admittere cupiunt, vt aduersarios Papistas sibi aequiores faciant. Sed renera pharisaicum fermentum sunt haec omnia, de quo verissime illud Pauli dicitur: Paululum fermenti totam massam inficit. Idem in Republica in Republica faciunt, qui bonis legibus insidiantur, & morum disciplinam subuertere cupiunt. Initium faciunt a legibus, quæ non vsq; adeo magni momenti videntur. Sed his sublatis, ad alias itur & paulatim legum omnium authoritas vilescit. Nihil ergo permittendum est intempestiuis illis nouatoribus, & potius anniti omnes decet, vt in ijs quæ bene constituta sunt non perseuerent modo, sed quotidie in melius quoq; proficiant, ne dum quæ prius bene destruxerunt, rursus ædificant, transgressores seipsos constituant, vt Apostolus dicebat, Galat.2.
units.tr: Since individuals must each guard themselves privately against false teaching and wicked opinions, how much more does this care pertain to those who are set over the Church or the commonwealth, so that they do not allow anything to be forced upon those entrusted to their faith which smacks of Pharisaic or Sadducean leaven. Impostors sometimes corrupt the purer teaching with new additions, and likewise adulterate the simplicity of external worship with new ceremonies, and commend their inventions with honeyed words. Thus many make the doctrine of justification by faith uncertain, while they extol human powers and works too much. Others want some use of images in the churches, to serve the teaching and instruction of the laity; they restore Papist altars and lights, bring back sacred vestments, and desire to admit superfluous and useless rites, in order to make the Papist adversaries more favourable to themselves. But in truth all these things are Pharisaic leaven, of which that saying of Paul is most true: "A little leaven leavens the whole lump." The same happens in the commonwealth when men lie in wait for good laws and wish to subvert the discipline of morals. They begin with laws which seem not to be of great importance. But once these are removed, they proceed to others, and gradually the authority of all laws becomes worthless. Nothing therefore is to be conceded to those untimely innovators, and all ought rather to strive not only to persevere in those things that have been well established, but to progress daily for the better, lest, while they rebuild what they had earlier well destroyed, they make themselves transgressors, as the Apostle said. Galatians 2.

units.la: Quid autem ad istam admonitionem discipuli? Non intelligunt quid sibi velit Dominus, sed de panibus ipsum loqui arbitrantur, & ideo de victu seu commeatu solliciti, inter se disceptant, quod panes nullos sumpserint. Concurrit hic multiplex error. Primus ignorantiæ est, quæ excusari nequit. Quia enim alibi Euangelij doctrinam fermentum dixerat, nō difficile erat hoc ad Pharisæorum & Sadducæorum traditiones extendere, de quibus non itapridem disseruerat. Sed et ipsius Christi exemplum interpretis loco esse poterat, qui antehac nihil huius vetuerat, & ipsemet solebat ad Pharisæorum mensas accedere. Ignorantiam anxia solicitudo de victu comitatur, quam supra capite sexto multis rationibus & exemplis ille prohibuit. Hac fidei infirmitatem arguit, & quod beneficiorum atq; miraculorum eius non satis meminissent. Est hoc euidens exemplum cæcitatis nostræ, qua in diuinis ac cœlestibus laboramus, cum ijs quæ huius seculi sunt, sagacissimi simus. Recte ergo quidam noctuarum similes dixerunt homines nondum in Christo renatos. Vt enim illæ noctu vident, interdiu autem cæcuti sunt: ita animalis homo inter tenebras mundi huius oculatissimus est in obeundis tenebrarum operibus, ad Solem iustitiæ autem, IESVM CHRISTVM, qui vera lux mundi est, oculi nostri caligant, & idem nobis ænigmata loqui videtur, quando regni sui mysteria proponit, quibus nihil est iucundius, nihil clarius & perspicacius. Si tausam quæras, non alia est, quam quod religionem ex carnis affectibus metimur, qui nos a Dei Verbo transfuersos abripiunt, & longe alia diffant, quam illo doceantur. Hinc fit quod qui alijs religiosiores sunt, nouos cultus instituunt contra Verbum Dei, & externis ritibus eum placari posse putant, qui Spiritus est, & non aliter quam in Spiritu potest coli. Alij vero non alia quam quæ carnis sunt, quærunt, & quando de cœlestibus dapibus & libertate filiorum Dei sermo est, ipsi animum in patinis habent, aut sub prætextu religionis immunitatem & licentiam quærunt. Semper ergo nobis suspecta esse debent, quæcunq; carnis ratio dictat, hanc autem per fidei obedientiam Verbo Dei subijciamus, quod fano sensu secundum analogiam fidei acceptum nos a veritatis scopo & salutis tramite aberrare non sinet.
units.tr: But what do the disciples make of this warning? They do not understand what the Lord means, but think he is speaking about bread, and so, anxious about food and provisions, they dispute among themselves because they had taken no bread. Multiple errors meet here. The first is ignorance, which cannot be excused. For since Christ had elsewhere called the teaching of the Gospel leaven, it was not difficult to extend this to the traditions of the Pharisees and Sadducees, of which he had not long before spoken. Moreover, the example of Christ himself could have served them as an interpretation, for he had hitherto forbidden nothing of this kind, and he himself used to go to the tables of the Pharisees. Ignorance is accompanied by anxious care for food, which in the sixth chapter above he forbade with many reasons and examples. This argues weakness of faith, and that they had not sufficiently remembered his benefits and miracles. This is a clear example of the blindness with which we labour in divine and heavenly things, while we are most keen-sighted in the things of this age. Rightly therefore some have called men not yet reborn in Christ like owls. For as owls see by night but are blind by day, so the natural man is most keen-sighted among the shadows of this world in carrying out the works of darkness, but towards the Sun of righteousness, Jesus Christ, who is the true light of the world, our eyes grow dim, and he seems to us to speak in riddles when he sets forth the mysteries of his kingdom, than which nothing is more pleasing, nothing clearer and more perspicacious. If you ask the cause, it is none other than that we measure religion by the affections of the flesh, which drag us away, turned aside from the Word of God, and they carry us far from what is taught there. Hence it happens that those who are more religious than others institute new worships against the Word of God, and think that God, who is Spirit and can be worshipped only in Spirit, can be appeased by external rites. Others, on the contrary, seek only what belongs to the flesh, and when there is talk of heavenly dainties and the freedom of the sons of God, they have their minds on the dishes, or under the pretext of religion they seek immunity and licence. Therefore whatever the reasoning of the flesh dictates ought always to be suspect to us; let us subject this reasoning to the Word of God through obedience of faith, which, taken in a sound sense according to the analogy of faith, will not allow us to wander from the goal of truth and the path of salvation.

units.la: Sed Christum audiamus, qui quam ipsi displiceant crassæ illæ disceptationes, quas caro fugerit, abundè docet grauissima correptione, qua aduersus discipulos vsus est. Sæpe quidem eos peccauisse, sæpe etiam ab illo reprehensos fuisse legimus: at nullam correptionem illis simul omnibus, hac præsenti grauiorem adhibitam fuisse constat. Initio enim manifesto indicio diuinitatem suam exerit, dum disceptationes, quas inter se priuatim habebant, arguit: nimirum magis vt percellerentur, quando videbant, quo cum ipsis res esset. Mox autem grauissimis verbis eos compellans ait: Quid disceptatis inter vos, exigua fide præditi, quod panes non sumpseritis? Accusat ergo, quod in fide vacillent, & ideo de ventre soliciti lites inter se habeant superuacaneas & a fui nominis professione alienas. Deinde fontem & originem huius mali indicat, dicens: Nondum intelligitis, neq; memini stis quinq; illos panes hominum quinquies mille, & quot cophinos acceperitis? neq; septem illos panes, &c. Quasi diceret: Adeo ne stupidi estis, vt non intelligatis in quem finem nuper miraculose multa millia hominum paucis panibus atq; piscic ulis saturauerim? Nimirum, vt promissio mea fidem facerem, qua iampridem pollicitus sum, nihil vnquam defuturum ijs, qui me vocant sequuntur, & regnum Dei ferio quærunt? Quid ergo solicita & odiosa disceptatione opus est tibi, qui in meo comitatu estis? Sed video vos non modo stupidos esse, sed beneficiorum & operum meorum parum memores, & pro his male gratos. Si enim horum meminissetis, quæ nuper admodum facta sunt: si ea grato animo vnquam recondidissetis, nullus apud vos diffidentia, nullus huic disceptationi aut altercationi locus esset. Quin ergo istorum recordatione excitati intelligitis, me quando a Pharisæorum & Sadducæorum fermento cauere iussi, non de panibus & commeatu, sed de illorum doctrina locutum esse?
units.tr: But let us hear Christ, who abundantly shows, by the very grave rebuke with which he addressed the disciples, how much those coarse disputes, which the flesh should flee, displease him. We read that they had often sinned and often been reproved by him; yet it is clear that no rebuke harsher than this present one was ever administered to them all together. At the outset he displays his divinity by a manifest sign, when he rebukes the disputes which they were holding privately among themselves; no doubt so that they might be the more startled when they saw with whom they had to do. Then, addressing them in the most serious words, he says: "Why do you dispute among yourselves, you of little faith, because you have taken no bread?" He accuses them, therefore, of wavering in faith, and so of holding vain quarrels about their belly, quarrels foreign to their profession of his name. Then he points out the source and origin of this evil, saying: "Do you not yet understand, nor remember the five loaves for five thousand men, and how many baskets you took up? Nor the seven loaves, etc.?" As if he said: "Are you so dull that you do not understand for what purpose I recently satisfied many thousands of men with a few loaves and fishes? Clearly, to make good my promise, which I made long ago, that nothing will ever be lacking to those who follow me and seek the kingdom of God first. Why then do you need anxious and hateful dispute, you who are in my company? But I see that you are not only dull, but little mindful of my benefits and works, and ungrateful for them. For if you had remembered those things which were done so recently, and if you had ever stored them up in a grateful mind, there would be no place among you for distrust, or for this dispute or wrangling. Why then, roused by the remembrance of these things, do you not understand that when I bade you beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees, I was speaking not of bread and provisions, but of their teaching?"

units.la: Note marginal "Discipuli non intelligunt Christi" "Luc.7.14.etc" "Humanæ mentis cæcitas" "Ioan.4" "Christus discipulos corripit" printed in the right margin, beside the text.
units.tr: Marginal notes: "The disciples do not understand Christ" "Luke 7.14, etc." "The blindness of the human mind" "John 4" "Christ rebukes the disciples"

units.la: Est haec tam acris correptio digna, quae diligenter consideretur, & saepe nobis in mentem veniat. Nam de causis ὀλιγοπιστίας aut diffidentiae nos admonet, simulque decet, ut huic malo, quo non aliud nocentius est, remedium adhibeamus. Ut enim operibus ac beneficiis suis nostram fidem Deus confirmat: ita nisi in horum recordatione ac meditatione frequenter nos exerceamus, non possumus in fide firmi & constantes esse, sed quouis periculo aut casu, qui praeter expectationem nobis accidit, territi vacillamus, & nostris rationibus nosipsos euertimus, ut neq; obsequium Deo praestemus quod ei debetur. Exempla in veteri Iudaeorum gente plurima videmus, quae hoc docent. Etenim divinus ille Psaltes illorum scelera, quibus sub Mose & deinceps peccarunt, narraturus, hanc causam praemittit. Statim obliti sunt operum eius, neque expectauerunt consilium eius. Et author libri Iudicum idem dicit, quod tota haec natio, quae opera Domini in Aegypto & deserto vi derat, collecta sit ad patres suos, & alia surrexerit, quae opus Domini ignorauit. Fecerunt ergo (in quit) filij Israel malum in oculis Domini, &c. Non temere ergo illos Moses monuerat: Caue tibi & custodi animum tuum diligenter, ne vnquam obliuiscaris eorum, quae viderunt oculi tui, & ne vnquam recedant a corde tuo, &c. Similes admonitiones frequenter in Psalmis occurrunt: Cantate Domino, psallite ei, loquimini de omnibus mirabilibus eius. Mementote mirabilium eius, quae fecit, prodigiorum eius & iudiciorum eius. Et alibi dicitur Deus hoc statuisse in Israele, ut patres opera ipsius filijs & nepotibus narrent, ut in Deo ipsum ponant, & eius mandata obseruent. Quin ipse Deus opera memorabilia posteris commendauit semper, & solennes eorum memorias instituit. Sic Iridem diluuij simul & in hoc seruati generis humani monumentum esse voluit. Et Sacramentorum hic vsus est, quod & promissiones suas illis obsignat, & redemptionis nostrae beneficium perpetuam memoriae consecrat. In his ergo exerceamus nos diligenter, ne vnquam nobis excidant, quae olim cum patribus aut nobiscum egit Dominus, & nullum periculum tam graue incidet, quin habituri simus vetera exempla, quibus in fide confirmemur.
units.tr: This sharp rebuke is worthy of careful consideration, and it should often come to mind. For it warns us about the causes of little faith (ὀλιγοπιστία) or distrust, and at the same time it is fitting that we apply a remedy to this evil, than which none is more harmful. As God strengthens our faith by his works and benefits, so unless we frequently exercise ourselves in remembering and meditating on them, we cannot be firm and constant in faith. Instead, terrified by any danger or chance that befalls us beyond expectation, we waver, and we undo ourselves by our own reasoning, so that we do not render to God the obedience that is owed to him. We see very many examples in the ancient Jewish nation that teach this. For that divine Psalmist, about to narrate the sins by which they sinned under Moses and afterwards, first sets down this cause: "They soon forgot his works, and did not wait for his counsel." And the author of the book of Judges says the same, that the whole nation which had seen the works of the Lord in Egypt and in the desert was gathered to its fathers, and another generation arose which did not know the work of the Lord. "The children of Israel therefore," it says, "did evil in the eyes of the Lord," and so on. Moses had not warned them for nothing: "Take heed to yourself and keep your soul diligently, lest you ever forget the things your eyes have seen, and lest they ever depart from your heart," and so on. Similar admonitions occur frequently in the Psalms: "Sing to the Lord, sing psalms to him, speak of all his wonderful works. Remember his marvellous works that he has done, his wonders and the judgments of his mouth." And elsewhere it is said that God established this in Israel, that the fathers should tell their children and grandchildren of his works, so that they might set their trust in God and keep his commandments. Indeed God himself always commended memorable works to posterity and instituted solemn memorials of them. Thus he willed the rainbow to be a memorial of the flood and of the preservation of the human race. And the use of the sacraments is of this kind: they seal his promises to them and consecrate the benefit of our redemption to perpetual memory. Let us therefore exercise ourselves diligently in these things, so that the things which the Lord once did with our fathers or with us never slip from us; and no danger so grave will befall us but we shall have ancient examples by which we may be strengthened in faith.

units.la: Restat correptionis Dominicae effectus apud discipulos, de quibus dicit Euangelista: Tunc intellexerunt eum non dixisse, ut cauerent a fermento panis, sed a doctrina Pharisaeorum & Sadducaeorum. Ergo mentis oculi aperti sunt correptione ista vehementiori, ut de re tota caeperint diligentius cogitare. Quod enim de pueris dixit Solomon, stultitia esse in cordibus illorum infixam, expelli autem ferula: id in omnibus hominibus locum habet. Natura enim diuinorum ignorantes fumus, & plerunq; veternus & securitas mentibus nostris obrepunt, quae non sinit nos mentem ad altiora attollere: excutitur autem haec, si liberior Verbi praedicatio accedat, sicuti in Dauidis & multorum aliorum exemplis est videre. Et haec certissima nota est, ex qua electi agnosci possunt. Qui ergo ne correpti quidem resipiscunt, sed respondent, & suas rationes, vel potius cupiditates, Verbo Dei praeferunt, atq; indies in peius proficiunt, ipsi se ex impiorum ac reproborum numero esse eo ipso testantur. Hinc apparet, quid iudicari debeat de iis, qui hodie neq; scelera sua argui volunt, neq; a superstitionibus discedere, quae nulla alia ratione, quam humanarum traditionum fermento nituntur. Nos ergo hanc Domini nostri IESV CHRISTI admonitionem nobis applicemus, & ipsi credamus atq; seruiamus in fide & charitate non fucata. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: There remains the effect of the Lord's rebuke upon the disciples, of whom the Evangelist says: "Then they understood that he had not told them to beware of the leaven of bread, but of the doctrine of the Pharisees and Sadducees." So the eyes of their minds were opened by this more vehement rebuke, so that they began to think about the whole matter more diligently. For what Solomon said of children, that foolishness is fixed in their hearts and must be driven out by the rod, holds true for all people. For by nature we are ignorant of divine things, and drowsiness and carelessness, which do not allow us to raise our minds to higher things, often creep over our minds. This is shaken off if a freer preaching of the Word comes, as can be seen in the examples of David and of many others. And this is a most certain mark by which the elect can be recognised. Those, then, who do not even repent when rebuked, but reply, and prefer their own reasonings, or rather their desires, to the Word of God, and daily advance for the worse, by this very fact testify that they are of the number of the wicked and reprobate. Hence it is clear what ought to be judged concerning those who today are unwilling either to have their sins rebuked or to depart from superstitions, which rest on no other foundation than the leaven of human traditions. Let us therefore apply to ourselves this admonition of our Lord Jesus Christ, and let us believe in him and serve him in faith and unfeigned charity. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCIIII.
units.tr: HOMILY CCIIII.

units.la: Cum venisset autem IESVS in partes Caesareae Philippi, interrogauit discipulos suos, dicens: Quem me dicunt homines esse, Filium hominis? Illi vero dixerunt: Alij quidem Ioannem Baptistam, alij vero Eliam, alij vero Ieremiam, aut vnum ex Prophetis. Dicit eis: Vos autem quem me dicitis esse? Respondens vero Simon Petrus dixit: Tu es Christus ille Filius Dei viuentis.
units.tr: When Jesus came into the region of Caesarea Philippi, he asked his disciples, saying: "Whom do men say that I, the Son of man, am?" They answered: "Some say John the Baptist, others Elijah, others Jeremiah, or one of the prophets." He said to them: "But whom do you say that I am?" Simon Peter answered and said: "You are Christ, the Son of the living God."

units.la: Quamuis Dominus noster IESVS CHRISTVS per doctrinam & miracula sese inter Iudaeos abundè manifestaris, varia tamen & multum inter se diuersa fuerunt hominum de illo iudicia. Qui enim aperti eius hostes erant, Pharisæi ac Scribæ cum toto Sacerdotum collegio vini potorem & helluonem, Samaritanum, dæmoniacum atq; iuratum Satanæ socium dicebant. Meliores autem ex vulgo, in ipso vel Ioannem Baptistam, vel Eliam, vel aliquem alium ex Prophetarum veterum numero resurrexisse arbitrabantur. Discipuli vero domestici, qui ipsum Messiam esse credebant, errore communi safinati, in ipso regnū terrenū somniabant: quæ causa fuit, ut quam primum aliquid aduersum accideret, in fide fluctuarent. Exemplū eius infirmitatis nuper vidimus, quando propter commeatus penuriam inter se disceptarunt. Quia autem hoc admodum frequens est, quod electi quoq; sibi ipsis nebulas offendunt, quæ fidem ipsorum labefactant, dum vel Christum alium sibi finguut, quam reuera sit, vel in aliorum iudicia respectant, ipse nunc actionem cum discipulis memorabilem instituit, qua eos aduersus falsa mundi de fide & religione iudicia instruit, & quid de se credi debeat, docet. Estq; eò diligentius considerandα hæc tractatio, quòd Lucas eum preces huic præmisisse scribit, quibus haud dubie fidei verae lumen discipulis aPa tre posjulauit. Nobis autem vsus totius actionis esse debet, ut discamus, quæ nam fides vere Apostolica & Catholica sit, quam eos tenere oportet, qui se Christianos esse profitentur, & Ieruari volunt. Quia ergo de re maximi momenti hic agitur, diligenter historiam narrat Matthæus: Et primo vbi hoc cum discipulis colloquium Dominus habuerit, docet. Deinde quæ eius fuerit occasio, quam ipse Christus præbuit. Tertiò discipulorum responsionem narrat, qua aliorum de Christo iudicia exponunt. Quartò qualem ipsi de illo fidei confessionem ediderunt.
units.tr: Although our Lord Jesus Christ made himself abundantly known among the Jews through his teaching and miracles, opinions about him among people were nevertheless varied and very different from one another. For those who were his open enemies, the Pharisees and scribes together with the whole college of priests, called him a winebibber and glutton, a Samaritan, a demoniac, and a sworn ally of Satan. But the better sort among the common people thought that in him had risen either John the Baptist, or Elijah, or some other one of the old prophets. The disciples of his household, who believed him to be the Messiah, were deceived by the common error and dreamed that his kingdom was an earthly one; this was the reason that, as soon as something adverse happened, they wavered in faith. We recently saw an example of that weakness, when they quarrelled among themselves over the lack of provisions. Since it is very common that even the elect bring clouds upon themselves which weaken their faith, while they either fashion for themselves a Christ other than he really is, or look to the judgments of others, he now sets up a memorable exchange with the disciples, by which he instructs them against the false judgments of the world about faith and religion, and teaches what ought to be believed about himself. This discussion deserves to be considered the more carefully because Luke writes that he had prefaced it with prayers, by which he undoubtedly sought for the disciples the light of true faith. For us the use of the whole action ought to be that we learn what faith is truly apostolic and catholic, which those must hold who profess themselves Christians and wish to be saved. Since a matter of the greatest importance is treated here, Matthew narrates the history carefully. First, he teaches where the Lord held this conversation with the disciples. Then, what its occasion was, which Christ himself provided. Thirdly, he narrates the disciples' answer, by which they set out the judgments of others about Christ. Fourthly, what confession of him they themselves made.

units.la: Locus fuit Cæsarea Philippi, in cuius finibus Christus peruenit, postquam a Pharisæis & Saddu- cæis abijt, qui signum de cœlo postularant. Fuit autem Cæsarea hæc Phœnicia vrbs inter riuos fontium Iordanis eo fere loco vbi hi confluunt, sita. Antiquitus Paneas dicebatur. Postea a Philippo Herodis Magni filio instaurata & aucta Cæsareæ nomen accepit in laudem Cæsaris Tiberij, cui hac re gratificari voluit Philippus tetrarcha. Ideo etiam Cæsarea Philippi dicitur ad differentiam eius, quam pater in honore Augusti Cæsaream appellauit, cum prius turris Stratonis dicere tur. Appareat autem ex hac loci notatione, Christum nuper ferio a Pharisæis & Sadducæis fecesi onem fecisse, cum in Phœniciam vsq; ad gentes abierit. Et illic voluit a Petro nomine omnium discipulorum confessionem fieri, vt rursum adumbraret regnum suum ad gentes transferendum esse, apud quas sedem firmiorem, quàm apud Iudæos incredulos atq; contumaces, habiturus sit. Vt enim ipse reliquis Iudæis in fines gentium secessit: ita Apostoli quoq; Iudæa pulsi, idem, quam hic confessi sunt, feliciori successu inter gentes prædicarunt, initio facto in his ipsis locis, vt Actorum liber docet. Obseruari hoc debet propter eos, qui fidem & Ecclesiam certis locis alligant: quod hodie faciunt, qui successionem Ecclesiæ veram & perpetuam Romæ alligatam esse clamant: qui si interrogentur, cur non potius Cæsarea eam constituant, vbi confessionem suæ fidei Petrus edidit: aut Antiochiæ, vbi nomen Christianorum primum cœpit, non habebunt quod respondeant. Sed hoc in præsenti obiter dixisse sufficiat.
units.tr: The place was Caesarea Philippi, into whose region Christ came after he had departed from the Pharisees and Sadducees, who had demanded a sign from heaven. This Caesarea was a city of Phoenicia, situated among the streams of the springs of the Jordan, roughly where they flow together. In ancient times it was called Paneas. Afterwards it was restored and enlarged by Philip, son of Herod the Great, and it took the name Caesarea in honour of Caesar Tiberius, to whom Philip the tetrarch wished to show favour by this act. It is also called Caesarea Philippi, to distinguish it from the one which his father named Caesarea in honour of Augustus, when it had previously been called the Tower of Straton. Now it appears from this indication of place that Christ had recently withdrawn from the Pharisees and Sadducees, since he went away into Phoenicia as far as the Gentiles. And there he wished the confession to be made by Peter in the name of all the disciples, so that again he might foreshadow that his kingdom was to be transferred to the Gentiles, among whom he would have a firmer seat than among the unbelieving and obstinate Jews. For just as he himself withdrew from the rest of the Jews to the borders of the Gentiles, so the Apostles too, driven out of Judea, preached among the Gentiles, with a more fortunate success, the same confession which they made here, a beginning being made in these very places, as the book of Acts teaches. This ought to be noted on account of those who tie the faith and the Church to certain places, as those do today who cry out that the true and perpetual succession of the Church is bound to Rome. If they are asked why they do not rather locate it at Caesarea, where Peter made his confession of faith, or at Antioch, where the name of Christians first arose, they will have nothing to answer. But it is enough to have said this in passing for the present.

units.la: Nunc præsentis actionis occasionem videamus, quam Dominus Christus præbuit discipulos interrogans: Quem me dicunt homines esse, Filium hominis? Quærit autè non ex ignorantia (non potuerunt enim vulgi seruones ipsum latère, qui cordium cogitationes perspectas habebat) nec am bitiosè, quòd laudum suarum commemorationem audire cupiuerit, sed potius vt occasione habeat discipulos prouocandi ad veram fidei confessionem, quæ scandalo medeatur, quod hæc iudiciorum de ipso diuersitas pariebat. Et Filium hominis seipsum dicit, vt exprimat offensionis & erroris omnis circa fidem causam: quæ est quod plerique nihil homine maius de ipso sentiant. Quia autem de aliorum sententijs discipulos, qui orbis doctores esse debebant, interrogat, non obscure monet, verbi administros, non modo veritatis doctrinam simpliciter proponere debere, verumetiam in a- liorum opiniones inquirere, vt eas confutare possint, & imperitiores monere, vt ab erroribus sibi caueant. Id quod hodie plus quam necessarium est, quando & veteres hæreses postliminio reuocantur, & noua quotidie absurdissimorum dogmatum portenta quidam ambitiosi rixatores parient. Nec audiri debet, qui errores & falsa dogmata argui indigne ferunt: quasi sufficiat veritatis doctrinam simpliciter tradidisse. Atqui cõstat plures esse hoc seculo, qui hanc audire dedignantur, & quorum mentes ad mendacia & impostauras propendant. Vide 2. Tim. 3. & 4. Discipuli Christo respondent, & eorum iudicia atq; sententias narrant, qui honestius de illo sentiebant, de Pharifaeorum autem & Scribarum calumnijs nihil dicunt, quod ha nemini ignota erant, & Christus ipse illorum conuitia quotidie audiret. Et laudem meretur hac ipsorum modestia, quod ea nolint abfq; causa exagitare. Interim quoad alios, nihil dissimulant, neq; etiam aliquid affingunt, vt solent qui feruiliter illis adulantur, quos sibi patronos delegerunt. Simpliciter ergo respondent: Alij quidem Ioannem Baptistam te esse dicunt, alij vero Ieremiam, aut vnum ex Prophetis. Et hi quidem omnes etsi honorifice senserint de Christo, multum tamen diuersa fuerunt illorum sententia, omnes autem ex eodem fonte erroris manarunt, qui tunc inter Iudaeos receptus fuit: quod putarent (vt alibi diximus) animas defunctorum in alia corpora migrare, & novis donis augeri. Quia ergo Dominum videbant eodem Spiritus ardore Dei negotium agere, eadem dicendi libertate vitta magnatum & antistitum arguere, qua olim veteres Prophetae, & non itaque pridem Ioannes vsi erant, illorum aliquem in illo reuixisse sibi persuadebant. Et licet vehementer errent, tamen Sacerdotum & Pharifaeorum improbitatem suo exemplo arguunt, qui illum calumniari & horrendis conuitijs lacessere audebant, in quo homines plebei & illiterati Spiritus Dei specimina obseruare poterant. Non ergo miremur si hodie etiam vulgus hominum melius de veritate iudicat, & ea videt, quae ambitione excaecati Praesules atq; Theologi videre nolunt.
units.tr: Now let us look at the occasion of the present action, which the Lord Christ provided when he questioned the disciples: "Whom do men say that I, the Son of man, am?" He asks not out of ignorance (for the chatter of the crowd could not be hidden from him, who knew the thoughts of hearts), nor ambitiously, as though he wished to hear a recital of his own praises, but rather so that he might have an occasion to provoke the disciples to a true confession of faith, which would remedy the scandal that this diversity of judgments about him was producing. He calls himself the Son of man so as to express the cause of all offence and error about the faith, which is that most people think nothing greater of him than of a man. Now because he asks the disciples, who were to be teachers of the world, about the opinions of others, he plainly warns that ministers of the Word ought not only to set forth the doctrine of truth simply, but also to inquire into the opinions of others, so that they can refute them and warn the more unskilled to beware of errors. This is more than necessary today, when both old heresies are being recalled and some ambitious brawlers bring forth new monsters of absurd dogmas every day. Nor should he be heard who takes it ill that errors and false dogmas are argued against, as if it were enough simply to have handed down the doctrine of truth. Yet it is plain that there are many in this age who disdain to hear this, and whose minds incline toward lies and impostures. See 2 Tim. 3. and 4. The disciples answer Christ and relate the judgments and opinions of those who thought more honourably of him, but they say nothing of the slanders of the Pharisees and scribes, because these were known to no one, and Christ himself heard their reproaches every day. Their modesty deserves praise, in that they are unwilling to stir these up without cause. Meanwhile, as regards the others, they conceal nothing and add nothing, as those do who slavishly flatter the men they have chosen as their patrons. So they answer simply: "Some say you are John the Baptist, others Jeremiah, or one of the prophets." And although all these thought honourably of Christ, their opinions were very different; yet all flowed from the same source of error which was then accepted among the Jews, namely that they thought (as we have said elsewhere) that the souls of the dead migrate into other bodies and are enriched with new gifts. Therefore, since they saw the Lord doing God's work with the same ardour of the Spirit, and rebuking the lives of great men and of the high priests with the same freedom of speech which the old prophets, and John not long before, had used, they persuaded themselves that one of those had come back to life in him. And although they err greatly, nevertheless by their example they condemn the wickedness of the priests and Pharisees, who dared to slander him and assail him with horrible reproaches; in these things the common and unlettered people could observe signs of the Spirit of God. Let us not wonder, then, if even today the crowd of men judges better about the truth, and sees what the prelates and theologians, blinded by ambition, are unwilling to see.

units.la: At quod praecipuum huius loci caput est, obseruemus, omnibus seculis varias & diuersas fuisse de religione & fidei doctrina hominum sententias. Nec enim aliter fieri potest, quando animalis homo non percipit quae sunt Spiritus Dei, & proinde mundus (vt ille dicebat) opinione regitur. Fit ergo vt plerique suis figmentis indulgeant, & qui meliores sunt & Veritatis amantes interdum inter se dissentiant. Neminem ergo offendant nostri seculi differentiones. Imo nimium ridiculi sunt, qui vniuersalem consensum se expectare velle dicunt, priusquam aliquid de religione statuat. Expectant illi quod nunquam fuit, neq; vnquam erit quoad mundus hic steterit. Nec enim mutabit hic ingenium suum, & sectas esse oportet (vt Paulus ait) vt qui probati sunt, manifesti fiant. Et ipse Dominus cum de nouissimis temporibus vaticinaretur, non modo falsos Prophetas, verum etiam falsos Christos exorituros praedixit, quos nimirum illi fingant. Non ergo in alios respicere, sed in hoc totiincumbere debemus, vt nos sidem habeamus veram & orthodoxam de Filio Dei, qui solus verba vitae aeternae habet.
units.tr: But let us observe the chief point of this passage: in all ages there have been various and differing opinions of men about religion and the doctrine of faith. For it cannot be otherwise, since the natural man does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God, and therefore the world (as that man said) is ruled by opinion. So it happens that most people indulge their own fictions, and that those who are better and lovers of the truth sometimes disagree among themselves. Let the differences of our age therefore offend no one. Indeed, those are too ridiculous who say they wish to await a universal consensus before anything is settled about religion. They wait for what has never been and never will be, as long as this world stands. For this world will not change its nature, and there must be sects (as Paul says) so that those who are approved may become manifest. And the Lord himself, when prophesying about the last times, foretold that not only false prophets but also false Christs would arise, whom of course they would invent. Therefore we ought not to look to others, but to devote ourselves wholly to this, that we hold a true and orthodox faith concerning the Son of God, who alone has the words of eternal life.

units.la: Et de eo admonet Dominus, quando quid discipuli de ipso sentiant, quaerit. Ergo non eiusmodi est causa fidei, in qua aliorum sententijs stare debeamus. Nam si hoc Deo probaretur, omnes isti excusari poterant, cum Regus sui Herodis eadem fere esset sententia, vt supra audiuimus cap. 14. Qui ite pessime de Christo sentiebant, eos Sacerdotum & Scribarum authoritas excusauisset, qui in cathedra Mosis sedebant, & illu iampridem damnauerant. Nec etiam quenquam excusat, quod se dicit illiteratum esse. Nam cum vnusquisq; sua fide viuat, vnumquenq; etiam de sua sententia certum esse oportet, sicuti Apostolus monet. Itaq; quisq; sibi a Domino dici putet: Tu autem quem me dicis esse?
units.tr: The Lord also warns about this when he asks his disciples what they think of him. So the cause of faith is not one in which we ought to rest on the opinions of others. For if this were approved by God, all those men could have been excused, since the opinion of his king Herod was almost the same, as we heard above in chapter 14. The authority of the priests and scribes, who sat in Moses' seat and had long since condemned him, would have excused those who thought most wickedly of Christ. Nor does it excuse anyone that he says he is unlearned. For since each lives by his own faith, each ought to be certain of his own opinion, as the Apostle warns. So let each one think that the Lord is saying to him: "But you, who do you say that I am?"

units.la: Caeterum ad hanc Domini quaestionem Petrus, qui vtiq; alijs feruentior se praebuit, omnium nomine respondet, dicens: Tu es Christus ille, Filius Dei viuentis. Est haec vere Apostolica Confessio, quam Petrus omnium Apostolorum nomine (vt diximus) edidit, & quam Christus elogio praeclaro probauit, vt suo loco audiemus. Constat autem duabus partibus, quarum prima quis sit ille Filius hominis quoad officium, docet: altera quid de ipsius persona siue substantia aut essentia sentiri debeat.
units.tr: Now, in answer to this question of the Lord, Peter, who was certainly more fervent than the others, replies in the name of all: "You are that Christ, the Son of the living God." This is truly the Apostolic confession, which Peter, as we have said, set forth in the name of all the Apostles, and which Christ approved with a splendid commendation, as we shall hear in its place. It consists of two parts: the first teaches who that Son of Man is with respect to his office; the second, what ought to be thought of his person or substance or essence.

units.la: Ad primam pertinet: Tu es Christus ille. Christi vox respondet Hebraeae Messiae: & vtraq; vnctum significat. Vngebantur autem olim Sacerdotes & Reges oleo, quod gratiae Dei symbolum erat, cuius donis omnes ornari ac instrui necesse est, qui vel Ecclesiae vel Reipub. praesse volunt. Multus etiam in medicina olei vsus est, eo quod illius virtute vena ac nerui confirmantur, & membra rigentia motum & agilitatem suam recipiunt. Adhaec Orientalibus populis vnctiones balneorum loco sunt, & corporis sordibus abstergendis seruiunt. Vnctione ergo admonebantur Sacerdotes & Reges, se a Deo vocatos esse, & proinde huius gratia sibi opus esse, vt fidelium medicorum instar omnibus mederi possent, & singulos in officio continere, vt gloria Dei prouehatur, & publica salus conseruetur.
units.tr: The first part concerns the words "You are that Christ." The Christ in Greek [Χριστός] corresponds to the Hebrew Messiah [משיח], and both signify "anointed." Priests and kings were formerly anointed with oil, which was a symbol of the grace of God, and all who wish to preside over the Church or the commonwealth must be adorned and equipped with its gifts. Oil is also much used in medicine, because by its power veins and sinews are strengthened, and stiff limbs regain their motion and agility. Moreover, among eastern peoples anointings take the place of baths and serve to wipe away the filth of the body. By anointing, therefore, priests and kings were reminded that they had been called by God, and that they therefore needed his grace, so that they might be able to heal all as faithful physicians, and to keep each one in his duty, so that the glory of God might be advanced and the public welfare preserved.

units.la: Vnctio regum et sacerdotum. conseruetur. Quia vero Deus aeterno decreto Filium suum vnigenitum, qui praefinito tempore ex Virgine homo nasci debuit, praedestinauit, vt populi sui Rex & Sacerdos esset, eundem Hebraicè Messiam, Graecè Christum dici voluit, quod nomen, quia in nouo Testamento illi tribuitur, in alijs quoq; linguis vsurpatur, proprie autem Vnctum significat. Ratio autem eius est, non quòd ipsum oleo aliquo materiali inungi oportuerit, sed quòd (vt Psaltes canit) Deus illum oleo laetitiae (id est, Spiritu sancto, qui solus mentes vere exhilarat & confirmat) vnxerit prae consortibus suis, id est, prae cunctis mortalibus, adeo vt ex eius plenitudine dona Spiritus in nos quoq; redundent. Dum ergo Christum dicit Petrus, Sacerdotem & Regem Ecclesiae & omnium credentium esse confitetur. Et vtriusque officio eum fungi Scriptura passim docet. Nam Sacerdotem agit, docendo & ministros surrogando Ecclesiae suae, benedicendo item, intercedendo, & in primis, quod semetipsum pro nobis peccatum, id est, hostiam pro peccato fecit, cuius meritum durat in aeternum, vt in ipso remissionem peccatorum omnium inueniant, qui eum vera fide apprehendunt. Sed & Regem agit fortem & fidelem, dum suos ex diaboli tyrannide vindicauit, eosdem tuetur, sceptro Veri sui regit, bonorum suorum caelestium thesauros inter eos distribuit, & olim ad iudicium venturus est, & vnicuique retribuet in corpore suo, prout bonum aut malum fecerit.
units.tr: Anointing of kings and priests. preserved. But since God, by an eternal decree, predestined his only-begotten Son, who was to be born of a Virgin at a appointed time as a man, that he should be the King and Priest of his people, he willed that the same one be called Messiah in Hebrew and Christ in Greek. This name, because it is applied to him in the New Testament, is also used in other languages, and properly means "Anointed." The reason for it is not that he had to be anointed with any material oil, but that (as the Psalmist sings) God anointed him with the oil of gladness (that is, the Holy Spirit, who alone truly cheers and strengthens minds) above his fellows, that is, above all mortals, so that from his fullness the gifts of the Spirit overflow also upon us. When Peter calls Christ this, he confesses that he is the Priest and King of the Church and of all believers. And Scripture teaches everywhere that he discharges the office of both. For he acts as Priest, by teaching and by appointing ministers for his Church, likewise by blessing and interceding, and above all because he offered himself for us as a sin, that is, made himself a sacrifice for sin, whose merit endures for ever, so that all who grasp him by true faith may find in him the forgiveness of all their sins. But he also acts as a strong and faithful King, in that he has rescued his own from the tyranny of the devil, protects them, rules them with his sceptre of truth, distributes among them the treasures of his heavenly goods, and will one day come to judgment and render to each one in his body according to what he has done, good or evil.

units.la: Altera parte personam Christi describit Petrus, quando priori addit, Filius Dei viuentis. Repetenda autem particula T V, qua emphaticè vtitur Apostolus. Quasi diceret: Tu qui te Filium hominis dicis, & reuera homo es, ex Maria Virgine natus, imo qui (vt Isaias de te dixit) ab ieiunissimus virorum esse videris, & vir dolorum, simul es Filius Dei, & quidem viuentis, id est, veri Dei, qui in Iehuda notus est, qui omnia creauit, & regit, & qui solus viuit in secula sempiterna. Huius (inquam) Filius es aeternus, verus, eiusdem cum Patre essentiae, potentiae, gloriae ac Maiestatis. Agnoscit ergo Petrus in vna eademq; indiuisa persona Christi, Deum & Hominem: Deum videlicet (vt Diuus Athanasius ait) ex substantia Patris ante secula genitum, & Hominem ex substantia matris in seculo natum: perfectum Deum, perfectum hominem ex anima rationali & humana carne subsistentem, &c. Et talem esse oportebat, qui Mediator inter Deum & nos esse debebat, vt coram illo pro nobis intercedere, & idem nostram tandem in se recipere posset, nosq; illi fidere possemus, vt sacerdoti fideli, qui nostris infirmitatibus afficeretur & condoleret.
units.tr: In the second part Peter describes the person of Christ, when he adds to the former: "the Son of the living God." The particle "You" must be repeated, which the Apostle uses emphatically, as if he said: "You who call yourself the Son of Man, and are truly man, born of the Virgin Mary, nay, who (as Isaiah said of you) seem to be the most abject of men and a man of sorrows, you are at the same time the Son of God, and indeed of the living God, that is, of the true God, who is known in Judah, who created and governs all things, and who alone lives for ever and ever. You are (I say) his eternal and true Son, of the same essence, power, glory and majesty as the Father." Peter therefore acknowledges in the one and the same undivided person of Christ God and Man: God, indeed (as the divine Athanasius says), begotten from the substance of the Father before the ages, and Man, born in time from the substance of his mother: perfect God and perfect man, subsisting of a rational soul and human flesh, and so on. And he had to be such a one as would be the Mediator between God and us, so that he could intercede for us before him, and at the same time take our cause upon himself, and so that we could trust in him as a faithful priest, who is touched with our infirmities and feels compassion for them.

units.la: Hac igitur Petri Apostoli fides est, quam ex Patris reuelatione (vt mox sequetur) didicit, & quam omnium discipulorum nomine confessus est, quam item Apostoli omnes (vt Diuus Vigilius scribit) postea tradiderunt, Martyres roborauerunt, & fideles nunc vsque custodiunt: quae deniq; Conciliorum prisco rum decretis stabilita, & Imperatorum Christianorum legibus Ecclesiae commendata est. Et quia haec sola Catholica fides est, Catholici sunt, qui illam corde toto ampletun tur, & ore confitentur.
units.tr: This, then, is the faith of the Apostle Peter, which he learned from the Father's revelation (as will follow shortly), and which he confessed in the name of all the disciples. All the Apostles likewise handed it down afterwards (as the divine Vigilius writes), the martyrs strengthened it, and the faithful keep it to this day. Finally, it was established by the decrees of the ancient Councils and commended to the Church by the laws of the Christian emperors. And because this alone is the Catholic faith, those are Catholics who embrace it with their whole heart and confess it with their mouth.

units.la: Itaq; Confessionis huius hic nobis vsus esto: Primum, vt inter tristes & infelices huius seculi controuersias, vnum IESVM, qui ex Maria Virgine natus est, credamus CHRISTVM illum esse, & aeternum Dei Filium, quem Pater in mundum misit confituto tempore, vt hominem verum ex Virgine Maria assumeret, & in vna indiuisa persona Deum & Homo noster Sacerdos & Rex, id est, seruator, vindex ac Mediator esset. Apud hunc ergo, extra quem nullum est nomen, in quo ieruari possimus, quaeramus quae salutis sunt. Solus enim hic (vt alibi Petrus ait) habet verba vitae aeternae: quod dictum cum Petro omnibus opponere debemus, qui defectionem ab hac fide nobis suadere non verentur. Est enim IESVS CHRISTVS idem heri, hodie & in aeternum. Deinde vt hanc fidem non ore modo & verbis publice confiteamur, verumetiam obedientia & omni obseruantiae genere testemur. Etenim quia olim Sacerdotis summi authoritatem tantam esse voluit Deus, vt mortis supplicio multari debuerit, qui eius sententiae aut decreto relucta retur: similiter si huius seculi Regibus & magistratibus obedire tenemur, non solum propter iram, sed etiam propter conscientiam, eò quòd Dei ministri sunt: Quanto magis aeterno Dei Filio hic homos & obsequium debetur, quem Pater aeterno suo decreto praedestinauit, vt Ecclesiae suae Rex sit & Sacerdos in aeternum secundum ordinem Melchisedech. De illo certè olim Deus per Isaiam pronuntiauit: Gens & regnum, quae tibi seruire noluerint, peribunt, & Ioannes Baptista dicebat. Pater diligit Filium, & omnia dedit in manum eius: Qui credit in Filium, habet vitam aeternam; qui autem non paret Filio, non videbit vitam, sed ira Dei manet super eum. Praterea consolatio
units.tr: Let us therefore make this use of the confession here: first, that amid the sad and unhappy controversies of this age, we believe that the one Jesus, who was born of the Virgin Mary, is that Christ, and the eternal Son of God, whom the Father sent into the world at the appointed time, so that he might assume true manhood from the Virgin Mary, and so that in one undivided person he might be God and our Man, our Priest and King, that is, our Saviour, Defender and Mediator. Let us therefore seek with him, outside whom there is no name by which we can be saved, the things that pertain to salvation. For he alone (as Peter says elsewhere) has the words of eternal life. We ought to set this saying of Peter against all who do not hesitate to persuade us to fall away from this faith. For Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today and for ever. Next, we should confess this faith not only publicly with the mouth and words, but also bear witness to it by obedience and every kind of observance. For since God wished the authority of the high priest of old to be so great that whoever resisted his sentence or decree ought to be punished with death, so, if we are bound to obey the kings and magistrates of this world, not only for fear of wrath but also for conscience' sake, because they are ministers of God, how much more is obedience due here to the eternal Son of God, whom the Father, by his eternal decree, predestined to be King and Priest of his Church for ever, according to the order of Melchizedek. Of him God surely declared long ago through Isaiah: "The nation and kingdom that will not serve you shall perish." And John the Baptist said: "The Father loves the Son, and has given all things into his hand. He who believes in the Son has eternal life; but he who does not obey the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him." Furthermore, let us seek consolation from him in every kind of temptation. The gravest of these arise from a conscience of sin. Set against them the priesthood of Christ, who is a faithful High Priest and has made atonement for our sins; moreover, having himself been tested in our infirmities, he can feel compassion and sympathy for us. There are also temptations which arise from...

units.la: nem hinc petamus in omni tentationum genere. Oriuntur hæ grauissimæ ex peccati conscientia. His oppone Sacerdotium Christi, qui fidelis est Pontifex, & pro peccatis nostris perlitauit: ad-hæc nostras infirmitates expertus nobis potest condolere & compati. Sunt item tentationes, quæ ex cruce & aduersis, seu tribulationibus nascuntur, quibus obnoxij sunt omnes, qui volunt in illa pie viuere. Sed his opponamus hunc Regem nostrum, cui omnis potestas data est in cælo & in terra. Habet ergo imperium in omnes creaturas, in morbos item & quæcunque alia nobis molesta & inimica sunt, ut ea a nobis depellere, & vicissim largiri possit, quæ nobis iucunda & salutaria sunt. Huic itaque fidamus & constanter seruiamus ex toto corde. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: ...consolation from this source in every kind of temptation. The most grievous temptations arise from the consciousness of sin. Against these set the priesthood of Christ, who is a faithful High Priest and has made atonement for our sins; moreover, having himself been tested in our infirmities, he is able to sympathise with us and have compassion on us. There are also temptations that arise from the cross and from adversities or tribulations, to which all are subject who wish to live godly lives in these things. But against these let us set this King of ours, to whom all power has been given in heaven and on earth. He therefore has dominion over all creatures, over diseases too and whatever else is troublesome and hostile to us, so that he can drive these away from us and in turn bestow what is pleasant and salutary for us. Let us therefore trust in him and serve him constantly with the whole heart. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCV.
units.tr: HOMILY CCV.

units.la: Tunc respondens IESVS dixit eis: Beatus es Simo Bar Iona: quia caro & sanguis non reuelauit tibi hoc, sed Pater meus, qui est in cœlis. Sed & ego tibi dico, tu es Petrus, & super hanc petram ædificabo Ecclesiam meam: & portæ inferorum non prævalebunt aduersus eam.
units.tr: Then Jesus answered and said to them: "Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jona, for flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven. And I also say to you, you are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell will not prevail against it." (Matt. 16:17-18)

units.la: Quemadmodum Deus in Filio suo Vnigenito IESV CHRISTO omnes gratiæ suæ & salutis thesauros nobis offert: ita æquum est, ut huic vnifidamus, & fidem in hunc oriè & factis profiteamur. Requirit hoc ille graui præcepto, cuius rationem Paulus reddit, dicens: Corde enim creditur ad iustitiam, ore autem confessio fit ad salutem. At peccatur hic a multis ignorantia, qui quid de Christo debeant confiteri, nesciunt: multi item sufficere arbitrantur, si aliis consentiant, qui authoritate præstant, & apud plerosque in pretio sunt. Sæpe ergo nos in Scripturis de hac causa instituit Spiritus sanctus: In primis autem huc facit præsens hæc Christi cum discipulis actio. Requisiuit ab his super, quid de ipso homines sentiant & loquantur: non autem illi satis fuit, quod aliorum sententias referre poterant, sed insuper quid ipsi credant interrogat. Ibi vero Petrus omnium nomine respondens ait, Tu es Christus ille Filius Dei viuentis. Quo loco discimus, vnumquenque de sua fide certum esse debere, non autem ab aliorum iudicio pendere. Deinde fidei Christianæ summam in eo consistere, vt IESVM hunc, qui ex Maria virgine verus homo natus est, etiam verum & æternum Dei viuentis Filium, adhæc Vnigenitum Dei, id est, Regem & Sacerdotem nostrum esse credamus. Sequitur nunc huius responsio, qua Petri Confessionem magnificè commendat, & fidei huius effecta siue fructus exponit. Tradit ergo locus hic vniuersam salutis nostræ rationem, & simul argumenta solidissima suggerit, quibus nosipsos aduersus omnis generis tentationes in vera fide confirmemus.
units.tr: Just as God offers all the treasures of his grace and salvation to us in his only-begotten Son Jesus Christ, so it is right that we trust in him alone and profess our faith in him with our mouths and by our deeds. The serious precept that requires this, and whose reason Paul gives, says: "For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation." Yet many sin here through ignorance, since they do not know what they ought to confess about Christ. Many also think it enough if they agree with those who hold authority and are highly esteemed among most people. The Holy Spirit therefore often instructs us about this matter in the Scriptures, but this present action of Christ with his disciples especially bears on it. He asked them what men think and say about him. But it was not enough for him that they could report the opinions of others; he further asks what they themselves believe. Then Peter, answering in the name of all, says: "You are Christ, that Son of the living God." From this place we learn that each one ought to be certain of his own faith, and not depend on the judgment of others. Next, the sum of the Christian faith consists in this: that we believe this Jesus, who was born a true man of the Virgin Mary, to be also the true and eternal Son of the living God, and moreover the only-begotten of God, that is, our King and Priest. Now follows his reply, in which he greatly commends Peter's confession and sets out the effects or fruits of this faith. This passage therefore presents the whole account of our salvation, and at the same time suggests most solid arguments by which we may strengthen ourselves in true faith against every kind of temptation.

units.la: Primum Beatus (inquit) es Simon Bar Iona, id est, Iona fili. Est hæc manifesta fidei, quam professus erat, approbatio, quando illum propter eius confessionem beatum pronunciat. Obseruari debet ergo hic locus propter Iudæos & Turcas, adeoque omnes alios, qui æternā Christi diuinitatem negant, & nos contra Dei mandatum homini mortali & crucifixo fidere clamitant. Etenim si Petrus ideo beatus dicitur, quod IESVM hunc, quem hominem & filium hominis esse probe sciebat, verum & naturalem Dei Filium professus est, hanc eius confessionem verissimam fuisse constat. Nam si falsa aut mendax fuisset, ex diabolo fuisset, qui mendacij pater est, & propter illam Petrus non beatus, sed potius infelix & damnationis reus dici merebatur. Itaque ex hoc Christi dicto sequitur, damnatos & perditos esse, qui Filio huic Dei fidere dedignantur, & eiusdem diuinitatem negare audent. De illis enim intelligi debet Ioannis Baptistæ sententia: Qui non paret Filio, non videbit vitam, sed ira Dei manet super ipsum. Ioan.3.
units.tr: First, he says, "Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jona," that is, son of Jona. This is a clear approval of the faith he professed, when he pronounces him blessed on account of his confession. This passage ought to be noted for the sake of the Jews and Turks, and indeed all others who deny the eternal divinity of Christ and cry out that we trust in a mortal and crucified man, against God's command. For if Peter is called blessed because he professed that this Jesus, whom he knew well to be a man and the Son of man, is also the true and natural Son of God, it is clear that this confession was most true. For if it had been false or lying, it would have come from the devil, who is the father of lies, and Peter would have deserved to be called not blessed but rather unhappy and guilty of damnation. Hence it follows from this saying of Christ that those are damned and lost who disdain to trust in this Son of God and dare to deny his divinity. For the saying of John the Baptist must be understood of them: "He who does not obey the Son will not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him." John 3.

units.la: Interim indicatur his Christi verbis primus fidei fructus, qui est, quod credentes per hanc beati fiunt, & proinde iustificantur. Sunt enim connexa inter se beatitas & iustificatio, vt Paulus in epistola ad Romanos Cap.4. docet, & illa ex hac sequitur. Natura quippe omnes homines peccatores, & propter peccatum irafilij atque damnati sunt: neque aliqua in nobis iustitia est, quæ
units.tr: Meanwhile, by these words of Christ the first fruit of faith is indicated, namely that believers through it become blessed, and therefore are justified. For blessedness and justification are connected with each other, as Paul teaches in his epistle to the Romans, chapter 4, and the former follows from the latter. For by nature all men are sinners, and on account of sin they are under the wrath of God and condemned. Nor is there any righteousness in us that

units.la: {Rom.10.} Rom. 10. nos in Dei conspectu tueatur. Agnouerunt hoc & confessi sunt palam sanctissimi quiq;, & Deum feriis precibus orarunt, ne in iudicium cum ipsis ingredi, aut delictorum, quae a pueritia patrarint, meminisse velit. Nec temere Solomon dicebat: Quis dicet, Mundum est cor meum? purus sum a peccato meo? Et grauius adhuc Apostolus pronuntiat: Si dixerimus, nos non peccasse, nosipsos fallimus, imo mendacem facimus Deum, & sermo eius non est in nobis. Itaq; aliena iustitia nobis opus est: ea nimirum, quam ipse Deus nobis in Filio suo dilecto IESV CHRISTO offert per Euangelium. Is vero non alia ratione quam per fidem apprehenditur, qua sola ad eum veniunt, & idem manducatur, ut nostrae fiat. Quia ergo in eum credebat Petrus, & fidem hanc ingenue ac intrepide confitebatur, non immerito illum Christus beatum dicit. At hic nos eius meminisse oportet, quod Paulus de Abrahamo scribit. Ut enim huic fides in promissum semen adiustitiam imputata est: id vero non propter Abrahamum solum scriptum est, sed etiam propter nos, quibus similiter imputabitur ad iustitiam, si crediderimus in eum, qui excitauit IESVM Dominum nostrum a mortuis: Ita qui Petrum propter fidem & liberam eius confessionem beatum dixit, nos quoq; in beatorum censu numerabit, si eandem fidem synceram & inconcussam seruauerimus. Vide Paulum ad Rom.4.
units.tr: Rom. 10. could protect us in the sight of God. The holiest people have acknowledged this and openly confessed it, and they have prayed to God with many prayers not to enter into judgment with them, nor to remember the offences that they committed from childhood. Solomon did not say without reason: "Who can say, My heart is clean, I am pure from my sin?" And the Apostle declares it even more strongly: "If we say that we have not sinned, we deceive ourselves, and indeed we make God a liar, and his word is not in us." Therefore we need an alien righteousness, namely that which God himself offers us in his beloved Son Jesus Christ through the Gospel. This righteousness is not laid hold of in any way other than through faith, by which alone people come to him, and by which he is eaten so that he becomes ours. Since Peter believed in him and openly and fearlessly confessed this faith, Christ rightly calls him blessed. But here we ought to remember what Paul writes about Abraham. For as faith was imputed to Abraham for righteousness in the promised seed, and this was written not for Abraham alone but also for us, to whom it will likewise be imputed for righteousness if we believe in him who raised up Jesus our Lord from the dead, so he who called Peter blessed on account of his faith and free confession will also number us among the blessed, if we keep this same faith sincere and unshaken. See Paul to the Romans, chapter 4.

units.la: At ne quis Petrum fidem hanc ex se ipso habuisse, & proinde sua industria beatitatem iflam consecutum esse putet, addit Dominus: Caro & sanguis non revelauit tibi hoc, sed Pater meus qui est in coelis. Carnis & sanguinis vocabulis hominem cum omnibus facultatibus intelligit, & eodem sensu Paulus illis vtitur, quando se non cum carne & sanguine consuluisse scribit, ut demonstret, se Euangelium non ex vllo hominum didicisse, sed ab ipso Deo fuisse edoctum. Sensus ergo verborum est: Quod me Filium Dei, & Vnctum illum siue promissum Seruatorem esse agnoscis & confiteris Petre, id non tui ingenij acumine & propria industria didicisti, neq; ex parentibus hausisti, aut ab vllis hominibus edoctus es, sed Pater meus caelestis ex singulari gratia, qua te pro sequitur, suo Spiritu mentem tuam illuminauit, ut sub vili & mortali carne latentem Dei Filium, & humani generis redemptorem videas & agnoscas. Docet ergo hic locus, fidem sublimius & angustius quiddam esse, quam quod humana ratio videre aut inuestigare possit: sed Dei donum esse, in quo sensus nostri omnes caecutiunt, donec ille mentis oculos nobis aperiat. Etenim si IESV CHRISTI mysteria ad nostrae rationis calculum examines, non solum obscura & intricata illi videbuntur, verumetiam stultitia illi erunt, neq; vnquam intelligere poterit, in illius morte vitam inueniri, qui pauper & egenus vixit, & ignominiose in cruce est mortuus. Itaq; ut diuinitus illuminemur & trahamur opus est: sicuti olim per Isaiam, & postea proprio ore Christus testatus est olim, dicens: Erunt omnes a Deo docti. Ite: Nemo venit ad me, nisi Pater meus traxerit eum. Ex eo autem apparet, totum redemptionis & salutis nostrae beneficium ex gratuita Dei misericordia manare, neq; aliquid in eo nostris viribus aut meritis tribui debere. Falluntur ergo turpiter, vel potius seipsos miserè fallunt, qui in cotrouerfijs, quae nostro saeculo inter plerosque agitantur, ad homines respectant, qui eruditionis & doctrinae, aut potentiae summae atq; authoritatis existimationem sustinent. Enimuero si idfecissent Apostoli, nunquam venissent ad Christi cognitionem, neq; Confessionem hanc edidissent, quae ipsis salutem attulit, & quam Dominus tam praeclaro elogio dignatus est.
units.tr: But lest anyone think that Peter had this faith from himself, and so obtained that blessedness by his own diligence, the Lord adds: "Flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven." By the words flesh and blood he understands man with all his faculties, and Paul uses them in the same sense when he writes that he did not consult with flesh and blood, to show that he had learned the Gospel from no men, but had been taught it by God himself. The sense of the words, therefore, is this: "That you, Peter, acknowledge and confess that I am the Son of God and that promised Anointed Savior, you have not learned by the sharpness of your own wit and your own diligence, nor have you drawn it from your parents, nor been taught by any men. Rather, my heavenly Father, by his singular grace with which he has chosen you, has illuminated your mind by his Spirit, so that you may see and acknowledge the Son of God, hidden under lowly and mortal flesh, to be the Redeemer of the human race." This passage therefore teaches that faith is something higher and more exclusive than human reason can see or search out, but is the gift of God, in which all our senses are blinded until he opens the eyes of our mind to us. For if you weigh the mysteries of Jesus Christ by the reckoning of our reason, they will not only seem obscure and intricate to it, but will even seem foolish, and it will never be able to understand that life is found in the death of one who lived poor and needy and died shamefully on the cross. Therefore we need to be enlightened and drawn by God, as Christ himself long ago bore witness through Isaiah and afterwards with his own mouth, saying: "They shall all be taught by God," and "No one comes to me unless my Father draws him." (Isa. 54:13; John 6:44-45) From this it is clear that the whole benefit of our redemption and salvation flows from the free mercy of God, and that nothing in it should be attributed to our own strength or merits. Therefore those are shamefully deceived, or rather they miserably deceive themselves, who in the controversies that are stirred up among many in our age look to men who hold a reputation for learning and teaching, or for the highest power and authority. Indeed, if the Apostles had done this, they would never have come to the knowledge of Christ, nor would they have made this confession that brought them salvation and that the Lord deemed worthy of such a splendid commendation.

units.la: Nemo tamen ex eo occasionem arripiat, quadoctrinam & institutionem omnem tam publicam quam priuatam reijcere velit. Nam etsi fides Dei donum sit, qui solus in mentes nostras ius habet, ut eas mutet & illustret suo Spiritu: eiusdem tamen ordinarium medium atq; organum est Verbi publica praedicatio, qua Spiritus in cordium recessus penetrat. Ideo alibi dicebat Christus: Amen amen dico vobis, qui sermonem meum audit, & credit ei qui misit me, habet vitam aeternam. Et iam in coelos abiturus idem dicit: Ite in orbem vniuersum, & praedicate Euangelium toti creaturae: Qui crediderit & baptizatus fuerit, seruabitur. Idem etiam doctores & ministros excitat, quibus ad reuelationem Euangelij erga alios vtatur, sicuti Paulus de seipso scribit. Et hoc adeo solenne est Deo, ut idem alibi dicat: Quomodo credent ei, de quo non audierint? quomodo autem audient absq; praedicante? Et postea multa concludit: Fides ergo ex auditu est, auditus autem per Verbum Dei. Ut vero in agricultura, nihil est qui plantat aut serit & rigat, sed Deus solus est, qui incrementum dat: ita etiam de Verbi ministerio & huius praeconibus nos sentire debemus, ut omnis effectus solius Dei virtuti & gratiae transcribatur. Vide 1.Cor.3.
units.tr: No one, however, should take occasion from this to reject all teaching and instruction, public and private. For although faith is a gift of God, who alone has the right to change and enlighten our minds by his Spirit, the ordinary means and instrument of that same faith is the public preaching of the Word, by which the Spirit penetrates the recesses of the heart. So Christ said elsewhere: "Verily, verily I say unto you, he who hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life." And when he was about to go up to heaven he said the same: "Go into all the world and preach the gospel to the whole creation; he who believes and is baptized will be saved." He also raises up teachers and ministers through whom he uses the revelation of the gospel toward others, as Paul writes of himself. And this is so customary with God that he says elsewhere: "How shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? And how shall they hear without a preacher?" Afterwards he concludes at length: "So faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God." But just as in agriculture, the one who plants, sows and waters is nothing, but God alone gives the increase, so we ought to think the same of the ministry of the Word and its heralds: every effect is to be ascribed to the power and grace of God alone. See 1 Cor. 3.

units.la: Caeterum pergit Dominus, & dicit: Tu es Petrus. In mentem ei reuocat, quod ei sub initium suae vocationis ipso primum visio dixerat: Tu es Simon filius Iona, tu vocaberis Cephas: quod declaratur Petrus vel lapis. Nunc autem cognomen hoc ei imponit & confirmat, occasione ex eo arrepta, quod ipsum, qui spiritualis illa Petra est, cui Ecclesia (ut paulo post sequetur) eu fundamento solido & inconcusso innititur, tam liberè erat confessus. Quasi diceret: Quia tu sprætis omnium aliorum de me iudicijs & sententijs, me credis æternum ac Vnigenitum esse Dei Filium, Christum item illum patribus promissum, id est, Regem & Sacerdotem Ecclesiae siue populi Dei, adeoque huius caput & fundamentum, ex quo salus omnis manat, ego quoque vicissim propter hanc fidei constantiam & intrepidam eius confessionem, Petri nomen tibi confirmo, & te pro tali agno fico & prædico, qui in mea domo siue Ecclesia lapis viuus & solidus esse debeas ad mei nominis gloriam & multorum aliorum ædificationem. Hæc dicendo præstat Christus promissionem veterem Dei: Qui me honorauerit, eum & ego honorabo. Item: Omnis qui confitebitur me coram hominibus, eum & ego confitebor coram Patre meo, qui in cœlis est. Matth.10.
units.tr: Moreover the Lord goes on and says: "You are Peter." He recalls to Peter's mind what he had said to him at the beginning of his calling: "You are Simon son of Jonah; you shall be called Cephas," which is interpreted Peter or stone. Now he imposes this surname on him and confirms it, the occasion being taken from the fact that Peter, who is that spiritual rock on which the Church rests on a solid and unshaken foundation (as will follow shortly), had so freely confessed him. It is as if he were saying: "Because you, having scorned the judgments and opinions of all others about me, believe that I am the eternal and only-begotten Son of God, and that Christ promised to the fathers, that is, King and Priest of the Church or people of God, and so its head and foundation from whom all salvation flows, I in turn, on account of this constancy of faith and his fearless confession, confirm to you the name Peter, and I make you and proclaim you such a stone, who ought to be a living and solid stone in my house or Church, for the glory of my name and the building up of many others." In saying this Christ fulfils the old promise of God: "Whoever honors me, I will also honor." Likewise: "Everyone who confesses me before men, I will also confess before my Father who is in heaven." Matt. 10.

units.la: At ne quis in solius Petri persona hæreret, ipse posteà quod sibi dictum fuerat omnium credentium institutioni applicans, in priori suaepistola scribit: Si quidem gustauistis quod benignus est Dominus, ad quem accedentes, qui est lapis viuus, ab hominibus quidem reprobatus, apud Deum vero electus ac pretiosus, ipsi quoque veluti viui lapides ædificemini, domus spiritualis, sacerdotium sanctum, ad offerendum spirituales hostias, acceptas Deo per IESVM CHRISTVM. Quotquot ergo volunt germani esse Christi discipuli, ij primò ad Christum accedere debent, neque fefalsis & iniquis aliorum iudicijs ab illo avocari sinant. Deinde super hunc ceu viui lapides ædificentur vna cum alijs credentibus, ut pars sint aliqua domus illius spiritualis, Ecclesiae nimirum in qua sola Deus recte colitur hostijs spiritualibus, quæ illi propter Christum grata & acceptæ sunt. Meminerint autem credentes & electos, non stipulis, fœno, ligno putrido, alij materiæ fragili, sed lapidibus viuis, siue silicibus, conferri: nimirum quod in fide & eius confessione solidos & firmos esse conueniat, qui sese non sinant arundinum instar a quouis vento doctrinæ aut opinionum circumferri. Hæc si diligenter expendas, mox videbis non dignos esse Christianorum nomine eos, quotquot extra Christum vagantur, mundo addicti sunt, & in fide vacillant, nec quicquam solidum aut stabile habent in religione & salutis negotio.
units.tr: But lest anyone cling to the person of Peter alone, he himself afterwards applied to the instruction of all believers what had been said to Peter, and writes in his first epistle: "If indeed you have tasted that the Lord is gracious; coming to him, who is a living stone, rejected indeed by men but chosen and precious before God, you also, like living stones, are built up as a spiritual house, a holy priesthood, to offer spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ." So whoever wishes to be a true disciple of Christ must first come to Christ, and must not allow himself to be drawn away from him by the false and unjust judgments of others. Then let him be built upon him, like a living stone, together with the other believers, so that he may be part of that spiritual house, namely the Church, in which alone God is rightly worshipped with spiritual sacrifices that are pleasing and acceptable to him for Christ's sake. Let believers and the elect remember, however, that they are compared not to straw, hay, rotten wood or other fragile material, but to living stones or flints: that is, they ought to be solid and firm in faith and its confession, and not allow themselves to be carried about by every wind of doctrine or opinion like reeds. If you weigh these things carefully, you will soon see that those who wander outside Christ, who are given over to the world and waver in faith, and who have nothing solid or stable in religion and in the business of salvation, are not worthy of the name of Christians.

units.la: Porrò apertius ad totam Ecclesiam extendit Dominus, quod de Petro dixerat, nimirum quod præuideret, quid futurum esset nouissimis temporibus, quando personati successores Petri, Romani pontifices, eius verbis in alienum & impium sensum detortis, seipsos Ecclesiae fundamentum simul & caput constituerunt. Dicit aut: Et super hanc petram ædificabo Ecclesiam meam, & portæ inferorum non præualebunt aduersus eam. Primò Ecclesiae meminit, ut discipulos conso-letur, qui tunc numero pauci & (ut alibi ait) pusillus grex erant, & terreri poterant aduersariorum multitudine & potentia. Docet ergo fore breui, ut in immensum crescant, & impleatur quod olim Prophetæ de gentium omnium accessione ad Ecclesiam prædixerunt. Et obseruari hoc debet ut discamus, velle Deum, ut electi cœtum proprium a reliquo mundo separatu & sibi consecratum constituant. Ita olim Iudæorum gentem suum peculium fecit, & in illa coli voluit: adhæc Legem ei dedit, & cultus sui sedem certam constituit, ad quam solenniter diebus festis conuenirent ex ter ris omnibus, ne in sectas scinderentur. Et in nouo Testamento diserte Christus testatur, vnum ouile & vnum gregem fore, cuius ipse vnicus & communis pastor sit. Et hæc est Ecclesia illa Catholica siue Vniuersalis, quam in Symbolo Apostolico profitemur, & communionem Sanctorum dicimus, id est, omnium qui per fidem in Christum sanctificati sunt. Huic ergo se coniungant, qui cunque Deo placere, & eius domestici censeri atque seruari cupiunt. Et quia Catholicae illius Ecclesiae partes sunt cœtus illi fidelium, qui hinc inde per Verbi prædicationem colliguntur, & in quibus Deus Pater per nomen Filij sui IESV CHRIST i innocatur, diligenter hos frequentare debent Christiani homines, adeo ut cum Dauide dicant: Lætor cùm mihi dicunt, Eamus ad domum Domini, &c. Prophani autem renera sunt, & seipsos a Christi & salutis, quæ in ipso habetur communione
units.tr: Further, the Lord extends more openly to the whole Church what he had said about Peter, foreseeing what would happen in the last times, when the successors of Peter in name only, the Roman pontiffs, twisting his words into an alien and impious sense, have made themselves both the foundation and the head of the Church. He says: "And upon this rock I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it." First he mentions the Church, to comfort the disciples, who were then few in number and (as he says elsewhere) a little flock, and who could be terrified by the multitude and power of their adversaries.
