He teaches, therefore, that before long they will grow immensely, and that what the prophets long ago foretold about the coming of all the nations to the Church will be fulfilled. And this should be observed so that we may learn that God wills the elect to form a community of their own, separated from the rest of the world and consecrated to himself. Thus of old he made the Jewish nation his own possession and wished to be worshipped in it; he gave them the Law and established a fixed seat of his worship, to which they would solemnly gather from all lands on feast days, lest they be split into sects. And in the New Testament Christ clearly testifies that there will be one fold and one flock, whose sole and common shepherd he is. This is that Catholic or universal Church which we profess in the Apostles' Creed, and which we call the communion of saints, that is, of all who have been sanctified through faith in Christ. Therefore let those who wish to please God, and to be counted and kept as his household, join themselves to it. And since the parts of that Catholic Church are those assemblies of the faithful which are gathered here and there through the preaching of the Word, and in which God the Father is invoked through the name of his Son Jesus Christ, Christians ought diligently to attend them, so that with David they may say: "I rejoiced when they said to me, Let us go into the house of the Lord," etc. Those, however, who are truly profane, and who by their own act cut themselves off from the communion of Christ and of the salvation that is had in him, are those who neglect the sacred assemblies and prefer the pursuits of this unhappy world to the exercises of the Christian faith and religion.

units.la: Psal.122 mNtione excludunt, qui coetus sacros negligunt, & infelicis mundi studia, exercitijs fidei & religionis Christianæ præferunt: digni, vt cum Israelitis carnes Ægyptias Manna præferentibus in huius mundi deserto male pereant.
units.tr: Psal.122 They are worthy, like the Israelites who preferred Egyptian meat to manna, to perish miserably in the wilderness of this world.

units.la: Deinde Ecclesiæ suæ architectum simul & fundamentum indicat. Ego (inquit) Ecclesiam meam ædificabo super hanc petram. Ipse ergo Christus verus architectus est, & ideo suam dicit esse Ecclesiam: quo Paulus respiciens dicebat Dei arum, Dei ædificatio estis. Hominibus quidem administris vtitur, qui interdum architecti Ecclesiæ dicuntur, sed ex gratia, qua eos dignatur Dominus, cum idem (vt Paulus de Apostolis simul omnibus fatetur, ex semetipsis ne ad cogitandum quidem idonei sint. Et voluit diserte in præsenti dicere, Ecclesiam meam, vt eorum ambitioni occurreret, quos nonnisi temporibus dominium in Ecclesiam vsurpaturos sciebat. Atqui Christus solus est Dominus, qui gloria suam dat nemini: & cum idem ille Ecclesiam, sui sanguinis pretio redemerit, et sibi consecrarit, inexcusabile sacrilegium est, si quis illa sibi ipsi vendicare audeat.
units.tr: Next he indicates the architect and foundation of his Church. "I," he says, "will build my Church upon this rock." Christ himself is therefore the true architect, and that is why he calls it his Church; looking to this, Paul said: "You are God's field, God's building." He does use human ministers, who are sometimes called architects of the Church, but this is by the grace with which the Lord deigns to honor them, since, as Paul confesses of all the apostles together, they are not of themselves even fit to think anything. And he wished to say plainly "my Church" here, to meet the ambition of those whom he knew would later seize dominion over the Church. But Christ alone is Lord, who gives his glory to no one; and since he redeemed that same Church at the price of his own blood and consecrated it to himself, it is an inexcusable sacrilege if anyone dares to claim it for himself.

units.la: Porro non architectus modo & Dominus Ecclesiæ est Christus, verumetiam fundamentum, quod satis perspicue docet, dicens: Tu es Petrus, & super hanc petram ædificabo, &c. Quæ verba Romani Pontifices de Petro exponunt, qui simul petra ipsa dicatur, & super hunc Ecclesiam ædificacam dicunt, vt eadem opera seipsos propter successionem Apostolicam, quæ falso gloriari solent, Ecclesiæ illius fundamentum constituant. Sed & huius loci contextu, & rei ipsa conuincuntur. Cum enim apud Græcos Petrus & Petra, quoad significationem idem sint & vtrumque significet lapidem, & verisimile sit, Christum cum Syriace loqueretur, vtrobique Cephæ vocabulo vsum fuisse, non tamen abs numine factum est, quod Matthæi interpres (quisquis is fuerit) distincte loqui voluit: Tu es Petrus, & super hanc petram: nimirum vt inter Petrum & petram, quæ Ecclesiæ fundamentum constituitur, distinguaret, & hoc esse doceret petram illam, quam Petrus confessus fuerat, & a qua cognomen suum acceperat. Atqui non alium ille quam <bl>IESVM CHRISTVM</bl> confessus est: Ergo de semetipso loquitur Dominus, & pollicetur, quod ipse Ecclesiæ suæ fundamentum esse velit, cui tuto inniti possint omnes, qui eandem fidem cum Petro ex corde sincero profitentur. Et vt ita intelligamus hunc locum, res ipsa (vt diximus) & totius Scripturæ consensus docet. Nam fundamentum Ecclesiæ oportet esse solidum, firmum, immobile, quod neque loco moueri, neque corruere possit, ne illo euerso Ecclesia collabatur. At omnis homo natura mendax est, qui & falli potest & fallere: adhæc affectibus obnoxij sunt homines, qui ipsos non sinunt in eadem semper sententia perseuerare, sæpe etiam metu aut alio affectu superati ea faciunt & dicunt, quæ illicita esse & male fieri norunt, & a propria conscientia arguuntur: quod ipsi Petro accidisse scimus, quando Christum, quem ante confessus fuerat, turpiter abnegauit. Ergo qui hominem Ecclesiæ fundamentum constituunt, ij Ecclesiam fingunt, cuius salus dubia & incerta sit, & dulcissima consolatione spoliant credentes, quam ipsis hic locus exhibet. Ideo Scriptura passim in vno Domino hoc fundamentum monstrat. Moses Deum vocat petram salutis nostræ, & Iudæos hoc nomine accusat, quod illo relicto, ad alia præsidia conuersi sint. Dauid item in Psalmis solum Deum petram & rupem suam frequenter profitetur. Quis est Deus (inquit) præter Iehouam? & quis Zur, id est, petra præter Deum nostrum? Paulus vero Christum vocat fundamentum Prophetarum & Apostolorum, eo quod tam hi quam illi ad vnum illum remittunt, & illi vni confidere docent. Idem ad Corinthios scribens ait: Fundamentum aliud nemo potest ponere præter id quod positum est, quod est IESVS CHRISTVS. Sed & ipse Petrus Christum dicit lapidem illum viuum, siue petram esse, super quam credentes ædificari debeant, & de illo exponit locum Isaiæ: Ecce pono in Zion lapidem in summo ponendum angulo, electum, pretiosum, cui qui credit non pudefiet. Nimis ergo impudentes sunt, qui Christi verba de Petro, aut de personatis eius successoribus exponunt. Nihil iam dicimus de ementita illa successione, qua prorsus nulla est, neque testimonijs aut argumentis vllis potest probari. Quomodo enim Petri successores Romani pontifices dici possunt, cum Petrus non posset Episcopus dici, nisi eum deserta sua statione accusare libeat. Apostolum enim fecit Christus, non Episcopum, qui in vno aliquo loco resideret, & Paulus illi prædicationem Euangelij inter Iudæos creditam fuisse scribit. Romæ quidem crucifixum fuisse Petrum negare nolum, cum id vetustissimi Scriptores vnanimi fere consensu testentur: sed num idem primatus Ecclesiæ Româ debet adscribi, & non potius Hierosolymæ, vbi Dei Filium in cruce mortuum esse constat? Atqui iniquum est vel hanc vel illam propter cædes indignas, imo propter parricidia aliis civitatibus præferre. At quamvis Petrus Romæ Episcopum egisset, quid hoc ad nostri seculi Pontifices, qui à Petri & eorum, qui hunc proxime secuti sunt, vestigijs ita degenerarunt, vt Neronis & Domitiani potius, quàm Petri successores dici mereantur. Quod ergo Paulus in fidei Romanæ commendationem scribit, quod item de veterum episcoporum fide & constantia, qui doctrinam suam proprio sanguine obsignarunt, & martirij coronam meruerunt, in historijs narratur, non magis ad nostros illos, qui hodie Romæ triplici corona & regali paludamento aut trabea superbi dominantur, pertinet, quam ad Annam & Caiaphan referri possunt, quæ de summi Sacerdotis authoritate in Lege, aut de veterum Sacerdotum fide apud Malachiam commemorantur. Itaque firmiter teneri debet, Ecclesiam non alio fundamento niti, quàm Filio Dei IESV CHRISTO, a quo etiam illius cives Christiani dicuntur, vt meminerint, hunc vnicum nostræ salutis authorem ac mediatorem esse, cuius nomine fidere debeant. Nam qui hunc honorem in alios transferunt, a quibus denominari volunt, ij Christum discerpunt (vt Paulus ait) & eo ipso testantur, se a corpore eius, quod est Ecclesia secessionem fecisse. Vide 1.Cor.1.
units.tr: Moreover, Christ is not only the architect and Lord of the Church but also its foundation, as he makes quite plain when he says: "You are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church," etc. The Roman Pontiffs explain these words as referring to Peter, saying that he is both the rock and the one on whom the Church is built, so that by this means they themselves, on the strength of their so-called apostolic succession, of which they habitually boast falsely, become the foundation of that Church. But the context of the passage and the matter itself refute them. For among the Greeks Petrus [Πέτρος] and petra [πέτρα] have the same meaning and both signify a stone. It is likely that Christ, speaking in Syriac, used the word Cephas in both places, but it was not without purpose that the translator of Matthew (whoever he was) chose to write distinctly, "You are Peter, and upon this rock." Evidently he wished to distinguish between Peter and the rock on which the Church is established, and to teach that this rock is the one Peter had confessed and from which he had received his surname. But the one whom Peter confessed was none other than <bl>JESUS CHRIST</bl>. Therefore the Lord speaks of himself, and promises that he himself will be the foundation of his Church, on which all may safely rest who profess the same faith as Peter with a sincere heart. And that we may so understand this passage, the matter itself, as we have said, and the agreement of all Scripture teach it. For the foundation of the Church must be solid, firm and immovable, able neither to be shifted from its place nor to collapse, lest the Church fall in ruin when it is overthrown. But every man is by nature a liar, able both to be deceived and to deceive. Besides, men are subject to passions, which do not allow them to persevere always in the same opinion; often, overcome by fear or some other passion, they say and do things which they know to be unlawful and wrong, and their own conscience condemns them. We know this happened to Peter himself, when he shamefully denied Christ, whom he had earlier confessed. Therefore those who make a man the foundation of the Church imagine a Church whose salvation is doubtful and uncertain, and they deprive believers of the most sweet consolation which this passage offers them. For this reason Scripture everywhere points to the one Lord as this foundation. Moses calls God the rock of our salvation, and charges the Jews with turning away from him to other protections. David too, in the Psalms, frequently professes that God alone is his rock and fortress. "Who is God," he says, "apart from Jehovah? And who is Zur, that is, a rock, apart from our God?" Paul, indeed, calls Christ the foundation of the Prophets and Apostles, because both the one and the others refer us back to him alone and teach us to trust in him alone. Writing to the Corinthians, he says the same: "No one can lay any other foundation than that which has been laid, which is Jesus Christ." But Peter himself also calls Christ the living stone or rock upon which believers ought to be built, and he explains the passage of Isaiah concerning him: "Behold, I lay in Zion a stone, chosen and precious, to be placed at the chief corner; whoever believes in him will not be put to shame." Therefore those men are extremely shameless who explain Christ's words as referring to Peter or to his so-called successors. I say nothing yet of that fabricated succession, which is wholly non-existent and cannot be proved by any testimonies or arguments. For how can the Roman pontiffs be called successors of Peter, when Peter could not be called a bishop unless one were to accuse him of having deserted his post? For Christ made him an apostle, not a bishop, who would reside in one particular place; and Paul writes that the preaching of the gospel among the Jews had been entrusted to him. It is indeed no secret that Peter was crucified at Rome, since the most ancient writers testify to this with almost unanimous agreement. But should the same primacy of the Church be ascribed to Rome, rather than to Jerusalem, where it is established that the Son of God died on the cross? Yet it would be unjust to prefer either this city or that one to the others on account of unworthy slaughters, or rather parricides. But even if Peter had served as bishop at Rome, what has this to do with the Pontiffs of our age? They have so degenerated from the footsteps of Peter and of those who most closely followed him that they deserve to be called successors of Nero and Domitian rather than of Peter. As for what Paul writes in commendation of the Roman faith, and what is related in histories about the faith and steadfastness of the early bishops, who sealed their teaching with their own blood and earned the crown of martyrdom, these refer no more to those who today rule proudly at Rome with a triple crown and royal mantle or toga than they could be applied to Annas and Caiaphas, whose authority as high priest under the Law, and the faith of the early priests, are recalled in Malachi. Therefore it must be firmly held that the Church rests on no other foundation than the Son of God, Jesus Christ, from whom its citizens are also called Christians, so that they may remember that he is the only author and mediator of our salvation, and that they ought to trust in his name. For those who transfer this honour to others, and wish to be named after them, tear Christ apart (as Paul says), and by that very fact they testify that they have separated themselves from his body, which is the Church. See 1 Cor. 1.

units.la: Præterea de Ecclesiæ suæ in terris conditione nos admonet Dominus, quando addit: Et portæ inferorum non prævalebunt aduersus eam. Est ergo certaminibus perpetuis obnoxia, quæ illi aduersus mundū & huius principe decertanda sunt. Ideo quoad in terris agit, militaris dicitur: neque hic multa demonstratione opus est, quando res ipsa loquitur, & ipse Christus paulo post dicet: Si quis vult post me venire, abneget semetipsum, & tollat crucem suā & sequatur me. In præsenti autem portas inferorum nominat, vt partim offendat, quo cum hoste nobis res sit, nimirum cum tenebrarum rectore & principe, Satana nimirum, qui ad sempiternos infernalium tormentorum cruciatus iam olim damnatus, hoc perpetuo agit, vt quam plurimos sui exitij & pœnæ socios habeat: partim vt doceat, quibus armis ille aduersus nos pugnet. In portis fere munitiones vrbium excitantur, aggeres fiunt, disponuntur bombardæ & militū præsidia: In portis item iudicia exercebantur olim. Innuit ergo Dominus, Satanam aduersus Ecclesiam & eius singulos cives primum aperta vi & omni armorum genere, deinde calumniis quoque & obtrectationibus, iniquis denique iudicijs pugnaturū esse. Et vtrunque iam olim factum fuisse, docent historiæ, & idem hodie experiuntur quicunque Christo ser-uire, & in eo pie viuere cupiunt. Et tanta est factellitiū Satanæ rabies, vt eos nullius sceleris & calumniæ pudeat, quæ religione & Ecclesiam expugnari & cuerti posse existimant. Itaque plerunque in calumniis & mendacijs, in proditorijs consilijs, in cædibus & crudelisanguinis effusione laudem quærunt, & (quod fore Dominus prædixit) se Deo cultum præstare sibi persuadet, si quam plurimos ex ferum illius horrendis suppliciorum exemplis e medio sustulerint. Imò tanta est hostis nostri calliditas, vt cordibus electorum sese insinuare, & illic graues contra illos accusationes instituere norit, vt dignos esse persuadeat, qui a Deo dereliĉti male pereant. Aduersus omnes istas machinationes nos in præsenti consolatur Dominus, & testatur, nulla mundi & principis eius potentiam, nullas vires, nullos conatus tantos, nullas insidias aut calumnias tam callidas aut astutas fore, vt Ecclesiam & germana huius membra expugnare possint. Nam iampridem vicit hostē nostrum ipse Dei Filius & caput illius coterminus. Idē mundo quoque superior factus, de omni aduersaria potestate triumphauit. Et quia Electi per fidē ipsi inseruntur, ijdem in ipso etiam omnia possunt: & vt gloria ipsorum est fides illa, qua illum apprehenderunt. Itaque perpetuo fit, quod olim vaticinatus est Zacharias, vt Ecclesia sit quidem lapis ille, in quo tollendo omnes tyranni & hostes Christi fatigantur, manet tamen salua, pereuntibus interim omnibus, qui certamen aduersus illam suscipiunt. Est item catinus terreus in fornace ardens & totus candens, non disrumpitur autem, sed dum ligna & pruna in cineres & fauillas rediguntur, aurum igni vi defæcatum purgatur, vt splendidius & pretiosius fiat. Est hoc demonstratum omnium seculorum exemplis, quæ alibi recitauimus: & quotidie multa fiunt, quæ istis possunt fidem facere. Itaque fortes in fide stemus, & teneamus stationem nostram, nobis deniq; applicemus in omni tentatione, quod Apostolus quasi latum pæana aut tiλixior canens, dicit: Quis intentabit crimina aduersus electos Dei? Deus est qui iustificat: quis est qui condemnet? Quis nos separabit à charitate Christi? num oppressio? num an gustiaq gustia? num persecutio? num fames? num nuditas? num periculum? num gladius? Imo in his omnibus plus quàm victores sumus per eum qui dilexit nos, &c. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: Furthermore, the Lord reminds us of the condition of his Church on earth when he adds: "And the gates of hell shall not prevail against it." It is therefore liable to perpetual conflicts, which it must wage against the world and its prince. For this reason, as long as it lives on earth, it is called militant. Nor is much demonstration needed here, since the matter speaks for itself, and Christ himself will say shortly afterwards: "If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me." Yet at present he names the gates of hell, partly to show us what enemy we have to deal with, namely the ruler and prince of darkness, Satan, who was long ago condemned to the everlasting torments of hell and who constantly labours to have as many companions as possible in his ruin and punishment; and partly to teach us with what weapons he fights against us. Fortifications of cities are generally raised at the gates, mounds are made, cannons and garrisons are stationed there; and formerly, too, judgments were held in the gates. The Lord therefore intimates that Satan will fight against the Church and each of its citizens first by open force and every kind of weapon, then also by slanders and detractions, and finally by unjust judgments. That both of these have already happened in the past, the histories teach, and the same things are experienced today by all who desire to serve Christ and to live piously in him. And so great is the fury of Satan's malice that his followers are not ashamed of any crime or calumny by which they think religion and the Church can be overthrown and destroyed. Thus they very often seek glory in slanders and lies, in treacherous plots, in murders and cruel bloodshed, and they persuade themselves (as the Lord foretold they would) that they render worship to God if they remove as many as possible from the midst by the horrible examples of their punishments. Indeed, our enemy is so skilful that he knows how to insinuate himself into the hearts of the elect and to bring grave accusations against them there, so as to persuade them that they deserve to perish, being forsaken by God. Against all these machinations the Lord now comforts us and testifies that neither the power of the world and its prince, nor any strength, nor any attempts so great, nor any snares or calumnies so crafty or cunning, will be able to overcome the Church and its true members. For long ago the Son of God, the head of the Church who is one with us, has already conquered our enemy; he too, having risen above the world, has triumphed over every hostile power. And since the elect are grafted into him through faith, they are also able to do all things in him, and that faith by which they have laid hold of him is their glory. Thus it constantly happens what Zechariah prophesied long ago: the Church is indeed that stone, in lifting which all the tyrants and enemies of Christ are wearied, yet it remains safe, while all who take up the struggle against it perish. Likewise, there is an earthen vessel glowing in a furnace, all aglow, yet it is not broken; rather, while the wood and embers are reduced to ashes and cinders, the gold, purged by the fire, is refined so that it becomes more brilliant and precious. This has been shown by the examples of all ages, which we have recounted elsewhere, and many things happen daily that can give confidence in these matters. Therefore let us stand firm in the faith, hold our ground, and apply to ourselves in every temptation what the Apostle sings as a triumphal paean: "Who will bring any charge against the elect of God? It is God who justifies; who is he who condemns? Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Will tribulation? Or distress? Or persecution? Or famine? Or nakedness? Or danger? Or the sword? Nay, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us," etc. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCVI.
units.tr: Homily 206.

units.la: Et tibi dabo claues regni cœlorum. Et quicquid ligaueris in terra, erit ligatū in cœlis: & quicquid solueris in terra, erit solutum in cœlis.
units.tr: "And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven. And whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven."

units.la: Sicuti Petrus ex Spiritus Sancti revelatione Dominum IESVM confessus est, esse æternum Dei Filium, & Christum illum, id est, promissum humani generis Seruatorem: Ita vicißim hic illum beatū pronuntiauit, & propter ingenuā & intrepidā fidei huius confessionē ei nomen Petri imposuit, quod initio promiserat. At ne quis solū Petrū beatū putaret, simul pollicitus est, quòd super hanc petrā, quam ille confessus erat, seipsum videlicet, Ecclesiā suā velit ædificare, & eandem ita munire suo præsidio, vt ne portæ quidē inferorū ipsam superare possint. Vbi discimus, Christum Ecclesiam habere, ad quā eos colligi oporteat, qui in ipso seruari volunt: Deinde eorū, qui ad hanc colliguntur, salutē certam esse ac solidā, vt nullis mundi huius aut principū eius machinationibus superari possit. Nam quicquid hic moliatur, firmū tamē ratumq; erit, quod Deus decreuit: et quia hic nobis in Filio suo placatus est, in eodē etiam victores erunt, quicunq; ad eius Ecclesiam pertinent.
units.tr: Just as Peter, by the revelation of the Holy Spirit, confessed that the Lord Jesus is the eternal Son of God and that he is the Christ, that is, the promised Saviour of the human race, so in turn Christ pronounced him blessed. On account of this frank and fearless confession of faith he gave Peter the name he had promised at the beginning. But lest anyone think that Peter alone was blessed, he promised at the same time that he would build his Church upon this rock which Peter had confessed, namely himself, and would so fortify it with his protection that the gates of hell itself could not overcome it. Here we learn that Christ has a Church, to which all who wish to be saved in him must be gathered. Then we learn that the salvation of those who are gathered to this Church is certain and secure, so that it cannot be overcome by any schemes of this world or of its princes. For whatever they plan, what God has decreed will stand firm and remain valid; and since he is reconciled to us in his Son, all who belong to his Church will also be victorious in him.

units.la: His commodè subtexit hunc locum Dominus, quo docet, qua ratione Ecclesiam suam regat, & qua via siue ratione nos miseri mortales, qui natura peccatores, & propter peccatum a Deo & eius domo alieni, imò irę filij sumus, ad illius confortiū peruenire possimus, & bonorum eius cœlestium participes fieri. Estq; huius loci doctrina admodum memorabilis, & necessaria consideratu: quia vniuersam nostrę salutis rationem, & vt hæc per Ecclesiæ ministerium dispensetur, tradit.
units.tr: The Lord added this passage fittingly to what he had said, teaching by what method he governs his Church, and by what way or means we wretched mortals, who are sinners by nature and, on account of sin, estranged from God and his household, and indeed children of wrath, may come into fellowship with him and become partakers of his heavenly goods. The teaching of this passage is very remarkable and worthy of careful consideration, because it sets out the whole plan of our salvation and how this is dispensed through the ministry of the Church.

units.la: Tibi dabo (inquit) claues regni cœlorum, &c. Petro loquitur Christus, at quæ illi dicuntur, ad alios quoq; discipulos pertinere, docet totius historiæ seu narrationis contextus. Nam illos omnes interrogauerat Dominus, quę nam ipsum esse diceret? Omnū etiā nomine respondit Petrus, & fidei communis confessione edidit. Ergo quæ illi Christus dicit, communiter ad omnes illos debent referri. Deinde quod in præsenti pollicetur, postea omnibus exhibet. Nam infra Cap. 18. ait: Amen dico vobis, quæcunq; ligaueritis in terra, erunt ligata in cœlo: et quæcunq; solueritis in terra, erunt soluta in cœlo. Et post resurrectione, cum se illis rediuiuū sisteret, in ipsos sufflans dicit: Accipite Spiritū sanctū: Quorumcunq; remiseritis peccata, remittuntur eis: quorumcunq; retinueritis, retenta erunt.
units.tr: "I will give you," he says, "the keys of the kingdom of heaven," and so on. Christ is speaking to Peter, but the context of the whole narrative shows that what is said to him pertains also to the other disciples. For the Lord had questioned all of them about who they said he was, and Peter answered on behalf of all and declared the common confession of faith. Therefore what Christ says to him should be referred to all of them together. Moreover, what he promises here in the present he afterwards gives to all. For in chapter 18 he says: "Truly I say to you, whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven." And after the resurrection, when he presented himself to them as one restored to life, he breathed upon them and said: "Receive the Holy Spirit. Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them; whose sins you retain, they are retained."

units.la: Debet hoc diligenter obseruari propter eos, qui Petro soli claues regni cœlorum datas esse contendunt, vt Pontificis Romani primatu et dominium stabiliat. Debet ergo hæc promissio in genere accipi, & ad omnes Apostolos & legitimos eorū successores extendi, vt cogeret hos audiendos esse, si qui ad illius possessione & hæreditate peruenire cupiūt. Vt autē restius locū hunc totū intelligamus, primo videbimus quid p Claues intelligi debeat. Deinde quomodo hæ Apostolis datæ sint: tertiò quomodo his vti debuerint Apostoli? et quis hodie legitimus earū vsus sit: quartò quanta illarū sit authoritas. Ex quibus patebit vt locus hic tā ministrorū, quā auditorū institutioni ac cosolationi seruiat.
units.tr: This must be carefully observed on account of those who maintain that the keys of the kingdom of heaven were given to Peter alone, in order to establish the primacy and lordship of the Roman Pontiff. This promise must therefore be understood in general terms and extended to all the apostles and their lawful successors, so that it obliges them to be heard by anyone who desires to attain that possession and inheritance. So that we may understand this passage fully, we shall first see what ought to be understood by the keys. Second, how these were given to the apostles. Third, how the apostles ought to have used them, and what the lawful use of them is today. Fourth, how great their authority is. From these points it will become clear that this passage serves both the instruction and the comfort of ministers and of hearers alike.

units.la: Clauis proprie est instrumentum, quo ædes, conclauia, arca et quæcunq; eius generis sunt, claudūtur vel aperiuntur. Vnde nonnulli a præpositione Clam dictam volunt, quod illa clauduntur, quæ celata esse, et non omnibus patere volumus. Et quia ei qui claues habet, ad ea penetrare licet, eadē potestatis credita aut comissæ symbolū sunt. Ita quando maritus vxori claues tradit, hanc se pro consorte sua agnoscere eo ipso testatur, & eidem domus administranda curam cum illis impo-nit. Ad eundem modum, œconomis & dispensatoribus claues committuntur, qui cum his eorū, quæ sub eis latent, potestatē accipiunt. Et principibus claues vrbiū offerunt, qui se illis dedunt, aut eorum imperio subijciunt. Metaphoram hanc in præsenti Christus ad Ecclesiam & regnū cœlorum transfert, cuius claues cum Petro & condiscipulis eius pollicetur, illius œconomos aut dispensatores fore docet, qui eius thesauros recludere & aperire debeant ijs, qui ad eorum possessionem vel vsum fructum admitti debent: eosdem vero occludere indignis & prophanis, quos procul ab eis arceri vult Deus. Facit ad huius sententiæ confirmationem, quòd infra doctores œconomis confert, quos domui suæ præfecerit. Et ita Paulus intellexit, qui de se & aliis Apostolis atq; viris A-
units.tr: A key, properly speaking, is an instrument by which houses, rooms, chests and whatever things are of this kind are locked or opened. Hence some derive the word from the preposition "clam" (secretly), because those things are locked which we want to be hidden and not open to all. And since it is permitted to the one who holds the keys to enter those things, the keys are a symbol of power entrusted or committed. Thus when a husband gives his wife the keys, he thereby testifies that he acknowledges her as his partner, and he places upon her the care of administering the household. In the same way, keys are committed to stewards and managers, who receive with them power over the things hidden under their charge. Keys of cities are also offered to princes by those who surrender themselves to them or submit to their rule. In the present passage Christ transfers this metaphor to the Church and the kingdom of heaven. When he promises its keys to Peter and his fellow disciples, he teaches that they will be its stewards or managers, who ought to unlock and open its treasures to those who are to be admitted to their possession or enjoyment, and likewise to shut them against the unworthy and profane, whom God wants kept far away from them. What supports this interpretation is that, below, the Lord compares teachers to stewards whom he has set over his household. Paul also understood it so, when he wrote of himself and the other apostles and men of apostolic rank:

units.la: {D} 4 postolicis scribit: Sic nos æstimet homo, vt ministros Christi & dispensatores mysteriorum Dei. Quòd si quæras, quo medio ./ postoli regnum Dei patefecerint, & eius mysteria dispensarint, nihil præter Euangelij prædicationem inuenis. Hæc igitur clauis est, qua regnum cœlorum aperitur, via & ratio ad illud perueniendi monstratur in Christo, qui solus est Via, Veritas & Vita. Eadem clauditur regnum Dei per accidens, quando alienis à Christo illud negatur, & eisdem pœnæ infernales & sempiternæ denuntiantur. Ideo Verbi doctrina alibi Clauis scientiæ dicitur, quia homines intellectum illustrat, & quasi aperit mentis oculos, vt mysteria hæc cernant, qui suæ rationis acumine illa percipere non possent. Itaq; patet ex his omnibus, Apostolis non aliud quàm Euangelij prædicatione creditam esse, cuius ministerium cùm in Ecclesia perpetuum esse velit Christus, & hoc omnes obire debeant, qui legitimè vocati sunt, iniqui & nimium audaces sunt Pontifices, qui clauium potestatem sibi solis vendicant.
units.tr: "Let a man so regard us as ministers of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God." But if you ask by what means the apostles disclosed the kingdom of God and dispensed its mysteries, you will find nothing except the preaching of the gospel. This, then, is the key by which the kingdom of heaven is opened: the way and means of attaining it is shown in Christ, who alone is the Way, the Truth and the Life. The kingdom of God is shut by implication when it is denied to those who are alienated from Christ, and eternal punishments of hell are threatened against them. Therefore elsewhere the teaching of the Word is called the key of knowledge, because it illuminates people's minds and, as it were, opens the eyes of the mind so that they may perceive these mysteries, which they could not grasp by the keenness of their own reason. Thus it is clear from all of this that the apostles were entrusted with nothing other than the preaching of the gospel. Since Christ wishes the ministry of this gospel to be perpetual in the Church, and since all who have been lawfully called ought to perform it, those Pontiffs are unjust and excessively bold who claim the power of the keys for themselves alone.

units.la: Quomodo autem datæ sunt? Num vt pro sua libidine claudant siue aperiant? Nequaquam. Imò Christus Ioannis Cap.20. ait: Sicut me misit, ita & ego mitto vos. Non debet autem hoc simpliciter intelligi, vt Apostolos quoad dignitatem & potestatē Christo æquemus. Hic enim missus est, vt noster Redemptor & Seruator esset, & idem clauem Dauidis gestat cum absoluta potesta te, sic vt ipso claudente nemo aperiat, ipso aperiente nemo claudat, quam gloriam nulli creaturæ concedit. Itaq; hoc dictum ad ea debet restringi, quæ Apostolis & omnibus legitimis Ecclesiæ ministris cum illo communia sunt. Missus est Christus, non vt suam voluntatem faceret, sed Patris: & ideo dicit, Doctrina mea non est mea, sed Patris qui misit me. Ita Apostoli non suam, sed Dei voluntatem prædicare debuerunt, & ab huius solius ore pendere. Ideo cum hoc dixisset illis Christus, mox flauit in eos, dicens: Accipite Spiritum Sanctum. Et vt Lucas annotauit, simul aperuit eorum mentem, vt intelligerent Scripturas. Quibus consentit, quod apud Matthæum habetur: Profecti docete omnes gentes, baptizantes eos in nomine Patris & Filij & Spiritus Sancti, docentes eos seruare omnia, quæ mandaui vobis. Non ergo pro vt ipsis visum fuit prædicare debuerunt Apostoli, sed limitata fuit eorum potestas, quam Clauium nomine eis Dominus tradidit. Quapropter hic quoque falsi conuincuntur Pontifices, qui sub Clauium prætextu licentiam quidus statuendi & nouas leges condendi in Ecclesia vsurparunt: quod Antichristi proprium esse, olim Daniel prædixit. Danielis vndecimo.
units.tr: But how were the keys given? Was it so that they might lock or open as they pleased? By no means. Rather, in John 20 Christ says: "As the Father has sent me, so I also send you." This, however, should not be understood simply as if we made the apostles equal to Christ in dignity and power. For he was sent to be our Redeemer and Saviour, and he bears the key of David with absolute power, so that when he locks, no one opens, and when he opens, no one locks; this glory he grants to no creature. Therefore this saying must be restricted to those things which are common to the apostles and all lawful ministers of the Church along with him. Christ was sent not to do his own will but the Father's, and so he says: "My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me." Thus the apostles too were bound to preach not their own will but God's, and to depend on his mouth alone. Therefore, when Christ had said this to them, he immediately breathed upon them, saying: "Receive the Holy Spirit." And as Luke noted, he at the same time opened their minds so that they might understand the Scriptures. This agrees with what is found in Matthew: "Go and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you." The apostles therefore were not bound to preach as seemed good to themselves, but their power, which the Lord gave them under the name of keys, was limited. Wherefore the Pontiffs are also proved false here, who under the pretext of the keys have usurped licence to set up laws of their own and to enact new laws in the Church, which Daniel long ago foretold to be the proper mark of Antichrist: Daniel 11.

units.la: Ideo modum quoque & rationem præscribit Dominus, quam in prædicando seruare aut sequi debeant. Nam apud Lucam ait: Ita scriptum est, & ita oportuit Christum pati, & resurgere a mortuis tertio die, & prædicari in nomine eius remissionem peccatorum in omnes gentes, &c. Vnde apparet, eos quæ Christus pro humani generis redemptione fecit ac passus est, & eiusdem resurrectionem prædicare debuisse: idq; in eum finem, vt simul omnes homines peccati reos agerent, conuictos ad resipiscentiam & vitæ totius nouitatem hortarentur, contritis autem corde remissionem peccatorum gratuitam in illius nomine & merito non obiter modò monstrarent, sed prædicationi huic credentibus serió quoq; pollicerentur. Ideo apud Marcum ait: Profecti in orbem vniuersum, prædicate Euangelium omni creaturæ: Qui crediderit, & baptizatus fuerit, seruabitur: qui verò non crediderit, condemnabitur. Et hunc ordinem Apostolos in prædicando secutos fuisse, in Actis & sermonibus illorum apparet, vt paulo post dicetur.
units.tr: Likewise the Lord also prescribes the manner and the method that they ought to observe or follow in preaching. For in Luke he says: "Thus it is written, and thus it behoved Christ to suffer and to rise again from the dead on the third day, and that repentance and remission of sins should be preached in his name to all nations," etc. From this it is clear that they ought to have preached what Christ did and suffered for the redemption of the human race, and his resurrection, and to do so with this aim: that they should at the same time show all people to be guilty of sin, exhort those convicted to repentance and a renewal of their whole life, and, to those who are contrite of heart, not merely point out in passing the free remission of sins in his name and through his merit, but also solemnly promise it to those who believe this preaching. Therefore in Mark he says: "Go into all the world and preach the gospel to every creature. Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved; but whoever does not believe will be condemned." And that the apostles followed this order in preaching appears in the Acts and in their sermons, as will be said shortly.

units.la: Nunc qua authoritate illos Dominus instruxerit, videamus: In præsenti Petro dicit: Quicquid ligaueris in terra, erit ligatum in cœlo: & quicquid solueris in terra, erit solutū in cœlo. Quæ verba alibi (vt nuper diximus) omnibus applicat, vt eiusdem cum Petro authoritatis in suo ministerio omnes esse demonstret. At si in Clauiū parabola insistere libuisset, dicendū erat: Cuicunq; aperueritis fores regni cœlorū in terra, illi aperta erunt in cœlo: & è contra cuicunq; clauseritis regnū cœlorum in terra, illi occlusum erit in cœlo. Sed soluendi & ligandi vocabulis vtitur: quæ parabola proposita non male conueniunt, si veterum morem spectes, qui (vt Eustathius scribit) cum nondum inuentus esset ferarum & clauium vsus, funibus & loris, sine ligamentis fores & arcas astringebant, quæ solui oportebat ad aperiendum. Sed cùm Christi tempore, & multò etiam ante eius incarnationem (vt ex Iudicum libro & Isaia patet) fera & claues in vsu fuerint, his vocabulis illum vsum arbitror, vt clarius doceret, quæ sit hominū conditio, & cur nobis non pateat ad regnum cœlorum aditus: Nimirum quia non modò peccatores, sed peccati mancipia, & vitiosa aut peccantis naturæ vinculis constricti sumus, adeò, ut si nobis fores illæ paterent, nos tamen per eas non possemus ingredi. Et hæc etiam illa vincula sunt, quibus in Euangelio eorum pedes & manus constringuntur, qui in tenebras exteriores merentur eici. Hoc vt infelicem humani generis conditionem adumbrat, ita ministerij Euangelici authoritatem mirificè extollit, per quod his nexibus soluimur, qui nulla humana potentia aut industria dissolui possunt. Huc facit, quod in præsenti Petro, & in huius persona omnibus Apostolis dicitur: Quicquid ligaueris in terra, ligatum erit in cœlo: & quicquid solueris in terra, solutum erit in cœlo. Apud Ioannem verò eadem clarius exponens, ait: Quorumcunq; remiseritis peccata, remittuntur eis: & quorumcunq; retinueritis, retenta sunt. Cauendum tamen, ne eo sensu hæc verba accipiantur, quasi peccatorum remissio aut retentio a ministri arbitrio pendeat: quæ perfuasio Pontificiu potentiam in immensum auxit, & miserorum conscientijs laqueos iniecit. Etenim quia peccatum noxa est aduersus Dei Legem admissa, nemo præter hunc illam remittendi potestatem habet: quod Pharisæos quamtumuis confidentes & excæcatos, intelliexisse supra vidimus. Itaq; ministerij ratione hoc dicitur: neq; aliter peccata remittunt aut retinent Euangelij prædones, quam olim Sacerdotes (vt Diuus Hieronymus annotauit) leprosos mundabant, aut leprææ damnabant. Quare peccata remittere dicitur, eo quod pœnitentibus, & ad Christi veram fide conuersis remissionem pollicentur: & e contra peccata retinent, quando contumacibus ac pœnitere nescijs sententiam damnationis denuntiant. Et in cœlo ratum est, quod ministri legitimi pronuntiant: quia cum Christi decreto illud conuenit, dicentis: Qui crediderit, saluabitur: qui non crediderit, condemnabitur. Exempla in vtranq; partem in Apostolorum Actis inueniuntur. Cum Petrus prima concione, quam accepto Spiritu Sancto habuit, Iudæos sceleris in Dei Filium commissi conuicisset, & hi totis animis compuncti quærerent: Quid faciemus viri fratres? Respondit Petrus: Resipiscite, & baptizetur vnusquisq; vestrum in nomine IESV CHRISTI in remissionem peccatorum: & accipietis donum Spiritus Sancti. Et in cœlo ratam fuisse sententiam, euentus probauit. Nam qui libenter acceperunt sermonem eius, baptizati sunt, & addita sunt Ecclesiæ die illo animæ quasi ter mille. Eiusdem generis est, quod apud Philippenses cum carceris publici custode actum est. Et ante natum Christum eandem fuisse Verbi Dei efficaciam, Dauidis exemplum docet, cui peccatum suum confitenti, & per fidem in promissum Seruatorem respicienti, Nathan dicebat: Et nunc transtulit Dominus peccatum tuum. E contra Iudæorum peccata retenta sunt, quando incurabili pertinacia Christum reiecerunt, & Apostoli excussò super illos pedum puluere, ab illis se ad gentes converterunt. Nec dubitemus etiam hodie ratum esse apud Deu quoad omnes pœnitere nescios, quod Paulus scribit: Neq; fornicatores, neq; idololatræ, neq; mœchi, neq; molles, neq; qui concumbunt cum masculis, neque fures, neq; auari, neq; ebriosi, neq; conuiciatores, neq; rapaces, regni Dei hæreditatem consequentur. Constat enim sibi ipsi Verbum Dei, & quod hic semel statuit, nulla vel ætas, vel consuetudo, vel authoritas hominum abrogabit.
units.tr: Now let us see with what authority the Lord instructed them. To Peter in the present passage he says: "Whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven." Elsewhere, as we lately said, he applies these words to all, to show that all have the same authority as Peter in their ministry. But if it had pleased him to keep to the parable of the keys, he should have said: "To whomever you open the gates of the kingdom of heaven on earth, they will be opened to him in heaven; and conversely, to whomever you shut the kingdom of heaven on earth, it will be shut to him in heaven." But he uses the words "loose" and "bind," and these fit the parable proposed quite well if you look at the custom of the ancients, who (as Eustathius writes), before the use of keys and locks was discovered, fastened doors and chests with cords and thongs, without fastenings, which had to be loosed in order to be opened. But since in Christ's time, and indeed long before his incarnation (as is clear from the book of Judges and from Isaiah), bars and keys were in use, I think he used these words in order to teach more clearly what the human condition is and why the way into the kingdom of heaven is not open to us. Clearly, this is because we are not only sinners but slaves of sin, bound by the chains of sin or of a sinful nature, so that even if those doors were open to us, we still could not enter through them. These are also the bonds with which the feet and hands of those who deserve to be cast into outer darkness are bound in the Gospel. Just as this shadows forth the unhappy condition of the human race, so it marvellously extols the authority of the evangelical ministry, through which we are loosed from those fetters which no human power or effort can undo. To this point is what is said in the present passage to Peter, and in his person to all the apostles: "Whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven." But in John, explaining the same thing more clearly, he says: "Whose sins you remit, they are remitted to them; and whose sins you retain, they are retained." Yet care must be taken that these words are not understood in such a sense as if the remission or retention of sins depended on the will of the minister. This notion has vastly increased the power of the Papists and cast snares upon the consciences of the wretched. For since sin is an offence committed against the law of God, no one except God alone has the power of remitting it; as we saw above, the Pharisees, however confident and blinded, understood this. Therefore it is said in terms of the ministry: the preachers of the Gospel remit or retain sins in no other way than the priests of old, as Saint Jerome observed, cleansed lepers or condemned them to leprosy. Hence sins are said to be remitted when ministers promise remission to penitents and to those who are converted to Christ by true faith; and conversely they retain sins when they pronounce a sentence of condemnation on the obstinate and those who do not know how to repent. And what the lawful ministers pronounce is ratified in heaven, because it agrees with the decree of Christ, who says: "Whoever believes will be saved; whoever does not believe will be condemned." Examples of both kinds are found in the Acts of the Apostles. When Peter, in the first sermon he delivered after receiving the Holy Spirit, had charged the Jews with the crime committed against the Son of God, and they, pricked to the heart, asked: "What shall we do, brothers?" Peter replied: "Repent, and let each one of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit." And that his sentence was ratified in heaven the outcome proved: for those who gladly received his word were baptized, and on that day about three thousand souls were added to the Church. Of the same kind is what happened at Philippi with the keeper of the public prison. And that the same efficacy of the Word of God existed before Christ was born, the example of David teaches, to whom, confessing his sin and looking by faith to the promised Saviour, Nathan said: "And now the Lord has taken away your sin." On the other hand, the sins of the Jews were retained when, with incurable obstinacy, they rejected Christ, and the apostles, shaking the dust of their feet against them, turned away from them to the Gentiles. Nor let us doubt that even today what Paul writes is ratified before God with regard to all who do not know how to repent: "Neither fornicators, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor effeminate persons, nor sodomites, nor thieves, nor covetous, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor robbers, will inherit the kingdom of God." For the Word of God is consistent with itself, and what it has once decreed, no age, custom or authority of men will abrogate.

units.la: Itaq; huius loci vsus hic debet esse, vt primùm ministri Ecclesiæ animentur & confirmentur aduersus Verbi contemptores, qui comminationes eiusmodi rid0ent, correptiones ferre nolunt, disciplinam deniq; omnè oderūt, & vel silentiũ ipsis mandant, vel dicedi leges præscribūt. His omnibus illi authoritatè, qua Christos illos armauit, constanter opponant, & sibi dicta putent, quod olim Paulo trepidanti & solicito dicebatur: Ne timeas, sed loquere, & ne taceas. Improbis autem illis & confidentibus cũ eodem Apostolo respondeant: Nũ experimentũ quæritis Christi in me loquentis? Deniq; ad se pertinere putent prophetica illa: Speculatorem constitui te: audies igitur Verbũ ex ore meo, & diserte monebis ex me, &c. Ite: Clama ex gutture, ne parcas, extolle instar tubæ vocem tuam, & annuntia populo meo præuaricationem suam, &c. Et ex his cũ Amos colligat: Leo fugiat, quis nõ timebit, Dominus Deus locutus est, & quis nõ prophetaret? Interim meminerint, potestate sua certis finibus circumscriptam esse, & ipsos nihil ex priuato arbitrio, sed omnia secundum Verbi diuini regulam facere debere ad ædificationem: quod Paulus ipse testatur, qui se gloriari dicit ea potestate, quam Dominus Apostolis dederit ad ædificationem, non ad alicuius subuersionem: Et idem ad Romanos scribit: Non sustinuerim loqui quicquam, quod non effecerit
units.tr: Therefore the use of this passage ought to be this: first, that the ministers of the Church be encouraged and strengthened against the despisers of the Word, who laugh at threats of this kind, are unwilling to bear reproofs, hate all discipline at last, and either impose silence on the ministers or prescribe laws for them to speak by. Against all these the ministers should constantly oppose the authority with which Christ armed them, and let them think that what was once said to Paul, when he was trembling and anxious, applies to themselves: "Do not fear, but speak, and do not keep silent." But to those wicked and presumptuous men they should answer with the same apostle: "Do you seek a proof of Christ speaking in me?" Finally, let them think that those prophetic words pertain to them: "I have appointed you a watchman; you shall therefore hear the word from my mouth, and warn them faithfully from me," etc. "Go: cry from the throat, do not spare, lift up your voice like a trumpet, and declare to my people their transgression," etc. And from these words Amos infers: "The lion roars; who will not fear? The Lord God has spoken; who will not prophesy?" Meanwhile let them remember that their power is circumscribed within certain limits, and that they must do nothing from private judgement, but everything according to the rule of the divine Word, for edification. Paul himself bears witness to this, who says that he glories in the power which the Lord gave the apostles for edification, not for the destruction of anyone. And he writes the same to the Romans: "I would not presume to speak of anything which Christ has not accomplished through me."

units.la: Matth.12. Matth.9. Marc.16. Act.2. Act.16. 2.Sam.12. Act.13.18. 1.Cor.6. Ministri vt hoc loco vti debeant. Act.18. 1.Cor.3. Ezech.3. Isa.58. Amos 3. 2.Cor.10. Rom.15. Christus per me, &c. Quod si omnes obseruauissent, qui Apostolorum successores dici voluerunt, nunquam ea tyrannis in Ecclesiam introducta esset, quae doctrinam puritatem & religionem omnem corrupit, & multorum conscientias turbauit, & hodie adhuc multos salutis suae incertos reddit. Sed iam olim coepit hoc malum. Nam Diuus Hieronymus in huius loci interpretatione scribit: Illum locum Episcopi & presbyteri non intelligentes, aliquid sibi de Pharisaeorum assumunt superciliō, ut vel damnent innocentes, vel soluere se noxios arbitrentur, cum apud Deum non sententia sacerdotum, sed reorum vita quaeratur: Nimirum ut qui peccarunt, resipiscant, & per fidem ad illum conuertantur. Quod si illo saeculo non ininsta fuit neque superuacanea querela ista, quid hodie fiat, quando ementita haec clauium potestas, quam inter insignia sua & in vexillis militaribus plus quam Pontifex fastu ostentant Romani Pontifices, iampridem non vulgo solum Christianorum, sed Regibus & Imperatoribus intolerabilis facta est? Sed meminerint illi, Deo Ecclesiam curae esse, qui non patitur eos hominum seruos fieri, quos Filii sui sanguine in libertatem asseruit.
units.tr: Matth. 12. Matth. 9. Mark 16. Acts 2. Acts 16. 2 Sam. 12. Acts 13. 18. 1 Cor. 6. How ministers ought to use this passage. Acts 18. 1 Cor. 3. Ezek. 3. Isa. 58. Amos 3. 2 Cor. 10. Rom. 15. Christ speaking through me, etc. If all had observed this, who wished to be called successors of the apostles, that tyranny would never have been introduced into the Church, which has corrupted the doctrine, purity and all religion, has troubled the consciences of many, and even today makes many uncertain of their salvation. But this evil began long ago. For the blessed Jerome, in his interpretation of this passage, writes: "Bishops and presbyters, not understanding that passage, assume for themselves something of the Pharisees' haughtiness, so that they either condemn the innocent or think they can absolve the guilty, whereas before God the judgement is not the sentence of priests but the life of the guilty; namely, that those who have sinned should repent and be converted through faith to him." If this complaint was not unfounded or superfluous in that age, what must happen today, when this fabricated power of the keys, which the Roman pontiffs display with more than pontifical pomp among their insignia and on their military banners, has long since become intolerable not only to the common mass of Christians but also to kings and emperors? But let them remember that God cares for his Church, and does not suffer those to become slaves of men whom he has freed by the blood of his Son.

units.la: Sed & qui Christiani dici & esse volunt, de Verbi ministerio & ministrorum dignitate recte indicare discant, & Verbo Dei se accommodent, ut hoc in honore & pretio habeant, vera fide amplexentur, & per illud admoniti aut correpti serio resipiscant. Est quidem Euangelij praedicatio clauis illa, quae fores regni caelorum peccatoribus aperit, & conscientias vinculis peccatorum ac mortis terroribus liberat. Sed nos clauem illam digne admittere oportet, ut in animos penetret, & intellectum aperiat, ut regni caelorum mysteria percipere possimus, & eorundem amore atque studio accensi vitam & mores secundum Verbi doctrinam instituamus. Ut enim fera, nisi clauem admittat, non aperitur: ita si qui non locum dant Euangelij praedicationi, eorum neque intellectus illuminatur, neque peccata remittuntur, & proinde ijsdem clausae manent regni caelorum fores, quae solis credentibus patent.
units.tr: But those who wish to be and to be called Christians should also learn to judge rightly about the ministry of the Word and the dignity of ministers, so that they accommodate themselves to the Word of God, hold it in honour and esteem, embrace it with true faith, and, admonished or corrected by it, repent in earnest. The preaching of the Gospel is indeed that key which opens the gates of the kingdom of heaven to sinners and frees consciences from the chains of sin and the terrors of death. But we must receive that key worthily, so that it penetrates our minds and opens our understanding, that we may grasp the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven and, kindled by love and zeal for them, shape our life and conduct according to the doctrine of the Word. For just as a wild beast is not opened unless it admits the key, so those who do not make room for the preaching of the Gospel have their understanding left unenlightened and their sins unforgiven, and therefore the gates of the kingdom of heaven, which stand open only to believers, remain shut to them.

units.la: Quoad vero eorum tractationem, quae hucusque cum discipulis acta sunt, utile est praecipua illius capita probe tenere, ac in eorum meditatione sedula versari. Primum ex his est, ne opinionum de fide & religione diuersitate offendamur. Nec enim fieri potest, ut idem de regno Dei sentiant homines, quorum intellectus, nisi a Deo illuminetur, diuina non percipit. Deinde perspexerimus nobis sit, unam modo fidem catholicam esse, in qua seruari possumus: eam videlicet, quam Diuus Petrus omnium Apostolorum nomine confessus est, quae IESVS vt docet esse aeternum Dei Filium, & vnicum humani generis redemptorem. Qui hac praediti sunt, super Christum ceu viui lapides aedificantur in domum Dei spiritualem, quae Ecclesia illa est, extra quam nemo feruatur. In hac Euangelij sui ministerium sanciuit Dei Filius, per quod regni caelorum ianua credentibus reseratur, claudiuntur autem incredulis & poenitere nescijs. Credamus igitur Euangelio, & per hoc peccatorum connubii, ad vnum IESVM CHRISTVM conuerji, in ipso viuamus vitam nouam, & ipse certa confirmati per aduersa omnia contendamus ad regni caelestis possessionem. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: As for the treatment of those matters which up to this point have been dealt with in the company of the disciples, it is useful to hold fast to their chief heads and to dwell on them with diligent meditation. The first of these is that we should not be offended by the diversity of opinions about faith and religion. For it cannot happen that men, whose understanding, unless it is enlightened by God, does not perceive divine things, should all think the same about the kingdom of God. Next, we must recognise that there is only one catholic faith in which we can be saved: namely, that which blessed Peter confessed in the name of all the apostles, teaching that Jesus is the eternal Son of God and the only redeemer of the human race. Those who possess this faith are built upon Christ, as living stones, into the spiritual house of God, which is that Church outside of which no one is saved. In this Church the Son of God established the ministry of his Gospel, through which the door of the kingdom of heaven is unlocked to believers, but shut to unbelievers and to those who know not how to repent. Let us therefore believe the Gospel, and, turning from our sins through it to the one Jesus Christ, let us live in him a new life; and, confirmed by him in all adversity, let us press on toward possession of the heavenly kingdom. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power forever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCVII.
units.tr: HOMILY CCVII.

units.la: Tunc interdixit discipulis suis, vt nemini dicerent, ipsum IESVM esse illum CHRISTVM. Ex eo tempore coepit IESVS indicare discipulis suis, quod oporteret ipsum abire Hierosolymam, & multa pati a Senioribus, & principibus Sacerdotum & Scribis, & occidi, & tertio die suscitari.
units.tr: Then he ordered his disciples not to tell anyone that he, Jesus, was the Christ. From that time Jesus began to show his disciples that he must go to Jerusalem and suffer many things from the elders, the chief priests and the scribes, be killed, and on the third day be raised again.

units.la: Quacunque Dominus noster IESVS CHRISTVS cum Apostolis suis egit, ita a nobis accipi debet, vt meminerimus, illa non minus nostrae quam illorum institutioni seruire. Ideo enim illos elegit, sed ipsum illis familiarius manifestauit, vt sua doctrina et exemplo omnes gentes in ipsius cognitione atque fide institueret. Debet hoc in primis obseruari in ista actione, quae hucusque audiuimus. Vbi primum occurrit, quod a Domino requisiti Apostoli, per Petrum fidei suae confessionem ædunt, ex qua discimus, quid de illo credere ac sentire debeant, qui in ipso seruari volunt: Nempe quod sit aeternus Dei Filius, qui ideo ex Maria Virgine hominem assumpsit, ut CHRISTVS fieret, id est, Rex & Sacerdos aeternus Ecclesiae Dei, denique ut petra illa pretiosa esset & inuicta, super quam aedificari oporteat Ecclesiam, ut aduersus inferorum portas posset consistere. Deinde docuit etiam, qua ratione Ecclesiam suam aedificet atque regat, & ut nos huius ciues aut membra fieri possimus? Nimirum si Euangelio credamus. Huius enim praedicatione Apostolis commendauit, quod ceu claue regnum caelorum & huius thesauros referent, & peccatorum remissionem atque certam salutem omnibus polliceantur, qui in ipsum credunt. At quia discipulis multa adhuc deerant, sequitur quid deinceps cum illis egerit, ut eos plenius instrueret & armaret aduersus Crucis scandalum, quod breui secuturum esse sciebat.
units.tr: Whatever our Lord Jesus Christ did with his apostles must be received by us in such a way that we remember it serves our instruction no less than theirs. He chose them for this purpose, but he revealed himself to them more intimately, so that by his teaching and example he might instruct all nations in knowledge of him and in faith. This must be noted first of all in the action we have heard so far. Where the apostles, questioned by the Lord, first give through Peter the confession of their faith, from which we learn what those who wish to be saved in him ought to believe and think about him: namely, that he is the eternal Son of God, who for this reason took on man from the Virgin Mary, so that CHRIST might become, that is, the eternal King and Priest of God's Church, and finally that he might be that precious and unconquered rock on which the Church must be built, so that it could stand against the gates of hell. Then he also taught by what method he builds and governs his Church, and how we may become its citizens or members. Clearly this happens if we believe the Gospel. For by its preaching he entrusted to the apostles the kingdom of heaven and its treasures, to be unlocked as with a key, and promised forgiveness of sins and certain salvation to all who believe in him. But since the disciples still lacked much, the narrative goes on to tell what he then did with them, so that he might instruct and arm them more fully against the scandal of the cross, which he knew would soon come.

units.la: Principio grauiter & cum increpatione (ut Lucas annotauit) interdixit discipulis, ne cui dicant, ipsum esse CHRISTVM illum, promissum humani generis Seruatorem. Atqui in eum finem illos elegerat, ut sui testes essent, & alibi iubet, ut quae ipsis in aurem, id est, familiarius & in occulto dicta erant, ex tectis diuulgent. Adhaec ipsos & nos omnes hortatur, ut ipsum coram mundo hoc ingenue confiteamur. At obseruari debet, mandatum hoc, quod nunc dat, temporariu fuisse, & praesenti modo tempori seruiuisse. Nam si discipulos spectes, erant quidem iam ante emissi ad praedicandum per Iudaeam & Galilaeam, sed eo fine, ut populum passim excitarent, & aliquo modo praepararent ad excipiendum Christum, qui interea per doctrinam & miracula sese manifestabat: non autem, ut ipsi eius cognitionem solidam traderent. Nec enim hoc potuissent, cum praecipua illius mysteria adhuc ignorarent, & in illo regnum terrenum somniarent, pro quo inter se frequenter altercabantur. Quoad vero populum Iudaeorum, ne hic quidem doctrinae illius adhuc capax erat, utpote communi errore cum Apostolis fascinatus. Non potuissent ergo eum pro Messia agnoscere, in quo nihil magnificum & regium cernebant. Itaque procul dubio omnibus ludibrium fastidiosum fuissent Apostoli, si eum praedicauissent Seruatorem & Regem, qui non multo post debebat in crucem suffigi: & eo gravius fuisset crucis scandalum, quo altius in spem futurae liberationis omnium animos erexissent. Necesse igitur erat, ut ipse Dominus prius moreretur, et gloriosa ex mortuis resurrectione scandalum illud Crucis remoueret, quando se peccati & mortis atque omnis aduersariae potestatis victorem esse, reipsa testabatur. Quae etiam causa fuit, quod iam semel atque iterum Iudaeis ingratis & contumacibus signum insidiose ab ipso poscentibus, signum Ionae Prophetae promisit, qui mortis & resurrectionis suae typus olim fuerat.
units.tr: First, he sternly and with rebuke (as Luke noted) forbade the disciples to tell anyone that he was the Christ, the promised Saviour of mankind. Yet to this end he had chosen them, that they might be his witnesses, and elsewhere he bids them proclaim from the housetops what had been said to them in the ear, that is, more intimately and in secret. Besides, he exhorts them and all of us to confess him openly before the world. But it must be observed that this command, which he now gives, was temporary and served the present moment. For if you look at the disciples, they had indeed already been sent out to preach through Judea and Galilee, but with the aim of stirring the people everywhere and preparing them in some measure to receive Christ, who in the meantime was making himself known through his teaching and miracles; not, however, so that they might deliver to others a solid knowledge of him. For they could not have done this, since they were still ignorant of his chief mysteries and dreamed of an earthly kingdom, about which they often quarrelled among themselves. As for the Jewish people, they too were not yet capable of that teaching, being bewitched by the common error together with the apostles. They could not therefore have acknowledged him as the Messiah, since they saw nothing splendid or royal in him. Thus, without doubt, the apostles would have become a tiresome laughingstock to everyone if they had preached as Saviour and King one who was not long afterwards to be nailed to a cross; and the scandal of the cross would have been all the greater, the more highly they had raised the hopes of all for a future deliverance. It was therefore necessary that the Lord himself should first die, and that by his glorious resurrection from the dead he should remove that scandal of the cross, when he in fact proved that he was the conqueror of sin, death and every hostile power. This was also the reason why, when the unthankful and obstinate Jews again and again asked him for a sign in a treacherous way, he promised them the sign of the prophet Jonah, who long before had been a type of his death and resurrection.

units.la: Docemur igitur hoc exemplo, non temere ad docendum prosilire debere eos, qui aliquem habent gustum rerum diuinarum, non autem adhuc solide instituti sunt: sed legitimam vocationem & missionem expectant, de qua Spiritus ipsos certiores faciet, si plenius instituti fuerint, & Deus ipsorum opera uti velit. Facit ad huius praecepti confirmationem, quod Christus, cum iam mortuus, & a mortuis refusitatus esset, atque per dies quadraginta cum Apostolis crebra habuisset de regno Dei colloquia, noluit tamen ut ipso in caelum digressso, statim ad praedicandum prodirent, sed adhuc eos Hierosolymae subsistere & promissum a Patre Spiritum expectare iussit. Non temere ergo Iacobus monebat, scribens: Ne fiatis multi magistri, fratres mei, scientes quod grauius iudicium auferemus: In multis enim labimur omnes, & omnium facillimus lapsus est linguae. At qui hac peccant inter docendum, ij non sibi soli peccant, sed multis alijs etiam errores & perditiones interdum occasionem praebent. Et videmus frequenter fieri, ut praecocis ingenij homines, dum prauato affectu moti ad docendi munus aspirant, aut etiam inter priuatos de rebus sublimibus disputationes instituunt, aduersariorum argumentis non semper respondere possunt, non modo infantiam suam turpiter prodant, sed doctrinam fidei atque religionem omnem impijs illusoribus deridendam propinent. Debebant hoc obseruare diligentius Anabaptistae, qui cum neque linguas norint, neque Scripturas unquam recte expenderint, eo tamen confidentia progrediuntur, ut in sua infscitia sibijpsis mirifice placeant, eoque magis idoneos se esse putent, quo sunt indoctiores. Vere igitur implertur in illis, quod vulgo dicitur, nihil arrogantius esse infscitia.
units.tr: We are taught by this example, therefore, not to rush rashly into teaching those who have some taste of divine things but are not yet soundly instructed; rather they should await a lawful calling and sending, of which the Spirit will assure them if they have been more fully instructed and if God wishes to use their work. To confirm this precept, it is relevant that Christ, when he had already died and been raised from the dead, and had held frequent conversations with the apostles about the kingdom of God over forty days, nevertheless did not want them to come forward at once to preach after he had departed into heaven; instead he ordered them to remain still in Jerusalem and await the Spirit promised by the Father. So James was not without reason warning in his letter: "Let not many of you become teachers, my brothers, knowing that we shall receive a stricter judgment. For we all stumble in many ways, and the slip of the tongue is the easiest of all." But those who sin in this way while teaching do not sin against themselves alone; they also sometimes give occasion for many others to fall into errors and ruin. And we often see that men of precocious talent, when moved by a perverse desire they aspire to the office of teaching, or even hold disputations about lofty matters among private persons, cannot always answer the arguments of their opponents. Not only do they shamefully betray their own immaturity, but they also offer to impious mockers the faith's teaching and all religion to be laughed at. The Anabaptists ought to have observed this more carefully. Since they neither know languages nor have ever properly weighed the Scriptures, yet they proceed with such confidence that they take wonderful pleasure in their own ignorance, and think themselves the more fit the less learned they are. Truly, then, in them is fulfilled what is commonly said: there is nothing more arrogant than ignorance.

units.la: Praeterea legitimi quoque & ordinarij Ecclesiarum ministri ex hoc loco discant, non temere semper & ubique, vel inter omnes effutienda esse quae probe didicerunt & optime perspecta habent:
units.tr: Furthermore, let the lawful and ordinary ministers of the churches also learn from this passage not to pour out rashly, always and everywhere, or before everyone, the things they have learned thoroughly and hold in clear view.

units.la: Christus prohibet ne ipsum Apostoli manifestent. Ioan. 15. Act. 1. Matth. 10.
units.tr: Christ forbids that the apostles make him known. John 15. Acts 1. Matt. 10.

units.la: Non temere docendi munus debet suscipi. Act. 1. Iac. 3.
units.tr: The office of teaching must not be undertaken rashly. Acts 1. James 3.

units.la: Non semper omnia debent praedicari. sed diligentem temporis, loci & personarum rationem habere debere: non quidem, vt cuiusuis affectui sese accommodent, aut doctrinae capita mutent, sed vt prudenter circumspiciant, quibus rationibus aut argumentis quisque moueri & lucrifieri possit, quid item praesentis temporis & loci, in quo agunt, ratio requirat, quidque ad Ecclesiae communis ac singulorum aedificationem faciat. Etenim omnia tempus habent, vt Solomon dicebat, neque semper correptione acriori opus est, sed interdum amica institutione plus proficitur: vt vicissim interdum prospiritu lenitatis virga aut baculo vtendum fuerit. Et vt in agricultura non omnis fert omnia tellus, ita in hac animorum cultura non omnes omnia capiunt, & ingenia multum inter se dissimilia sese obtulerunt. Itaque Dominus alibi in domus suae dispensatore fidem simul & prudentiam requirit, vt familiae suae alimentum in tempore depromat. Et Paulus Ecclesiae ministrum eiusmodi esse vult, qui sermonem veritatis recte secare norit, vt omnium institutioni & aedificationi seruiat. Obseruauit hoc ipse diligenter in Corinthijs suis, quos initio lacte aluit, quando cibi solidioris nondum capaces videbat: postea autem alios mitius, alios seueri^us tractauit, quorum contumacia merebatur, vt experimentum Christi in ipso loquentis sentirent. 2. Cor. 13.
units.tr: Not everything must always be preached; but there must be careful regard for time, place and persons. This is not so that they may adapt themselves to anyone's passions or change the heads of doctrine, but so that they may prudently consider by what reasons or arguments each person can be moved and won, and likewise what the nature of the present time and place, where they are working, requires, and what contributes to the edification of the Church as a whole and of its individual members. For "to everything there is a time," as Solomon said, and sharper rebuke is not always needed; sometimes more is achieved by friendly instruction, just as at other times the rod or staff must be used with a spirit of gentleness. And as in farming not every soil bears every crop, so in this cultivation of souls not all receive all things, and minds very different from one another present themselves. Accordingly, the Lord elsewhere requires of the steward of his house both faithfulness and prudence, so that he may give out food to his household in due time. And Paul wants the minister of the Church to be of such a kind that he knows how to handle the word of truth rightly, so that he serves the instruction and building up of all. He himself observed this carefully with his Corinthians, whom at first he fed with milk, when he saw they were not yet able to take solid food; later he dealt with some more gently and with others more severely, whose stubbornness deserved that they should feel the proof of Christ speaking in him. 2 Cor. 13.

units.la: Porro ipse Dominus non obscure sui illius mandati causam indicat, dum discipulis praedicit, quid de se futurum sit: de quo illi nunquam hucusque cogitarunt. Facit autem hoc, vt Messiae officium proprium, quod adhuc ignorabant (vt postea in Petri exemplo videbimus) illos doceat, & simul scandalo occurrat, quod ex eius morte sciebat enasciturum esse. Et huc potissimum facit tam diligens circumstantiarum omnium annotatio. Ex eo tempore (inquit Matthaeus) capit IESVS indicare discipulis suis, quid ipsi esset euenturum. Monet ergo eum ingenua Petri confessio, quae elogium illud praeclarum meruerat, Beatus es Simon Bar Iona, etc. Et ne confidentiores facti, ea negligerent, quae cognitu & obseruatu quam maxime necessaria erant, sic illis loquitur. Oportet me abire Hierosolymam, & multa pati a Senioribus & principibus Sacerdotum & Scribis, & occidi, & tertio die suscitari. Primo locum denotat, vbi haec fieri debeant, Hierosolymam nimirum. Quia enim Iudaeis praecipue promissus ex ipsdem carnem assumpserat, Hierosolyma autem gentis illius caput & diuini cultus sedes erat, illic ipsum immolari oportuit, vbi sacrificia publica & priuata peragebantur, vt magis nota esset illius mors, et eius nuntium facilius & citius per totum orbem terrarum diuulgaretur: quod fore, olim Prophetae praedixerant. Adhaec oportebat Hierosolymam indigna Christi nece implere mensuram patrum suorum, qui antehac Prophetas & Dei seruos innumerabiles occiderant. Hinc apparet, quam stulte faciunt, qui religionem & cum hac salutem aeternam loci certis alligare solent. Etenim nulla ciuitas vnquam fuit in terris, quae vetustate, vi- ribus, potentia, religionis & cultus diuini maiestate Ierosolymam superarit. Quae causa est, quod eam Dominus ciuitatem magni Regis vocat, & vulgo apud Euangelistas Ciuitas sancta dicitur. At eadem sanguine Prophetarum maduit, & Filij Dei indigna nece excidium horribile cum sempiterna infamia sibi accersiuit. Quid igitur de Roma aut aliis vrbibus dicamus, quae in hoc vno Hierosolymam imitantur, quod similiter impietate contra Deum insaniunt, nullis aliis praerogatiuis aut virtutibus celebres?
units.tr: Moreover, the Lord himself clearly indicates the reason for this command of his, when he foretells to the disciples what is to happen to him, something they had never yet thought about. He does this so as to teach them the proper office of the Messiah, which they still did not know (as we shall see later in the example of Peter), and at the same time to meet the scandal which he knew would arise from his death. This is the main purpose of the very careful noting of all the circumstances. "From that time" (says Matthew) "Jesus began to show his disciples what would happen to him." So the frank confession of Peter, which had earned that splendid commendation, "Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jona," etc., gave him warning. And lest they, having become overconfident, should neglect things most necessary to know and to observe, he speaks to them thus: "I must go to Jerusalem and suffer many things from the elders and chief priests and scribes, be killed, and on the third day be raised again." First he indicates the place where these things must happen, namely Jerusalem. For since he had taken on flesh from them especially, as promised, and Jerusalem was the head of that nation and the seat of divine worship, it was fitting that he should be sacrificed there, where public and private sacrifices were performed, so that his death might be better known and the news of it might spread more easily and quickly through the whole world, as the prophets had long since foretold. Besides, Jerusalem had to fill up the measure of her fathers by the unworthy murder of Christ, since they had before this killed countless prophets and servants of God. From this it appears how foolishly those act who are accustomed to bind religion, and with it eternal salvation, to certain places. For there was never any city on earth that surpassed Jerusalem in antiquity, strength, power, or the majesty of religion and divine worship. This is why the Lord calls it the city of the great King, and in the Evangelists it is commonly called the holy city. Yet that same city was soaked with the blood of the prophets, and by the unworthy killing of the Son of God it brought upon itself a dreadful destruction together with everlasting infamy. What then shall we say of Rome or of other cities, which in this one respect imitate Jerusalem, that they likewise rave in impiety against God, and are famous for no other privileges or virtues?

units.la: Deinde oportet me (inquit) illic multa pati. Etenim non simplici aut vulgari morte obijt Christus, sed concurrunt hic omnia, quae acerba & dira sunt, & mortem possunt infame facere. Etenim a domestico discipulo proditus est, quo nomine in vltima Coena prae dolore infremuit, vt Ioannes scripsit. Deinde cum laternis & facibus atque assumpta militum cohorte ad illum capiendum egressi sunt, tanquam ad hominem facinorosum, qui dignus sit, vt publico omnium concursu opprimatur. Captus Concilio Seniorum & Sacerdotum sistitur, qui vt scismaticum examinant, atque violatae religionis patriae condemnant. Inde Pilato praesidi traditur, apud cuius tribunal regni affectati & seditionis accusatur. A Pilato ad Herodem deducitur, qui illum Pilato remittit, & quasi de ipsius capite ludentes duo isti sibi mutuo gratificantur. Adhaec innocentem Praesides cum Barraba latrone & seditioso confert, & hunc infelix populus illi praefert. Innocens damnatur ad dirum & infame Crucis supplicium, primum autem spineo ferto coronatur, confutitur, caeditur in faciem, & per ludibrium irridetur. Mox ducitur in publicum supplicij locum, nomine & aspectu terribilem, & crucem propriam humeris gestat. Illuc vbi ventum est, amarissimum illi potum propinant. pinant milites, & mox vestibus exutum in crucem suffigunt, medium inter latrones. Accedunt his omnis generis contumelię & opprobria, quorum omnium tanta vis fuit, vt exclamarit: Deus meus, Deus meus, vt quid me dereliquisti? Tandem inter dolores acerbissimos animam Patri reddens, expirat. Reuera igitur multa dira & nefanda passus est.
