units.tr: "Then," he says, "I must suffer many things there. For Christ did not die a simple or ordinary death. Everything bitter and dreadful comes together here, everything that can make a death shameful. He was betrayed by a disciple from his own household, and in the last supper he groaned in grief over it, as John wrote. Then they went out with lanterns and torches, and with a cohort of soldiers, to seize him, as though he were a criminal who deserved to be overpowered in the sight of everyone. Taken, he is brought before the council of elders and priests, who examine him as a schismatic and condemn him for violating the religion of the fathers. From there he is handed over to Pilate the governor, before whose tribunal he is accused of aspiring to kingship and of sedition. From Pilate he is led to Herod, who sends him back to Pilate, and these two, as if playing with his very head, gratify each other. Next the governors set the innocent man against Barabbas, a robber and a seditious man, and the unhappy people prefer the robber to him. The innocent man is condemned to the dreadful and infamous punishment of the cross. First he is crowned with a crown of thorns, spat upon, struck in the face, and mocked for sport. Soon he is led to the public place of execution, terrifying in its name and in its sight, and he carries his own cross on his shoulders. When they arrive there, they give him a most bitter drink. The soldiers drink, and soon, stripped of his clothes, they nail him to the cross, in the middle between two robbers. Added to these are every kind of insult and reproach, and their force was so great that he cried out: My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? Finally, amid most bitter pains, giving up his spirit to the Father, he expires. Truly, then, he suffered many dreadful and wicked things.

units.la: Qui vero horum omnium fuerunt authores? Nominat ipse Seniores, Sacerdotes & Scribas, sub quibus omnes comprehendit, qui in Republica & Ecclesia authoritatis, sanctitatis & eruditionis existimationem aliquam sustinebant: quod ipsum per se mortem hanc illi acerbam reddere potuit, & supplicij infamiam augere. Nominantur autem isti, quod totius negotij duces fuerunt, adeo vt illis acceptum ferri debeat, quicquid alij fecerunt. Nam ab his conductus est Iudas, vt illum proderet. Ipsi miserunt suos seruos cum militibus, qui illum captiuum facerent. Ipsi captum Concilio sisterunt, testes falsos subornarunt, captio e confessione Veritatis ex eius ore elicuerunt, vt eius damnandi occasionem inuenirent. Illi eum damnarunt, damnatum seruis suis improbissimis illudendum tradiderunt. Illi eundem Pilato adduxerunt, ad cuius tribunal falsis criminibus insontem grauarunt, populo denique persuaserunt, vt huic Barrabam latronem praeferret, & sua improbitate Pilatum coegerunt, vt inuitus capitalem contra illum ferret sententiam. Atqui hoc est, quod olim Dauid praedixerat, fore, vt architecti lapidem illum pretiosum, qui Ecclesiae funda mentum & caput anguli futurus sit, reprobent atque reiciant. Et haec quidem omnia in praesenti Apostolis praedicit, & se tertio die resurrecturum ex mortuis pollicetur, ne iis offenderentur postea, & animos suos aduersus scandalum obfirmarent sepe laeta resurrectionis, quae mox secuta illum mortis victorie esse ostendit. Nobis ante in tota hac narratione duo potissimum consideranda sunt.
units.tr: But who were the authors of all these things? He names the elders, the priests and the scribes, under whom he includes all who held some reputation for authority, holiness and learning in the commonwealth and the Church. This alone could make his death bitter for him and add to the infamy of the punishment. These men are named because they were the leaders of the whole affair, so that whatever the others did must be credited to them. For it was by them that Judas was hired to betray him. They sent their servants with the soldiers to take him captive. They themselves brought him, once seized, before the council, suborned false witnesses, and drew from his mouth a confession of the truth, so that they might find an occasion to condemn him. They condemned him, and, once condemned, handed him over to their most wicked servants to be mocked. They brought him to Pilate, before whose tribunal they burdened the innocent man with false charges. Finally they persuaded the people to prefer the robber Barabbas to him, and by their wickedness they compelled Pilate, against his will, to pronounce the capital sentence against him. And yet this is what David had long ago foretold would happen: the builders would reject and cast away that precious stone which was to be the foundation of the Church and the head of the corner. And indeed he foretells all these things to the apostles at this time, and promises that he will rise from the dead on the third day, so that they would not later be offended and would fortify their minds against the scandal by the joyful memory of the resurrection, which he showed would soon follow as the victory over death. In this whole narrative, two things chiefly must be considered by us.

units.la: Primum est, redemptionis nostrae negotium, quod in his consistit, & ita hic proponitur, vt abunde demonstret se esse CHRISTVM sive Vnicum Dei, id est, Sacerdotem & Regem Ecclesiae, cui omnis salus accepta ferri debeat. Hoc initio statim innuit, quando dicit OPORTET me ire Hierosolymam. Passus igitur est ista, quia ita fieri oportuit. Non debet autem hoc dictum ita accipi, quasi ipse nolens & inuitus, vel ab aliquo hostium suorum coactus ista tulerit. Nam volens passus & mortuus est, sicuti verbis & re ipsa testatur. Nam apud Ioannem ait: Nemo tollit animam meam a me, sed ego pono eam a me ipso, &c. Deinde cum quid sibi euenturum esset, non ignoraret, tamen sponte & volens Hierosolyma abijt, & dehortantibus ipsum discipulis multoties, faciem suam ad illud iter obfirmauit: & postea in hortum sponte exiit, vbi se capiendum sciebat, & neque discipulorum armis, neque Angelorumope & auxilio defendi voluit contra vim hostilem. Itaque huius necessitatis ratio, quam hic allegat in aeterno Patris decreto quaeri debet: vt dicamus, haec ita fieri oportuisse, quia Pater ita voluit, & nobis miseris mortalibus aliter subuenire non poterat. Omnes enim peccaueramus, & propter peccatum mortis rei eramus: neque nos ipsos poteramus liberare, eo quod in peccatis concepti & nati, ne ad cogitandum quidem ex nobis ipsis idonei sumus. Non proderat etiam sanguis pecudum, qui inter gentes & Iudaeos quotidie magna copia fundebatur. Nulla enim inter pecudes & nos vel naturae vel delictorum communio est, & ex diuinae iustitiae decreto, non pecudes, sed nos ad supplicium poscebamur. Non etiam saluti nostrae consuli poterat, etiamsi quidam homines ceu καθάρματα seu piacula fierent: quod inter gentes aliquas barbaras magna cum crudelitate sub religionis praetextu fieri solitum fuit. Quia enim vna omnium noxa erat, vno reatu item omnes tenebamur, nemo alterius culpa praestare, aut aliorum scelera expiare poterat. In ista igitur rerum humanarum angustia Deus, quia hanc calamitatem, priusquam esse mus, praeuidit, nostri miserti ab aeterno praedestinauit Filium suum Vnigenitum, qui homo factus ex Virgine, omnium hominum peccata in se transferret, & eadem sanguine suo pretioso expiaret. Idem hic praefinito tempore ex Maria natus, hoc omne praestitit, & volens quidem Patri obediens factus vsq; ad mortem crucis, seipsum ceu fidus Pontifex pro nobis obtulit: vt quemadmodum per vnius Adami patris omnium nostrum inobedientiam peccatum in mundum introierat: ita per illius obedientiam iustificaremur, & hac noxa soluaremur. Quia vero non satis erat peccata nostra expiari & tolli, nisi & poena peccati, Mors, deuinceretur, quae per peccatum nobis dominabatur, hanc quoque Resurrectione sua gloriosa vicit, & stimulo seu aculeo suo exarmatam quasi aboleuit, vt quae olim peccati poena erat, nunc in illum credentibus felix et laetus transitus sit ex hac lachrymarum valle in vitam æternam. Itaq; Regis instar deuictis hostibus nostris, peccato, morte, inferis, diabolo, cœlos ascendit triumphans, & illic nobis mansionem parauit, in quam ipsi quoq; olim transferemur, cum ipse venerit ad iudicandum viuos & mortuos. Hæc (inquam) nostræ redemptionis summa est, quæ in Scripturis fusissimè tractatur: quarum testimonia cum vbiq; occurrant, & alibi sæpius adducta sint, non opus est eam in præsenti repetere. Prodest autem de his crebrò cogitare, vt agnoscamus peccati atrocitatem, neq; eius blanditias admittamus, quibus nobis Satan insidiatur, vt in suum seruitium retrahat. Quid enim in illo leuiculum, quid iucundum censeri potest, quod non alio pretio quàm innocenti sanguine Filij Dei expiari potuit? Deinde meminerimus, non aliam inueniri posse rationem, quà seruemur. Si quæ enim esset, procul dubio non latuisset ea Deum, cuius oculi vniuersam terram percurrunt, & qui abstrusa tenebrarum scrutatur. Idem quia ipsa charitas & iustitia est, noluisset hanc potius salutis nostræ viâ sequi, quæ et iniusta et crudelis dici poterat, si quæ alia potuisset singi. Huic ergo nos insistamus, nec excidat Apostolicū illud de Christo dictū: Nō est in alio quoquā salus: Nec enim aliud nomen est sub cælo, quod datū sit inter homines, per quod oporteat nos seruari. Act.4. Præterea quia hæc Apostolis dixit Dominus, vt eos contra crucis scandalum præmuniret, nobis quoq; huius loci vsus esto, vt discamus, quæ semper in terris sors futura sit seruorum illius, qui ipsum cum side amplexantur, neq; offendamur, si quid durius nobis accidat. Nec enim melius potest esse membris quàm capiti, discipulis & seruis quàm magistro & hero. Habent ergo etiam illi aduersarios & hostes ex eorum numero, qui Filiū Dei exosculari, & eius seruos souere & iuuare debebant: inter hos autem facile principes sunt, qui Ecclesiæ antistites volunt haberi, & Spiritualiū nomine gloriantur. Et hi ijsdem artibus ac armis pugnāt, quibus veteres illi calumniis nimirum, mendaciis & dolis: neq; eos vllius iniustitiæ aut sceleris pudet, dummodo Ecclesiæ & Christo possint officere. Adhæc crudeles sunt, neq; vllis supplicijs piorum exsaturari possunt. Experti sunt tales Apostoli olim, & tales hodie passim credentibus negotium faciunt. Non ergo offendamur eorum conatibus, neq; vt re peregrina ac insolita percellamur exploratione illa, quæ per ignem fit ad nostri experimentum. Soletur autem nos resurrectio Christi. Vt enim non diuturna fuit huius perpessio, neq; eum mors detinere potuit, sed tertio die ad vitam immortalem resuscitatus est, atq; mirabili consilio Dei factum est, vt inepti illi ac perfidi architecti, qui lapidem illum pretiosum reprobarunt, eum in caput Anguli euexerint: Ita hisce etiam postremus tem poribus fieri solet, vt qui petram illam inuistam, IESVM CHRISTVM expugnare, & super hanc extructos vere credentes euertere ac destruere volunt, illius regnum suis conatibus prouehant, & illustrius reddant. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: The first is the business of our redemption, which consists in these things, and is so set forth here that it abundantly shows him to be CHRIST, that is, the only Son of God, the Priest and King of the Church, to whom all salvation must be credited. He hints at this at the outset when he says, "It is necessary for me to go to Jerusalem." So he suffered these things because it had to be so. Yet this statement should not be taken as if he endured these things unwillingly and against his will, or as if he were compelled by one of his enemies. For he suffered and died willingly, as he testifies both by words and in fact. In John he says: "No one takes my life from me, but I lay it down of myself," and so on. Again, though he was not ignorant of what would befall him, nevertheless he went up to Jerusalem freely and willingly. Many times, when the disciples dissuaded him, he set his face firmly on that journey. Afterwards he went out voluntarily into the garden, where he knew he would be seized, and he would not be defended against hostile force either by the weapons of his disciples or by the help of angels. The reason for this necessity, which he here alleges, must therefore be sought in the eternal decree of the Father. We should say that these things had to happen in this way because the Father willed it, and because he could not otherwise help us wretched mortals. For we had all sinned, and on account of sin we were liable to death. Nor could we free ourselves, since, conceived and born in sin, we are not even capable of thinking anything good from ourselves. The blood of beasts, which was poured out every day in great quantity among the nations and the Jews, did not help either. For there is no community between beasts and us, either in nature or in guilt, and by the decree of divine justice it was not beasts but we who were demanded for punishment. Nor could our salvation be secured even if certain men were made as καθάρματα [offscourings] or expiatory victims, as was customary among some barbarian nations with great cruelty under the pretext of religion. For since the guilt of all was one, all were bound by one liability, and no one could answer for another's fault or expiate the crimes of others. In this straitened condition of human affairs, therefore, God, who foresaw this calamity before we existed, took pity on us and from eternity predestined his only-begotten Son, who, made man from the Virgin, would take upon himself the sins of all men and expiate them by his precious blood. This same Son, born of Mary at the appointed time, accomplished all this. Willingly obedient to the Father, he became obedient even unto the death of the cross, and offered himself for us as a faithful High Priest. Thus, just as through the disobedience of one man, Adam, the father of us all, sin entered the world, so through the obedience of the one we are justified and freed from this guilt. But since it was not enough that our sins be expiated and taken away, unless the punishment of sin, death, which ruled over us through sin, was also overcome, he conquered this too by his glorious resurrection, and as though disarmed of its sting, he abolished it, so that what was once the punishment of sin might now be a happy and joyful passage for those who believe in him, from this valley of tears into eternal life. And so, like a king, having conquered our enemies, sin, death, the underworld and the devil, he ascended triumphantly into the heavens and prepared a dwelling there for us, to which we too shall one day be transferred when he comes to judge the living and the dead. This, I say, is the sum of our redemption, which is treated most fully in the Scriptures. Since its testimonies occur everywhere and have often been cited elsewhere, there is no need to repeat it at present. It is profitable, however, to think often on these things, so that we may recognize the atrocity of sin and not admit its allurements, by which Satan lies in wait for us to drag us back into his service. For what in sin can be considered trivial or pleasant, when it could be expiated only at the price of the innocent blood of the Son of God? Then let us remember that no other way of our salvation can be found. For if there were another, it would certainly not have been hidden from God, whose eyes run through the whole earth and who searches out hidden things of darkness. Since he is love and justice itself, he would not have wished to follow this way of our salvation, which could be called unjust and cruel, if another could have been devised. Let us therefore cling to this, and let not that saying of the apostle about Christ fall from our minds: "There is salvation in no one else; for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved" (Acts 4). Moreover, since the Lord said these things to the apostles to fortify them against the scandal of the cross, let us also make use of this passage for ourselves, so that we may learn what the lot of his servants will always be in this world, those who embrace him with faith, and that we may not be offended if anything harsher befalls us. For the members cannot fare better than the head, nor disciples and servants better than their master and lord. So they too have adversaries and enemies from among those who ought to have kissed the Son of God and cherished and helped his servants. Among these, the chief are easily those who want to be considered the bishops of the Church and glory in the name of spiritual men. And they fight with the same arts and weapons as those ancient enemies: calumnies, lies and tricks. Nor are they ashamed of any injustice or crime, provided they can harm the Church and Christ. Moreover, they are cruel, and can never be satisfied by any punishments of the godly. Such men tested the apostles long ago, and such men today everywhere make trouble for believers. Therefore let us not be offended at their attempts, nor be struck down as by a strange and unusual trial, that testing which is done by fire to prove us. Let the resurrection of Christ console us. For although his suffering was not lasting, and death could not hold him, but on the third day he was raised to immortal life, and by the wonderful counsel of God it came about that those foolish and faithless builders who rejected that precious stone lifted it up to be the head of the corner, so also in these latter times it is customary for those who wish to overthrow Jesus Christ, the unconquered rock, and to destroy and ruin the true believers built upon him, to advance his kingdom by their own efforts and make it more illustrious. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCVIII.
units.tr: HOMILY 208.

units.la: Et præhensum eum Petrus cœpit obiurgare, dicens: Propitius tibi sis Domine: nequaquam erit tibi hoc. At ille conuersus, dixit Petro: Abscede a me Satana, scandalo es mihi: Nam non sapis quæ sunt Dei, sed quæ sunt hominum.
units.tr: And Peter, taking him aside, began to rebuke him, saying: "Far be it from you, Lord; this shall never happen to you." But he turned and said to Peter: "Get behind me, Satan; you are a stumbling block to me, for you do not savour the things of God, but the things of men."

units.la: Quamuis Apostoli scirent IESVM esse CHRISTVM, id est, promissum humani generis Seruatorem, Sacerdotem æternum, & Regem illū gloriæ, cui omnes gentes obedire ac subiici debeant: hoc tamen illis defuit, quòd ignorarunt, in quo redemptio & salus nostra consistat, & quale regnum ille in terris habeat. Nam vt sæpe diximus, regnum terrenum in illo somniabant, in quo omnem huius sæculi felicitatem sibi ipsis pollicebantur. Quæ causa fuit, quòd postea eius cruce & morte grauiter offensi sunt. Ideò ille, vt eos aduersus crucis scandalum confirmaret, nuper ex ordine diligenter recensuit, quid sibi Hierosolymæ authoribus Sacerdotibus & Scribis, euenturum, & vt ex morte ad vitam resurrecturus sit, vt & nos suæ mortis merito redimat, & per hanc in gloriam Patris ac cœlestis regni possessionem ingrediatur. Quàm vero necesse fuerit, illoq illos de hu præmoneri, hic locus docet, ex quo apparet, illos hæc omnia finistrè intellexisse. Nam Petrus ipsum dehortatur, ne id faciat quod in primis sui officij erat, & hoc nomine ab eo acerrimè corripitur. Quia autem error iste Apostolorum hodie etiam vulgaris est, & locus iste de multis admonet, quæ nobis cognitu necessaria sunt, videamus primùm, in quo peccarit Petrus: Deinde vt eum Christus corripuerit.
units.tr: Although the Apostles knew that Jesus is the Christ, that is, the promised Saviour of the human race, the eternal Priest, and that King of glory to whom all nations ought to submit and be subject, yet this was lacking in them: they did not understand in what our redemption and salvation consist, or what kind of kingdom he has on earth. For, as we have often said, they dreamed of an earthly kingdom in which they promised themselves all the happiness of this world. This was the reason why they were later gravely offended by his cross and death. Therefore, in order to strengthen them against the scandal of the cross, he recently went through the whole sequence carefully, telling them what would befall him at Jerusalem at the hands of the chief priests and scribes, and that he would rise from death to life, so that he might redeem us by the merit of his death and, through this, enter into the glory of the Father and the possession of the heavenly kingdom. How necessary it was that they be forewarned of these things this passage teaches, from which it appears that they understood all of this wrongly. For Peter dissuades him from doing what belonged especially to his office, and for this he is sharply rebuked. Since this error of the Apostles is still common today, and this passage warns us about many things that we need to know, let us consider first where Peter erred, and then how Christ rebuked him.

units.la: Quoad illum, dicitur, quòd prehenderit Christum, vel (vt Græcum verbum innuit) eum adse assumptum seorsim, cæperit obiurgare, &c. Atqui non dubium est, illum, quicquid fecit, bona animi intentione fecisse. Nam impense Christum amauit, vt ab eo diuelli non posset. Itaq; ne mentionem quidem ferre potest eorum, quæ ipsi euentura esse audiebat. At quia zelus hic siue intentio non regebatur scientia vera, in vno hoc facto errores & vitia multa concurrunt. Primò quasi aliquod in eum ius & imperium habeat, prehensum abducere vult seorsim. Deinde inexcusabilis est confidentia, quòd non contentus monuisse, eum insuper obiurgat & corripit, cùm ipse potius ab illo discere deberet, cur ipsum ista perpeti oporteat. Sed & verba Petri accusationem temeritatis spirant, cùm dicat: Propitius tibi sis Domine, nequaquam erit tibi hoc. Quasi diceret: Tu quidem ista fieri oportere dicis: sed quis te coget ad ista, si tu nolis? Enimuero cùm alios seruaris hastenus, & morbis, ventis, fluctibus, spiritibus item immundis imperes, & ex mortis faucibus, quos vis extra has, facile tibi fuerit teipsum seruare. Adhæc cùm norit quàm infenso in te sint animo Seniores & Sacerdotes cum tota coniuratorum suorum cohorte, consultius erit, vel non abire illuc vbi illi dominantur, vel illos non irritare. Nam etsi illi digni sint, qui durius tractentur, tu tamen tuipsius rationem habere debes, ne ista tam dira & iniqua tibi accidant. Addit his postremò: Nequaquam erit tibi hoc. Idem est, & si velis tu salutem tuam negligere, nos tamen ista fieri non patiemur, nec deerunt alij etiam, qui sese illorum hominum furoribus opponent, &c. Omnium verò istorum hic finis & status est, vt Christum ab eo renocet, cuius ergo in mundum venerat, & homo erat factus.
units.tr: As to Peter, it is said that he took hold of Christ, or (as the Greek word suggests) took him aside privately, and began to rebuke him, and so on. Yet there is no doubt that whatever he did, he did with a good intention of mind. For he loved Christ intensely, so that he could not be torn away from him. Therefore he could not even bear to hear of the things that he was told would happen to him. But because this zeal, or intention, was not governed by true knowledge, many errors and faults meet in this one act. First, he wants to take Christ aside privately, as if he had some right and authority over him. Next, his presumption is inexcusable: not content with having warned him, he rebukes and chides him besides, when he himself ought rather to have learned from him why he must suffer these things. But Peter's words also breathe an accusation of rashness when he says: "Far be it from you, Lord; this shall never happen to you." It is as if he said: "You indeed say that these things must happen, but who will compel you to them if you do not wish it? Indeed, since until now you have saved others and commanded diseases, winds, waves, and also unclean spirits, and have snatched whom you wished from the jaws of death, it will be easy for you to save yourself." Besides, since he knows how hostile the elders and priests, with their whole band of conspirators, are towards you, it will be wiser either not to go there where they rule, or not to provoke them. For although they deserve to be treated more harshly, you ought nevertheless to take thought for yourself, lest such dreadful and unjust things befall you. Finally he adds: "This shall never happen to you." It is the same as if he said: "Even if you wish to neglect your own safety, we will not allow these things to happen, and there will be others too who will oppose themselves to the fury of those men," and so on. Now the aim and purpose of all these words is to call Christ back from that which he had come into the world for, and for which he had been made man.

units.la: Vnde autem tanta illi fiducia venit? Non aliunde, quàm quòd carnis rationibus ducitur, quæ illum non sinunt animi oculos altius attollere. Et erant hæ in specie plansibiles. Nam Filius Dei viuentis erat, in quem mors nihil iuris habebat. Deinde Messias erat qui regnū Dei inter homines debebat instaurare. Cur ergo seipsum sponte morti obijceret? Præterea innocens erat, & nō solùm ab omni maleficio alienus, verumetiā beneficijs incomparabilibus quotidie omnes adse venientes cumulabat. Ex istis colligit Petrus, indignum & iniquum esse vt infamē mortem subeat, neq; ratas fore promissiones de Messia, si ista fiant, quæ fieri oportere dixerat. Et eandem fuisse discipulorum omnium sententiā certò constat. Nam cum ista omnia, quæ prædixerat, ei euenijssent, non prædictionum eius recordati, sed morte eius offensi sunt, vt ex duorū sermonibus appáret, qui ipso resurrectionis die Emaunte profecturi in ipsum inciderunt. Cū enim ipsi ceu peregrino & rerum ignaro ex posuissent, quæ cum Iesu acta erant, addunt tandē: Nos autē sperabamus eum esse illum, qui redem speurus esset Israelem. Atqui hic lapis ille est, ad quem Iudæi omnes olim offenderunt, Paulo teste, & adhuc hodie offendunt, vt non possint eum pro Seruatore promisso agnoscere, quem acerbam & crudelem morte sustinuisse audiunt. Sed & Turcæ, cū de illo alioqui honorificè sentiant, nos tamen eo potissimū nomine oderunt atq; persequuntur, quòd illum in cruce suffixum esse, & medium inter latrones expirauisse credimus. Id enim indignissimū putant esse, vt de eo dicatur, quæ illi Dei verbum & Animam, adhæc maximū omnium Prophetarum, quotquot ante Mahumetē fuerunt, appellant. Inter Christianos autē nihil tam vulgare est, quàm quòd pleriq; qui in cruce Iesu Christi spem salutis omnē habere gloriantur, ipsi ad illū offendant, si quid pro illo ferendā est. Et hoc tunc maximè fit, quando interea huius seculi filios & apertos Christi hostes feliciter agere & florere vi dent. Tunc enim de Euangelij promissionibus dubitare, adhæc de Dei iudicijs conqueri, & (vt Asaph de semetipso dicebat) omnē filiorum Dei generationē damnare incipiunt: neq; credere possunt, illorum fide atq; cultum Deo probari, quos hic perpetuis persecutionibus & aduersis exerceat. Cæterum omnes isti cogitare debebant, non temerè a Christo dictum esse, OPORTET me abire Ierosolymam, & multa pati a Senioribus, &c. Item, ita OPORTVIT Christum pati & resurgere a mortuis tertio die, &c. Nimirū quòd non alia esset ratio, quasi simul iustitia Dei satisfieret pro peccatis nostris, & nos eiusdē gratuita misericordia seruaremur. Neq; ignominiosum hoc fuit Dei Filio, qui Patri obediuit, & excusso mortis aculeo, gloriosa resurrectione hanc vnà cum inferno &c.
units.tr: But whence came such confidence in him? From nothing else than that he was led by considerations of the flesh, which did not allow him to raise the eyes of his mind higher. And these considerations were plausible in appearance. For he was the Son of the living God, over whom death had no right. Then he was the Messiah, who ought to restore the kingdom of God among men. Why, then, should he expose himself willingly to death? Moreover, he was innocent, and not only free from all wrongdoing, but he daily heaped incomparable benefits upon all who came to him. From these things Peter concludes that it is unworthy and unjust that he should undergo an infamous death, and that the promises about the Messiah would not stand if these things were to happen which he had said must happen. And it is certain that all the disciples held the same opinion. For when all those things that he had foretold had come to pass, they remembered none of his predictions but were offended by his death, as appears from the words of the two men who, on the very day of the resurrection, set out for Emmaus and met him. For when they had explained to him, as a stranger and ignorant of what had happened, what had been done with Jesus, they finally add: "But we were hoping that he was the one who would redeem Israel." Yet this is the stone over which all the Jews once stumbled, as Paul testifies, and still stumble today, so that they cannot acknowledge him as the promised Saviour, since they hear that he endured a bitter and cruel death. But the Turks too, although otherwise they think honourably of him, hate and persecute us chiefly for this reason: that we believe he was fastened to the cross and died between two thieves. For they think it most unworthy that such things be said of one whom they call the Word of God and the Spirit, and moreover the greatest of all the prophets who have existed before Muhammad. Among Christians, however, nothing is so common as that many who boast that all their hope of salvation rests in the cross of Jesus Christ take offence at him when something must be borne for his sake. And this happens especially when they see the sons of this age and open enemies of Christ living happily and flourishing. For then they begin to doubt the promises of the gospel, to complain of God's judgements, and (as Asaph said of himself) to condemn the whole generation of God's sons. Nor can they believe that the faith and worship of those whom God here exercises with constant persecutions and adversities are pleasing to him. But all these men ought to have considered that it was not said rashly by Christ: "I must go to Jerusalem and suffer many things from the elders," and so on. Likewise: "Thus it was necessary for Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day," and so on. Surely because there was no other way, as if at the same time the justice of God might be satisfied for our sins and we might be saved by his free mercy. Nor was this a disgrace to the Son of God, who obeyed the Father and, having shaken off the sting of death by his glorious resurrection, conquered it together with hell and the devil, and now lives and reigns in the heavens.

units.la: Luc. 24. | 1. Cor. 1 | Psal. 73. diabolo vicit, & nunc in cœlis viuit & regnat. Eadem nostrorum quoque afflictionum est ratio. Quia enim in sanctis quoq; & credentibus peccata hærent, iustum ac æquum est, vt quando Deus mundum punire vult, iudicium a suo domo inchoet, ne in suis ea probare putetur, quæ in aliis graui ssime vlciscitur. Deinde hoc nostræ salutis ratio requirit, vt a Domino castigemur ad pœnitentiam, ne cum mundo incurabili æternum damnemur. Nobis autem hoc gloriosissimum est, quod æternus Dei Filius suæ crucis socios facere dignatur nos, qui propter delicta nostra multiplicari merebamur. Hinc enim fiet, vt si cum eo toleramus, cum eodem regnemus: si item cum eo moriamur, cum eodem viuamus. 2. Tim. 2.
units.tr: Luc. 24. | 1. Cor. 1 | Psal. 73. The reason for our afflictions is the same. For since sins cling even to the saints and believers, it is just and right that, when God wishes to punish the world, he should begin judgement at his own house, lest he be thought to approve in his own people what he most severely avenges in others. Next, the reasoning of our salvation requires that we be chastised by the Lord unto repentance, lest we be condemned eternally along with the incurable world. But for us this is most glorious: that the eternal Son of God deigns to make us, who deserved to be multiplied on account of our sins, partners in his cross. For from this it will come about that, if we endure with him, we shall reign with him; likewise, if we die with him, we shall live with him. 2. Tim. 2.

units.la: Porrò alteram huius loci partem videamus, quæ responsionem Christi continet, qui conuersus, discipulos simul omnes (vt Marcus annotauit) intuitus est, nimirum quod (vt paulò ante dixi mus) eodem affectu omnes effent præditi, Petrũ obiurgauit, dicens: Abscede post me Satana, &c. Verba per se clara & perspicua sunt, quibus Petrum vt pessimum consultorem a se reiicit: quam obrem res ipsas, quæ hic continentur videamus: Primò videlicet, cui loquatur, & quid iubeat: Deinde quam sui mandati rationem afferat: Postremò, quo argumento hoc totum confirmet.
units.tr: Let us next consider the other part of this passage, which contains Christ's reply. Turning round and looking at all the disciples together (as Mark noted), since, as I said a little earlier, they were all affected in the same way, he rebuked Peter, saying: "Get behind me, Satan," etc. The words are clear and plain in themselves, by which he rejects Peter as the worst of counsellors. So let us look at the matters contained here: first, to whom he speaks and what he commands; then the reason he gives for his command; and lastly, by what argument he confirms the whole.

units.la: Primò, etsi causa hæc ad omnes pertineat, præcipuè tamen Petro loquitur, qui aliis feruenti or sibi tantum iuris in illum sumpserat, vt non requisitus ipsi consilium daret, aut ab instituto dehortaretur. Dicit autem ei: Abi post me Satana. Non Petri aut Simonis nomine eum compellat, sed Satanam dicit, quod communis hostis nostri nomen est proprium, & aduersarium significat. Ita vero vocat Petrum, partim quod sua dehortatione ipsi aduersaretur, & obstaret, quo minus quod ipsi a Patre iniunctum erat faceret: partim quod Satan ipse hoc consilium ei suggessisset, vt Petri simplicitati atq; zelo bono abuteretur, & per hunc efficeret, quod se a Christo nunquam im petraturū esse sciebat. Nam ante quidem simili tentatione ipsum aggressus erat, quando ei omnia huius mundi regna pollicebatur, si prostratus ipsum adoraret: Sed ab eo cum graui correptione re pulsus, ex arena discessit, nec quicquã tale præterea ausus fuit, eò quod Christus quotidie diuinam suam virtutem operibus miraculosis declararet, & ipsum ex obsessis magna cum virtute eijceret. Itaque vt olim non Adamum, sed Euam aggressus est, quam infirmiorem esse sciebat, vt per hanc illius fidem expugnaret: ita nunc per Petrum conatur ipsum Christum deuincere, & illius simpli citate & zelo abutitur. Itaque non tam Petro, quàm ipsi Satanæ ista dicit, & vtrumque posse se abire iubet.
units.tr: First, although this admonition concerns everyone, he speaks chiefly to Peter, who, in his fervour, had taken such authority over Christ that he gave advice without being asked and tried to dissuade him from his undertaking. He says to him: "Go behind me, Satan." He does not address him by the name Peter or Simon, but calls him Satan, which is the proper name of our common enemy and means adversary. He calls Peter this partly because by his dissuasion he opposed and hindered him from doing what the Father had enjoined, and partly because Satan himself had suggested this counsel to him, so as to abuse Peter's simplicity and good zeal and through him to bring about what he knew he could never obtain from Christ. For Satan had indeed attacked him earlier with a similar temptation, when he promised him all the kingdoms of this world if he would fall down and worship him. But repulsed by him with a severe rebuke, Satan withdrew from the field and did not dare to attempt anything like that again, because Christ daily declared his divine power by miraculous works and cast out demons from the possessed with great power. Therefore, just as Satan once attacked not Adam but Eve, whom he knew to be the weaker, in order to overcome his faith through her, so now he tries to subdue Christ himself through Peter, abusing his simplicity and zeal. Thus he says these things not so much to Peter as to Satan himself, and bids both of them to depart.

units.la: Debet autē obseruari, quòd hic, qui eadem hora inuictum Petri nomen accepit, quem beatum dixit, & cui claues regni cœlorum promisit, nunc Satan dicitur, quo nomine nihil abominabilius & magis exosum Christianis hominibus esse debet. Elucet in hoc exemplo communis infirmitas, quæ in Sanctis quoque locum inuenit propter Legë peccati, quam in membris suis circumferunt. Docent hoc innumera exempla, quæ passim occurrunt. Abraham, pater credentium, qui Deo vocante, intrepidus patrios lares & cognatos simul omnes reliquerat, & qui Ifaacum filiū, illo mandante, immolare voluit: non multò post ignauo metu superatus vxorem Saram abnegat, & mendacio illo turpissimo eam in præsens pudicitiæ suæ periculum adducit. Moses mortalium, quotquot vn quam fuerunt, mitissimus & patientissimus, populi tamen improbitate vincitur, vt Deo non det gloriam, & indignus iudicetur qui in terra promissam ingrediatur. Dauid vir secundum cor Dei, quando minime putabat, turpis adulter & populi Dei proditor fit. Idem in Petro factum fuisse hoc loco videmus, qui insuper Christum tandem turpissimè abnegauit. Et huius generis infinita passim occurrunt: quorum omnium hic nobis vsus esse debet, ne securitati nos dedamus, sed vt qui sibi videtur stare, caueat ne cadat. 1. Cor. 10.
units.tr: It must be observed that this man, who at that same hour had received the invincible name of Peter, whom he called blessed and to whom he promised the keys of the kingdom of heaven, is now called Satan. Nothing should be more hateful and detestable to Christians than that name. In this example the common weakness shines forth, which finds a place even in the saints, on account of the law of sin that they carry about in their members. Countless examples that occur everywhere teach this. Abraham, the father of believers, who at God's call fearlessly left his native home and all his kinsfolk, and who was willing to sacrifice his son Isaac at God's command, was not long after overcome by cowardly fear and denied his wife Sarah, and by that most shameful lie brought her into immediate danger to her chastity. Moses, the meekest and most patient of all mortals who have ever lived, was nevertheless overcome by the wickedness of the people, so that he did not give glory to God, and was judged unworthy to enter the land of promise. David, a man after God's own heart, when he least expected it, became a shameful adulterer and a betrayer of the people of God. We see that the same happened to Peter in this place, who moreover at last shamefully denied Christ. Countless examples of this kind occur everywhere, and we ought to make use of all of them so that we do not give ourselves over to complacency, but that whoever thinks he stands may take care lest he fall. 1 Cor. 10.

units.la: Iubet autem Petrum post se abire: Ipsi Satanæ, qui ei regna orbis terrarum omnia pollicebatur, vt ipsum ab obedientia Patris auocaret: simpliciter dicebat: Abi Satana. Petrum vero post se abire, id est, se sequi vult. Id vero eius confidentiæ opponit, qui ipsum manu prehendere, & se ei ducem præbere ausus fuerat: quasi melius quàm ipsi prospiceret, quid ipsi effet agendū. Iubet ergo vt suæ inscitiæ & infirmitatis memor, intra discipuli terminos sese contineat, ipsum obseruet & eius vestigijs insistat. Est hoc generale præceptum, quod omnibus mandatur, & quod singuli sibijpsis applicare debent. Quàm primum enim Christo præire volumus, ex discipulis in Satanas degeneramus, & similem correptionem meremur.
units.tr: Now he bids Peter go behind him. To Satan himself, who promised him all the kingdoms of the world in order to turn him away from obedience to the Father, he simply says: "Go, Satan." But he wants Peter to go behind him, that is, to follow him. He sets this against Peter's confidence, who had dared to take hold of him by the hand and offer himself as his guide, as if he knew better than Christ what ought to be done. Therefore he bids him, mindful of his own ignorance and weakness, to keep within the limits of a disciple, to observe him, and to follow in his footsteps. This is a general precept, given to all, and each one should apply it to himself. For as soon as we wish to go before Christ, we degenerate from disciples into Satans and deserve a similar rebuke.

units.la: Sed diligentius consideretur causa, quae Dominum movit, ut qui prohibet fratrem fatuum aut Racha vocare, Petrum Satanam nominarit. Quia (inquit) scandalo es mihi, id est, me impedire vis, ne in Patris vocatione pergam, et lapsus occasionem mihi praebere. Etenim Patris decretum erat, ut ea patefieret Christus, quae se passurum dixerat, neque aliter poterat consuli humanae saluti. Et Dei decreta nullo humano consilio, nulla vi aut machinatione impediri possunt.
units.tr: But let us consider more carefully the cause that moved the Lord, who forbids calling a brother a fool or Raca, to name Peter Satan. Because (he says) you are a stumbling block to me, that is, you want to hinder me so that I do not proceed with the Father's calling, and you offer me an occasion of falling. For it was the Father's decree that Christ should make known what he had said he would suffer, and human salvation could not otherwise be secured. And the decrees of God cannot be hindered by any human counsel, by any force or contrivance.

units.la: Quia tamen Petrus, quantum in ipso erat, obstare conabatur ne illa fierent, quae omnino fieri oportebat, recte eum sibi obstaculo esse dicit, et ideo Satanae nomen ei tribuit. Rursus autem suo exemplo docet, quo loco habendi sint, quotquot nos ab officio revocant, aut quacunque ratione obstant, ne Deo obsequium praestemus.
units.tr: Yet because Peter, as far as lay in him, tried to prevent those things from happening which had to happen altogether, Christ rightly says that he is an obstacle to him, and therefore gives him the name of Satan. Again, by his own example he teaches what place should be given to all those who call us back from duty, or in any way stand in the way so that we do not render obedience to God.

units.la: Faciunt hoc saepe amici coniunctissimi bono zelo et intentione, sed non secundum scientiam: quando dum nobis metuunt, et nos quam diutissime incolumes manere volunt, vel cessationem ab officio, vel fugam turpem suadent. Ita nonnunquam Verbi ministri fideles monentur, ut sibi parcant quo ad labores et curas, aut alio se conferant: et in eo Satan frequenter pijssimorum hominum opera abutitur, ut suo regno consulat, ne libera et assidua Verbi praedicatione expugnetur ruat. Ide solet principibus fidis accidere, quos similiter otiari vellet Satan, ne ex illis suo regno aliquid incommodi accidat.
units.tr: Very often this is done by the closest friends, out of good zeal and good intention, but not according to knowledge: when, fearing for us and wishing us to remain safe for as long as possible, they advise either that we cease from our duty or that we flee shamefully. Thus faithful ministers of the Word are sometimes urged to spare themselves from labours and cares, or to betake themselves elsewhere; and in this Satan often abuses the works of the most godly men, so that he may consult for his own kingdom, lest it be overthrown by the free and constant preaching of the Word. The same is wont to happen to faithful princes, whom Satan would likewise wish to be idle, so that nothing harmful may befall his kingdom from them.

units.la: Et est quidem laudanda piorum hominum intentio, qui ex charitate non fucata fidei Christi ministris consultum volunt: sed quod agunt ex Satana est, qui illorum pietate abutitur, et ideo eorum consiliis non semper obedire debent, qui in publica aliqua functione constituti sunt, sed videre quo ipsos vocet Deus, ne officio suo desint, quoad hic bene agendi occasiones atque vires suppeditat.
units.tr: Indeed the intention of pious men is to be praised, who from sincere love wish to provide for the ministers of Christ's faith; but what they do is from Satan, who abuses their piety. Therefore those who are placed in some public office ought not always to obey the counsels of such people, but rather see where God calls them, so that they may not fail in their duty, as long as he supplies the opportunities and strength to act well here.

units.la: Exemplum Christi secutus est Paulus Apostolus, qui etsi in postrema sua profectione in Syriam, per singulas prope civitates moneretur a pijs et sanctis fratribus, ne Hierosolymam ascenderet, et ipse sciret sibi illic vincula parata esse, nulla tamen periculi denuntiatione se ab instituto revocari passus est, quo minus Spiritus Dei vocationem sequeretur.
units.tr: The Apostle Paul followed the example of Christ, who, although on his last journey into Syria, was warned by godly and holy brothers in nearly every city not to go up to Jerusalem, and he himself knew that chains were prepared for him there, nevertheless allowed himself to be turned from his purpose by no threat of danger, so as not to follow the calling of the Spirit of God.

units.la: Quod si vero a piorum et sanctorum consiliis incon-sideratis cavere nobis debemus, quanto magis cavere debent ij, quos nescio quae species quidem aliqua pietatis commendat, et qui sub amicitiae praetextu suadent, quae palam turpia, inhonesta et iniusta sunt. Tales sunt, qui ut Tyrannorum offensam, et praesens vitae periculum vitemus, nos idola colere, et superstitionibus impijs communicare, aut alio profugere iubent. Habent hi rationes carni quidem plausibiles, dum monent, ut nos melioribus temporibus referuemus, neque nostra ope et consolatione fraudemus eos, quibus aliquo modo prodesse possumus. Sed revera obstaculo nobis sunt, et Satanae oratores censeri debent (Amasiae similes) qui hoc quaerit, ut nos a fidei confessione, et vero Dei cultu abster-reat, et nostro exemplo etiam ad alios sedu-cendos abutatur.
units.tr: But if we ought to beware of the ill-considered counsels of the pious and holy, how much more ought those to beware whom some appearance of piety commends, and who under the pretext of friendship urge what is plainly shameful, dishonourable and unjust? Such are those who bid us, in order to avoid the displeasure of tyrants and present danger to life, to worship idols, to take part in impious superstitions, or to flee elsewhere. These men have arguments that are indeed plausible to the flesh, when they advise us to save ourselves for better times, and not to deprive those to whom we can in some way be of help of our aid and comfort. But in truth they are an obstacle to us, and ought to be counted as ambassadors of Satan (like Amasiah), who seeks to turn us away from the confession of the faith and the true worship of God, and to use our example also to seduce others.

units.la: Similes horum sunt, qui puellarum et matronarum pudicitiae insidiantur, et miris blanditiis ac lenocinijs ad scorta-tionem eas sollicitant: qui item ut cum mundo communemur, ludamus, castra sequamur, venurarias artes sectemur nos admonent. Volunt hi videri ex amicorum numero, qui nobis bene esse cupiant: sed revera Satanae sunt, et indigni, quibus aures praebeant, qui fidem in Christum profitentur. Et debet hoc propter eos quoque observari, qui indignius ferunt, si scelera et scandalorum publicorum authores suis nominibus appellentur.
units.tr: These are like those who lie in wait for the chastity of girls and matrons and with wonderful flatteries and enticements urge them toward harlotry; likewise they advise us to join with the world, to play, to follow the camp, and to pursue the hunter's arts. These men want to seem to be among our friends, who wish us well; but in truth they are Satan's agents, and unworthy to be listened to by those who profess faith in Christ. This should also be observed on account of those who take it ill if the authors of crimes and public scandals are called by their proper names.

units.la: Quid enim contra hos nimium dici potest, quando Petrum Dominus Satanam vocavit, qui pio et sancto zelo ipsum ab officio abducere conabatur?
units.tr: For what can be said too strongly against these men, since the Lord called Peter Satan, when he was trying, with a pious and holy zeal, to turn him away from his duty?

units.la: Sed audiamus quo argumento ipse hoc suum dictum confirmet: Nam non sapis (inquit) quae sunt Dei, sed quae sunt hominum. Primus Patris suggestionem secutus fuit Petrus, quando Christum confessus est, et ideo beatum hic pronuntiavit, et dignum iudicavit, cui domus sua dispensationem, et claves regni caelorum committeret. Nunc Satanam vocat, quod carnis rationem secutus, non quid Deus velit, sed quod sibi commodum aut utile videbatur, spectavit. Unde colligimus, ad regnum Dei non idoneos fore, qui non quae Dei sunt sapiunt, sed humanam prudentiam in consilium adhibent.
units.tr: But let us hear by what argument he himself confirms this saying of his: "For you do not savour" (he says) "the things of God, but the things of men." Peter first followed the suggestion of the Father when he confessed Christ, and therefore here he pronounced him blessed and judged him worthy to whom his house's stewardship and the keys of the kingdom of heaven should be committed. Now he calls him Satan, because, following the reasoning of the flesh, he looked not to what God wills but to what seemed convenient or useful to himself. From this we gather that those who do not savour the things of God, but bring human prudence into their counsel, will not be fit for the kingdom of God.

units.la: Rationem huius dicti Paulus monstrat, scribens: Propterea quod intelligentia carnis, inimicitia est adversus Deum. Carnis autem vocabulo hominem nondum renatum intelligit, quem alibi animalem dicit, quod nihil norit aut sapiat, quam quod natiuus intellectus suggerit.
units.tr: Paul shows the reason for this saying, writing: "Because the mind of the flesh is enmity against God." By the word flesh he understands the man not yet reborn, whom elsewhere he calls the natural man, who knows and savours nothing beyond what his native understanding suggests.

units.la: Itaque sensus iflorum verborum est. Quicquid homo ex se ipso sapit, novit, intelligit, vult et cupit, illud omne Deo inimicum est, cui ille, quantus quantus est, reluctatur, et obstiliter resistit. Et ne hoc durius aequo dixisse putetur, alia ratione id quoque confirmat, addens: Legi enim Dei non subijcitur, nam ne potest quidem. Ergo non voluntas modo prava est in homine, sed eidem neque vires aliquae sunt, quibus illam corrigat, aut Deo obedire cogat. Quod idem Apostolus suo exemplo probat, quando se videre ait Legem aliam in membris suis rebellantem Legi mentis suae, quae ipsum captivum reddat Legi peccati. Et posteaquam graue certamen quod intra se sensit, tandem exclamat. Miser ego homo, quis me eripiet ex isto corpore mortis? Et mox subjicit: Gratias ago Deo per IESVM CHRISTVM Dominum nostrum. Discimus ergo ex his Domini verbis, aliam esse sapientiam Dei, aliam hominum. Dei sapientia est, quam ex verbi femine renati per fidem consequuntur in Christo, qui nobis a Patre sapientia factus est. Et haec quia in solum Deum respicit, et eius Verbo atque Spiritu ducitur, neque ipsa fallit, neque fallit alios: Humana vero sapientia est, quae huius saeculi filii superbiunt, quibus summa prudentia videtur, aliorum placitis et exemplis se accommodare, curare ut tibi bene sit, et proxima quaeque pericula declinare, stultos autem putare eos, qui ipsi futurorum praesentia negligunt, et contemptis huius saeculi commodis in cruce Christi gloriari. Quam turpiter autem et misere fallantur, qui ita sentiunt, quotidianis exemplis docemur. Itaque procul relictis omnibus caecae carnis et infelicis mundi placitis, in Filium Dei IESVM CHRISTVM respiciamus, et hunc ducem secuti aspiremus ad caelestia bona, quae illi nobis meruit. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria et potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: So the sense of these words is this: whatever man savours, knows, understands, wills and desires from himself, all that is hostile to God, and against him, however great he may be, he struggles and resists stubbornly. And lest this be thought said more harshly than is fair, he confirms it also by another reason, adding: "For it is not subject to the law of God, for indeed it cannot be." Therefore the will in man is not only depraved, but neither does he have any powers by which he might correct it or compel it to obey God. The same Apostle proves this by his own example, when he says that he sees another law in his members rebelling against the law of his mind, which makes him captive to the law of sin. And after the grievous struggle he felt within himself, at last he cries out: "Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from this body of death?" And soon he adds: "I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord." We learn therefore from these words of the Lord that the wisdom of God is one thing, and the wisdom of men another. The wisdom of God is that which those reborn through the seed of the word obtain through faith in Christ, who has been made wisdom to us from the Father. And since this looks only to God and is led by his Word and Spirit, it neither deceives nor misleads others. Human wisdom, however, is that which the sons of this age pride themselves on, who think it the highest prudence to accommodate themselves to the pleasures and examples of others, to take care that things go well for them, and to avoid every nearby danger, while regarding as fools those who neglect present things for the sake of future ones and who, scorning the advantages of this age, glory in the cross of Christ. How shamefully and wretchedly those who think this way are deceived, we are taught by daily examples. Therefore, leaving aside all the pleasures of blind flesh and the unhappy world, let us look to the Son of God Jesus Christ, and following him as our leader, let us aspire to the heavenly goods which he has merited for us. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCIX.
units.tr: HOMILY 209.

units.la: Tunc IESVS dixit discipulis suis: Si quis vult post me venire, abneget semetipsum, et tollat crucem suam, ac sequatur me.
units.tr: Then Jesus said to his disciples: If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me.

units.la: Quamuis Dominus et Seruator noster IESVS CHRISTVS nuper suis discipulis, qui ipsum Dei Filium et VNCTVM Dei id est, promissum humani generis Seruatorem, Regem et Sacerdotem populi Dei esse confessi erant, aperte praedixisset, quid sibi Ierosolymae eventurum sit, nimirum quod ipsum infame et diram mortem subire oporteat: pollicetur tamen, quod tertio die a mortuis resurrecturus sit. Causa huius praedictionis est, ut illos in fide sua confirmet et adversus futurum crucis scandalum praemuniat.
units.tr: Although our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ had recently told his disciples plainly what would happen to him at Jerusalem, namely that he must suffer an infamous and dreadful death, these disciples had confessed that he was the Son of God, the Anointed One, that is, the promised Saviour of mankind, the King and Priest of God's people. Yet he also promised that he would rise from the dead on the third day. The purpose of this prediction was to strengthen them in their faith and to arm them in advance against the scandal of the coming cross.

units.la: {y} Prodest ante omnia diligenter videre, qua occasione et quibus ista dixerit Dominus. Matthaeus ijs, quae proxime praecesserunt, hunc locum connectens ista tunc dicta esse scribit, quando Petrus Christum increpare et ab instituto suo dehortari ausus, et ideo graviter correptus fuit. ciunt, eius solius gloriam quærunt, neq; se ab illo diuelli sinunt: quales scimus fuisse Apostolos, qui etsi suos tunc errores & nævos haberent, tamen licuit eis vere dicere: Ecce nos reliquimus omnia, & secuti sumus te. E contra erant alij, qui non tam post Christum veniebant, quàm post regni terreni spem, aut miracula, quibus quotidie multorum morbis medebatur, & interdum gratuito epulo senatores suos excipiebat: quod eis apud Ioannem exprobrat. Et hodie multi passim inueniuntur, qui cum post Christum venire se simulent, nihil aliud tamen, quàm priuatum commodum, dignitates, sacerdotia opima, vel carnis licentiam quærunt. Vt ergo inter hos & germanos discipulos discernat, in publico omnibus loquitur: Si quis vult post me venire, abneget semetipsum, &c.
units.tr: {y} It is useful, before all else, to see carefully on what occasion and to whom the Lord said these things. Matthew, connecting this passage with what came just before, writes that these words were spoken when Peter dared to rebuke Christ and to dissuade him from his purpose, and for this he was sharply rebuked. They follow, seek his glory alone, and do not allow themselves to be torn away from him. Such, we know, were the Apostles, who, although they still had their errors and blemishes, could nevertheless truly say: "Behold, we have left all things and followed you." On the other hand, there were others who came after Christ not so much from attachment to him as from hope of an earthly kingdom, or for the sake of the miracles by which he daily healed many people, and sometimes he even entertained his senators with a free feast; John reproaches them for this. And today many are found everywhere who, while pretending to come after Christ, seek nothing else than private advantage, dignities, rich benefices, or licence for the flesh. So, in order to distinguish these from his true disciples, he speaks in public to all: "If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself," and so on.

units.la: Est autem probè obseruandum, quòd indefinitè loquitur. Quasi diceret: Quisquis ille est, qui meus vult esse discipulus, siue ille doctus aut indoctus, diues vel pauper, herus aut seruus, mas aut fœmina fuerit, vt intelligat non sufficere externam mei nominis professionem, sed vt huic respondeat opus esse. Traditur ergo hic vniuersalis regula, quæ ex æquo ad omnes pertinet, qui Christiani censeri volunt, cuiuscunque sint loci aut ordinis. Nam vt sæpè diximus, sicut in CHRISTO IESV non est Iudæus aut Græcus, non Scytha aut barbarus, non seruus aut herus: sic vitæ genus nullum est, nulla personæ conditio, quæ aliquem ab obsequio, quod illi debetur eximat. Ad fidei enim obedientiam vocantur, quotquot Euangelium eius audiunt. Quia vero ad vnam & eandem regulam omnes obstringuntur, abolentur vtiq; omnes aliarum sectarum regulæ, quæ salutem extra Christum monstrant, & contra Apostoli præceptum hominum discipulos & Iudæos faciunt eos, qui in Baptismo Christo nomen dederunt. Et sane cum hi omnes non ex illo bibant, qui solus est fons aquæ viuentis, perpetua siti æfluent oportet. At quicunq; (vt Paulus scribit) ad hanc regulam, quam Christus hoc loco tradit, gressum suum dirigunt, super eos erit pax & misericordia, & super Israelem Dei, Id est, hi veri Israelitæ sunt, in quibus non est dolus (vt de Nathanaele Christus pronunciauit) & tales pro suis Deus agnoscit, qui non inani nominis professione ducitur, sed corda inspicit, & nos in Filio suo nouam Creaturam vult fieri. Porrò videamus regulæ huius capita, quæ tria sunt.
units.tr: It must be carefully observed that he speaks indefinitely. As if he were saying: whoever he is who wishes to be my disciple, whether he be learned or unlearned, rich or poor, master or servant, male or female, let him understand that an outward profession of my name is not enough, but that there must be a corresponding deed. Here, therefore, a universal rule is laid down, which applies equally to all who wish to be counted Christians, of whatever place or rank. For, as we have often said, in Christ Jesus there is neither Jew nor Greek, neither Scythian nor barbarian, neither slave nor free; so there is no way of life and no condition of person that exempts anyone from the obedience that is owed to him. For all who hear his gospel are called to the obedience of faith. But because all are bound to one and the same rule, all the rules of other sects are surely abolished, those which show salvation outside Christ, and which, contrary to the Apostle's precept, make disciples of men and Jews of those who have given their name to Christ in Baptism. And indeed, since they do not drink from him, who alone is the fountain of living water, they must flow away in perpetual thirst. But whoever (as Paul writes) direct their steps by this rule which Christ gives in this place, "peace and mercy will be upon them, and upon the Israel of God." That is, these are the true Israelites, in whom there is no guile (as Christ declared of Nathanael), and God acknowledges as his own those who are not led by an empty profession of name, but who look upon the heart, and who wishes us to become a new creature in his Son. Let us now look at the heads of this rule, which are three.

units.la: Primum est, vt semetipsum homo abneget. A nobis ipsis ergo nos vult initium facere, & hoc præcepto totam hominis naturam damnat cum omnibus suis viribus & desiderijs. Quia enim in peccato, quod ex primo parente in nos deriuatum est, concepti & nati sumus, non solum peccatores, sed serui peccati sumus, quorum cogitationes, figmenta, & affectus prauì sunt a pueritia. Ex hac naturæ corruptione philautia originem ducit, cuius tanta vis est, vt in nostris studijs pessimis nobismetipsis delitias faciamus, & ne Dei quidè Verbum patienter feramus, quod vt illis relictis aliam vitæ rationem instituamus, nos admonet. Ideò Paulus (sicuti nuper diximus) carnis intelligentiam dicebat esse inimicitiam aduersus Deum, eò quòd Legi Dei non solùm non subijciatur, sed ne possit quidem illi subijci. Cùm ergo, qui in carne viuunt, id est, qui innatis sibi affectibus & studijs ducuntur, non possint Deo placere, necesse est, vt nosmetipsos abnegemus, id est, vt renuntiemus carnis rationi, intellectui, affectibus, denique placitis nostris omnibus, nosque totos humiliemus sub potenti Dei manu, & huic nos consecremus per fidei obedientiam. Idem ergo hic Christus præcepit, quod alibi per regenerationis mysterium docet, item per mortificationem membrorum terrestrium. Paulus, quæ in eo consistit, vt omnem vitiosæ naturæ, quæ nos a Dei obedientia & cœlestium meditatione abstrahit, vim atq; affectus frangamus, ne illa in nobis dominetur. Exempla huius abnegationis multa in Scripturis extant, inter quæ admodum memorabile est Abrahami patris credentium, qui Deo vocante patrios lares & natale solum cum cognatis & affinibus charis reliquit, ignarus quò nam se conferre deberet, & vbi ei sedem quietis parasset Deus. Idem in extremam vsque senectam, filium ex Sara nascituum sperauit, cùm ipsa rerum naturam sibi omnem negaret: & eundem proprijs manibus mactare voluit, cùm itaiuberet Deus. At nihil horum fecisset, nisi φοβας quoque & naturales cordis affectiones abnegauisset. Idem Mosem fecisse constat, quando relicta aula & huius delitijs ad Israelitas transfuit, ex quibus nihil lætum aut vtile sperare poterat. Seipsum quoq; Paulus abnegauit, quando omnia quæ mundo eximia putantur, pro stercoribus & damnis habuit, vt Christum lucrifaceret. Et vt hoc ipsum faciant, qui germani discipuli IESV CHRISTI esse volunt, plus quàm necesse est, quando vbiq, sese offerunt, quæ fidem oppugnant, & nos ne in Dei semitis progrediamur, remorari solent. Opus igitur est assiduis precibus, vt ipse Dominus nos reluctantes postea se trahat, sicuti sponsa apud Solomonem canit. Proderit etiam diligens rerum huius sæculi meditatio, in quibus nihil est, quod Dei vocationi præferri mereatur. Minus etiam hic laborabunt, qui a pueris disciplinæ assueuerunt. At cum ea sit nostri sæculi calamitas, vt pleriq; terrenis studijs addicti cælestia negligant, imò pauci credant cælos esse, in quibus vitam aliam postea hanc sinus vituri, disciplinam vero neq; parentes adhibeant filijs adhuc tenerioribus, neq; illam admittant pueri, quid mirū est, si rari admodum sint, qui non impingant ad primum hunc Christianæ professionis gradum, quo nosmetipsos abnegare iubemur.
units.tr: The first is that a man deny himself. He wills, therefore, that we make a beginning with ourselves, and by this precept he condemns the whole of human nature with all its powers and desires. For since we were conceived and born in the sin that has been derived to us from our first parent, we are not only sinners but slaves of sin, whose thoughts, imaginings and affections have been evil from childhood. From this corruption of nature self-love takes its origin, and its force is so great that in our most wicked pursuits we make ourselves our own delight, and cannot patiently bear even the Word of God, which admonishes us to abandon these things and to adopt another manner of life. Therefore Paul (as we said recently) called the understanding of the flesh enmity against God, because it is not subject to the Law of God, and indeed cannot be made subject to it. Since, then, those who live in the flesh, that is, who are led by affections and pursuits innate in them, cannot please God, it is necessary that we deny ourselves, that is, that we renounce the reason of the flesh, the intellect, the affections, and finally all our own pleasures, and that we humble ourselves entirely under the mighty hand of God, and dedicate ourselves to him through obedience of faith. So Christ here commands the same thing that he teaches elsewhere through the mystery of regeneration, and likewise through the mortification of earthly members. This consists in breaking the force and affections of the corrupt nature, which draws us away from obedience to God and from meditation on heavenly things, so that it may not rule in us. There are many examples of this self-denial in the Scriptures, among which the memorable example of Abraham, father of believers, is especially notable, who, when God called him, left his ancestral home and native soil with his dear kinsfolk and relatives, not knowing where he should go, or where God would prepare a resting place for him. The same man hoped, even into extreme old age, for a son to be born of Sarah, although nature itself denied him all this; and he was willing to slay that same son with his own hands when God so commanded. Yet he would have done none of these things unless he had also denied fears [φόβους] and the natural affections of the heart. It is agreed that Moses did the same, when he left the court and its pleasures and went over to the Israelites, from whom he could hope for nothing joyful or profitable. Paul too denied himself, when he counted all those things that are thought outstanding by the world as dung and loss, so that he might gain Christ. And so, those who wish to be the true disciples of Jesus Christ must do the same, more than is necessary, when, whenever they present themselves everywhere, those things which assail the faith, and which are wont to hinder us from advancing in the paths of God. Therefore there is need of constant prayer, so that the Lord himself may draw us after him when we resist, as the bride sings in Solomon. Careful meditation on the things of this world will also help, in which there is nothing that deserves to be preferred to God's calling. Those will also labour less who have been accustomed to discipline from boyhood. But since it is the calamity of our age that most people, given over to earthly pursuits, neglect heavenly things, and indeed few believe that there are heavens in which they will live another life after this one, and since parents do not impose discipline on their children while they are still tender, nor do the children themselves admit it, it is no wonder that very few fail to stumble at this first step of Christian profession, by which we are commanded to deny ourselves.

units.la: Alterum regulæ Christi caput est: Et tollat crucem suam, Lucas addit, Quotidie. Crux olim infame & acerbissimum mortis genus fuit, & a Deo maledictū, quod ipse Christus pro nobis sufferre debuit. Sub huius igitur vocabulo omnis generis afflictiones continentur: quarum vita hæc plena est. Nam per peccatum cum morte omnes eius satellites ingressi sunt, labor, cura, morbi, fames, sitis, & quæcunq; vitam hanc nobis acerbam faciunt. Habent tamen pij afflictiones proprias, quæ fidem in Christum comitantur. Quia enim Veritatis lucem mundus odit, non potest non eos etiam odisse ac persequi, penes quos illa lucet, & qui in ea ambulant. Admonet de hoc Dominus frequenter in Evangelio, & quæcunq; propter ipsius nomen nobis accidunt, Crucis nomine dignatur, vt doceat, nos in his perferendis ipsius sactos fieri, neq; nobis graue aut iniquum debere censeri, si acerbissima quæq; subire cogamur. Quid enim tam graue, tam iniquum, tam acerbum nobis accidere potest, quod cum ijs conferri possit, quæ Dei Filius pro nobis pertulit? At quia propter innatam nobis impatientiam hic multa instituitione opus est, proderit singulas voces expendere.
units.tr: The second head of Christ's rule is: "And let him take up his cross." Luke adds: "daily." The cross was once an infamous and most bitter kind of death, and was accursed by God, and Christ himself had to suffer it for us. Under this name, therefore, every kind of affliction is included, and of these this life is full. For through sin death entered with all its attendants: toil, care, sickness, hunger, thirst, and whatever else makes this life bitter for us. Yet the godly have their own afflictions, which accompany faith in Christ. For since the world hates the light of truth, it cannot but hate and persecute also those in whom that light shines and who walk in it. The Lord often reminds us of this in the Gospel, and whatever befalls us on account of his name he honours with the name of cross, so that he may teach us that we are made like him in bearing these things, and that we ought not to think it grievous or unjust if we are compelled to undergo the most bitter things. For what can happen to us so grievous, so unjust, so bitter, that it can be compared with what the Son of God suffered for us? But because, on account of the impatience innate in us, much instruction is needed here, it will be useful to weigh the individual words.

units.la: Primo, tollat (inquit) crucem SVAM. Sua cuiusq; crux est, quam cuiq; Deus imponit. Solet enim hic huius sæculi aduersa dispensare, & (vt alio simili docet Scriptura) singulis suum calicem propinare, quem bibant. Et nouit ille quæ cruce nobis sit opus. Itaq; suam ferant singuli, neq; de ea permutanda aut excutienda cogitent. Peccatur hic multum a nonnullis, qui cum audiunt, Christianos homines necessario Crucem ferre oportere, non expectata vocatione Dei, non necessarios labores & aduersa sibi accersunt. Sic in Papatu Monachi, inter Evangelij professores Anabaptistæ faciunt, dum illi quidem vitam cælibem aut eremiticam, adhæc voluntariam paupertatem vouent, vel vigilijs, cilicijs & alijs se affligunt, quibus abstinere poterant, cum nullo Dei præcepto ad illa adigantur: hi vero relictis coniugibus & liberis atq; re domestica, & interdum patrio solo quoq; homines impie morosos sectantur, qui proprium vitæ genus, vt olim Esaiæ, sibi delegerunt. Vidi ego mulierem, quæ cum multis annis cum marito honeste vixisset, hoc furore percitam relictis septem liberis, & quidem minimo natu adhuc lactente, ad Anabaptistas profugisse, nec aliam sui facti excusationem prætexuisse, quam quod Christus nos ad crucem vocet. At qui habet vnum quodq; vitæ genus suam crucem, & vnusquisq; suam crucem ferre iubetur, eam nimirum, quam ipsi Deus in sua vocatione ambulanti imponit, nō alienam accersere. Neq; etiam tam iniquus aut morosus est Deus, vt nullas ferias, & otium omnino nullum suis concedat: sed sæpissime eos indulgentius tractat, quando vel eos infirmiores esse novit, quam vt laboribus & aduersis durioribus sufficiant, vel vt promissionibus suis fidem faciat, & alij exempla habeant, quibus se consolentur. Discant ergo omnes suam crucē gestare, vt neq; eam cum alijs commutare, neq; nouam pro suo arbitrio formare velint, aut nō necessarijs periculis se obijciendo Deum tentent, & superstitionis suæ pœnas dent.
units.tr: First, he says, let him take up HIS cross. Each person's cross is his own, which God lays on each one. For God is accustomed here to dispense the adversities of this age, and (as Scripture teaches in another similar place) to give each one his own cup to drink. And He knows what cross we need. So let each one bear his own, and let them not think of exchanging it or shaking it off. Many people go wrong here: when they hear that Christians must of necessity bear the cross, they bring upon themselves, without waiting for the call of God, labours and hardships that are not necessary. So among the Papists the monks do this, and among the professors of the Gospel the Anabaptists do it, while the monks vow celibate or eremitical life and voluntary poverty, and afflict themselves with night watches, hair shirts and other things, which they could have refrained from, since no command of God compels them to these things; and the Anabaptists, having left their wives and children, their household affairs and sometimes even their native soil, follow impiously morose men who, like Isaiah of old, have chosen for themselves a particular way of life. I have seen a woman who, having lived honourably with her husband for many years, was seized by this madness, abandoned seven children, the youngest still nursing, and fled to the Anabaptists; nor did she put forward any other excuse for her action than that Christ calls us to the cross. But each way of life has its own cross, and each one is commanded to bear his own cross, namely the one which God lays upon him in his calling as he walks, and not to seek out another's. Nor is God so unjust or morose that He grants his people no holidays and no rest at all; rather He very often treats them more gently, either when He knows they are too weak to endure harder labours and adversities, or so that He may make good his promises, and so that others may have examples by which to console themselves. Let all therefore learn to carry their own cross, so that they neither wish to exchange it with others, nor to devise a new one at their own pleasure, nor tempt God by exposing themselves to needless dangers, and so pay the penalty of their superstition.

units.la: Deinde tollendi verbo vtitur Dominus, quo alacritatem & voluntariam obedientiam nobis commendat, qualis in famulis frugi & fidelibus cernitur. Hi si onera aut sarcinas ab heris suis aliquo deferre iubeantur, mox sese operi accingunt, illas sponte in lumeros subleuant, & quo iussi sunt pergūr, licet nō semper ipsis constet, quod heri sui instituturi sit: Ita Christianum hominem facere conuenit. Nec enim semper Deus suorum præceptorum rationem nobis reddit: ius autem & imperium in nos habet mandandi quod vult. Meminerimus tunc nostri officij esse, vt faciamus quod ille iubet, qu bet, qui nihil temere mandat, cum sit sapientissimus, neq; non necessarijs oneribus nos grauat, cum nostri amans sit, & nostrae saluti consulcum velit, & ideo nos supra vires tentari non sinat. Vehementer ergo peccatur ab iis, qui si quid ferendum est, Deo litem intendunt, aut cur alios mitius tractet, interrogant: in quo Petrum aliquando offendisse legimus, quando quid de dilecto discipulo Ioanne Dominus constituisset, quaerebat. Sed quod illi tunc respondit Christus, hoc singuli sibi dictum putent: Si illum velim manere donec veniam, quid ad te? tu me sequere. Ioan.21.
units.tr: Next, the Lord uses the word "take up", by which He commends to us the eagerness and willing obedience which is seen in faithful and honest servants. If they are told to carry burdens or loads from their masters to some place, they at once set themselves to the task, lift them willingly onto their shoulders, and go where they were sent, even though it is not always clear to them what their master intends. So a Christian ought to act. For God does not always give us the reason for his commands; but He has the right and authority to command us what He wills. Let us remember that it is then our duty to do what He orders, since He who commands nothing rashly is most wise, and does not burden us with unnecessary weights, since He loves us and wishes to care for our salvation, and therefore does not allow us to be tried beyond our strength. Those therefore sin grievously who, if something must be borne, go to law with God, or ask why He treats others more gently. In this matter we read that Peter once gave offence, when he asked what the Lord had decided about his beloved disciple John. But let each one take to himself what Christ then answered: "If I wish him to remain until I come, what is that to you? Follow me." John 21.

units.la: Praeterea non temere iubet Christus, ut QVOTIDIE crucem nostram tollamus. Habet enim unaquaeq; dies suam afflictionem (ut Christus monet) neq; satis est manum aratro admouisse, sed ut in finem usq; perseueremus necesse est. Sic crucem suam indefesso studio tulerunt Patriarchae, inter quos Iacob, cum iam vitae annum centesimum tricesimum attigisset, & dies omnes sibi tristes & acerbos accidisse posset dicere, nullum tamen animi impatientis indicium praebuit. Sic Moses totis annis quadraginta crucem suam tulit, etiamsi ex contumaci & rebelli gente noua illi molestiae quotidie exorirentur. Idem de Prophetis plerisq; dici potest, quorum multi annos quadraginta & amplius in ministerio suo laborarunt. Fecerunt idem Apostoli, & inter hos Paulus in primis, qui per annos triginta & septem assiduis laboribus, curis & periculis exercitatus est. Arguitur hus exemplis eorum ignauia, qui ut serui malae frugis sibi ipsis ferias indicunt, priusquam opus suum absoluerunt: aut ut milites ignaui coronari volunt, priusquam victoriam assecuti sunt. Meminerint ergo discipuli Christi, non feriandum sibi esse, quoad ipsorum feriitio Deus uti voluerit. Et quia id carni durum & graue est, in Dei prouidentiam respiciant, sine cuius voluntate & decreto nihil eis accidit. Idem cum iustus sit, nemini facit iniuriam: magni aut beneficij loco censeri debet, quod nos Crucis filij sui socios facit, ut cum eodem olim glorificemur: in certaminibus autem iustus confirmet nos, quod quae in praesenti saeculo perpetimur, non paria sunt futurae gloriae, quae omnem sensum & intellectum hominis superat. Rom.8. Isa.64.
units.tr: Moreover, Christ does not command us to take up our cross DAILY without reason. For each day has its own affliction (as Christ warns), nor is it enough to have put one's hand to the plough; it is necessary to persevere to the end. In this way the Patriarchs bore their cross with unwearied zeal, among whom Jacob, when he had already reached the hundred and thirtieth year of his life, and could say that all his days had been sad and bitter, nevertheless showed no sign of an impatient spirit. So Moses bore his cross for the whole of forty years, although new troubles arose for him every day from a stubborn and rebellious people. The same can be said of most of the Prophets, many of whom laboured in their ministry for forty years and more. The Apostles did the same, and among them Paul above all, who for thirty-seven years was exercised by constant labours, cares and dangers. By these examples the idleness of those is condemned who, like wicked and unprofitable servants, grant themselves holidays before they have finished their work, or like lazy soldiers wish to be crowned before they have won the victory. Let the disciples of Christ therefore remember that they must not take rest until God chooses to use their rest. And since this is hard and burdensome to the flesh, let them look to God's providence, without whose will and decree nothing happens to them.
