Since He is just, He does injury to no one; it ought to be counted a great and good thing that He makes us companions of His Son's cross, so that we may be glorified together with Him; and in our conflicts the just God will strengthen us, for the sufferings of the present age are not equal to the future glory, which surpasses all the sense and understanding of man. Rom. 8; Isa. 64.

units.la: Restat tertium regulae Christi membrum, quod est: Ac sequatur me. Id vero non debet de corpore intelligi, quo ille in coelos abiit, quo nobis non licet illum sequi, quoad vitae huius metam attigerimus. Spiritualem ergo sequelam nobis commendat, quae in duobus consistit. Primum fides est, qua ille apprehenditur, qui ipsissima Lux est, quam qui sequuntur, errare non possunt. Huc pertinet quod ipse dicit: Ego sum Lux illa mundi: qui me sequitur, non ambulabit in tenebris, sed habebit lumen vitae. Item, ambulate donec Lucem habetis, ne vos tenebrae deprehendant. Vbi expositionis loco subijcit: Dum Lucem habetis, credite in Lucem, ut filij Lucis sitis. Ergo in Christum credamus oportet, si illu sequi volumus. In hunc autem credunt, qui (ut alibi docuimus) firmo & constanti animi assensu talem agnoscunt, qualis in Scriptura describitur, & qualem in Symbolo Apostolico profitemur: Aeternum scilicet Dei Filium, qui propter nos ex Virgine homo factus, unicus mundi redemptor & noster apud Patrem Mediator est. Obseruari hoc debet diligenter propter eos, qui se Christi sectatores esse dicunt, quando nouum vitae genus eligunt, & superstitiones frigidissimas sequuntur, quae ab illo abducunt ad humanae iustitiae, quae nulla est, fiduciam. Alterum in quo Christi sequela consistit, est imitatio exempli, quo ille nobis praeiuit. Sunt quidem in illo, quae imitari non possumus, qualia sunt diuinae virtutis opera, quibus se aeterna Dei viuentis Filium, & promissum Seruatorem esse demonstrauit. At praeter ista habemus in illo exemplar perfectissimum obedientiae, quam Patri praestitit usq; ad mortem crucis: Innocentia item, quam nulli hostes suis calumniis, nulli falsi testes suis mendacijs denigrare potuerunt: Charitatis incomparabilis, qua miseros nos, qui filij irae & inimici eramus, ita complexus est, ut seipsum pro nobis in mortem dederit: Patientiae, qua iniurias omnes vicit, ut vindictae cupiditatem ne verbulo quidem vno prodiderit: Fidei denique constantis, qua Patrem inter diros animi & corporis dolores inuocauit, & eidem iam morituros animam commendauit. In his illum imitemur, si post eum venire, & germani eius discipuli esse volumus. Neq; nos illius periculi metus, neq; rei difficultas terreat. Qui enim haec praecipit, idem vires dat, ut ea praestemus: qui nos ad se vocat, idem manum nobis porrigit, & post se trahit. Denique nobis in hac valle umbrae mortis ambulantibus, non dux modo, sed pastor quoq;, fidelis, lux item, panis & fons vitae est, in quo nihil nobis deerit. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: There remains the third part of Christ's rule, which is: "And let him follow me." This must not be understood of the body, by which He went up into heaven, so that we may not follow Him in that way until we have reached the goal of this life. He therefore commends to us a spiritual following, which consists of two things. The first is faith, by which He is apprehended, who is the very Light itself, and those who follow Him cannot go astray. To this belongs what He Himself says: "I am the Light of the world; he who follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life." Likewise, "Walk while you have the Light, lest darkness overtake you." Where, by way of explanation, He adds: "While you have the Light, believe in the Light, that you may be sons of the Light." Therefore we must believe in Christ, if we wish to follow Him. Now they believe in Him who (as we have taught elsewhere) acknowledge with a firm and steadfast assent of mind such a one as is described in Scripture, and as we profess in the Apostles' Creed: namely, the eternal Son of God, who for our sake was made man of the Virgin, the only Redeemer of the world and our Mediator with the Father. This ought to be carefully observed on account of those who say they are followers of Christ when they choose a new way of life, and follow the coldest superstitions, which lead them away from Him to a confidence in human righteousness, which is no righteousness at all. The other element in which the following of Christ consists is the imitation of the example which He has set before us. Indeed there are things in Him which we cannot imitate, such as the works of divine power, by which He showed that He is the eternal Son of the living God and the promised Saviour. But besides these we have in Him the most perfect example of obedience, which He rendered to the Father even unto the death of the cross; likewise of innocence, which no enemies could blacken by their calumnies, and no false witnesses by their lies; of incomparable charity, by which He embraced us, wretched as we were, sons of wrath and enemies, so that He gave Himself for us to death; of patience, by which He overcame all injuries, so that He did not betray the desire for vengeance even by a single word; and finally of steadfast faith, by which, amid the dreadful anguish of soul and body, He called upon the Father and commended His spirit to Him as He was about to die. In these let us imitate Him, if we wish to come after Him and to be His true disciples. Let neither the fear of that danger nor the difficulty of the matter terrify us. For He who commands these things also gives the strength to perform them; He who calls us to Himself also stretches out His hand to us and draws us after Him. Finally, as we walk in this valley of the shadow of death, He is not only our leader but also our faithful shepherd, and also our light, bread and fountain of life, in whom nothing will be lacking to us. To Him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: Phil.2. Rom.5. Psal.23.
units.tr: Phil. 2; Rom. 5; Psal. 23.

units.la: HOMILIA CCX.
units.tr: HOMILY CCX.

units.la: Quisquis enim voluerit animam suam seruare, perdet eam: quisquis autem perdiderit animam suam mea causa, inueniet eam. Quid enim prodest homini si totum mundum lucratus fuerit, anima vero sua multetur? aut quam dabit homo compensationem animae suae? Futurum est enim ut filius hominis veniat in gloria patris sui cum angelis suis: & tunc reddet unicuique secundum facta eius. Amen dico vobis, sunt quidam ex iis qui hic astant, qui nequaquam gustabunt mortem, vsque dum viderint Filium hominis venientem in regno suo.
units.tr: For whoever wishes to save his life will lose it; but whoever loses his life for my sake will find it. For what does it profit a man if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul? Or what will a man give in exchange for his soul? For the Son of Man is going to come in the glory of his Father with his angels, and then he will repay each one according to his deeds. Truly I say to you, there are some of those standing here who will by no means taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom.

units.la: Quoniam aeternus Dei Filius propter nos sese exinanivit & homo factus est, & ita nos dilexit, ut seipsum pro nobis in mortem tradiderit, aequum est, ut nos vicissim ita eum diligamus, ut si opus sit, non dedignemur propter illum extrema quaeque perpeti. Ideo nuper generalem regulam praescripsit, quam omnes sequi debent, quotquot ipsius discipuli censeri, & in ipso seruari cupiunt. Ea est, ut seipsos abnegent, crucem suam, id est, quicquid ipsis Deus imponit, quotidie animo prompto & alacri in humeros suos recipiant, & in ipsum intenti per fidem, eius exemplum, quo nobis praeiuit, intrepide sequantur. At sunt haec carni dura & aspera, eo quod propter innatam nobis philautiam omnes quoad hoc seculum sibi bene esse volunt, & a cruce atque aduersis abhorrent. Itaque, etsi iure optimo nos totos sibi vindicet Christus, multa tamen sunt, quae nos ab eo avocant. Alij enim vitae suae metuunt, alij opes & alia vitae huius commoda amittere, aut de dignitatibus suis periclitari nolunt, & magnorum atque potentum hominum fauorem caelestibus bonis praeferunt. Omnium vero efficacissimum scandalum est, quod multi num quae vita post hanc mortalem alia sit, dubitant, & proinde nouissimum Christi aduentum & retributionem, quae tunc fiet, vel omnino negant, vel saltem in dubium vocant. Ideo Dominus aduersus haec omnia argumentis validissimis nos confirmat.
units.tr: Since the eternal Son of God emptied himself for us, became man, and loved us so much that he gave himself up to death for us, it is only right that we in turn love him, so that, if need be, we do not refuse to suffer any extremity for his sake. Therefore he recently laid down a general rule, which all must follow who wish to be counted his disciples and to be preserved in him. It is this: that they deny themselves and take up their cross daily, that is, whatever God lays upon them, on their shoulders, with a ready and eager mind, and that, fixing their eyes on him through faith, they boldly follow his example, by which he has gone before us. But these things are hard and bitter to the flesh, because, through our innate self-love, everyone wants to be well off in this age and shrinks from the cross and from adversity. Thus, although Christ rightly claims us wholly for himself, there are many things that draw us away from him. Some fear for their lives; others do not want to lose wealth and other comforts of this life, or to risk their positions, and they prefer the favour of great and powerful men to heavenly goods. But the most effective stumbling block of all is that many doubt whether there is any life after this mortal one, and therefore either altogether deny Christ's final coming and the retribution that will then take place, or at least call it into question. So the Lord strengthens us against all these things with most powerful arguments.

units.la: Principio aduersus mortis metum nos instruit. Est quod doctrina ista admodum necessaria, eo quod vitae cupiditas omnibus inhaeret, & nisi recte gubernetur, causa praecipua est, ut multi suae dignitatis & officij immemores ea faciant, quorum illos postea vehementer pudet & poenitet. In primis autem fidei verae abnegatione multi hoc argumento excusant, quod vita nihil pretiosius esse, & semel amissam nulla ratione recuperari posse dicunt. Ostendit ergo periculum, quod isti sibi ipsis accersunt, & docet nullos vitae suae penas consulere, quam eos qui illam cum fidei suae abnegatione seruare volunt. Ait enim: Quisquis voluerit animam suam seruare, perdet eam. Quisquis autem perdiderit animam suam mea causa, inueniet eam. Apud Ioannem hanc sententiam sic enuntiat: Qui amat animam suam, perdet eam: & qui odit animam suam in hoc mundo, in vitam aeternam custodiet eam. Anima autem in praesenti sumitur pro vita, quam in hoc seculo viuimus: quod frequens est in sacris literis. Hanc amant & seruare volunt homines carnales & delicatuli, qui nihil praeter huius seculi delitias & commoda nouerunt, & proinde ne illam amittant, aut sibi amaram & acerbam reddant, Christum potius & eius Euangelium volunt relinquere. Econtra vitam odisse dicuntur mundi iudicio, qui quando de Christo agitur, omnia huius seculi commoda vna cum vita amittere malunt, quam ab illo diuelli, quem ceu sponsum animae suae super omnia diligunt. Sed videamus quid de vtrisque dicatur.
units.tr: First, he instructs us against the fear of death. This teaching is very necessary, because the desire for life clings to everyone, and unless it is rightly governed, it is the chief cause why many, forgetful of their dignity and duty, do things for which they later feel deep shame and regret. Above all, in denying the true faith, many excuse themselves with this argument: that life is the most precious thing, and once lost cannot be recovered by any means. He therefore shows the danger that such people bring upon themselves, and teaches that no one takes less care of his life than those who want to keep it by denying their faith. For he says: "Whoever wants to save his life will lose it; but whoever loses his life for my sake will find it." In John he states this saying thus: "He who loves his life will lose it, and he who hates his life in this world will keep it to eternal life." Now "soul" in the present passage is taken for the life we live in this age, which is common in the sacred writings. Carnal and effeminate men, who know nothing but the delights and comforts of this age, love this life and want to preserve it; so, lest they lose it or make it bitter and harsh for themselves, they prefer to abandon Christ and his Gospel. On the contrary, those are said to hate their life by the judgment of the world who, when it comes to Christ, prefer to lose all the comforts of this age along with life rather than be torn away from him whom above all they love as the bridegroom of their soul. But let us see what is said of each of these.

units.la: De primis illis ait: Quisquis animam suam ita amat & seruatam cupit, vt nulla futurae & caelestis vitae cura habita, me abnegat, & verbi mei disciplina coerceri nolit, perdet eam. Rationes huius dicti multae & graues sunt. Primo inutili cura & solicitudine sese ipsi fatigant. Nam etsi periculum praesens declinent, adhuc tamen communi lege moriendi tenentur, quam omnibus impositum Deus, & quae via est, vniuersae terrae: adhaec nesciunt dierum suorum numerum, & plerunque nihil huius cogitantibus, & omni opinione citius ipsis hora mortis obrepit. Deinde idem conscientiae carnificinam sibi ipsis accersunt, quae nihil acerbius homini accidere potest, & quae non modo vitam acerbam facit, sed multos huius cursum violenta morte abrumpere cogit. Quod si conscientiae terrores ad tempus excutiant, & simul omni etiâ Dei timore posito securi in delictis pergant, qui viuentes mortui sunt, vt de vidua luxuriante Paulus scribit, & nihil a brutis differunt. Adhanc Christum abnegando, qui solus vita est, mortis mancipia fiunt & morituri sentiunt quid fe-cerint, incerti autem salutis de animae etiam interitu cum infelice Adriano Imperatore quiritan-tur: Animula vagula blandula, Quae nunc abibis in loca, &c? Et idem apud posteros infamem sui nominis memoriam relinquunt. Deniq; non consistere possunt in resurrectione iustorum, neque eos profuis tunc Christus agnoscet, sed ad sempiternos corporis & animae cruciatus damnabun-tur: vt paulo post dicetur. Itaque vitam praesentis saeculi male feruando & hanc & aeternam amittunt.
units.tr: Of the first he says: whoever loves his soul so much, and wants it kept safe, that, taking no thought for the future and heavenly life, he denies me and is unwilling to be restrained by the discipline of my word, will lose it. There are many weighty reasons for this saying. First, (1) they wear themselves out with useless care and anxiety. For even if they avoid the present danger, they are still bound by the common law of dying, which God has imposed on all, and which is the way of all the earth. Besides, they do not know the number of their days, and for the most part, when they do not think of this, the hour of death creeps upon them more quickly than any expectation. Second, (2) they bring upon themselves the torture of conscience, which can befall a man nothing more bitter, and which not only makes life miserable but often forces many to cut its course short by a violent death. But if the terrors of conscience are for a time shaken off, and, with all fear of God laid aside, they go on securely in their sins, they are living dead, as Paul writes of the wanton widow, and differ in nothing from brute beasts. By denying Christ, who alone is life, they become slaves of death; and when they are about to die, they feel what they have done, and, uncertain of their salvation, they lament even the loss of the soul, like the unhappy Emperor Hadrian: "Little wandering, charming soul, where now will you go?" Third, (3) they leave behind an infamous memory of their name for posterity. Finally, (4) they cannot stand in the resurrection of the just, nor will Christ then acknowledge them as profitable, but they will be condemned to eternal torments of body and soul, as will be said shortly. Thus, by badly preserving the life of the present age, they lose both it and eternal life.

units.la: E contra qui vitam hanc mortalem odit respectu Christi: & vt hunc retineat, illam amittit, amittendo inuenit eam & vere in aeternum feruat. Etenim qui id faciunt, ij se totos Christo con-secrant, in quo vere viuunt, & idem in ipsis viuit, vt cum Apostolo possint dicere: Viuo non am-plius ego, sed viuit in me Christus: vitam autem quam nunc viuo, per fidem Filij Dei viuo, qui dilexit me, & tradidit semetipsum pro me. Et haec demum vera hominis vita in hoc saeculo dici meretur, cum prophani (vt nuper diximus) non aliam viuant, quam quae eis cum brutis animan-tibus communis est. Deinde inter afflictiones & pericula confirmantur Dei spiritu, qui salutis arrhabo est, & (vt Psaltes ille diuinus canit) pro multitudine cogitationum, quibus distrahun-tur consolationes dulcissimas suggerit, quibus animam suam exhilarent. Praeterea per veteris ho-minis mortificationem seipsos infinitis molestijs liberant, & vitae fructus ferunt. Morituri autem spem vitae melioris habent in Christo repositam, qui mortis terrores discutit, vt sciant se a morte in vitam transfire: Itaq; animam illi commendant, & laeti in vitae aeternae & caelestis possessionem transeunt. Verissimè ergo hoc dicitur, quòd isti dum vitam oderunt & amittunt, eandem inueniât, imò custodiant extra omne periculum. Etenim Paulo teste vita eorum cum Christo in Deo ab-scondita est: quando igitur Christus, vita illa nostra, patefactus fuerit, tunc & ipsi cum eo decla-rabuntur vere gloriosi. Nam & corpora illis restituentur, & Christo venienti in nubibus caeli ob-viam rapientur per aerem, vt cum eodem in caelis viuant & regnent. Et haec illa beata spes est, qua Martyres olim confirmati diros omnium tormentorum cruciatus inuicto animi robore su-perarunt.
units.tr: On the other hand, he who hates this mortal life for the sake of Christ, and loses it in order to keep Christ, finds it by losing it and truly preserves it for eternity. For those who do this consecrate themselves wholly to Christ, in whom they truly live, and he lives in them, so that with the Apostle they can say: "I no longer live, but Christ lives in me; and the life that I now live, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me." And this is rightly deemed the true life of man in this age, since the profane (as we said just now) live no other life than that which they share with the brute animals. Then, amid afflictions and dangers, they are strengthened by the Spirit of God, who is the pledge of salvation, and (as that divine Psalmist sings) according to the multitude of thoughts by which they are distracted, he supplies the sweetest consolations with which to cheer their souls. Moreover, by mortifying the old man they free themselves from countless troubles and bear the fruits of life. Those who are about to die have the hope of a better life laid up in Christ, who dispels the terrors of death, so that they know they are passing from death into life; so they commit their souls to him and go gladly into possession of eternal and heavenly life. Most truly, then, it is said that these people, while they hate and lose life, find it, or rather keep it entirely safe beyond all danger. For, as Paul testifies, their life is hidden with Christ in God; therefore, when Christ, our life, is revealed, they too will be revealed with him as truly glorious. For their bodies will be restored to them, and they will be caught up to meet Christ coming in the clouds of heaven, through the air, so as to live and reign with him in heaven. This is that blessed hope by which the martyrs of old, strengthened, overcame the dreadful tortures of every kind with an unconquered firmness of spirit.

units.la: Quod autem de vita dicitur, ad omnia alia extendi debet. Nulla enim alia ratio augendi & feruandi quae habemus, melior & tutior est, quàm si ea propter Christum expendamus aut amit-tamus. Ita enim illa in Dei manus deponimus, qui remunerator est fidelissimus. Ideo alibi dicit: Nullus est qui reliquerit domum, aut fratres, aut sorores, aut parentes, aut vxorem, aut liberos, aut agros mea causa & Euangelij, quin accipiat centuplicia nunc in tempore hoc, ac in saeculo su-turo vitam aeternam. Qui autem propter Christi nomen pauperibus sua erogant, ipsi Deo faene-rantur, & olim hic sibi factum reputabit, quod illis factum fuerit. Sed & ipsa pietas per se cum animo sua forte contento quaestus est vberrimus, vt pote promissiones habens praesentis & futuri saeculi. Exempla passim occurrunt, quibus ista probantur. Inter alia memorabile est Lothi, qui Deo vocante Sodomas & cum his opes suas omnes reliquit, sed harum iactura vitam suam rede-mit: quam eiusdem vxor infelix amisit, dum in illas respicit. Huius ergo memores (vt Christus monet) non diligamus mundum, neque ea quae in mundo sunt, sed ad caelestia bona toto corde aspi-remus, quorum spes certa & possessio stabilis est.
units.tr: What is said of life must be extended to everything else. For there is no better or safer way to increase and preserve what we have than to weigh it out, or to lose it, for Christ's sake. In this way we place it in the hands of God, who is the most faithful rewarder. So he says elsewhere: "There is no one who has left house, or brothers, or sisters, or parents, or wife, or children, or fields for my sake and the sake of the gospel, who will not receive a hundredfold now in this time, and in the age to come eternal life." Those who give to the poor for the sake of Christ's name lend to God himself, and he will one day reckon as done to himself what was done to them. Godliness itself, too, when joined with a contented mind, is a most abundant gain, since it holds promises for the present and the future age. Examples of this are found everywhere. Among others, the case of Lot is memorable: when God called him out, he left Sodom and all his wealth with it, but by losing these he redeemed his life, which his unhappy wife lost when she looked back at them. Mindful of this (as Christ admonishes), let us not love the world, nor the things that are in the world, but turn our eyes with our whole heart to heavenly goods, whose hope is sure and whose possession is stable.

units.la: Sed ad eos transeamus, qui opes & huius saeculi fortunas Christo praeferunt, quorum maximus est numerus. Nam plerique in opum abundantia felicitatem omnem consistere sibi persuadent: quae causa est, quod circa illas varie peccetur. Dum enim eas acquirere studeant, in tentationum laqueos incidunt, & paucos inuenias, qui non peccent in charitatis & iustitiae leges. Qui ve-rò iam diuites facti sunt, ij aut fiduciam in diuitijs collocant, & idololatrae fiunt, aut illis ad lu-xum & factum abutuntur. Quod si periculum eas amittendi oriatur, multi quidem faciunt, aut sibi persuaderi sinunt, dummodo opes suas retinere possint, & si tunc de religione agatur, pleriq; in ea ludunt, & vel fidem aperte abnegant, aut quidem simulando et dissimulando tepidi illi fiunt. quos Christus euomere solet, sicuti de Laodicenfibus ait. Sed de his omnibus in præsenti loquitur. Quid prodest homini, si totum mundum lucratus fuerit, anima vero sua multetur, vel animæ aut vitæ iacturam faciat? Habent verba ista speciem Cocessionis, & duplex argumentum continet, quod utrumque ex communi sensu sumitur, qui docet, hominem in hoc sæculo nihil sibi ipso & vitæ præsentis habere. Primum ad vitam huius sæculi refertur, & tale est. Esto, possit quis non solum crucis declinare, sed simul omnes totius orbis terrarum opes coquirere, nihil tamen hæc proderunt, si vitæ iacturam faciat. At qui propter opes me abnegant, & mea disciplinæ iugum excutiunt, ut vitam suam perdunt: Ergo etiamsi opes suas retineant, & simul eadem vehementer augeant, nullam tamen ex eis utilitatem percipient. Maior ex eo probatur, quod nullus post hanc vitam opum huius sæculi usus est. Etenim nudi ex utero matris (ut Iob dicebat) egredimur, & nudi ex hoc mundo abimus, nec quicquam nobiscum efferimus: ex opibus autem hunc solum fructum percipimus, quod alimenta & vestitum cum tecto nobis subministrant: quibus cum nobis post mortem nō opus sit, cum item ignoremus, quibus illæ cedant, frustra laborant, qui, ut opes feruet, vitæ iacturam faciunt. Damnatur hoc argumento insanum ditescendi studium, quo plerique homines accensi vitam sibi ipsis amaram faciunt, & eius commodis sese defraudant, adhæc eam in præsens diserimen adducunt. At quando fatalis illa hora inflat, nullis opibus vita hæc prolongari potest, multo minus ex morte redimi. Alterum argumentum ad animæ vitam, sub qua beatitudo vera comprehenditur, referri potest. Id paucis enuntiat Dominus, dicens: Quam dabit compensationem animæ suæ? A minori ad maius argumentatur. Quasi diceret: Stulte faciunt, qui propter opes vitam corporis huius mortalis amittunt, cum nullis pecuniis ea recuperari possit. Quanto ergo stultius est propter illas de anima vita immortali periclitari? Quid enim pro huius redemptione dabitur, si semel perdita fuerit? Certe vniuersa totius mundi diuitiæ ad vnius animulæ redemptionem non sufficient. Est hoc per se graue, & recte consideratum immane illud & insatiabile studium colligendi & feruandi opes reliquere poterat. Sed multo grauius est, quod animarum saluti diuitiæ officiunt, & plerunque damnationis causa sunt. Etenim contra eos, qui eas illicitis modis contra charitatis leges coaceruarunt, ad Deo pro vindicta clamant mercenarii, opifices & alij, quos illi defraudarunt. Contra eos de tectum tinea vestium & aruga pecuniarum, quibus neque ipsi vti sunt, neque alios vti permiserunt. Et licet dum in otio & pace viuunt, clamorem illos facile negligunt, tamen moriturii obuersantur viduæ, pupilli, pauperes, & ipsis omnia infesta reddunt, ut neque Dei promissis credere, neque de salute serio cogitare possint. Frequenter ergo fit, ut hunc aurum & argentum omne oderint, & e conspectu remoueri velint, & cum diuitiis ipsem omne vitæ æternæ abijciant, ut Iudas olim, qui cum pecuniis Christo, & vita propria chariores haberet, tandem & illas abiecit, & vitam sibi ipsi horribili & violento mortis genere eripuit. Prodest autem hæc Christi verba sæpe & diligenter in mentem reuocare propter eos, qui per fas & nefas opes congregerunt, & secuti in suis rapinis, vsuris & sanguine multo sibi ipsis omnia tollicentur, quod peccata omnia per sacra pro defunctis expiari posse putant. Sed negat Dominus quicquam dari posse pro animarum compensatione, & olim omnis quidem generis sacra Deus instituit, sacrificiorum autem pro defunctis nulla prorsus mentio fit in Lege, opera autem, quæ vi- decerunt ex fide, sequuntur eos, qui in eadem fide hinc migrarunt. Est ergo error hic gentilitius, neque absque sacrilega fraude imperitum vulgus illo decipiunt sacrifici & monachi, dum se pro defunctorum salute Missas facere & precari dicunt, qui iam eo loco sunt, ut nullis sacris iuuari possint, aut nullis opus habeant. Taceo nunc, quod aliorum salute curare se pollicentur, qui propriam negligunt. Itaq; omnes, quibus sua salus cordi est, reliquis nugiuendis illis impostoribus IESVM CHRISTVM audiant, & in huius fide constantes sint, qui nobis hoc meruit, ut a morte transeamus in vitam æternam. Ioan. 5.
units.tr: But let us turn to those who prefer the riches and fortunes of this age to Christ, and they are the greater number. For most people persuade themselves that all happiness lies in an abundance of wealth, and this is why they sin in various ways over it. For while they strive to acquire it, they fall into the snares of temptation, and you will find few who do not sin against the laws of love and justice. Those who have already become rich either place their trust in their riches and become idolaters, or misuse them for luxury and display. If there is danger of losing them, many indeed act, or allow themselves to be persuaded, so long as they may keep their wealth; and if religion is then at stake, most of them trifle with it, and either openly renounce the faith or, by pretending and dissembling, grow lukewarm. Such people Christ is accustomed to spew out, as he says of the Laodiceans. But he speaks of all these in the present. "What does it profit a man to gain the whole world and suffer the loss of his soul, or to forfeit his soul or his life?" These words have the appearance of a concession, and they contain a twofold argument, each drawn from common sense, which teaches that a man in this age has nothing of his own apart from the life of the present. The first refers to the life of this age, and runs thus: granted that someone could not only avoid the cross but also gather together all the riches of the whole world, these will profit him nothing if he suffers the loss of his life. But those who deny me for the sake of riches and cast off the yoke of my discipline, so that they lose their lives: therefore, even if they keep their wealth and greatly increase it, they will gain no advantage from it. The major premise is proved by the fact that after this life there is no use of the riches of this age. For we come naked out of our mother's womb (as Job said), and naked we depart from this world, nor do we carry anything away with us. From riches we gain only this fruit, that they supply us with food, clothing and shelter; and since we have no need of these after death, and do not know to whom they will pass, they labour in vain who, in order to keep their wealth, suffer the loss of their life. By this argument the mad desire to grow rich is condemned, the desire by which many people, inflamed, make their own lives bitter and defraud themselves of its benefits, and moreover bring it into present peril. But when that fatal hour strikes, this life cannot be prolonged by any riches, much less redeemed from death. The second argument can be referred to the life of the soul, in which true blessedness is comprehended. The Lord states this in a few words, saying: "What will he give in exchange for his soul?" He argues from the less to the greater, as if to say: foolish are those who, for the sake of riches, lose the life of this mortal body, since it cannot be recovered with any money. How much more foolish, then, is it to imperil the immortal life of the soul for their sake? For what will be given for its redemption if it is once lost? Surely all the riches of the whole world will not suffice to redeem a single little soul. This is grievous in itself, and rightly considered, that monstrous and insatiable zeal for gathering and keeping riches should have been abandoned. But it is much more grievous that riches stand in the way of the salvation of souls and are for the most part a cause of damnation. For against those who have heaped them up by unlawful means, against the laws of love, hired labourers, craftsmen and others whom they have defrauded cry out to God for vengeance. Against them cry the moth-eaten garments and the rust of their money, which they neither use themselves nor have allowed others to use. And although while they live in ease and peace they readily disregard that outcry, yet when they are about to die, the widows, orphans and poor confront them and make everything hostile to them, so that they can neither believe God's promises nor think seriously about salvation. Frequently, therefore, it happens that they come to hate all gold and silver, wish to have them removed from their sight, and cast away with their riches all hope of eternal life, as Judas once did, who held money dearer than Christ and his own life, and at last threw it away and took his own life by a dreadful and violent kind of death. It is useful, however, often and diligently to call these words of Christ to mind, on account of those who have gathered wealth by right or by wrong, and who, pursuing their plunder, usury and much blood, take everything upon themselves, because they think all sins can be expiated by sacred rites for the dead. But the Lord denies that anything can be given in exchange for souls. Although God instituted sacrifices of every kind long ago, no mention at all is made in the Law of sacrifices for the dead; rather, the works that have been done through faith follow those who have departed hence in that same faith. This error, then, is a heathen one, and priests and monks deceive the unlearned crowd with it, not without sacrilegious fraud, when they say that they perform Masses and pray for the salvation of the dead, who are already in such a place that they cannot be helped by any sacrifices, or have no need of them. I say nothing now of their promise to look after the salvation of others while neglecting their own. Therefore let all those to whom their own salvation is dear set aside those trifling impostors and hear JESUS CHRIST, and remain steadfast in his faith, who has won for us this, that we pass from death into eternal life. John 5.

units.la: At multos est videre, qui sibi ipsis blanditias faciunt, dum Deum res hominum non curare, neque iudicium aliquod vnquam fore existimant, in quo dictorum & factorum ratio cuiquam reddenda sit. Quapropter huic etiam errori occurrit Dominus, & magna cum gravitate dicit: Futurum est enim, ut Filius hominis veniat in gloria Patris sui cum Angelis suis, & tunc reddet vnicuique secundum facta eius. Habent singula verba Emphasim suam. Primum de seipso loquens, Filium
units.tr: But there are many who flatter themselves, while they think that God does not care for human affairs and that there will never be any judgment in which an account of their words and deeds must be given to anyone. Therefore the Lord also meets this error and says with great seriousness: "For the Son of man is to come in the glory of his Father with his angels, and then he will render to each according to his works." Each word carries its own emphasis. First, speaking of himself, he says the Son

units.la: Apo. 3. Iob 1. 1 Tim. 6. Luc. 12. Psal 49. Luc. 5. Matth. 27. Apo. 14. Filium hominis dicit. Quasi diceret: Etsi homo sim, & hominum contemptissimus videar, nec dignus, propter quem aliquis de suis fortunis, multo minus de vita periclitetur. Veniam tamen in die vniuersalis illius iudicij. Deinde modum & apparatum, quo venturus sit, describit. Veniet (inquit) in gloria Patris sui, coelestis nimirum, vtpote Dei Filius, & ipse Deus verus, eiusdem cum Patre virtutis, maiestatis & potentiae. Tertio, cum Angelis suis, quorum multas myriades adducet (vt apud Danielem habetur) qui eius apparitores & iudicij illius executores erunt: quorum quanta vires sint, multis exemplis constat. Quid vero faciet Filius ille hominis in aduentu suo? Reddet vnicuique secundum facta eius: Nimirum (vt alibi exponit) electis suis, qui ipsum coram mundo hoc confessi sunt, & ipsi fideliter seruierunt, gloriam & honorem & immortalitatem quando eos pro suis fratribus & coheredibus agnoscet coram Patre suo: prophanis vero huius saeculi filijs, quos coram mundo hoc prauo & adultero ipsius & Euangelij sui puduit, & qui ipsum negauerunt, sempiternam ignominiam cum nunquam finiendis cruciatibus coniunctam, quando eos cum diabolo & Angelis suis ad tartara vel tenebras exteriores ablegabit.
units.tr: Apo. 3. Iob 1. 1 Tim. 6. Luc. 12. Psal 49. Luc. 5. Matth. 27. Apo. 14. He calls himself the Son of man, as if to say: although I am a man and seem the most despised of men, and not worthy that anyone should risk his fortunes, much less his life, for my sake, nevertheless I will come on the day of that universal judgment. Then he describes the manner and the retinue in which he will come. He will come, he says, in the glory of his Father, that is, heavenly glory, as the Son of God and himself true God, of the same power, majesty and might as the Father. Third, he will come with his angels, of whom he will bring many myriads (as is found in Daniel), who will be his attendants and the executors of that judgment; how great their strength is is clear from many examples. What, then, will that Son of man do at his coming? He will repay each man according to his deeds: namely (as he explains elsewhere), to his elect, who have confessed him before this world and faithfully served him, he will give glory, honour and immortality, when he acknowledges them before his Father as his brothers and co-heirs; but to the profane sons of this age, whom he was ashamed of before this perverse and adulterous world, and of his Gospel, and who denied him, he will give everlasting shame joined with torments that will never end, when he sends them away with the devil and his angels to Tartarus or the outer darkness.

units.la: Caeterum vt supra Christus generalem regulam tradidit, quam omnis loci & ordinis homines qui eius discipulos se profitentur, sequi debent: ita rationes etiam, quibus illam confirmat, omnibus communes sunt, & quidem postrema haec ab eius nouissimo aduentu petita, in primis ad omnes pertinet. Nam, vt Apostolus testatur, omnes homines manifestari oportet ad eius tribunal, vt vnusquisque reportet secundum ea quae in corpore fecit, vel bona vel mala. Requirit hoc iustitia Dei. Quia enim ea est praesentis vitae conditio, vt non semper boni virtutis ac pietatis suae praemia recipiant, mali item & impij non omnes vt meruerunt puniantur, sed saepe per omnem vitae cursum felices sint: aliud saeculum fit oportet, quo vnicuique retribuatur, prout dignus est. Hoc qui negant, & doctrinam de Christi ad iudicium aduentu scurriliter eludunt (quod multos factu- ros esse, Petrus olim praedixit) hi eadem opera Dei iustitiam negant. At si haec negetur, Deus ipse e me dio tollitur, aut, quod gravius est, tyrannus fingitur. Quia vero Deum esse, & eundem iustum remuneratorem & vindicem esse constat, singuli quoad suam vocationem sibi ipsis iam doctrinam applicent, & nunquam non meminerint, fore aliquando diem, quo de omni suo facto & dicto rationem reddituri sint, & quo vicissim Deus omnibus retribuat. Haec consideratio in aduersis patientes, in mortis articulo intrepidos, in secundis autem humiles & prouidos facit, & carnis desideria restinguit, ne his nos irretiri ac seduci sinamus.
units.tr: Moreover, as Christ above gave a general rule, which all men of every place and rank who profess themselves his disciples ought to follow, so too the reasons by which he confirms it are common to all; and this last one, taken from his final coming, pertains above all to everyone. For, as the Apostle testifies, all men must be made manifest before his judgment seat, so that each may receive what he has done in the body, whether good or evil. The justice of God requires this. For since the condition of the present life is such that the good do not always receive the rewards of their virtue and piety, and the wicked and impious are not all punished as they deserve, but are often happy throughout the whole course of their life, another age must come in which each will be repaid as he deserves. Those who deny this, and scoffingly mock the teaching about Christ's coming to judgment (as Peter long ago foretold that many would do), by that very act deny the justice of God. But if this is denied, God himself is removed from the midst, or, what is worse, is pictured as a tyrant. Since, however, it is established that God exists and is the same just rewarder and avenger, let each one apply this teaching to himself according to his own calling, and never cease to remember that a day will come when they must render an account of every deed and word, and when God in turn will repay all. This consideration makes men steadfast in adversity, fearless at the point of death, and humble and provident in prosperity, and it quenches the desires of the flesh, so that we do not allow ourselves to be ensnared and seduced by them.

units.la: Porro quia nunquam desunt illusores, qui haec in dubium vocant, & discipulis multa consola tione opus erat propter tristem & periculosam rerum huius saeculi faciem, quae Domini mortem et ascensionem in coelos erat secutura: promissionem hanc confirmat, & ait: Amen dico vobis, sunt quidam ex ijs qui hic astant, qui nequaquam gustabunt mortem, vsq; dum viderint Filium hominis venientem in regno suo. Certum experimentum & specimen pollicetur, quo discant ipsum in coelis regnare, & iudicem venturum, qui suos remuneretur, incredulis autem & contumacibus retribuat. Potest autem hic locus bifariam intelligi, & recte fecerit, si vtrumq; sensum coniungas. Primo enim paucis ab eo quod haec dixit diebus, coram tribus discipulis, Petro, Iacobo & Ioanne clarificatus est, & illis gustum quendam coelestis gloriae & maiestatis, in qua ad iudicium olim venit, praebuit: de quo prolixius proximo capite dicetur. Deinde postquam in coelos ascendit, Spiritum sanctum misit, qui per Apostolos & viros Apostolicos regnum Christi longe lateq; per totum orbem propagauit.
units.tr: Furthermore, since there are always mockers who call these things into doubt, and the disciples needed much consolation because of the sad and dangerous state of affairs in this world, which was to follow the death of the Lord and his ascension into heaven, he confirms this promise and says: Truly I say to you, there are some of those who stand here who shall in no way taste death until they see the Son of man coming in his kingdom. He promises a certain and visible proof, by which they may learn that he reigns in heaven, and will come as judge to reward his own and to repay the unbelieving and obstinate. This passage may be understood in two ways, and you will do well to join both senses. For first, a few days after he said these things, he was made glorious before three disciples, Peter, James and John, and gave them a foretaste of the heavenly glory and majesty in which he once came to judgment; of this more will be said at greater length in the next chapter. Then, after he had ascended into heaven, he sent the Holy Spirit, who through the Apostles and apostolic men spread the kingdom of Christ far and wide throughout the whole world.

units.la: Quod plerisq; Apostolis adhuc viuentibus factum fuit, adeo vt Paulus ad Colossen. scribat, Euangelium praedicatum esse omni creaturae, quae sub coelo est. Ex eo autem luce clarius apparuit, iam venisse illum, qui regnum diaboli euertere, & regnum Dei inter homines instaurare debuit. At primus ille aduentus Christi in carnem & Euangelij eius per totum orbe pro pagatio nobis certissimi argumenti loco esse debet, quod nouissimo etiam die in gloria Patris venturus sit, vt nostram redemptionem perficiat. Quia ergo hodie etiam Euangelium passim praedicatur & regnum Dei per illud instauratur, adhaec quotidie fiunt signa, quae ille finem mundi praecessura praedixit, attollamus capita nostra, & praeparemus nos in occursum eius, vt vbi nos fidorum seruorum instar paratos inuenerit, cum ipso ingrediamur ad regni sui gaudia. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: This was done while most of the Apostles were still living, so that Paul writes to the Colossians that the Gospel has been preached to every creature which is under heaven. From this it appeared more clearly than light that he had now come who was to overthrow the kingdom of the devil and restore the kingdom of God among men. But this first coming of Christ in the flesh, and the spreading of his Gospel throughout the whole world, ought to serve us as the most certain proof that he will also come on the last day in the glory of his Father, to complete our redemption. Therefore, since the Gospel is today also preached everywhere and the kingdom of God is restored through it, and daily there occur those signs which he foretold would precede the end of the world, let us lift up our heads and prepare ourselves to meet him, so that when he finds us ready, like faithful servants, we may enter with him into the joys of his kingdom. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen.

units.la: CAPVT XVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVII.

units.la: HOMILIA CCXI.
units.tr: HOMILY CCXI.

units.la: SExto autem post die accepit IESVS Petrum & Iacobum & Ioannem fratrem eius, & subducit eos priuatim in montem sublimem. Transformatus est coram eis, & splenduit facies eius vt Sol: vestimenta autem eius facta sunt alba, vt lux. Et ecce conspecti sunt eis Moses & Elias, cum eo colloquentes. Respondens autem Petrus, dixit IESV: Domine, bonum est nos hic esse: si vis faciamus hic tria tabernacula, tibi vnum, & Mosi vnum, & Eliae vnum.
units.tr: Six days later Jesus took Peter, James, and John his brother, and led them up privately into a high mountain. He was transfigured before them, and his face shone like the sun, and his garments became white as the light. And behold, Moses and Elijah appeared to them, talking with him. Then Peter answered and said to Jesus, "Lord, it is good for us to be here. If you wish, let us make three tabernacles here, one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah."

units.la: VONIAM plerique homines aut praesentis seculi illecebris, aut cruce & aduersis afflicti de vera & obedientia IESV CHRISTI abducuntur, docuit hic nuper discipulos suos aliam vitam esse in futuro seculo, in qua caelestium bonorum retributionem recepturi sint pij, qui in praesenti propter ipsum opes, dignitates, vitam denique reliquerunt. Rursus autem ira & ignominia sempiterna eos maneat, qui propter fluxa & terrena bona ab ipsius fide & obedientia recesserint. At non ignorabat Dominus nouissimus temporibus paucos fore, qui ista credant, ideo nuper promisit, se nonnullis ex discipulorum numero specimen praebere velle eius gloriae & maiestatis, qua olim ad iudicium vniuersale venturus sit. Id in praesenti historia praestat, & ita quidem vt primum demonstretur, Iesum hunc esse Dei Filium & promissum Seruatorem, cui omnes consecrari oporteat qui seruari volunt: deinde quae huius sit in caelis conditio, & qualis ibidem cum ipso nostra quoque futura sit. Totius vero historiae hic nobis praecipuum vsus esse debet, vt neque ipsius Christi indigna morte & cruce offendamur, neque aduersis quae nobis accidunt, nos ab ipso diuelli patiamur, sed constantes simus in eius obsequio, neque dubitemus exoriturum suo tempore diem illum resitutionis omnium, quo omnibus rependatur in corpore suo, prout vel bonum vel malum fecerint.
units.tr: Since many people are drawn away from the true obedience of Jesus Christ, either by the allurements of the present age or by being afflicted with the cross and adversity, the Lord recently taught his disciples that there is another life in the age to come, in which the godly will receive the reward of heavenly goods, they who in this present life have left behind wealth, honours, and even life itself for his sake. On the other hand, eternal wrath and shame will remain for those who have fallen away from his faith and obedience for the sake of fleeting and earthly goods. But the Lord did not fail to know that in the last times few would believe these things, and so he recently promised that he would show some of his disciples a sample of that glory and majesty with which he will one day come to the universal judgement. He does this in the present narrative, and in such a way that, first, it is shown that this Jesus is the Son of God and the promised Saviour, to whom all must be consecrated who wish to be saved; and then what his condition is in heaven, and what ours will be there with him. The chief use of the whole narrative for us ought to be this: that we should be neither offended by the unworthy death and cross of Christ himself, nor allow ourselves to be torn away from him by the adversities that befall us, but that we should be steadfast in his service, and not doubt that the day of the restoration of all things will dawn in its time, on which each will be repaid in his body, according as he has done good or evil.

units.la: Quae omnia vt rectius & maiori cum fructu intelligantur, omnes totius historiae circumstantias Matthaeus describit, & a tempore exorsus, Christi mox promissis fetiisse docet. Sexto autem post die (inquit) accepit Iesus Petrum, &c. Lucas hoc post dies circiter octo factum scribit, nimirum eum quoque numerans, quo cum discipulis de fidei & vitae Christianae regula disseruit, vna cum eo, quo haec ipsius transfiguratio facta est. Quia enim haec magni momenti res erat, non diu eam differre voluit, sed cum adhuc in recenti discipulorum memoria erat eius promissio, eam ad oculum demonstrare voluit. Apparet autem ex hac tam diligenti temporis notatione promissionum Christi fides & veritas. Sunt huius generis exempla multa alia in Euangelio. Huc enim referri possunt promissiones Spiritus sancti, resurrectionis item ex mortuis, & aliae similes: quas omnes reuera impletas fuisse legimus. Debet ergo hinc generalis consolatio peti, ne in tentationibus de promissis Dei auxilio dubitemus. Sicuti enim promisit, ita reuera non relinquet nos orphanos, sed nobis aderit vsque ad consummationem seculi, & eius fidei neque temporis diuturnitas, neque graues huius mundi motus quicquam derogare poterunt. Enimuero, qui paulo ante discipulis de morte sua ignominiosa concionatus fuerat, & illos omnes ad crucem ferendam vocarat, nunc se illis in caelesti gloria videndum sistit, & se in caelis simul atque in terris regnare testatur.
units.tr: So that all these things may be understood more correctly and with greater profit, Matthew describes all the circumstances of the whole narrative, and beginning with the time, shows that the event followed closely upon Christ's promises. "Six days later," he says, "Jesus took Peter," and so on. Luke writes that this happened about eight days after, evidently counting also the day on which he spoke with the disciples about the rule of faith and of the Christian life, together with the day on which this transfiguration took place. For since this was a matter of great importance, he did not wish to delay it long, but while the memory of his promise was still fresh in the minds of the disciples, he wished to set it before their eyes. Now the faithfulness and truth of Christ's promises appear from this so careful notation of time. There are many other examples of this kind in the Gospel. To this class belong the promises of the Holy Spirit, likewise that of the resurrection from the dead, and others like them, all of which we read were indeed fulfilled. From this, therefore, a general consolation should be drawn, that we should not doubt in our temptations the help of God promised to us. For just as he has promised, so he will indeed not leave us orphans, but will be with us even to the end of the age; and neither the length of time nor the heavy upheavals of this world will be able to diminish this faith. Indeed, he who had shortly before preached to the disciples about his own ignominious death, and had called them all to bear the cross, now presents himself to them in heavenly glory to be seen, and testifies that he reigns in heaven as well as on earth.

units.la: Secundo testes nominantur, quos Dominus adhibuit: nimirum tres numero, quorum testimonium legitimum esse, Lex vetus docet. Et hos quidem non temere ex aliis delectos fuisse constat, cum hi ipsi sistantur, quos alibi quoque in rebus grauioribus sibi adiunxit: Petrum videlicet, Iacobum & Ioannem, quos miraculi in filia Iari ex mortuis resuscitata facti testes esse voluit, & coram quibus postea ad monte oliueti extremae suae infirmitatis conscios facere dignatus est. Quae exemplo obseruari debent, vt discamus nullum quidem personarum respectum esse in Christo, quoad ater nam salutem, veruntamen quoad Spiritus sancti dona, inter electos discrimina esse, vt alij alijs praesent: quod alibi Paulus vasorum similitudine docet, quae in magna & diuite domo varia & multa. multum inter se diuersa sunt. Et huius meminisse debent, qui vel ad Ecclesiæ vel Reipublicæ gu-bernacula sedent, vt muneribus publicis eos adhibeant, quos a Deo peculiaribus & necessarijs donis instructos esse vident. Reliqui vero in seipsos descendant, & suo sepe metiantur, vt nec maiora viribus temere aggredi, neque alios præ fe contemnere velint, neque etiam aliquis aduer-sus eos fremat, quos sibi præferri videt: omnes autem in commune conferant quod a Domino acceperunt, & alij alios honore præueniant.
units.tr: Second, the witnesses whom the Lord took with him are named: namely three in number, whose testimony the ancient Law teaches to be lawful. And it is clear that these were chosen not at random from the others, since these same men are set forth, whom he also associated with himself on other weightier occasions: namely Peter, James, and John, whom he wished to be witnesses of the miracle when the daughter of Jairus was raised from the dead, and in whose presence afterwards on the Mount of Olives he deigned to make them sharers of his extreme anguish. These things ought to be observed as an example, so that we may learn that in Christ there is indeed no respect of persons as regards salvation, yet as regards the gifts of the Holy Spirit there are differences among the elect, so that some excel others; this Paul teaches elsewhere by the similitude of vessels, which in a great and rich house are various and very different from one another. And those who sit at the helm of the Church or of the commonwealth ought to remember this, so that they employ in public offices those whom they see to be endowed by God with special and necessary gifts. The rest, on the other hand, should descend into themselves and often measure themselves by their own standard, so that they neither rashly undertake greater things than their strength allows, nor wish to despise others in comparison with themselves, nor let anyone rage against those whom he sees preferred to himself; but all should bring into common use what they have received from the Lord, and let each go before the others in showing honour.

units.la: Tertiò locus quoq; indicatur, vbi ista facta sunt. Subduxit enim discipulos Dominus in montem altissimum, quem Thabor dictum fuisse Diuus Hieronymus annotauit. Et alias quoq; solitus fuit montes frequentare, & in illis ea agere, quæ maioris momenti erant: Ita nimirum admonens, vt qui fidei & regni Dei mysteria tractare volunt, animos a terrenis cogitationibus in cælos attollant, neq; carnis rationem in consilium adhibeant. Non sunt enim cogitationes Dei vt no ftræ cogitationes, sed (vt apud Ifaiam dicit Dominus) quantum cœli terra sublimiores sunt, tanto superant Dei placita nostras intentiones: nec superant modo, sed etiam eis repugnant, quemadmodum vicifim omnis carnis intelligentia Deo aduersatur, vt alibi diximus. Et huc in primis facit, quod Lucas precationis meminit, quæ plus quàm necessaria est, vt animi diuino Spiritu illuminati cœlestia meditari discant.
units.tr: Third, the place where these things were done is also indicated. For the Lord led the disciples up into a very high mountain, which Saint Jerome noted was called Tabor. He was also accustomed on other occasions to frequent mountains, and to do there those things which were of greater importance: thus evidently admonishing that those who wish to handle the mysteries of the faith and of the kingdom of God should lift their minds from earthly thoughts to heaven, and should not take the counsel of the flesh into account. For the thoughts of God are not our thoughts; but, as the Lord says through Isaiah, as much as the heavens are higher than the earth, so much do God's purposes surpass our intentions; and they not only surpass them, but even oppose them, just as in turn all human understanding is hostile to God, as we have said elsewhere. And to this above all pertains what Luke says about prayer, which is more than necessary, so that minds illumined by the divine Spirit may learn to meditate on heavenly things.

units.la: Sequitur ipsa clarificatio Christi, cuius modum Euangelistæ diligenter exponunt. Initio summam rei comprehendit Matthæus, quando ipsum coram discipulis transformatum fuisse scribit. Et mox modum describens, dicit eius faciem instar Solis splenduisse, quod ipsum de corpore toto intelligi debere, ex eo apparet quod additur: Vestimenta autem eius facta sunt alba, vt lux. Apud Marcum nitè candidiora fuisse dicuntur, vt nemo fullo sua arte aut industria potuisset talia facere. Vnde vero vestium fulgor, quàm ex corporis corruptione enatus est? Visuntur autem cum illo Moses & Elias, qui cum ipso differunt de eius excessu (vt Lucas dicit) id est, de eius morte, quàm Hierosolymæ erat subiturus. Quod in tempore factum fuit, cùm non multò ante mortis tam acerbæ mentione Petrus fuisset offensus. Oportuit ergo eum doceri, nihil hic euenturum nouum & insolens, neq; obstituram mortis ignominiam, quo minus per hanc in regni cœlestis gloriam transeat. Sed de eo postea suo loco plura dicentur.
units.tr: There follows the very glorification of Christ, the manner of which the Evangelists describe carefully. At the beginning Matthew comprehends the sum of the matter, when he writes that he was transfigured before the disciples. And soon describing the manner, he says that his face shone like the sun, which must be understood of his whole body, as appears from what is added: "and his garments became white as the light." In Mark they are said to have been far whiter, so that no fuller by his art or industry could have made them such. But whence did the brightness of the garments arise, if not from the body's transformation? Moses and Elijah are seen with him, and they speak with him about his departure (as Luke says), that is, about his death, which he was about to undergo at Jerusalem. This took place at the right time, since Peter had been offended not long before by the mention of so bitter a death. It was therefore necessary for him to be taught that nothing new and strange would happen here, and that the ignominy of death would not stand in the way of his passing through it into the glory of the heavenly kingdom. But more will be said about this at its proper place.

units.la: Nunc quo corpore & qualis ad iudicium Christus venturus fit, consideremus. Sermo est de IESV, qui ex Maria Virgine natus, paulò ante fe Hierosolymæ multa acerba & indigna passurum esse prædixerat, in montem vero istum ascenderat, vt tribus istis discipulis ostenderet, quo habitu venire velit ad iudicandum viuos & mortuos. Hic transformatus esse dicitur. Ergo nulla substantiæ, sed solius formæ mutatio facta est. Et vt facies nominatur, cuius substantia mansit, splendore autem nouo & radijs, quales Solis esse solent, illustrata refulsit: ita neq; aliorum membrorum aut corporis substantia abolita est. Sed & vestes manserunt, quibus similiter fulgor ille cœlestis communicatus est. Ex quibus apparet, non alium quàm IESVM illum CHRISTVM venturum in nouissimo die, qui ex Maria verum hominem affumpfit, & in illo corpore venturum in quo passus est & mortuus, sed clarificato, id est, repurgato ab omni corruptione & vitiofitate non autem exinanito aut in spiritum couerfo, multò minus Deificato, vt i im vna cum diuinitate, in omnibus locis fit, & omnia in cœlo & in terris corporaliter impleat. Nam vt Diuus Augusti-nus ait, eandem corporis fui substantiam in resurrectione retinuit, cui immortalitatem dedit, naturam non abstulit. Ideo nuper de suo aduentu loquens, Filium hominis sese dixit, quod alibi quoque illum facere legimus, quotiefcunq; fui aduentus meminit. Et Daniel in nubibus cœli vidit ve-nientem Filium hominis. Angeli itemqui Ascensionis testes & interpretes esse debuerunt, simul venturum testantur, non inuisibili aut ineffabili modo fiue forma, sed ea, qua ipsum abire in cœlum viderint discipuli. Procul ergo facessunt fanatici, qui hodie ex Eutychianorum scholis nobis Christum nouum fingunt, & contra omnis Vetustatis regulam, quam Diuus Augustinus tradidit, Filij hominis diuinitatem ita afstruunt, vt veritatem corporis auferant.
units.tr: Let us now consider with what body and in what form Christ will come to judgement. The discourse concerns Jesus, who, born of the Virgin Mary, had shortly before foretold that he would suffer many bitter and unworthy things at Jerusalem, and had ascended this mountain in order to show to those three disciples in what appearance he wishes to come to judge the living and the dead. Here he is said to have been transfigured. Therefore no change of substance took place, but only of form. And he is called a face, whose substance remained, yet shone forth illumined with a new splendour and rays, such as the sun is wont to have; so likewise the substance of his other members and of his body was not abolished. And the garments remained, to which that heavenly brightness was similarly communicated. From these things it appears that the Christ who will come on the last day is none other than that Jesus who took true manhood from Mary, and that he will come in the same body in which he suffered and died, but made glorious, that is, cleansed from all corruption and defect; not emptied, nor turned into spirit, much less deified, so that he is everywhere together with his divinity, and fills all things in heaven and earth bodily. For, as Saint Augustine says, he retained in the resurrection the same substance of his body, to which he gave immortality but did not take away its nature. Therefore, speaking recently of his coming, he called himself the Son of man, as we read that he did elsewhere whenever he mentioned his coming. And Daniel saw the Son of man coming in the clouds of heaven. Likewise the angels, who ought to have been the witnesses and interpreters of the Ascension, testify that he will come at the same time, not in an invisible or unutterable manner or form, but in that in which the disciples saw him depart into heaven. Far away, therefore, be those fanatics who today, out of the schools of the Eutychians, fashion for us a new Christ, and, against the whole rule of antiquity which Saint Augustine handed down, so assert the divinity of the Son of man as to take away the truth of his body.

units.la: At quia nos secum esse vult Christus, & idem (vt Paulus scribit) corpus nostrum humile transformabit, vt conforme faciat corpori suo glorioso, simul quæ nostra in cœlesti vita conditio fit cœlis conuersa tura fit, hac historia adumbratur. Vt ergo Christus vero suo corpore resurrexit, & eiusdem natu-tio fit futura. rales & essentiales proprietates retinuit: ita nos quoq; nostris corporibus resurgemus, & vt hoc fiat, iustitiæ lex iubet, ne alia corpora gloriæ cœlesti paritcipent, quàm quæ perpessionibus Christi communicarunt. Resurgent autem illa corusca & radiantia, qualem Mosis faciem fuisse scribi-tur, cum ex Dei colloquio rediret. Deinde vt discipuli tres Christum viderunt, & eius conspestu ita delectati sunt, vt eos omnium quæ in terris habebant, obliuio cæperit (sicuti paulò post Petri verba docebunt) ita nos illum coram videbimus, & in eius facie omnium bonorum satietate fruemur, vt Dauid in Psalmis ait. Et hoc illud est, quo Iob seipsum consolatur, dicens: Et rursum circundabor hac mea cute & spestabo Deum e carne mea: Quem ego mihi contemplabor, & oculi mei videbunt, & non alius, &c. Vt deniq; Mosem & Eliam cum Christo viderunt discipuli, & illos licet nunquam antea visos potuerunt dignoscere: ita nos olim in cœlesti gloria omnes electos Dei videbimus & eosdem agnoscemus, sicuti Adam Euam suam primo slatim intuitu agnouit. Procul autem aberit omnis vitiosus affectus, qui cogitationes vel tristes vel inhonestas & indecoras posset parere. Deniq; exhibebitur hic dulcissimus typus lætæ illius & beatæ consuetudinis, quam sanctii in cœlesti patria cum Christo & ipsi simul omnes inter se fruentur: cum e contra impij corruptibilitatem quidem exuent quoque, sed vt sempiternis pœnis possint sufficere, & vnà omnes ad eum locum ablegabuntur, qui Satanæ & eius angelis destinatus est, vt alibi ipse Dominus testatur.
units.tr: But since Christ wills us to be with him, and since (as Paul writes) he will transform our lowly body to make it conformable to his glorious body, this story shows at the same time what our condition will be in the heavenly life, which is to be turned to the heavens. Just as Christ rose again in his true body and kept the natural and essential properties of that same body, so we too will rise again in our bodies. For this to happen, the law of justice requires that bodies not share in heavenly glory unless they have shared in the sufferings of Christ. Those bodies will rise shining and radiant, like the face of Moses is written to have been when he returned from speaking with God. Then, just as the disciples saw Christ with three (senses), and were so delighted by the sight of him that they forgot all the things they had on earth (as the words of Peter soon will show), so we too will see him face to face, and in his presence we will enjoy the fullness of every good, as David says in the Psalms. This is also what Job consoles himself with, saying: "And again I shall be surrounded by this my skin, and in my flesh I shall see God; whom I shall behold for myself, and my eyes shall see, and not another, etc." Finally, just as the disciples saw Moses and Elijah with Christ, and could recognise them although they had never seen them before, so one day in heavenly glory we will see all the elect of God and will know them, just as Adam recognised his Eve at the first glance. Every sinful affection, which could produce sad or dishonourable and indecent thoughts, will be far away. Finally, here is shown the sweetest type of that joyful and blessed fellowship which the saints will enjoy together with Christ and with one another in the heavenly fatherland, whereas the wicked will indeed also put off corruptibility, but so that they may be able to endure eternal punishments; and they will all be sent away together to that place which is appointed for Satan and his angels, as the Lord himself testifies elsewhere.

units.la: Sed vt discipuli his affecti fuerint, præstat videre. Lucas initiò somno grauatos fuisse dicit, & cum eugilassent, vidisse gloriam IESV, & duos illos viros cum eo stantes. Adumbratur hoc exemplo infirmitas carnis nostræ, & eius tarditas in percipiendis regni Dei mysterijs: a qua nisi Deus ipse nos excitet suo Spiritu, nihil vnquam proficiemus. Prodest autem obseruare illius erga nos studium, vt quando hic nobis aurem vellicat, nos eius monitis accommodemus. Caterùm addit Lucas, Mosem & Eliam ab illo discessisse, & tunc dulcedine visionis abreptum Petrum exclamauisse: Domine bonum est nos hic esse: si vis, faciamus hic tria tabernacula, tibi vnum, & Mosi vnum, & Eliæ vnum. Tantum in illo potuit beatæ immortalitatis gustus, quem percipie bat, vt iam neq; domus neque coniugis suæ aut eorum recordaretur, quæ hastenus magni facere solitus fuerat. Interim hic quoq; carnis ingenium sese prodit. Audiuit illos cum Christo de morte sua colloquentes, & eadem dicentes, quæ nuper ipse dixerat: Oportere nimirum se ire Ierosolymam, & illic multa pati & mori, &c. Cùm ergo hos iam abiisse videt, & Christum absq; mora secatu-rum suspicatur, vt morti obuiâ quasi procedat, ad eundé lapidem, vt prius offendit: & monet, vt potiùs inter delitias & gaudia illa gloriæ cœlestis maneant, & ineptam illam vocem de tribus tabernaculis illic extruendis profert, quam (vt Marcus & Lucas annotarunt) ne ipse quidem intelligebat. Ita solet caro crucem detrectare & fugere quantum potest, & triumphos sibi ante-quam pugnarit, polliceri. Sed longè alia est regni Christi conditio. Vt enim hic per multas affli-ctiones & acerbam mortem crucis in gloriam Patris ingressus est: ita nobis eadem via pergen-dum est, & oportet eos qui in ipso pie viuere volunt persecutiones multas sufferre, vt in regnum Dei ingrediantur. Non ergo nos illi nouum vitæ genus præscribere, aut viam nouam nobis ipsis quærere debemus, sed hoc bonum & vtile putare, quod ipse nobis monstrat aut imponit. Quod vt nobis facilius persuadeatur, proderit frequenter & assiduè versari in consideratione bonorum cælestium, quæ Deus præparauit diligentibus ipsum. Est horum tanta excellentia, vt omnem comparationem transcendat. Nam vt Isaias ait, non oculus vllus hominis talia vnquam vidit, neque auris audiuit, neque cogitatio aliqua potest simile quid percipere. Et vt hic Petrus omnium, quæ habebat oblitus in monte manere, & illic firmas sedes figere cupit: ita qui illa olim assequentur, ij etiam excussa omnium, quæ vnquam tristissima passa sunt, recordatione, omnes lachrymas abstergent, & cum Filio Dei IESV CHRISTO nunquam finiendis gaudijs fruentur.
units.tr: But it is worth seeing how the disciples were affected by these things. Luke says that at first they were weighed down with sleep, and when they woke up they saw the glory of Jesus and the two men standing with him. This example shows the weakness of our flesh and its slowness in grasping the mysteries of the kingdom of God; unless God himself rouses us by his Spirit, we will never make any progress. It is useful, however, to observe his zeal toward us: when he here tugs at our ear, we should adapt ourselves to his warnings. But Luke adds that Moses and Elijah departed from him, and then Peter, carried away by the sweetness of the vision, exclaimed: "Lord, it is good for us to be here; if you wish, let us make here three tabernacles, one for you, one for Moses and one for Elijah." So great was the taste of blessed immortality which he was perceiving that he no longer remembered his house or his wife, or the things which he had hitherto been accustomed to value highly. Meanwhile here too the nature of the flesh shows itself. He had heard them talking with Christ about his death, saying the very things which he himself had lately said: that he must indeed go up to Jerusalem, and there suffer many things and die, and so on. So when he sees these two now departing, and supposes that Christ will set out without delay, as if to go to meet death, he stumbles again over the same stone as before, and advises that they rather remain amid the delights and joys of heavenly glory, and utters that foolish word about building three tabernacles there, which (as Mark and Luke have noted) he himself did not even understand. Thus the flesh is accustomed to shrink from the cross and flee it as far as it can, and to promise itself triumphs before it has fought. But the condition of Christ's kingdom is quite different. For just as he entered into the glory of the Father here through many afflictions and a bitter death on the cross, so we too must go by the same way, and those who wish to live godly in him must suffer many persecutions, so that they may enter into the kingdom of God. Therefore we ought not to prescribe for him a new kind of life, nor to seek for ourselves a new way, but to consider good and useful whatever he shows or imposes on us. So that this may be more easily persuaded to us, it will be helpful to dwell frequently and constantly on the contemplation of the heavenly goods which God has prepared for those who love him. Their excellence is so great that it surpasses every comparison. For, as Isaiah says, no eye of man has ever seen such things, nor has ear heard, nor can any thought perceive anything similar. And just as Peter here, forgetting all that he had, wishes to remain on the mountain and fix firm dwellings there, so those who will one day attain those things, with the memory of all the most sorrowful things they have ever suffered wiped away, will dry all their tears and will enjoy, with the Son of God Jesus Christ, joys that never end.

units.la: Quæ vt facilius assequamur, proderit quotidie obliuisci omnium, quæ hic mundus in pretio habet, & in illū vnū respicere, qui nobis illa acquisiuit suæ mortis & sanguinis suæ merito. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: So that we may attain these more easily, it will help us daily to forget all that this world holds in esteem, and to look upon him alone who acquired those goods for us by the merit of his death and his blood. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: Iob. 19
units.tr: Job 19

units.la: HOMILIA CCXII.
units.tr: HOMILY 212.

units.la: Adhuc eo loquente, ecce nubes lucida inumbrauit eos: & ecce vox ex nube dicens: Hic est Filius ille meus dilectus, in quo mihi bene complacitum est: ipsum audite. Et cum haec audissent discipuli, ceciderunt in faciem suam, & timuerunt vehementer. Tunc accedens IESVS tetigit eos, dixitq;: Surgite, & ne timete. Sublatis autem oculis suis neminem viderunt, nisi IESVM solum.
units.tr: While he was still speaking, behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them, and behold, a voice out of the cloud said, "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear ye him." And when the disciples heard this, they fell on their faces and were terribly afraid. Then Jesus came and touched them and said, "Arise, and be not afraid." And when they lifted up their eyes, they saw no one but Jesus only.

units.la: Historia de clarificatione IESV CHRISTI praeter multa alia, quae nostrae institutioni & consolationi seruiunt, duo continet confideratu valde necessaria. Nam primo docet, quomodo ille in nouissimo die ad iudicandum viuos & mortuos venturus, & quae tunc electorum omnium conditio in caelesti patria futura fit. Deinde euidenter demonstrat, illum esse promissum humani generis Seruatorem, quem omnes ampletl & sequi oporteat, quotquot seruari volunt. De priori nuper dictu est, quod venturus fit vero & naturali corpore, quod ex virginis Mariae substantia assumpfit, sed clarificato, impijs quidem terribilis, pijs autem & credentibus laetus, qui ipsi confor mes facti, in conspectu Dei satietate bonorum caelestium cum beatis omnibus fruentur. Sequitur nunc alterum, quo ipsius Dei Patris voce caelitus delata explicatur. Eftq; locus hic dignissimus, cuius singulae circumstantiae ex ordine considerentur.
units.tr: The narrative of the glorification of Jesus Christ, besides many other things that serve our instruction and comfort, contains two points that are very necessary to consider. For first it teaches how he will come on the last day to judge the living and the dead, and what the condition of all the elect will then be in the heavenly fatherland. Then it clearly shows that he is the promised Saviour of the human race, whom all must embrace and follow who wish to be saved. About the first we have recently spoken: that he will come in a true and natural body, which he took from the substance of the virgin Mary, but glorified, terrible indeed to the unbelieving, but joyful to the godly and believers, who, made like him, will enjoy in the sight of God the fullness of heavenly goods together with all the blessed. Now follows the second point, in which the voice of God the Father himself, sent down from heaven, is explained. And this passage is most worthy, and its individual circumstances should be considered in order.

units.la: Videamus igitur principio oraculi huius authorem, quae non obscure indicat: Matthaeus, quando nubem lucidam discipulos & Christum inumbrauisse scribit, ex qua vox ista audita sit. Nam vt alibi diximus, nubes praesentiae Dei symbolum siue indicium sunt, & ideo nubes olim tabernaculu adumbrabat, quando illic Dei responsum quaerebatur, aut hic se praesentem adesse significabat. Petrus certe postea ex hoc loco probauit, Apostolos non arte compositas fabulas secutos Ecclesiae notam fecisse Domini nostri potentiam & aduentu, sed ipsos suis oculis aspexisse illius maiestatem, & audiuisse ex caelo ad illum delatam. Itaq; Dei hac vox fuit, qui Filio suo Vnigenito testimonium voluit perhibere. Et cum alibi caliginis & atrarum nubium mentio fiat, quibus ille maiestatem suam terribilem adumbrat (quemadmodum in Legis promulgatione & saepe alias factum fuisse legimus) in praesenti lucida nubes istos inumbrauisse dicitur, ex qua denuo audita est vox illa, quae in Baptismo quoq; Christi prius sonuit, & qua nullam suauiore & iucundiorem vnquam mundus audiuit. Etenim olim tristes illae sententiae audiebantur: Paenitet me fecisse hominem: Maledictus qui non fecerit quaecunq; scripta sunt in libro Legis huius, & aliae similes, quae peccatorum conscientia grauatis terrorem diru incutiut. At his omnibus ista opponitur, qua Deus fe propter Filium suum nobis placatu esse testatur, & seipsum cu bonis suis omnibus nobis offert.
units.tr: Let us therefore look first at the author of this oracle, which he does not obscurely indicate: Matthew, when he writes that a bright cloud overshadowed the disciples and Christ, out of which this voice was heard. For, as we have said elsewhere, clouds are symbols or signs of the presence of God, and so a cloud once overshadowed the tabernacle when God's answer was sought there, or signified that he was present here. Peter certainly later used this passage to prove that the Apostles, not following cleverly devised fables, made known to the Church the power and coming of our Lord, but had seen his majesty with their own eyes and heard the voice sent to him from heaven. So this was the voice of God, who wished to bear witness to his only-begotten Son. And although elsewhere mention is made of darkness and dark clouds, by which he signifies his terrible majesty (as we read was often done also at the promulgation of the Law), here he is said to have overshadowed them with a bright cloud, out of which again was heard that voice which also sounded earlier at the baptism of Christ, and which the world has never heard more sweet and pleasant. For formerly those grim sentences were heard: "It repenteth me that I have made man," and "Cursed is he that continueth not in all things which are written in the book of this Law," and others like them, which strike dreadful terror into consciences burdened with sin. But against all these is set this word, by which God testifies that he is appeased toward us for the sake of his Son, and offers himself to us with all his goods.

units.la: Diligenter autem obseruari debet quod supra quoq; monuimus, quod cum longe aliis verbis Deus vti posset, ea repetit, quae olim per seruos suos Prophetas pronunciarat, & quae iam pridem literis erant mandata. Etenim per Dauidem olim dixerat praedestinato humani generis Seruatori: Filius meus es tu, hodie ego te genui. Per Isaiam autem de eode testatus erat: Ecce seruus meus, quo nitar: electus meus, quo placatur anima mea. Et cum eunde sub magni illius & catholici Prophetae nomine pollicebatur per Mosem, similiter addidit: Ipsum audite. Quapropter vt Moses & Elias, qui omniu feruorum Dei veteris Testamenti personam sustinuerunt, hic cum illo coparuerunt: ita eorunde quoq; verbis loqui voluit. Facit hoc plurimum ad Scripturae veteris commendationem, vt no dubitemus, eam (quod Paulus postea diserte affirmauit) a Deo inspiratam esse, & Dei Verba esse quae in illius libris describuntur. Ad hos ergo recurrant, quotquot Deum loquentem audire cupiunt, neq; (vt dies ille epulo) doctores alios ex alio mundo mitti postulent. Nam si ipse Deus nobis vt olim humana voce loqui vellet, no alia diceret, quam quae olim dixit. Constat enim sibi ipsi semper eius voluntas, & proinde Verbu quoq; eius manet in aeternu. Ideo Dei Filius Scripturas allegauit, & no solu priusquam moreretur, verietia ex mortuis resuscitatus ex Mose & Prophetis & Psalmis desumpsit concionum suarum argumenta. Stulte ergo nimis faciunt, qui nouum doctrinae genus requirunt: Qui vero praeterid quod euangelizatu est, praedicare audent, eos Christiani homines anathema debent censere, etiamsi Angeli de caelo, aut Apostoli fuerint. Videamus ergo oraculum hoc, quod tribus partibus constat.
