For, by the testimony of Christ himself, he has been a murderer from the beginning, and he seeks nothing but to destroy those whom he has enticed into his snares. Nor is it enough for him to have destroyed the body; he also plots the perdition of souls. For if he has cast the snares of vices upon anyone, to what precipices, immortal God, does he drag such people? With what dreadful and horrible torments does he rack them! They foam among their wicked desires, which at last drive them headlong into ruin; the same people are loud in unlawful things, and dumb before God in prayers and in other things that could help our salvation or be honourable to us.

units.la: ❦ esse poterant. Eiusmodi imagines quotidie, prob dolor, nobis repræsentant libidinosi, quos scortan di licentia abripit: ebriosi ite, iracundi, & vindictæ cupiditate flagrantes, auari, et si qui alij excusso diuinæ disciplinæ iugo in scelerū licentiam effunduntur. Et vtinam diligentius consideraremus hanc hostis nostri rabiem, vt nobis ab ea magis caueremus, & in precibus essemus ardentiores, qui bus ille quàm maximè profligari potest, vt in sequenti sermone dicetur. Nunc vero obseruemus plus quam paternam Dei bonitatem, qui hosti nostro non tantum permittit, quantu ipse vult, sed occultis habenis rabiē eius coercet. Quid enim obstitisse putas, ne infelix ille, de quo hic agitur, iam pridē perierit, nisi quòd Deus Satanam constrinxit, vt sibi præscriptos limites non auderet transgredi. Eiusdem generis est exemplum, quod in Iobo habemus. At quid vetera referre opus est, quando Deus quotidie pro nobis excubat? Etenim huic debemus, quòd hostis hic nos neq; insomnis iugulat, neq; inter pocula occidit, aut libidini cæcæ vacates, aut securitati nimiæ immersos per dit infinitis modis: quod facile poterat, nisi occulta Dei virtute in officio contineretur. Hæc cōsidē ratio nos ad gratiarū actionem excitet, & simul animosos faciat, ne nobis ab hoste illo, aut eius mancipijs, quales sunt Magi, incantatores, venefici, metuamus. Quid enim hi possent contra electos Dei, in quos ne principi quidem ipsorum ius est? Memorabilia sunt, quæ de Ägyptijs Magis, de Balaamo, Elyma, Simone & alijs commemorantur.
units.tr: ❦ ...could be. Such images, alas, present themselves to us every day: the lustful, whom the licence of the brothel carries off; the drunkards, the wrathful, those burning with a desire for revenge, the greedy, and whoever else, having shaken off the yoke of divine discipline, pours himself out into a licence for sin. And would that we considered more carefully this rage of our enemy, so that we might be more wary of it and more fervent in prayer, by which he can be most of all overcome, as will be said in the following sermon. But now let us observe the more than fatherly goodness of God, who does not allow our enemy as much as he wishes, but restrains his rage with hidden reins. For what do you think has kept that unhappy man, of whom we are speaking here, from perishing long ago, except that God bound Satan so that he would not dare to cross the limits set for him? The example we have in Job is of the same kind. But why recall old examples, when God keeps watch for us every day? For it is to him that we owe the fact that this enemy neither slaughters us in our sleep, nor kills us over our cups, nor destroys us in countless ways, immersing us in blind lust or excessive security, which he could easily do were he not held in check by the hidden power of God. This consideration should stir us to give thanks, and at the same time make us bold, so that we need not fear that enemy or his servants, such as magicians, enchanters and poisoners. For what could these do against the elect of God, over whom not even their prince has any right? Memorable are the things recorded of the Egyptian magicians, of Balaam, Elymas, Simon and others.

units.la: Sed ad Dominum Christum redeamus, qui paterno cum dolore queritur de isto rum omnium incredulitate & contumacia: O natio (inquit) incredula & peruersa, quousq; tandē ero vobiscū? quousq; tandē tolerabo vos? Indignes dicit, quibus cū ipse diutius versetur. Dura vox & digna, ad quam omnes exhorrescant, qui non omnes sensum pietatis exuerunt. Etenim quos Dei Filius, qui propter nos in mundū venit & homo factus est, Juo commercio indignos iudicat, eosdē ab Ecclesia simul & salutis societate excludit. Et magnū quid sit oportet, quo ille tantopere cōmoueatur, qui nullos vnquā peccatores fastidiuit. Quid vero illud est? O natio (inquit) incredula & peruersa vel distorta. Primo incredulitate eorū accusat, qua ipsum reijciebant, & quæ hactenus neq; doctrina neq; signis expugnari aut corrigi potuerat. Peruersam vero natione aut distortam dicit, qualis Moses olim dixit: quod legibus nullis sese in ordine adduci sinerent. Ideo alibi cœlos & terra aduersus illos producit testes, alibi vero eos ad boues & asinos, ad ciconias item, hirundines, grues & turtures remittit, vt in brutorū animantiū schola fecundū leges naturæ discant vi ue re, qui Dei legibus parere nolint. Quòd si quæras, quos nā tam duriter coepellet Dominus, ego omnes, qui aderat, vno reatu inuolui existimo, quàmuis alij alijs graniū peccauerint. Etenim discipulorum diffidentia manifestior est, quam vt illam multis demonstrari oporteat. De parente lunatici huius Marcus scribit, vt sua incredulitate ipse cōfessus sit, & huic succurri petierit. Interim certū est, increpatione illa in primis aduersus Scribas dirigi, quorū contumacia incurabilis erat, adeò vt cū Christo certamē suscepisse videri possent, cū quotidie in peius proficerent. Incredulitate ergo regnū Dei maximè stabilitur & promouetur, & hanc potissimū cauēant oportet, qui illius tyrannide liberari cupiunt: vt in sequenti sermone prolixius dicetur.
units.tr: But let us return to the Lord Christ, who with a fatherly grief complains of the unbelief and obstinacy of them all: "O unbelieving and perverse generation" (he says), "how long shall I be with you? How long shall I endure you?" He says that they are unworthy of his company, since he is with them for so long. It is a harsh word, and a worthy one, at which all must shudder who have not cast off all sense of piety. For those whom the Son of God, who came into the world for our sake and was made man, judges unworthy of his fellowship, he at the same time excludes from the Church and from the fellowship of salvation. And there must be something great by which he is so deeply moved, he who never despised any sinners. But what is that word? "O unbelieving and perverse, or distorted, generation." First he accuses them of unbelief, by which they rejected him, and which until now could be overcome or corrected neither by teaching nor by signs. But he calls the generation perverse or distorted, as Moses once did, because they would not allow themselves to be brought into order by any laws. Therefore elsewhere he calls heaven and earth as witnesses against them, and elsewhere he sends them to oxen and asses, and likewise to storks, swallows, cranes and turtledoves, so that in the school of the brute animals they may learn to live according to the laws of nature, since they refuse to obey the laws of God. But if you ask whom the Lord so harshly rebuked, I think that all who were present were bound by one and the same guilt, although some sinned more gravely than others. For the distrust of the disciples is too plain to need to be shown by many examples. Mark writes of the father of this lunatic boy that he confessed his unbelief and sought help for him. Meanwhile it is certain that this rebuke was directed above all against the scribes, whose obstinacy was incurable, so that they might seem to have entered into a contest with Christ, since they grew worse every day. Therefore the kingdom of God is above all established and advanced by unbelief, and those who wish to be freed from its tyranny ought especially to guard against this, as will be said more fully in the following sermon.

units.la: In præsenti hoc addemus, quod Dominus, etsi reliqui omnes acrius corripi mererentur, tamen puerum sibi adducere iubet: nimirum, vt ipsi medeatur. Est hoc nouum & irrefragabile bonitatis argumentū, quæ iustam indignatione vincit, vt licet reliqui omnes diffidentia hucusq; peccarint, nolit tamen horū culpa fraudi esse misero huic, quò minus huic succurrat. Indulgentiæ huius exempla quotidie cernimus. Etenim ingratitudine & intemperantia sua meretur mundus, vt fruges nobis neget Deus. Nō tamen quid pleriq; merentur respicit, sed quid communis necessitas postulet, & ideo Sol suū super iustos et iniustos oriri finit, & super bonos & malos de cœlo pluit. Quin tanta est Patris nostri cœlestis indulgetia, vt propter paucos credetes totis ciuitatibus parcat, et si omnino puniri oporteat incurabiles, tamē suos inter medias pœnas tueri et mirificè ex tētatione eripere nouit. Exēpla, quibus hoc demonstratur, in Noe, Lotho, Daniele extat, et similia multa quotidie fiunt. Ne ergo facile de Dei bonitate desperemus, multò minus nos exemplo multitudinis abripi patiamur. Nouit Dominus nostrer IESVS CHRISTVS qui sint fui, et sibi fideles nunquā deseret.
units.tr: To the present point we add this: although all the others deserved to be rebuked more sharply, the Lord nevertheless bids the boy be brought to him, namely so that he might heal him. This is a new and irrefutable proof of his goodness, which overcomes just indignation, so that, although all the others have sinned until now through their distrust, he is unwilling that their fault should be a hindrance to this wretched boy, so as to prevent him from helping him. We see examples of this indulgence every day. For the world, by its ingratitude and intemperance, deserves that God should deny us the fruits of the earth. Yet he does not look to what most people deserve, but to what common necessity requires, and therefore he lets the sun rise on the just and the unjust, and rain from heaven on the good and the evil. Indeed, so great is the indulgence of our heavenly Father that, for the sake of a few believers, he spares whole cities; and even if the incurable must altogether be punished, he nevertheless knows how to protect his own in the midst of the punishments and wonderfully snatch them from temptation. Examples by which this is shown are found in Noah, Lot and Daniel, and many similar things happen every day. Therefore let us not easily despair of the goodness of God, and much less let us allow ourselves to be carried away by the example of the multitude. Our Lord Jesus Christ knows who are his, and will never forsake those who are faithful to him.

units.la: Apparet hoc in huius historiæ catastrophe. Nam postquam (vt Marcus scripsit) aliquā tum cum patre huius pueri collocutus est, vt & huius diffidentiam argueret, & suam virtutem facere illustriorem, atq; nobis fidei cum diffidentia luctantis exemplu consolationis plenum proponeret, mox opus ipsum aggreditur, et magna cum authoritate miseru liberat. Nam primo obiurgat Daemoniu, ut se hostē Diaboli esse ostendat, qui eius deuincendi et destruendi causa in mundum venerit. Deinde superbu & arrogante titulis proprijs et ipso dignu compellat dicens: Tu spiritus mute & surde. Reuera autem talis est, cum nec Deum patienter audiat, nec ea loquatur, qua huic placere possint. Et vult, ut tale omnes agnoscant, neq; se ab eo decipi sinant. Tertio, Ego (inquit) tibi iniungo, exi ex eo, & ne amplius ingrediaris in eu. Et hoc dicendo ius omne Diabolo abdicat, quod in illum homine vsurparat. Nec mora, cogitur mandato Christi obedire improbus ille. Itaq; horrendum exclamans puerū laniat & discerpit, atq; eo seminece relicto abit, ut pleriq; ex circum stantibus illum mortuu esse dicerent. At IESVS praehensa manu pueri erigit eu, & sanitati restitutum patri restituit. Quo exemplo docemur, ut nobis quoq; cum illo hoste pugnandu sit. Sanciuit hanc militiam Deus in Paradiso inter serpente vetere & omnes Eua filios in ipsa rerum origine: & huic nomen damus, quando Baptismi aqua tingimur in Christi nomine, qui et ipse quam primum ab Ioanne baptizatus est, cum Diabolo in certamen descendit. Huius ergo exemplum imitemur, & prima cura sit, ne quas ei demus inducias, sed tergiuersante & moras nectente feruide vrgeamus. Deinde eunde depingamus suis coloribus, et proprijs titulis compellemus, ut se agnoscifentiat. Id enim ad eius audaciam frenanda efficacissimum est. Adhaec non obiter eum relegemus, sed procul a nobis repellamus, neq; ei ad nos redeundi aliquam potestate relinquamus. Nec enim aliqua esse debet nobis cum eo hoste societas, qui toties clamauit: Quid mihi rei tecum est? IESVS Fili Dei? Neq; terreant nos eius furores, quos iam discessurus ciet. Est enim hic postremus eius conatus, & quando omnia pessundaturus videtur, manu nobis porrigit Christus Dominus, et suo contactu nos sanat. Ideo enim hic in mundum venit & homo factus est, ut nos sibi uniret, & idem Draconem illum olim sub nostris pedibus conculcabit. Rom.6.
units.tr: This appears in the outcome of this story. For after (as Mark writes) he had spoken for a while with the father of this boy, both to rebuke his distrust and to make his own power more illustrious, and to set before us an example of faith struggling with distrust, full of comfort, he at once takes up the work itself and frees the wretched boy with great authority. For first he rebukes the demon, so as to show that he is the enemy of the devil, who came into the world to overcome and destroy him. Then he addresses him with his own titles, proud and arrogant, and such as befits him, saying: "You dumb and deaf spirit." And indeed he is such, since he neither listens patiently to God nor speaks anything that could please him. And he wills that all should recognise him as such, and not allow themselves to be deceived by him. Thirdly, "I," he says, "command you: come out of him, and enter him no more." And by saying this he strips the devil of every right that he had usurped over that man. Without delay that wicked one is compelled to obey the command of Christ. So, crying out terribly, he tears and mangles the boy, and leaves him almost dead, so that many of the bystanders said he was dead. But Jesus, taking the boy by the hand, raises him up and restores him to his father, healed. From this example we are taught that we too must fight with that enemy. God sanctioned this warfare in Paradise between the old serpent and all the sons of Eve, at the very origin of things; and we give it its name when we are washed with the water of Baptism in the name of Christ, who himself, as soon as he was baptised by John, entered the contest with the devil. Let us therefore imitate his example, and let our first care be not to give him any truce, but to press him hard as he shifts and delays. Then let us portray him in his own colours and address him by his proper titles, so that he may recognise himself. For this is most effective in restraining his audacity. Moreover, let us not dismiss him carelessly, but drive him far from us, and leave him no power to return to us. For there ought to be no fellowship between us and that enemy, who so often cried out: "What have I to do with you? Jesus, Son of God?" Nor let his raging frighten us, which he stirs up as he is about to depart. For this is his last attempt, and when he seems about to ruin everything, Christ the Lord stretches out his hand to us and heals us by his touch. For this reason he came into the world and was made man, so that he might unite us to himself, and he will tread that dragon under our feet as he did long ago. Rom. 6.

units.la: Restat miraculi effectus, quem apud populum circumstantem habuit. De hoc ita scribit Lucas: perctellebantur autem omnes super magnifica virtute Dei. Agnouerunt ergo virtute diuinam in Christo. At cum ea ipsis solatio esse deberet, terrori fuit, eo quod eius officium ignorarent. Terruit autem eos triste pueri a malo Daemone rapti & lacerati conditio. Etenim miserabile & terroris plenum spectaculum est, hominem a Satana tam indignis modis tractari. Deinde procul dubio eos terruit mens male sibi conscia, quando cogitarunt, quam parum honorifice Christum tractarint in suis discipulis, in quo tam luculenta diuinae potentia indicia elucebant. Docet autem hoc exemplum, quam facile fit Domino hostiu fuoru petulantia compescere. Paulo ante discipulis insultarunt Scribae, et videtur in his Diabolus contra Christum triumphare. Populus item priorum signorum oblitus stupet & haeret. Sed ecce vno verbo Diaboli eijcit Dominus, puerum patri in fide labascenti restituit, & hunc confirmat. Scribas autem confundit, ut perculsi et attoniti nesciant quid porro dicant. Huius generis exempla passim occurrunt, & haec perpetua Ecclesia IESV CHRISTI fors est, quam hic discipulis pollicetur, dicens: Amen amen dico vobis, flebitis & lamentabimini vos, mundus autem gaudebit, vos vero tristes fietis, sed tristitia vestra euadet in gaudium. In ipso igitur fortes teneamus stationem nostram, & ipsi seruiamus in fide syncera & sanctimonia. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: The effect of the miracle remains, which it had on the crowd standing around. Luke writes about this as follows: "But all were astonished at the majesty of God." They therefore recognised the divine power in Christ. Yet although this ought to have been a comfort to them, it became a terror, because they did not know his office. The wretched condition of the boy, seized and mangled by the evil demon, also frightened them, for it is a pitiable and terrifying sight to see a man handled by Satan in such shameful ways. Next, without doubt, a conscience aware of its own guilt terrified them, when they considered how dishonourably they had treated Christ in his disciples, in whom such clear signs of divine power shone forth. This example teaches, however, how easily the Lord can restrain the insolence of his enemies. A little before, the scribes had mocked the disciples, and in this the Devil seemed to triumph over Christ. Likewise the people, forgetting the earlier signs, stood amazed and hesitant. But see, with a single word the Lord casts out the Devil, restores the boy to his father, who was wavering in faith, and confirms him. He confounds the scribes, so that, struck dumb and astonished, they do not know what to say further. Examples of this kind occur everywhere, and this is the constant lot of the Church of Jesus Christ, which he promises to the disciples here, saying: "Verily, verily, I say unto you, that ye shall weep and lament, but the world shall rejoice; and ye shall be sorrowful, but your sorrow shall be turned into joy." Therefore let us hold our position firmly in him, and serve him in sincere faith and holiness. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCXV.
units.tr: HOMILY 215.

units.la: Tunc accedentes discipuli IESVM priuatim dixerunt: Quare nos non potuimus illud eijcere? IESVS autem dixit eis: Propter incredulitatem vestram. Amen quippe dico vobis, si habeatis fidem quantulum est granum sinapis, dicetis monti huic, Demigra hinc illuc: & demigrabit, & nihil impossibile erit vobis. Hoc vero genus daemoniorum non egreditur nisi per precationem & ieiunium. Versantibus autem ipsis in Galilaea, dixit eis IESVS: Futuru est ut Filius hominis tradatur in manus hominum, & trucidabunt eum, sed tertio die suscitabitur. Et contristati sunt vehementer.
units.tr: Then the disciples came to Jesus privately and said, "Why could we not cast it out?" Jesus said to them, "Because of your unbelief. For truly I say to you, if you have faith as small as a grain of mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, 'Move from here to there,' and it will move, and nothing will be impossible for you. But this kind of demon does not come out except by prayer and fasting." While they were staying in Galilee, Jesus said to them, "The Son of Man is going to be handed over into the hands of men, and they will kill him, but on the third day he will be raised." And they were exceedingly distressed.

units.la: CAP.XVII.
units.tr: Chapter 17.

units.la: QVamuis Dei Filius IESVS CHRISTVS commune humani generis hostem Satanam sua mortis merito & resurrectione gloriosa superatu ex regno suo foras expulerit, & nos ex eius tyrannide vindicarit, ne tame nos innata nobis confidentia & securitate circumuenti, nobis ipsis exitium pariamus, permittit illi, vt adhuc Leonis rugientis instar obambulet, & variis tentationibus nos infestet. Itaque admodum necesse est, vt probe teneamus, quomodo cum illo nos pugnare oporteat, & quibus armis vinci possit. Docet hoc ipse Christus proprio exemplo, & nuper non obscure docuit, hostem illum nostra diffidentia & incredulitate potissimum armari, ideoq; nobis fide firma & constanti opus esse, si adversus illum victoria velimus potiri. At quia discipuli rem nondum recte intelligebant, & nos omnes natura tardiores sumus in divinis, vt nulla institutio nobis nimia sit, in praesenti apertius et gravius cum illis agit, & simul quae alias multoties de to to redemptionis nostrae mysterio illis dixerat, denuo in mentem eis revocat.
units.tr: Although the Son of God, Jesus Christ, has overcome Satan, the common enemy of mankind, by the merit of his death and his glorious resurrection, and has driven him from his kingdom and rescued us from his tyranny, he still permits him to prowl like a roaring lion and to harass us with various temptations. Lest we, lulled by the confidence and security innate in us, bring ruin upon ourselves, it is therefore very necessary that we hold firmly how we ought to fight against him and with what weapons he can be conquered. Christ himself teaches this by his own example, and lately taught plainly that this enemy is armed chiefly by our distrust and unbelief, and that we therefore need a firm and constant faith if we wish to gain the victory over him. But because the disciples did not yet rightly understand the matter, and because we all are by nature slow in divine things, so that no instruction can be too much for us, he now deals with them more openly and more seriously, and at the same time calls back to their minds what he had on many other occasions told them about the whole mystery of our redemption.

units.la: Occasionem huic tractationi praebuerunt discipuli, qui illu priuatim domi interrogarunt, quid obstiterit, quod ipsi daemonium ex puero lunatico, de quo audiuimus, non potuerint expellere. Causae, quae ipsos potuerunt mouere, variae fuerunt. Nam procul dubio doluit ipsis, quod non sine scandalo multorum Scribis ludibrio fuerant. Et fortasis timebant etiam, ne Dominus potestatem, quam antea ipsis in spiritus immundos & omnis generis morbos dederat, omnino auferre vellet. At si quae Christus parenti istius pueri dixerat, propius attendissent, non multa quaestione opus erat. Sed tmpofuit eis, quod se in fide satis instructos esse, neque incredulitatis vitio notari debere putauerunt, & ideo culpam omnem in alios transferre cupiunt. Est hoc commune vitium humani ingenij, quo fit, vt quando nobis ipsis aliquod malum aut incommodum accersiuimus, minime tamen videri velimus, id nostra culpa factum esse, sed causas mali in aliis quaeramus, vel etiam temere in quosdam alios reijciamus. Fecit hoc parens noster Adamus, & hodie multi in salutis aeternae negotio idem faciunt, qui ignorantiam praetexunt, & huius causam esse queruntur mysteriorum regni Dei obscuritatem, cum tamen ad lucem Euangelij, quam eis Deus benigne offert, ipsi oculos malitiose claudant. Ad eundem modum multi quoad rem domesticam de egestate & penuria sua queruntur, & huius causam omnem reijciunt in aliorum inhumanitatem atque auaritiam, cum ipsi sua prodigalitate & luxu, adhaec impio admonitionum omnium & legum contemptu se in eas angustias adducant, vt ab vsurarijs & faeneratoribus cogantur opem petere, quorum vngues & insatiabilem rapacitatem facile euitare poterant, si temperantius viuerent, & bonis legibus obedirent. Sed audiamus Christi responsum, quo tria agit.
units.tr: The disciples provided the occasion for this discussion, for they asked him privately at home why they had not been able to cast out the demon from the lunatic boy of whom we have heard. There were various causes that could have moved them. For without doubt it grieved them that they had become a laughingstock to the Scribes, to the scandal of many. And perhaps they also feared that the Lord might wish to take away entirely the power he had previously given them over unclean spirits and every kind of disease. But if they had paid closer attention to what Christ had said to the boy's father, there would have been no great question. Yet they were deceived into thinking that they were sufficiently instructed in faith and could not be marked with the fault of unbelief, and so they wish to shift all the blame onto others. This is a common vice of human nature: when we bring some evil or inconvenience upon ourselves, we do not want it to seem that we did so through our own fault, but seek the causes of the evil in others, or even rashly cast them upon certain people. Our father Adam did this, and today many do the same in the matter of eternal salvation. They plead ignorance and complain that the cause of it is the obscurity of the mysteries of God's kingdom, although they maliciously close their eyes to the light of the Gospel which God kindly offers them. In the same way many complain about their poverty and want in domestic affairs and lay the whole cause of it on the inhumanity and avarice of others, whereas by their own prodigality and luxury, and moreover by their impious contempt of all warnings and laws, they bring themselves into such straits that they are forced to seek help from usurers and moneylenders, whose claws and insatiable rapacity they could easily have avoided had they lived more temperately and obeyed good laws. But let us hear Christ's answer, in which he does three things.

units.la: Primum, quod paulo ante de totius gentis ἀπιστία seu incredulitate in genere quaestus erat, ad ipsos quoque pertinere ostendit, dicens: Propter incredulitatem vestram. Quasi diceret: Quid opus est quaerere? Iam ante dixi, incredulitate vestrum omnium immundos spiritus armari, vt pelli non possint. Sed quia video vos velle extra culpam esse, aperte dico, vos non minus illius reos esse quam cateros: nec enim tantum adhuc profecistis in fide, quantum debebant profecisse, qui mihi tam diu conuersati sunt, &c. Suo autem exemplo docet quomodo tractari debeant, qui quae in genere de vitijs publicis, quorum culpa ipsi quoq; tenentur, pro concione publica dicuntur, nolunt agnoscere, & tanquam nihil ad se pertinentia surdis auribus praetereunt. In facie dicatur eis quod res est, vt se tangi sentiant. Ita olim Prophetae fecerunt, qui non veriti sunt clamare: Audite capita Iacob, et principes domus Israelis, qui a iudicio abhorretis & quicquid rectum est peruertitis. Principes pro munere eius dicunt, et sacerdotes pro pretio docent, prophetae pro pecunia diuinant: Idcirco propter vos Sion vt ager arabitur, & Ierusalem acerrimus erit, &c. Va securis in Sione, & confidentibus in monte Samariae, &c. Audite verbum Domini principes Sodomai, & tu populae Gomorrhae legem Dei nostri: Quomodo meretrix facta est vrbs fidelis, aequitatis plena, in qua iustitia habitabat, nunc autem parricida? Ad eundem modum Pharisaei & Scribis laruam Christus detraxit. Et ita Paulus publice peccantes iubet coram omnibus argui, vt si ipsi incurabiles sunt, saltem alij timore aliquo percellantur. 1. Tim.5.
units.tr: First, he shows that the unbelief (ἀπιστία [apistia]) of the whole people, which he had mentioned a little before in general terms, pertains also to them, saying: "Because of your unbelief." As if he said: Why is there need to ask? I said before that by the unbelief of you all the unclean spirits are armed so that they cannot be driven out. But since I see that you wish to be free of blame, I say openly that you are no less guilty of it than the others; for you have not advanced in faith as far as you ought to have advanced, you who have been with me so long, etc. He teaches by his own example how those should be treated who refuse to acknowledge what is said in general from the pulpit about public vices, in which they too are implicated, and who pass by with deaf ears as if these things had nothing to do with them. Let it be said to their face what the truth is, so that they feel themselves touched. So the prophets of old did, not fearing to cry out: "Hear, you heads of Jacob and princes of the house of Israel, who abhor judgment and pervert all that is right. The princes teach for a bribe, the priests for pay, the prophets divine for money. Therefore for your sake Zion shall be ploughed like a field, and Jerusalem shall become a heap of ruins," etc. "Woe to the careless in Zion, and to those who trust in the mountain of Samaria," etc. "Hear the word of the Lord, princes of Sodom, and you people of Gomorrah, the law of our God. How has the faithful city become a harlot, full of justice, in which righteousness dwelt, but now murderers?" In the same way Christ tore off the mask from the Pharisees and Scribes. And so Paul bids that those who sin publicly be rebuked before all, so that if they are incurable, at least others may be struck with some fear. 1 Tim. 5.

units.la: Docet autem hic locus, ἀπιστίαν siue incredulitatem praecipuam in rebus gerendis remoram esse, vt minus proficiatur, neq; successum optatum habeant. Est autem illa duplex. Prima, quam propriè diffidentiam vocant, qua fit, vt nec Dei Verbo credamus, neque eius auxilio fidamus. Altera potest perfidia vel infidelitas dici, qua peccatur, quando non bona fide, sed negligenter res nobis mandatas agimus: quod ex priori sequitur, & plerunq; eius comes est. Itaq; quotquot se parum proficere vident in sua vocatione, hoc Christi dictum sibi applicent, & in seipsos descendendo, qua fide agant, considerent. Queruntur hodie Ecclesiarum ministri nihil profici apud plerosq; homines praedicando, docendo, monendo, hortando, corripiendo, minando denique. Sed vtinam omnes diligentius seipsos intuerentur, & fere viderent, se non ea, qua decebat, fide in ministerio suo versari. Plerique enim non satis intenti sunt lectioni Scripturarum, in docendo item negligentes, in monendo frigidi & remissi, in precibus languidi sunt, adhaec mundo & hominibus potius placere cupiunt quam Deo, multi denique perfidum illum dispensatorem imitantur, quem Christus cum ebrijs edere & bibere, conservos percutere & familiam suae fidei creditam suo dimenso fraudare dicit. Quid ergo aliud de iis fiat, quam quod Ieremias dicit: Maledictus, qui facit opus Domini maligne? Transferant itaque ad se etiam qui ad Respublicae gubernacula sedent, & similiter videbunt, non in omnibus tantum fidei Zelum & in rebus curandis feruorem esse, quantum functio ista requirit. Similem languorem & negligentiam, imo infidelitatem in opificibus manuarijs, in agricolis, in heris & patribus familias, in servis item & mercenarijs deprehendes. Quid ergo mirum si hos omnes suo fauore & benedictione Deus destituat, ut successu nullo fruantur? Meretur omne genus calamitatum publica ista omnis loci et ordinis hominum infidelitas, nec rebus passim omnibus cofuli poterit, nisi Deo et hominibus fideles sint omnes in sua vocatione aut functione, qua fungitur.
units.tr: This passage teaches that unbelief (ἀπιστίαν [apistian]), or lack of faith, is the chief hindrance in carrying out our tasks, so that less progress is made and we do not obtain the success we desire. This unbelief is twofold. The first, which is properly called diffidence, is when we neither trust God's word nor rely on his help. The second may be called perfidy or infidelity, by which we sin when we carry out the tasks entrusted to us not in good faith but carelessly; this follows from the former and is usually its companion. Therefore, as many as see that they make little progress in their calling should apply to themselves this saying of Christ, and by descending into themselves consider with what faith they act. Today the ministers of the churches complain that nothing is gained among most people by preaching, teaching, admonishing, exhorting, rebuking, and finally threatening. But I wish that all would look more diligently at themselves, and would see that they do not conduct their ministry with the faith it deserves. For most are not sufficiently intent on the reading of Scripture, are negligent in teaching, cold and remiss in admonishing, and languid in prayer; moreover, they desire to please the world and men rather than God. Finally, many imitate that faithless steward whom Christ describes as eating and drinking with drunkards, beating his fellow servants, and cheating the household entrusted to his care of its portion. What else, then, should be done with them than what Jeremiah says: "Cursed is he who does the work of the Lord deceitfully"? Let those too who sit at the helm of the commonwealth apply this to themselves, and they will likewise see that there is not in all things so much zeal of faith, nor such fervour in handling affairs, as that office requires. You will find a similar languor and negligence, indeed unfaithfulness, in craftsmen, in farmers, in masters and heads of households, and likewise in servants and hired workers. Why then is it a wonder if God deprives all these of his favour and blessing, so that they enjoy no success? This general unfaithfulness of every rank and order of men deserves every kind of calamity, and affairs cannot be set right anywhere unless all are faithful to God and to men in the calling or office which they discharge.

units.la: At respondere poterant discipuli: Cur incredulitatis accusamur, qui non ita prudenter fidei confessionem addidimus, quae ita tibi probata fuit, ut Simonem ideo beatum dixeris? Imo poterant alij Apostolis infirmiores sibi omnem abiicere, & Deum nimis iniquum aut morosum putare, cui nulla fides sufficiat, & ita secum rationem inire: Si Apostolorum fides non sufficiens fuit, ut daemonium illud posset eicere, qui omnibus reliquis Christum secuti sunt, qui cum ipso permanserunt in omnibus tentationibus suis, quos suos testes, lucem mundi, salem terrae dixit, & publicos totius orbis doctores esse voluit: quid de te fiet, cuius fides cum Apostolis nullo modo comparari potest? Sed ad omnes eiusmodi obiectiones per Praeoccupationem respondet Dominus, dicens: Amen dico vobis, si habeatis fidem quantulum est granum sinapis, dicetis monti huic, Demigra hinc illuc: & demigrabit, & nihil impossibile erit vobis. Quasi diceret: Exigit a servis suis Deus fidem, sine qua ei nemo placere potest. Idem tamen non adeo difficilis et morosus est, ut nihil ipsi sufficiat. Novit enim qui sint homines, & quod dum in carne viuunt, longissime absunt a perfectione. Itaq; fides modica ipsi probatur, modo vera sit, non fucata: & instar grani sinapis acris & viuax, non frigida et mortua sit. Hanc qui habent, & eius professione constanter retinent, & (ut per Prophetam ait) sabbata sua custodiunt, & quae ipsi placet eligunt, atq; facta sua firmiter apprehendunt, hos ille vicissim excolit, & viribus nouis instaurat ac auget, ut si necesse sit montes loco mouere & alio transferre, id ipsis non sit impossibile futurum. At hoc dicendo discipulos conuincit sua infirmitatis & imperfectionis, ne sibi nimium placeant. Interim hoc non rigide accipi debet secundum literam, ut vel confidenter nimis tentemus res absurdas & non necessarias, ut olim Simon Magus, qui se volaturum pollicebatur: vel eos damnemus mendacij & erroris, qui non omnium postulatis aut votis satisfaciunt. Nam sunt quidem fidei omnia possibilia, sed eadem uni Deo nituntur, & ab eius Verbo pendet. Nihil ergo tentat aut conatur, quam quod ei placere novit, & quod is iubet: ipso denique iubente ea perficit, quae vires humanas superant, quod in epistola ad Hebraeos Apostolus exemplis infinitis demonstrat. Nihil denique tam arduum & graue est, nihil homini incumbit tam intolerabile, quod non superet & procul remoueat fides, si necesse fit. Et quod in praesenti pollicetur Christus, Apostoli non multo post experti sunt, & ipsi laeto admodum successu perfecerunt. Cum enim accepto Spiritu Sancto Euangelium IESV CHRISTI praedicaret, montes altissimos & grauissimos ipsis Satan obiecit, Iudaeorum Sacerdotes & Seniores, gentium philosophos, Romanos Imperatores et horum minacia edicta, scismata item intra Ecclesiae parietes excitata: Sed haec omnia Euangelij praedicationi cesserunt, quae inuito mundo & eius principe per totum orbe feliciter propagata est. Es quotidie sentiunt Christiani homines, qui vere credunt, montes grauissimos ab illorum ceruicibus atque humeris subito remoueri & auferri, quibus ferendis sese impares esse paulo ante arbitrabantur. Porro ad praesentem causam iflud omne applicans, addit: Hoc vero genus daemoniorum non egreditur nisi per precationem & ieiunium. Vbi non putabimus illum de certo daemoniorum genere loqui, quod caeteris sit contumacius ac ferocius, multo minus loco fidei preculas certas aut exorcismos cum ieiunijs superstitiosis commendat, sed partim in genere ostendit, eam esse daemoniorum omnium pertinaciam, ut non nisi fide viua & efficaci possit expelli: partim quibus praescribis fidem confirmari oporteat, docet: denique & generalem doctrinam tradit, quid nobis agendum sit, si quando Satan ita pedem fixisse & regnum suum confirmauisse videtur, ut nunquam cessuru putemus: quod in hoc puero fecit, quem a pueris occupauerat, & hodie in multis facit, qui vel superstitionibus vel scelerum licentia ita adiuuerunt, ut quoad humanas rationes, de ipsorum salute prorsus desperandum sit: Quando item fidem in nobis labascere & tantumnon succumbere sentimus, sicuti de pueri huius parente nuper dictum est. Tunc nihil proficitur nuda ac otiosa fidei professione, sed eam precibus assiduis & ardentibus adiuuari oportet. Ne aut frigeant preces, & nos carnis vel securitas vel lasciuia alio vocet, ieiunij eam in ordinem redigi, adeoq; mortificari necesse est, ut Paulus loquitur. Ieiunia autem non in incerto & superstitioso ciborum delectu consistunt, sed in omnium eorum abstinentia, quae carnem ferociorem reddunt, & eius lasciuiam augent, aut in causa sunt, ut securA salutis nimium sibi parcat indulgeat. Itaque, ipsum quisque examinet, & vel otium sibi subducat, quod aliqui pulmunt Satanae dixerunt, vel vestes luxuriosas deponat, qui bus animi fastus & superbia augetur, vel etiam a legitimo coniugij vsu sibi temperet, ne libido in precibus remissiorem reddat. Ideo in paenitentia publica Prophetae sacciis aut cilicijs nos induì, & coniuges secubare, atque sponsum e thalamo suo exire iubent: & huius postremi Paulus quoq; meminit. Haec si probe considerentur, non mirabimur, cur in tanta Euangelij luce, quando fides vera in Christum omnes gloriantur, tantae diaboli vires sint, ut passim regnum suum obtineat & instauret per superstitiones in multorum cordibus repullulantes, vel per effrenem & sceleratam quiduis agendi licentiam. Frigent enim apud plerosq; fidei verae exercitia. Verbi studium languet, preces negliguntur, cupiditatibus carnis indulgetur, a compotationibus, vestium luxu, fastu, libidinum licentia ne ij quidem omnes prorsus alieni sunt, qui in Ecclesiae ministerio constituti alios ad pietatem & preces indefinentes doctrina & exemplo suo excitare debebant. Est ergo fides in terris rara, sicuti Dominus de nouissimis faculis praedixit, & ideo Satan vbique regnat & triumphat.
units.tr: But the disciples could answer: "Why are we accused of unbelief? We did not make our confession of faith so rashly. It was so well approved by you that you called Simon blessed for it." Others, weaker than the Apostles, might have cast off all such thoughts, thought God too unjust or too difficult, to whom no faith is enough, and reasoned with themselves: "If the faith of the Apostles was not sufficient to cast out that demon, those who followed Christ with everyone else, who stayed with him through all his trials, whom he called his witnesses, the light of the world and the salt of the earth, and wanted to be the public teachers of the whole world, what will become of you, whose faith cannot be compared with the Apostles' at all?" But the Lord answers all such objections in advance, saying: "Truly I say to you, if you have faith no bigger than a grain of mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, 'Move from here to there,' and it will move, and nothing will be impossible for you." It is as if he said: God requires faith from his servants, and without it no one can please him. Yet he is not so hard to please or so exacting that nothing satisfies him. For he knows what men are, and that while they live in the flesh they are very far from perfection. So a small faith pleases him, provided it is true and not feigned, and is sharp and lively like a grain of mustard seed, not cold and dead. Those who have this faith, and hold firmly to its profession, and (as the Prophet says) keep their sabbaths, and choose what pleases him, and firmly grasp his works, these he in turn cultivates and renews and increases with fresh strength, so that, if it should be necessary to move mountains and carry them elsewhere, this will not be impossible for them. But in saying this he convicts the disciples of their weakness and imperfection, so that they will not be too pleased with themselves. Meanwhile, this must not be taken rigidly according to the letter, so that we rashly attempt absurd and unnecessary things, as Simon Magus once did, who promised that he would fly; nor should we condemn as liars and deceivers those who do not obtain all that they ask or wish for. For all things are indeed possible to faith, but faith rests on the one God alone and depends on his Word. So it attempts and undertakes nothing except what it knows pleases him and what he commands; and at his command it accomplishes those things that exceed human strength, as the Apostle demonstrates in his Epistle to the Hebrews with countless examples. In short, nothing is so arduous or heavy, nothing so intolerable weighs upon a man, that faith does not overcome it and remove it far away, if need be. What Christ promises in the present passage, the Apostles experienced not long afterwards, and they themselves accomplished it with very happy success. For when, having received the Holy Spirit, they preached the Gospel of Jesus Christ, Satan set before them very high and heavy mountains: the priests and elders of the Jews, the philosophers of the Gentiles, the Roman emperors and their threatening edicts, and likewise schisms stirred up within the walls of the Church. Yet all these yielded to the preaching of the Gospel, which, against the wishes of the world and its prince, was happily spread throughout the whole earth. And every day Christian people who truly believe feel that very heavy mountains are suddenly lifted and taken from their necks and shoulders, which shortly before they thought themselves unequal to bearing. Moreover, applying all this to the present case, he adds: "This kind of demon does not go out except by prayer and fasting." Here we should not think he is speaking of a certain class of demons that is more stubborn and fierce than the rest, much less does he commend to faith fixed prayers or exorcisms together with superstitious fasts. Rather, he shows in general that such is the obstinacy of all demons that they cannot be cast out except by a living and effective faith; and partly he teaches by what means faith ought to be strengthened; and finally he gives a general teaching about what we must do whenever Satan seems to have fixed his foot and confirmed his kingdom so firmly that we think he will never give way. He did this in the case of this boy, whom Satan had possessed from childhood, and he does it today in many who have been so aided by superstitions or by licence in wickedness that, as far as human reasoning goes, their salvation must be entirely despaired of. He does it also when we feel faith wavering in us and nearly giving way, as was said recently about the father of this boy. Then the bare and idle profession of faith achieves nothing, but faith must be helped by constant and fervent prayers. Lest our prayers grow cold, and the security or wantonness of the flesh call us elsewhere, it is necessary to bring faith into order by fasting, and so to mortify it, as Paul says. Fasts, however, do not consist in an uncertain and superstitious choice of foods, but in abstinence from all those things that make the flesh more fierce and increase its wantonness, or that cause a man to spare and indulge himself too much in a false sense of security. So let each one examine himself, and either withdraw from idleness, which some have rightly called the devil's pillow, or lay aside luxurious clothing, by which pride and haughtiness of spirit are increased, or even refrain for a while from the lawful use of marriage, so that lust does not make his prayers less earnest. That is why, in public repentance, the Prophets bid us put on sackcloth and ashes, and bid spouses live apart and the bridegroom come out of his bridal chamber; and Paul too makes mention of this last. If these things are duly considered, we shall not be surprised why, in such a great light of the Gospel, when all glory in true faith in Christ, the power of the devil is so great that he holds and renews his kingdom everywhere, through superstitions sprouting again in the hearts of many, or through unbridled and wicked licence to do whatever one pleases. For the practices of true faith grow cold among most people. Zeal for the Word languishes, prayers are neglected, the desires of the flesh are indulged; and not even all of those are wholly free from drinking bouts, luxury in dress, pride and licence in lusts, who have been placed in the ministry of the Church and ought to have stirred others to godliness and unceasing prayer by their teaching and example. Faith is therefore rare on earth, as the Lord foretold of the last times, and so Satan reigns and triumphs everywhere.

units.la: His subtexit Dominus nouam eorum commemorationem, quae ipsi euenturae erant, & de quibus intra paucos dies prius tertio dixerat: Primo nimirum postea fidei confessionem a Petro aedi tam: deinde quando ex monte descendens prohibuit ne tres discipuli, quod illic viderant, cuiquam diuulgent: tertio quando sibi idem quod Ioanni Baptistae euenturum esse dixit. Idem nunc quoq; repetens ait: Futurum est vt Filius hominis tradatur in manus hominum, & trucidabunt eum, sed tertio die suscitabitur. Et ista quidem tunc dixit, quando diuina eius virtute omnes perculsi fuerant (vt nuper ex Luca dictum est) & iam per Galilaeam transiens contendebat Hierosolymam ad crucem. Apparet autem ex circumstantiis, cur de his rursus differat. Primo videlicet propter seipsum, vt frequenti passionis & mortis meditatione sese ad patientiam praeparet: Deinde propter discipulos, qui toties de his admoniti, adhuc de illo & regno eius carnalia sapiebant: quae causa erat, vt quoties vulgi applausum ex eius miraculis exoriri videbant, in ipsem regni futuri erigerentur: quod tunc quoq; factum fuisse patebit, ex illorum de primatu contentione, quae sub initium sequentis Capitis describetur. Vult ergo illos ab hac spe regni terreni reuocare, & insuper docere, quis ipsis miraculorum omnium vsus esse debeat: Vt nimirum ex illis virtutem eius diuinam agnoscant, nec crucis ignominia offendantur, quin potius seipsos quoque ad crucem ferendam praeparent. At ex eo generalis doctrina peti debet, vt quando res secundae sunt, ad certamina nos armemus diligenti eorum meditatione, quae de Ecclesiae persecutionibus olim praedictae sunt. Similiter in priuata fortuna memores simus vicissitudinis rerum humanarum, in quibus nihil certum & stabile est. Consolationem vero petamus ex Resurrectione Christi, qua hic peccatum, mortem & inferos vicit, nobisq; in caelis gloriam & vitam aeternam meruit.
units.tr: To this the Lord added a new reminder of what was about to happen to them, and of which he had spoken a few days before, a third time: first, when Peter made his confession; then, when, coming down from the mountain, he forbade the three disciples to tell anyone what they had seen there; and third, when he said that what was to befall John the Baptist would also befall him. Now, repeating it again, he says: "The Son of Man is going to be delivered into the hands of men, and they will kill him, but on the third day he will be raised." He said these things at the time when all had been struck with amazement at his divine power (as was said just now from Luke), and while he was passing through Galilee on his way to Jerusalem and the cross. The circumstances make clear why he again speaks of these things. First, for his own sake, so that by frequent meditation on his passion and death he might prepare himself for patience. Second, for the sake of the disciples, who, though so often warned about these things, still thought fleshly thoughts about him and his kingdom; and this was the reason that whenever they saw the crowd's applause arise from his miracles, they were lifted up in hope of the kingdom to come. That this also happened on that occasion will become clear from their contention over primacy, which will be described at the beginning of the following chapter. He therefore wants to call them back from this hope of an earthly kingdom, and moreover to teach them what use all his miracles ought to have for them: namely, that from them they might recognise his divine power, and not be offended by the shame of the cross, but rather prepare themselves to bear the cross. From this a general teaching ought to be sought: that when things go well for us, we should arm ourselves for struggles by diligently meditating on what was foretold long ago about the persecutions of the Church. Likewise, in our private fortunes, let us remember the changeableness of human affairs, in which nothing is certain or stable. But let us seek consolation from the resurrection of Christ, by which he has overcome sin, death and hell here, and has won for us glory and eternal life in heaven.

units.la: Quam necessaria sit haec meditatio, Apostoli suo exemplo docent. Nam his auditis contristati stati sunt vehementer. Causam tristitiæ huius Lucas indicat, quòd dictum istud ignorarint, neq; intellexerint mentem Christi. Nam, vt sæpè diximus, caro a cruce abhorret: quia ergo fructum mortis Christi discipuli ignorabant, resurrectionis autem mysterium illis prorsus absconditum erat, non potuerunt non contristari istorum commemoratione. Auxit dolorem, quòd Lucas addit, ipsos non ausos fuisse interrogare Dominum: quòd fortassis correptionem verentur, exemplo Petri territi, de quo supra audiuimus. Debet hic obseruari carnis ingenium, quæ fere gaudet & spes magnas concipit, quando de cruce cogitandum erat: vicissim autem dolet, quando debebat exultare. Causa huius peruersi iudicij præcipua est, quòd Christum sibi alium fingit quàm reuera sit. Nos ergo talem agnoscamus, qualem Scripturæ proponunt. Si quid nos latet, alacri & intrepida mente ad ipsum accedamus, & audiamus in Euangelio nobis loquentem. Quicquid autem accidat, consolari nos debet, quòd vt propter nos in mundum venit Dei Filius & hominem verum induit: ita propter nos mortuus est, nobis item resurrexit, nobis vicit mortem & diabolum, noster item Mediator & intercessor ad dexteram Patris considet, nec tamen nos relinquit orphanos, sed nobiscum manet, vt nos tueatur, feruet & alat vsq; ad consummationem seculi. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: How necessary this meditation is, the Apostles teach by their own example. For when they heard these things, they were greatly saddened. Luke indicates the cause of this sadness: they did not understand that saying, nor did they grasp the mind of Christ. For, as we have often said, the flesh shrinks from the cross; so because the disciples were ignorant of the fruit of Christ's death, and the mystery of the resurrection was entirely hidden from them, they could not help being saddened by the mention of these things. Luke adds that the sorrow was increased by the fact that they did not dare to ask the Lord, perhaps fearing a rebuke, frightened by the example of Peter, of whom we heard above. Here we should observe the nature of the flesh, which almost rejoices and conceives great hopes when it ought to be thinking of the cross, and in turn grieves when it ought to exult. The chief cause of this perverse judgment is that it fashions for itself a Christ other than he really is. Let us therefore acknowledge him as the Scriptures set him forth. If anything about him is hidden from us, let us approach him with a cheerful and fearless mind, and let us hear him speaking to us in the Gospel. Whatever happens, this should console us: that just as the Son of God came into the world for our sake and put on true manhood, so he died for our sake, and likewise rose again for us, conquered sin, death and the devil for us, and likewise our Mediator and intercessor sits at the right hand of the Father, and yet he does not leave us orphans, but remains with us, to protect, nourish and sustain us until the end of the age. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCXVI.
units.tr: HOMILY CCXVI.

units.la: Cum autem venissent Capernaum, venerunt ad Petrum qui didrachma accipiunt, dixerunt s: Magister vester non soluit didrachma? Dicit, Etiam. Et cum ingressus fuisset domum, præueniteum IESVS, dicens: Quid tibi videtur Simon? Reges terræ a quibus accipiunt tributa aut censum? a filiis suis, an ab alienis? Dicit ei Petrus: ab alienis. Ait ei IESVS: Nempe igitur liberi sunt filij. Sed ne offendamus eos, profectus ad mare, mitte hamum: & eum piscem qui ascenderit primus, tolle: & aperto ore eius, inuenies staterem: acceptum illum da eis pro me & pro te.
units.tr: When they had come to Capernaum, those who collect the didrachma came to Peter and said: "Does your Master not pay the didrachma?" He said, "Yes." And when he had gone into the house, Jesus anticipated him, saying: "What do you think, Simon? From whom do the kings of the earth take tribute or tax: from their own sons, or from strangers?" Peter said to him, "From strangers." Jesus said to him, "Then indeed the sons are free. But so that we do not offend them, go to the sea, cast a hook, and take the first fish that comes up; when you open its mouth you will find a stater. Take that and give it to them for me and for you."

units.la: NOn ignorauit Dei Filius, Dominus & redemptor noster IESVS CHRISTVS omnibus seculis plures fore, qui sub fidei & libertatis Christianæ prætextu carnis licentiam & immunitatem ab onerib. ciuilibus, tributis nimirum, censibus & vectigalibus, quærant. Quia verò hæc causa est periculosorum motuum & turbarum in Republica, quas omnes boni & honesti merito oderunt, Euangelij quoq; doctrina & fides Christiana multis hoc nomine suspecta & exosa est. Ideò Dominus non verbis modò, verumetiam proprio exemplo docet, se non abolere legitimum Magistratu & ciuiles constitutiones, sed perpetuò ratum esse velle quod semel dixit: Reddite Cæsari quæ sunt Cæsaris, & Deo quæ sunt Dei: quod Paulus diligentius explicans ait: Reddite omnibus quod debetis: cui tributum debetur, tributum: cui vectigal, vectigal: cui timorem, timorem: cui honorem, honorem. Ad cuius doctrinæ confirmationem cumprimis pertinet hæc historia, quæ commodissime hoc loco interseritur. Quia enim discipuli, qui etiam ipsi in Christo regnū terrenum & liberationem ex Romana tyrannide sperabant, partim per clarificationem eius nuperrime factam: partim populi exemplo, qui totius miraculo in lunatici pueri curatione edito perculsus fuerat, in errore suo confirmari poterant, nouo exemplo docere voluit, quid omnes homines Magistratibus suis debeant. Insunt autem huic historiæ alia nonnulla consideratu dignißima, & proinde illam diligenter inspexisse proderit. Partes eius duæ sunt: prior occasionem huius facti indicat, vbi colloquium narratur, quod Petro cum publicanis aut census exactoribus intercessit: posterior Domini Christi cum Petro colloquium continet, ex quo miraculi historia potest intelligi, quod ille in censu aut didrachma persoluendo edidit.
units.tr: The Son of God, our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ, did not fail to know that in every age there would be many who, under the pretext of faith and Christian liberty, seek licence for the flesh and immunity from civil burdens, namely tributes, taxes and duties. Since this is the cause of dangerous uprisings and disturbances in the commonwealth, which all good and honourable people rightly hate, the teaching of the Gospel and the Christian faith are on this account viewed with suspicion and hatred by many. Therefore the Lord teaches not only by words but also by his own example that he does not abolish the lawful magistracy and civil ordinances, but wishes what he once said to stand for ever: "Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's." Paul, explaining this more carefully, says: "Render to all what you owe: tribute to whom tribute is owed, custom to whom custom, fear to whom fear, honour to whom honour." This story, which is most fittingly inserted here, serves above all to confirm this teaching. For the disciples, who themselves hoped in Christ for an earthly kingdom and deliverance from Roman tyranny, could be confirmed in their error, partly by his recent transfiguration and partly by the example of the crowd, which had been struck by the miracle wrought in the healing of the lunatic boy. So he wished to teach by a new example what all people owe their magistrates. Moreover, there are several other matters in this history worthy of consideration, so it will be useful to examine it carefully. It has two parts. The first indicates the occasion of this event, and narrates the conversation that Peter had with the publicans or tax collectors. The second contains the conversation of the Lord Christ with Peter, from which can be understood the miracle he performed in paying the census or didrachma.

units.la: Prioris narrationum a loco, vbi hæc facta sunt, exorditur Euangelista, & IESVM cum discipulis Capernaum venisse scribit, quam supra Capite nono ipsius ciuitatem dixit. Et verisimile est, tunc tempus fuisse, quo census annuus a singulis exigi ac colligi solebat. At hic obseruari debet Iudæorū gentem olim liberam fuisse, neq; alium censum cuiquam dedisse, nisi quem Deus adsarta tecta tabernaculi seu templi, & cultus externi conseruationem dari iusserat: quo cen publico testi monio testabantur, fe Dei peculium esse, neq; alium habere Regem praeter Deum, qui fe totu ipsis obstrinxerat, & ideo Sanctus Israelis dicebatur. Erat hic siclus dimidius, quae viritim singuli pen debant, fiue drachmas aut denarios duos. At cum Romani Iudaeam in prouincia redegissent, cen- sum hunc ad fe transtulerunt, quod sub natalem Christi factum fuisse, Lucas annotauit, & ab eo tempore quottannis illum exegerunt. Et tanta fuit in censu hoc exigendo illorum seueritas, vt post euersam vrbem & templum, cum Iudaei per orbem totum dispersi effent, Vespasianus auarissimus princeps, cui (vt Suetonius scribit) dulcis erat lucri odor ex re qualibet, legem sanciret, vt singuli Iudaei vbicunq; terrarum viuerent, binas drachmas tributi annui loco penderent Capitolio. Neq; abfq; Dei prouidentia hoc accidit, qui hoc indicio testatum voluit, fe populum istum abdicauisse, neq; eum amplius pro suo peculio agnoscere. Quod etiam hodie obseruare debebant Iudaei, quando tributis & censibus maximis grauantur a principibus, in quorum terris habitant, neq; alia de causa recipi solent, quam vt census & tributa soluant immodica, quae ab hominibus Christianis vix possent extorqueri. Vtile autem effet, fi diligentius omnes expenderet, qua Iudaeis huius calamitatis praecipua causa fiue initium fuerit, nimirum sacerdotum ambitio, qui sacerdotium contra Dei institutum in regnum conuerterant, vel cum sacerdotio regiam potestatem coniunxerant, vt ijdem Sacerdotes & Reges effent. Inde factum est, vt Hircanus & Aristobulus fratres de hoc regno sacerdotali hostiliter inter fe pugnantes, populum quoq; in partes distraherent, & belli ciuilis authores effent, quod eo vfq; exarsit, vt viriq; externa auxilia quererentur, & Pompeius magnus hac occasione Hierosolymam caperet, & tandem Iudaea tota Romani fubiurentur. Est hoc memorabile exemplum, quo docetur, quantum noceant dissensiones ciuiles, & praealijs quidem ha, quas sacerdotum & praesulum personatorum auaritia & ambitio excitat. Et vtinam huius meminissent Germani hodie, quando nonnulli pro Romani Pontificis authoritate contra cives & fratres arma gerunt, & bella ciuilia accendunt. Etenim periculum est, ne du pro istorum regno pugnant, qui sacra tractare debebant, & regnorum administratione huius saeculi principibus relinquere, tandem libertate amissa, seipsos & communem patriam miserrimae seruituti, & exterorum tyrannidi subijciant.
units.tr: The evangelist begins the first part of the narrative from the place where these things were done, and writes that Jesus came with the disciples to Capernaum, which above, in chapter nine, he called his own city. It is likely that it was the time when the annual census was customarily demanded and collected from each person. But here it must be observed that the Jewish nation was formerly free, and gave no census to anyone except that which God had commanded to be given for the repair of the torn coverings of the tabernacle or temple and the upkeep of external worship. By this public tax they bore witness that they were God's own possession, and had no king besides God, who had bound himself wholly to them; and therefore he was called the Holy One of Israel. This was the half-shekel, which each man paid individually, equal to two drachmas or denarii. But when the Romans had reduced Judea to a province, they transferred this census to themselves. Luke notes that this was done around the birth of Christ, and from that time they exacted it every year. Their severity in exacting this census was so great that, after the city and temple were overthrown and the Jews were dispersed throughout the whole world, the emperor Vespasian, a most avaricious prince, to whom (as Suetonius writes) the sweet smell of profit from any source was pleasing, decreed a law that each Jew, wherever on earth he lived, should pay two drachmas annually to the Capitol in place of the tribute. This did not happen without God's providence, who wished by this sign to attest that he had renounced that people and no longer acknowledged them as his own possession. Jews ought to observe this even today, when they are burdened by very heavy tributes and taxes from the princes in whose lands they live, and they are not usually admitted for any other reason than to pay immoderate censuses and tributes, which could scarcely be extorted even from Christians. It would be useful, however, if everyone weighed more carefully the principal cause or origin of this calamity among the Jews: namely the ambition of the priests, who, against God's institution, had turned the priesthood into a kingdom, or had joined royal power to the priesthood, so that the same men would be both priests and kings. Hence it happened that Hyrcanus and Aristobulus, brothers fighting hostilely over this priestly kingdom, also divided the people into factions and became the authors of civil war. It blazed to such an extent that each sought foreign aid, Pompey the Great took Jerusalem on this occasion, and at last all Judea was subjected to the Romans. This is a memorable example, which teaches how greatly civil dissensions harm, especially those stirred up by the avarice and ambition of priests and masked prelates. Would that the Germans remembered this today, when some bear arms against citizens and brothers for the authority of the Roman Pontiff, and kindle civil wars. For there is danger that they fight for the kingdom of those who ought to handle sacred things, and, leaving the administration of the kingdoms of this age to princes, they may at last, liberty lost, subject themselves and their common fatherland to the most wretched slavery and to the tyranny of foreigners.

units.la: Caeterum accedamus ad exactorum census cum Petro colloquium. Interrogant illi Petrum de Christo, dicentes: Magister vester non soluit didrachma? Fidei & integritatis opus est, quod viritim censum a quibusuis exigunt, neq; vlli parcunt ex priuato arbitrio. Ita enim decet facere minifros publicos, qui a Magistratu aliquid in mandatis acceperunt. At simul laude meretur illorum moderatio & humanitas, cuius indicium est, quod non insolenter & rigide exigunt a Christo censum. Sed prius quaerunt, num ipse etiam communi lege teneatur. Solebant enim Romani viros illustres & beneficos interdum immunitate donare: & videntur exactores isti nuper deleti & constituti fuisse, vt nondum probe noffent omnes, a quibus census deberet exigi. Quia ergo magna erat apud omnes Christi authoritas, neq; certam aut fixam sedem habebat, non temere dubitant de eius conditione, neq; sua potestate aduersus illum volunt audacius abuti: quin potius ea aequitate vtuntur, quam Baptista publicanis praecepit, dicens: Nihil amplius quam quod constitutum est vobis, exigite. Arguit ergo istorum modestia ferociam & iniquitatem multorum, qui hodie cum Christiani dici volint, quiduis insolenter a quibusuis exigunt, & sepe lites iniquissimas hominibus optime meritis mouent, vt sub Reipublicae nomine & pratextu quaftum priuatum faciant. Et sane in eo nulli infolentiores sunt Episcoporum & Abbatum feruis, qui vt herorum inexplebili cupiditati satisfaciant, nemini parcunt, ne mortuis quidem, quin ab his quoq; tributum exigant, egentibus sepe defunctorum liberis, paruulis & viduis.
units.tr: But let us come to the conversation of the tax collectors with Peter. They question Peter about Christ, saying: "Does your Master not pay the didrachma?" It is a mark of fidelity and integrity that they collect the census individually from whomever, and spare no one by private judgment; for it is fitting that public ministers who have received instructions from the magistrate should act so. At the same time their moderation and courtesy deserve praise, as is shown by the fact that they do not demand the census from Christ insolently and harshly. But first they ask whether he too is bound by the common law. For the Romans sometimes granted immunity to illustrious and beneficent men, and these collectors seem to have been recently appointed, so that they did not yet properly know all from whom the census should be exacted. Therefore, since Christ's authority was great among all, and he had no fixed or settled abode, they do not rashly question his status, nor do they wish to abuse their power against him more boldly. Rather they use that fairness which the Baptist prescribed to the publicans, saying: "Exact nothing more than what has been fixed for you." The modesty of these men therefore reproaches the arrogance and injustice of many who today, though they wish to be called Christians, demand whatever they like insolently from anyone, and often bring most unjust lawsuits against the best of men, so that under the name and pretext of the commonwealth they may make private profit. Indeed in this no one is more insolent than the servants of bishops and abbots, who, to satisfy the insatiable greed of their masters, spare no one, not even the dead, but exact tribute from these too, often from the children of the deceased, the needy, the little ones and widows.

units.la: Quid vero Petrus? Ingenue respondet, & Christum didrachma dare affirmat. Vnde appa- ret, hunc ita solitum fuisse haftenus. Et cur de eo aliquis dubitet, quando illum sub censu nasci vo luisse legimus. Petrus autem boni & fidelis ciuis officium facit, dum nihil dissimulat, neque tergiuersatur, quo minus Magistratus debitum tributum a suo praeceptore recipiat. Et debent illius exemplum imitari, quotquot viri boni dici & esse volunt. Etenim magnum scelus est in hac re fraudem committere. Quia enim magistratus a Deo institutus est, qui huncfuorum iudicio- tum tiorum vindicem & custodem constituit: quia item viri principes in Republica sunt, quod pastor est in grege, pater in familia, adhæc quia tributa, vectigalia, census & quæcunque sunt huius generis nervi sunt Reipublicæ, quam absque magnis impensis gubernari & ferunt impossibile est: quicunque illos defraudant, hi & in Dei leges peccant, & Rempublicam iniuria & damno afficiunt, & peculatus crimine se polluunt, quod apud gentes omnes semper gravissimum fuit, inter Christianos autem non multum a sacrilegio differt, eo quod inter Ecclesiam & Rempublicam tanta coniunctio est, ut neutra sine altera possit diu consistere. Et si sceleus est, seruum mercenarium debita mercede fraudare, quanto gravius peccare putabitur publicos iuris & legum administros & patriæ patres ijs fraudare, quæ ipsis ex lege Dei debentur? Nec est, quod qui istud faciunt, de Magistratuum iniquitate vel ignavia quiritentur, qui officium non faciant. Non enim ideo subditis licet a suo officio discedere, Deo rationem reddent mali principes, qui functionem suam non bona fide obeunt: & meminerint cives, magistratus iniquos aut ignavos non absque Dei decreto & voluntate dari, quando tales populi improbitas meretur. Patienter ergo tales ferri debent, & orandus est Dominus, ut hic rebus afflictis opem ferat.
units.tr: But what of Peter? He answers frankly and affirms that Christ pays the didrachma. From this it appears that he had been accustomed to do so until then. And why should anyone doubt it, when we read that he wished to be born under the census? Peter performs the duty of a good and faithful citizen, in that he dissembles nothing and does not evade, so that the magistrate would not receive the tribute owed by his teacher. All who wish to be, and be called, good men should imitate his example. For it is a great crime to commit fraud in this matter. The magistrate is instituted by God, who appointed him avenger and guardian of good and evil deeds; likewise princes stand in the commonwealth as the shepherd does in the flock and the father in the family. Moreover, tributes, customs duties, censuses and whatever is of this kind are the sinews of the commonwealth, which cannot be governed and sustained without great expense. Whoever defrauds them sins both against God's laws and injures and harms the commonwealth, and defiles himself with the crime of embezzlement, which among all nations has always been most grave, and among Christians differs not much from sacrilege, because there is so close a conjunction between Church and commonwealth that neither can long subsist without the other. If it is a wicked thing to defraud a hired servant of his due wage, how much more grievously will it be judged to sin by defrauding the public administrators of the law and the fathers of the fatherland of what is owed them by the law of God? Nor have those who do this any reason to complain of the iniquity or sloth of magistrates who do not perform their office. For subjects are not thereby permitted to depart from their own duty; evil princes who discharge their function without good faith will render account to God. Let citizens remember that unjust or slothful magistrates are not given apart from God's decree and will, when the wickedness of the people deserves such. Such men must therefore be borne patiently, and the Lord must be prayed to bring help to these afflicted affairs.

units.la: Sed transeamus ad alteram historiæ partem, quæ Christi cum Petro colloquium continet. Initium huic præbet Dominus, qui prævenit Petrum, quem sciebat ipsi narraturum ea, quæ ei ab exactoribus de censu solvendo dicta fuerant. Ubi rursus habemus argumentum divinitatis Christi, nihil ignorantis eorum, quæ de ipso dicuntur: quale supra capite nono vidimus. Sed ne alia quidem ignorat quæ fiunt aut dicuntur. Et quid illum lateret, quem neque cogitationes hominum fugiunt, & qui de futuris nos tam fideliter præmonuit? Seruiat autem huius loci exemplum institutioni nostræ, ne quid temere loquamur aut agamus, sed nos ab eo videri & audiri meminerimus, qui olim iudex veniet, & cui rationem reddere oportebit de quovis verbo otioso. Vicissim consolationem quoque ex eo petamus, quod illum ea etiam cernere & audire constat, quæ calumniatores & obtrectatores improbi de nobis mentiuntur, aut proditorie consultant, vel etiam insidiose & hostiliter machinantur in nostram perniciem. Licebit ergo nobis ad eius tribunal provocare, & illum nostræ innocentiæ testem sistere, orare deinque ut iniqua hostium consilia & crudeles machinationes dissipet. Elucet item in hoc exemplo propensa illius erga nos voluntas. Sciebat discipulus suis in hac causa adhuc ampliori institutione opus esse. Non expectat ergo donec ipsi quærant, sed illos prævenit. Fit idem frequenter nobiscum, quando errore aut scelere aliquo præoccupatos prævenit, & quamvis in institutionem & consilium non petamus, ipse tamen nos docet, monet, corripit, hortatur ne salutem propriam negligamus. Tunc vero curare nos decet, ne nobis ipsis desimus, sed nos ipsi accommodemus obsequentes & morigeros. Sed plura de his alibi.
units.tr: But let us turn to the other part of the narrative, which contains Christ's conversation with Peter. The Lord himself begins it, anticipating Peter, who he knew would report what the tax collectors had said to him about paying the census. Here again we have evidence of Christ's divinity, since nothing that is said of him escapes his knowledge, as we saw earlier in chapter nine. Nor does he fail to know the other things that are done or said. What could be hidden from him, whom people's thoughts do not escape, and who has warned us so faithfully about the future? This passage should also shape our own conduct: we should not say or do anything rashly, but remember that we are seen and heard by him who will one day judge us and to whom we must give account for every careless word. In turn, we may also take comfort from the fact that he sees and hears even those things which wicked slanderers and detractors falsely say about us, or plot in secret, or devise treacherously and hostilely for our ruin. We may therefore appeal to his judgment seat, call him as witness of our innocence, and pray that he will scatter the wicked counsels of our enemies and their cruel schemes. The passage also shows his favourable disposition towards us. The disciple needed fuller instruction in this matter, so Christ does not wait for Peter to ask but anticipates him. This often happens with us too: when we are caught by some error or sin, he anticipates us, and even though we do not ask for instruction or advice, he teaches, warns, rebukes and exhorts us not to neglect our own salvation. Then it is fitting that we take care not to fail ourselves, but to make ourselves obedient and compliant. But more on these matters elsewhere.

units.la: Nunc quid Petro dixerit, audiamus. Stetit suis actionis est docere, se immunem esse a censu & vectigalibus solvendis. Interrogatione autem vitur, ut respondeat ex ipsius Petri ore eliciat. Quid tibi videtur (inquit) Simon? Reges terræ a quibus accipiunt tributa aut censum? an a filijs suis an ab alienis? Et respondente Petro, ab alienis tributa exigi. Infert: Nempe igitur liberi sunt filij, &c. Argumentum est eiusmodi: Filij regum a tributis & censu immunes sunt in regno patris, cuius ipsi hæredes sunt: Ego sum Filius Dei, qui Rex regum & Dominus dominantium est, qui omnes gentes ad extremos fines vsque orbis terrarum mihi addixit, ut mea sint hæreditas atque peculium: Ergo immunis sum a tributis & vectigalibus, ubicunque terrarum sim. Et facit ad confirmationem huius argumenti, quod Deus Iudæam Romanis subiecerat, & suum in Iudæos ius quasi resignarat illis, ut quod prius templo impenderant, nunc Capitolio Romano dare cogerentur. Initium ergo erat, Romanos censum a Filio Dei exigere, a quo ipsi non Iudæa modo, sed omnia alia quoque regna, ut eius beneficiarij tenebant. Addit tamen Christus: Sed ne offendamus eos, profectus ad mare, &c. Quod ergo tributum sive censum solvit, voluntarius fecit, non ex debito, aut a quoquam coactus. Et de eo Petrum & reliquos discipulos admoneri oportuit, ne ipsi offenderentur, et Messia esse dubitaret. Quia enim de illo prædictum erat, quod virgam exactoris cofringere debebat, absurdum videri poterat hunc pro Messia cognoscere, qui ipse censum exactoribus persolueret. Et diligenti observatione dignum est, quod vitandi scandali causa hoc fecit, quod non tenebatur facere. Nam eo exemplo docet, non semper faciendum esse quod licet, sed proximi rationem haberi debere, vt alij per nos aedificentur, ne cui scandalum demus non necessarium: de qua reprolixè & graviter Paulus ad Corinthios disputat, de idolothytorum esu differens, & inter alia ait: Omnia mihi licent, sed non omnia conferunt: omnia mihi licent, sed non omnia aedificant. Item, cum liber sim ab omnibus, omnibus meipsum seruum feci, vt plures lucrifaciam. Et rursus: Si esca facit, vt offendat frater meus, non vescar carnibus in aeternum, ne faciam vt frater meus offendatur. Qui animus si in omnibus esset hodie, qui fidem in Christum profitentur, minus esset scandalorum, & Euangelij doctrina maiori successu ad alios longe latè propagaretur.
units.tr: Now let us hear what he said to Peter. His purpose in this action is to teach that he is exempt from paying the census and tributes. He proceeds by question, so that he may draw the answer from Peter's own mouth: "What do you think, Simon? From whom do the kings of the earth take tribute or census: from their own sons, or from strangers?" When Peter answers that tribute is exacted from strangers, Christ concludes: "Then indeed the sons are free," and so on. The argument runs like this: the sons of kings are exempt from tributes and census in the kingdom of the father whose heirs they are. I am the Son of God, who is King of kings and Lord of lords, who has bound all nations to me to the farthest ends of the earth, so that they are my inheritance and property. Therefore I am exempt from tributes and taxes wherever I am on earth. In confirmation of this argument, God had made Judea subject to the Romans and had, as it were, surrendered his own right over the Jews to them, so that what they had once given to the temple they were now compelled to give to the Roman Capitol. The Romans were therefore beginning to demand the census from the Son of God, although they themselves, like all other kingdoms, held not only Judea but every other realm as his beneficiaries. Yet Christ adds: "But so that we do not offend them, go to the sea," and so on. Therefore, whatever tribute or census he paid, he paid voluntarily, not from obligation or because anyone compelled him. Peter and the other disciples had to be warned about this, so that they would not be offended and doubt that he was the Messiah. For it had been foretold of him that he would break the rod of the exactor, and it might have seemed absurd to recognise as the Messiah one who himself paid the census to tax collectors. It is also worth careful notice that he did this to avoid giving offence, though he was not obliged to do it. By this example he teaches that one should not always do what is permitted, but must have regard for one's neighbour, so that others may be built up through us and we do not give anyone unnecessary offence. Paul discusses this at length and gravely in his letter to the Corinthians, when treating of eating meat sacrificed to idols, and among other things he says: "All things are lawful for me, but not all things are helpful; all things are lawful for me, but not all things edify."
