Likewise: "Though I am free from all, I have made myself a servant to all, that I might gain the more." And again: "If food causes my brother to stumble, I will eat no meat for ever, lest I make my brother stumble." If this spirit were present today in all who profess faith in Christ, there would be fewer scandals, and the doctrine of the gospel would be spread far and wide with greater success.

units.la: Quod vero praecipuum huius loci caput est, demonstrat hoc facto Dominus, Euangelicam libertatem, quam ipse nobis meruit, non abrogare magistratus, neq; constitutiones similes abolere, quas a Deo institutas esse alibi Scriptura docet. Quia enim regnū eius non est de hoc mundo, non inuadit petulanter regna huius mundi, neq; ea tollit, sine quibus nulla Respublica aut regnū potest consistere. Ideo alibi noluit iudicem agere inter fratres, qui de hereditate inter se contendebant: interim non prohibet, quo minus apud ordinarios iudices ius suum persequatur is, cui iniuria fiebat. Arguit hoc Anabaptistarum furores, qui hominibus Christianis magistratu opus esse negant, neq; illos magistratum posse gerere contendunt: & loco Psalmi abutuntur, qui populum Christi vltroneum fore ait, qui obsequium voluntarium illi praestet. Enimuero fatemur, eos qui Christo verè & ex animo nomen dederunt, a Spiritu Sancto moueri & impelli, vt sponte officium faciant. At quia ijdem homines sunt, sentiunt & ipsi legem peccati in membris suis, quae illos sibi captiuos facit, & ducit quo non volunt. Itaq; interdum ipsis etiam disciplina necessaria est. Deinde quia in mundo viuunt, in quo plures mali sunt, vt Bias ille sapiens dicebat, cui Scriptura Sacra astipulatur, ipsis etiam in Magistratu opus est, cuius praesidio contra malorum iniurias defendantur. Et hoc tam manifestum est, vt si quis negare velit, exemplis quotidianis, & ipsa rerum experientia conuincatur. At quae illorum hominū contumacia est, aiunt illi nefas esse Magistratus defensione vti, & exempla extant eius sesta hominum, quos illi non alia de causa excommunicarunt, quàm quod Magistratus sui opem implorarent. Sed nos illis Paulum Apostolum opponimus, qui non semel ad legum Romanorum praesidium confugit, & praesidiū Romani armato praesidio vsus est aduersus vim iniustam. Act. 16. 22. 23. 25. &c.
units.tr: What is the chief point of this passage is that by this deed the Lord shows that the evangelical liberty which he himself has earned for us does not abolish the magistrates, nor does it do away with similar institutions, which Scripture teaches elsewhere were established by God. For his kingdom is not of this world, so he does not wantonly attack the kingdoms of this world, nor does he remove those things without which no commonwealth or kingdom can stand. Thus elsewhere he refused to act as judge between brothers who were disputing over an inheritance; yet he does not forbid the one who has been wronged from pursuing his right before the ordinary judges. This refutes the frenzy of the Anabaptists, who deny that Christian men need a magistrate and maintain that they cannot hold that office, and who misuse a psalm which says that the people of Christ will be willing, offering him voluntary obedience. Indeed we grant that those who have truly and sincerely given their name to Christ are moved and impelled by the Holy Spirit to perform their duty willingly. But since they are still the same men, they too feel the law of sin in their members, which makes them captives and leads them where they do not wish to go. Therefore discipline is sometimes necessary even for them. Moreover, since they live in a world in which many are evil, as that wise man Bias said, and Holy Scripture agrees, they too need the magistracy, by whose protection they are defended against the injuries of the wicked. This is so plain that anyone who wished to deny it would be refuted by daily examples and by the very experience of affairs. Yet how obstinate these people are! They say it is unlawful to use the protection of the magistrate, and there are examples of their sect whom they excommunicated for no other reason than that they begged the help of their magistrate. But against them we set the apostle Paul, who more than once took refuge in the protection of Roman law, and who used the armed protection of the Romans against unjust violence. Acts 16:22, 23, 25, etc.

units.la: Sed modum quoq; & rationem videre oportet, qua Christus in hoc tributo persoluendo vsus est. Iubet Petrum ad mare abire, & hamo in aquas proiecto piscari: ac pollicetur, quòd in primi piscis, quem praehensurus sit, ore inuenturus sit staterem (quem quatuor drachmas valere alij annotarunt) & vt hunc pro vtroq; exactoribus numeret, praecipit. Atqui multa aliae rationes erant quibus pecunias sibi pararet. Alibi a pijs matronis accepit, quae ipsi erant necessaria. Poterat ite ex nihilo pecuniam creare, aut pauculas illas, quas in loculis suis habebat Iudas quaestor, mirabiliter augere, quemadmodū prius panes inter suas & discipulorum manus auxit, vt multis missibus alendis ac saturandis sufficerent. Sed novo hoc & insolito modo voluit agere: primum vt re ipsa demonstraret quod dixerat, se nimirū Regis aeterni ac supremi Filium esse, cui creatura omnes obediant, & qui immunis sit a censu & tributo. Enimuero pisces sine duce & lege viuere videntur, & tale quid de illis dicit Habakuk: at Christo iubente vel ducente hic piscis ad Petri hamum festinat. Quis ergo de aliarum creaturarum erga Filium Dei obseruantia dubitet? Deinde exemplo hoc obedientiam, quae magistratibus debetur, suis discipulis commendat, docens, Deum eorum laboribus ac studijs benedicere, qui suis principibus fideles & obsequentes sunt, etiamsi lo: seueriores aequo, & in multis iniquos etiam experiantur: quales scimus fuisse Romanorum Imperatores & horū praesides. Et diuina huius benedictionis exempla hodie passim cernimus in multis, qui a Regibus per immodicas exactiones ita expilantur, vt mirū sit eos viuere posse. Attamen et ipsi viuunt, & liberos honestè educant: egentibus interim multis alijs, qui in libera Respub. magistratuum optimorum legibus aequissimis obedire nolunt, & dolo malo vtuntur in ijs persoluendis, quae iure ab ipsis postulantur.
units.tr: But we must also consider the manner and reason by which Christ acted in paying this tribute. He bids Peter go to the sea, cast a hook into the water and fish; and he promises that in the mouth of the first fish that he catches he will find a stater (which others have noted was worth four drachmas), and he orders him to pay it for both of them to the tax collectors. Yet there were many other ways by which he could have obtained money. Elsewhere he received from pious women what he needed. He could have created money out of nothing, or miraculously multiplied the few coins which Judas the treasurer kept in his purse, just as he had earlier multiplied the bread in his own and the disciples' hands, so that it sufficed to feed and satisfy many thousands. But he wished to act in this new and unusual way: first, so that he might demonstrate in fact what he had said, namely that he is the Son of the eternal and supreme King, to whom all creatures are obedient, and who is exempt from census and tribute. Indeed fish seem to live without leader or law, and Habakkuk says something like this of them; yet at Christ's command, or under his guidance, this fish hastens to Peter's hook. Who then could doubt the obedience of the other creatures towards the Son of God? Second, through this example he commends to his disciples the obedience owed to magistrates, teaching that God blesses the labours and efforts of those who are faithful and obedient to their princes, even though they experience rulers who are too severe and often unjust, such as we know the Roman emperors and their governors were. We see today the divine evidence of this blessing in many people who are so stripped by kings through excessive exactions that it is a wonder they can live at all. Yet they do live, and they bring up their children honourably; meanwhile many others, in free commonwealths, refuse to obey the most just laws of the best magistrates, and use fraud in paying what is rightfully demanded of them.

units.la: Praeterea non temere factum putabimus, quòd non pro se modo didrachma soluit Dominus, verumetiam vt Petrus illud soluat, iubet. Voluit hoc exemplo procul dubio eorū insolentiam consutare, qui sub religionis & successionis Apostolicae praetextu immunitatem sibi vendicarunt: Romanos manos
units.tr: Moreover, we need not think it was without purpose that the Lord paid the didrachma not only for himself but also commanded Peter to pay it. Undoubtedly he wished by this example to refute the insolence of those who, under the pretext of religion and apostolic succession, have claimed immunity for themselves: the Romans, [manos].

units.la: 1. Cor. 10. 8. & 9. manos nimirum Pontifices & abbas vnctos & rasos sacrificos atq; monachos. Clamat illi, absurdum & iniquum esse, vt spirituales secularibus & laicis tributum dent, aut vectigal: adhæc non se modo immunes esse cotendunt, sed insuper principes & magistratus omnes vna cum subditis sibi tributarios fecerunt. At velim dicant nobis, quis superbum illud spiritualium nomen ipsis ceu proprium impo fuerit, quod Paulus omnibus Christianis comune facit, dicens: Si quis Spiritum Christi nô habet, non est eius? Idem omnibus in Christum credentibus spiritum adoptionis tribuit, cuius instinctu clament, Abba Pater. Quæro item quis vnquam spiritualior fuerit IESV CHRISTO, quem Pater vnxit oleo lætitiæ præ consortibus suis, & de cuius plenitudine nos omnes accepimus? Quis item in Ecclesiæ ministerio feruentior & sacris additior fuit vnquam Apostolis, qui omnibus aliis reliquis Christum secuti sunt, & Ie totos huic & Ecclesiæ consecrarunt? At Christus tempore censùs natsci, & matrem Virginem sacratissimum illud Spiritus Sancti templum, quo nullum vnquam inter homines sanctius fuit, cum sponso suo Iosepho in censum venire voluit: in præsenti item tributum pro seipso & Petro dedit, & vt id posset, miraculum fecit, quo totam hanc actionem toti mundo magis commendaret. Vnde apparet, illum neq; sibi ipsi immunitatem vsurpasse, neq; Apostolis dedisse. Qui ergo hanc sub Apostolicæ successionis prætextu sibi vendicant, ij plus sibi arrogant, quam vel Christus vel Apostoli eius habuerint. At Regum priuilegia allegant, qui ipsos immunitate ista donarint. Nos vero respondemus, non quid homines in hac causa fecerint spectandum esse, sed quid Deus statuerit. Hic per Filium Iudæos, qui suum peculiu erant, iubet reddere Cæsari quæ sunt Cæsaris. Idem per Paulum Apostolum clamat: Omnis anima potestatibus superemineni tibus subiecta esto. Et dum omnem animam nominat, neminem excipit, sed (vt Diuus Chrysostomus interpretatur) sacerdotibus quoq; & monachis loquitur. Deniq; addit Pater iste: Siue Apostolus fuerit, siue Euangelista, siue Propheta, aut quisquam alius, subiectus esto: Nec enim ista subiectio pietatem euertit, &c. Imò si verum dici debeat, isti homines dum immunitate gloriantur, & se a principum subiectione eximunt, sibi vendicant, quod ipsorum professioni repugnat, & illis dici potest, quod Diocletianus Imperator olim philosopho cuidam immunitatem petenti, respondebat: Professio tua multum a tua petitione discrepat. Philosophia enim tua docet vincendos esse affectus: tu autem ostendis te plane victum esse cupiditate & avaritia. Ita spirituales illi Clerici, cum præ aliis religionem profiteantur, quæ nos ad humilitatem & charitatis officia obstringit, & Dei præceptis omnibus obedire iubet, tamen supra reges sese efferunt, & ab oneribus publicis immunes esse volunt, cum tamen communi iure & defensione fruantur: & in omnibus sibi præroga- tiuam quandam superbe ac insolenter vendicent. Neminem ergo moueant istorum hominum præstigiæ, quin potius Christiani principes in ordinem illos redigant, vt Christi regulæ & exemplo obedire discant. Idem faciant alij quoq; fidei Christianæ professores, neq; sub religionis prætextu aliquid machinentur, quod Rempublicam turbare possit. Qui vero libertatis beneficio fruuntur, hoc Dei donum esse agnoscant, eodem bene vtantur, vt se totos Deo consecrent, pacem & charitatem colant cum omnibus, quantum in ipsis est, quoad mores autem & reliqua vitæ studia, honeste & temperanter viuant, ne luxu & petulantia seruitutis iugum sibi accersant, quod multis accidisse legimus. In primis autem libertatem spiritus tueamur, quam nobis sanguinis sui pretio acquisiuit æternus Dei Filius IESVS CHRISTVS, cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: 1 Cor. 10. 8 & 9. Namely the Roman pontiffs, abbots anointed and shaven, sacrificing priests and monks. He cries out that it is absurd and unjust for spiritual persons to pay tribute or tax to secular and lay people. Moreover, they contend not only that they themselves are immune, but they have also made princes and magistrates, together with their subjects, tributary to themselves. But I would like them to tell us who imposed upon them that proud name "spiritual" as if it were their own, when Paul makes it common to all Christians, saying: "If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he is not his" [Rom. 8. 9]. The same Paul gives the spirit of adoption to all who believe in Christ, by whose prompting they cry, "Abba, Father." I ask again, who was ever more spiritual than Jesus Christ, whom the Father anointed with the oil of gladness above his fellows, and from whose fullness we have all received? Who was ever more fervent in the ministry of the Church and more devoted to sacred things than the Apostles, who followed Christ when all others had left him and devoted themselves wholly to him and to the Church? Yet Christ wished to be born at the time of the census, and went up to be enrolled with his betrothed Joseph, together with the Virgin mother, that most holy temple of the Holy Spirit, than which none among men was ever holier. At present, too, he gave tribute for himself and for Peter, and in order to be able to do so he worked a miracle, by which he might commend this whole action more widely to the whole world. From this it is clear that he neither claimed immunity for himself nor gave it to the Apostles. Therefore those who claim it for themselves under the pretext of apostolic succession arrogate to themselves more than either Christ or his Apostles ever had. They allege the privileges of kings who granted them this immunity. But we reply that in this matter we must look not at what men have done, but at what God has decreed. Here, through the Son, he commands the Jews, who were his own people, to render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's. Through the Apostle Paul he likewise cries out: "Let every soul be subject to the higher powers" [Rom. 13. 1]. And when he says "every soul," he excepts no one, but (as the blessed Chrysostom explains) he speaks also to priests and monks. Finally that same Father adds: "Whether he be an Apostle, or an Evangelist, or a Prophet, or anyone else, let him be subject; for such subjection does not overthrow piety," and so on. Indeed, if the truth must be told, these men, while they boast of immunity and exempt themselves from subjection to princes, claim for themselves what is contrary to their own profession, and what the Emperor Diocletian once replied to a certain philosopher who sought immunity may be said to them: "Your profession differs greatly from your petition. For your philosophy teaches that the passions must be conquered, but you show yourself plainly conquered by desire and avarice." So those spiritual clerics, although they profess a religion above others that binds us to humility and duties of charity and orders us to obey all of God's precepts, nevertheless raise themselves above kings and wish to be free from public burdens, though they enjoy the common law and protection, and in everything they arrogantly and insolently claim a certain privilege for themselves. Let no one, therefore, be moved by the deceits of these men; rather, Christian princes should bring them back into line, so that they learn to obey the rule and example of Christ. Let other professors of the Christian faith do likewise, and let them not contrive under the pretext of religion anything that could disturb the commonwealth. Those who enjoy the benefit of liberty should acknowledge that it is a gift of God and use it well, so that they devote themselves wholly to God, cultivate peace and charity with all, as far as lies in them, and, as to morals and the other pursuits of life, live honestly and temperately, lest by luxury and wantonness they bring upon themselves the yoke of servitude, as we read has happened to many. Above all, let us guard the liberty of the spirit, which the eternal Son of God, Jesus Christ, acquired for us at the price of his own blood, to whom be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPVT XVIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVIII.

units.la: HOMILIA CCXVII.
units.tr: HOMILY CCXVII.

units.la: EO ipso tempore adierunt IESVM discipuli, dicentes: Quis nam maximus est in regno cœlorum? Et cum aduocasset puerulum IESVS, statuit eum in medio eorum, & dixit: Amen dico vobis, nisi conuersi fueritis, & fiatis vt pueruli, nequaquam ingrediemini in regnum cœlorum. Quisquis igitur demiserit semetipsum sicut est puerulus iste, is est maximus ille in regno coelorum. Et quisquis receperit aliquem puerulum talem in nomine meo, me recipit.
units.tr: At that same time the disciples came to Jesus and said, "Who then is greatest in the kingdom of heaven?" And Jesus called a little child to him, set him in the midst of them, and said: "Truly I say to you, unless you turn and become like little children, you will by no means enter the kingdom of heaven. Whoever therefore humbles himself like this little child, the same is greatest in the kingdom of heaven. And whoever receives one such little child in my name receives me."

units.la: OTO hoc Capite Matthaeus insigne Domini nostri IESV CHRISTI cum discipulu suis colloquium describit, in quo utilis ac omnibus necessaria doctrina proponitur quales esse oporteat eos qui in regno Christi excellere, & veri eius cives esse, & tandem coelestis regni haereditatem adire volunt. Vbi haec requiruntur: primum ut depositio ambitionis & superbiae affectu humilitati studeant, & quibusfuis inseruiant: deinde ut neminisscandalum praebeant, & in primis, ne qui simpliciores sunt aliquo ipsorum dicto aut facto offendantur, curent: tertio ut fratres qui peccarunt pijs admonitionibus non solum priuatim, sed publice etiam, si opus sit, corrigere & in viam reducere studeant: quarto ut omnibus iniurias atque offensas suas benigne condonent.
units.tr: In this chapter Matthew describes the remarkable conversation of our Lord Jesus Christ with his disciples, in which a useful teaching, necessary for all, is set forth: what sort of people those must be who wish to excel in the kingdom of Christ, to be his true citizens, and at last to enter the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom. Here the following are required: first, that they put off ambition and pride and devote themselves with humility to the service of all; second, that they give offence to no one, and above all take care that the simpler sort are not hurt by any word or deed of theirs; third, that they strive to correct, not only privately but also publicly if need be, brothers who have sinned, with godly admonitions and to bring them back to the right way; fourth, that they graciously forgive everyone their wrongs and offences.

units.la: Ad primum pertinet hic locus, quem modo recitauimus, de discipulorum quaestione de primatu. Quia vero Matthaeus breuitati studet, hist oriae contextus ex aliis farciendus erit. Hanc ita narrat Marcus, ut appareat, discipulos in itinere versus Capernaum inter se disceptauisse, quis ex illis maximus censeri debeat in regno coelorum. At Dominus, quem ipsorum disceptatio non latuit, vbi domum ingressus est, interrogat eos: Quid in via inter vos disceptabatis? Ipsi vero perculsi silenuerunt initio: nimirum quod ipsos sui facti puderet: sed tandem ad illum referunt hanc quaestionem, & interrogant: Quis nam maximus est in regno coelorum? Vocant autem regnum coelorum exemplo Christi regnum quod ipsi in illo somniabant, non quod illum in coelis fore crederent, sed quod illud coelitus promissum in terris expectarent. Origo contentionis fuit falso cocepta de regno Christi in terris opinio, in quo sibi ipsis honores & dignitates pollicebantur. Et ut tunc disceptatio ista inter ipsos exoriretur, multiplex causa potest indicari. Primo quod Dominus intra paucos dies (ut nuper quoque monuimus) ter & quater de sua morte disseruerat. Cogitant ergo sibi duce aut antistite opus fore, qui in alios ius habeat atque imperium, & sua authoritate illos regat. Aemulationis autem & rixae occasionem praebuit, quod ille Petrum aliis anteposuisse videbatur, quando ei claues regni coelorum promisit, & paulo post eum cum duobus aliis, Iacobo & Ioanne, in montem seorsum subduxit: quod item proillo didrachma soluerat non sine miraculo: ex quo hodie etiam personati successores Petri primatum in Ecclesia sibi vendicant. Ex his aemulatio accensa est, quae disceptationem iam peperit, in qua multifariam peccarunt. Primum ambitione & superbia: deinde quod immemores eorum, quae de cruce ferenda dixerat nuper Dominus, de iis quaerunt, quae ille nunquam promiserat: & licet promissiffet, error tamen in eo fuisset non leuis, quod triumphare volunt priusquam pugnauerant: tertio quod qui coniunctius animis & studiis debebant pro Christi gloria pugnare, inter se committuntur. Concurrunt praeterea, ut inter tales fieri solet, aemulatio, inuidia, odium, simultas, aperta rixae: quae ut multis regnis exitium pererunt, ita a regno Dei excludunt. Ita solet fere fieri omnibus qui ambitione accensi de rebus arduis & nihil ad nos pertinentibus quaerunt: ut hodie qui de caelo & conditione caelitum disputant, quae tunc demum perfecte cognoscemus, vbi hac carne soluti in patriam peruenerimus. Itaque hoc discipulorum exemplo admonemur, quae & quanta sit natura & ingenii nostri vitiositas, & quam parum tribui debeat nostris viribus. Sunt hi discipuli, quos Christus sibi in peculium elegerat, sed non hic modo peccant, verumetiam post institutionem & correptionem, quam hoc loco eis ille adhibuit, non semel iterum ambitionis aestro sese vinci passi sunt. Nisi ergo singulari gratia seruasset Dominus, & pro illis intercessisset apud Patrem (sicuti in vltima Cena Petro dicit) prorsus defecissent illorum fides, & toti perijssent. Nemo enim sibi ipsi aut dignitati, in quam eutus est, fidat. Nam quo altiori gradu consistimus, eo periculosius & grauius labimur, nisi Deus suo Spiritu & manu potenti nos sufflulciat. Factum hoc in successoribus Apostolorum, ut in Apocalypsi per stellam magnam adumbratur, quae coelo decidit, cui data est clauis putei abyssi, &c. Vide homiliam in Lucam nostrum 92.
units.tr: This passage we have just read belongs to the first of these, namely the disciples' question about primacy. Because Matthew aims at brevity, the context of the story must be filled out from the others. Mark relates it thus: that the disciples, on the road to Capernaum, had disputed among themselves which of them ought to be counted greatest in the kingdom of heaven. But the Lord, who was not unaware of their dispute, when he had entered the house asked them: "What were you arguing about on the way among yourselves?" But they, struck with shame, were silent at first, no doubt because they were ashamed of what they had done; yet at last they refer this question to him and ask: "Who then is greatest in the kingdom of heaven?" They call it the kingdom of heaven, following the example of Christ, meaning the kingdom which they dreamed of in this world, not that they believed he would be in heaven, but that they expected in this earth the kingdom promised from heaven. The source of the contention was a false opinion, conceived about the kingdom of Christ on earth, in which they promised themselves honours and dignities. And several causes may be given for why this dispute arose among them. First, because the Lord, within a few days (as we lately noted), had spoken three and four times about his death. They therefore thought that they would need a leader or chief, who would have right and authority over the others and rule them by his authority. But the occasion of rivalry and quarrel was given by the fact that he seemed to put Peter before the others, when he promised him the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and shortly afterwards took him aside into a mountain with two others, James and John; and likewise when he paid the didrachma for him, not without a miracle. From this, even today, the so-called successors of Peter claim primacy in the Church for themselves. From these things rivalry was kindled, which has already produced the dispute, in which they sinned in many ways. First, by ambition and pride; then, forgetful of what the Lord had lately said about bearing the cross, they ask about things which he had never promised; and even had he promised them, their error would still have been no small one, in that they wished to triumph before they had fought; third, that those who ought to have fought together with united minds and efforts for the glory of Christ were set against one another. Moreover, as usually happens among such people, there came together rivalry, envy, hatred, enmity and open quarrelling, which, as they have destroyed many kingdoms, so they exclude from the kingdom of God. This commonly happens to all who, fired with ambition, inquire about lofty matters that have nothing to do with us, as today those who dispute about heaven and the condition of the heavenly beings, which we shall know perfectly only when, released from this flesh, we have come to our fatherland. Therefore by this example of the disciples we are warned what and how great is the sinfulness of our nature and mind, and how little our own strength ought to be trusted. These disciples were those whom Christ had chosen for his own possession, yet they not only sinned here, but even after the instruction and correction which the Lord gave them in this place, they did not once but again allowed themselves to be overcome by the fever of ambition. Unless therefore the Lord had kept them by singular grace and interceded for them with the Father (as he says to Peter at the last supper), their faith would have utterly failed and they would all have perished. For no one should trust in himself or in the dignity to which he has been raised. For the higher the rank we stand on, the more dangerously and gravely we fall, unless God supports us by his Spirit and his mighty hand. This happened to the successors of the Apostles, as is foreshadowed in the Apocalypse by the great star which fell from heaven, to which was given the key of the bottomless pit, and so on. See our homily on Luke, 92.

units.la: Sed Christum videamus, quem non latuit disceptatio, quam inter se mouerunt discipuli, & interrogant eos arguit, imo tacentes & tergiuersantes fateri cogit, & sententiam ex ipso requirere. Est hoc nouum
units.tr: But let us look at Christ, who was not unaware of the dispute which the disciples had stirred up among themselves; he confronts them with it, indeed, forces them to confess when they are silent and evasive, and requires their opinion from them. This is a new

units.la: Matth.18. Marc.9. Luc.22. 1.Cor.13. nouum diuinitatis indicium, qualia iam multa vidimus: & simul hoc exemplo admonemur, quàm displiceant Deo amulatio & ambitio. Qui enim occultam redargutione & correptione dignam iudicanit, minimè inultos sinet aut impunitos eos, qui priuatae gloriae aut commodi studio accensi in Ecclesia & Republica turbas excitant, & scandalorum nocentissimorum authores sunt,
units.tr: Matth. 18; Mark 9; Luke 22; 1 Cor. 13. A new token of his divinity, such as we have already seen many of; and at the same time we are warned by this example how displeasing to God are rivalry and ambition. For he who judges secret rivalry worthy of rebuke and correction will by no means leave unpunished those who, inflamed by the desire of private glory or advantage, stir up tumults in the Church and the commonwealth and are the authors of most harmful scandals.

units.la: Quoad causam vero, non directè ad quaestionem propositam respondet Dominus, vt quis nam sit maximus ille in regno suo offendat, sed docet potius quid eos facere, quidue vitare oporteat, qui in illo volunt locum habere. Enimuero quis maximus sit in regno caelorum quaerere ridiculū est, quando hunc esse IESVM CHRISTVM constat, cui datum nomen, quod est supra omne nomen, &c. Nobis hac praecipua cura esse debet quaerere, vt nos eius consortes fiamus. Itaq; praesenti discipulorum affectui responsionem accommodas, ambitionem ipsorum diserte damnat, dum nisi illi longum valere renuntient, regnum suum nequaquam ingressuros esse minatur. Nec nudis verbis rem agit, sed Christus vtitur, sicut postea quoq; fecit, quando cum eandem contentionem in vltima Caena instauraffent, pedum ablutione ipsis humilitatem commendat. Voluit autem tanto studio in hac causa vti, quo d sciret, quàm difficile sit ex hominum animis superbia spiritum eximere, quem ex primis parentibus hausimus, qui illo decepti peccarunt: quae causa est, quòd superbiam peccati principium Sirachides dixit. Ideo in praesenti magna cum gravitate causam hanc agit Dominus. Nam puerulum vocat, & (vt Marcus annotauit) hunc in vlnas acceptum complectitur: deinde statuit in medio discipulorum, & non sine gravissima asseueratione ait: Amen dico vobis, nisi conuersi fueritis, & fiatis vt pueruli, nequaquam ingredieminin regnum caelorum. Quasi dicat: Quaeritis, quis in regno caelorum maximus, adeoq; aliorum princeps futurus sit, & ambitiose ad principatum istum omnes aspiratis. Sed tam abest, vt hic alicui veñrum debeatur, vt nulli ex vobis in regno meo locus futurus sit, nisi toti conuertamini, & depòsito spiritu ambitionis, qui vos nunc agit, puerulorum similes fiatis. Idem ergo hic dicit, quod Nicodemo: Nisi quis fuerit renatus, non potest videre regnum Dei. Itaq; non modo discipulorum factum reprehendit, sed totam hominis naturam damnat, quando necesse esse dicit esse, vt conuertantur. Et vt norint qualis hac conuersio esse, & quousq; progredi debeat, puerulorum nos vult similes fieri.
units.tr: As for the matter itself, the Lord does not answer directly the question put, namely who is that greatest one in his kingdom, but rather teaches what those who wish to have a place in it ought to do and avoid. Indeed it is ridiculous to ask who is greatest in the kingdom of heaven, when it is plain that this is Jesus Christ, to whom has been given the name which is above every name, and so on. Our chief concern ought to be to seek how we may become partakers with him. So he adapts his answer to the present feeling of the disciples: he plainly condemns their ambition, threatening that unless they renounce it and bid it farewell, they will by no means enter his kingdom. Nor does he deal with the matter in bare words, but Christ uses an action, as he later did too, when, after the same contention had been renewed at the last supper, he commended humility to them by washing their feet. He wished to use such earnestness in this matter because he knew how difficult it is to remove from men's minds the pride of spirit which we have drawn from our first parents, who were deceived by it and sinned; this is why Jesus the son of Sirach called pride the beginning of sin. Therefore in the present case the Lord handles the matter with great seriousness. For he calls a little child, and (as Mark noted) takes him up into his arms and embraces him; then he sets him in the midst of the disciples and says, with the most solemn assurance: "Truly I say to you, unless you turn and become like little children, you will by no means enter the kingdom of heaven." As if he said: You ask who will be greatest in the kingdom of heaven, and who will be the prince of the others, and you all aspire ambitiously to that leadership. But far from any of you being owed the first place here, none of you will have a place in my kingdom unless you are wholly converted and, having put off the spirit of ambition which now drives you, become like little children. He therefore says here what he said to Nicodemus: "Unless one is born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God." So he not only rebukes the disciples' conduct but condemns the whole nature of man, since he says that it is necessary for men to be converted. And so that they may know what kind of conversion this is, and how far it ought to go, he wishes us to become like little children.

units.la: At hic quoq; diligenter videre oportet, in quo nos puerulos imitari oporteat. Nam si de pueris simpliciter dicendum sit, omnes in peccato conceptos & natos esse constat, & ideo figmenta cordis humani ab ipsa infantia praua esse Deus ipse pronunciat. Et in pueris quoq; affectus superbia, aemulationis & invidiae non obscuris indicijs sese prodit. Sed meminerimus, similitudinem omnem (vt vulgò dicitur) claudicare, & ideò non ad viuum illas debere resecari. Et Christus simpliciter ad hoc respicit, quod etsi lex peccati & naturae vitiositas in pueris locum habeat, quae eos etiam mortis reos facit, tamen nondum in eis dominantur affectus praui, vt in opus erumpant, neq; adhuc norunt dignitatum gradus, multò minus aliis dominari cupiunt, vt pro imperio cum quoquam digladientur: sed sua forte & parentum complexu atq; fauore contenti, nihil praeterea expetunt: adhaec disciplinam facile admittunt, si in tempore illis adhibeatur: offensi ad parentes recurrunt, & facile placantur. In his puerulos imitari debemus. Et hoc Paulus quoq; monet, Corinthijs scribens: Fratres, ne fitis pueri intelligentia: sed malitia pueri, intelligentia verò adulti fitis. Et alibi quoad fidem & agnitionem Filij Dei nos adolescere vult in virum perfectum, qui non fluctuemus, & puerorum instar incerti circumferamur quouis vento doctrinae. Et Christus Dominus praesenti argumento solum puerulorum exemplum applicat, cum dicit: Quisquis igitur demiserit seipsum, sicut est puerulus iste, is est maximus ille in regno caelorum. Et apud Lucam addit: Qui minimus est inter vos, iste erit magnus. Haec autem dicendo non damnat legitimos dignitatum gradus in Republica & Ecclesia, sed docet, ad quid hi nobis seruire debeant, qua ratione item ad eos peruenire & quomodo retineri possint: Si nimirum ad seruiendum aliis prompti & parati simus, & quò altius quis supra alios eminet, eò plus aliis seruiat. Hic enim proprius donorum Dei visus est. Consentit his quod alibi dicit Dominus: Qui maximus est inter vos, sit sicut qui minimus est: & qui princeps est, sicut qui ministrat. Et hoc ipsum proprio exemplo confirmat, addens: Nam vter maior est, qui accumbit, an qui ministrat? nonne qui accumbit? At ego in medio vestrum sum, vt qui ministrat. At quid multis opus est, quando res ipsa loquitur, omnes
units.tr: But here too we must look carefully at the respect in which we ought to imitate little children. For if we were to speak of children without qualification, it is agreed that all are conceived and born in sin, and therefore God himself declares that the imaginations of the human heart are evil from infancy. In children too, pride, rivalry and envy show themselves by clear signs. But let us remember that every comparison, as the common saying goes, limps, and so these things should not be pressed to the quick. Christ looks simply to this: although the law of sin and the corruption of nature have their place in children, which also makes them liable to death, nevertheless the evil passions have not yet taken hold of them so as to break out into action; nor do they yet know the grades of dignity, much less desire to rule over others, so that they fight with anyone for power. Rather, content perhaps with their own things and with the embrace and favour of their parents, they seek nothing further. Moreover, they readily accept discipline, if it is applied to them in good time; when offended, they run back to their parents, and are easily appeased. In these respects we ought to imitate little children. Paul also advises this, writing to the Corinthians: "Brethren, do not be children in understanding, but in malice be children, yet in understanding be grown men." And elsewhere, with regard to faith and the knowledge of the Son of God, he wants us to grow up into a perfect man, so that we are not tossed about and carried like unstable children by every wind of doctrine. And Christ the Lord, in the present argument, applies only the example of the little child, when he says: "Whoever therefore humbles himself as this little child is, he is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven." And in Luke he adds: "He who is least among you, he will be great." Yet in saying these things he does not condemn the lawful grades of dignity in the commonwealth and the Church; rather, he teaches for what purpose these ought to serve us, and by what reasoning we may likewise attain to them and how they may be kept: namely, if we are ready and prepared to serve others, and the higher anyone stands above others, the more he serves them. For this is the proper character of the gifts of God. He agrees with what the Lord says elsewhere: "Whoever is greatest among you, let him be as the one who is least, and the one who is chief, as the one who serves." And he confirms this very thing by his own example, adding: "For which is greater, the one who reclines at table, or the one who serves? Is it not the one who reclines? But I am among you as the one who serves." But why need many words be spent, when the thing itself speaks, that all

units.la: Luc.9 publicorum officiorum aut munerum dignitates cum ministerio coniunctas esse, & vt in domo bene constituta nemo magis seruus est, quam paterfamilias, qui pro omnibus solicitus est, & toti domui prospicit: ita in Republica & Ecclesia qui supra alios eminent, ad Dei exemplum se demittere debent, vt omnia inspiciant, & pro omnibus vigilent atque laborent.
units.tr: Luke 9. Public offices and positions of rule are joined with service; and, as in a well-ordered household no one is more of a servant than the father of the family, who is anxious for everyone and watches over the whole house, so in the commonwealth and the Church those who stand above others ought to humble themselves after the example of God, so that they may oversee all things and keep watch and labour for all.

units.la: Efta, hoc diligenter obseruandum, vt in quo nam vera humilitas consistat, intelligamus. Nam hic vehementer errant hypocritae, qui illam vt olim Pharisaei, vestitu & gestibus metiuntur, cum interim superbiae spiritu inflati supra Deum fere efferantur, & omnes homines prae se contemnant. Sed quae Deo probatur humilitas, in eo consistit: vt primum coram ipso & sub eius potenti manu humiliemur, neque nobis ipsis aut nostris viribus aliquid tribuamus, ex quo illius gratia quicquam derogetur.Imitemur ergo patrem nostrum Abrahamum, qui etsi ipsum Deus sibi foedere iunxisset, & sui contra Sodomaeos decreti conscium fecisset, tamen se puluerem & cinerem esse fatebatur.Et vt Dauid in regio throno sedens non obliuiscebatur caulae, ex qua ipsum Deus extraxerat: vt item Paulus, cum plus omnibus Apostolis laborauisset in Verbi ministerio, pristinae suae conditionis non fuit immemor: ita nos qui & quales simus natura meminerimus etiam tunc, quando nos supra multos Deus euexit. Hic certa vera pietatis fons, & ad eandem stimulus est acerrimus.
units.tr: Next, we must carefully observe in what true humility consists. For hypocrites greatly err here: like the Pharisees of old, they measure humility by clothing and gestures, while meanwhile, puffed up with a spirit of pride, they exalt themselves almost above God and despise all people in comparison with themselves. But the humility that is pleasing to God consists in this: that we first humble ourselves before him and under his mighty hand, and that we ascribe nothing to ourselves or to our own strength, by which anything would be taken from his grace. Let us therefore imitate our father Abraham, who, although God had bound himself to him by covenant and had made him a partner in his decision against the Sodomites, nevertheless confessed that he was dust and ashes. And just as David, sitting on the royal throne, did not forget the sheepfold from which God had drawn him; and as Paul, though he had laboured more than all the Apostles in the ministry of the Word, was not unmindful of his former condition; so let us remember what and what kind of people we are by nature, even when God has raised us above many others. Here is the certain and true fountain of piety, and the sharpest spur to it.

units.la: Ex eo alterum sequitur, ne quem prae nobis contemnamus. Etenim vt id a nobis fiat, nulla causa est. Si qui enim nobis inferiores sunt, eo plus illis debemus: quod Apostolus eleganter docet simi litudine membrorum corporis nostri. Quod si qui nobis & multis aliis praestant, aequum est, vt in eis dona Dei exosculemur. Cogitent deniq; singuli, nullum esse inter homines, qui solus sibi ipsi sufficiat. Idcirco mutuis officijs indigemus: & exempla sunt potentissimorum regum, quos a servis, aut piscatoribus aut aliis obscuris hominibus seruatos fuisse legimus. Nec exemplis veteribus opus est, cum quotidie huius generis multa fiant. Dehis qui diligenter cogitant, hi facile deposito superbiae spiritu sese humiliabunt, vt omnibus inseruiant. Hos autem Dominus exaltat, vt alibi Christus loquitur: & tunc mutuis officijs fouetur charitas & concordia, quae inter ambitiosos & superbos non potest consistere.
units.tr: From this follows the second point: that we should despise no one in comparison with ourselves. For there is no cause for us to do so. If there are some who are inferior to us, we owe them all the more; as the Apostle teaches elegantly by the likeness of the members of our body. But if there are some who excel us and many others, it is fitting that we should embrace the gifts of God in them. Let each one finally consider that there is no one among men who is sufficient for himself alone. Therefore we stand in need of mutual services; and there are examples of the most powerful kings whom we read to have been saved by servants, or fishermen, or other obscure men. Nor is there need of old examples, since many things of this kind happen every day. Those who think carefully about these things will easily lay aside the spirit of pride and humble themselves, so as to serve all. But the Lord exalts these, as Christ speaks elsewhere; and then charity and concord are nourished by mutual services, which cannot exist among the ambitious and the proud.

units.la: Porro ne cui turpe aut indecorum videretur, Apostolos orbis totius doctores ad puerulum mittrum remisit, Dominus hunc magnifice commendat. Nam, vt diximus, in vlnas eum accipit, & eundem quasi suo loco subsistuit, dicens: Quisquis receperit aliquem puerulum talem in nomine meo, me recipit. Recipiunt puerulos Christi nomine, qui ab ipso commendatos fouent, tuentur, iuuant, instituunt, & vicissim eosdem imitantur, quatenus nobis abillo ceu exemplar propositi sunt. Quod si fiat, ipsum Christum recipimus doctorem. Nemo igitur doctrinam Veritatis aspernetur propter vilem & contemptibilem eius administrum. Vt enim alibi diximus, solet Deus humilia eligere, vt Verbo suo consistet authoritas ex se ipso: & vt nostram insolentiam deprimat, non ad pueros modo aut homines obscuros, sed saepe ad asinos & boues nos remittit: ad aues item omnis generis, & ad flores temere in agris nascentes. Confutantur etiam huius loci authoritate Anabaptistae, qui pueros indignos iudicant, qui in Ecclesiae societatem recipiantur, & ideo symbolum Christianae imitationis infantibus negant. Clamant, illos non intelligere mysteria regni coelorum. Quid tum? At haec ad illos pertinere sequenti Capite Dominus testabitur, & in praesenti iubet nos eorum similes fieri, si illius cives & haeredes velimus fieri. Sed plura de hac re alibi. Nunc discamus humiliari sub potenti manu Dei, & alij alijs seruiamus. Quod si pudet a puerulis discere,
units.tr: Moreover, lest it should seem shameful or unseemly to anyone, the Lord commends the little child highly, even though he sent the apostles, the teachers of the whole world, back to a little child. For, as we have said, he takes him into his arms and, as it were, sets him in his own place, saying: "Whoever receives one such little child in my name, receives me." They receive little children in the name of Christ who cherish, protect, help and instruct them, which were commended by him, and in turn imitate them, insofar as they have been set before us by him as an example of the purpose. If we do this, we receive Christ himself as teacher. Let no one therefore despise the doctrine of truth on account of its base and contemptible minister. For, as we have said elsewhere, God is accustomed to choose lowly things, so that the authority of his Word may stand of itself; and to humble our arrogance, he sends us not only to children or obscure men, but often to asses and oxen, likewise to birds of every kind, and to flowers growing carelessly in the fields. The Anabaptists also are refuted by the authority of this passage; they judge children unworthy to be received into the fellowship of the Church, and therefore deny the sign of Christian discipleship to infants. They cry out that these do not understand the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven. So what? But the Lord will testify in the following chapter that these things pertain to them, and in the present passage he bids us become like them, if we wish to be his citizens and heirs. But more on this matter elsewhere. Now let us learn to be humbled under the mighty hand of God, and let us serve one another. But if we are ashamed to learn from little children,

units.la: IESVM CHRISTVM imitemur, qui cum esset aeternus Dei Filius, humiliauit se, & Patri obediens factus est vsq; in mortem Crucis, vt nos exaltaret, & regni sui caelestis haeredes faceret. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Let us imitate JESUS CHRIST, who, although he was the eternal Son of God, humbled himself, and became obedient to the Father even unto the death of the Cross, so that he might exalt us and make us heirs of his heavenly kingdom. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCXVIII.
units.tr: HOMILY 218.

units.la: Quisquis autem offenderit aliquem ex paruis istis, qui in me credunt, praestiterit ei vt mola asinaria suspendatur in collo eius, ac demergatur in profundo maris: Vae mundo ab offendiculis. Necesse est enim vt veniat offendicula; veruntamen vae homini illi, per quem offendiculum venit. Si vero manus tua vel pes tuus facit vt tu offendas, excinde ea, & abijce abs te. Bonum est tibi ad vitam ingredi claudum, quàm duas manus aut duos pedes habentem conijci in ignem æternum. Et si oculus tuus facit vt tu offendas, erue eum, & abijce abs te. Bonum est tibi luscum ingredi in vitam, quàm duos oculos habentem conijci in gehennam ignis.
units.tr: Whoever shall offend one of these little ones who believe in me, it were better for him that a millstone were hanged about his neck and that he were drowned in the depth of the sea. Woe to the world because of offences! For it must needs be that offences come; but woe to that man by whom the offence comes. If your hand or your foot causes you to offend, cut it off and cast it from you. It is better for you to enter into life maimed or lame than having two hands or two feet to be cast into everlasting fire. And if your eye causes you to offend, pluck it out and cast it from you. It is better for you to enter into life with one eye than having two eyes to be cast into the fire of hell.

units.la: Oniam discipuli Domini nostri IESV CHRISTI ambitionis affectu accensi de prima tu inter se disceptabant, hic ad humilitatem ita eos hortatus est, vt puerulo in medium pro-ducto graviter minatus sit, ipsos nullum omnino locum in regno suo habituros esse, nisi excusso prorsus superbiae spiritu humilientur, & puerulorum similes fiant. Et ne cui indignum hoc videretur, eos qui tam diu in Christi schola instituti, & orbis totius doctores futuri erant, nunc ad puerulos remitti, vt ab his discant quae sui sint officij, hos tanti abs se fieri monet, vt seipsum recipi putet, si qui eos in suo nomine receperint. Quia vero ambitiosi illi primatus affectatores, qui sese alijs praeferunt, factu suo multos offendunt, prae caeteris aut simpliciores & qui nondum in fide confirmati sunt, vehementer offendi solet, si Verbi ministros, qui alijs modestiae & humilitatis doctores esse, & cato huius mundi factu ad caelestia aspirare debebat, ambitione & superbia turgere, ac inter se amulatione caeca committi videat: Dominus ex eo occasione arrepta, in doctrina de Scandalis digredi tur: & primum admonet, quam graue scelus sit, si quis alicui scandalum praebeat: deinde quantum periculi mundo a scandalis immineat, praedicit: postremo vt illa possint cauteri & vitari, docet.
units.tr: When the disciples of our Lord Jesus Christ, inflamed with a desire for ambition, were disputing among themselves about who should be first, he exhorted them to humility in this way: he brought a little child into their midst and solemnly warned them that they would have no place at all in his kingdom unless, with the spirit of pride wholly cast out, they humbled themselves and became like little children. And lest anyone think this unworthy, he told them, who had been trained so long in the school of Christ and were to be teachers of the whole world, that they were now being sent back to little children, to learn from them the duties of their office; and he so valued these children that he considered himself received if they were received in his name. But because those ambitious seekers of primacy, who set themselves above others, cause many to stumble by their conduct, and because the simpler folk, and those not yet confirmed in faith, are especially wont to be offended when they see ministers of the Word, who ought to be teachers of modesty and humility to others and, being strangers to this world, ought to aspire to heavenly things, swollen with ambition and pride and engaged in blind rivalry among themselves: the Lord, seizing the occasion from this, digresses into a teaching about offences. First he admonishes how grave a crime it is if anyone gives offence to another; then he foretells how great the danger from offences hanging over the world; finally he teaches how they can be guarded against and avoided.

units.la: Vt vero rem omnem rectius intelligamus, initio de scandalo, quid hoc proprie & quam multiplex sit, dicendum erit. Graecis scandala & σκανδαλα dicuntur ligna, quibus in decipulis aut laqueis tendicula alligatur vel suspenditur, ad quae fera offendens aut obruitur aut capitur. Deinde in genere accipitur scandali vox pro omni eo, ad quod iter facientes offendunt, vt vel cadant, vel laesi impediuntur, vt minus possint progredi. Inde vero per Metaphoram ad vitae conversationem transfertur et scandalum dicitur quicquid in Domini viis sive praeceptis ambulatibus obstaculo est, aut delinquendi occasione praebet. Nos Germani proprio vocabulo id exprimimus & Ergernus vocamus illud, quo homo deterior fit. Est igitur scandalum dictu aut factu quodcunque, ad quod alii qui in suo officio aut salutis via impediuntur, aut peccandi occasione inde arrepta deteriores fiunt.
units.tr: In order to understand the whole matter more rightly, we must first say what a scandal properly is and how manifold it is. Among the Greeks, skandala [σκανδαλα] are called the sticks to which a small trap or snare is fastened or hung, into which a beast, stumbling, is either caught or taken. Then, in a general sense, the word scandal is applied to anything over which travellers stumble, so that they either fall or, being injured, are hindered and can make less progress. Further, by metaphor it is transferred to the conduct of life, and whatever is an obstacle to those walking in the ways or precepts of the Lord, or offers an occasion for sinning, is called a scandal. We Germans express this by a proper word and call it Ergernus, that by which a man becomes worse. A scandal, then, is whatever is said or done by which others are hindered in their duty or in the way of salvation, or, taking occasion from it, become worse by sinning.

units.la: Est autem scandalum multiplex in dictis & factis, quoad item religionem & mores, aut alia vitae studia. Nocentissima sunt scandala, quae in religione obijciuntur, quia ex hac omnis fa-lus hominis dependet. Et hic praecipuum est doctrina falsa, quae Deos novos aut alienos praedicat, cultus item novos tradit, & idololatras facit: vel alioqui ineptis & absurdis quaestionibus religionis causam implicat & obscurat, vt simplicioribus dubia & suspecta fiat. Deinde non minus hic peccant principes, qui vel superstitione & falsa doctrina fascinati eandem populo obtrudunt: aut vt regnum suum stabiliant, cultus novos & illicitos instituunt; & eiectis Dei seruis falsos doctores & suae libidini seruientes mystas sibi accersunt, adhuc leges condunt, quibus inuitos cogunt, vt superstitiones absurdissimas sectentur: quod olim Ieroboamum primum Israelitarum Regem, deinde Herodem Magnum fecisse legimus. Neque extra culpam sunt principes, qui etsi verum Dei cultum non abrogent, in aliorum tamen gratiam permittunt, vt simul idola & superstitiones introducantur. Sic Solomon toti Iudaeorum genti scandalum posuit sua indulgentia, qua uxoribus alienigenis permisit, vt suis Dijs excelsa aedificarent & sacra facerent. Scandalum etiam sibi ipsis aut suis in religione obijciunt, qui seipsos imparibus coniugijs obstringunt, aut filias suas alienis a vera fide elocant. Scandalum quoque patiuntur non leve infirmiores, quando vera fidei professores superstitionibus communicare, aut in ijs quae indifferentia & media sunt, libertate sua nimium licenter abuti videntur. Et huc referri debent Encaenia, Carnisprivij ludi, vel potius Bacchanalia & Lupercalia, saltationum item & chorearum licentia, & alia eius generis quae ex Papatu, vel potius gentilismo ad nos deriuata, magno cum multorum scandalo quidam retinent, qui Euangelij doctrinam profitentur. Sunt praeterea vitae & morum scandala, quae dictis & factis praebentur. Etenim corrumpunt bonos mores colloquia prava. Multi enim ex obscaenis sermonibus, aut cantu lasciuo libidinis occasionem arripiunt. Ideo Apostolus scortationem, obscaenitatem, stultiloquium & quaecunque scurrilitatem redolent, inter Christianos ne nominari quidem volunt. Scandalum quoque multis praebent, qui sacro sancto Dei nomine ad execrationes & deierationes impie abutuntur: qui absentibus obtrectant, aut piis magistratibus & fidis Ecclesiae ministris conviciantur, aut calumniis virulentis illos in odium & contemptum adducunt: quod hodie apud multos nimis vulgare est. Graviùs peccant, qui ne a factis quidem turpibus abstinent, & eo nocentiora sunt scandala; quo maior est eorum, qui illa praebent, authoritas. Gravissimè igitur peccant parentes, dum sua petulantia & improbitate liberis tenellis pessimarum cogitationum materiam obiiciunt, & cupiditatum illicitarum scintillas in eorum cordibus excitant: Ministri item Ecclesiarum, qui sua intemperantia, libidine, avaritia, fastu & scurrilitate ministerium Verbi contemptum reddunt. Quibus adnumerari debent Magistratus, qui sua licentia bonas leges eneruant, & existimationem suam turpiter prostituunt. Ad eundem modum diuites pauperibus & egenis impatientia & murmurationis aduersus Deum scandalum proponunt, dum in horum conspectu voluptuantur, comessantur & vestitu luxurioso superbiunt. Vicissim hi egentium multorum exemplo offensi ex beneficiis immites & duri fiunt, quando multos ex mendicatione quaestum facere, & eleemosynis bonorum turpiter ad ignauum otium & omnem licentiam abuti conspicantur. Denique foecundissima est scandalorum seges, & latissimè per omnes hominum ordines extenditur: & omnibus applicari debet quod in praesenti dicit Dominus.
units.tr: Scandal is manifold in words and deeds, both as regards religion and morals, or other pursuits of life. The most harmful scandals are those given in religion, because the whole salvation of man depends on this. Here the chief is false teaching, which proclaims new or strange gods, likewise hands on new forms of worship and makes idolaters; or else it entangles and obscures the cause of religion with foolish and absurd questions, so that doubts and suspicions arise for the simpler folk. Next, no less do princes sin here, who, bewitched by superstition and false doctrine, impose the same on the people; or who, in order to establish their kingdom, institute new and unlawful forms of worship, and, having driven out the servants of God, summon to themselves false teachers and mystics who serve their own lust, and further enact laws by which they compel unwilling subjects to pursue the most absurd superstitions. We read that Jeroboam, the first king of Israel, did this, and afterwards Herod the Great. Nor are princes free of blame who, though they do not abolish the true worship of God, nevertheless permit, for the sake of others, that idols and superstitions be introduced at the same time. So Solomon gave a scandal to the whole Jewish nation by his indulgence, in that he allowed his foreign wives to build high places for their gods and to offer sacrifices. Those also give scandal to themselves and to their own households in religion who bind themselves in unequal marriages, or give their daughters in marriage to men alien from the true faith. The weaker suffer no slight scandal also when professors of the true faith seem to join in superstitions, or to abuse their liberty too freely in those things which are indifferent and middling. To this must be referred the Encaenia, the Carnival games, or rather the Bacchanalia and Lupercalia, and likewise the licence of dances and choruses, and other things of this kind, derived to us from Papacy, or rather from heathenism, which some who profess the doctrine of the Gospel retain, to the great scandal of many. Moreover, there are scandals of life and manners, which are given by words and deeds. For wicked conversations corrupt good morals. Many take occasion for lust from obscene speech or wanton song. Therefore the Apostle does not even wish fornication, obscenity, foolish talk, or whatever smells of buffoonery, to be named among Christians. Many also give scandal who impiously abuse the holy name of God for curses and oaths; who slander the absent, or revile godly magistrates and faithful ministers of the Church, or with virulent calumnies bring them into hatred and contempt, which today is far too common among many. They sin more gravely who do not even abstain from shameful deeds, and the scandals are the more harmful the greater the authority of those who give them. Parents therefore sin most gravely when by their wantonness and wickedness they set before tender children the material of the worst thoughts, and kindle sparks of unlawful desires in their hearts. Likewise the ministers of the Churches, who by their intemperance, lust, avarice, arrogance and buffoonery make the ministry of the Word contemptible. To these must be added magistrates, who by their licence weaken good laws and shamefully prostitute their own reputation. In the same way the rich, by feasting, revelling and boasting in luxurious clothing before the eyes of the poor and needy, offer them a scandal of impatience and murmuring against God. In turn, many of the needy, offended by the example of such people, become harsh and hard-hearted towards those who would help them, when they see many making a trade of begging and shamefully abusing the alms of the good for idle sloth and every licence. In short, the crop of scandals is most abundant and spreads very widely through all orders of men; and what the Lord now says must be applied to all.

units.la: Docet hic primum, quam grave scelus sit, si quis alijs scandalo sit, & magna cum grauitate ait: Quisquis offenderit aliquem, vel vnum ex paruis istis, qui in me credunt, praestiterit ei, vt mola asinaria suspendatur in collo eius, ac demergatur in profundo maris. Primo, QVIS QVIS, ait: vt vniuersale hoc decretum esse offendat, quo omnes cuiuscunque loci aut ordinis homines comprehendantur: vt nemo sit, qui se immunem possit dicere, cui in hac re plus quam alijs liceat. Deinde addit: ALIQVEM vel vnu ex paruis istis: & hic quoque indefinitè loquitur, ne quæ excipiat, qui impune offendi possit. Et vt nuper primo de puerulo quae in medio discipulorum stiterat, locutus est: dein de ad omnes, qui per fidem puerulorum similes facti sunt, orationem extendit, dicens: Quisquis receperit aliquem puerulum talem: Ita hic vtrosque comprehendit: nimirum quod qui credunt, mundi iudicio parui & nullius pretij homines sunt, imo (vt Paulus ipsos Apostolos vocat) purgamenta & rameta mundi censentur. Paruos aut hic nominare voluit, vt ijs occurrat, qui contemptu peccant, quod sibi put tent quiduis licere in eos, quorum nulla est in mundo authoritas. Ideo etiam addit, Qui in me credit: vt moneat, non spernendum esse, quis quisque sit quoad suam conditionem, sed qualis quoad fidem sit: nimirum Christi discipulus & frater, & proinde Filius Dei atque Christi cohæres. Est multa obseruatione dignum, quod pueruulos quoque credentibus in ipsum adnumerat, non vtique quod aliu credant, sed proculdubio propter gratiam foederis, quo eos Deus complexus est, quæ causa est, quod ijde ad Ecclesiae credentium societatem pertinent, & (vt in sequenti Capite dicetur) ad ipsos quoque pertineat regni caelorum haereditas. Sufficit hoc ad confutandum Anabaptistas, qui infantibus Baptismum negant, eo quod neque credere possint, neque fidem fateri. Nam etsi hoc vere dicant, non tamen hoc obstat, quo minus fidei symbolum accipiant, & in Ecclesiae societatem adscribantur, cum Dei Filius, qui & Baptismi author & Ecclesiae caput atq; sponsus est, eos credentibus adnumeret. Quo ad aut causam praesentem, scelerius huius, de quo agitur, atrocitatem supplicij comminatione dento tat, quod apud Palaestinos grauissimum fuisse, Diuus Hieronymus testatur. Qui enim lapide molari ex collo suo suspenso demergebantur in maris abyssum, indigni iudicabantur, qui vnquam Sulla huius aut aeris beneficio fruerentur. Quod si vero praestaret hoc supplicio multari scandalorum authores, non obscure docet, eos in futuro quoque saeculo poenis sempiternis excruciandos fore. Et cos uenit cum Christi dicto, quod in Lege pronuntiat Deus: Maledictus qui caecum errare aut impingere facit in via: & dicet omnis populus, Amen. Quod si maledictionem meretur (qua nihil atrocius dici & fingi potest) qui quoad corpus offendere facit caecum, quid de illo fiet, qui scandalum infirmis & incautis ponit, quo anima hominis in perditionis sempiternae periculum adducitur? Rationes tam dirae comminationis alibi ex Pauli ad Corinthios epistola priori adduximus.
units.tr: He first teaches how grave a crime it is if anyone is a scandal to others, and he says with great solemnity: Whoever shall offend anyone, even one of these little ones who believe in me, it were better for him that a millstone were hanged about his neck and that he were drowned in the depth of the sea. First he says WHOEVER, so that this decree may be seen as universal, embracing men of every place and rank, so that there is no one who can call himself exempt, to whom in this matter more is allowed than to others. Then he adds ANYONE, or ONE of these little ones; and here too he speaks indefinitely, so that he excludes no one who might offend with impunity. Just as he had recently spoken of the little child who stood in the midst of the disciples, he then extends his words to all who, through faith, have become like little children, saying: Whoever receives one such little child. So here he includes both: for those who believe are, in the judgement of the world, small and worthless men; indeed (as Paul calls the Apostles themselves) they are reckoned the refuse and off-scouring of the world. He chose to name them "little ones" to meet those who sin through contempt, thinking they may do whatever they like to those who have no authority in the world. Therefore he also adds, Who believe in me: to warn that we should not despise anyone because of his condition, but consider what he is in respect of faith, namely a disciple and brother of Christ, and therefore a son of God and joint heir with Christ. It is worthy of much attention that he also counts the little children among those who believe in him, not indeed because they believe, but undoubtedly because of the grace of the covenant by which God has embraced them. This is the reason that they belong to the fellowship of the believing Church, and (as will be said in the following chapter) the inheritance of the kingdom of heaven pertains to them too. This is enough to refute the Anabaptists, who deny baptism to infants on the ground that they can neither believe nor confess the faith. For although they say this truly, it nevertheless does not hinder them from receiving the sign of the faith and being enrolled in the fellowship of the Church, since the Son of God, who is both the author of Baptism and the head and bridegroom of the Church, counts them among believers. As to the present matter, the enormity of this crime, which is under discussion, is shown by the threat of a punishment, which Saint Jerome testifies was most severe among the Palestinians. For those who were drowned in the depth of the sea with a millstone hung from their necks were judged unworthy ever to enjoy the light or the benefit of the air. And if this punishment were to be inflicted on the authors of scandals, it clearly teaches that they will also be tormented with everlasting punishments in the age to come. And it agrees with the saying of Christ, when God pronounces in the Law: Cursed is he who makes the blind to wander or stumble in the way; and all the people shall say, Amen. But if he deserves a curse (than which nothing more atrocious can be said or imagined) who causes the blind man to stumble in body, what will become of him who sets a scandal before the weak and the unwary, by which the soul of a man is brought into danger of everlasting perdition? We have elsewhere brought forward the reasons for so dreadful a threat from Paul's first Epistle to the Corinthians.

units.la: Etsi vero hoc sufficere debeat vere pio, vt sibi a scandalis caveat, vt tamen magis excitemur, de periculi
units.tr: Although this should be enough for a truly pious person to guard himself against scandals, so that we may be stirred up all the more, concerning the danger of

units.la: Scandali periculum frequens. de periculo communi admonet, dicens: Væ mundo ab offendiculis: qua imprecatione partim scan- dalorum authoribus maledicit, partim monet à nulla re magis cauendum esse, quàm a scandalis. Et causam tam seriæ admonitionis indicat: Necesse est enim, ut veniant offendicula. Et ne quis ob- ijceret: Ergo excusati sunt qui illa dant, cum necessitate peccent: Præoccupat: Veruntamen væ homini illi, per quem offendiculum venit. Non ergo hic aliquis necessitatem fatalem fingat, cuius prætextu sese excusent, qui alios offendunt. Nam necessitas illa ex nobis est. Quia enim mundus hic totus in malo iacet, & homo animalis no percipit ea quæ sunt spiritus Dei, ubiq; occasiones in- uenit Satã, per quas scandala obijciat incautis. Quid enim aliud in mundo occurrit, præter illece- bras omnis generis, quæ carnis cupiditates accendere, libidine oculorum inflammare, & latenté in nobis fastum siue superbiam inflare possunt? Et adiuuat Satanæ conatu vulgi mos, qui hodie pas- sim regnat, quod plerique, sua scelera mundi exemplo excusant. Fieri ergo non potest, quin alius a- lium offendat, & vitia grauissima cum contagione quadam latissime propagentur. Quid de vitijs dico? Tanta est in huius sæculi filijs nequitia, ut scandala ipsi arripiant ex eo, quo ad virtutis studium & pietatem excitari debebant. Exepla huius malitiæ alibi in Caino, Ejauo, Iosephi fra- tribus, Pharaone, Saule & similibus vidimus. Et nihil hodie vulgarius est, quàm quod multi ex aliorum felicitate, & prospera Euangelij propagatione sibi scandala fabricant, & ad Christu of- fendunt (sicuti Simeon prædixit) ut ipsis fiat offendiculi lapis, qui electis salutis author est. Si- militer Euangelium odor mortis est multis ad mortem, quod vere credentibus odor vitæ est ad vitam. Quia autem tanta est hominum peruersitas, quanto magis ipsi ea faciunt & loquuntur, quæ sibi ipsis & aliis scandalo sunt? Permittit autem ista Deus, ut interea electi probentur, & fidei exercendæ materiam habeant. Admonet autem ista consideratio, quàm prouidos oporteat eos esse, qui salutem suam tueri volunt, ne vel aliis scandalum ponant, aut ipsi temerè accipiant. Et in primis horum nos meminisse decet aduersus eos, qui infide & religione patrũ vestigiis, aut multitudinis exemplo insistendũ esse clamitant. Quia enim in mundo semper plures mali sunt, & ratio nostra in diuinis cæca est, errent atq; offendant oportet, quotquot mundi authoritate ducun tur. Non temerè ergo factum putabimus, quòd Dominus admonitionem hanc apud Lucam breui quidem, sed graui admodum Epiphonemate concludit: Cauete vobis.
units.tr: The danger of scandal, frequently. He warns of the danger that all share, saying: "Woe to the world because of offences!" By this curse he pronounces judgment on the authors of scandals, and he warns that we must beware of nothing more than scandals. He also gives the reason for so serious a warning: "For it must needs be that offences come." Lest anyone object, "So those who give offences are excused, since they sin out of necessity," he anticipates it: "Nevertheless woe to that man through whom the offence comes." Therefore let no one invent some fated necessity and use it as a pretext to excuse himself for offending others. For that necessity comes from us. Because the whole world lies in evil, and the natural man does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God, Satan finds opportunities everywhere by which to place stumbling blocks before the unwary. For what else meets us in the world but allurements of every kind, which can kindle the desires of the flesh, inflame the lust of the eyes, and puff up the pride or arrogance hidden within us? And the custom of the crowd, which today reigns everywhere, helps Satan's efforts, since most people excuse their sins by the example of the world. It is therefore impossible that one should not offend another, and grievous vices spread very widely with a kind of contagion. Why do I speak only of vices? Such is the wickedness among the children of this age that they seize upon scandals from the very things by which they ought to have been stirred up to the pursuit of virtue and godliness. We have seen examples of this malice elsewhere, in Cain, Esau, Joseph's brothers, Pharaoh, Saul and others like them. And nothing is more common today than that many people manufacture scandals for themselves from the good fortune of others and from the prosperous spread of the Gospel, and so stumble at Christ (as Simeon foretold), so that he becomes for them a stone of stumbling, though he is the author of salvation for the elect. Likewise the Gospel is a savour of death to death for many, while to those who truly believe it is a savour of life to life. But since human perversity is so great, how much more do they do and say those things which are a scandal both to themselves and to others? God permits these things so that the elect may meanwhile be proved and have matter for exercising their faith. This consideration also teaches how cautious those ought to be who wish to keep their salvation safe, so that they neither give scandal to others nor take it up rashly themselves. And in the first place we ought to remember this against those who cry out that one must cling to the faith and religion of the Fathers or to the example of the multitude. For since there are always more wicked people in the world, and our reason is blind in divine matters, all who are led by the authority of the world must necessarily go astray and stumble. We shall not think, then, that it was without reason that the Lord concludes this warning in Luke with a brief but very weighty exclamation: "Take heed to yourselves."

units.la: In præsenti autem rationem quoq; tradit, quam secuti scandalum omne euitare possumus: Si manus tua vel pes tuus facit ut tu offendas, excinde ea, & abijce abs te, &c. Et mox idem de oculo quoq; præcipit. Simili utitur a chirurgis petito, qui si totius corporis salus & vita periclitetur ob membrũ aliquod vitiosum, illud resecare solent, ut hominis saluti consulant: Ita hic nobis facien dum esse monet, ut tam sedulo resistamus scandali occasionibus, ut ne membris quidem proprijs par- camus, si nos illis offendi sentimus. Non autem simpliciter oculos eruere, manus & pedes abscin- dere iubet, sed ut affectus prauos coerceamus necesse est, qui nos ad scelera solicitant. Lasciuiunt plerunq; oculi, dum mundi fastu delestantur, aut in speciandis formis alienis occupati sunt. Erue tunc illos, id est, auerte ab illicitorũ contemplatione, & malam concupiscentiam, quæ ex illa con- cipitur, gladio Verbi iugula. Sentis manus tuas, id est, naturales agendi facultates: pedes item, id est, affectus carni insitos ad illicita propendere, & ijs offendi, quæ Satan & mundus obijcit. Mox igitur eundem illum gladium stringito, ut (quod Paulus monet) membra hæc terrestria mor- tifices, & corpus totum in seruitutem redigas. Quod autem singulis præcipitur, publice etiam in Republica & Ecclesia obseruari debet. Quia enim ista non omnes sponte faciunt, Verbi prædica- tione & legibus opus est: Verbi ministri item & magistratibus, qui opus Dei apud omnes vrge- ant, & disciplina quoq; vel castigatione seueriori in officio contineant eos, quos alijs scandalo esse vident. Sint igitur hi seduli in commissio sibi munere, ut neq; oculis, neq; manibus, aut pedibus parcant. Oculi in Ecclesia sunt Verbi præcones, qui ideo Speculatoribus conferuntur, & Episcopi dicuntur. Oculorum instar etiam sunt magistratus, qui morum disciplinæ præfecti sunt, quos ideo Lacedæmonij Ephoros dixerunt. Manuũ loco sunt officiales publici. Pedes & crura dicere possumus populum totum, qui nisi saluus sit, Respublica non potest consistere. His omnibus adhi- beri debet hæc Christi regula, ut nemini propter sua merita aut dignitatem parcatur, si alicuius scandali author sit: nemo etiam propter vilem & abiectam conditionem negligatur, ut ipsi im-
units.tr: He also gives in the present passage the principle by which, if we follow it, we can avoid every scandal: "If your hand or your foot causes you to stumble, cut it off and cast it from you," and so on. And soon he gives the same command about the eye. He uses a comparison taken from surgeons, who, when the health and life of the whole body are endangered on account of some diseased member, are accustomed to cut it away so as to care for the man's health. So here he warns us that we must act in such a way as to resist the occasions of scandal so resolutely that we spare not even our own members, if we feel that we are stumbling over them. He does not, however, command us simply to tear out our eyes or cut off our hands and feet, but that we must restrain the depraved affections which entice us to crimes. The eyes often run wild while they are delighted by the pride of the world, or are busy gazing at the forms of others. Tear them out then, that is, turn them away from contemplating forbidden things, and with the sword of the Word slay the evil lust which is conceived from that contemplation. You feel your hands, that is, your natural powers of acting; likewise your feet, that is, the affections implanted in the flesh which lean toward unlawful things and stumble over those things which Satan and the world put in our way. Therefore, immediately, draw that same sword, so that (as Paul admonishes) you may mortify your earthly members and bring your whole body into bondage. But what is commanded to individuals must also be observed publicly in the commonwealth and the Church. For since not everyone does these things willingly, there is need of the preaching of the Word and of laws. Ministers of the Word likewise, and magistrates, who press the work of God upon all and by discipline, or by more severe correction, keep in their duty those whom they see to be a scandal to others, must do so. Let them therefore be diligent in the office committed to them, so that they spare neither eyes, nor hands, nor feet. In the Church the eyes are the heralds of the Word, who for this reason are compared to watchmen and are called bishops. Magistrates, who are set over the discipline of morals, are in the likeness of eyes, and for this reason the Lacedaemonians called them ephors. The public officials take the place of hands. We may call the whole people the feet and legs, which unless they are sound the commonwealth cannot stand. This rule of Christ must be applied to all of these: no one should be spared on account of his merits or dignity if he is the author of some scandal; and no one should be neglected on account of a base and humble condition, so that it may be allowed to him to sin with impunity.

units.la: {*} ... pune peccare liceat. Etenim nullius hominis tanta possunt esse merita, ut propter ipsum scandalum publicum ferri debeat: nec etiam securè negligi debet, quisquis suo exemplo vel minimum offendere potest. Breuius ista nunc annotamus, quia Capite quinto haec eadem verba, prolixius interpretati sumus. Nunc monuisse sufficiat, communem ac generalem doctrinam hic tradi, quam si bijpsis singuli applicent, & primo quidem curent, ne ipsi quoquam dicto aut facto offendant: deinde pro sua vocationis & officij ratione apud alios quoque scandalorum licentiam coerceant: Ita deniq; viuant omnes, ut in ipsis Dei nomen glorificetur. Alij vero cum quibus versantur, in fide & pietate per eos proficiant, & ut in nouissimo illo Domini nostri IESV CHRISTI aduentu coram illo consistere, & regni caelestis haereditatem, cum eo adire possint. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: ... For no man's merits can be so great that they should be allowed to excuse public scandal, nor should anyone who can offend even in the smallest degree by his example be safely overlooked. We note these things more briefly now, because we have already explained these same words more fully in the fifth chapter. Now it is enough to have admonished that a general and common teaching is set forth here, which each one should apply to himself: first, that he take care not to offend by any word or deed; then, according to the nature of his calling and office, that he also restrain the licence of scandals among others; and so let all live that the name of God may be glorified in them. And let others, among whom they live, advance through them in faith and godliness, and so be able to stand before him at that last coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, and to enter with him into the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCXIX.
units.tr: HOMILY CCXIX.

units.la: Videte ne contemnatis aliquem exparuis istis: dico enim vobis, quod Angeli eorum in coelis semper vident faciem Patris mei, qui in coelis est. Venit enim Filius hominis, ut feruet quod perierat. Quid vobis videtur?
