Si fuerint alicui homini centum oues, & errauerit vna ex eis, nonne relictis ipsis nonaginta nouem, profectus in montes quaerit eam quae aberrauerat? Quod si acciderit ut inueniat eam, amen dico vobis, gaudet super ea magis quam super illis nonaginta nouem, quae non aberrarunt. Ita non vult Pater vester, qui in coelis est, ut pereat vnus ex paruis istis.
units.tr: See that you do not despise one of these little ones. For I tell you that their angels in heaven always see the face of my Father who is in heaven. For the Son of man came to save what was lost. What do you think? If a man has a hundred sheep, and one of them goes astray, does he not leave the ninety-nine, go up into the mountains and seek the one that went astray? And if it happens that he finds it, truly I say to you, he rejoices over it more than over the ninety-nine that did not go astray. So it is not the will of your Father who is in heaven that one of these little ones should perish.

units.la: Dominus & Seruator noster IESVS CHRISTVS non abfq; graui causa discipulos suos & in his omnes qui nomen eius profitentur, monuit, ut sic vita sua instituant, ne quis ipsorum dictis aut factis offendatur. Quia enim peccatum (ut Ioannes definit) ἀνομία est, id est, legis transgressio, & ideo per se omnes damnat, qui in illo perseuerant, grauior est eorum culpa, qui insuper aliis peccadi occasione praebet. At quia ea est ingenij humani prauitas, ut no possint no in mundo scandala quotidie noua incidere, redit ad id Christus, unde praesentis disceptationis initiu exortum fuit, ut fonte scandalorum obturet. Est hic superbia, qua quisq; se aliis praefert. Parit haec aliorum contemptu, qui causa est, quod eos, quibus cum nobis res est, non putamus dignos, in quorum gratiam aliquid facere aut omittere debeamus. De hoc vitio igitur grauem admonitionem subtexit.
units.tr: Our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, not without grave cause, warned his disciples, and in them all who profess his name, to order their lives so that none of them be offended by their words or deeds. For since sin, as John defines it, is lawlessness [ἀνομία], that is, transgression of the law, it condemns by itself all who persist in it; the guilt of those who moreover offer an occasion of sin to others is graver. But since human perversity is such that stumbling-blocks cannot fail to arise in the world daily, Christ returns to the point from which the beginning of the present discussion arose, so that he may stop up the source of stumbling-blocks. Here the vice is pride, by which each person sets himself above others. This produces contempt for others, which is the reason we do not think those with whom we have dealings worthy of having anything done or left undone for their sake. Against this vice, therefore, he adds a serious admonition.

units.la: Propositio fiue summa est: Videte ne contemnatis aliquem ex paruis istis. Rursus paruos nominat, & horum nomine partim aetate paruulos intelligit, partim eos qui paruulorum similes facti ab ipso vno pendet, & ideo apud mundum contemptui sunt, & tales censentur, quorum nulla ratio haberi debeat. Videre aut iubet, ut hic multa cura & solicitudine opus esse doceat.
units.tr: The proposition, or summary, is: See that you do not despise any of these little ones. Again he calls them little, and by this name he understands partly those who are little in age, and partly those who have become like little children and depend on him alone, and who are therefore held in contempt by the world and counted as those whom no regard need be shown. He bids them to be looked at, which he teaches requires great care and concern.

units.la: Quasi diceret: Scio quale sit hominis ingenium, Sublimia spectat, & no cotentu sua forte, subinde ad altiora cotendit: cuius vti exemplu habemus in primis paretibus, qui cum foli essent, neq; aliquē ipsis praestantiore haberet praeter vnū Deum, huius similes fieri voluerunt. Est hoc vitium ita commune omnibus, ut qui optimi sunt, & ab iniuriis facile abstinet, tamen alios prae se contemnunt, quos se inferiores esse videt, et ut id faciat, sibi licere arbitrantur. Et hoc iam in vobis ipsis experimini, dicit Dominus. Vnde enim haec de primatu disceptatio exorta est? None ex eo, quod vnusquisq; vestrum se aliis praestare sibi persuadet. Quod si inter vos, qui omnes discipuli mei domestici, imo fratres estis, quos ego omnes hac stenus pari studio et amore coplexus sum, hoc fit, quid fiet quoad alios, nisi de reprimendo hoc superbia spiritu serio cogitetis? Itaq; quam chara vobis est falsa vestra, videte quaeso, ne huic vitio locum detis: ut deniq; ne quae ex paruis istis, quos vobis nequaquam coferendos esse, palam constat, contemnatis: Sed potius, quo quisq; minor & indignior, vel infirmior videtur, eo magis illu omni dile ctionis officio prosequamini. Etenim, ut alias monui, hoc charitatis proprium est, quod aliorum miseriis afficitur, & his non superbe ac inhumaniter insultat, sed amice condolet. Hic inquam verborum Christi Christifenfus est. Et quod breui dicto hic monet Dominus, Paulus ad Philippenses prolixe & ad modum modu pathetice explicat,dicens: Si qua est cofolatio in Christo,id est, Christiana,fi quod solatium charitatis,fi qua comunio spiritus,fi qua viscera ac miserationes: explete meu gaudium,vt itidem fitis affecti, eandem charitatem habetes,id est,parem aut mutuam,vnanimes,vt sententijs vni, nihil gerite per contentionem,aut per inanem gloriam,sed ex modestia quisq; aliu se praestantiorem existimet,neq; sua quisq; spectetis,sed vnusquisq; etiā quae sunt aliorū. Et his Christi exemplu addit,qui cum esset in forma Dei,adeoq; vnum cum Deo Patre,tamen vt nostrae saluti consuleret, demisit se,&c. Eodem pertinet,quod alibi monet,vt alij alios honore praeueniant. Rom.12.
units.tr: As if he said: I know what kind of nature a human being has. He looks to lofty things and, not content with his own lot, strives upward toward higher things. We have an example of this in the first parents, who, when they were alone and had no one more excellent than the one God, wanted to become like him. This vice is so common to all that even those who are best, and who easily abstain from wrongs, nonetheless despise others in comparison with themselves, whom they see to be inferior, and think it permitted them to do so. And this you now experience in yourselves, says the Lord. For whence has this dispute about primacy arisen? Is it not from the fact that each of you persuades himself that he excels the others? If this happens among you, who are all my domestic disciples, indeed brothers, whom I have hitherto embraced all with equal zeal and love, what will happen as regards others, unless you think seriously about restraining this spirit of pride? Therefore, however dear your own salvation is to you, see, I beg you, that you do not give place to this vice; so that, finally, you do not despise any of these little ones, whom it is plainly agreed are in no way to be compared with you. Rather, the more humble, unworthy or weaker anyone seems, the more you should attend to him with every office of love. For, as I have admonished elsewhere, it is the property of charity to be moved by the miseries of others, and not to insult them proudly and inhumanely, but to sympathise with them in friendship. This, I say, is the sense of Christ's words. What the Lord here admonishes in a brief saying, Paul explains at length and with some pathos in his letter to the Philippians, saying: "If there is any consolation in Christ, that is, Christian comfort; if any comfort of love, if any fellowship of the Spirit, if any bowels and mercies: fulfil my joy, that you may be of the same mind, having the same love, being of one accord and one mind; do nothing through contention or vainglory, but in lowliness of mind let each esteem the other better than himself; look not each on his own things, but each also on the things of others. Let this mind be in you which was also in Christ Jesus, who, being in the form of God, and thus one with God the Father, nevertheless, to consult our salvation, humbled himself," etc. To the same end pertains what he elsewhere admonishes, that they should go before one another in honour. Rom. 12.

units.la: Quia autem in hac causa nihil nobis nimium dici potest, propter innatam nobis Philauti- am & ambitionem,rationem huius praecepti aut admonitionis grauissimam adducit,paruulos ita Deo Patri curae esse,vt nolit aliquem ex illis perire. Vnde sequitur,in Deum ipsum eos peccare, qui illos contemnunt,& ex contemptu eis scandalum praebent. Id vero duobus argumentis confir mat,quae mox parabola eleganti & consolationis plena illustrat.
units.tr: But since in this matter nothing can be said too much against us, on account of the self-love and ambition innate in us, he brings forward the most weighty reason for this precept or admonition: that the little ones are so cared for by God the Father that he is unwilling that any of them should perish. Hence it follows that those who despise them, and give them offence by their contempt, sin against God himself. He confirms this by two arguments, which he soon illustrates with an elegant parable full of consolation.

units.la: Primum argumentum a Dei protectione petit,qui Angelorum ministerio parvulos custodiat. Nam ait: Angeli eorum in coelis semper vident faciem Patris mei,qui in coelis est. Paruulorum Angelos dicit,qui ipsorum custodiae ac defensioni deputati sunt. Et hi(inquit) illi ipsi sunt,qui per petuo vident faciem Patris mei,id est,quos Pater suo seruitio destinauit,vt perpetuo in eius conspectu coapareant,ac ipsius mandata exequantur. Argumentu est eiusmodi: Qui custodes & defensores habet potentes & robustos,ij nō temere contemni aut offendi debet: Paruuli & mundo contemp ti custodes & tutores habent Angelos,& quidē non vulgares,sed eos quos Deus sibi quasi domesticos famulos delegit: Ergo non sunt contemnendi. Quis enim nō dicat iniquū esse,vt ij a quoquā hominū parui fiant & negligantur,quos Deus in suam tutelā recepit, & pro quibus Angeli excubant. De hoc Angelorū praesidio Scriptura saepe loquitur. Meminit huius Abraham,quando feruo suo,qui in Mesopotamiā ablegabat pro vxore Isaaco filio quaereda,dixit: Dominus Deus coeli,qui tulit me de domo patris mei,& mihi dixit: Semini tuo dabo terram istam, is mittet Angelum suum ante te,&c. Et in Psalmis habentur ista Dauidis: Castrametatur Angelus Domini circa eos qui timent eum,& eripit eos. Ite, Angelis suis praecepit de te,vt in omnibus viis tuis custodiant te,&c. Quo Paulus respexit,quādo Angelos scripsit esse ministratores spiritus,qui ministerij causa mittuntur propter eos,qui haeredes erunt salutis. Exempla praesidij huius aut defensionis Angelicae passim occurrunt in historia sacra,quae alibi recitauimus. Et si de infantibus dicendum sit,res ipsa testatur,periculis tam multis tamq; grauibus eos esse obnoxios,vt nulla parentum cura illis defendendis aut seruandis sufficeret,nisi illis Angeli custodes adessent. Idē de nobis ipsis possumus dicere,qui multoties ex periculis grauissimis,quae ipsi ignoramus,etiam praeter animi nostri voluntatem subducimur: nimirum Angelorum ministerio,qui se nobis insinuant.
units.tr: The first argument he takes from God's protection, who guards the little ones through the ministry of angels. For he says: Their angels in heaven always see the face of my Father who is in heaven. He speaks of the angels of little ones, who have been appointed to their custody and defence. And these, he says, are the very ones who continually see the face of my Father, that is, whom the Father has assigned to his service, so that they may always appear in his sight and carry out his commands. The argument runs thus: whoever has guardians and defenders who are powerful and strong ought not to be rashly despised or offended. Little ones, despised by the world, have guardians and tutors, angels, and indeed not ordinary ones, but those whom God has chosen, as it were, as his household servants. Therefore they are not to be despised. For who would not say it is unjust that those whom God has taken into his protection, and for whom angels keep watch, should be made little and neglected by anyone among men? Scripture often speaks of this protection of angels. Abraham mentioned it when he said to his servant, who was sent into Mesopotamia to seek a wife for his son Isaac: "The Lord God of heaven, who brought me from my father's house and spoke to me, saying, To your seed I will give this land, he will send his angel before you," etc. And in the Psalms there are these words of David: "The angel of the Lord encamps around those who fear him, and delivers them." And: "He has commanded his angels concerning you, that they keep you in all your ways," etc. Paul had this in view when he wrote that angels are ministering spirits, sent for the sake of ministry on account of those who will be heirs of salvation. Examples of this angelic protection and defence occur everywhere in sacred history, which we have recited elsewhere. And if one must speak of infants, the thing itself bears witness that they are exposed to dangers so many and so grave that no care of parents would suffice to defend or preserve them unless guardian angels were present. We can say the same of ourselves, who are often withdrawn, even against our will, from very grave dangers that we ourselves do not know: surely by the ministry of angels, who insinuate themselves to us.

units.la: Cauendus tamen est illorū error,qui vnicuiq; ab ipsa infantia duos Angelos,bonum & malum affingunt. Nam nihil de eo affirmat Scriptura,quae interdum toti alicui genti vnum Angelum assignat: vt quando Daniel Michaelis meminit,quem alius Angelus principe siue duce populi Iudaici vocat: alias vero vni homini plures adfuisse docet,vt Iacobo,qui vidit castra siue cohortes Angelorum: Elisaeo item,quem innumerabiles Angeli,qui curruum & equitum igneorum speciem referebat,contra Syros defenderut. Multo magis caueri debet superstitio,qua nonnulli decepti Angelos idcirco colunt & adorant,quod nos ab eis iuuari aut defendi audiunt. Quod olim quoq; aliquos fecisse,author est Theodoretus in suis in epistola Pauli ad Colossenses commentarijs,vbi scribit,eos qui Legis iustitiam defendebant, Angelorum quoq; cultum docuisse,eo quod Legem per hos datam esse dicerent. Et licet Synodus Laodicena hanc superstitionem damnasset, tamen adhuc suo tempore in Phrygia & finitimis locis oratoria Sancti Michaelis visa fuisse. Hodie apud multos Angeli cum Diuis coelitibus coluntur. Sed his confutandis sufficere nobis debet,quod Angelus ille Sanctus,qui Ioanni reuelationis illius nobilissimae,qua Christus eum dignatus est,interpres fuit,ipsi ad pedes eius prostrato vt eum adoraret,dixit: Vide ne feceris: conseruus enim tuus sum & fratrum tuorum,habentium testimonium IESV. Apo.19.& 22.
units.tr: Yet the error of those must be guarded against, who attribute to each person from infancy two angels, a good one and an evil one. For Scripture affirms nothing of this; it sometimes assigns a single angel to a whole nation, as when Daniel mentions Michael, whom another angel calls the prince or leader of the Jewish people; at other times it teaches that several were present to one man, as to Jacob, who saw the camp or companies of angels; likewise Elisha, whom innumerable angels, looking like chariots and horsemen of fire, defended against the Syrians. All the more must that superstition be guarded against, by which some, deceived, worship and adore angels on the ground that they hear we are aided or defended by them. That some did this in former times also, Theodoret is the authority, in his commentary on Paul's epistle to the Colossians, where he writes that those who defended the righteousness of the Law taught the worship of angels too, because they said the Law had been given through them. And although the Synod of Laodicea had condemned this superstition, nevertheless in his own time oratories of Saint Michael were still seen in Phrygia and the neighbouring places. Today among many, angels are worshipped along with the saints in heaven. But to refute these things it should suffice us that that holy angel, who was the interpreter of that most noble revelation to John, with which Christ deigned to favour him, when John prostrated himself at his feet to worship him, said: "See that you do not do it: for I am your fellow servant and of your brothers who have the testimony of Jesus." Rev. 19 and 22.

units.la: Vsus autem huius doctrinae de Angelorum custodia & ministerio nobis hic esto,vt primo Dei bonitate agnoscamus,qui non solum terrestres creaturas,verumetiam coelestes spiritus nobis (vt
units.tr: The use of this teaching about the guardianship and ministry of the angels is to be found here for us, so that first we may acknowledge the goodness of God, who has subjected to us (so to speak) not only earthly creatures but also the heavenly spirits, so that they too are his servants and ours,

units.la: Phil.2. ita dicam subiecit) vt ijdem ipsius & noltri serui sint, & ex eo petamus consolatione, qua nos arma memus aduersus metum in tentationibus, quas Satan aut mundus nobis mouent: vt cum Paulo dicamus, Persuasum mihi est, quod neque mors neque vita, neque angeli neque principatus, neque potestates, neque instantia neque futura, neque sublimitas neque profunditas, neque vlla res creata, poterit nos separare a charitate Dei, quae est in CHRISTO IESV Domino nostro. Deinde nostra huius dignitatis memores solicite caueamus, ne morum impuritate aut sermonibus impijs siue obscœnis nos ipsos tam necessario Angelorum praesidio spoliemus: sed perpetuo meminerimus, illos nobis adesse, ideoque quae puderet coram hominibus honestis dicere aut facere, multo minus faciamus in illorum conspectu, quos Deus nobis custodes addidit.
units.tr: Phil.2. and from this we may seek the consolation by which we arm ourselves against fear in the temptations that Satan or the world stirs up against us, so that with Paul we may say: I am persuaded that neither death nor life, neither angels nor principalities, neither powers, nor things present nor things to come, neither height nor depth, nor any other created thing, will be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord. Then, mindful of this dignity of ours, let us carefully take care that we do not, by impurity of conduct or by impious or obscene talk, deprive ourselves of the protection of the angels, which we so greatly need. Rather, let us always remember that they are present with us, and therefore what we would be ashamed to say or do before honest men, let us much less do in the sight of those whom God has added to us as guardians.

units.la: Sed vt ad praesentis loci tractationem redeamus, alterum argumentum adducit Christus, a proprio exemplo & fine sui in mundum aduentus siue incarnationis desumptum, quod hoc dicto comprehendit: Venit Filius hominis, vt feruet quod perierat. Si totius loci contextum consideres, dicere debebat: Veni vt seruem paruulos, & eos qui coram mundo propter me pro nullius pretij hominibus habentur. Sed eorum meminit qui perierunt, vt argumentu comparatione firmius fiat: quod ita formabit: Qui mei discipuli censeri volunt, non debent eos contemnere quorum causa ego in mundum veni, vt per me feruentur: Veni autem vt seruè eos qui perierant: Ergo non debent contemni etiam ij, quorum salus omnino deplorata est quoad mundi iudicium. Hoc vero si praesenti causae applicabis, irrefragabili consequentia concludes, multo minus paruulos contemni aut offendi debere, qui eo ipso nomine Deo acceptiores & charior sunt, quod in hoc mundo abiectissimi censentur.
units.tr: But to return to the treatment of the present passage: Christ brings forward a second argument, drawn from his own example and from the purpose of his coming into the world, that is, of his incarnation, which he sums up in this saying: The Son of man has come to save what was lost. If you consider the whole context of the passage, he ought to have said: I have come to save the little ones, and those who in the eyes of the world are held in no esteem for my sake. But he mentions those who have perished, so that the argument may be made more forceful by comparison. It may be framed thus: Those who wish to be counted as my disciples ought not to despise those for whose sake I came into the world, that they might be saved through me. Now I came to save those who were lost. Therefore those too ought not to be despised, whose salvation is utterly given up as far as the judgment of the world goes. If you apply this to the present case, you will conclude with an unanswerable inference that little ones ought much less to be despised or offended, since by that very name they are more acceptable and dearer to God, in that they are reckoned most abject in this world.

units.la: Argumentum vero hoc ratione ex communi hominum more petita confirmat, quo fit, vt plus gaudeamus de ijs, quae cum amissa essent & perdita, recuperauimus, quam de ijs, quae nobis semper salua & integra manserunt. Id vero eleganti parabola illustrat, quae vt magis moueat animos discipulorum, initio ait: Quid vobis videtur? Id est, vos iudices appello, dicite quid ipsi de casu, quem proponam, sentiatis: & fatebor, quod idem mecum dicturi estis. Si fuerint alicui homini centum oues, & vna ex eis errauerit relicto grege, nonne ipse relictis alijs omnibus, profectus per montes & valles, quaeret perditam, quae aberrauit? Id certe vulgo solent facere, qui boni pastores sunt aut frugi patresfamilias, cum sciant rem domesticam non in eo consistere totam, vt quae hanc augeat et ornant, acquiramus, sed non minus opus esse, vt quae nobis parta & acquisita sunt tueamur, aut amissa & perdita recuperemus. Quod si perditam & amissam ouem ille inuenerit, sanctè vobis affirmo, quod super ea magis gaudet, quam super omnibus alijs, quae non aberrauerunt. Etenim dolor & solicitudo, quae ex amissione obortae fuerat, ex recuperatione conceptu gaudium augere solet. Ista vero ad causam praesentem applicans, concludit: Itanon vult Pater vester, qui in caelis est, vt pereat vnus ex paruis istis. Et quia perditorum salute gaudet, non potest eos probare, qui superbo contemptu aliquos ita negligunt, vt eis scandali aut lapsus authores sint.
units.tr: This argument, moreover, he confirms by a reason taken from the common custom of men, by which it comes about that we rejoice more over those things which, having been lost and perished, we have recovered, than over those which have always remained safe and whole with us. He illustrates this by an elegant parable, which, in order to move the minds of the disciples more, he introduces by saying: What do you think? That is, I call you as judges: say what you yourselves feel about the case I shall propose, and I shall confess that you will say the same as I do. If a man has a hundred sheep, and one of them has strayed away from the flock, does he not leave all the others and go off over the mountains and valleys to seek the one that has gone astray? Certainly this is what ordinary men do who are good shepherds or thrifty heads of households, since they know that the management of a household does not consist wholly in acquiring and adding to what enriches it, but that it is no less necessary to guard what has been gained and acquired, or to recover what has been lost and perished. And if he finds the lost and straying sheep, I solemnly assure you that he rejoices over it more than over all the others, which have not gone astray. For the grief and anxiety that arose from the loss usually increases the joy conceived from the recovery. Applying these things to the present cause, he concludes: So it is not the will of your Father who is in heaven that one of these little ones should perish. And since he rejoices in the salvation of the lost, he cannot approve of those who, in proud contempt, so neglect some that they become the authors of scandal or stumbling for them.

units.la: Apud Lucam eadem parabola aliquantum diuersio sensu & in alium finem repetitur, & additur alia eiusdem generis vel argumenti de drachma vna ex decem amissa, vt Pharisaeorum insolentem confidentiam confutet, qui indignius ferebant, quod publicanos & peccatis infames recipiebat, & cum eis etiam vescerentur. Quibus per parabolas istas ita respondet, vt doceat, hoc abs se recte fieri. Nam & Deum Patre ita velle, & in caelis Angelos gaudere, si peccatores, quorum salus desperata videbatur, in viam redeant ac salui fiant. Ita vero Pharisaeos potius impios esse probat, quam sanctitatis amantes, cum Dei voluntati aduersentur, & eos perditos velint, quorum salute debebant gaudere. Et hoc sensu considerata parabola ista doctrinam & consolationem dulcissimam continent, qua vniuersum humanae salutis mysterium ceu in tabula adumbratur.
units.tr: In Luke the same parable is repeated with somewhat different meaning and for another purpose, and another of the same kind or subject is added, about the one drachma out of ten that was lost, in order to refute the insolent confidence of the Pharisees, who took it more indignantly that he received publicans, infamous for their sins, and even ate with them. To these men he responds through these parables in such a way as to teach that he rightly does this. For the Father himself wishes it so, and the angels in heaven rejoice if sinners, whose salvation seemed hopeless, return to the way and are saved. And he proves that the Pharisees are rather impious than lovers of holiness, since they oppose the will of God and wish those to be lost over whose salvation they ought to have rejoiced. Understood in this sense, this parable contains a doctrine and a most sweet consolation, in which the whole mystery of human salvation is, as it were, sketched out on a tablet.

units.la: Vbi primum occurrit, quae sit omnium nostrum conditio, si quales natura simus, consideres. Eadem nimirum, quae ouis perdita & extra gregis septa vagantis. Est ouis animal stolidum, & futuri ignara neque seipsam iuuare potest, neque si a grege secesserit, ad eum redire, nisi pastoris cura & studio reducatur: Ita homo ex semetipso nou sapit ea quae sunt Spiritus Dei, & praesentibus intentus futura neglegit. Adhaec si semel a via veritatis aberret, & ab Ecclesia societate auellatur, nec redire spote eo vt de abierat. Imo vt ouis alias per praecipitia sequitur, & in exitium propriae voluntatis impulsu ruit: ita homo suorum affectuum libidine excaecatus in omne vitium prolabitur, & ne exemplis quidem eorum, qui bus hoc primùm peßimè ceßit, terretur, vt de salute sua serio cogitet. Et hoc illud est, quod Isaias olim dixit: Omnes tanquàm oues errauimus, quisque ad viam suam respeximus. Itaq; pastore opus erat, qui nos quaereret: quod de semetipso Dauid fatetur, dicens: Erraui sicut ouis perdita, quaere seruum tuum.
units.tr: Here, first of all, we meet with the condition of all of us, if we consider what kind of creatures we are by nature. It is the same as that of the lost sheep wandering outside the fold of the flock. The sheep is a stupid animal, unaware of the future, and it cannot help itself, nor, if it has strayed from the flock, return to it unless it is brought back by the care and diligence of the shepherd. So man of himself does not understand the things of the Spirit of God, and, intent on the present, neglects the future. Moreover, if he once wanders from the way of truth and is torn away from fellowship with the Church, he cannot return of his own accord to where he had departed. Indeed, like a sheep, he follows other paths over precipices and rushes to destruction by the impulse of his own will. So man, blinded by the lust of his own affections, slips into every vice, and is not even frightened by the examples of those to whom this first turned out very badly, so that he might seriously think about his own salvation. This is what Isaiah said long ago: We have all gone astray like sheep; each of us has turned to his own way. Therefore there was need of a shepherd to seek us; this David also confesses about himself, saying: I have gone astray like a lost sheep; seek your servant.

units.la: At hic elucet Dei erga nos studium, qui cùm quales futuri essemus, praeuideret, ab aeterno pastorem nobis praedestinauit Filium suum Vnigenitum, sicut promissiones veteres docent & Prophetae vaticinantur. Et qualis nam ille pastor est? Qualem parabola haec adumbrat. Primùm de certo numero ouium agitur. Habet ergo suos in numerato, & (vt Paulus ait) nouit qui sint sui. Deinde nō eas modò oues nouit, quae cum grege manent, sed errantes quoq; et temerè vagantes. Ita olim oues se habere dixit, quae inter gentes & superstitiones absurdissimas dispersae palabantur. Tertiò, vnà quoq; & solitaria non negligit. Ita Christus singulos quaerit & nominatim vocat, sicut ti olim Adamum fugitiuū & latebras quarentē, & Dauidem inter libidines suas securè sese volu- tantem quaesiuit & vocauit. Sic postea face Euangelij accensa totum orbem terrarum lustrauit, vt filios Dei inter gentes dispersos colligeret. Quarto, quid agit cum inuentis ouibus? Num ferox & iratus terrae illidit, pugnis & calcibus ferit, laniat & miseras ad necem vsq; multat? Imò in humeros attollit, & (vt Isaias olim praedixit) brachio suo congregat agnos & in gremio suo gestat, fa- tas autem suauiter ducit. Non alio autem quàm ad gregem suum reducit, id est, ad Ecclesiam suam societatem colligit, in qua sola pascua illa inueniuntur, quae Dauid commendat. Psal.23.
units.tr: But here God's concern for us shines forth. Foreseeing what we would be, he predestined for us from eternity his only-begotten Son as Shepherd, as the ancient promises teach and the prophets foretell. And what sort of shepherd is he? Such as this parable sketches. First, it speaks of a certain number of sheep. He therefore has his own, counted up, and (as Paul says) he knows who are his own. Then he knows not only those sheep that remain with the flock, but also those that wander and stray at random. So long ago he said that he had sheep that were scattered among the nations and the most absurd superstitions and were wandering. Third, he does not neglect even the one that is alone and apart. Thus Christ seeks out each one and calls him by name, just as he once sought and called Adam, the fugitive seeking his hiding place, and David, who was wallowing securely in his own lusts. So afterwards, with the light of the Gospel kindled, he has gone through the whole world to gather the children of God dispersed among the nations. Fourth, what does he do with the sheep once found? Does he, fierce and angry, dash them to the ground, strike them with fists and kicks, mangle them and punish the wretched creatures to death? Rather, he lifts them onto his shoulders and (as Isaiah once foretold) gathers the lambs with his arm and carries them in his bosom, and gently leads those that are with young. He leads them back to nothing other than his own flock, that is, he gathers them into his Church, his fellowship, in which alone those pastures are found that David commends. Psal.23.

units.la: Simul autem nos officij ista admonent, vt primùm non desperemus in tentationibus de Dei erga nos bonitate, qui Filium suum nobis pastorem & Seruatorem dedit, & nunquam excidat nobis quod Paulus ex hoc Domini dicto desumpsit, dicens: Fidus sermo, & modus omnibus dignus quem ampletamur, quòd CHRISTVS IESVS venit in mundum, vt peccatores seruaret. Deinde vt huic nos accommodemus, & licet frequenter aberremus, non tamen incurabili contumacia in errore pergamus, sed nos inueniri, & ad Ecclesiam colligi patiamur, atque nominis Christiani profeßioni respondeamus: neq; nos terreat nostra indignitas, quae nos mundo contemptibiles reddit, & saepe causa est, vt nobis ipsis ita displiceamus, vt ipsi etiam Deo nos displicere putemus. Etenim vt omnes Christi simus, non diuitijs, non exquisita eruditione, non huius saeculi prudentia, honoribus, dignitatibus, splendore, amicitijs aut clientelis opus est, sed pastorem nostrum agnosce re & eius vocem audire atq; sequi oportet. Hoc si fiat, hic vicissim nos agnoscet, vocabit item, & Spiritu suo ducet, vt voluntarium obsequium ipsi praestando Angelos caelestes exhilaremus. Qui vero secus agunt, vt impij & contumaces efficiunt, & alijs quoque scandalo sint, ij Spiritum Sanctum tristitia afficiunt, & amisso salutis signaculo infeliciter in peccatis pereunt. Postremò, qui huius loci scopus est, deprimamus superbiam cristas, & ne quem contemnamus, sed vnusquisq; se alijs debitorem esse agnoscat, atq; alij alios iuuemus, vt sancto & indefesso pietatis studio diguitate filiorum Dei retinere possimus, quà sua mortis merito nobis acquisiuit IESVS CHRISTVS Dominus noster, cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: At the same time, this duty also reminds us, first, not to despair in temptations of God's goodness toward us, who gave us his Son as our shepherd and Saviour; and let never slip from us what Paul took from this saying of the Lord, saying: "This is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptation, that CHRIST JESUS came into the world to save sinners." Next, that we should adapt ourselves to this: even though we often go astray, we should not persist in error with incurable obstinacy, but let ourselves be found and gathered into the Church, and answer to the profession of the Christian name. Nor should our unworthiness frighten us, which makes us contemptible to the world and often causes us to be so displeasing to ourselves that we think we also displease God himself. For in order for us all to be Christ's, we have no need of riches, of exquisite learning, of the wisdom of this age, nor of honours, dignities, splendour, friendships or patronage; rather, we must acknowledge our shepherd and hear and follow his voice. If this is done, he in turn will acknowledge us, will also call us, and will lead us by his Spirit, so that by rendering him willing obedience we may gladden the heavenly angels. But those who act otherwise become impious and obstinate, and are also a scandal to others; they grieve the Holy Spirit, and having lost the seal of salvation, they perish unhappily in their sins. Finally, which is the aim of this passage: let us humble pride, the crest of arrogance, and let no one despise another, but let each acknowledge that he is a debtor to others, and let us help one another, so that by a holy and tireless zeal for godliness we may retain the dignity of the sons of God, which Jesus Christ our Lord has won for us by the merit of his death, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCXX.
units.tr: HOMILY CCXX.

units.la: Si vero peccauerit in te frater tuus, abi & arque eum inter te & ipsum solum: si te audierit, lucratus es fratrem tuum. Sin vero te non audierit, accipe tecum adhuc vnum aut duos, vt in ore duorum aut trium testium stabile sit omne verbum. Quod si neglexerit eos audire, dic Ecclesiae. Quòd si Ecclesiam audire neglexerit, sit tibi vt lut quispiam ethnicus & quispiam publicanus.
units.tr: "Moreover, if your brother sins against you, go and show him his fault between you and him alone. If he listens to you, you have gained your brother. But if he will not listen, take with you one or two more, so that every matter may be established by the testimony of two or three witnesses. If he refuses to listen to them, tell it to the Church. And if he refuses to listen even to the Church, let him be to you as a Gentile and a tax collector."

units.la: Dvlcißima consolationis plena vox est Domini nostri IESV CHRISTI, qua nuper dixit: Venit Filius hominis, vt feruet quod perierat. Debet autem nos non solū consolari in conscientia terroribus aduersus peccatū et Satana: verumetiā officij admonere, vt ipsi quoq; aliorū saluti consulamus quantū in nobis est neq; putemus aliquē a nobis impunè negligi posse, quē tanti fecit Dei Filius, vt propter ipsum Filius hominis fieri, & in cruce mori dignatus est. Caeterū obstat hic nobis vehementer duo vitia, quae plerisq; ex natura nostra vitiositate inhaeret. Primū est seueritas in mia, qua in eos vtimur, qui nos offenderunt, & quam multi zelo pietatis & iustitiae palliant, dum scelerum impatientes videri volunt, eo tamen praetextu vindictae cupiditati plus quam hominem Christianum decet, indulgent. Alterum est contumacia, quae admonitionum impatientes facit, & causa est, quod multis non satis est offendisse fratres, sed insuper admoniti irascuntur, & eos fer re nolunt, quorum reconciliationem ipsi supplicitier quaerere deberent. Itaque fit, ut & priores, qui laesi sunt, exasperentur, et simultates augeantur, atque scandala in immensum crescant. Quapropter Dominus hoc loco doctrinam utilem & necessariam subtexit, quomodo cum fratribus, qui nos laese runt, agi debeat. Vbi etiam discemus, quanta sit fraterna correctionis utilitas, si admittatur: quod item de eius contemptoribus statui & iudicari debeat.
units.tr: The voice of our Lord Jesus Christ, which he recently spoke, is most sweet and full of comfort: "The Son of Man has come to seek and to save what was lost." Indeed, it ought not only to console us, troubled in conscience, against sin and Satan, but also to admonish us in our duty, that we too should care for the salvation of others as far as lies in us, and not think that anyone whom the Son of God valued so highly, that he deigned to become the Son of Man for his sake and die on the cross, can be neglected by us with impunity. But two vices, which cling to most people from our corrupt nature, strongly hinder us here. The first is severity in the way we treat those who have offended us. Many cover this with a pretence of zeal for piety and justice, since they wish to appear impatient of wickedness, yet under this pretext they indulge their desire for revenge more than a Christian ought. The other is obstinacy, which makes people impatient of admonition. It is the cause of why, for many, it is not enough to have offended their brothers; besides, when admonished, they grow angry and refuse to tolerate those whose reconciliation they ought to seek humbly. And so it happens that those who were wronged first are exasperated, enmities grow, and scandals increase beyond measure. For this reason the Lord, in this place, adds a useful and necessary teaching on how one ought to act toward brothers who have wronged us. Here too we shall learn how great is the usefulness of brotherly correction, if it is accepted, and likewise how those who despise it ought to be regarded and judged.

units.la: Vt autem huius loci sensus & usus melius & rectius intelligatur, videre oportet initio statim, ad quos pertineat doctrina ista, & de quibus peccatis aut delictis agatur. Sunt enim nonnulli, qui dum Christi praeceptum ad Verbi ministros & magistratus usque extendunt, sub eius praetextu publicas scelerum correptiones abolent, dum aduersus publicorum scandalorum authores nihil vel publice dici, vel statui volunt, nisi prius hoc ordine procedatur. Anabaptistae vero, qui Magistratum omnem abrogatum vellent, totum hunc locum ad Excommunicationem suam detorquent, & nisi haec observetur, Ecclesiam non consistere posse clamant. At Christus hic cum discipulis, vt cum hominibus privatis loquitur, sicuti ex toto contextu patet. Nec enim quicquam hic dicitur, quod non ex aequo ad omnes Christianos pertineat, quorum omnium est, humiliter de se ipsis sentire, omnem scandali occasionem vitare, neminem contemnere, et cuiusvis saluti consulere. Deinde non simpliciter ait: Si peccauerit quis: Sed, si peccauerit in fratem. Itaque de privatis iniuriis agitur, quae singulis fiunt, & quarum remissio in nostra potestate est. Quare ne vindictae cupiditati indulgeamus prohibet, & vt eos, qui in nos peccando charitatis legem violarunt, lucri facere potius studeamus, quam vlcisci aut diffamare. Conuenit ergo hic locus (vt alibi diximus) cum eo quod in Lege iubemur: Ne oderis in corde tuo fratrem tuum, sed libere reprehendas proximum tuum, ne feras propter eum peccatum: Ne vlciscaris, nec item fis iniuriarum memor erga filios populi tui: sed diliges proximum tuum vt teipsum. Minime ergo detorqueri debet locus hic contra ordines a Deo institutos, quibus publica scelerum correptio & scandalorum extirpatio mandata est: Quales sunt Ministri siue praecones Verbi, qui excubitorum instar, quid fiat obseruare, & (vt Paulus iubet) eos qui publice peccant, & scandali alicuius authores sunt, publice arguere debent, vt caeteri admoniti ab exemplo malo sibi caveant. Et ad illos pertinet quod Isaiae dicit Dominus: Clama ex gutture, ne parcas, attolle instar tubae vocem tuam, & annuntia populo meo praevaricationem suam, & domui Iacob peccata sua. Eiusdem generis sunt magistratus, qui in Lege scelera excindere iubentur, & iudicia Dei sic exequi absque omni personarum respectu, vt neque diuites aut potentes reuereantur, neque pauperum misericordia tangantur, si hos poenam meruisse intelligant. Etenim exemplis multis docemur, Respublica & Ecclesia semper infeliciter cessisse indulgentiam nimiam, qua sceleratis & scandalorum authoribus parcitur. Inter quae cum primis memorabilia sunt Heli summi Pontificis & Iudicis, Dauidis item, quorum vterque dum filios sceleratos indulgentius tractat, Israelem totum in clades & calamitates grauissimas adduxit. Itaque qui in publico munere constituti sunt, fideliter faciant, quod in mandatis habent, neque obliuiscantur eius, quod Solomon non minus vere quam graviter dixit: Ex aequo abominatur Dominus tam eum, qui sceleratum absoluit, quam eum qui innocentem damnat. Item, Qui dicit impio Iustus es, huic maledicunt populi, hunc nationes detestantur. Caeterum in priuatis iniuriis, ex quibus nihil damni aut scandali ad alios redundet, neque disciplina publica labefactatur, singuli ordinem hic a Domino praescriptum sequantur, qui tres gradus habet.
units.tr: But so that the meaning and use of this passage may be understood better and more rightly, we must see at the outset to whom this teaching pertains and of what sins or offences it speaks. For there are some who, while they extend Christ's precept to ministers of the Word and to magistrates, abolish public corrections of wickedness under its pretext, since they wish that nothing be said or decided publicly against the authors of public scandals unless this order is first followed. The Anabaptists, who would have all magistracy abolished, twist this whole passage to their own excommunication, and cry out that unless this is observed the Church cannot stand. But Christ here speaks with his disciples as with private persons, as is clear from the whole context. For nothing is said here that does not apply equally to all Christians, whose duty it is to think humbly of themselves, to avoid every occasion of scandal, to despise no one, and to care for the salvation of everyone. Then he does not simply say, "If anyone sins," but, "If your brother sins against you." Thus it is about private injuries, which are done to individuals and whose forgiveness lies in our power. Therefore he forbids us to indulge the desire for revenge, and bids us be eager to gain those who have violated the law of charity by sinning against us, rather than to take revenge on them or defame them. This passage therefore agrees (as we have said elsewhere) with what is commanded in the Law: "You shall not hate your brother in your heart, but you shall surely rebuke your neighbour, lest you bear sin because of him. You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people, but you shall love your neighbour as yourself." Hence this passage must by no means be twisted against the orders instituted by God, to which the public correction of sins and the extirpation of scandals have been entrusted. Such are the ministers or heralds of the Word, who, like watchmen, must observe what is happening, and (as Paul bids) must publicly rebuke those who sin publicly and are the authors of some scandal, so that others, warned by the bad example, may take care for themselves. To them belongs what the Lord says through Isaiah: "Cry aloud, do not spare; lift up your voice like a trumpet, and declare to my people their transgression, and to the house of Jacob their sins." Of the same kind are the magistrates, who are commanded in the Law to cut off wickedness and to carry out God's judgments without any regard for persons, so that they neither revere the rich or powerful nor are moved by pity for the poor, if they understand that these have deserved punishment. For we are taught by many examples that the commonwealth and the Church have always fared badly through excessive indulgence shown to the wicked and to the authors of scandals. Among these, the cases of Eli, the high priest and judge, and likewise of David are especially memorable; each of them, while treating his wicked sons too leniently, brought all Israel to ruin and most grievous calamities. Therefore let those who are placed in public office faithfully do what they have been commanded, and let them not forget what Solomon said no less truly than seriously: "The Lord abhors equally him who acquits the wicked and him who condemns the innocent." Likewise: "He who says to the wicked, 'You are righteous,' peoples will curse him, and nations will detest him." But in private injuries, from which no harm or scandal redounds to others and public discipline is not weakened, let individuals follow the order prescribed here by the Lord, which has three steps.

units.la: Primus de priuata admonitione est. Si peccauerit in te (inquit) frater tuus, abi & argue eum inter te & ipsum solum, &c. Quo loco singula verba considerationem merentur. Primum abi re iubet, nimirum ad fratrem, qui te laesit, & de eo tibi reconciliando cogitare. Non ergo expectabis, donec ipse ad mentem redeat, et sponte veniens culpam deprecetur, sed tu prior de illo lucrade cogita. Conuenit hoc cum pastoris boni exemplo, de quo nuper dixit, qui oue perdita quaerit per montes & valles, & inuentam reportat ad gregem, & de ea laetatur. Et supra Capite quinto tale quid monet quando iubet munus ad altare relinquere, & cum fratre in gratiam redire, priusquam illud offeras. Est hoc factu necessarium. Ita enim plerosq; philautia excaecat, ut non obseruent iniurias, quas aliis fecerunt: vel alios has non animaduertere arbitrantur: vel non tantam esse iniuriam sibi per suadet, ut de ea sarcienda multum soliciti esse debeat. Necesse igitur est, ne frater du hisce perjua sionibus sibijpsi delitias facit, induretur & pereat, ut ipsi illu quaeramus, qui iam a nobis alienus factus est. De hoc igitur studiose cogitet, qui si illud faciat, exiſtimationi suae multu decedere vere tur. Sed nihil ex eo periculi est. Fecit idem Deus, quando Adamu perduellem, & diuinitatis asse- ctatae reum quaesiuit, & fugitiuu retraxit, clamans: Adam vbi es? Fecit idem Dei Filius, qui (ut initio dictu est) in mundu venit, ut peccatores, qui ipsum offenderant, nec quicquam de sua salute cogitabant, saluos faceret. Ide hodie adhuc accensa Euangelij sui face nos quaerit, & per ministros suos (ut Apostolus scribit) ipse nos precatur, ut Deo reconciliemur. Cur ergo te eius pudeat, quod tua salutis ergo fecit Dei Filius, & quod nisi quotidie faceret, nemo nostrum seruaretur?
units.tr: The first concerns private admonition. "If your brother sins against you," he says, "go and rebuke him between you and him alone," and so on. Here each word deserves consideration. First he bids you go, namely to the brother who has wronged you, and think about being reconciled to him. You therefore should not wait until he comes to his senses and, coming of his own accord, begs pardon for his fault; rather, you yourself should think first of gaining him. This agrees with the example of the good shepherd, of whom he spoke recently, who seeks the lost sheep over mountains and valleys, carries the one found back to the flock, and rejoices over it. In the fifth chapter also he gives similar advice when he bids a man leave his gift at the altar and first be reconciled to his brother before offering it. This is necessary to do. For self-love blinds many so that they do not notice the injuries they have done to others, or they think others do not notice them, or they persuade themselves that the injury to them is not so great that they ought to be very anxious to make amends for it. It is necessary therefore, lest the brother, indulging these persuasions and pampering himself, grow hardened and perish, that we seek him who has already become estranged from us. Let him therefore consider this carefully, since if he does so he will fear that his reputation suffers much. But there is no danger in it. God did the same when he sought out Adam, the rebel and guilty of aspiring to divinity, and drew back the fugitive, crying, "Adam, where are you?" The Son of God did the same, who (as was said at the beginning) came into the world to save sinners who had offended him and gave no thought to their own salvation. Even today he still seeks us, with the torch of his Gospel kindled, and through his ministers (as the Apostle writes) he himself entreats us to be reconciled to God. Why then should you be ashamed of what the Son of God did for the sake of your salvation, and what none of us would be saved by unless he did it every day?

units.la: Deinde argue eum (inquit) inter te & illum solum. Non iuber, ut ei supplex fias, vel ut illi blandiaris, iniuriam tibi factam excusses, vel etiam factum laudes. His enim ille contumacior factus, in scelere periret. Sed arguere debemus eum qui peccauit, id est, peccati grauitatem, & quam indigne hoc fecerit, ei demonstrare debemus. Et quia plerunq; fit, ut qui peccarunt, hominum iudicia facile contemnant, tales ad Dei tribunal, si opus sit, citari debent, ut quid Deus de ipsis iudicet, & ut olim similia delicta punierit, intelligat. Errant ergo vehementer, qui hoc contra charitatis legem fieri existimant, & ne quo offendant, ab omni redargutione aut correptione abstinent. At iubet hoc Dominus de fratribus fieri, ut inter hos locum habere possit charitas, aut violata instauretur. Ideo ut priuatim arguamus iubet, ut nimirum ex eo intelligant, nos non infamiam aut ignominiam, sed emendationem & salutem ipsorum quaerere. Est hoc proprijssimum charitatis opus, quo nullum vtilius & salutarius fingi potest.
units.tr: Then he says, "Rebuke him between you and him alone." He does not command you to plead with him, to flatter him, to excuse the wrong done to you, or even to praise what he did. Such treatment would only make him more obstinate, and he would perish in his sin. Rather, we ought to rebuke the one who has sinned: we should show him the gravity of his sin and how unworthy the deed was. Since those who have sinned often easily despise human judgments, such people should, if necessary, be summoned before the tribunal of God, so that they may understand what God judges about them and how he once punished similar offences. Those therefore greatly err who think this is against the law of love, and who, lest they give offence, abstain from all rebuke or correction. But the Lord commands this to be done among brothers, so that love may have a place among them, or, if it has been violated, may be restored. Therefore he commands us to rebuke privately, so that they may understand from this that we seek not their disgrace or shame, but their amendment and salvation. This is the most proper work of charity, and no more useful or healthful work can be imagined.

units.la: Idcirco addit Dominus: Si te audierit, id est, si admiserit redargutionem, ut culpam admissam agnoscat, & deprecetur, lucratus es fratrem tuum. Breui dicto multiplex lucru comprehendit. Etenim primo fratrem sibi lucratus es, qui alioqui periturus erat, nisi tu hoc officio illum praeuenisses. Sed de eo Iacobus admonet, dicens: Fratres, si quis inter vos aberrarit a veritate, & conuerterit eum quispiam, sciat quod qui auerterit peccatorem ab errore viae suae, seruabit animam a morte, &c. Quod ergo beneficium maius & salutarius homini conferri poterit? Deinde tibi ipsi lucraris fratrem, ut qui iam alienus esse coeperat, tibi reconciliatus verus & germanus frater fit. Itaq; amicum fidelem tibi hoc officio paras, quo nullum thesaurum pretiosiorem esse, gentium quoq; sapientes tradiderunt. Etenim amicus verus (ut Solomon ait) tenacius adhaeret quam frater. Est quidem inter fratres amor, quem natura inter eos conciliat. At quia haec vitiosa est, facile amor iste extinguitur, imo in odium vertitur, si quid incommodi ex fratre fit metuendum. Hinc est, quod in haereditatis diuisione vterini & germani fratres rixantur, quod item aemulatione accensi, alij alijs inuident, & tunc (quod prouerbio dicitur) fratrum irae sunt acerrimae, & fere implacabiles. Exempla huius rei in primis fratribus Cainus, deinde Ismael, Esau, Iosephi item fratres, & innumeri alij ediderunt, quorum mentio fit in sacris & prophanis historijs. Amicitiae autem verae ea vis est, ut in periculis maxime sese exerat, & tunc animos magis inflammet, quando amicos in aliquo discrimine videt constitutos. Exemplo est Ionathas, quem neq; patris Saulis reuerentia, neq; regni maiestas & spes, a qua se excidisse videbat, neq; pericula vlla a Dauide auellere potuerunt. Magnum ergo quaestum fecit, qui amica & fraterna correptione sibi ipsi amicum fecit ex eo, qui iam inimicus esse coeperat. Accedit tamen adhuc maius, quod Deo officium longe gratissimum praestamus, qui hominum salute & conuersione gaudet: Huic enim lucramur eum, qui iam ouis perdita erat, & qui charitatem fraternam violando in diaboli castra transfierat. Huius consideratio Paulum olim monuit, ut omnibus omnia fieret, quo plures Christo lucrifaceret. Cur ergo cuiquam graue sit cum fratre reconciliari, a quo iniuriam accepit, cum hoc officio eum sibi ipsi & Deo lucrari possit? Ideo apud Lucam addit Christus: Si peccauerit frater, remitte ei. Quo dicto ijs occurrit, qui fratribus ita reconciliantur, ut interim ab illis satisfactionem aliquam exigant, quae plerunq; simultatem veterem in cordibus fouet, vel etiam nouam offensa & inimicitia causa est. Vult ergo Dominus, ut quando correctio privata finem suum attigit, qui est fratris repiscentia, hac contenti, imo ea exhilarati, nihil praeterea quaeramus. Quod si observaretur ab omnibus, minus offensionum & turbarum esset inter homines. At quaerit quis, quid fieri debeat cum eo, qui privatim admonitus & correptus, non agnoscit culpam, sed redargutione illa exasperatur? Enimvero sunt, qui tunc se omni officio defunctos esse putant, nec amplius quicquam volunt agere cum ijs, quos praefractiores esse vident. At hoc animum arguit non vera charitate praeditum, sed ambitiosulum, quem passae repulsae injuria magis ac cruciat. Ideo Christus nos pergere iubet, & assumptis testibus aut arbitris idoneis denuo homine aggredi, si forte horum reverentia motus se mitiorem & magis placabilem praebeat. Deinde vult hoc fieri secundum Legis institutum, quo in causis dubijs testes adhibebantur, ut si quando iure agendi sit, idoneis testibus demonstrari possit, te charitatis officio prius functum esse, neque illum implacabilem habere, quod de tuo rigore quiritetur. Est enim admodum officiosa charitas, & qui huius studio ardent, omne offensionis novae causam diligenter solent vitare. Interim admonemur hoc loco, eos etiam officium charitatis Deo gratum facere, qui se arbitros aut sequestros adhiberi sinunt in componendis fratrum dissidijs. Nam, ut testete Solomone, eum odit & detestatur Dominus, qui inter fratres dissidia ferit, eorundem vero consensione gaudet, & concordibus benedicit: ita non potest non probare eos, qui in illis conciliandis seduli sunt. Quod vtinam diligentius observarent, qui dissidia publica & privata linguis suis venenatis, & calumniandi aut obtrectandi licentia magis accendunt.
units.tr: Therefore the Lord adds: "If he listens to you," that is, if he admits the rebuke, so that he acknowledges the fault he committed and asks forgiveness, "you have gained your brother." In a brief saying he comprehends many gains. For first, you have gained a brother for yourself, who otherwise would have perished unless you had anticipated him with this duty. James admonishes about this, saying: "Brethren, if anyone among you wanders from the truth, and someone turns him back, let him know that whoever turns a sinner from the error of his way will save a soul from death," and so on. What greater or more healthful benefit can be conferred on a man? Next, you gain a brother for yourself, so that one who had already begun to become a stranger to you is reconciled to you and becomes a true and genuine brother. Thus by this duty you prepare for yourself a faithful friend, and the wise men of the nations too have taught that no treasure is more precious. For, as Solomon says, a true friend clings more closely than a brother. Indeed, there is love between brothers, which nature establishes between them. But because this is corrupted, that love is easily extinguished, or rather turns into hatred, if any inconvenience from a brother is to be feared. Hence it is that in the division of an inheritance full brothers quarrel, and likewise, kindled by rivalry, some envy others; and then (as the proverb says) the anger of brothers is most fierce and nearly implacable. Examples of this appear first in the brothers Cain, then Ishmael, Esau, and likewise the brothers of Joseph, and countless others, whose mention is made in sacred and profane histories. The power of true friendship, however, is that it shows itself most in dangers, and then inflames the hearts of friends most, when it sees them placed in some peril. Jonathan is an example: neither reverence for his father Saul, nor the majesty of the kingdom and the hope he saw slipping from him, nor any danger, could tear him away from David. He therefore made a great gain who, by a friendly and brotherly rebuke, made a friend for himself out of one who had already begun to be an enemy. Yet something greater is added: we perform a service most pleasing to God, who rejoices in the salvation and conversion of men. For we gain for him one who was already a lost sheep, and who, by violating brotherly love, had gone over to the camp of the devil. Paul once reminded us of this consideration when he taught that he became all things to all men, so that he might gain more for Christ. Why then should it be burdensome to anyone to be reconciled with a brother by whom he has been wronged, when by this duty he can gain him for himself and for God? Therefore Christ adds in Luke: "If your brother sins, forgive him." By this saying he meets those who are reconciled to brothers in such a way that meanwhile they exact some satisfaction from them, which often nourishes an old resentment in the heart, or is even the cause of a new offence and enmity. The Lord therefore wills that when private correction has reached its end, which is the brother's repentance, we should be content with this, or rather rejoice in it, and seek nothing further. If this were observed by all, there would be fewer offences and disturbances among men. But someone asks what ought to be done with one who, privately admonished and corrected, does not acknowledge his fault but is exasperated by that rebuke. Indeed, there are those who then think they have discharged every duty, and want to do nothing more with those whom they see to be more stubborn. But this shows a mind not endowed with true charity, but rather a somewhat ambitious one, which is hurt more by the injury of a rejected approach. Therefore Christ bids us to go on, and, taking with us witnesses or suitable arbitrators, to approach the man again, in case perhaps out of reverence for them he may show himself milder and more easily appeased. Then he wills this to be done according to the institution of the Law, by which witnesses were used in doubtful cases, so that if ever there is need to act at law, it may be shown by suitable witnesses that you first performed the duty of charity and that he is not implacable, so that he cannot complain of your harshness. For charity is very dutiful, and those who burn with zeal for it are accustomed to avoid carefully every cause of new offence. Meanwhile we are reminded here that those also perform a work of charity pleasing to God who allow themselves to be employed as arbitrators or mediators in settling disputes between brothers. For, as Solomon testifies, the Lord hates and abhors the one who stirs up discord among brothers, but rejoices in their agreement and blesses those who are of one mind; so he cannot but approve those who are diligent in reconciling them. Would that those who inflame public and private quarrels with their venomous tongues, and with a license to slander and disparage, would observe this more carefully!

units.la: Quid vero (inquis) si neque testes aut arbitros reverearur, ut admonitiones fraternas admittat? Tunc dic (ait Christus) Ecclesiae. Loquitur autem pro eius saeculi more; quando iudicia in publico exercebantur, & quidem totius Ecclesiae nomine, quam Iudicum confessum referebat. Ideo in gravioribus causis non obiter vocabantur ad forum indicus, sed simul totius populi coeuntis cum tumulto solenni indicebatur, sicuti in Nabothi historia est videre. Hinc locutio illa, qua nonnulli prohibentur in Ecclesiam ingredi, id est, pro Ecclesiae civibus censeri, quibus solis ad honores aut dignitates publicas accessus patebat. Sensus ergo verborum Christi est, licere ad iudices publicos eius causam referre, & iure cum eo agere, qui omne reconciliationis modum sive rationem respuit. Ex quo apparet Christum hoc loco nolle patrocinari contumacibus & poenitere nescijs, multo minus prohibere, quo minus ius suum persequatur, qui aduersarium sua indulgentia abuti & contumaciam rem fieri animadvertit. Scio equidem Paulum Corinthios hoc nomine reprehendere, quod iure contenderent alij cum alijs, & inter alia dicere: Cur non potius iniuriam patimini? Sed illis haec dicit, qui apud ethnicorum tribunalia causas suas persequebantur non sine scandalo & publica Christiani nominis infamia. Adhaec eos reprehendit, qui temerarias lites movebant de rebus ad vitam pertinentibus, de quo Christus etiam solicitos esse vetat. Quia autem multae aliae offensae sunt & iniuriae, quas homo Christianus non potest neque debet dissimulare, eo quod cum publico scandalo coniunctae sunt, & saepe ad nominis divini ignominiam tendunt, in illis hoc ordine procedendum est, quem hoc loco Christus praescribit.
units.tr: "But what," you say, "if the offender does not respect witnesses or arbitrators, so that he will not admit brotherly admonitions?" Then, says Christ, "tell it to the Church." He speaks according to the custom of that age, when judgments were conducted in public, and indeed in the name of the whole Church, which the assembly of judges represented. Therefore in more serious cases the judges were not summoned to the court casually, but were announced with the solemn tumult of the whole people gathering together, as can be seen in the history of Naboth. Hence the expression by which some are forbidden to enter the Church, that is, to be counted among the citizens of the Church, to whom alone access to public honours or offices was open. The sense of Christ's words, therefore, is that it is lawful to bring his case before public judges and to proceed legally against one who rejects every mode or method of reconciliation. From this it appears that Christ in this place does not wish to defend the obstinate and those who do not know how to repent, much less to forbid a man from pursuing his right when he sees that his adversary abuses his forbearance and makes an obstinate thing of it. I know indeed that Paul rebukes the Corinthians on this account, because some went to law with others, and among other things he says: "Why do you not rather suffer wrong?" But he says this to those who were pursuing their causes before the tribunals of the heathen, not without scandal and public infamy to the Christian name. Besides, he rebukes those who stirred up rash lawsuits about matters pertaining to this life, about which Christ also forbids us to be anxious. But since there are many other offences and injuries which a Christian cannot and ought not to overlook, because they are joined with public scandal and often tend to the dishonour of the divine name, in these cases the procedure must follow the order Christ prescribes in this place.

units.la: Porro adhuc quaerat aliquis, quid fieri opus sit, si neque Ecclesiam & ab hac constitutos indicesquam contumax ille audiat? Huic respondet Dominus: Sit tibi velut quispiam ethnicus, & quispiam publicanus. Id est, hoc indicio agnosce eum non esse civem aut membrum germanum Ecclesiae: & quia ipse se ab Ecclesiae societate segregat, dum huius iudicio refragatur, sit tibi ethnici & publicani loco, cui quo nihil porro cofortij habeas, sed Dei iudicio illum permitte, qui tanta contumacia multa minime sinet. Hunc ordine observarunt olim Christiani homines, cum nullos haberet magistratus Christianos, durum autem esset fratres, qui eandem cum ipsis fidem profitebantur ethnicorum iudicio subijcere, qui alias omne in credentes saeviendi occasionem avide captabant. Itaque in aliis quoque casibus ab Ecclesiae consortio excludebant publicis sceleribus infames, si incurabiles esse viderentur, ne illis patrocinari viderentur, & religione Christianam diffamarent. Interdum etiam Satanae tradebant tales: quod non ex paucorum arbitrio fiebat, sed cum publico Ecclesiae totius consensu, cum authoritatem Apostolicam accedere oporteba t, eo quod hac potestate Apostolos peculiariter Christus armaverat, sicuti in hominis incesti causa, qui apud Corinthios fuit, est videre. 1. Cor.5.
units.tr: Further, someone may ask: what must be done if the contumacious man does not listen even to the Church and to the judges appointed by it? The Lord answers this: "Let him be to you as a heathen and a publican." That is, by this sign recognise that he is not a citizen or true member of the Church; and since he separates himself from the fellowship of the Church while he rejects its judgment, let him be to you in the place of a heathen and a publican, so that you have no further dealings with him, but leave him to the judgment of God, who will not suffer such stubborn obstinacy to go unpunished. Christians of old observed this order, when they had no Christian magistrates; for it would have been hard to hand over brethren who professed the same faith as themselves to the judgment of heathens, who otherwise eagerly seized every occasion to rage against believers. So too in other cases they excluded from the fellowship of the Church those notorious for public crimes, if they seemed incurable, lest they should appear to defend them and bring the Christian religion into disrepute. Sometimes they even handed such people over to Satan; and this was not done at the will of a few, but with the consent of the whole Church, when the apostolic authority had to be added, because Christ had armed the Apostles with this power in a special way, as can be seen in the case of the incestuous man who was among the Corinthians. 1 Cor. 5.

units.la: Quod Quòd autem hoc omne ad suam Excommunicationem Anabaptistæ detorquent, nimium inepte & ridiculè (vt alia omnia) faciunt. Nam primò insolenter vendicant, quod Apostolis datum fuit, & Satanæ tradere volunt homines sua Excommunicatione, qua ne culicem quidem possunt occidere. Deinde eandem in cœnam inuehunt, sine Christi instituto & exemplo. Plus item hic exigunt, quàm Paulus a Corinthijs omni modo corruptissimis olim requisierit: quos contentus fuit monuisse, vt quisq; seipsum probaret, & ita de pane Domini ederet, & eusdem poculo biberet. Sed plura de hac re alibi dedimus. In præsenti sufficiat monuisse, intra cancellos verborum Christi no bis subjiciendum esse, ne temerarijs iudicijs ad disipationem eo abutamur, quod hic charitatis fraterna vinculum esse voluit. Interea studeant singuli eos, qui contra leges fidei & charitatis peccant, in viam reducere, & Ecclesiarum vnitatem inuiolatam seruare sub capite & sponso IESV CHRISTO, cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: That the Anabaptists twist all this to their own excommunication is done very foolishly and ridiculously, as everything else they do. For first they arrogantly claim for themselves what was given to the Apostles, and they want to hand men over to Satan by their own excommunication, when they cannot even kill a gnat by it. Then they carry this over to the Lord's Supper without Christ's institution or example. They also demand more here than Paul once required of the Corinthians, although they were most corrupt in every way; he was content to admonish them that each should examine himself, and so eat of the Lord's bread and drink of his cup. But we have given more on this matter elsewhere. For the present it is enough to remind you that we must be bound within the limits of Christ's words, lest by rash judgments we abuse for division what he meant to be the bond of brotherly love. Meanwhile let each strive to bring back to the way those who sin against the laws of faith and charity, and to keep the unity of the Churches inviolate under the head and bridegroom Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCXXI.
units.tr: HOMILY CCXXI.

units.la: Amen dico vobis, quæcunque ligaueritis in terra, erunt ligata in cœlo: & quæcunq; soluerítis in terra, erunt soluta in cœlo. Rursum dico vobis, si duo ex vobis consenserint in terra, quodcunq; in omni re petierint, fiet eis a Patre meo, qui in cœlis est. Vbi enim sunt duo aut tres congregati in nomine meo, illic sum in medio eorum.
units.tr: Verily I say unto you, Whatsoever ye shall bind on earth shall be bound in heaven: and whatsoever ye shall loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven. Again I say unto you, That if two of you shall agree on earth as touching any thing that they shall ask, it shall be done for them of my Father which is in heaven. For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them.

units.la: Paulus IESV CHRISTO nihil valere ait, quàm fidem, quæ per charitatem agit, & ideò hæc propria nota est, ex qua veri & germani discipuli Christi agnoscuntur, si alij alios diligamus, sicut ille nos dilexit. Non temere ergo omnis scriptura charitatem passim commendat. Et quia ex innata nobis philautia quotidie multa fiunt, quibus illa turbatur, docet etiam quibus rationibus inter homines foueri & conseruari possit. Huc pertinet, quod nuper Christus docuit, quomodo cum ijs, qui nos læserunt, debeat agi, vt concordia instauretur, neue simultates & odia perpetua inde surgant. Summa eius doctrinæ est, vt fratre, qui sua culpa a nobis alienus est factus, ita lucrifacere conemur, vt quoad eius fieri potest, honori & existimationi illius consulatur. Ideo iubet, vt initio priuatim cum illo agas, neq; apud alios quiriteris de facta tibi iniuria. Deinde, vt si ille fit contumacior, arbitros adhibeas idoneos. Præterea si neq; horum authoritati quicquam tribuat, causa verò eiusmodi fit, quæ seueriorem actionem mereatur, tunc demum illam referas ad Ecclesiæ iudicium. Et si hoc quoq; contemnat, & omnem satisfactionem improbè detrectet, ethnici & publicani loco nobis sit, neq; porrò pro Ecclesiæ membro habeatur, a qua sese propria contumacia sponte abalienauit.
units.tr: Paul says that nothing avails in Jesus Christ except faith, which works through love, and therefore this is the proper mark by which true and genuine disciples of Christ are recognised: if we love one another as he loved us. It is not without reason, then, that all Scripture commends charity everywhere. And because much is done every day out of the self-love innate in us, by which charity is disturbed, Scripture also teaches by what means it may be fostered and preserved among men. To this belongs what Christ taught recently about how we ought to deal with those who have wronged us, so that concord may be restored and enmities and hatreds may not arise and last. The sum of his teaching is that we should try, by winning back a brother who has become estranged from us through his own fault, to look after his honour and reputation as far as that can be done. So he commands that at first you deal with him privately, and not complain of the wrong done to you before others. Then, if he becomes more obstinate, you should call in suitable arbiters. Moreover, if he gives no weight to their authority, and the case is of a kind that deserves a more severe proceeding, then at last you should refer it to the judgement of the Church. And if he despises this too, and shamelessly refuses all satisfaction, let him be to us as a heathen and a tax collector, and let him no longer be regarded as a member of the Church, from which by his own obstinacy he has voluntarily alienated himself.

units.la: Cæterum quia non ignorauit Christus, non defuturos, qui hoc quoq; non multum vereantur, si ab Ecclesia consortio separentur, sed exclusionem illam scurrilibus iannis eludant, adeoq; gaudeant sibi ita maiore licentia fieri, nunc cum his grauiter agit, vt & illorum audaciam retundat, & animum addat pijs, ne illorum proteruia se frangi aut vinci sinant. Nam initio graui sententia docet illis non cum hominibus solis, sed cum ipso Deo rem esse, dicens: Amen amen dico vobis, quæcunq; ligaueritis in terra, erunt ligata in cœlo: & quæcunq; soluueritis in terra, erunt soluta in cœlo. Repetit hoc loco, quod supra Petro, & in hoc omnibus Apostolis promisit, & quod post suam ex mortuis resurrectionem eis præstitit. Differt tamen hic locus ab aliis, quoad materiam. Illic enim de Apostolorum doctrina & Euangelij prædicatione agitur, ratas nimirum fore apud Deum æternæ salutis promissiones, quæ credentibus in Christum fiunt: nec minus ratas fore comminationes, quibus damnatio & sempiternæ pœnæ denuntiantur incredulis & pœnitere nescijs. In præsenti autem de morum disciplina sermo est, & idem applicatur actionibus iniuriarum, quæ nobis cum hominibus improbis & temerarijs intercedunt, qui nos contra charitatis leges offenderunt. Itaq; quod Apostolis dictum, vt prædicationis authoritas confirmetur, id in præsenti Christianis omnibus ituur: & ad omnes gradus actionum illarum, de quibus nuper dictum est, hoc debet applicari, vt non dubitemus, coram Deo mtum fore, quicquid in eiusmodi casu vel priuatim, vel per arbitros, vel coram Ecclesia & eius ordinarijs iudicibus actum fuerit.
units.tr: But since Christ was not unaware that there would be men who would not greatly fear even this, if they were separated from fellowship with the Church, but would mock that exclusion with buffoonish jests, and would rejoice that things were thus done with greater licence, he now deals severely with them, both to blunt their audacity and to encourage the godly, so that they do not allow themselves to be broken or overcome by their insolence. For at the beginning he teaches, in a solemn sentence, that these men have to do not with men alone but with God himself, saying: Verily, verily, I say unto you, whatsoever you shall bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatsoever you shall loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven. He repeats here what he earlier promised to Peter, and in this respect to all the apostles, and what he granted them after his resurrection from the dead. This passage differs from the others, however, in its subject matter. There the discussion concerns the teaching of the apostles and the preaching of the gospel, namely that the promises of eternal salvation made to those who believe in Christ will be ratified before God, and no less that the threats by which damnation and everlasting punishment are announced to unbelievers and to those who do not know how to repent will be ratified. Here, however, the discourse concerns the discipline of morals, and the same principle is applied to the actions of injuries which arise between us and wicked and rash men who have offended against the laws of charity. Therefore, what was said to the apostles to confirm the authority of their preaching applies in this case to all Christians. And this principle ought to be applied to all the stages of those actions of which we have just spoken, so that we may not doubt that whatever is done in such a case, whether privately, through arbiters, or before the Church and its ordinary judges, will be ratified before God.

units.la: I
units.tr: I

units.la: Etenim quoad priuatam actionem, dixerat Dominus: Si te audierit frater, ut culpam agno-scat, deprecetur, & tecum in gratiam redeat, lucratus es fratrem tuum. Id in præsenti expomitur & confirmatur: quod scilicet non tibi modo fratrem lucratus sis amicum fidum & constantem, verumetiam Deo, ut hic in cœlis ratam habeat offensæ & iniuriæ remissionem per te factam. Rationes huius dicti multæ & graues sunt. Primò solet Deus, qui iustus iudex est, vlcisci iniurias, quæ iustis præter omne meritum fiunt, in primis autem, quæ fiunt peregrinis, viduis, pupillis aut aliis eiusmodi hominibus, quibus nulla ad se defendendum vires sunt, & idcirco querelas suas in ipsius sinum effundere coguntur. Testatur hoc ipse in Lege, & huc pertinet quod de mercenariis mercede sua fraudatis & ad Deum clamantibus Apostolus scribit, & quod Syrachides admodum graviter ait: Supplicationem pupilli minime negliget Deus, nec preces fundentem viduam. Nonne cum lachrymæ viduæ ad maxillam eius defluunt, aduersus cientem eas auxilium inuocat? Oratio afflicti nubes penetrat, non conquiescit, non deficit, donec peruenerit ad altissimum, qui agit causam eius, & iuste iudicabit, &c. Ex quo sequitur, quod iram suam tunc quoq; remittat Deus, si qui iniuriam passus est, ad ipsum clamare destinat, & eiusdem preces exaudire soleat pro eo, qui ipsi iniuriam fecit. Deinde vniuersalis promissio est, quod Deus omnibus, qui ipsum inuocant, & aliis offensas remittunt, sua delicta remittere velit. Quanto magis ergo id fiet, quando qui iniuriam fecerat, & qui hanc passus erat, inter se reconciliati coniunctis animis & precibus illius gratiam implorant? Etenim delectatur Deus fratrum concordia, & eius mandatum est, ut tales benedictionem & vitam æternam percipiant. Admonet hoc omnes eos officij, qui alios offenderunt, ut quam chara ipsis est salus sua, cum ipsis in gratiam redire studeant: quia nisi id faciant, qualescunq; illi sint, seipsos a Dei gratia excludunt, ut nullam apud hunc delicti sui remissionem sperare possint. Elucet præterea hoc loco, quam magna sit hominum Christianorum dignitas, & quod non temere in Apocalypsi scriptum sit, IESVM CHRISTVM nos Deo & Patri suo fecisse Reges & Sacerdotes. Etsi enim Reipub. gubernatio & Ecclesiæ ministerium publicum nequaquam promiscue ad omnes pertineant, vnusquisq; tamen in sua causa sibi ipsi Rex & Sacerdos est, & Regis instar ea libertate vtitur, ut sibi facta iniurias condonet, & ut Sacerdos culpam omnem ei remittat, a quo læsus est. Quod si fecerit, in cœlo quoq; apud Dei tribunal rata erit ista remissio. Hoc sensu veteres quoq; hunc locum intellexerunt, ut videre est in Theophylacto, qui inter alia scribit: Non solum quæ sacerdotes soluunt, soluta sunt: sed etiam quæ nos, qui iniurijs læsi sumus, vel ligamus vel soluimus, ea soluta vel ligata sunt. Porro eadem ratio est, si frater læsus actionem reconciliationis per arbitros instituat. Etenim ut nuper diximus, faciunt hi opus Deo gratissimum. Si quis ergo talibus more gerit, ut sibi persuaderi sinat, ut cum ijs, quos offendit, in gratiam redeat, & culpam admissam deprecetur, hic obsequium illud Deo præstat, qui similiter in cœlis ratum habebit, quod isti pacis & concordiæ ergo in terra statuunt.
