E contra si quis se contumacem & implacabilem præbeat, Deum ipsum non vno modo offendit. Nam primum iniuriam nouam facit arbitris illis, quos reuereri debebat. Deinde scelus prius admissum impiopia & fraternæ admonitionis contemptu auget & aggrauat. Præterea in propriam animam peccat, quia preces & omnem cultum externum coram Deo sibi ipsi inutilem reddit. Etenim dum fratri, quem læsit, reconciliari non vult, odiū implacabile prodit, quod aut nulla iusta causa accensus concepit, aut quo excæcatus dilectionis obliuiscitur, sine qua Dei filij non possumus censeri. Itaq; proprijs precibus seipsum damnat, et quia quisquis fratre suo odit (teste Apostolo) homicida est, ijs adnumerari meretur, qui inter precandum manus sanguine plenas attollunt. Quis ergo dubitet in cœlo ratam fore sententiam, qua arbitri illi iram Dei & damnationem sempiternam improbo & contumaci denuntiant. At quanto magis valet hæc ratio, si quis non contentus omnes reconciliationis vias priuatim respuisse, insuper vel Ecclesiæ totius, vel eorum qui ab hac constituti iudices sunt, sententiam siue intercessionem contemnit? Hic certè non obscure reipsa testatur, se legum & iudiciorum Dei contemptorem esse, et proinde indignum, cui in populi Dei communione locus detur. At quia hic consessibus iudicium medius interesse solet, non potest impunitum dimittere ordinis abs se instituti prophanum contemptum. Itaq; etsi ne tota quidem Ecclesia tam præfracti hominis cotumacia frangere aut superare potest, tamen legitime aduersus illu pronuntiata sententia pondus habebit apud bit apud Deum, qui facile viam inueniet, qua & in hoc præsenti & futuro sæculo illius contumaciam vlciscetur.
units.tr: Indeed, as regards private action, the Lord had said: If your brother hear you, and acknowledge his fault, and beg pardon, and be reconciled to you, you have gained your brother. This is explained and confirmed here: namely, that you have gained not only a faithful and constant friend for yourself, but also for God, so that in heaven he may ratify the remission of the offence and injury made by you. There are many and weighty reasons for this saying. First, God, who is a just judge, is wont to avenge injuries which are done to the innocent beyond all deserts, and especially those done to strangers, widows, orphans, or other people of this kind, who have no strength to defend themselves and are therefore compelled to pour out their complaints into his bosom. He bears witness to this himself in the Law, and to this belongs what the apostle writes about labourers defrauded of their wages who cry out to God, and what the son of Sirach says very gravely: God will not neglect the supplication of the orphan, nor the widow when she pours out her prayer. Does not she who causes her tears to run down her cheek call upon him against the one who causes them? The prayer of the afflicted penetrates the clouds; it does not rest nor give up until it reaches the Most High, who will plead her cause and judge justly, etc. From this it follows that God also remits his anger when the one who has suffered the injury appeals to him, and he is accustomed to hear the prayers of that person even on behalf of the one who did the injury. Next, there is a universal promise that God is willing to remit the sins of those who call upon him and who remit offences to others. How much more, then, will this happen when the one who did the injury and the one who suffered it are reconciled to each other and together with united hearts and prayers implore his grace? For God delights in the concord of brothers, and it is his command that such people receive his blessing and eternal life. This admonishes all those who have offended others of their duty: that, as their own salvation is dear to them, they should strive to be reconciled to those whom they have offended, because unless they do so, whatever they may be, they exclude themselves from the grace of God, so that they can hope for no forgiveness of their sin from him. Moreover, this passage makes plain how great is the dignity of Christian people, and that it was not without reason written in the Apocalypse that Jesus Christ has made us kings and priests to God and his Father. For although the government of the commonwealth and the public ministry of the Church do not belong to all men without distinction, yet each person is, in his own cause, a king and a priest to himself. Like a king, he uses that liberty to pardon the injuries done to him, and like a priest, he remits every fault to the one by whom he has been wronged. If he does so, that remission will also be ratified in heaven before the tribunal of God. The ancients also understood this passage in this sense, as may be seen in Theophylact, who writes among other things: Not only are the things that priests loose loosed, but also the things that we, who have been injured, bind or loose are bound or loosed. Moreover, the same reasoning holds if an injured brother brings about reconciliation through arbiters. For, as we said recently, these men do a work most pleasing to God. Therefore, whoever so conducts himself that he allows himself to be persuaded to be reconciled to those whom he has offended and to beg pardon for the fault he has committed, renders that obedience to God, who in heaven will in the same way ratify what these men decide on earth for the sake of peace and concord. On the other hand, if anyone shows himself obstinate and implacable, he offends God himself in more than one way. For first, he commits a new injury against those arbiters whom he ought to revere. Then he increases and aggravates the earlier crime by impiety and by contempt of fraternal admonition. Moreover, he sins against his own soul, because by his refusal he renders his prayers and all outward worship useless to himself before God. For while he is unwilling to be reconciled to the brother whom he has wronged, he shows an implacable hatred, which he has conceived either from no just cause or from which, blinded, he forgets love, without which we cannot be counted children of God. Thus he condemns himself by his own prayers, and since whoever hates his brother (as the apostle testifies) is a murderer, he deserves to be numbered among those who lift up hands full of blood while praying. Who then could doubt that the sentence by which those arbiters announce the wrath of God and eternal damnation to the wicked and obstinate man will be ratified in heaven? But how much more does this reasoning hold if someone, not content to have rejected all the ways of reconciliation in private, further despises the sentence or intercession of the whole Church, or of those who have been appointed judges by it? Here he certainly bears witness, by his very deed, that he is a despiser of the laws and judgements of God, and therefore unworthy to be given a place in the fellowship of the people of God. And because the judgement usually is set in the midst of the assembled elders, he cannot let pass unpunished the profane contempt of the order that they have established. Therefore, even if the whole Church cannot break or overcome the obstinacy of such a stubborn man, nevertheless the sentence lawfully pronounced against him will have weight before God, who will easily find a way by which he will avenge that obstinacy both in this present age and in the age to come.

units.la: Cæterum, ne pij, quibus cum eiusmodi hominibus res est, eorū contumacia fracti succumbant, promissionem istam amplius confirmat Dominus, & illis apud Deum præsidium certum paratum esse docet, qui ipsorum precibus minime defuturus sit. Nam rursum dico vobis (ait) si duo ex vobis consenserint in terra, quodcunq; petierint, fiet eis a Patre meo, qui in cælis est. Sumit argumentum ab axiomate generali, Deum non deesse votis suorum credentium, si quid pio & vnanimi consensu cum nominis sui invocatione faciant. Ergo fieri no posse, quin firmum atq; ratū habeat, quicquid in causa reconciliationis inter fratres aliqui statuerint, licet numero pauci sint. Et indefinitè loquitur, si duo ex vobis. Quasi diceret: modo ex credentium numero sint, non obstabit conditio, etiamsi non magnæ sint coram mundo hoc existimationis. Et hoc quoq; alio argumento confirmat: Vbi enim sunt duo aut tres congregati in nomine meo, illic sum in medio eorum. Enimuero vbi Christus præsens adest, illic necesse est exaudiri preces: At qui in meo nomine conuenerunt (inquit) ijs ego præsens adsum: Exaudientur ergo, & a Patre meo quod petent impetrabunt. Maior confirmatur, quod Christus Filius ille Dei dilectus est, quem hic Mediatorem fecit, & propter quem nobis placatus est. Idem iam mortem aditurus promissione hanc amplius stabiliuit, dicens: Amen amen dico vobis quæcunq; petieritis a Patre meo in nomine meo, dabit vobis.
units.tr: Moreover, lest the godly, who have to do with such men, give way and be broken by their obstinacy, the Lord reinforces that promise further and teaches that a sure defence is laid up for them with God, who will by no means fail their prayers. For he says: "Again I say to you, if two of you agree on earth, whatever they ask will be done for them by my Father who is in heaven." He takes his argument from a general principle: God does not fail the prayers of his believers when they do something with a godly and united agreement and with the invocation of his name. Therefore it cannot be that whatever some have decided in a matter of reconciling brothers should not be firm and ratified, even though they be few in number. He speaks indefinitely, "if two of you." As if he were saying: provided they are from the number of believers, the condition will not stand in the way, even if they are of little account in the eyes of the world. He also confirms this by another argument: "For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them." Surely where Christ is present, prayers must necessarily be heard. But those who have gathered in my name (he says), I am present with them. They will therefore be heard, and they will obtain from my Father what they ask. The major premise is confirmed because Christ is that beloved Son of God whom he has here made Mediator, and on account of whom he is reconciled to us. Now about to go to death, he established this promise still more firmly, saying: "Verily, verily I say to you, whatever you ask of my Father in my name, he will give you."

units.la: Docemur autem simul hoc loco, quàm serio & studiose Christiani homines agere debeant in causis ad aliorum salutem pertinentibus. Etenim Christus de reconciliatione inter duos fratres, vel potius de vnico homine, qui sese difficiliore præbet, quàm par sit, differens, tamen contentus in suo nomine facti, adhæc precum meminit. Idem Paulus facit, quando quid in hominis incesti causa fieri debeat, monet. Nam Corinthios reprehendit, quod non publico luctu testati sint, quàm ipsis scelus hoc displiceret, & quantopere eis cordi esset hominis istius salus: deinde no obiter & vt quotidie solebant, illos conuenire iubet, sed ait: Vobis & meo Spiritu congregatis in nomine Domini nostri IESV CHRISTI, cum potestate Domini nostri IESV CHRISTI, tradatur eiusmodi homo Satanæ, &c. Quod si in vnius hominis causa tanto studio opus est, quanto magis hoc observari debet, quando totius Ecclesiæ causa agitur, aut propter publicum scandalum salus multorum periclitatur? Ibi cauendum in primis, ne quid ex vnius priuato arbitrio fiat, sed Ecclesiæ consensus habeatur. Nemo enim tantæ authoritatis aut existimationis est, vt sibi dominium in clerum siue hæreditatem Domini, id est, in Ecclesiam vendicare debeat. Deinde omnia fiant in nomine Domini. Quod tunc fiet, quando reliquis affectibus priuatis, omnes ab vno Christo pendent, hunc vnum audiunt, eius Verbo sese subijciunt, & actionum suarum hunc finè sibi proponunt, vt illius gloria illustretur. Et quia ex nobis ipsis nihil possumus, publicæ preces instituantur, vt Deus suo Spiritu consilia nostra & omnium mentes atq; sententias dirigat. Hunc morem olim Apostoli obseruarunt in ministrorum Verbi & diaconorum Ecclesiæ electione. Et huius etiam meminisse debebant: qui in Magistratu constituti ad Reipub. gubernacula sedent. Etenim hi quoq; in Dei consp. ectu & in eius nomine conueniunt, qui sua iudicia ipsis credidit, & medius illis adest. Hunc ergo obseruent & audiant in suo Verbo loquentem: Finis autem & scopus consiliorum omnium sit Dei gloria & publica salus: & ad Solomonis exemplū seriò precentur Dominum, vt suo spiritu mentes ipsorum illuminet atq; regat. Hæc si obseruentur in conuentibus Ecclesiasticis & politicis, non dubium est, quin Dei gloriam & regnū quærentibus Deus adsit, & illorum deliberationes moderetur. At quid vulgo fiat, & quales fere cætus sint eorū, qui rebus præfecti sunt, res ipsa loquitur: vt nemo mirari debeat, rem Christianam vbiq; locorum periclitari.
units.tr: At the same time we are taught in this passage how earnestly and zealously Christians ought to act in matters that concern the salvation of others. For Christ, speaking of the reconciliation of two brothers, or rather of a single man who shows himself more stubborn than is right, nevertheless, content with what was done in his name, also mentions prayer. Paul does the same when he admonishes what ought to be done in the case of an incestuous man. For he rebukes the Corinthians because they did not show by public mourning how much this crime displeased them, and how greatly the salvation of that man was dear to them; then, not casually and as they were accustomed to do daily, he bids them assemble, saying: "When you are gathered together, and my spirit, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, with the power of our Lord Jesus Christ, let such a man be delivered to Satan," etc. If such diligence is needed in the case of a single man, how much more ought it to be observed when the cause of the whole Church is at stake, or when the salvation of many is endangered on account of public scandal? In such matters one must above all take care that nothing is done by the private judgment of one person, but that the consent of the Church be obtained. For no one is of such authority or repute as to claim for himself lordship over the clergy, or the inheritance of the Lord, that is, over the Church. Next, let all things be done in the name of the Lord. This will happen when, with other private affections set aside, all depend on Christ alone, hear him alone, submit themselves to his Word, and set before themselves as the sole aim of their actions that his glory be made illustrious. And since we can do nothing of ourselves, public prayers should be made, so that God by his Spirit may direct our counsels and the minds and opinions of all. The Apostles observed this custom in the election of ministers of the Word and deacons of the Church. And those who are set in magistracy and sit at the helm of the commonwealth ought also to remember this. For they too gather in the sight of God and in his name, who has entrusted his judgments to them and is present in their midst. Let them therefore observe and listen to him speaking in his Word: "Let the end and aim of all counsels be the glory of God and the public good;" and, following the example of Solomon, let them earnestly pray the Lord to illuminate and rule their minds by his Spirit. If these things are observed in ecclesiastical and civil assemblies, there is no doubt that God will be present to those who seek his glory and kingdom, and will govern their deliberations. But what generally happens, and what sort of gatherings those are who are set over affairs, the matter itself speaks: so that no one should wonder that the Christian cause is everywhere in peril.

units.la: Deinde priuati quoq; homines admonentur, quanti facere debeant cætus Ecclesiasticos, in qui bus conuenitur in nomine Christi, vt eius Verbum audiatur, Sacramenta administrentur & preces fiant pro publicis totius Ecclesiæ & priuatis singulorum necessitatibus. Quid enim in horum commendationem præclarius dici potest, quàm quod Dei Filius pollicetur, se illis interesse velle, & preces quæ in illis fiunt, a Patre suo exaudiri? Id vero non temere ille pollicetur. Etenim vt Deus vnus est, ita vt nos in ipso vnum simus, & vnitatē istam cætibus publicis testemur, requirit. Ideo olim vnum modo tabernaculū esse voluit, ad quod populus suus conueniret, in cuius locum postea templum successit, quod & ipsum vnicum fuit. Vnum etiam fuit altare, in quo sacrificabatur. Festa quoq; publica in eum maxime finem instituta fuerunt, vt ter in anno ex diuersis locis conuenirent omnes, qui in Dei populo volebant censeri. Damnantur autem Excelsa, & ij qui in illis sacrificando Ecclesiæ vnitatem scindebant. In nouo testamento vnitatem hanc Christus quæ que commendat, & quàm hæc ipsi placeat, in feria illa precatione testatur, quam habuit iam mortem aditurus. Pater sancte (inquit) serua eos per nomen tuum, quos dedisti mihi, vt sint vnum, sicuti & nos. Et rursum: Non pro eis tantum rogo, sed & pro iis qui creduturi sunt per sermonem eorum in me: VT OMNES VNVM SINT, sicut tu Pater in me, & ego in te, vt & ipsi in nobis vnu sint. Et vt solent qui rem in primis necessariam suis commendando nunquam sibi ipsis satisfaciunt, mox addit: Ego gloriam quam dedisti mihi, dedi eis, VT SINT VNV M, sicut & nos vnum sumus. Et facit hoc quod Paulus scribit: Studete seruare vnitatem spiritus per vinculum pacis: Vnum est corpus (nimirum Ecclesiæ) & vnus spiritus, sicut & vocati estis in vnam spem vocationis vestræ: vnus Dominus, vna fides, vnū baptisma, vnus Deus & Pater omnium. Et alibi per cœnam mysticam quoq; huius vnitatis mysterium nobis commendans ait: Vnus panis, vnum corpus multi sumus: nam omnes vnius panis sumus participes. Cum vero in cœtibus sacris hæc omnia in oculos incurrant, & sensibus nostris quasi repræsententur, non possunt illos non magni facere, qui salutis propriæ & gloriæ Dei cura serio tangitur. Superat tamen hæc omnia, quod ex hoc loco discimus, nos in ipsius Filij Dei conspectu venire, quoties in illis conuenimus, qui nobiscū loquitur, seipsum & meritū suum nobis communicat, & preces nostras Patri acceptas facit. Horum consideratio olim sanctos mouit, vt si quando longius abessent a tabernaculo, aut ad sacros cœtus non possent accedere, non sine maximo animi dolore clamarent: Sitit anima mea Deũ, Deum viuũ: quando tandem veniam, vt appareain conspectu Dei? Et nota est Dauidis vox: Lætor cum mihi dicunt: Eamus ad domum Domini. Quales ergo censeri debent, qui ad templu raro veniunt, Verbi prædicationem fastidiunt, & nulla precum publicarum cura tanguntur, neq; Sacramentorum vsu sibi opus esse existimant? Sunt hi prophani homines, & ab ingenio filiorum Dei alienissimi, cum Patris huius conspectum oderint, & eisdem vocem audire dedignentur.
units.tr: Next, private persons too are admonished how highly they ought to value ecclesiastical assemblies, in which people gather in the name of Christ, so that his Word may be heard, the sacraments administered, and prayers offered for the public needs of the whole Church and the private necessities of individuals. For what can be said more splendidly in commendation of these than that the Son of God promises that he wishes to be present with them, and that the prayers offered in them will be heard by his Father? He does not promise this rashly. For as God is one, so he requires that we be one in him, and bear witness to that unity in public assemblies. Therefore of old he willed that there be only one tabernacle, to which his people should come together, and in its place later succeeded the temple, which was also unique. There was also one altar on which sacrifice was offered. Public feasts too were instituted chiefly for this end, that three times a year all who wished to be counted among God's people should gather from different places. Moreover, the high places are condemned, and those who by sacrificing in them divided the unity of the Church. In the New Testament Christ commends this unity everywhere, and bears witness how pleasing it is to him in that prayer, full of feeling, which he made when about to go to death. "Holy Father," he says, "keep through your name those whom you have given me, that they may be one, as we are." And again: "I pray not for these only, but also for those who will believe in me through their word: THAT ALL MAY BE ONE, as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be one in us." And as those do who, in commending something most necessary, never feel they have said enough, he adds at once: "The glory which you have given me I have given to them, THAT THEY MAY BE ONE, as we are one." And he does what Paul writes: "Be eager to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. There is one body (that is, of the Church) and one Spirit, just as you were called into one hope of your calling: one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all." And elsewhere, commending to us the mystery of this unity also through the mystical supper, he says: "One bread, one body, we who are many: for we all partake of one bread." Since all these things are plainly before our eyes in sacred assemblies and are, as it were, set before our senses, those who are seriously concerned for their own salvation and the glory of God cannot but hold them in high esteem. Yet what we learn from this passage surpasses all these things: that we come into the very sight of the Son of God whenever we assemble in those gatherings in which he speaks with us, communicates himself and his merit to us, and makes our prayers acceptable to the Father. The consideration of these things once moved the saints, so that if at any time they were far from the tabernacle, or could not come to the sacred assemblies, they cried out, not without the greatest grief of mind: "My soul thirsts for God, the living God: when at last shall I come and appear in the sight of God?" And the voice of David is well known: "I rejoice when they say to me: let us go to the house of the Lord." What, then, must be thought of those who seldom come to the temple, who despise the preaching of the Word, who are moved by no concern for public prayers, and who think they have no need of the use of the sacraments? They are profane men, and most alien to the disposition of the children of God, since they hate the sight of this Father and disdain to hear his voice.

units.la: Porrò turpiter & nefarie huius loci authoritate abutuntur Pontifices, vt sua tyrannide stabiliant, quando sua decreta Ecclesiæ obtrudunt, & priuato arbitrio quosuis soluunt aut ligant, sua deniq; excommunicatione non vulgus modo hominū, sed reges quoq; perterrefaciunt. Etenim sibi vendicant, quod ad totā Ecclesiā pertinet. Et de suis conciliabulis intelligi volunt, quod Dominus dixit: Si duo ex vobis consenseriat in terra, quodcunq; petierint, fiet eis a Patre meo, qui in cœlis est. Item: Vbi sunt duo aut tres congregati in nomine meo, illic sum in medio illorū. Atqui Christus de credentibus loquitur, qui in illo consentiunt, non de prophanis Verbi sui illusoribus, qui contra ipsum & Ecclesiam conspirando hanc traditionibus nouis & eius Verbo contrarijs grauant. Adhæc se ijs adesse velle pollicetur, qui in ipsius nomine congregatur: Nihil ergo hoc ad eos, qui vt suæ auaritiæ consulant, & male vsurpatam tyrannidem stabiliant, Concilia indicunt, in quibus nemini nisi qui in ipsorum verba iurarunt, sententiam dicere licet, & quorū finis fere nō alius est, quàm quod bellis ciuilibus orbem terrarum turbant. Nec est quod Ecclesiæ titulo sese palliet, a cuius communione se alienissimos esse produnt. Hæc enim non leges nouas condit, sed asponso suo Christo acceptas solicitè seruat, neq; vllius voce audit, quàm sponsi, cui se totam consecrauit. Psal.45.
units.tr: Moreover, the Popes shamefully and wickedly abuse the authority of this passage in order to establish their tyranny: when they force their own decrees upon the Church, and at their private discretion loose or bind whomever they please, and by their excommunication terrify not only the common people but kings as well. For they claim for themselves what pertains to the whole Church, and they wish what the Lord said to be understood of their own conventicles: "If two of you agree on earth, whatever they ask will be done for them by my Father who is in heaven." Likewise: "Where two or three are gathered together in my name, there I am in the midst of them." Yet Christ speaks of believers, who agree with him, not of the profane mockers of his Word, who by conspiring against him and the Church burden it with new traditions contrary to his Word. Moreover, he promises to be present with those who are gathered in his name. Therefore this has nothing to do with those who, in order to serve their own greed and to shore up a tyranny wrongly seized, summon councils in which no one is allowed to give an opinion unless he has sworn to their words, and whose aim is almost nothing other than to disturb the whole world with civil wars. Nor is there any reason for them to cloak themselves in the title of the Church, from whose communion they show themselves to be utterly estranged. For she does not make new laws, but carefully keeps the things received from her Bridegroom Christ, and hears no voice but that of the Bridegroom, to whom she has consecrated herself entirely. Psalm 45.

units.la: Priusquam vero dicendi finem faciamus, obseruari debet argumentum diuinitatis Christi euidens & irrefragabile, quod in his verbis continetur: Vbi sunt duo aut tres cōgregati in nomine meo, illic sum in medio illorum. Etenim vbiq; præsentem esse solius Dei proprium est, qui dixit: Amon cœlum & terram ego impleo? Item: Cœlum mihi thronus est, terra vero scabellū pedum meorum. At Christus præsens est, vbicunq; duo aut tres in ipsius nomine conueniunt: & idem Ecclesiæ suæ, quæ per omnes orbis terrarum partes dispersa, & nulli certo loco alligata est, dixit: Ecce ego vobiscum sum vsq; ad consummationem sæculi. Ergo Deus verus & æternus sit, oportet. At hic meminisse conuenit, personam eius ex Deo & homine constare, & Deum quidem esse ab æterno, hominem autem factũ esse præsinito tempore, neq; vnquam deposuisse, quàm semel assum sit, ho-
units.tr: Before we make an end of speaking, the argument for the divinity of Christ, evident and irrefutable, which is contained in these words, ought to be noted: "Where two or three are gathered together in my name, there I am in the midst of them." For to be present everywhere is proper to God alone, who said: "Do I not fill heaven and earth?" Likewise: "Heaven is my throne, and the earth is the footstool of my feet." But Christ is present wherever two or three come together in his name; and he said to his Church, which is scattered through all parts of the world and bound to no certain place: "Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age." Therefore he must be the true and eternal God. Yet here it is fitting to remember that his person consists of God and man, and that he indeed is God from eternity, but became man at a predetermined time, and never laid aside the nature of man, once assumed.

units.la: Matth.28. psit, hominis naturam. Itaque secundum D. Augustini dictum, cauendum nobis esse, ne ita diuinitatem hominis astruamus, vt veritatem corporis auferamus. Perperam ergo & inepte (ne quid grauius dicam) hæc Christi verba detorquent, qui ex illis omnipræsentiam corporis eius colligunt, & hoc vbique esse contendunt. De hoc enim ille dixit: Me non semper habebitis: Confert vobis, vt abeam: Iam non sum in mundo: Et innumera alia, quæ in Euangelio & scriptis Apostolicis occurrunt: quæ cum ijs quæ de eius omnipræsentia dicuntur, non aliter conciliari possunt, quàm vt in vnitate personæ Christi naturas distinctas diuinitatis & humanitatis obseruemus, & cum Augustino dicamus: Secundum præsentiam maiestatis, semper habemus Christum: secundum præsentiam carnis recte dictum est, Me autem non semper habebitis. Habuit enim illum Ecclesia secundum præsentiam carnis paucis diebus, modo fide tenet, oculis non videt, &c. Conueniunt hæc articulis Symboli Apostolici, quibus nos insistere decet, ne verba Christi in sensum alienum detorqueamus. Soletur autem nos, quod qui propter nos hominem assumpsit, vt ea faceret & pateretur, quæ propter humani generis redemptionem fieri oportebat, eundem hominem post peractum nostræ redemptionis mysterium in cœlos euexit, vt viam sanctorum nobis patefaceret, & noster esset apud Patrem intercessor. Idem vero quoad diuinitatem nobis adest, vt nos seruet, regat, alat & defendat vsque ad eum diem, quo corpore suo glorioso redibit in nubibus cœli ad iudicandum viuos & mortuos, vt superatis & subiectis omnibus hostibus, & ipsa quoq; morte abolita, credentes suos ad se recipiat, & regni sui cœlestis consortes faciat. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Matth. 28. According to the saying of Saint Augustine, we must take care that in asserting the divinity of the man we do not take away the truth of the body. Therefore they twist these words of Christ wrongly and foolishly (to say nothing harsher), who from them gather the omnipresence of his body and contend that it is everywhere. For he spoke of this: "You will not always have me"; "It is expedient for you that I go away"; "Now I am no longer in the world"; and countless other things which occur in the Gospel and the apostolic writings. These cannot be reconciled with what is said of his omnipresence in any other way than by observing, in the unity of Christ's person, the distinct natures of divinity and humanity, and by saying with Augustine: "According to the presence of majesty we always have Christ; according to the presence of the flesh it was rightly said, 'But you will not always have me.'" For the Church had him according to the presence of the flesh for a few days; now she holds him by faith, does not see him with her eyes, and so on. These things agree with the articles of the Apostles' Creed, to which we ought to hold fast, lest we twist the words of Christ into a foreign sense. Yet we are comforted by this: he who for our sake assumed a man, that he might do and suffer what had to be done for the redemption of the human race, after the mystery of our redemption was accomplished, lifted that same man up into the heavens, so that he might open the way of the saints to us and be our intercessor with the Father. And according to his divinity he is present with us, to keep, rule, nourish and defend us until that day on which he will return in his glorious body in the clouds of heaven to judge the living and the dead, so that, all enemies being overcome and subdued, and death itself abolished, he may receive his believers to himself and make them partners of his heavenly kingdom. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCXXII.
units.tr: Homily 222.

units.la: Tunc adiens eum Petrus dixit: Domine, quoties peccabit in me frater meus, & remittam ei? Num vsq; septies? Dicit ei IESVS: Non dico tibi vsq; septies, sed vsq; septuagies septies.
units.tr: Then Peter came to him and said: "Lord, how often shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? Up to seven times?" Jesus says to him: "I do not tell you up to seven times, but up to seventy times seven."

units.la: Omnibus hominibus innata est vindicta cupiditas, cuisi indulgeatur, odia & simultates parit & quæcunque alia dilectioni fraternæ aduersantur, sine qua fides & religio Christiana non potest consistere. Ideò Dominus noster IESVS CHRISTVS non temere multis docuit, vt cum fratribus, qui nos læserunt, ipsi reconciliationem quæramus: & vt ipsi eandem admittant, graviter monuit quid eos maneat, qui hic sese difficiles aut implacabiles præbent: Quod nimirum non possint nec debeant pro Ecclesiæ membris censeri, & quòd Deus in cœlis ratum habeat, quicquid vel Ecclesia tota, vel pauculi fideles de illis statuerint. Quia vero de illis solis dixit haben-tes, qui cum ipsi alios offenderint, de reconciliatione non cogitant, nisi ab ijs requirantur, quibus ipsi supplices fieri debebant, & tamen tunc quoq; non possunt adduci, vt culpam deprecentur, nihil autem de melioribus egit, qui sponte culpam agnoscunt & cum ijs, quos læserunt, in gratiam redire cupiunt, nunc quomodo cum his agi debeat, docet: Summa totius tractationis est, necesse esse vt qui seruari volunt, ex animo offensas & iniurias omnes condonent ijs, qui sibi ignosci petunt, & nobiscum reconciliari cupiunt.
units.tr: Vengeance is a desire born in all human beings, and if it is indulged it gives rise to hatred and quarrels, and to everything else that opposes brotherly love, without which the Christian faith and religion cannot stand. For this reason our Lord Jesus Christ taught many people, not rashly, that they should themselves seek reconciliation with the brothers who have wronged them. And so that they would grant it in return, he solemnly warned what awaits those who show themselves hard or unforgiving here: namely, that they cannot and ought not to be counted among the members of the Church, and that God in heaven ratifies whatever the whole Church, or even a few faithful people, decides about them. But because he spoke only of those who, after offending others, do not think of reconciliation unless they are sought out by the very people before whom they ought to have humbled themselves, and even then cannot be brought to beg pardon for their fault, and because he said nothing about better people, who freely acknowledge their fault and wish to be restored to favour with those they have wronged, he now teaches how such people ought to be dealt with. The sum of the whole discussion is this: those who wish to be saved must from the heart forgive all offences and injuries to those who ask to be pardoned and wish to be reconciled with us.

units.la: Præmittitur autem doctrinæ huius occasio, quam Petrus & reliqui discipuli Christo præbuerunt. Hi enim cum audirent, quàm multa lenitate & indulgentia cum præsrattiis illis & implacabilibus agi debeat, & simul sentirent, quàm hoc graue sit carni, quæ (vt initio diximus) vindicta cupidissima est, pio animi affectu in preces erumpunt (sicuti Lucas annotauit) & clamant: Domine adijce nobis fidem. Quasi dicerent: Audimus equidem quid iubeas, & obsequi cupimus: sed senti-mus quam multa hic nobis obstent, & tanta est nostra infirmitas, vt ne fidem quidem tuis dictis possimus habere, nisi tu hanc largiaris. Precamur ergo, vt hanc augeas, & quod iubes, ipse largiris, &c. At Petrus, qui passim reliquis discipulis seruentior introducitur, longius procedit: et quia facile ex ijs, quæ audierat, colligere poterat, adhuc maiori indulgentia tractandos esse eos, qui vbi nos læserunt, sponte veniunt, & culpa deprecando nobiscum reconciliari cupiunt. Quærit, quoufq; cum his sit procedendum? Quoties (inquit) peccabit in me frater meus, & remittam ei? Causa huius Petri quæstionis est, quod sciret, multos qui reconciliatione quærunt, non ex animo illud facere, sed sui commodi causa, & hos facile alio affectu abripi, ut iniurias suo offensas iterent: & licet id sæpius faciant, semper tamen sibi ignosci velint. Id vero pijs quoq; interdum bilem mouet, ut arbitrentur, indulgentiam istam, & condonandi facilitatem necessario restringendam esse, ne qui ea ferociores fiant, & in nimiam licentiam effundantur. In primis vero qui natura ad vindictam proclivores sunt, hoc prætextu plausibili in speciem sese palliant, & seueritatem nimiam, qua iniurias totiesque sibi factas vlcisci student, zelo gloriæ Dei & charitatis fraternæ excusant. Idem affectus ergo etiam Petrum impulit, ut hanc quæstionem moueat, qua hoc omnino vult dicere: Recte quidem mones Domine, ne læsi ab aliquo, eum mox damnemus, sed potius lucrifacere studeamus, ut quamuis intractabilior sit, quam tuum discipulum deceat, tamen omnia priuatim & publice tentemus, priusquam pro ethnico & publicano habeatur. Quid vero cum ijs agendum erit, qui ipsi sponte culpam agnoscunt, & nobiscum in gratiam redire cupiunt? Enimuero maiori indulgentiæ tractandi sunt. Veruntamen cauendum esse arbitror, ne dum hæc nimia est, illi non lucrifiant, sed potius ut pueri deprauatæ indolis, ea corrumpantur & insolentiores fiant. Annon ergo sufficiet, si septies remisero ei, qui iniurias subinde iterat, &c.? Hic quæstionis Petri sensus esse videtur, qui procul dubio putauit, se magnum quid præstare, si hoc faciat, & omni hominis Christiani officio abunde defungi.
units.tr: The occasion for this teaching is given first, provided by Peter and the other disciples to Christ. For when they heard with how much gentleness and indulgence one must deal with those obstinate and unforgiving people, and at the same time perceived how hard this is for the flesh, which (as we said at the beginning) is most eager for vengeance, they broke out in prayer with a devout feeling of the heart (as Luke noted) and cried: "Lord, increase our faith." As if they were saying: We indeed hear what you command, and we wish to obey, but we feel how many things stand in our way, and our weakness is so great that we cannot even have faith in your words unless you grant it. We therefore pray that you increase it, and that you yourself give what you command, and so on. But Peter, who is everywhere introduced as more fervent than the other disciples, goes further. And because he could easily gather from what he had heard that those who, when they have wronged us, come of their own accord and wish to be reconciled to us by begging pardon for their fault, must be treated with still greater indulgence, he asks how far we must go with such people. "How often," he says, "will my brother sin against me, and I forgive him?" The reason for Peter's question is that he knew many who seek reconciliation do so not from the heart but for their own advantage, and that such people are easily carried off by another disposition, so that they repeat their offences against us; and although they do this often, they still want to be forgiven each time. This sometimes stirs even good people to anger, so that they think this indulgence and readiness to forgive must necessarily be restrained, lest such people become bolder and pour themselves out into excessive licence. Above all, those who are naturally more inclined to revenge hide behind this plausible pretext and excuse the excessive severity with which they strive to avenge the injuries done to them, however often, by appealing to zeal for God's glory and brotherly love. So the same feeling also moved Peter to raise this question, which means in effect: Rightly do you warn, Lord, that we should not condemn at once someone who has wronged us, but rather strive to win him back; yet, however unmanageable he may be, which is unfitting for your disciple, we should still try everything, in private and in public, before he is regarded as a heathen and a tax collector. But what must be done with those who freely acknowledge their fault and wish to be restored to favour with us? Surely they must be treated with greater indulgence. Nevertheless, I think we must take care lest, while such indulgence is excessive, they are not won back but rather, like children of a corrupt disposition, are spoiled by it and become more insolent. Will it not then be enough if I forgive him seven times, the one who repeatedly renews his injuries, and so on? This seems to be the sense of Peter's question, for he doubtless thought he would be doing something great if he did this, and would have fully discharged every duty of a Christian.

units.la: Cæterum si rem ipsam propius consideres, videbis illum, dum de re bona & sancta quæstionem mouet, & germanus Christi discipulus videri vult, non uno modo peccare. Nam primum affectui priuato indulgens, præiudicio suo fallitur, & hoc a Christo probari & confirmari cupit. At boni discipuli est, simpliciter quærere de præceptoris sui sententia. Deinde animum vindictæ cupidum prodit, dum scire cupit, quis ignoscendi & condonandi finis esse debeat, & quando liceat fratrem vlcisci, qui non contentus semel & iterum nobis iniuriam fecisse, novas subinde prioribus accumulat. Sunt tales hodie multi, qui etsi Verbi Dei studiù pleno ore profitentur, tamen de multis rebus similes quæstiones eodem plane animi proposito mouent. Faciunt hoc, qui tantū ne scelus sit scortatio, quantum nonnulli dicunt, interrogant, & anno præsertim lupanaria esse publica, ne iuuenes & cœlibes virginum aut matronarum pudicitiam insidientur, aut libidinibus longe fœdioribus sese polluant? Vel annon durior æquo & crudelis nimium sit eorum sententia, qui adulterium capite plectendum esse fententiunt? Num vitium tam immane sit ebrietas & perpetrandi studium, ut legibus publicis coerceri mereatur? Num qui ut rei domesticæ consulant, pecuniam suam dant fœnori, & vsuris fratres grauant, digni censeri debeant, qui a regno Dei excludantur? Et si quæ alia hodie inter Christiani nominis profitentes in quæstionem veniunt. At isti omnes, ut tut pietatem & religionis studium simulent, non aliud quam licentiam quærunt, ut excusso Christi iugo pessimis suis cupiditatibus indulgeant. Nisi enim hoc agerent, facile viderent, in his omnibus non multa quæstione opus esse. Etenim Lex Dei est: Ne sit scortum in Israele. Et in novo testamento Apostoli clamant: Scortatio & omnis impuritas, ne nominetur quidem inter vos. Item: Propter fornicationes suam quisque uxorem habeat, & proprium quæque virum habeat. Et rursus de alieni thori violatoribus Deus pronunciauit: Qui adulterium committit cum uxore proximi sui, morte moriatur, tam ipse quam adultera. Idem Væ illud horrendum ebriosis per prophetas denuntiat, & non solum deportationem in alienas terras, sed infernales quoque pœnas eis minatur. Vt iuras vero morsum vocat Deus qui nemini inferri debeat, & inter montis sanctos iniuriae numerantur, qui ab illis abstinent. Et notum est, quid de his omnibus Christus per elegantem illum organum, Paulum Apostolum, dixerit: Ne erretis, neque scortatores, neque idololatræ, neque mœchi, neque molles, neque qui cum masculis concumbunt, neque fures, neque auari, neque ebriosi, neque conuiciatores, neque rapaces regni Dei hæreditatem consequentur, &c. Quid ergo quæreret aut disputare opus est de ijs, de quibus iam olim Deus suam sententiam tam diserte protulit? Rata hæc erit in æternum, neque nostris disputationibus aut iudicijs mutari vel aboleri poterit. Quin ergo in hoc speculo partim quæ contra Dei leges designauimus, contemplamur, partim agnitasi mul infirmitate nostra cum Apostolis precamur, ut Deus fidem nobis augeat, & vires largiatur, ut posthac præceptis eius obedire possimus.
units.tr: Yet if you consider the matter itself more closely, you will see that Peter, while raising a question about a good and holy thing, and wishing to appear a true disciple of Christ, did not sin in only one way. For first, by indulging a private feeling, he was deceived by his own prejudice and wanted Christ to approve and confirm it. But it is the mark of a good disciple simply to ask about his teacher's opinion. Next, he revealed a mind eager for vengeance, while he wished to know what limit of forgiving and pardoning there ought to be, and when it is permitted to avenge a brother who, not content to have wronged us once or twice, keeps piling new injuries upon the old. Today there are many like this who, although they profess the study of God's Word with full voice, nevertheless raise similar questions about many matters with exactly the same purpose of mind. Those do this who ask whether fornication is really so great a crime as some say, and especially whether brothels ought to be public, so that young unmarried men do not lie in wait for the chastity of virgins or matrons, or defile themselves with far more foul lusts? Or is the opinion of those who think adultery should be punished by death too harsh and excessively cruel? Is drunkenness, and the eagerness to commit it, such a monstrous vice that it deserves to be restrained by public laws? Should those who lend their money at interest, to look after their domestic affairs, and burden their brothers with usury, be judged worthy to be excluded from the kingdom of God? And if there are other matters today that are called into question among those who profess the Christian name. But all these people, though they pretend piety and zeal for religion, seek nothing but licence, so that, having shaken off the yoke of Christ, they may indulge their worst desires. For if they were not doing this, they would easily see that in all these cases there is no great need for question. For the Law of God says: "Let there be no whore in Israel." And in the New Testament the Apostles cry out: "Fornication and all impurity, let it not even be named among you." Likewise: "Because of fornication let each man have his own wife, and each woman her own husband." And again, God pronounced against violators of another's marriage bed: "He who commits adultery with the wife of his neighbour shall surely die, both he and the adulteress." The same God through the prophets pronounces that dreadful woe upon drunkards, and threatens them not only with deportation to foreign lands but also with infernal punishments. Indeed, God calls the bite of usury something that ought to be inflicted on no one, and among the injustices of the holy mountain are counted those who abstain from it. And it is well known what Christ said about all these things through that eloquent instrument, the Apostle Paul: "Do not be deceived: neither fornicators, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor men who lie with men, nor thieves, nor the covetous, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor extortioners, will inherit the kingdom of God," and so on. Why then is there any need to ask or dispute about things on which God long ago declared his judgment so plainly? This judgment will stand for ever, and it cannot be altered or abolished by our disputes or opinions. Let us then, therefore, look in this mirror at what we have partly marked as contrary to God's laws, and, acknowledging our weakness, pray with the Apostles that God would increase our faith and grant us strength, so that from now on we may be able to obey his precepts.

units.la: Deut.23. Eph.5. 1.Cor.7. Leu.20. Amos 6. Isa.5. Deut.23, Psal.15. 1.Cor.6. Sed audiamus quid Dominus Petro respondeat: Non, dico tibi, septies, sed septuagies septies. Corrigit primò Petri praeiudicium, adeoque nullius aestimat hoc, in quo ille sibi mirifice placebat: Qua si diceret: Quid de septenaria remissione dicis o bone? Etenim si legi charitatis satisfacere, et meus discipulus atque regni mei haeres esse velis, ei qui in te peccavit et vt sibi ignoscas precatur, septua gies septies remittere oportet: qui numerus quadringenta et quadraginta nouem facit. Apud Lucam, vt in die septies remittamus iubet. Ponitur ergo numerus finitus pro infinito, et sensus est: Remissione delictorum, quibus in nos peccatur, nulli certo numero astringi debere, sed quotiescunque illa a nobis petunt qui nos offenderunt, et nos ad ignoscendum faciles et promptos esse debere. Idq; simpliciter affirmat, vt omnem praetextu eripiat ijs, qui sibi plus quidda quam aliis licere putat.
units.tr: Deut.23. Eph.5. 1.Cor.7. Leu.20. Amos 6. Isa.5. Deut.23, Psal.15. 1.Cor.6. But let us hear what the Lord answers Peter: "I tell you, not seven times, but seventy times seven." First he corrects Peter's presumption, and so judges of no account the very thing in which Peter took such pleasure. It is as if he said: "What do you say about forgiveness seven times, my good man? If you wish to satisfy the law of love and to be my disciple and heir of my kingdom, you must forgive seventy times seven the one who has sinned against you and asks you to pardon him." That number makes four hundred and ninety. In Luke he bids us forgive seven times in a day. A finite number is therefore put for an infinite one, and the meaning is this: the forgiveness of offences committed against us should be bound to no fixed number, but whenever those who have offended us ask for it, we ought to be ready and prompt to forgive. He states this plainly so as to take away every pretext from those who think they may claim more licence than others.

units.la: At quia carnis ingenium est, difficilem admodum sese praebere, et benefaciendo mox fatigari, prodest certas rationes in promptu habere, quibus nosipsos exhortemur. Inter has primum occurrit, nihil iniqui a nobis exigi, neque aliud Deum iubere, quam quod ipse facit. Etenim non possunt homines contra nos aliquid designare, quod non ipsi prius in Deum perpetrauerimus, vt supra cap. 6. demonstratum est. Attamen, vt tibi ille ignoscat precanti, et hoc ille liberaliter facit ijs, qui eius gratiam serio implorant. Cur igitur tu ijs, qui eiusdem sortis et conditionis sunt, te duriorem praebeas? Deinde meminerit, nihil tibi accidere insscio aut nolente Deo, qui vt alij nos offendat, iusto iudicio permittit, vel alicuius boni causa, quod ex eo sequetur, vel quod nos iam ita meruimus, aut quod carnis nostrae petulantiam sic coerceri opus est. Prioris exemplum in Iosepho habes, quem a fratribus vendi et in Aegypto seruum fieri voluit Deus, vt ea occasione eueniret ut seruaret populum multum: Et hoc ille perpendens fratribus culpam deprecantibus facile ignouit. Posterius vero Dauid obseruans, patienter ferebat maledici Semei conuitia, et quaecunque aduersus ipsum improbi hostes designabant. In primis hoc tenere oportet, quando conuitijs petimur atrocioribus. Quia enim vitia nostra ipsi non agnoscimus, amici vero nostri eadem dissimulant, vel prae amore etiam non vident, vel prae metu ignavo non audent carpere, hostium linguas in nos acuit Deus, vt ex his audiamus quae nobis cognitu sunt necessaria. Captemus ergo hanc vtilitatem ex inimicis (vt gentium sapientes monuerunt) nec patienter modò feramus quod faciunt aut dicunt, sed ex animo condonemus reprehensionibus. Quanta enim vtilitas ex amicis sperari potest, qui cum inimici essent, nobis beneficium non vulgare contulerunt? Tertio cogitemus, nos nobis vix alia ratione melius consulere posse quoad huius seculi vitam. Ita enim nos liberamus odio et inuidia, pessimis affectibus, qui vbi dominantur, cor exedunt, vitam amaram reddunt, imò dum valetudini officiunt, illius cursum abrumpunt. Postremò, vt Christi praecepto obediamus necesse est. Quia enim vita haec iniuriarum plena est, quas alij alijs scientes et ignorantes, volentes et nolentes faciunt, nisi ad condonandum propensi simus, nulla inter homines amicitia, nulla concordia, nulla pax consistere poterit. At quid iste sublatus, in vita hac iucundum erit? Solem e mundo tollunt (dicebat Cicero) qui amicitiam e vita tollunt. Accedit, quòd nisi alij alijs offensas remittamus, nos ipsos Deo inuisos facimus, et regni coelestis haereditatem amittimus, de quo in sequenti parabola ipse Christus prolixè differet. Nunc suffi-ciat has rationes breuiter annotauisse, vt harum consideratione innatam nobis vindictae cupiditatem restinguamus, si quando iniuriarum impatientia nos sentimus tentari.
units.tr: But because it is the nature of the flesh to be very hard to move, and to grow weary soon of doing good, it helps to have ready reasons by which we may encourage ourselves. Among these, the first to occur is that nothing unjust is demanded of us, and that God commands nothing other than what he himself does. For men cannot devise anything against us which we have not first committed against God, as was shown above in chapter 6. Yet when you ask him to pardon you, he does this freely for those who earnestly implore his grace. Why, then, should you show yourself harder toward those who are of the same lot and condition as you? Next, let him remember that nothing happens to him without God's knowledge or against his will. God, by a just judgement, allows one man to offend another either for the sake of some good that will follow from it, or because we have already so deserved it, or because our fleshly wantonness needs to be restrained in this way. As an example of the first you have Joseph, whom God willed to be sold by his brothers and made a slave in Egypt, so that by that occasion he might preserve a great people. Joseph, weighing this, readily forgave his brothers when they begged pardon for their fault. As an example of the second, David, observing it, patiently bore the reproaches of Shimei the cursing man and whatever the wicked enemies devised against him. Above all, this must be kept in mind when we are assailed with the most grievous reproaches. For since we do not recognise our own faults, and our friends either overlook them, or from love do not see them, or from cowardly fear do not dare to censure them, God sharpens the tongues of enemies against us, so that from these we may hear what it is necessary for us to know. Let us therefore draw this benefit from our enemies (as the wise men of the nations have advised), and not only bear patiently what they do or say, but forgive their rebukes from the heart. For how much benefit can we hope for from friends, who, when they were enemies, conferred on us no small kindness? Thirdly, let us consider that we can scarcely look after our own good better, as far as the life of this age is concerned, by any other means. For thus we free ourselves from hatred and envy, the worst passions, which, where they rule, eat away the heart, make life bitter, and indeed, while they harm our health, interrupt its course. Lastly, we must obey the precept of Christ. For since this life is full of injuries, which one man inflicts on another, knowingly and unknowingly, willingly and unwillingly, unless we are inclined to forgive, no friendship, no harmony, no peace can exist among men. But what will be pleasant in this life if that is taken away? "They take the sun out of the world," Cicero used to say, "who take friendship out of life." Moreover, unless we remit offences to one another, we make ourselves hateful to God and lose the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom, about which Christ himself will speak at length in the following parable. For now let it suffice to have noted these reasons briefly, so that by considering them we may quench the desire for revenge that is innate in us, if at any time we feel ourselves tempted by impatience at injuries.

units.la: Porrò quod alibi monuimus, hic quoque repetendum est, Christum de priuatis iniurijs et offensis loqui, quarum remissio nostri iuris est, vt sic dicam, vt nulla ex hac ad alios iniuria aut noxa redundet. Cauendum ergo, vt ita illas condonemus, ne probare videamur ea, quae per se iniqua sunt, et Deo displicent. Nam si hoc fiat, et proximo nocemus, qui adulatione ista in scelere confirmatur, et Dei gloriae derogamus. Multò minus ergo doctrinam hanc ad se transferre debent, qui in Magistratu ad Reipub. gubernacula sedent, et quibus iudicia sua Deus commisit, vt scelera puniant, et malum e medio populi sui extirpent. Etenim vt alij aliis ignoscamus necesse est, et culpam deprecantibus propitij simus in ijs quae ad nos priuatim spectant. At alia est magistratuum conditio, qui ex officio, quod eis Deus impossuit, iniurias et malefacta punire debent, et licet nemo accusset, improborum petulantiam, impostura et violentiam dignis supplicijs coercere. Vehementer ergo peccant illi, si quod priuatis hominibus dicitur, ipsi sibi applicent nulla sui munerus aut officij ratione habita. Excusant quidè sese nonnulli, dum impostoribus et iniquis vel scelerati...
units.tr: Furthermore, what we have stated elsewhere must be repeated here too: Christ is speaking of private injuries and offences, the remission of which is within our own right, so to speak, so that no harm or damage to others follows from it. Care must therefore be taken that we forgive them in such a way that we do not seem to approve what is in itself unjust and displeasing to God. For if this happens, we harm our neighbour, who is confirmed in wickedness by such flattery, and we detract from the glory of God. Far less, then, ought this teaching to be applied to themselves by those who sit at the helm of the commonwealth in the magistracy, and to whom God has committed his judgements, so that they may punish crimes and root out evil from the midst of his people. For we must forgive one another, and be merciful to those who beg pardon for their fault, in those matters which concern us privately. But the situation of magistrates is different: by the duty which God has laid upon them, they ought to punish injuries and wrongdoings, and even if no one brings an accusation, to restrain the insolence, deceit and violence of the wicked with fitting punishments. Those therefore sin grievously if they apply to themselves what is said to private persons, without any regard to the nature of their office and function. Some indeed excuse themselves, when they spare impostors and the unjust or the wicked…

units.la: Ratione quae ad condonandum nos excitent. ratis parcunt eo pratextu, quòd nemo de illis conqueratur, nemo accuset aut vt puniantur petat. Atqui calua plane est ista excusatio: Laudem merentur illi, qui sibi fastas iniurias condonant, & hominis Christiani officium faciunt. Ignauia autem & iniusta dissimulatione peccat iudex, si peripsum scelera impune grassentur: nam & improborum audaciam auget, & impunitatem inue- hit, quæ Reipublicæ nocet, & eos negligit, quorum fortunas, famam, corpus tueri debebat. Ideo Salomon dicebat, æque Deo exosum esse eum qui sontem absoluit, & eum qui insontem damnat. Pro uerb, 17.
units.tr: Reasons that stir us to forgive. Some spare them under this pretext: that no one complains about them, no one accuses them, or asks that they be punished. Yet this excuse is plainly worthless. Those who forgive injuries done to themselves deserve praise, and perform the office of a Christian man. But a judge sins by sloth and unjust dissimulation if wicked deeds run riot before him with impunity. For he increases the audacity of the wicked and brings in impunity, which harms the commonwealth, and he neglects those whose property, reputation and body he ought to protect. Therefore Solomon said that he who acquits the guilty and he who condemns the innocent are equally abominable to God. Prov. 17.

units.la: Praeterea consoletur nos locus hic aduersus conscientiæ tentationes, quas Satan mouet, si quando in peccata relabimur. Tunc enim persuadere conatur, indignos nos esse, quorum rursus misereatur Deus, vt iterum in gratiam recipiat, quam ipsi turpiter prostituerimus. At tunc memi nerimus, Deum ipsum hoc facere, quod a nobis exigit. Nec enim a nobis superari vult misericor- dia, bonitate, & gratuita debitorum remissione, quæ propria ipsius opera sunt, & (vt sæpe dixi- mus) in omnibus iudiciis eius eminent. Perpetuæ item sunt promissiones illæ: Viuo ego, nolo mor- tem peccatoris, sed vt conuertatur & viuat. Ego ego sum ille ipse, qui transgressiones tuas deleo, idque propter me, & peccatorum tuorum non recordabor. Et illud Christi semper ratum erit: Veni- te ad me omnes qui laboratis & onerati estis, & ego refocillabo vos: Si quis sitit, veniat ad me & bibat. Quæ omnia sic prædicantur, vt nulla vel conditio vel exceptio adiiciatur, quæ gratiam hanc restringat, aut aliquem eorum excludat, qui seria peccatorum pœnitentia tangitur, & cum fide vera ad throuum gratiæ Dei recurrit. Exempla quoque passim extant eorum, qui etsi ad eun- dem lapidem sæpius offenderint, tamen Dei misericordia seruati sunt, si ad illum conuersi hanc non sictis lachrymis expetiuerunt. Testatur hoc totus Iudicum liber, vt priuatorum hominum exem- pla præteream. Sed & ex Filii Dei mandato quotidie precamur: Remitte nobis debita nostra: quæ precatio friuola & irrita esset, si relabentibus in peccata remissio negaretur. Confutatur igitur hoc loco Nouatianorum error, qui relapsis post Baptismum pœnitentiam & remissionem peccatorum negabant, quod ipsum fere nostro seculo Anabaptistæ faciunt. Contra quos olim ex præsentis loci authoritate rectè dicebat Chrysostomus: ... quin millies refi- piscens ingredere. Sed plura de hac re in parabola dici poterunt, quæ proximè sequetur. Nunc im- mensam Dei bonitatem agnoscamus, qui fores gratuitæ misericordiæ nulli resipiscenti claudit, & eundem precemur cum Apostolis, vt sidem nobis confirmet & augeat, vt erga quosuis officio cha- ritatis defungamur in hoc seculo, in cœlis autem viuamus olim & regnemus cum æterno Filio IESV CHRISTO, cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Moreover, this passage will comfort us against the temptations of conscience which Satan stirs up whenever we fall back into sin. For then he tries to persuade us that we are unworthy that God should show mercy to us again, so that he would receive us once more into the favour which we ourselves have shamefully forfeited. But then let us remember that God himself does what he requires of us. For he does not want his mercy, his goodness, and the free remission of debts to be surpassed by us; these are his own proper works, and (as we have often said) they stand out in all his judgements. Likewise those promises are everlasting: "As I live, I do not desire the death of a sinner, but that he turn and live." "I, I am he who blots out your transgressions, and for my own sake, and I will not remember your sins." And that saying of Christ will always stand: "Come to me, all you who labour and are heavy laden, and I will refresh you. If anyone thirst, let him come to me and drink." All these things are proclaimed in such a way that no condition or exception is added which would restrict this grace, or exclude any of those who are touched by a genuine repentance for sins and with true faith have recourse to the throne of God's grace. There are also everywhere examples of those who, though they had stumbled over the same stone many times, were nevertheless preserved by the mercy of God, if they turned to him and sought it with unfeigned tears. The whole book of Judges bears witness to this, to say nothing of the examples of private men. And daily, too, by the command of the Son of God, we pray: "Forgive us our debts." This prayer would be frivolous and vain if forgiveness were denied to those who fall back into sin. This passage therefore refutes the error of the Novatians, who denied repentance and forgiveness of sins to those who had lapsed after baptism, which the Anabaptists in our own age nearly do as well. Against them Chrysostom rightly argued from the authority of this passage: "...nay, return a thousand times, repenting, and enter in." But more about this matter can be said in the parable which follows next. For now let us acknowledge the immense goodness of God, who closes the doors of free mercy to no one who repents, and let us pray to him with the Apostles that he would confirm and increase our faith, so that we may discharge every office of love toward whomever in this age, and in heaven hereafter may live and reign with the eternal Son Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCXXIII.
units.tr: HOMILY CCXXIII.

units.la: Propterea simile est regnum cœlorum homini Regi, qui voluit conferre rationem cum seruis suis. Et cum cœpisset conferre, obla- tus est quidam debitor decies mille talentorum. Cum autem is non posset hæc reddere, iussit eum dominus eius venundari, & vxorem eius & liberos, & omnia quæ habebat, & reddi debitum. Procidens ergo seruus ille adorabat eum, dicens: Domine, esto longanimis er- ga me, & omnia tibi reddam. Commotus autem misericordia domi- nus serui illius, dimisit eum, & debitum remisit ei.
units.tr: Therefore the kingdom of heaven is like a king who wished to settle accounts with his servants. When he began to settle them, one was brought before him who owed ten thousand talents. Since he could not pay, his lord ordered that he be sold, together with his wife, his children and all he possessed, and that the debt be paid. The servant therefore fell down and worshipped him, saying: "Lord, have patience with me, and I will repay you everything." Moved with compassion, the lord of that servant let him go and forgave him the debt.

units.la: Et si charitate fraterna nihil iucundius, nihil salutarius & magis necessarium sit, multa ta- men quotidie fiunt ex innato hominibus philautia & priuata vindicta cupiditatis vitio, quæ illam dissoluunt & turbas pariunt. Aduersus ea remedium nullum præsentius est, quam vt absq; mora reconciliemur cum iis qui nos offenderunt. Vt enim ignis subito accensus facilè reslin- guitur, si confestim aquam infundas: idem vero si cunctéris, vires acquirit & incendium parit in- extinguibile: ita non magni laboris est dissidia componere, si in tempore iis occurratur, prius- quam ira in odium & hoc in inimicitias implacabiles exarserit. Idcirco Dominus noster IESVS CHRISTVS
units.tr: Although nothing is more pleasant, more wholesome and more necessary than brotherly love, many things happen every day from the self-love that is innate in human beings and from the vice of private revenge and desire, which dissolve love and produce disturbances. Against these there is no more ready remedy than to be reconciled at once with those who have offended us. For just as a fire, suddenly kindled, is easily put out if you pour water on it at once, but if you delay it gains strength and becomes an unquenchable blaze, so it is no great labour to settle quarrels if they are met in time, before anger has flared into hatred and hatred into implacable enmity. For this reason our Lord Jesus Christ

units.la: offensis cita reconciliatio ne opus est.
units.tr: has no need of a quick reconciliation of offences.

units.la: CHRISTVS, qui discipulos suos in dilectione mutua synceros & constantes esse vult, de duobus illos admonuit observatu necessarijs: Primum, ut si qui te laesit, cunctetur, tu prior illum convenias, & omnia tentes, quibus possit lucrifieri. Deinde, ut si ipse facti poenitentia ductus petat, ut culpam admissam ipsi condones, tu te facilem praebeas & placabilem: & licet iniuriam iteret, rursus autem veniam sibi dari petat, tunc quoq; illam impetret, adeo ut ne septuages septies repetitis offensis te superari sinas, quo minus conversum & culpam deprecantem benigne suscipias. Argumenta, quae nos ut hoc faciamus monere debent, multa sunt, inter quae gravissimum merito censeri debet, quod nisi id fiat, salus nobis constare non potest, cum proprijs precibus nosipsos damnemus, quoties dicimus: Remitte nobis debita nostra, sicut & nos remittimus debitoribus nostris. At quoniam in hoc certamine cito fatigamur, si iniurius in nos esse pergat is, cui aliquoties signo-uimus, totam hanc causam eleganti parabola illustrat Dominus, qua ipsius Dei exemplum nobis proponit, & hoc ita tractat, ut communis sensus unumquemq; admonere possit, inexcusabiles esse eos, qui illud imitari dedignantur.
units.tr: Christ, who wills that his disciples be sincere and steadfast in mutual love, warned them about two things that must be observed. First, that if someone has wronged you, you should not delay but go to him first and try every means by which he may be gained. Second, that if he, moved by repentance for what he has done, asks that you pardon the fault he committed, you should show yourself easy to appease and ready to forgive; and even if he repeats the injury and again asks to be pardoned, you should then grant it too, so that you do not allow yourself to be overcome by offences repeated seventy times seven, but receive kindly the one who turns back and asks pardon for his fault. There are many reasons that ought to move us to do this, among which the weightiest, rightly reckoned, is this: unless we do so, our salvation cannot stand, since we condemn ourselves by our own prayer whenever we say: "Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors." But since in this struggle we soon grow weary if the one whom we have often pardoned goes on wronging us, the Lord illustrates this whole matter by an elegant parable, in which he sets before us the example of God himself, and treats it in such a way that common sense can admonish each one that those who disdain to imitate it are inexcusable.

units.la: Partes parabolae tres sunt.
units.tr: The parable has three parts.

units.la: Prima Dei bonitatem commendat, qui miseris nobis debita quantumuis multa & magna gratis remittit, si id seriò petamus. Secunda communem malitiam & ingratitudinem arguit, plerique in Deum & homines peccant, dum se immites & inexorabiles praebet fratribus & conservus suis, qui ipsos offenderunt. Postrema poenam istis denuntiat. Primam partem modo recitauimus, quam ita proponit Dominus: Propterea simile est regnum caelorum homini Regi, qui voluit conferre rationem cum servis suis, &c. Regnum caelorum vocat totum Ecclesiae & salutis, quae in hac sola inuenitur, mysterium sive dispensatione. Sensus itaq; verborum Christi est: Negotiu salutis aeternae inter Deum & homines ita se habet, ut inter herum & servos solet fieri quoad dispensationem pecuniarum & aliarum rerum temporalium. Estq; haec parabolae pars diligenti consideratione dignissima, quia universum nostrae iustificationis mysterium, ex quo omnis salus nostra dependet, ceu in tabula spectandum proponit. Ut ergo res illustrior fit, & melius seruiat institutioni nostrae, singula illius membra ex ordine inspiciemus.
units.tr: The first commends the goodness of God, who freely forgives us wretched people debts however many and great, if we seriously ask it. The second rebukes the common malice and ingratitude of people, since many sin against God and men when they show themselves merciless and unforgiving toward their brothers and fellow servants who have offended them. The last announces punishment to these. We have just recited the first part, which the Lord sets forth thus: Therefore the kingdom of heaven is like a king who wished to settle accounts with his servants, etc. By the kingdom of heaven he means the whole mystery and dispensation of the Church and of salvation, which is found in this alone. The sense of Christ's words therefore is: the business of eternal salvation between God and men stands as it usually does between a master and his servants in the management of money and other temporal goods. And this part of the parable is most worthy of careful consideration, because it sets before us, as on a tablet to be looked at, the whole mystery of our justification, on which all our salvation depends. So that the matter may be clearer and better serve our instruction, we shall examine its individual members in order.

units.la: Principio Deus homini Regi confertur, rationem cum servis suis conferenti. Rex dicitur Deus, utpote omnium creator & Dominus, cuius nutu omnia reguntur, quae in caelo & in terra sunt. Talem se ipse profitetur, dicens: Caelum thronus meus est, terra vero scabellum pedum meorum. Idem vero homo dicitur, partim propter amore, quo genus humanum complectitur, & quo se sese demittit, & nostro captui accommodat, ut pleraq; de illo in Scripturis ἀνθρωπομόρφως dicantur: partim quod aeternus ille Filius, qui unum cum Patre est, hominem in persona unitatem assumpsit, ut idem Deus & Homo fit. Is in servos suos inquirit, & rationem cum illis conferre dicitur: Non est ergo otiosus, quale Epicurus fingebat, neq; securus eorum quae in terris fiunt, ad cardines caeli obambulat: sed ut omnia Verbo suo omnipotente creauit, ita omnia videt, seruat & gubernat. Idem quia sapientissimus & iustissimus est, nihil temere, sed omnia certa cum ratione facit, neminem item ἀχρίτως, id est, indicta causa damnat, sed omnium quae fiunt aut iam facta sunt, rationes & causas inspicit & aequa lance examinat. Adhaec ut bonus paterfamilias a servis suis: ita ille ab hominibus, quorum seruitio vitur, dictorum & factorum omnium rationes exigit. Quo loco in primis meminisse oportet, neminē mortalium tantae authoritatis aut tam potente seu aflutum esse, ut sese subducere, aut quo minus rationem reddat, subterfugere possit. Citat enim ille nos quando cunq; vult, & citati se ipsi sistere coguntur. Fit hoc nobis sanis & integris corpore inter graues consci-entiae tentationes, quae omnium quae vnquam fecimus aut diximus memoriam renouant. Fit idem in mortis articulo, & olim publicè in totius mundi conspectu fiet in gloriose Filij Dei aduentu, quando non factis modo nostris, verumetiam quouis verbo otioso ratione reddemus. Neq; hic testibus aut indicijs opus erit Deo, qui nihil ignorat, sed corda & renes scrutatur, & unumquemq; propriae conscientiae testimonio convincit. De eo omnes perpetuò cogitare debebat in sua vocatione, ut actiones suas secundum illius voluntatē instituerent, cui olim de illis ratio erit reddenda. At hic plerique offenduntur, dum alij carnis suae rationes sequuntur, alij mundo placere studet, multi principibus suis obsequuntur. Atqui caro concupiscit aduersus spiritum & qui hominibus vel mundo placere volunt, Dei serui non sunt, imò amicitia mundi huius est inimicitia cum Deo. Deinde ad
units.tr: First, God is compared to a king who settles accounts with his servants. The king is God, as the creator and Lord of all, by whose nod all things are governed that are in heaven and on earth. He himself professes to be such, saying: Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool. Yet he is called a man, partly on account of the love by which he embraces the human race, and by which he humbles himself and adapts himself to our capacity, so that many things about him in the Scriptures are said [in human form, ἀνθρωπομόρφως]; partly because that eternal Son, who is one with the Father, has assumed a human being into unity of person, so that he is both God and man. He inquires into his servants and is said to settle accounts with them. He is therefore not idle, as Epicurus imagined, nor careless of what happens on earth, wandering about the corners of heaven; but as he created all things by his all-powerful Word, so he sees, preserves and governs all things. And because he is most wise and most just, he does nothing rashly, but does all things with certain reason, and he condemns no one [without judgment, ἀκρίτως], that is, without a hearing of the case, but examines the reasons and causes of all things that are done or have been done, and weighs them with an even balance. Moreover, as a good householder demands accounts from his servants, so he demands from the men whose service he uses an account of all their words and deeds. Here above all we must remember that no mortal is of such authority or so powerful or so clever that he can escape or evade giving an account. For he summons us whenever he wishes, and those summoned are compelled to present themselves. This happens to us while we are sound and whole in body, amid the grave temptations of conscience, which renew the memory of everything we have ever done or said. It happens also at the moment of death, and one day it will happen publicly, in the sight of the whole world, at the coming of the glorious Son of God, when we shall give an account not only of our deeds but of every idle word. Nor will God need witnesses or evidence here, for he knows all things, searches hearts and kidneys, and convicts each one by the testimony of his own conscience. Everyone ought always to think of this in his calling, so that he may order his actions according to the will of him to whom an account of them must one day be given. But here many go astray: some follow the reasons of their own flesh, others strive to please the world, many obey their rulers. Yet the flesh lusts against the Spirit, and those who want to please men or the world are not servants of God; indeed, friendship with this world is enmity with God. Then to
