units.la: Gal.5.1 Iac.4 Dei tribunal omnes sistemur, vbi neq; mundi fautor, neq; principū authoritas nos tuebitur: imò te-cum coram illo iudice sistentur hi quos tu tibi patronos fore speras, & illis ipsis testibus cōuincēris, te mundum & eius amicitiam plurīs fecisse quàm Deum & Verbum eius: ideoq; dignum esse, qui cum mundo incurabili & eius principe condemnēris. Vide Matt.10. Mar.8.
units.tr: Gal. 5.1; Jas. 4. We shall all be brought before the tribunal of God, where neither the favour of the world nor the authority of princes will protect us; indeed, those whom you hope will be your patrons will stand with you before that judge, and you will be convicted by those very witnesses that you valued the world and its friendship more than God and his Word, and therefore deserve to be condemned along with the incurable world and its prince. See Matt. 10; Mark 8.

units.la: Porrò rationem conferenti cum feruis hero isti offertur quidam debitor decies mille talento-rum. Talentum non eiusdem valoris apud omnes gentes fuit, vsitatissimum vero fuit Atticum, quod Coronatos Gallicos sexcentos valere ex eorum calculo conflat, qui antiquitatis inuestigato res diligentissimi fuerunt. Itaq; decies mille talenta milliones coronatorum sex, conficiunt. Notatur ergo summa, quam nemo seruus posset soluere, vtpote qui iam ante seipsum, & omnia sua hero debeat. Est autem seruus hic typus humani generis, & quae omnium nostrum conditio sit, docet.
units.tr: Moreover, to that lord, settling accounts with his servants, there is brought a certain debtor who owed ten thousand talents. The talent was not of the same value among all nations, but the most common was the Attic talent, which, as those who have investigated antiquity most diligently agree in their calculation, was worth six hundred French crowns. Thus ten thousand talents make six million crowns. The sum is therefore marked out, which no servant could pay, since he already owes himself and all his possessions to his lord. This servant, moreover, is a type of the human race, and shows what the condition of all of us is.

units.la: Sumus omnes Dei serui, & vt tales sumus, ab illo conditi: Vt autem in istis rationibus omnes ferui debitores fuerunt, ita de nobis fiet, si rationes nobiscum Deus subducat. Vt enim viri principes & opulenti in rationum suarum codicibus habent titulos varios & diuersos: ita Deus in Lege praecepta habet omnis generis, quibus quid ipsi debeamus docet. Sut prima tabula praecepta, inter quae praecipuum est, vt vnum Deum agnoscamus, in quo omnis salutis fiducia nobis repositā sit: & ad huius praecepti expositionē facit, quod Moses dicit: Audi Israel, Dominus Deus tuus Deus vnus est. Diliges igitur Dominum Deum tuum ex toto corde tuo, ex tota anima tua, & ex omnibus viribus tuis. Item Dominum Deum tuum timebis, & ei soli seruies. Alterum praeceptum est, ne Deo alicuius rei similitudinem affingamus, neq; cultum aut honorem aliquem simulachris quali-bus unq; tribuamus. Tertium, ne sacrosanctum Dei nomen temere vsurpemus, multò minus eo impie ad dolum & scelus aliquod abutamur. Quartum, vt Sabbatu sanctificemus, & quod Deus sibi consecratum esse voluit otiū nullo labore non necessario, nullo item scelere profanemus. Sunt deinde praecepta secunda tabula, quae omnia sub fraterna charitatis Lege continentur, quae vt proximum sicuti nosipsos diligamus iubet. Vt etiam ergo cades, adulteria & stupra, furta & rapinas, testimonia falsa & calumnias. At omnia ista ad postremum praeceptum, quod de concupiscentia est, refert optimus interpres Christi s, & reos agit omnes, qui aliquid concupiscunt, quod Lex tangere prohibet. At si Legis codice siue tabulas proferat Deus, & a primo praecepto exorsus, rationes dilectorum & factorum nobis cōferat, nos in omnibus illis transgressores, & proinde debitores Dei esse patebit, eoq; grauius & infolubilius esse hoc debitum, quod cum a Deo quotidie nouis beneficiis accumulemur (vt qui in illo viuimus, mouemur & sumus) nō modò nihil pro illis repetimus, sed neq; debita officia illi praestamus, quibus sumus obstricti. Quotus enim quisq; est, qui vni & soli Deo fidat in omni periculorum genere? cuius cor non alio interdum respiciat? qui illū ex toto corde amet & ueneretur? qui non aliquando illi mundum, honores, opes, voluptates praeferat? Quem item dabimus, qui non interdum Deo formam & imaginem alienam affingat, aut idolafi-bi fabricet ex ijs, quae in hoc mundo veneratur & suspicit? Quis vero gloriari poterit, se nunquā Dei nomine abusum esse, aut saltem incogitantius quàm decebat illud nominasse? Aut quis ille est, qui dicat, se Sabbatū semper sanctificasse? aut qui negare possit, se illo die sapius fecisse, quae nunquam fieri debebant? Idem dici poterit, si ad secunda tabulae praecepta vitam anteactam, & nosipsos examinemus. Nam etsi obsequium & honore debitū praestemus parentibus & ijs, qui parentum loco sunt, etsi neminem occidamus, nullius thorum violemus, nullius pecunias aut facultates praeter ius rapiamus, linguam deniq; contineamus ne quem laedat, quis se ab omni cupiditate immune dicere poterit? In multis labimur omnes, vt Apostolus ait, & septies in die cadit iustus: & quia cum bonis nostris operibus carnis cupiditates, & cogitationes praue concurrunt, iustitiae etiam nostrae in star sordidorum centonum polluta sunt. Ergo in Dei are sumus, & omnibus dicī potest, quod olim Iudaeis dicebat Moses: Hoccine rependis Domino populestulte & non sapiens? Sumus autem debitores decies mille talentorum; Id est, peccata nostra tam multa & tam grauia sunt, vt non simus soluendo. Superant enim (vt Dauid ait) omnes nostras vires & facultates, quae reuera nullae sunt. Intelle&us hominis animalis non percipit quae sunt spiritus Dei. Voluntas igitur ad malum propendet, & omnia cordis figmenta ab ineunte aetate praua sunt: neq; ipsi his morbis possumus mederi, qui ex nobis ipsis ne ad cogitandum quidem idonei sumus. Et hac quidem ita se habere, fatebuntur omnes, qui in Dei rationario vel Legis speculo sese paulò diligentius contemplati fuerint.
units.tr: We are all servants of God, and as such we were created by him. But just as in those accounts all the servants were debtors, so it will be with us if God reckons accounts with us. For just as great and wealthy men have various and different titles in the account books of their affairs, so God in the Law has precepts of every kind, by which he teaches what we owe him. The first tablet contains the precepts, the chief of which is that we acknowledge the one God, in whom all confidence of salvation is placed for us. To the explanation of this precept belongs what Moses says: "Hear, Israel, the Lord your God is one God. You shall therefore love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your strength." Likewise: "You shall fear the Lord your God and serve him alone." The second precept is that we should not fashion any likeness of God, nor ever give worship or honour to any images whatsoever. The third is that we not rashly use the holy name of God, much less abuse it impiously for deceit or any crime. The fourth is that we sanctify the Sabbath, and not profane the rest that God wished to be consecrated to himself, with any unnecessary labour or any wickedness. Then there are the precepts of the second tablet, all of which are contained under the law of brotherly love, which bids us love our neighbour as ourselves. So also murders, adulteries and fornications, thefts and robberies, false witness and calumnies are forbidden. But the best interpreter of Christ refers all these to the last precept, which concerns concupiscence, and makes guilty all who desire anything the Law forbids them to touch. But if God should bring forward the codex or tablets of the Law, and beginning from the first precept, should set before us the reckoning of our words and deeds, it will be plain that we are transgressors in all those things, and therefore debtors of God. This debt is all the more serious and insoluble, since although we are daily heaped with new benefits from God (for in him we live, move and have our being), we not only repay nothing for them, but do not even render him the due duties to which we are bound. For how few are there who trust in the one and only God in every kind of danger? Whose heart does not sometimes look elsewhere? Who loves and reveres him with all his heart? Who does not at some time prefer the world, honours, wealth and pleasures to him? Again, whom will we find who does not sometimes fashion for God a strange form and image, or make an idol for himself from those things which he venerates and admires in this world? Who indeed can boast that he has never abused the name of God, or at least has not named it more thoughtlessly than was fitting? Or who is he who says he has always sanctified the Sabbath? Or who can deny that on that day he has more often done things that should never have been done? The same can be said if we examine our past life and ourselves by the precepts of the second tablet. For although we render the obedience and honour owed to parents and to those who stand in their place, although we kill no one, violate no one's bed, seize no one's money or property beyond right, and finally restrain our tongue lest it harm anyone, who can say he is free from every desire? We all stumble in many things, as the Apostle says, and the righteous falls seven times a day; and because fleshly desires and wicked thoughts run together with our good works, even our righteousnesses are polluted, like a rag stained with filth. So we stand in debt to God, and it can be said to all what Moses once said to the Jews: "Is this how you repay the Lord, foolish and unwise people?" We are indeed debtors of ten thousand talents; that is, our sins are so many and so grave that we cannot pay. For they exceed (as David says) all our strength and resources, which in truth are nothing. The natural man does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God. The will therefore inclines towards evil, and all the imaginations of the heart are wicked from youth. Nor can we ourselves heal these diseases, since we are not even fit to think of good from ourselves. And all who have looked somewhat more carefully into God's account book or the mirror of the Law will confess that these things are so.

units.la: Quid ergo meremur, si Rex & Herus noster Deus ius suum persequi velit? Hoc in praesenti Christus docet, de seruo isto dicens: Cum autem non posset haec reddere, iussit eum dominus eius venundari, & vxorem eius & liberos, & omnia quae habebat, ac reddi debitum. Quae verba non eo sensu accipi debent, quasi hac ratione hero isti satisfieri, ac debitum omne dissolui potuerit. Quem enim seruum dabis tanti pretij, qui etsi cum vxore, liberis & omnibus suis fortunis vendatur, pro tanta summa aris alieni possit satisfacere? Enimuero cum & ipse & quaecunq; habet, seruitij iure ad herum pertineant, hic quidem quod suum est repetere poterit, de summa vero debiti nihil decedet. Eadem plane est omnium nostrum ratio. Etenim Deo nosipsos & omnia nostra debemus, nec aliquid habemus quod non ab eo acceperimus. Peccando autem debitores & rei mortis sumus.
units.tr: What then do we deserve, if our King and Lord God wishes to pursue his right? Christ teaches this in the present passage, speaking of that servant: "But when he could not repay, his lord ordered him to be sold, along with his wife and children and all that he had, and the debt to be paid." These words ought not to be taken in the sense that by this means the master could be satisfied and the whole debt discharged. For what servant will you find of such worth that, even if he were sold with his wife, children and all his possessions, he could satisfy so great a sum of debt? Indeed, since both he and all that he has belong to the master by right of service, the master can reclaim what is his, but nothing will be taken off the sum of the debt. It is plainly the same reckoning for all of us. For we owe God ourselves and all that is ours, nor do we have anything that we have not received from him. But by sinning we become debtors and liable to death.

units.la: Quia vero vnumquodq; peccatum mortem sempiternam meretur (Dei enim dictum siue decretum est: Quacunq; die ex arbore hac comederis, morte morieris: Item, Maledictus qui non fecerit omnia quae scripta sunt in libro Legis huius) quid fiat, si tot millia peccatorum concurrant, quae ab ineunte aetate cogitando, concupiscendo, dicendo item & faciendo, imo etiam tacendo & otiando, id est, debitum obsequium aut officium negligendo, commisimus? Nulla ergo spes satisfactionis reliqua est. Vendatur totus mundus, eius tamen pretio ne vnius quidem hominis anima redimi poterit, teste Christo, qui nuper dixit: Quid prodest cuipiam si totum mundum lucratus fuerit, anima vero sua mulctetur? aut quam dabit homo compensationem animae suae. Nemo igitur ex hoc loco satisfactionis meritum colligat, quod omnino nullum est. Etenim pro more veterum loquitur Christus, qui erat, vt debitores qui soluendo non erant, vel vinculis constringebantur, vel vendebatur, aut etiam si pluribus deberent, in partes secarentur. Fuerunt enim antiqui iustitiae & fidei datae acerrimi vindices, & inter gentes fere omnes grauiter animaduersum fuit in eos, qui sub mutui praetextu creditores fallebat. Nam vt apud Gellium legitur, adimi vel e medio tolli putauerunt sub fidium hoc inopiae temporariae, quo communis hominum vita maximè indiget, si perfidia debitorum sine graui poena eluderet. Caeterum Christus in praesenti venditionis meminit, vt doceat, quid mereamur, si Deus stricto iure nobiscum agere velit, & (vt ex sequentibus patebit) quam necesse nobis sit ad misericordiae Dei thronum supplices confugere. Venditio enim haec alienatione a Deo & regno eius denotat, quae aequissimo iure debetur iis, qui seipsos sub peccatu vendiderunt, & cum Dei serui esse deberent, Satanae sese manciparunt. Atqui hoc de omnibus hominibus dici potest, si quales natura sua sint spectes, Apostolus testatur, de seipso loquens: Lex spiritualis est, at ego carnalis sum, venundatus sub peccatum, &c. Rom.7.cap.
units.tr: Since indeed each sin deserves eternal death (for it is God's word or decree: "On whatever day you eat from this tree, you shall die the death"; also, "Cursed is he who does not do all that is written in the book of this Law"), what happens if so many thousands of sins coincide, which from youth we have committed by thinking, desiring, speaking and doing, indeed even by keeping silent and idling, that is, by neglecting the obedience or duty owed? No hope of satisfaction is therefore left. Let the whole world be sold; yet not even the soul of one man can be redeemed with its price, as Christ attests, who recently said: "What does it profit a man if he gains the whole world and forfeits his soul? Or what will a man give in exchange for his soul?" Let no one therefore gather from this passage the merit of satisfaction, which is entirely nonexistent. For Christ speaks after the manner of the ancients, when it was the custom that debtors who could not pay were either bound in chains or sold, or even, if they owed to several creditors, cut into pieces. For the ancients were keen avengers of justice and good faith, and among almost all nations those who deceived creditors under the pretext of a loan were severely punished. For, as is read in Gellius, they thought that this temporary lack of means, which common human life especially needs, should be taken away or removed from the midst if the faithlessness of debtors could escape without grave punishment. Otherwise, Christ in the present passage mentions the sale in order to teach what we deserve if God wishes to deal with us by strict right, and (as will be clear from what follows) how necessary it is for us to flee as suppliants to the throne of God's mercy. For this sale denotes alienation from God and his kingdom, which by the most just right is owed to those who have sold themselves under sin, and who, when they ought to be servants of God, have handed themselves over to Satan. And indeed this can be said of all men, if you look at what they are by nature; the Apostle bears witness, speaking of himself: "The law is spiritual, but I am carnal, sold under sin," and so on. Rom. 7.

units.la: Quid ergo faciamus aliud, quam quod de isto seruo dicitur? qui procidens ad heri pedes adorat eum, dicens: Domine, esto longanimis erga me, & omnia tibi reddam. Agnoscit se miserum esse cui gratuita remissione opus sit: Petit autè dilationem, & omnia se reddere velle pollicetur; quod de more debitorum dicitur, qui soluendo sunt: vel potius arguitur vulgaris obaeratorum leuitas, qua non pudet eos polliceri, quod se nunquam praestituros esse norunt. Itaq; hoc minimè in exemplum trahi debet, quoad causam hanc, quae nobis apud Deum agenda est, cui (vt paulò ante diximus) nemo potest satisfacere. Itaq; in eo solo imitemur seruulum hunc, vt primo toto corde contriti procidamus coram Deo & sub eius potenti manu humiliemur. Non desperemus autem, sed adoremus illum, & precibus testemur, nos de eius misericordia spem bonam animo concepisse. Quoad vero solutionem debitorum nostrorum, nihil polliceamur, sed fateamur ingenuè, haec plura & graviora esse, quàm vt simus soluendo. Velle quidem & optare ex animo debemus, vt Deo possimus satisfacere: sed quia ad eam perfectionem nunquam peruenire possumus, quoad in carne hac viuimus, fateamur Deo quod res est, ne Pharisaeorum confidentiae similes efficiamur, qui dum suorum meritorum enumeratione & ementitis satisfactionibus Deo volunt fucum facere, seipsos fallunt, & debitorum summam magis aggrauant. Nos cum Dauide & aliis sanctis Dei seruis dicamus: Ne intres Domine in iudicium cum seruo tuo: quia non iustificabitur in conspectu tuo vllus viuens. Si iniquitates obseruees ô Deus, Domine quis subsistet? Delictorum iuuentutis meae & transgressionum mearum ne memineris: sed secundum clementiam tuam memento mei, propter bonitatem bonitatem tuam. Huius generis exempla in nouoetiam Testamento occurrunt, vt peccatrici, quae ad Christi pedes confidens, eos lachrymis ex contrito corde manantibus abluit: publicani item, qui non ausus oculos ad Deum attollere clamabat, Domine, propitius esto mihi peccatori, &c. Lucae 7. & 18.
units.tr: What then shall we do, other than what is said of that servant? He fell down at his lord's feet, worshipped him, and said: "Lord, have patience with me, and I will pay you everything." He acknowledges that he is wretched and needs free forgiveness. But he asks for time, and promises that he will repay everything, as debtors commonly say when they are able to pay; or rather, this shows the common levity of debtors, who are not ashamed to promise what they know they will never deliver. Therefore this should by no means be taken as an example in the case that we have to deal with before God, for which (as we said a little while ago) no one can make satisfaction. So in this respect alone let us imitate this little servant: first, crushed in our whole heart, let us fall down before God and humble ourselves under his mighty hand. Yet let us not despair, but worship him and by our prayers bear witness that we have conceived good hope in his mercy. As for paying our debts, let us promise nothing, but frankly confess that these are too many and too great for us to be able to pay. We ought indeed to wish and desire from our hearts that we might satisfy God; but since we can never attain that perfection while we live in this flesh, let us tell God the truth, lest we become like the confidence of the Pharisees, who, while they wish to deceive God by reckoning up their merits and by feigned satisfactions, deceive themselves and rather increase the sum of their debts. Let us say with David and the other holy servants of God: "Enter not into judgment with your servant, for no living man shall be justified in your sight" (Ps. 143); "If you, O God, should mark iniquities, Lord, who could stand?" (Ps. 130); "Remember not the sins of my youth and my transgressions, but according to your mercy remember me, for your goodness' sake" (Ps. 25). Examples of this kind also occur in the New Testament: the sinful woman who, falling at Christ's feet, washed them with tears flowing from a contrite heart (Luke 7); and likewise the publican, who did not dare to lift his eyes to God but cried out: "Lord, be merciful to me, a sinner" (Luke 18).

units.la: Horum vestigijs si insistamus, nostrae saluti consultum erit. Docet hoc Cataftrophe huius loci, plena consolationis. Dicit enim Christus: Commotus autem misericordia Dominus ferui illius, dimisit eum, & debitum remisit ei. In quibus verbis primo obseruari debet, salutem nostram ex gratuita Dei misericordia pendere, vt modo diximus. Non enim temerariae & stultae promissionis ergo, qua debiti solutione seruulus iste pollicitus fuit, herus illi pepercit, sed misericordia motus hoc fecit. Ita nullo nostrorum operum aut meritorum respectu, sed ex gratia nostri miseretur Deus. Eo autem argumento eius bonitas commendatur, quod licet inter precandum multa temere & inepte effutiamus, multa etiam indigne faciamus, quando optimi sumus, non tamen illa nobis fraudi esse vult Pater ille indulgentissimus, qui nos ex terra & puluere factos esse nouit, & proinde infirmitatis nostrae ratione habet. Deinde modus & ordo salutis indicatur, quando seruum hunc dimisit herus, & debitu ei remisit. Dimissione opus habebat, quia iam vinctus tenebatur, vt abduCtus ve nundaretur. Rursus vt dimissio illa securu faceret, remissione debiti opus erat. Ita nobiscum agit Deus. Nam, vt nuper monuimus, sumus nos quoq; vinculis peccati & vitiosae naturae constricti: sed dimittit nos Deus & libertate donat: neue peccatorum conscientia nos salutis incertos & animos perpetuo detineat, illa liberaliter remittit & condonat. Postremo ne Deus hic aliquid temere aut leuiter, vel etiam iniuste agere putetur, meminisse oportet, remissione peccatorum gratis quidem fieri quoad nos, qui non sumus soluendo, interim aut iustitiae Dei tampridem satisfactum esse per Filium Vnigenitum, qui homo factus debitum illud peccati quo tenebamur, in se recepit, pro eodem mortis & sanguinis sui merito satisfecit, & chirographum Legis, quod aduersum nos erat, cruci affixum e medio sustulit. Et hoc illud est, quod olim per Isaiam promisit Deus: Ego ego ille ipse sum, qui deleo transgressiones tuas, idque propter me, & peccatorum tuorum non recordabor. Itaq; nobis horum omnium vsus esto, vt primum agnoscamus nos peccatores esse ac mortis aeternae reos. Deinde ne ideo desperemus, sed confugiamus ad thronum gratiae Dei per fidem in IESVM CHRISTVM, cuius sanguine peccata nostra deleta sunt, & qui via est vnica, qua ad Patrem venitur. Non dubitemus autem de satisfactione eius, ne forte illam non ratam habeat Pater. Hic enim ipsum nobis Seruatorem praedestinauit ab aeterno, eundem prisci Patribus promisit, & de eode caelitus testatus est, dicens: Hic est Filius ille meus dilectus, in quo placatus sum. Idem ille omnes, qui laborant & onerati sunt, ad se vocat, & neminem ad se venientem reiicit. Huic debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: If we follow in their footsteps, it will be good for our salvation. This is taught by the outcome of this passage, which is full of consolation. For Christ says: "The lord of that servant, moved with compassion, released him and forgave him the debt" (Matt. 18). In these words, first, it must be observed that our salvation depends on the free mercy of God, as we have just said. For the lord did not spare that servant because of his rash and foolish promise, by which he undertook to pay the debt, but he did it moved by mercy. Thus God has compassion on us not from any regard to our works or merits, but out of grace. Moreover, his goodness is commended by this argument: although in praying we utter many things rashly and foolishly, and also do many things unworthily while we are at our best, that most indulgent Father does not want these to be held against us; he knows that we were made out of earth and dust, and therefore takes account of our weakness. Next, the manner and order of salvation is indicated, when the lord released the servant and forgave him the debt. He needed release, because he was already held bound, so that he would be led away and sold. Again, for that release to make him secure, forgiveness of the debt was necessary. So God deals with us. For, as we recently warned, we too are bound by the chains of sin and of our corrupt nature; but God releases us and grants us liberty; and lest the awareness of our sins keep us uncertain of salvation and perpetually troubled in spirit, he freely remits and pardons them. Lastly, lest God be thought to act rashly or lightly, or even unjustly, here we must remember that the forgiveness of sins is indeed free so far as we are concerned, since we cannot pay; yet meanwhile the justice of God was long ago satisfied through the Only-begotten Son, who, made man, took upon himself that debt of sin by which we were held, and by the merit of his death and blood made satisfaction for it, and nailed to the cross and took out of the way the handwriting of the Law, which was against us. This is what God promised long ago through Isaiah: "I, I am he who blots out your transgressions, and for my own sake I will not remember your sins" (Isa. 43). Therefore make use of all these things for this purpose: first, that we recognise that we are sinners and liable to eternal death; then, that we should not on that account despair, but flee to the throne of God's grace through faith in Jesus Christ, by whose blood our sins have been blotted out, and who is the only way by which one comes to the Father. Let us not doubt his satisfaction, lest perhaps the Father should not accept it. For he himself appointed him from eternity to be our Saviour, promised the same to the ancient fathers, and bore witness from heaven concerning him, saying: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased." He himself calls to himself all who labour and are burdened, and he rejects no one who comes to him. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCXXIIII.
units.tr: HOMILIA CCXXIIII.

units.la: Egressus vero seruus ille inuenit vnum ex conferuis suis, qui debebat ei centum denarios: & praehensum illum suffocabat, dicens: Redde quod debes. Procidens ergo conseruus eius ad eius pedes, precabatur eum dicens: Esto longanimis erga me, & omnia reddam tibi. Ille vero noluit: sed abiens coniecit eum in carcerem, quoufq; redderet debitum. Cum autem vidissent conserui eius quae facta fuerant, contristati sunt vehementer: & cum venissent declararunt domino suo omnia quae facta fuerant. Tunc eo aduocato dominus ipsius, dixit ei: Serue male, totum debitum illud remisi tibi, quia precatus es me. Nonne oportuit & te miserieri conseruo tui, vt & ego tui miser- tus sum? Tunc iratus dominus eius tradidit eum tortoribus, vsque quo redderet illud omne quod sibi debebatur. Ita & Pater meus coelestis faciet vobis, nisi remiseritis suo quisq; fratri ex cordibus vestris offensas eorum.
units.tr: But when that servant went out, he found one of his fellow servants who owed him a hundred denarii; and seizing him, he throttled him, saying: "Pay what you owe." So his fellow servant fell down at his feet and begged him, saying: "Be patient with me, and I will repay you everything." But he would not; instead he went away and threw him into prison, until he should repay the debt. When his fellow servants saw what had been done, they were deeply grieved, and they came and reported to their lord all that had happened. Then his lord summoned him and said to him: "You wicked servant, I forgave you all that debt, because you begged me. Should you not also have had mercy on your fellow servant, as I had mercy on you?" And in anger his lord handed him over to the torturers, until he should repay all that was owed to him. So also will my heavenly Father do to you, unless each of you forgives his brother from your hearts their offences.

units.la: DOminus noster & Seruator IESVS CHRISTVS parabola ista docet, vt fratribus, qui nos offenderunt, iniurias & offensas debeamus remittere. Est, doctrina haec plus quam necessaria, partim quia offensarum plena sunt omnia, & ideo nisi alij alijs condonemus, pax & concordia inter homines nulla esse poterit: partim quod neq; quoad animas salui erimus, eo quod talis erga nos Deus est, quales nos sumus erga alios, & idcirco hunc quoq; implacabilem sentient, qui cunq; fratribus veniam petentibus se duros & difficiles praebent. Quia vero natura vindicta cupidi sumus, & plerunq; homines spectamus, qui ex illa fortitudinis laudem aucupantur ad exemplum Patris sui caelestis nos revocat Dominus, cuius paterna bonitate nuper ceu in tabula nobis spectandam propositum est. Etenim eadem omnium nostrum conditio est, si rationem nobiscum conferre & inire agere velit Deus, quae serui illius, qui decem millia talentorum debuit. Debebamus ergo prorsus alienari a familia Dei, & Satanae tradi, vt aeternum multaremur. Sed remittit nobis debitum omne Deus ex gratuita misericordia propter Filium suum Vnigenitum, qui pro nobis spopondit & satisfecit. Huius ergo nos meminisse decet, vt cum Dei filij esse & dici velimus, patris nostri bonitatem imitemur.
units.tr: Our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ teaches in this parable that we ought to remit injuries and offences to brothers who have wronged us. This teaching is more than necessary, partly because all things are full of offences, and so unless we pardon one another, there can be no peace or harmony among people. Partly also because we shall not be saved in our souls if God is towards us such as we are towards others. For that reason, those who show themselves hard and difficult towards brothers who ask forgiveness will also find God implacable. Since we are by nature eager for revenge, and most people look to those who win praise for their strength by it, the Lord calls us back to the example of our heavenly Father, whose paternal goodness has just been set before us as if on a tablet to be looked at. Indeed, the condition of all of us is the same as that of the servant who owed ten thousand talents, if God is willing to reckon with us and call us to account. We ought therefore to have been wholly cut off from the household of God and handed over to Satan, to be punished eternally. But God, out of free mercy, remits to us the whole debt, for the sake of his only-begotten Son, who undertook and made satisfaction for us. We should therefore remember this, so that, since we wish to be and be called children of God, we may imitate our Father's goodness.

units.la: At sequitur secunda parabolae pars, qua in illo ipso seruo, qui tantam heri clementiam expertus fuit, communem hominum malitiam & ingratitudinem arguit, qua plerique non in homines modo, verumetiam Deum ipsum peccant. Etenim seruus ille egressus ab hero, mox vnum ex conseruis inuenit, ex quo peccandi occasionem arripit, qua heri offensam rursus incurrit. Vbi primum obseruari debet, quod a conspectu & domo heri exiuisse dicitur, quando haec fecit. Indicatur causa omnis mali quae est, quod non manemus in Deo. Qui enim in hunc intenti sunt, & perpetuo in consideratione bonitatis eius versantur, ij quocunq; oculos circumferunt, clara & perspicua illius testimonia vident, quae ipsos non sinunt duriùs & inhumanius eos tractare, qui ipsis aliquam iniuriam fecerunt. Nam communis sensus eos admonet, non decere vt Deo seueriores sint qui omnem salutis fiduciam in illius misericordia sibi repositam esse sciunt. Discant ergo cum Deo & in huius domo, quae est Ecclesia manere, & in hac per verbum suum nobis loquentem audire, quotquot seipsos in officio continere cupiunt. Quam primum enim alio diuertimus, mox multiplices peccandi occasiones occurrunt.
units.tr: Now follows the second part of the parable, in which, in that very servant who had experienced such great clemency from his lord the day before, he rebukes the common wickedness and ingratitude of men, by which most people sin not only against other men but against God himself. For that servant, having gone out from his lord, soon found one of his fellow servants, and from this he seized an opportunity for sin, by which he again incurred his lord's displeasure. Here one must first observe that he is said to have gone out from his lord's sight and house when he did this. The cause of every evil is indicated, which is that we do not remain in God. For those who are intent on him, and constantly dwell in the contemplation of his goodness, wherever they turn their eyes they see his clear and manifest testimonies, which do not allow them to treat harshly and inhumanely those who have done them some injury. For common sense warns them that it is not fitting for those who know that all their confidence of salvation is laid up in God's mercy to be harsher than God. Let all who desire to keep themselves in their duty, therefore, learn to remain with God and in his house, which is the Church, and to hear him speaking to us in it through his Word. For as soon as we turn aside elsewhere, many occasions for sin immediately present themselves.

units.la: Accidit hoc isti infelici seruo. Nam mox inuenit vnum ex conseruis, qui ipsi debebat centum denarios. Hunc subito apprehensum obtorto collo violenter rapit, & non minus importune quam inhumaniter debitum ab eo exigit. Quo loco typus communis nostrae sortis & conditionis proponitur. Sumus omnes eiusdem heri serui, Dei nimirum, qui cum abs q; nobis vniuersam hanc mundi machinam crearit, & nullius indigeat, nos tamen eo honore dignatur, vt nostro seruitio vti velit, vt ipsius σωτῆρες, siue administri simus, alius quidem in verbi sui praedicatione, alius in iudiciorum suorum executione, alius in puerorum educatione ac institutione, alij in aliis functionibus quas ipse inter homines instituit. Idem quoq; donis necessariis vnumquenq; instruit pro ratione functionis suae, sicuti in talentorum parabola suo loco dicetur. Debebat hoc nos admonere officij, vt etsi alij alijs praestent, nemo tamen alium prae se contemneret, sed alij alios iuuarent. Etenim vt Apostolus monet, sunt quidem discrimina donorum, sed idem est spiritus: sunt discrimina ministeriorum, sed idem est Dominus: sunt discrimina facultatum, sed idem est Deus, qui omnia agit in omnibus. Quid vero fit? Pleriq; horum immemores, simul officij quoq; sui obliviscuntur, & quia inuidia & odio vel alijs priuatis cupiditatibus indulgent, quotidie alij alios offendunt. At hic quoq; meminisse oportebat, offensas illas leues esse, si cum ijs conferantur, quibus nos in Deum peccauimus. Etenim huic debemus ipsi, decies mille talenta, id est, sexagies millia coronatorum. Huic summae opponuntur centum denarij, qui vix octo coronatos conficiunt, si ad hodiernae monetae calculum illos reuoces. Quae autem est inter duas has summas proportio? Nulla equidem. Non temerè autem hanc comparationem a Christo fieri, fatebuntur quotquot rem ipsam diligentius expendunt. Etenim contra Deum quotidie & in horas peccamus, neq; aliter fieri potest, cum ne ad cogitandum quidem idonei simus, & illicitis desiderijs intra animos nostros aestuemus. At non ita sem per in nos peccant alij, & si quando nos offendunt, sunt tamen beneficia quoq; non rara, quae per illos nobis Deus confert, in nobis autem culpa est, qui illis non semper volumus vti. Iniuriae item
units.tr: This befell that unhappy servant. For at once he found one of his fellow servants who owed him a hundred denarii. Seizing him suddenly by the throat, he violently drags him along, and demands the debt from him no less insistently than inhumanely. In this place the type of our common lot and condition is set before us. We are all servants of the same lord, namely God, who, although he created this whole machinery of the world without any help from us, and needs nothing, nevertheless deigns to honour us so far that he wishes to make use of our service, so that we may be his helpers or ministers [σωτῆρες]: some in the preaching of his Word, some in the execution of his judgements, some in the education and instruction of children, and others in the other functions which he has established among men. He also equips each one with the gifts necessary for the discharge of his function, as will be said in its place in the parable of the talents. This should have reminded us of our duty: that although some excel others, no one should despise another in comparison with himself, but each should help the others. For, as the Apostle warns, there are differences of gifts, but the same Spirit; there are differences of ministries, but the same Lord; there are differences of operations, but the same God, who works all things in all. What, however, happens? Most people, forgetful of these things, also forget their own duty, and because they indulge in envy and hatred or other private desires, they daily offend one another. Yet here too one ought to have remembered that those offences are light if they are compared with those by which we have sinned against God. For to him we owe ten thousand talents, that is, sixty thousand crowns. Against this sum are set a hundred denarii, which scarcely make up eight crowns, if you reckon them by the present currency. What, then, is the proportion between these two sums? None at all. Indeed, all who weigh the matter more carefully will confess that this comparison was not made by Christ without reason. For we sin against God every day and every hour, and it cannot be otherwise, since we are not even fit to think, and we seethe with unlawful desires within our minds. But others do not always sin against us in this way, and if they ever offend us, there are nevertheless also not rare benefits which God confers on us through them; the fault is in us, because we do not always wish to use them. Likewise the injuries

units.la: K & offensæ, quas nobis homines faciunt, vel opes & fortunas huius sæculi, vel famam & exstli‑matione nostram, vel corpus & vitam hanc mortale concernūt, & proinde facile sarcrı possunt. At nos in Adamo patre nostro læsæ maiestatis diuinæ reifactı fuimus, & quotidie ea designa‑mus, quæ non alia satisfactione, quā indigna filij Dei morte & eius sanguine expiari potuerut. Ista ergo comparatio nos mitigare debebat, ne qui grauissimorum & infolubiliū debitorū remissio‑nem gratuitam a Deo obtinuimus, duros & inexorabiles nos præbueremus fratribus, qui nos leui‑bus iniurijs offenderunt.
units.tr: and offences which men do to us concern either our wealth and fortunes in this age, or our reputation and standing, or this mortal body and life, and therefore they can easily be made good. But we, in our father Adam, were made guilty of violating the divine majesty, and every day we commit those deeds which could not be expiated by any other satisfaction than the unworthy death of the Son of God and his blood. This comparison, therefore, ought to have moderated us, so that we who have obtained free remission from God of the most grievous and insoluble debts should not show ourselves hard and unyielding towards brothers who have offended us with slight injuries.

units.la: Sed hic exerit sese innatum nobis philautiæ vitium, quando pleriq; faciunt, quod de seruo isto dicitur. Agit hic omnium inhumanissime. Et primò qui paternam plane heri erga se indulgentiam expertus erat, conseruum hunc subito adorsus, de debito reddendo duriter compellat. Deinde ceu hostis manu inietā in collum tantum non suffocat. Tertiò deprecantem, & quidem iisdem verbis, quibus ipse ad herum vsus erat, non audit: quo argumento testatur, se iam oblitum esse eius angu‑stiæ, in qua paulò ante constitutus fuerat. Quarto miserum in carcerem coniicit ea conditione, vt inde nou exeat, donec debitum totum reddiderit. Sunt hæc per se dura & reprehensione digna, sed auget culpam, quòd propter debitum tam leue ita secit, cum ipsi summam tam magnam remisisset herus: quòd item sui loci & ordinis homine ita tractat, in cuius corpus ipsi nullum ius erat. Nam etsi centum denarios ipsi deberet, non tamen ideo herum eius seruitio fraudare debuit. Hæc autē ita narrantur a Christo, vt imagine ista doceat, quid fieri soleat, quando carnis affectui homines indulgent. Primum immemores gratiæ Dei, quam quotidie sentiunt, importune & inhumaniter agunt, imò hostiliter, cum iis, quos pro conseruis agnoscere & amare debebant. Surdi item siunt, vt deprecantes non audiant, neq; videant in illis, quid de ipsis futurum esset, si suum ius vellet Deus contra ipsos persequi. Ita vero non in eos modo peccant, qui ipsos offenderunt, verumetiam in eorundem coniuges, liberos & multos alios, quibus illi suam operam præstare debebant. Taceo eos, qui iram suam eo vsq; fouent, vt in posteris quoq; vlciscantur sibi factam iniuriam. At dum hoc faciunt, pleruncq; in ipsum Deum iniuria ista redundat. Nam miseris illis authores sunt, vt impatientius fortem suam ferant, in vindictæ cupiditatem ipsi quoq; exardescant, & cum preci‑bus assiduis Deum inuocare, & eidem gratias agere deberent, querelis impijs & murmurationi‑bus in illum peccent, & contra charitatis legē diris execrationibus eos deuoueant, quorū salutem debebant quærere. Itaq; in hac imagine seipsos contemplentur omnes homines, & quando serui istius inhumanitatem odio dignam esse vident, meminerint eadem culpa ipsos quoq; teneri, quādo sibi factas iniurias vlcisci volunt.
units.tr: But here the vice of self-love, innate in us, shows itself, when most people do what is said of that servant. He acts most inhumanely of all. First, although he had himself experienced his lord's fatherly indulgence, he suddenly attacks this fellow servant and harshly demands repayment of the debt. Then, like an enemy, he seizes him by the neck and all but throttles him. Thirdly, he does not listen to him when he begs, and that in the very words with which he himself had addressed his lord. By this argument he shows that he has already forgotten the distress in which he had been placed a little before. Fourthly, he throws the wretched man into prison on the condition that he shall not come out until he has paid back the whole debt. These things are in themselves harsh and deserving of reproof, but his guilt is increased by the fact that he acted thus over so small a debt, when his lord had forgiven him so great a sum; and also that he treats a man of his own rank and standing in this way, on whose person he had no right at all. For even if the other owed him a hundred denarii, he ought not on that account to have defrauded his lord of his service. Christ relates these things so that by this image he may teach what usually happens when men indulge the desires of the flesh. First, forgetful of the grace of God, which they feel every day, they act troublesomely and inhumanely, indeed hostilely, towards those whom they ought to acknowledge and love as fellow servants. Likewise they become deaf, so that they do not hear those who beg them, nor see in those people what would become of themselves if God wished to pursue his right against them. And so they sin not only against those who have offended them, but also against their wives, children, and many others, to whom they ought to have given their help. I say nothing of those who nurse their anger to such an extent that they take vengeance for the injury done to them even on their descendants. But while they do this, that injury very often recoils upon God himself. For they are the authors of misery for those people, in that they bear their lot more impatiently, and they themselves burn with desire for revenge; and whereas they ought to invoke God with constant prayers and give him thanks, they sin against him with impious complaints and murmurings, and against the law of charity they curse with dire execrations those whose salvation they ought to seek. Therefore let all men contemplate themselves in this image, and when they see that the inhumanity of that servant is worthy of hatred, let them remember that they too are bound by the same guilt whenever they wish to avenge the injuries done to them.

units.la: At quia de his pleriq; rarius cogitant, tertiam parabolæ partem Christus subtexit, qua docet ista non impune fieri, dicens: cum autem vidissent conserui eius quæ facta fuerant, cōcristati sunt vehementer: & cum venissent declarant domino omnia quæ facta fuerant. Dicuntur ista de Deo ἀνθρωπο̈πάθως. Etenim ei minime opus est nuntijs, qui quæ in terris inter homines fiunt, ad ipsum referant, cum ipse cœlum & terram impleat, & vbiq; præsens, omnia videat & norit. Sen‑sus ergo est, inhumanos illos, innumeros testes habere aduersarios, qui apud Deū de ipsorum im‑probitate testentur, & huius vindictam strictò iure postulent. Faciunt hoc hi ipsi, qui læsi sunt, quo‑rum clamores & gemitus Deus clementer exaudit, etsi ipsi vindictam non petant. Quia enim ipsa charitas est, non potes non irasci, si quos iniquè & iniustè affligi videat. Sic lachrymæ viduā‑rum in cœlum redundare dicuntur, & Dauid suas lachrymas a Deo colligi dicit, & in huius con‑spectu semper coparere. Sed & pij quiq; quando vident aliquos ex conseruis suis inhumanius tra‑ctari, ijs condolent, & Deam pro eis precantur, vt miseros & afflictos vindicet. Sunt etiam con‑seruinostri Angeli (quod ipsimet fatetur) & quia nos amant, & couersione atq; salute nostra gau‑dent, Christo teste, non possunt non contristari, quando ea fieri conspiciantur, quæ nos ab officio re‑vocant, & quò minus in via salutis pergamus, impediunt. De his cogitare debebat stulti illi Na‑bales, qui se Dei oculos latere putant, & dū non solum iniurias sibi factas inhumaniter vlciscun‑tur, verumetiam innoxios insolenter affligunt & atterunt, dicere audent: Dominus non videt, Deus Iacob non intelligit. At audiant illi ipsis respondentem Spiritum Sanctum: Intelligite & insipientes
units.tr: Since most people think about these things only rarely, Christ adds the third part of the parable, in which he teaches that such conduct does not go unpunished, saying: "When his fellow servants saw what had been done, they were deeply grieved, and they came and told their lord all that had happened." These things are said of God in human terms [ἀνθρωποπάθως]. For God has no need of messengers to report to him what happens among men on earth, since he fills heaven and earth, is present everywhere, and sees and knows all things. The sense, then, is that those inhumane men have countless witnesses against them, who testify before God to their wickedness and rightly demand that it be punished. Those who have been wronged do this themselves, and God graciously hears their cries and groans, even if they do not seek vengeance themselves. For since God is love itself, he cannot help being angry when he sees anyone afflicted unjustly and wrongfully. So the tears of widows are said to pour into heaven, and David says that God gathers his tears and that they always appear before his sight. Also, when the godly see some of their fellow servants treated more cruelly, they grieve with them and pray to God for them, that he would avenge the wretched and afflicted. Our fellow servants the angels (as they themselves confess) also love us and rejoice in our conversion and salvation; Christ is our witness. They cannot but be saddened when they see things done that call us back from our duty and hinder us from pressing on the way of salvation. Those foolish Nabals ought to have considered these things, who think that God's eyes are hidden from them. While they not only take inhuman vengeance for wrongs done to them but also insolently crush and afflict the innocent, they dare to say: "The Lord does not see; the God of Jacob does not understand." But let them hear the Holy Spirit answering them: "Understand, and you foolish,

units.la: Ier.23. Psal.113. / 1.Ioh.an.4. Eccli.35. Psal.56. / Apo.19.22. Luc.15. Psal.94. insipientes in populo & o stulti, quando sapietis? Num qui aurem plantauit, non audiet, num qui oculum finxit, non videbit? Meminerimus ergo tot coram Deo testes contra nos stare, quot nobiscum viuunt homines: & si nulli essent Angeli, inanimes creaturae, caeli deniq; & terra exhorrescunt ad eorum crudelitatem & ingratitudinem, qui Dei miserentis bonitatem, toties experti, in conseruos & fratres suos iniqui & inhumani esse pergunt.
units.tr: Jer. 23. Ps. 113. / 1 John 4. Ecclus. 35. Ps. 56. / Rev. 19.22. Luke 15. Ps. 94. "...foolish among the people, and you fools, when will you be wise? He who planted the ear, shall he not hear? He who formed the eye, shall he not see?" Let us therefore remember that as many witnesses stand against us before God as there are men living with us. And if there were no angels, the lifeless creatures, and indeed heaven and earth, shudder at the cruelty and ingratitude of those who, having so often experienced the goodness of a merciful God, continue to be unjust and inhumane toward their fellow servants and brothers.

units.la: Sed quid porro factum sit, audiamus. Herus aduocato seruo illo, eius improbitatem duriter arguens, dixit ei: Serue male totum debitum illud remisi tibi, quia precatus es me, &c. Habent singula verba suam Emphasim. Seruum malum vocat. Quasi diceret: Seruus frugi & fidelis esse debebas, ac mihi gratiam bonam rependere: sed revera seruus nequam & malitiosus es, qui mihi & aliis molestiam facis. Et talem esse probat: Ego tibi remisi totum illud debitum tam magnum & graue, cui non eras soluendo: etiamsi cum vxore & liberis omnibus fuisses venundatus. Et hoc feci qui herus sum, tibi seruo, in quem ius & potestatem absolutam habeo: nec alia de causa feci, quam quod me precatus es. Nonne ergo oportuit te misereri conserui, qui eiusdem tecum loci esset, & qui suam operam tibi vicissim praestare poterat? & in quem quia meus est, non tantum iuris tibi vendicare debebas, ut me inscio aut nolente aliquid duriùs de illo statueres. Quae ergo haec audacia est, qua tuae potius cupiditati iniquissimae indulgere, quàm meae misericordiae exemplum imitari voluisti? His infert sententiam, qua illum tortoribus tradere iubet, a quibus crucietur, vsquequo totum debitum reddiderit. Ita vero dicuntur ista, ut communis sensus doceat hoc decreto nihil iustius aut aequius pronuntiari potuisse. Id vero praesenti causae applicans Dominus, sermonem hunc concludit: Ita & Pater meus caelestis faciet vobis, nisi remiseritis suo quisq; fratri ex cordibus vestris offensas eorum: vt nimirum ipsum quoq; iratum & implacabilem sentiatis, adeoq; irrita fiat vobis delictorum vestrorum remissio, quam per Euangelij praedicationem in me vobis offert. Vt ergo seruus iste nequam tortoribus esset traditus ea conditione, vt non liberetur, nisi prius soluto omni debito: ita neq; vobis aliqua salus speranda, nisi pro peccatis vestris omnibus iustitiae Dei satisfeceritis. Hoc autem non eo sensu dicit, quod peccata nostra poenis certis expiari possint, quibus exactis feruemur, sed potius docere vult, sempiternis inferorum tormentis excruciandos fore eos qui fratribus suis offensas remittere nolunt. Tortores enim isti sunt diaboli, quorum ministerio in puniendis hostibus suis & omnibus poenitere nescijs Deus vtitur. Et si de peccati poena simpliciter dicendum sit, esset haec mors aeterna, quae perpetua est hominis totius alienatio a Deo atq; regno eius: eiectio deniq; in tenebras exteriores, vbi est sempiternus ploratus, & stridor dentium penes damnatos, quorum vermis non moritur, & ignis non extinguitur. Ridiculi ergo sunt, qui ex hoc loco ignem purgatorium colligunt esse carcerem illum, in quo animae defunctorum propecatis suis satisfacere possint, vt tandem ad beatae immortalitatis sedes transferantur. Sed de hac re supra Cap.5. homilia 66. diximus, vt plura hoc loco addere non sit opus.
units.tr: But let us hear what was done next. The lord, summoning that servant, sharply rebuked his wickedness and said to him: "Wicked servant, I forgave you all that debt because you begged me, etc." Each word has its own emphasis. He calls him a wicked servant, as if to say: "You ought to have been a worthy and faithful servant and to repay me with good favour, but in truth you are a worthless and malicious servant, who causes trouble both for me and for others." And he proves that he is such: "I forgave you that whole debt, so great and so heavy, which you were not able to pay, even if you had been sold with your wife and all your children. And I did this, I who am the lord, to you my servant, over whom I have full right and absolute power. Nor did I do it for any other reason than that you begged me. Ought you not then to have had pity on your fellow servant, who was in the same position as you and who could in turn render you his service? And since he is mine, you ought not to have claimed for yourself such a right that, without my knowledge or against my will, you should decide something harsher about him. What, then, is this audacity, by which you chose to indulge your most unjust greed rather than to imitate the example of my mercy?" He then pronounces a sentence upon him, ordering that he be handed over to the torturers, by whom he is to be tormented until he has paid the whole debt. These things are spoken in such a way that common sense teaches nothing more just or fair could have been decreed. The Lord applies this to the present case and concludes his discourse: "So also will my heavenly Father do to you, unless each of you forgives his brother from your hearts their offences." Thus you will feel that he too is angry and implacable, and the remission of your sins, which he offers you through the preaching of the gospel in me, will become void. Just as that wicked servant was handed over to the torturers on the condition that he would not be freed until he had paid off every debt, so no salvation is to be hoped for by you unless you have satisfied the justice of God for all your sins. He does not say this in the sense that our sins can be expiated by certain punishments, after which we are released; rather, he wants to teach that those who are unwilling to forgive offences to their brothers will be tormented with eternal torments of hell. For these torturers are the devils, through whose ministry God uses, in punishing his enemies and all who know not how to repent, the punishment. And if one must speak simply of the punishment of sin, this would be eternal death, which is the perpetual estrangement of the whole man from God and his kingdom, and finally being cast into outer darkness, where there is everlasting weeping and gnashing of teeth among the damned, whose worm does not die and whose fire is not quenched. Those therefore are ridiculous who gather from this passage that purgatory fire is that prison in which the souls of the dead can make satisfaction for their sins, so that at last they may be transferred to the abodes of blessed immortality. But we spoke about this matter above, in chapter 5, homily 66, so there is no need to add more here.

units.la: Itaq; huius loci doctrinae insistamus, quae vt luculentius nobis pateat, singula verba conclusionis Christi, quam ex parabola recitata infert, consideremus. His enim docemur primò, quibus haec mandet, & qui nam debeat sibi factas iniurias aut offensas remittere? Nimirum omnes, qui se discipulos eius esse profitentur, & seruari volunt. Nam ait: Nisi remiseritis QVISQVE, id est, cuiuscunq; loci aut conditionis fueris, diues vel pauper, herus vel seruus, nobilis aut obscurus. Omnes enim peccatores sumus, & quotidie precamur, Remitte nobis debita nostra, sicuti & nos remittimus debitoribus nostris. Obseruandum hoc superbis, quos sui generis aut dignitatis fiducia in flat, vt homines plebeios & obscuros impune laedi, & postea negligi posse sibi persuadeant. Deinde cui remittere debeamus, docet: Nimirum quisq; fratri suo. Poterat dicere, CONSERVO, sed vult nos oculos altius attollere, vt cogitemus, omnes homines non solum eiusdem conditionis & seruos Dei, sed insuper eiusdem naturae & dignitatis, vtpote filios Dei esse, qui humiles & obscuros adeò non fastidit, vt filium vnigenitum propter nos pauperem & contemptum fieri voluerit, vt nos eueheret & diuites faceret. Tertiò quid remitti debeat, monet: Offensae eorum scilicet. Indefinitè loquitur, vt omne id comprehendat, quo aliqui nos offenderunt. Nam, vt antea diximus, qualecunque illud sit, nullo modo cum ijs conferri potest, quibus nos Deum offendimus. Quartò modum quoq; remissionis exprimit, dicens: Ex CORDIBVS vestris, id est, non verbis nudis,
units.tr: Let us therefore keep to the teaching of this passage. So that it may lie open to us more clearly, let us consider the individual words of Christ's conclusion, which he draws from the parable just recited. For through these words we are taught, first, to whom he gives this command, and who ought to forgive the injuries or offences done to them. Clearly all who profess themselves to be his disciples and wish to be saved. For he says: "Unless each one forgives," that is, whatever place or condition you are in, rich or poor, master or servant, noble or humble. For we are all sinners, and every day we pray: "Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors." This should be noted by the proud, whom confidence in their own family or rank puffs up, so that they persuade themselves that common and humble people can be injured with impunity and afterwards be disregarded. Next, he teaches whom we ought to forgive: "Each one his brother," that is, each one his brother. He could have said "fellow servant," but he wants us to lift our eyes higher, so that we may consider that all men are not only of the same condition and servants of God, but also of the same nature and dignity, as sons of God. He does not despise the humble and obscure so much that he willed his only-begotten Son to become poor and despised for our sake, so that he might raise us up and make us rich. Thirdly, he warns what ought to be forgiven: "their offences," that is. He speaks indefinitely, so that it embraces everything by which anyone has offended us. For, as we said before, whatever it may be, it can in no way be compared with the offences by which we have offended God. Fourthly, he also expresses the manner of forgiveness, saying: "from your HEARTS," that is, not with bare words,

units.tr: Punishment of the implacable.

units.tr: The whole reason for forgiving brothers.

units.la: 2. Cor. 8. non simulato aut fucato animo, sed vere & ferio, ut nulla odij aut invidia vel rancoris scintillae in corde remaneant. Arguitur hac particula eorum contumacia, qui se remisisse dicunt, at si mulrop testantur, se iniuria acceptae non posse nec velle obliuisci: & in conspectum juum venire nolunt eos a quibus offensi sunt. Hi no ex corde condonant aut ignoscunt, sed verbis modo: imo ne verbis quidem, cum μνησικακίαν corde foueant, & hanc non dissimulent. Vult ergo ἀμνησίκακον & obliuionem omnium offensarum sancire Christus, qua posit graues motus & periculosas mutationes in Republica opus esse interdum, prudentissimi quique inter Ethnicos intellexerunt, & laudatur in historijs Thrasibulus, qui illam post eiectos triginta tyrannos Athenis fanciuit, & hac ratione Rempub. pacauit & seruauit, quae nunquam quieuisset, nisi iniuriarum acceptarum memoria fuisset abolita. Ut vero id inter eos fiat magis necesse est, qui Ecclesiae aut regni Dei ciues esse volunt. Etenim ut in condonando Dei exemplum imitemur, oportet. At is ita delet omnes iniquitates nostras, ut ea rum non amplius recordetur. Et ut ita fiat necesse est: quia quamdiu peccata nostra in memoriam veniunt apud Deum, non poterit nobis spes salutis certa & solida constare. Ideo Dauid precatur: Delictorum iuuentutis meae & transgressionum mearum ne meminerit. Quod ergo a Deo petere necessitas iubet, ipsi quoque praestemus omnibus, quibus cum nobis res est. Nam etsi remissionem peccatorum omnibus in filio suo offerat Deus, ea tamen indignos sese faciunt, qui fide per charitatem agente deflituuntur. Atqui hoc verissime in eos copetit, qui erga fratres se rigidos & implacabiles praebent. Damnantur enim hi natura lege, quae est: Qua mensura vos metimini, eadem vobis reddetur. Vidit hoc Sirachides, quando scripsit: Cupidum vltionis vltio manet a Domino, qui peccata eius sedulo conseruabit. Remitte iniuriam proximo tuo, tunc tibi quoque oranti peccata condonabuntur. An ne homo iram alat aduersus hominem, & a Domino salutem postulet? aut num peccata sua deprecetur, qui sui similis hominis misereri dedignatur. Quod si homo mortalis iram fouet et veniam petit a Deo, qui eius peccata expiet? Disputant hic aliqui de peccatorum pecuniario remissione, & nu magistratibus liceat capitalium scelerum reos, culpam agnoscentes et deprecantes occidere. At intempestiua mihi videntur haec disputationes. Etenim non venit Christus, ut lege aboleret, sed impleret: Regnum item eius non est ex hoc mundo: idcirco neque Respub. neque domestica abolet, sed vult, ut & Magistratus officium faciant, & singuli domui suae prospiciant: quod fieri nequit, nisi & homines facinorosi puniantur, & contractus fiant, ad quos mutuum & fideiussiones & alia huius generis pertinent.
units.tr: 2 Cor. 8. not with a feigned or pretended mind, but truly and sincerely, so that no spark of hatred, envy or rancour remains in the heart. This phrase exposes the obstinacy of those who say they have forgiven, yet testify with many words that they cannot and will not forget the wrong they received, and refuse to come into the presence of those by whom they were offended. These do not forgive or pardon from the heart, but only in words; indeed, not even in words, since they nourish a grudge [μνησικακίαν] in their hearts and do not hide it. Christ therefore wishes to establish a forgetting [ἀμνησίκακον] and oblivion of all offences. The wisest men among the pagans understood that sometimes serious disturbances and dangerous upheavals in a commonwealth make this necessary. Thrasybulus is praised in histories for having enacted such an oblivion at Athens after the thirty tyrants were driven out, and by this means he brought peace to the state and preserved it; it would never have been quiet unless the memory of the injuries received had been abolished. But it is all the more necessary for those who wish to be citizens of the Church or of the kingdom of God that this be done among them. For if we are to imitate God's example in forgiving, we must do so. And he so blots out all our iniquities that he no longer remembers them. For this to happen it is necessary, since as long as our sins come to mind before God, no sure and solid hope of salvation can stand for us. Therefore David prays: "Remember not the sins of my youth and my transgressions." What necessity bids us ask of God, let us also show to all those with whom we have dealings. For although God offers the forgiveness of sins to all in his Son, those who refuse to forgive their brothers make themselves unworthy of it, since they lack faith working through love. And this applies most truly to those who show themselves hard and implacable toward their brothers. For these are condemned by the law of nature, which is: "With what measure you measure, it will be measured back to you." The son of Sirach saw this when he wrote: "The one who seeks vengeance will find vengeance from the Lord, who will keep his sins carefully. Forgive your neighbour the wrong, and then your sins will be forgiven when you pray. Can a man harbour anger against a man and seek healing from the Lord? Can he who has no mercy on a man like himself pray for his own sins? If a mortal man nurses wrath, who will make atonement for his sins?" Here some dispute about the remission of sins by money payment, and whether magistrates may put to death those guilty of capital crimes who acknowledge their guilt and beg for it. But these disputes seem to me out of place. For Christ did not come to abolish the law but to fulfil it; nor is his kingdom of this world. Therefore he abolishes neither the commonwealth nor the household, but wishes both that magistrates do their duty and that each man care for his own house. This cannot happen unless criminals are punished, and contracts are made, to which loans, sureties and other things of this kind belong.

units.la: Parabolae ergo huius nobis hic vsus esto, ut primum agnoscamus nos peccatores, et in aere Dei esse, qui soluendo non simus. Deinde ad thronum gratiae Dei supplices recurramus per fidem in Filium Dei IESVM CHRISTVM, cuius sanguine debita nostra deleta sunt. Memores autem gratiae quae nobis facta est, Deo nos gratos praebeamus: quod tunc fiet, si libertate nostram tanto pretio emptam tueamur, & simul in Christo omnes homines amore fraterno copulamur, atque pro cuiuslibet iniuriarum omnium memoria, Dei Patris bonitate imitemur, ut huius filij & fratres germani IESV CHRISTI simus, qui hanc dignitatem nobis meruit. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Let us therefore make use of this parable here, so that first we may recognise that we are sinners and are in debt to God, unable to pay. Then let us come as suppliants to the throne of God's grace through faith in the Son of God, Jesus Christ, by whose blood our debts have been wiped out. Mindful of the grace that has been done to us, let us show ourselves thankful to God; this will happen if we guard the liberty bought for us at so great a price, and at the same time are joined together in Christ with brotherly love toward all men, and, forgetting every injury done to us, imitate the goodness of God the Father, so that we may be true brothers of this Son, Jesus Christ, who earned this dignity for us. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPVT XIX. HOMILIA CCXXV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIX. HOMILY CCXXV.

units.la: ET factum est cum finiuisset IESVS sermones istos, soluit a Galilaea & venit in fines Iudaeae, trans Iordanen. Et secuta est eum turba multa, sanauitque eos illic. Tunc adierunt eum Pharisaei, tentantes eum, & dicentes ei: Licet ne homini dimittere vxorem suam quauis ex causa.
units.tr: And it came to pass, when Jesus had finished these sayings, that he departed from Galilee and came into the coasts of Judaea beyond Jordan. And great multitudes followed him, and he healed them there. Then the Pharisees came unto him, tempting him, and saying unto him: Is it lawful for a man to put away his wife for every cause?

units.la: ESCRIBITVR hoc cap. postremus Domini nostri IESV CHRISTI ex Galilaea in Iudaeam aduentus, & initio quidem breuiter narratur, ut illic a vulgo exceptus sit, & ut vicissim ille cum populo ad se veniente egerit. Deinde eius actiones & colloquia aliquot narratur, quae ipsi cū nonnullis priuatim intercesserunt, in quibus de diuersis vitae generibus, siue hominum conditionibus disseruit: Vtpote de coniugio & diuortio: de liberorum educatione, & vt hi ad ipsum adduci debeant: de vita totius secundum Dei praecepta institutione, vbi cū diuite quodam de re domestica & diuitiis huius saeculi disseruit, & vt [his] priuatim vti debeant, quot-quot germani ipsius discipuli esse, & vitam aeternam consequi volunt. Vbi discemus, Dei Filium, etsi vt regnum Dei inter homines instauraret, in mundū venerit, non tamen aboluisse a DeoPatre institutas olim vocationes siue status, sine quibus vita haec in terris non potest honestè & pacificè conseruari. Itaq; nos ex Euangelio non solum aeternae salutis doctrinam percipere, verum-etiam in hoc intentos esse debere, vt quisq; in sua vocatione ita viuat secundum Christi regulam atq; praecepta, ne quam ore profitetur fidem, vitae & morum licentia abneget. Et sic Christi exemplum Apostoli imitati sunt, qui in suis epistolis cum doctrina fidei & salutis aeternae praecepta moralia & oeconomica atq; politica coniunxerunt. Esq; hoc obseruatu valde necessarium propter fanaticos, qui sub religionis praetextu coiugij leges, rei item domesticae curā, deniq; legitimam magistratuum potestatem, adeoq; rempub. omnem abolent, vt confusionem plus quam Platonicam inuehant. Caeterum in praesenti haec habentur.
units.tr: This chapter describes the final coming of our Lord Jesus Christ from Galilee into Judaea. At the beginning it is briefly related that he was received there by the crowd, and how in turn he dealt with the people who came to him. Then several of his deeds and conversations are narrated, which he had privately with certain persons, and in which he discussed different ways of life or human conditions: namely marriage and divorce; the upbringing of children, and that they ought to be brought to him; the arrangement of a whole life according to God's precepts, where he discussed with a certain rich man household affairs and the riches of this age, and how they are to be used privately by all who wish to be his true disciples and to attain eternal life. Here we learn that the Son of God, although he came into the world to restore the kingdom of God among men, did not abolish the callings or states instituted long ago by God the Father, without which this life on earth cannot be preserved honourably and peacefully. Therefore from the Gospel we should not only learn the doctrine of eternal salvation, but also take care that each person lives in his own calling according to Christ's rule and precepts, so that no one denies by a licence of life and morals the faith he professes with his mouth. And so the apostles imitated Christ's example, for in their epistles they joined moral, domestic and political precepts with the doctrine of faith and eternal salvation. This is very necessary to observe on account of the fanatics who, under the pretext of religion, abolish the laws of marriage, the care of household affairs, and finally the lawful power of the magistrates, and indeed every commonwealth, so as to bring in a confusion greater than Plato's. But for the present these things are held.

units.la: Principio aduentus Christi Domini in Iudaeam narratur: & factum est, cum finiuisset IESVS sermones istos, quibus discipulos hucusq; in vera fide aduersus omne genus scandalorū instituerat, soluit a Galilaea, quae ipsi instar patriae fuit, cum in ea educatus esset, & maximam vitae partem illic transegisset, & recta in Iudaeam contendit, cuius fines traiecto Iordani ingressus est. At-qui non ignorabat, quid illic ipsi esset euenturum, & eo non semel discipulos suos admonuit. Nihilominus faciem suam (vt Lucas scribit) obfirmauit, vt Ierosolymā iret, id est, constanti & obfirmato animo illuc perrexit, vbi se moriturum sciebat. Et causa huius instituti indicatur, quod tempus illud fatale appropinquaret, quando ipsum ex hoc mundo sursum recipi, & (vt alibi dicitur) ad Patrē redire oportebat. Apparet in eo inuicta animi constantia & fortitudo in Christo, et ardentissimum studium siue desiderium salutis humanae, quod ipsum mouit, vt omni periculo contempto hoc vnum caperet, vt Patris decreto obsequeretur, & seipsum daret pro mundi vita. De hoc postea testatus est, quando in vltima coena discipulis dicebat: Desiderio desideraui hoc pascha vesci vobiscum, &c. Interim hoc ipsum carni graue & molestū fuisse constat, & hoc ipse confessus est, quando mortis acerbissimae consideratione turbatus dicebat: Nunc anima mea turbata est, & quid dicā? Pater conserua me ab hac hora. At mox animum recolligens iterum, addit: Sed propterea veni in horam hanc. Debent haec a nobis saepius & diligenter considerari, quia dulcissimam consolationem pariunt in tentationibus, neq; nos sinunt dubitare de salute nostra, quae Filio Dei ita curae fuit, vt pro nobis mori tantopere desiderauerit. Deinde exemplum illius imitari di-scamus, vt quemadmodum ipse constanter perrexit in Patris sui vocatione: ita nos intrepide sequamur qua Deus nos vocat. Enimuero multa occurrunt in Dei vocatione ambulantibus, quae ipsis impedimento sunt: quod olim in Israelitis ex Aegypto in terram promissam contendentibus adumbratū fuit. Nam vt hi primum, quando res adhuc secundae erant, Aegypti delitijs inescati, & idololatria seductifuerunt, deinde a Pharaone oppressi triste seruitutem seruierunt, quae quo propinquior fuit redemptio ipsorum, eo magis aggrauata est: tandem vero iam iter ingressos pericula vndiq; circumsteterunt, cum a tergo illis cū copijs militaribus Pharao imminueret, a fronte mare esset, & vtrinq; montes praerupti surgerent, & quocunq; se verterent plurima mortis imago miseris obuersaretur: ita adhuc fieri solet, vt in huius vitae curriculo versantibus omnis generis obstacula obijciat Satan, quibus eos reuocat, ne in Dei viis progrediantur. Sed tunc exemplum Domini nobis ob oculos ponamus, & meminerimus dicti Apostolici: Per multas tribulationes nos ingredi oportere in regnum Dei, hunc vero etsi per ignem & aquam adeoq; per vallem vmbrae mortis ambulandum sit, suis adesse, vt metam optatam attingere, & cursum suum consummare possint, & iustitiae coronam assequi. Vide Psal.66.23.2. Tim.4.
units.tr: At the beginning, the arrival of Christ the Lord in Judaea is narrated: "And it came to pass, when Jesus had finished these sayings," by which he had so far instructed his disciples in true faith against every kind of stumbling-block, "he departed from Galilee," which was to him like a homeland, since he had been brought up there and had spent the greater part of his life there, and he went straight into Judaea, whose borders he entered after crossing the Jordan. Yet he was not unaware of what would happen to him there, and more than once he warned his disciples of it. Nevertheless, as Luke writes, "he set his face" to go to Jerusalem, that is, he went there with a steadfast and resolute mind, where he knew he would die. And the reason for this resolve is indicated: that the fatal time was drawing near, when he had to be taken up out of this world and, as he says elsewhere, return to the Father. In this there appears in Christ an unconquered constancy and courage of mind, and the most ardent zeal or desire for human salvation, which moved him to take up this one thing, setting aside every danger, so that he might obey the Father's decree and give himself for the life of the world. He later bore witness to this, when at the last supper he said to his disciples: "With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you," and so on. Meanwhile it is clear that this was grievous and burdensome to his flesh, and he himself confessed it, when, troubled by the thought of most bitter death, he said: "Now my soul is troubled, and what shall I say? Father, save me from this hour." But soon gathering his spirit again, he adds: "But for this cause I came to this hour." These things ought to be considered by us more often and diligently, because they bring the sweetest consolation in temptations, and do not allow us to doubt our salvation, which was of such concern to the Son of God that he so earnestly desired to die for us. Then let us learn to imitate his example, so that as he steadfastly persevered in the calling of his Father, so we may fearlessly follow wherever God calls us. Indeed many things stand in the way of those who walk in God's calling, and this was foreshadowed long ago in the Israelites as they hastened from Egypt to the promised land. For at first, when their circumstances were still prosperous, they were enticed by the delights of Egypt and seduced into idolatry; then, oppressed by Pharaoh, they served in a sad servitude, which grew heavier the nearer their redemption drew. At last, when they had already set out on their journey, dangers surrounded them on every side: Pharaoh pressed behind them with his military forces, the sea lay before them, and steep mountains rose on both sides, and wherever they turned the wretched people were confronted with the image of death. So it still happens that Satan, in the course of this life, throws every kind of obstacle in the way of those who are travelling, by which he tries to call them back from advancing in God's ways. But then let us set the Lord's example before our eyes, and remember the apostolic saying: that "through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God." And even if one must walk through fire and water, and so through the valley of the shadow of death, yet the Lord is present with his own, so that they may reach the desired goal, complete their course, and obtain the crown of righteousness. See Psalm 66:23; 2 Timothy 4.

units.la: Sed ad Christum redeamus, quem turba multa secuta est. Nam vt ex Luca est videre, secum habuit non Apostolos modò, verumetiam LXX. discipulos: & quia priuatim & publicè non semel praedixerat, quid ipsi euenturū esset, & multi in Galilaea in ipsum credebant, nō dubium est, quin
units.tr: But let us return to Christ, whom a great crowd followed. For as is seen from Luke, he had with him not only the apostles but also seventy disciples. And since he had foretold privately and publicly, more than once, what would happen to him, and many in Galilee believed in him, there is no doubt that

units.la: Ioan.13. Christi constantia, Luc.9., Luc.22., Ioan.12., Actō.14., Comites Christi multi. Luc.10. & 23. plerique ex illis ipsum secuti sint. Inter hos certè fuerunt mulieres illæ religiosæ, quarum Lucas in mortis & resurrectionis eius historia meminit: & (vt fieri solet) rei nouitas alios quoq; mouit, vt se comites adiungerent. Vt primum verò Iudææ fines attigit, ex his quoq; multi confluxerunt, cùm non ignotus veniret, & doctrinæ ac miraculorum eius fama iam pridem effet ad omnes diuulgata. Quales autem pleriq; horum fuerint, ex eo colligi potest, quòd illos sanauisse dicitur. Fuerunt ergo inualidi, claudi, cæci, muti, & diuersis morborum generibus obnoxij, vel ex suis habuerunt tales, quos ad Christum adduxerunt. Est autem hoc obseruatu dignissimum, quòd ad mortem abiturus Christus, comites tam multos habuit. Fuit hic typus, quo docemur, regnum et Ecclesiam eius cruce ac persecutionibus nō minui aut euerti, sed potius crescere & augeri. Etenim potest illi, qui corda hominū nouit, & in sua potestate habet, trahere quoscunq; vult & ita pollicitus est, quòd exaltatus aut sublimatus de terra, velit omnia ad se trahere. Docet etiā historia, Ecclesia sub cruce & persecutionibus semper floruisse, & eandē fere decreuisse, quando otio & pace abundauit. Ex eo igitur consolationem petamus, ne facile offendamur, aut desperemus, si quando aduersa & pericula incidunt, quibus pij exercetur. Docet præterea locus hic, qui pra alijs maximè idonei sint ad regnum Christi: Claudi nimirum, cæci, mâci, id est, peccatores, qui vitia & infirmitates suas non possunt dissimulare, & eorum sensu tanguntur, vt & illa agnoscāt, & salute ferè quærant. Etenim vt ægrotus, qui vim morbi non agnoscit, neq; videri vult cui medicina opus sit, medicum nō admittit: ita qui se iustos & sanctos esse sibi persuaserunt, vix adduci possunt, vt ad Christum accedant, qui laborantes & oneratos ad se vocat. Et perpetuò ratio erit, quòd Paulus de Iudæis dicit, quòd qui propriam iustitiam constituere volunt, iustitiæ Dei non subiiciuntur, quæ in eius Filio habetur, & sola nos ad eius tribunal defendit. Ideò Euangelij prædicationem ab articulo pœnitentiæ Christus inchoare iubet, & hoc primū Spiritus Sancti opus sine officiū in Ecclesia fore ait, quòd mundum debeat arguere de peccato. Sunt ergo reuera stulti & miseri, qui hoc indignè ferunt, similes nimirum eorum, qui a medico petunt, vt morbo, quo laborant, medeatur, eundem verò de illo vt bafacere nolunt, nec vt eius causas & vim ipsis declaret.
units.tr: John 13. The constancy of Christ. Luke 9; Luke 22; John 12; Acts 14. Many companions of Christ. Luke 10 and 23. Many of them followed him. Among these were certainly those pious women whom Luke mentions in the story of his death and resurrection. And (as usually happens) the novelty of the thing moved others too to join themselves to him as companions.
