But as soon as he reached the borders of Judaea, many of these also flocked together, since he was coming not unknown, and the report of his teaching and miracles had long since spread to everyone. What sort of people most of these were can be gathered from the fact that he is said to have healed them. So there were the infirm, the lame, the blind, the dumb, and those subject to various kinds of diseases, or they had among their own people such as they brought to Christ. It is most worthy of note that Christ, about to go to his death, had so many companions. This was a type by which we are taught that his kingdom and Church are not diminished or overthrown by the cross and persecutions, but rather grow and increase. For he who knows the hearts of men and holds them in his power can draw whomever he wills, and he has promised that, once lifted up from the earth, he will draw all things to himself. History also teaches that the Church has always flourished under the cross and persecutions, and has nearly always declined when it abounded in leisure and peace. Let us therefore draw consolation from this, and not be easily offended or despair if adversities and dangers befall us, by which the godly are exercised. This place further teaches which people are most fit for the kingdom of Christ: namely the lame, the blind, and the sick, that is, sinners, who cannot disguise their faults and infirmities, and are moved by a sense of them, so that they both acknowledge them and seek salvation almost in spite of themselves. For just as a sick man who does not recognise the force of his disease, and does not wish to appear to need medicine, refuses the physician, so those who have persuaded themselves that they are righteous and holy can scarcely be brought to come to Christ, who calls to himself those who labour and are burdened. And the principle will always hold that Paul says of the Jews: that those who wish to establish their own righteousness do not submit themselves to the righteousness of God, which is found in his Son, and alone defends us before his tribunal. Therefore Christ bids the preaching of the Gospel begin with the article of repentance, and he says that this will be the first work and office of the Holy Spirit in the Church, that it should convict the world of sin. They are therefore truly foolish and wretched who take this badly, like those who ask a physician to heal the disease from which they suffer, but are unwilling to have it examined in them, nor to have its causes and force declared to them.

units.la: Quid verò cum istis egit Christus? Marcus scribit, ipsum eos docuisse. Est hoc præcipuū munus, cui potissimum vacauit, quàm diu in terris versatus est, & ad quod se vnctum esse & in mundum venisse, ipsemet non semel testatus est. Quia enim in ignorantia tenebris versabatur humanum genus, doctrina & institutione veritatis omnino opus fuit, quæ a nemine poterat melius præstari, quàm a magno illo Propheta, quem Deus olim promiserat, & quem Filium illum Vnigenitum esse, Pater ipse cœlitus pronunciauit. At quia Iudæis hoc proprium fuit, quòd signa petierunt, hæc subinde doctrinæ coniunxit, quibus hanc confirmaret, ne dubitarent eum esse, quem se profitebatur. Et opus erat in hoc postremo suo in Iudæam aduentu publicè demonstrari, eum adesse, de quo olim Isaias dixerat: Deus ipse veniet, & seruabit nos: Tunc aperientur oculi cæcorum, & aures surdorum reserabuntur: tunc saltabit claudus instar cerui, & lingua muti iubilabit. Nobis autem obseruandū venit hoc loco indefessum Christi studium in salute nostra promouenda, de quo ante etiam diximus. Etenim etsi morti obuiam eat, quam mox acerbissimam erat subiturus, non tamen sui officij immemor est: sed perpetuò inter eos docet, & eorum ægrotos curat, in quibus plerique ingrati ac contumaces, mortis deniq; eius authores futuri erant. Consoletur hoc nos, & in fide confirmet trepidantes, ne illum erga nos difficilliorem fore putemus. Qui enim inuitis & reluctantibus salutem liberaliter obtulit, qua ratione eos fastidiat, qui illam totis animis esurimus, & ipsum pro Seruatore ac Redemptore nostro agnoscimus. Etenim qui ad se inuitat omnes, qui conscientia peccatorum presi laborant, idem pollicetur quoq; quod neminem, qui ad ipsum venit, velit reiicere. Ioan.6.
units.tr: But what did Christ do with these people? Mark writes that he taught them. This was his chief office, to which he devoted himself above all while he lived on earth, and he himself testified more than once that he had been anointed for it and had come into the world for it. Because the human race lay in the darkness of ignorance, it needed teaching and instruction in the truth, and no one could provide this better than that great Prophet whom God had promised long before, and whom the Father himself declared from heaven to be his Only-begotten Son. But since it was characteristic of the Jews to seek signs, Christ often joined signs to his teaching, to confirm it, so that they would not doubt that he was the one he professed to be. And in this last coming of his into Judea it was necessary to show publicly that he was present, of whom Isaiah had long before said: "God himself will come and save us. Then the eyes of the blind will be opened, and the ears of the deaf unsealed; then the lame will leap like a deer, and the tongue of the dumb will sing for joy." Here we should observe Christ's tireless zeal for promoting our salvation, of which we have spoken before. For although he was going to meet death, which he was soon to undergo in its bitterest form, he did not forget his office. Rather, he kept teaching among these people and healing their sick, even though most of them would prove ungrateful and obstinate, and would in the end be the authors of his death. Let this comfort us and confirm us when we tremble, so that we do not think him harder toward us. For he who freely offered salvation to those who were unwilling and resisting, how could he scorn those of us who hunger for it with our whole souls and acknowledge him as our Saviour and Redeemer? Indeed, he who invites all who labour under the burden of their sins also promises that he will refuse no one who comes to him. John 6.

units.la: Porrò dum alij longo itinere Dominum sequuntur, alij ex locis diuersis ad illum confluunt, vt eius beneficio feruentur, qui se omnibus facilem atque benignum præbuit, iamque spes bona esse poterat, regnum eius breui longè lateq; potens futurum esse, ecce subito aduersus illum veteres hostes Pharisæi insurgunt, qui eum tentant quæstione insidiosa. Quo exemplo docemur, quòd vt vbique & semper discipulos habebit Christus, ita nunquam defuturi sunt hostes, qui se ipsi opponant. Perpetuò enim durabit inimicitia, quam inter ipsum & veterem serpentem fauciuit Satan, quod Simeon ille diuinus prædixit, illum positum esse in casum & resurrectionem multorum, & in signum cui contradicatur. Quod ergo hic fecerunt Pharisæi, hoc alibi quoq; accidit, & in posterum quoq; fiet. Est enim Ecclesia Christi (vt sæpe monuimus) instar nauiculæ in medio maris. Vt ergo γαλιον siue tranquillitas in mari non potest diuturna esse, eò quòd hoc & proprio æstu monetur, & a ventis vndique incumbentibus turbatur: ita Ecclesiæ in terris accidere solet, quia intra huius parietes sæpè falsi fratres sunt, qui turbas (vt ita dicam) domesticas excitant, & foris ab hostibus apertis vel ex insidijs vel aperta vi infestatur. Et prodest de eo sæpe cogitare, ne quis sþe otij & pacis perpetuæ seipsum decipiat, & postea turbis & periculis ex improuiso incidentibus offendatur. In præsenti hostes Christi introducuntur Pharisæi, qui quales fuerint sæpè dictu est: hypocritæ nimirum, qui suorum operum iustitia freti, doctrinam de gratia Dei & Mediatore Christo, de fidei item iustitia, vt inutile & minimè necessaria contemnebant, imò hostiliter oderant, quòd illius luce ipsis larua detraheretur, & ita ipsorum existimationi multum derogaretur, & quæstus quoq; fieret, quem ex sacrorum nundinatione faciebant. Erant ergo similes Monachis nostri sæculi, quos idem hypocrisis spiritus inflat & decipit, vt passim turbas dent Euangelij ministris ac sectatoribus: nec est, quod meliora speremus de illis, qui suam gloriam priuatam diuinæ præferunt. Ioan. 5.
units.tr: Meanwhile, while some followed the Lord on a long journey and others flocked to him from various places, to be helped by him who had shown himself easy of access and kind to all, and while good hope could already exist that his kingdom would soon become powerful far and wide, behold, suddenly the old enemies, the Pharisees, rose up against him and tested him with a treacherous question. From this example we are taught that, just as Christ will always and everywhere have disciples, so enemies who set themselves against him will never be lacking. For the enmity that Satan wounded between him and the old serpent will last forever, as that divine Simeon foretold, that he was set for the fall and rising again of many, and for a sign that would be spoken against. So what the Pharisees did here has happened elsewhere too, and will happen again in the future. For the Church of Christ (as we have often warned) is like a little boat in the middle of the sea. Just as calm [γαλήνη] cannot last long on the sea, since it is disturbed by its own tides and is stirred by winds pressing from every side, so it usually happens with the Church on earth: within its walls there are often false brothers who stir up, so to speak, troubles at home, and from outside it is attacked by open enemies, either by plots or by open force. It is useful to think often of this, so that no one deceives himself with the idea of lasting leisure and perpetual peace, and is then overwhelmed when troubles and dangers fall upon him unexpectedly. In the present passage Christ's enemies, the Pharisees, are introduced. What sort of men they were has often been said: they were hypocrites, who, relying on the righteousness of their own works, despised, indeed hated with hostility, the doctrine of God's grace and of Christ the Mediator, and likewise the doctrine of righteousness by faith, as useless and in no way necessary. They hated it because its light would strip away their mask, so that their reputation would be greatly diminished, and the profit they made from trading in sacred things would be lost. They were therefore like the monks of our age, whom the same spirit of hypocrisy puffs up and deceives, so that they stir up disturbances everywhere against the ministers and followers of the Gospel. Nor is there reason to hope for better things from those who prefer their own private glory to the divine. John 5.

units.la: Sed audiamus, quomodo illi Christum aggressi sint. Mouent quæstionē de iure diuortij. Liceat ne (inquiunt) homini dimittere vxorem suam quauis ex causa? Impudens & absurdissima quæstio, quam nemo honestus inter ethnicos facile mouisset. Nam perinde est, ac si quærerent, num quisque nulla de causa, ex priuata libidine vxorem eijcere debeat? Atqui vulgo iniquus & inhumanus iudicatur, qui famulum aut ancillam quauis de causa domo exturbat. Num ergo id fiat de vxore, quæ qualiscunque sit, tamen tua consors aliquando fuit, & fortunam omnem tecum communem habuit. Portento igitur simile est, in ea gente, quæ Dei peculium erat, & quæ olim sola sapiens dicta fuerat, quæstionem hanc moueri ab ijs, qui summam virtutis & sapientiæ existimationem sustinebant. Sed occasionem arripuerunt ex licentia diuortiorum, quæ tunc inter Iudæos regnabat. Quia enim Moses permiserat, vt si quis aliquid fœdum & sibi displicens in coniuge sua inuenisset, eam dato libello repudij dimitteret, hoc priuilegio, seu potius licentia, non minus turpiter quam inhumaniter abutebantur. Et vetus hoc vitium fuisse, ex ijs patet, quæ post reditum ex Babylone facta sunt: quando vt Ezræ & Nehemiæ libris traditur, multi non ex vulgo solum, verumetiam ex sacerdotibus & proceribus populi, vxoribus, quæ ipsis exilij & calamitatum maximarum sociæ fuerant, atq; ideò curis & laboribus exhaustæ & minus formosæ aut delicatæ erant, inhumanissimè repudiatis, nouas ex ethnicis in otio & delitijs aducatas ducebant: Quod Malachias ceu immane & omni execratione dignum scelus in illis accusat. Nec dubium est, licentiam illam postea sub Romanorum imperio creuisse, cùm hi illis αυτονομιαν concessissent, vt nimirum suis legibus vterentur. Et cur in Iudæis pœna & reprehensione dignum iudicassent Romani, quod apud ipsos vulgò fiebat? Quo loco obseruari merito debet, quousque tandem libidines vagæ eos arripiant, qui eis assueuerunt? vt nimirum non solum omnes æquitatis, iustitiæ, honestatis, dilectionis item & pudoris leges transgressi, bellorum instar inter nefarios concubitus volutentur, verumetiam crudeles fiant in eas quarum impudicitiæ, honori & vitæ non minus quam sibi ipsis debebant consulere. Exempla, quibus hoc demonstrari posset, quotidie occurrunt.
units.tr: But let us hear how they came at Christ. They raise a question about the right of divorce: "Is it lawful for a man to put away his wife for any cause whatever?" It is a shameless and most absurd question, which no decent person among the heathen would easily have raised. For it is just as if they asked whether anyone may cast out his wife for no reason, out of private lust. Yet by common judgment a man is considered unjust and inhuman who throws out a male or female servant for any cause whatever. Should it then happen with a wife, who, whatever she is, has nonetheless once been your partner and has shared all your fortune with you? It is therefore a monstrous thing that this question should be raised among that nation which was God's own possession, and which had once been called the only wise nation, and that it should be raised by men who claimed the highest reputation for virtue and wisdom. But they seized the opportunity offered by the licence for divorce that then prevailed among the Jews. For since Moses had permitted that if anyone found in his wife something foul and displeasing to him, he might dismiss her by giving a bill of divorce, they abused this privilege, or rather this licence, no less shamefully than inhumanly. That this was an old vice is clear from what happened after the return from Babylon. When, as the books of Ezra and Nehemiah record, many people, not only of the common folk but also of the priests and leaders of the people, cruelly put away their wives, who had shared their exile and their greatest calamities, and who for that reason were worn out with cares and labours and were less beautiful or delicate, and took new wives brought up among the heathen in ease and pleasure. Malachi accuses them of this as a monstrous crime deserving every curse. Nor is there any doubt that this licence later grew under Roman rule, since the Romans had granted the Jews autonomy [αὐτονομίαν], so that they might use their own laws. And why should the Romans have judged the Jews worthy of punishment and rebuke for what was commonly done among themselves? Here it ought rightly to be observed how far wandering lusts will carry those who have become accustomed to them: they not only transgress all the laws of fairness, justice, honour, love, and modesty, and roll like beasts of war in wicked couplings, but also become cruel toward those women whose chastity, honour, and life they ought to have cared for no less than their own. Examples by which this could be shown occur every day.

units.la: Caeterum vt ad Pharisæos redeamus, ex hac diuortiorum licentia occasionem arripiunt, & quasi illa ipsis ex animo displiceat, quærunt, num honestum, æquum & Verbo Dei conueniens sit, vt quis pro suo arbitrio ob quamlibet causam vxorem suam dimittat? At dum honestatis & coniugalis iuris studium simulant, Christum improbè tentant: vt scilicet hac quæstione irretitum vel illaqueatum in præsens vitæ aut existimationis suæ discrimen adducant. Etenim si dicat sibi probari quod vulgo fiebat sub Legis prætextu, mox eum sibi ipsi contradicere, & vagarum libidinum patronum esse clamabunt. Nec enim ignorare poterant ea, quæ supra cap. 5. de diuortijs publicè dixerat. Quod si idem nunc repetat, & licentia hanc damnet, tum Mosi contrarium esse calumniabuntur, & odium ei conflabunt apud populum, qui licentia iam assueuerat. Est ergo hoc incurabilis pertinacia & impudentiæ argumentum, quòd illi insidiantur, quem publicè omnibus benefacere.
units.tr: But to return to the Pharisees: they seize on this licence for divorce as an occasion, and, as if they were truly displeased by it, they ask whether it is honourable, equitable, and in agreement with the Word of God, for a man to dismiss his wife at his own discretion for any cause at all. Yet while they pretend a zeal for honesty and for the law of marriage, they tempt Christ wickedly, namely so that by this question they may entangle or ensnare him and bring him into danger of his life or his reputation. For if he should say that what was commonly done under the pretext of the Law pleased him, they would at once cry out that he contradicted himself and was a defender of wandering lusts. Nor could they be ignorant of what he had publicly said about divorces in chapter 5 above. And if he now repeated the same and condemned this licence, they would slander him as opposed to Moses and would stir up hatred against him among the people, who were already accustomed to the licence. So this is a proof of incurable obstinacy and shamelessness, that they lay snares for him who publicly does good to all.

units.la: Quæstio de iure diuortij.
units.tr: The question concerning the right of divorce.

units.la: Quæstio insti-diosa. re videbant, & quem ab omni sceleris suspicione alienum esse sciebant. Nec minus apparet, quam profundo astu hypocritae suas insidias celare possint, & quod non absque causa Dominus serpentinam prudentiam a suis requirit, quibus cum eiusmodi hominibus res est. Quae nos ita observare conuenit, ut tamen non terreamur, si quid huius nobis quoque accidat. Etenim ut Dominus noster IESVS CHRISTVS hinc occasione arrepta doctrinam saluberrimam contexit, qua de coniugij prima institutione, dignitate & vsu disserit, & improbos istos cum tota hominum libidinosorum cohorte confutat: Ita in suis etiam membris suo spiritu agere solet, ut quae aduersarij moliuntur, ut ipsos contemptos aut exosos faciant, ipsis honorifica sint & salutaria. In illo ergo fortes simus, cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: The insidious question. ...they saw, and whom they knew to be free from all suspicion of crime. Nor does it appear any less how deeply cunning hypocrites can hide their snares, and why the Lord rightly requires serpent-like prudence from his people, since they have to deal with men of this kind. We ought to observe this in such a way that we are not terrified if anything of the kind happens to us as well. For just as our Lord Jesus Christ, seizing the occasion, set out most wholesome teaching on the first institution, dignity and use of marriage, and refuted those wicked men together with the whole crowd of lustful people, so he is accustomed to act in his members by his Spirit, so that what the adversaries contrive in order to make them despised or hated turns out to be honourable and beneficial for them. Therefore let us be strong in him, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCXXVI.
units.tr: Homily CCXXVI.

units.la: IESVS vero respondens dixit eis: Non legistis, quod qui fecit [hominem] ab initio, marem & foeminam fecit eos, & dixit: Praeterea relinquet homo patrem & matrem, & agglutinabitur vxori suae: & qui duo erant, fient caro vna. Itaque non amplius sunt duo, sed vna caro. Quod ergo Deus coniunxit, homo non separet.
units.tr: Jesus answered and said to them: "Have ye not read, that he which made them at the beginning made them male and female, and said, For this cause shall a man leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife: and they twain shall be one flesh? Wherefore they are no more twain, but one flesh. What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder."

units.la: CVm ad Dominum nostrum IESVM CHRISTVM, qui in Iudaea redierat, populus vndique confluceret, & hunc ille magno successu doceret, mox eum aggressi sunt Pharisaei, qui vt eius concionem interrumperent, quaestionem insidiosam mouerunt de iure diuortij: Quo exemplo docemur, nunquam defuturos aduersarios, qui sese Christo & eius Euangelio opponant, & hos plerunque futuros eos, qui praecipuam sanctitatis existimationem in mundo iustinent. Tales erant isti, qui simulant quidem disputare sibi licentiam diuortiorum, quae sub praetextu Legis, vel potius priuilegij per Mosem concessi, inter Iudaeos vulgo regnabat: interim hoc agunt, vt eum tanquam Moysi contrarium populo exosum reddant, vel vt sibi ipsi contradicentem in contemptum adducant, sicuti alias quoque fecerunt. Et prodest exempla eiusmodi obseruare, vt non offendamur, si quid simile fit hodie, vigilemus autem & nos ad certamina fortiter & prudenter excipienda praeparemus. Et docet hoc proprio exemplo Dominus, qui praesenti animo & fortiter Pharisaeis respondet: & primo eos ad coniugij institutionem reuocat: deinde quae ratio Mosem mouerit, docet, vt hoc patribus permitteret, quo ipsi tunc non minus inhumaniter quam turpiter abutebantur: postremo suam de diuortijs sententiam diserte explicat.
units.tr: When the people came flocking from every quarter to our Lord Jesus Christ, who had returned to Judea, and he was teaching them with great success, the Pharisees immediately set upon him. In order to break up his sermon, they raised a captious question about the right of divorce. From this example we learn that there will never be lack of adversaries who set themselves against Christ and his Gospel, and that they will for the most part be those who hold the highest reputation for holiness in the world. Such were these men, who pretended to dispute about the liberty of divorce, which under the pretext of the Law, or rather of the privilege granted through Moses, was commonly practised among the Jews. Meanwhile their aim was to make him hateful to the people as opposed to Moses, or to bring him into contempt by showing him to contradict himself, as they had done on other occasions too. It is useful to observe examples of this kind, so that we are not offended if anything similar happens today, and so that we too keep watch and prepare ourselves to meet contests bravely and wisely. The Lord himself teaches this by his own example: he answers the Pharisees with presence of mind and courage. First he recalls them to the institution of marriage; then he explains the reason which moved Moses to permit this to the fathers, a permission they were then abusing no less inhumanly than shamefully; and finally he sets out plainly his own judgment on divorce.

units.la: Quod ad primam responsionis partem, ab acri & vehementi interrogatione exorditur, qua voluntariam & crassam ignorantiam ipsi exprobrat, dicens: Non legistis, quod qui fecit, &c. Legerant vtique, neque ignorabant prorsus, quomodo totam hanc mundi machinam, & postea hominem quoque creasset Deus: sed negligenter (vt omnia alia quae in scripturis traduntur) legebant ista, & quam uis scirent inexcusabilem esse licentiam istam diuortiorum, & Domini de illa sententiam iampridem audiuissent, odium tamen eius ita ipsos excaecabat, vt non attenderent. Tales hodie etiam multi sunt, qui scripturas legunt, canunt & audiunt quotidie, neque possunt improbare, quae illis tradunter, attamen odio Veritatis fascinati tergiuersantur, & omnes contradicendi occasiones aucupando sibi ipsis tenebras offundunt, vt videntibus oculis caecutiant. Quia vero interim rudi populo fucum faciunt, digni sunt, qui acrius corripiantur, vt omnes intelligant, non tantum eis tribui debere, quantum sibi vendicant. Cur enim illis parcatur, qui sui nominis existimationem & commodum priuatum gloriae Dei ac publicae saluti praeferunt?
units.tr: As for the first part of his answer, he begins with a sharp and vehement question, by which he reproaches them for their wilful and gross ignorance, saying: "Have ye not read, that he which made them, etc.?" They had certainly read it, and they were not wholly ignorant of how God had made this whole machinery of the world and afterwards man also. But they read these things carelessly, as they read all the other things that are handed down in the Scriptures; and although they knew that this licence of divorce was inexcusable, and had long since heard the Lord's judgment on it, their hatred blinded them so that they did not pay attention. There are many such people today too, who read the Scriptures, sing them and hear them every day, and cannot disapprove of what is taught them; yet, bewitched by hatred of the truth, they shuffle off, and by seeking out every opportunity for contradiction they throw darkness over themselves, so that their eyes grow dim while they are looking. Yet because they meanwhile deceive the simple people, they deserve to be rebuked more sharply, so that everyone understands they should not be granted as much as they claim for themselves. For why should we spare those who put their own reputation and private advantage before the glory of God and the public good?

units.la: Admonet praeterea exemplo suo Christus, quid fieri debeat, si quando controuersiae incidunt, de quibus iam olim suam sententiam Deus exposuit. Quaerunt isti de iure diuortij, & Mosis authoritate nituntur. Sed Dominus ad primam coniugij institutionem prouocat, vt ex ea colligant quid de diuortijs sit statuendum. Ita Paulum fecisse legimus apud Corinthios, cum hi Coenam Domini mysticam in vsum prophanum conuertissent. Idem ergo fiat in omnibus articulis controuersis, & mox sopitis contentionibus rei Veritas patefiet. Disputant hodie de imaginibus & harum vsu homines superstitiosi, & miris exceptionibus fucu faciunt imperitis, ut illas in templis retineat, & eiectas reducant. At si Deum in Lege sua loquentem audiamus, mox disputandi finis erit. Pro hibet enim Deus, ne sibi vllam imaginem affingamus, & se in nulla forma viri aut foemina, aut alicuius rei creatae apparere voluisse testatur, ne quae occasio inde arriperetur, alicuius imaginis ipsi affingendae. Monet praeterea, ut si qui alij imagines faciant, nullum illis cultu aut honore tribuamus, sed ut vanitates, ut sordes & stercora, ut abominationes deniq; reiciamus: Doctrinam vero & admonitiones ex Verbo suo petere iubet, non ex simulachris, quae mendacij doctores & magistri a Propheta dicuntur. Quod si hoc omnes insisterent, abruptam mox videremus omnem de hoc contendendi materiam.
units.tr: Moreover, Christ by his example shows what ought to be done if controversies arise about matters on which God long ago set out his judgment. These men ask about the right of divorce and rest on the authority of Moses. But the Lord appeals to the first institution of marriage, so that from it they may gather what must be decided about divorces. So we read that Paul did among the Corinthians, when they had turned the Lord's Supper to profane use. Let the same be done in all controverted articles, and once the contentions are laid to rest, the truth of the matter will be made plain. Today superstitious men dispute about images and their use, and by wonderful exceptions they deceive the unlearned, so that they keep images in the churches and bring back those that have been cast out. But if we hear God speaking in his Law, the dispute will soon be at an end. For God forbids us to make any image for ourselves, and he declares that he did not wish to appear in the form of man or woman, or of any created thing, lest any occasion should be seized from this for making an image of him. He further warns that if others make images, we should give them no worship or honour, but reject them as vanities, filth and dung, and finally as abominations. He orders us to seek doctrine and admonitions from his Word, not from the statues, which the Prophet calls teachers of lies. If everyone kept to this, we would soon see every matter of contention on this subject cut off.

units.la: Idem dici potest de diebus festis & feriis, de quibus non minori contentione animorum disputa tur abijs, qui Iudaico more dies & tempora observant: adhaec Diuorum meritis & cultui plus tri buunt, quam fidei Christianae puritas permittat. Sed hi quoq; ad primam Sabbati institutionem revocandi sunt, quam omnibus ceremonijs, imo omnibus praeceptis alijs Dei antiquiore esse constat. Nam in ipsa rerum origine, cum Deus sex diebus perfecisset creationem caeli & terrae, atq; omnium quae his continentur, quieuit die septimo, & huic benedixit atq; sanctificauit eu, ut nobis quoq; operum eius meditationi & verae pietatis exercitijs consecratus esse debeat. Neq; ab eo tempore ferias alias instituit. Enimuero multa posteris temporibus facta sunt, quorum memoria nobis perpetua & sancta esse debet, ut pote humani generis conseruatio tempore diluuij, fœderis quod tunc abolitum videri poterat, instauratio cum Abrahamo facta, Iacobi in Ægyptum deductio, & alia huius generis innumera: attamen cum Legem daret, nullas nouas ferias instituit. Sed Sabbati diem horum omni um meditationi sufficere voluit, & illius obseruatione praecepto peculiari commendauit, cuius par tes duae sunt: Prima, ut sex diebus faciamus, quaecunq; nobis facta necessaria sunt: Altera, ut se ptimo die ab omni opere seruili feriemur. Ut ergo Sabbati otium nobis mandatur: ita no minus praecipitur, ut sex totis & continuis diebus operi intenti simus, ne videlicet otium sub religionis praetextu vel in superstitionem degeneret, vel licentiam peccandi pariat, ad quam natura proclives sumus. Quid ergo quaestione multa opus est de feriis Diuorum, quando nullas Deus instituit, quam quae ipsi consecratae sint, & vicissim reliquis diebus nos operari, non feriari iussit. Sed haec exempli loco adduxisse sufficiat.
units.tr: The same can be said about feast days and holy days, over which, with no less contention of spirits, dispute is carried on with those who observe days and seasons in the Jewish manner; moreover they attribute more to the merits and worship of the saints than the purity of the Christian faith allows. But these too must be recalled to the first institution of the Sabbath, which is known to be older than all the ceremonies, indeed older than all the other precepts of God. For at the very origin of things, when God had finished the creation of heaven and earth and all that they contain in six days, he rested on the seventh day, and blessed it and sanctified it, so that it should be set apart for us too for meditation on his works and for the exercises of true piety. Nor from that time did he institute any other festivals. Indeed many things have happened in later times, the memory of which ought to be perpetual and holy for us: such as the preservation of the human race at the time of the flood, the renewal of the covenant made with Abraham, when it might have seemed to have been abolished, the bringing of Jacob into Egypt, and countless other things of this kind. Yet when he gave the Law, he instituted no new feasts. Rather he willed that the day of the Sabbath should suffice for the meditation on all these things, and he commended its observance by a special precept, which has two parts. The first is that we should do in six days whatever deeds are necessary for us; the second is that on the seventh day we should abstain from all servile work. Thus, just as rest on the Sabbath is commanded us, so too it is no less commanded that we be busy at work for six whole and continuous days, so that rest under the pretext of religion does not degenerate into superstition, or give licence to sin, to which by nature we are prone. Why then is there any need for much questioning about the feasts of the saints, when God has instituted none except those that are consecrated to himself, and has ordered us to work and not to rest on the other days? But it will be enough to have adduced these things by way of example.

units.la: Audiamus nunc quid de coniugij institutione prima dicat Dominus. Sunt illa eiusmodi, ut singula prope verba doceant licentiam diuortiorum nequaquam cum Dei instituto conuenire, & proinde nullo modo probari posse. Primum ait: Qui fecit ab initio mare & foeminam fecit eos. Graece est ὁ ποιήσας, id est, qui creator & opifex est omnium, qui hominem quoq; fecit, ut initio statim non vnum solum, sed binos creauit, mare videlicet & foeminam, ut hisimul coniuncti viuerent. Ex quo sequitur, non debere illos duos temere seiungi. Ad confirmationem huius facit, quod Deus ipse de Adamo dixit: Non bonum est hominem esse solum, faciamus ei adiutorium, quod sit coram illo, &c. Secundò, Propterea relinquet homo patrem & matrem, & agglutinabitur uxori suae. Inter homines nulla videtur arctior esse coniunctio, quam quae inter parentes & filios est, qui ex his progeniti eius vitam suam debent: & hoc gentium sapientes obseruarunt, qui parem gratiam parentibus reddi posse negauerunt. At arctius multo est vinculum coniugij, cui quae parentibus debetur pietas, cedere iubetur. Etenim cum ex omnibus animantibus nullum inueniretur, quod Adamo conueniret, & ex eius sopiti latere Eam creauisset Deus, mox hac visa quasi exultans ille clamat: Hoc nunc os ex ossibus meis, & caro ex carne mea: ideo vocabitur Ischa, id est, virago, quia de viro sumpta est. Et mox ex Spiritus sancti suggestione hanc coniugij legem fert, cuius in praesenti meminit Dominus, ut eam perpetuam & inuiolabilem manere debere doceat. Cum enim impij merito dicantur, qui debitum officium parentibus negant, quales merentur dici, qui coniugij ius violat, aut coniuges temere abs se dimittunt, quorum gratia, si opus sit parentes debet deseri? Ne tamen dicitur hoc Adamo temere excidisse putetur, eius ratione reddit Dominus, et addit: Qui duo erant, fiemt caro vna, id est, ea conditione coiunguntur vir & foemina, ut qui duo interse distin cti & separati erat, vna caro, id est, vnus homo fiat. Ut ergo homo no potest in partes diuidi, quin totus intereat, zita neq; coniuges temere diuortiu facere possunt, quin Dei institutum violetur, & illi de salute periclitentur. Ex his firmissime concludit: Quod ergo Deus coniunxit, homo ne separet: & hoc dicens, turpem illam & crudelem uxores repudiandi licentiam ita damnat & abrogat, ut nemo quantumuis malitiosus, contradicere audeat, nisi primam coniugij institutionem damnare, & in Deum ipsum linguam habenas laxare velit. At quia de diuortijs postea ipse plura addet, quando Pharisaei priuilegium a Mose concessum obijcientibus respondebit, haec modo de hac causa dicta sufficiant. Interim hac occasione excitati discant Christiani homines, quanto grauius scelus sit, si qui abs quo omni iuris praetextu, turpi & impudenti scortandi aut moechandi licentia vinculum coniugij abrumpant. Quod tunc demum intelligemus, si quanta sit coniugij dignitas videamus, & quam multifariam peccent, qui illius leges adulteris & vaga libidine violant.
units.tr: Let us now hear what the Lord says about the first institution of marriage. The words are such that almost each one teaches that the licence of divorce by no means agrees with God's institution and therefore cannot be approved in any way. First he says: "He who made them from the beginning made them male and female." In Greek it is [ὁ ποιήσας], that is, he who is the creator and maker of all things, who also made man, so that at the very beginning he created not one alone but two, male and female, to live together joined in this way. From this it follows that those two should not be rashly separated. This is confirmed by what God himself said of Adam: "It is not good for man to be alone; let us make him a help meet for him," etc. Secondly, "For this cause shall a man leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife." Among men no closer bond seems to exist than that between parents and children, who, having been begotten by them, owe their life to them; and the wise men of the nations observed this, and denied that an equal return of gratitude could be made to parents. Yet the bond of marriage is much closer, and the duty of piety owed to parents is commanded to give way to it. For when among all living creatures none was found that suited Adam, and God had created Eve from his side while he slept, Adam, seeing her, cried out as if exultant: "This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh; therefore she shall be called Ischa, that is, woman, because she was taken out of man." And immediately, under the prompting of the Holy Spirit, he laid down this law of marriage, which the Lord now recalls, so as to teach that it must remain perpetual and inviolable. For if those are rightly called wicked who deny the duty owed to parents, what should we call those who violate the right of marriage, or rashly put away their spouses, for whose sake parents must be forsaken if need be? Lest it be thought that this came from Adam rashly, the Lord gives the reason for it and adds: "They twain shall be one flesh," that is, a man and a woman are joined on this condition, that the two who were distinct and separate from each other become one flesh, that is, one man. Just as a man cannot be divided into parts without perishing as a whole, so spouses cannot rashly divorce without violating God's institution and putting their own salvation in danger. From these things he draws the firmest conclusion: "What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder." And in saying this he condemns and abrogates so completely that shameful and cruel licence to repudiate wives, that no one, however malicious, dares to contradict it, unless he wishes to condemn God's first institution of marriage and to let loose his tongue against God himself. But because he will himself add more about divorce later, when he answers the Pharisees who object the privilege granted by Moses, let what has been said on this point for now suffice. Meanwhile, Christian people, stirred up by this occasion, should learn how much more grave a crime it is when anyone, under no pretext of right, breaks the bond of marriage out of a shameful and shameless licence to whore or commit adultery. We shall understand this only if we see how great the dignity of marriage is, and how many ways those sin who violate its laws by adultery and wandering lust.

units.la: Coniugium est legitima & a Deo instituta unius viri & unius feminae coniunctio, cum v-trius consensu, ut se mutuo iuuent, sobolem generent, & illicitis libidinibus remedium inueniant. Conuenit haec definitio cum scripturis sacris. Etenim, ut paulo ante diximus, Deus pronuntiauit non esse bonum, ut homo solus sit, sed adiutorio opus esse, quo cum vitam transigat. Idem ipse Adamo Euam ut nymphagogus adduxit, & nuptijs eorum benedixit: Crescite & multiplicamini, & implete terram, & subiugite eam, &c. Et Paulus ait: Propter fornicationes suam quisque uxorem habeat, & proprium quaeque virum habeat. Haec omnia coniugij dignitatem commendant. Primum ab authore Deo, qui cum solus bonus & sanctus sit, nihil quam bonum & sanctum instituit & iubet. Huc respexit Solomon, cum diceret: Domus & diuitiae ex parentum haereditate obueniunt, uxor autem prudens a Domino. Et vulgo dicitur, coniugia Dei dispensatione contrahi. Deinde a vetustate, qua omnia alia hominum instituta & vitae genera superat: & ne propter molestias, quae postea irrepserunt, inter peccati poenas numeraretur, ante hominis lapsum coepit. Itaque perfecta sanctitas coniugium, & thorus coniugium impollutus: impij vero sunt & daemoniorum dogma fouent, qui illud inter carnis opera numerant. Quo ad finem & vsum, tale est, ut sine eo nec commodè nec honestè viui, neque genus humani legitimè conseruari ac propagari possit. Et ut illius author est Deus, ita suo spiritu idem hanc notitiam omnium hominum cordibus inscripsit, ut quod Apostolus ait, apud omnes omnibus saeculis honorabile fuerit, & inter gentes quoque non omnino barbaras, & ab omni honestatis sensu alienas poenis grauibus punitis sint, qui alienos thoros libidine sua polluerunt. Et enim quanti coniugium ante legem latam fecerint gentes, Pharaonis & Abimelechi Regum exempla docent, qui scelus inexcusabile iudicarunt, si Abrahami, hominis peregrini, uxorem violauissent. Iob quoque, inter scelera grauissima, a quibus se immunem fuisse testatur, adulterium numerat, dicens: Si concupiscentia uxoris alienae obnoxium fuit cor meum, & ante ostium sodalis mei insidiatus sum, permolat uxorem meam alius, & subiugant eam alij. Hoc enim grande flagitium est, & iniquitas capitali actione persequenda, &c. Vnde apparet Deum, priusquam in lege Moysis capitis poenam adulteris decerneret, hanc notitiam per legem naturae cordibus hominum inscriptam esse, ut scelus hoc capitale esse intellexerint.
units.tr: Marriage is the lawful union, instituted by God, of one man and one woman, entered into with the consent of both, so that they may help one another, produce offspring, and find a remedy for unlawful lusts. This definition agrees with the holy Scriptures. For, as we said a little earlier, God declared that it is not good for man to be alone, but that he needs a helper with whom to spend his life. The same God brought Eve to Adam as a go-between, and blessed their marriage: "Be fruitful and multiply, and fill the earth, and subdue it," etc. And Paul says: "Because of fornications, let each man have his own wife, and each woman her own husband." All these things commend the dignity of marriage. First, it has God as its author, who, since he alone is good and holy, institutes and commands nothing but what is good and holy. Solomon had this in mind when he said: "House and riches come by inheritance from parents, but a prudent wife is from the Lord." And it is commonly said that marriages are contracted by the providence of God. Second, it has antiquity, by which it surpasses all other human institutions and ways of life. So that marriage would not be counted among the punishments of sin because of the troubles which later crept in, it began before the fall of man. Therefore marriage is perfect holiness, and the marriage bed is undefiled; but those who count it among the works of the flesh are impious and foster the doctrine of demons. As to its end and use, it is such that without it one can neither live conveniently and honourably, nor can the human race be lawfully preserved and propagated. And as God is its author, so by his Spirit he has written this knowledge on the hearts of all men, so that, as the Apostle says, it has been honourable among all people in all ages. Even among nations not altogether barbarous, and alien from every sense of honesty, those who have polluted other men's beds by their lust have been punished with severe penalties. How highly the nations valued marriage before the law was given is taught by the examples of the kings Pharaoh and Abimelech, who judged it an inexcusable crime if they had violated the wife of Abraham, a foreigner. Job also, among the gravest crimes from which he testifies that he was free, counts adultery, saying: "If my heart has been enticed by another man's wife, and I have lain in wait at my neighbour's door, let another grind for my wife, and let others bow down over her. For this is a great wickedness, an iniquity to be punished by judgment," etc. Hence it appears that God, before he decreed the death penalty for adulterers in the law of Moses, had this knowledge written on men's hearts through the law of nature, so that they understood this to be a capital crime.

units.la: Hodie quidem, quae nostri saeculi calamitas & nequitia est, leuiculum putatur, & multis lusus & iocus risu potius quam poena aliqua dignus videtur, si & vxori propriae fidem datam improbè fallant, & alterius coniugę insuper polluant. At si quis omni carnis affectu posito rem penitius inspiciat, tam multiplex hoc scelus esse patebit, ut ne mors quidem vna illi expiando sufficiat. Etenim primo multifariam in Deum peccatur primum coniugij authorem, quo auspice illud contrahitur atq; confirmatur. Multiplex etiam est iniuria, quae fit non coniugi modo, verumetiam affinibus & toti eius cognationi: et item, qua ad satiandam libidinem suam adulteri abutuntur: liberis item proprijs, quorum salus ipsis propria vita charior esse debebat: adeò ut, si adulterium cum alijs sceleribus conferas, vix aliquod inuenias, quod cum illo conferri possit, eo quod reliqua omnia fere illud comitantur, aut ex illo emanant, ut non absque ratione multiceps hydra omnis generis scelerum possit dici. At quia de his prolixè dictum est supra capite quinto, homilia 67. minimè opus est hic eadem repetere. De eo autem admonendi sunt Christiani homines, ne eorum argutijs & sophisticae se decipi sinant, qui veteris Legis rigorem in nouo testamento abrogatum esse dicunt. Nam hos falsi arguit Christus, qui se non ideo venisse ait, ut legem aboleat aut soluat, sed ut impleat. pleat. Idem non adulterium modo, sed concupiscentiam quoq; alienæ mulieris prohibet, & per Apo stolos ex regno cælorum adulteros excludit. Deniq; quotidianis exemplis docemur verissimè ab Apostolo dictum esse: Adulteros & scortatores iudicabit Deus. Nam etsi ferè leges & iudicia publica sileant, & ideo libidines vagæ passim impunè grassentur, non dormitat tamen iudicium Domini, qui illarum sectatores & patronos multat in fortunis, corpore & anima. Huius ergo memi nerint Christiani homines, & vasa sua ab omni pollutione ferunt in sanctitate in diem Domini nostri IESV CHRISTI, cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Today, indeed, which is the calamity and wickedness of our age, it is thought a trifle. To many it seems a joke and a jest deserving laughter rather than any punishment, if a man deceitfully breaks faith given to his own wife and moreover defiles another's spouse. But if anyone sets aside all fleshly feeling and looks more deeply into the matter, it will be clear that this sin is so manifold that not even one death suffices to atone for it. For first, sin is committed in many ways against God, the first author of marriage, under whose auspices it is contracted and confirmed. The injury is also manifold: it is done not only to the spouse but also to in-laws and to her whole kindred; likewise, adulterers abuse the marriage to sate their own lust; likewise it is done to their own children, whose safety ought to have been dearer to them than their own life. So much so that if you compare adultery with other sins, you will hardly find any that can be compared with it, since almost all the others accompany it or flow from it, so that not without reason it can be called the many-headed hydra of every kind of wickedness. But since these things were treated at length above in chapter five, homily 67, there is no need to repeat them here. Christians should, however, be warned not to allow themselves to be deceived by the cleverness and sophistry of those who say that the rigour of the Old Law has been abrogated in the New Testament. For Christ refutes these men, saying that he came not to abolish or loosen the law, but to fulfil it. He forbids not only adultery but also the desire for another's wife, and through the Apostles he excludes adulterers from the kingdom of heaven. Finally, we are taught by daily examples that what the Apostle said is most true: "God will judge adulterers and fornicators." For even if laws and public courts for the most part keep silent, so that wandering lusts run riot everywhere unpunished, the judgment of the Lord does not sleep, but punishes the followers and patrons of those lusts in their fortunes, body and soul. Let Christians therefore remember this, and let them keep their vessels in holiness and honour, free from all pollution, until the day of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCXXVII.
units.tr: HOMILY 227.

units.la: Dicunt ei: Cur ergo Moses mandauit dare libellum discessionis, & eam dimittere? Dicit eis: Moses pro duritia cordis vestri permisit vobis dimittere vxores vestras: cæterum a principio non fuit ita. Dico autem vobis, quicunq; dimiserit vxorem suam, nisi ob scortatio-nem, & aliam duxerit, cum mœchari; & qui dimissam duxerit, mœ-chari.
units.tr: They said to him: Why then did Moses command to give a certificate of divorce, and to dismiss her? He said to them: Moses, because of the hardness of your hearts, permitted you to dismiss your wives; but from the beginning it was not so. And I say to you, whoever dismisses his wife, except for fornication, and marries another, commits adultery; and whoever marries her who is dismissed commits adultery. (Matth. 19.)

units.la: INterrogarunt nuper Pharisæi IESVM Dominum & seruatorē nostrum, an liceat viro vxo-rem suam quauis de causa dimittere? Ille verò quia eos sciebat malitiosè agere, nec aliud quàm calumniandi occasionem captare, non statim diserte aut Categoricè (vt Dialectici loquuntur) re-spondet, sed initio eos ad primam coniugij institutionem remittit, & suo exemplo docet, quid fieri debeat in controuersis articulis, & tunc quidem cumprimis, quando nobis res est cum aduersarijs malignis, qui non de veritate institui cupiunt, sed contradicendi ansam solicitè quærunt. Nam etsi cum talibus nihil proficias, vt qui ne Deo quidem cedant, prodest tamen cum illis methodum hanc sequi, quam Christus suo exemplo nobis commendat, vt simpliciores intelligant, nos Dei authori-tate niti, & illorum contumacia minus offendantur. Porrò de coniugij institutione prima sic disse-ruit Dominus, vt ex ea recte concludat, non recte facere eos, qui priuata autho-ritate vinculum coniugij dissoluunt, quod Deus indissolubile esse voluit.
units.tr: Recently the Pharisees questioned Jesus the Lord and our Saviour, whether it is lawful for a man to dismiss his wife for any cause at all. But he, because he knew they were acting maliciously, and were seeking nothing but an occasion to slander him, does not reply at once plainly or categorically (as the logicians put it), but at the start refers them back to the first institution of marriage, and by his own example teaches what ought to be done in disputed matters. This is especially so when we have to deal with malicious adversaries, who do not wish to be instructed in the truth but diligently seek an occasion for contradiction. For although you accomplish nothing with such people, since they will not yield even to God, it is still useful to follow with them the method which Christ commends to us by his example, so that the simpler sort may understand that we rest on the authority of God, and that they may be less offended by the obstinacy of those men. Moreover, the Lord spoke about the first institution of marriage in such a way that he rightly concludes that those do not act rightly who dissolve the bond of marriage by private authority, a bond which God willed to be indissoluble.

units.la: Sequitur Pharisæorum responsio, qui nouam quæstionem mouent: Cur ergo Moses mandauit dare libellum discessionis, & vxorē dimittere? Vbi apparet, illos probè intellexisse Christi senten-tiam, neq; hanc potuisse improbare: non tamē cedunt Veritati, sed odij contra hunc concepti virus produnt, dum Mosis authoritatem illam premunt. Quasi diceret: Tu quidem dicis, non esse seiungen-dos eos, quos Deus coniunxit: nec de eo iam disputare volumus. At alius nos scrupulus angit: nimi-rum quod longè alia videtur esse Mosis sententia, qui mandauit, vt si quis vxorem habeat sibi minus acceptam aut gratiosam, dato repudij libello eam dimittat. Et hoc dicendo non aliud quæ-runt, quàm vt apud populū illi inuidiā & odium conflent, quasi Mosi contradicat, & eo sanctior & sapientior haberi velit. Interim improbissimè agunt, & non tam Christo quàm Mosi iniuriā faciunt, dum eius verba in alienum sensum detorquent, et illum dicunt mandasse, quod præter ani-mi voluntatē certis de causis concesserat. Etenim nusquam ille iussit, vt quis vxorem suam quauis de causa ex priuata libidine dimittat. sed (vt postea sequetur) cum videret id in illa gente nō pos-se omnino prohiberi, modū præscripsit, quæ sequerentur ij, qui vxores eijcere volebant. Id vero isti dissimulant, & vt rudi ac simplici populo imponant, ex permissione præceptum siue mandatū sin-gunt. Itasolent hodie facere multi rixatores, dum aliquem scripturæ locum pertinaciùs secundum literam vrgent, neq; vllas rationes ex ore Dei & institutis eius desumptas admittunt. Fit hoc in altercatione illa sacramentaria circa Cœnam Dominicam & alijs prope omnibus, de quibus con-tenditur. Itaq; magna cautione simul & fortitudine opus est ijs, quibus cum talibus res est.
units.tr: There follows the reply of the Pharisees, who raise a new question: Why then did Moses command to give a certificate of divorce and to dismiss the wife? Here it is clear that they had understood well Christ's sentence and could not refute it; yet they do not yield to the truth, but betray the venom of the hatred they have conceived against him, while they press the authority of Moses. As if they said: You indeed say that those whom God has joined are not to be separated, and we do not now wish to dispute about that. But another scruple troubles us, namely that the opinion of Moses seems quite different, for he commanded that if anyone has a wife less acceptable or pleasing to him, he should dismiss her by giving a bill of divorce. And in saying this they seek nothing else than to stir up envy and hatred against him among the people, as if he contradicted Moses, and they wish to be thought holier and wiser than he. Meanwhile they act most shamelessly, and do injury not so much to Christ as to Moses, while they twist his words into a foreign sense and say that he commanded what, beyond his own intention, he had permitted for certain reasons. For he nowhere ordered that anyone should dismiss his wife for any cause at all out of private lust; but (as will follow later) when he saw that this could not be prohibited altogether among that people, he prescribed the manner in which those who wished to cast out their wives should proceed. These men, however, conceal this, and in order to impose upon a rude and simple people, they invent a command out of a permission. So many quarrelsome men are accustomed to do today, when they press some passage of Scripture stubbornly according to the letter, and admit no reasons drawn from the mouth of God and his institutions. This happens in that sacramentarian controversy about the Lord's Supper, and in almost all the other matters over which contention arises. Therefore great caution and at the same time firmness are needed by those who have to deal with such people.

units.la: Exemplum, quod sequamur, hic quoq; præbet Dominus, qui Pharisæis dicit: Propter duritia cor-dis vestri permisit vobis Moses dimittere vxores vestras. Permissionem aut concessionem nu-dam esse docet, quod illi mandatum esse dicebant, & insuper Mosem ita excusat & defendit, vt culpam omnem in Iudæos reijciat, atq; simul ostendat, illum etiamsi hoc permiserit, minimè tamen licentiam diuortiorum probauisse, quæ tunc inter Iudæos regnabat. Quasi diceret: Quid opus est Mosem mihi obijcere, qui de patrum vestrorum contumacia toties conquestus est, venon possit negari, ipsum in hac quoque causa illis praeter animi voluntatem indulsisse. Videbat enim plerosque ingenio tam feroci & implacabili esse, vt vxores, quas semel odisse coepissent, occisuri essent, si eas retinere cogerentur, vel ita tractaturi, vt illas mori praestaret. Permisit ergo, vt dimitterent abs se, sed cum conditione eiusmodi, quae deliberationem grauem & diligentem requirebat, & quasimul vxorum absq; causa iusta repudiatarum honori consulebatur. Addit autem ex prima coniugij institutione: A principio non fuit ita. Id est, Deus non ita fieri voluit, neq; in coniugio ita luserunt sancti patres, qui ante Mosem vixerunt, &c. Itaq; ciuilis dispensatio fuit, quod Moses permisit, maioris mali vitandi causa instituta: quales multae in legibus ciuilibus praesertim municipalibus, inueniuntur, quas si quis ad viuum resecare velit, & cum Christi praeceptis conferre, ab his illas non parum differre patebit. In illis ergo meminisse oportet Christianos homines, ipsis non semper licitum esse coram Deo, quod per leges ciuiles licet: & ideo in omnibus actionibus suis suae vocationis ratione habeant, & potius quid fides & charitas requirat, cogitent, quam quid priuilegia eiusmodi hominibus prophanis & saeculo deditis concedant. Peccatur in eo hodie a multis non solum ex vulgo, verumetiam Ecclesiarum ministris & scholarum praefectis, qui se inter eos versentur, quibus per leges conceditur perpotare alea ludere, licentius vestiri, & alia huius generis, mox sibi quoq; ista licere existimant, & pessimo vitae exemplo authoritatem suam turpiter prostituunt, atque ita salsiunt infatuatus, qui extra Ecclesiam eiici & conculcari meretur.
units.tr: The Lord here also provides an example for us to follow, for he says to the Pharisees: Because of the hardness of your hearts Moses permitted you to dismiss your wives. He teaches that it was a bare permission or concession, which they were saying was a command; and further he excuses and defends Moses in such a way as to throw all the blame upon the Jews, and at the same time to show that Moses, even though he permitted this, nevertheless did not approve the licence of divorces which then reigned among the Jews. As if to say: What need is there to object Moses to me, who so often complained of the obstinacy of your fathers, when it cannot be denied that he too, in this matter as well, indulged them beyond his own will? For he saw that most men were of such a fierce and implacable temper that, once they began to hate the wives they had, they would kill them if they were compelled to keep them, or would treat them so that death would be preferable for them. He therefore permitted them to put them away from themselves, but under a condition of such a kind as required a grave and careful deliberation, and at the same time provision was made for the honour of wives who had been repudiated without just cause. He adds, moreover, from the first institution of marriage: From the beginning it was not so. That is, God did not wish it to be done so, nor did the holy fathers who lived before Moses act so in marriage, and so on. Therefore what Moses permitted was a civil dispensation, instituted to avoid a greater evil; many such provisions are found in civil laws, especially in municipal laws, and if anyone wished to cut them down to the quick and compare them with the precepts of Christ, it will be plain that they differ not a little from them. Christians ought therefore to remember in regard to such laws that what civil laws permit is not always lawful for them before God; and so in all their actions they should take account of their calling, and think rather about what faith and charity require than about what privileges of this kind grant to profane men given over to the world. Many today sin in this respect, not only among the common people but also among ministers of the Church and prefects of schools, who live among such people; since the laws allow them to drink to excess, play dice, dress more freely, and other things of this kind, they soon think these things are permitted to themselves as well, and by a most wicked example of life they shamefully prostitute their authority, and so become foolish and insipid, deserving to be cast out of the Church and trampled underfoot.

units.la: Iterum ne Christus tergiuersari & luce subterfugere putaretur, suam de diuortiis sententiam diserte proferet: quod factu opus erat, cum procul dubio licentia illa, quae olim caperet, sub Romanis, qui tunc Iudeam per praesides suos gubernabant, in immensum creuerat. Et ex verbis eius colligere possumus, frequens hoc fuisse, vt mulieres, quae se maritis suis displiceret, sententiam ferebant, saepe alijs aures praeberent, qui ipsis si dimitterentur, coniugij spem faciebant: quod item multi eas, quas dimiserant, ex nouo coniugio opulentiores factas, postea ad se reciperent: quod non multis ante Filij Dei incarnationem annis, Romae fecerat Cato, grauissimus (scilicet) honestatis publicae vindex. Nam vxorem Martiam, ex qua filios genuerat, & tunc quoq; praegnantem, sub artis-ris amicitiae praetextu Hortensio concessit, & cum hic moriens illam haeredem scripsisset, eandem denuo ad se recepit. Et ex historiis constat, quam turpi leuitate multi ex Iudaeis tunc gentium moribus atq; opinionibus sese accommodarent. Quid enim non facerent, quando inter eos publice sua placita professi Saducaei, qui Epicuraeorum similes animarum immortalitatem & mortuorum resurrectionem negabant, & quaecunq; de spiritibus tam bonis quam malis traduntur, ludibrio habebant. Quapropter quod supra in lege explicatione dixerat Dominus, in praesenti repetit, dicens: Dico autem vobis, quicunq; dimiserit vxorem suam, nisi ob sornicationem, & aliam duxerit, eum moechari, & qui dimissam duxerit, moechari. Adulteria vocat, quae ipsi coniugia dicebant, imo sub vno diuortio tria adulteria latere, vel potius palam committi, testatur. Nam qui vxorem dimittit, & aliam ducit, eo ipso adulter fit. Deinde vxorem quoq; adulteram facit, dum data repudij libello potestatem illi facit, vt alteri nubat. Tertio adulterium quoq; committit, qui dimissam ducit. Ratio huius dicti est, quod in nullius priuata potestate sit, coniugij legitime facti vinculum dissoluere. Ex eo sequitur, quod etsi quis vxorem ita dimittat, apud Dei tribunal tamen adhuc firmum ratumq; est coniugium illud: & qui illud facit, plus iuris sibi sumit, quam Deus ipsi dederit, adeoq; vxorem prostituit, quae eius caro est, & cui se totum debet.
units.tr: Again, lest Christ be thought to evade the matter and flee from the light, he plainly sets forth his opinion about divorces; this had to be done, since without doubt that licence which had once been taken had grown immensely under the Romans, who then governed Judea through their governors. And from his words we can gather that it was common for women who were displeased with their husbands to pronounce sentence, and often lent their ears to others who, if they were dismissed, held out hope of marriage to them; likewise many who had dismissed their wives later took them back when they had become richer through a new marriage. Cato, the most serious guardian (to be sure) of public decency, did this at Rome not many years before the incarnation of the Son of God. For he gave his wife Martia, by whom he had begotten sons, and who was then even pregnant, to Hortensius under the pretext of close friendship; and when Hortensius died after naming her his heir, Cato took her back to himself again. And from the histories it is evident with what shameful levity many of the Jews at that time conformed themselves to the customs and opinions of the Gentiles. For what would they not do, when the Sadducees openly professed their opinions among them, men who, like the Epicureans, denied the immortality of souls and the resurrection of the dead, and held in mockery whatever is taught about spirits, both good and evil? Therefore what the Lord had said above in the explanation of the law, he now repeats, saying: But I say to you, whoever dismisses his wife, except for fornication, and marries another, commits adultery, and whoever marries her who is dismissed commits adultery. He calls adulteries what they called marriages, and he testifies that under a single divorce three adulteries lie hidden, or rather are plainly committed. For he who dismisses his wife and takes another becomes an adulterer by that very act. Next, he also makes the wife an adulteress, since by giving her a bill of divorce he gives her the power to marry another. Thirdly, he who marries her who has been dismissed also commits adultery. The reason for this saying is that the bond of a lawfully contracted marriage is not in any private person's power to dissolve. It follows that even if someone dismisses his wife in this way, that marriage nevertheless remains firm and valid before the tribunal of God; and he who does this takes to himself more right than God has given him, and so prostitutes the wife, who is his flesh and to whom he owes himself entirely.

units.la: At hic probe obseruari debet, Christum de diuortiis illegitimis & temerarijs loqui, qualia tunc inter Iudaeos ex cuiusq; priuata libidine fiebant quauis de causa. Hoc enim dum quidam non obseruant, omne diuortium damnant, & dum coniugij & honestatis vindices strenui esse volunt, sortationis & adulteriorum patroni siunt. Clamant quidem cum Christo. Quod Deus coniunxit, homo ne seiungat: sed dum absq; omni exceptione ad omnes extendunt, quod Dominus de iniquis & temerarijs vinculi coniugalis abruptoribus dixit, illi ipsi palam contradicunt, qui in praesenti exceptione diserte ponit, dicens: NISI OBSCORTATIONEM. Hac enim particula causam exprimit, ob quam diuortiū fieri debeat, adulterium videlicet. Conuenit hac cum natura lege, &c. lege, & ideo Imperatorie quoq; leges adulterii iustam diuortij causam esse sentiunt. Etenim adultera, dum sui copiam alteri facit, vinculum coniugij ipsa abrumpit, nec habet quod de maritii iniquitate queratur: huic autem iniuria grauis, & honesto viro intolerabilis fit, si adulteram retinere cogatur. Eadem est ratio inter vxorem probam & adulterum maritum. Quod si quaeras, cur in lege inter causas diuortij nulla adulterij mentio fiat? facilis est responsio, quod haec adulterium capite plecti iubebat: quod si fiat, omnis diuortij quaestio abrumpitur. Quia vero hodie inter Christianos quoq; lex Dei in hac causa fere silet, & imperatorie etiam plerisq; duriores aequo videntur, cauendum tamen est magistratibus, ne indulgentia, qua adulteris parcunt, innocenti coniugi fraudi sit: & illi (vt modo diximus) fornicationis & adulteriorum patroni fiant. Vt vero Christus diuortij iusti causam tradit adulterium, sub quo alia graviora scelera comprehendi, alibi diximus: ita alterius etiam causa Paulus meminit, quae est religionis diuersitas, quando infidelis coniunx fidelem tam contumaciter infestat, vt ei cohabitare nolit, nisi fidem in vnum Christum abneget. Hic enim locum apud nos habere debet illud Christi, quo nos parentes & vxorem cum liberis, imo vitam pro patriam, odisse iubet, si nos ab ipso velint abducere. Attamen fidelis curet, ne ipse diuortij author sit, sed haereat cum infideli, quoad eius fieri potest. Quod si vero infidelis aut discedat, aut fidelem exturbet, aut extorrem facium sequi nolit, non est (vt Apostolus ait) seruituti subiectus frater aut soror in huiusmodi. Deo igitur causam commendet, & libertate sua vel iure qua infidelis coniugis contumacia ei concedit, pie vtatur. Poterat de his omnibus prolixe dici, sed breuiter ista perstringimus, quia eadem supra capite quinto expositia sunt. Nunc sufficiat monuisse, vt Christiani homines de coniugio honorifice sentiant, eius fidem sancte colant, patienter ferant eius molestias nullam diuortij causam alteri praebeant, multo minus temere a suo compare discant. Interim omnibus huius saeculi commodis & amoribus praeferant Seruatorem & sponsum suum IESVM CHRISTVM, vt huic fidem seruent, & cum eodem in caelis viuant. Huic debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: But here it must be carefully observed that Christ is speaking of illegitimate and reckless divorces, such as then took place among the Jews at each man's private whim, for whatever reason. For while some do not observe this, they condemn every divorce; and while they want to be vigorous defenders of marriage and decency, they become patrons of fornication and adultery. They indeed cry out with Christ: What God has joined together, let not man put asunder. But while they extend without any exception to all cases what the Lord said about the wicked and reckless breakers of the marriage bond, they openly contradict that very text, which expressly adds the exception: EXCEPT FOR FORNICATION. For this particle states the cause for which divorce ought to be made, namely adultery. This agrees with the law of nature, and therefore the imperial laws too hold that adultery is a just cause of divorce. For an adulteress, by giving her body to another, herself breaks the bond of marriage, and has no ground to complain of her husband's wrongdoing; but for an honest man it is a grave injury, and intolerable, to be compelled to keep an adulterous wife. The reasoning is the same for a virtuous wife and an adulterous husband. But if you ask why adultery is not mentioned among the causes of divorce in the law? The answer is easy: that law ordered adultery to be punished by death, and once that is done, no question of divorce arises. But since today among Christians too the law of God is nearly silent on this matter, and the imperial laws seem to many rather harsher than is fair, magistrates must nevertheless take care that the indulgence with which they spare adulterers does not become a loss to the innocent spouse, and that they do not (as we just said) become patrons of fornication and adultery. Just as Christ gives adultery as the just cause of divorce, under which other more grievous crimes are included, as we have said elsewhere, so Paul also mentions another cause, which is difference of religion, when an unbelieving spouse so obstinately harasses the believing one that he will not live with him unless he renounces his faith in Christ alone. For here that saying of Christ ought to have its place among us, by which he bids us hate parents, wife and children, indeed even life itself for the fatherland, if they wish to draw us away from him. Yet the believer should take care not to be the author of the divorce himself, but should stay with the unbeliever as far as that can be done. But if the unbeliever either departs, or drives the believer out, or refuses to follow when the believer is expelled, then (as the Apostle says) a brother or sister is not under bondage in such cases. Let him therefore commend the matter to God, and use with a pious mind the liberty, or right, which the obstinacy of the unbelieving spouse grants him. All this could be discussed at length, but we touch on it briefly, because these matters were set out fully above in the fifth chapter. For now it suffices to have admonished that Christians should think honourably of marriage, keep its faith holy, patiently bear its troubles, give no cause of divorce to the other, and much less lightly seek separation from their mate. Meanwhile, above all the comforts and loves of this age, they should prefer their Saviour and bridegroom Jesus Christ, so that they may keep faith with him and live with him in heaven. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCCXXVIII.
units.tr: HOMILY 328.

units.la: Dicunt ei discipuli eius: Si tale est negotium hominis cum vxore, non expedit contrahere matrimonium. Ipse vero dixit eis: Non omnes capiunt hoc verbum, sed quibus datum est. Sunt enim eunuchi, qui ex matris utero nati sunt ita: & sunt eunuchi qui castrati sunt ab hominibus: & sunt eunuchi, qui seipsos castrarunt propter regnum coelorum. Qui potest capere, capiat.
units.tr: His disciples said to him: "If such is the case of a man with his wife, it is not expedient to marry." But he said to them: "Not all can receive this saying, but only those to whom it is given. For there are eunuchs who were born so from their mother's womb; and there are eunuchs who were made eunuchs by men; and there are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. He who can receive it, let him receive it."

units.la: Dominus noster IESVS CHRISTVS ad duas Pharisaeorum quaestiones respondit, quarum prima fuit: An liceat homini vxorem quauis de causa dimittere. Altera, cur Moses patribus mandarit, vt vxores, quae dimittebant, dato dimissionis aut repudij libello ablegarent. Summa responsionis Christi est, coniugij vinculum sacrosanctum esse, quod nemo ex priuato affectu authoritate dissoluere debeat. Mosem vero ita excusauit, vt culpam omnem in ipsorum contumaciam reiecerit, simul autem docuit, diuortia, quae hactenus fecerint, non solum non probari Deo, sed multiplicium adulteriorum causam siue seminarium esse, quibus Deus offendatur. Etsi vero haec ita tradiderit Dominus, vt Pharisaei non haberent quod ipsi opponerent, discipulis tamen non per omnia satisfecit, qui quaestionem de caelibatu mouerunt, de quo in praesenti agitur. Est locus hic dignissimus consideratu, eo quod hodie multi religionem & pietatem in caelibatu magna ex parte consistere putant.
units.tr: Our Lord Jesus Christ answered two questions of the Pharisees. The first was whether it is lawful for a man to put away his wife for any cause. The second was why Moses commanded the fathers that wives who were being put away should be dismissed with a bill of divorce or writ of repudiation. The sum of Christ's answer is that the bond of marriage is sacred, and that no one may dissolve it out of private inclination or by his own authority. He excused Moses in such a way that he laid all the blame on their stubbornness; at the same time he taught that divorces, as they had been practised until then, were not only not approved by God, but were the cause and seedbed of many adulteries, by which God is offended. Yet although the Lord taught this in such a way that the Pharisees had nothing to set against it, he did not fully satisfy his disciples, who raised the question of celibacy, which is the matter now under discussion. This passage is most worthy of consideration, because many today think that religion and piety consist for the most part in celibacy.

units.la: Occasio, quae discipulos mouit, vt de hoc quaerent, haec fuit, quod ita apud Iudaeos inualuerat diuortiorum licentia, vt eius abrogatio ipsis quoque iniqua & intolerabilis videretur. Ideo dicunt: Si negotium hominis cum vxore tale est, id est, si haec coniugij lex est, vt cum vxore quam quis duxit, perpetuo viuere cogatur, adeo vt nisi illa prior maechando coniugij vinculum abrumpat, tam ferre oporteat, etiam si rustica, morosa, iurgatrix, prodiga, deformis, denique omnibus modis molesta sit, non expedit matrimonium contrahere, sed profuerit absque hoc vitam caelibem viuere, vt molestijs eiusmodi te liberes, &c. Et credibile est, in mentem illis venisse ea, quae de eiusmodi coniugijs a Solomone dicta sunt: Praestat habitare in pinna tecti, aut in terra deserta, quam cum muliere rixosa & iracunda. Item vxor rixosa est instar tecti iugiter perstillantis. Nam vt tecta pertusa & stillantia molestiam die noctequeexhibent, adhaec domui incommodant, tabulata, trabes & supellectilem corrumpunt: ita mulier contentiosa & rixis assueta viro intolerabilis est, eiusdem existimationi derogat, domo quoque eum frequenter eijcit non sine rei domesticae iactura. Ideo sapiens quoque Sirachi filius dicebat: Apud leonem & draconem habitare optarim potius, quam cum improba muliere. Et quia dicta haec quotidie confirmantur exemplis multarum, quae vitam ipsam viris suis acerbam reddant, non mirum est discipulos in haec verba erupisse.
units.tr: The occasion that moved the disciples to ask about this was that the licence of divorce had so taken hold among the Jews that its abolition seemed to them unjust and intolerable. So they say: "If the case of a man with his wife is such," that is, if this is the law of marriage, that a man is forced to live with the wife he has taken for the rest of his life, so that unless she breaks the bond of marriage by adultery he must put up with her, even if she is boorish, peevish, quarrelsome, extravagant, ugly, and in every way troublesome, then it is not expedient to marry, but it is better to live a single life without this, so that you may free yourself from such troubles, and so on. And it is likely that the words Solomon spoke about such marriages came into their minds: "It is better to dwell in a corner of the housetop, or in a desert land, than with a contentious and angry woman." Likewise, "a contentious wife is like a roof that constantly drips." For just as leaking and dripping roofs cause trouble by day and by night, and also harm the house, ruining the floors, beams and furnishings, so a contentious woman, accustomed to quarrels, is intolerable to her husband, diminishes his reputation, and often drives him out of the house, not without loss to the household's property. So too the wise son of Sirach said: "I would rather dwell with a lion and a dragon than with a wicked woman." And since these sayings are confirmed every day by the examples of many women who make life bitter for their husbands, it is no wonder that the disciples burst out with these words.

units.la: Caeterum imponit illis communis error, quo fere in omnibus vitae generibus vulgo peccatur: qui est, quod plerique incommoda sola, quae ad ipsos redundant obseruant, aliorum non item: incommoda vero in vniuersum negligunt, quae in vnaquaque conditione Deus nobis propinat. Ita fit in agricultura, de cuius laboribus & molestijs quaeruntur agricolae, non obseruant autem laboris sui fructus vberrimos, quos ex terra prouentu percipiunt, animi item securitate & conscientiae tranquillitate, quae illam comitatur, dum alij inter opes suas & delitias otio ignauo contabescunt, aut curis mordacibus discrutiantur, atque noctes quoque insomnes agunt. Ita solet inter heros & seruos fieri, dum hi quidem de solo seruitutis ugo quaeruntur, quae autem heros grauant incommoda non expendunt. In primis autem in coniugio hic error cernitur. Mulierum rixositate aut morositatem indignissime ferunt mariti, interim non cogitant, quanto grauior sit mulierum seruitus, quibus rei domesticae cura & educationis liberorum labores potissimum incumbunt, & quae viros qualescunque ferre coguntur, qui saepe seipsos & rem domesticam sua insolentia & libidine pessundant. Cur item non recordantur vtrinque coniugium per se sanctum & vtile, imo ad vitam commode conseruandam ne caesarium esse, incommoda autem & molestias, quae concurrunt, ex peccato accesisse, & facile mitigari posse, si Deus obseruetur & timeatur, qui primus illius author est, & pijs coniugibus benedicit. Huius si omnes in sua conditione meminissent, minus sentirent molestiae, & ex laboribus quoque & curis, quas sentiunt, fructum percipere non poenitendum.
units.tr: Moreover, a common error affects them, the one by which people commonly go wrong in almost every walk of life: most people observe only the inconveniences that fall on themselves, and not those that fall on others, and in general they overlook the troubles that God hands to us in every condition. So it happens in farming: farmers complain about the labours and hardships of their work, but they do not notice the very abundant fruits of their labour that they receive from the earth, nor the peace of mind and tranquillity of conscience that go with it; while others waste away in idle sloth amid their wealth and pleasures, or are tormented by biting cares, and spend sleepless nights. It is so too between masters and servants: the latter complain only of the yoke of servitude, and do not weigh the troubles that weigh on the masters. Above all this error is seen in marriage. Husbands bear with great impatience their wives' quarrelsomeness or peevishness, and meanwhile do not consider how much heavier is the servitude of wives, on whom the care of the household and the labours of raising children chiefly fall, and who are forced to bear husbands of whatever sort, who often ruin themselves and the household by their arrogance and lust.
