Why do they also not remember that marriage on both sides is in itself holy and useful, and indeed not least for keeping life decently ordered; and that the troubles and annoyances that arise have come from sin, and can easily be softened if God is observed and feared, who is the first author of marriage and blesses godly couples? If all remembered this in their own condition, they would feel the troubles less, and it would not be a thing to regret to gain fruit also from the labours and cares they do feel.

units.la: Ante omnia vero obseruari debet in hoc discipulorum Christi exemplo Satanae ingenium, qui non definit bonis Dei institutis insidiari, vt ea vel aboleat omnino, vel hominibus exosa aut contempta reddat. Facitu hoc omnibus saeculis in coniugio. Scit enim improbus ille quadruplator, sanctimoniae opus esse ijs, qui cum Deo conciliari & eius gratia frui volunt: non posse autem illam constare, vbi fides & amor coniugalis non rite colitur: eo quod innata omnibus generandi cupiditas incontinentes reddit, & vagas libidines parit, nisi hoc remedio sine fraeno, quod Deus ipse dedit, coerceatur. Itaque vbi coniugiorum reuerentia nulla est, ibi fornicationis sordibus polluuntur, qui Spiritus sancti templa aut vasa esse debebant. Itaque a prima rerum origine in eo fuit Satan, vt matrimonia vulgo inuisa faceret, aut illorum vsum legitimum corrumperet. Huius suggestio ne factum est, quod primus parens Adamus transgressionis suae culpa Euae coniugi acceptam ferre, & ipsi Deo dicere ausus est: Mulier, quam dedisti mihi, dedit mihi de arbore, & comedi. Deinde mox bigamia inter Caini posteros coepit, quae in polygamiam tandem erupit, neque inter prophanas gentes solum, verumetiam in populo Dei locum inuenit, & multa incommoda peperit.
units.tr: Above all, in this example of Christ's disciples we must observe the cunning of Satan, who never ceases to lay snares for God's good institutions, either to abolish them altogether or to make them hateful and despised among men. He does this in marriage in every age. For that wicked pimp knows that holiness is necessary for those who wish to be reconciled to God and enjoy his grace, but that holiness cannot exist where the faith and love of marriage are not properly cultivated; for the innate desire to beget makes men incontinent and gives birth to wandering lusts, unless it is restrained by this remedy, which God himself gave, without a bridle. So where there is no reverence for marriages, there men are polluted with the filth of fornication, who ought to have been temples or vessels of the Holy Spirit. Thus from the very beginning of things Satan worked to make marriages generally hated, or to corrupt their lawful use. At his suggestion it came about that the first parent Adam, by the guilt of his transgression, dared to lay the blame on Eve his wife, and to say to God himself: "The woman whom you gave me gave me of the tree, and I ate." Soon after, bigamy began among the posterity of Cain, which at last broke out into polygamy, and found a place not only among the profane nations but also among the people of God, and brought many troubles.

units.la: Nunc Noui testamenti tempore, dum legem Dei pristino nitori, & eidem germanum sensum restituit Dominus, imo dum de coniugij prima institutione disserit, & huius nocentissimam pestem, diuortiorum licentiam coercere studet, inconsiderato zelo Apostoli decepti, consultissimum esse arbitrantur, si qui vitam caelibem viuant, neque sese indissolubili hoc vinculo astringi sinant, ex quo se non possint postea absque scelere extricare. Et licet hi a Christo edocti postea Ecclesiam diligenter praemonuerint, vt ab hoc errore sibi caueant Christiani homines, illis tamen mortuis, illum magno studio & miris artibus ferere et omnibus persuadere conatus est Satan. Hoc enim authore Tacianus coniugium aperte damnauit, & hunc secuti Encratitae & Seueriani mulieres non a Deo, sed a diabolo factam, atque eos qui matrimonio iungantur diabolico operi vacare dixerunt. Exorti sunt etiam etiā alij hæretici, qui idem senserunt, & inter hos etiā qui Apostolici dici voluerūt, & Apotactici a renuntiando, quasi procul relictis omnibus huius sæculi studijs, soli Deo se consecrauissent. Et in ipsa Ecclesia reperti sunt, qui de coniugio minus honorifice sentirent. Ex horum numero fuere, qui in Concilio Nicæno Ecclesiæ ministros ad cælibatū astringere voluerunt, quibus se se vir sanctus Paphnutius oppositus, & consuetudine coniugalem dixit castitate esse. Licet autem huic Synodus assentiretur, tamen non multis annis post sub Constantino exortus est Eustathius Sebastiæ in Armenia episcopus, qui se ceciderat quæsiuit, vt monachus, & coniugij vsu abrogandū esse cesuit. Et quā-uis hic quoq; a Gangrensi Synodo exauthoraretur, nō cessauit tamen Satan hanc Camarinam movere, & tantum potuit simulatæ castitatis, quæ in cælibatu coli putabatur, perfuasio, vt inter pios quoq; & non male meritos de Ecclesia inuenti sint nonnulli, qui coniugio se iniquiores præbuerunt: ex quorum numero D. Hieron. fuit, qui virginitatem ita extollit, vt coniugibus non satis propitiū illum fuisse appareat. Eodem tempore, viuente adhuc Hieronymo, Syricius Romanus pontifex, qui Damaso successit presbyteros vxoratos a ministerio remouere, & verba Pauli: Qui in carne sunt, Deo placere non possunt, &c. nō minus impio quam falso sensu de coniugibus exponere ausus est, sicuti in Decretorū lib. Distinct. 81. est videre. Ab eo tempore decreta de cælibatu exasperata sunt, & mysterium iniquitatis Antichristi spiritus indies liberius & maiori licentia pergit, donec impurum cælibatum Ecclesiæ obtrusit, monachorum & sacrificulorum agmina auxit, & ita impletum est quod olim Daniel & Paulus Apostolus prædixerunt. Nos autem ista ideo commemoramus, vt constet, Satanam omnibus sæculis apud omnes gentes: in primis autem in Ecclesia, coniugio insidiatum esse, vt huius vsu legitimo abolito aut corrupto, vagis libidinibus locum faceret, & publicam morum honestatem aboleret. Quo magis aduigilandum est ijs, quos per Euangelij prædicationem Deus vocauit in admirabilem lucem suam, ne impostores admittant, qui sub ementitæ castitatis prætextu miseros circumuenire studeant, & Satanæ tentandos propinant.
units.tr: Now in the time of the New Testament, while the Lord restores God's law to its former purity and its true meaning, and indeed while he discourses on the first institution of marriage and strives to restrain the most harmful plague of it, the licence of divorce, some, deceived by the ill-considered zeal of the Apostles, think it most wise that those who live a single life should not let themselves be bound by this indissoluble bond, from which they cannot afterwards free themselves without sin. And although these men, taught by Christ, afterwards carefully warned the Church that Christians should beware of this error, nevertheless, after they were dead, Satan strove with great zeal and wondrous arts to sow that error and to persuade everyone of it. For under his leadership Tatian openly condemned marriage, and the Encratites and Severians who followed him said that wives were made not by God but by the devil, and that those who marry are busy with a diabolical work. There also arose other heretics who held the same view, and among them those who wished to be called Apostolic, and Apotactites from renouncing, as if, having left behind all the pursuits of this age, they alone had consecrated themselves to God. And there were also found within the Church itself some who thought less honourably of marriage. Among these were those who at the Nicene Council wished to bind the ministers of the Church to celibacy; against them the holy man Paphnutius stood up and said that marital chastity is chastity in accordance with custom. But although the Synod assented to him, nevertheless not many years later, under Constantine, there arose Eustathius, bishop of Sebaste in Armenia, who sought to be a monk, having fallen away, and held that the use of marriage must be abolished. And although he too was deposed by the Synod of Gangra, Satan did not cease to stir up this Camarina, and the persuasion of a pretended chastity, which was thought to be cultivated in celibacy, prevailed so far that some were found even among the godly, and among those who had deserved well of the Church, who showed themselves less favourable to marriage. St Jerome was among their number, who so exalted virginity that he appears not to have been sufficiently kind to married people. At the same time, while Jerome was still living, Siricius, Roman bishop, who succeeded Damasus, dared to remove married elders from the ministry, and to expound the words of Paul, "Those who are in the flesh cannot please God," and so on, in a sense no less impious than false, as may be seen in the Decretum, part 1, distinction 81. From that time the decrees on celibacy grew harsher, and the mystery of iniquity and the spirit of Antichrist went on daily more freely and with greater licence, until it forced the impure celibacy of the Church upon it, increased the companies of monks and sacrificing priests, and so what Daniel and the Apostle Paul had long before foretold was fulfilled. We record these things so that it may be plain that Satan has in every age, among all nations, and above all in the Church, laid snares for marriage, so that, by abolishing or corrupting its lawful use, he might make room for wandering lusts and destroy public decency of morals. All the more must we keep watch over those whom God has called through the preaching of the Gospel into his wonderful light, lest they admit impostors who, under the pretext of a feigned chastity, strive to deceive the wretched and offer them up to be tempted by Satan.

units.la: Sed audiamus, quid discipulis suis Christus Dominus responderit. Primo summam suæ doctrinæ proponit, dicens: Non omnes capiunt verbum istud, sed quibus datum est{a}. Habent verba ista aliquam Concessionis speciem. Nec enim negat, commodius & minori cum molestia vitam institui posse, si ea esset hominum natura & conditio, vt nullo libidinis affectu titillaretur, & cælibes possent caste & sancte viuere. Sed longe aliud esse docet carnis ingenium, vt non omnes ad cælibatum idonei sint, sed ij soli, quibus hoc cælitus datum est, & ideo matrimonium necessarium esse & perperam facere eos, qui continentiæ legem vel sibi ipsis vel aliis velint imponere. Et ad hunc locum respexit Apostolus, quando Corinthijs scripsit: Bonum fuerit viro mulierem non attingere: sed propter fornicationes, suam quisque vxorem habeat, & proprium quæque virum habeat. Fatetur Apostolus coniugium suas habere curas, solicitudines & molestias, & proinde hos liberatos commodius & quietius vitam traducere eos quibus datum est continentiæ donum: Sed addit: Propter fornicationes, id est, quia donum hoc rarum est, & aliud postulat carnis natura, eo remedio vtantur homines, quod Deus ipse dedit: & ne fornicationis spiritu feduti, sanctitatem suam polluant, aut indefinenti libidinis æstu vrantur, matrimonium contrahant. Et hoc diligentius explicans, monet, ne quis etiam sub religionis prætextu secus agat. Vxori (inquit) vir debitam benevolentiam reddat, similiter autē et vxor viro. Benevolentia nomine omne coniugij officiū comprehendit, hoc nimirum volens, vt quod alter alteri debet, fideliter præstet. Et hoc ipsum in epistola ad Ephesios per exemplū Christi & Ecclesiæ illustrat, quo nullum castius & sanctius fingi potest, & quod solum sufficit confutandis impuris illis, qui coniugalem consuetudinem damnare non verentur. Rationem autem, qua sententiam suam confirmet, ex communi lege naturæ profert, quæ vnicuiq; quod suum est iubet reddere: Vxor (inquit) proprium corpus non habet in potestate, sed vir: similiter autem & vir proprium corpus non habet in potestate, sed vxor. Et ex eo infert: Ne fraudetis alius alium, nisi fi quid ex consensu, ad tempus, vt vacetis ieiunio & orationi: & rursum in vnum conuenire, ne tentet vos Satanas propter incontinentiam vt stram. Rursus ergo Paulus periculi timendum esse docet ex secubatione coniugū, quam ex moderato coniugij vsu, & tunc quoq; imbecillitatis nostræ nos meminisse iubet, quando propter priua-
units.tr: But let us hear what Christ the Lord answered his disciples. First he sets out the sum of his teaching, saying: "Not all men can receive this saying, but only those to whom it is given"{a}. These words have a certain appearance of concession. For he does not deny that life could be lived more conveniently and with less trouble if human nature and condition were such that no passion of lust stirred us, and the unmarried could live chastely and holily. But he teaches that the nature of the flesh is quite otherwise, so that not all are fit for celibacy, but only those to whom this is given from heaven; and therefore marriage is necessary, and those who wish to impose a law of continence on themselves or on others act wrongly. The Apostle had this passage in view when he wrote to the Corinthians: "It is good for a man not to touch a woman; but because of fornications, let each man have his own wife, and let each woman have her own husband." The Apostle admits that marriage has its own cares, anxieties and troubles, and that therefore those to whom the gift of continence has been given lead their lives more conveniently and quietly, being freed from them. But he adds "because of fornications": since this gift is rare and the nature of the flesh demands something else, people should use the remedy that God himself has given, and, lest they be seduced by the spirit of fornication and pollute their holiness, or burn with the heat of unbridled lust, they should contract marriage. Explaining this more carefully, he warns that no one should act otherwise even under the pretext of religion: "Let the husband render to the wife the due kindness; likewise also the wife to the husband." By the name of kindness he comprehends every duty of marriage, plainly wishing that each faithfully render to the other what is owed. He illustrates this very point in the epistle to the Ephesians by the example of Christ and the Church, than which nothing more chaste and holy can be imagined, and which alone is enough to refute those impure men who do not hesitate to condemn the conjugal life. He sets out the reason for his opinion from the common law of nature, which bids each to render what is his: "The wife does not have power over her own body, but the husband; likewise also the husband does not have power over his own body, but the wife." And from this he infers: "Do not defraud one another, except perhaps by consent for a time, that you may be free for fasting and prayer; and come together again, lest Satan tempt you because of your incontinence." Paul therefore again teaches that there is more danger from the separation of spouses than from the moderate use of marriage, and bids us, even then, to remember our weakness, when on account of private

units.la: {a} Matth. 19. tas aut publicas afflictiones nos totos religioni & precibus dedimus: ne ea occasione circumuen- tos Satan in fornicationis laqueos pertrahat.
units.tr: {a} Matth. 19. or public afflictions we have given ourselves wholly to religion and prayer, lest Satan, seizing the occasion, draw us into the snares of fornication.

units.la: Caeterum ne quis hic nimium sibi ipsi tribuat, probat Dominus, non omnibus datum esse, ut abs- que coniugio caelibes & caste viuat. Sunt enim eunuchi, qui ex matris vtero nati sunt: et sunt eunuchi, qui castrati sunt ab hominibus: & sunt eunuchi, qui seipsos castrauerunt propter regnum caelorum. Eunuchos vocat eos, quibus coniugij vsu non opus est, & ideo ad caelibatum idonei sunt. Horum tria genera facit. Primum eorum, quos natura tales creauit, ut frigidiores sint, & ad generandum inepti. Alterum eorum, qui vel propter vitium aut morbum corporis, qui aliunde accidit, vel etiam violenter castrantur, ut reginis & virginibus custodiendis idonei sint: quod olim apud barbaros vulgare fuit, & hodie etiam apud Turcas in vsu est: & hi proprie spadones dicuntur. Tertij sunt, qui seipsos castrauerunt propter regnum caelorum. Eos intelligit, quos Dei spiritus efficaciter trahit, ut se totos ipsius seruitio consecrent, & ut expeditiores sint ad regni caelorum munera obeunda, neque curis domesticis distrahantur, perfectiones item & aduersa commodius ferant, a coniugio abstinent. Talis fuit Paulus, qui ius vxorem habuerit, sine non habuerit, eam tamen non secum duxit, ut reliqui fecerunt: idque haud dubie ex illius consensu, & quod vtrique datum esset a Deo, ut caste possent viuere absque incontinentia aut tentationis grauioris periculo. Idem animus aliis quoque apostolis fuit, qui etsi vxores suas secum circumduxerunt, quando id commode fieri potuit, tamen ii quae necessitas grauior incidit, has quoque reliquerunt, ne per eas in suo ministerio impedirentur, sed expeditiores essent ad regnum Dei per totum orbem propagandum, sicuti Christus illus iniunxerat. Et tales esse decet Christianos omnes, ut si opus sit, propter regnum Dei & Dominum nostrum IESVM CHRISTVM, non modo omnes huius saeculi facultates, verumetiam parentes, fratres, sorores, coniuges & liberos relinquant. Notum est enim illud Christi: Si quis venit ad me, nec odit patrem suum ac matrem, & vxorem ac liberos, & fratres & sorores, amplius autem etiam animam suam, non potest meus esse discipulus. Luc.14.
units.tr: Moreover, lest anyone here attribute too much to himself, the Lord proves that it has not been given to all to live unmarried and chastely without marriage. For there are eunuchs who were born so from their mother's womb, and there are eunuchs who have been made so by men, and there are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. He calls eunuchs those who have no need of the use of marriage and are therefore fit for celibacy. He makes three kinds of these. The first are those whom nature created such that they are more cold and unfit for begetting. The second are those who are castrated either because of a defect or disease of the body arising from elsewhere, or even by violence, so that they are fit for guarding queens and virgins; this was once common among the barbarians and today is still in use among the Turks; these are properly called eunuchs (spadones). The third are those who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. He means those whom the Spirit of God effectively draws, so that they devote themselves wholly to his service, and so that they may be more ready to discharge the duties of the kingdom of heaven, not distracted by domestic cares, and may bear privations and adversities more easily; these abstain from marriage. Such was Paul, who may have had a wife or may not have had one, yet did not take her with him as the others did; and this was without doubt by mutual consent, and because it had been granted by God to both that they could live chastely without incontinence or the danger of heavier temptation. The same spirit was in the other apostles too, who, although they led their wives about with them when that could conveniently be done, nevertheless, when a heavier necessity fell upon them, left these also behind, lest they be hindered in their ministry through them, and might be more free to spread the kingdom of God throughout the whole world, as Christ had enjoined. And all Christians ought to be such, so that, if need be, for the sake of the kingdom of God and our Lord Jesus Christ, they leave behind not only all the goods of this age, but even parents, brothers, sisters, spouses and children. For that saying of Christ is well known: "If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father and mother, and wife and children, and brothers and sisters, and moreover even his own life, he cannot be my disciple." Luc.14.

units.la: Porro ne quis ex eo, quod dictum est, esse eunuchos, qui seipsos castrauerunt propter regnum caelorum, legem communem statueret, & in propria cuiusque potestate esse putaret, ut seipsum castrare, & ad caelibatum possit idoneum reddere, concludit locum hunc Dominus graui epiphonemate: Qui potest capere, capiat: Quasi diceret: Sunt quidem nonnulli, quibus datum est, ut continenter viuere, & tantum non seipsos castrare possint, ut nihil ipsis a Satana periculi sit, ne ab eius tentationibus superentur, non tamen hoc commune est omnibus electis, & ideo nemo temere sibi ipsi aut aliis hanc legem imponere debet: sed qui potest hoc capere, id est, qui sibi hoc datum esse sentit, capiat, & Dei dono religiose vtatur: qui vero se infirmiore esse videt, vs coniugium contrahat, quod Deus omnibus commune remedium esse vult, quo imbecillitati suae medeantur. Non ergo Legem vniuersalem hic sancit Christus, sed liberum cuique facit, ut quod sibi conducibilius esse sentit, eligat. Idem postea quoque fecit Apostolus, qui cum dixisset: Velim omnes homines esse vt & ipse sum: Mox addit: Sed vnusquisque proprium donum habet ex Deo, alius quidem ita, alius autem ita, &c. Vide 1.Cor.7.
units.tr: Further, lest anyone from what has been said, that there are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven, should establish a general law and think that it is in each person's own power to castrate himself and make himself fit for celibacy, the Lord concludes this passage with a weighty epiphonema: "He who can receive it, let him receive it." As if he were saying: there are indeed some to whom it has been given to live continently, and who are able, as it were, to castrate themselves, so that there is no danger to them from Satan, that they should be overcome by his temptations; yet this is not common to all the elect, and therefore no one should rashly impose this law on himself or on others; but he who can receive this, that is, he who feels that it has been given to him, let him receive it and use God's gift religiously; but he who sees that he is weaker, let him marry, which God wishes to be a common remedy for all, by which they may heal their weakness. Christ therefore does not here enact a universal law, but leaves it free to each to choose what he feels to be more suitable for himself. The Apostle afterwards did the same, who, having said, "I would that all men were even as I myself am," immediately adds: "But each has his own gift from God, one indeed in this way, another in that way," etc. See 1 Cor. 7.

units.la: Debet ex his doctrina generalis peti, in nullius priuata potestate esse, ut se ad caelibatum obstringat, sed vnumquemque diligenter vires suas expendere debere, ut quid Deus ipsi dederit intelligat. Enimuero quis non dicat ridiculè nimis eum facere, qui volare velit, cum Deus homines implumes crearit, & terra, non aeris, incolas fecerit? At non minus ridiculè quàm stultè faciunt, qui cum Deus primo nostro parenti, adhuc in statu perfectionis agenti dixerit: Non est bonum, ut homo solus sit, &c. ipsi caelibes & solitarij viuere instituunt, cum quotidie carnis vitiosa, & ad libidinem procliuis affectibus se tentari sentiant. Arguitur ergo huius loci authoritate tyrannis Pontificum Romanorum, qui Ecclesiarum ministrus coniugio interdicunt: & in primis confutantur monastica vota, quibus ad caelibatum perpetuum fere obstringunt pueri & puellae, hi inquam, qui sane per aetatem nondum scire possunt, quid de ipsis Deus statuerit, multo minus vires suas examinare possunt. Etenim Pontifices legem certam & necessariam obseruatu ex eo faciunt, quod Deus liberum esse voluit, imo publica authoritate prohibent, quod ille iusserit: qui vero monasticam vitam profitentur, non exploratis viribus vouent quod non est in ipsorum potestate. Olim sub veteri lege non valebant vota, quae filiae & vxores absque patrum & virorum consensu nuncupassent, & his illa rescindere licebat. Quae ergo iniquitas est, votis temerarijs & non solum inuito Deo, verumetiam reluctante natura factis perpetuo obstrictos tenere homines, ne libertate per Christum nobis parta fruantur? Est haec inconsulta nimis temeritas, cum impio coniugij a Deo instituti contemptu coniunctia. Non finit ergo hanc inultam abire Deus, qui plerunque iusto iudicio tales in sensum reprobum tradit, vt illicitis libidinibus seipsos polluant & infames reddant, qui coniugio, cuius thorum sanctum & immaculatum esse, Apostolus testatur, vt inolunt. Accidit hoc olim Eusthathij, cuius supra meminimus, sectatoribus, qui cum matrimonia damnarent, aliorum vxores ad se pertraxerunt, quarum multae sub virili veste apud illos latebant, & cum quibus illi stupri consuetudinem habuerunt. Quid inter Christianos factum sit post stabilitum sacerdotum caelibatum, omnibus notum est. Ex eo certe tempore scortandi & machandi licentia inualuit, vt multis lusus & iocus videretur, virgines constuprare, alienos thoros polluere, & absque omni pudore quarumuis pudicitiam insidiari. Quid enim facerent aliud, qui suos pastores & doctores publice scortari videbant? Quod si quis de ijs loqui instituat, quae clam in coenobijs facta sunt, & adhuc fiunt, nemo honestus ista patienter audire, nemo bonus de illis cogitare poterit, quin totus exhorrescat. Non temere ergo Apostolus doctrinam esse dixit, quae nubere prohibet: & Scriptura, vt his scandalis medeatur, passim coniugium magnifice commendat, cuius vsum gentes etiam prophanae non honestum modo, verumetiam necessarium esse intellexerunt. Etenim commendatur in historijs Metellus Numidicus, quem dixisse ferunt: Si sine vxore possemus viuere Quirites, omnes ea molestia careremus: sed quoniam ita natura tradit, vt nec cum ijs satis commode, nec sine illis vllo modo viui possit, salutiperpetua prius quam breui voluptati consulendum est. Pudeat ergo sua infinitia & temeritatis Christianos homines, qui cum Dei Filium in Euangelio loquentem audiant, simul tamen impuri caelibatus patronis aures praebent, qui cum Verbo Dei publica etiam honestatis leges impie conculcant, & religionem Christianam Iudaeorum atque Turcarum ludibrijs exponunt. Nos vero fratres IESVM CHRISTVM secuti coniugij leges sanctae colamus, & huius authorem Deum glorificemus in corpore nostro, & in spiritu nostro. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: From these things a general doctrine ought to be drawn: that it is in no one's private power to bind himself to celibacy, but that each ought to weigh his own powers carefully, so that he may understand what God has given him. Indeed, who would not say that he acts all too ridiculously who wishes to fly, since God created men unfeathered and made them dwellers on the earth, not in the air? Yet no less ridiculously and foolishly do those act who, when God said to our first parent, still in the state of perfection, "It is not good for man to be alone," etc., set about living unmarried and solitary, though they feel themselves tempted every day by the sinful affections of the flesh, inclined to lust. By the authority of this passage, therefore, the tyranny of the Roman Pontiffs is refuted, who forbid the ministers of the Churches to marry; and above all the monastic vows are confuted, by which boys and girls are almost bound to perpetual celibacy, those who, truly, because of their age cannot yet know what God has decided about them, much less examine their own powers. For the Pontiffs make a certain and necessary law to be observed out of what God willed to be free, and by public authority forbid what he has commanded; but those who profess the monastic life vow, without testing their powers, what is not in their own power. In the past, under the old law, vows which daughters and wives had made without the consent of their fathers and husbands were not valid, and these could be annulled by them. What unfairness, then, is it to keep men bound forever by rash vows, made not only against God's will but even against nature's resistance, so that they may not enjoy the liberty won for us through Christ? This is a most ill-advised rashness, joined with impious contempt of the marriage instituted by God. God does not allow this to go unpunished; for very often, by a just judgment, he gives such men over to a reprobate mind, so that, as they are unable to contain themselves, they defile themselves with unlawful lusts and make themselves infamous. The Apostle testifies that the marriage bed is holy and undefiled. This once happened to the followers of Eustathius, whom we mentioned above: since they condemned marriages, they drew other men's wives to themselves, many of whom were hiding among them in men's clothing, and with whom they had illicit intercourse. What happened among Christians after the celibacy of priests was established is known to all. From that time certainly the licence of whoring and adultery prevailed, so that to many it seemed a game and a joke to violate virgins, defile other men's beds, and without any shame to lay snares for the chastity of anyone at all. For what else would they do, when they saw their own ministers and teachers openly whoring? And if anyone undertakes to speak of those things which have been done in secret in the monasteries, and are still done, no honest person will be able to hear them with patience, and no good person can think of them without shuddering all over. Not without reason, therefore, did the Apostle call doctrine that forbids marriage a doctrine of demons; and Scripture, to heal these scandals, everywhere commends marriage magnificently, whose use even profane nations understood to be not only honourable but necessary. For in the histories Metellus Numidicus is commended, who is reported to have said: "If we Romans could live without a wife, we would all be free of that trouble; but since nature has so arranged things that one can live neither conveniently with them nor in any way without them, we must care for lasting well-being rather than for brief pleasure." Christians, then, should be ashamed of their own ignorance and rashness, who, when they hear the Son of God speaking in the Gospel, at the same time lend their ears to the patrons of impure celibacy, who impiously trample under foot, together with the Word of God, even the public laws of honesty, and expose the Christian religion to the mockery of Jews and Turks. But we, brothers, following Jesus Christ, should cultivate the holy laws of marriage, and glorify God, its author, in our body and in our spirit. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCXXIX.
units.tr: HOMILY CCXXIX.

units.la: Tunc oblati sunt ei pueruli, vt manus eis imponeret, & precaretur. Discipuli autem obiurgarunt eos. IESVS autem ait: Sinite pueruli, & ne prohibite eos ad me venire: talium est enim regnum caelorum. Et cum imposuisset eis manus, profectus est illinc.
units.tr: Then little children were brought to him, that he should lay his hands on them and pray. And the disciples rebuked them. But Jesus said: Suffer the little children, and do not forbid them to come to me, for of such is the kingdom of heaven. And when he had laid his hands on them, he departed from there.

units.la: Postquam Dominus noster IESVS CHRISTVS de coniugio egit, & huius dignitatem argumentis ex prima eius institutione petitis non solum aduersus diuortiorum & adulteriorum licentiam, verumetiam aduersus impuri caelibatus & ementita castitatis patronos asseruit: sequitur nunc ordine commodissimo & naturali (vt sic dicam) historia de pueruli, quos quidam ad illum attulerunt. Sunt enim pueri siue infantes proprius & praecipuum coniugij fructus, & quia ex his legitima humani generis propagatio dependet, idem etiam Reipub. & Ecclesiae seminarium sunt: Itaq; non minus necesse quam vtile est, scire, quae illorum dignitas sit coram Deo, quomodo item educari et instituti debeant. Est ergo historia haec consideratu dignissima, quia de his omnibus admonet, & simul consolatione duplice continet: Prima quidem speciale, qua parentes sese consolentur aduersus educationis molestias, dum audiunt, se inter has Deo seruire, ad cuius regnum illi pertinent. Alteram vero generalem, qua in conscientia tentationibus nos confirmemus, ne quis facile de Dei gratia desperet, quando constat, hanc ad parvulos vsque extendi, qui de illa ne cogitant quidem, neq; ea sibi opus esse norunt, nedum vt eam precibus expetant. Et haec causa est, quod Lucas hanc historiam hanc subiicit parabolae de Pharisaeo & publicano, qua docet Christus, salute nobis ex nulla
units.tr: After our Lord Jesus Christ had discoursed on marriage, and had asserted its dignity by arguments drawn from its first institution, not only against the license of divorce and adultery but also against the patrons of impure celibacy and feigned chastity, the story now follows in the most fitting and natural order (as I may say) about the little children whom certain people brought to him. For children, or infants, are the proper and chief fruit of marriage, and since the lawful propagation of the human race depends on them, they are also the seedbed of the commonwealth and the Church. It is therefore no less necessary than useful to know what their dignity is before God, and likewise how they ought to be brought up and instructed. This story is therefore most worthy of consideration, because it admonishes us about all these things and at the same time contains a twofold consolation. The first is particular: parents may console themselves against the troubles of upbringing, since they hear that in these very troubles they serve God, to whose kingdom their children belong. The second is general: we may strengthen ourselves in conscience against temptations, so that no one easily despairs of the grace of God, since it is established that this grace extends even to little ones, who do not think of it at all, nor know that they need it, much less ask for it in prayer. And this is why Luke places this story after the parable of the Pharisee and the publican, in which Christ teaches that salvation comes to us from no

units.la: vide homil. 81 in Marcum. operum nostrorum merito, sed gratuita Dei misericordia obtingere, & ideo neminem suaiussitia cum aliorum contemptu superbire, neminem item de gratia Dei & salute propria desperare debere. Quae omnia vt rectius intelligamus, singulas historiae partes ex ordine videbimus.
units.tr: See homily 81 on Mark. merit of our works, but from the free mercy of God; and therefore no one should be puffed up with his own righteousness with contempt for others, and likewise no one should despair of the grace of God and of his own salvation. So that we may understand all these things more rightly, we shall look at the individual parts of the story in order.

units.la: Primum occasio totius actionis narratur, quae fuit, quod Christo pueruli oblati sunt, vt eis manus imponeret, & precaretur. Qui fuerint illi, qui eos obtulerunt, no exprimitur, sed haud dubie parentes fuerunt, aut qui ex parentum rogatu hoc fecere. Causa quae illos mouit, fuit, quod haberent eius contactum multis salutare fuisse, & verba eius vim & effectum coniunctum habere. Itaque sibi certam conceperant, suis quoque infantibus hoc salutare fore, si manibus impositis fausta illis imprecaretur. Habemus in illis exemplum fidei, imperfectae quidem, sed quae multa habet, imitatione digna. Nam primo liberis suis consultu cupiunt, quod argumento est, locum in illis habuisse sop γὰρ, id est, naturales animi affectiones, quas Deus parentum cordibus infeuit, vt molestias educationis, quae multae & graves sunt, facilius ferant. Habuerunt ergo dilectione, per quam fides in eletis agit. Deinde vt infantibus suis consulant, nō alio quam ad Christum illos afferunt. Vnde apparet, illos de eo magnifice sentisse: quamuis fidei quaedam infirmitas & imperfectio concurrat, quae in eo cernitur, quod vt illos tangat, & pro eis precetur petunt. Non ergo eo vsq; progressi sunt, vt illum verum Deum agnoscant, qui suo nutu quiduis faciat: qualem Centurio agnouit, de quo ca.8. dictum est. Rursum tamen fidei robur & vis sese in eo profert, quod ipsos non pudet Christi, quem principibus suis exosum esse sciebant, sed fortes & intrepidi eum accedunt, & se de illo maiora quam de homine vulgari sentire & sperare profitentur. Plus ergo laudis merentur, quam parentes caeci illius apud Ioannem quos post beneficium amplißimum, quod filius a Domino acceperat, ad huc eius puduit propter Pharisaeos, ne in horum offensam incurrerent. Vide Ioan.9.
units.tr: First the occasion of the whole action is related: little children were brought to Christ, so that he would lay his hands on them and pray. Who they were who brought them is not stated, but they were without doubt parents, or people doing this at the parents' request. The cause that moved them was that they thought contact with him was beneficial to many, and that his words carried power and effect with them. So they had firmly conceived that it would also be salutary for their own infants, if he prayed good things over them with his hands laid on. In them we have an example of faith, imperfect indeed, but one with much worthy of imitation. For first they desire what is good for their children, which is evidence that the natural affections, which God has implanted in parents' hearts, had a place in them, so that they bear more easily the troubles of upbringing, which are many and grievous. They therefore had love, through which faith works in the elect. Then, to look after their infants, they bring them to Christ and to no one else. From this it appears that they thought highly of him, although a certain weakness and imperfection of faith is mingled in, seen in their asking that he touch the children and pray for them. They had not progressed so far as to acknowledge him as the true God, who by his nod could do whatever he wished, as the centurion acknowledged, of whom it was said in chapter 8. Yet again the strength and power of faith show themselves in them, in that they were not ashamed of Christ, whom they knew to be hated by their rulers, but approach him boldly and fearlessly, and profess that they think and hope greater things of him than of an ordinary man. They therefore deserve more praise than those blind parents in John, who, even after the very great benefit their son had received from the Lord, were still ashamed of him because of the Pharisees, lest they incur their displeasure. See John 9.

units.la: Secunda pars discipulorum de hoc parentum facto iudicium narrat. Dicuntur autem illos obiurgauisse, quod satis pro imperio fecerunt. Nec enim illos Dominus ianitorum aut satellitum in star esse voluit, qui ab eius congressu arcerent eos, quos ipsi indignos iudicassent, sed potius ad hoc destinati erant, vt quosuis ad eu adducerent, qui omnes adse inuitabat, qui sua opus se indigos esse sentiebant. At erroris causa est, quod carnis rationem in consilium admittunt. Hinc fit, vt primum infantes solos respiciant, & quia hi (vt apparet) non aliquibus morbis laborabant, qui eius opem medicam requirerent: per ætatem vero doctrinae nondum capaces erant, non vident causam aliquam grauem & iustam, cur ad illum debeant afferri. Deinde ipsum Christum aliter sibi imaginabantur, quam par erat. Nam regem huius saeculi fore sperabant, & sibi ipsis in illo dignitates & principatus promittebant. Ergo indignißimum eis videtur, tantum virum circa puerulos aut infantes occupari, quorum cura ad mulieres potius quam viros pertinet, & a negotiis grauioribus & magis necessarijs auocari. Est hoc memorabile exemplum, quo docemur, quid eis accidat, qui in iis, quae Christi sunt & ad regnum Dei spectant, carnis rationem audiunt. Quia enim haec non percipit ea quae sunt Spiritus Dei, non possunt non in errores multiplices incidere. Exempla quotidie occurrunt in sapientibus huius saeculi, qui dogmata absurdissima, quibus fundamenta Christianae fidei & religionis conuelluntur, humanis rationibus propugnant, & ita sibiipsis & aliis imponunt, nec in Veritatis cognitionem perueniant.
units.tr: The second part relates the disciples' judgment of this action of the parents. They are said to have rebuked them, because they went beyond what was fitting for them. For the Lord did not wish his disciples to be doorkeepers or guards, to keep away from him those whom they themselves judged unworthy; rather they were appointed to bring to him whoever they could, for he invited all who felt they had need of him. But the cause of their error is that they admitted the reasoning of the flesh into their counsel. Hence it happens that first they looked only at the infants, and since these (as appears) were not suffering from any disease that would require his healing help, and because by reason of age they were not yet capable of being taught, they saw no grave and just cause why they should be brought to him. Then they imagined Christ himself otherwise than was fitting. For they hoped he would be a king of this age, and promised themselves dignities and principalities in him. Therefore it seemed most unworthy to them that so great a man should be occupied with little children or infants, whose care pertains to women rather than to men, and that he should be called away from weightier and more necessary business. This is a memorable example, by which we are taught what happens to those who, in matters that belong to Christ and concern the kingdom of God, listen to the reasoning of the flesh. For since it does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God, it cannot but fall into manifold errors. Examples meet us daily among the wise of this age, who defend with human reasons the most absurd dogmas, by which the foundations of the Christian faith and religion are overthrown, and so deceive both themselves and others, and never come to the knowledge of the truth.

units.la: In primis autem obseruari debet hoc loco indefessum diaboli studium, qui ab ipsa rerum origine infantium saluti semper insidiatus est. Nam vt nihil de eo dicamus, quod institutione mala & prauis exemplis multi corrumpuntur, religionis praetextu plerumque abutitur, vt illos perdat. Etenim inter gentes olim multos ita dementauit, vt proprios infantes Deo Moloch immolarent, & in impietate omnium crudelißima pietatis laude quaerent. Et ne hoc alicui mirum & incredibile putetur, Iudaeis quoque, qui veri cultus formam ab ipso Deo acceperant, tantum sceles persuasit, inter quos non vulgus modo hominum, verumetiam viri principes & Reges sese illo pollue runt: sicuti de Achaz & Manasse sacra historia perhibet. Hic per Apostolos Christum suspe&ctum facere conatur, ac si is pueruios reijcere & fastidire soleat. Etsi vero hic illius fraudem detegat, posteris temporibus tamen effecit, vt pleriq; dum suos liberos Christo consecrare voluerunt, ipsi Moloch eos sacrificauerint: quando nimirum votis monasticis obstrictos in Coenobia detruserunt, vbi inter horribiles libidinum ignes miserrimè arserunt: et multi adhuc ita ardet, vt felices dici possent, si accelerata morte subito tollerentur. Hodie, quando hanc quoque carnificinam Deus per EuangeEuangelij prædicationem euertit, Satan e contra Anabaptistas excitauit, qui dum infantibus Baptismum negant, eadem ratione eos a communione Ecclesiæ excludunt: quod non aliud est, quàm illius insidijs eos obijcere. Quò magis nos adiuigilare decet, vt Christo consecremus eos, quos communis ille hostis sibi vendicare cupit.
units.tr: Above all, in this place we ought to observe the tireless zeal of the devil, who from the very origin of things has always lain in wait against the salvation of infants. To say nothing of the fact that many are corrupted by bad upbringing and evil examples, he very often abuses religion as a pretext to destroy them. Indeed among the nations of old he drove many so mad that they sacrificed their own infants to the god Moloch, and sought the praise of piety in the most cruel of all impieties. And lest anyone think this strange and incredible, he persuaded the Jews too, who had received the form of true worship from God himself, to such wickedness that not only the common people but also their princes and kings defiled themselves with it, as sacred history reports of Ahaz and Manasseh. Here he tries, through the Apostles, to make Christ suspected, as if he were accustomed to reject and despise little children. Yet although here he is exposed in his deceit, in later times he has brought it about that many, while they wished to consecrate their children to Christ, sacrificed them to Moloch themselves: namely when they thrust them, bound by monastic vows, into cloisters, where they burned most miserably amid the horrible fires of lust; and many still burn so, that they could be called happy if they were carried off by a speedy death. Today, when God overturns this slaughterhouse too through the preaching of the Gospel, Satan on the contrary has stirred up the Anabaptists, who, while they deny baptism to infants, on the same principle exclude them from communion in the Church; which is nothing other than to throw them into his snares. All the more it becomes us to be vigilant, so that we consecrate to Christ those whom that common enemy desires to claim for himself.

units.la: Et huc cum primùm pertinet postrema huius historiæ pars, qua quid Dominus fecerit, narratur. Primò indignatus est discipulis, quod illum rarissimè fecisse constat, cum ipsissima sit charitas. Indignationis autem causas iustas & graues habuit. Nam parentum fides labefactari poterat, quando videbant eos sibi aduersari, quos Christo familiarissimos esse videbant. Deinde quantum in ipsis erat, infantum saluti obstabant, quasi eos Dominus ab Ecclesiæ suæ communione arceat. Præterea regno Christi derogabant. Quota enim pars Ecclesiæ sunt infantes ex Christianis parentibus geniti? Hos igitur omnes a Christo arcendo, ab Ecclesia excludunt & hanc suo seminario spoliant, quo sublato non posset diu consistere. Vt enim parentum sterilitas & orbitas famili is nobilissimis interitum affert, vt paulatim intermoriantur & occidant: ita nisi infidelium de functorum locum liberi ex his geniti succedant, breui tempore de Ecclesia actum erit, & nulli erunt, qui IESVM CHRISTVM Regem & Seruatorem suum agnoscant. Recte ergo & merito discipulis suis irascitur Dominus, & idem proculdubiò nunquam feret eos, qui regni sui pomeria finibus angustioribus includere, & eos arcere satagunt, qui serio salutis desiderio accensi cum ipso reconciliari cupiunt. Vide Psal. 2.
units.tr: And since the last part of this history, which tells what the Lord did, belongs here first: first he was indignant with the disciples, which is recorded as something he very rarely did, since he is love itself. He had just and serious reasons for his indignation. The faith of parents could be shaken when they saw that those whom they knew to be closest to Christ were opposing them. Moreover, as far as the disciples were concerned, they stood in the way of the salvation of infants, as if the Lord would shut them out from his Church. Besides, they were detracting from the kingdom of Christ. For how small a part of the Church are the infants born of Christian parents? By shutting out all these from Christ, they exclude them from the Church and strip her of her nursery, and without it she could not long survive. For just as the barrenness and childlessness of parents bring ruin upon the noblest families, so that they gradually die out and perish, so unless children born of these families succeed to the places of the unbelieving dead, the Church will soon be undone, and there will be none left who acknowledge Jesus Christ as their King and Saviour. Rightly and justly, therefore, the Lord is angry with his disciples, and he will certainly never tolerate those who strive to confine the boundaries of his kingdom within narrower limits and to keep out those who, kindled with a serious desire for salvation, wish to be reconciled with him. See Psalm 2.

units.la: At non modò discipulis indignatur, sed simul puerulis, qui ad ipsum deferebantur, & horum parentibus aditum facit liberum, dicens: Sinite pueruulos, & ne prohibete eos ad me venire. Et ne hæc vox irato excidisse videretur, ratione grauissima eam confirmat: Talium est enim regnum cœlorum. Id est, tales sunt regni mei ciues & Ecclesiæ meæ membra: Ergo non arcendi sunt, quò minus ad me veniant. At ne quis in vocabulo τοιούτων, id est, talium, cauillandi occasionem quærat, & dictum hoc non ad eos, qui ætate paruuli sunt, pertinere contendat, sed ad eos qui iam adulti & fidem in ipsum professi, puerulorum similes simplicitati, humilitati & obedientiæ student (quo sophismate Anabaptistæ vtuntur, vt paruulos a Baptismo & Ecclesiæ contubernio excludant) apud Marcum & Lucam addit: Amen amen dico vobis, quicunque non acceperit regnum Dei tanquam puerulus, nequaquam introibit in illud. Et mox puerulos istos vlnis suis complexus est, & manibus suis super eos impositis benedixit eis. Quæ ratio ergo iubet vt eos ad regnum Christi per tinere & in Ecclesiam recipi debere negemus, quos ipse Dei Filius complexu & benedictione sua dignatus est?
units.tr: But he is indignant not only with the disciples, but at the same time he also makes free access for the little children who were brought to him and for their parents, saying: "Suffer the little children, and do not forbid them to come to me." And lest this word should seem to have fallen from him in anger, he confirms it with the weightiest reason: "For of such is the kingdom of heaven." That is, such are the citizens of my kingdom and the members of my Church. Therefore they are not to be kept away from coming to me. But lest anyone seek an occasion for quibbling in the word τοιούτων [of such], and contend that this saying refers not to those who are young in age, but to those who are already grown and have professed faith in him, and who strive after the simplicity, humility and obedience of little children (this sophism the Anabaptists use to exclude little children from Baptism and from fellowship in the Church), he adds in Mark and Luke: "Verily, verily I say unto you, whoever does not receive the kingdom of God as a little child shall by no means enter into it." And immediately he embraced those little children in his arms, and laying his hands upon them he blessed them. What reason, then, bids us deny that they belong to the kingdom of Christ and must be received into the Church, those whom the Son of God himself has deigned to embrace and bless?

units.la: Debet igitur ex hoc loco generalis doctrina peti, Christianorum esse, vt infantes ex se genitos IESV CHRISTO adducant. Id verò bifariam fit. Primò quando per Baptismum initiantur, vt Ecclesiæ, quæ Christi corpus est, membra fiant. Non negamus equidem propriam & veram rationem, qua homines Christo adducuntur, doctrina & institutione constare. At in præsenti diserte de infantibus loquitur Dominus, & vt hi ad se adducantur iubet: qui cùm doctrinæ & prædicationis non sint capaces, eo medio & ratione cum illis agendum est, cuius capaces sunt. Est hæc Baptismus, vt in V. Testamento Circumcisio, qua masculi octauo a par. u die insigniti in Ecclesiæ societate adoptabantur. Obseruarunt hoc Apostoli, qui ideò totas familias baptizauisse legantur, quòd scirent diuini fœderis gratiam ad credentium infantes quoq; extendi, secundum promissionem: Ero Deus tuus & seminis tui. Et cur non baptizauissent eos, quos sanctos & Spiritus sancti capaces, Ecclesiæ stè & regni Dei ciues esse sciebant? Et hunc morem ab Apostolis acceptum postea obseruauit Ecclesia, teste D. Augustino, qui non veritus est scribere, paruulorum Baptismum esse tradition em Apostolicam, & Ecclesiæ vniuersitatem ideò hunc retinere dicit, & insuper addit: Si quisquam in hac re authoritatem diuinam quærat (quanquam quod vniuersa tenet Ecclesia, nec Concilijs institutum, sed semper retentum est, non nisi authoritate Apostolica traditum rectissimè creditur) tamen veraciter conijcere possumus, quid valeat in paruulis Baptismi sacramentum, ex circumcisione carnis, quæ prior populus accepit,, etc. Et ibidè postquàm Abrahami & Corneli Centurionis exempla adduxit, diserte testatur, quod vt Abraham prius fide iustificatus est, et postea demum iustitiæ fidei sigillum, Circumcisionem videlicet accepit, in Isaaco autē e contra Circumcisio iustitiam fidei præcessit, quam adultus demùm & institutus in fide obtinuit: ita etiam cum Christianorum infantibus fieri quoad Baptismum, ut regenerationis sacramentu praecedat, & si Christianam tenuerint pietatem, sequatur etiam in corde conuersio, cuius mysterium praecessit in corpore. Idem pater in alio libro scribit, vniuersam Ecclesiam antiquitus hoc constanter tenere, fideles pa-rulos originalis peccati remissionem per Christi Baptismum consequi. Et huius sententiae testem adducit Cyprian, qui idcirco paruulos a materno vtero recentissimos iam idoneos esse asseruit ad percipiendu Christi Baptismum. Hic certe epistola de baptizandis infantibus ad Fidu presbyterum, qui non baptizandos censebat ante diem octauum, quo olim circumcidi solebant, nomine Coni-lij scriptam, concludens ait: Idcirco frater charissime, haec fuit in Concilio nostra sententia, a Baptismo atq; a gratia Dei, qui omnibus misericors atq; benignus & pius est, neminem per nos debere prohiberi. Quod cum circa vniuersos obseruandum sit atq; retinendum, tum magis circa infantes ipsos & recens natos obseruandum putamus, qui hoc ipso de ope nostra, ac de diuina misericordia plus merentur, quod in primo statim nativitatis suae ortu plorantes ac flentes nil aliud faciunt, quam deprecantur. Et vt ad D. Augustinum redeamus, hic in libro contra Iulianum Pelagianum eiusdem sententiae alios etiam testes citat ex orthodoxis patribus, qui ante ipsum floruerunt, Basilium Capadocem, Gregorium Nazianzenum, Hilarium Gallum, & ex sui iaculi scriptoribus Innocentium Romanum, Ambrosium Mediolanensem & Ioannem Chrysostomum: ex quo apparet eandem fuisse olim omnium ecclesiarum per totum orbem doctrinam. Haec autem propter Anabaptistas annotamus, qui non minus pertinaciter quam impie contendunt, neminem baptizari debere, priusquam in Christum credere & fidem profiteri possit: ad quorum argumenta cum in Marco nostro respondemus, eadem nunc repetere non est opus. Sufficiat vere pijs & non contentiosis, quod Christus pueros quoq; sibi adduci vult, & cum id non possit alia ratione fieri, quam vt per Baptismum in corporis sui mysticis societatem cooptentur, id religiose fiat, & illum precemur, vt quae ex vi foederis in illis obsignatur, iustitiam fidei, ipsefuo tempore eis largiri & confirmare dignetur.
units.tr: From this passage, therefore, a general doctrine ought to be drawn, that it is the duty of Christians to bring the infants born of them to Jesus Christ. This is done in two ways. First, when they are initiated through Baptism, so that they become members of the Church, which is the body of Christ. We do not deny that the proper and true way in which men are brought to Christ consists in teaching and instruction. But in the present case the Lord speaks expressly of infants and commands that they be brought to him; since they are not capable of teaching and preaching, they must be dealt with by that means and in that manner of which they are capable. This is Baptism, as in the Old Testament circumcision was, by which males, marked on the eighth day, were adopted into the fellowship of the Church. The Apostles observed this, and it is read that they baptized whole households, because they knew that the grace of the divine covenant, according to the promise, "I will be your God and the God of your seed," extended also to the infants of believers. And why should they not have baptized those whom they knew to be holy and capable of the Holy Spirit, and citizens of the Church and of the kingdom of God? And this custom, received from the Apostles, was afterwards observed by the Church, as witnessed by Saint Augustine, who did not hesitate to write that the baptism of infants is an apostolic tradition, and says that the whole Church therefore keeps it, and he adds further: "If anyone in this matter seeks divine authority (although what the whole Church holds, not instituted by councils but always retained, is most rightly believed to have been handed down by apostolic authority alone), nevertheless we can truly conjecture what the sacrament of Baptism is worth in infants, from the circumcision of the flesh which the earlier people received," and so on. And there, after he had adduced the examples of Abraham and Cornelius the centurion, he clearly testifies that just as Abraham was first justified by faith and afterwards received circumcision, the seal of the righteousness of faith, whereas in Isaac on the contrary circumcision preceded the righteousness of faith, which he obtained later as an adult instructed in the faith, so also it happens with the infants of Christians as regards Baptism: that the sacrament of regeneration comes first, and if they keep the Christian piety, the conversion of the heart also follows, whose mystery went before in the body. The same Father writes in another book that the whole Church has held from antiquity, consistently, that faithful infants obtain remission of original sin through the Baptism of Christ. And he cites as a witness of this opinion Cyprian, who asserted that for this reason infants, even newly born from the mother's womb, are already fit to receive the Baptism of Christ. Indeed, in the letter on the baptizing of infants, written in the name of Cyprian's council to Fidus, the presbyter, who thought that they should not be baptized before the eighth day, when they used to be circumcised in former times, he concludes by saying: "Therefore, dearest brother, this was our opinion in the Council, that no one should be kept by us from Baptism and from the grace of God, who is merciful, kind and loving to all." Which we must observe and retain with regard to all, and we think it must be observed all the more with regard to the infants themselves and the newly born, who, by that very fact, deserve more from our help and from divine mercy, because at the very first moment of their birth, weeping and crying, they do nothing other than entreat. And to return to Saint Augustine: in his book against Julian the Pelagian he also cites other witnesses of the same opinion from the orthodox Fathers who flourished before him, Basil of Cappadocia, Gregory of Nazianzus, Hilary of Gaul, and from the writers of his own time Innocent of Rome, Ambrose of Milan and John Chrysostom. From this it appears that the same doctrine was once held by all the churches throughout the whole world. We note these things, however, on account of the Anabaptists, who contend no less obstinately than impiously that no one ought to be baptized before he is able to believe in Christ and profess faith. Since we have answered their arguments in our Mark, there is no need to repeat the same things now. It is enough for truly pious and not contentious people that Christ wishes children also to be brought to him, and since this cannot be done in any other way than by their being incorporated through Baptism into the mystical fellowship of his body, let this be done devoutly, and let us pray him that he may deign to bestow and confirm in them, in his own time, the righteousness of faith which is sealed in them by the power of the covenant.

units.la: Interim ipsi etiam non desinamus officio nostro, & vt primum per aetatem doctrinae atq; institutionis capaces sunt, hanc illis adhibeamus. Fecit hoc pater credentium Abrahamus, & idem populo Iudaico in lege Deus diligenter mandat: & nota sunt Apostolorum praecepta de hac re. Arguuntur hic prophani homines, qui filiorum, qui ex ipsis nati sunt, minorem rationem habent, quam iumentorum & pecorum, imo quam canum & accipitrum, quos diligentissime ad venationem & aucupium instituunt, filios autem turpissime negligunt, quoad ea, quae ad religionem & salutem aeternam pertinent: Nihil nunc de illis dicam, qui illos consulto corrumpunt, & teneram aetatem pessimis moribus imbuunt, vt iurare & execrari, potare, obscoena loqui & canere discant, priusquam quid ista sint intelligant: Deinde vbi aetate profecerunt ijs vitae generibus infelices mancipant, in quibus non possunt non perire, nisi eorum Deus misertus denuo illos educat. De illis loquor, qui in monasteria suos detrudunt, in militiam mercenariam mittunt, coniugijs imparibus implicant, vsurarijs artibus destinant: qui deniq; hoc vnu quaerunt, vt in mundo hoc diuites & honorati sint, neq; illis cura est, si Deo displiceant & aeternum damnentur. Peccant hi in leges naturae, & Reipub. atq; Ecclesiae pessime consulunt, cuius seminarium (vt initio diximus) corrumpunt. Itaq; vt Christiani magistratus suam authoritatem interponant, necesse est. Excitet hos Solomonis exemplu, qui in prouerbijs non aliud magis vrget, quam vt pueri recte instituantur. Qui vero scholarum praefecti sunt, meminerint quam arduam functionem suscipiant, & suae fidei creditos pueros qui Reipub. & Ecclesiae ipsi sunt, in veri Dei cognitione & fide syncera ad pietatem instituant, vt Christo insiti in eo adolescant. Ita enim & huic officium longe gratissimum praestant, & de tota Republ. & Ecclesia optime merentur. Interea omnes ad se pertinere putet, quod in hac actione dixit Dominus, neminem ingressurum in regnum Dei, nisi qui hoc vt puerulus acceperit. Exponit hoc Petrus Apostolus scribens: Depositu omni malitia & omni dolo & simulationibus & inuidentijs, & omnibus obtrectationibus, vt modo nati infantes lac illud sermonis syncerum expetite, vt per illud adolescatis. Quibus verbis tria monet Apostolus: Primum, vt quia natura mali, mendaces, philauti, & proinde inuidi sumus, quae obtrectationum, maledicentia & aliorum sceler um causa est malitia hac deposita in alios homines transformemur, & noua fiamus creatura, vtra, vt Paulus scribit. Deinde vt lac verbi Dei, quo nihil syncerius est & sanctius ex animo appetamus, & vt infantes nihil charius habent vberibus maternis: ita nobis nihil antiquius & exoptatius sit verbo Dei, quod vt semen est ex quo nos renasci oportet, sic nutrimentum quoq; ad vitam nobis suppeditat. Postremum non solum incipiamus officium facere, sed in eo proficiamus quod ex Dei verbo didicimus, vt ex infantibus tandem euadamus in virum perfectum, in mensuram statura adulti Christi, ne puerorum instar fluctuemus, sed veritatem facientes cum charitate, adolescamus in illum per omnia, qui est caput, nempe Christus. In his (inquam) nos esse oportebat. At quae nostri seculi calamitas est, plerique se Christianos esse sibi persuadent. Etiamsi in perdita & peccatrice conditione maneant, & peccato servire pergant: imo ijdem si quando aliquo vsque profecerunt, leuissima quaq; occasione relabuntur. Et hi sunt, quibus lac illud Verbi Dei sordet, & aut Circaum poculum appetunt, quod magna illa mater scortationum illis miscet, aut omni religionis cura depositta, mundi studijs sese totos dedunt, & tunc sibi felices videntur, si pessimis affectibus abrepti omnia pro sua libidine faciant. Oremus ergo Vnigenitum Filium Dei IESVM CHRISTVM, vt ex verbi sui semine renatis manum medicam adhibeat, atque nobis benedicat, vt in ipso adolescamus & feruemur. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Meanwhile let us not cease from our duty toward the children themselves, and as soon as by age they are capable of teaching and instruction, let us apply this to them. Abraham, the father of believers, did this, and God commanded the same thing to the Jewish people diligently in the law; and the precepts of the Apostles on this matter are well known. Here profane men are rebuked, who have less regard for their own children, born of themselves, than for beasts of burden and cattle, indeed than for dogs and hawks, which they train most diligently for hunting and fowling, while they shamefully neglect their sons in what pertains to religion and eternal salvation. I will say nothing now of those who deliberately corrupt them and steep their tender age in the worst habits, so that they learn to swear and curse, to drink, to speak and sing obscene things, before they understand what these things are. Then, when they have grown in years, they hand them over, unhappy, to those ways of life in which they cannot but perish, unless God in his mercy leads them out again. I speak of those who thrust their sons into monasteries, send them into mercenary soldiery, entangle them in unequal marriages, or destine them for usurious trades; who, finally, seek only this, that in this world they be rich and honoured, and do not care whether they displease God and are damned for ever. Such people sin against the laws of nature, and they consult most badly for the commonwealth and the Church, whose seminary (as we said at the beginning) they corrupt. Therefore it is necessary that Christian magistrates interpose their authority. The example of Solomon should stir them, who in the Proverbs urges nothing more than that children be rightly instructed. As for those who are set over the schools, let them remember how arduous a function they undertake, and let them train the boys entrusted to their faith, who are themselves the hope of the commonwealth and the Church, in the knowledge of the true God and in sincere faith, unto godliness, so that, grafted into Christ, they may grow up in him. For in this way they both perform a most pleasing duty and deserve very well of the whole commonwealth and Church. Meanwhile, let everyone think that what the Lord said in this action applies to him: that no one will enter the kingdom of God unless he receives it as a little child does. The Apostle Peter explains this when he writes: "Put away all malice and all guile and hypocrisies and envies and all evil speaking, and as newborn babes, desire the sincere milk of the word, that you may grow thereby." In these words the Apostle gives three admonitions. First, that since by nature we are evil, deceitful, self-loving, and therefore envious, which is the cause of backbiting, slander and other crimes, we should put off this malice and be transformed into other men, and become a new creature, as Paul writes. Then, that we should desire from the heart the milk of God's word, than which nothing is purer or holier, and that as infants have nothing dearer than their mother's breasts, so nothing should be dearer or more longed for by us than the word of God, which, as seed, is that from which we must be born again, and likewise supplies us with nourishment for life. Last, that we should not only begin the duty, but make progress in what we have learned from God's word, so that from infants we may at last grow into a perfect man, into the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ, lest we waver like children, but, speaking the truth in love, grow up in all things into him who is the head, namely Christ. It is in these things (I say) that we ought to be. But what a calamity of our age it is, that most persons persuade themselves that they are Christians, even though they remain in a lost and sinful condition and go on serving sin; indeed, if at any time they have advanced somewhat, they fall back at the slightest occasion. These are the ones for whom that milk of God's word is distasteful, and who either seek the cup of Circe, which that great mother of harlotries mixes for them, or, having cast off all care of religion, give themselves wholly to the pursuits of the world, and then they think themselves happy if, carried away by the worst affections, they do everything according to their lust. Let us therefore pray the Only-begotten Son of God, JESUS CHRIST, that he would apply a healing hand to those reborn from the seed of his word, and bless us, that we may grow and be strengthened in him. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCXXX.
units.tr: HOMILY CCXXX.

units.la: Et ecce, quidam accedens dixit ei: Magister bone, quid boni faciam, vt habeam vitam aeternam? Ipse vero dixit ei: Cur me dicis bonum? Nullus est bonus, nisi vnus, nempe Deus. Si vis autem ad vitam ingredi, serua mandata. Dicit ei: Quae? IESVS autem dixit: Non occides, Non moechaberis, Non furaberis, Non dices falsum testimonium, Honora patrem & matrem, Et diliges proximum tuum vt teipsum.
units.tr: And behold, a certain man came up and said to him, "Good Teacher, what good thing shall I do, that I may have eternal life?" But he said to him, "Why do you call me good? No one is good but one, that is, God. If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments." He said to him, "Which ones?" And Jesus said, "You shall not kill. You shall not commit adultery. You shall not steal. You shall not bear false witness. Honour your father and mother. And you shall love your neighbour as yourself."

units.la: QVamuis regnum Domini nostri IESV CHRISTI non sit de hoc mundo, sed in eo constat, vt per illum ex peccati seruitio redempti, & ex semine verbi eius renati, noux creaturae simus, in quibus ille regnet & viuat: idem tamen non abolet huius vitae conditiones, sine quibus in terris neq; genus humanum conseruari, neq; commode & honeste viui possit, quales sunt, Coniugium, liberorum procreatio & educatio, oeconomia, ad quam agricultura cum opificijs manuarijs & mercatura pertinet, Magistratus item & quaecunq; in pace & bello sunt necessaria. Vt enim ista omnibus seculis inter electos Dei cultores in vsu fuerunt: ita quid in his omnibus fieri & obseruari debeat, Spiritus sanctus in Scripturis diligenter docet. Et hoc facit totum hoc Caput, in quo huc vsq; de Coniugio disseruit Christus, & liberorum institutione. Sequitur nunc actio memorabilis cum iuuene opulento & magnae dignitatis, qua docemur, quis nam adultis & in quocunq; vitae genere versantibus studiorum & actionum omnium scopus esse debeat: Nimirum vt non solum in hoc seculo commode viuant, sed huius vitae curriculum emensi aeternam assequantur. De quasic loquitur, vt ea occasione ostendat, quantum impedimentum ad vitam aeternam aspirantibus diuitiae obiiciunt, nisi in fide vera recte simus instituti. Itaque traditur hic primum quae vera sit vitae aeternae assequendae ratio: deinde quis nobis opum vsus esse, & quid in tota re domestica & omnibus, quae ad praesentem vitam faciunt, obseruari debeat. In praesenti primam historiae partem videamus, & breuitati quidem studebimus, quia prolixius de his dictum est in Marco nostro homilia 83.
units.tr: Although the kingdom of our Lord Jesus Christ is not of this world, yet it is in this world that, redeemed by him from the bondage of sin and born again of the seed of his Word, we become new creatures, in whom he reigns and lives. Nevertheless, he does not abolish the conditions of this life, without which the human race cannot be preserved on earth, nor can anyone live decently and honourably. These conditions are marriage, the procreation and upbringing of children, household management (to which agriculture, manual trades and commerce belong), and likewise the magistracy and all things necessary in peace and war. For just as these have been in use among the elect worshippers of God in every age, so the Holy Spirit teaches diligently in the Scriptures what ought to be done and observed in all these matters. And this whole chapter does exactly that, in which Christ has so far discoursed about marriage and the instruction of children. Now follows a memorable action with a wealthy young man of great standing, by which we are taught what should be the aim of all studies and actions for adults and for those engaged in any kind of life: namely, that they should not only live well in this age, but, having run the course of this life, attain eternal life. He speaks of these things so that, on this occasion, he may show how great a hindrance riches present to those who aspire to eternal life, unless we are rightly instructed in the true faith. Accordingly, here we are taught first what is the true way of attaining eternal life, and then how we should use our wealth, and what ought to be observed in the whole management of the household and in all things that pertain to the present life. For now, let us look at the first part of the story, and we will be brief, since this was discussed at greater length in our homily 83 on Mark.

units.la: Primus vero occurrit, qui toti actioni occasionem praebuit. Initio quendam accessisse ait Matthaeus, & mox eundem dicit νεανίσκον, id est, iuuenem. Lucas principem siue primatem fuisse scribit: Certe diuitem & opulentum fuisse constat: quae fortasse (vt in mundo fieri solet) causa fuit, vt in ea aetate ad Magistratum & publicas functiones eueheretur. Hic ad Christum accessisse dicitur. Non autem obiter, & quasi aliud agens, accessit, sed Marco teste, accurrit & accidit ad genua, vel cum genuum inflexione eum compellauit: quod magni studij & obseruantiæ indicium est. Dicit autem: Magister bone, quid boni faciam, vt habeam vitam æternam? Et hæc illum non ficto animo, aut malitiose fecisse tentandi ergò, ex eo constat, quòd Christus eum dilexisse dicitur apud Marcum. Itaq; operæ pretium fuerit, singula quæ fecit diligentius inspicere.
units.tr: The first thing to notice is the man who gave occasion for the whole action. Matthew says that at the outset a certain man came up, and soon he calls him a young man [νεανίσκον], that is, a youth. Luke writes that he was a ruler or chief man. Certainly it is clear that he was rich and wealthy, which perhaps (as usually happens in the world) was the reason he had been raised at that age to the magistracy and public offices. He is said to have approached Christ. Yet he did not come casually, as if busy with something else, but, according to Mark, he ran up and fell at his knees, or at least addressed him with a bending of the knees; this is a sign of great zeal and reverence. He says: "Good Teacher, what good thing shall I do, that I may have eternal life?" And that he did this not with a feigned mind, nor out of malice to test him, is clear from the fact that Mark says Christ loved him. Therefore it will be worth our while to examine carefully each thing he did.

units.la: Principio de vita æterna quærit. Ergo non fuit ex Sadducæorum numero, qui cum animarum immortalitatem & corporum resurrectionem negarent, vitam æternam esse non credebant. Hanc ille non credidit modo, sed beatam esse credidit, & ad solos pios pertinere, qui virtuti & sanctissimæ studeant. Magnum autem animi vere pij argumentum est, quod neq; ætas, neq; diuitiæ, neq; dignitates illum potuerunt auocare, quo minus de vita futura & æterna sollicitus fit. Et in eo qui dem omnes, qui Christum sequebantur, superat. Nam si eius discipulos domesticos spectes, hi tunc regnum terrenum somniabant. Reliqui propter miracula accedebant, vt morbis suis remedium inuenirent, aut epulo gratuito exciperentur. Multos inanis curiositas trahebat. Solus hic inuenitur, qui de vita æterna interrogat. Est hoc memorabile exemplum, quod iuuenes imitentur, & ij qui dem in primis, qui aliquando magnates futuri sunt. Existimant pleriq; vitæ æternæ curam ad iuniores nequaquam pertinere: sed aliud res ipsa loquitur. Quia enim Dei opus sumus, qui nos in vero finxit, & in quo sumus, viuimus & mouemur, nos totos illi debemus, & nullum vitæ tempus est quod non debeat illi consecratum esse. Deinde cum iuuenes perinde vt senes morti sint obnoxij, imo pauciores ad senectam peruenient, necesse est, vt assiduis de vita æterna meditationibus sese ad abitum præparent. Præterea quia iuuenes cupiditatibus feruentioribus ardent, correctione quoq; & disciplina seueriori & continua opus est, quæ illos in officio contineat, ne quid in ætate illa lubrica desiguent, quod aliquando in gradu sublimiori constitutis, existimationi ipsorum aliquid deroget. Semper ergo sibi ipsis occinant illud Dauidis: Qui nam emendabit adolescens viam suam? Si custodiat verbum tuum. Et illud Sirachidis: Memento finis tui, & non vnquam peccabis. Nec desunt exempla sanctissimorum iuuenum in utroq; Testamento, quorum vestigijs potius insistant iuniores, quàm vt mundi illecebras sectentur, aut hominum prophanorum & illusorum voces audiant.
units.tr: First, he asks about eternal life. Therefore he was not of the number of the Sadducees, who, denying the immortality of souls and the resurrection of bodies, did not believe in eternal life. He not only believed in it, but believed it to be blessed, and to belong only to the godly, who strive after virtue and holiness. Moreover, it is a great proof of a truly pious mind that neither youth, nor riches, nor dignities could draw him away from being anxious about the future and eternal life. In this respect he surpasses all who followed Christ. For if you look at his household disciples, they were at that time dreaming of an earthly kingdom. Others came because of the miracles, to find a remedy for their diseases, or to be received at a free feast. Many were drawn by idle curiosity. Only this man is found asking about eternal life. This is a memorable example for young people to imitate, and especially those who will one day be great men. Most people think that care for eternal life does not pertain to the young at all, but the matter itself speaks otherwise. For since we are God's workmanship, who formed us truly, and in whom we live, move and have our being, we owe ourselves wholly to him, and there is no time of life that ought not to be consecrated to him. Next, since young people are subject to death just as the old are, indeed fewer of them reach old age, it is necessary that they prepare themselves for departure by constant meditation on eternal life. Moreover, because young people burn with more fervent desires, they also need correction and stricter, continual discipline, which keeps them in their duty, lest in that slippery age they commit anything which, when they are later placed in a higher rank, may detract from their reputation. Let them therefore always repeat to themselves that saying of David: "How shall a young man cleanse his way? By taking heed to your word." And that saying of the son of Sirach: "Remember your end, and you will never sin." Nor are there lacking examples of the most holy young men in both Testaments, whose footsteps younger people should rather follow than pursue the allurements of the world or listen to the voices of profane and deceitful men.

units.la: Deinde obseruatu dignum est, quòd de vita æterna Christum interrogat, non scribas aut Pharisæos: nimirum quòd hos diu nequicquam audiuisset. Etenim, vt alibi dictum est, frigidè isti docebant, neq; ipsorum dictis aliqua aderat Spiritus sancti gratia, qualis in Christi labijs erat diffusa. Deinde nihil fere præter externo sacrificiorum ritus, oblationes, ieiunia, ablutiones, & alia corporalia exercitia tradebant, quæ ad veram pietatem parum conferunt, neq; cor stabilire possunt. Ergo sitiebat ille adhuc, quod omnibus euenire dicit Dominus, qui alibi quàm ex ipso bibunt. Itaq; quia haud dubiè ex fama, quæ longè lateq; spargebatur, præclaram de Christo sibi concepisset, ad hunc contendit, vt certum quid & solidum ex illo audiat. Imitentur hunc quotquot veritatis & falsitatis studio tenentur. Etenim qui ab hominum authoritate pendent, aut Conciliorum determinationes expectant, ij semper dubij pendent, & tandem miserè falluntur.
units.tr: Next, it is worth noting that he asks Christ about eternal life, and not the scribes or Pharisees; clearly because he had heard them for a long time to no purpose. For, as has been said elsewhere, those men taught coldly, and there was no grace of the Holy Spirit in their words such as was poured out on the lips of Christ. Moreover, they taught almost nothing beyond the outward ritual of sacrifices, offerings, fastings, washings and other bodily exercises, which contribute little to true godliness and cannot establish the heart. Therefore he was still thirsting, which the Lord says happens to all who drink anywhere other than from him.
