Accordingly, since he had doubtless conceived a high opinion of Christ from the report that spread far and wide, he hastens to him, so that he may hear from him something certain and solid. Let all those who are eager to know truth from falsehood imitate him. For those who depend on the authority of men, or who await the decisions of councils, always remain in doubt and at last are miserably deceived.

units.la: Præstat vero quæstionem ipsam audire: Magister bone (inquit) quid boni faciam, vt habeam vitam æternam? Pia quæstio & quæ ex zelo bono mota fuit: sed concurrit hic duplex error, quem ex Pharisæorum institutione hauserat. Primus est, quòd vitam operibus & horum merito acquiri posse putat: alter, quòd se proprijs viribus aut ex seipso aliquid boni posse facere, sibi persuasit. Vtrumq; docebant Pharisæi, vt alibi demonstrauimus. Non agnouit ergo ipse adhuc in seipso tam vitiositatem, qua fit vt ex nobisipsis ne ad cogitandum quidem idonei simus. Et hic error ille communis est, qui non Iudæos solos perdidit, dum proprietatem Dei iustitia suam constituere voluerunt, verumetiam omnibus seculis in toto orbe omnium superstitionum causa fuit: & hodie ad hunc lapidem offendunt omnes, qui Euangelij doctrinæ sese opponunt, quòd pro suorum operum iustitia & merito pugnant. Et nocentissimi doctores sunt, qui Pharisæos secuti miseros peccatores ad opera sua remittunt. Faciunt hic perinde, ac si medicus ineptus paralyticum & omnium virium admini culo destitutum currere aut saltare iuberet, & ex eo salutem ei polliceretur: Itaq; a nostrijpsius cognitione initium fieri oportet: quod ipsum Christus sua responsione docet, cuius partes sunt duæ.
units.tr: Let us now hear the question itself: "Good Teacher," he says, "what good thing shall I do, that I may have eternal life?" It is a pious question, and one moved by good zeal. Yet there is a double error here, which he had drawn in from the teaching of the Pharisees. The first is that he thinks life can be acquired by works and by their merit; the second is that he has persuaded himself that he can do anything good by his own strength or from himself. The Pharisees taught both, as we have shown elsewhere. He did not yet recognise in himself that vice by which we are so unfit that we cannot even think anything of ourselves. This error is common, and it has destroyed not only the Jews, who wanted to establish their own righteousness in place of the justice of God, but has also in every age and throughout the whole world been the cause of all superstitions; and today all who oppose themselves to the doctrine of the Gospel stumble over this stone, because they contend for the righteousness and merit of their own works. And there are very harmful teachers who, following the Pharisees, send miserable sinners back to their works. They do just as if an incompetent physician ordered a paralytic, who is deprived of all strength and support, to run or leap, and promised him health on that basis. Therefore the beginning must be made with knowledge of ourselves, which Christ himself teaches in his answer, which has two parts.

units.la: Priori quæstionem nouam opponit, dicens: Cur me dicis bonum? Et mox huius rationem reddens, addens, addit: Nullus est bonus, nisi unus, nempe Deus. At haec dicendo, non negat se bonum aut Deum esse. Multo minus subtili argutia suam Deitatem asserere vult (ut quidam interpretantur) sed simpliciter ad iuvenis errorem respiciens, ut huic medeatur, occasionem ei dare voluit altius quid de hac ipsa quaestione cogitandi. Quasi diceret: Quaeris quid boni facere debeas, ut vitam aeternam possis assequi. Atqui ipsa Boni vox te docere poterat. Quia enim nemo ex seipso bonus est praeter unum Deum, nihil utiq; bonum dici poterit, quam quod ipsi placet, quod item ipse iubet, et in nobis agit. Quin ergo ad illum totus converteris, et depositá confidenti illa de tuis operibus persuasione, ad divinae gratiae thronum recurris per eum, quem ille inter seipsum et homines Mediatorem constituit, &c. Hic huius dicti proprius sensus et usus est.
units.tr: He sets before him a new question, saying: "Why do you call me good?" And soon, giving the reason for this, he adds: "No one is good except one, namely God." Yet by saying this he does not deny that he himself is good or God. He does not wish, by subtle cleverness, to assert his Deity (as some interpret it), but simply looking to the young man's error, he wanted to give him, in order to heal it, an occasion to think more deeply about this very question. As if he said: "You ask what good you ought to do so that you may attain eternal life. Yet the very word good could have taught you. For since no one is good of himself except the one God, nothing can rightly be called good except what pleases him, what he likewise commands, and what he works in us. Why not then turn wholly to him, and, having laid aside that confidence in your works, have recourse to the throne of divine grace through him whom he has appointed as Mediator between himself and men, etc." This is the proper sense and use of this saying.

units.la: Interim diligenti consideratione dignum est, Deum revera solum bonum esse, neq; extra hunc aliquid esse, quod ex seipso bonum dici mereatur. Etenim, ut Apostolus scribit, peccatum ex uno homine Adamo in omnem posteritatem deriuatum est, et ideo omnes in peccato concipimur et nascimur, adeo ut ad omnes pertineat quod dicit Deus: Non contendet spiritus meus perpetuo cum homine: quia caro est. Figmentum cordis humani malum est a pueritia sua. Item, non est iustus, ne unus quidem, non est qui intelligat, non est qui exquirat Deum: Omnes declinauerunt, simul inutiles facti sunt: non est qui exerceat bonitatem, non est usque ad unum. Sepulchrum apertum guttur eorum, linguis suis ad dolum utuntur, venenum aspidum sub labiis eorum: Quorum os maledictione et amaritudine plenum est: veloces pedes eorum ad effundendum sanguinem, contritio et calamitas in viis eorum: et viam pacis non cognouerunt, &c. Adhaec propter nos uniuersa haec mundi machina laborat et vanitati obnoxia suspirat, ut liberetur. Solus ergo Deus ex seipso bonus, et omnis boni fons est. Istorum vero hic nobis usus esse debet: Ut primum Deo uni fidamus, et ab illo uno petamus quod nobis bonum et salutare est. Deinde ne efferamur donis eius, si quae in nobis ipsis inuenimus, sed nobis ipsis dicamus: Quid habes quod non accepisti? &c. Simul etiam cogitemus, in quem finem acceperimus: Nimirum ut Dei gloriae et aliorum hominum utilitati seruiat. Praeterea si Deus solus bonus, homines autem mali sunt, cur offendimur, aut iras implacabiles concipimus, si qui nos dicto aut facto laeduntur? Quid enim aliud faciat homo, qui natura malus est? Socrates olim a temerario et petulante quodam temere et iniuste percussus, cum ab astantibus iuberetur illum in ius trahere, respondebat: si asinus me calce feriret, num me huic actioni forensem intendere iuberetis? Non arbitror. At nisi hic asinus et vere rationis usu destitutus esset, nunquam fecisset quod fecit. Si in ethnico philosopho tantum potuit innatae omnibus vitiositatis consideratio, quid non eadem possit apud homines Christianos, si simul Dei bonitatem cum illa conferamus, quaesit, ut hunc diligentibus omnia adiumento sint in bonum? Roman. octavo Cap.
units.tr: Meanwhile it is worth careful consideration that God alone is truly good, and that outside him there is nothing which deserves to be called good of itself. For, as the Apostle writes, sin passed from one man, Adam, into all his posterity, and therefore we are all conceived and born in sin, so that what God says applies to all: "My spirit shall not strive with man forever, because he is flesh. The imagination of the human heart is evil from its youth." Likewise: "There is not even one righteous, there is none who understands, there is none who seeks God. All have turned aside, together they have become useless; there is none who does good, no, not one. Their throat is an open sepulchre; they use their tongues for deceit; the venom of asps is under their lips; their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness; their feet are swift to shed blood; destruction and misery are in their ways; and the way of peace they have not known," etc. Moreover, on our account this whole machinery of the world labours and sighs under the bondage of vanity, that it may be set free. Therefore God alone is good of himself, and he is the fount of all good. From these things the use for us ought to be this: first, that we trust in the one God alone and ask from him alone what is good and salutary for us. Then, that we not be puffed up by his gifts, if we find any in ourselves, but say to ourselves: "What have you that you did not receive?" etc. Let us also consider at the same time to what end we have received them: surely that they may serve the glory of God and the usefulness of other men. Furthermore, if God alone is good, and men are evil, why are we offended, or conceive implacable anger, if anyone injures us by word or deed? For what else can a man do who is evil by nature? Socrates once, when struck rashly and unjustly by a certain reckless and insolent fellow, and when the bystanders urged him to drag the man into court, replied: "If an ass had kicked me, would you urge me to bring a suit against it in court?" I think not. Yet unless this ass were destitute of the use of reason, he would never have done what he did. If in a heathen philosopher the consideration of the vice innate in all men could have such force, what might not the same achieve among Christian men, if we were to set alongside it the goodness of God, who makes all things work together for good for those who love him? Romans, chapter eight.

units.la: Sequitur altera responsionis Christi pars, qua directe ad quaestionem iuvenis istius respondet, dicens: Si vis ad vitam ingredi, serva mandata. Et illo quaerente, Quae? secundae tabulae praecepta recenseт: Non occides, Non moechaberis, &c. Quibus compendium omnium addit: Et diliges proximum tuum ut teipsum. Vbi quis miretur, cur hunc ad legis praecepta remittat Christus, qui alias fidem exigit ab omnibus, hoc unum itidem inculcans: Amen dico vobis, qui credit in me, habet vitam aeternam, &c. Num ergo sibi ipsi contradicit? Aut num duae diversae ad vitam aeternam viae sunt? Vna per fidem in Christum, altera per operum legis iustitiam? Nequaquam. Etenim Christus, qui ipsissima veritas est, sibi ipsi non potest esse contrarius: et idem solus est Via et ostium, ut nemo sine illo ad Patrem veniat: neq; est aliud nomen sub caelo datum inter homines, per quod nos oporteat saluos fieri. Et quia hic non alia ratione quam per fidem apprehenditur, recte et proprie ille dicit: Qui credit in me, habet vitam aeternam: proprie item loquuntur Apostoli, quando nos fide in Christum absque operibus Legis iustificari et seruari docent. At quia hunc propriae iustitiae fiducia decipiebat, ut aliena sibi non opus esse putaret, quae per fidem in promissum Seruatorem acquiritur, Dominus ad Legem remittit, ceu ad speculum in quo infirmitatem suam siue defectum, et latentem in carne naturae vitiositatem videat, et ea visa humilieтur. Et hanc Christi sententiam siue mentem fuisse, ex sequentibus patebit, quando de horum praeceptorum obseruatione gloriantem ad perfectissimum charitatis opus remittit,
units.tr: There follows the second part of Christ's answer, in which he responds directly to this young man's question, saying: "If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments." And when he asks, "Which?", he recounts the precepts of the second table: "You shall not kill, you shall not commit adultery," etc. To these he adds the summary of them all: "And you shall love your neighbour as yourself." Here someone may wonder why Christ sends him back to the precepts of the law, he who elsewhere requires faith from all, inculcating this same thing: "Amen, I say to you, he who believes in me has eternal life," etc. Does he then contradict himself? Or are there two different ways to eternal life, one through faith in Christ, the other through the righteousness of the works of the law? By no means. For Christ, who is the very truth, cannot be contrary to himself; and he alone is the Way and the Door, so that no one comes to the Father without him; nor is there any other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved. And since here he is apprehended in no other way than through faith, he rightly and properly says: "He who believes in me has eternal life." The Apostles likewise speak properly when they teach that we are justified and saved by faith in Christ without the works of the Law. But because the confidence in his own righteousness was deceiving this man, so that he thought he had no need of that righteousness which is acquired through faith in the promised Saviour, the Lord sends him back to the Law, as to a mirror in which he may see his weakness or defect, and the vice of nature hidden in the flesh, and, having seen these, be humbled. And that this was the meaning or mind of Christ's saying will be clear from what follows, when, to a man who boasts of the observance of these precepts, he sends him on to the most perfect work of charity.

units.la: Christus quo modo boni non men reijciat. & ut omnibus diuenditis & in pauperes distributis, se sequatur postulat. Adde huc praeceptorum istorum interpretationem, quam supra capite quinto audiuimus, & mox patebit, neminem esse mortalium, qui quae istis requiruntur praestare possit. Vehementer ergo errant, qui ex hoc dicto Christi, Si vis ad vitam ingredi, serua mandata: operum iustitiam colligunt. Nam recte quidem hoc dictum est, sicut & illud in lege, Custodite iudicia mea, quae faciens homo viuet in eis: Sed hu minorem propositionem subijcere oportet. At nemo ista facere & perfectam obedientiam eis praestare potest. Et irrefragibili demonstratione sequetur, Nemmem ex praeceptorum legis obserua tione iustificari aut seruari posse.
units.tr: How Christ rejects the boast of goodness, and requires him, having sold all and distributed to the poor, to follow him. Add to this the interpretation of these precepts which we heard above in chapter five, and it will soon be plain that there is no mortal who can perform what these things require. They err greatly, therefore, who from this saying of Christ, "If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments," gather a righteousness of works. For this saying is indeed correct, just as that in the law, "Keep my judgements, which if a man does he shall live in them," is correct; but the minor premise must be added. Yet no one can do these things and render perfect obedience to them. And by an irrefutable demonstration it follows that no one can be justified or saved by the observance of the precepts of the law.

units.la: Quis ergo (inquis) vsus est legis? Magnus & multiplex o fratres: Primus, de quo nunc dixi mus, vt speculi instar sit, quod nostram vitiofitatem & imperfectionem arguat, & conuictos peccati, in star pædagogi deducat ad Christum, qui solus ei medetur. Alter, vt nos de Dei voluntate edoceat & quae vere bona opera sint, ostendat, ne hominum traditiones secuti eorum specie & splendore sal lamur, quae secundum illas fiunt. Postremus, vt in officio contineat homines, ne qui praetextu fidei abutantur ad peccandi licentiam: quod multi (proh dolor) non sine publico multorum scandalo fa ciunt. Discimus ergo ex hoc loco, doctrinam de sola fide in Christum iustificante & seruante, neque cum Legis doctrina pugnare, neque bonis operibus inimicam esse, sed ad hac nos potius per illam ob stringi. Est enim fides certa & indubitata de gratia Dei in Filio suo IESV CHRISTO no bis facta persuasio, qua hunc ita apprehendimus, vt ipse in nobis viuat & agat, & nos ceu pal mites ei insiti fructum multum feramus. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeter num. Amen.
units.tr: What then (you ask) is the use of the law? Great and manifold, brethren. The first, of which I have just spoken, is that it may be like a mirror which shows up our vice and imperfection, and, having convicted us of sin, leads us as a schoolmaster to Christ, who alone heals us. The second is that it may teach us the will of God and show which works are truly good, lest, following human traditions, we be deceived by the appearance and splendour of those works which are done according to them. The last is that it may keep men in check, lest they abuse the pretext of faith for a licence to sin, which many (alas!) do, not without public scandal to many. We learn therefore from this passage that the doctrine of faith alone in Christ, which justifies and saves, neither fights against the doctrine of the Law nor is hostile to good works, but rather binds us to them. For faith is the certain and undoubted persuasion, wrought in us by God, concerning his grace in his Son Jesus Christ, by which we so apprehend him that he lives and acts in us, and we, grafted into him like branches, bear much fruit. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCXXXI.
units.tr: HOMILY 231.

units.la: Dicit ei adolescens: Omnia haec obseruaui a iuuentute mea: quo adhuc deficior? Ait ei IESVS: Si vis perfectus esse, abi, vende quae habes, & da pauperibus: & habebis thesaurum in coelo: Et veni, seque re me. Cum audisset autem adolescens eum sermonem, abiit contri status: Habebat enim bona multa.
units.tr: The young man said to him: "All these things I have kept from my youth; what do I still lack?" Jesus said to him: "If you want to be perfect, go, sell what you have, and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven. And come, follow me." But when the young man heard that saying, he went away sorrowful, for he had many possessions.

units.la: Quamuis omnes hominea natura non solum peccatores, verumetiam ita vitiosi sint, vt ne ad cogitandum quidem idonei sint ex semetipsis, ea tamen confidentia illis innata est, vt suorum operum meritis vitam aeternam se consequi posse sibi ipsis persuadeant. Est haec causa omni um superstitionum, in quas mundus scinditur. Vt ergo Deus Seruatorem humano generi vnicum praedestinauit, Filium suum vnigenitum: ita speculum commune dedit, legem nimirum, in quo nosi ptos contemplando vitiofitatem nostram agnoscamus, & intra animos nostros conuictiinFilio suo oblatam salutem amplexemur. Idcirco hic nuper iuuenem istum, de vita aeterna quaerentem, ad praecepta legis remisit. Sed quid tunc quoq; fieri soleat, altera historiae pars in praesenti docet: vbi discemus, non sufficere vt Legis speculum obiter intueamur, sed efficaci spiritus virtute opus esse, qua in animos nostros ille penetret.
units.tr: Although all men by nature are not only sinners but so corrupt that they are not even fit to think good thoughts of themselves, they are nonetheless born with a confidence that they can persuade themselves they will attain eternal life by the merits of their works. This is the cause of all the superstitions into which the world is split. So God, who appointed one Saviour for the human race, his only-begotten Son, has also given a common mirror, namely the law, in which we may contemplate our wickedness and recognise it, and, convicted within our hearts, embrace the salvation offered in his Son. For this reason he recently sent this young man, who was asking about eternal life, back to the precepts of the law. But what usually happens then, the other part of the story shows at this point, where we learn that it is not enough to glance briefly at the mirror of the law, but that the effective power of the Spirit is needed to penetrate our hearts.

units.la: Nec enim intelligit Christi consilium iuuenis iste, sed hoc audito in errore & propria iustitia fiducia potius confirmatur: vt hodie multi qui ex eo, quod Lex nobis a Deo data est, colligunt, nobis vires inesse, quibus illi possimus satisfacere: & si quis hoc neget, Deum nobiscu ludere aiunt. Tale quid hunc quoq; sensisse apparet. Nam confidenter responder: Omnia haec obseruaui a iuuen tute mea. Neq; dicto tam arrogante, quo & suijpsius & Legis diuinae ignorantiam prodit, conten tus, addit insuper: Quo adhuc deficior. Quod nunquam dicturus erat, si eum Legis sensum & vsum tenuisset, quem Christus supra Capite quinto tradidit. Sed non alium legis vsum esse putauit, quam vt ad politicam obedientiam nos instituat. Interim huic plus tribuit quam sanctissimi quiq; omni bus suis virtutibus, quae in ipsis comendantur, vnquam tribuerint. Omnium enim horum vox fuit: Ne ingrediaris Domine cum seruo tuo in iudicium: Cor mundum crea in me Deus: Conuertenos, & conuertemur. Sed eo vsq; progrediuntur, qui semel incipiunt suis operibus fidere. Quia tamen non malitia aut impia confidentia peccauit, non prorsus abijci meretur: sed sunt aliqua in ipso ob feruanda, quae laudem & imitationem merentur.
units.tr: This young man does not understand Christ's counsel; rather, on hearing it, he is confirmed in his error and in confidence in his own righteousness. So today many who infer from the fact that the law was given us by God that we have the strength within us to satisfy it, and who say that God is mocking us if anyone denies this. It appears that this man too thought something of this kind. For he answers confidently: "All these things I have kept from my youth." Not content with this boast, which betrays both his own and the divine law's ignorance, he adds further: "What do I still lack?" He would never have said this if he had grasped the sense and use of the law that Christ set out in the fifth chapter above. But he thought the use of the law was only to train us in civil obedience. Meanwhile he attributed to himself more than the holiest men ever attributed to their virtues. For the voice of all of them was: "Enter not into judgement with your servant, O Lord" (Ps. 143); "Create in me a clean heart, O God" (Ps. 51); "Turn us, and we shall be turned" (Lam. 5). But those who once begin to trust in their works go so far. Yet since he sinned not from malice or impious confidence, he does not deserve to be cast off altogether; there are some things in him worth preserving, which deserve praise and imitation.

units.la: Primum, quod diu hac aetate & fortuna, inter opes nimirum & dignitates non vulgares, sic vitam suam transegit, ut legi Dei se obedientiam politicam praestitisse gloriari possit. Nam vere hoc illu dixisse, ex eo colligat, quod Dominus eu non arguit falsi quoad externa vitae officia, sed eundem dilexit, ut nuper quoq; ex Marco annotauimus. Habemus igitur in eo exemplum eius, quod Dauid ait: In quo emendabit adolescens viam suam? In eo, si verbum tuum custodiat. Huius certe studium hunc in officio continuit, ut licet vitam aeternam non potuerit mereri, ciuilis tamen probitatis siue integritatis laudem assecutus sit. Et qui huic animo syncero studeant, horum pietas Deo grata est, qui eam praemijs suis in hoc saeculo remunerat, & eadem conscientiam placat, & in aduersis consolationes suggerit non contemnendas, sicuti in Iobis exemplo est videre. At quae nostri saeculi calamitas est, plures inuenias hodie, qui praecepta Decalogi ne numerare quidem, ne dum de illorum obedientia gloriari possint.
units.tr: First, that for so long in this age and station, among considerable wealth and no mean dignities, he so conducted his life that he could boast of having rendered civil obedience to God's law. For that he said this truly, one may infer from the fact that the Lord did not accuse him of falsehood in respect of the outward duties of life, but loved him, as we noted recently from Mark. So we have in him an example of what David says: "Wherein shall a young man cleanse his way? By taking heed to it according to your word" (Ps. 119). Certainly his zeal kept him in his duty so that, although he could not merit eternal life, he obtained the praise of civil uprightness and integrity. And those who strive for this sincere disposition, their piety is pleasing to God, who rewards it with his blessings in this age, calms the conscience, and offers no small consolations in adversity, as may be seen in the example of Job. But it is a calamity of our age that today you will find many who cannot even count the precepts of the Decalogue, let alone boast of obeying them.

units.la: Obseruari praterea debet, quod etsi de externa siue politica praeceptorum Dei obseruatione sibi bene conscius esset, nihilominus tamen ad Christum venit, quaerens, quid ipsum facere oporteat, ut vitam aeternam consequi possit, & nunc quid porro sibi faciendum sit, quaerit. Ergo legis iustitia, qua plerisque suis loci & ordinis hominibus praestabat, ipsius conscientiae satisfacere aut salutis certum reddere non potuit. Fit hoc omnibus qui abs Christo ex operibus suis iustificari & seruari volunt. Etenim opus Dei, quod animum hominis facit & tranquillum reddit, vnicum est, ut Filium eius IESVM CHRISTVM fide vera apprehendamus, quem ille misit, ut non fier redemptor fieret. Veruntamen laude meretur, quod proficere cupit. Etenim quia natura vitiosi sumus, nisi indies progrediamur, mox vel ignaui torpemus, vel in peius relabimur. Vidit hoc Paulus, qui etsi in Pharisaismo prae aequalibus suis profecisset, & postea in Christi seruitio plus aliis Apostolis laborauisset, tamen non dubitauit de seipso scribere: Non quod iam apprehenderim aut perfectus sim, sed persequor experiens an quoq; apprehendam, &c. Turpiter ergo seipsos fallunt, qui sibi nihil deesse arbitrantur, & quasi metam perfectionis iam attigerint, ignauo otio se dedunt. Etenim si serui inutiles sunt, qui omnia fecerunt, quae ipsis mandata sunt, quales dici merebuntur, qui vix dum coeperunt officium facere? Vide Luc.17.
units.tr: It should further be observed that, although he was well aware of his external or civil observance of God's precepts, he nevertheless came to Christ, asking what he must do to attain eternal life, and now asks what more he must do. Therefore the righteousness of the law, by which he surpassed most men of his rank and order, could not satisfy his conscience or make his salvation certain. This happens to all who wish to be justified and saved by Christ through their own works. For the work of God, which makes the human heart tranquil, is one thing only: that we lay hold by true faith on his Son Jesus Christ, whom he sent that he might become our redeemer. Yet he deserves praise for desiring to advance. For since we are by nature sinful, unless we make progress daily, we soon either grow lazy or slide back for the worse. Paul saw this; although he had advanced beyond his peers in Pharisaism, and afterwards had laboured more than the other apostles in the service of Christ, he did not hesitate to write of himself: "Not that I have already attained, or am already perfect, but I follow after, if I may apprehend" (Phil. 3). So those deceive themselves shamefully who think they lack nothing, and as if they had already reached the goal of perfection, give themselves over to idle ease. For if servants are unprofitable when they have done all that was commanded them (Luke 17), what must be said of those who have scarcely begun to do their duty?

units.la: Sed Christum audiamus, qui (vt Marcus annotauit) iuuenem hunc amice intuitus est, ac dilexit: Nimirum quod licet ex ignorantia errare, proficere tamen cuperet, & ipso magistro vtetur. Quod probe obseruari debet, ne animi nostri intentionem bonam sufficere putemus. Etenim tunc demum probatur Deo intentio nostra, si quod ille iubet, facere cupimus. Et haec causa est, quod istum nimis arroganter de seipso sentientem amico respondit dignetur Dominus. Nam apud Marcum ait: Vno deficeris. Quasi diceret: Videris tibi multum praestitisse, & laudo tuum institutum, sed adhuc vnum tibi deest, & quidem praecipuum: Nimirum obedientia fidei, ut omnibus alijs relictis ab vno Deo pendeas per fidem in me, qui vnicus sum inter ipsum & homines Mediator. Itaque si vis perfectus esse, abi, vende quae habes, & da pauperibus, & habebis thesaurum in coelo: & veni, sequere me.
units.tr: But let us listen to Christ, who (as Mark noted) looked upon this young man kindly and loved him. Clearly, although through ignorance he was in error, he desired to advance, and he would make use of the Master himself. This must be carefully observed, lest we think a good intention is enough. For our intention is approved by God only if we desire to do what he commands. And this is why the Lord responded to this man who thought too arrogantly of himself. For in Mark he says: "One thing you lack." As if he were saying: "You seem to yourself to have done much, and I commend your purpose, but one thing is still lacking to you, and indeed the chief thing: namely, the obedience of faith, so that, having left all else, you depend on the one God through faith in me, who alone am the Mediator between him and men. Therefore, if you want to be perfect, go, sell what you have, and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me."

units.la: In quibus verbis diligenter videre oportet, quis scopus Christo propositus fuerit. Nam qui hunc non obseruant, hi praeceptum generale dari putant, in quo perfectio Christiana consistat. At non omnibus praecipi, quod huic dicitur, ex eo colligitur, quod alijs permittitur, res suas sibi seruare, vt Zachaeo, Iosepho Arimathaeo, Lazaro Bethanienfi & sororibus: multi item iubentur domum abire, & suis adesse. Quid ergo in praesenti vult Christus? Defectu suo indicare vult cofidenti adulescentulo, vt sentiat quam procul absit a perfectione. Itaque quia se hactenus legi obediuisse, & ad hanc implendam se satis instructum esse putabat, altius in eius cor penetrat, vt intelligat, Deum in lege non solum politicam obedientiam, sed totum hominem requirere, vt quantus quantus est, ad ipsius obsequium paratus sit, vt vel propter ipsum omnia relinquat, vel ipso sic iubente omnia egenis distribuat. Et hunc scopum Christo propositum fuisse, apparet ex eo, quod addidit: Et sequere me: Ita nimirum innuens, ne illud quidem profuturum ad vitam aeternam, nisi quis reliquis omnibus, quae prius eximia duxit, & seipso abnegato, se totum illi consecret. Ideo opponuntur inter se diuitiæ huius seculi & thesaurus, qui in cœlis nobis repositus est: Christus item & pauperes, quos sibi ipsi substituit, vt alibi monuimus. Et huius nos semper meminisse oportet, vt beneficentia in pauperes testemur, quanti faciamus Deum, qui illos nobis commendauit. Nam hic ille Lydius lapis est, ad quem fides vera per dilectionem agens, probari & cognosci potest.
units.tr: In these words we must carefully see what aim was proposed to Christ. For those who do not observe this think that a general precept is being given, in which Christian perfection consists. But that what is said to this man is not commanded to all is gathered from the fact that others are permitted to keep their possessions, as Zacchaeus, Joseph of Arimathea, and Lazarus of Bethany and his sisters were; many also are told to go home and attend to their own. What, then, does Christ intend in the present case? He wishes to show the self-confident young man his deficiency, so that he may perceive how far he is from perfection. Therefore, because he thought he had obeyed the law so far and was sufficiently equipped to fulfil it, Christ penetrates more deeply into his heart, so that he may understand that God in the law requires not only civil obedience but the whole man, so that, whatever he is, he be ready to obey him: to leave everything for his sake, or, at his command, to distribute everything to the needy. That this was Christ's aim is clear from what he added: "And follow me." He thus signifies that even that would not avail for eternal life unless someone, having left all those things which he had held in high esteem, and having denied himself, consecrates himself wholly to him. Hence the riches of this age and the treasure laid up for us in heaven are set against each other; so too Christ and the poor, whom he has substituted for himself, as we have pointed out elsewhere. We must always remember this, so that by our beneficence towards the poor we may show how highly we esteem God, who has commended them to us. For this is that Lydian touchstone by which true faith, working through love, may be tested and known.

units.la: Exemplo nobis sit hic iuuenis, qui audito Christi præcepto, abijt contristatus. Tristitiæ causa indicatur, quod dies esset & bona multa haberet, fide autem in Christum adhuc deflituere-tur, quæ sola leuem nobis reddit, non modo opum, verumetiam proprij sanguinis & vitæ iacturam: vt exempla sanctorum Martyrum abundè testantur. Huic autem diuitiarum iactura difficillima visa est, quia vt operum suorum meritis sidebat, quoad vitam æternam: ita spem & fiduciam omnem in diuitijs sitam habebat, quoad vitam huius seculi: ita vero pudefiunt iustitiarij, qui sibi ipsis fidunt: & simul apparet, quantum impedimentum ad vitam æternam afferant opes, nisi in Christo diuites simus per fidem: de qua re in sequenti Sermone prolixius dicetur.
units.tr: Let this young man be an example to us, who, having heard Christ's command, went away sorrowful. The cause of his sorrow is indicated: he was rich and had many goods, but he still lacked faith in Christ, which alone makes the loss not only of wealth but even of one's own blood and life seem light to us, as the examples of the holy martyrs abundantly attest. The loss of his riches seemed to him most difficult, because just as he relied on the merits of his works for eternal life, so he placed all his hope and confidence in riches for the life of this age. Thus those who trust in themselves, the self-righteous, are put to shame; and at the same time it becomes clear how great an obstacle riches are to eternal life, unless we are rich in Christ through faith. We will speak of this matter more fully in the following sermon.

units.la: Nunc autem obseruatu dignum est animi pij specimen, quod ipse præbet. Tristis quidem discedit, quod carnis & infirmitatis humanæ proprium est, quasi, vt (quod Satyricus dicebat) ploretur lachrymis amissa pecunia veris. Attamen non miserabiliter queritur de sua sorte, multo minus fremit & murmurat contra Dominum. Etenim sentit nihil iniquum abs se peti, dolet autem ipsi, quod se infirmiorem esse sentit, quàm vt officium posset facere. Itaque non vereor affirmare, quod licet nunc a Christo abierit, non tamen totum ex animo expuit, nec euanidus fuit huius amor, quo illum dilexit: sed suo tempore ipsum quoq; efficaciter vocauit Dominus. Quapropter etsi interdum dura & grauia nobis videntur, quæ nobis mandat Dei Filius IESVS CHRISTVS, tamen ipsum imitemur, & contemptis omnibus, quæ hic mundus admiratur, illum magnis passibus sequamur, qui sanguinis sui pretio thesaurum incorruptibilem nobis in cœlo parauit. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Now, however, the example of a godly mind which he displays is worth noting. He indeed departs sad, which is the nature of the flesh and human weakness, as if (as the satirist said) the lost money must be wept over with true tears. Yet he does not complain wretchedly about his lot, much less does he rage and murmur against the Lord. For he perceives that nothing unjust is demanded of him, but he grieves that he feels himself too weak to be able to perform the duty. Therefore I do not hesitate to affirm that although he has now gone away from Christ, he has not wholly spat him out of his heart, and his love by which he loved him was not extinguished; but at its proper time the Lord also effectually called him. Wherefore, although the things which the Son of God, Jesus Christ, commands us sometimes seem hard and heavy to us, let us nevertheless imitate him, and, despising all that this world admires, follow him with great strides, who by the price of his own blood prepared for us an incorruptible treasure in heaven. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCXXXII.
units.tr: Homily 232.

units.la: IESVS autem dixit discipulis suis: Amen dico vobis, diues difficile introibit in regnum cœlorum. Rursum vero dico vobis, facilius est camelum per foramen acus transfire, quàm diuitem in regnum Dei introire. His autem auditis discipuli eius perculsi sunt valde, dicentes: Quis ergo poterit saluus fieri? Intuitus autem eos IESVS dixit eis: Apud homines hoc impossibile est, apud Deum autem omnia possibilia sunt.
units.tr: Jesus said to his disciples: "Truly I say to you, a rich man will enter the kingdom of heaven with difficulty. Again I say to you, it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God." When the disciples heard this, they were greatly astonished and said: "Who then can be saved?" Jesus looked at them and said: "With men this is impossible, but with God all things are possible."

units.la: Historia diuitis adolescentis, qui Dominum IESVM CHRISTVM de ratione vitam æternam assequendi interrogauit, inter alia admonet, quantum impedimentum diuitiæ huius seculi ijs obijciant, qui ad vitam veram & cœlestem contendunt, nondum autem in fide sunt recte instituti. Idq; primum exemplo illius iuuenis adumbratur: qui etsi a pueris in Lege institutus esset, & ferio regni Dei studio teneretur, tamen cum iubetur omnia sua diuendere & nudus nudum Christum sequi, tristis & toto animo perturbatus discedit, qui paulo ante ad omne officium se alacrem & paratum præbuerat. Cæterum vt quod cum illo factum fuit, communi omnium infirmitati seruiat, hac occasione in generalem doctrinam digreditur Dominus, qua diuites primum de conditione sua periculosa admonet, deinde ijsdem consolationem adhibet, ne de salute sua desperent. Ejusdem summa loci totius: Diuites agre quidem seruari, adeoq; quoad ipsos & diuitiarum naturam, vt feruentur impossibile esse: quoad Deum vero, id factu facillimum esse, si eius voluntati se accommodent. Sed videamus singula.
units.tr: The story of the rich young man, who asked the Lord Jesus Christ how he might obtain eternal life, warns, among other things, how great a hindrance the riches of this world present to those who strive for the true and heavenly life, but who are not yet rightly instructed in the faith. This is first shown by the example of that young man. Although he had been brought up in the Law from childhood and was earnestly devoted to the pursuit of the kingdom of God, yet when he is told to sell all that he has and follow naked Christ, he goes away sad and deeply troubled, though a little earlier he had shown himself eager and ready for every duty. But so that what happened to him may serve the common weakness of all, the Lord turns from this occasion to a general teaching. First he warns the rich about their perilous condition, and then he offers them comfort, so that they do not despair of their salvation. The sum of the whole passage is this: the rich can be saved only with difficulty, indeed, as far as they themselves and the nature of riches are concerned, it is impossible for them to be saved; but as far as God is concerned, it is very easy, if they submit themselves to his will. But let us look at the details.

units.la: Christus vbi istum tristem abire videt, & procul dubio hoc mirum videretur omnibus, qui ipsum prius accurrisse, & nihil non de seipso polliceri viderant, ipse etiam astantes circumspiciens (vt Marcus annotauit) admirabundus, & non sine animi dolentis significatione ait: Quàm difficile qui opes habent, in regnum Dei introibunt. Et mox hoc ipsum graui assueratione confirmans, addit: Amen dico vobis, diues difficilè introibit in regnum coelorum. Et discipulis ad hoc dictum expauescentibus, hoc ipsum comparatione illustrans non amplificat modò, sed prorsus impossibile esse docet, inquiens: Rursum dico vobis. Quasi diceret: Nemo hoc mihi temerè excidisse putet, sed quod dixi repeto: Facilius est camelum per foramen acus transfire, quàm diuitem in regnum Dei introire. Est hoc graue dictum, & carnis iudicio intolerabile: Sed cogitandum hoc a Filio Dei dici, penes quem est omnis regni Dei potestas, qui item veritas ipsa & nostri amans est, nofq; saluos cupit: adhæc discipulis dici, quos amicorum loco habuit, & quos in præsenti apud Marcum filiolorum nomine compellauit. Nihil ergo affectui tribuit, sed ideo hoc dicit, quia verum & cognitu atq; obseruatu necessarium est. Vt autem institutioni nostræ melius omnia seruiant, duo tenere oportet.
units.tr: When Christ sees this sorrowful man going away, and this surely seemed remarkable to all who had seen him run up earlier and promise everything, he looks around at those standing by (as Mark notes) in wonder, and says, not without a sign of sorrowful feeling: "How hard it is for those who have wealth to enter the kingdom of God!" And soon after, confirming this with a solemn assurance, he adds: "Truly I say to you, a rich man will enter the kingdom of heaven with difficulty." And when the disciples are alarmed at this saying, he illustrates the point with a comparison, and not only enlarges on it but teaches that it is quite impossible, saying: "Again I say to you." As if he were saying: let no one think that I have spoken rashly, but I repeat what I have said: it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God. This is a hard saying, and intolerable to human judgement. But we must consider that it is spoken by the Son of God, in whose power is the whole kingdom of God, who is truth itself and loves us and desires our salvation. Moreover, it is spoken to the disciples, whom he regarded as his friends, and whom he here, in Mark, addresses as his little sons. He therefore gives nothing to feeling, but says this because it is true, and necessary to know and to observe. So that all things may serve our instruction better, two things must be held.

units.la: Primum, de quibus ista dicat. Etenim, vt alibi diximus, diuitiæ multæ sunt iustæ, quæ ex Dei benedictione obtingunt, & quas seruis suis ille largitur, vt de Iobo, Salomone & multis aliis legitur. Et inter Christi amicos scimus aliquos fuisse diuites, vt Zachæum, Lazarum cum sorori bus, Iosephum Arimathæum, Centuriones, vt iam nihil de illis dicam, qui Apostolorum tempore Ecclesiis totis adiumento & ornamento fuerunt, cum ditissimi essent. Sed sufficiat omnium loco exemplum Abrahami, qui etsi ditissimus fuerit, tamen pater credentium est, & in eius sinu in cælis recumbit pauper Lazarus: multi denique ab Oriente & Occidente venient, vt in regno Dei accumbant cum Abrahamo, Isaaco & Iacobo, qui omnes diuitiis in hoc seculo abundarunt. Itaq; non simpliciter de omnibus hoc dictum intelligi debet, sed de illis, de quibus Dominus ipse illud interpretatur, qui apud Marcum discipulis illo consternatis dicit: Filij quàm difficile est eos qui confidunt opibus, in regnum Dei ingredi. Non ergo opes ipsæ per se, sed fiducia opum nocet: Hæc enim idolatria est, & quia Mammona seruos facit, Deo seruire non finit. Deinde qui fiduciam in opibus habent, ij vt has consequantur, iustitiæ & charitatis leges violant, quia fere malis artibus undique corradunt, neq; aliorum penuria aut calamitatibus mouentur, imò ex eorum spoliis ditescunt, quorum egestatem ipsi suâ liberalitate debebant subleuare. Accedit fastus & luxus, qui opum abundantiam comitantur, vt pleriq; diuitis illius epulonis similes, de quo Christus apud Lucam loquitur, pauperes ac egenos inhumaniter negligunt, vel si quid his largiuntur ad ostentationem id faciunt, vt ab hominibus conspiciantur, ideoq; (vt alibi monuit Dominus) mercedem suam in hoc seculo recipiunt. Et vt acquirendo & possidendo peccatur, ita non minor peccandi occasio occurrit, si quando aliquo casu improuiso amittuntur, aut si quod illas amittendi periculum instat. Tunc enim alij creditores fallunt, & conuasatis omnibus se alio recipiunt. Multi ex his patriæ hostes fiunt, & huic turbas dant. Alij contra Deum fremunt, neque a conuitijs abstinent. Taceo nunc curas mordaces, quæ auaros excruciant, & ita cordibus insident, vt nec in mortis quidem articulo excuti possint. Fit ergo vt nihil acerbius sit memoria mortis ijs, qui opes summum bonum esse arbitrantur, aut luxui & voluptatibus huius seculi assuefuerunt, quarum materiam diuitiæ ipsis suppeditant. Quod sapiens ille obseruauit, cùm diceret: Quàm amara est ô mors tui memoria homini quieto in bonis suis, viro vacuo negotijs, felici per omnia & adhuc cibum sumere valenti. Quòd si verò mors amara est homini securo, quid de ijs dicemus, quos mens sibi male conscia vexat, & iam morituris exprobrat, quæcunq; contra æquitatis & dilectionis leges iniustè ac crudeliter designarunt. Non temerè ergo Christus ait, diuites eiusmodi ægrè in regnum coelorum ingredi. Quomodo enim per tot difficultates & obstacula eluctabuntur? quomodo per viam illam asperam & portam angustam penetrabunt cameli illi, qui seipsos tot tamque grauibus curarum sarcinis onerarunt? O si hæc omnes diligentius expenderent, qui felicitatem omnem in opum abundantia collocant, cui tam male cum regno coelorum conuenit, pauperta tem verò tantopere odérunt, quæ viam ad cælos nobis facilem & expeditam reddit ijs, qui Deo fidunt, & forte sua contenti viuunt, quem quæstum multò vberrimum esse Apostolus docet, priori ad Timotheum sexto capite.
units.tr: First, we must consider of whom he is speaking. For, as we have said elsewhere, there are many lawful riches, which come from the blessing of God, and which he bestows on his servants, as we read of Job, Solomon and many others. And among Christ's friends we know that some were rich, such as Zacchaeus, Lazarus with his sisters, Joseph of Arimathea, and the centurions. I say nothing more of those who, though very wealthy, were in the time of the apostles a help and ornament to whole churches. But the example of Abraham will suffice for all: though he was exceedingly rich, yet he is the father of believers, and in his bosom in heaven the poor Lazarus reclines. Finally, many shall come from east and west to recline in the kingdom of God with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, all of whom abounded in riches in this world. Therefore this saying must not be understood simply of all, but of those of whom the Lord himself explains it, when, to the disciples dismayed by it, he says in Mark: "Children, how hard it is for those who trust in riches to enter the kingdom of God!" It is not, then, riches in themselves that harm, but trust in riches. For this is idolatry, and because Mammon makes slaves of men, it does not allow them to serve God. Next, those who place their trust in riches, in order to obtain them, violate the laws of justice and charity, for they usually gather them on all sides by evil arts, and are not moved by the want or calamities of others, but grow rich from the spoils of those whose need they ought to relieve by their generosity. Added to this are pride and luxury, which accompany an abundance of wealth. So many, like that rich glutton of whom Christ speaks in Luke, cruelly neglect the poor and needy; or if they give anything to them, they do it for show, so as to be seen by men, and therefore (as the Lord has warned elsewhere) they receive their reward in this world. And just as sin is committed in acquiring and possessing, so no less an occasion for sin arises if at some time they are lost by an unforeseen accident, or if there is danger of losing them. For then they deceive other creditors, and, having stirred up everything, they withdraw elsewhere. Many of them become enemies of their country and cause disturbances in it. Others rage against God and do not refrain from reproaches. I say nothing now of the gnawing cares which torment the avaricious and so sit in their hearts that they cannot be shaken off even at the point of death. So it comes about that nothing is more bitter to those who think that wealth is the highest good, or who are accustomed to the luxury and pleasures of this world, for which riches supply the means, than the remembrance of death. This the wise man observed when he said: "How bitter is the remembrance of death to a man who is at rest in his possessions, free from business, prosperous in all things, and still able to take food!" But if death is bitter to a man who is secure, what shall we say of those whom a conscience ill at ease torments, and whom, now about to die, it reproaches for whatever they have unjustly and cruelly devised against the laws of equity and love? Christ did not speak rashly, then, when he said that such rich men enter the kingdom of heaven with difficulty. For how will they struggle through so many difficulties and obstacles? How will those camels, who have loaded themselves with so many and such heavy burdens of cares, pass through that rough way and narrow gate? Oh, if only all who place all happiness in abundance of wealth would weigh these things more carefully! Wealth agrees so badly with the kingdom of heaven, while they hate poverty so greatly, which makes the way to heaven easy and open for those who trust in God and live contented with what they have. The Apostle teaches that this gain is far more abundant, in the sixth chapter of his first letter to Timothy.

units.la: Alterum est, vt sui officij diligenter meminerint diuites, quod in hus fere consistit. Primum, ut ab vnius Dei benedictione pendeant, neque ipsi suis curis & laboribus opes acquirere velint. Nec enim temere cecinit diuinus Psaltes: Nisi Dominus ædificet domum, frustra laborant qui ædificant. Frustra est vobis mane sedentibus surgere, sero quiescere, & comedere panem doloris, &c. Deinde si Deo benedicente opes abundè affluant, non tamen ijs cor apponant. Est enim instabilis illarum possessio, & cum minimè putes auferuntur, vel tibi ab illis discedendum est. Adhæc non nisi præsentis vitæ vsibus seruiunt, quæ breuis est, & singulis momentis ad suum finem decurrit. Mortem verò diuitiæ (vt modò dictum est) non arcere possunt, sed accelerant potius, & eius memoriam acerbam reddunt. Miseri ergo renera sunt, qui illis fidunt. Interim non opus est, vt illas cum Cratete Thebano in mare abijcias, aut superstitione stolida deceptus omnibus temerè relictis egestatem non necessariam tibi accersas, sed quoad licet salua fide & religione, illis cum gratiarum actione vtitor, & simul charitatis fraternæ memor beneficentiæ studeto, vt thesaurum in cœlis tibi recondas nullis fortunæ casibus & iniurijs obnoxium. Qui his studeut, ij ad omnem euentum parati omnem fortunam intrepidè & constanter ferunt, nemini item molesti sunt, multos autem sua pietate adiuuant. At quia his negligentibus plerique insano & insatiabili ditescendi studio tumultuantur, sibijpsis atque aliis laborum & curarum authores sunt, & dum alij alios deglubunt atque devorant, egestatem publicam sibijpsis atque aliis omnibus accersunt, quæ tandem multis sempiterni exitij & interitus causa est.
units.tr: Second, the rich must carefully remember their duty, which consists mostly in the following. First, that they depend on the blessing of the one God alone, and do not wish to acquire riches by their own cares and labours. For the divine Psalmist did not sing in vain: "Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labour in vain. It is vain for you to rise early and sit up late, and to eat the bread of sorrow," and so on. Next, if riches flow in abundantly with God's blessing, they should nevertheless not set their hearts on them. For the possession of them is unstable, and when you least expect it they are taken away, or you must leave them. Moreover, they serve only the uses of the present life, which is brief and runs to its end at every moment. Riches cannot, as has just been said, keep off death, but rather hasten it and make its remembrance bitter. Those who trust in them are therefore truly wretched. Meanwhile there is no need to cast them into the sea, as Crates of Thebes did, or, deceived by foolish superstition, to abandon everything rashly and bring upon yourself unnecessary poverty. Rather, so far as is permitted with faith and piety preserved, use them with thanksgiving, and at the same time, mindful of brotherly love, be zealous in beneficence, so that you may store up for yourself a treasure in heaven, exposed to no chances of fortune and no injuries. Those who are devoted to these things, prepared for every event, bear every fortune fearlessly and steadfastly, are troublesome to no one, and assist many by their piety. But because most people, neglecting these things, are stirred up by a mad and insatiable desire to grow rich, they become the authors of labours and cares for themselves and others; and while they strip and devour one another, they bring upon themselves and all others a public poverty, which in the end is for many the cause of eternal destruction and death.

units.la: Hæc certè in mentem venerunt discipulis, qui ideo perculsi dixerunt. Quis ergo poterit seruari? Haud tenus quidem regni Dei mysterium non tam arduum esse putarunt: Nunc autem vbi voluntariam omnium facultatum amissionem & animos ab omni cupiditate alienos requiri audiunt, timent & turbantur. Etsi enim quæ de diuitibus dicta erant, nihil ad ipsos pertinere videri poterant, pauperculi erant, & iam pridem reliquis suis scaphis & retijs Christum secuti fuerant, sentiebant tamen inhærentes cordibus suis ambitionis & æmulationis affectus, qui hucusque contentionum & rixarum de primatu & regno huius seculi causam dederant. Deinde doluit eis procul dubio, quòd viderent plerosque homines diuitijs, luxui & cupiditatibus huius seculi ita deditos atque addictos esse, vt cœlestia secure negligant, vt de salute æterna periclitentur. Vt ergo ipsi vitæ æternæ & regni Dei studio atque desiderio flagrarunt, ita alios quoque bominess illius participes fieri voluerunt, multum dissimiles eorum, qui suam egestatem impatienter ferunt, & e contra alijs meliorem fortem inuid…
units.tr: Certainly these thoughts had come into the minds of the disciples, which is why they were struck with dismay and said: "Who then can be saved?" Up to then they had not thought the mystery of the kingdom of God so very difficult. But now, when they hear that a voluntary surrender of all possessions and minds free from every desire are required, they are afraid and troubled. For although what had been said about the rich seemed to have nothing to do with them, since they were poor and had long since followed Christ, leaving behind their boats and nets, they nonetheless felt ambition and rivalry lodged in their hearts, the very feelings which until then had given cause for quarrels and disputes about primacy and rule in this age. Next, no doubt, it grieved them that they saw most people so devoted and addicted to riches, luxury and the desires of this age that they carelessly neglect heavenly things and are endangered in their eternal salvation. So just as they themselves burned with zeal and longing for eternal life and the kingdom of God, so they wished others also to become sharers in it, quite unlike those who bear their own poverty impatiently and, on the contrary, envy others a better lot...

units.la: Solus Dei Filius IESVS CHRISTVS suæ egestatis merito nobis regni cœlorum thesauros acquisiuit, qui ijs solis debentur, qui pauperes sunt spiritu, & de seipsis desperantes illi vnì fidunt.
units.tr: Only the Son of God, IESVS CHRISTVS, by the merit of his own poverty, has won for us the treasures of the kingdom of heaven, which are owed only to those who are poor in spirit and, despairing of themselves, trust in him alone.

units.la: Vide 1. Tim.5.
units.tr: See 1. Tim.5.

units.la: Porrò Christum audiamus, qui hanc actionem dulci consolatione concludit, dicens: Apud homines hoc impossibile est, apud Deum autem omnia possibilia sunt. ex verbi sui semine regenerare & novas creaturas facere potest, coelestium item bonorum desiderio accendere, ut spontè & cum gaudio renuntiemus omnibus, quae in hoc mundo carni magnifica videntur. Exempla sanctorum hominum, qui illud olim fecerunt, multa in Scripturis & historia Ecclesiastica occurrunt, & hodie non pauca videmus inter illos, quos persecutio premit, ut domi fidem non possint profiteri, neque salutis rebus suis alibi abire. Cum ergo hodie etiam Spiritus sancti gratia in multis efficaciter agat, nemo temere de alicuius salute desperet. Potest Deus fulcire infirmos, & eos etiam qui lapsi sunt, erigere. Agnoscant autem singuli suam infirmitatem, ne quid arrogantius de seipsis sentiant, sed in Dei gratiam respiciant per fidem in IESVM CHRISTVM, cuius spiritu confirmati omnia poterunt. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Furthermore, let us hear Christ, who concludes this matter with sweet consolation, saying: "With men this is impossible, but with God all things are possible." He can regenerate by the seed of his word and make new creatures, and likewise kindle the desire for heavenly goods, so that we renounce willingly and with joy all those things in this world that seem splendid to the flesh. Examples of holy men who once did this occur in abundance in the Scriptures and in ecclesiastical history, and today we see not a few among those whom persecution presses so hard that they cannot profess the faith at home, nor leave their goods behind and go elsewhere for safety. Since, therefore, the grace of the Holy Spirit still works effectively in many today, no one should rashly despair of anyone's salvation. God can support the weak and raise up even those who have fallen. Let each one, however, acknowledge his own infirmity, lest he think anything too proud of himself, but look to the grace of God through faith in IESVS CHRISTVS, by whose Spirit strengthened we shall be able to do all things. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCXXXIII.
units.tr: HOMILY CCXXXIII.

units.la: Tunc respondens Petrus dixit ei: Ecce nos reliquimus omnia, & secuti sumus te: Quid ergo erit nobis? IESVS autem dixit eis: Amen dico vobis, vos qui secuti estis me in regeneratione, cum sederit Filius hominis in throno gloriae suae, sedebitis etiam vos super thronos duodecim, iudicantes duodecim tribus Israelis.
units.tr: Then Peter answered him: "Behold, we have left everything and followed you. What then shall we have?" And Jesus said to them: "Truly I say to you, you who have followed me in the regeneration, when the Son of Man shall sit on the throne of his glory, you also shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel."

units.la: Dominus & Seruator noster IESVS CHRISTVS, qui idem nobis doctor a Patre datus est, non absque causa sapius inter discipulos de diuitiis huius seculi & periculoso diuitum statu disserit. Quia enim plerique in illarum abundantia omnem felicitatem consistere putant, plurimum in illis peccatur, & fere fit, ut qui zelum regni Dei habent, & in omni vita integritatem student, graviter offendant, si quando propter Christum & Euangelium eius opes suas relinquere aut aliquam iacturam facere debeant. Exemplum eius rei memorabile vidimus in opulento iuvene, qui etsi regnum Dei serio quaereret, & a pueris legem Dei sedulo observasset, ut de externa obedientia gloriari posset, tamen quando iubetur omnibus diuenditis & in pauperes distributis, Christum sequi, toto animo consternatus discessit. Quia vero vitium hoc omnibus commune est, quoad non regeneramur, Dominus adversus illud nos amplissimis promissionibus instruit, quarum summa est, nihil eorum nobis perire, quae propter ipsum amittimus, sed retributionem amplissimam nos accepturos esse tam in praesenti quam futuro seculo.
units.tr: Our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, who was given to us as teacher by the Father, not without reason often speaks among the disciples about the riches of this age and the dangerous condition of the rich. For since most people think that all happiness consists in their abundance, very much sin is committed in this regard, and it often happens that those who have zeal for the kingdom of God and strive for integrity in all of life are gravely offended if at any time, for the sake of Christ and his Gospel, they must give up their wealth or suffer some loss. We saw a memorable example of this in the wealthy young man who, although he earnestly sought the kingdom of God and had diligently kept the law of God from boyhood, so that he could boast of his outward obedience, nevertheless, when he was told to sell everything, distribute it to the poor, and follow Christ, he departed dismayed in his whole soul. But since this fault is common to all, as long as we are not regenerated, the Lord arms us against it with the most ample promises, the sum of which is that nothing we lose for his sake will perish, but that we shall receive a most abundant reward both in the present age and in the age to come.

units.la: Occasionem huic actioni praebuit Petrus, qui eorum, quae cum iuvene acta erant, consideratione excitatus, quaestionem novam ad discipulos omnes pertinentem movet, dicens: Ecce, nos reliquimus omnia, & secuti sumus te: Quid ergo erit nobis? Quaestionis huius causa proculdubio fuit periculosa de regno terreno Christi, quod illos sperauisse, saepe diximus. Cum ergo in illo non opes modo, sed regnum quoque sibi hucusque polliciti essent, non potuerunt non perturbari ijs, quae de periculosa diuitum conditione dixerat, eo quod huius spem omnem ipsis negare videretur. Ideo omnium nomine quaerit Petrus. Quasi diceret: Enimuero quia te vnum Dei & olim promissum Seruatorem & Regem esse credimus, vocationem tuam secuti sumus, reliquis rebus nostris omnibus, spe bona pleni, nos remunerationem accepturos, quae omnem iacturam nobis abunde farciat. At si ea est diuitum conditio, scire cupimus, quid nobis porro sperandum sit, &c.
units.tr: Peter provided the occasion for this discussion. Stirred by consideration of what had happened with the young man, he raises a new question concerning all the disciples, saying: "Behold, we have left everything and followed you. What then shall we have?" Without doubt the cause of this question was the perilous notion of Christ's earthly kingdom, which, as we have often said, they had hoped for. Since they had been promised not only riches but also a kingdom, they could not help being disturbed by what he had said about the perilous condition of the rich, since that seemed to deny them all hope of it. So Peter asks on behalf of all. As if he were saying: "Indeed, since we believe that you alone are the God-promised Saviour and King, we have followed your calling, having left all our other possessions, full of good hope that we shall receive a reward which will abundantly make up for every loss. But if that is the condition of the rich, we wish to know what we may further hope for," etc.

units.la: Elucet in hac quaestione humani ingenij vitiositas, quae in sanctissimis Dei seruis locum habet. Elegit ipsos Dei Filius ex toto humano genere, & amicorum loco habuit atque instituit, ut sal terrae & lux mundi essent: ijdem ipsum alacriter secuti sunt, & multis alijs deficientibus hucusque constantes perseuerauerunt. Attamen non pauca hic concurrunt, quae docent, multa adhuc ipsis de fuisse. Nam primum, ut diximus modo, adhuc titillantur spe regni, quae superbia spiritu ipsos inflauit, quem paulo ante Dominus seueriter corripuit. Deinde satis ambitiose iactat, quid propter Christum fecerint. Ecce, reliquimus omnia, & secuti sumus te. Quasi diceret: Quod iuuenis iste facere dedignatur, id nos iam praestitimus. Quae vero fuerunt omnia illa, de quibus reliquis gloriantur? Domus piscatoria, vel casae potius, scapha aliquot, remi, conti, retia, hami, ipsa deniq; paupertas,& durus manuum labor,quo duriter & parce vexitarunt. Interim in Filij Dei comitatu nihil ipsis defuit,sicuti in vltima cœna postea confessi sunt,& viderunt atq; audiuerunt, quae multi sancti & Prophetae videre & audire olim gestierunt. Adhac conscientias habebant liberas a traditionibus Scribarum & Pharisaeorum,qui intolerabiles sarcinas folebant miseris & incautis imponere. Ergo iam nunc plus receperant quam reliquerunt:sed apparet,non satis digne aestimauisse eximia illa Christi beneficia,quae omnes mundi opes & dignitates superant. Quod vitium hodie nimis vulgare est,vt multi Deum adhuc sibi debitorem faciant in hoc seculo,etiamsi ille liberaliter omnia suppeditet,quae ad vitae sustentationem faciunt,& insuper plus quam aurea animarum libertate fruantur. Addunt hic tertium vitium,quod de premio quaerunt priusquam ad metam peruenerunt adeoq; cum nondum scirent,num ad illam vnquam essent peruenturi. Quod ipsum hodie etiam a multis fit,vt mercedem sibi reddi velint, quando de fide & perseuerantia in suo officio potius cogitare debebant. Quid vero de illis dicemus,qui priusquam Christo nomen dederunt,aut aliquid fecerunt laude dignum,omnia Dei verba & praecepta ad suae rationis calculum reuocant, neq; sibi aliquid faciendum putant,nisi de eventu & premio prius certiores sint facti. Discamus ergo suspeetum habere carnis ingenium,& Deo simpliciter credamus.
units.tr: In this question the fault of human nature shows itself, which has a place even in the most holy servants of God. The Son of God chose them out of the whole human race, held them and appointed them as friends, so that they might be the salt of the earth and the light of the world. They followed him eagerly, and when many others fell away, they have remained steadfast until now. Yet several things here show that much of them is still lacking. First, as we have just said, they are still tickled by hope of the kingdom, a pride which has puffed up their spirit, which the Lord had recently rebuked sharply. Then they boast rather ambitiously of what they have done for Christ: "Behold, we have left everything and followed you." As if he were saying: "What this young man refuses to do, we have already done." But what were all those things about which they boast? A fishing house, or rather huts, a few boats, oars, poles, nets, hooks, and finally poverty and the hard labour of their hands, with which they toiled hard and sparingly. Meanwhile, in the company of the Son of God they lacked nothing, as they afterwards confessed at the last supper, and they saw and heard what many saints and prophets had long desired to see and hear. Moreover, they had consciences free from the traditions of the Scribes and Pharisees, who used to lay intolerable burdens on the wretched and unwary. So they had already received more than they had left behind; but it is clear that they had not sufficiently valued those outstanding benefits of Christ, which surpass all the riches and dignities of the world. This fault is today far too common, so that many make God still in their debt in this age, even though he gives generously all that serves the sustaining of life, and besides this they enjoy a freedom of soul that is more than golden. Here they add a third fault: they seek the reward before they have reached the goal, and indeed while they do not yet know whether they will ever reach it. Today too many do this too, wanting their wages paid to them, when they ought rather to think about faith and perseverance in their duty. But what shall we say of those who, before they have given their name to Christ or done anything worthy of praise, bring all the words and commands of God back to the reckoning of their own reason, and think they must do nothing unless they have first been informed of the outcome and the reward? Let us therefore learn to be suspicious of the nature of the flesh, and simply to believe God.

units.la: Sed Christum nunc audiamus,qui etsi correptionem mererentur discipuli,amice tamen illis respondet. Quia enim non abfq; causa turbatos videbat,infirmitatis ipsorum rationem habet,& promissionibus amplissimus eos erigit. Debet hoc consolari eos,qui suae vitiositatis sibi ipsis conscii mentur,ne ipsos Deus fastidiat. Potest enim nobis compati,qui natura est pater indulgentissimus, & Filius Dei homo verus factus est,vt fidelis pontifex esset, & nostras infirmitates non modo agnosceret,verumetiam eis mederetur. Quod nos ita consolari debet,vt exemplo quoq; seruiant, quod imitemur,& eadem lenitate vtamur in fratres,qui aliquid praeter officium dicunt aut faciunt. Quoad vero responsionem Christi,constat ea duabus promissionibus, quarum prior ad Apostolos proprie pertinet,altera vniuersalis est,& ad omnes vere credentes extenditur. His postremo admonitionem subiicit,qua & ipsa omnes monet,ne efferantur,si bene ceperunt,sed in eo perganterint,& in finem vsq; perseuerent.
units.tr: But let us now hear Christ, who, although the disciples deserved correction, answers them kindly. For since he saw that they were troubled not without cause, he takes account of their weakness and raises them up with most ample promises. This ought to console those who, being conscious of their own faults, fear that God may despise them. For he who is by nature a most indulgent Father can have compassion on us, and the Son of God was made true man so that he might be a faithful high priest, and not only know our infirmities but also heal them. This should console us in such a way that it also serves us as an example to imitate, and that we use the same gentleness toward brethren who say or do anything beyond their duty. As for Christ's answer, it consists of two promises, of which the first properly pertains to the Apostles, the second is universal and extends to all who truly believe. Finally he adds a warning to these, which also admonishes all not to become puffed up if they have made a good beginning, but to persevere in it and continue to the end.

units.la: Apostolis cum grauiisimi eueneratione ait: Amen dico vobis,vos qui secuti estis me,in regeneratione,cum sederit Filius hominis in throno gloriae suae,sedebitis etiam vos super thronos duodecim, iudicantes duodecim tribus Israelis. Regenerationis meminit,quae particula bifariam exponitur,vt vel ad praecedentia vel sequentia referatur. Si ad praecedentia referas,de primo suo in carnem aduentu loquitur,cuius hic finis fuit,vt homines ex peccati seruitute & Satanae tyrannide redempti,& ex perditis Adami filijs in filios Dei regenerati vitam nouam viuant, quam olim aeternam & caelestis sequatur. Quod si ad sequentia referas,de nouissimo suo aduentu hoc dicit,in quo mortui resurgent,qui aut tunc vivi & superstites erunt, in momento immutabuntur. Et dicitur hic dies regenerationis,vel(vt Petrus postea locutus est) restitutionis omnium, eo quod resurrectio ipsa regenerationis erit, in qua corpora nostra corruptibilia & mortalia incorruptibilitatem & immortalitatem induent,vt conformia fiant glorioso Christi corpori, & simul tota creatura, quae nunc vanitati & corruptibilitati subiecta ingemiscit,liberabitur, & terra noua & caeli noui fient,adeoq; omnia in melius restituentur. Non absurde autem fecerit meo iudicio,si vtrumque sensum comungas,& tunc ita dixit Dominus: Nolo vos de premio folicitos esse,quaesi opera & impensa vobis perierit,si in hoc seculo fortunas omnes mea causa relinquere oporteat. Quia enim me,qui regenerationis author et doctor sum,secuti estis,et ex verbi mei semine in alios homines renati,relictis prioribus iudicijs,vos mihi consecrauistis, ego quanti vos faciam, olim in magno illo die vniuersalis regenerationis & restitutionis omnium toti mundo patefaciam. Cum enim ego,qui nunc non alius quam Filius hominis,imo abiectissimus hominum esse videor,in nubibus caeli venero cum sanctis Angelis meis, & confedero in gloria Patris ad iudicandum vivos & mortuos,tunc vos quoq; sedebitis super duodecim thronos & iudicabitis duodecim tribus Israelis. Conuenit hoc cum eo,quod in vltima cœna discipulis dixit: Ego pacisco vobis, prouti pactus est mihi Pater regnum, vt edatis & bibatis super mensam meam in regno meo, & sedeatis super thronos,iudicantes duodecim tribus Israelis. Regnum pollicetur, caelestem nimirum & aeternum.
units.tr: To the Apostles he says, with the most serious solemnity: "Truly I say to you, you who have followed me in the regeneration, when the Son of Man shall sit on the throne of his glory, you also shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel." He mentions the regeneration, a phrase which can be explained in two ways, so that it may refer either to what precedes or to what follows. If you refer it to what precedes, he speaks of his first coming in the flesh, the purpose of which was that men, redeemed from the bondage of sin and the tyranny of Satan, and regenerated from the lost sons of Adam into sons of God, might live a new life, which would afterwards be followed by eternal and heavenly life. But if you refer it to what follows, he is speaking of his last coming, in which the dead will rise, and those who are then alive and remaining will be changed in a moment. And this day is called the day of regeneration, or (as Peter later spoke) the restoration of all things, because the resurrection itself will be the regeneration, in which our corruptible and mortal bodies will put on incorruptibility and immortality, so that they may be made like the glorious body of Christ; and at the same time the whole creation, which now groans subject to vanity and corruptibility, will be set free, and there will be a new earth and new heavens, and so all things will be restored to something better. In my judgment it would not be absurd to combine both senses, and then the Lord spoke thus: "I do not want you to be anxious about reward, as if your labour and expense were lost, if you must leave all your fortunes in this age for my cause. For since you have followed me, who am the author and teacher of regeneration, and since, born again from the seed of my word into other men, you have, leaving behind your former judgments, consecrated yourselves to me, I will show the whole world someday on that great day of universal regeneration and restoration of all things how much I value you. For when I, who now seem to be nothing but the Son of Man, and indeed the most abject of men, come on the clouds of heaven with my holy angels, and sit in the glory of the Father to judge the living and the dead, then you too shall sit upon twelve thrones and judge the twelve tribes of Israel." This agrees with what he said to the disciples at the last supper: "I make a covenant with you, just as the Father has covenanted the kingdom to me, that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom, and sit upon thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel." He promises a kingdom, namely a heavenly and eternal one.

units.la: Luc.22. & aeternum, nullis huius mundi casibus obnoxium, in cuius consortium Apostolorum animæ, ut & aliorum credentium, receptæ sunt, ut primum ex corporis ergastulo emigrarunt, & iam nunc ad mensam Christi in cælis edunt, & bibunt, id est, ea fruuntur gloria & beatitate, in quam ille aspectu: cuius ipse Paulus confirmatus cupiebat hinc soluere, ut cum Christo esset. Deinde huius gloriæ manifestationem publicam promittit, quæ in nouissimo suo aduentu fiet, & hanc quoque humano more describit, ut res fit illustrior & melius intelligatur. Etenim Reges & Monarchæ res magnas acturi, in throno sublimi considerent, & affinitores habent principes cognatos aut consanguineos, proceres item regni & consiliarios, quorum fideli opera aliquando usi sunt. Sensus ergo est, quod ipsos similiter suæ gloriæ socios habere velit, qui in terris hi fuerunt ipsius amici & regni sui administri fuerint. Adhæc igitur verba respexisse videtur Paulus ad Colos. scribens: Quando Christus, vita illa nostra, patefactus fuerit, tum & vos cum eo declarabimini gloriosi. Et dilectus ille discipulus: Carissimi, nunc filii Dei sumus, sed nondum apparuit, quod erimus: scimus autem, quod cum ipse patefactus fuerit, similes ei erimus, &c. 1. Ioan. 3.
units.tr: and eternal, subject to none of the chances of this world. The souls of the apostles, and of other believers as well, have been received into this fellowship. As soon as they have departed from the prison-house of the body, they now eat and drink at Christ's table in heaven; that is, they enjoy that glory and blessedness which Paul, strengthened in faith, longed to attain when he desired to depart hence and be with Christ. Then he promises a public manifestation of this glory, which will take place at his last coming, and he describes this too in human fashion, so that the matter may be made clearer and better understood. For kings and monarchs, about to undertake great affairs, sit on a lofty throne; and princes have kinsmen and blood relations as their in-laws, as well as nobles and councillors of the realm, whose faithful service they have at times used. The sense, therefore, is that he likewise wishes to have as sharers in his glory those who were his friends on earth and the ministers of his kingdom. Paul seems to have had these words in mind when he wrote to the Colossians: "When Christ, who is our life, shall be revealed, then you also will be revealed with him in glory." And that beloved disciple: "Beloved, now we are the children of God, but it has not yet appeared what we shall be; we know, however, that when he shall be revealed we shall be like him, etc." 1 John 3.

units.la: Est autem diligentius considerandum, quo sensu Apostoli super thronos duodecim sedebunt & tribus Israeliticas iudicaturi sint. Nam si proprie loqui velimus, Pater omne iudicium dedit Filio, qui suam gloriam dat nemini. Dicuntur autem iudicare Apostoli trifariam: Primum quoad doctrinam & verbi prædicationem: quia secundum hanc sententiam illa nouissima pronuntiabitur, quæ omnes condemnabit, qui Euangelio non crediderunt. Docebit hoc Christus postea, quando appropinquante mortis hora dicet: Qui reijcit me, nec recipit verba mea, habet qui iudicet ipsum: sermo quem locutus sum, ille iudicabit eum in ultimo illo die. Quia ergo hunc prædicarunt Apostoli, rectè dicuntur iudicaturi non modo Israeliticas tribus, verumetiam omnes gentes, ad quas ipsorum doctrina diuulgata est. Deinde testimonio suo iudicabunt, imò etiam damnabunt Iudæorum gentem, cui omnem excusationis prætextum eripient. Solet hic fieri ex ignorantia peti, id, in primis in religionis & æternæ salutis causa. Et in nouissimo die multos neglecta pietatis officia perigno rantiam excusaturos esse, ipse Dominus testatur, quando ipsi ita responsaturos ait: Domine, quando te vidimus esurientem aut sitientem, aut hospitem, aut nudum, aut inualidum, aut in custodia, & non ministrauimus tibi? At conuincentur illi omnes conspectu Apostolorum, quando propria conscientia horum doctrinam ipsis in mentem reuocabit cum omnibus iis, quæ illi inter eos dixerunt & fecerunt. Ad huius confirmationem facit, quod Christus alibi ait, Euangelium in testimonium prædicari iis, qui non credunt: quod item Apostolos iubet puluerem ex vestibus & pedibus excutere, & hunc testimonij locofore ait, quod regnum Dei illis appropinquauerit. Præterea exemplo suo iudicabunt Apostoli Iudæos. Nec enim poterit quis illorum de Euangelij obscuritate aut difficultate conqueri, quando in totius mundi conspectu aderunt Apostoli, qui cum rudes & illiterati fuerint, illud tamen intellexerunt & ex eo renati ac filij Dei facti sunt. Erit ergo hæc magna Apostolorum dignitas, quod qui cum viuerent, omnibus ludibrio & contemptui fuerunt, sua doctrina & exemplo omnes iudicabunt, qui ipsos contempserunt. In præsenti autem duodecim tribus Israelis nominantur, quia ex his electi fuerunt Apostoli, & ad illas primum missi: & quidem duodecim numero, ut vel inde constaret, Christum esse promissum illum Seruatorem, qui filios Dei dispersos congregare debebat. At quod de Apostolis dicitur, idem de omnibus Euangelij ministris dici poterit, qui officio suo fideliter fungentur. Nam & hi sua diligentia damnabunt omnes incredulos & pœnitere nescios, ipsi vero (ut Daniel prædicit) splendebunt ut splendor firmamenti, & ut stellæ sempiternis temporibus.
