units.tr: It must be considered more carefully in what sense the apostles will sit on twelve thrones and judge the tribes of Israel. For if we wish to speak strictly, the Father has given all judgment to the Son, who gives his glory to no one. The apostles are said to judge in three ways. First, as to doctrine and the preaching of the Word: for according to this teaching that final sentence will be pronounced, which will condemn all who have not believed the Gospel. Christ himself will teach this afterwards, when, as the hour of death approaches, he says: "He who rejects me and does not receive my words has one who judges him; the word which I have spoken will judge him on the last day." Since the apostles preached this, they are rightly said to judge not only the tribes of Israel but also all the nations to which their teaching has been spread. Second, by their testimony they will judge, indeed even condemn, the Jewish nation, depriving them of every pretext of excuse. Here it is usually asked whether ignorance can be pleaded, especially in matters of religion and eternal salvation. The Lord himself testifies that on the last day many will plead ignorance for their neglect of the duties of piety, when he says that they will answer him thus: "Lord, when did we see you hungry or thirsty, or a stranger, or naked, or sick, or in prison, and did not minister to you?" But all of them will be convicted in the sight of the apostles, when their own conscience brings to mind the apostles' teaching, together with all that those men said and did among them. In support of this, Christ says elsewhere that the Gospel is preached to those who do not believe as a testimony against them; likewise he bids the apostles shake the dust from their clothes and feet, and he says that this will be a testimony to them, because the kingdom of God has drawn near to them. Third, the apostles will judge the Jews by their example. For none of them will be able to complain of the obscurity or difficulty of the Gospel, when the apostles, who were rude and unlettered, stand in view of the whole world, and yet understood it, and through it were born again and became sons of God. This will therefore be the great dignity of the apostles: that those who, while they lived, were a laughingstock and an object of contempt to all, will judge by their doctrine and example all who despised them. Now, they are named the twelve tribes of Israel because the apostles were chosen from these and first sent to them; and indeed they were twelve in number, so that this itself might show that Christ was the promised Saviour who was to gather the scattered children of God. But what is said of the apostles can be said of all ministers of the Gospel who faithfully discharge their office. For these too, by their diligence, will condemn all unbelievers who refuse repentance; and they themselves (as Daniel foretold) will shine like the brightness of the firmament, and like the stars for ever and ever.

units.la: Hæc ut Apostolorum doctrinam commendant, & ipsos a contemptu vindicant: ita in genere omnes homines admonent, nullam excusationem in nouissimo die fore impiis et contumacibus. Vt enim, Verbum Dei omnibus prædicatur, ita ex eo omnes iudicabuntur: et simul habent tunc omnis loci & ordinis homines exempla, quæ ipsis condemnandis sufficient. Iudæos iudicabunt non modo Apostoli, qui ex ipsis oriundi fuerunt, verumetiam Regina Sabæ, Niniuitæ & quotquot alij Euangelio crediderunt, & a peccatis conuersi sunt. Pharisæos iudicabunt Nicodemus & Paulus: Veri pracones infidos & improbos, non modo Prophetæ & Apostoli damnabunt, verumetiam ex pleh multi, qui zelo Dei yruntur, & religiosius quam illi viuus. Diuites Abrahamus, Iobus & simi-
units.tr: These things commend the teaching of the apostles and vindicate them from contempt; and in the same way they warn all men in general that there will be no excuse on the last day for the impious and the obstinate. For just as the Word of God is preached to all, so by it all will be judged; and at the same time, men of every place and rank will then have examples that will suffice for their condemnation. The Jews will be judged not only by the apostles, who sprang from their own stock, but also by the Queen of Sheba, the Ninevites, and all the others who believed the Gospel and turned from their sins. The Pharisees will be judged by Nicodemus and Paul, true heralds of the Word; the unfaithful and wicked will be condemned not only by the prophets and apostles, but also by many from among the Gentiles, who are zealous for God and live more devoutly than they did. The rich will be judged by Abraham, Job and their like; kings and princes by David, Hezekiah, Josiah; the poor who murmur and are shameless by Lazarus; and so it will be with the rest.

units.la: Col 3. les: Reges & principes Dauid, Ezechias, Iosias: pauperes murmurantes & impudentes Lazarus: & ita de reliquis fiet. Discant ergo omnes magni facere Euangelij doctrinam, & diligenter obser uare exempla eorum, qui olim crediderunt, neque sibi ipsis delitias faciant in sua contumacia. Vna fides in IESVM CHRISTVM seruabit, qui vt iudex seuerus veniet impijs sui Verbi contemptoribus: ita suorum fidus aduocatus & testis erit, atque eosdem ad se recipiet in regnisui caelestis consortium. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Col 3. Let all therefore learn to hold the teaching of the Gospel in high regard, and carefully observe the examples of those who believed in former times, and let them not indulge themselves in their obstinacy. Faith in Jesus Christ alone will save; he who will come as a stern judge to those who despise his Word, so he will be a faithful advocate and witness to his own, and will receive them into the fellowship of his heavenly kingdom. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCXXXIIII.
units.tr: HOMILIA CCXXXIIII.

units.la: Et quisquis reliquerit domos, aut fratres, aut sorores, aut patrem aut matrem, aut uxorem, aut liberos, aut agros, causa nominis mei, centuplicia accipiet, & vitam aeternam haereditatis iure possidebit. Multi autem primi, erunt vltimi: & vltimi primi.
units.tr: And everyone who has left houses, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or fields, for my name's sake, shall receive a hundredfold and shall possess eternal life as an inheritance. But many who are first will be last, and the last first.

units.la: Dicuus Paulus in priori ad Timotheum graviter & vere pronuntiat: Pietas ad omnia vtilis est, vt quae promissionem habeat vitae praesentis ac futurae. Nam licet Deus electis suis, qui ipsi ex fide vera seruiunt praecipue caelestium bonorum & vitae aeternae praemia praeparauerit, simul tamen infirmitatis nostrae rationem habet, & quia huius saeculi vita afflictionum plena est, atque eos qui in Christo volunt pie viuere, persecutionem perpeti oportet, quoad illum quoque solatia nobis praebet, quibus ad ferendam crucem confirmemur. Fit hoc etiam in praesenti tractatione. Interrogauit Petrus omnium discipulorum nomine, quid praemij sperare debeant ipsi, qui relictis omnibus facultatibus suis ipsum secuti sint? Respondet ad hanc quaestionem Dominus, & quia illi orbis totius doctores & ideo alijs perfectiores esse debebant, interim vero terreni regni spe falsa seipsos lactabant, prima responsionis parte illos a terrenis ad caelestia remittit, & regni sui beati consortium pollicetur, quod item in nouissimo die coram totius mundi conspectu gloriosi futuri sint, quam do ipsos adfuturos habere velit, vt Iudaeos contumaces suo exemplo & testimonio iudicent & condemnent.
units.tr: The apostle Paul in his first letter to Timothy says it seriously and truly: "Godliness is profitable for all things, since it has the promise of the life that now is and of that which is to come." For although God has prepared the rewards of heavenly goods and eternal life especially for his elect, who truly serve him from genuine faith, he nevertheless takes account of our weakness. Since the life of this age is full of afflictions, and those who want to live godly lives in Christ must suffer persecution, he also offers us consolations by which we may be strengthened to bear the cross. This is also the case in the present passage. Peter, speaking for all the disciples, asked what reward they ought to expect, who had left all their possessions to follow him. The Lord answers this question. Since those men were to be teachers of the whole world and therefore ought to be more mature than others, yet in the meantime were deluding themselves with a false hope of an earthly kingdom, he first turns them from earthly things to heavenly ones in the first part of his answer, and promises them a share in his blessed kingdom. He also says that they will be glorious in the last day, before the eyes of the whole world, and that he wishes them to be present there, so that by their example and testimony they may judge and condemn the obstinate Jews.

units.la: Sequitur altera responsionis pars, quae latius extenditur: Quia enim non soli Apostoli suis relictis Christum secuti sunt, sed hoc ipsum ab omnibus exigitur, qui illi nomen dederunt, ac in ipso seruari volunt, vniuersali promissione hos omnes confirmat, dicens: Quisquis reliquerit domos aut fratres aut sorores, aut patrem aut matrem, aut uxorem aut liberos, aut agros causa nominis mei, centuplicia accipiet (nimirum in hoc saeculo, vt Marcus & Lucas annotauerunt) & in futuro vitam aeternam haereditatis iure possidebit. Sensus huius promissionis est, eos qui sua propter Christum amiserint, adeo nullam iacturam facturos esse, vt potius quoad huius saeculi vitam, feliciores futuri sint ijs, qui sua seruarunt: & olim regni caelestis haereditatem accessuros. At quia hic non pauca occurrunt, ad quae carnis ratio offendere potest, necesse est singula paulo diligentius expendere: Et primo quidem, ad quos promissio ista pertineat: Deinde quid facere conueniat eos, qui ea frui volunt: Tertio quae retributio nobis speranda sit, & qua conditione haec Dominus polliceatur.
units.tr: There follows the second part of the answer, which is extended more fully. For not only the apostles left their households and followed Christ, but this is required of all who have given their name to him and wish to be kept in him. With a universal promise he encourages all of them, saying: "Whoever has left houses, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or fields, for my name's sake, shall receive a hundredfold" (namely in this age, as Mark and Luke noted), "and in the future world shall possess eternal life as an inheritance." The sense of this promise is that those who lose their goods for Christ's sake will suffer no loss at all; indeed they will be happier than those who kept their possessions, as far as the life of this age is concerned, and in time they will attain the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom. But since many matters arise here to which human reason can take offence, it is necessary to weigh each point rather carefully. First, to whom this promise pertains; second, what those who wish to enjoy it ought to do; third, what reward we may hope for, and on what condition the Lord promises these things.

units.la: Quoad primum, in praesenti de illis loquitur, qui causa sui nominis relinquunt, domos, agros, fratres, sorores, &c. Apud Marcum autem ait: Propter me & Euangelium. In Luca vero: Causa regni Dei. At in idem haec omnia recidunt, eo quod per Euangelium Christus praedicatur, qui regnum Dei in nobis instaurat, & huius haeredes facit omnes, qui constanti fide ipsum amplexantur. Itaque ad eos pertinet haec promissio, qui vt regnum Dei assequi & seruari possint, Christo ita adhaerent, vt hunc omnibus quae in hoc saeculo habent, praeferant, adeo vt ipso vocante, abiqu omni mora aut tergiuersatione ipsum quo vocat sequantur, & si opus sit, vitam quoque amittere malint, quam ab illo diuelli. Talis olim fuit Abrahamus, qui gestiuit videre diem Domini, & per fidem eo cognito & apprehenso ita exultauit, vt illo vocante e domo paterna discesserit, & sponte nuas exul sit factus: iussus item filium Isaacum immolare, obsequentem sese praebuerit. Idem fecerunt Apostoli, qui suas naviculas, retia, domus, telonia mox reliquerunt, vt primum ab illo vocati sunt.
units.tr: As to the first point: in the present passage he speaks of those who, for the sake of his name, leave houses, fields, brothers, sisters, and so on. In Mark, however, he says: "for my sake and the gospel's"; and in Luke: "for the sake of the kingdom of God." But all these things come to the same thing, because through the gospel Christ is preached, who restores the kingdom of God in us and makes heirs of it all who embrace him with steadfast faith. Therefore this promise pertains to those who so cling to Christ, in order to attain and be kept in the kingdom of God, that they prefer him to everything they have in this age, so that when he calls, they follow him where he calls without delay or evasion, and if necessary would rather lose their lives than be torn away from him. Abraham was such a man of old: he longed to see the day of the Lord, and having known and grasped it by faith, he rejoiced so much that when he was called he left his father's house and became a voluntary exile. Likewise, when commanded to sacrifice his son Isaac, he showed himself obedient. The apostles did the same: as soon as they were called by him, they immediately left their little boats, nets, houses, and tax offices.

units.la: Ioan.8. Gen.12.22. Matth.4.9 sunt. Et hos imitatus postea Paulus, audita Christi voce coelitus conante, dicebat: Domine quid me vis facere. Nihil ergo haec ad eos faciunt, qui facultates suas non tam relinquunt, quam dila-pidant, & turpiter consumunt, adeoq; egestate non necessaria petulanter sibi accersunt. Glorian-tur hi illa saepe, & se Deo propter hanc magis acceptos esse sibi persuadent. At talibus adeo nihil cum Christo negotij est, ut infidelibus deteriores esse dicat Apostolus, & ne in Ecclesia eius locus detur, monet, nisi ad frugem redeant. Non etiam ad eos pertinent ista, qui superstitionis causa facultates suas relinquunt, & eo se beatiores putant. Quia enim in paupertate ista voluntaria (ut ipsi loquuntur) salutis meritum collocant, Christum sibi ipsis inutilem reddunt. Probe ergo observari debet causa haec, qua Dominus allegat, dicens: Quisquis reliquerit suas facultates causa nominis mei, aut propter me & Euangelium, vel causa regni Dei, &c. non autem, Quisquis sua dilapidarit, aut reliquerit propter superstitionem aut hypocrisim, aut sub voluntaria paupertatis praetextu opes amplissimas, & dignitates huius saeculi vanetur: quod plerosq; istorum facere cōstat.
units.tr: (John 8; Gen. 12.22; Matth. 4.9 are the passages cited.) After them Paul also imitated them, when he heard the voice of Christ speaking from heaven and said: "Lord, what do you want me to do?" Therefore these things have nothing to do with those who do not so much leave their goods as squander them and wastefully consume them, and who thus shamelessly bring upon themselves a needless poverty. Such people often boast of this, and persuade themselves that they are more acceptable to God because of it. But to such people Christ has so little to do that the apostle says they are worse than unbelievers, and warns that no place is to be given them in his Church unless they return to sobriety. Nor do these words pertain to those who leave their possessions for the sake of superstition, and think themselves the more blessed for doing so. For since they place the merit of salvation in this voluntary poverty (as they themselves call it), they make Christ useless to themselves. The cause which the Lord cites must therefore be carefully observed, when he says: "Whoever has left his possessions for my name's sake, or for my sake and the gospel's, or for the sake of the kingdom of God, etc." He does not say: "Whoever has squandered or left his goods on account of superstition or hypocrisy, or who, under the pretext of voluntary poverty, pursues the vast wealth and honours of this age"; which is what many of them are known to do.

units.la: Deinde, quid relinqui, & quando id fieri debeat, videamus. Nec enim abfq; causa tam diligenti enumeratione vtitur Dominus, qua domus, fratres, sorores, parentes, coniuge, liberos, agros recenset. Sunt haec omnibus, qui sensum communem non prorsus exuerunt, charissima: imo necessaria sunt, eo quod vita haec sine illis neq; commode neq; honeste sustentari potest: ideoq; sine ignominia vix possunt relinqui. Quod si de parentibus, liberis, coniugibus, fratribus, sororibus dicendum sit, hos Dei Lex & natura ipsa nobis ita deuincit, ut merito impietatis summa damnentur, quicunq; ab eis temere discedunt, aut suam illis opem abfq; causa necessaria negant. Quoad ergo domus, praedia & facultates honeste partae, vna cum Christo & salua fide retineri possunt, non temere relinqui debent. At si aut ista relinquere, aut Christum & fidem in hunc abnegare oportet, tunc pro noxijs habenda sunt, & illorum iactura pro lucro deputari debet. Eadem est personarum, quae hic nominantur, ratio. Quoad parentibus, coniugibus, liberis, fratribus & cognatis, patriae domini, communi & civibus, debita officia praestare possumus, salua pietate & religione, qua Christo sumus obstricti, impij & fidei abnegatores, atq; infidelibus (ut paulo ante dictum est) sceleratiores erimus, si illos deseramus. Quod si vero isti a Christo nos auocent, iam eos no modo relinquere, sed odisse debemus. Luc. 14. Non ergo commune mandatum hic praescribitur, sed quid fieri debeat, indicatur, si necessitas vrgeat. Docet hic Dominus reipsa, quando multis hoc permisit, ut cum suis manerent, & rem domesticam curarent, quos tamen amicorum loco habuit: quales fuerunt Zachaeus, Lazarus Bethanienses cum sororibus, & alij similes: quibus adde daemoniacum illum, ex quo totam legionem daemoniorum eiecerat, quē cum precaretur, ut cum ipso manere posset, noluit in comitatum suum recipere, sed domum remisit, ut suis renuntiaret beneficium, quod ab ipso acceperat. Quoad coniuges & liberos, nota est Pauli sententia, qui ne fidelis ab infideli sub religionis praetextu discedat, graviter prohibet, si ea sit infidelis coniugis modestia & humanitas, ut fidelem amice ferat, neq; fidem abnegare cogat. De hoc eo diligentius admonemus propter eos, qui ab Anabaptistis fascinati, relictis coniugibus & liberis discedunt, etiam si inter eos habitent, qui publicae Euangelij praedicationi locum dant, & inter quos fidem profiteri & pie viuere ipsis licet. Hi sub pietatis praetextu impijssimi sunt, & revera Satanae spiritu agitantur, qui ἀσόρυς facit, quales nouissimis temporibus multos fore, Apostolus praedixit. Vidi talem aliquando mulierem, quae cum per multos annos honeste cum marito vixisset, & septem liberorum mater esset, quorum minimus adhuc lactebat, ab Anabaptistis persuasa maritum vere Christianum, cū omni prole sua reliquit, & cum intra biduum a vicinis inuenta, ac domum reducta esset, ita ςoρyac, & omnem matris affectum tam breui temporis spatio exuerat, ut liberos ne aspicere quidem dignaretur, & paruulum illum ad ipsam brachia tendentem, & vbera materna cum vagitu requirentē abs se repelleret, & haec quidem siccis oculis, cum alij qui praesentes aderant, a lachrymis non possent abstinere. Interim illa non aliud in ore habebat, quam hunc Christi locum, & quod idē alibi dicit: Si quis venit ad me, nec odit patrem suum ac matrem, & vxorē ac liberos, & fratres & sorores: amplius item animam suam, non potest meus esse discipulus, &c. Quis vero Dei spiritum esse credat, qui omne charitatis sensum in hominibus restinguit? Quis Christi fideles esse dicat eos, qui a charitate, quae propria discipulorum eius nota est, tam sunt alieni, ut nulla infantulorum ex ipsis natorum commiseratione tangantur? Exemplorum autem eiusmodi usus hic esto Christianus hominibus, ne huius loci abusu sibi imponi sinant, ut temere eos relinquant, quorum curam ipsis Deus commendauit.
units.tr: Next, let us see what is to be left behind, and when this ought to happen. The Lord does not use such a careful enumeration without reason, listing houses, brothers, sisters, parents, spouse, children, and fields. All these are very dear to everyone who has not entirely cast off common sense; indeed they are necessary, since this life cannot be sustained decently or honourably without them, and so they can scarcely be abandoned without disgrace. If we speak of parents, children, spouses, brothers, and sisters, the law of God and nature itself binds us to them so firmly that whoever rashly departs from them, or without necessary cause denies them his help, deservedly stands condemned of the greatest impiety. Therefore, as far as houses, estates, and goods honourably acquired can be kept along with Christ and with faith intact, they ought not to be rashly abandoned. But if one must either give up these things or deny Christ and faith for their sake, then they are to be regarded as harmful, and their loss is to be counted as gain. The same reasoning applies to the persons named here. As to parents, spouses, children, brothers, relatives, the lord of one's country, the community, and fellow citizens, we can render them their due duties, provided that piety and religion, by which we are bound to Christ, remain intact. If we desert them, we shall be impious and deniers of the faith, and more wicked than unbelievers (as was said a little earlier). But if these people draw us away from Christ, then we ought not merely to leave them, but to hate them. (Luke 14.) Therefore this is not a general command that is prescribed here; rather, it shows what ought to be done if necessity presses. The Lord himself teaches this by his own practice, since he allowed many to remain with their own households and attend to domestic affairs, and yet he regarded them as friends: such as Zacchaeus, Lazarus, and the sisters at Bethany, and others like them. To these add that demoniac from whom he had cast out the whole legion of demons, who, when he asked to be allowed to remain with him, was not willing to receive him into his company, but sent him home so that he might proclaim to his own people the benefit he had received from him. As to spouses and children, Paul's judgment is well known: he strictly forbids a believer to leave an unbeliever under the pretext of religion, if the unbelieving spouse is of such a disposition and gentleness as to bear the believer kindly and not compel him to deny the faith. We remind of this more carefully because of those who, bewitched by the Anabaptists, leave their spouses and children, even though they live among those who allow the public preaching of the gospel, and among whom they are free to profess the faith and live piously. Under the pretext of piety such people are most impious, and in truth they are driven by the spirit of Satan, who makes them "without natural affection [ἄστοργοι]," as the apostle foretold that many would be in the last times. Once I saw such a woman. She had lived honourably with her husband for many years and was the mother of seven children, the youngest of whom was still nursing. Persuaded by the Anabaptists that her husband was a true Christian, she left him with all her children. When she was found within two days by neighbours and brought back home, she had become so unfeeling [ἄστοργος], and had put off all maternal feeling in so short a time, that she did not deign even to look at her children. She pushed away from herself that little one who reached out its arms to her and cried for its mother's breast. She did this with dry eyes, while the others who were present could not refrain from tears. Meanwhile she had nothing else on her lips but this saying of Christ, and the one he gives elsewhere: "If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father and mother, and wife and children, and brothers and sisters, and even his own life as well, he cannot be my disciple," etc. But who would believe that such a spirit is from God, one that extinguishes every sense of charity in human beings? Who would say that those are faithful to Christ who are so far removed from that charity, which is the distinctive mark of his disciples, that they are not moved by compassion for the infants born of themselves? The use of examples of this kind should be Christian for people here, so that they do not allow themselves to be deceived by an abuse of this passage into rashly abandoning those whose care God has entrusted to them.

units.la: Sed ad Christi verba redeamus, qui de premio quod illi debetur, qui facultates suas et homines sibi charos propter illum relinquit, loquens ait, illum in hoc saeculo centuplam retributionem ac ceperturum, in altero autem saeculo vitae aeternae hereditatem aditurum. Habemus ergo hic (ut initio monuimus) promissionem praesentis et futurae vitae. Quod autem de centupla remuneratione Matthaeus annotauit, Lucas sic expressit: Multiplicia recipiet in hoc saeculo. Ponitur ergo hic numerus finitus pro infinito. Videtur autem Christo contradicere ipsa experientia, quando quotidie videmus multos pios omnibus facultatibus exutos, quod reliquum vitae superest, in summa egestate transigere: quae causa est, quod prophani homines nos ridnext, ut olim Iulianus faciebat, ut Dei Filium mendacij arguerent. Sed observari debet, non unu esse huius retributionis modum.
units.tr: But let us return to the words of Christ, who, speaking of the reward due to those who leave their possessions and dear ones for his sake, says that such a person will receive a hundredfold return in this present age, and will enter into the inheritance of eternal life in the age to come. We have here, then (as we noted at the beginning), a promise of both the present and the future life. Matthew noted the hundredfold reward, but Luke expressed it thus: they will receive manifold in this present age. A finite number is therefore put here for an infinite one. Yet experience itself seems to contradict Christ, since we see every day many pious people stripped of all their goods, who spend the rest of their lives in utter want; and this is the reason why profane men mock us, as Julian once did, to prove that the Son of God is a liar. But it must be observed that this reward is not of one kind only.

units.la: In nonnullis hoc fit κατὰ τὸ ρητόν, vel secundum literam, ut dignitatibus amplissimis donentur, qui Dei vocationem secuti aliquam bonorum suorum iacturam fecerunt. Factum hoc est in Abrahamo, patre credentium, quem postea eius ex natali solo discessum in terra peregrina opibus auxit Deus, et principibus virum charum et societum fecit. Similem benedictionem Iobus accepit, ut cum omnium facultatum iacturam patienter tulisset, illas cumulatiores reciperet. In Ecclesiastica autem historia Valentinianum habemus, qui a Iuliano propter Christi confessionem, et quod sacerdotem idololatrae, a quo aqua lustrali aspersus fuerat, pugno percussisset, balteo militari spoliatus, post illius obitum ad Imperatoriam dignitatem evectus est. Sed et vulgo videmus fieri, ut qui propter fidem Christi extorres fiunt, in exilio innumeros fratres inveniunt, qui ipsis omnia Christianae dilectionis officia praestant, adeoque omnia cum ipsis communia habent. Quod ipsum olim Apostolis accidit, quibus in Christi seruitio nihil unquam defuit, sicuti in ultima Cena confessi sunt. In aliis vero rata est promissio Christi quoad animi affectionem. Etenim vere dives est, qui praesenti bus, quae Deus largitur, contentus, nihil praeterea cupit, et ideo Paulus maximum quaestum dicebat pietatem cum animo sua sorte contento. Atqui hunc reuera soli credentes habent, qui Christum omnibus huius saeculi bonis praeferunt. Illi enim de nulla re foliciti, ante omnia quaerunt regnum Dei, et norunt cum Apostolo, in quibus sunt, ipsis contenti esse, et cum Dauide dicunt: Iehoua est pars portionis meae et calicis mei: Tu Domine sustentas sortem meam: Funes ceciderunt mihi in locis amoenis: etiam hereditas pulchra est mihi. Denique haec causa est, quod tantillum boni, quod pijs inter huius vitae molestias accidit, eos maiori gaudio recreat, quam impios diuitiae vndique affluentes, inter quas illi Tantali instar perpetuo sitiunt et ferunt, curis deniq; mordacibus torquentur. Et huc referri possunt ista Solomonis: In domo iusti thesaurus multus, at in prouentibus impij turbatio. Item, Melius est buccella siccacum tranquillitate, quam domus plena victimis contentionis. Prouerb. 15. et 17.
units.tr: In some cases it happens according to the letter (κατὰ τὸ ρητόν), that is, literally, so that those who have followed God's call and suffered some loss of their goods are rewarded with the highest dignities. This happened to Abraham, the father of believers, whom God, after his departure from his native soil into a foreign land, enriched with wealth and made a dear and esteemed companion of princes. Job received a similar blessing: after he had patiently borne the loss of all his possessions, he received them back in greater abundance. In ecclesiastical history we have Valentinian, who, because he confessed Christ and had struck with his fist a priest of the idols, by whom he had been sprinkled with lustral water, was stripped of his military belt by Julian; after Julian's death he was raised to the imperial dignity. Yet we also commonly see that those who become exiles for the faith of Christ find in exile countless brothers who perform for them all the offices of Christian love, and hold all things in common with them. This happened in the past to the Apostles themselves, who never lacked anything in the service of Christ, as they confessed at the last supper. In others, however, Christ's promise is fulfilled with respect to the disposition of the mind. For he is truly rich who is content with the blessings God bestows, and desires nothing beyond them; and therefore Paul said that godliness with contentment is great gain. Indeed, only believers truly have this, those who prefer Christ to all the goods of this world. For they, anxious about nothing, seek above all the kingdom of God, and know with the Apostle to be content with what they have, and they say with David: The LORD is the portion of my inheritance and of my cup; you, O Lord, uphold my lot; the lines have fallen to me in pleasant places; indeed, I have a goodly heritage. Finally, this is the reason why the small good that befalls the godly amid the troubles of this life refreshes them with greater joy than the riches of the wicked, which flow in from every side, and amid which they thirst perpetually like Tantalus and are at last tormented by gnawing cares. To this may also be referred the sayings of Solomon: In the house of the righteous is much treasure, but in the revenues of the wicked is trouble. Likewise: Better is a dry morsel with tranquillity than a house full of sacrifices with strife. Prov. 15 and 17.

units.la: Porro diligenter obseruari debet conditio, quam Marcus annotauit, quod nimirum retributionem hanc Dominus promiserit cum persecutionibus, quae fidei perpetui sunt comites. Nec enim aequum est, ut discipulorum et seruorum fors melior sit, quam Christi Domini et praeceptoris fuit in terris. Neq; mutabit mundus ingenium suum, quod est odisse lucem et huius filios persequi. Id vero fieri finit Deus, quia sic nobis prodest, ne cum mundo polluamur, sed ut afflictiones, quibus quotidie nouis infestamur, illius fastidium nobis pariant. Debemus de eo semper cogitare, ut animum a terrenis auocemus ad caelestium meditationem. Ideo Dominus veram retributionem in illis monstrat, quando Vitam aeternam pollicetur, cuius hereditatem adituri sumus. Incipit hac per fidem in terris, dum adhuc in mortali corpore agimus, perficietur autem in caelis: Vult enim nos secum esse Christus, et illic abstergit omnibus curis et lachrymis, fruemur bonis illis, quae oculus non vidit, neq; auris audiuit, neq; in cor hominis ascenderunt. Qui de his serio cogitant, ijs leuicula est omnium fortunarum huius saeculi iactura: imo hi cupiunt vitam quoque hanc mortalem cum immortali commutare, &c.
units.tr: Moreover, the condition which Mark noted must be carefully observed: namely, that the Lord promised this reward together with persecutions, which are the constant companions of faith. For it is not fitting that the lot of the disciples and servants should be better than that of Christ the Lord and Teacher was on earth. Nor will the world change its nature, which is to hate the light and to persecute its children. God, however, permits this to happen because it profits us so: lest we be polluted together with the world, but so that the afflictions by which we are daily assailed in new ways may produce in us a distaste for it. We ought always to think of this, so that we turn our minds away from earthly things to the meditation of heavenly ones. Therefore the Lord shows the true reward in those things when he promises eternal life, whose inheritance we shall enter. It begins here on earth through faith, while we still live in a mortal body, but it will be perfected in heaven. For Christ wills that we be with him, and there he will wipe away all cares and tears; we shall enjoy those good things which the eye has not seen, nor the ear heard, nor have entered into the heart of man. To those who think seriously about these things, the loss of all the fortunes of this age is a trifle; indeed, they desire to exchange even this mortal life for an immortal one, etc.

units.la: Caeterum nouerat Dei Filius confidentiam discipulorum, Petri in primis, qui omnium nomine quaestionem illam mouerat. Ergo ut eos intra modestiae limites et in metu contineret, ne vel alios alios præse contemnerent, vel securitati se dederent, quæ multis in salutis negotio nocet. Epipho- nemate graui & acuto istam tractatione concludit, dicens: Multi autem primi, erunt vltimi: & vltimi primi. Quo dicto eos, qui bene cæperunt ad strenuè pergendum hortatur, ne in medio cursu deficiant. Quasi diceret: Enimuero bene cæpistis, & aliquousque progressi estis hucusque, vt multos alios anteuerteritis. Sed nondum metam attigistis, multo minus præmiũ consecuti estis. Itaq; quod in stadio currentibus accidit, semper in animum reuocate. Solent illic sæpe qui initiò alijs omnibus præcurrunt, vel ex lapsu improuiso, vel spiritus interclusione, aut virium defatigatione impediri, vt a postremis vincantur, & ipsi postremi fiant. Ita hic fieri solet. Et exempla sunt publica et priuata, quibus hoc dictum confirmatur: Inter primos cucurrit Iudas, sed idem non vltimus modò discipulorum, sed proditor quoq; factus est: E contra postremus illis ceu abortiuus accessit Paulus, qui & Iudam anteuertit, & plus alijs omnibus laborauit. Publicè vero primi in toto genere humanum Iudæi fuerunt, quibus ipse Christus manifestauit: sed sua confidentia & securitate decepti exciderunt, & a gentibus superati sunt. Qui vero ex gentibus primi ad fidem Christianam accesserunt Asiatici nimirum, Africani, & ex Europæis Græci: ij nunc omnes sub duro & impio Mahumetis seruitio laborant, libertate autem in Christo fruuntur quibus hic postremis est prædicatus. Et si ciuitates spectes, quanta olim fuit Romæ dignitas, quando fides eius per totum orbem prædicabatur? & quam illa nunc infamis & misera est, dum Christi loco personatus huius vicarius illic regnat? Quod si eos consideraro libeat, quibus primis nostro sæculo Euangelium prædicatum est, & qui fidei feruore & zelo omnibus alijs palmam præripuerunt, non absq; causa multi metuunt, ne hoc Domini dictum illis quoq; conueniat. Discant igitur illud sibi ipsis applicare, quotquot in hoc stadio Euangelico currunt, nec quantum spacij confecerint, sed quàm procul adhuc a meta absint, respiciant, neq; illis vnquam excidat quod Dominus dixit. Nemo qui manu sua admota aratro, respexerit ea quæ a tergo sunt, aptus est regno Dei: sed qui perseuerat in fine, saluus erit: Qui vero (vt D. Basilius scribit) progressum in bonis actionibus fecerit, deinde ad pristinam consuetudinem reuersus fuerit, non modò laborum præteritorum mercede priuatur, sed etiam acerbiore condemnatione dignus iudicatur. Quam diu ergo in hac carne viuimus, cum Apostolo cogitemus, nos metam nondum apprehendisse, pergendum vero nobis esse, vt certamen illud bonum decertemus, cursum consumemus, fidem seruemus: ad constantiam vero nos excitet perpetua iustitiæ corona re cordatio, quam Dominus IESVS CHRISTVS, iustus ille iudex, in magno illo die reddet omnibus, qui illustrem illum aduentum ipsius expetierint. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Moreover, the Son of God knew the confidence of his disciples, especially of Peter, who had raised that question in the name of all. Therefore, in order to keep them within the limits of modesty and in fear, lest they either despise others or give themselves over to security, which harms many in the business of salvation, he concludes this discourse with a weighty and sharp epiphonema, saying: But many who are first will be last, and the last first. By these words he exhorts those who have begun well to press on vigorously, lest they fail in the middle of the course. As if he said: Indeed you have begun well, and so far have progressed so that you have outstripped many others. But you have not yet reached the goal, much less obtained the prize. Therefore, keep always in mind what happens to those who run in the stadium. There it often happens that those who at the start run ahead of all others are hindered, either by an unforeseen fall, or by a loss of breath, or by exhaustion of strength, so that they are overtaken by the last and become last themselves. So it commonly happens here too. Both public and private examples confirm this saying. Among the first, Judas ran; yet the same man became not only the last of the disciples but also a traitor. On the other hand, Paul came to them as the last, as if untimely born, and yet he outstripped Judas and labored more than all the others. Publicly, the Jews were first among the whole human race, to whom Christ himself revealed himself; but deceived by their own confidence and security, they fell away and were overcome by the Gentiles. Those of the Gentiles who first came to the Christian faith, namely the Asiatics, the Africans, and from among the Europeans the Greeks, all these now labor under the harsh and impious servitude of Mahomet; yet those who were last preached to here enjoy liberty in Christ. And if you look at cities, how great once was the dignity of Rome, when its faith was preached throughout the whole world! And how infamous and wretched it is now, while its vicar, masquerading in Christ's place, reigns there! But if it pleases us to consider those to whom the gospel was first preached in our age, and who have snatched the palm from all others by the fervor and zeal of their faith, not without cause many fear that this saying of the Lord applies to them as well. Let all who run in this gospel stadium therefore learn to apply it to themselves; let them look not at how much of the course they have covered, but how far they still are from the goal; and let there never slip from their minds what the Lord said: No one who has put his hand to the plough and looked back at what is behind is fit for the kingdom of God; but he who perseveres to the end will be saved. Whoever (as St. Basil writes) has made progress in good works and then returned to his former habits is not only deprived of the reward of his past labors, but is also judged worthy of a more severe condemnation. Therefore, as long as we live in this flesh, let us think with the Apostle that we have not yet laid hold of the goal, but that we must press on, that we may fight that good fight, finish the course, and keep the faith; and let the continual remembrance of the crown of righteousness, which the Lord Jesus Christ, that righteous judge, will give on that great day to all who have longed for his glorious coming, stir us to constancy. To him be blessing, honor, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPVT XX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XX.

units.la: HOMILIA CCXXXV.
units.tr: HOMILY 235.

units.la: SImile enim est regnum cœlorum patrifamilias, qui exijt cum prima luce ad conducendos operarios in vineam suam. Pactus autem cum operarijs denario in diem, misit eos in vineam suam. Et egressus circa horam tertiam, vidit alios stantes in foro otiosos. Et iis dixit: Abite & vos in vineam, & quodcunq; iustum fuerit, dabo vobis: Illi autem abierunt. Rursus egressus circa sextam & nonam horam, fecit itidem. Circa horam autem vndecimam egressus, invenit alios stantes otiosos, ac dicit eis: Cur hic statis totum diem otiosi? Dicunt ei: Quia nemo nos conduxit. Dicit eis: Abite & vos in vineam; & quicquid fuerit iustum, accipietis.
units.tr: For the kingdom of heaven is like a householder, who went out early in the morning to hire workers for his vineyard. When he had agreed with the workers for a denarius a day, he sent them into his vineyard. Going out again about the third hour, he saw others standing idle in the marketplace, and said to them: "Go you also into the vineyard, and whatever is right I will give you." And they went. Again he went out about the sixth and the ninth hour, and did likewise. And about the eleventh hour he went out and found others standing idle, and said to them: "Why do you stand here idle all day?" They said to him: "Because no one has hired us." He said to them: "Go you also into the vineyard, and whatever is right you will receive."

units.la: OMINVS & Seruator noster IESVS CHRISTVS, nuper suis discipulis, qui relictis omnibus ipsum secuti fuerant, amplissima præmia promiserat. Quia vero omnibus hominibus innatum est, quod si aliquousque progressi laudem merentur, sibi ipsis mi-
units.tr: Our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ had recently promised very great rewards to his disciples, who had left everything and followed him. But because it is innate in all men that, when they have advanced somewhat and earned praise, they take wonderful pleasure in themselves,

units.la: . rifice placent, & ipsius Petri quaestio, quam omnium discipulorum nomine moverat, dicens: Quid erit nobis? abunde testabatur, illos altius quid spirare & sapere, ac ideo confidentiores & securi fieri poterant, graviem admonitionem subiecit isti promissioni, qua eos ad modestiam & humilitatem hortatus est, hoc argumento: Fieri posse, ut qui primi sunt, postremi fiant, nisi diligenter sibi cauant, & in eo quod bene coeperunt, constanter perseverent. Continet autem gnome ista generalem admonitionem, & omnibus admodum necessariam, eo quod (ut alibi dictum est) qui retrabuntur, eorum postrema primis deteriora fiunt. Ideo quod breviter dixit, nunc eleganti parabola illustrat & confirmat: in primis autem docet, qui nam primi illi sint, quibus periculum incumbit, ne fiant postremi, id est, ne a regno Dei prorsus excludantur, & salute omni excidant. Hi nimirum, qui suorum meritorum fiducia elati, alios prae se contemnunt, securi deniq; & confidentes Deum sibi ipsis debitorem faciunt, & eius iudicis obloqui audent. Est horum magnus numerus hodie, qui cum ex hac ipsa parabola occasionem arripiant disputandi de merito, eo diligentius illa considerari debet, ut quid velit Dominus, recte intelligamus.
units.tr: and because Peter's own question, which he had raised in the name of all the disciples ("What shall we have?"), clearly showed that they were thinking and feeling somewhat loftily and could therefore become overconfident and complacent, he added a grave warning to that promise, exhorting them to modesty and humility with this argument: that those who are first may become last, unless they take careful heed for themselves and persevere steadily in what they have begun well. This saying contains a general admonition, most necessary for everyone, since (as was said elsewhere) the last state of those who turn back becomes worse than the first. What he has said briefly he now illustrates and confirms with an elegant parable; but first he teaches who those first are who are in danger of becoming last, that is, of being utterly excluded from the kingdom of God and cut off from all salvation. These are, of course, those who, puffed up by confidence in their own merits, despise others in comparison with themselves, and, being secure and confident, make God their debtor and dare to find fault with his judgment. There is a great number of such people today, who seize on this very parable as an occasion for disputing about merit; so it ought to be considered all the more carefully, that we may rightly understand what the Lord intends.

units.la: Summa parabolae est, regni coelorum eandem esse conditionem, quae est vinea, in quam paterfamilias mittit ad opus faciendum, operarios certa mercede conductos, deinde ipsidem alios diversis horis submittit de nullo certo pretio cum illis pacisecens: at ubi vespera venit, quam primis illis pactus est mercedem, omnibus ex aequo largitur, nec illorum murmura curat, qui postremos inique sibi aequari quaeruntur, cum quod illis debetur, acceperint. Imo docetur horum exemplo iustitiarios murmuratores indignos esse, quos bonus ille paterfamilias porro inter suos numeret, cum eius liberalitatem caeteris invideant, ex qua nulla iniuria aut damnum ad ipsos redijt. Vocatur autem hoc loco Regnum coelorum Ecclesia, in qua Deus regnat, & universos salutis aeternae thesauros inter suos non minus iuste quam liberaliter dispensat.
units.tr: The sum of the parable is this: the kingdom of heaven is in the same condition as a vineyard, into which a householder sends workers hired for a fixed wage to do the work. Then he sends others at different hours, agreeing with them on no fixed price. But when evening comes, he gives equal pay to all, the same wage he had agreed with the first. He pays no heed to the grumbling of those who unjustly complain that the last have been made equal to them, since they have received what was owed to them. Indeed, by their example it is taught that grumbling men who judge by strict justice are unworthy to be counted further among that good householder's people, since they begrudge the generosity of another, from which no wrong or loss has come back to them. Here the kingdom of heaven means the Church, in which God reigns and dispenses all the treasures of eternal salvation among his people, no less justly than generously.

units.la: Confertur autem vinea Ecclesia, quae similitudo in utriusque testamenti libris admodum frequens est. Huius enim Moses meminit de Iudaeis loquens, Dauid item, qui eosdem vites ex Aegypto perditas & transplantatas nominat. Et praeter Prophetas Isaiam & Ieremiam Christus non hoc solum loco, verum etiam in sequenti cap. veterem Ecclesiam Vineam, Sacerdotes autem colonis male fidis confert. Et alibi seipsum verant vitem, credentes autem palmites dicit, quarum curam habeat Pater, quo nullus melior est vinitor sine agricola. Quia vero in praesenti non de vinea nova aut nuperrime demum plantata loquitur, sed simpliciter vineam Dei Patris nominat, in quam hic operarios miserit, non obscure docet, Deum omnibus saeculis habuisse et porro habiturum Ecclesiam suam, cui illi prospiciat, & quam gubernet ac servet.
units.tr: The Church is compared to a vineyard, and this likeness is very frequent in the books of both Testaments. Moses mentions it when speaking of the Jews, and David likewise, who names the vine that was brought out of Egypt and planted. Besides the Prophets Isaiah and Jeremiah, Christ, not only in this place but also in the following chapter, compares the old Church to a vineyard, and the priests to wicked tenants. Elsewhere he calls himself the vine, and says that believers are the branches, whose care the Father has, since there is no better vinedresser than the husbandman. But because here he is not speaking of a new vineyard or one recently planted, and simply calls it the vineyard of God the Father, into which he sends the workers here, he clearly teaches that God has had his Church in all ages, and will continue to have it, which he watches over, governs and preserves.

units.la: Est ea, Sicuti in Symbolo Apostolico profitemur, Sanctorum communio sive societas, in qua doctrina de Filio Dei IESV CHRISTO praedicatur, Deus ex fide Christi invocatur, & Sacramenta, quae hic salutis promissae olim & iam quasi aut partae signa esse voluit, rite secundum eius institutionem dispensantur. Coepit Ecclesia ista in primis parentibus, qui promissionem de semine mulieris a Deo acceperunt, & eandem posteris suis fideliter tradiderunt, cuius signa tunc erant sacrificia, quae illis visitata fuisse, ex Caini & Abelis historia constat. Et licet eius seminarium in Abele per Cainum infando parricidio extinctum videri posset, mox tamen illius loco alium substituit Deus, Sethum videlicet: ex quo filiorum Dei prosapia usque ad Noa propagata est, cum quo Ecclesiae reliquiae tempore Diluvij in arca servatae, & inde ad Abrahamum usque deductae sunt, cum quo foedus suum Deus instauravit. Ab eo tempore Ecclesia aut Vineae Domini nomen sive titulus penes Iudaeorum gentem manssit usque ad exhibitionem Messiae vel Filij Dei adventum in carnem: Sed illis propter incredulitatem & ingratitudinem suam repudiatis, gentes vocatae sunt, & Ecclesia per Euangelij praedicationem in toto orbe terrarum propagata est, sicuti olim Prophetae praedixerunt. Atq; toto Veteris Testamenti tempore inter continuas fere persecutiones & varios orbis terrarum motus admirabili Dei protectione servata durauit usque ad Christi nativitatem: ita posse eius in coelum Ascensionem quoq; inter crudeles tyrannorum conatus, non modo sed verumetiam creuit, & adhuc hodie durat, atq; salua manebit, usque ad Christi ad iudicium universale nouissimum aduentum. Ita enim pollicetur: Ecce ego vobiscum sum omnibus diebus usque ad consummationem saeculi: Oportet enim perpetuo verum ratum esse, quod Dauid praedixit,
units.tr: This Church is, as we profess in the Apostles' Creed, the communion or fellowship of the saints, in which the doctrine concerning the Son of God, Jesus Christ, is preached, God is called upon through faith in Christ, and the sacraments, which he willed to be signs of the salvation promised long ago and now as if already obtained, are rightly administered according to his institution. This Church began with our first parents, who received from God the promise concerning the seed of the woman, and faithfully handed it on to their posterity. Its signs were then sacrifices, which we know were in use among them from the history of Cain and Abel. And although its seed in Abel might seem to have been extinguished by Cain's unspeakable murder, God soon put another in his place, namely Seth. From him the line of the sons of God was propagated down to Noah, with whom the remnants of the Church were preserved in the ark at the time of the Flood, and from him were led on down to Abraham, with whom God renewed his covenant. From that time onward the name or title of the Church, or of the Lord's vineyard, remained with the Jewish nation until the manifestation of the Messiah, or the coming of the Son of God in the flesh. But when they were rejected for their unbelief and ingratitude, the Gentiles were called, and the Church was spread through the preaching of the gospel throughout the whole world, just as the Prophets had foretold long ago. And throughout the whole time of the Old Testament, amid almost continual persecutions and various upheavals of the world, it endured, preserved by the wonderful protection of God, down to the birth of Christ. So too, after his ascension into heaven, it grew not only amid the cruel attempts of tyrants, but even more so, and it still endures today and will remain safe until the last universal judgment, at the coming of Christ. For he promises: "Behold, I am with you all days, even to the end of the age." For it must always be true and firm what David foretold, that Christ would reign in the midst of his enemies.

units.la: Matth. 12. 1. Pet. 2. pradixit, Christum regnaturum in medio inimicorum suorum. Habet hæc Ecclesia perpetui-tas dulcissimam consolationem, qua nos infide confirmemus. At quia Ecclesiæ titulum alij e-tiam sibi vindicant, non tam vtile quàm necessarium est, proprias notas veræ Ecclesiæ Chri-sti obseruasse, ne alij nos meritricio suo fuco & ornatu decipiant. Comprehendit illas Lucas, quan do de Apostolica Ecclesia scribit: Erant perdurantes in doctrina Apostolorum & communicatio-ne (quam fraterna charitas peperit) & fractione panis (id est, in ysu Cœna Dominicæ) & preca-tionibus. Ergo Ecclesiæ veræ notæ sunt: doctrina Euangelicæ puritas, vnius Dei veri invocatio per vnicum Mediatorem IESVM CHRISTVM, Sacramentorum vsus, qui primæ institu-tioni respondeat: Charitatis fraterna ardor, qui mutua auxilia parit, et cui cohaeret disciplina mo-rum & totius vitæ, quæ obstat, ne propter nos fides Christiana male audiat. Vbi hæc habentur, ibi est Vinea Domini, ibi Ecclesia est, ibi Sanctorum communio, a qua nemo auelli debet, qui vult salvus fieri.
units.tr: Matth. 12. 1. Pet. 2. This perpetuity of the Church holds the sweetest consolation, by which we may strengthen one another in faith. But because others also claim for themselves the title of the Church, it is not so much useful as necessary to have observed the proper marks of the true Church of Christ, lest others deceive us with their harlot's paint and finery. Luke sets these out when he writes about the Apostolic Church: "They continued steadfastly in the doctrine of the apostles and in fellowship (which brotherly love brought about), and in the breaking of bread (that is, in the use of the Lord's Supper), and in prayers." Therefore the marks of the true Church are: purity of evangelical doctrine; the invocation of the one true God through the one Mediator, Jesus Christ; the use of the sacraments, corresponding to their first institution; the ardour of brotherly love, which brings forth mutual help; and the discipline of morals and of the whole life, which is bound up with it, and which prevents the Christian faith from being badly spoken of because of us. Where these things are found, there is the vineyard of the Lord, there is the Church, there is the communion of the saints, from which no one who wishes to be saved should be torn away.

units.la: Cæterum quantopere Ecclesia Deo cura sit, parabola ista pulchre docet. Et huc facit initio, quòd patrisfamilias personam illi Christus tribuit, vt illam sub eius potestate & dominio esse, & ab eodem fideliter innisi & curari ostendat. Etenim licet in alto habitet, & eius gloria cœlis sublimior sit, demittit tamen se, vt videat quæcunque in cœlo & in terra sunt. Et quæ ratio fingi potest, vt cogitemus, illum Ecclesiam negligere posse, quam Filij Vnigeniti sanguine redemit, qui nos singulos pascit, aues cœli & pullos coruorum alit, flores in agris vestit, capillos denique nostros in numerato habet? Christus certè apud Lucam ita illum describit, vt eum vineam suam quottannis peculiari studio inuisere dicat, & velle, vt arbores inutiles aut sterilies excindantur, ne vitibus officiant aut terram inertem reddant. In præsenti autem, illum primo diluculo exiuisse dicit, ad vocandum operarios, quos in vineam suam mitteret: Deinde rursus idem fecisse hora diei tertia, quæ nostræ nonæ antemeridianæ respondet: Rursus etiam alios misses esse hora sexta & nona, id est, in ipsa meridie, & sub tertiam horam pomeridianam. Denique sub vndecimam quoque quando iam ferus vesper instabat, & vnica modo hora diei superarat, adhuc de quibusdam operarijs mittendis solicitum fuisse. Quo admonemur, nullam diei partem, nullam horam, imò ne momentum quidem vllum elabi, quo Dei cura pro Ecclesia sua cesset. Nam vt Propheta ait, oculi Domini discurrunt per vniuersam terram: Et non dormitat, neque dormiet custos Israelis. Quoad verò huius parabolæ argumentum & statum, hæc nobis ex ordine consideranda veniunt.
units.tr: Moreover, how greatly God cares for the Church, this parable teaches beautifully. And to this purpose it contributes at the outset that Christ gives him the person of a householder, to show that the Church is under his power and lordship, and is faithfully watched over and cared for by him. For although he dwells on high, and his glory is more sublime than the heavens, yet he humbles himself so that he may see whatever is in heaven and on earth. And what reason can be imagined for thinking that he could neglect the Church, which he redeemed with the blood of his only-begotten Son, who feeds each one of us, feeds the birds of the heaven and the young ravens, clothes the flowers in the fields, and finally has even the hairs of our head numbered? Christ certainly describes him in Luke in such a way that he says he visits his vineyard every year with special care, and wishes unfruitful or barren trees to be cut down, lest they harm the vines or make the ground useless. In the present passage he says that the householder went out at early dawn to call the workers whom he would send into his vineyard; then again he did the same at the third hour of the day, which corresponds to our nine o'clock in the morning; again he sent others at the sixth and the ninth hour, that is, at midday and about three in the afternoon. Finally, at the eleventh hour as well, when the cruel evening was already coming on and only one hour of the day remained, he was still anxious about sending some workers. By this we are reminded that no part of the day, no hour, nor even any moment passes in which the care of God for his Church ceases. For, as the Prophet says, "The eyes of the Lord run through the whole earth; and he who keeps Israel neither slumbers nor sleeps." As to the subject and state of this parable, the following points are to be considered in order.

units.la: Primum, quòd ipse Paterfamilias exit, vt vocet quos mittat in suam vineam. Docet hæc particula, solius Dei esse in Ecclesia consortium vocare quos vult, & in illa certam cuique fun-ctionem siue ministerium assignare. Etenim quia omnes in peccato concipimur & nascimur, ex nobis ipsis ad nihil idonei sumus, ne ad cogitandum quidem, vt Paulus scribit. Quoad ergo nos non vocat & suo seruitio Deus destinat, stamus in huius mundi foro siue theatro otiosi spectatores, nec habemus, quod vtiliter agamus. Affectant quidem multi munera publica, & philautia philtro fascinati, se ad quæuis obeunda idoneos esse, sibi persuadent. Sed nisi a Deo efficaciter vocentur, nunquam ad Ecclesiæ & Christi societatem accedent & licet aliquo priuato cæterum affectu moti accedant, & rebus agendis se immisceant, absque fructu & laude id faciunt. Quod enim de doctoribus, qui sua sponte currunt, dixit Apostolus, Quomodo prædicabunt, nisi missi fuerint, id de magistratibus, de officialibus publicis, de omnibus denique debet intelligi, qui ad aliquas functiones temerè aspirant. Debet hoc omnes homines admonere, ne ex suo arbitrio genus vitæ sibi deligant, quod vel priuati commodi, vel gloriæ studium, vel cæca animi libido dictat: sed quisque suo se modulo metiatur, & propriæ infirmitatis memor vocationem Domini expectet: qui quos vocat, eos donis quoque necessarijs instruit, & idoneos reddit, vt suum officium recte possint facere.
units.tr: First, that the householder himself goes out to call those whom he sends into his vineyard. This little phrase teaches that it belongs to God alone, within the Church, to call whom he wills and to assign to each a definite function or ministry in it. For since we are all conceived and born in sin, we are of ourselves fit for nothing, not even for thinking, as Paul writes. Therefore, as long as God does not call us and destine us for his service, we stand in the forum or theatre of this world as idle spectators, with nothing useful to do. Many indeed seek public offices, and bewitched by self-love they persuade themselves that they are fit for any task. But unless they are effectively called by God, they will never come into the fellowship of the Church and of Christ. Even if they come, moved by some private desire, and mix themselves into the business at hand, they do so without fruit and without praise. What the Apostle said of teachers who run of their own accord, "How shall they preach unless they be sent?", must be understood of magistrates, of public officials, and finally of all who rashly aspire to any office. This should admonish all people not to choose for themselves a way of life according to their own judgement, as dictated by private advantage, a zeal for glory, or a blind desire of the mind. Rather, each should measure himself by his own measure, remember his own weakness, and wait for the Lord's call. He who calls them also equips those whom he calls with the gifts they need, and makes them fit to perform their duty rightly.

units.la: Deinde quos & quales vocet, videndum est. Operarios nimirum, Ergo non otiosos ventres, non inutiles sponsos Penelopes, non inertia tellurus pondera & fruges consumere natos, qui non aliud agunt, quàm vt otientur, saltu se ostentent, tempus omne in delitijs & voluptatibus transfigant, vel vt ditescant, aut titulis ambitiosis omne sibi in Ecclesiam ius atque imperium vsurpent: qua
units.tr: Next, we must consider whom and what sort of men he calls. Workers, certainly: not idle bellies, not useless suitors of Penelope, not men born to consume the earth's weight and its fruits while doing nothing but lounging about, showing off in idleness, and spending all their time in pleasures and luxuries, or else growing rich, or seizing by ambitious titles every right and rule over the Church. Such men there are today in great number, who wish to be called not only the leaders and rulers of the Church but the Church itself, so much so that they dare to thrust upon all people in the name of the Church whatever they themselves decree or determine. Such men, I say, the good and thrifty householder does not send into his vineyard; he sends workers who diligently do some task that serves the building up of the whole Church and of its individual members, both in public and in private.

units.la: Rom. 10. les hodie pleriq; sunt, qui non solum Præsules & Ancistites Ecclesiæ, sed ipsissima Ecclesia dicł volunt: adeo, vt quod ipsi statuunt aut decernunt, omnibus hominibus Ecclesiæ nomine obtrudere ausint. Tales (inquam) non mittit in suam vineam bonus ille & frugi Paterfamilias, sed operarios, qui opus aliquod sedulo faciant, quod publice ac priuatim totius Ecclesiæ & singulorum ædificationi seruiat. Sunt hic Apostolo teste ministrorum discrimina, idem tamen Spiritus, idem Deus, qui dona largitur, & in omnibus agit. Primum gradum tenent administri Verbi: quorum est non obiter modo docere, sed exemplar præbere fidelium in sermone, in conuersatione, in charitate, in spiritu, in fide, in puritate: prædicare item sermonem, instare tempestiuè & intempestiuè, arguere, obiurgare, exhortari cum omni lenitate & doctrina. Deniq; fidos excubitores, industrios pastores, laboriosos colonos & architectos agere. Proximi his sunt viri principes, qui ad Reipub. clauum sedent, quos Deus Ecclesiæ suæ nutritios, patronos & tutores constituit. Horum manus & pedes quasi sunt, quibus officia reliqua, legum item & iudiciorum siue decretorum exeeutio commissa est. Qui nisi in suo munere diligentes sint, non possunt fideles operarij censeri in vinea Domini. Habent præterea singuli priuatim quod agant, diuites, pauperes, coniuges, beri & serui, opifices, summi, infimi. Nec enim aliquem cuiuscunq; sit loci aut ordinis otiosum esse vult in sua vinea ille Paterfamilias, aut infrugiferos, sed vt quisq; seipsum priuatim excolat, vt vel ficus fæcunda sit, vel palmes virens, qui fructum ferat, quo Dei nomen glorificetur, & alij emendentur. Et huc referri debent quæcunq; in Scripturis passim de sanctimonia & innocentia vitæ, de iusticia & æquitate, de dilectione mutua traduntur, quibus studere oportet eos, qui in Ecclesia censeri volunt.
units.tr: Rom. 10. There are, as the Apostle witnesses, differences of ministries, yet the same Spirit, the same God, who bestows the gifts and works in all. The first rank belongs to the ministers of the Word. It is their task not merely to teach in passing, but to set an example to the faithful in speech, in conduct, in love, in spirit, in faith, and in purity; likewise to preach the word, to press on in season and out of season, to reprove, rebuke and exhort with all gentleness and teaching; and finally to act as faithful watchmen, diligent shepherds, and hard-working farmers and builders. Next to these are the men in authority who sit at the helm of the commonwealth, whom God has appointed as nurses, patrons and guardians of his Church. They are, as it were, its hands and feet, to whom the remaining duties are entrusted, together with the execution of the laws, judgements and decrees. Unless they are diligent in their office, they cannot be counted as faithful workers in the Lord's vineyard. Besides these, each person has his own private work to do: rich and poor, husbands and wives, masters and servants, craftsmen, the highest and the lowest. For the householder does not wish anyone, of whatever place or rank, to be idle or unfruitful in his vineyard, but that each should cultivate himself privately, so that he may be a fruitful fig tree or a green branch that bears fruit, by which the name of God is glorified and others are improved. To this must be referred everything that the Scriptures everywhere teach about holiness and innocence of life, about righteousness and fairness, and about mutual love. Those who wish to be counted in the Church ought to strive for these things.

units.la: Tertiò obseruatu dignum est, quod præter communem morem operarij isti non omnes simul summo mane conducuntur & mittuntur in vineam, sed diuersis horis, & quidem nonnulli sub vesperum demum, aut die iam ad occasum declinante. Hoc alij de patribus priscis, de ijs item qui sub Mose vixerunt, exponunt, ad Prophetarum itẽ, Christi & Apostolorum tempora, ad nos denique qui in hac mundi senesta viuimus, & a Domino vocamur, referunt. Qui sensus et non omnino reijci debeat, & in se verum sit quod isti dicunt, simplicius tamen illud intelligo, quod nimirum doceat Christus, nos omnes homines vt primum nati sunt, aut a pueris statim vocari, vt veri serui & cultores Dei sint, & membra Ecclesiæ vtilia, sed Deus prout ipsi placet vnumquenq; vocare, quando vult. Fit hoc quoad publicas functiones tam politicas et Ecclesiasticas, Nam alij ex pe culiari Dei consilio a pueris statim in suo seruitio educantur & instituuntur, quod de Samuele & filijs Prophetarum dici potest, quorum in libris Regum mentio fit: alij postquam ex ephebis egressi virilem ætatem attigerunt, & bonam ætatis partem in alio vitæ genere transegerunt, ad Dei & Ecclesiæ suæ seruitium vocantur. Sic Moses in aula Ægyptiaca vixit priusquam populi Dei curam susciperet: Eliæus & Amos rusticam & pastoritiam vitam sectati sunt, priusquam Prophetæ fierent, Apostoli piscatores et publicani fuerunt: Paulum etsi ab vtero matris segregatus esset ad Euangelium, tamen Pharisæorum lacunis immergi & Ecclesiæ persecutore fieri passus est, ac postea demum inde extraxit, vt Apostolum organum eleCtum faceret. Similia siunt in priuatis hominibus quoad vitæ actiones, mores & studia. Nam alij ex pijs parentibus nati fidem & religionem veram a pueris discunt, & in pietatis officijs instituuntur: alij dum pueri sunt ita negliguntur, vt ne precari quidem possint, & in adolescentia demum præceptores inueniant, a quibus docen- tur: multi illam quoque in ignorantia transigunt, & virilem quoque ætatem vitijs & scelerum sententia consecrant, quando autem ad limen senesta appropinquant, tunc demum de salute propria incipiunt cogitare, vt in vinea Domini opus faciant Christiana professione dignum. Sunt qui sub mortis horam demum vocantur, vt latro ille Christi in cruce socius. Vidimus itẽ fieri, vt quidam quando iam duodecima vitæ hora illis instat, & morbis confecti vires deficere, & vitæ finem appropinquare sentiunt, a spiritu Domini illuminentur, vt seriam vitæ male transactæ pœnitentiam agant, peccata cum lachrymis confiteantur, misericordiam Dei implorent, suos de pietate admoneant, & iam morituri bonam operam præstent in vinea Domini, dum exemplo suo multos docent & officij admonent. Et hæc quidem omnia certa cum ratione facit Deus, cui licet in suis facere quod lubet. Nos vero horum consideratio admonet, nullum vitæ tempus esse, quod non aptum & idoneum sit Dei seruitio, & huius gratiam non esse astrictam legibus vllis, quo minus in quauis aetate & conditione ijs affulgeat, quos ille vocare dignatur. Non temere ergo de alicuius salute desperemus, sed potius precemur sedulo Deum, vt eos qui otiosi adhuc stant, aut etiam in Satanae palaestra tempus suum impie non abfq; publico scandalo transigunt, efficaciter vt cet & suo Spiritu trahat, vt ipsi seruire discant.
units.tr: Thirdly, it is worth noting that, contrary to common custom, these workers are not all hired and sent into the vineyard at early morning, but at different hours, some only towards evening, or when the day is already drawing to its close. Some interpret this of the ancient fathers and of those who lived under Moses, others refer it to the times of the Prophets, of Christ and of the Apostles, and finally to us who live in this old age of the world and are called by the Lord. This sense ought not to be altogether rejected, and what they say is true in itself. Yet I understand it more simply: Christ teaches that all men are called to be true servants and worshippers of God, and useful members of the Church, either as soon as they are born or straight from childhood; but that God calls each one whenever and however it pleases him. This holds for public offices, both civil and ecclesiastical. For some, by a special counsel of God, are brought up and trained in his service from boyhood, as may be said of Samuel and of the sons of the prophets, who are mentioned in the books of Kings. Others are called to the service of God and his Church only after they have left youth behind, reached manhood, and spent a good part of their life in another way of living. So Moses lived at the Egyptian court before he took up the care of the people of God; Elisha and Amos followed a rustic and pastoral life before they became prophets; the apostles were fishermen and tax collectors. Paul, although he had been set apart for the Gospel from his mother's womb, nevertheless allowed himself to be plunged into the pits of the Pharisees and to become a persecutor of the Church, and only afterwards did God draw him out, so that he might make him a chosen vessel and apostle. Similar things happen with private persons in respect of the actions, morals and pursuits of their lives. For some, born of godly parents, learn the true faith and religion from boyhood and are trained in the duties of piety. Others are so neglected while they are children that they cannot even pray, and only in adolescence find teachers who instruct them. Many spend even that time in ignorance, and dedicate their manhood too to vices and wicked opinions; then, when they approach the threshold of old age, they finally begin to think about their own salvation, so as to do some work in the vineyard of the Lord worthy of the Christian profession. Some are called only at the hour of death, like that thief who was Christ's companion on the cross. We have also seen it happen that some, when the twelfth hour of life is upon them, and their strength fails them worn out by sickness, and they feel the end of life drawing near, are enlightened by the Spirit of the Lord, so that they repent seriously of their misspent life, confess their sins with tears, implore the mercy of God, admonish their families to godliness, and, though about to die, do good work in the vineyard of the Lord, teaching many by their example and reminding them of their duties. God does all these things with a certain reason, and it is his to do in his own affairs as he pleases. But from the consideration of these cases we are admonished that there is no time of life that is not fit and suitable for the service of God, and that his grace is bound by no laws that would prevent it from shining upon those whom he deigns to call, at any age or in any condition. Therefore let us not rashly despair of anyone's salvation, but rather pray earnestly to God that he may effectively draw by his Spirit those who still stand idle, or who even now spend their time impiously in the wrestling-ground of Satan, not without public scandal, so that they may learn to serve him.

units.la: Interim omnes cuiuscunque loci aut aetatis sint, hac parte admonentur officij. Etsi diuersis horis ijsti vocentur, nemo tamen illorum Patrisfamilias respondauit: primi non queruntur, se nimis mane, vix dum Sole exorto, vocari, quando, qua coeli facies futura sit ignoretur: medij non cau-fati sunt aestum, quem meridies pariturus sit: postremis denique non ridiculum visum esset, si imminente iam crepusculo ad opus exeant: sed heri mandato omnes paruerunt: Idem faciant omnes, quandocunque vocantur a Deo. Si qui in pueritia statim destinentur ad Dei cultum & Ecclesiae ministerium, agnoscant Domini singularem bonitatem, qua ipsos prae multis alijs dignatur, dum non vult illos vllum vitae tempus inutiliter transigere. Similiter qui serius florente iam ipsorum iuuenta, dum aetas illos alio vocat, a Domino reuocantur, non detrectent officium. Qui vero vitae genus iam fuscepepunt non omnino laudabile, in quo fibijpsis potius, quam Deo seruierunt, aut otio suo consulere voluerunt, ijs non graue fit, illo relicto in Domini vineam abire, si ab eo mittantur. Deniq; si qui in extrema senecta demum vocentur, hos quoq; non pigeat mores & vitae genus mutare: pudeat potius, tam diu otiosam & inertem vitam egisse, aut diabolo seruiuisse, & agnoscant Dei beneficium, qui iam breui morituros gratia & honoris sui organa facere dignatur. Itaq; vt fidus & strenuus operarius, quo serius ad opus accedit, eo magis operari instat, vt breue illud temporis spacium, quod illi restat, bene collocet: ita facere decet Dei seruos, quando se breui hinc ad meliorem vitam migraturos esse sentiunt.
units.tr: Meanwhile, all men, of whatever place or age they are, are admonished in this part of their duty. Although those men were called at different hours, none of them answered the householder: the first did not complain that they were called too early in the morning, when the sun had scarcely risen and it was not known what the face of the sky would be; the middle workers did not complain of the heat the noon would bring; and it would not have seemed ridiculous even to the last, if they had gone out to work when dusk was already coming on; but all obeyed the master's command. Let all men do the same whenever they are called by God. If some are destined from childhood at once for the worship of God and the ministry of the Church, let them acknowledge the Lord's singular goodness, by which he deigns to honour them above many others, in that he does not wish them to spend any time of their life uselessly. Likewise, those who are called later by the Lord, when their youth is already in full flower and their age calls them elsewhere, should not shrink from the duty. But those who have already taken up a way of life that is not wholly praiseworthy, in which they have served themselves rather than God, or have chosen to look after their own leisure, should not find it hard to leave that behind and go into the Lord's vineyard, if he sends them. Finally, if some are called only in extreme old age, let them not be reluctant to change their habits and way of life; let them rather be ashamed to have lived so long an idle and useless life, or to have served the devil, and let them acknowledge the favour of God, who deigns to make instruments of his grace and honour those who are soon to die. Therefore, just as a faithful and diligent workman, the later he comes to the work, the more eagerly he works, so that he may make good use of the short span of time left to him, so the servants of God ought to act when they feel that they will soon migrate hence to a better life.

units.la: Quarto videamus quomodo & qua conditione isti operarij in vineam missi sint. Cum primis pacisci tur Paterfamilias denario in diem, cum alijs non item, sed simpliciter illis dicit: Quodcunque iustum fuerit dabo vobis, &c. Quoad primos, sunt qui meritum operum nostrorum hoc exemplo stabiliri contendunt, sed hi dum singulas parabolae partes curiosius examinant, extra oleas (quod dicitur) currunt, & multa diuinunt a Christi instituto & scopo aliena. Etenim si proprie loquendum sit, Deus nemini quicquam debet, suo autem iure ab omnibus hominibus debitum obsequium exigit: vtpote omnium creator & Dominus, in quo viuimus, monemur & sumus, & qui omnia agit in omnibus. Et licet ipsi praestemus quaecunque ille praecipit, serui tamen inutiles sumus, qui ex nobis ipsis nihil eorum fecimus, neque aliud fecimus, quam quod debuimus facere, ne aeternum periremus. Bonitatis ergo gratuita est, quod nobiscum pacisicitur Deus, & promissionibus laetat eos, quibus mandandi ius habet. In eo enim patres fidos imitatur, qui liberis munuscula pollicentur, vt sibi obsequentiores faciant eos, qui puerilibus desiderijs ab officio reuocari solent. In praesenti vero Paterfamilias ille bonus cum primis patius esse dicitur, vt postea illis ob gratiam alijs factam murmurantibus, constaret, nullam ipsis iniuriam fieri, cum pactam mercedem acceperint, sed ipsos potius iniuriam hero & socijs facere, qui illum in ordinem redigere consentur, ne quod vult de suo faciat, his vero inuideant illius liberalitatem, ex qua nihil damni adipsos redundabat. Alteros vero in vineam mittit, nulla certa mercede conductos, vt partim doceat, Deo liberum esse, vt nobiscum agat pro sua bona voluntate: partim vt nos officij admoneat, quod est ipsius vocationi simpliciter parere, non autem confidenter quaerere cum Petro: Quid erit nobis? quid praemij dabitur? Sed de hoc plura in ijs quae sequentur. Nunc discamus, nihil ex nobis instituere, sed Dei vocationem expectare: hac audita, simpliciter illi obedire, & eius voluntati nos subijcere. Ipsi denique fidere, qui iustius, verax, beneficus & liberalissimus remunerator est. Dedit hic nobis iam pridem Filium suum Vnigenitum, IESVM CHRISTVM, qui nobis ab illo factus est sapientia, iustitia, sanctificatio & redemptio. Is nos secum esse vult, vbi ipse est, & ad suam mensam in regno suo accumbere. Quid ergo praeterea quaerimus? Sufficiat, nos in suorum operariorum numero censeri & vt filius ille perditus non aliud quaerebat, quam vt in patris domo locum qualemcunque haberet: ita nobis
units.tr: Fourthly, let us consider how and on what terms these workers were sent into the vineyard. The householder agrees with the first group on a denarius a day, but with the others he makes no such agreement and simply tells them: "Whatever is right I will give you," and so on. As for the first group, there are some who try to establish the merit of our works from this example, but while they examine each part of the parable too closely, they wander off the track, as the saying goes, and draw many conclusions foreign to Christ's purpose and aim. For if we speak strictly, God owes nothing to anyone, but by his own right he demands the obedience owed to him from all people, since he is the creator and Lord of all, in whom we live, move and have our being, and who works all things in all. And even though we perform whatever he commands, we are still unprofitable servants, since we have done none of it by our own power and have done no more than our duty, so that we might not perish forever.
