It is therefore out of goodness, and not by obligation, that God makes a bargain with us and encourages those to whom he has the right to give orders with promises. In this he imitates good fathers, who promise small gifts to their children so as to make them more obedient, since children are usually called away from their duty by childish desires. In this parable, however, the householder is described as having first agreed on wages, so that when the others later grumbled at the grace shown to them, it would be clear that no wrong was done to them, since they had received the wage agreed upon, and that they rather did wrong to the master and to their fellow workers, who are judged to be trying to bring him into line, so that he may not do what he wishes with his own, and who begrudge his generosity, from which no loss came to them. The others, however, he sends into the vineyard, hired without any fixed wage, to teach partly that it is free for God to deal with us according to his good will, and partly to remind us of our duty, which is simply to obey his call, and not to ask with confidence, as Peter did: "What will there be for us? What reward will be given?" But more on this in what follows. Now let us learn that we should undertake nothing on our own initiative, but await God's call; once we have heard it, we should simply obey him and submit ourselves to his will. Finally, we should trust him, who is the most just, truthful, bountiful and most generous rewarder. He has long since given us his only-begotten Son, Jesus Christ, who has been made by him our wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption. He wishes us to be with him where he is, and to recline at his table in his kingdom. What more, then, do we seek? Let it suffice that we are counted among his workers, just as that lost son sought nothing more than to have some kind of place in his father's house. So let us think ourselves

units.la: Deum vocantem omnes ie qui debent. abunde satisfactum putemus, si nos Deus vilissimorum seruulorum loco habere dignetur: nec de premio nostro, sed potius de nostro officio soliciti simus. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Calling God to all who owe. fully repaid if God deigns to count us as the lowliest of servants, and let us be concerned not about our reward but rather about our duty. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power forever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCXXXVI.
units.tr: HOMILY 236.

units.la: Cum autem serum diei esset, dicit Dominus vineae procuratori suo: Voca operarios, & redde eis mercedem, incipiens ab vltimis vsque ad primos. Et cum venissent qui circa vndecimam horam exierant, acceperunt singuli denarium. Venientes autem & primi, existimarunt se plus esse accepturos: sed acceperunt, ipsi quoque singuli denarium. Et cum accepissent, murmurabant aduersus patrem familias, dicentes: Isti vltimi vnam horam opus fecerunt, & eos aequales nobis fecisti, qui portauimus pondus diei & aestum. Ipse vero respondens dixit vni eorum: Amice, non facio tibi iniuriam: nonne denario pactus es mecum? Tolle quod tuum est, & abi. Volo autem huic vltimo dare, vt & tibi. An non licet mihi quod volo facere in meis? An oculus tuus malus est, quia ego bonus sum? Sic erunt vltimi primi, & primi vltimi. Multi enim sunt vocati, pauci vero electi.
units.tr: When evening had come, the lord of the vineyard said to his steward: "Call the workers and pay them their wages, beginning with the last and ending with the first." And when those who had been hired about the eleventh hour came, each of them received a denarius. But when the first also came, they thought they would receive more; yet each of them likewise received a denarius. And when they had received it, they grumbled against the householder, saying: "These last men have worked only one hour, and you have made them equal to us, who have borne the burden of the day and the heat." But he answered one of them: "Friend, I am not wronging you. Did you not agree with me for a denarius? Take what is yours and go. But I wish to give this last man as much as I give you. Am I not allowed to do what I wish with what is mine? Or is your eye evil because I am good?" So the last will be first, and the first last. For many are called, but few are chosen.

units.la: Audiuimus nuper primam huius parabolae partem, in qua Deus adumbratur sub persona frugi ac fidi patrisfamilias, qui diuersis horis toto pene die operarios conduxit, quos ad opus faciendum misit in suam vineam. Vbi didicimus, Deo omnibus saeculis fuisse Ecclesiam, cuius ille curam diligentem semper habuit, vt ei de operarijs siue colonis prospiceret. Mittuntur autem isti non omnes eadem hora, sed diuersis horis (vt diximus) vt doceat, de nullius hominis salute temere desperandum esse. Potest enim fieri, vt qui nondum vocatus ad opus Domini magnam vitae suae partem in otio ignauo & inhonesto transegit, adhuc vocetur: Curent modo omnes, vt quando vocantur, se Deo obsequentes praebeant, & pro suae vocationis aut functionis ratione in opere suo fideles sint & indefessi. Ad omnes enim pertinet, quod Ieremias dicit: Maledictus, qui fecerit opus Domini maligne. Sequitur altera parabolae pars, quae narratur, vt operarijs singulis mercedem redderit paterfamilias, quid item fecerint primi illi, qui mane vocati plus alijs laborauerant, & vt his murmurantibus ille responderit. Qui locus docebit, qui fiat, vt ex primis vltimi fiant: imo vt qui reliquis praestare videntur in opere Domini, a salute prorsus excidant.
units.tr: We heard the first part of this parable recently, in which God is shadowed forth under the figure of a thrifty and faithful householder, who hired workers at different hours, almost throughout the whole day, and sent them to do the work in his vineyard. There we learned that the Church has existed for God in every age, and that he has always taken diligent care of it, so that he might provide for it workers or tenants. These men, however, are not all sent at the same hour, but at different hours (as we said), to teach us that no one's salvation should be rashly despaired of. For it can happen that a man who has not yet been called to the work of the Lord, and has spent a great part of his life in idle, lazy and dishonourable leisure, may still be called. Let everyone take care only that, when they are called, they present themselves obedient to God, and that, according to the nature of their calling or office, they be faithful and untiring in their work. For what Jeremiah says applies to all: "Cursed is he who does the work of the Lord deceitfully." There follows the second part of the parable, which tells how the householder paid each of the workers, what those first men did who, being called in the morning, had laboured more than the others, and how he answered them when they grumbled. This passage will teach how it comes about that the last become first, or rather, how those who seem to excel the rest in the work of the Lord may fall utterly from salvation.

units.la: Ier. 48.
units.tr: Jer. 48.

units.la: Cum iam ferum esset diei, procurator suo in mandatis dat herus, vt operarijs singulis mercedem reddat, initio facto a postremis, qui sub horam vndecimam demum in vineam missi erant, & quoad morem vulgo receptum, non poterant multum sperare, cum vix horam vnam fuissent in opere. Ab his (inquam) procurator initium facere, & ad primos vsq; progredi debuit, cum quibus paterfamilias denario in diem pactus erat. Procurator iste Dei est IESVS CHRISTVS, aeternus Dei Filius, cui omnis potestas data in caelo & in terra, & qui solus habet clauem domus Dauidis, siue regni caelorum. Hic in fine mundi veniet, vt suam mercedem reddat omnibus, tam bonis quam malis. In praesenti vero docere vult, salute non pro meritorum nostrorum ratione coniunctus, sed prout Deo placet, & qui nam operarij prae caeteris ipsi placeant. Primi certa mercede conducti fuerunt, vtpote homines venales, & (vt ex eorum murmure postea colligi potest) fortasse non abituri in vineam, nisi hanc pactus illis effet herus. At caeteri omnes, cum nihil certum ipsis polliceretur, sed simpliciter eis diceret, Quodcunque iustum fuerit, dabo vobis: eius bonitate & aequitate confisi abierunt. Qui tales sunt, ij reipsa testantur, se indutios esse & operis faciendi cupidos, ne-
units.tr: When it was already late in the day, the master ordered his steward to pay each of the workers their wage, beginning with the last, who had been sent into the vineyard only at the eleventh hour and, by the usual custom, could not expect much, since they had scarcely been at work for one hour. It was from these (I say) that the steward ought to begin and proceed as far as the first, with whom the householder had agreed on a denarius a day. This steward is Jesus Christ, the eternal Son of God, to whom all power in heaven and on earth has been given, and who alone holds the key of the house of David, that is, of the kingdom of heaven. He will come at the end of the world to pay his wage to all, good and bad alike. Yet in the present he wishes to teach that salvation is not joined to the measure of our merits, but is given as pleases God, and that it is those workers whom he likes above the rest who receive it. The first were hired at a fixed wage, as men who worked for money and (as can later be gathered from their grumbling) perhaps would not have gone into the vineyard unless the master had agreed this with them. But all the others, since he promised them nothing certain and simply said, "Whatever is just I will give you," went off trusting in his goodness and fairness. Those who are such show by their deeds that they are diligent and eager to work, and they neglect no opportunity to do so. And these now receive their wage first. So they please God above the rest. Though they may stand idle for a long time and seem about to do nothing, yet they are held by an earnest desire to labour, and as soon as they are called they eagerly seize the opportunity offered, and they do what he commands with all the strength he gives. Nor do they look to the wage in a servile way, but depend on God's goodness, whom they firmly believe to be a generous rewarder, yet so that they prescribe nothing to him. Hence they are content with what is given, since they know they have deserved nothing, but are unprofitable servants who have done only what duty required. Surely this is true piety, this is the character of sincere faith, without which no one can please God, and which alone lays hold of the life and salvation that Christ has acquired for us. Therefore those endowed with these qualities are reckoned the first in the kingdom of heaven.

units.la: Matth. 18. Apoc. 3. 2. Cor. 4. Operarij qui Deo placeant prae alijs. dos, neque aliquam eius occasionem negligunt. Et ijdem nunc primi mercedem recipiunt. Itaque prae caeteris placent Deo, qui etsi diu otiosi stent, nec quicquam facturi videntur, tamen serio illi jerkuendi desiderio tenentur, & quam primum vocantur, occasionem oblatam avidè arripiunt, & quantum ille virium largitur sedulò faciunt quod iubet, nec seruiliter ad mercedem respiciunt, sed a Dei bonitate pendent, quem liberalem remuneratorem esse firmiter credunt: ita tamen, ut nihil illi praescribant. Contenti ergo sunt eo quod datur, utpote quod sciant se nihil meruisse, sed seruos inutiles esse, qui nihil quam quod ex officio debebant, fecerint. Atqui haec vera pietas, hoc fidei syncerae ingenium est, sine qua nemo potest Deo placere, & quae sola apprehenditur vita salusque, quam nobis Christus acquisiuit: ideoque, qui haec praediti sunt, primi in regno coelorum censentur.
units.tr: Matth. 18. Apoc. 3. 2. Cor. 4. Workers who please God above others. Those who are such truly show that they are diligent and eager to work, and they neglect no opportunity to do so. And these now receive their wage first. So they please God above the rest. Though they may stand idle for a long time and seem about to do nothing, yet they are held by an earnest desire to labour, and as soon as they are called they eagerly seize the opportunity offered, and they do what he commands with all the strength he gives. Nor do they look to the wage in a servile way, but depend on God's goodness, whom they firmly believe to be a generous rewarder, yet so that they prescribe nothing to him. Hence they are content with what is given, since they know they have deserved nothing, but are unprofitable servants who have done only what duty required. Surely this is true piety, this is the character of sincere faith, without which no one can please God, and which alone lays hold of the life and salvation that Christ has acquired for us. Therefore those endowed with these qualities are reckoned the first in the kingdom of heaven.

units.la: His opponuntur primi, quibus certam mercedem pactus est paterfamilias, & quales se gesserint, narratur. Primum visa illius erga alios liberalitate, sperant se plus accepturos esse. Unde hoc? nimirum quod de suo labore, quem sustinuerunt magnificè sentiunt, & se aliis omnibus praeferunt. Deinde etsi recipiant quod ipsis ex pacto debebatur, eo tamen non contenti murmurant ad uerbus patremfamilias, a quo se duplici iniuria affectos putarunt: cum vltimos sibi praeferri viderent, quoad ordinem; & quod idem ipsis aequentur quoad mercedem diurnam, qui non totum diem cum ipsis in opere fuerant. Ex quo sequitur, quod dicta quaeruntur de hero, ut ne socijs quidem parcant, sed contemptim de his loquuntur, isti vltimi (inquiunt) vnam horam opus fecerunt & eos aequales nobis fecisti, &c. quasi dicerent: Isti totum diem otiosi steterunt, & ut solent ignaui, subduxerunt se, ne ab aliquo ad opus faciendum conducerentur: Quae ergo haec iniquitas est, quod nunc nobis aequantur, qui totius diei laborem & aestum magna cum molestia sustinuimus?
units.tr: Opposed to these are the first, with whom the householder agreed a fixed wage, and the narrative tells how they behaved. First, seeing his generosity toward others, they hope to receive more. Whence this? Plainly because they think highly of their own labour, which they have endured, and they prefer themselves to all others. Then, although they receive what was owed to them by agreement, they are not content with it but grumble against the householder, by whom they thought themselves wronged twice over: since they saw the last placed before them in order, and that they were made equal to them in daily wage, though those had not been with them in the work the whole day. From this it follows that they complain about the master and do not even spare their fellow-workers, speaking of them with contempt: "These last (they say) did one hour's work, and you have made them equal to us," and so on, as if they said: "These men stood idle all day, and like lazy fellows kept themselves away so that no one would hire them for work. What injustice is this, that they are now made equal to us, who have borne the labour and heat of the whole day with great trouble?"

units.la: Exprimuntur hic ceu in speculo hypocritarum iustitiariorum mores & ingenium. Nituntur hi suorum operum meritis, & ideo haec magni aestimant. Exemplum habes apud Isaiam, qui tales cum a Deo corriperentur, ita huic respondentes introducit: Quare ieiunauimus, & tu non aspicis? affligimus animas nostras, & tu ignoras? Et apud Micheam superbe quaerunt, quid porro facere debeant, tantumno dicentes: Si non sufficiunt quae fecimus, age dic quid praeterea velis, nec in nobis mora erit, qui & volumus & possumus quicquid iusseris. Quorum similis Pharisaeus ille, quem Christus apud Lucam producit, dicentem: Gratias ago tibi, quod non sum ut reliqui homines rapaces, iniusti, moechi, vel etiam ut iste Publicanus: Ieiuno bis in hebdomade, decimo omnia quae possideo, &c. Et huius generis multa hodie audiuntur ex ore hypocritarum nostri saeculi. At si diligentius examinentur omnia illorum opera, quae tantopere illi iactant, fere nullius pretij illa esse patebit. Nam si quid faciunt boni, ex debito faciunt. Non habent ergo, quo glorientur: idque eo minus, quod non suis viribus illud faciunt, sed a Dei Spiritu excitati, qui certis de causis interdum in hypocritis vel palam impijs quoque agit. Caeterae ferè eiusmodi sunt, ut neque ad Dei gloriam faciant, neque vllis hominibus prosint, & ne illis ipsis quidem qui eis fatigantur. Quod enim de Iudaeorum ieiunijs olim Deus per Zachariam dixit: Quando ieiunastis & planxistis mense quinto & septimo per annos istos septuaginta, num ieiunando mihi ieiunastis? Et cum comeditis et bibitis, annon vobis comeditis, & vobis bibitis? Hoc ipsum de feriis, de peregrinationibus, vigiliis, cucullis, cantionibus & omnibus aliis potest dici, quae ab illis nullo Dei mandato, sed ex humanarum traditionum praescripto fiunt. Adde quod multa faciunt, quae Deo vehementer displicent, ut quando idola colunt, sacra cauponantur, vsum Coenae Dominicae peruertunt, ex mortuis tributa exigunt, et in his aliisque multis meritu aeternae salutis collocant, non sine atroci iniuria, quae Christo faciunt, cui soli haec gloria debetur: Verumtamen tanti ista faciunt, ut coelum sibi soli deberi existiment, & aliis omnibus salute inuideant, neque ferre possint eius doctrinae praedicationem, quae peccatoribus gratuitam omnium delictorum remissionem in nomine IESV CHRISTI annuntiat. Et hac causa est, quod contra bonum illum Patremfamilias impie murmurant, cuius bonitatem gratuitam exosculari & praedicare debebant. Hoc alibi fecisse scimus Pharisaeos, quando Christum cum publicanis familiarius versari videbant. Et hodie passim audiuntur sermones istorum hominum, quos non pudet dicere: Si propter solam fidem in Christum gratis iustificamur, si nullum est nostrorum operum meritum, frustra vtique seruitur Deo, frustra bonis operibus studetur, nequicquam carnis lasciuientis nequitia castigatur: Quin ergo facimus quicquid carnis libido dicat, ut locum habeat gratia Dei, & abundantior fiat? Denique Euangelij doctrinam isti homines bonis operibus inimicam esse clamitant, adeoq; Christum omnis licentiae scelerum authorem fingunt: Quia blasphemia nulla atrocior fingi poterat. Annon ergo digni sunt isti, qui ex primis vltimi fiant, & ab Ecclesia & regni Dei societate prorsus excludantur? Haec certe causa fuit, quod Christus sacerdotibus & senioribus Iudaeorum postea dixit: Amen dico vobis, quod publicani & meretrices praecedunt vos in regnum Dei. Matth.21.
units.tr: Here, as in a mirror, the character and disposition of hypocritical self-righteous men are displayed. They rely on the merits of their works, and therefore they value them highly. You have an example in Isaiah, who introduces such men, when they were rebuked by God, answering him thus: "Why have we fasted, and you do not look? We afflict our souls, and you take no notice?" And in Micah they proudly ask what further they ought to do, saying only: "If what we have done is not enough, come, tell us what else you want, and there will be no delay on our part, for we are willing and able to do whatever you command." Like them is that Pharisee whom Christ brings forward in Luke, saying: "I thank you that I am not like other men, grasping, unjust, adulterers, or even like this tax collector. I fast twice a week, and I give a tenth of all that I possess," etc. And many such things are heard today from the mouths of hypocrites in our own age. But if all their works, which they boast of so greatly, are examined more carefully, it will be clear that they are almost of no worth at all. For if they do anything good, they do it as a debt owed. They have, therefore, nothing to boast of, and all the less so because they do it not by their own strength, but by being stirred up by the Spirit of God, who for certain reasons sometimes also works even in openly impious men. The rest of their works are for the most part of such a kind that they serve neither the glory of God nor any men, not even those who are wearied by them. For what God once said through Zechariah about the fasts of the Jews applies: "When you fasted and mourned in the fifth and seventh months, for these seventy years, did you truly fast for me? And when you eat and drink, do you not eat and drink for yourselves?" The same can be said of holy days, pilgrimages, vigils, cowls, chants, and all the other things which they do, not by any command of God, but by the prescription of human traditions. Add to this that they do many things which greatly displease God: as when they worship idols, make merchandise of sacred things, pervert the use of the Lord's Supper, exact tributes from the dead, and place in these and many other things the merit of eternal salvation, not without a dreadful wrong done to Christ, to whom alone this glory is owed. Yet they hold these things in such high esteem that they think heaven is owed to themselves alone, and they envy all others their salvation, and cannot bear the preaching of that doctrine which announces to sinners the free remission of all sins in the name of Jesus Christ. And for this reason they grumble impiously against that good householder, whose free goodness they ought rather to embrace and proclaim. We know that the Pharisees did the same elsewhere, when they saw Christ associating too familiarly with tax collectors. And today such talk is heard everywhere from these men, who are not ashamed to say: "If we are justified freely by faith alone in Christ, if our works have no merit at all, then surely it is in vain that we serve God, in vain that we strive after good works, to no purpose that the wickedness of the lascivious flesh is restrained. Why then should we not do whatever the lust of the flesh says, so that the grace of God may have room and become more abundant?" In short, these men cry out that the doctrine of the Gospel is hostile to good works, and so they imagine Christ to be the author of every licence and sin. Since no more atrocious blasphemy could be invented, are not these men worthy to become last from being first, and to be utterly excluded from the Church and from fellowship in the kingdom of God? This was certainly the reason why Christ later said to the priests and elders of the Jews: "Truly I say to you, that tax collectors and harlots go before you into the kingdom of God." Matth. 21.

units.la: Sed audiamus quid herus ipse mercenarijs istis responderit? Vni eorum dixisse illum, ait Dominus: Amice, non facio tibi iniuriam, &c. Exprimitur rursum paterna Dei bonitas ac indulgentia, qui adhuc amicos vocare dignatur, iniquos illos murmuratores, qui in ipsum & socios laborum injurii erant: Huic simile est, quod Christus Iudae proditori in osculum eius ruenti postea dixit: Amice, ad quid addes? Debent exempla eiusmodi non ofcitanter observari, ut pudeat Christianos homines, quae impotentia, qui ob lenissimam offensam charitati fraternae renuntiant, & insuper linguas ad contumelias & execrationes laxant, quibus in Deum simul & homines graviter peccatur. Porro responsionis huius partes sunt tres: Prima suum factum excusat Paterfamilias: Secunda obiectioni respondet, quam murmuratores poterant praetexere: Postrema acriter corripit illorum nequitiam, qui ex eius bonitate invidiae, odij & murmuris occasionem arripiant.
units.tr: But let us hear what the master himself answered those hired workers. The Lord says that he spoke to one of them: "Friend, I do you no wrong," and so on. Here again God's fatherly goodness and kindness is expressed, since he still deigns to call friends those unfair grumblers who were angry with him and with their fellow labourers. Similar is what Christ later said to Judas the traitor when he rushed to kiss him: "Friend, why have you come?" Examples like these should not be passed over carelessly, so that Christians may be ashamed of how impatient they are, who renounce brotherly love over the slightest offence, and who loose their tongues in insults and curses, by which they sin gravely against God and against men. Moreover, this answer has three parts. First, the householder excuses his own action. Second, he answers the objection the grumblers might have raised. Last, he sharply rebukes the wickedness of those who seize on his goodness as an occasion for envy, hatred and complaint.

units.la: Prima partis propositio est, Non facio tibi iniuriam. Unde sequitur, illum iniustum esse, qui murmuret & de ipso quaeritur. Id vero evidenti ratione probat, dicens: Nonne denario pactus es mecum? Poterat dicere: Si qui accipiant quod eis ex pacto debetur, non habent illi iustam quiritandi occasionem: Atqui ego denario in diem operam tuam conduxi: Ergo cum hunc tibi reddam iniquè tu contra me murmuras. Quin accipis quod tuum est, & eo contentus me mittum facis? Voluit autem interrogatione vrgere murmuratorem iniquum, ut proprio testimonio convictum magis confunderet. Possunt autem hoc argumento in genere omnes conuinci, qui de Deo conqueruntur & aduersus illum murmurant, si non omnia ex sui animi voto accipiunt. Nam si iniuste queruntur qui quod ipsis debetur, accipiunt: quanto maior est eorum iniquitas, qui cum plura, quam quae debentur, recipiant, nihilominus tamen de Dei bonitate aut iniustitia quiritantur? Atqui nemo est mortalium, qui non plura acceperit, & quotidie adhuc accipiat a Deo, quam ipsi debetur. Etenim hic nos omnes condidit, cum nulli effemus: hic nobis spiritum vitae largitur, & in ipso viuimus, movemur & sumus: hic nos alit, vestit, feruat, imo in nobis alendis & feruandis omnes creaturas occupatas habet, adeo ut Angelos quoq; nobis ministros & defensores adhibeat. Sunt haec magna, & omnem gratiarum actionem superant, nedum ut aliquid horum nobis deberi, dicere possimus. Accedunt tamen his maiora, quae omnem quoq; humani ingenij captum excedunt: quod nimirum Filium suum Vnigenitum pro nobis dedit, qui aeternam mortem merebamur, quod illum nobis fecit iustitiam, sanctificationem & redemptionem nostram: quod in eodem nos adoptauit, ut ex irafilijs, filij gratia & bonorum eius omnium haeredes fieremus: quod eundem nobis ingratis, inobedientibus, & vix vnquam serio de salute cogitantibus, per Euangelium offert, & plerunq; reluctantes ad regni sui caelestis possessionem inuitat. An non ergo plura dat Deus, quam mereamur? annon plura ab eo accepimus, & quotidie adhuc recipimus, quam ille nobis debeat? Imo si nihil horum daret, si nos fame et siti emori sineret, si perpetuis morbis discrucciaret, si quoad animam & corpus perderet, dicendum nobis esset, si quidem quod verum est vellemus dicere: Iustus es Domine, & iudicia tua sunt iustitia & veritas. Quae ergo improbitas & nequitia est, patri tam indulgenti obloqui, & de eius iustitia conqueri, qui si pro meritis nos tractaret, in aeternum nobis pereundum esset.
units.tr: The first part of his reply is the statement, "I do you no wrong." From this it follows that the one who grumbles and complains against him is unjust. He proves this by an evident argument, saying: "Did you not agree with me for a denarius?" He could have said: those who receive what is owed to them by agreement have no just cause to complain. But I hired your labour for a denarius a day. Therefore, when I give you this, it is wrongly that you complain against me. Why do you not take what is yours and be content, and send me on my way? He chose to press the unjust grumbler with a question, so that, convicted by his own testimony, he would be more thoroughly put to shame. And in general, all who complain about God and murmur against him, if they do not receive everything according to the desire of their own heart, can be convicted by this same argument. For if those who receive what is owed to them complain unjustly, how much greater is the injustice of those who, though they receive more than is owed, still complain about God's goodness or injustice? Yet there is no mortal who has not received more, and does not still receive every day from God, than is owed to him. For here he created us all when we were nothing; here he gives us the breath of life, and in him we live, move and have our being; here he feeds, clothes and preserves us; indeed, in feeding and preserving us he employs all creatures, so that he also uses angels as our ministers and defenders. These are great gifts, and they surpass all thanksgiving, so that we could not say any of them is owed to us. Yet there are greater things added to these, which exceed even the grasp of human understanding: that he gave his only-begotten Son for us, though we deserved eternal death; that he made him our righteousness, sanctification and redemption; that in the same Son he adopted us, so that from children of wrath we might become children, heirs of grace and of all his good things; that he offers the same Son to us through the gospel, though we are ungrateful and disobedient and scarcely ever think seriously of salvation, and he often invites us, though we resist, to possess his heavenly kingdom. Does God not then give more than we deserve? Have we not received, and do we not still receive every day, more from him than he owes us? Indeed, if he gave none of these things, if he let us die of hunger and thirst, if he tormented us with constant sickness, if he destroyed us in soul and body, we would have to say, if we wished to speak the truth: "You are righteous, O Lord, and your judgments are just and true." What wickedness and depravity is it, then, to speak against so kind a Father and to complain about his justice, when, if he dealt with us according to our deserts, we would have to perish for ever?

units.la: Sed Iosmachum monuit mercenarijs illis, quod ipsis pactam mercedem postremis quoque reddit, qui minus operis fecerant in vinea, quod iniuste & contra iustitiae distributiuae leges factum arbitrantur. Et hoc est, quod hodie quoq; multos offendit. Etenim audiuntur obiectiones non tam iniquae quam acerbae, quibus Deum tantum non in ius vocant aliqui, dum quaerunt: Cur hic serua-tur, & iam moriturus in gratiam recipitur, qui praeteritam vitam omne in sceleribus transegit? Cur hunc diuitijs beat Deus, ad honores euehit, me vero cum inopia conflictari, contemptum & exosum plerisque in sordibus iacere sinit? Cur denique bonis & malis, iustis & iniustis benefacit? Cur eadem gratia mecum dignatur multos, qui non tam multa pro eius nomine fecerunt aut passi sunt, quàm multa ego feci & pertuli? Sed his quoq; breuiter respondet Dominus: Volo huic vltimo dare vt & tibi. Liberam suam voluntatem allegat, & hac omnes ratiocinationes carnis abrumpit, vt se eum esse offendat, qui nemini teneatur rationem reddere, vtpote qui omnium Dominus, & proinde nulli legi subiectus sit. Ideo addit: An non licet mihi quod volo facere in meis? Enimuero hæc natura lex est, quæ communi sensu probatur, & vulgo inter homines recepta est, quacunq; licet de suis statuere vt libet, & prout sibi utile ac commodum videtur, si quidem id absque alterius fraude & iniuria fiat: Id autem ego facio, inquit Dominus. Tu iam recepisti quod tibi debebatur, neq; vllo iure amplius quid a me potes exigere. Quid vero ad te, quod tantundem aliis quoq; largior, cum id ex meo faciam, & absq; tuo incommodo? Debent hoc respönsum sibi ipsis applicare, quotquot rationem iudiciorum suorum a Deo exigere audent, & si quid eis iniquius aut absurdius esse videtur, cogitent omnia illius nutu gubernari, qui non solum omnipotens, sed etiam perfecte bonus & iustus est. Hic (vt mater Samuelis canebat) neci dat, & vitæ restituit: deiicit & eneruit: pauperem facit & ditem: In ipsius deniq; manu sumus vt lutum figuli. Cur ergo ei non liceat de nobis statuere pro suo arbitrio, sicuti figulo licet facere ex luto vas qualecunq;, ipsi placuerit. Hæc consideratio multis quæstionibus finem imponit, quæ circa prouidentiam & prædestinationis diuinæ negotium ab hominibus vel prophanis vel impiè curiosis moventur & simul patientia nos armat, & ne quid temerè contra Deum dicamus aut faciamus prohibet, si quid nobis præter animi voluntatem accidit.
units.tr: But he reminded those workers that he pays the agreed wage to the last too, even to those who had done less work in the vineyard, which they judge to have been done unjustly and against the laws of distributive justice. And this is what still offends many today. For there are heard objections, not so much unfair as bitter, by which some almost summon God to court, asking: Why is this man spared, and why is he received into grace when he is about to die, though he has spent his whole past life in wickedness? Why does God enrich this man, raise him to honours, while he lets me struggle in poverty, lying despised and hated by most in squalor? Why, finally, does he do good to both good and bad, just and unjust? Why does he deign to show the same grace to many who have not done or suffered so much for his name as I have done and endured? But the Lord answers these briefly too: "I wish to give to this last one as much as to you." He claims his free will, and by this he cuts off all the reasonings of the flesh, showing that he is one who owes an account to no one, since he is Lord of all and therefore subject to no law. So he adds: "Is it not lawful for me to do what I wish with my own?" Indeed, this is a law of nature, approved by common sense and generally accepted among men: that anyone may decide about his own things as he pleases, and as seems useful and convenient to himself, provided this is done without fraud or injury to another. "But I do this," says the Lord. "You have already received what was owed to you, and by no right can you demand anything more from me. But what business is it of yours that I give as much to others also, since I do this with what is mine and without any loss to you?" All who dare to demand an account of God's judgments should apply this answer to themselves, and if anything seems to them unjust or absurd, let them consider that all things are governed by the nod of him who is not only almighty but also perfectly good and just. He (as the mother of Samuel sang) kills and makes alive; he brings down and raises up; he makes poor and rich; in short, we are in his hand like clay in the potter's hand. Why then should it not be lawful for him to decide about us at his own will, just as a potter may make of clay whatever vessel he pleases? This consideration puts an end to many questions which profane men, or those impiously curious, raise about providence and the matter of divine predestination; it also arms us with patience, and forbids us to say or do anything rashly against God if something happens to us contrary to our desire.

units.la: His subiicitur acris & vehemens correptio, quam omnes merentur, qui in Dei iudiciis affectui carnis indulgent. Aic enim sub patrisfamilias persona: An oculus tuus malus est, quia ego bonus sum. Oculum malum dicit pro inuido & aliorum commoda dolente. Vt enim visus inter sensus corporis nobilissimus habetur, ita animi affectiones per illum in oculis maximè se produnt: quales sunt, ira, amor, tristitia sive dolor, gaudium, & in primis inuidia seu odium. Itaq; sensus verborum est: Eiusmodi ne est, vt tu alijs inuidendi occasionem ex mea bonitate vel liberalitate arripias? Perstringitur autem hoc dicto præcipua causa murmurationum & querimoniarum, quibus contra charitatis fraternæ leges in proximum, & in Deum ipsum peccatur. Est hæc inuidia, quam innatam nobis philautia pririt. Perhincfit, quòd dum nobis melius esse volumus quàm aliis, nobis debere patemus quæcunq; alij obtinguunt commoda. Quæ causa est, vt aliis inuideamus, & simul Deum iniustitiæ accusemus, vt qui nobis negletis beneficia sua in ingratiores conferat. Id vero sine manifesta impietate & atroci, quæ Deus ipse affligitur, iniuria non potest fieri. Itaque hæc maximorum scelerum causa est, & diaboli filios facit, sicuti in Caini exemplo est videre. Quotquot ergo inuidiæ fascino se tenere sentiunt, primò cogitent bonorum omnium quæ vel ipsis vel aliis obtingunt, auctorem esse Deum, qui vt natura bonus est, erga omnes, ita iustus quoque est, & ideo iniquos esse, qui eius beneficentiam reprehendunt. Deinde meminerint, inuidos non tam alijs, quàm sibi ipsis nocere. Ethnicus error est, quo creditur inuidos aut maleficos homines oculorum fascino infantibus aut etiam pecoribus nocere posse. Ideò pastor ille Vergilianus dicebat: Nescio quis teneros oculos mihi fascinet agnos.
units.tr: To this is added a sharp and vehement rebuke, which all deserve who indulge the desires of the flesh in judging God's judgments. For he speaks in the person of the householder: "Is your eye evil because I am good?" By "evil eye" he means the envious man who grieves at the advantages of others. For just as sight is considered the noblest of the bodily senses, so the affections of the mind show themselves especially in the eyes: such as anger, love, sadness or grief, joy, and above all envy or hatred. So the sense of the words is: Is it your disposition to seize on my goodness or generosity as an occasion for envying others? This saying singles out the chief cause of murmurings and complaints, by which men sin against the laws of brotherly love towards their neighbour and against God himself. This is the envy which self-love produces in us by nature. It comes from this, that while we want to be better off than others, we think we ought to have all the advantages that others obtain. This is the reason why we envy others and at the same time accuse God of injustice, as if he were conferring his benefits on the more ungrateful while neglecting us. But this cannot happen without manifest impiety and a grievous injury, by which God himself is wounded. Therefore this is the cause of the greatest crimes, and it makes men children of the devil, as is seen in the example of Cain. Therefore, all who feel themselves held by the spell of envy should first consider that God is the author of all the good things that come either to themselves or to others; that as he is good by nature towards all, so he is also just, and therefore those are unjust who find fault with his beneficence. Then let them remember that envious people harm not so much others as themselves. It is a pagan error to believe that envious or malicious men can harm infants or even cattle by the spell of the evil eye. Hence that shepherd of Virgil said: "I know not who is bewitching my tender lambs with his eye."

units.la: At pij & quæcunq; ad eos pertinent, sub Dei tutela sunt, vt neque Satan ipse, qui inuidiæ & odij parens est, illis possit nocere. Quid ergo homines inuidi aut malitiosi faciant aliud, quàm quòd sibi ipsis nocent, & cor proprium exedunt, atque alijs inuidendo contabescunt. Recte igitur poeta Satyricus dixit: Inuidia Siculi non inuenere tyranni Tormentum maius. Et alius item de illo cecinit: Et videt ingratos intabescitq; videndo Successus hominum carpitq; & carpitur vnà.
units.tr: But the godly, and all that belongs to them, are under God's protection, so that not even Satan himself, the parent of envy and hatred, can harm them. What, then, do envious and malicious men achieve, except that they harm themselves, eat away at their own heart, and waste away by envying others? Rightly, therefore, the satirical poet said: "The tyrants of Sicily have not invented a greater torment than envy." And another poet likewise sang of him: "He sees the ungrateful, and wastes away by seeing the successes of men; he gnaws and is gnawed at the same time."

units.la: Procul ergo hanc pestem arceant Christiani homines, quorum nota propria est fraterna & mutua dilectio, cuius exemplum ipsis Dei Filius præbuit.
units.tr: Let Christian people therefore keep this plague far away, since their distinguishing mark is brotherly and mutual love, of which the Son of God himself has given them the example.

units.la: In primis vero moneat, quod Christus postquam hoc Patrisfamilias responsum exposuit, statum parabola totius repetit, dicens: Sic vltimi erunt primi, & primi vltimi. Quo dicto non solum vt prius ad humilitatem & diligentem salutis curam hortatur eos, qui aliquo vsque profecerunt, verum etiam docet, quae causa sit, quae vltimos faciat in regno Dei, vel etiam prorsus ab eo exclu-dat multos, qui primi esse videbantur: superba nimirum propria dignitatis & meritorum fiducia, quae inuidiam parit erga eos, quorum saluti nos congratulari decebat, & simul linguas contra Deum laxat, vt huius misericordiam gratuitam carpant, quibus vniuersa salutis spes in illa debebat esse reposita. Quis vero neget salute indignos esse eos, qui talia desiganant? Quia vero haec vitia fere innata sunt hominibus, & in plerisque dominantur, quoad non renascuntur ex verbi femine in nouas creaturas, aliud dictum aeque graue & vehemens subtexit, quo huius parabolae doctrinam concludit: Multi enim sunt vocati, pauci vero electi: qui videlicet Dei vocationem fide syncera sequantur, professioni suae respondeant, & fideles sint in vinea eius operarij. Sed quia de hac sententia commodius infra dicetur in nuptiarum & inuitatorum parabola, sufficiat nunc tenuisse, quanta sit bonitas Dei, qui nos in Ecclesiam suam vocare, & donis necessariis instruere dignatur: sequamur ergo vocantem, & huic fidele praestemus officium, vt olim cum Filio Dei aeterno, IESV CHRISTO, in caelis vinamus & regnemus, cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Above all, let them take note that Christ, after he had set out this answer of the householder, repeats the statement of the whole parable, saying: "So the last will be first, and the first last." By these words he not only exhorts to humility and to a diligent care for salvation those who have advanced to some degree, as he did before, but also teaches what the cause is that makes men last in the kingdom of God, or even wholly excludes from it many who seemed to be first: namely, the proud confidence in one's own dignity and merits. This gives rise to envy towards those on whose salvation we ought rather to rejoice, and at the same time it loosens the tongue against God, so that men carp at his free mercy, in which the whole hope of salvation ought to have been placed. Who, indeed, would deny that those who harbour such feelings are unworthy of salvation? Because these vices are almost innate in men, and rule over most of them, until they are born again from the seed of the Word into new creatures, he adds another saying no less weighty and forceful, with which he concludes the teaching of this parable: "For many are called, but few are chosen." That is, those who follow God's calling with sincere faith, answer to their profession, and are faithful workers in his vineyard. But since this saying will be discussed more fittingly below, in the parable of the marriage feast and of the invited guests, it is enough for now to have grasped how great is the goodness of God, who deigns to call us into his Church and to equip us with the necessary gifts. Let us therefore follow the one who calls, and render him faithful service, so that we may one day live and reign in heaven with the eternal Son of God, Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCXXXVII.
units.tr: HOMILY 237.

units.la: Et ascendens IESVS Hierosolymam, assumpsit duodecim discipulos suos priuatim in via, & dixit eis: Ecce ascendimus Ierosolymam, & Filius hominis tradetur principibus sacerdotum ac scribis, & condemnabunt eum morte. Tradentque eum gentibus, vt illudant & flagellent, & crucifigant: sed tertia die resurget.
units.tr: And Jesus, going up to Jerusalem, took the twelve disciples apart on the way and said to them: Behold, we go up to Jerusalem, and the Son of man shall be delivered to the chief priests and scribes, and they shall condemn him to death. And they shall deliver him to the Gentiles, to mock and scourge and crucify him; but on the third day he shall rise again.

units.la: Summa vitae Christianae & verae pietatis, quae promissionem habet praesentis & futuri seculi in eo consistit, vt communem regulam sectemur, quam Dei Filius IESVS CHRISTVS omnibus, qui eius discipuli censeri volunt, praescribit, dicens: Si quis vult post me venire, abneget semetipsum, & tollat crucem suam quotidie, & sequatur me. Quia vero carni nihil acerbius & magis aduersum est cruce, & plerique non ijs modo offenduntur, quae ipsis ferenda sunt, verum etiam ipsius Christi crux, vt olim Iudaeis, sic hodie multis scandalo est, qui sibi ipsis in illo omnia laeta & fecunda pollicentur: ipse frequenter de illa apud discipulos suos sermonem habuit, & quidem tunc potissimum, quando tempus illud praefinitum appropinquabat, quo mori debuit. Factum hoc nuper, quando illustrem illam fidei in ipsum confessionem omnium discipulorum nomine Petrus edidit. Nec multo post cum in monte Thabor se in clarificationis gloria speciandum exhibuisset discipulis tribus, inde descendens, ter mortis & resurrectionis suae mentionem repetijt. Et nunc idem facit denuo, quando iter Ierosolymitanum ingressus Ierichuntidi appropinquabat. Non pigeat ergo nos eadem saepius audire & meditari, de quibus ille, qui aeterna Dei sapientia est, toties verba facere dignatus est. Id vero vt in praesenti commodius fiat, hoc ordine locum iustum excutiamus: vt primum de loco dicatur, vbi ista Christus dixit: Deinde quibus haec dixerit, & qua occasione. Postremo, qua diligentia hoc factum sit.
units.tr: The sum of the Christian life and of true godliness, which has the promise of the present and future age, consists in this: that we follow the common rule which the Son of God, Jesus Christ, prescribes to all who wish to be counted his disciples, saying: If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross daily, and follow me. But because nothing is more bitter or more opposed to the flesh than the cross, and because many are offended not only by what must be borne by themselves, but also by the cross of Christ itself, which is a stumbling block to some today as it was to the Jews of old, who promise themselves everything joyful and fruitful in him, Christ often spoke of it with his disciples, and especially then, when the appointed time drew near in which he had to die. This happened lately, when Peter, speaking for all the disciples, made that famous confession of faith in him. Not long after, when he had shown himself to three of the disciples on Mount Tabor in the glory of his brightness to be gazed upon, and was coming down from there, he again three times mentioned his death and resurrection. And now he does the same again, when, having entered upon the journey to Jerusalem, he drew near to Jericho. Let us not be weary, then, of hearing and meditating often upon the things which he, who is the eternal wisdom of God, deigned to speak of so often. So that this may be done more profitably at present, let us examine the passage in this order: first, the place where Christ said these things is to be spoken of; then to whom he said them and on what occasion; and finally, with what care this was done.

units.la: Ad primum pertinet, quod Euangelista haec Christum dixisse scribit, cum ascenderet Ierosolymam. Ergo in via, quam fecit, vt Hierosolymae moreretur. Solet autem Scriptura fere Ascendendi verbo vti, quando de Hierosolyma loquitur, eo quod haec in monte sita, & circumquaque montibus cincta fuit (vt Psalmi docent) qui superandi fuerunt, si quis ad illam vellet peruenire. Fuit autem Hierosolyma typus caelestis patriae, vel etiam Ecclesiae triumphantis, quae (vt Paulus scribit) sursum vel in sublimi est, neque huius mundi vicibus incertis obnoxia. Sed & Ecclesia vniuersa caelestis & de caelo descendisse dicitur, eo quod caelitus ex Verbo Dei virtute Spiritus sancti regenerantur eius filij, qui ex corruptis & maledictis Adami filijs, Dei filios facit & caelestis regni haeredes: Quotquot ergo illius membra germana fieri & esse volunt, eos non terrenis inhaerere, sed animis in caelum per fidem euectis quae sursum sunt quaerere & sapere oportet. Illic enim (ut Apostolus ait) vita nostra abscondita est cum Christo in Deo, reuelabitur autem cum gloria in magno illo die, quando hic veniet ad iudicandum vivos & mortuos. Vide priorem Epistolam Ioannis 3. Cap.
units.tr: As to the first point, the Evangelist writes that Christ said these things as he was going up to Jerusalem. So he was on the way he took in order to die at Jerusalem. Scripture usually uses the word "to go up" when it speaks of Jerusalem, because the city lies on a mountain and is surrounded on every side by mountains (as the Psalms teach), which had to be climbed by anyone who wished to reach it. Jerusalem was a type of the heavenly fatherland, or even of the triumphant Church, which (as Paul writes) is above, on high, and not subject to the uncertain changes of this world. But the whole Church is also said to be heavenly and to have come down from heaven, because its sons are born again from heaven by the power of the Spirit through the Word of God, and he makes sons of God and heirs of the heavenly kingdom out of the sons of the corrupt and cursed Adam. Therefore, all who wish to be true members of that body ought not to cling to earthly things, but to seek and savour the things that are above, with their minds lifted up to heaven by faith. For there, as the Apostle says, our life is hidden with Christ in God, but it will be revealed with glory on that great day when he comes to judge the living and the dead. See the first Epistle of John, chapter 3.

units.la: Debet autem non officianter obseruari, quod Ierosolymam ad crucis supplicium ascendens Dominus discipulis suis de sua morte concionatur. Ita enim docet, quia via nos omnes ad caelestem patriam, quae beata immortalitatis sedes est, contendere oportear. Per crucem nimirum, quae in hoc mundo, quem vallem lachrymarum Scriptura vocat, nobis ferenda est. Etenim de eo nos admonere potest communis sensus, non alia via nos illuc peruenire posse, quam quae illue iuit, qui nobis illustrius suo merito acquisiuit. Ideo ipse ait: In mundo afflictionem habebitis. Et Apostoli eius Spiritu illuminati dixerunt: Per multas tribulationes oportet nos ingredi in regnum Dei. Item omnes qui volunt pie viuere in CHRISTO IESV, persecutionem patientur. Nec temere (ut initio diximus) ad crucem ille vocat omnes, qui eius discipuli esse cupiunt. Et sane ita fieri necesse est, ut mundi fastidium possimus concipere, qui carni nostrae ita adlubescit, ut si omnia in eo nobis iucunda acciderent, de caelesti patria nunquam cogitaturi eramus. Sed dum per huius mundi salebras & inhospita tesqua, per Labyrinthos item periculi plenos & per mille mortes nobis iter est, soletur nos, quod aeternus Dei Filius, non solum viam nobis monstrat, sed seipsum nobis viam facit, & eiusdem ducem, qui nobis praeit, & simul manum porrigit, atque grassius nostros dirigit, ne procul a tergo relicti deficiamus. Nouit enim bonus ille pastor oues suas, neque eas sibi ex manibus eripi finit. Idem vires suggerit infirmis, defendit item ab hostili vi, ne quid nocere possit ijs, qui ipsum fide intrepida sequuntur. Deniq; is est, qui omnia huius vitae aduersa & difficultates crucis merito sanctificauit, ut ipsum diligentibus omnia adiumento sint in bonum. Haec qui diligenter meditantur, ijs nulla afflictio tristis aut noxia esse poterit.
units.tr: Moreover, it should not be overlooked that the Lord, as he goes up to Jerusalem to the punishment of the cross, preaches to his disciples about his death. For he teaches that all of us must make our way by the road to the heavenly fatherland, which is the blessed seat of immortality. Namely, by the cross, which in this world, which Scripture calls a valley of tears, must be borne by us. Indeed, common sense can remind us of this: that we cannot reach that place by any other way than the one by which he went, who acquired it for us by his merit, more gloriously than anyone else. So he himself said: In the world you will have tribulation. And his Apostles, enlightened by his Spirit, said: We must enter the kingdom of God through many tribulations. Likewise, all who wish to live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution. Nor does he call all who wish to be his disciples to the cross without reason (as we said at the beginning). And indeed it must be so, that we may come to despise the world, which so pleases our flesh that, if everything in it turned out pleasantly for us, we would never think of the heavenly fatherland. But since our way lies through the rough places and inhospitable wastes of this world, and through labyrinths full of danger and a thousand deaths, we are consoled by the fact that the eternal Son of God not only shows us the way but makes himself the way for us, and is the leader who goes before us, and at the same time stretches out his hand and more firmly directs our steps, so that we, left behind, do not fail. For that good Shepherd knows his sheep, and does not allow them to be snatched from his hands. The same one supplies strength to the weak, and also defends them from hostile force, so that nothing can harm those who follow him with fearless faith. Finally, he is the one who has sanctified all the adversities of this life and the difficulties of the cross by his merit, so that all things work together for good to those who love him. For those who diligently meditate on these things, no affliction can be sad or harmful.

units.la: Secundo videamus, quibus & qua occasione Christus in praesenti locutus sit. Dicitur autem duodecim discipulos suos in via assumpsisse priuatim, & ista dixisse. Atqui ex alijs locis constat, magnam hominum multitudine in hac postrema profectione ipsum fuisse comitatum. Cur ergo solus discipulis mysterium hoc patefacit, cuius cognitio omnibus est necessaria? Cur non publice omnibus conuocatis de illo disseruit? Atqui vt id fieret, non necesse erat, & fortassis non profuisset. Quia enim pleriq; regnum terrenum somniabant, & huius seculi commoda penes illum quaerebat, pleriq; dilapsuri fuissent, si quid ipsi euenturum esset audiuissent. Atqui oportebat eius in vrbem ingressum illustrem esse, ut olim Zacharias praedixerat, & proderat quam plurimos esse spectato res mortis suae ex illis, qui ipsius miracula in Galilaea plurima viderant. Discipulorum vero duodecim longe alia ratio fuit. Nam hi testes delecti & designati erant omnium, quae illum facere & pati oportuit. Ergo nihil eos celari oportuit, ut certius de omnibus testari possent. Deinde Marcus annotauit, illos in ea profectione expauisse & timuisse. Etenim sciebant Ierosolymae crudelissimos Christi hostes regnare, qui non multo ante eum semel atque iterum lapidibus obruere conati fuerant: & ideo illi profectionem illam difuasisse leguntur alibi. Quia vero nihilominus ipsum sequebantur, neque erat defectionis periculum, aequum erat, ut de ijs, quae prius saepe audierant, rursus admoniti in fide confirmatiores fierent, qui prima pro illo certamina subituri erant. Praeterea de omnibus eos praemonuit Dominus, ut quando in morte videbant omnia, sicuti praedixerat, accidere, postea de resurrectione minus dubitarent, sed huius promissionem animo repeterent. Et hanc causam non obscure Angelus annotat, quando mulieribus ipsum in sepulchro quaerentibus ait: Quid inter mortuos quaeritis eum qui viuit. Non est hic, sed surrexit: mementote vt locutus sit vobis, cum adhuc in Galilaea esset. Et ipse Christus horum repetitione discipulos hortantes confirmat, dicens: Hi sunt sermones, quos locutus sum vobis, cum adhuc essem vobiscum, &c. Et mox: Ita scriptum est, & ita oportuit Christum pati, & resurgere a mortuis tertio die, &c.
units.tr: Second, let us see to whom and on what occasion Christ spoke at this point. He is said to have taken the twelve disciples apart on the way and to have said these things. Yet from other passages it is clear that a great multitude of people accompanied him on this last journey. Why then does he disclose this mystery to the disciples alone, when the knowledge of it is necessary for all? Why did he not speak of it publicly, calling everyone together? But to do this was not necessary, and perhaps would not have profited. For since most men dreamed of an earthly kingdom and sought the advantages of this age from him, most would have deserted him if they had heard what was going to happen to him. Yet it was fitting that his entry into the city should be notable, as Zechariah had foretold long before, and it was of great benefit that very many should witness his death, from among those who had seen his many miracles in Galilee. But the case of the twelve disciples was quite different. For these were chosen and appointed witnesses of all that he had to do and suffer. So nothing had to be hidden from them, that they might bear more certain witness to everything. Next, Mark noted that in that journey they were astonished and afraid. For they knew that the most cruel enemies of Christ reigned at Jerusalem, who not long before had twice tried to stone him; and therefore they are read elsewhere to have dissuaded him from that journey. But because they nevertheless followed him, and there was no danger of their falling away, it was right that, being reminded of what they had often heard before, they should become more firmly confirmed in faith, since they were about to undergo the first conflicts for him. Moreover, the Lord forewarned them about all these things, so that when they saw everything happen in his death as he had foretold, they would afterwards doubt less about the resurrection, but would call its promise back to mind. The Angel plainly notes this same reason when he says to the women seeking him in the tomb: Why do you seek the living among the dead? He is not here, but has risen: remember how he spoke to you when he was still in Galilee. And Christ himself, exhorting and confirming the disciples by repeating these things, says: These are the words which I spoke to you while I was still with you, etc. And soon after: Thus it is written, and thus it behoved Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day, etc.

units.la: Habemus autem in discipulis hoc loco infirmitatis humanae exemplum. Viderunt hucusq; innumera diuinae potentiae exempla in Christo, & licet multi ab illo defecerint aliquoties, ipsi haenus cum eo perseuerauerunt in omnibus tentationibus, quo nomine ab illo in vltima cœna commendantur: deniq; quod diues ille iuuenis facere dedignabatur, ipsi præstiterunt, & eò vsq; profecerant, vt quasi re omni confecta interrogarent: Ecce nos reliquimus omnia, & secuti sumus te, quid erit nobis? At ijdem etsi Christum penes se habeant ducem & protectorem, timent tamen, vt ipsis noua consolatione & institutione opus sit. Quòd si causam quæras, nō alia reddi potest, quàm quòd admonitiones priores, quas multas audierant, & quacunq; hactenus viderunt, non ea qua decebat attentione consideratunt, adeò vt quod de sua morte dicebatur, ipsis adhuc nouum esset ac insolens: nimirum quòd adhuc regnum terrenum somniarent, sicut ex actione filiorum Zebedæi patebit, quæ mox sequetur. Itaq; ex ambitione falsa concepta perfuasio obstitit, vt sub illius crucé latens redemptionis mysterium nec videre, nec ex eo vires aduersus metum hunc concipere potuerint, vt animos fide constanti erigerent. Nemo igitur sibi ipsi nimium tribuat, in primis autem caueant sibi, qui Christi discipuli esse volunt, ne in illo quærant, quæ huius sæculi sunt. Nam qui id faciunt, ij sibi persuadent, posse fieri, vt quis Christum sequatur, & Euangelio credat, & tamen mundo placeat, vt nihil periculi sit metuendum. Qua perfuasione in regno Dei nihil nocentius excogitari potest. Nam ea fit vt mundi amicitiam quærant ij, qui terrenis omnibus renuntiare, adeoq; seipsos abnegare debebant, vt Deo placere possent. At qui mundo placere volunt, huic indulgeant oportet, & proinde (vt de seipso Paulus dicebat) Christi serui esse nō possunt: & reuera in illis fit, quod Iacobus scribit, amicitiam huius mundi esse inimicitiam cum Deo: neq; potest aliter fieri, quando mundus totus in malo iacet, & lucem veritatis odit. Deus autem summe bonus & ipsa veritas est. Et vt nihil aliud maioris mali accedat, saltem tepidi fiunt eiusmodi homines, vt Dei zelus in ipsis paulatim intermoriatur. Itaq; dum in partem vtramq; claudicant, non possunt Deo placere, qui ipsos vt cibum insipidum & noxium euomit. Est magnus horum numerus hodie, & tales fere sunt, qui regni Dei mysteria humana sapientia modulo metiuntur, & nō aliter se tutos fore existimant, quàm si mundu sibi amicu habeant. Et hïs non satis est, si ipsi ignaui & tepidi sint: sed insuper oderunt vere pios, qui zelo Dei ardent, & mundi corruptis studijs se opponunt. Ideo in peius multi proficiunt, & fere regnu Christi in ijs locis deficit, vbi luce Euangelij primùm accendit Deus: & ita postremi fiunt, qui primi fuerūt. Semper ergo meminerimus eorum, quæ Dominus dixit: Si de mundo fuissetis, mundus quod suum est amaret: quia verò de mundo non estis, sed ego elegi vos ex mundo, propterea odit vos mundus. Etenim res ipsa docet, tantum esse hoc odium mundi, quo Christum & eius fideles persequitur, vt nō aliter, quàm Christi abnegatione redimi queat. Sed o miseros, qui vt mundo amico vtantur, Christum abnegat, qui semetipsum pro nobis tradidit, & extra quem salus nulla inuenitur. Quotquot ergo infirmitate alij quàm in seipsis sentiunt, ij cum ea luctari discant, & discipulos imitentur, qui hoc nomine laudandi sunt, quod etsi timeant, non tamen ideò Dominum deserunt, sed sibijpsis quodammodo vim faciunt, & illum trepidi licet comitantur.
units.tr: We have in the disciples here an example of human weakness. They had so far seen countless examples of divine power in Christ, and although many have at times fallen away from him, they themselves have so far persevered with him in all temptations, for which they are commended by him at the last supper. Finally, they did what that rich young man refused to do: they have come so far that, as if everything were already accomplished, they ask: "Behold, we have left everything and followed you; what will there be for us?" Yet even though they have Christ as their leader and protector, they are still afraid, and so they need fresh consolation and instruction. If you ask the cause, none other can be given than this: they had heard many earlier warnings and had seen much, but they did not consider it with the attention it deserved, so that what was said about his death was still new and strange to them; indeed, they were still dreaming of an earthly kingdom, as will be clear from the action of the sons of Zebedee that follows soon after. Thus a persuasion conceived from false ambition stood in the way, so that they could neither see the mystery of redemption hidden beneath his cross, nor draw from it strength against this fear, so as to raise their minds with steadfast faith. Let no one therefore think too highly of himself; above all, let those who wish to be Christ's disciples take care lest they seek in him the things of this age. For those who do so persuade themselves that it is possible to follow Christ and believe the Gospel and yet please the world, so that there is nothing to fear in danger. Nothing more harmful than this persuasion can be devised in the kingdom of God. For it makes those who ought to renounce all earthly things, and indeed deny themselves in order to please God, seek the friendship of the world. But those who wish to please the world must indulge it, and so (as Paul said of himself) they cannot be servants of Christ; and in truth what James writes happens to them, that the friendship of this world is enmity with God; nor can it be otherwise, since the whole world lies in evil and hates the light of truth. God, however, is supremely good and is truth itself. And so that no greater evil follows, such men at least become lukewarm, so that the zeal of God gradually dies out in them. Thus, while they limp to both sides, they cannot please God, who spews them out like tasteless and harmful food. The number of such people is great today, and nearly all of them measure the mysteries of God's kingdom by the measure of human wisdom, and think they will be safe only if they have the world as their friend. And it is not enough for these people to be idle and lukewarm themselves; moreover, they hate those who are truly godly, who burn with zeal for God and oppose the corrupt pursuits of the world. Therefore many make progress for the worse, and the kingdom of Christ almost fails in those places where God first kindled the light of the Gospel; and so those who were first become last. Let us therefore always remember what the Lord said: "If you were of the world, the world would love what is its own; but because you are not of the world, but I have chosen you out of the world, therefore the world hates you." For the thing itself teaches that this hatred of the world, with which it pursues Christ and his faithful, is so great that it can be redeemed only by the denial of Christ. But how wretched are those who, to use the world as a friend, deny Christ, who gave himself up for us and outside whom no salvation is found. Therefore, however many feel weakness in others rather than in themselves, let them learn to struggle with it and imitate the disciples, who are to be praised for this, that although they were afraid, they did not on that account desert the Lord, but in some measure forced themselves, and trembling, nevertheless accompanied him.

units.la: Quod vt a nobis quoq; fiat, proderit Christi facilitatem obseruasse, qui infirmos & nunc trepidantes tam patienter fert. Petrum quidè nuper acerrimè corripuit, qui confidenter nimis ab officio reuocare conabatur, cui illum Pater deflinauerat. At idem verò non abijcit eos, qui ex carnis infirmitate humanu quid patiebantur, nihilominus tamen statione suam tenebant: sed prius tim assumptos instituit & consolatur. Est ergo reuera fidelis ille Pontifex & mitis Seruator, qui nobis infirmis condolere potest, neq; extinguit linum fumigans, neq; arundinem rimas agentem comminuit. Itaq; ex eo consolationem petant, qui se metu & formidine tentari sentiunt, & licet Christum non possint paribus vestigijs sequi, sequantur tamen vt possunt, & Deu sero orent, vt hic ipsis vires sufficiat. Imitentur quoq; Filij Dei facilitatem Christiani homines, ne infirmos & meticulosos temere abijciant, sed assumant potius in spiritu lenitatis non ad certamina disputationum, sed ad ædificationem. Potest enim Deus (vt Apostolus monet) infirmos confirmare, & lapsos erigere: & in primis hic locum habet, quod vulgo dicitur: Vir fugiens denuo pugnabit. Exemplo est Petrus, qui cùm Christum turpissimè abnegasset, postea accepto Spiritu Sancto primus in actiem prodijt, & eundem magno cum successu prædicauit. Vide Actorum secundum, tertium & quartum Cap. &c. Porrò videamus, quomodo cum discipulis egerit Dominus? Diserte & plenè omnia prædi-cit, quæ passuri erat, neq; vllis verborum phaleris vtitur, quibus periculum mitiget. Quo exem-plo docemur, admoneri debere quosuis homines de periculis imminentibus, vt sibi ipsis prospiciant in tempore, ne si quid ex improuiso accidat, grauius offendantur. Imitati sunt præceptoris sui exemplum Apostoli, quando quid pij & credentes passuri, quæ item Ecclesiæ fors nouissimis temporibus futura sit, ex Spiritus sancti suggestione diligenter ac sæpè prædixerunt. Stultè autem & male faciunt, qui pericula dissimulant, & promissis inanibus securos faciunt eos, quos piis adhortationibus & præceptis instruere atq; ad certamina præparare debebant. Solent hoc nonnulli apud eos facere, qui lethalibus morbis correpti, iam iam vitam hanc mortalem cum immortali commutaturi sunt. Fit idem interdum, quando Euangelium aliquibus prædicatur, & omnia lætain hoc sæculo promittuntur ijs, quibus certissima crux propter veritatis professionem imminet. Atqui ex proprio carnis ingenio homines sibi ipsis sponte eiusmodi ipses fingunt, quibus seipsos lætant & fallunt, vt minimè opus sit securos facere eos, qui plus satis ad securitatem & confidentiam natura proclives sunt. Vt ergo bonus imperator militibus indicat, quæ hostium vires & quanta eorundem astutia sit, vt vigilantes & prouidos reddat: ita Ecclesiarum ministri privatim & publicè Christianos homines de mundi & principis eius conatibus diligenter præmonere debent, & eosdem armis spiritualibus instruere, vt in fide constantes pericula omnia facilius vincant. Cæterum audiamus sermonem Christi, quem ad discipulos habuit. Propositio & status eius, timidos & trepidantes consolari, quod facit hoc ordine. Primùm in genere docet, sibi euentura quæcunq; olim Prophetæ vaticinati sint. Annotauit hoc Lucas, qui illum scribit dixisse: Ecce, ascendimus Ierosolymam, & perficientur Filio hominis omnia, quæ scripta sunt per Prophetas. De hoc illos ante omnia admoneri oportebat, ne quid fortuito fieri aut tantas hostium vires esse putarent, sed omnia ex Dei decreto fieri intelligerent, eoq; minus offenderentur. Deinde ex ordine omnia prædixit, vt nullas circumstantias prætermittat: vt ex eo colligerent, nihil sibi ignoranti aut præter voluntatem accidere, sed ipsum necessario quidem ex Patris decreto mori, attamen id voluntarium facere, neq; aliquem esse, qui ipsum possit cogere. Erat hoc euidens diuinitatis argumentum, quod vnum sufficiebat ad remouendum crucis scandalum. Ideo alibi quoq; eadem prædixit, & simul diserte testatus est: Ego pono animam meam, vt rursus sumam eam. Nemo tollit eam a me, sed ego ponam eam a meipso: Potestatem habeo ponendi eam, & potestatem habeo rursus sumendi eam. Præterea se tertia die ex mortuis resurrecturum dicit. Quasi diceret: Faciant hostes mei quod lubet, nihil tamen regno meo aut gloriæ derogabunt. Etenim licet omni consuetudinis genere me obruant, occidant, sepeliant denique, & armato milite sepulchrum custodiant, ego tamen, qui vitæ & mortis Dominus sum, resurgam, vt sicuti in Psalmo olim prædictum est, cum extremè humiliatus ex torrente in via bibero, caput attollam. Ex his peti debent consolationis argumenta, quibus nosipsos aduersus pericula & ex his nascentes tentationes confirmemus. Primò enim nobis quoq; nihil fortuitu accidit. Etenim tempora nostra (vt Dauid ait) sunt in manu Domini, qui pilos capitis nostri numerauit, & cuius prouidentia adflores in agro nascentes & coruorum pullos atq; passeres extenditur. At quia idem bonus & fidelis est, non sinit nos supra vires tentari, sed vt perpessiones Christi in nobis redundant, ita abundat etiam consolatio nostra in Christo. Sed & ipse Christus nobis perpetuò adest suo spiritu, neq; nos orphanos relinquit. Finis deniq; idem nobis cum illo propositus est: Vult enim nos secum esse. Itaq; quando hostes nos captos tenere arbitrantur, Dominus alas dat (vt in Apocalypsi legitur) quibus ex draconis illius rufi faucibus & vnguibus feruemur. Possumus ergo cum tota Ecclesia canere: Benedictus Iehoua, qui non dedit nos in prædam dentibus hostium. Anima nostra sicut auis euasit ex laqueo aucupis: laqueus ruptus est, & nos liberati sumus. Nam etsi vario mortis genere pij tollantur, veniet tamen dies ille, quando mare, mors & infernus mortuos suos reddent, & cum Christo æternum viuent atq; regnabunt, qui cum illo & pro eius nomine mortui sunt. Apo.10. Sed vt diximus, quid sibi euenturum sit, diligenter & perspicuè exponit, vbi totum nostræ redemptionis & salutis negotium completur, quod in morte & resurrectione eius consistit. Nam vt Apostolus scribit, in mortem traditus est Dei Filius propter offensas nostras, vt has sua mor-tis merito expiaret: & excitatus est propter iustificationem nostri, id est, vt & nos in ipso iusti-ficati feruemur. De vtroq; in praesenti agitur, & de morte quidem omnia dicuntur, qua eius men-tionem potuerunt acerbam ac triste m facere. Nam Filius hominis (inquit) tradetur fiue prode-tur: nimirum a discipulo domestico & mensa eiusdem socio. Est hoc per se acerbissimum, & quam graue Christo fuerit, Ioannes non obscure docet, quando scribit, eum cum de Iuda sermonem insti-tueret in vltima coena spiritu, id est, toto animo turbatum atq; commotum fuisse. Deinde quibus i-psum tradi oporteat, dicit: Principibus nimirum Sacerdotum ac Scribis: quos hostes eius acerrimos fuisse constat, eo quod illo viuente & eius doctrina salua, neq; existimationem, neq; quaestum suum consistere possent. Tertio, quid de ipso facturi sint, praedicit: Condemnabunt eum morte. Quod in concilio factum fuisse, suo loco audiemus, eo contumeliosior fuit illa condemnatio, quod totius concilij authoritate confirmabatur. Nec condemnabunt modo, sed tradent gentibus, vt il-ludant, flagellent, crucifigant. Ita vero fieri oportuit, vt Iudaei simul & gentes mortis Christi rei fierent: neq; caruit mysterio, quod Iudaei Messiam suum, qui ipsis peculiariter promissus & ex ipsis natus erat, gentibus tradiderunt, quas vt prophanas fastidiebant & summe oderant. Neminem ergo moueant vel offendant posthac infelicium Iudaeorum conuicia & execrationes, quibus in nos virus odij fui euomunt. Ipsi enim nobis illum tradiderunt, in quo benedicuntur omnes gentes ter-ra, vt ita impleretur, quod de regno Christi ad gentes propagando olim praedictum fuit.
units.tr: That we too may do this, it will help to observe Christ's gentleness, for he bears so patiently with the weak and the now trembling. He recently rebuked Peter sharply, who was rashly trying to turn Christ aside from the office for which the Father had destined him. Yet he did not cast off those who, through the weakness of the flesh, suffered something human and nevertheless kept their post. Rather, he first took them up and comforted them. He is therefore truly that faithful High Priest and gentle Saviour who can sympathise with us in our weakness, who does not quench the smoking flax or break the bruised reed. Let those who feel themselves tempted by fear and dread therefore seek consolation from him. Although they cannot follow Christ with equal steps, let them nonetheless follow as best they can, and pray earnestly to God that he will give them strength. Let Christians also imitate the gentleness of the Sons of God, so that they do not rashly cast off the weak and the timid, but rather take them up in a spirit of gentleness, not for contests of disputation but for edification. For God (as the Apostle warns) can strengthen the weak and raise up the fallen; and in particular that saying which is commonly repeated applies here: a man who flees will fight again. Peter is an example: when he had shamefully denied Christ, he afterwards, having received the Holy Spirit, was the first to come forward into the battle line and preached Christ with great success. See the second, third and fourth chapters of the Acts, etc. Moreover, let us see how the Lord dealt with his disciples. He foretold plainly and fully everything that he was going to suffer, and he used none of those verbal embellishments by which danger is softened. From this example we are taught that people of every kind ought to be warned of impending dangers, so that they may provide for themselves in good time, and that if anything should happen unexpectedly they may not be more grievously offended. The Apostles imitated the example of their teacher when they carefully and often foretold, under the prompting of the Holy Spirit, what the godly and believing would suffer, and what the lot of the Church might be in the last times. But foolish and wicked are those who conceal dangers and, by empty promises, make secure those whom they ought to instruct with pious exhortations and precepts and prepare for conflicts. Some people do this among those who have been seized by deadly diseases and are about to exchange this mortal life for the immortal. The same thing sometimes happens when the Gospel is preached to some and all joys in this world are promised to those for whom the most certain cross hangs over them on account of professing the truth. Yet men, by the natural bent of the flesh, devise for themselves such fictions of their own accord, by which they flatter and deceive themselves, so that there is hardly any need to make secure those who are by nature far too inclined to complacency and overconfidence. Therefore, just as a good commander tells his soldiers what the strength of the enemy is and how great their cunning is, so as to make them watchful and prudent, so the ministers of the Churches, both privately and publicly, ought to forewarn Christians carefully about the attempts of the world and its prince, and to arm them with spiritual weapons, so that, constant in faith, they may more easily overcome all dangers. But let us hear the words that Christ addressed to his disciples. The purpose and situation of this discourse is to comfort the timid and trembling, and he does it in this order. First, he teaches in general that whatever the Prophets once foretold would happen to him. Luke noted this, writing that he said: Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and all the things that have been written by the Prophets concerning the Son of Man will be accomplished. It was necessary above all that they be warned of this, so that they would not think anything happened by chance, or that the enemies' power was so great, but would understand that everything happens by the decree of God, and so be less offended. Then he foretold everything in order, so as to omit no circumstances; so that from this they might gather that nothing happens to him unknowingly or against his will, but that he would indeed die of necessity by the Father's decree, yet would do so voluntarily, and that there was no one who could compel him. This was a clear proof of his divinity, and that alone was enough to remove the offence of the cross. Therefore he also foretold the same things elsewhere, and at the same time testified plainly: I lay down my life, that I may take it again. No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of myself. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again. Moreover, he says that on the third day he will rise again from the dead. As if he were saying: Let my enemies do what they please; they will nonetheless detract nothing from my kingdom or my glory. For although they may overwhelm me with every kind of insult, kill me, and finally bury me, and guard the tomb with armed soldiers, yet I, who am the Lord of life and death, will rise again, so that, as was once foretold in the Psalm, when I am utterly humbled, I shall drink from the torrent in the way and lift up my head. From these things we ought to draw arguments of consolation, by which we may strengthen ourselves against dangers and the temptations arising from them. For first, nothing happens to us by chance either. Indeed, our times (as David says) are in the hand of the Lord, who has numbered the hairs of our head, and whose providence extends to the flowers growing in the field and to the young ravens and sparrows. And because he is good and faithful, he does not allow us to be tempted beyond our strength, but, as the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so also our consolation abounds in Christ. Moreover, Christ himself is always present with us by his Spirit, and does not leave us orphans. Finally, the same end is set before us as before him: for he wills us to be with him. Therefore, when the enemies think they hold us captive, the Lord gives us wings (as we read in the Apocalypse) by which we are carried away from the jaws and claws of that red dragon. We can therefore sing with the whole Church: Blessed be the LORD, who has not given us as prey to the teeth of our enemies. Our soul has escaped like a bird from the snare of the fowler: the snare is broken, and we are set free. For although the godly may be taken away by various kinds of death, that day will nonetheless come when the sea, death and hell will give up their dead, and those who died with Christ and for his name will live and reign with him eternally. Rev. 10.
