But, as we have said, he sets out carefully and clearly what is going to happen to himself, where the whole business of our redemption and salvation is accomplished, which consists in his death and resurrection. For as the Apostle writes, the Son of God was delivered to death because of our offences, to atone for them by the merit of his death; and he was raised for our justification, that is, so that we also might be justified in him. Both are treated here, and indeed everything is said about his death, by which they could make the mention of it bitter and sad. For the Son of Man, he says, will be delivered up or betrayed, certainly by a disciple of his household and a companion at his table. This in itself is most bitter, and how grievous it was for Christ John does not obscurely teach, when he writes that when he was speaking about Judas at the last supper he was troubled and moved in spirit, that is, in his whole mind. Then he says to whom he is to be delivered: namely to the chief priests and scribes, who are known to have been his most bitter enemies, because while he lived and his teaching stood, neither their reputation nor their profit could endure. Third, he foretells what they will do to him: they will condemn him to death. That this was done in the council we shall hear in its place; that condemnation was all the more insulting because it was confirmed by the authority of the whole council. And they will not only condemn him, but will deliver him to the Gentiles, to mock him, scourge him and crucify him. It had to happen in this way, so that both the Jews and the Gentiles would become guilty of the death of Christ; and there was a mystery in the fact that the Jews handed over their Messiah, who had been promised especially to them and was born of them, to the Gentiles, whom they disdained as profane and hated intensely. Let no one, therefore, be moved or offended hereafter by the reproaches and curses of the unhappy Jews, with which they pour out the poison of their hatred against us. For they themselves delivered to us him in whom all the nations of the earth are blessed, so that what was once foretold about the propagation of Christ's kingdom among the Gentiles might be fulfilled.

units.la: Hus alterum addit, Resurrectionem ex mortuis, quam vno quasi verbo absoluit: quia omnem humani ingenij captum excedit eius mysterium, & per se illustre est & plenum consolationis ar-gumentum, quo redemptio nostra asseritur, & omnia tentationum tela eluduntur & hebetantur, quibus fidem nostram Satan oppugnat. In hoc enim, Apostolo teste, Christus & mortuus est & resurrexit & reuixit, vt & mortuus ac viuentibus dominetur. Siue igitur viuimus siue morimur, Domini sumus. Porro omnium istorum hic nobis vsus esse debet: Primum, vt vni Christo fida-mus, & ipso vno contenti simus. Etenim quia haec tam dira, tam acerba, tam iniqua fieri oportuit, satis apparet, nullam aliam rationem fuisse, qua nostrae saluti possit consuli. Neque vt huic ali-quid addatur necesse est. Quia enim Christus in aeternum manet, perpetuum quoq; habet sacer-dotium: & proinde perfecte seruare potest eos, qui per ipsum accedunt ad Deum, semper viuens ad hoc vt interpellet pro nobis. Ideo iam moriturus in cruce dicebat: Consummatum est. Deinde tanto merito & pretio liberati, libertatem nostram tueamur, vt neq; superstitionibus, neq; peccatis & horum seruitio nos mancipemus, quin potius peccato mortui, & vna cum Christo in mortem eius sepulti per Baptismum, cum eodem resurgamus, vt in vita nouitate ambulemus. Sunt haec perspicua & plenissima consolationis. Sed arguitur hic nostra natura infelicitas. Nam discipu-los nihil horum intellexisse, Lucas scribit: nimirum quod partim metu, partim falsa de regno eius terreno perfuasione erant praeoccupati. Atqui eadem ignorantia & caecitas adhuc regnat inter eos qui Christiani dici & haberi volunt. Quam pauci enim sunt, qui mysterium mortis & resurrectionis eius intelligunt? Si enim hoc intelligerent, vno illo contenti effent, adhaec peccata, quae tanto pretio expiari oportuit, odissent. At cum apud omnes loci & ordinis homines regnet atrocissimo-rum scelerum licentia, horum autem remissionem & satisfactionem in abfurdissimis superstitio-nibus plerique quaerant, quis illos mysterium hoc vel intelligere vel credere dicat, quod ore prosi-tentur, quoties Symboli Apostolici articulos recitant? Vides ergo quam multo studio opus sit, in primis vero ardenter oremus Patrem luminum, vt vera Filij sui IESV CHRISTI cognitio-ne animos nostros illustret, vt hic inhabitet per fidem in cordibus nostris, vt in charitate radicati & fundati valeamus assequi cum omnibus sanctis, quae sit latitudo & longitudo, & profunditas & sublimitas, id est, quam sit opus illud nostrae in Christo reconciliationis omnibus suis numeris & partibus absolutum, ideoq; illo vno contenti, in ipso viuamus & fer-uemur: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: The other thing he adds is the resurrection from the dead, which he disposes of in a single word, because its mystery exceeds the grasp of human understanding; yet in itself it is an illustrious argument, full of consolation, by which our redemption is established and all the darts of temptation with which Satan assails our faith are turned aside and blunted. For in this, as the Apostle witnesses, Christ both died and rose and returned to life, that he might be Lord both of the dead and of the living. Whether we live or die, therefore, we are the Lord's. Moreover, of all these things the use for us ought to be this: first, that we trust in Christ alone and be content with him alone. For since these things so dire, so bitter and so unjust had to happen, it is sufficiently plain that there was no other way by which our salvation could be secured; nor is it necessary to add anything to this. For since Christ remains for ever, he also holds an everlasting priesthood, and therefore he is able to save perfectly those who come to God through him, living always to make intercession for us. For this reason, already about to die on the cross, he said: "It is finished." Next, having been freed at so great a price and cost, let us guard our liberty, so that we do not surrender ourselves to superstitions, or to sins and slavery to them; rather, dead to sin, and buried with Christ in his death through Baptism, let us rise with him again, that we may walk in newness of life. These things are clear and very full of consolation. But here the unhappiness of our nature is exposed. For Luke writes that the disciples understood none of these things, doubtless because they were preoccupied partly by fear, partly by a false persuasion about his earthly kingdom. And yet the same ignorance and blindness still reigns among those who wish to be and be called Christians. How few, indeed, are those who understand the mystery of his death and resurrection? For if they understood it, they would be content with that one thing alone, and they would hate those sins which had to be expiated at so great a price. But since licence for the most atrocious crimes reigns among people of every place and rank, and most men seek the remission and satisfaction of these sins in the most absurd superstitions, who would say that they understand or believe this mystery, which they profess with their mouths whenever they recite the articles of the Apostles' Creed? You see, therefore, how much zeal is needed; and above all let us pray earnestly to the Father of lights that by the true knowledge of his Son Jesus Christ he may illuminate our minds, that he may dwell in our hearts through faith, and that, rooted and grounded in love, we may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length and depth and height, that is, how complete that work of our reconciliation in Christ is in all its parts and aspects; and so, content with him alone, may we live and be kindled in him, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCXXXVIII.
units.tr: HOMILY CCXXXVIII.

units.la: Tunc venit ad eum mater filiorum Zebedæi cum filijs suis, adorans & petens aliquid ab eo. Ipse vero dixit ei: quid vis? Ait ei. Dic, vt sedeant isti duo filij mei, vnus ad dextram tuam, & alter ad sinistram, in regno tuo. Respondens autem IESVS dixit: Nescitis quid petitis. Potestis bibere poculum quod ego bibiturus sum, & baptismate, quo ego baptizor, baptizari. Dicunt ei: Possumus. Tunc dicit eis: Poculum quidem meum bibetis, & baptismate, quo ego baptizor, baptizabimini: sedere autem ad dextram meam & sinistram meam non est meum dare, sed dabitur quibus paratum est a Patre meo.
units.tr: Then the mother of Zebedee's sons came to him with her sons, bowing down and asking something of him. And he said to her, "What do you want?" She said to him, "Grant that these two sons of mine may sit, one at your right hand and the other at your left, in your kingdom." But Jesus answered, "You do not know what you are asking. Can you drink the cup that I am going to drink, and be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized?" They said to him, "We can." Then he said to them, "You will indeed drink my cup, and be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized; but to sit at my right hand and at my left is not mine to give, but it will be given to those for whom it has been prepared by my Father."

units.la: QVamuis Dominus & Seruator noster IESVS CHRISTVS dilectis suis discipulis, qui omnibus reliquis ipsum secuti fuerunt, nuper amplißimam remunerationem pollicitus sit, scilicet vt quando ipse sedeat in throno gloriæ suæ, illi quoq; tanquam sui assessores sedeant in thronis duodecim, & tribus Israelis iudicent: mox tamen ne istud secundum carnis sensum de huius seculi gloria & otio ignauo intelligerent, de regno suo ita disseruit, vt abundè doceat, longè aliam esse huius quàm regnorum huius mundi conditionem. Nam primo parabolam vineæ recitauit, in quam a Patre Deo operarij mittantur, non otiosi fuci aut ventres ignaui, qui carnis suæ desiderijs indulgeant, sed qui seipsos & alios excolant ad ferendum fidei fructus. Deinde quæ ipse Ierosolymæ passurus sit, ex ordine illius prædixit, vt suo exemplo doceat, nobis quoq; crucem ferendam esse, si ipsius discipuli & regni eius consortes aut ciues esse velimus. Consentiunt his, quæ passim in Scripturis de piorum afflictionibus habentur, per quas illos in regnum Dei ingredi oportet. Cæterum in hac causa potissimum cernitur, quam vere Paulus dixerit, animalem hominem non percipere ea, quæ sunt Spiritus Dei, & quàm non sufficiat nobis vlla externa institutio, nisi Spiritus mentes nostras illuminet ac trahat. Exemplum eius rei euidens exhibet historia, quam modò recitauimus, & qua primum in præstantissimorum discipulorum postulatione ostendit, quid caro in Christo & eius regno potissimum quærat: Deinde quæ sint Christiani hominis officia, ad quæ seipsos præparare oporteat eos, qui regnum illius possidere volunt. Quæ vt rectius & maiori cum fructu intelligamus, singulas actionis istius partes ex ordine videbimus.
units.tr: Although our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ had recently promised his beloved disciples, who had followed him when all the others had left, a very great reward, namely that when he himself sat on the throne of his glory, they too would sit as his assessors on twelve thrones and judge the twelve tribes of Israel, nevertheless, lest they should understand this in a carnal sense, as referring to the glory and idle ease of this present age, he then spoke about his kingdom in such a way as to teach abundantly that its condition is quite different from that of the kingdoms of this world. For first he recited the parable of the vineyard, into which the Father God sends labourers, not idle drones or lazy bellies who indulge the desires of the flesh, but people who cultivate themselves and others so as to bear the fruits of faith. Then he foretold in order what he himself was going to suffer at Jerusalem, so as to teach by his own example that we too must bear the cross, if we wish to be his disciples and fellow citizens of his kingdom. These things agree with what is found everywhere in the Scriptures about the afflictions of the godly, through which they must enter the kingdom of God. Moreover, in this matter one especially sees how truly Paul said that the natural man does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God, and how no external instruction suffices for us unless the Spirit illuminates and draws our minds. The story we have just recited provides a clear example of this, and first it shows, in the request of the most outstanding disciples, what the flesh chiefly seeks in Christ and his kingdom; then it shows what the duties of a Christian are, for which those who wish to possess his kingdom must prepare themselves. So that we may understand these things more correctly and with greater profit, we shall look at the individual parts of this action in order.

units.la: Principio producuntur duo Zebedæi filij, Iacobus & Ioannes, quorū mater a Domino IESV supplex postulat, vt ipsi velit dare quod petitura sit. Marcus ipsos filios postulationem hanc Christo proposuisse scribit: Nimirum quod ipsi matrem vt hoc faceret, subornarint. Fuit hæc (vt veteres tradiderunt) Salome Josephi filia ex priori vxore aut soror, & ideò idonea visa est, quæ ex iure cognationis & familiaritatis, quæ ipsi cum IESV a pueris fuerat, hoc facilè impetratura esset quod illi cupiebant. Qua vero occasione id fecerit, temporis circumstantia indicat. Dicit enim Euangelista: Tunc venit ad eum mater filiorum Zebedæi, &c. quando nimirum vineæ parabolam recitarat, quâ ad modestiam & humilitatem discipulos adhortatus fuit: & mox ijsdem quid Ierosolymæ euenturum esset prædixerat. His ergo auditis coniciunt, nunc tempus esse, quo regnum suum constituere & inchoare velit, & proinde ipsis maturandum esse, ne qui hastenus inter Apostolos ex primis fuerant, ab alijs præueniantur. Credibile item est extimulatos etiam fuisse æmulationis affectu, quod non ita pridem claues regni cœlorum Petro promissas esse audierant, & quia discipulos simul omnes suos assessores fore dixerat in regeneratione, sibi in hoc consessu aliquam prærogatiuam deberi putarunt. Petunt ergo vt vnus ad dextram Christi, alter ad sinistram collocetur, id est, vt primos post ipsum dignitatis gradus in eius regno obtineant. Quia vero pudor & reuerentia eos nonnihil absterrebat, per matris intercessionem impetrare cupiunt, quod ipsimet non audebant petere. Venit ergo hæc, & primo adorat Christum, vt gestu indicet cansam hanc sibi quàm maximè cordi esse. Deinde tam est audacula, vt Christi assensum postulet, priusquam quid velit proponat. Quod non vulgaris confidentiæ argumentum est, dum sibi peculiari promisso eum obstringere vult, de cuius fide & bonitate omnia quæ honestè & vtiliter peti & dari possunt, simpliciter debebat sperare.
units.tr: At the beginning, the two sons of Zebedee, James and John, are brought forward, and their mother makes a humble request of the Lord Jesus that he would grant them what she is about to ask. Mark writes that the sons themselves put this request to Christ, and that they had persuaded their mother to do it. This woman (as the ancients have handed down) was Salome, the daughter of Joseph by a former wife, or his sister, and so she seemed a suitable person to obtain easily, by right of kinship and the familiarity which the sons had had with Jesus from boyhood, what they desired. The circumstances of the time indicate the occasion on which she did this. For the Evangelist says: "Then the mother of the sons of Zebedee came to him," and so on, namely when he had just recited the parable of the vineyard, by which he had exhorted the disciples to modesty and humility, and had soon afterwards foretold to them what would happen at Jerusalem. Having heard these things, they concluded that the time had now come when he wished to establish and begin his kingdom, and that therefore they must hasten, lest those who had hitherto been among the first of the Apostles should be forestalled by others. It is also credible that they were stirred by a feeling of rivalry, since they had recently heard that the keys of the kingdom of heaven had been promised to Peter, and since he had said that all the disciples would be his assessors at the regeneration, they thought that some pre-eminence was due to them in this assembly. They therefore ask that one be placed at Christ's right hand and the other at his left, that is, that they may obtain the first places of dignity after him in his kingdom. But because shame and reverence somewhat deterred them, they desire to obtain through their mother's intercession what they themselves did not dare to ask. So she came, and first she worships Christ, so that by her gesture she might show that this cause lay very close to her heart. Then she is so bold as to seek Christ's assent before she sets out what she wants. This is no ordinary proof of confidence, since she wishes to bind him by a special promise, from whose faith and goodness she ought simply to hope for everything that can rightly and profitably be asked and given.
1 Tim. 3. Acts 14. 1 Cor. 4.

units.la: Filij Zebedæi per matrem petunt primatū.
units.tr: The sons of Zebedee, through their mother, ask for primacy.

units.la: Habemus ergo hic primò ambitionis muliebris exemplum, quæ plerunq; matres extimulat, ut neglectus ijs, sine quibus filij vere beati & felices non possunt esse, alia petunt, quæ illis neq; vtilia neq; satis honesta sunt. Etenim si quæ Christus discipulus dixerat, recte expendisset, amplissima erat occasio longè alia filijs ab illo petendi, ut nimirum fidos in sua vinea operarios faceret, & Spiritus sui donis instrueret atq; confirmaret, ne inter Crucis certamina succumberent, sed in fide effent constantes. At quasi nihil aliud desit filijs, ut primum in regno Christi, quod illa terrenum sonabat, locum teneant, petit: nec expendit, quam periculosa sit eorum, qui in gradum sublimiorem ascendunt, conditio. Est vitium hoc nimis vulgare, & paucos parentes inuenire licet, qui non ad hunc lapidem offendant. Etenim prima fere cura omnibus est, ut liberis suis de coniugijs opulentis & honoratis, de vita genere quæstuoso, de huius mundi fauore & amicitijs prospiciant, nihil aut parum solliciti, num in Dei cognitione vera instituti sint? num Deo pie & sanctè seruiant? num honestè viuant? Adeò ut omnium cordibus inscriptum videri possit Satyricum illud:
units.tr: Here, then, we have first an example of womanly ambition, which mothers commonly stir up, so that, neglecting the things without which their sons cannot truly be blessed and happy, they seek other things which are of no use to them and not honourable enough. Indeed, if she had duly weighed what the disciple of Christ had said, there was a very ample occasion for her to ask quite different things for her sons from him, namely that he would make them faithful labourers in his vineyard, and would equip and strengthen them with the gifts of his Spirit, so that they would not give way amid the struggles of the cross, but would be steadfast in faith. But, as if nothing else were lacking to her sons, she asks that they may first hold a place in Christ's kingdom, a phrase which sounded earthly to her; nor does she consider how dangerous is the condition of those who climb to a higher rank. This fault is far too common, and one may find few parents who do not stumble on this stone. For almost everyone's first concern is to provide for their children with wealthy and honourable marriages, a profitable way of life, and the favour and friendships of this world; they are little or not at all anxious whether they have been instructed in the true knowledge of God, whether they serve God piously and holily, whether they live honestly. So much so that one might think that Juvenal's saying is written on everyone's heart:

units.la: O ciues ciues quærenda pecunia primum,
units.tr: O citizens, citizens, money must be sought first,

units.la: Virtus post nummos. Et hæc causa est, cur liberi male educentur, & morum licentia passim regnet, non sine manifestus irae Dei indicijs.
units.tr: virtue comes after money. And this is the reason why children are badly brought up, and licence of morals reigns everywhere, not without clear signs of God's anger.

units.la: Occurrit præterea hoc loco memorabile peruersitatis humanæ exemplum, quæ in electis quoque locum inuenit. Fuerunt Iacobus & Ioannes ex primis qui Christi vocationem secuti sunt, & hoc eos ex fide fecisse, ex eo constat, quòd patre Zebedæo & rebus omnibus relictis, hactenus illi constanter adhæserunt, neq; aliorum leuitate, qui quotidie ab illo deficiebant, moti sunt, ut idem facerent. Eosdem Dominus propter Spiritus sancti virtutem & zelum qui in ipsorum concionibus se proferebat, filios tonitrui dixit. Attamen ad hunc lapidem offendunt, ut petant quod a Christi regno alienissimum erat, & de quo ille omnes discipulos admodum graviter admonuerat non multo ante, ut Cap. 18. audiuimus. Quòd si tanti erroris causam quæras, non alia reddi potest, quam quod de regno illius non recte iudicant, sed terrenum somniant, quod instar regum huius seculi habiturus sit. Et hoc illud est, quod hodie multis imponit, & ideo sub prætexta Euangelij IESV CHRISTI opes & diuitias quærunt, honores & dignitates, voluptates item & morum licentiam, scelerum deniq; immunitatem. Idcirco multa passim inepte, indigne, inhoneste & cum publico scandalo fiunt, & propter eos fere male audit Euangelium & fides Christiana, qui suo exemplo alios ædificare & Christo adducere debebant. Quamobrem necesse est, ut preces ad Deum Patrem luminum assiduas fundamus, ut non semel modo veritatis cognitione nos illuminet, verum etiam cogitationes & greßus nostros dirigat, ut animis in cælos euectis ea, quæ supra sunt quæramus, vbi vita nostra abscondita est in Deo cum Christo, ut cum hic patefactus fuerit, nos cum illo declaremur gloriosi, &c. Vide Col. 3.
units.tr: Here there also occurs a memorable example of human perversity, which finds a place even among the elect. James and John were among the first who followed Christ's call, and that they did this from faith is clear from the fact that, having left their father Zebedee and all their possessions, they had hitherto clung to him steadfastly, and were not moved by the fickleness of others, who daily fell away from him, to do the same. The Lord called these same men sons of thunder, on account of the power of the Holy Spirit and the zeal which showed itself in their preaching. Yet they stumble on this stone, in asking for what was most alien to Christ's kingdom, and about which he had admonished all the disciples quite severely not long before, as we heard in chapter 18. If you ask the cause of so great an error, none can be given other than that they did not judge rightly about his kingdom, but dreamed of an earthly one, which would be like the kingdoms of this age. And this is what today deceives many, and therefore under the pretext of the Gospel of Jesus Christ they seek riches and wealth, honours and dignities, pleasures too and licence of morals, and finally immunity from crimes. Hence many things are done everywhere foolishly, unworthily, dishonourably and with public scandal, and because of those people the Gospel and the Christian faith are badly spoken of, people who ought to have built up others by their example and led them to Christ. Therefore it is necessary that we pour out constant prayers to God the Father of lights, that he may not only illuminate us once with the knowledge of the truth, but also direct our thoughts and steps, so that, our minds being lifted up to heaven, we may seek those things which are above, where our life is hidden in God with Christ, so that when he has been revealed, we too may be revealed with him in glory, and so on. See Col. 3.

units.la: Porrò quid Christus, hac postulatione audita, fecerit, videamus. Non statim annuit, ut fe fa-eturum promittat, quicquid petierit, sed quærit, quid velit? Quo exemplo docemur non temere pro mittendum esse cuiq; mortalium, priusquam scias quid petatur, ut si opus sit, de re tota diligentius cogitare possis. Est enim inscrutabile cor hominis (ut per Ieremiam ait Dominus) & multorum insatiabilis cupiditas, quos nihil pudet petere, modo ipsorum desiderijs & libidini satisfiat. Exemplum eius rei in Herode & Herodiade exhibet Ioannis Baptista decollati historia. Et si Christus in præsenti annuisset temerè huius mulieris postulationi similiter faßurus erat, quod ipsum non decebat, sicuti ex eius verbis intelligemus. Nam postquam mater ista petitionem suam proposuit, sermone ad filios conuerso, se illud factum negat. Respondet autem non matri, sed filijs, quos totius negotij authores esse sciebat, & quos in regni sui cognitione melius instituto esse decebat. Rursum ergo docet suo exemplo, quod si quid vitij committitur, quod reprehensione & correctione dignum est, eos cum primis peti debere præ alijs, qui illius præcipui authores sunt. Enim uero canes absq; iudicio lapides qui in ipsos proijciuntur, mordicus inuadunt. At non ita decet homines facere, quos intellectu & ratione instruxit Deus. Nec etiam temerè negat Dominus, sed simul argumentis graribus illorum postulationem confutat.
units.tr: Let us see, then, what Christ did when he heard this request. He did not at once consent, promising that he would do whatever they asked, but asked what they wanted. From this example we learn that one should not promise anything rashly to any mortal before knowing what is being asked, so that, if necessary, one can think the whole matter over more carefully. For the heart of man is inscrutable (as the Lord says through Jeremiah), and many people have insatiable desires, and are not ashamed to ask for anything provided their wishes and lusts are satisfied. The story of the beheading of John the Baptist shows an example of this in Herod and Herodias. If Christ had consented rashly, as he would have done to this woman's request, he would have acted unworthily, as we shall understand from his words. For after the mother set out her request, he refused it, turning his speech to the sons. He answered not the mother but the sons, whom he knew to be the authors of the whole business, and who ought to have been better instructed in the knowledge of his kingdom. Once again, then, he teaches by his own example that if any fault is committed which deserves rebuke and correction, those who are its chief authors should be called to account before others. For dogs, without judgment, bite fiercely at the stones thrown at them. But men, whom God has endowed with understanding and reason, should not act so. Nor does the Lord refuse rashly, but at the same time he confutes their request with weighty arguments.

units.la: Primum ab illorum persona petit, dicens: Nescitis quid petitis. Quo dicto ita vult argumentari: Qui quid petant, aut quæ sit petitionis ipsorum vtilitas, nò intelligunt, indigni sunt qui exaudiantur.
units.tr: First he addresses their persons, saying: "You do not know what you are asking." By these words he argues as follows: those who do not understand what they are asking, or what use the request would be to them, are unworthy to be heard.

units.la: At yo… At vos petitis quod nescitis: Ergo vestrae postulationi non debeo satisfacere. Minor facile probatur. Etenim arbitrabantur illi, se rem æquam, iustam, honestam, utilem atq; salutarem petere. Sed error multiplex concurrebat, quem ipsi ambitione fascinati non poterant in seipsis agnoscere. Nam primò ignorabant conditionem regni Christi, quod hic de mundo esse negat iam moriturus, ipsi verò terrenum esse sibi persuaserunt. Deinde officio & muneri, cui ipsos Deus destinarat, contrarium erat quod petebant. Nam Euangelium praedicare, non more huius saeculi regnare debebant. Praeterea ipsis vehementer nocuisset. Qui enim plus satis superbiebant, maiorem sese efferen di habuissent occasionem, si quod iam animo conceperant, impetrassent. Accedit his quod in fratres & socios iniqui & iniurij sunt, dum supra alios eminere volunt, cum potius humiliter de seipsis sentire, & mutuis officijs inter se certare deberent. Recte ergo dicit Dominus, eos ignorare quid petant, & indignos esse quorum votis satisfiat.
units.tr: But you ask what you do not know. Therefore I ought not to satisfy your request. The minor premise is easily proved. For those men thought that they were asking something fair, just, honourable, useful and salutary. But a manifold error was involved, which they, bewitched by ambition, could not recognise in themselves. For first, they did not know the nature of Christ's kingdom, which he, about to die, declares is not of this world, whereas they had persuaded themselves that it was earthly. Next, what they asked was contrary to the office and duty to which God had appointed them. For they were to preach the Gospel, not to reign after the manner of this age. Moreover, it would have greatly harmed them. For those who were already puffed up with pride would have had a greater occasion for lifting themselves up, if they had obtained what they had already conceived in their minds. To these things must be added that they were unfair and unjust toward their brothers and companions, while they wished to stand out above the others, when they ought rather to think humbly of themselves and to vie with one another in mutual services. Rightly, therefore, the Lord says that they do not know what they ask, and that they are unworthy to have their prayers granted.

units.la: Debet autem ex hoc loco generalis doctrina peti, quales esse oporteat eos, qui in precibus suis exaudiri volunt? & quae causa sit, quod interdum precantes non exaudiat Deus. Extant quidem promissiones eius: In die afflictionis invoca me, & liberabo te. Item: Fiet, ut priusquam invocent, ego respondeam, & adhuc illis loquentibus, ego exaudiam. Et ipse Dominus in Euangelio ait: Petite, & dabitur vobis: quaerite & invenietis: pulsate & aperietur vobis. Item: Amen amen dico vobis, quaecunq; petieritis a Patre meo in nomine meo, dabit vobis. Verùijs solis ratae sunt promissiones ijs, qui certa cum ratione petunt, quae licita sunt, & sibi salutaria esse sciunt. Nihil ergo ad eos faciunt, qui affectibus abrepti & ignorantes petunt inepta, absurda, indigna, iniusta, & proinde noxia quoq;. Etenim cum Deus summè sapiens & bonus sit: adhæc hominum amans, atq; nos salvos velit, non potest neq; vult iniqua & noxia petentes exaudire. Possunt hoc proprio exemplo intelligere parentes, quibus liberi sunt ex ipsis nati. Nam etsi illi suapte natura mali & toti corrupti sint (ut Christus alibi ait) norunt tamen dona utilia & salutaria dare suis filijs, neq; lapidem pro pane, scorpium pro ouo, serpentem pro pisce porrigunt: ijdem parvulos cultrum improbius poscentes virgis caedunt potius, quam ut ipsorum cupiditati indulgeant. Quanto magis ergo Deus, qui ipsa bonitas est, nihil dabit, quam quod nobis utile & bonum esse novit? Inter homines item qui ratione sana utuntur, furioso non dant gladium, ne vel seipsum vel alios laedat. Cur ergo miramur, si Deus nobis neget ea, quibus ceu gladio nocentissimo abuteremur. Atqui gladij instar auaro sunt divitiae, ebrioso vinum & aliarum frugum abundantia, superbo dignitates, crudeli & sanguinario potentia, libidinoso corporis forma & sanitas. Itaq; his omnibus loquitur Iacobus, dum quorundam preces damnat & reijcit, dicens: Petitis & non accipitis, eo quod male petatis, ut in voluptates vestras insumatis. Quod ne nobis dici possit, has precandi regulas observare oportet: Ut primò petamus quae nostrae vocationi, & praesenti conditioni conveniunt. Deinde ut ne quid praescribamus temerè Deo, sed eius voluntati bonae & iustae vota nostra subijciamus: de quo Dominus nos in orationis formula ab ipso tradita, adhæc proprio exemplo admonet, quando dirum crucis supplicium deprecans dicebat: Non mea Pater, sed tua voluntas fiat. Precemur praeterea, ut sua gratia & spiritu nos Deus dignetur, ut ab ipso acceptis donis rectè utamur ad sui nominis gloriam atq; nostri & multorum aliorum aedificationem. Haec si observentur, procul dubio ratae erunt preces nostrae, & licet non det Deus quod petimus, maiora tamen dabit, fidei nimirum constantiam, patientiam, consolationem, ut quaecunq; etiam aduersa accidunt, nobis ad bonum adiumento sint.
units.tr: From this passage a general teaching ought to be drawn: what sort of people they must be who wish to be heard in their prayers, and why God sometimes does not hear those who pray. There are indeed his promises: "In the day of affliction call upon me, and I will deliver you." Likewise: "It shall come to pass that before they call I will answer, and while they are still speaking I will hear." And the Lord himself says in the Gospel: "Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and you shall find; knock, and it shall be opened to you." Likewise: "Truly, truly I say to you, whatever you ask of my Father in my name, he will give it to you." Yet these promises are fulfilled only for those who ask with sound reason for what is lawful, and whom they know to be salutary for themselves. Therefore they have nothing to do with those who, carried away by their passions and ignorant, ask for what is foolish, absurd, unworthy, unjust, and therefore also harmful. For since God is supremely wise and good, and moreover loves mankind and wishes us to be saved, he can neither nor will he hear those who ask for what is unjust and harmful. Parents, whose children have been born of them, can understand this from their own experience. For although they are by nature evil and wholly corrupt (as Christ says elsewhere), yet they know how to give useful and salutary gifts to their sons, and they do not offer a stone for bread, a scorpion for an egg, or a serpent for a fish. Likewise, when little children demand a knife more wantonly, they beat them with rods rather than indulge their desire. How much more, then, will God, who is goodness itself, give nothing except what he knows to be useful and good for us? Likewise among men who use sound reason, they do not give a sword to a madman, lest he harm either himself or others. Why, then, do we wonder if God denies us those things with which we would abuse ourselves as with a most harmful sword? Indeed, riches are like a sword to the greedy, abundance of wine and other produce to the drunkard, dignities to the proud, power to the cruel and bloodthirsty, and bodily beauty and health to the lustful. Therefore James speaks to all these when he condemns and rejects the prayers of certain people, saying: "You ask and do not receive, because you ask amiss, that you may spend it on your pleasures." So that this cannot be said of us, we ought to observe these rules of prayer: first, that we ask for what agrees with our calling and present condition; then, that we do not rashly prescribe anything to God, but subject our prayers to his good and just will. The Lord reminds us of this in the form of prayer he himself delivered, and also by his own example, when, praying against the dreadful torment of the cross, he said: "Not my will, Father, but yours be done." Let us further pray that God will deign to grant us his grace and Spirit, so that we may rightly use the gifts received from him for the glory of his name and for our own and many others' edification. If these rules are observed, our prayers will undoubtedly be heard, and even if God does not give what we ask, he will give greater things, namely constancy of faith, patience, and consolation, so that whatever adversities befall us may serve us for good.

units.la: Alterum argumentum a credentium sive fidelium communi conditione petitur, quae est, ut Cruce exerceantur, & per multas tribulationes introeant in regnum Dei. Quia vero discipulos confidentiores esse sciebat, per interrogationem illud proponit, dicens: Potestis ne bibere poculum, quod ego bibiturus sum? & baptizari baptismate, quo ego baptizor? Poculi vocabulo fors quae unicuiq; a Deo decreta sive destinata est, intelligitur: & frequens est in Prophetis ista similitudo, quando de calice irae aut furoris loquuntur, quem Deus Iudaeis & gentibus propinare vellit. Et infra de sua morte, quam in Cruce subire debuit, loquens Dominus precatur: Pater si possibile est, transeat a me poculum istud. Eodem sensu Baptismi quoq; meminit, & eodem baptis-
units.tr: The second argument is taken from the common condition of believers, or the faithful, which is that they are exercised by the cross and enter into the kingdom of God through many tribulations. But since he knew the disciples to be rather over-confident, he sets this forth by a question, saying: "Can you drink the cup that I am about to drink, and be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized?" By the word "cup" is understood the lot which has been decreed or appointed for each person by God. This likeness is frequent in the Prophets, when they speak of the cup of wrath or fury, which God wished to give to the Jews and the Gentiles to drink. And later, speaking of his own death, which he had to undergo on the cross, the Lord prays: "Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me." In the same sense he also mentions baptism, and in the same way

units.la: Ioan. 18. mo secum baptiʒari dicit eos, qui eandem cum ipso crucem ferunt. Præsenti autem instituto ista locutio melius convenit, quia in Baptismo militiæ Christianæ initiamur, & Christo quasi nomen damus, vt eius auspicijs sub Crucis vexillo contra mundum & eius principem militemus. Itaq; hic verborum sensus est: Vos de regno meo & dignitatibus, quas vobis in regno meo pollicemini, quæritis. Atqui longè alia sunt, de quibus vos solicitos esse & quærere decebat. Etenim qui militiæ adscripti sunt, non debent de triumpho quærere, priusquam ex hoste victoriam referant. At vos meæ militiæ nomen dedistis, & dura vos certamina manent: Ergo de his potius, & quibus armis victoria obtineri possit, quærere debebatis.
units.tr: John 18. he says that those who bear the same cross with him are baptized with him. But this expression fits the present purpose better, because in baptism we are initiated into Christian warfare, and as it were we take Christ's name, so that under his auspices we may fight under the banner of the cross against the world and its prince. Thus the sense of his words here is: "You seek positions and dignities in my kingdom which you hope to receive from me. Yet quite different things are those about which you ought to be concerned and to seek. For those who have been enlisted in an army must not seek the triumph before they have won victory over the enemy. But you have given your names to my warfare, and hard struggles await you. Therefore you ought rather to seek these, and by what arms victory may be obtained."

units.la: Arguitur autem hoc argumento communis hominum ignauia, qui priusquam vicerint hostem, triumphos agere, & otio se dedere cupiunt. Nunquā ergo excidat, electos ad certamina asti-dua vocari, quæ ipsis sub Crucis vexillo decertanda sunt. Neq; finit nos meliorem fortem sperare mundi peruerfitas, qui lucem odisse no desinet, quoad steterit: & vt itafiat propria carnis praui-tas requirit, quæ nisi per Crucem & afflictiones in ordinem redigatur, nunquam emendabitur. Soletur autem nos in istis certaminibus, primum prouidentia Dei: in cuius manu sunt diesnoftri, & qui vnicuiq; suum calicem certa mensura distribuit, adeo, vt nihil nobis fortuitum accidat, neq; etiam cum fidelis & hominum amans sit, nos amplius quam ferre possimus, tentari finit. Deinde quod Christi poculum bibimus, & eodem Baptismate cum illo baptizamur: Id est, illius in cruce ferenda socij sumus, & vt olim Simon Cirenæus illius crucem ferimus, qui remunerator est liberalissimus. Itaq; si cum illo morimur, cum eodem vinemus, si cum illo sufferimus, cum eodem regnabimus. In horum meditatione nos sedulos & assiduos esse decebat. Sed pleriq; Bacchi & Sileni, Veneris & Mammonæ calicem sibi deligunt, & cum indefessi & insatiabiles sint in exhauriendis poculis, quæ illis Satan propinat, aconitis & toxico lethali mixta, magnam sibi iniuriam fieri arbitrantur. Si bonestè & pie viuere iubentur, & pro Christi nomine persecutionem aliquam sufferre debent.
units.tr: This argument also rebukes the common laziness of men, who want to celebrate triumphs and give themselves to leisure before they have defeated the enemy. Let it never slip from our minds that the elect are called to constant struggles, which they must fight under the banner of the Cross. Nor does the perversity of the world allow us to hope for a better lot, for it will not cease to hate the light as long as it stands. And the depraved nature of our own flesh requires that it be brought into order through the Cross and afflictions, for otherwise it will never be amended. In these struggles we are comforted, first, by the providence of God, in whose hand are our days, and who distributes to each one his cup in a fixed measure, so that nothing happens to us by chance. Since he is faithful and loves mankind, he does not allow us to be tempted beyond what we can bear. Second, we drink Christ's cup and are baptized with the same Baptism. That is, we are partners in his bearing of the cross, and, like Simon of Cyrene, we carry his cross, and he is the most generous rewarder. So if we die with him, we shall live with the same; if we suffer with him, we shall reign with the same. We ought to be diligent and constant in meditating on these things. But most people choose for themselves the cup of Bacchus and Silenus, of Venus and Mammon. Although they are tireless and insatiable in draining the cups that Satan pours out for them, mixed with aconite and deadly poison, they think a great wrong is done to them if they are told to live honourably and piously and to endure some persecution for the name of Christ.

units.la: Sed ad Zebedæi filios redeamus, qui non minori confidentia, quàm qua primatum sibi dari postularant, se posse affirmant idem cum Christo poculum bibere, & eodem cum illo Baptismate baptizari. At quàm temere hoc dixerint, euentus docet, quando ad montem oliueti ne vnus quidem horulæ spacio cum illo vigilare potuerunt, & illo capto vnà cum alijs metu superati & turpi fuga dilapsi sunt. Nouum ergo humanæ confidentiæ & temeritatis speciem exhibent, nec mo-res sunt, hominem ex seipso ne ad cogitandum quidem idoneum esse, neq; aliquid habere, quod non acceperit. Quia tamen aliquando futurum erat, vt nouis viribus confirmati pro Christo multa sufferrent (etenim Iacobus ab Herode Agrippa cæsus est gladio, Ioannem autem sub Domitiano feruenti oleo immersum miraculosè quidem seruauit Dominus, at idem vsq; ad extremam senectam multa & grauia certamina sustinuit) ne ex præsenti actione aliquam meriti fiduciam conciperent, tertium argumentum sub Correctionis specie adducit Dominus, dicens: Poculum quidem meum bibetis, & Baptismate, quo ego baptizor, baptizabimini: sedere autem ad dextram meam & sinistram meam, non est meum dare, sed ijs dabitur, siue contingent, quibus paratum est a Patre meo. Sumitur argumentum ab illa cælestis regni conditione, & ipsius Christi persona, duplex est: Primo enim sic colligit. Regnum Dei, & qui in eo sunt dignitatis atq; beatitudinis gradus non pro meritorum ratione aut cognationis iure, sed ex gratuita misericordia distribuuntur: Ergo etsi multa pro me sufferatis, non tamen ex merito aliquid postulare, sed potius vos inutiles seruos esse debetis fateri, vt alias monui. Deinde ita quoq; ratiocinatur. Deus Pater ab æterno elegit quos mihi daret, vt mei regni coheredes & confortes facerè, & illius dona & vocatio firma sunt, vt horum non posset illum pœnitere: Ergo non meum est, vt negletta illius electione ex personarum aut meritorum respectu ista bona inter meos distribuam. Summa istorum huc redit, ipsos postulare quod minimè eos deceat, & quod ipse non possit dare. Non debet autem hoc ita accipi, quasi non eadem sit Filij cum Patre diuinitas atq; potestas (perpetuò enim ratum manet quod alibi dixit: Ego & Pater vnum sumus: Qui me videt, Patrem videt, &c. sed in persona Mediatoris loquitur, & adsumta dispensationis mysterium respicit, quod in assumpta carne debuit obire, & quod in electorum redemptione, nō in cœlestis gloriæ distributione perfabatur. Et necesse erat discipulorum errorem confutari, qui propter cognationis ius & propria merita sibi ipsis aliquam prærogatiuam vendicabant.
units.tr: But let us return to the sons of Zebedee, who, with no less confidence than that with which they had demanded the first place, declared that they could drink the same cup as Christ and be baptized with the same Baptism. How rashly they spoke, the outcome shows: when they could not even keep watch with him for the space of one hour at the Mount of Olives, and when he was taken, they were overcome by fear along with the others and slipped away in shameful flight. So they display a new form of human confidence and rashness. Nor is it the custom for a man to be fit even to think of anything from himself, or to have anything that he has not received. Yet since it was going to happen at some time that, strengthened by new powers, they would suffer much for Christ (for James was struck down by the sword by Herod Agrippa, and John, though the Lord miraculously saved him when he was plunged into boiling oil under Domitian, nevertheless endured many grave struggles until extreme old age), so that they would not conceive from their present action any confidence in merit, the Lord brings forward a third argument under the guise of correction, saying: "You indeed will drink my cup, and be baptized with the Baptism with which I am baptized; but to sit at my right hand and at my left is not mine to give, but it will be given to those for whom it has been prepared by my Father." The argument is taken from the condition of that heavenly kingdom and from the person of Christ himself, and it is twofold. For first he reasons thus: the kingdom of God, and the degrees of dignity and blessedness among those who are in it, are distributed not according to the measure of merits or by the right of kinship, but from free mercy. Therefore, even if you suffer many things for me, you ought not to claim anything on the ground of merit, but rather to confess yourselves unprofitable servants, as I have admonished elsewhere. Next he reasons in this way also: God the Father from eternity chose those whom he would give me, to make them co-heirs and partners of my kingdom, and his gifts and calling are firm, so that he cannot repent of them. Therefore it is not mine, by disregarding his election, to distribute these goods among my people according to regard for persons or merits. The sum of these points comes to this: they ask for what is not at all fitting for them, and for what he himself cannot give. But this should not be taken as if the Son did not have the same divinity and power as the Father (for what he said elsewhere remains forever valid: "I and the Father are one; he who sees me sees the Father," etc.). Rather, he speaks in the person of the Mediator, and looks to the mystery of the dispensation which he had to undertake in the assumed flesh, and which was carried out in the redemption of the elect, not in the distribution of heavenly glory. And it was necessary that the error of the disciples be refuted, who claimed for themselves some prerogative on account of the right of kinship and their own merits.

units.la: Hoc igitur firmiter teneamus, hæreditatem regni cælorum a gratuita & libera Dei electione pendere, nec aliquid hominum dignitati aut meritis deberi. Etenim Filij Dei non ex carnis voluntate nascuntur, neq; ex viribus aut meritis, sed per fidem fiunt, quæ Dei donum est, vt re ste Paulus dixerit: Non est volentis aut currentis, sed miserentis Dei. Vt ergo hic nostri meriti fiducia euertitur, & Dei gratia asseritur: ita de salute nostra nos certos facit hæc consideratio, & inter tentationes nos validissime confirmat atq; consolatur. Præterea de officio admonet, vt humiliemur sub potenti manu Dei, deq; nobisipsis modeste sentiamus, Deo autem gratissimus, & (vt Petrus monet) vocationem & electionem nostram firmam efficiamus effectus fidei, quæ nos gratiam Dei in Christo vere apprehendisse testantur. Interim nihil nobisipsis tribuamus, neq; huius mundi gloriam sectemur, vt nos supra alios efferamus, sed cælestia & æterna bona quæramus per fidem in IESVM CHRISTVM, qui vnicus redemptor est, cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Let us therefore hold firmly that the inheritance of the kingdom of heaven depends on God's free and gracious election, and that nothing is owed to human dignity or merits. For the sons of God are not born of the will of the flesh, nor of powers or merits, but are made through faith, which is the gift of God; as Paul says in these words: "It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy." Thus, just as here confidence in our own merit is overturned and the grace of God is asserted, so this consideration makes us certain of our salvation, and strongly confirms and consoles us amid temptations. Moreover, it admonishes us of our duty: that we be humbled under the mighty hand of God, think modestly of ourselves, and be most pleasing to God, and (as Peter warns) make our calling and election firm by the fruits of faith, which testify that we have truly laid hold of the grace of God in Christ. Meanwhile let us attribute nothing to ourselves, nor pursue the glory of this world so as to exalt ourselves above others, but seek heavenly and eternal goods through faith in JESUS CHRIST, who is the only Redeemer, to whom blessing, honour, glory and power are due for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCXXXIX.
units.tr: HOMILY 239.

units.la: Et cum hæc audissent alij decem, indignati sunt de duobus fratribus. IESVS autem cum eos aduocasset, ait: Scitis quòd principes gentium dominantur in eas, & qui magni sunt licentia vtuntur in eas: Verum non ita erit inter vos; sed quicunq; voluerit inter vos magnus fieri, sit vester minister: Et quicunq; voluerit inter vos primus esse, sit vester seruus. Sicut Filius hominis non venit vt sibi ministraretur, sed vt ministraret, daretq; animam suam in redemptionis pretium pro multis.
units.tr: When the other ten heard this, they were indignant at the two brothers. But Jesus called them to himself and said: You know that the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and that those who are great exercise authority over them. It shall not be so among you. Whoever wishes to become great among you, let him be your minister; and whoever wishes to be first among you, let him be your servant. Just as the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.

units.la: IN prima huius historiæ parte Dominus IESVS CHRISTVS cum duobus Apostolis, Iacobo & Ioanne egit, qui per matrem suam postularant, vt in regno eius primatum tenerent, & graviter docuit, longe aliam esse regni sui conditionem, quàm regnorum huius seculi: Se enim per Crucem in illud ingressurum, quam viam omnes sequi oporteat, qui ipsius consortes velint fieri. Sequitur altera pars, in qua Dominus eandem doctrinam omnibus discipulis applicat, & ad omnes, qui suum nomen profitentur, pertinere docet ea, quæ Iacobo & Ioanni dixerat. Debet autem hoc observari in vniuersa doctrina Euangelij, ne quis sibi ipsi immunitatem in aliquo illius arti culo pollliceatur. Præcipua eius capita sunt, fides in vnum Deum per vnum Mediatorem Christum, dilectio fraterna, vitæ sanctimonia & honestas. Adista ergo omnes obstringuntur, quotquot Christo in Baptismo nomen dant, & in Ecclesiæ societatem adoptantur, cuiuscunq; in hoc seculo sint loci aut ordinis. Quoad vero locum, quem recitauimus, Christus humilitatis studium in genere omnibus commendat, & vt alij alijs seruiant: & simul monet, hanc esse viam, qua ad veram regni cælestis gloriam perueniatur.
units.tr: In the first part of this story, the Lord Jesus Christ dealt with the two apostles, James and John, who through their mother had asked that they might hold the first place in his kingdom, and he taught them firmly that the condition of his kingdom is quite different from that of the kingdoms of this world. He would enter it through the Cross, and everyone who wishes to be his companions must follow that same way. The second part follows, in which the Lord applies the same teaching to all the disciples and shows that what he had said to James and John pertains equally to all who profess his name. This teaching of the gospel must be observed throughout, so that no one promises himself an exemption from any article of it. Its principal heads are faith in one God through one Mediator, Christ, brotherly love, and holiness and integrity of life. All who are given the name of Christ in Baptism and are adopted into the fellowship of the Church are bound by these, whatever place or rank they hold in this world. As for the passage we have cited, Christ commends to all a zeal for humility in general, and that they should serve one another; and at the same time he warns that this is the road by which one arrives at the true glory of the heavenly kingdom.

units.la: Initio occasionem narrat Euangelista, quæ Dominum mouit, vt cum discipulis denuo de re eadem disputaret. Fuit hac, quòd alij decem indignius tulerunt duorum postulationem, & animi indignationem haud dubiè verbis odiosis testati sunt, ex quibus inter illos contentio aut lis exorta est. Indignantur autem, non quòd ipsis displiceat ambitio, sed quòd simili affectu accensi, non possunt eos ferre, qui primatum, ad quem ipsi aspirabant, & quem sibi tanquam præstantioribus deberi, sibi iam pridem perfuaderant, ipsis præripere conati fuerant. Venit hic obseruanda deplorata humani ingenij vitiositas. Acriter modò corripit Dominus duos discipulos, & postulationem eorum docuit absurdam, iniustam & a regni sui conditione alienissimam esse: adhæc de cruce eos admonuit, idque suo exemplo, ne fortem meliorem possent sperare: & de his ita locutus est, vt facile intelligere potuerint, ista ad omnes ex æquo pertinere. At ecce alij omnes eo ipso morbo laborant, cui ille modò mederi voluit, neq; illos pudet in corde latentem ambitionem apertis verbis & gestibus ipso audiente & videnteprodere. Est hoc vulgare admodum in aliis quoq; sceleribus, vt ea in aliis damnemus, eadem autem nobis licita putemus esse, & ijs abfq; omni pudore indulgeamus. Sic Iecortatores & vagis libidinibus addicti riualibus suis indignantur, & hos praeter ius & fas agere clamitant, quando violata coniugali fide hoc faciunt, quod ipsi quotidie designant. Ita auari monopolis & vsurarijs sese inimicos praebent, milites militibus mercenarijs male dicunt, quòd sibi hoc obstare vident, quòd ipsi cupiditatibus suis minus possint satisfacere. Et qui vitia in aliis magno illorum merito accusari fatentur, & hoc nomine gaudent, eadem in semetipsis non agnoscunt. Debent hoc diligenter obseruare verbi administri, quos Deus Ecclesiae sua excitatores constituit, vt discant sibi magno & acri studio opus esse, neq; se officio suo satisfecisse putent, si in genere scelera corripiant, sed singulis applicent Verbum, vt fidis admonitionibus, correptionibus item & minus, si opus sit, quosfuis in viam reuocent. Iniquissimè quidem hoc plerique ferunt, & vt aegroti & male habentes ringi solent, si chirurgi sectione & cauteriis vtantur: itafremunt & murmurant homines, qui peccatorum licentiae assuefuerunt, si per Dei verbum liberius arguantur: sed eo ipso suam ignorantiam produnt cum inexcusabili confidentia coniunctam, quando discipulis Christi meliores & perfectiores censeri volunt, quibus quotidiana institutione & correptio ne opus fuit.
units.tr: At the beginning the evangelist relates the occasion that moved the Lord to discuss the same matter again with his disciples. It was this: the other ten took the request of the two badly, and without doubt they expressed their indignation in hateful words, from which a quarrel or dispute arose among them. They were indignant, however, not because they disliked ambition, but because, fired by the same desire, they could not bear that others should get ahead of them and seize the primacy to which they themselves aspired and which they had long persuaded themselves was owed to them as the more distinguished. Here we must note the deplorable wickedness of the human mind. The Lord now sharply rebukes the two disciples and shows that their request was absurd, unjust, and wholly foreign to the condition of his kingdom. Moreover, he warns them about the cross, and by his own example, so that they might not hope for a better lot; and he spoke about these things in such a way that they could easily understand that they apply equally to all. But look, all the others suffer from the very disease which he had just wished to cure, nor are they ashamed to betray, in plain words and gestures, the ambition hidden in their hearts, while he hears and sees. This is quite common in other sins too: we condemn them in others, yet think the same things permissible for ourselves, and indulge in them without any shame. Thus adulterers and those given to wandering lusts are indignant at their rivals and cry out that these men act against right and law, when they do the very thing, breaking their marriage vows, that they practise every day. So too the greedy, who engage in monopolies and usury, show themselves enemies of others; soldiers curse fellow mercenaries because they see them standing in their way, so that they cannot satisfy their own desires as well. And those who admit that vices in others deserve severe censure, and rejoice in this, do not recognize the same vices in themselves. The ministers of the Word, whom God has appointed as stirrers-up of his Church, must observe this diligently, so that they learn that they need great and keen zeal, and do not think they have done their duty if they rebuke sins in general terms, but apply the Word to individuals, so that by faithful admonitions, and also by rebukes, and by more severe measures if need be, they may call them back to the right way. Most people take this very ill, and, like the sick and the unwell, they are wont to groan when surgeons use the knife and cautery; so men accustomed to the licence of sin rage and mutter when they are reproved more freely through the Word of God. But by this very thing they reveal their ignorance, joined with an inexcusable self-confidence, when they wish to be judged better and more perfect than the disciples of Christ, who needed daily instruction and correction.

units.la: Apparet praeterea in exemplo discipulorum, quàm pertinax & noxium sit ambitionis malum, si semel mentes hominum occuparit. Fuerunt Apostoli fere aequales a pueris, homines nimirum obscuri, & qui duro manuum labore sibi ipsis victum quaesiuerunt. Et si qui ex illis lautiori fortuna fuerunt, ij fere ex telonijs & vectigalibus quaestum fecere prius, eoque magis exosi erant & contempti vulgo, vt qui Romanae tyrannidis administri aliquando fuissent. Nullam ergo habebant occasionem aut causam grauem qua alij aduersus alios superbirent. Deinde ab omnibus quotidie charitatem fraternam requirebat Dominus, & hanc dicebat propriam notam esse, ex qua sui discipuli dignosci possint. Est autem haec ambitioni quàm maximè contraria. Quod enim de prophano amore dixit Poeta: Non bene conueniunt, nec in vna fede morantur Maiestas & amor: hoc ipsum de Christiana dilectione multò verius potest dici, quae, vt Apostolus scribit, non inuidet, non est insolens, non inflatur, non fastidit, non quaerit quae sua sunt, non irritatur.
units.tr: Moreover, the example of the disciples shows how stubborn and harmful the evil of ambition is once it has taken hold of men's minds. The apostles were nearly equal from boyhood, obscure men certainly, who earned their living by hard manual labour. And if some of them were in better circumstances, they had mostly earned their living before from tolls and customs duties, and for that reason they were all the more hated and despised by the common people, as men who had at one time served Roman tyranny. They therefore had no occasion or serious cause for one to lord it over another. Next, the Lord daily required brotherly love from all, and said that this was the proper mark by which his disciples might be known. But this is most contrary to ambition. What the poet said of profane love, that majesty and love do not agree well nor remain in one faith, is far more truly said of Christian love, which, as the Apostle writes, does not envy, is not arrogant, is not puffed up, does not despise, does not seek its own, is not provoked.

units.la: Quae omnia ab ambitiosis fiunt, neq; possunt abesse, vbicunque inanis gloria & dominandi studium regnat. Quod alius Poeta similiter obseruauit, cum diceret: Nulla fides regni sociis, omniq; potestas Impatiens consortis erit, nec gentibus vllis Credite, nec longe fatorum exempla petantur, Fraterno primi maduerunt sanguine muri.
units.tr: All these things are done by the ambitious, and they cannot be absent wherever empty glory and the desire to rule hold sway. Another poet observed the same thing, when he said: There is no trust among partners in a kingdom; all power will be impatient of a companion. Trust no nations, and do not seek far for examples of fate: the first walls were soaked with brotherly blood.

units.la: Cum ergo discipuli non eiusdem potestatis & regni consortes esse, sed alij supra alios eminere voluerunt, latis apparet, quàm parum quotidianae de mutua & fraterna dilectione admonitiones apud eos profecerint. Quod eo magis reprehensionem meretur, quod ne pericula quidem magna, quae vndique ab hostibus struebantur, ipsos mouerunt, vt sibi vnanimi consensu & concordia opus esse cogitarent. Et si nihil horum fuisset, saltem vnius Christi praeceptoris exemplum, quod in oculos quotidie incurrebat, illos in officio continere debebat. Sed quia ambitioni locum dant, non conditionis modo communis & officij, sed periculi quoque imminentis & quotidianae institutionis immemores, inuident, alij alios oderunt, rixantur, & hostiles cogitationes alij contra alios concipiunt, quae proculdubio maius aliquod incendium peperissent, nisi Deus sua gratia & Spiritu illis adfuisset. Exempla huius generis, & quidem atrocissima, passim in sacris & prophanis historijs occurrunt, & vtinam non hodie experiremur magno nostro malo, minis trorum Ecclesiarum contentionibus ambitiosis, Ecclesias passim turbari, & Euangelij cursum impediri, multos item simpliciores offendi, vt a fide deficiant, in qua progressus magnos facturi videbantur. Quotquot ergo propriae simul & publicae saluti consultum volunt, ambitionis pestem detestari & odisse discant, stadeant autem humiliati & parvuli illi fiat, quibus regni sui mysteria Deus revelare dignatur. Matth.11.
units.tr: Since, then, the disciples were not willing to be partners in the same power and kingdom, but wished some to stand out above others, it is plain how little the daily admonitions about mutual and brotherly love had profited them. This deserves all the more reproof because not even the great dangers that were being plotted on every side by enemies moved them to think that they needed unanimous agreement and concord. And even if none of these things had occurred, the example of their one teacher, Christ, which daily came before their eyes, should have kept them in their duty. But because they gave room to ambition and forgot not only the condition and duty they shared, but also the impending danger and their daily instruction, they envied one another, hated one another, quarrelled, and conceived hostile thoughts against one another, which would undoubtedly have produced some great conflagration, had God not helped them by his grace and Spirit. Examples of this kind, and indeed most atrocious ones, occur everywhere in sacred and profane histories; and would that today we were not experiencing to our great harm how the Churches of our ministers are everywhere disturbed by ambitious contentions, how the course of the gospel is impeded, and how many of the simpler folk are offended, so that they fall away from the faith in which they seemed about to make great progress. Therefore, all who wish to consult both their own salvation and the common good should learn to detest and hate the plague of ambition, and let them strive to become humble and little like those to whom God deigns to reveal the mysteries of his kingdom. Matt. 11.

units.la: Porrò quid fecerit Christus, videamus. Principio convocat discipulos, & hoc ipso attentos reddit & dociles, utpote ostendens, quod de re gravi & cuius cognitio ad omnes pertineat, cum ipsis velit agere. Deinde etsi magna & iustam habeat seueritas ipsos corripiendi occasionem, amice tamen & humaniter eos instituit, ut litem inter eos exortam componat. Status vero totius actionis est, ut ad humilitatem & mutua officia illos adhortetur, quae fidissima dilectionis & concordiae nutrix est. Ita vero novum mansuetudinis & patientiae exemplum praebet, quando discipulos tam carnaliter affectos tam diu pertulit, & adhuc ipsorum mores tam benigne fert: & ut idem nos quoque faciamus monet. Hunc exempli Christi ipsum Apostolus tradit, ad Romanos scribens: Debemus nos qui firmi sumus, imbecillitates infirmorum portare, ac non indulgere nobis ipsis: ut scilicet nostro animo morem geramus, ut solent qui nulla aliorum cura tanguntur. Unusquisque enim noštrum proximo indulgeat in bonum, id est, ad eius aedificationem: Etenim Christus non indulsit sibi ipsi, &c. In primis autem exemplo suo commendat pacis studium. Quia enim tam cito, & a nemine requisitus suam authoritatem interponit, ut dissidentes conciliet, evidenter demonstrat, se nihil minus ferre posse, quam suorum dissidia. Ideo tam ardenter precatur iam mortem aditurus: Rogo Pater, ut omnes unum sint, sicut tu Pater in me, & ego in te, ut & ipsi in nobis unum sint: ut credat mundus, quod tu me misisti: Et ego gloriam, quam dedisti mihi, dedi eis, ut sint unum, sicut & nos unum sumus, &c. Imitentur ergo Christi exemplum omnes, qui aliis mandandi ius habent, ut nimirum consensionem animorum inter illos foveant. Hac ratione & hominibus maximum beneficium conferent, & Deo officium praestabunt longe gratissimum, qui (ut David docet) concordia fratrum delectatur, & benedictionem suam illis non sine expresso mandato pollicetur, quae ex illis in multos alios redundat. Et notum est illud Christi: Beati pacifici, quoniam filii Dei vocabuntur. Porrò quoad sermonem Domini ad Apostolos, constat hic tribus partibus.
units.tr: Let us now consider what Christ did. First, he calls the disciples together, and by this very act makes them attentive and teachable, since he shows that he wishes to deal with them about a weighty matter, one whose knowledge concerns everyone. Then, although he had a great and just occasion to rebuke them severely, he instructs them kindly and humanely, so as to settle the quarrel that had arisen among them. The whole aim of his action is to urge them to humility and to mutual duties, which is the most faithful nurse of love and concord. In this way he also offers a new example of gentleness and patience, since he bore so long with disciples so carnally disposed and still bears their conduct so kindly; and he bids us do the same. The Apostle hands down this example of Christ in his letter to the Romans: "We who are strong ought to bear the weaknesses of the weak, and not to please ourselves," that is, we should not follow our own inclination as those do who are moved by no care for others. "Let each of us please his neighbour for good, that is, for his building up. For Christ did not please himself," and so on. Above all, by his own example he commends the pursuit of peace. For since he so quickly, and without anyone asking, interposes his authority to reconcile those who disagree, he plainly shows that he can bear nothing less than the dissensions of his own people. Therefore, about to go to his death, he prays so earnestly: "Father, I ask that they may all be one, as you, Father, are in me and I in you, so that they too may be one in us, that the world may believe that you sent me. And the glory that you gave me I have given to them, that they may be one, as we are one," and so on. Let all who have the right to command others therefore imitate Christ's example, so as to foster agreement of minds among those under them. In this way they will both confer the greatest benefit on men and render to God a service far more pleasing, for God (as David teaches) delights in the concord of brothers, and promises his blessing to them, not without an express command, a blessing which flows from them to many others. And that saying of Christ is well known: "Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God." Now, as regards the Lord's speech to the Apostles, it consists of three parts.

units.la: Primò ad fontem mali accedit, ut hunc obturet. Erat hic, quòd nesciebant quae esset regni sui conditio. Docet ergo hanc longe aliam esse quam quae est regnorum huius mundi. Ex eo colligit, ipsos aliter affectos esse debere quam homines prophani sint, quibus voluptas est alijs imperare. Nam quod in praesenti dicit: Scitis quod principes gentium dominantur in eas: id apud Marcum sic enunciatur: Scitis, quod quibus placet imperare gentibus, dominantur eis, &c. Obiter ergo perstringit tyrannicos & feroces ambitiosorum hominum animos, qui cum cupiant imperare, fere potestate concessa abutuntur, ut se dominari ostendant. Itaque ut hic loquitur Dominus, licentia vtuntur in subditos, & quidvis pro suo arbitrio faciunt, nulla iuris aut aequi ratione habita. Ideo horum quasi propria vox est: Sic volo, sic iubeo, sit pro ratione voluntas.
units.tr: First, he goes to the source of the evil, so as to stop it up. The cause here was that they did not know what the condition of his kingdom was. He therefore teaches that it is far different from the condition of the kingdoms of this world. From this he concludes that they ought to be disposed otherwise than profane men are, for whom it is a pleasure to rule over others. For what he says in the present place, "You know that the princes of the Gentiles lord it over them," is expressed in Mark thus: "You know that those who are considered to rule over the Gentiles lord it over them," and so on. Incidentally, then, he touches upon the tyrannical and fierce spirits of ambitious men, who, since they desire to rule, mostly abuse the power granted to them, so as to show that they are masters. And so, as the Lord speaks here, they use license against their subjects and do whatever they please, with no regard for law or equity. Hence their very own saying is: "Thus I will, thus I command; let my will stand in place of reason."

units.la: Cum vero his Apostolos suos Christus opponat, & dicat: Verum non ita erit inter vos: adhunc modum argumentatur: Quicunque mei discipuli, & mei regni administri esse volunt, ij non debent imitari Reges gentium prophanos, qui nullam subditorum rationem habent, sed ambitiose sese ad uersus omnes efferunt: Atqui vos ego elegi, ut mei discipuli, & regni mei caelestis administri ac dispensatores sitis: Ergo non ambitiose debetis vos alijs praeferre, sed potius quisque quae aliorum sunt sperare & quaerere.
units.tr: But when Christ sets his Apostles over against these, and says, "But it shall not be so among you," he argues in this way: whoever wish to be my disciples and ministers of my kingdom ought not to imitate the profane kings of the Gentiles, who take no account of their subjects but ambitiously lift themselves up against everyone. But I have chosen you to be my disciples, and ministers and stewards of my heavenly kingdom. Therefore you ought not to set yourselves ambitiously above others, but rather each one should hope for and seek what is good for others.

units.la: Ubi observaveris, nominari quidem hic Reges gentium, & his licentiam tribui, qua potestate sua male abutantur: at non ideo magistratus legitimos a Christo damnari, multò minus huncordinem prorsus aboleri. Sed ita loquitur, ut partim perstringat Apostolorum ambitionem, qua ita sese alij contra alios efferebant, ut a prophanis principibus non multum differrent, quoad animi affectum: partim inter magistratus politicos & Ecclesiasticam functionem, quae illis committedebat, distinguit. Nam (ut saepe monuimus) turpiter & seditiose errat, qui per religionem Christia nam magistratum & iura politica abrogari sentiunt. Non enim venit Filius Dei, ut Lege abolea t, sed ut impleat & confirmet. Atqui huius iudicia legitimis magistratibus credita sunt, ut secundum illa ius dicant. Deinde ijsdem Ecclesiae suae curam Deus commendat, & eiusdem nutritios & patronos fecit,sicuti Prophetæ passim docent. Vt deniq; Prophetæ de Regum & Principum conuersione ad fidem Christi vaticinantur: ita non legimus hunc aut Apostolos eius alicui ad fidem conuersio mandasse, vt si Christianus haberi velit, Magistratus functionem relinquat, & vitam viuat priuatam. Neminem ergo offendant furores Anabaptistici, sed meminerint magistratus, se Dei seruos esse, & huius Filium osculentur: & quia hic consessibus ipsorum interesse solet, ius sanctè dicant, leges bonas condant, & eas sedulò tueantur, vt Dei gloria in ipsis illustretur, & Ecclesia quotidie in melius proficiat: Vide Psal.2. & 72. Item 2. Paral.19.
units.tr: Here you may observe that kings of the Gentiles are indeed named, and license is granted to them, by which they abuse their power; yet Christ does not on that account condemn lawful magistrates, much less does he abolish this order altogether. He speaks rather so as partly to rebuke the ambition of the Apostles, by which they lifted themselves up against one another so that they differed little from profane princes in their state of mind; and partly to distinguish between the political magistrates and the ecclesiastical function committed to the Apostles. For (as we have often warned) they err shamefully and seditiously who think that the magistracy and political rights are abrogated by the Christian religion. For the Son of God did not come to abolish the Law, but to fulfil and confirm it. Moreover, judgments of this kind have been entrusted to lawful magistrates, so that they may declare justice according to them. Then God has also committed the care of his Church to these same magistrates, and has made them its nursing fathers and patrons, as the Prophets teach everywhere. And just as the Prophets foretell the conversion of kings and princes to the faith of Christ, so we do not read that he or his Apostles ever commanded anyone, when converted to the faith, to give up the office of magistrate and live a private life if he wished to be counted a Christian. Let not the Anabaptist frenzies offend anyone; rather let the magistrates remember that they are servants of God, and let them kiss the Son; and because he is accustomed to be present at their assemblies, let them rightly declare justice, enact good laws, and diligently protect them, so that the glory of God may shine forth in them and the Church may daily advance for the better. See Psalm 2 and 72. Likewise 2 Chronicles 19.

units.la: Sed aliud hoc loco occurrit non leui admiratione dignum: Vnde nimirum qui hodie Apostolici dici & esse volunt, regna sua habeant & subditos, quibus more principum huius seculi dominantur: cum Christus illud omne neget Apostolis, & postea quoq; in vltima cœna, cum litem istam ambitiosam instaurarent, iterum dicat: Verum non ita erit inter vos. Vel, Vos autem non sic. Ipsi quidem regna & iurisdictiones sibi vendicant primò ipsius Christi nomine, cui Pater dixerit: Postula a me, & dabo tibi gentes, vt sint hereditas tua. Item: Gens & regnum quod tibi non seruierit, peribunt. Et qui ipse in Euangelio pronunciarit: Data est mihi omnis potestas in cœlo & in terra. Deinde Petrum Apostolum allegant, quem ille sum Vicarium fecerit, & cuius ipsi sint legitimi successores. Sed vtrumq; friuolum est. Nam quoad primum, etsi Christo gentes obedire debeant, & eidem omnis potestas data sit, idem tamen de regno interrogatus, respondit: Regnum meum non est de hoc mundo. Quoad alterum, alibi demonstrauimus futile esse illud Vi cariatus Christi commentum, nec plus potestatis Petro datum esse quam aliis Apostolis: quo etiam huius loci authoritate abunde demonstrari poterat, si opus esset. Sed prolixa demonstratione nö est opus, vbi res ipsa loquitur. Nam etsi ipsi longum Catalogum terrarum & vrbium contexant, quas Petri patrimonium dicunt, constat tamen neq; hunc, neq; collegas eius quicquam huius habuisse. Etsi Constantini, Pipini itè & Caroli Magni atq; Ludouici donationes prætexant, nos hunc locum illis opponimus: ex quo apparet, ipsos ista non debuisse accipere, cum Christus tam diserte interdicat, ne in stat principum huius seculi cuiquam dominentur aut imperent. Vnde ergo ista habent? Ex eo nimirum, quod in hac etiam parte Romanos Pontifices palam testari oportuit, ipsos magni illius ἀντιχριστοῦ siue Antichristi spiritu agitari, cui ambitionem & fastam intolerabilem cum insatiabili auaritia coniunctum Propheta Daniel & Apostoli tribuunt. De Christo legitur, quod cum ipsi totius mundi regna Satan offerret, & vicisset vt prostratus se adoraret, pe teret, cum magna indignatione eum reiecerit, dicens: Discede a me Satana, &c. Petrus itèa Simone Mago oblatam pecuniam recipere noluit, & Centurioni Cornelio ipsum adorare volenti, dicebat Surge, & ego ipse homo sum. At non ita Pontifices, qui vt rebus suis melius consuluerunt, primatum in Ecclesia a latrone Phoca ipsis concessum auide amplexi sunt: deinde terras alienas sibi donatas similiter acceperunt, & sublimes aliorum humeris gestari, reges ad pedum suorum osculabantur procumbere volunt. Itaq; non Christi exemplum sectantur, sed Giezi spiritu ducuntur, qui quæ herus Heliæus a Naamano Syro oblata munera accipere noluit, ipse mox heri nomine impudenter postulauit. Huius ergo vestigijs cum insistunt Pontifices, & ab his facti Episcopi & Abbates, non pro Apostolicis haberi debent, sed digni sunt, qui cum Giezi leprosio ab Ecclesia consortio excludantur, & quibus idem dicatur, quod Petrus olim Simoni Mago: Argentum vestrum, & primatus vester, & omne regnum vestrum vobiscum pereat, &c. Act.8.
units.tr: But another matter presents itself here, not unworthy of no small wonder: whence is it that those who today wish to be called and to be Apostolic have kingdoms and subjects, over whom they lord it in the manner of the princes of this age, when Christ denies all of this to the Apostles, and afterwards also at the last supper, when they renewed that ambitious quarrel, again says: "But it shall not be so among you," or "But you shall not be so." They claim for themselves kingdoms and jurisdictions, first in the name of Christ himself, to whom the Father said: "Ask of me, and I will give you the nations for your inheritance." Likewise: "The nation and kingdom that will not serve you shall perish." And he who in the Gospel declared: "All power is given to me in heaven and on earth." Then they cite the Apostle Peter, whom Christ made his vicar, and of whom they are the legitimate successors. But both of these are frivolous. For as to the first, although nations ought to obey Christ, and all power has been given to him, yet when asked about his kingdom he answered, "My kingdom is not of this world." As to the second, we have demonstrated elsewhere that this invention of a vicariate of Christ is futile, and that Peter was given no more power than the other Apostles; this could also be sufficiently shown by the authority of this very passage, if there were need.
