But there is no need of a lengthy demonstration where the thing itself speaks. For although they weave together a long catalogue of lands and cities, which they call the patrimony of Peter, it is nevertheless certain that neither he nor his colleagues ever had any such thing. Although they pretend the donations of Constantine, Pepin, and Charlemagne and Louis, we oppose to them this passage: from it it appears that they ought not to have accepted these things, since Christ so plainly forbids that any of them should lord it over anyone or rule, in the manner of the princes of this age. Whence then do they have these things? Clearly from this: that in this part too the Roman Pontiffs had to bear public witness that they are driven by the spirit of that great Antichrist [ἀντιχριστοῦ], to whom the Prophet Daniel and the Apostles attribute ambition and intolerable pride, joined with insatiable greed. Of Christ it is read that when Satan offered him the kingdoms of the whole world, and sought that he, having been overcome, would fall down and worship him, he rejected him with great indignation, saying: "Get behind me, Satan," and so on. Peter likewise refused the money offered by Simon the Magician, and to the centurion Cornelius, who wished to worship him, he said, "Rise up, I myself am also a man." But not so the Pontiffs, who, as they have looked better to their own affairs, have eagerly embraced the primacy in the Church conceded to them by the thief Phocas; then they likewise accepted foreign lands given to them, and they want to be carried high on the shoulders of others, and kings to prostrate themselves to kiss their feet. Therefore they do not follow the example of Christ, but are led by the spirit of Gehazi, who, when his master Elisha would not accept the gifts offered by the Syrian Naaman, himself shamelessly demanded them soon after in his master's name. Therefore, since the Pontiffs, and the bishops and abbots made by them, tread in these footsteps, they ought not to be regarded as Apostolic; rather they deserve to be excluded from the fellowship of the Church together with leprous Gehazi, and to be told what Peter once said to Simon the Magician: "May your silver and your primacy and all your kingdom perish with you," and so on. Acts 8.

units.la: Sed ad Christum redeamus, qui secunda fui sermonis parte, quæ discipulorum conditio aut fuit ἐλιοφιτ, docet: Quicunq; voluerit (inquit) inter vos primus esse, sit vester seruus. Quod non eo sensu accipi debet, quasi ipsos seruire iubeat, vt primi aut aliis superiores fiat: sed in regno Dei eos magnos censeri dicit, qui plurimis seruiunt. Vnde sequitur, domus spiritualibus adeo neminem superbire debere, vt potius qui plura alijs acceperunt, eò magis se alijs obstrictos ac debitores esse meminisse debeant. Et hanc esse donorum Dei rationem, Dominus apud Lucam in dispensatoris parabola docet. At hic obseruari debet, de quo seruitij genere loquatur: Nimirum non de sordido illo, quod reuera seruile dicitur, quando nos ad vniuscuiusq; arbitrium demittimus, vt omnibus gratificemur: sed de eo, vt pro nostra vocationis ratione omnibus seruiamus ad ædificationem ipsorum, vt salui fiant. Ita omnibus seruierunt Apostoli, dum omnibus omnia facti sunt, vt omnes Christo lucrifa-
units.tr: But let us return to Christ, who in the second part of his discourse, which describes the condition of the disciples [ἐλιοφιτ], teaches: "Whoever wishes to be first among you, let him be your servant." This should not be understood as if he ordered them to serve so that they might become first or superior to others. Rather, he says that in the kingdom of God those are counted great who serve the most. From this it follows that spiritual men ought not to be proud at all; rather, those who have received more from others should remember all the more that they are bound and indebted to others. The Lord teaches this same principle of God's gifts in Luke, in the parable of the steward. But we must observe what kind of service he means. It is certainly not that sordid service, which is truly called servile, when we submit ourselves to each person's will so as to please everyone. It is rather that we serve all, according to the nature of our calling, for their edification, so that they may be saved. In this way the Apostles served all, since they became all things to all, that they might win all to Christ.

units.la: {} lucrifacerent.Ita toti populo & singulis subditis seruiunt viri principes, dum omnibus ius dicunt, bonas leges tuentur, & Christiana disciplina peccandi licentiam coercere studrent, ne quis sibijpsi exitium temerè accersat. Ad hunc modum omnium in familia seruus est paterfamilias frugi & fidelis. Et qui ita omnibus seruiunt, simul Dei serui sunt, qui hominum salute potissimum delectatur.
units.tr: ...that they might win them. Thus princes serve the whole people and each of their subjects, when they render justice to all, uphold good laws, and labour through Christian discipline to restrain the licence to sin, so that no one rashly brings ruin upon himself. In this way the wise and faithful householder is the servant of all in his family. And those who serve all in this way are at the same time servants of God, who takes especial delight in the salvation of men.

units.la: At quia carnis nostrae ea est ambitio, ut quando nos prae aliis instructos sentimus donis eximijs, aegrè nos demittamus ad aliorum seruitia, multi etiam sibi iniuriam fieri putent, si hoc ab ipsis exigatur, proprio exemplo discipulos vrget & stimulat Christus, dicens: Sicut Filius hominis non venit, ut sibi ministraretur, sed ut ministraret. Quasi diceret: Cur cuiquam vestrum graue sit, quod me quotidie videtis facere, qui studio indefesso omnibus omne officium praesto, ut saluti omnium consulam? Enimuero si in mundum venissem, ut Regis terreni instar dominarer, satellitu & seruorum turba stiparer, qui omnes in meo seruitio occupati essent, merito tale quid vobis quoq; polliceremini, & primatum someniaretis. Sed cum maiestate & regno, quod mihi ab aeterno cum Patre commune est, me quasi abdicarim, & ex Patris decreto Filius hominis, adeo; hominum infimus & miserrimus factus sim, forma serui assumpta, nulla vobis excusatio reliqua erit, si sub mei nominis praetextu alijs vos imperare velitis.
units.tr: But because our flesh is so ambitious that, when we feel ourselves endowed with outstanding gifts beyond others, we are reluctant to stoop to the service of others, and many even think they are wronged if this is demanded of them, Christ urges his disciples and spurs them on by his own example, saying: "Just as the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve." As if he were saying: Why should it be hard for any of you to do what you see me doing every day, I who with tireless zeal stand ready to perform every duty for all, so that I may care for the salvation of all? Indeed, if I had come into the world to rule like an earthly king, surrounded by a crowd of attendants and servants, all occupied in my service, you would rightly promise yourselves something of the sort too, and aspire to primacy. But I have, as it were, laid aside majesty and the kingdom which is common to me with the Father from eternity; by the Father's decree the Son of Man has become the lowest and most wretched of men, having taken the form of a servant. Therefore you will have no excuse left if you wish to lord it over others under the pretext of my name.

units.la: Caeterum omissis alijs seruitijs, quae docendo & miraculose multos sanando quotidie praestitit omnibus ad se venientibus, praecipuum allegat, quo omnium saluti consuluit, & cuius meritum atq; virtus etiam hodie omnibus salutaris est, qui illud cum fide apprehendunt. Nam se venisse ait, ut daret animam suam in redemptionis pretium pro multis. Superat hoc omnia officia, quae inter homines alij alijs praestare possunt. Nam, ipso teste, maiorem hac charitatem nemo habet, quam ut animam suam ponat pro amicis suis. At ipse pro inimicis quoque mori dignatus est, ut eos qui natura filij irae erant, Patri reconciliaret. Et fieri potest, quis pro alijs se vitae periculo exponat & moriatur, attamen illos non seruet, sed ipsi quoq; vna cum illo pereant. At Christus pro nobis moriendo nobis vitam contulit: eo quod mors eius λύτρον, id est, redemptionis pretium sufficiens est pro peccatis totius mundi. Ideo enim qui non nouerat peccatum, & in cuius ore non inuentus est dolus aut fraus, peccatum, id est, hostia pro peccato factus est, ut nos efficeremur iustitia Dei in eo, dum quae in illo est iustitia, nobis propter fidem, qua ipsum apprehendimus & ei vni mur, imputatur. Et facit ad huius beneficij amplificationem, quod non pro vno aut paucis seipsum dedit, sed pro multis, id est, pro omnibus credentibus, siue hi Iudaei sint, aut Graeci, serui aut heri, diuites & pauperes. Non est enim persona respectus apud Deum, & in CHRISTO IESV non est Graecus & Iudaeus, Circumcisio & praeputium, barbarus, Scytha, seruus, liber, sed omnia in omnibus Christus. Coloss. 3. Gal. 3.
units.tr: Moreover, setting aside the other services which he daily rendered to all who came to him, by teaching and by healing many through miracles, he names the chief one, by which he cared for the salvation of all, and whose merit and power is still salutary for all who lay hold of it with faith. For he says that he came to give his life as a ransom [λύτρον] for many. This surpasses all the duties which some men can render to others. For, by his own testimony, no one has greater love than to lay down his life for his friends. But he deigned to die even for his enemies, so that he might reconcile to the Father those who by nature were children of wrath. It can happen that someone exposes himself to peril of life and dies for others, yet does not save them, but perishes together with them. But Christ by dying for us has given us life, because his death is a ransom [λύτρον], that is, a price of redemption sufficient for the sins of the whole world. For he who did not know sin, in whose mouth no deceit or fraud was found, was made sin, that is, a sacrifice for sin, so that we might be made the righteousness of God in him, since the righteousness which is in him is imputed to us on account of faith, by which we apprehend him and are united to him alone. It also adds to the greatness of this benefit that he gave himself not for one or a few, but for many, that is, for all believers, whether they are Jews or Greeks, slaves or free, rich or poor. For there is no respect of persons with God, and in CHRIST JESUS there is neither Greek nor Jew, circumcision nor uncircumcision, barbarian, Scythian, slave, free, but Christ is all in all. Col. 3. Gal. 3.

units.la: Porrò vsus huius loci nobis est: Ut primò ad statum praesentis actionis referatur, & doceat exemplum Christi imitari, ut procul depositia omni alios excellendi cupiditate, humiliemur in conspectu Dei, et (ut Paulus monet) nihil per contentionem geramus, aut per inanem gloriam, sed ex modestia alium quisque se praestantiorem existimet: neq; sua quisque spectet, sed vnusquisq; etiam quae sunt aliorum. Est enim hoc praecipuum, quod in Christi exemplo nos imitari decet: de quo nos non solum in praesenti, verumetiam alibi admonuit, dicens: Discite a me, quod mitis sum & humilis corde. In primis autem huc referri debet, quod postremam Coenam discipulorum pedes abluit, & se exemplum praebuisse testatur, quod imitentur quicunq; sui discipuli censeri voluntt. Et sane, si cogitemus quis sit ille, quid item fecerit pro nobis, & qua facultate se ad nos quotidie demittat, mox patebit, inanem, imo turpem esse omnem praetextum, quo ambitiosi & superbi se supra alios efferunt. At quia de hac re alibi fusius dictum est, haec in praesenti dicta sufficiant.
units.tr: Moreover, the use of this passage for us is this: first, it is to be applied to the state of the present action, and it teaches us to imitate the example of Christ, so that, putting far away every desire to excel others, we may humble ourselves in the sight of God, and (as Paul admonishes) do nothing through strife or vainglory, but in lowliness of mind let each esteem others better than himself; and let each look not only to his own things, but also to the things of others. For this is the chief thing which we ought to imitate in Christ's example, and he admonished us of it not only here but also elsewhere, saying: "Learn from me, for I am meek and lowly in heart." Above all, this should be referred to the fact that at the last Supper he washed the feet of his disciples, and bore witness that he had set an example for those who wish to be considered his disciples to imitate. Indeed, if we consider who he is, what he has done for us, and by what power he daily stoops down to us, it will soon become clear that every pretext by which the ambitious and proud raise themselves above others is empty, or rather shameful. But since this matter has been discussed more fully elsewhere, let what has been said suffice for the present.

units.la: Deinde de tota salutis ratione nos hoc Christi dictu admonet. Etenim quia redemptionis meminit, qua opus fuit, non obscure docet, nos omnes sub peccatum venundatos (ut Paulus ait) & non huius modo mancipia, verumetiam morti obnoxios fuisse. Dum vero redemptionis pretium in se monstrat, hoc nusquam alibi inueniri innuit. Si quod enim aliud fuisset, vtiq; non opus erat aternum Filium Dei infamem & acerbam mortem in Cruce sufferre. Itaque atrocem illi iniuriam faciunt, quotquot redemptionem humani generis extra illum quaerunt, & hanc suis vel aliorum meritis tribuunt. Nobis autem illa applicatur, vel nostra fit, per fidem, vt paulo ante diximus. Et certa est redemptio ista, adeo vt de illa dubitare nefas sit. Nam Patris testimonio confirmatur, dicentis: Hic est Filius ille dilectus, in quo placatus sum. Et ipse iam moriturus dicebat: Consummatum est. Quis item suspicetur, illum nos negligere posse, aut perditos velle, quos tanto pretio redemit, & pro quibus animam suam dedit? Contenti ergo simus tanto redemptore, qui oues suas nouit, neque eas ex manibus suis eripi sinit. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Next, this saying of Christ reminds us of the whole reason of salvation. For since he mentions the redemption which was needed, he clearly teaches that we all were sold under sin (as Paul says) and were not only slaves of it but also liable to death. When he shows the price of redemption in himself, he implies that this is found nowhere else. For if there had been any other price, there would surely have been no need for the eternal Son of God to suffer an infamous and bitter death on the Cross. Therefore they do a grievous wrong to him, as many as seek the redemption of mankind outside him and ascribe it to their own or others' merits. But that redemption is applied to us, or becomes ours, through faith, as we said a little before. And this redemption is so certain that it is wicked to doubt it. For it is confirmed by the Father's testimony, who says: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased." And he himself, about to die, said: "It is finished." Who, moreover, could suspect that he could neglect us, or wish to lose those whom he redeemed at so great a price, and for whom he gave his soul? Let us therefore be content with so great a Redeemer, who knows his sheep and does not allow them to be snatched from his hands. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCXL.
units.tr: HOMILY 240.

units.la: Tunc egredientibus ipsis ex Iericho, secuta est eum turba multa. Et ecce duo caeci sedentes iuxta viam cum audissent IESVM praeterire, clamarunt dicentes: Miserere nostri Domine, Fili Dauid. Turba autem obiurgabat eos, vt tacerent. Illi vero magis clamabant, dicentes: Miserere nostri Domine, fili Dauid. Et cum substitisset IESVS, vocauit eos, & ait: Quid vultis faciam vobis? Dicunt ei Domine, vt aperiantur oculi nostri. Misericordia autem commotus IESVS tetigit oculos eorum, & statim visum receperunt oculi eorum, & secuti sunt eum.
units.tr: As they went out from Jericho, a great crowd followed him. And behold, two blind men sitting by the road, when they heard that Jesus was passing by, cried out, saying: "Have mercy on us, Lord, Son of David." The crowd rebuked them, telling them to be quiet. But they cried out all the more, saying: "Have mercy on us, Lord, Son of David." And Jesus stood still, called them, and said: "What do you want me to do for you?" They said to him: "Lord, that our eyes may be opened." Moved with compassion, Jesus touched their eyes, and at once they received their sight, and they followed him.

units.la: Quoniam parens noster Adam peccando non solum a dignitate sua excidit, verum etiam intellectus lumine, quo donatus fuerat, amisso, seipsum et posteros perdidit, vt homo anima lis non percipiat, quae sunt Spiritus Dei: nō temere inter promissi Seruatoris IESV CHRISTI beneficia non postremum celebratur, quod ipse Sol ille iustitiae sit, in cuius alis est sanitas, & Lux illa mundi, qui sola mentes illuminat, vt possint videre, quomodo in hoc saeculo viuere debeant, vt aeternam salutem assequantur. De hoc Dauid in Psalmo loquitur: Penes te est fons vitae, in luce tua videbimus lucem. Item, Iehouah lux mea, a quo timebo? Et Isaias de Christo vaticinans: Populus positus in tenebris vidit lucem magnam, & constitutis in regione & vmbra mortis lux exorta est: Quem locum supra Matthaeus annotauit, & de illo interpretatus est. Ioannes item de illo scribens: In ipso vita erat, et vita illa erat Lux hominum. Ipse deinde Christus apud Ioan, publice exclamat: Ego sum Lux illa mundi: Qui sequitur me, non ambulabit in tenebris, sed habebit lumen vitae. Et rursus: Dum Lucem habetis, credite in lucem, vt filij lucis sitis. Quia vero tanta est homum prauitas, vt plerique tenebris gaudeant: & ideo quasi sibi pfis sufficiant, sibi non putent alia luce opus esse. Christus quod verbis profitetur, signis & miraculis multis demonstrauit, dum secundum promissionem veterem, cuius Isaias meminit, multis caecis oculos aperuit. Ex quibus aliqua hucusque vidimus, quibus accedit quod in praesenti narratur: vt nimirum Ierichuntem transiens duos caecos visu donarit vrbem egressus, cum prius in vrbis ingressu (vt Lucas scribit) idem beneficium cuidam contulisset. Quia enim ia inflabat mortis hora, signa accumulare voluit, & ideo postquam Ierosolymam venit multos caecos & claudos sanauit in templo (sicut proximo cap. dicetur) vt scandalo crucis mederetur, & doceret penes se quaeri debere, quaecunque ad salutem sunt necessaria. Sed quia miraculi huius descriptio multa habet, quae nostrae institutioni seruiunt, praefat omnes historiae circumstantias ex ordine videre: Primo nimirum, qui fuerint ij, in quibus miraculum est editum, & quid fecerint? Deinde, quid cum illis egerit Christus? Postremo, vt beneficium ipsis collatum acceperint?
units.tr: Since our first parent Adam, by sinning, not only fell from his dignity but, having lost the light of understanding with which he had been endowed, ruined himself and his descendants, so that the natural man does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God, it is no small matter that among the benefits of the promised Saviour Jesus Christ this is celebrated: that he is that Sun of righteousness, in whose wings is healing, and that Light of the world, who alone illumines minds, so that they may see how they ought to live in this age in order to attain eternal salvation. David speaks of this in the Psalm: "With you is the fountain of life; in your light we shall see light." Likewise: "The LORD is my light; whom shall I fear?" And Isaiah, prophesying of Christ: "The people who sat in darkness have seen a great light, and on those who dwelt in the region and shadow of death a light has dawned." Matthew noted this passage above and interpreted it concerning him. John, too, writing of him, says: "In him was life, and that life was the light of men." Then Christ himself, in John, cries out publicly: "I am that Light of the world; whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life." And again: "While you have the Light, believe in the Light, so that you may be sons of light." But because human wickedness is so great that most people delight in darkness, and therefore think themselves sufficient for themselves, they do not suppose that they need any other light. Christ demonstrated by signs and many miracles what he professed in words, when, according to the ancient promise of which Isaiah speaks, he opened the eyes of many blind men. We have already seen some of these cases, and to them is added what is related in the present passage: namely, that as he passed through Jericho he gave sight to two blind men as he left the city, although earlier, on entering the city (as Luke writes), he had conferred the same benefit on another man. For since the hour of his death was now approaching, he wished to pile up signs, and therefore, after he came to Jerusalem, he healed many blind and lame people in the temple (as will be told in the next chapter), to remedy the scandal of the cross and to teach that whatever is necessary for salvation must be sought with him. But since the account of this miracle contains many things that serve our instruction, let us look at all the circumstances of the history in order. First, who they were in whom the miracle was performed, and what they did; then, what Christ did with them; and finally, how they received the benefit conferred upon them.

units.la: Quoad primum, caeci fuerunt: & licet non exprimat Euangelista, ex natiuitate nec caeci fuerint (vt ille, de quo Ioannes nono cap. scribit) aut ex casu aliquo vel morbo hoc vitium contraxerint, constat caecitatem ingens malum esse, eo quod visus ad res agendas tam necessarius est, vt nullo alio sensu minus possimus carere: quae causa est, quod caecus, etsi nihil aliud mali accedat, vulgo homo miser & calamitosus dicatur: Blind man/arm man. At istos simul dura egestas pressit, quae eos in publico via obsidere coegit, ut a praetereuntibus stipem peterent ad vitam sustentandam. Ut vero alibi annotauimus, quoties mendicantium meminerunt Euangelista, populi Iudaici corruptus status perstringitur, qui Legis Dei immemor egenos & pauperes immisericorditer neglexit. Etenim aliter illam Remp.instituerat Deus, cuius constitutio erat: Ne sit in te mendicus. Nimirum, quod ut mendicitas publica animos immites & a dilectione fraterna alienos arguit: ita morum honestati & religioni, disciplinae denique officit, quam nulli minus ferunt, quam qui abstersó pudore mendicitati assuenerunt. Ideo primitiua Ecclesia ex Apostolorum institutione hoc vitium correxit, quod Sacerdotum auaritia inuexerat, & ita egenis ius prospexit, ut non esset inter eos, qui Christo nomen dederant, qui victum mendicando sibi parare cogeretur. At hodie impossibile putatur, quod olim factum est, quando nullas opes habuit Ecclesia, quam quas quotidie credentes conferebant. At conuincunt illos nostri saeculi mores, cum plerisque ad luxum sufficiat, multi etiam ex ijs ditescant, quae olim viri principes & pij contribuerunt, ut Ecclesiae ministris & egenis prospiceretur.
units.tr: As to the first point: they were blind. Although the Evangelist does not state it, they were not blind from birth (like the man about whom John writes in chapter nine), nor had they contracted this defect from some accident or disease. It is certain that blindness is a great evil, because sight is so necessary for doing the things of life that we can least of all do without any other sense. This is why a blind man, even if nothing else bad befalls him, is commonly called a wretched and miserable man: Blind man/arm man. But these men were at the same time pressed by harsh poverty, which forced them to beg by the road, so that they might seek alms from passers-by to sustain their lives. As we have noted elsewhere, whenever the Evangelists mention beggars, the corrupt state of the Jewish people is exposed, which, forgetful of the Law of God, neglected the needy and the poor without mercy. For God had established the commonwealth otherwise, and its constitution was: "Let there be no beggar among you." Indeed, just as public begging betrays hard hearts alienated from brotherly love, so it also hinders good morals, religion and, finally, discipline, which no one bears less than those who, having cast off shame, have grown accustomed to begging. Therefore the early Church, following the institution of the Apostles, corrected this evil which the greed of priests had introduced, and so provided for the needy that among those who had given their name to Christ there was no one compelled to get his living by begging. But today it is thought impossible what was once done, when the Church had no resources except those that the believers contributed daily. Yet the morals of our age prove them wrong: while most people have enough for luxury, and many of them grow rich on what godly and upright rulers once contributed so that the ministers of the Church and the needy might be provided for.

units.la: Porro quia isti totius humani generis typum gerunt, & nostram miseriam repraesentant, qui mente & intellectu caeci & omnium indigi sumus (ut initio dictum est) videamus quid fecerint, ut quid nobis in hac nostra conditione misera ac deplorata faciendum sit. Primo, quando audiunt IESVM per illam viam transire, mox illum inuocant. Unde apparet, illos prius de Domino & miraculosis eius operibus audiuisse, & bona spe concepta occasionem captauisse, ut eius beneficio fruerentur. Est hoc salutis initium, ut Euangelium de IESV CHRISTO audiamus, & audito credamus. Etenim ex auditu fides est, quae nos serio salutis desiderio accendit, & industrios reddit, ne quam illius occasionem negligamus. Quicunque ergo Verbum audire detrectant, salutis nunquam participes fient. Deinde forma inuocationis exprimitur: Miserere nostri Domine, Fili David. Ita Messiam vulgo vocabant Iudaei propter promissiones Dauidi factas, quae in secundo Samuelis libro capite septimo, & in Psalmis aliquibus extant: In Prophetis item, qui illum germen Isai & Dauidis vocant. Agnoscunt ergo illum esse promissum & diu expectatum humani generis Seruatorem: & plus vident ex Spiritus Sancti suggestione, quam Sacerdotes & Scribae, qui sibi ipsis occultatissimi videbantur, hactenus autem neque doctrina neque miraculis eius moueri potuerant, ut de illo ampliendo cogitarent. Est autem fidei verae certum indicium, quod quem Filium Dauidis agnoscunt in morbo incurabili & deplorato inuocant. Ex eo enim apparet, ipsos altiora & sublimiora de illo sibi pollicitos esse, quam vulgus Iudaeorum, qui non aliud quam regnum huius saeculi & liberationem ex Romana tyrannide ex illo sperabant. Praeterea solam illius misericordiam implorant: quod modestiae argumentum est, quae animi quoque facultate & omni merito se deflitutos esse sentiunt, & proinde spem omnem in gratuita illius bonitate habent repositam. Accedit his constantia fidei. Nam etsi a populo obiurgarentur, in quo alios improbos clamor fortasse offendit, alij Christo in via festinanti remoram obici nolebant, multi etiam ingenuam fidei confessionem, qua Filium Dauidis esse testabantur, indignius ferebant: pergunt tamen illi, nec propterea ab inuocatione abstinent, neque eius formulam mutant. Et haec quidem diligentius annotantur ab Euangelista, ut ex illis exemplum petamus. Itaque ipsi quoque agnita nostra miseria, captemus & quaeramus studiose omnes salutis occasiones, & per Christum oblatas auide arripiamus: In sola aute misericordia eius gratuita speremus. In primis vero meminerimus, nobis perseuerantia opus esse. Nunquam enim deerunt, qui fidei confessionem & quae ex illa fit Christi inuocationem impedire conentur. Odit enim lucem hanc mundus infelix, & ideo extinctam cupit. Hypocritae iustitiarij fremunt, si solius Christi misericordiae & merito tribuatur, quod ipsi suis meritis solent ascribere. Sunt item ex nostris saepe, qui in aduersariorum gratiam nos dissimulare vellent quod in corde sentimus: Accedunt conscientiae terrores, qui inter precandum nos dubios reddunt, & nostram nobis indignitate exprobrant. Multos etiam in precibus remissiores reddit, quod Deus interdum opem differt, & quasi nos non audiat, contemptim praeterire videtur. Sed aduersus omnia ista constanter eluctari nos oportet. Cur enim mundi iudicium audiant, quos ex hoc mundo Christus selegit, ut sibi illos consecraret? Cur vero hypocritas timeant, qui Christo nomen dede-
units.tr: Moreover, since these men bear the image of the whole human race and represent our misery, we who are blind in mind and understanding and in need of everything (as was said at the beginning), let us see what they did, so that we may learn what must be done by us in this our wretched and desperate condition. First, when they hear that Jesus is passing by that road, they immediately invoke him. From this it appears that they had earlier heard about the Lord and his miraculous works, and, having conceived good hope, they seized the opportunity to enjoy his benefit. This is the beginning of salvation: that we hear the Gospel of Jesus Christ and, having heard it, believe. For "faith comes from hearing," and it is faith that kindles in us a serious desire for salvation and makes us diligent, so that we do not neglect any opportunity of it. Therefore, whoever refuses to hear the Word will never become a partaker of salvation. Then the form of invocation is expressed: "Have mercy on us, Lord, Son of David." The Jews commonly called the Messiah thus, on account of the promises made to David, which are found in the seventh chapter of the second Book of Samuel and in some Psalms, and also in the Prophets, who call him the shoot of Jesse and of David. They therefore recognised that he was the promised and long-expected Saviour of the human race, and they saw more, by the prompting of the Holy Spirit, than the priests and scribes, who seemed to themselves most wise, but who until then had been moved neither by his teaching nor by his miracles to think about acknowledging him. It is a sure sign of true faith that they, acknowledging him as Son of David, call upon him in an incurable and desperate disease. For from this it appears that they had promised themselves higher and loftier things from him than the common crowd of Jews, who hoped from him for nothing but the kingdom of this age and deliverance from Roman tyranny. Besides, they implore his mercy alone, which is a mark of humility: they feel that they are destitute of any ability of mind and of any merit, and therefore they have placed all their hope in his free goodness. Added to these is steadfastness of faith. For although they were rebuked by the crowd, in which perhaps the loud cry offended some wicked people, and others did not want an obstacle placed in the way of Christ as he hastened on his journey, and many even took more indignantly the open confession by which they testified that he was the Son of David, yet they persisted, and did not on that account abstain from invoking him or change the form of their prayer. And these things the Evangelist notes more carefully so that we may take an example from them. Therefore, let us too, having recognised our misery, seize and eagerly seek all opportunities of salvation, and eagerly grasp those offered through Christ; and let us hope in his free mercy alone. Above all, let us remember that we need perseverance. For there will never be lacking those who try to hinder the confession of faith and the invocation of Christ that comes from it. For this unhappy world hates this light and therefore desires it extinguished. The self-righteous hypocrites rage if what they are accustomed to ascribe to their own merits is given to the mercy and merit of Christ alone. There are also often some among our own people who would wish us to conceal, for the favour of our opponents, what we feel in our hearts. Then there are the terrors of conscience, which make us doubtful while we pray and cast our unworthiness in our faces. Many also become more sluggish in prayer because God sometimes defers help and seems to pass us by with contempt, as if he did not hear us. But against all these things we must struggle on steadfastly. For why should they listen to the judgement of the world, whom Christ has chosen out of this world to consecrate to himself? And why should they fear hypocrites, who have given their name to Christ?

units.la: Ioan.15. & 10. runt, qui oues suas tuetur, nec eas sibi ex manibus eripi finit? Cur intra conscientias suas trepidè ij, quorum infirmitas, satisfactio, sanctificatio & redemptio est {Dei Filius, qui Patrem nobis placauit? Quòd si aliquando cunctetur Dominus, cogitemus nostro bono id fieri, vt maiori gratiæ Dei desiderio accendamur, in fide exerceamur & confirmemur, & illustrior fit tandè Dei nos seruantis bonitas & potentia.
units.tr: Ioan.15. & 10. ...who guards his sheep and does not allow them to be snatched from his hands? Why should those tremble inwardly in their consciences whose weakness, satisfaction, sanctification and redemption is the Son of God, who reconciled the Father to us? But if the Lord sometimes delays, let us consider that this is for our good: so that we may be kindled with a greater desire for the grace of God, be exercised and strengthened in faith, and the goodness and power of God, which preserves us, may at last shine more brightly.

units.la: Facit ad horum confirmationem altera pars historiæ istius, qua quid Christus fecerit, narratur. Primum subsistit ad clamorem cæcorum. Bonitatis eximiæ argumentum, quæ neminem fefellit: quando gradum sistit propter mendicos, ex quibus non aliud, quàm molestiam & laborem sperare poterat. Docet præterea hoc exemplum, quanta sit efficacia precationis ardentis, & ex fide vera manantis. Etenim cœlos penetrat, & patent illi aures Domini. Sistit ergo cursum fiue executionem iudiciorum Dei, & iam a nobis discessurum, quasi manu iniecta retinet. Exempla, quibus hoc confirmetur, multa passim occurrunt. Illa certè maris rubri alueum aperuit & exsiccauit Moses, vt tutum transitum Israelitis daret. Eadem Iosue Solu & Lunæ cursum cohibuit: Elias item cœlum clausit & aperuit: vt tam taceamus omnia, quæ in Euangelio innumera huius generis narrantur. Quòd hodie minus proficitur, ex eo est, quòd in precibus pleriq; frigent, & abfq; fide precantur: aut pietatis sensu destituti circa inutilia, aut ea, quæ carni seruiunt, occupantur.
units.tr: The other part of this story, which tells what Christ did, serves to confirm these points. First, he stops at the cry of the blind men. This is a sign of outstanding goodness, which never fails anyone: he halts his step on account of beggars, from whom he could expect nothing but trouble and labour. This example also teaches how effective is an ardent prayer that springs from true faith. For it penetrates the heavens, and the ears of the Lord are open to it. So he halts the course, or the execution, of God's judgments, and holds back, as if with a hand laid on him, the one who was about to depart from us. Many examples confirming this occur everywhere. Moses indeed opened the bed of the Red Sea and dried it up, to give the Israelites a safe passage. Joshua likewise restrained the course of the sun and moon; Elijah also shut and opened the heavens. I say nothing of the countless things of this kind related in the Gospel. That less is achieved today comes from the fact that most people grow cold in prayer and pray without faith, either destitute of a sense of piety and occupied with useless things, or with the things that serve the flesh.

units.la: Secundò, vocat eos ad se. Atqui absentes sanare poterat, vt Centurionis famulum, & regij illius aulici filium, & Syrophœnissæ filiam. Sed ad se vocat istos, partim vt miraculum a pluribus obseruetur, & vt eos arguat, qui illos ipsum invocantes fatis pro imperio obiurgarunt: partim vt doceat, ad se accedere oportere eos, qui illuminari & salutem consequi cupiunt. Ad ipsum vero accedunt, qui Verbum eius audiunt, & in hoc sese offerentem fide non fucata amplexantur. Sic ipse hoc exponit apud Ioannem. Cum enim dixisset: Si quis sitit, veniat ad me, & bibat. Mox per Expositionem subijcit: Qui credit in me, sicut dixit Scriptura, flumina aquæ viuæ fluent ex ventre eius. Nam fidei effectus est, quòd in illo vno acquiescimus, & reliquis omnibus alijs rebus, cœlestia quærimus, & erga quosuis beneficentiæ studemus. Non mirum ergo, hodie paucos illuminari in tanta Euangelij luce, quæ se omniù oculis ingerit. Pauci enim fyncero corde ad Christum accedunt, imò pleriq; sibi iniuriam fieri putant, si propter ipsum vel superstitiones veteres vel carnis ac mundi studia relinquere iubeantur.
units.tr: Second, he calls them to himself. Yet he could have healed those who were absent, as he did the centurion's servant, the son of that royal official, and the daughter of the Syrophoenician woman. But he calls these men to himself, partly so that the miracle might be observed by many, and so that he might rebuke those who, when they invoked him, had too harshly scolded them for their importunity; partly to teach that those who wish to be enlightened and to obtain salvation must come to him. Indeed, those come to him who hear his Word and embrace with unfeigned faith the One who offers himself in it. So he himself explains this in John. For when he had said, "If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink," he at once added by way of explanation, "He who believes in me, as Scripture has said, out of his belly will flow rivers of living water." For it is the effect of faith that we rest in him alone, seek heavenly things, set aside all other things, and devote ourselves to every kind of goodness. No wonder, then, that today so few are enlightened in such a great light of the Gospel, which forces itself upon the eyes of all. For few approach Christ with a sincere heart; indeed, most think they are wronged if they are ordered to give up, for his sake, either old superstitions or the pursuits of flesh and world.

units.la: Tertiò, quid sibi fieri velint, interrogat. Poterat hoc ridiculum videri: Sed ex mendicorum numero erant, qui plerunq; ex morbis quæstum facere solent, multi quoq;, vt hunc vberiorem faciant, corporis vitia sibi ipsis improbè accersunt, aut ex se natorum infantium membra luxant: digni quouis supplicio, cum nihil a parricidio differat scelus illud: imò atrocius multò sit, eò quòd istorum mendicitas cum sacrilego nominis diuini abusu sit coniuncta. Et qui ista faciunt, hi curari noluint, sed turpem quæstum corporis saluti præferunt. Interrogat ergo illos Christus, primò vt pateret eos non esse ex nebulonum & erronum istorum societate: deinde vt fides ipsorum manifesta fieret, ne adulatorie clamauisse putentur: Miserere nostri Domine, fili Dauid: cùm ea abillo petant, quæ præter Messiam nemo dare poterat. Seriò ergo salutis studiù requirit Dominus, neque eos probat, qui in tenebris desidere malunt, & perire quàm vera luce illuminati Veritatem profiteri & sequi. Quin abominatur eos, qui errores semel conceptos tanta cum contumacia tuentur, vt non pudeat publicè testari, se cum illo aut illo errare & perire malle quàm cum ijs recte sentire, quos semel odisse cœperunt. Sunt hi digni, qui in erroribus suis animo & corpore pereant.
units.tr: Third, he asks what they want done for them. This might seem a ridiculous question. But these men were among the beggars, who usually make their gain from diseases; many of them, to make their takings larger, wickedly bring bodily defects upon themselves, or dislocate the limbs of the infants born to them. Such people deserve any punishment, since that crime differs in nothing from parricide; indeed, it is far more atrocious, because their begging is joined with a sacrilegious abuse of the divine name. Those who do these things are unwilling to be cured, preferring shameful gain to bodily health. Christ therefore asks them, first so that it would be clear they were not of the company of these scoundrels and vagabonds, and second so that their faith might be made manifest, lest they be thought to have cried out with flattery, "Have mercy on us, Lord, Son of David," when they were asking from him what no one but the Messiah could give. Therefore the Lord earnestly seeks the pursuit of salvation, and does not approve of those who prefer to sit in darkness and perish rather than, once enlightened by the true light, profess and follow the truth. Indeed he abhors those who defend errors once conceived with such obstinacy that they are not ashamed to testify publicly that they would rather err and perish with this or that person than think rightly with those whom they have once begun to hate. Such people deserve to perish in body and soul in their errors.

units.la: Cæterum istis non aliud petentibus, quàm vt oculi ipsorum aperirentur, misericordia motus Dominus oculos eorum tangit, & statim illuminati visum receperunt. Diuina ergo virtute hoc factum est, causa autem, quæ illam mouit, est gratuita Dei misericordia, qua hic omnes dignatur, qui ex fide ipsum inuocant. Et quidè hac opus est, quæ sola apprehendit ea, quæ ingenij nostri captum superant: & fine qua Verbum quoq; Dei non potest intelligi. Fide autem percipimus quis Deus, quæ eius voluntas, quæ vera salutis ratio, Quæ omnia in solo Dei Filio IESV CHRISTO habentur, qui cùm sit splendor gloriæ, & character diuinæ substantiæ aut persona expressus, adeoq; vnum cum Patre, recte olim Philippo dixit: Qui videt me, Patrem videt. Non temerè ergo nobis fides commendatur, ut qua sola iustitiae & salutis participes faciat.
units.tr: Moreover, since these men asked for nothing else than that their eyes be opened, the Lord, moved by mercy, touches their eyes, and at once they, enlightened, received their sight. This was done by divine power, but the cause that moved it is the free mercy of God, by which he deigns to show favour to all who call upon him in faith. And indeed this faith is needed, for it alone grasps those things that exceed the capacity of our intellect, and without it the Word of God also cannot be understood. But by faith we perceive who God is, what his will is, and what the true way of salvation is. All these things are held in the only Son of God, Jesus Christ, who, since he is the brightness of glory and the express image of the divine substance or person, and so one with the Father, rightly once said to Philip, "He who sees me sees the Father." Not without reason, then, is faith commended to us, since it alone makes us partakers of righteousness and salvation.

units.la: At praestat postremò videre, quid caeci isti fecerint. Primò vocati mox veniunt ad Christum, etsi nihil ipsis pollicetur. Est hoc nouum fidei verae indicium, quo abundè testantur, se de illo omnia sperare, quae saluti conferant. Simpliciter ergo illi obediunt: quod ita ab omnibus exigitur, ut necesse sit omnia relinquere, ut Christum vocantem sequamur. Facit huc Bartimaei caeci exemplum, de quo Marcus narrat, quod relicto pallio suo exilierit, & ad Dominum festinarit. Ita nihil eorum nos retineat, quae carni iucunda, aut etiam necessaria videntur. At hic sano de rebus huius saeculi iudicio opus est, ne caro nos fascinet, quae mundum hunc, & quae in mundo sunt, admirari solet. Quid vero in illis omnibus admiratione aut amore dignum est? Fortunae bona incerta & fluxa sunt. Corporis forma, valetudo, vires fragiles sunt. Animi dotes fallunt, nisi Spiritu Dei dirigantur. Itaque si haec omnia simul cum iustitia nostra coniungas, revera nihil nisi centones sunt, quibus fere mendici vestiuntur, & ideo neque ornare nos, neque tueri possunt. Sunt ergo revera stulti & miseri, qui Christo ipsos vocante, rebus cadacis & friuolis inhaerent, quae non solum inutiles, sed noxiae sunt, quando ab illo nos abducunt, qui solus seruat & gaudio solido exhilarat.
units.tr: But it is worth finally seeing what those blind men did. First, when they were called, they came at once to Christ, although he promised them nothing. This is a new sign of true faith, by which they abundantly attest that they hope from him for everything that conduces to salvation. They therefore obey without hesitation, which is demanded of all, so that we must leave everything behind if we are to follow Christ when he calls us. The example of the blind Bartimaeus is relevant here, of whom Mark tells that, having cast off his cloak, he leapt up and hurried to the Lord. So let nothing hold us back of those things that seem pleasant to the flesh, or even necessary. But here a sound judgment about the things of this age is needed, lest the flesh bewitch us, for the flesh is wont to admire this world and what is in it. But what in all those things is worthy of admiration or love? The goods of fortune are uncertain and fleeting. Beauty of body, health and strength are fragile. Gifts of the mind deceive unless they are directed by the Spirit of God. So if you join all these things together with our righteousness, they are in truth nothing but patchwork, such as beggars mostly wear, and therefore they can neither adorn nor protect us. Those are truly foolish and wretched who, when Christ calls them, cling to fleeting and frivolous things, which are not only useless but harmful, since they draw us away from him who alone saves and gladdens us with solid joy.

units.la: Praeterea, ut ad Christum ipsos vocantem caeci isti accedunt, & non aliud petunt, quam ut oculi ipsorum aperiantur: ita postquam hic eos voti compotes fecit, illum secuti sunt, & eo segregatos pro accepto beneficio, adhaec non tam corpore quam animo illuminatos esse testantur. Est, eò laudabilior illorum promptitudo, quod eum sequuntur, qui (ut paulo ante diximus) nihil quod mundo magnificum est suis sectatoribus pollicebatur, & quos pauperes, obscuros & huius saeculi potentibus exosos esse videbant. Itaque faciunt, quod ab omnibus ille requirit, qui ipsius discipuli esse volunt, dicens: Si quis vult post me venire, abneget seipsum, & tollat crucem suam quotidie, & sequatur me. Quod ergo isti faciunt, hoc omnes, qui illi nomen dederunt, in exemplum sibi factu esse existimant, ut ipsi quoque abnegatis & mortificatis vitiosae naturae desiderijs et procul relictis mundi improbi studijs, toti innocentur, & post IESVM CHRISTVM in ipsius vijs ambulent, ut hic in ipsis glorificetur, cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: Moreover, just as these blind men came to Christ when he called them, and sought nothing but that their eyes be opened, so, after he had granted their request, they followed him, and, separated from their former life for the benefit received, they testify that they were enlightened not so much in body as in mind. Their readiness is the more praiseworthy because they followed him who (as we said a little before) promised his followers nothing that is splendid in the world's eyes, and whom they saw to be poor, obscure, and hateful to the powerful of this age. So they do what he requires of all who want to be his disciples, saying, "If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross daily, and follow me." What these men did, all who have given their name to him should consider an example for themselves as well: that, having denied and mortified the desires of corrupt nature and put far away the pursuits of the wicked world, they should be wholly renewed, and walk after Jesus Christ in his ways, so that he may be glorified in them, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.tr: HOMILY 241.

units.la: ET cum appropinquassent Ierosolymis, & venissent Bethphage ad montem Olearum: tunc IESVS misit duos discipulos, dicens eis: Ite in vicum, qui vobis est ex aduerso, & statim inuenietis asinam ligatam, & pullum cum ea: Soluite, & adducite mihi. Et si quis vobis aliquid dixerit, dicite: Domino his opus est: Et statim mittet eos.
units.tr: And when they drew near to Jerusalem, and were come to Bethphage, unto the mount of Olives, then Jesus sent two disciples, saying unto them: Go into the village over against you, and straightway ye shall find an ass tied, and a colt with her: loose them, and bring them unto me. And if any man say ought unto you, ye shall say, The Lord hath need of them; and straightway he will send them.

units.la: TIESVM CHRISTVM recte agnoscamus, probe tenendum est, cum non solum Sacerdotem esse aeternum, qui sui corporis & sanguinis sacrificio peccata mundi expiarit, & pro nobis apud Patrem intercedat: verumetiam quod Rex sit, qui nos ex diaboli potestate vindicarit, & regnum habeat aeternum cuius non sit finis. Talem passim Prophetae describunt, quorum vaticinia olim Iudaei norant quidem, sed in eo non solum vulgus, verumetiam domestici illius discipuli errabant, quod regnum in illo terrenum somniarent: quae causa erat, quod alij quidem IESVM hunc, qui pauper & inops nullo splendore commendabatur, non possent pro Messia agnoscere, discipuli vero regni terreni spe decepti inter se ambitiose de primatu rixarentur, & postea eius vinculis offensi diffugerent. Itaque ille cum iam mortis suae hora instaret, re ipsa docere voluit, se Regem esse, & quae sit regni sui conditio. Nam urbe non ut antea solitus fuerat, pedes ingreditur, sed pullo asinae insidens, se publicis populi acclamationibus celebrari finit, & toti urbi, hostibus autem maxime, terrorem incutit, & multa facit, quibus maiestatem
units.tr: If we are rightly to acknowledge Jesus Christ, we must firmly hold that he is not only an eternal Priest, who by the sacrifice of his body and blood has expiated the sins of the world and intercedes for us with the Father, but also that he is a King, who has delivered us from the power of the devil and who has an eternal kingdom without end. The Prophets everywhere describe him thus, and the Jews of old indeed knew their prophecies; but in this matter not only the common people but even his own familiar disciples went astray, dreaming that his kingdom was an earthly one. This was why others could not recognise this Jesus, who was poor and destitute and commended by no splendour, as the Messiah, while the disciples, deceived by hope of an earthly kingdom, quarrelled ambitiously among themselves about primacy, and afterwards, offended by his sufferings, scattered. So when the hour of his death was now at hand, he wished to teach by deed that he was a King, and what the condition of his kingdom was. For he did not enter the city on foot as he had been accustomed to do before, but, sitting upon a colt of an ass, he allowed himself to be celebrated with the public acclamations of the people, and he struck terror into the whole city, and most of all into his enemies, and did many things by which he displayed his kingly majesty.

units.la: P regiam exerit. Interim apparatus est eiusmodi, qui satis ostendit, regnum eius non esse de hoc mundo: tandem vero capitur quoque, & iniquo iudicio damnatus in cruce moritur, sed ex mortuis resuscitatus caelos conscendit, unde misso Spiritu Sancto Apostolos totius orbis doctores fecit, quorum praedicatione regnum suum inter gentes longe lateque propagavit. Ex quo appareat, illum eiusmodi Regem esse, qui per Crucem de mundo & eius principe triumpharit, & in caelestem gloriam euectus omnes hostes pedibus suis subiecerit. Nobis autem historia ipsius hic vsus esse debet, ut non offendamur illius crucem, neque etiam aduersis, quae nobis accidunt. In praesenti, quomodo se ad ingressum in urbem praepararit, narratur, ubi multa concurrunt, quae nos in eius cognitione instituunt.
units.tr: He displays royal majesty. Meanwhile the preparation was of such a kind as sufficiently shows that his kingdom is not of this world. At last indeed he was also taken, and condemned by an unjust judgment, and died on the cross; but raised from the dead he ascended into heaven, whence, having sent the Holy Spirit, he made the apostles teachers of the whole world, and by their preaching he spread his kingdom far and wide among the nations. From this it appears that he is the kind of King who through the Cross has triumphed over the world and its prince, and, carried up into heavenly glory, has subjected all enemies under his feet. But his history ought to be used by us here, so that we are not offended at his cross, nor at the adversities that befall us. In the present passage it is narrated how he prepared himself for entering the city, where many things come together that instruct us in knowledge of him.

units.la: Principio cum Dominus comitantibus ipsum turbis appropinquasset Ierosolyma, ubi mortem ignominiosam obiturus erat, & Bethphagen venisset, quae ad radices montis olearum sita fuit, misit duos ex discipulis, qui ex proximo vico ipsi adducant asinam cum pullo suo, cui insidens postea urbem ingressus est. Poterat hoc ridiculum videri, vili nimirum iumento, & eo quidem precario sumpto illum vehi, qui se promisisset illum Regem gloriae esse docere volebat.
units.tr: First, when the Lord, with crowds accompanying him, had drawn near to Jerusalem, where he was about to undergo an ignominious death, and had come to Bethphage, which lies at the foot of the Mount of Olives, he sent two of the disciples to bring him from the nearby village an ass with her colt, and mounting this he afterwards entered the city. This might seem ridiculous: that he who had promised to show that he was the King of glory should be carried on a lowly beast of burden, and one that was borrowed at that.

units.la: Et enim huius saeculi Reges si unquam alias superbiunt, seipsos tamen quasi superant fastu & luxu, si quando vrbes, regnorum suorum praecipuas sedes, ingrediuntur, ut in regni possessionem veniant. At Christus nunc proprio exemplo confirmat, quod nuper Apostolos monuit, non debere ipsos Reges gentium imitari, sed potius modestia & humilitati studere. Ita tamen hoc facit ipse, ut in sua humili ac vili specie earum virtutum specimen edat, quae in Regibus praecipue commendantur, imo quae cum laude regnare volentibus necessariae sunt: quales sunt, Sapientia, Potentia & Iustitia, de quibus singulis dicemus.
units.tr: For if kings of this age ever show pride, they surpass themselves in arrogance and luxury when they enter cities, the chief seats of their kingdoms, in order to take possession of their realm. But Christ now confirms by his own example what he lately taught the apostles, that they ought not to imitate the kings of the nations, but rather to devote themselves to modesty and humility. Yet he does this in such a way that, in his humble and lowly appearance, he displays a pattern of those virtues which are especially commended in kings, and indeed which are necessary for those who wish to reign with praise: such as wisdom, power and justice, each of which we shall discuss.

units.la: Quoad sapientiam, in primis ea a Regibus requiritur, ut nimirum norint quae in genere ad Rempub. pertinent, & quibus Legibus opus sit: deinde qui populi, qui ipsorum fidei creditus est, mores sint, & quomodo ipsum regere oporteat. Sut enim instar capitis in corpore humano. At nisi illud sapiat, recordetur, vel visu, auditu, olfactu, gustu praeditum sit, capitis officium nunquam praestare, nec maior eius, quam pedum aut alterius vilissimi membri dignitas erit. Imo idolorum simulacra sunt principes, qui nihil sapiunt, nihil vident, neque audiunt, nullam deniq; rerum praesentium & futurarum habent rationem. Quod Solomon observans, cum optionem a Deo haberet postulandi quod vellet, sapientiam sibi dari petijt, ut posset ingredi & exire coram Domino, & ea facere, quae populi tam magni & multi salus exigebat. Atque in eo Christus omnes Reges superat, quotquot unquam fuerunt, aut adhuc sunt. In eo enim reconditi sunt omnis scientiae & sapientiae thesauri: quod (ut nunc alia omittamus) haec historia abunde docet. Qui enim modo ex Galilaea veniebat, videt & novit quid fiat in vico illo, & quid illic inventuri sint discipuli, praedicere poterit. Id vero consolationi seruiat, quando Satan suggerit, nos abillo negligi, aut etiam ignorari. Quomodo enim ouium suarum non haberet curam, qui auiculas & coruorum pullos, adhaec asinos respicit? Videt ergo nos in quovis periculo. Novit innocentiam nostram, quando calumniis improborum hominum premimur: videt vim apertam, quae nobis fit. Et quia ita nos dilexit, ut seipsum pro nobis tradiderit, non sinet nos tentari supra quam ferre possumus. Deinde ad vitae etiam institutionem facit haec consideratio, ut memores nos illi curae esse, qui olim in nubibus caeli veniet ad iudicandum vivos & mortuos, sanctitatem tueamur & sectemur, ne eius oculos offendamus, qui nos sanguinis sui lauacro abluere dignatus est.
units.tr: As to wisdom, first of all it is required of kings that they know what pertains in general to the commonwealth, and what laws are needed; then what manners the people entrusted to their faith have, and how it is fitting to rule them. For they are like the head in the human body. But unless the head is wise, and remembers, or is endowed with sight, hearing, smell and taste, it never performs the office of a head, nor will it have any greater dignity than the feet or some other most lowly member. Indeed, princes who understand nothing, see nothing, and hear nothing, and who in the end take no account of present or future things, are like images of idols. Solomon, observing this, when he had the choice from God of asking for whatever he wished, asked that wisdom be given him, so that he might go in and come out before the Lord, and do those things which the welfare of so great and so numerous a people required. And in this Christ surpasses all kings, as many as have ever been or still are. For in him are hidden all the treasures of knowledge and wisdom; and this history, to say nothing of other things, teaches this abundantly. For he who was now coming from Galilee sees and knows what is happening in that village, and can foretell what the disciples will find there. And this serves for consolation, when Satan suggests that we are neglected by him, or even unknown to him. For how would he not have care of his sheep, who regards the little birds and the young ravens, and asses besides? He therefore sees us in every danger. He knows our innocence when we are oppressed by the slanders of wicked men; he sees the open violence that is done to us. And because he has loved us so much that he gave himself for us, he will not allow us to be tempted beyond what we can bear. Furthermore, this consideration also serves for the training of our life: that, mindful that we are a care to him who will one day come on the clouds of heaven to judge the living and the dead, we may guard and pursue holiness, lest we offend the eyes of him who has deigned to wash us in the laver of his blood.

units.la: Deinde evidens potentiae suae specimen hic edit Dominus, qua Regibus & omnibus, qui Magistratum gerunt, opus est, ut contumaces in ordinem cogere possint, & vim apertam a populo suo depellere, ac bonos tueri. Ideo eos gladio & authoritate armavit Deus, quam gentes omnes, etiam barbarae agnoscunt. At quoad hanc quoque omnibus potentior est Christus, ut qui corda quoque hominum in sua manu habet, & ex inutiis voluntarios facit. Huius enim opus fuit, quod ipsi asinam cum pullo abduci sinunt ab hominibus peregrinis, & ut videtur, ignotis. Simile quid in ipsis discipulis factum fuit prius, quando ab illo vocati, alij sua negotia, alij quaestum suum & munera publica subito reliquerunt, & ipsum secuti sunt. Sic Paulus ex lupo rapace in momento ouis factus, sese ad omne obsequium sponte offerebat, dicens: Domine, quid me vis facere? Ideo David de illa vatici vaticinabatur olim: Populus tuus vltroneus in die ostentationis copiarum tuarum. Nam Paulo teste, idem ille in omnibus agit velle & facere. Quod similiter nos consolari debet. Poterit enim ho die etiam mentes hominum flectere, vt nobis egentibus benefaciant: & hostes placare iratos, vt a vindicta abstineant, & qui paulo ante nostrum sanguinem sitiebant, cum lachrymis culpam deprecentur: quod Saulem in Dauidis causa aliquando fecisse legimus. Efauum item, quando Iacobo obuiam venit, quem prius coegerat in oras longinquas profugere. Quod si qui non mutent ingenia, tamen freno suae potentiae eos coercere potest, ne tantum noceant, quantum volunt: cuius rei exem plain Achabo, Zedechia & similibus tyrannis extant. Quid enim non possit in homines ille, qui mari terminum suum posuit, qui item daemones in officio continet, ne abfq; ipsius nutu aliquid possint? Sin vero vel hos vel illos aliquid aduersus nos permittit, nostro bono illud fit, quos castigari prodest, ne cum mundo infelici condemnemur. 1.Cor.11.
units.tr: Next, the Lord here gives a clear pattern of his power, which kings and all who hold magistracy need, so that they may be able to bring the unruly into order, to repel open violence from their people, and to protect the good. For this reason God armed them with the sword and with authority, which all nations, even barbarous ones, acknowledge. But Christ is more powerful than all in this respect as well, since he holds the hearts of men in his hand and makes the unwilling willing. For it was his doing that the men who were strangers and, as it seems, unknown, allowed the ass with her colt to be led away. Something similar happened earlier with the disciples themselves, when they were called by him: some left their affairs, others their gain and public offices, and suddenly followed him. So Paul, from a ravening wolf turned in a moment into a sheep, offered himself willingly to every obedience, saying: "Lord, what wilt thou have me to do?" Therefore David long ago prophesied of this: "Thy people shall be willing in the day of thy power." For, as Paul testifies, the same one works in all men both to will and to do. This ought similarly to console us. For even today he can bend the minds of men so that they do good to us in our need, and appease enemies who are angry so that they refrain from vengeance, and those who a little before thirsted for our blood may beg pardon for their fault with tears; as we read that Saul once did in the cause of David, and Esau likewise when he came to meet Jacob, whom previously he had forced to flee to distant regions. But if some do not change their dispositions, yet he can restrain them with the bridle of his power, so that they do not harm as much as they wish; examples of this exist in Ahab, Zedekiah and similar tyrants. For what could he not do against men, he who set the sea its bound, and who also keeps the demons in check, so that they can do nothing without his nod? But if he allows either these or those to do anything against us, it is done for our good, whom it profits to be chastised, lest we be condemned together with the unhappy world. 1.Cor.11.

units.la: Praeterea iustitiae etiam exemplum hic edit, sine qua nulli Reges vel Magistratus consiste- re, aut regna sua feruare possunt. Ideo enim instituti sunt, vt iudicia Dei enuntient, & absq; omni personarum respectu ius dicant. Quod nisi faciant, in tenebrarum potestatem degenerat ipsorum authoritas, neq; diu ipsi durare possunt. Nam Deo inuisi fiunt, qui iniusta iudicia abominantur, & abalienantur ab illis hominum animi, quae causa est, vt fere contemptissimi hominum fiant, et tandem male pereant. Exempla huius generis multa in historijs occurrunt cum sacris tum prophanis. Quare non absq; causa olim Solomon dixit: Qui iudicat pauperes in veritate, huius solium perpetuo firmum erit. Item iudicio Rex ditionem confirmat: at qui tributis & exactionibus inhiat, euertit eam. Porro quoad hoc quoq; Christus omnibus praestat. Etenim etsi hic omnium dominus sit, & legitimam a Patre potestatem acceperit omnium quae sunt in coelo & in terra: attamen nullius domo aut bonis vnquam vsus est, illo nolente, aut reluctante: & in praesenti discipulos iubet ratio-nem sui facti reddere, si interrogentur, cur asinos abducant. Ergo vel hoc etiam nomine regnum eius aeternum est. Arguit autem suo exemplo fanaticos turbatores, qui sub Euangelij & Christianae aut fraternae communionis praetextu Platonicam aut Anabaptisticam bonorum omnium communionem introducere studeant: & in hunc finem primitiuae Ecclesiae exemplo abutuntur: quod tamen ipsos validissime confutat, si omnes circumstantiae propius inspiciantur: sicuti suo loco demonstrauimus. Sufficiat nobis vnius Christi exemplum, neq; in aliorum fortunas nobis plus licere putemus, quam ille sibi licere voluit, qui optimo iure omnibus, ceu proprijs vti poterat. Itaq; singuli egenis ex suis facultatibus benefaciant, alijs autem sua relinquant, ne dum Christiani perfectissimi videri volunt, fures & raptores fiant. Huius autem loci hic nobis vsus est, vt IESVM CHRISTVM agnoscamus Regem sapientissimum & omnificum, omnipotentem & iustum, & proinde ipsi fidelitatem & obsequamur.
units.tr: Furthermore, this passage also provides an example of justice, without which no kings or magistrates can stand or preserve their realms. For they have been appointed so that they may pronounce the judgments of God and render justice without any regard for persons. If they do not do so, their authority degenerates into the power of darkness, and they cannot last long. For those who abhor unjust judgments become hateful to God, and men's minds are alienated from them; this is the cause why such rulers become the most despised of men and at last perish miserably. Many examples of this kind occur in histories, both sacred and profane. Hence Solomon rightly said long ago: "He who judges the poor in truth, his throne will be firm for ever." Likewise, "a king establishes his realm by judgment, but he who greedily seeks tributes and exactions overthrows it." Moreover, in this respect too Christ excels all others. For although he is the Lord of all, and has received from the Father lawful power over all things in heaven and on earth, yet he never used anyone's house or goods against the owner's will or in spite of his resistance; and now he orders the disciples to give an account of their action, if they are asked why they are untying the donkeys. Therefore, for this reason too, his kingdom is eternal. Moreover, by his own example he refutes the fanatical troublemakers who, under the pretext of the gospel and of Christian or brotherly fellowship, strive to introduce a Platonic or Anabaptist communion of all goods, and to this end abuse the example of the primitive Church; yet this very example refutes them most strongly, if all the circumstances are examined more closely, as we have shown in its proper place. Let the example of Christ alone suffice for us, and let us not think that we may take more liberty with the fortunes of others than he wished to take for himself, he who could rightly use everything as if it were his own. Therefore let each one do good to the needy from his own means, and leave the goods of others to others, lest, while wishing to appear the most perfect Christians, they become thieves and robbers. The purpose of this passage for us is that we may acknowledge Jesus Christ as the most wise and all-powerful King, almighty and just, and therefore render him faith and obedience.

units.la: De hoc discipuli isti duo nos suo exemplo admonent. Erant enim multa quae ipsos abstererepo terant, quo minus huic Christi mandato obedirent. Inhonestum, suspectum & periculosum erat, ho mines peregrinos insalutatis heris asina alligata soluere, & cum pullo suo abducere. Sed vt primus omnibus suis rebus relictis illum secuti sunt, & ipsi ad praedicandum eos mittenti abfq; comeatu & viatico simpliciter paruerunt: ita nunc quoq; non respondent, neq; tergiuersantur, sed abfq; contradictione faciunt, quod iusti erant. Est hoc praeclarum obedientiae fidei exemplum, quod imitari debemus, eo quod sine illa germani IESV CHRISTI discipuli esse non possumus. Etenim frequenter fit, vt quae ille iubet, carnis rationi & mundi iudicio absurda, indecora, iniqua, periculosa deniq; & noxia videantur. Sed tunc sensus nostros cum intellectu per fidei obedientiam Dei Verbo subijcere debemus, & sola illius authoritas nobis sufficiat. Qui enim ipsa iustitia, adhaec omniscius & nostri amantissimus est, nihil iubet quod iniustum, quod inhonestum, quod superuacaneum aut cum periculo non necessario coniunctum sit: & idque cum Dominus exercituum sit, & ipsi omnes creaturae obediant, in suis praeceptis incedentes tueri potest, ne vllis periculis succumbant. Itaq; aduersus illius mandata disputare, impium & sceleratum est. Quia id non potest fieri, quin stultitia & iniquitatis insimuletur. Et exempla sunt, quae docent, quam infeliciter haec audacia multis ceciderit. E contra qui Dei mandatis obediunt, & in eius vocatione ambulant, ijs leuia & tuta ille facit, & faciliafactu, quae impossibilia & plena periculi videbantur.
units.tr: These two disciples admonish us about this by their example. For there were many things that could have deterred them from obeying this command of Christ. It seemed dishonourable, suspicious and dangerous for men who were strangers to untie a donkey tied up without the knowledge of its owners and to lead it away with its colt. But just as they had first left all their possessions and followed him, and had simply obeyed when he sent them out to preach without provisions or travel money, so now too they do not hesitate or make excuses, but without objection do what they were bidden. This is an outstanding example of the obedience of faith, which we ought to imitate, since without it we cannot be true disciples of Jesus Christ. For it often happens that what he commands seems to human reason and worldly judgment absurd, unbecoming, unjust, and finally dangerous and harmful. But then we must subject our feelings and understanding to the word of God through obedience of faith, and his authority alone should suffice for us. For he who is justice itself, and moreover all-knowing and most loving toward us, commands nothing that is unjust, dishonourable, pointless, or necessarily bound up with danger; and since he is the Lord of hosts, and all creatures obey him, he is able to protect those who walk in his commands, so that they do not succumb to any dangers. Therefore to dispute against his commands is impious and wicked, because this cannot be done without being charged with folly and iniquity. And there are examples that teach how unhappily this audacity has fallen upon many. On the contrary, those who obey God's commands and walk in their calling, for them he makes light and safe what seemed impossible and full of danger, and easy to do.

units.la: Imitemur ergo discipulos istos, & simul confirmet nos illorum exemplu, ad quos asini isti pertinebant. Nam, ut Marcus annotauit, quidam ex illis discipulos compellarunt, dicentes: Quid facitis qui soluitis pullum? Quod non temere factum est. Nimium enim rerum suarum securus & negligens esset, qui eiusmodi facientes homines peregrinos alto silentio praeteriret. Sed audito discipulorum responso, qui Domino suo IESV hoc opus esse dixere, mox eos abduci passi sunt: ita nimirum animos illorum mouente Domino, cui (ut nuper diximus) in omnium corda ius est. Docemur autem hoc exemplo, ne quid Christo negemus eorum, quae a nobis requirit. Ipse quidem nullius eget, cum sit bipfi abunde sufficiat, utpote aeternus & omnipotens Dei Filius: sed ex immensa & gratuita boni tate nos suae gratiae & gloriae vasa facere, & ut suum regnum proueheret, nostro ministerio uti digna tur. Et quia ipse ita vult, opus est ei administrus Euangelij sui, quorum praedicatione homines ipsi adducantur: opus est principibus viris, qui Ecclesiae suae nutritij sint & defensores: opus est eis patrentum studio & fide, qui ex se natos in eius cognitione instituant, & disciplina seueriori in officio retineant. Isti ergo omnes fideles ipsi obsequiu praesent, neque eos alicuius laboris aut indulstria pigeat: & meminerint sibi etiam dictum esse, quod olim Propheta pronuntiauit: Maledictus, qui facit opus Domini maligne. Eget item, sunt, aliget & exulat saepe Christus in membris suis, & tunc ipsi nostro hospitio, pecunijs, vestitu & amictu opus est. Tunc ergo similiter erga eum benefici et liberales simus. Quis enim honestior, in fliorum quaestuosior opum huius saeculi vsus est, quam ut eum alamus, vestiamus, in aedes nostras recipiamus, qui nos creauit, qui omnes alit, vestit, feruat, quique nobis in caelo mansiones parauit, in quibus aeternum viuamus et regnemus? Et hic excitet nos promissio eius, qua se in suas rationes adscribere velle pollicetur beneficia, quae vel minimis et vilissimis hominibus, in ipsum credentibus praestiterimus. Ideo Solomo dicebat: Domino foenerantur quisquis bene facit pauperi. In primis vero nostri officij esse meminerimus, ut nosipsos, qui natura ad simus ex frenes, obstinati & omnis ingi impatientes, ipsi adducamus, & eius seruitio consecremus: Ut item aliis idem praestemus officium, & si quos asinorum instar sub scelerum sarcinis succumbere, & ut boues reliifo hero suo vagari & obberare cernimus, eos pijs admonitionibus subleuemus, & Domino adducamus. Sed o socordiam, o duritiem incurabilem, quae passim regnat. Laborant passim & egent non priuati modo homines, sed tota Ecclesia periclitantur, dissipantur, euertuntur: discipulorum labascit, famelici & sitientibus verbi pabulu & consolatio subducitur, & clamat vbiq; Christus, opus sibi esse ministrorum fide & industria, principum forti defensione, patrumfamilias diligentia & seueritate, nostrum omnium conuersione. Sed quotus quisq; clamantem audit, & egenti opem fert? Et ut rursum de singulis loquamur, quoties ille mittit suos seruos, qui nos ad ipsum addu cant, qui ut asini refragatores in vijs praeceptorum suorum subsistimus, qui voracitate & gulae studio in porcos, libidinibus vagis in canes, inuidia, odijs, truculentia in lupos, vrsos, serpentes degeneraui mus? At paucos inuenias, qui vocantem sequantur: sed plerique huius mundi Loto inescati in Circaeo stabulo grunire malunt, & in turpissimorum scelerum caeno voluntari, quam ad Ecclesiae sepia colligi, ut Deo viuant, & filiorum eius libertate fruantur. Est haec praecipua & propria malorum omnium causa quae nos vndiq; circumstant. Imitemur ergo istorum exemplu, & quando nos a Filio Dei IESV CHRISTO per suos seruos vocari sentimus, voluntarium illi praestemus obsequium, ut eius freno gubernati, in hoc saeculo vitam viuamus nostrae professioni conuenientem, & tandem cum illo in caelis regnemus, cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Let us therefore imitate these disciples, and let the example of those to whom these donkeys belonged also strengthen us. For, as Mark noted, some of those standing there said to the disciples: "What are you doing, untying the colt?" This was not done without reason. For a man who passed by in deep silence while others did such things to strangers would be too careless and negligent of his own property. But when the disciples' answer was heard, that they said the Lord Jesus had need of it, they were at once allowed to take it away; so truly the Lord moved their hearts, to whom (as we said recently) belongs the right over the hearts of all. We are taught by this example not to deny Christ anything of what he requires from us. He indeed needs nothing, since he is sufficient in himself, being the eternal and almighty Son of God; but out of his immense and free goodness he deigns to make us vessels of his grace and glory, and to use our ministry to advance his kingdom. And because he so wills, he needs servants of his gospel, through whose preaching men are brought to him; he needs princes who are nurses and defenders of his Church; he needs fathers who, with zeal and faith, instruct the children born of them in the knowledge of him and keep them in duty by stricter discipline. Let all the faithful therefore offer him obedience, and let no toil or labour weary them; and let them remember that what the prophet once declared is also said to them: "Cursed is he who does the work of the Lord deceitfully." Christ also is often in need, is hungry, is naked and is an exile in his members, and then we ourselves need to offer him our hospitality, money, clothing and covering. Then let us likewise be kind and generous toward him. For what more honourable or more profitable use of worldly wealth could there be than to feed, clothe, and receive into our houses him who created us, who feeds, clothes and preserves all, and who has prepared for us dwelling places in heaven, where we shall live and reign for ever? And let his promise stir us up, by which he pledges to credit to his own account the kindnesses we show even to the humblest and most lowly men who believe in him. Hence Solomon said: "Whoever does good to the poor lends to the Lord." Above all let us remember that it is our duty first to bring ourselves, who by nature are wild, stubborn, and impatient of every yoke, to him, and to consecrate ourselves to his service; and likewise to show the same duty to others, and when we see some, like donkeys, sinking under the burdens of their sins, or wandering and straying like oxen that have left their master, to relieve them with pious admonitions and bring them to the Lord. But, O the sloth, O the incurable hardness that reigns everywhere! Everywhere men labour and are in need, not only private persons but the whole Church is in peril, scattered and overthrown; the disciples' flock totters, the hungry and thirsty are deprived of the food and comfort of the word; and everywhere Christ cries out that he needs the faith and diligence of ministers, the strong defence of princes, the care and strictness of heads of households, and the conversion of us all. But how few hear the one crying out and bring help to the needy? And, to speak again of individuals, how often does he send his servants to lead us to himself, while we, like stubborn donkeys, stand in the ways of his precepts; how often have we degenerated, through greed and love of the belly, into swine, through wanton lusts into dogs, through envy, hatred and savagery into wolves, bears and serpents? Yet you will find few who follow the one calling; most people, allured by the Lotus of this world, prefer to grunt in the Circean stall and to wallow in the mire of the most shameful crimes, rather than be gathered into the fold of the Church, to live for God and enjoy the liberty of his children. This is the chief and proper cause of all the evils that surround us on every side. Let us therefore imitate the example of these disciples, and when we feel that we are being called by the Son of God, Jesus Christ, through his servants, let us render him willing obedience, so that, guided by his bridle, we may live a life in this world fitting our profession, and at last reign with him in heaven, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCXLII.
units.tr: HOMILY 242.

units.la: Hoc autem totum factum est, ut impleretur quod dictum est per Prophetam, dicentem: Dicite filiae Zion, Ecce Rex tuus venit tibi mansuetus, & insidens asinę, ac pullo filio subiugis. Profecti sunt autem discipuli, fecerunt, sicut imperarat eis IESVS, Et adduxerunt asinam ac pullum, & imposuerunt eis pallia sua, & collocarunt ipsum super ea. Plurima autem turba straverunt pallia sua in via: alij vero caedebant ramos ex arboribus, & sternebant in via. Porro turba quæ præibat & quæ sequebatur, clamabat, dicens: Hosanna Filio Dauid: Benedictus, qui venit in nomine Domini: Hosanna in excelsis.
units.tr: All this was done that what was spoken by the prophet might be fulfilled, saying: "Tell the daughter of Zion, Behold, your King comes to you, meek, and sitting on an ass, and on a colt, the foal of a beast of burden."
