units.tr: When the chief priests and the scribes saw the wonders that he did, and the children crying out in the temple, "Hosanna to the Son of David," they were indignant and said to him, "Do you hear what these are saying?" Jesus said to them, "Yes. Have you never read, 'Out of the mouths of infants and nursing babes you have prepared praise'?" And leaving them, he went out of the city to Bethany and lodged there.

units.la: Quoniam principes Sacerdotum & Scribae Iudaeorum, hostes Domini nostri IESV CHRISTI acerrimi fuerunt, & ijdem principum authoritate & fauore defendebantur, non immerito quis miretur, cur passi sint, illum in urbem instar Regis ingredi, populi acclamationibus laetis excipi, & ex templo eijcere quaecunque ipsi contra Dei Verbum privati quaestus causa instituerant. Sed causam nuper annotavit Matthaeus, quando ad eius introitum totam urbem commotam & territam fuisse dixit, ut nihil contra auderent. Estque hoc evidens divinae eius potentiae argumentum, ex quo apparet eum esse, quem olim David inter medios hostes dominaturum esse praedixit. Caeterum licet interdum impij intra animos suos conuicti trepident, non tamen serio respipiscunt, sed quam primum respirare ipsis licet, mox ad ingenium redeunt, sicuti in Pharaone, Saule, Achabo & similibus esse videre: quibus Sacerdotes & Scribas ipsos merito adnumerauerit. Nam etsi Christi potentem manum senserint, neque quicquam contra illum verbo audeant, tamen postquam terror ille transijt, ipsum calumnijs & quaestionibus insidiosis aggrediuntur, & tandem nefaria de illo occidendo consilia ineunt. Initium istorum fuit quod modo recitavimus: & serviet locus hic multum nostrae institutioni & consolationi, si primo, quae totius actionis occasio fuerit, deinde quid illi fecerint, & ut Christus se adversus illos tutatus sit, ex ordine videamus.
units.tr: It is not surprising that someone should wonder why the chief priests and the scribes of the Jews, the most bitter enemies of our Lord Jesus Christ, and men who were defended by the authority and favour of the rulers, allowed him to enter the city like a king, to be welcomed by the joyful acclamations of the people, and to have driven out of the temple everything they had set up against God's Word for private gain. But Matthew has recently noted the reason, when he said that at his entry the whole city was stirred and frightened, so that they did not dare to do anything against him. This is a clear proof of his divine power, from which it appears that he is the one whom David long ago foretold would rule in the midst of his enemies. Moreover, although the wicked sometimes tremble when their consciences are convicted, they do not seriously repent; as soon as they are allowed to breathe again, they quickly return to their nature, as we see in Pharaoh, Saul, Ahab and others like them, among whom the chief priests and scribes are rightly to be counted. For although they have felt the mighty hand of Christ and dare to say nothing against him openly, yet once that terror has passed, they attack him with slanders and insidious questions, and at last they form wicked plans to kill him. The beginning of these things was what we have just read. This passage will serve greatly to our instruction and comfort if we consider in order: first, what was the occasion of the whole action; then, what they did to him; and how Christ protected himself against them.

units.la: Occasio fuit, quod Domino publice in templo docente, & doctrinam miraculis confirmante, pueri Ierosolymitani ijsdem vocibus, quas ex populo audierant, illum pergunt celebrare, & clamant: Hosanna filio David. Fuit autem hoc quoque singulare Dei opus, qui pueros istos excitavit ut non veriti sint praesentibus Scribis & Sacerdotibus id facere, & simul hos cohibuit, ne illos punire auderent. Interim exemplo isto docemur, quantum prosit ad puerorum institutionem, si ex parentibus & aliis, quibus cum versantur, ea audiant & videant, quae ipsos in Dei cognitione & pietate instituere possunt. Etenim proprium hoc est aetati huic, ut aliorum dicta & facta facile imitentur, idque in primis si quid praeter solitum fiat. Ideo Deus olim praecepit, ut patres familias inter suos de praeceptis suis & operibus atque iudiciorum eius exemplis dissererent & eosdem in usu mysterio rum instituerent. Et memorabile est Mariae virginis & Iosephi exemplum, qui puerum IESVM Ierosolymam ad festum illic peragendum deducere soliti fuerunt. Debebat hoc diligenter observari quoad religionem & mores. Sed multam reprehensionem meretur eorum lenitas, qui audientibus liberis suis, Verbi ministris conuiciantur, conciones sacras contemptim & odiose carpunt, male gistratibus pijs obtrectant, adhaec deierant, execrantur temere, denique obscaenis dictis & cantionibus lascivis teneros animos imbuunt. Audiunt ista pueri & imitantur, & de ijs cogitandi occasionem arripiunt, quae per aetatem adhuc ignorant. Estque haec praecipua corruptela morum causa, quae hodie passim regnat. Discant ergo Christiani homines ea in conspectu puerorum loqui, canere & facere, quæ ipsorum animos ad Dei laudes & morum probitatem possunt excitare.
units.tr: The occasion was this: while the Lord was teaching publicly in the temple and confirming his teaching with miracles, the boys of Jerusalem, using the same words they had heard from the people, went on to celebrate him and cried out, "Hosanna to the Son of David." This too was a singular work of God, who stirred up these boys so that they were not afraid to do it in the presence of the scribes and priests, and at the same time restrained the priests so that they did not dare to punish the boys. Meanwhile, from this example we are taught how much it helps the training of children if they hear and see, from their parents and others with whom they associate, things that can form them in the knowledge and piety of God. For it is characteristic of this age to imitate easily the words and deeds of others, especially if something out of the ordinary is done. Therefore God long ago commanded that heads of households should discuss with their families his precepts, his works and the examples of his judgements, and should instruct them in the use of the mysteries. And the example of the virgin Mary and Joseph is memorable, who were accustomed to take the boy Jesus up to Jerusalem to keep the feast there. This ought to be carefully observed with respect to religion and morals. But the leniency of those deserves great reproach who, while their children are listening, revile the ministers of the Word, scornfully and spitefully carp at sacred sermons, slander the godly magistrates, moreover swear oaths and curse rashly, and finally imbue tender minds with obscene talk and lewd songs. Children hear these things and imitate them, and seize upon occasions to think about things which, because of their age, they still do not know. And this is the chief cause of the corruption of morals that now reigns everywhere. Let Christians therefore learn to speak, sing and do, in the sight of children, those things which can stir their minds to praise God and to goodness of life.

units.la: Quid autem de Sacerdotum principibus & Scribis dicitur? Vident hi miracula Christi, quæ cæcorum oculos aperiebat, claudis item medebatur: cuius generis multa prius quoq; non semel vi-derant: adhæc puerorum acclamationes audiunt, & utroq; offenduntur. Nec dubium est ipsos miraculis potissimum offensos fuisse, quæ a populo in admirationem trahebantur, ut plures ad illum confluerent. Sed quia hæc tam illustria erant, ut neq; negari, neq; reprehendi possent, præteritis illis ex puerorum vocibus calumniandi ansam arripiunt, quas prius etiam in disciplinis cum urbe appropinquaret, reprehenderant, & ipsum, ut eos sic clamantes obiurgaret, monuerat, sicut Lucas annotavit. Itaq; ipsum aggressi, dicunt: Audis, quid isti dicant? Quæstione autem ista ipsum non obscure carpunt, quod ambitiosius quam tantum virum deceat, laudem ex pueris aucupetur. Qua si dicerent: Miramur equidem, quod hæc fieri patiaris. Etenim voces istæ de Mesia olim dictæ sunt, cui Spiritus sanctus divinitatis testimonium perhibere voluit, ut illum non vulgarem hominem fore doceret. At ignobile & stolidum vulgus his acclamationibus te celebrauit, nunc stul-ti pueruli idem faciunt, qui quid dicant non intelligunt. Etsi vero id ferri poterat, & per ignorantiæ prætextum excusari suum tamen erat ista prohibere, ne vel inanis gloriæ affectator putaris, aut Romano præsidi aliquid gravius tentandi occasionem præbeas.
units.tr: But what is said of the chief priests and scribes? They see the miracles of Christ, which opened the eyes of the blind and likewise healed the lame; they had seen many things of this kind before, not just once. Moreover, they hear the acclamations of the boys, and they are offended by both. There is no doubt that they were offended chiefly by the miracles, which drew the people into admiration so that more of them flocked to him. But because these were so remarkable that they could be neither denied nor found fault with, they seize upon the boys' cries as an occasion for slander, which they had already found fault with, even before he drew near the city, and he had already warned them to stop shouting in that way, as Luke noted. So they confront him and say, "Do you hear what these are saying?" By this question they openly carp at him, as though he sought glory from boys more ambitiously than such a man should. It is as if they said: "We are certainly surprised that you allow these things to be done. For these words were spoken long ago about the Messiah, to whom the Holy Spirit wished to bear witness of divinity, to teach that he would not be an ordinary man. But a base and foolish crowd has praised you with these acclamations, and now silly little boys do the same, who do not understand what they are saying." Yet even if this could be tolerated, and could be excused by the pretext of ignorance, it was nevertheless his duty to forbid it, lest you be thought a seeker of empty glory, or give the Roman governor an occasion to attempt something more serious.

units.la: Quo exemplo docemur, Christo nunquam defuturos adversarios, qui ei suum honorem invidere, & Euangelij prædicationem sopitam & extinctam velint. Est enim (ut beatus ille Simeon prædixit) positus in signum, cui contradicatur. Id vero præ aliis faciunt, quos alijs veræ fidei & pietatis magistros esse oportebat, religionis autem prætextu adsum quæstum abutuntur. Non possunt hi ferre, ut suæ existimationi aliquid derogetur, quæ ita ipsis cordi est, ut potius Dei gloriam velint obscurari. Quod si insuper quæstum suum minui aut funditus evertí videant, toti in rabiem aguntur. Experimur istud bodie, quoad Monachos & inquisitores, quorum nequitia eo intollerabilior est, quod non coram minoribus Christi aggrediuntur, sed calumniis & obtrectationibus suis apud rude vulgus in contemptum & odium adducunt, & falsis criminationibus principum iras aduersus innocentes accendunt.
units.tr: From this example we are taught that Christ will never lack adversaries, who begrudge him his honour and want the preaching of the gospel to be stifled and extinguished. For (as that blessed Simeon foretold) he is set for a sign which is spoken against. And they do this more than others, who ought to have been teachers of true faith and piety, but who abuse religion as a pretext for their gain. These men cannot bear to have anything taken away from their reputation, which is so dear to them that they would rather have the glory of God obscured. And if moreover they see their profit diminished or utterly overthrown, they are driven to a frenzy. We experience this today in the case of the monks and the inquisitors, whose wickedness is all the more intolerable because they do not attack Christ's ministers face to face, but by their slanders and detractions bring them into contempt and hatred among the uneducated crowd, and by false accusations stir up the anger of princes against the innocent.

units.la: Præstat autem diligentius videre, quæ arte illi vsi sint? Non pueros modo Christum latis acclamationibus celebrantes audierant, sed miracula quoq;, quibus hic se Saluatorem esse docebat, ut derant: At his præteritis & dissimulatis, ex puerorum vocibus calumniam illi struunt. Ita hodie qui Euangelium Christi oppugnant, beneficia, quæ ex illo præclara ad omnes redundant, malitiose tacent: utpote quod simplicium & cæcorum mentes veritatis luce illuminantur, in salutis viam reducuntur, qui prius incerti claudicabant, conscientiæ afflictæ terroribus diris liberantur, & confracto tyrannidis iugo in libertatem filiorum Dei vindicantur, qui superstitionibus friuolis servient, &c. De his (inquam) & infinitis aliis altum silentium est apud ipsos homines, qui semel contra Christum & eius Ecclesiam coniurarunt. Atsi qui vel per incogitantiam, vel zeli Christiani ardore abrepti, aliquid dicunt aut faciunt, quod aliquam motus publicis speciem præferat, aut in suspicionem aliquo modo trahi possit, id mirifice amplificant, adeoq; ex musca (quod aiunt) elephantem faciunt, & pericula quæ nulla vspiam apparent, dira & horrenda fingunt, ut non solum vulgo ignobili, verumetiam Regibus fucum faciant. Fit hoc si quis liberius aduersus Papæ tyrannidem loquatur, si Conciliorum decretum aliquod contemptim reiiciat, manifestos abusus reprehendat, imagini ligneæ aut lapideæ seruandi vim inesse neget, aut etiam illam demoliatur & e medio tollat, ne porro scandalo sit imperitis & ignorantibus. Tunc illi in furorem conuersi, perinde agunt, ac si noui gigantes exortisunt, qui Dei Filium a dextera Patris detrahere, & cœlos ipsos expugnare conentur. Sed tunc eorum, quæ olim facta sunt, nos meminisse oportet, ne clamoribus & calumniis istorum hominum offendamur.
units.tr: It is worth looking more carefully at the craft they used. They had heard not only the boys joyfully celebrating Christ, but also the miracles by which he showed that he was the Saviour, as they had seen. Yet passing over and ignoring these, they build a charge against him from the boys' cries. So today those who attack the gospel of Christ maliciously keep silent about the blessings that flow from it to all people in abundance: namely, that the minds of the simple and blind are illuminated by the light of truth, that those who before were uncertain and limping are brought back to the way of salvation, that afflicted consciences are freed from dreadful terrors, and that, the yoke of tyranny being broken, people are restored to the liberty of the sons of God, who had been enslaved to frivolous superstitions, and so on. Of these things, I say, and of countless others, there is deep silence among those very men who have once conspired against Christ and his Church. But if any people, either through thoughtlessness or swept along by the fervour of Christian zeal, say or do something that carries some appearance of public disturbance, or that could in some way bring suspicion upon them, these men magnify it wonderfully, and so, as the saying goes, make an elephant out of a fly, and invent dreadful and horrible dangers that appear nowhere, so as to deceive not only the common people but even kings. This happens if anyone speaks more freely against the tyranny of the Pope, if he scornfully rejects some decree of the Councils, if he points out manifest abuses, if he denies that a wooden or stone image has any power to be venerated, or even if he tears it down and removes it, lest it be a stumbling block to the unskilled and ignorant. Then those men, turned into a fury, act as if new giants had arisen who try to drag the Son of God from the right hand of the Father and to storm heaven itself. But then we ought to remember what was done long ago, so that we are not wounded by the clamours and slanders of these men.

units.la: In primis autem in Christi exemplo respicere oportet, de quo in præsenti Matthæus scribit, quod libere affirmarit, se audire quid pueri dicant. Non ergo puduit illum puerorum, & praeconij quo hi ipsum celebrarunt. Qui in mundo alijs præstare volunt, & huius seculi gloria aucupantur a viris magnis & illustribus prædicari cupiunt, vulgi vero ignobilis & pauperis de se iudicia facile contemnunt. contemnunt. At non ita Christus, qui parvulorum & ignobilium laudibus gaudet, & supra his gratulatur, & spiritu suo exultans Patri gratias agit, quod mysteria regni sui abscondenit a sapi-entibus & intelligentibus, & detexerit ea infantibus: & in hoc Patris placito siuit consilio se prior sus acquiescere testatur. Id vero plurimum consolari potest homines ignobiles, qui coram mundo plerisque contemptui sunt: Ne videlicet se a Deo quoque negligi arbitrentur. Ut enim istorum pueror um voces audiuit Christus, & eas sibi placere voluit, ut etiam si propter has a Sacerdotibus & Scribis accusetur: ita omnium eorum officia grata & accepta habet, qui ipsum syncero animo colunt & praedicant. Sufficiat ergo nobis propria conscientia testimonium, & licet toti mundo displiceat nostra fides, in illo gaudeamus & exultemus, qui nos eo honore dignatus est, ut per nos praedicari velit.
units.tr: First of all, in Christ's example we must consider what Matthew writes of him in this passage: that he openly declared he heard what the children were saying. He was therefore not ashamed of the children, or of the praise with which they honoured him. Those who want to excel others in the world, and who chase the glory of this age, wish to be praised by great and distinguished men, and readily disregard the judgments of the common and poor. They disregard them. But Christ is not like that. He rejoices in the praises of little children and the lowly, takes delight in them, and, exulting in his Spirit, gives thanks to the Father that he has hidden the mysteries of his kingdom from the wise and understanding and revealed them to infants. In this he testifies that he gladly acquiesces in the Father's good pleasure and plan. This can greatly comfort lowly people, who are despised by most people in the world, so that they do not think God also neglects them. For just as Christ heard the voices of these children and was pleased to accept them, so that he was accused by the priests and scribes because of them, so he holds acceptable and pleasing the services of all who worship and proclaim him with a sincere heart. Let the testimony of our own conscience be enough for us. Even if our faith displeases the whole world, let us rejoice and exult in him who has deigned to honour us so much that he wishes to be proclaimed through us.

units.la: Porro probat quoque puerorum acclamationes Dominus, & simul seipsum omni culpa liberat. Nam vicissim Scribas & Sacerdotes interrogans ait: Nunquam legistis, Ex ore infantium & lactantium perfecisti laudem? Ad Scripturas eos remisit, sic ut harum ignorantiam illis exprobret. Quasi diceret: Cum sacerdotum principes sitis, ex quorum ore Lex requiri debet, Scripturas vos probe & exacte nouisse oportebat. Sed quantum video, vel non legistis, vel non observauistis attente, quod ad hanc causam in primis facit, & vobis scrupulum omne eximere poterat. Etenim olim David hoc nomine Dei bonitatem & potentiam celebrauit, quod laudem suam ex infantium & lactentium ore proferat, adeoque perfectam & illustrem reddat. Si ergo infantes, qui sermonis vsu adhuc destituuntur, Dei bonitatem praedicant, cur indignamini istis, qui hoc vocibus disertis faciunt. Enimuero non aliud isti faciunt, quam quod debitum officium mihi praestant: neque ego reprehendi debeo, qui illud recipio, sed vos potius culpandi estis, qui quod pueri isti vident, non videtis, & ab illis superamini, quibus ad pietatem magistri esse debebatis.
units.tr: Moreover, the Lord also approves the acclamations of the children, and at the same time frees himself from all blame. For in turn he questions the scribes and priests: "Have you never read, 'Out of the mouths of infants and sucklings you have perfected praise'?" He sends them back to the Scriptures, so that he reproaches them for their ignorance of them. It is as if he said: "Since you are the leaders of the priests, from whose mouth the law ought to be sought, you ought to know the Scriptures well and accurately. But as far as I can see, you either have not read them or have not observed them carefully, which especially bears on this cause and could have removed all your scruples. For long ago David celebrated God's goodness and power on this very point, that he brings forth his praise from the mouths of infants and sucklings, and thus makes it perfect and illustrious. If, then, infants, who as yet lack the use of speech, proclaim God's goodness, why are you angry with these children, who do it with clear voices? Indeed they are doing nothing other than rendering me the duty owed to me, and I ought not to be blamed for accepting it. Rather, you are the ones to be blamed, who do not see what these children see, and are surpassed by those to whom you ought to have been teachers of piety."

units.la: Est autem observatu dignum, quod Scripturas allegat, cum miraculis & signis, quae in omnium oculis versabantur, seipsum & pueros istos tueri posset. Calumniam ei struunt Sacerdotes ex eo, quod voces istas admittat, quae ipsi nequaquam conueniant, dum sibi acclamari sinat, Hosanna, id est, serua nos quaeso, &c. At miraculis docebat se esse Seruatorem illum promissum, cum claudos sanaret, caecorum oculos illuminaret, & alios quoque morbos humana arte immedicabiles sua virtute pelleret. Sed quasi nihil huius vnquam fecisset, Verbo Dei ex Scripturis deprompto sese tuetur: & ita docet, ut ipsi quoque ex ipsdem argumenta petamus, quibus in fidei & religionis causa nos aduersus calumnias impiorum tueamur: Etenim illarum authoritas miraculis longe praestat, quae nisi cum Verbo Dei in Scripturis comprehenso consentiant, falsa sunt, & horum factores pro impostoribus haberi debent. Vide Deut. 13. Cap.
units.tr: It is worth noticing that he appeals to the Scriptures, although the miracles and signs, which were before the eyes of all, could have defended both himself and these children. The priests plotted a charge against him because he allowed those words to be addressed to him, which did not at all suit them, when he let himself be acclaimed with "Hosanna," that is, "save us, we pray," and so on. Yet by his miracles he showed that he was the promised Saviour, when he healed the lame, gave sight to the blind, and by his power drove out other diseases that were incurable by human skill. But as if he had never done any of these things, he defends himself by the Word of God taken from the Scriptures, and so teaches that we too should seek from the same sources the arguments by which we defend ourselves against the slanders of the impious in the cause of faith and religion. For the authority of the Scriptures far surpasses miracles, which, unless they agree with the Word of God contained in the Scriptures, are false, and their workers ought to be regarded as impostors. See Deut. 13.

units.la: Quoad vero locum, quem Dominus adducit, extat hic in Psalmo 8. Praedicat eo Dauid Dei laudes, in primis autem huius bonitatem, qua homines prosequitur, commendat, & initio statim hanc tantam esse dicit, ut ex ore infantium & lactentium sibi fundarit robur, id est (ut in praesenti Christus interpretatur) laudem sibi perfecerit. Et sane licet infantes & lactantes lingua & sermonis vsu destituantur, reipsa tamen Dei prouidentiam praedicant, quae in illorum conceptione, conseruatione in vtero matris, partu item vel natiuitate, alimento deniq;, quod recens nati in uberibus maternis paratum inueniunt, ita sese exerit, ut de illius paterna erga humanum genus cura nemo possit dubitare. Ut ergo caeli dicuntur gloriam Dei annunciare, licet locutione & voce destituantur, si quis admirabilem illorum structuram & Solis atque Lunae aliorumque syderum motus consyderet: sic infantium & lactentium consideratio nos excitat, ut non possimus non paternam Dei curam & fidem laudibus euehere. Haec denique Dei laudem perficit, dum validissime per hanc confutantur Epicurei Nabales, qui vel Deum nullum esse, vel res mortalium non curare garriunt. In primis autem eorum arguitur vecordia, qui de Dei cura dubitant, cuius tot indicia in semetipsis deprehendere poterant, si suam generationem & educationem sibi in mentem reuocarent.
units.tr: As for the passage which the Lord cites, it stands here in Psalm 8. There David proclaims God's praises and especially commends his goodness, by which he cares for human beings. At the very beginning he says that it is so great that out of the mouths of infants and sucklings he has founded strength for himself, that is (as Christ interprets it here) he has perfected praise. And indeed, although infants and sucklings lack tongue and the use of speech, in fact they proclaim God's providence. This shows itself in their conception, their preservation in the mother's womb, likewise their birth, and finally in the nourishment which newborns find prepared at their mother's breasts, so clearly that no one can doubt his fatherly care for the human race. Just as the heavens are said to declare the glory of God, although they lack speech and voice, so if anyone considers the wonderful structure of these and the motions of the sun, the moon and the other stars, so the consideration of infants and sucklings stirs us up, so that we cannot help but extol God's paternal care and faithfulness with praises. Finally, this perfects the praise of God, since the Epicurean Nabals, who either babble that there is no God or that he does not care for mortal things, are most powerfully refuted by it. Above all, the folly of those is exposed who doubt God's care, of which they could find so many signs in themselves if they called to mind their own generation and upbringing.

units.la: Ex eo autem apparet, incassum laborare eos omnes, qui Christi gloriam oppugnant, & Euangelij praedicationem suppressam volunt. Persuadent hi sibi ipsis interdum, se effecturos quod volunt, si vel aliquos e medio tollant, qui docendi dexteritate & dicendi libertate aliis praestant, vel minacibus editis alios terreant, ut linguas suas cohibeant. Sed quamuis omnium ora obturentur & omnes linguæ sileant, non tamen propterea silebit diuinæ bonitatis prædicatio, quando ad hæc commendandam infantiū, adhuc a materno uberibus pendentiū, cōsideratio suffi ciet. Et huc in primis referri debet, quod apud Lucam Pharisæis rogantibus, ut discipulis silentiū imponeret, Christus respondit: Dico vobis, si illuerint isti, mox lapides clamaturos. Quia enim Dei decretum est, ut Filij regnum surgat, & Euangelium in toto orbe prædicetur, quis illud irritum faciet? Quis Spiritum Dei, quo minus spiret, remorabitur? Quod si omnium hominum linguæ cessent (ut modo diximus) pecudum & aliorum brutorum ora Deus aperire poterit, ut in Balaami asina factum est olim, vel lapidibus & truncis inanimatis nouas linguas formare, ut veritati testimonium ferant. Factum hoc Ierosolymæ, quando ei ectis Apostolis, lapides murorum disiecti doctrinam Christi confirmarunt: & hoc in Cruce pendente, omnibus tacentibus, petræ scissæ illi testimonium perhibuerunt. Et huius generis hodie multa fiunt. Nam ut ad Balaami historiam redeamus, annon Germanorum linguas & ora Deus soluit, ut Romanis Pontificibus, qui nos a sinorum & bestiarum loco habuerunt, obloqui & IESV CHRIST gloriam prædicare cœperint?
units.tr: From this it appears that all those labour in vain who attack the glory of Christ and want the preaching of the Gospel suppressed. Sometimes such people persuade themselves that they will achieve what they want if they remove from the midst those who excel others in skill in teaching and freedom of speech, or if they frighten others with threatening edicts, so that they hold their tongues. But although the mouths of all are stopped and all tongues are silent, the proclamation of divine goodness will nevertheless not be silent, since the consideration of infants still hanging at their mothers' breasts is enough to commend it. And especially relevant here is what Christ answered in Luke, when the Pharisees asked him to order his disciples to be silent: "I tell you, if these were silent, the stones would immediately cry out." For since it is God's decree that the kingdom of the Son should rise and the Gospel be preached throughout the whole world, who will make it void? Who will hold back the Spirit of God from breathing where he wills? And if the tongues of all men should cease (as we have just said), God will be able to open the mouths of cattle and other brute beasts, as once happened with Balaam's donkey, or to form new tongues from stones and lifeless logs, so that they bear witness to the truth. This happened at Jerusalem, when the Apostles had been cast out, and the stones of the walls, thrown down, confirmed the doctrine of Christ; and when he hung on the Cross, and all were silent, the split rocks bore witness to him. And many things of this kind happen today. For to return to the story of Balaam, has not God loosed the tongues and mouths of the Germans, so that they have begun to speak against the Roman pontiffs, who have treated us as dogs and beasts, and to proclaim the glory of Jesus Christ?

units.la: Cæterum quia sciebat Dominus sibi rem esse cum incurabilibus, ijs relictis abijt in Bethaniam, & illic diu versatus est, ubi amicos habuit fidos, Lazarum cum sororibus Martha & Maria: Si monem item leprosum & similes. Cuius in discipulis huius Lucas indicat, quod primarij Sacerdotes cum Scribis & Senioribus illum perdere conati sint. Itaq; nullam noctem in urbe mansit, præter eam, in qua captus est, ne ante tempus illis occasionem daret aliquid aduersus ipsum tentandi, quod prius quoque illum aliquoties fecisse legimus. Arguitur autem Ierosolymitanorum ingratitudo, qui tam multis tamque magnis beneficijs per Christum affecti, tam inhumaniter eum negligunt, ut nemo sit in urbe opulenta & populosa, qui illi cutum hospitium præbeat, nedum qui ipsum contra hostium insidias defendat. Sunt horum similes multi hodie pastum: quorum eadem fors est, quæ Ierosolymæ fuit. Ut enim ab ingratis Christus discessit, ita hodie ab ijs discedit, qui ipsi contumaciter reluctantur: discedens vero secum aufert benedictionem omnem, & ingratos dignus supplicijs multat. At consolationem dulcem in eo nobis hic locus exhibet, quod ita ab ingratis & contumacibus abit Dominus, ut tamen sua Ecclesia rationem habeat, quæ tunc Bethaniæ erat. Non ergo offendamur, si hodie quoque eos relinquat, qui authoritate & potentia superbi Euangelium auersantur. Non enim horum contumacia fraudi erit electis, qui Bethaniam vilem & afflictam incolunt. In his enim implebitur, quod alibi dicit Dominus: Beati qui lugent, quoniam ipsi consolationem accipient. Et quamuis a mundo reijciatur IESVS CHRISTVS, in suis tamen regnat ac triumphat. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: But since the Lord knew that he had to do with incurable people, he left them and went away to Bethany, and stayed there for a long time, where he had faithful friends, Lazarus with his sisters Martha and Mary, and Simon the leper and others like him. Luke indicates this in the case of his disciples, when the chief priests with the scribes and elders tried to destroy him. Therefore he stayed in the city no night, except the one in which he was taken, so that he would not give them an opportunity to try anything against him before the appointed time, which we read he had also done several times before. But the ingratitude of the Jerusalemites is exposed, who, though they had been favoured by Christ with so many and such great benefits, neglected him so inhumanely that there was no one in that wealthy and populous city who would offer him a modest lodging, let alone defend him against the plots of his enemies. Many today are like them, and their fate is the same as Jerusalem's was. For just as Christ departed from the ungrateful, so today he departs from those who stubbornly resist him; and in departing he takes away with him every blessing, and punishes the ungrateful with the penalties they deserve. But this passage offers us a sweet consolation in this, that the Lord departs from the ungrateful and stubborn in such a way that he nevertheless takes account of his Church, which at that time was in Bethany. Therefore let us not be offended if today too he leaves those who, proud in their authority and power, turn away from the Gospel. For the obstinacy of these will not be a loss to the elect, who dwell in lowly and afflicted Bethany. For in them will be fulfilled what the Lord says elsewhere: "Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall receive comfort." And although Jesus Christ is rejected by the world, he nevertheless reigns and triumphs in his own. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCXLV.
units.tr: Homily 245.

units.la: Mane autem rediens in urbem, esurijt. Et cum vidisset ficum quandam in via, venit ad eam, & nihil inuenit in ea, nisi folia solum. Tunc dicit ei: Ne amplius ex te fructus nascatur in æternum. Et exaruit illico ficus.
units.tr: Now in the morning, as he was returning to the city, he was hungry. And when he saw a certain fig tree by the way, he came to it, and found nothing on it but leaves only. Then he said to it, "Let no fruit grow on you ever again." And immediately the fig tree withered.

units.la: Iohannes Apostolus & Euangelista scribit æternum & omnipotens Dei verbum carnem factum esse, & ad suos venisse, id est, ad Iudæos, quibus peculiariter promissum, & ex quibus homo natus erat, hos autem ipsum non receperunt. Apparet hoc in tota historia Euangelica, maxime tamen in ijs, quæ eius mortem proxime precesserunt. Et enim ne ignorantiam pratexere possent, post innumera miracula, quibus se illis cognoscendum præbuit, Ierosolymam ut Rex ingressus est, apparatu quidem contemptibili, sicuti olim Zacharias prædixerat, sed ita, ut diuinæ potentiæ indicia præclara præbuerit: dum populum ad ipsum cum applausu excipiendum excitat, urbem totam terrore concutit, magnates quoque continet, ne quid aduersus ipsum ausint: Adhæc in templum diuertit, sicuti Malachias vaticinatus fuit, & ibi purgat & eiectos filios Leui, & quæcunque contra Dei verbum inuenta fuerunt, eijcit. Neue ipsum aliquid hostile aut inimicum moliri putarent, ad docendum confidet, & cæcis ad ipsum venientibus visum, claudis valetuvaletudinem integram largitur, ut ita celebretur, se promissum illum Seruatorem esse, quem venturum Prophetae praedixerant. At omnibus istis non aliud profecit, quam quod Sacerdotes primarij et Scribae primo calumnijs ipsum aggrediuntur, ut populo suspectum et iniuisum reddant: deinde occisum voluit. Et ut nuper monuimus, in urbe populosa et opulenta nemo est, qui ipsum hospitio dignetur, aut apud quem tuto pernoctare possit. Itaque relicta ciuitate, Bethaniam se recepit: eo exemplo docens, quid suos hostes et verbi sui contemptores maneat. Discedit ab eis ille, et secum aufert benedictionem et gratiam Dei omnem, cuius ipse Mediator est. Id vero non intelligebant, neque eo multum mouebantur Iudaei, quos templi et cultus externi fiducia fascinabat, ut in sua contumacia perseuerarent. Ideo nunc miraculo nouo et exemplo euidenti docet, hunc adeo non profuturum, ut potius hanc laruam illis ereptur us sit Deus, ne sub ea porro latere possint, et cum illo ipsos quoque male perituros esse. At quia in Iudaeorum persona commune exemplum proponitur, quo docemur, quid hypocritas omnes maneat, digna est haec historia, quae diligentissime consideretur.
units.tr: The apostle and evangelist John writes that the eternal and almighty Word of God was made flesh and came to his own, that is, to the Jews, to whom he was especially promised and from whom he was born as a man; yet they did not receive him. This appears throughout the whole Gospel history, but most of all in the events that immediately preceded his death. For so that they could not plead ignorance, after countless miracles by which he made himself known to them, he entered Jerusalem as king, with a humble display indeed, as Zechariah had foretold long ago, but in such a way as to give clear signs of divine power. While he stirs up the people to receive him with applause, he shakes the whole city with fear, and restrains the magnates too, lest they dare anything against him. Moreover, he turned aside into the temple, as Malachi had prophesied, and there he cleansed it, cast out the sons of Levi, and threw out whatever had been introduced contrary to the word of God. Lest they think he was planning anything hostile or unfriendly, he teaches openly, and to the blind who come to him he gives sight, and to the lame he restores full health, so that it might be proclaimed that he is that promised Saviour whom the prophets foretold would come. But from all these things nothing else resulted except that the chief priests and scribes first attack him with accusations, so as to make him suspect and hateful to the people; then they wished him killed. And, as we recently noted, in the populous and wealthy city there is no one who would honour him with hospitality, or with whom he could safely pass the night. So, leaving the city, he withdrew to Bethany, thereby teaching by example what awaits his enemies and despisers of his word. He departs from them, and takes with him the blessing and all the grace of God, of which he himself is the Mediator. The Jews, however, did not understand this, nor were they much moved by it, since they were bewitched by confidence in the temple and external worship, so that they persevered in their obstinacy. Therefore now, by a new miracle and a plain example, he teaches that this will profit them nothing; rather, God has snatched away this mask from them, so that they can no longer hide beneath it, and that they too will perish miserably along with it. But since in the person of the Jews a common example is set before us, by which we are taught what awaits all hypocrites, this history is worthy of the most careful consideration.

units.la: Occasio historiae totius fuit, quod minime in urbem reuersus est Dominus, ut populum doceret: quod illum quotidie fecisse constat ex Luca, qui scribit: Docebat autem interdin in templo, noctu vero exiens diuersabatur in monte, qui vocatur Olearum. Ergo non ita discessit ex urbe, ut hostili in ipsam animo fuerit, neque eo vnquam voluerit redire, sed fecit hoc, ut partim admoneret, quid de ipsis futurum sit, si ingrati esse pergant: partim (ut nuper diximus) ne ipsis ante horam fatalem praeoccuparet aliquid turbulentius contra ipsum designandi. Interim rationem habet electorum, qui in illa reliqui erant, et peregrinorum, qui sancto diuini cultus studio ad diem festum venerant, ut quae in cordibus suis iam conceperant pietatis verae femina, quotidianis admonitionibus excoleret. Est autem multa obseruatione dignum hoc Christi studium. Fuit enim Ierosolymitanus populus contumax et incurabilis: hostili item erga ipsum animo, ut nihil ei inter illos tutum esset. Quotidie tamen in urbem redit, ne doctrinae cupidos frustretur, et ne mortis quidem propinquae metu se reuocari finit, ut a Patre sibi comissum docendi munus deferat. Et mane quidem venit, ut idem hic fiat, quod olim, quando, cum urbis excidium et populi deportatio in Babylonem instaret, Deus multis iurrexisse, et Prophetas misisse dicitur, per quos admoniti imminentes poenas matura respicere sententia subterfugerent. Sic alias quoque illud fecisse legimus, quando vel ex Iudaea, vel aliquibus Galilaeae locis fecerit, ut sibi strages in insidias demitaret, eodem tamen semper cum faeno re redijt, ut suos confirmaret, qui aliqua habebant pietatis ac fidei principia. Vere ergo potuit dicere: Ierusalem Ierusalem, quae trucidas Prophetas, et eos lapidas, qui ad te missi sunt: quoties volui congregare liberos tuos, quemadmodum gallina congregat pullos suos sub alas, et noluisti? Matth. 23. Cap.
units.tr: The occasion for the whole story was that the Lord did not return to the city to teach the people, which we know he did daily from Luke, who writes: "And by day he was teaching in the temple, but at night he went out and lodged on the mount called the Mount of Olives." So he did not leave the city with hostility towards it, nor did he ever wish to return to it for that reason; rather he did this partly to warn them what would become of them if they persisted in ingratitude, and partly (as we said recently) so that they would not anticipate the fatal hour by plotting something more violent against him. Meanwhile he takes account of the elect who remained among them, and of the strangers who had come up for the feast out of holy zeal for the divine worship, so that he might cultivate by daily admonitions the seeds of true godliness they had already conceived in their hearts. This zeal of Christ is indeed well worth noting. The people of Jerusalem were stubborn and incurable, and so hostile towards him that nothing was safe for him among them. Yet he returns to the city every day, so as not to disappoint those eager for teaching, and he does not allow himself to be recalled even by fear of imminent death, so that he might discharge the office of teaching committed to him by the Father. And he comes in the morning, so that the same thing may happen as once, when the destruction of the city and the deportation of the people to Babylon were at hand, and God is said to have risen early and sent prophets, through whom the people, warned, might turn to repentance with timely judgment and escape the impending punishments. We read that he did the same at other times too, when he withdrew from Judea or from some places in Galilee to avoid the slaughter and snares set for him; yet he always returned again to the same place, so as to strengthen those who had some beginnings of piety and faith. Truly, then, he could say: "Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those sent to you! How often I wanted to gather your children together, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were unwilling!" Matt. 23.

units.la: Initentur autem esse Christi exemplum omnes Ecclesiarum ministri, ne in docendi munere cessent, si pauciores esse videant qui respiscant, adeoque nulli videantur reliqui esse, qui Verbum Dei admittant. Etenim ea est in mundo hominum conditio, ut (quod Bias ille ex Graecia sapientibus olim dixit) plures sint mali: non tamen ideo omnes incurabiles sunt, sed habet vbique suos Deus, apud quos aliquem fructum fert Verbi doctrina. Etenim, ut terra locis incultis, scopulis et rupibus abundat, quae pluuijs frustra irrigantur, non desunt autem propterea agri fertiles et horti, qui caelitus compluti fructus ferunt: et ut semen quidem aliud in viam cadit, aliud in loca lapidosa, aliud inter spinas, ex quibus omnibus spes nulla est, non autem desunt, quae in terram bonam seminata fructum ferunt copiosum: Ita nunquam omnino perit Verbi praedicatio, quin sint, qui illo audito respiscant, et de sua salute serio cogitent. De hoc olim Deus ipse Eliam tempore Achabi, et Paulum apud Corinthios agentem admonuit, cum vterque de statione sua deferenda cogitaret. Imo etsi omnes deplorati sint, nihilominus tamen in officio pergere debent Dei serui, ut suo studio excusationem omne contumacibus eripiant, et (ut Ezechieli dicebatur) suas ipsorum animas feruent: quod qui faciunt, nae illi non paruum sui laboris praemium reportant. In primis autem curent omnis loci et ordinis homines, ne periculi alicuius metu vocationem suam deserant, quoad aliqua datur eius obeunda occasio. Etenim facile Deus seruos suos tueri, hostium vero conatus impedire, et rabiem mitigare potest. Et ut Dominus monet, sunt vnicuique duodecim hora diei constituta, nec quisquam obstabit, quo minus ad metam sibi præfixam quisq; per ueniat. Deeo diligenter cogitent non solum Verbi administri, verumetiam qui ad Rempublicam gubernacula sedent, & Dei auxilio atq; præsidio freti, non timeant improborum hominum minas atq; conatus.
units.tr: All ministers of the churches should take Christ's example, so that they do not cease in the office of teaching if they see only a few who repent, and it seems there are none left who receive the Word of God. For this is the condition of men in the world: as the sage Bias of Greece once said, the wicked are more numerous. Yet they are not therefore all incurable; God has his own everywhere, among whom the teaching of the Word bears some fruit. For just as the earth abounds in uncultivated places, crags and rocks, which are watered by rains in vain, and yet there are not lacking fertile fields and gardens which, watered from heaven, bear fruit; and just as some seed falls on the path, some on stony ground, some among thorns, from all of which there is no hope, and yet there is not lacking seed sown in good soil that bears abundant fruit: so the preaching of the Word never utterly perishes, but there are always some who, on hearing it, repent and think seriously about their salvation. God himself once admonished Elijah of this in the time of Ahab, and Paul among the Corinthians, when each of them was thinking of giving up his post. Indeed, even if all have been given up as hopeless, nevertheless the servants of God ought to persevere in their duty, so that by their zeal they may deprive the obstinate of every excuse, and (as was said to Ezekiel) save their own souls. Those who do this will surely reap no small reward for their labour. Above all, men of every place and rank should take care not to abandon their calling out of fear of some danger, as long as an opportunity to discharge it is given. For God can easily protect his servants and check the attempts of enemies and restrain their rage. And, as the Lord warns, each person has twelve hours of the day appointed, and no one will hinder anyone from reaching the goal set before him. Let not only the ministers of the Word but also those who sit at the helm of the commonwealth consider this carefully, and, relying on the help and protection of God, not fear the threats and attempts of wicked men.

units.la: Sed ad Christum & huius loci historiam reuertamur. Hic cum iter in vrbem faceret, esu- rijt. Vere autem esurijt, neq; se esurire simulauit, vt quidam admodum incogitanter dixerunt. Nec enim simulatio in eum cadit, qui ipsa est veritas, & in cuius ore non est inuentus dolus. Nec defuerunt esuriei causæ naturales & propriæ. Etenim diem, quæ præcesserat, totam in ne- gotijs arduis transegerat, vt ne cibum quidem sumendi, tempus haberet: quod alias quoque ipsi ac cidisse scimus. Et inexpectatus hospes Bethaniam reuersus frugalius cœnauisse videtur. Adhæc maiorem noctis partem pro more in precibus consumpsit. Nunc primo diluculo ad iter sese accin- xit. Itaque non mirum, si fames ipsi obrepserit. Docent autem eiusmodi loci, verum homi- nem fuisse illum, qui cum carne infirmitates quoque nostras, teste Apostolo ad Hebræos, su- sceperit. Sic alibi eum exitinere defessum ad fontem Iacobi consedisse, spiritu turbatum suis- se, exultauisse, sitiuisse, legimus. Quorum omnium nobis hic vsus esse debet, vt primo meminerimus, illum Pontificem esse misericordem, & fidelem in iis, quæ pro nobis apud Deum sunt agenda, qui cum tentatus sit, nobis etiam, qui tentamur, possit succurrere: Deinde vt eius exemplo admoniti & confirmati, patienter feramus communis naturæ incommoda. Etenim si Dei Filius, qui nihil huius meruit, fatigationem corporis, famem, sitim, animi dolores & tristitiam propter nos sustinere voluit, nulla venia digni erimus, si delicati nimis nostram sortem velimus meliorem esse quam ipsius fuit. Proderit autem, vt temperantiæ & frugalitati in vitu assue- scamus. Hæc enim laborum, inediæ, vigiliarum patientes reddit, vt minus offendamur, si quid præter animi sententiam accidit. Puduit ergo Christianos homines gulæ indulgere, & intempe- rantius viuere. Etenim primo diluculo esuriens Christus, satis euidenter ostendit, quam fruga- liter cœnatus fuerit: & simul euidenter docet, quam alieni esse debeant Christianorum hominum mores ab iis, qui in multam noctem comessantur, aut perpotant, vt mane adhuc crapulam hester- nam eructent.
units.tr: But let us return to Christ and to the history of this passage. Here, as he was making his way to the city, he was hungry. He truly was hungry, and did not pretend to be, as some have rather thoughtlessly said. For pretence cannot fall upon him who is truth itself, and in whose mouth no deceit was found. Nor were there lacking natural and proper causes of his hunger. For he had spent the whole previous day in arduous business, so that he had no time even to take food, as we know happened to him on other occasions too. And the guest who had unexpectedly returned to Bethany seems to have dined rather frugally. Besides, he had spent most of the night in prayer, as was his custom. Now, at first dawn, he set out on his journey. So it is no wonder if hunger crept upon him. Such circumstances, moreover, show that he was a true man, who, as the Apostle says to the Hebrews, took upon himself our infirmities along with our flesh. Thus elsewhere we read that he, wearied from his journey, sat down by Jacob's well, that he was troubled in spirit, that he rejoiced, that he thirsted. From all of these we ought to draw this use: first, that we remember that he is a merciful and faithful High Priest in those things that are to be performed for us before God, who, since he himself was tempted, is able also to help us who are tempted. Then, that, admonished and strengthened by his example, we may patiently bear the troubles common to our nature. For if the Son of God, who deserved none of this, was willing to endure bodily weariness, hunger, thirst, the sorrows and sadness of the soul for our sake, we shall deserve no pardon if, being too pampered, we wish our lot to be better than his was. It will also be profitable for us to accustom ourselves to temperance and frugality in diet. For this makes us patient of labours, fasting and wakefulness, so that we are less offended if anything happens contrary to our wish. Christians should therefore be ashamed to indulge the palate and to live intemperately. For Christ, hungry at first dawn, shows quite plainly how frugally he dined; and at the same time he plainly teaches how far the manners of Christians ought to be from those who carouse far into the night, or drink to excess, so that in the morning they still belch up yesterday's drunkenness.

units.la: Simul autem consolationi seruit hæc Christi esuries. Nec enim corpore solum esuriuit, verum etiam animo. Quia enim ideo in mundum venit, vt homines quos primorum parentum intemperan tia perdiderat, salsos faceret, nostrum omnium salutem ille stiuit & esurinit. Ideo apud Ioannem colloquium cum Samaritide habitum, discipulis ipsum vt comederet hortantibus dicebat: Ego cibum habeo quo vescar, quem vos nescitis. Et mox: Esca mea est, exequi voluntatem eius qui misit me, & perficere ipsius opus. Et alibi: Hæc autem est voluntas eius qui misit me, vt omnis qui videt Filium, & credit in eum, habeat vitam æternam. Vt ergo Deus Pater vult omnes homines salvos fieri, & in Veritatis cognitionem peruenire, & Filium eo nomine in mundum misit: Ita hic salutem hominum esurit ac sitit, atque ideo tanta eius cupiditate arsit, vt ne mortis quidem acerbissimæ metus eum absterrere potuerit, quo minus de illa nobis acquirenda cogitaret.
units.tr: Yet this hunger of Christ also serves for our comfort. For he did not hunger only in body but also in spirit. Since he came into the world for this reason, to save the people whom the intemperance of our first parents had destroyed, he thirsted and hungered for the salvation of us all. Hence in John, when the conversation with the Samaritan woman had taken place and the disciples urged him to eat, he said: "I have food to eat that you do not know." And soon after: "My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to finish his work." And elsewhere: "This is the will of him who sent me, that everyone who sees the Son and believes in him should have eternal life." Just as God the Father wills that all people be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth, and for that name sent his Son into the world, so here he hungers and thirsts for the salvation of men, and was therefore so burning with desire for it that not even the fear of most bitter death could deter him from thinking about obtaining it for us.

units.la: Testatur hoc quando vltimam cœnam ab his verbis exorditur: Desiderio desideraui hoc pascha vobiscum edere. Et in cruce iam moriturus se sitire clamauit, & gustato aceto ait: Consummatum est, & inclinato capite tradidit spiritum, vt pote peraɛtis iam omnibus, quorum ergo in mundum venerat. Quoties ergo Christum esuriuisse aut sitiuisse legimus, semper cogitemus, ei omnium quæ vnquam passus est, causam fuisse ardens illud salutis humanæ studium, quo motus seipsum pro nobis tradidit. Consoletur hoc afflictas conscientias, ne quis se propter anteacta ab illo negligi pu- tet. Etenim non possumus nos salutem tam ardenter sitire, quin maiori nos seruandi desiderio Christus ardeat: simul autem nos excitet eius erga nos studium, vt nos ipsius voluntati accommodemus, ne nostram salutem esurientem improbe frustremur. Et huc referri debet ficus exemplum, quod modo sequitur.
units.tr: He bears witness to this when he begins the last supper with these words: "With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you." And on the cross, about to die, he cried out that he thirsted, and after tasting the vinegar said: "It is finished," and bowing his head he gave up his spirit, since all the things for which he had come into the world were now accomplished. So whenever we read that Christ hungered or thirsted, let us always think that the cause of all that he ever suffered was that burning zeal for human salvation by which he was moved to give himself up for us. This should console troubled consciences, lest anyone think that he is neglected by Christ on account of past sins. For we cannot thirst so ardently for salvation without Christ burning with an even greater desire to save us; and at the same time his zeal toward us should stir us to accommodate ourselves to his will, lest we wickedly disappoint his hunger for our salvation. The example of the fig tree that follows now should be referred to this.

units.la: Nam videns ficum ad viam, accedit ad eam, si quid in ea inueniat: At nihil inueniens nisi folia solum, illi maledicit, inquiens: Ne amplius ex te fructus nascatur. Et illico ficus ista exa- ruit. Caterum cum constet vernum tempus tunc fuisse, quo fructus in arboribus nulli adhuc inueniuntur (quod diserte Marcus annotauit) poterat factum hoc ridiculum & absurdum, vel animi praecipitis & impotentis opus videri, quod virum graue minime decuerit, nedum aeternum Dei Filium. Sed cum nihil vnquam absq; certa ratione fecerit, qui ipsissima est Dei Patris Sapientia, hic quoq; eum nihil ex caeco & temerario affectu fecisse putabimus. Nam etsi ficuum tempus non esset, poterat tamen ex anno praeterito reliquias quales cunq; sperare, quibus famem aliquo modo sedaret. Deinde videtur ficus ista non tunc modo fructus nullos habuisse aptos esui, sed natura sterilis fuisse, aut a multis annis fructus nullos tulisse. Digna igitur erat, cui malediceret Dominus, & ut foliorum quoq; honore destituta excinderetur, ne porro inanis specie quenquam falleret. Adhaec etsi ficuum tempus non esset, erat tamen tempus, quo Iudaei matura respiscentia imminens sibi exitium debebant auertere. Itaq; quod saepe hypocritis minatus fuerat, fore, ut ablato ab illis regno Dei, excindantur, id nunc exemplo isto confirmare, & ad oculum demonstrare voluit, sic in mentem eis reuocans, quod alibi fusius expositum erat per parabolam ficus, quae Lucae 13. cap. habetur.
units.tr: For seeing a fig tree by the road, he approached it to see whether he might find anything on it; but finding nothing except leaves, he cursed it, saying: "Let no fruit grow from you any more." And immediately the fig tree withered. Yet since it is agreed that it was then spring, when no fruit is yet found on the trees (which Mark carefully noted), this deed could seem ridiculous and absurd, or the work of a hasty and unrestrained mind, which would hardly befit a grave man, let alone the eternal Son of God. But since he who is the very Wisdom of God the Father never did anything without a sure reason, we shall think that he did nothing here either from blind and rash emotion. For even if it was not the season of figs, he could still hope for some remnants of the past year, by which he might somehow relieve his hunger. Next, this fig tree seems not only to have had no fruit fit for eating at that time, but to have been barren by nature, or to have borne no fruit for many years. It was therefore worthy that the Lord should curse it, and that, stripped even of the honour of its leaves, it should be cut down, lest it deceive anyone any longer with its empty show. Besides, even if it was not the season for figs, it was nevertheless a time when the Jews ought to turn away the destruction hanging over them by timely repentance. Therefore what he had often threatened to the hypocrites, that the kingdom of God would be taken from them and they would be cut off, he now wished to confirm by this example and show to the eye, thus recalling to their minds what had been set out more fully elsewhere through the parable of the fig tree, which is found in Luke chapter 13.

units.la: Etenim reuera ficus in vinea Domini fuerunt Iudaei, quam ipse ex singulari gratia plantatam & excultam sapius inusit, ut ex ea fructus dignos colligeret: Primo per Mosem, cuius ministerio illos ex Aegypto eduxit, Legem dedit & non cultum modo externum, qui totus mysteriis erat conspicuus tradidit, verumetiam sacerdotium & in hoc perpetuum Verbi sui ministerium inter eos sanciuit, ut per hoc in officio continerentur. De hac cura loquitur Asaph in Psalmis: Vitem ex Aegypto traduxisti, expulisti gentes & plantasti eam: Expurgasti coram ea, radicasti radices eius, & impleuit terram, &c. Deinde extraordinarie Prophetas excitauit, qui Sacerdotibus & Leuitis in suo munere cessantibus, eos vrgerent & professione sua dignos fructus ferrent. Tandem Filium misit Vnigenitum, quem humanae salutis fames & sitis impulit, ut toto illo tempore, quo in terris vixit, ea requireret, quae ad ipsorum salutem facerent. At nequicquam haec facta sunt. Et licet Regis persona assumpta iam ad illos veniisset, & manum quoq; ferio admouisset, illi tamen nudis foliis, id est, inani religionis professione & speciosa populi Dei titulo superbi, illum fructu sitiente frustrati sunt: adeo ut ure cum Prophetas exclamare potuerit: Vae mihi, quia idem mihi accidit, quod collectis iam fructibus aestiui, & quod vindemia peracta in racematione fieri solet: maturos fructus desiderauit anima mea, sed non est botrus ad comedendum. Quia ergo incurabilis erat illorum contumacia, interim vero inani specie externi cultus Ecclesiae nomen mentiebantur, ut Deo & hominibus fucum facerent: tempus illud fatale praesoribus erat, ut laruam hanc speciosam ipsis detraheret Deus, & simul securi ad radices arboris foliosae admota stirpitus excinderentur, quod per Ioannem Baptistam prius quoq; interminatus fuerat. Id vero non multo post factum est, quando Romanos adduxit, qui vrbem cum templo demoliti sunt, & simul cultus externi exercitium omne abrogarunt. Itaq; iam multis diebus, id est, annis amplius mille quingentis fuerunt filii Israel (vt Hosea praedixit) absq; rege, & absq; principe, sine sacrificio & statua, absq; Ephod & Teraphim, id est, absq; sacerdotio & omnis cultus legitimi simul & illegitimi exercitio. Qui ergo hypocrisi sua & superstitiosa inanis professionis fiducia Dei oculos diu offenderunt, tandem fuco illo suo nudati, totius orbis ludibrium facti sunt. Et hoc ficus istius exemplo demonstrare voluit Dominus, quae ad eius maledictionem subito exaruit: ut omnibus constaret, quam facile ipsi fiat hostes suos perdere, & proinde crucis ignominia, quam subiturus erat, nemo piorum offenderetur. At quia mox ipse hoc omne alia parabola fusius explicabit, haec modo dixisse sufficiat.
units.tr: For indeed the Jews were the fig trees in the vineyard of the Lord, which he himself, out of singular grace, planted and tended, and often visited so that he might gather worthy fruit from it. First through Moses, by whose ministry he led them out of Egypt, he gave them the Law, and handed down not only external worship, which was wholly conspicuous with mysteries, but also established among them the priesthood and in it the perpetual ministry of his Word, so that by this they might be kept in their duty. Asaph speaks of this care in the Psalms: "You brought a vine out of Egypt; you drove out the nations and planted it. You cleared the ground before it, you caused its roots to take hold, and it filled the land," etc. Then he raised up prophets extraordinarily, who were to urge the priests and Levites, when they neglected their office, and to bear fruits worthy of their profession. Finally he sent his only-begotten Son, whom the hunger and thirst of human salvation impelled, so that throughout the whole time in which he lived on earth he might seek those things which would serve their salvation. But these things were done in vain. And although he had come to them assuming the person of the King, and had even laid the axe to the tree, they nevertheless frustrated him, who thirsted for fruit, with bare leaves, that is, with the empty profession of religion and the proud boast of the splendid title of the people of God. So much so that he could cry out with the Prophet: "Woe is me, for it has happened to me as when, the summer fruits having been gathered, or the vintage finished, gleaning is usually done: my soul has desired ripe fruits, but there is no cluster to eat." Because therefore their obstinacy was incurable, while they falsely claimed the name of the Church by the empty show of external worship, so as to deceive God and men, that fateful time was at hand for the leaders, when God would tear this beautiful mask from them, and at the same time the axe would be applied to the roots of the leafy tree and they would be cut down to the stump, as he had previously threatened through John the Baptist. This indeed happened not long afterwards, when he brought the Romans, who demolished the city together with the temple and at the same time abolished every practice of external worship. Thus for many days now, that is, for more than fifteen hundred years, the sons of Israel have been (as Hosea foretold) without king and without prince, without sacrifice and pillar, without ephod and teraphim, that is, without priesthood and without any exercise of worship, whether lawful or unlawful. Those who therefore long offended God's eyes by their hypocrisy and the superstitious confidence of an empty profession, at last stripped of that pretence, were made the mockery of the whole world. By this example of the fig tree the Lord wished to show, which at his curse suddenly withered, how easily he can destroy his enemies, so that all might understand it, and therefore that no pious person would be offended by the shame of the cross which he was about to undergo. But since he himself will explain all this more fully in another parable soon, it is enough to have said these things for now.

units.la: Caeterum quia Iudaei olim Dei peculium fuerunt, & penes illos fuit Ecclesiae titulus, in quorum locum nos succesisimus, qui ex oleastro, id est, ex gentibus oriundi ex gratuita misericordia in hanc radicem sive stirpem insiti sumus, ad nos quoq; exemplum hoc pertinet, ut quid nobis sperandum sit discamus, si illorum similes reperiamur. Nam si Deus naturalibus ramis non pepercit, pro cul dubio multo minus nobis parcet, si ipsi quoq; infrugiferi simus. Et exempla extant in Ecclesiis Orientalibus, quae cum libertate etiam Christiani nominis professione amissa, hodie sub infelicis Mahumetis iugo durissimam seruitutem seruiunt. Singuli deniq; priuatim ista ad se transferant, & se ficus esse meminerint in vinea Domini vel Ecclesia. Ut vero nemo frugi & industrius paterfamilias arbores steriles & inutiles ferat in vinea, quae terram fructra occupent: ita neq; nos Deus feret, si fructus nostra professione dignos non feramus. De eo Christus ipse nos admonet alibi sub vitis & palmitum parabola dicens: Ego sum vitis illa vera, vos palmites, & Pater meus agricola est: Omnem palmitem in me non ferentem fructum, tollit: & omnem, qui fert fructum, purgat, vt plus fructus adferat. Venit autem quotidie ad nos bonus illePaterfamilias, & fructus per suos seruos exigit, quibus salutis nostrae desiderium, quo totus ardet, reflinguat. Quid vero inveniat, res ipsa loquitur. Etenim nudis foliis, id est, otiosa fidei professione, & theatrico Sacramentorum abusu plerique, se ostentant, fructibus autem omnino destituuntur. Sub Euangelij quidem praetextu, quae sua sunt, quaerunt multi, in aduersis vero & periculis, fides plane nulla est: refriguit item charitas, iniquitas abundat, regnat libido effrenis, intemperantia, luxus, avaritia: vt cum Prophetis dicere nobis liceat: Perijt beneficus de terra, non est inter homines rectus aut integer, vniuersi insidiantur sanguini, quisque fratrem suum reti venatur: peierare, mentiri, occidere, furari & moechari quasi aggere rupto perruperunt, & sanguines sanguines tetigerunt. Pepercit hucusque nobis Deus propter intercessionem boni illius coloni, Filij sui dilecti IESV CHRISTI. Attum respiscentia spes nulla vspiam sese ostendat, quid aliud speremus, quam maledictionem, quae nos quoque feriat, & qua percussi fuditus exarescamus. Non feret enim nomen suum per nos perpetuo prophanari Deus ille sanctus & iustus. Et iam pastim conspiciuntur irae Dei & iudicij eius vndiq; imminentis indicia. Occurramus ergo ei matura & feria respiscentia, & precemur, vt nos ad se conuertat, & indignorum licet misereatur propter nomen suum sanctum, & propter meritum Filij sui IESV CHRISTI: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Moreover, since the Jews were once God's peculiar people, and the title of the Church belonged to them, and we have succeeded in their place, we who, having sprung from the wild olive, that is from the Gentiles, have been grafted by free mercy into this root or stock, this example also pertains to us, so that we may learn what we ought to hope for if we are found like them. For if God did not spare the natural branches, without doubt he will much less spare us, if we too become unfruitful. And there are examples in the Eastern Churches, which, having lost even the freedom of professing the Christian name, now serve the harshest slavery under the yoke of the unhappy Mahomet. Finally, let each person apply these things privately to himself, and remember that he is a fig tree in the vineyard of the Lord or the Church. But just as no fruitful and diligent householder would bear sterile and useless trees in his vineyard, which occupy the ground to no purpose, so God will not bear us either, if we do not bear fruits worthy of our profession. Christ himself warns us of this elsewhere under the parable of the vine and the branches, saying: "I am the true vine, you are the branches, and my Father is the vinedresser. Every branch in me that does not bear fruit he takes away, and every one that bears fruit he prunes, so that it may bear more fruit." Now that good householder comes to us daily and demands fruit through his servants, by whom he kindles in us the desire for our salvation with which he himself wholly burns. What he finds, the thing itself speaks. For many display themselves with bare leaves, that is, with an idle profession of faith and a theatrical abuse of the sacraments, but are altogether destitute of fruits. Under the pretext of the Gospel many seek their own advantage; in adversity and dangers there is plainly no faith; charity has likewise grown cold, iniquity abounds, unbridled lust reigns, with intemperance, luxury and avarice; so that we may say with the Prophets: "The godly man has perished from the earth, there is none upright or honest among men; all lie in wait for blood, each hunts his brother with a net; they have burst out like a broken dam in perjury, lying, murder, theft and adultery, and bloodshed has followed bloodshed." Until now God has spared us on account of the intercession of that good husbandman, his beloved Son JESUS CHRIST. But if no hope of repentance appears anywhere, what else shall we hope for than the curse, which will strike us too, and by which, struck, we shall wither to the roots? For that holy and just God will not allow his name to be profaned by us forever. And already the wrath of God and the signs of his judgment, impending on all sides, are plainly seen. Let us therefore meet him with timely and earnest repentance, and let us pray that he turn us to himself and have mercy on us, though unworthy, for the sake of his holy name and for the merit of his Son JESUS CHRIST, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCXLVI.
units.tr: HOMILY CCXLVI.

units.la: Cum igitur hoc vidissent discipuli, mirati sunt, dicentes: Quomodo illico exaruit ficus? Respondens autem IESVS ait eis: Amen dico vobis, si habueritis fidem, neque haesitaueritis, non solum hoc quod factum est ficui, facietis: verumetiam si monti isti dixeritis, Tollitor, & proijcitor in mare, fiet. Et quaecunque precando petieritis, si credideritis, accipietis.
units.tr: When the disciples saw this, they marvelled and said: "How has the fig tree withered away so quickly?" Jesus answered them: "Truly I say to you, if you have faith and do not doubt, you will do not only what has been done to the fig tree, but even if you say to this mountain, 'Be taken up and cast into the sea,' it will happen. And whatever you ask in prayer, if you believe, you will receive."

units.la: POstquam Dominus noster IESVS CHRISTVS templum ab impia sacrorum nundinatione & abusibus aliis, qui irrepserant, repurgauit, mox in illo ipse docuit quotidie, & doctrinam suam miraculosa caecorum & claudorum curatione confirmauit: vt efficeret, salute omnem penes se solum inueniri, neque alios huius participes fieri, quam qui ipsum audiunt, & persidem in ipsum illuminati in via praeceptorum suorum ambulant. Quia vero Iudaei his minus attendebant, miraculo memorabili eos excitare voluit. Nam mane in vrbem reuertens cum esuriret, ad ficum quandam accessit fructum ex ea quaesituru s, nullo autem inuento, illam sterilitate perpetua damnauit. Et quia hoc fecit tempore alienissimo, cum non esset tempus ficuum, altiora docere voluit: sic nimirum propter ipsos venisse, vt qui salutem ipsorum esuriat. Itaque tempus esse, vt matura respiscentia respondeant eius desiderio nisi funditus perire velint, & aeternum a Deo reiecti. At non vulgus solum Iudaeorum non attenderunt quid hic ageretur, sed discipuli quoq; domestici hoc non fatis obseruarunt. Sequitur ergo hic locus, quo miraculi istius vsum illis Dominus exponit, vt differre doceat, quid fieri necesse sit, si iram Dei auertere, & ea omnia superare aut amoliri velint, quae hactenus impedimento fuerunt, quo minus profecerint in causa salutis.
units.tr: After our Lord Jesus Christ had cleansed the temple of the impious trade in sacred things and of the other abuses that had crept in, he then taught in it every day, and confirmed his teaching by the miraculous healing of the blind and the lame, so as to show that salvation is found in him alone, and that no one shares in it except those who hear him and, enlightened by faith in him, walk in the way of his commandments. But because the Jews paid little heed to these things, he wished to rouse them by a remarkable miracle. For returning to the city in the morning, he was hungry, and went to a certain fig tree to seek fruit from it; but finding none, he condemned it to perpetual barrenness. And because he did this at a most unseasonable time, when it was not the season for figs, he wished to teach higher things: namely, that he had come for their sake, as one who hungers for their salvation. Therefore it was time for them to answer his desire by timely repentance, unless they wished to perish utterly and be cast off by God for ever. But not only the common crowd of Jews failed to consider what was being done here; even the disciples, who were his household companions, did not sufficiently observe it. Therefore this passage follows, in which the Lord explains to them the use of this miracle, to teach what must be done if they wish to avert the wrath of God and to overcome or remove all those things which have hitherto hindered them from making progress in the cause of salvation.

units.la: Occasionem & causam nouae huic tractationi praebuerunt discipuli, qui ficum ad Christi imprecationem mox exaruisse, mirantur. Nam, vt Marcus annotauit, cum crastino mane rursus illac iterfacerent, viderunt illam radicitus exaruisse: quod ex eo cognosci potuit, quod iam folijs quoq; nudata stabat, vt nihil porro ex ipsa sperari posset. Itaq; omnium nomine Petrus de hoc euentu interrogat, dicens: Rabi, ecce quomodo ficus ista, cui imprecatus es, exaruit? Atqui multa hactenus miracula isto maiora viderant, & (vt nuper monuimus) sola temporis circumstantia ipsos dacere poterat Christum, qui nihil vnquam inconsiderate aut inconsulto fecerat, proculdubio hic quoque que altius quid spectauisse. Itaq; de causa potius quærere, quàm euentum rei admirari debuisset, in quo Christi omnipotentia elucebat, cuius documenta hucusque viderant infinita. Sed est hoc carnis ingenium, in externis hærere, causas vero rerum, quæ geruntur, negligere: quo fit, vt euentus admiremur, non tamen eorum consideratione excitemur, vt serio ad Deum conuersi resipiscamus. Ita hodie multi admirantur publicam et communem egestatem, qua omnis loci & ordinis homines laborant, adeo vt non familiæ modo priuatæ, verumetiam Respub. & regna, quæ primò florebant, passim vt arbores arefactæ, nefolia quidem retineant, quibus pristinum splendorem repræsentent. Interim non obseruant vitia illa plane contraria, quæ omnium fortunas depascuntur, auaritiam nimirum & prodigalitatem, quæ apud omnes regnant. Sic priuatim ebriosi vires suas debilitari & nouis quotidiè morbis corpus suum infestari mirantur, seipsos autem non inspiciunt, qui assiduo gulæ studio & crapulæ sibiipsis omnis mali authores sunt. Similis illorum stupor est, quibus mirum videtur, ad Euangelij prædicationem motus passim surgere, quibus orbis terrarum turbatur, non autem cogitant, aliter fieri non posse, quando pleriq; principem pacis, IESVM CHRISTVM, nolunt admittere.
units.tr: The disciples, who marvelled that the fig tree had immediately withered at Christ's curse, gave the occasion and cause for this new discussion. For, as Mark noted, when they passed that way again the next morning, they saw that it had withered from the root, which could be known from the fact that it now stood stripped even of its leaves, so that nothing more could be hoped from it. So Peter, speaking for all, asks about this event, saying: "Rabbi, see how the fig tree you cursed has withered!" Yet hitherto they had seen many miracles greater than this, and (as we lately observed) the mere circumstance of the time could have taught them that Christ, who never did anything thoughtlessly or without reason, surely had something deeper in view here as well. Therefore they ought to have inquired into the cause rather than marvelled at the event, in which the omnipotence of Christ shone forth, of which they had already seen countless proofs. But it is the nature of the flesh to cling to external things and to neglect the causes of things that happen; hence we marvel at events, yet are not moved by considering them to turn earnestly to God and repent. So today many marvel at the public and common poverty which afflicts men of every place and rank, so that not only private households but also commonwealths and kingdoms, which once flourished, are everywhere like withered trees, which still keep their leaves, by which they might show their former splendour. Meanwhile they do not notice those plainly contrary vices which devour the fortunes of all, namely avarice and prodigality, which reign among everyone. So individual drunkards marvel that their strength is weakened and their body is daily assailed by new diseases, but they do not look at themselves, who by their constant devotion to gluttony and drunkenness are the authors of every evil for themselves. Similar is the stupor of those who think it strange that movements arise everywhere at the preaching of the Gospel, by which the world is thrown into turmoil; they do not reflect that this cannot be otherwise, since most people are unwilling to admit Jesus Christ, the Prince of Peace.

units.la: Porrò Christus discipulis hoc, quod in ficu factum fuerat, admirantibus ita respondet, vt eadem de proprio miraculi vsu non obscure admoneat, simulq; doceat, fidem solam medium illud esse, quæ ipsos aduersus maledictionem omnem tutos reddere, omnia item vera pietatis atq; salutis obstacula remouere, & e contra fructibus Deo gratis & acceptis fœcundos reddere possit. Est ergo responsio ista digna, quæ per singulas partes diligenter consideretur.
units.tr: Moreover, Christ answers the disciples, who were marvelling at what had happened to the fig tree, in such a way as to give them a clear reminder about the proper use of the miracle, and at the same time to teach that faith alone is the means which can make them safe against every curse, likewise remove every obstacle to true piety and salvation, and on the other hand make them fruitful in works acceptable and pleasing to God. Therefore this answer is worthy of being considered carefully, part by part.

units.la: Matthæus illum a graui asseueratione exorsum fuisse scribit, & dixisse: Amen amen dico vobis, si habueritis fidem, neq; hæsitaueritis, &c. Fide opus sore docet, si negotium hoc rectè intelligere, & omnibus, quæ saluti officiunt, superiores fieri velint. Ideo apud Marcum, disertius aliquanto quid faciant, monet dicens. Habete fidem Dei. Fides Dei dicitur passiuè pro ea, quæ Deo habetur, & quæ huic itaque siditur, vt de eius dictis aut promissis minimè dubitemus. Itaq; sensus huius dicti est: Miramini, quòd ad meæ vocis imprecationem ficus exaruit. Ac hoc accidisse, non vsq; adeò ad mirabile censeri debet, quando qui verbis meis rectè confidunt, maiora multò, si opus sit, efficere poterunt. Itaq; vt fidem Dei habeatis, cura vobis præcipua sit. Ista enim ratione excidium euitabitis, ne hoc ipsum vobis accidat, quod exemplo ficus istius toti genti Iudæorum denunciari volui. Proderit autem singulas responsionis Christi partes diligentius inspicere.
units.tr: Matthew writes that he began with a solemn assurance and said: "Amen, amen, I say to you, if you have faith and do not doubt," and so on. He teaches that there must be faith, if they wish to understand this matter rightly and to rise above all things that stand in the way of salvation. Therefore Mark, somewhat more plainly, advises what they should do, saying: "Have the faith of God." "The faith of God" is spoken in a passive sense, for that which is held concerning God, and which is therefore trusted in, so that we should not in the least doubt his sayings or promises. So the sense of this saying is: "You marvel that the fig tree withered at my spoken curse. But this should not be thought so very wonderful, since those who rightly trust my words will be able to do far greater things, if need be. Therefore let it be your chief concern to have the faith of God.
