For by this means you will avoid ruin, so that the same thing does not happen to you that I wished to announce to the whole nation of the Jews by the example of this fig tree." It will be useful, however, to look more carefully at each part of Christ's answer.

units.la: Prima non obiter fidem commendat, sed disertè Dei fidem, id est, eam, quæ vni Deo habetur. Hanc passim Scriptura tradit. Etenim si fœdus Dei, quod cum Abrahamo fecit consideres, huius primum caput est, Ego sum El Schadai, id est, Deus omnipotens aut omnisufficiens. Ita verò se dicit, vt doceat, se non solùm omnia posse, aut sibiipsi sufficere ad omnia, vt nullius subsidio sibi opus sit: sed insuper eum esse, qui omnibus, quæ in cælo & in terra sunt, sufficiat, & ex quo creatu-ræ omnes hauriant, quæ ipsis sunt necessaria. Cur verò se talè esse dicit? Nimirum, vt Abraham ipsi vni fidat, ab ipso vno pendeat, neq; alibi quærat ea, quibus sibi opus esse sentit vel ad corpus vel ad animam. Ideò addit: Anbula coram me, id est, mihi seruire & placere stude, teq; totum mihi addicito, ne in vllum alium respicias. Quid hoc aliud est, quàm fides Dei, quæ in præsenti præcipitur? Eadè est in Lege primi præcepti sententia. Nam in eo etiam se Dominum Deum nostrum esse profitetur, qui nos eduxerit ex Ægypto. Quo beneficio reliqua omnia comprehendit, quorum fons & origo est libertas filiorum Dei, in quam ille suos asseruit. Quid verò vicissim a nobis exigit? Nefint tibi (inquit) dij alij coram me. Id est, me vnum pro Domino & Deo vestro ita agnoscite, vt omnibus alijs dijs, quos gentes prophanæ & superstitiosæ colunt, procul relictis, omnem fiduciam in me vno collocetis. Rursus ergo in Lege etiam fides illa Dei commendatur. Nec aliam in precationis formula suis discipulis tradit Dominus, quando nos ita precari iubet: Pater noster, qui es in cœlis. Atqui communis omnium nostrum Pater, & idem cœli Dominus, est vnus solus Deus, omnium conditor. Quia ergo hunc vnum inuocare iubet, & ab illo petere vita præsentis & futuræ subsidia, vtrique vt huic etiam vni fidamus, præcipit. Et hæc illa fides est, quam in Symbolo Apostolico profitemur, dicentes: Credo in vnum Deum Omnipotentem, creatorem cœli & terræ. Qua confessione religio Christiana ab omnibus alijs sectis distinguitur, teste Paulo, qui ad Corinthios scribit: Etiamsi sint qui dicantur dij, & in coelo & in terra (sicut sunt dij multi & domini multi) nobis tamen unus est Deus, Pater ille, a quo omnia, & nos in ipso: & unus Dominus IESVS CHRISTVS, per quem omnia, & nos per ipsum. Confutantur hi omnes, qui vel uno Deo relicto circa alienos occupantur, vel non uno illo contenti, alios ei coniungunt, quos sibi patronos & vindices fingunt, & in quos uni Deo debitam gloriam partiuntur, dum illos invocant in adversis, aut ex his erepti, illis gratias agunt. Pugnat hoc cum Christianae religionis professione, & simul cum veri cultus regula, quam Deus ipse, procul reiectis omnibus superstitionibus in Psalmis tradit, dicens: Invoca me in die tribulationis, & eruam te, & tu me glorificabis. Excusant se variis rationibus, & argumentis qui secus agunt: at nullum istorum pondus est apud Deum, qui solus ex fide vera coli vult, & in praesenti per Filium suum dilectum discipulis dixit: Habete fidem Dei. Glorientur ergo alij fide Petri & Pauli, vel etiam fide Ecclesiae: nos autem in fide Dei acquiescamus per Filium eius Unigenitum IESVM CHRISTVM. Illa fide omnes Prophetae & Apostoli seruati sunt, & hanc unam profitetur Ecclesia, quae nisi in ea constans permanserit, non meretur nomen Ecclesiae, sed fornicationis Synagogae similis est, quae religione Deo amatores suos olim secuta est, & hoc nomine a Deo damnatur.
units.tr: The first part commends faith not in passing but expressly the faith of God, that is, the faith which is held in the one God alone. Scripture hands this down everywhere. For if you consider the covenant of God which he made with Abraham, its first chapter is: "I am El Shaddai [אל שדי], that is, God Almighty or All-sufficient." He says this in such a way as to teach that he not only can do all things, or is sufficient for himself in all things, so that he needs no one's help, but moreover that he is the one who suffices for all things that are in heaven and on earth, and from whom all creatures draw what is necessary for them. But why does he say that he is such? Clearly so that Abraham may trust in him alone, depend on him alone, and not seek elsewhere those things which he feels he needs, whether for body or for soul. Therefore he adds: "Walk before me," that is, strive to serve and please me, and devote yourself wholly to me, lest you look to any other. What else is this than the faith of God, which is here commanded? The same sense is found in the first commandment of the Law. For there too he declares himself to be the Lord our God, who brought us out of Egypt. By this benefit he embraces all the rest, of which the source and origin is the freedom of the sons of God, into which he has claimed his own. And what in turn does he require from us? "You shall have no other gods before me," he says. That is, acknowledge me alone as your Lord and God, in such a way that, leaving far behind all the other gods which the profane and superstitious nations worship, you place all your trust in me alone. Thus that faith in God is commended again in the Law. Nor does the Lord hand down any other faith to his disciples in the form of prayer, when he bids us pray thus: "Our Father, who art in heaven." And indeed the common Father of us all, and the same Lord of heaven, is the one God alone, the creator of all. Therefore, since he bids us call upon this one alone, and ask from him the aids of this present life and of the life to come, he commands us to trust in this one alone as well. And this is that faith which we profess in the Apostles' Creed, saying: "I believe in one God, the Almighty, maker of heaven and earth." By this confession the Christian religion is distinguished from all other sects, as Paul witnesses, who writes to the Corinthians: "Even if there are those who are called gods, whether in heaven or on earth (as there are many gods and many lords), yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things, and we in him; and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and we through him." All those are refuted who either, having left the one God, busy themselves with strangers, or, not content with that one, join others to him, whom they imagine as their patrons and avengers, and among whom they divide the glory due to the one God alone, while they call upon them in adversity, or give thanks to them when they have been rescued by them. This clashes with the profession of the Christian religion, and at the same time with the rule of true worship, which God himself, having rejected all superstitions, hands down in the Psalms, saying: "Call upon me in the day of trouble, and I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me." Those who act otherwise make excuses by various reasons and arguments; but none of these has weight with God, who alone wishes to be worshipped from true faith, and who in the present passage said to his disciples through his beloved Son: "Have the faith of God." Let others therefore glory in the faith of Peter and Paul, or even in the faith of the Church; but let us rest in the faith of God through his only-begotten Son, Jesus Christ. By that faith all the Prophets and Apostles were saved, and the Church professes this one faith; unless the Church remains steadfast in it, it does not deserve the name of Church, but is like the fornicating Synagogue, which once went after its lovers by false religion, and for this reason is condemned by God.

units.la: At ne nudam & otiosam fidei professionem putemus sufficere, videre oportet, qualis haec fides Dei in nobis esse debeat. Admonet de eo quoque Dominus, dicens: Si habueritis fidem, & non haesitaveritis. Apud Marcum cordis dubij & fluctuantis meminit, quod a fide procul abesse debeat. Respicit ante ad carnis ingenium, quae si quid arduum aut grave oportet aggredi, intra seipsa altercare, & duersis sententijs aut cogitationibus diffrahi solet, ut modo in hanc, modo in alteram partem incliner, & nunc Dei promissis confidens obsequi velit, mox vero ipsi diffidens, obsequium illi neget. At fides vera & germana, neglectis omnibus aliis in unum Deum respicit, quae causa est, quod non haesitet aut fluctuet, licet ordo naturae & communis sensus diversum monere videatur. Et enim novit Dei bonitatem immensam & infinitam esse, atque in aeternum durare. Credit item eundem esse omnipotentem, & ideo eius decreta nec abrogari, aut vllis hominum viribus impediri posse. His veritatem coniunctam esse, certo sibi persuasit: unde colligit, fieri non posse, ut qui verax simul & omnipotens est, promissis suis velit deesse. Talem Abrahami, patris credentium, fidem fuisse, scribit Apostolus, quando illum promissioni de femine ex Sara nascituro contra spe sub spe credidisse ait, se videlicet fore patrem multarum gentium. Nam non imbecillis fide (inquit) non considerat suum ipsius corpus iam emortuum, nec emortuum uterum Sarae: adversus promissionem autem Dei non disceptauit, sed robustus factus fide, Deo gloriam tribuit, plane persuasum habens, eum quod promiserat, posse etiam facere. Exemplum hoc imitati sunt plures alij, quorum fides in Scripturis praedicatur. Idem ergo hodie faciant, quotquot Christiani dici & haberi volunt. Habemus enim pignus veritatis & gratiae Dei, IESVM CHRISTVM, in quo omnes promissiones sunt etiam & Amen. Huic ergo fi nitamur, nihil erit, quod nos ab eius charitate possit separare, sed in omnibus plus quam victores erimus. In primis autem hoc observari debet in aeternae salutis negotio, ubi mirifice fidem nostram oppugnat Satan, dum peccatorum nostrorum multitudine & propria conscientia testimonio nos territat, & Dei iustitiam ita nobis commendat, ut eiusdem bonitatem in dubium vocet. Nec desunt incauti doctores, qui in Ecclesia hoc dogma mordicus retinent & urgent, hominem quoad in carne viuit, non posse salutis suae certum fieri, & ideo nobis perpetuo dubitandum esse, num simus in gratia Dei: quod non aliud est, quam miseros peccatores in desperationis praecipitium adducere. Nos igitur Christum audiamus, qui nē haesitemus iubet. Et cur dubitent de salute sua Christiani homines, cuius origo ex Dei gratia manat, quam inexhaustā esse, Scriptura omnis testatur, & exempla beneficiorum quotidiana probant? Nec tamen in gratuita solum misericordia Dei, verum etiam in eiusdem iustitia salus iusta fundatur. Meruit enim hanc nobis aeternam ille & dilectus Filius, quem Pater nobis iustitiam, satisfactione & redemptione fecit, & in quo se nobis placatum esse caelitus publice testatus est. Idem pastor ille bonus est, qui non modo animam suam pro ovibus tradidit, sed sui sanguinis pretio redemptos fideliter custodit, neque aliquos ex manibus suis eripi finit. Et qui huic fidunt, super petram illam inexpugnabile aedificationis, quam neque portae quidem inferorum superare poterunt. Denique fides proprie coniunctum sibi habet πληροφορίαν, quæ certum est Spiritus sančti testimonium, quod nos de dilectione Dei, quæ nos hic complectitur, dubitare non sinit. Nascitur ex eo πεποίθησις, siue fiducia, qua fit, vt in medijs tentationibus clamemus Abba Pater, neq; de huius paterno erga nos amore dubitemus.
units.tr: But lest we think a bare and idle profession of faith is enough, we must consider what kind of faith in God ought to be in us. The Lord admonishes us about this too, saying: "If you have faith and do not doubt." In Mark he mentions a heart that is doubtful and wavering, which ought to be far from faith. He looks back to the nature of the flesh, which, when it must undertake something difficult or burdensome, is wont to argue within itself and be torn apart by opposing opinions and thoughts, so that it leans now to this side, now to that, and at one moment, trusting in God's promises, wishes to obey him, but soon, distrusting him, refuses obedience. But true and genuine faith, disregarding all other things, looks to the one God. This is why it does not hesitate or waver, even though the order of nature and common sense seem to advise otherwise. For it knows that God's goodness is immense and infinite and endures for ever. It likewise believes that he is almighty, and therefore that his decrees cannot be annulled or hindered by any human powers. It has firmly persuaded itself that truth is joined with these attributes, and from this it concludes that he who is at once truthful and almighty cannot be wanting to his promises. The Apostle writes that Abraham, the father of believers, had such faith, when he believed, against hope, in hope, that he would become the father of many nations through the seed to be born of Sarah. For, he says, "not weak in faith, he did not consider his own body, already dead, nor the dead womb of Sarah; but he did not dispute against the promise of God, but, made strong in faith, gave glory to God, being fully persuaded that what he had promised, he was also able to do." Many others, whose faith is proclaimed in the Scriptures, have imitated this example. Therefore, let all who wish to be and be called Christians do the same today. For we have the pledge of God's truth and grace, Jesus Christ, in whom all the promises are yes and amen. If we rest upon him, nothing will be able to separate us from his love, but in all things we shall be more than conquerors. Above all, this must be observed in the matter of eternal salvation, where Satan fiercely attacks our faith, terrifying us with the multitude of our sins and the testimony of our own conscience, and so sets before us God's justice that he calls God's goodness into doubt. Nor are there lacking unwary teachers in the Church who stubbornly hold to and press this dogma: that a man, as long as he lives in the flesh, cannot be made certain of his salvation, and that therefore we must always doubt whether we are in God's grace. This is nothing other than to drive wretched sinners over the precipice of despair. Let us therefore hear Christ, who bids us not to hesitate. And why should Christian people doubt their salvation, whose origin flows from the grace of God, which all Scripture testifies to be inexhaustible, and which the daily examples of his benefits prove? Yet salvation is founded not only on God's free mercy but also on his justice. For that dear Son, whom the Father made to us justification, satisfaction and redemption, has merited this eternal salvation for us, and in him he publicly testified from heaven that he was reconciled to us. He is that good shepherd who not only gave his soul for the sheep but faithfully keeps those redeemed at the price of his own blood, and he does not allow any to be snatched from his hands. And those who trust in him are built upon that rock, against which the gates of hell shall not prevail. Finally, faith has as its proper companion full assurance [πληροφορίαν], which is the sure testimony of the Holy Spirit, and which does not allow us to doubt the love of God that embraces us here. From this arises confidence [πεποίθησις], or trust, by which it comes about that, in the midst of temptations, we cry "Abba, Father," and do not doubt his fatherly love toward us.

units.la: Rom.8.

units.la: At quia hic cultus Deo gratissimus est, neq; honore maiori a nobis hic potest affici, quàm si talem esse constanter credamus, idem vicißim sibi fidentes non frustratur, sed (quod Christus sa- pius pollicetur) largitur, vt eorum fidei & spei euentus rerum respondeant. Nihil ergo impossibi le est credentibus. Id in præsenti exemplo probat, cuius occasione ex miraculo in ficu arefacta ædi- to petit, dicens: Si habueritis fidé, neq; hæsitaueritis, non solum hoc quod factum est ficui, facietis, veramentia si monti isti dixeritis, Tollitor, & proijcitor in mare, fiet. Hoc per hyperbolé enuntiat Christus: cuius hic sensus est, fide superari omnia obstacula, neq; aliquid tā arduum aut difficile esse, quod per illam non possit perfici, si opus sit. Nec enim promissionem hanc ideò dedit Dominus, vt nostræ curiositati indulgendo fidem nostram miraculis minimè necessarijs ostentemus, sed vt Dei potentia ac bonitate freti non succumbamus, etiamsi ea occurrant, quæ nulla hominum industria nullis item viribus superari posse videntur. Etenim vt montes loco moueamus, nequaquam opus est, neq; tale quid vel a Christo vel ab Apostolis factitatum esse legimus. Sed per salutis viam am bulantibus montes ardui & insuperabiles occurrunt, qui nisi e medio auferantur nō poterimus pro gredi. Etenim montis instar est caro, quæ vel cæcis affectibus, vel zelo inconsiderato inflata nobis negotium facit, vt nobisipsis difficultates fingamus, quæ nullæ essent, si rem ipsam rectiùs intuere mur. Mons arduus & altus est Satan, qui intus & foris multa mouet, vt vel securos, & propriæ salutis negligentes faciat, vel in desperationem coniectos salutis viam deferere cogat. Sed & ipse mundus, cum totus ex terræ filijs constet, nouos quotidie montes, vt olim de gigantibus poetæ fa- bulati sunt, congerit, quibus regnum cœlorum expugnare conatur, ne vllum in terris locū habeat. Typum huius rei in Zorobabele Zacharias proponit. Nā illi, cùm a reditu ex Babylone tem plum ædificaret, multa obijciebantur, quæ opus illud non difficile modò, verumetiā impossibile red debant. Quæ omnia in spiritu videns Propheta dicebat: Quis tu mons magne coram Zorobabele. Sed mox ipsi spiritus respondet: Ad campum planum videlicet redigeris. Quasi diceret: Insurgat populi vt volent, & montes montibus imponant, nunquā tamen effectum dabunt quod cupiunt, sed in planitie redigentur, imò in nihilum, & irritus erit eorum contra Dominum conatus, Et qui fidè Dei habent, montes omnes, quos vel caro, vel mundus, & huius princeps Satan obijcit, facilè vincunt. Fides enim est victoria nostra, quæ carnem vincit & Verbo Dei subijcit. Eadem mun- dum contemptui habet, vt neq; minis eius succumbat, neq; illecebris eiusdem capiatur. Sed & mundi principem vincit, & credentium pedibus calcandum subijcit. Itaq; omnibus aduersis & ten tationibus superiores siunt credentes, & (vt de seipso Paulus ait) omnia possunt in Christo, qui ipsos corroborat. Exempla, quibus hoc confirmetur, passim occurrunt: & multa Apostolus congerit in epistola ad Hebr. 11 quibus plura addere non opus est, cùm quotidie similia fiant apud eos, qui animos suos in fide obsirmarunt.
units.tr: But because this worship is most pleasing to God, and he cannot be honoured by us in a greater way than by steadfastly believing him to be such, he in turn does not disappoint those who trust in him, but (as Christ often promises) grants that the outcomes of their faith and hope correspond to the things they ask for. Nothing is impossible for believers. Christ proves this in the present example, on the occasion of the fig tree withered by the miracle, when he says to the disciples who marvelled: "If you have faith and do not hesitate, you will not only do what has been done to the fig tree, but if you say to this mountain, 'Be taken up and cast into the sea,' it will be done." Christ speaks this by hyperbole, and its meaning is that all obstacles are overcome by faith, and that nothing is so arduous or difficult that it cannot be accomplished through faith, if there is need. For the Lord did not give this promise so that, by indulging our curiosity, we might display our faith in miracles that are in no way necessary; rather, so that, relying on the power and goodness of God, we may not give way, even when there occur things which seem to be unable to be overcome by any human effort or by any strength. For we have no need at all to move mountains from their place, nor do we read that anything of this kind was done either by Christ or by the Apostles. But for those walking the way of salvation there appear steep and insurmountable mountains, which, unless they are removed from the midst, we cannot advance. For the flesh is like a mountain, which, puffed up by blind passions or by inconsiderate zeal, makes trouble for us, so that we invent for ourselves difficulties which would not exist if we looked at the matter more rightly. Satan is a lofty and high mountain, who stirs up many things within and without, either to make us secure and negligent of our own salvation, or to force us, cast into despair, to abandon the way of salvation. But the world itself, since it wholly consists of the sons of the earth, heaps up new mountains every day, as the poets once fabled of the giants, by which it tries to storm the kingdom of heaven, so that it may have no place on earth. Zechariah sets forth a type of this in Zerubbabel. For when he was building the temple after the return from Babylon, many objections were raised which made that work not only difficult but even impossible. Seeing all these things in spirit, the prophet said: "Who are you, great mountain, before Zerubbabel?" But straightaway the Spirit himself answers: "You shall be reduced to a plain." As if to say: let the peoples rise up as they wish, and heap mountains upon mountains, yet they will never achieve what they desire; rather they will be reduced to a plain, indeed to nothing, and their attempt against the Lord will come to nothing. Those who have faith in God easily overcome all the mountains which the flesh, or the world, and its prince Satan, throw in their way. For faith is our victory, which conquers the flesh and subjects it to the Word of God. It holds the world in contempt, so that it neither yields to its threats nor is caught by its allurements. It also conquers the prince of the world and subjects him to be trampled under the feet of believers. Thus believers become superior to all adversities and temptations, and (as Paul says of himself) "they can do all things in Christ, who strengthens them." Examples to confirm this occur everywhere, and the Apostle gathers many in his Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter 11, to which there is no need to add more, since similar things happen daily among those who have strengthened their minds in faith.

units.la: Cæterum quia fidei proprium opus est, Inuocatio, & qui hanc habent, eam precibus testan tur, vt primùm aliquid periculi imminet, de his quoq; agit, & fidem eo nomine nobis amplius com mendat, quòd preces nostras coram Deo acceptas & ratas faciat. Nam ait: Et quæcunq; pre- cando petieritis, si crediderit is, accipietis. Quo loco animaduerti debet, quòd etsi fidei omnia possi- bilia esse dixerit, non tamen ideo securos esse iubet, qui side freti, omnia pro imperio & nostro nutu agamus: sed quia Deus orari vult, vt fidem precibus assiduis absq; omni hæsitatione testemur, monet, & ad has nos promissione noua excitat. Confutatur ergo hic eorum calumnia, qui per do- strinam fidei preces & alia pietatis exercitia aboleri dicunt. Et consentiunt huic loco aliæ pro- missiones, quæ passim in Scripturis habentur, qualis est, quà nuper ex Psalmis adduximus, & quæ apud Isaiam extat, per quem Dominus ait: Fiet, vt priusquam inuocent, ego respondeam: & ad- huc illis loquentibus, ego exaudiam. Et Christus ipse, cùm iam mortem aditurus discipulos in fide & omnibus ijs instituisset, quæ adsalutem nobis necessaria sunt, eosdem ad preces excitat. Quic- quid petieritis (inquit) in nomine meo, hoc faciam: vt glorificetur Pater in Filio. Item, Amen
units.tr: Moreover, because prayer is the proper work of faith, and those who have faith bear witness to it by their prayers, he also deals with this matter when danger threatens. He commends faith to us more strongly on this account, that it makes our prayers acceptable and effective before God. He says: "And whatever you ask in prayer, if you believe, you will receive" (Matt. 21:22). Here it must be noted that although he has said that all things are possible to faith, he does not thereby bid those who rely on faith to act as if everything were at our command and nod. Rather, because God wishes to be called upon, he admonishes us to bear witness to our faith in prayer, constantly and without any hesitation, and he rouses us to this with a new promise. The calumny of those who say that prayer and the other exercises of piety are abolished by the doctrine of faith is therefore refuted here. Other promises that occur everywhere in the Scriptures agree with this passage, such as the one we recently brought forward from the Psalms, and the one found in Isaiah, through whom the Lord says: "It shall come to pass that before they call, I will answer; and while they are still speaking, I will hear" (Isa. 65:24). Christ himself, when he was about to face death and had instructed his disciples in faith and in all those things necessary for our salvation, likewise rouses them to prayer: "Whatever you ask in my name," he says, "I will do it, that the Father may be glorified in the Son" (John 14:13).

units.la: amen dico vobis, quaecunque petieritis a Patre meo in nomine meo, dabit vobis. Exempla, quae nos in fide iustarum promissionum confirment, innumera in Scripturis narrantur, quibus recitandis immorari non opus est, cum singuli in semetipsis multa inveniunt, si vitae suae curriculum a pueris examinarint. Huius modo meminerimus, precibus pondus suum ex fide accedere, neque Deo probari posse, nisi hanc sibi coniunctam habeant. Sola fide enim Christus apprehenditur: qui nobis Deum Patrem placavit. Adhac quia fidei meminit, ad eas quoque preces promissio ista referringi debet, quibus quae salutaria sunt, et cum Dei voluntate bona conveniunt, postulamus. Solet enim fides in Deum et huius Verbum respicere, et qui hac praediti sunt, inter precandum ex animo dicunt: Fiat voluntas tua quemadmodum in caelo, sic etiam in terra. Quia vero fides (ut Christus praedixit) in terris rara est, hodie, in precibus etiam plerique instar belluarum vlulant, neque alia requirunt, quam quae carni adlubescunt, non mirum est, non semper exaudiri omnes, et mundum calamitatibus atque periculis perpetuis exerceri. Applicemus ergo huius loci doctrinam nostris temporibus. Efficit salutem nostram Dominus, et quotidie ut frugi paterfamilias fructus quaerit, qui professioni nominis Christiani respondeant. Sed plerique sicut sunt steriles, sterilitatis autem huius causa est, quod plerique fide destituuntur, neque credunt Dei verbis. Urget ergo nos maledictio Domini, et quia plerique radicitus exaruerunt, securis ad radices arborum posita excidium graue omnibus minatur. Ut ergo sterilitati nostrae medeamur, et montes quos Satan ingentes contra Ecclesiam excitat, superare et procul a nobis arcere possimus, credamus Dei Verbo, et per hoc edocti fructus feramus, qui de fide nostra testantur, adhaec ex fide constanti precemur Patrem miserationum, ut nobis propitius montes ipsos in planitiem redigat, hostium concilia dissipet, et Ecclesias nobis feruet propter nomen Filii sui Unigeniti IESV CHRISTI, Seruatoris et Domini nostri, cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria et potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: "Amen, I say to you, whatever you ask of my Father in my name, he will give you" (Matt. 18:19). Examples that confirm us in faith in the just promises are told innumerable times in the Scriptures. There is no need to dwell on reciting them, since each person will find many in his own life if he examines the course of his life from boyhood. Let us remember this: prayers receive their weight from faith, and they cannot be pleasing to God unless faith is joined to them. For Christ, who reconciled God the Father to us, is laid hold of by faith alone. Moreover, since this promise speaks of faith, it must also be referred to those prayers in which we ask for what is salutary and agrees with the good will of God. For faith looks to God and to his Word, and those who are endowed with it, when they pray, say from the heart: "Your will be done on earth as it is in heaven." But because faith (as Christ foretold) is rare on earth, many today also howl in their prayers like beasts, and seek nothing but what pleases the flesh. It is no wonder, then, that not all are always heard, and that the world is afflicted with constant calamities and dangers. Let us therefore apply the teaching of this passage to our own times. The Lord effects our salvation, and every day, like a thrifty householder, he seeks the fruits that correspond to the profession of the Christian name. But many are barren, and the cause of this barrenness is that many are destitute of faith and do not believe the words of God. The curse of the Lord therefore presses upon us, and because many have withered to the root, the axe laid to the roots of the trees threatens all with grievous destruction. So, that we may remedy our barrenness, and be able to overcome the great mountains which Satan raises against the Church and keep them far from us, let us believe the Word of God, and, taught by it, bear fruits that bear witness to our faith. Moreover, let us pray with a steadfast faith to the Father of mercies, that he, being gracious to us, may reduce those mountains to a plain, scatter the councils of our enemies, and preserve his Churches for us, for the sake of the name of his only-begotten Son, Jesus Christ, our Saviour and Lord, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCXLVII.
units.tr: HOMILY 247.

units.la: Et cum venisset in templum, primarij Sacerdotes & Seniores populi eum docentem adierunt, dicentes: Qua authoritate facis ista? & quis tibi dedit istam authoritatem? Respondens autem IESVS dixit eis: Interrogabo vos & ego verbum unum: quod si dixeritis mihi, dicam & ego vobis, qua authoritate ista faciam. Baptisma Ioannis unde erat? e coelo, an ex hominibus? At illi ratiocinabantur apud se dicentes: Si dixerimus, E coelo: dicet nobis, Quare ergo non credidistis ei? Sin autem dixerimus, Ex hominibus: timemus turbam. Omnes enim habent Ioannem ut Prophetam. Et respondentes IESV, dixerunt, Nescimus. Ait eis & ipse: Nec ego vobis dicam, qua authoritate ista faciam.
units.tr: And when he was come into the temple, the chief priests and the elders of the people came unto him as he taught, and said, By what authority doest thou these things? and who gave thee this authority? And Jesus answered and said unto them, I will also ask you one thing, which if ye tell me, I in like wise will tell you by what authority I do these things. The baptism of John, whence was it? from heaven, or of men? And they reasoned with themselves, saying, If we shall say, From heaven; he will say unto us, Why then did ye not believe him? But if we shall say, Of men; we fear the people: for all hold John as a prophet. And they answered Jesus, and said, We cannot tell. And he himself said unto them, Neither tell I you by what authority I do these things.

units.la: Inter opera miraculosa, quibus Dominus noster IESVS CHRISTVS paulo ante mortem, sciens omnipotentem Dei Filium esse demonstrauit, non postremum est, quod etsi ex templo quasi suam sacrorum nundinationem cum aliis abusibus eiecisset, & omnia fecisset, quae aduersarios suos poterant offendere, eosdem tamen sine armis & praesidijs humanis occulta virtute ita coercuit, ut quamuis maxime vellent, non tamen auderent ipsi manus inijcere, neque etiam obstare possent, quo minus quotidie in templo doceret, & doctrinam suam miraculis confirmaret. Ex eo enim constat, illum esse Regem gloriae, cui Pater gentes subiecit, & qui in medio hostium suorum dominatur. Rursus autem in his fe prodit incurabilis hostium contumacia. Nam etsi manum eius potentem sentirent, non tamen quieuerunt: sed quem non ausi sunt aperta vi aggredi, eum quaestionibus & colloquijs insidiosis tentant, si quo modo eum apud Romanum Praesidem calumniari, aut populo suspectum facere possint. Inter haec colloquia primum est, quod hic narratur, & cuius status ipsis fuit, quod eius vocationem volunt in dubium vocare, quasi priuata authoritate omnia
units.tr: Among the miraculous works by which our Lord Jesus Christ, shortly before his death, showed that he was the almighty Son of God, this is not the least: when he had cast out of the temple, as if it were a market for sacred things, together with other abuses, and had done everything that could offend his adversaries, he nevertheless restrained them by a hidden power, without arms or human protection. Though they most eagerly wished to, they did not dare to lay hands on him, nor could they prevent him from teaching in the temple every day and confirming his teaching with miracles. For from this it is clear that he is the King of glory, to whom the Father has subjected the nations, and who rules in the midst of his enemies. Yet again, in these things the incurable obstinacy of his enemies is revealed. For although they felt his powerful hand, they did not keep quiet. Whom they did not dare to attack by open force, they now try to overcome with questions and insidious conversations, to see whether in some way they could bring a false charge against him before the Roman governor, or make him suspect to the people. Among these conversations, the first is the one recorded here. Its purpose for them was to call his calling into doubt, as if he did all things by private authority, and therefore did not deserve belief.

units.la: Luc.18
units.tr: Luke 18.

units.la: Psal.2.110 omnia faciat, & proinde fidem non mereatur. Quia vero hoc stratagemate adhuc pugnant Evangelij hostes, sciunt historia hæc aduersus eos, qui hodie similiter sibi omnem potestatem in Ecclesia vendicant, nec cuiquam licere volunt, vt doceat, aut aliquid agat, nisi ab ipsis ordinatus character bestiæ acceperit. Proderit ergo, vt singulas huius disputationis partes diligenter consideremus.
units.tr: Psalm 2; 110. He does all things, and therefore does not deserve belief. But since the enemies of the Gospel still fight with this stratagem, this story is known to be against those who today likewise claim for themselves all power in the Church, and will not allow anyone to teach or do anything unless he has received the mark of the beast from them. It will therefore be useful to consider carefully each part of this dispute.

units.la: Principio occasionem totius actionis exponit Euangelista, & eos producit simul, qui hanc ad uersus Christum instituerunt. Et cum venisset (inquit) in templum IESVS, primarij Sacerdotes & Seniores populi eum docentem adierunt. Occasio igitur fuit, quod quotidie primo mane (vt alibi diximus) in vrbem reuersus populum in templo docuit. Illic ergo eum adierunt Sacerdotum principes, quibus cura religionis & cultus diuini comissa erat, & Seniores populi, qui veterem Senatus politici formam referebant, & ius cuiq; dicere atq; innocentes tueri, homines vero malefi-cos & sceleratos dignis pœnis coercere debebant. Marcus Scribas quoq; his connumerat, qui iuris diuini cognitionem profitebantur, & eruditionis præcipuam existimationem sustinebant. Coniurarunt ergo contra Christum omnes tam Ecclesiastici quam politici, penes quos aliqua tunc erat inter Iudæos authoritas: & quidem in templo eum aggrediuntur docentem. Quia enim Sacerdotes sibi in templo ius omne vendicabant, religionem vero sibi ipsis quæstum fecerant, nullibi minus illum ferre potuerunt, quam in templo. Est hæc fors Veritatis, vt ibi potissimum oppugnetur, vbi regnare debebat, & illos aduersarios habeat acerrimos, quorum erat illam prædicare. Etenim non possunt huius lucem ferre Sacerdotes, qui quæstum quærunt ex religione. Cum enim per illam arguantur ipsorum impostura, non satis est illis, si ipsi in officio cessent, nisi officium facientibus sese opponant. Idem animus est ijs, quos eruditionis & humanæ sapientiæ perfuasio fascinauit. Indignum enim putant, si quæ ipsi hactenus tradiderunt, aut saltem exemplo & calculo suo approbarunt, falsi arguantur. At quia se solos non multum posse vident, magistratus & principes viros mirifico astu in suas partes trahunt, vt horum authoritate & viribus ad causæ suæ defensionem abutantur. Enimuero mirum videri poterat, hic & aliàs sæpe cum Christum cum Sacerdotibus collusisse Seniores, qui veterem libertatem populi, & quicquid ex hac adhuc reliquum erat debebant defendere. Nec enim legitimi fuerunt Sacerdotes, qui tunc in templo dominium & ius sibi vendicabant, sed (vt alibi diximus) ab Herode magno instituti erant, qui vt regnum suum stabiliret, extinctâ veterum Sacerdotum prosapia, nouos & obscuros homines ex sece vulgi ad Sacerdotij dignitatem euexerat, vt illis pro libito abuteretur. Deinde ijdem aprasidibus Romanis toti pendebant, qui Sacerdotium pro pecunia modo his, modo alijs conferebant. Sed licet his illi feruiliter adulantur, & Romanæ tyrannidis iugum grauius facerent priuati commodi ergo, illis tamen contra promissum a Deo vindicem & Seruatorem patrocinantur Seniores, qui vetera populi iura pro virili debebant tueri. Idem aliquot iam faculis factum est inter Christianos, postquam Episcopi omnem sibi in Ecclesia potestatem vendicarunt. Quis enim nescit, hos ex nobilium & principum oppressione creuisse, & potentissimos Reges a Pontificibus dolo circumuentos esse, vt horum iugo collum submiserint, adhac eosdem bellorum & seditionum fere omnium ab eo tempore fuisse authores? Attamen adhuc cum ipsis colludunt, qui publicæ libertatis vindices esse, & propriam dignitatem contra illos asserere debebant. Offendit hoc multos, & ideo de Euangelij fide dubitant. Sed meminerint Christiani homines, non nouum hoc esse & insolens. Fascinat summos reges & principes spiritus ille fornicationis, vt poculo magnæ illius meretricis inebriati, huic sese subiciant, nec aliquam suæ existimationis & fortunarum suarum habeant rationem. Nos interea IESVM CHRISTVM audiamus, qui suos vindicare pergit, & olim de impostoribus illis pœnas sumet, quas eorum improbitas meretur.
units.tr: At the outset, the Evangelist sets out the occasion of the whole action, and brings forward at the same time those who devised this plot against Christ. "And when he was come," he says, "into the temple, the chief priests and the elders of the people came to him as he taught." The occasion, then, was that, as we have said elsewhere, every morning he returned to the city and taught the people in the temple. There the leaders of the priests, to whom the care of religion and divine worship had been entrusted, came to him, along with the elders of the people, who represented the old form of the civil council and were obliged to give judgment to each person, to protect the innocent, and to punish evildoers and criminals with due penalties. Mark also counts the scribes among these, who professed knowledge of divine law and held the chief reputation for learning. So all of them, both churchmen and civil officials, who then held some authority among the Jews, conspired against Christ; and indeed they attack him while he is teaching in the temple. For since the priests claimed for themselves every right in the temple, and had made a profit out of religion, they could nowhere bear him less than in the temple. It is the lot of truth that it is attacked most of all where it ought to reign, and that it has its bitterest opponents among those whose task was to proclaim it. For the priests who make a living from religion cannot bear its light. When their imposture is exposed by it, it is not enough for them to neglect their own duty; they also set themselves against those who perform it. The same spirit is found in those whom the persuasion of learning and human wisdom has bewitched. For they think it shameful if what they themselves have taught up to now, or at least approved by their example and judgment, is shown to be false. But because they see that they alone cannot achieve much, they draw magistrates and princes to their side with remarkable cunning, so that they may misuse their authority and power to defend their cause. Indeed, it might seem strange here, and often elsewhere, that the elders colluded with the priests against Christ, when they ought to have defended the old liberty of the people and whatever remained of it. For the priests who then claimed dominion and right in the temple were not lawful priests; as we have said elsewhere, they had been appointed by Herod the Great. In order to strengthen his kingdom, after destroying the line of the old priests, he had raised new and obscure men from the common people to the dignity of the priesthood, so that he could use them as he pleased. Moreover, these same men depended entirely on the Roman governors, who gave the priesthood now to one man, now to another, for money. But although those priests fawned on them in a servile way, and made the yoke of Roman tyranny heavier for their own private advantage, the elders, who ought to have defended the ancient rights of the people as far as they could, nevertheless took the side of these men against the avenger and Savior whom God had promised. The same thing has happened among Christians for some centuries now, since the bishops claimed for themselves all power in the Church. For who does not know that they grew up out of the oppression of nobles and princes, that the most powerful kings were craftily entrapped by the pontiffs, so that they bowed their necks under their yoke, and that they have been nearly the authors of almost all wars and seditions since that time? Yet even now, those who ought to be the defenders of public liberty and to assert their own dignity against the bishops still collude with them. This offends many, and therefore they doubt the faith of the Gospel. But let Christians remember that this is not new or unusual. That spirit of fornication bewitches the greatest kings and princes, so that, drunk from the cup of that great harlot, they submit themselves to her and take no account of their own reputation and fortunes. Meanwhile, let us listen to Jesus Christ, who goes on defending his own, and who will one day exact from those impostors the punishment their wickedness deserves.

units.la: Porro videamus, quomodo Sacerdotes isti cum suis coniuratis Dominum aggrediantur. Dicunt ei, Qua authoritate facis ista? & quis tibi dedit hanc authoritatem? Non quærunt de doctrina, non de causis templi a sordibus turpis illius nundinationis & alijs abusibus repurgati, non item de miraculis. Nec enim audent ista attingere, cum doctrinam eius scirent cœlestem, & ipsum a Deo missum præceptorem venisse, sicuti Nicodemus diserte testatus fuerat. Miraculorum autem Veritas toti populo cognita & testata erat: nundinationis quoq; in templo tanta fuit fœditas, ut procul dubio eius ipsos puduerit. Quo iure ergo ista faciat quaerunt: unde nimirum haec illi authoritas data sit? & sub huius quaestionis praetextu novum crimen ei intentant: Quod nimirum authoritate privata rebus nihil ad se pertinentibus se immisceat. Etenim an tiquitus Leuitae sacris destinati fuerunt, & inter hos erant distinctae familiae, inter quas munera sacerdotalia erant distributa. Nota item erant exempla, quae olim in Coritas & Uziam Regem Deus edidit, quando illos quidem terra absorbuit, quod Pontificatum sibi vendicarent, hunc vero lepra percussit, quod suffitum adolere ausus fuisset. Inter Prophetas autem damnatur apud Ieremiam, qui non missi currebant. Quo Paulus respiciens, dixit: Quomodo praedicabunt, nisi missi fuerint? Itaq; Christum hac quaestione constringi posse putant, ut non habeat, quo se excusset. Nec enim poterat authoritatem humanam allegare, cum non effet ab ipsis ordinatus, qui hoc ius penes se solos esse volebant. Si diuinam adducat, illum nimis superbum, arrogantem, imo blasphemum dicent, & signum e cælo petent, quo se a Deo missum evidenter demonstret: quod ipsos alias fecisse in superioribus audiuimus. Ita vero suspectum toti populo volunt reddere, ut qui seditiose nouis rebus studeat, & sibi vsurpet, quod ad ipsos solos pertineat, ut pote legitimos Aaronis successores. Et hoc audent, qui potius ipsi cogendi erant, ut eorum quae ipsi contra expressum Dei Verbum faciebant, rationem redderent. Nec enim legitimi erant veterum Sacerdotum & filiorum Aaronis successores, ut paulo ante diximus. Et si maxime tales fuissent, nullo tamen iure ipsis licuisset Legis doctrinam falsis interpretationibus corrumpere, aut nouis traditionibus depravare: multo minus ex templo emporium facere, sacrum Dei cultum in speluncam latronum convertere, & infinita alia agere, quae iam diu impie & turpiter contra Dei praecepta designarunt.
units.tr: Let us now see how these priests, with their conspirators, attack the Lord. They say to him, "By what authority doest thou these things? and who gave thee this authority?" They do not ask about his teaching, nor about the cleansing of the temple from the filth of that shameful market and other abuses, nor likewise about his miracles. For they dare not touch these matters, since they knew his teaching was heavenly, and that he had come as a teacher sent by God, as Nicodemus had clearly testified. The truth of the miracles was known and attested to by the whole people; and the filth of the market in the temple was so great that, beyond doubt, they themselves were ashamed of it. So they ask by what right he does these things: from where, of course, did he get this authority? And under the pretext of this question they bring a new charge against him: that by private authority he meddles in matters that do not concern him. For in ancient times the Levites were set apart for sacred duties, and among them there were distinct families, among whom the priestly offices were distributed. Examples were also well known, which God once showed in Korah and in King Uzziah: the earth swallowed up the former, who claimed the high priesthood for himself, while leprosy struck the latter, who had dared to burn incense. Among the prophets, Jeremiah condemns those who ran without being sent. Paul, looking to this, said: "How shall they preach, except they be sent?" So they think they can bind Christ with this question, so that he has no way to excuse himself. For he could not allege human authority, since he had not been ordained by them, who wanted this right to rest with themselves alone. If he should appeal to divine authority, they will say that he is too proud, arrogant, indeed blasphemous, and will ask for a sign from heaven by which he may clearly demonstrate that he has been sent by God; this, as we heard earlier, they had done on other occasions. In this way they want to make him suspect to the whole people, as one who seditiously pursues new things and claims for himself what belongs to them alone, as the lawful successors of Aaron. And they dare to do this, when they themselves ought rather to have been compelled to give an account of what they did against the express word of God. For they were not the lawful successors of the old priests and the sons of Aaron, as we said a little while ago. And even if they had been such, they would have had no right to corrupt the teaching of the Law with false interpretations, or to pervert it with new traditions; much less to turn the temple into a marketplace, to change the sacred worship of God into a robbers' cave, and to do countless other things which for a long time they had impiously and shamefully carried out against the commands of God.

units.la: Habemus autem in hac historia speculum nostri temporis. Olim ministrorum Verbi electio penes Ecclesiam erat. Ab Ecclesia electus Matthias in locum Iudae proditoris substitutus est. Ecclesiae item suffragijs non sine ieiunio & publicis precibus designati Paulus & Barnabas inter gentes praedicarunt. In hunc quoq; finem conscripti sunt canones Apostolici, quos Ecclesia ministrorum electione sequeretur, ne quid ex priuato affectu fieret. Postea autem tempori bus hoc ius sibi vendicarunt Romani Episcopi, qui tandem alios Episcopos in sua verba iurare coegerunt, & per eosdem alijs quoq; parochijs & Ecclesijs insidiati sunt, nec cessarunt, donec omnes fere vbiq; terrarum sibi subiecerunt, ut pastores & ministros vel ab ipsis Pontificibus, vel ab Episcopis & Monachis, qui his obstrictl sunt, petere cogantur. Ex hoc fonte manauit postea omnis doctrinae & religionis corruptio. Quod si Deus excitet seruos suos, qui libera Verbi praedicatione ista arguunt, & per hos excitati principes & magistratus pij de reformatione facienda consilia capiunt, & operi huic non minus necessario quam pio & sancto manus admouent, non possunt illi manifestos errores & abusus negare, multo minus defendere possunt ex Scripturis sacris, quae contra Verbum Dei inuexerunt. Quare causae cognitione & disputationes omnes detrectant, ad hoc autem asylum sese recipiunt, ad quod Iudaei Sacerdotes & Scribae confugerunt. Clamat enim nullius vel ministro Ecclesiae vel magistratui politico licere, ut statum Ecclesiae mutet, aut doctrinae, siue cultus reformationem instituat abs Romani Pontificis consensu, aut Concilij vniuersalis determinatione. Et hic multa garriunt de Apostolica successione & donationibus regum, priuilegijs item & immunitatibus. Sed his nemo moueatur. Successio enim nihil probat, nisi de doctrina eiusdem successione constet. Cum ergo illi a doctrina Apostolorum iam pridem discesserint, frustra illorum successione gloriantur. Quoad immunitates & priuilegia, haec partim emetita & ficta sunt, partim malis artibus extorta, & talia sunt, quae neq; Reges & Imperatores dare debuerunt, neq; accipere ij, qui spirituales dici & haberi volunt. Et bene fecerunt nostro saeculo Germani principes & magistratus, qui portas suas Regi gloriae, IESV CHRISTO, aperuerunt, neq; se a coeptae reformationis instituto reuocari passi sunt. Fecerunt hi quod olim Asa, Iosaphat, Ezechias & Iosias fecere, quos hoc nomine Spiritus Sanctus commendat. Nos igitur & hos & illos imitemur, & fortiter tueamur libertatem fidei, quam illi nobis peperunt, & eadem bene vtamur, ut in nobis Deus glorificetur. Sed transeamus ad Christum, qui etsi illi respondere indigni essent, respondet tamen, sed obli-que, dum aliam quaestionem illis opponit, quae sola illos admonere poterat, ipsum divina authori-tate omnia facere. Interrogabo (inquit) vos & ego verbum unum: quod si dixeritis mihi, di-cam & ego vobis, qua authoritate ista faciam. Baptisma Ioannis unde erat? e caelo, an ex homi-nibus? Sub Baptismo totum Ioannis ministerium comprehendit. Quia enim Sacramenta doctri-nae appendices & sigilla sunt, haec ab illis nequaquam divelli debet. Quod Marcus observans, scri-bebat: Baptizabat Ioannes in deserto, & praedicabat Baptismum respiscentiae ad remissionem peccatorum. Itaq; Christus sic dicere videtur: Si vobis licet de me quaerere, qui meam vocationem hactenus innumeris signis probavi, non graue vobis videri debet, si ego quoq; ex vobis quaeram, quod ad vos cumprimus & ad huius causae declarationem pertinet. Dicite ergo, quid de Ioanne sentiatis. Fuit ne hic a Deo missus Veritatis praeco, aut ab hominibus subornatus, vel sua sponte currens impostor? Sic vero agit Christus, non quod rationem suae vocationis & eorum quae agebat reddere detrectet, sed ut eos proprio ipsorum testimonio convincat. Sciebat enim, quid de Ioanne sentirent, & simul huius de se testimonium illis in mentem revocat, quod est: Ecce Agnus Dei, qui tollit peccatum mundi. Qui superne venit, supra omnes est. Qui eius testimonium recipit, is obsignavit, quod Deus verax sit. Nam is quem misit Deus, verba Dei loquitur: non enim huic admetitur Deus spiritum. Pater diligit Filium, & omnia dedit in manum: Qui credit in Filium, habet vitam aeternam, &c. Haec (inquam) illis in mentem revocat. Similis locus est, qui alibi habetur: Vos misistis ad Ioannem, & is testimonium dedit veritati. At ego testimonium habeo maius testimonio Ioannis: opera enim, quae mihi dedit Pater, ut eaperficerem, ipsa (inquit) opera quae ego facio, testantur de me, quod Pater misit me, &c.
units.tr: We have in this history a mirror of our own time. Formerly the choice of ministers of the Word lay with the Church. Matthias, chosen by the Church, was put in the place of Judas the traitor. Likewise Paul and Barnabas, designated by the votes of the Church with fasting and public prayers, preached among the Gentiles. To this end the Apostolic canons were also drawn up, so that the Church would follow them in choosing ministers, lest anything be done from private feeling. Afterwards, however, the Roman bishops claimed this right for themselves in time. They at last compelled other bishops to swear to their words, and through these they laid snares for other parishes and churches as well. They did not stop until they had brought almost all places everywhere under their own control, so that men are compelled to seek pastors and ministers either from the Pontiffs themselves or from bishops and monks who are bound to them. From this source all corruption of doctrine and religion afterwards flowed. But if God raises up his servants, who by free preaching of the Word denounce these things, and through them pious princes and magistrates take counsel for making reformation and put their hands to this work, no less necessary than pious and holy, the Papists cannot deny the manifest errors and abuses, much less can they defend from the sacred Scriptures what they have introduced against the Word of God. Therefore they refuse every examination of the case and every disputation, and take refuge in that sanctuary to which the Jewish priests and scribes fled. For they cry out that it is lawful for no minister of the Church or political magistrate to change the state of the Church, or to institute a reform of doctrine or worship, without the consent of the Roman Pontiff or the decision of a universal council. And here they chatter much about apostolic succession and the donations of kings, and likewise about privileges and immunities. But let no one be moved by these things. For succession proves nothing unless agreement in doctrine is established. Since they have long since departed from the doctrine of the Apostles, they boast of their succession in vain. As for immunities and privileges, some of these have been invented and fabricated, some extorted by evil arts, and they are of such a kind that neither kings nor emperors ought to have granted them, nor should those who wish to be called and regarded as spiritual have received them. The German princes and magistrates of our age have done well, who opened their gates to the King of glory, Jesus Christ, and did not allow themselves to be called back from the undertaking of the reformation they had begun. They did what Asa, Jehoshaphat, Hezekiah and Josiah once did, whom the Holy Spirit commends for this very thing. Let us therefore imitate both these and those, and bravely defend the liberty of faith which they won for us, and use it well, so that God may be glorified in us. But let us pass on to Christ, who, though they were unworthy of an answer, nevertheless answers them, indirectly, while he puts to them another question, which alone could remind them that he does all things by divine authority. "I will ask you one thing," he says, "and if you tell me, I too will tell you by what authority I do these things. The baptism of John: whence was it, from heaven or from men?" Under baptism he includes the whole ministry of John. For since the sacraments are appendages and seals of doctrine, the one must by no means be separated from the other. Mark, observing this, wrote: "John was baptizing in the desert and preaching the baptism of repentance for the remission of sins." So Christ seems to say: If you are allowed to ask about me, who have hitherto proved my calling by countless signs, it should not seem burdensome to you if I too ask you something which concerns you and pertains to the declaration of this cause. Tell me then, what do you think of John? Was he a herald of the truth sent by God, or an impostor suborned by men, or a runner who came of his own accord? Christ acts thus not because he shrinks from giving an account of his calling and of what he was doing, but so that he may convict them by their own testimony. For he knew what they thought of John, and at the same time he calls to their minds John's testimony concerning himself: "Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world. He who comes from above is above all. He who receives his testimony has certified that God is true. For he whom God has sent speaks the words of God, for God does not give the Spirit to him by measure. The Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand. He who believes in the Son has eternal life," etc. These things, I say, he brings back to their minds. There is a similar passage elsewhere: "You sent to John, and he gave testimony to the truth. But I have a testimony greater than the testimony of John: for the works which the Father has given me to accomplish, these very works which I do bear witness concerning me, that the Father has sent me," etc.

units.la: Admonent haec, ut agi debeat cum apertis & praefractis Veritatis hostibus. Parati simus sequendum Petri praeceptum semper ad respondendum cuilibet petenti, neq; nos Christi & Euangelij eius pudeat. Interim prudenter agamus, memores dicti Solomonici: Ne respondeas stulto secundum stultitiam eius, ne & tu par eis fias. Cura ergo sit, ut non tam nostra dicamus, quam quae Dei sunt: & stemus in statione nostra, ut audiamus, quid in nobis loquatur Dominus, qui suum spiritum promisit illis, qui sistuntur iudicibus, ut fidei suae rationem reddant. Itaq; ad Dei tribunal citemus aduersarios, & nos vicissim interrogemus, quid ipsi de Prophetis & Apostolis sentiant? Annon hos agnoscant Dei seruos fuisse, qui huius Verbum fideliter tradiderint? Demonstrent ergo, nos ab his diuersum docere & sentire: Quod si id non possunt, nos missos faciant.
units.tr: These things admonish us how we ought to deal with open and stubborn enemies of the truth. Let us be ready always to follow Peter's precept, to give an answer to anyone who asks, and let us not be ashamed of Christ and his Gospel. Meanwhile let us act prudently, mindful of the saying of Solomon: "Answer not a fool according to his folly, lest you also become like him." Let care be taken that we say not so much our own things as those that are God's; and let us stand at our post, that we may hear what the Lord speaks in us, who promised his Spirit to those who are brought before judges to give an account of their faith. Therefore let us summon our adversaries to the tribunal of God, and in turn ask them what they think of the Prophets and Apostles. Do they not acknowledge that these were servants of God who faithfully handed down his Word? Let them demonstrate, then, that we teach and think differently from these. But if they cannot do that, let them dismiss us.

units.la: Quantum vero pondus habeant eiusmodi quaestiones, & quam profunde in corda hostium, quantumuis obstinati sint, penetrent, praesenti exemplo docemur. Etenim haerent Sacerdotes, illi & Seniores, & licet praemeditati ad hoc colloquium venerint, nunc dubij & perplexi secum rationes ineunt: Si dixerimus, E caelo fuisse totum Ioannis ministerium: dicet nobis. Cur ergo non credidistis ei? (Sciunt enim impij quoq;, Deo & eius seruis esse parendum. Et execrabilis est quorundam pertinacia, qui cum Scripturis Dei Verbum contineri fateantur, tamen illis obloqui non verentur.) Sin autem dixerimus, Ex hominibus fuisse Ioannis ministerium, ex populo nobis periculum imminet, cum omnibus perspicuum sit, Ioannem Prophetam fuisse diuinitus missum. Tenentur ergo conuincti propria conscientia testimonio: sed quia omnia potius metuunt quam Deum, seipsos omnium ludibrijs exponunt, & se nescire dicunt, quod omnibus vulgo notum erat: deniq; mentiri malunt cum certa existimationis suae iactura, quam Veritati cedere. Exprimuntur hoc exemplo mores antistitum, quos priuata gloria & commodi cupiditas fascinat. Ab una parte suae existimationi, ab altera populi furore metuunt, nihil interim de gloria Dei & populi fauore solliciti. His affectibus hodie etiam multi impediuntur quo minus credant. Sed plerunq; illis idem quod ipsis accidit: ut proprijs laqueis capiantur, seq; ipsos infames faciant, ut iam de vita aeterna iactura nihil dicatur, quam eis Dominus non obscure minatur, cum inferet: Neq; ego vobis dicam, qua authoritate ista faciam. Atqui facis iam dixerat, & ipso tacente res loquebatur. Sed quia scientes volentes nescThey ebant quod dicebatur, indigni erant pleniori institutione. Etenim talibus doctrina nequicquam adhibetur. Relinquuntur ergo in tenebris, quas sibi ipsis accersunt, ut in illis pereant, sicut merentur. Nobis autem huius historia vsus sit, ut discamus posthabito honoreris & quaestus priuati studio, Veritati cedere, & perfidei obedientiam subijci Filio Dei IESV CHRISTO, cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: How great a weight such questions carry, and how deeply they penetrate the hearts of enemies, however obstinate they may be, we are taught by the present example. For the priests and elders stick fast, and although they came to this conference prepared, now they reckon among themselves in doubt and perplexity: "If we say that John's whole ministry was from heaven, he will say to us: Why then did you not believe him?" (For even the wicked know that God and his servants must be obeyed. And the obstinacy of certain men is detestable, who, while admitting that the Word of God is contained in the Scriptures, nevertheless do not hesitate to speak against them.) "But if we say that John's ministry was from men, we are in danger from the people, since it is clear to all that John was a Prophet sent by God." They are therefore convicted by the testimony of their own conscience; but because they fear everything more than God, they expose themselves to the mockery of all, and say that they do not know what was commonly known to everyone. In the end they prefer to lie, with the certain loss of their reputation, rather than yield to the truth. By this example the character of the leaders is set forth, whom private glory and the desire for gain bewitch. On the one hand they fear for their reputation, on the other for the fury of the people, while meanwhile they are not at all anxious about the glory of God or the favour of the people. By these passions many are hindered today also from believing. But for the most part what happened to them happens to these men too: they are caught in their own snares, and make themselves infamous. Now there is no need to speak of the loss of eternal life, which the Lord does not obscurely threaten when he adds: "Neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things." Yet he had already said that he did them, and even in his silence the thing itself spoke. But because they knowingly and willingly did not know what was being said, they were unworthy of fuller instruction. For doctrine is applied to such people in vain. They are therefore left in the darkness which they bring upon themselves, so that they may perish in it, as they deserve. Let us, however, take from this history the use of learning, setting aside the desire for honour and private gain, to yield to the truth and to submit in faith's obedience to the Son of God, Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCXLVIII.
units.tr: HOMILY 248.

units.la: Quid autem vobis videtur? Quidam habebat duos filios: & accedens ad priorem, dixit: Fili abi, & hodie operare in vinea mea. Ille vero respondens ait: Nolo. Sed postea cum resipuisset, abiit. Et accedens ille ad secundum, dixit itidem. Is vero respondens ait: Ego abeo domine. Sed non abiit. Vter e duobus fecit quod voluit pater? Dicunt ei, Prior. Dicit eis IESVS: Amen dico vobis, publicani & meretrices praeeunt vobis in regnum Dei. Venit enim ad vos Ioannes in via iustitiae, & non credidistis ei: publicani vero & meretrices crediderunt ei: Vos autem qui hoc vidistis, non poenituistis postea, ut ei crederetis.
units.tr: "But what do you think? A man had two sons. He went to the first and said, 'Son, go and work today in my vineyard.' He answered, 'I will not.' But afterwards he repented and went. The man went to the second and said the same. He answered, 'I go, sir,' but he did not go. Which of the two did the father's will?" They said to him, "The first." Jesus said to them, "Truly I say to you, the tax collectors and the harlots go into the kingdom of God before you. For John came to you in the way of righteousness, and you did not believe him; but the tax collectors and the harlots believed him. And you, when you saw this, did not repent afterwards, so as to believe him."

units.la: Nter alia, quibus hypocritae & falsi antistites peccant, praecipuum fere est, quod cum omnem in Ecclesia potestatem sibi vendicent, non solum ipsi officium suum negligunt, verumetiam obstant, ne, si quos Deus excitat, ministri exequantur, quod in mandatis acceperunt. Exemplum huius rei in Sacerdotibus & Scribis Iudaeorum habemus. Hi cum neque doctrinam Christi, neque quod in templo fecerat, improbare possint, quaerunt tamen admodum imperiose, quis ei hanc authoritatem dederit? Nimirum, ut ipsum sed itione ex priuato arbitrio Ecclesiam inuadere oflendant, in qua nihil habeat iuris. Et cum Christus vicissim de Ioanne Bapt. quaerit, ut huius de se testimonia illis in mentem reuocet, illi mentiri malunt, quam Veritati cedere, & se nescire aiunt, quod omnibus ex vulgo erat notissimum.
units.tr: Among the other faults by which hypocrites and false leaders sin, the chief one is this: although they claim for themselves all authority in the Church, they not only neglect their own duty but also stand in the way, so that ministers whom God raises up cannot carry out what they have received in their commission. We have an example of this in the priests and scribes of the Jews. Since they could neither disapprove of Christ's teaching nor of what he had done in the temple, they nonetheless demand very imperiously, "Who gave you this authority?" Clearly they wish to show that he had invaded the Church on his own private judgement, and that he had no right in it. And when Christ in turn asks them about John the Baptist, so that they may recall John's testimony about himself, they prefer to lie rather than yield to the truth, and they say that they do not know what was most well known to everyone in the common people.

units.la: Falsorum antistitum mores.
units.tr: The morals of false leaders.

units.la: Christus Sacerdotibus larua detrahit. Initio quemadmodum qui causam optimam tuentur, ita Christus rem omnem aduersario-rum iudicio permittit, dicens: Quid autem vobis videtur? Dicitus vos nescire, num Ioannes Baptismus ex coelo sit, an ex hominibus. Aliam ergo quaestionem vobis propono, in qua vos iudices esse velim, & ingenue fateri quid animo sentiatis.
units.tr: Christ strips the priests of their mask. At the outset, as those who defend the best cause do, Christ leaves the whole matter to the judgement of his opponents, saying, "But what do you think?" He says that you pretend not to know whether John the Baptist was from heaven or from men. So I put before you another question, in which I wish you to be the judges, and to state frankly what you think in your minds.

units.la: Exo.4. Gen.3.8. Primum genus ergo est filiorum huius saeculi, qui mundi studijs immersi & carnis cupiditatibusediti, praecepta Dei aperte aspernantur, obedientiam omnem Deo negant, neque talem agnoscere volunt, qui mandandi ius in ipsos habeat. Et tales natura sunt omnes homines vtpote in peccato concepti & geniti, & ideo figmenta cordis eorum praua sunt a pueris. Isti si quid iubeant tur, quod ipsorum desiderijs repugnat, mox responsant, & de praeceptorum eius difficultate & iniquitate. quitate quaeruntur. Sed ijdem postea vel naturalibus notitijs, quas Deus omnium cordibus inscri-pfit, et cogitationibus, quas illæ pariunt, vel aliquo casu improuiso excitati incipiunt sentire, quàm indecorum sit Dei Patris indulgentissimi præceptis obloqui, & prioris vitæ pœnitentia ductì se-ipsos ad illius seruitium accingunt. Alterum genus filiorum hypocritas habet, qui auditis Dei mandatis, mox alacres respondent: Ego domine, scilicet præsto sum, vt quod iubes exequar: sed ab eius conspectu digressi nihil præstant. Et pulchrè exprimit sub huius filij typo Christus hypocritarum ingenium, atq; mores. Hi non contenti Deum patris nomine compellauisse, insuper Domi-num vocant, non tam huius reuerentia quàm propriæ dignitatis fiducia freti, quæ eos inflat, vt se dignos existiment, quos ille seruitijs suis adhibeat, & qui regni sui ministerijs obeundis sufficiant. Imò interdum de sua industria & studio gloriantur, & e contra de Deo queruntur, quasi hic parum æquus illorum censor sit, neq; dignis præmijs illa rependat. Tales describuntur apud Isaiam, qui ieiunia sua plenis buccis prædicabant, & talis fuit frater ille filij prodigi, qui patri audebat exprobrare, quod nunquam ab eo recepisset dignum suæ industriæ & obedientiæ præmium. At isti fere filios nequam agunt, qui parentibus ad oculum seruiunt, non autem Jyncera dilectione & reuerentia illos prosequuntur. Vt enim hi multa pollicentur de suo studio, & se ad opus paratos & accinctos esse simulant, postea autem vbi ex conspectu patris abierunt, in caupona aut ad sui similes diuertunt, & tempus terunt inter pocula & aleam, neq; cogitant de opere faciendo, quod ipsis mandatum est: ita isti relictâ sua vocatione, non in vineam Dei se conferunt, vt illic faciant, quæ gloriæ illius & aliorum ædificationi seruiunt, sed circa cæremonias inanes & inutilia corporis exercitia occupantur, quæ neq; cor stabilire, neq; proximum meliorem facere, neq; Deo probari possunt, cum secundum hominum traditiones fiant, & interea negligantur propria & germana fidei vera ac pietatis officia, in quibus Dei cultus & salus nostra atq; aliorum hominum consistit. Quia ergo hoc typo adumbrantur hypocritarum omnium mores in genere, discamus non in externa professione, aut cæremonijs & rituum larua hærere, sed penitius inspiciamus rem ipsam: nũ quæ fiunt, cum Dei mandatis & præceptis conueniant. Nisi enim id fiat, illud Christi locum habebit: Discedete a me qui operamini iniquitatem, &c. Matth.7.
units.tr: Ex. 4; Gen. 3:8. The first kind of sons, then, are those of this world, who, immersed in worldly pursuits and given over to the desires of the flesh, openly scorn God's commands, deny all obedience to God, and do not want to acknowledge anyone who has a right to command them. All men are naturally like this, since they are conceived and born in sin, and therefore "the imaginations of their hearts are evil from their youth." When such people are told to do something that goes against their desires, they at once object and complain about the difficulty and unfairness of God's precepts. But afterwards, stirred either by the natural knowledge that God has written in all hearts and by the thoughts that this knowledge brings forth, or by some unexpected event, they begin to feel how unseemly it is to speak against the commands of the most indulgent Father God. Led by repentance for their former life, they gird themselves for his service. The second kind of sons is that of hypocrites, who, when they hear God's commands, at once answer eagerly, "I am ready, sir," meaning that they are at hand to do what you command; but once they have gone out of his sight they do nothing. In the figure of this son Christ beautifully expresses the nature and manners of hypocrites. Not content with addressing God as Father, they also call him Lord. They rely not so much on reverence for him as on confidence in their own worth, which puffs them up so that they think themselves worthy to be employed in his service and fit to carry out the duties of his kingdom. Indeed, they sometimes boast of their own diligence and zeal, and on the other hand complain against God, as if he were too unfair a judge of them and did not repay them with due rewards. Such people are described in Isaiah, who proclaimed their fasts with full cheeks; and that elder brother of the prodigal son was such a one, who dared to reproach his father that he had never received from him a reward worthy of his diligence and obedience. But these men are almost like wicked sons, who serve their parents only for show and do not honour and respect them with sincere love. For just as these promise much about their zeal and pretend that they are ready and prepared for the work, but afterwards, once they have left their father's sight, turn aside to a tavern or to people like themselves, and waste their time among cups and dice, and do not think about doing the work that was entrusted to them, so these men, abandoning their calling, do not betake themselves into God's vineyard to do what serves his glory and the building up of others. Instead they busy themselves with empty ceremonies and useless bodily exercises, which can neither steady the heart, nor make a neighbour better, nor please God, since they are done according to human traditions; meanwhile the proper and genuine duties of faith and true piety, in which the worship of God and our salvation and that of other men consist, are neglected. Because the manners of all hypocrites in general are foreshadowed by this figure, let us learn not to cling to outward profession, or to ceremonies and the mask of rites, but to look more deeply into the thing itself: whether what is done agrees with God's commands and precepts. For unless this is so, that saying of Christ will apply: "Depart from me, you workers of iniquity," etc. Matt. 7.

units.la: Cæterum vt Sacerdotes & Scribæ atq; Seniores de se agi intelligerent, ad ipsos conuersus Christus, quid ipsi de filijs istis sentiant, quæris: Vter e duobus istis fecit quod voluit pater? Prior ne qui initiò proterue obsequium illi negauit, postea autem respuit, & illud præstitit: aut alter, qui alacriter & liberaliter promisit de sua obedientia, nihil autem fecit eorum, quæ pater mandarat? Ad quam quæstionem illi respondent quod res est, & priorem patri obediuisse dicunt. Itaq; quod prius noluerunt agnoscere, quando simpliciter interrogabantur, nunc sponte fatentur, & in alterius persona seipsos damnant, qui posterioris filij similes erant, vt mox audiemus.
units.tr: But so that the priests, scribes and elders might understand that they themselves are being spoken of, Christ turned to them and asked what they think of these sons: "Which of these two did the father's will?" Was it the first, who at the beginning boldly refused obedience to him but afterwards repented and carried it out; or the other, who eagerly and generously promised his obedience but did nothing of what the father had commanded? To this question they answer what is the case, and say that the first obeyed the father. So what they had been unwilling to acknowledge when they were asked plainly, they now freely confess, and in another's person they condemn themselves, since they were like the second son, as we shall soon hear.

units.la: Nunc obseruemus, quæ Veritatis fors sit & conditio. Est hæc perse euidens & efficax, vt quosuis arguat & conuincat. Sed plerunq; hominum vitio fit, vt non habeat suum effectum: quando hi aliis affectibus occupati vel non sentiunt de ipsis agi, vel admittere nolunt, quod illis aduersatur: qui postea quod in seipsis noluerunt agnoscere, mox intelligunt, si in aliena persona proponatur. Exemplum eius rei in Dauide historia sacra proponit, qui in iniqui diuitis & raptoris perso-na agnouit scelus suum, quod hactenus in semetipso non agnouerat. Itaq; arte & industria opus est Verbi administris, qua Dei Verbum rite secent, vt omnium redargutioni & emendationi seruire possit. Et in eo commendatur bonitas Dei, qui ad captum nostrum se demittens, doctrinam omnium ingenijs accommodat vt plures sibi lucrifaciat. Vicissim ergo nos illi aures & animos nostros accommodemus, ne ille in nobis instituendis operam perdat.
units.tr: Now let us observe what the nature and condition of the truth is. It is in itself evident and effective, so that it refutes and convicts anyone. But often through the fault of men it does not have its effect: when such people, occupied with other passions, either do not feel that they are being spoken of, or are unwilling to admit what is against them. Afterwards they understand what they would not acknowledge in themselves, when it is set forth in another person. The sacred history gives us an example of this in David, who recognised in the person of the unjust rich man and robber the crime that he had until then not recognised in himself. Therefore the ministers of the Word need skill and diligence, so that they may rightly divide the Word of God and it may be able to serve the refutation and correction of all. In this the goodness of God is commended, who, lowering himself to our capacity, adapts his teaching to all kinds of minds so that he may win more to himself. In turn, then, let us accommodate our ears and minds to him, so that he does not waste his labour in instructing us.

units.la: Porrò postquam ex illorum ore responsum elicuit, quale volebat, parabolam illis applicans, ipsos filij posterioris & improbi hypocritæ similes esse docet, & quia ei cum contumacibus res erat, magna cum grauitate sententia enuntiat: Amen dico vobis, publicani & meretrices præeunt vobis in regnum Dei. Quasi diceret: Itane in alijs fatemini, quod in vobisipsis hactenus noluistis agnoscere & fateri? Enimuero vos estis filius ille hypocrita & nequam. Vobis Lex data est, vos eius doctores estis, & cæcorum duces, lux item eorum qui in tenebris versantur, videri vultis: pro pria item sanctitatis & iustitiæ opinione turgidi, reliquum vulgus fastiditis, & in primis quidem publicanos & meretrices atq; similes horu,qui hactenus quodammodo in omne peccandi licentiam effusi,aperte responsarunt Deo,quod ipsi obedire nolint:adhac me eo nomine odistis,quod illis familiariter conuersor,& in meum comitatum illos admitto. At ego vobis sanctè affirmo & iuro, illos vobis praeire,id est,praestantiores vobis esse in regno Dei. Nam profitemini quidem veri Dei cultum,& in eo laboriosi atq; industrij haberi vultis,sed cum totus eiusmodi ritibus constet, qui peccatores ad promissum Messiam remittunt,& insuper carnis mortificatione & vitam nouam exigunt,quam homines in vniuersum Deo consecrati viuant in sanctitate & iustitia, vos circa vmbras occupati,re ipsam negligitis. Interim vobis cessantibus in officio,priores illi magno studio ad regnum Dei contendunt,& vitae anteactae feria poenitentia ducuntur. Itaq; vos praeuenient,qui procul a tergo reliçti vestrae hypocrisis & simulationis poenas graues dabitis.
units.tr: Moreover, after he had drawn from their mouths the answer he wanted, applying the parable to them he teaches that they are like the second, wicked son, the hypocrite; and since he was dealing with stubborn men, he pronounces the sentence with great gravity: "Truly I say to you, the tax collectors and the harlots go into the kingdom of God before you." As if he said: "Do you so confess in others what until now you have been unwilling to acknowledge and confess in yourselves? Indeed, you are that hypocritical and wicked son. The Law has been given to you, you are its teachers and leaders of the blind, and you wish to be seen as the light of those who dwell in darkness; swollen with your own opinion of holiness and righteousness, you despise the rest of the common people, and especially the tax collectors and harlots and others like them, who until now have, in a sense, poured themselves out into every licence of sinning and have openly answered God that they do not want to obey him. Besides, you hate me for this very reason, that I associate familiarly with them and admit them into my company. But I solemnly affirm and swear to you that they go before you, that is, they are better than you in the kingdom of God.
