For you do indeed profess the true worship of God and wish to be considered diligent and zealous in it, but since it consists entirely of such rites, which send sinners back to the promised Messiah, and moreover requires mortification of the flesh and a new life, the kind of life that men consecrated to God live in holiness and righteousness, you, occupied with shadows, neglect the reality itself. Meanwhile, while you are idle in your duty, those former sinners strive with great zeal toward the kingdom of God, and are led by repentance for their earlier life. So they will go before you, and you, left far behind, will pay the heavy penalties of your hypocrisy and pretence."

units.la: Quia vero sciebat sibi cum hypocritis rem esse,quibus nihil contumacius,nulli item disciplinae & reprehensionis impatientiores sunt,exemplo recenti,& quod in omnium memoria erat,quod dixit confirmat & illustrat. Venit ad vos(inquit) Ioannes in via iustitiae,&c. Quasi diceret: Simul latis vos nescire,vnde Ioannes venerit,at ego quod alias dixi, repeto:illū venisse a Deo missum, & venisse in via iustitiae,id est,iustum & integrum quoad doctrinam & mores: Nam iuste & sancte vixit,& simul viam rectam monstrauit,qua ad iustitiam peruenitur. Me etenim,qui via illa sum,digito monstrauit. Refipiscentiam docuit,& eius fructus ferio requisiuit. Exemplo ite vobis praeiuit,ab omni vanitate & petulantia alienus,modestiae autē & temperantiae ad miraculū vsq; studiosissimus: At non credidistis ei,vt vel me agnoscere tis esse Agnum illum Dei,vel vita emendaretis. Publicani vero & meretrices crediderunt ei,& qui prius in omni genere vitiorum volutabantur,& tantum non Deo in facie dicebant: Nolumus tibi obsequium praestare,etc:ij diligentius de officio suo & salute cogitare coeperunt,& ab illo consilium postularunt,qua ratione iram Dei effugere possent. Faciunt ad huius loci confirmationem quae Lucas scribit:milites & publicanos Ioannis praedicatione perculsos,ab eo salutis consilia petijfe: Christum ite aliquando Ioannis virtutem magnificè commendauisse,& hoc audito populum totum & publicanos iustificauisse Deum, eos nimirum qui ab illo baptizati fuerant: Pharisaeos autē & Legis interpretes consilium Dei reiecisse aduersus semetipsos. In praesenti vero,vt horum scelus amplificet,addit: Vos autem qui hoc vidistis,ne postea quidē poenituistis,vt ei crederetis,id est,etsi subitam & miraculo simile plurimorum conuersionem videritis,non potuistis tamen adduci,vt in tam memorabili exemplo agnoscere tis Dei opus,& ipsos imitaremini,quibus vos debebatis exemplo esse. Veniunt hic quaedam observanda,quae diligentem consideratione merentur,ne ipsi quoq; ad eundem lapidem cum Sacerdotibus istis & Scribis offendamus.
units.tr: Since he knew that he had to deal with hypocrites, who are the most stubborn of all and the least patient of discipline and rebuke, he confirms and illustrates what he has said by a recent example, one that was within everyone's memory. He says: "John came to you in the way of righteousness," etc. As if he were saying: you pretend not to know where John came from, but I repeat what I have said elsewhere: that he came sent by God, and came in the way of righteousness, that is, upright and blameless in both doctrine and conduct. For he lived justly and holily, and at the same time showed the right path by which one reaches righteousness. He pointed to me, who am that way, with his finger. He taught repentance and required its fruits. He went before you as an example, free from all vanity and wantonness, and most eager for modesty and temperance even to the point of wonder. But you did not believe him, so that you would either recognise me as the Lamb of God or amend your lives. The tax collectors and harlots, however, believed him, and those who had previously wallowed in every kind of vice and almost said to God's face: "We will not obey you," etc. These began to think more carefully about their duty and their salvation, and asked him what plan they might follow to escape the wrath of God. In confirmation of this place, Luke writes that soldiers and tax collectors, struck by the preaching of John, sought from him counsels of salvation; that Christ at one time commended John's virtue magnificently, and that on hearing this all the people and the tax collectors justified God, namely those who had been baptised by him; but the Pharisees and lawyers rejected the counsel of God against themselves. Here, however, to magnify their wickedness, he adds: "You, who saw this, did not even afterwards repent so as to believe him." That is, although you saw a sudden conversion of many, something like a miracle, you still could not be brought, by so memorable an example, to recognise the work of God and imitate those by whom you ought to have been an example. Some points deserve careful consideration here, lest we too stumble over the same stone as those priests and scribes.

units.la: Primum ex his est,quod illos contumaciae & inexcusabilis inobedientiae accusare & conuincere volens,Ioan.Bapt.allegat,& quales in illum fuerint eis exprobrat. Ita vero non solum Ioannis,sed in genere totius ministerij Verbi dignitas asseritur,& Deo rebelles esse docetur eos,qui legitimis Verbi ministris respondant aut contradicunt. Adomnes enim istos pertinet, quod alibi ait Dominus: Qui vos audit,me audit:& qui vos reicit,me reicit:qui vero me reicit,reicit eū qui misit me. Item: Quando aliquē misi,quisquis eum recipit,me recipit,&c. Debebat de his diligentius cogitare qui hodie laude ex eo quaerunt,si ministros Verbi non modo auersentur,verumetiā maledictis lacessat,et atrocibus minis territos procul abs se repellat. Cōstabit illis magno olim hac gloria,quando illum iudice videre & ferre cogentur,cuius seruos ta indignis modis tractarunt.
units.tr: The first of these is that, wishing to accuse and convict them of stubbornness and inexcusable disobedience, he cites John the Baptist and reproaches them with the kind of men they were towards him. In this way the dignity not only of John but of the whole ministry of the Word is asserted, and it is taught that those who answer or contradict the lawful ministers of the Word are rebels against God. For what the Lord says elsewhere applies to all of them: "He who hears you hears me, and he who rejects you rejects me; and he who rejects me rejects him who sent me." Likewise: "Whomever I send, whoever receives him receives me," etc. Those who today seek praise from this should think more carefully about it: if they not only shun the ministers of the Word but also assail them with abuse and, by terrifying threats, drive them away. This glory will cost them dearly one day, when they are compelled to see and endure him as judge, whose servants they treated with such unworthy violence.

units.la: Deinde Sacerdotum & Seniorum istorum exemplo admonemur,non nouum aut insolens censeri debere,si qui alijs ad pietatem duces & magistri esse debebat,pessimi & impijssimi sint hominum. Etenim si illi incipiant relicto Verbo Dei carnis cupiditatibus indulgere, Verbu Dei vsu apud eos vilescit(vt olim Chrysostomus dicebat)vt nihil ab ipsorum aut aliorum hominum comentis illud differre putent. Symmysitas monitores contemnunt scurriliter & oderunt. Adhac indecorē sibi esse persuadent,si ipsi laicos sequantur, qui potius in ipsos debebant respicere. Pudet deniq; ipsos postremos cōspici in via iustitiae,quā noluerunt priores ingredi. Fiunt ergo sal infatuatus, qui nulli alij vsui est,quā vt foras eiciatur,& conculcetur ab hominibus. Et tales quidē olim erant Iudaeorum antistites,& hodie multos horū similes videmus,quos non solum in vita & moribus nullius nullius sceleris pudet, sed errores quoq; manifestos impudenter excusant & tuentur, ne ipsorum existimatio periclitetur. Dicunt enim: Esto, errores & abusus plurimi in Ecclesia irrepserint, corruptissimi item sint mores Sacerdotum, monachorum libido, fastus, luxus & tyrannis plane intolerabilis: Haec (inquam) non omnino negamus, sed ut ista habeant, intolerabile & nulla venia dignum est, ministros Ecclesiarum privatos ista urgere, & laicos de reformatione consultare, & eosdem dignitatem totius cleri vilipendere. Dandum est aliquid dignitati ecclesiasticae, & praestat retinere manifestos errores & abusus, quam ut per importunos istos reformatores tota religio cum Pontificum & Episcoporum existimatione in dubium veniat. At qui ita sentiunt, ij consilium Dei spernunt & reiiciunt adversus semetipsos, id est, in proprium exitium. Consilio equidem Dei quod aeternum manet, nihil decedit: sed qui hoc non admittunt, ij fibijpsis interitum accersunt: quod infinitis exemplis tam politicis quam ecclesiasticis demonstrari poterat, si in rebus omnibus nota demonstratione opus esset.
units.tr: Next, the example of these priests and elders admonishes us that it should not be thought new or strange if those who ought to be leaders and teachers of others to piety are the worst and most impious of men. For if they begin, having abandoned the Word of God, to indulge the lusts of the flesh, the Word of God becomes cheap in their eyes (as Chrysostom once said), so that they think it differs in nothing from the inventions of themselves or other men. They despise and scornfully hate those who admonish them, their fellow-conspirators. Moreover, they persuade themselves that it is unseemly for them to follow the laity, when they ought rather to look up to them. Finally, they are ashamed to be seen last on the way of righteousness, which they were unwilling to enter first. So they become a tasteless salt, which is good for nothing except to be thrown out and trodden underfoot by men. Such indeed were the high priests of the Jews of old, and today we see many like them, who not only feel no shame at any wickedness in their life and conduct, but also shamelessly excuse and defend even manifest errors, lest their own reputation be put in danger. For they say: "Granted, many errors and abuses have crept into the Church, and the morals of the priests, the lust of the monks, their pride, luxury and a tyranny truly intolerable are very corrupt. These things, I say, we do not wholly deny; but however they stand, it is intolerable and worthy of no pardon that private ministers of the churches press these matters, and consult laymen about reform, and thereby cheapen the dignity of the whole clergy. Something must be conceded to ecclesiastical dignity, and it is better to keep manifest errors and abuses than to let the whole religion be called into doubt, with the esteem of the Pontiffs and bishops, by these troublesome reformers." But those who think this way spurn and reject the counsel of God against themselves, that is, to their own destruction. Indeed nothing is taken from the counsel of God, which remains eternal; but those who do not admit it bring ruin upon themselves. This could be shown by countless examples, both civil and ecclesiastical, if in all things a plain demonstration were needed.

units.la: Praeterea consolationis plenum est exemplum, quod hoc loco in publicanis & meretricibus pro ponitur. Estque, utrumque genus sceleratum & bonis omnibus abominabile, nec temere publicanos oderant Iudaei, cum illos ob quaestum Romanae tyrannidis ministros esse, & prophanis gentibus suam operam contra Dei populum locare viderent: meretrices vero abominabantur, quod Deus his in Israele locum omnem negauisse scirent, qui quaestum quoq; meretricium in domum suam inferri vetuit. Sed neq; his neq; illis gratia Dei fores occlusit. Ioannes Bapt. & Christus utrofq; benigne ad se admisit, & gratiae atq; gloriae suae organa ex illis fecit, qui prius Satanae erant mancipia. Exempla, quibus hoc confirmetur in Euangelio multa occurrunt. Consolentur ista peccatores in tentationibus, ne se repulsam passuros existiment. Etenim non venit Dei Filius vocatum iustos, sed peccatores ad resipiscentiam. Et memorabile est Pauli dictum: Fidus sermo, & modis omnibus dignus quem amplectamur, quod CHRISTVS IESVS venit in mundum, ut peccatores salvos faceret: quorum primus sum ego, sed ideo misertus est mei, ut in me primo ostenderet IESVS CHRISTVS omnem clementiam, ut essem exemplo credituris ipsi ad vitam aeternam. 1. Tim.1.
units.tr: Moreover, the example set forth here in the tax collectors and harlots is full of consolation. Both kinds of people are wicked and abominable to all good men. Nor did the Jews hate the tax collectors without cause, since they saw them serving the tyranny of Rome for gain, and hiring out their labour to profane nations against the people of God; and they abhorred the harlots because they knew that God had denied them any place in Israel, and forbade the wages of prostitution to be brought into his house. Yet the grace of God shut its doors neither to these nor to those. John the Baptist and Christ admitted both kinds kindly to themselves, and made instruments of their grace and glory from those who had previously been slaves of Satan. Many examples of this are to be found in the Gospel. Let these things console sinners in their temptations, so that they do not think they will suffer rejection. For the Son of God came not to call the righteous but sinners to repentance. And Paul's saying is memorable: "This is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptation, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the first. But for this reason I obtained mercy, that in me first Jesus Christ might show all long-suffering, for a pattern to those who should believe on him unto eternal life." 1 Tim. 1.

units.la: Verum non solum peccatores in gratiam receptos esse, sed etiam quid illi fecerint, Christus & Euangelistae narrant. Et huc in primis facit locus, quem nuper ex Luc.Cap.7. recitavimus. Illic dicuntur publicani cum toto populo audivisse Ioannem, & ab eodem baptizatos fuisse, quod nunquam facturi erant, nisi illi credidissent. Adhaec quando Christum magnifice de illo audierunt, testari iustificarunt Deum, & hunc celebrarunt, neq; poenituit eos conversionis, quam fecerunt ab Ioanne institutae & baptizati. Imitemur ergo horum exemplum, & primum accommodemus nos medijs, quibus erga nos utitur Deus, quando salute nobis offert. Sunt haec verbi praedicatio & Sacramenta. Per illam nos docet & instruit, promissionibus item invitat, & minis terrefacit. Per illa obsignat doctrinam salutis, & depromissionibus certos facit. Audiamus ergo verbum, Sacramentis autem pie & religiose utamur, secundum primam illorum institutionem, ut cum Paulo possimus dicere, nos a Domino accepisse quod facimus. Neq; offendamur, si effectus non statim sese prodat. Nam hic idem fieri solet quod in Semente, ut ipse Christus apud Marcum docet: quae ignorante agricola germinat, & primo herbam, deinde spicam, tandem suo tempore plenum frumentum in spica ferre solet. At fructus iste hic per id denotatur, quod Deum iustificasse dicuntur audito magnifico hoc Christi de Ioanne testimonio. Sensus est, quod Deo gratias egerunt, & hunc celebrarunt ut iustum, bonum, fidelem & misericordem. Hic autem opus est, ut primo nos agnoscamus peccatores esse, quibus aliena iustitia opus sit. Deinde ut quam Deus nobis in Filio suo offert, fide vera & constanti apprehendamus. Postremo ut eandem vita & moribus exprimamus, ac vitae sanctitate testemur nos per fidem iustificatos esse, adeoq; (quod Iacobus docet) fidem nostram operibus testatam faciamus. Et hoc illud opus Dei est, de quo Christus loquitur, quod facere debent quotquot cibum illum assequi volunt, qui non perit sed permanet in vitam aeternam. His ergo intenti simus, ne otiosa fidei professione nosipsos fallamus, dum Deo Patri, ut hypocritae solent, volumus fucum facere, sed vere & serio a peccatis ad illum conuertamur, ut in Filio eius unigenito servemur, qui nobis ab illo factus est sapientia, iustitia, sanctificatio & redemptio. Huic debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: Yet Christ and the Evangelists tell not only that sinners were received into grace, but also what they did afterwards. The passage I recently quoted from Luke chapter 7 bears especially on this. There it is said that the tax collectors, with all the people, heard John and were baptised by him, which they would never have done unless they had believed him. Moreover, when they heard Christ speak magnificently of him, they bore witness that they justified God, and praised him; nor did they regret the conversion which they had undergone, instituted and baptised by John. Let us therefore imitate their example, and first make use of the means by which God deals with us when he offers us salvation. These are the preaching of the Word and the Sacraments. Through the one he teaches and instructs us, and likewise invites us by promises and terrifies us by threats. Through the others he seals the doctrine of salvation and makes us certain of the promises. Let us therefore hear the Word, and use the Sacraments piously and reverently, according to their first institution, so that with Paul we can say that we have received from the Lord what we do. Nor let us be offended if the effect does not show itself at once. For here what usually happens is what happens with seed, as Christ himself teaches in Mark: it sprouts while the farmer does not know it, first the blade, then the ear, and at last, in its time, it is wont to bear full grain in the ear. This fruit is here signified by the fact that they are said to have justified God when they heard this magnificent testimony of Christ about John. The sense is that they gave thanks to God and praised him as just, good, faithful and merciful. Here, however, we must first recognise ourselves as sinners, in need of an alien righteousness. Then we must lay hold, with true and steadfast faith, of what God offers us in his Son. Finally, we must express the same in our life and conduct, and bear witness by the holiness of our life that we have been justified through faith; and so, as James teaches, make our faith evident by our works. This is that work of God of which Christ speaks, which all must do who wish to obtain that food which does not perish but remains unto eternal life. Let us therefore be intent upon these things, lest we deceive ourselves by an idle profession of faith, while we wish, as hypocrites are wont to do, to put on a show before the Father; but let us truly and seriously turn from our sins to him, that we may be preserved in his only-begotten Son, who has been made by God our wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAP. XXI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXI.

units.la: Aliam parabolam audite. Fuit quidam paterfamilias, qui planta-uit vineam, & sepem circumposuit ei, foditque in ea torcular, & aedifi-cauit turrim, & elocauit eam agricolis, ac peregre profectus est.
units.tr: Hear another parable. There was a certain householder who planted a vineyard, put a hedge around it, dug a winepress in it, built a tower, let it out to tenants, and went abroad.

units.la: Dominus & Seruator noster IESVS CHRISTVS quamdiu in terris docuit & Mes-siae munus obiit, cui a Patre destinatus erat, nullos habuit aduersarios acriores quam Iu-daeorum Sacerdotes & Scribas, qui multifariam illum oppugnarunt & tandem authores fuerunt vt in crucem suffigeretur. Fuit hoc cum magno scandalo coniunctum, & multos a fide absterruit, vt non possent pro Messia eum agnoscere, quem ab ijs reijci videbant, qui in Ecclesia summam tenebant doctrinae & religionis exstimationem. Quae causa est, quod ijsdem Dominus acriter re-stitit, atque nuper laruam illis ita detraxit, vt ostenderit, publicanos & meretrices ipsis praestare in regno Dei, eo quod his resipiscentibus ipsi contumaces esse pergant. Id quia haud dubie multis nouum & insolens videbatur, nunc alia parabola docet, eo neminem debere offendi: quia iam olim ipsorum antecessores similli impietate aduersus Deum pugnarint, quorum memoriam ipsi nunc im-pleant. Partes parabolae sunt tres. Prima Dei studium erga gentem Iudaeorum adumbrat, & in quam dignitatem Sacerdotes euexerit: Secunda horum ingratitudinem cum summa iniquitate & crudelitate describit: Postremo quid de illis futurum sit, docet, si ita pergant. In praesenti pri-mam parabolae partem recitauimus, qua studium Dei erga suam Ecclesiam describitur, in quo primum videbimus, vt hoc erga Iudaeorum gentem declarauit, deinde vt idem postea in Ecclesia elucescat.
units.tr: Our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, while he taught on earth and discharged the office of the Messiah to which the Father had appointed him, had no fiercer opponents than the priests and scribes of the Jews. They attacked him in many ways and at last were the authors of his being nailed to the cross. This was a great scandal and turned many away from faith, so that they could not acknowledge him as the Messiah when they saw him rejected by those who held the highest reputation for teaching and religion in the Church. For this reason the Lord opposed them sharply and recently stripped away their mask, showing that tax collectors and harlots went before them in the kingdom of God, because they remained stubborn while these repented. Since this seemed to many undoubtedly new and strange, he now teaches by another parable, so that no one should be offended: their own forefathers had long ago fought against God with the same impiety, and they themselves now fulfil the memory of those men. The parable has three parts. The first sets forth God's care for the Jewish nation and the dignity to which he raised the priests. The second describes their ingratitude with great wickedness and cruelty. Finally, it teaches what will become of them if they persist. Now we have recited the first part of the parable, which describes God's care for his Church. In it we shall see first how he showed this towards the Jewish nation, and then how the same care shines forth afterwards in the Church.

units.la: Porro a vinea parabolam sumit, quae in Scripturis frequens est. Hac enim Moses vtitur de Iudaeorum gente & beneficijs Dei in hanc collatis differens. Eandem in Psalmis adducunt pij, & Ieremias eiusdem meminit. Sed & Christus nuper per illam Ecclesiae suae conditionem illustrauit. Et apud Ioannem se vitem dicit, nos palmites. At in praesenti repetitur & illustratur, quod apud Isaiam olim adumbrauit sub hoc typo Spiritus sancti. Nec temere toties huius parabolae men-tio fit. Exprimitur enim per hanc Ecclesiae dignitas, & Dei erga hanc amor & studium. Etenim vt inter praedia, quae in terris habentur, pretiosissimae sunt vineae, & eadem summo studio & labore immenso coluntur: ita Deus nihil habet carius & pretiosius sua Ecclesia, quam Filij sui vni geniti sanguine redemit, & quam per homines sanctissimos non absque singulari Spiritus sancti auxilio excolit & Martyrum sanguine irrigat. Adhaec vel sola vinea appellatio nos officij ad-monet. Etenim vt fructum ferant, coluntur vineae, neq; aliquis in illis locus datur vel arboribus sterilibus, vel palmitibus aridis, ex quibus fructus nullus sperari potest. Vt enim ligni vitis nul-lius alius vsus est (vt apud Ezechielem Dominus ait) quam vt fructum ferat: ita neq; nos aliquid in Ecclesia prodesse possumus, nisi fructus feramus nostra professione dignos.
units.tr: Moreover, he takes the parable from a vineyard, a image frequent in the Scriptures. Moses uses it when he speaks of the Jewish nation and the benefits God conferred upon it. The godly also bring it up in the Psalms, and Jeremiah mentions it too. Christ himself lately illustrated by it the condition of his Church, and in John he calls himself the vine and us the branches. Here, however, is repeated and illustrated what Isaiah long before had shadowed forth under this type of the Holy Spirit. Nor is mention of this parable made rashly so often. For through it is expressed the dignity of the Church and God's love and care for it. Just as among the properties on earth vineyards are most precious, and are tended with the greatest care and immense labour, so God has nothing dearer and more precious than his Church, which he redeemed with the blood of his only-begotten Son, and which he tends through most holy men, not without the singular help of the Holy Spirit, and waters with the blood of the martyrs. Besides, the very name of vineyard reminds us of our duty. For vineyards are tended so that they may bear fruit, and no place is given in them either to barren trees or to dry branches from which no fruit can be expected. For just as the wood of the vine has no other use (as the Lord says through Ezekiel) than to bear fruit, so we too can be of no benefit in the Church unless we bear fruit worthy of our profession.

units.la: Porro multis & diligenter describitur patrisfamilias Dei circa vineam suam indulgria, vt ingratitudinis scelus, qua Sacerdotes peccarunt, magis aggraueretur. Et primo quidem ipse illam plantauisse dicitur: quo vno verbo multa comprehenduntur, quae absq; labore & studio non possunt fieri. Nam qui vineas plantant, de loco cogitant idoneo, quia non omnis fert omnia tellus, & inter vites delectum habent. Ideo apud Isaiam haec vinea dicitur consita in cornu filio olei, id est, in loco prominenti & aprico, pingui tamen ac fertili, consita item vite Sorec, quam prae alijs com-mendant veteres Hebraei, quod vuas gignat abscisas. Sed & elapidari solent loca, in quibus vineae plantantur, ne quid fertilitatem & prouentum remoretur. Et haec quidem omnia fecisse di-citur bonus ille paterfamilias, qui vineam spiritualem, id est, Ecclesiam plantauit. Deinde cir-cumposuit ei sepem. Sepium vsus duplex est, quod & distinguunt vineas ab aliorum praedijs ad-iacentibus, & insuper defendunt a bestijs, pecoribus & hominibus noxijs & inimicis. Ergo ne hac quidem in parte officium ille neglexit. Praeterea fodit torcular, quo ipsem bonam de vinea te-status est, quam non temere conceperat, cum in loco pingui ex vitibus nobilissimis consita, a lapi-dibus repurgata, & sepe diligenter munita esset, vt nihil ipsi posset officere. Nec his contentus tur-rim quoq rim quoq; ædificauit, quæ loco speculæ esset, & simul ornamentum vineæ adderet. Dicuntur hæc in genere, sed vt patrisfamiliàs istius cura & industria illustrior fit, videamus primùm, vt ista in Iudæis sint facta: deinde vt postea in gentibus aut noui Testamenti Ecclesia suum habuerint complementum, quæ in illorum locum successit.
units.tr: Next, the care of the householder for his vineyard is described at length and in detail, so that the crime of ingratitude committed by the priests may be made the more grievous. And first he is said to have planted it himself, a single word which comprehends many things that cannot be done without labour and zeal. For those who plant vineyards think about a suitable place, since not every soil bears everything, and they make a careful choice among the vines. So in Isaiah this vineyard is said to be planted on a horn, the son of oil, that is, in a prominent and sunny place, yet rich and fertile, and planted with the choice vine Sorek, which the ancient Hebrews commend above others because it yields grapes without seeds. Moreover, the places where vineyards are planted are usually cleared of stones, so that nothing may hinder fertility and yield. All these things, we are told, the good householder did, who planted the spiritual vineyard, that is, the Church. Then he put a hedge around it. A hedge has a twofold use: it distinguishes vineyards from the neighbouring estates of others, and it also defends them from wild beasts, cattle, and harmful and hostile men. Therefore in this part too he did not neglect his duty. Furthermore, he dug a winepress in it, having good hope of the vineyard, which he had not rashly formed, since it was planted in a rich place with the noblest vines, cleared of stones, and carefully fortified with a hedge, so that nothing could harm it. Not content with these, he also built a tower, which would serve as a lookout and at the same time add an ornament to the vineyard. These things are said in general terms; but so that the care and diligence of this householder may be seen more clearly, let us look first at how these things were done among the Jews, and then at how afterwards among the Gentiles, or in the Church of the New Testament, which succeeded to their place, they received their completion.

units.la: Quoad Iudæos plantauit hos Deus, quando ex Ægypto eductos adoptauit, & suum fecit peculium eos, qui ne populus quidem prophanus dici merebantur, cum Reipub. forma carerent, & omnibus ad hanc necessarijs destituerentur. Fuerunt autem tunc Iudæi vites generosæ, non quidem proprio merito, sed quòd ex patribus sanctissimis originem ducerent, cum quibus fœdus fecerat Deus, qui ratum esse voluit iuramentum, quo fidem suam illis obstrinxerat. Plantauit autem eos in cornu, filio olei, id est, in terra fertilißima, quam lacte & melle fluere dicit Scriptura. Et hanc elapidauit, eiectis Cananeis, qui prius ipsam superstitionibus nefarijs & omni scelerum genere polluerant. Quæ omnia paucis verbis pij in Psalmo comprehendunt, dicentes: Vitè ex Ægypto transtulisti, expulisti gentes, & plantasti eam. Deinde sepem circumposuit, quando ab alijs gentibus segregatos circumcisione & cultu proprio ceu finibus certis conclusit, ne alijs gentibus commisceretur: muniuit item & defendit contra hostes suos & omnes inimicorum insidias. Præterea turrim ædificauit, id est, Respub. & Ecclesiæ formam inter illos constituit, dum religionis antistites dedit sacerdotes & Leuitas, magistratus item politicos, Iudices primùm & heroes fortissimos: deinde Reges, qui omnes in excubijs steterunt, vt leges bonæ seruarentur, & his populus in officio continetur. Addidit torcular, disciplinâ legis, quæ sacerdotibus & Leuitis atq; iudicibus commissa fuit: interdum quoq; lasciuientes cruce & omni genere afflictionum coercuit, vt fructus sua profeßione dignos ab illis extorqueret. Nihil ergo omisit Deus eorum, quæ ad ipsorum incolumitatem tam in hoc præsenti quàm futuro seculo facere poterant: & constat felicissimam fuisse Iudæorum gentem quàm diu Dei legibus obediuit, & intra fines ab illo præscriptos sese continuit.
units.tr: As regards the Jews, God planted them when, having led them out of Egypt, he adopted them and made them his own special possession, though they deserved not even to be called a profane people, since they lacked a form of commonwealth and were destitute of all things necessary for one. The Jews were then generous vines, not indeed by their own merit, but because they sprang from most holy fathers, with whom God made a covenant, and he willed that the oath by which he had bound his faith to them should be kept firm. He planted them on a horn, the son of oil, that is, in a most fertile land, which Scripture says flows with milk and honey. And he cleared it, casting out the Canaanites, who had earlier polluted it with wicked superstitions and every kind of crime. The godly comprehend all these things briefly in the Psalm, saying: "You brought a vine out of Egypt; you cast out the nations and planted it." Then he put a hedge around it, when he enclosed his people, separated from other nations by circumcision and their own worship, as if by fixed boundaries, so that they might not mix with the other nations; he also fortified and defended them against their enemies and all the snares of their foes. Moreover, he built a tower, that is, he established among them a commonwealth and the form of the Church, when he gave priests and Levites as leaders of religion, and likewise political magistrates, first judges and most brave heroes, and then kings, who all stood on watch so that good laws might be kept, and by these the people were kept in duty. He added a winepress, the discipline of the law, which was entrusted to the priests, the Levites and the judges; at times also he restrained the wanton with the cross and every kind of affliction, so that he might wring from them fruit worthy of their profession. God therefore omitted nothing of those things which could be done for their welfare both in this present age and in the future. And it is clear that the Jewish nation was most happy as long as it obeyed God's laws and kept itself within the limits he had prescribed.

units.la: At ista non minus Ecclesiæ noui Testamenti conueniunt, & docent, quibus opus sit, vt ea nobis salua & incolumis maneat. Primùm illam quoq; plantauit Deus: & ante omnia plantatione opus est, per quam Christo inseramur, sine quo (vt ipse ait) nihil possumus. Huius initium est electio, quæ ab æterno facta est in Christo ex gratuita misericordia. De illa canitur in Psalmis: Beatus, quem tu elegeris, & tibi adiunxeris: habitabit ille in atrijs tuis, satiabitur bonis domus tuæ, & sanctuario palatij tui. Et hoc initium salutis singuli probè teneant. Quia enim natura omnes peccatores sumus, neq; ex nobis ipsis ad cogitandum idonei sumus, non poterit nobis certa & firma consistere salutis fiducia, nisi de electione nobis constet, cuius signum infallibile est fides, quæ nos Christo inserit, qui & liber vitæ est, nec expungi sinit eos, qui ipsi inscripti fuerint. Deinde quia ex hominibus constat vinea hæc, quæ est Ecclesia, elapidatio fiat oportet, per quam scandala expurgentur, quæ sunt falsa doctrina, superstitiones, morum corruptio, & quæcunq; vera pietatis fructus impediunt. Quid autem in his tollendis Deus fecerit apparet, si quales olim fuerint gentes consideremus. Obseruandum hoc propter eos, qui morum disciplinâ inter indifferentia numerant, & Deum nobis fingunt, qui res humanas, & quæ in terris geruntur non curet. Abutuntur hi loco Psalmi: Cœlum cœlorum Domino, terram verò dedit filijs hominum. Itaq; qui ita sentiunt, cum Nabale dicunt: Non est Deus, Deus non audit, non videt. E medio ergo remouendi sunt hi filii ces & obstacula ista, neq; excidat nobis, oculos Domini discurrere per omnem terram, & nos in eius conspectu versari, adeo vt nihil eorum, quæ facimus aut loquimur, illum lateat. Ita enim auferemus, quæcunq; oculos eius possunt offendere. Præterea septo quodam suos a reliquis gentibus & sectis segregauit Dominus, Baptismo nimirum, per quem in Ecclesiæ suæ externam societatem adoptamur, quæ alijs quoq; exercitijs fidei a mundo distinguitur. De quo sæpè cogitandum est, vt his quasi notis insigniti, & certis legibus circumscripti, intra Ecclesiæ fines nos contineamus, neq; aliquid commercij habeamus cum aliorum superstitionibus, neq; prophanorum hominum vitijs communicemus. Huic studio non deerit protectio Domini, qui procul etiam arcebit apros & alias feras, & in primis vulpes astutas, quæ florentibus vuis insidiantur, & de quibus Ecclesia canit: Capite nobis vulpes, vulpes (inquam) paruas, quæ vastant vineas, cum vineæ nostræ floreant. His turrim siue speculam addidit Deus, quando in Ecclesia ministerium verbi sui sanciuit, & vt olim promiserat, Reges & Principes dedit nutritios, deniq; omnibus prope seculi dedit spe-culatores non Ecclesiasticos modo, verumetiam politicos, qui verbi prædicatione & legibus bonis Ecclesiam excolant. Ideo olim duos istos ordines coniunctos esse voluit Deus, & initio cum Ecclesiam inter Iudæos primum constitueret, duos germanos fratres Mosem & Aaronem delegit, vt hunc sacris, illum iudicijs & legum executioni præficeret, & semper opus est, vt illi operas suas conferant, quando florere non potest Ecclesia, nisi inter ordines istos verus consensus sit in Domino. Vt ergo peccant sacrorum administri, qui Rempublicam inuadunt, & sub religionis prætextu regnum quærunt: ita non minor virorum principum culpa est, qui operam suam ministris negant & quæ Ecclesiæ sunt, nihil ad se pertinere arbitrantur. Etenim vt frustra excoletur vinea, & nul la vindemia vtilitas erit, nisi per torcular exprimantur botri: ita nec Verbi prædicatione, nec legibus bonis quicquam proficietur, nisi disciplina seria & seuera in officio contineantur homines, vt sæpe ab inuitis extorqueantur fructus boni & Iusti, qui de fide nostra testentur.
units.tr: But these things apply no less to the Church of the New Testament, and they teach what is needed for it to remain safe and sound for us. First, God planted this Church also; and before all else there is need of planting, by which we are grafted into Christ, apart from whom (as he himself says) we can do nothing. The beginning of this is election, which was made from eternity in Christ out of free mercy. Of this the Psalm sings: "Blessed is the one whom you choose and draw near to you; he will dwell in your courts, and be satisfied with the good things of your house and of the sanctuary of your palace." Let each of us hold firmly to this beginning of salvation. For since by nature we are all sinners, and are not of ourselves fit to think, a sure and firm confidence of salvation cannot stand for us unless we are assured of election, whose infallible sign is faith, which grafts us into Christ, who is also the book of life and does not allow those who have been written in it to be blotted out. Then, since this vineyard, which is the Church, consists of men, there must be clearing of stones, by which offences are removed: false doctrine, superstitions, corruption of morals, and whatever hinders the true fruits of piety. What God has done in removing these things appears if we consider what the nations once were like. This must be observed on account of those who count the discipline of morals among things indifferent, and who imagine a God who does not care for human affairs or for what happens on earth. They abuse the verse of the Psalm: "The heavens are the Lord's heavens, but the earth he has given to the sons of men." Therefore those who think thus say with Nabal: "There is no God; God does not hear, does not see." These sons must then be removed from the midst, and these obstacles must be cleared away; nor should it slip from our minds that the eyes of the Lord run through the whole earth, and that we live in his sight, so that nothing we do or say is hidden from him. For in this way we shall remove whatever could offend his eyes. Besides, the Lord has separated his people from the other nations and sects by a kind of hedge, namely baptism, through which we are received into the external fellowship of his Church, and which is also distinguished from the world by other exercises of faith. We must often think about this, so that, marked with these signs as with badges, and bounded by fixed laws, we may keep ourselves within the limits of the Church, and have no dealings with the superstitions of others, nor share in the vices of profane men. This endeavour will not lack the protection of the Lord, who will also keep far away the boars and other wild beasts, and above all the cunning foxes, which lie in wait for the flowering vines, and of which the Church sings: "Catch us the foxes, the little foxes, which ruin the vineyards, while our vineyards are in flower." To these he added a tower or lookout, when he sanctioned in his Church the ministry of his Word, and, as he had long promised, gave kings and princes as nursing fathers, and finally gave to almost the whole world watchmen, not only ecclesiastical but also civil, who cultivate the Church by the preaching of the Word and by good laws. Therefore God long ago willed these two orders to be joined, and at the beginning, when he first established the Church among the Jews, he chose two brothers, Moses and Aaron, to set the one over sacred things and the other over judgments and the execution of the laws. And it is always necessary that they should bring their labours together, since the Church cannot flourish unless there is true agreement between these orders in the Lord. Just as the ministers of sacred things sin when they invade the commonwealth and seek a kingdom under the pretext of religion, so the fault of princes is no less when they deny their help to the ministers and think that what belongs to the Church is no concern of theirs. For just as the vineyard is tended in vain and there is no benefit from the vintage unless the grapes are pressed in the winepress, so nothing will be gained either by the preaching of the Word or by good laws, unless men are kept to their duty by a serious and strict discipline, so that good and just fruits, which bear witness to our faith, are often wrung even from the unwilling.

units.la: Et hæc quidem præstat Deus fideliter, nofq; obseruare decet hæc ita dicit a Christo, vt istorum authorem faciat solum Deum, cui omnis gloria debeat transcribi. Etenim penes illum est eligendi & vocandi potestas, nec temere alibi dicit Dominus: Nemo venit ad me, nisi Pater meus traxerit eum. Idem solus animos purgat, & scandala remouet, quæ mundus plurima obijcit, & nostri nobis innumera quotidie fingimus. Ipse corda illuminat, & nouam voluntatem in nobis creat, vt intra obedientiæ fidei metas nos contineamus, nec nos prauis desiderijs & illicitis affectibus patiamur transuersos abripi. Ipse deniq; lupos & feras a septis Ecclesiæ arcet, & insuper authoritatem conciliat serius suis, vt quod ille mandat, exequi & cum laude obire possint. Deniq; (vt alibi Christus loquitur) illius est messis ista, qui solus ius habet extrudendi mercenarios idoneos, per quos ipse agit pro bona sua voluntate.
units.tr: And these things God indeed faithfully performs, and we ought to observe them in such a way that we ascribe the authorship of all of them to God alone, to whom all glory must be given. For the power of choosing and calling rests with him, and the Lord does not say this lightly elsewhere: "No one comes to me unless my Father draws him." He alone also cleanses minds and removes the stumbling-blocks which the world throws in our way in great number, and which we ourselves invent innumerable times each day. He illuminates hearts and creates a new will in us, so that we keep ourselves within the bounds of obedient faith, and do not allow ourselves to be dragged off course by wicked desires and unlawful affections. Finally, he keeps wolves and wild beasts away from the fold of the Church, and moreover gives authority to his servants, so that they can carry out what he commands and perform it with praise. Lastly (as Christ says elsewhere), that harvest belongs to him who alone has the right to send out suitable workers, through whom he himself acts according to his good pleasure.

units.la: Et huc pertinet clausula, quam primæ huic parti addit, dicens: Et elocauit vineam agricolis, ac peregre profectus est. Nouum industriæ argumentum est, quod non antea discedit paterfamilias iste, quam omnia perfecit, quæ ad vineæ absolutam constitutionem faciunt. Sunt enim opera Dei perfecta, nec vt malæ frugis & ignaui opifices solent, opus inchoatum intermittit, aut deserit. Sed & IESVS CHRISTVS non ante terras corpore suo deseruit, quàm opus nostræ redemptionis, cuius ergo in mundum venerat, absoluisset. Ideo iam moriturus dicebat, Consummatum est. In præsenti autem peregre profectus dicitur Deus, & vineam colonis locasse, non quòd ab Ecclesia sua vnquam discedat. Nam non minus ad nos pertinet quod olim in lege veteri populo pollicitus est, dicens: Ego ponam tabernaculum meum inter vos, & animus meus vos non fastidiet. Ego ambulabo inter vos, & ero Deus vester, & vos eritis populus meus. Et in cælum abiturus corpore suo Christus dicebat: Data est mihi omnis potestas in cælo & in terra, & ecce ego vobiscum sum vsq; ad consummationem seculi. Itaq; ex more communi & ratione parabolæ dicitur peregre profectus esse, vt ostendatur, illum vineam suam colonis ita locauisse, vt eis nulla in re molestus fuerit, nec obsiterit, quo minus possent officium facere. Et opponitur hoc illorum moribus, qui prædia locant quidem colonis, sed interim horum opera abutuntur ad alia negotia, conditiones subinde mutant, adhæc isdem molesti sunt, exactionibus, quas non messis modo aut vindemia tempore faciunt. Sed per totum annum quasi perpetuas exercent, vt miseri vix victum necessarium ex suo labore percipere possint. At non ita Deus egit, sed vineam suam, quam ex Iudæis plantauerat colonis Leuitis & Sacerdotibus locauit conditionibus certis & æquis, atq; eodem liberaliter tractauit. Nam cum summa dignitate coniuncta fuit vtilitas quoq;, quam ex functione sua maximam receperunt: qua de re multa apud Mosem leguntur, qui quid de decimis, primitijs & sacrificijs & alijs vestigalibus sacris ad illos debuerit redire, prolixè indicat. Imò sibi quodammodo illos substituit Deus, vt quæ ipsi debebantur, illi reciperent, & his tanquam proprijs fruerentur. Et in nouo Testamento similiter doctrinam salutis & ministerij regulam certam tradidit, simulq; hanc legem sanciuit Dominus, vt qui Euangelio seruiunt, ex eodem viuant. Facit autem ad hoc amplificandum scelus ingratitudinis & improbitatis Sacerdotum, quæ pecarunt, dum non contenti liberalitate Dei, vineam totam sibi vendicarunt, & suum ius et istipere conati sunt, vt posteà suo loco sequetur.
units.tr: To this belongs also the clause which he adds to this first part, saying: "And he let out the vineyard to farmers and went abroad." This householder's departure before he had completed everything needed for the full establishment of the vineyard is a new proof of his diligence. For the works of God are perfect, and he does not, as bad and lazy workmen usually do, leave an unfinished task half-done or abandon it. Indeed, Jesus Christ did not leave the earth in his body before he had finished the work of our redemption, for the sake of which he had come into the world. That is why, about to die, he said, "It is finished." Now God is said to have gone abroad and to have let the vineyard to tenants, not because he ever withdraws from his Church. For what he once promised the people in the old law is no less true for us: "I will set my tabernacle among you, and my soul will not loathe you. I will walk among you, and I will be your God, and you shall be my people." And Christ, about to go up to heaven in his body, said: "All power is given to me in heaven and on earth, and behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age." Therefore, according to the common custom and the logic of the parable, he is said to have gone abroad, to show that he so let out his vineyard to the tenants that he was in no way troublesome to them, nor hindered them from doing their work. This is contrasted with the ways of those who indeed let estates to tenants, but meanwhile misuse their labour for other business, change the terms from time to time, and besides trouble them with exactions, which they demand not only at harvest or vintage time but throughout the whole year, as if they were perpetual, so that the wretched people can hardly get the necessary living from their toil. But God did not act so. He let his vineyard, which he had planted from among the Jews, to the Levites and priests as tenants, on certain and fair conditions, and treated them generously in the same way. For a great advantage was joined to their high dignity, which they received as the greatest reward of their office; many things are read about this in Moses, who sets out in full what was to return to them from the tithes, firstfruits, sacrifices and other sacred dues. Indeed, God in some sense put them in his own place, so that they might receive what was owed to him and enjoy it as their own. And in the New Testament likewise he gave the teaching of salvation and a certain rule of the ministry, and the Lord also ordained this law, that those who serve the Gospel should live from the Gospel. Moreover, the wickedness of the priests, who sinned in their ingratitude and dishonesty, adds weight to this amplification: not content with the generosity of God, they claimed the whole vineyard for themselves and tried to seize their own right by force, as will follow in its proper place.

units.la: Nume. 18. Matth. 18. 1.Cor.9. In primis autem hoc loco considerari debet, qua ratione Deus Ecclesiam suam gubernet & administret. Ipsius quidem est omne opus, & ideo Paulus Corinthijs scribebat: Dei arum, Dei aedificatio estis. Idem tamen hominum opera & ministerio vtitur, eo quod infirmitas nostra non patitur, vt ille nobis immediate loquatur: cuius exemplum evidens in Israelitis extat, qui ad montem Sinai Deum ipsis concionantem audire non potuerunt. Vt ergo tunc Moses interpretes vsus est: ita postea has partes Sacerdotibus mandauit, vt ex horum ore legem & voluntatis suae cognitionem populus requireret. Et his in officio cessantibus, Prophetas extraordinarie excitauit, qui omnis loci & ordinis hominibus praedicarent. In nouo Testamento Apostolos substituit, in quibus Ecclesiae ministerium sanciuit, quod perpetuo seruari vult, & ideo caelitus dona Spiritus sui largitur, ne Ecclesiae desint operarij fidi, per quos excolatur & aedificetur. Est magna horum dignitas, quod ipsis Deus Ecclesiam suam locat, qua (vt initio diximus) nihil habet pretiosius, & quam non solum vt vineam, sed vt sponsam diligit. Id vero eosdem officij admonet: quod est, vt primo ipsi quoq; hanc cordi habeant, & eius zelo sancto ardeant, qualem in Paulo olim fuisse legimus. Interim meminerint, se non dominos vineae, sed colonos esse a Filio Dei constitutos, ad quem fructus omnis redire debeat. Colono non ius est aliquod, vt vites temere pro suo arbitrio extirpet, multo minus vt vineam vendat, aut alijs oppignoret, vel vt terminos transferat: Ita neq; sacerdotibus ista olim licuerunt, neq; postea Apostolis, qui nihil horum conati sunt, sed toti in eo fuerunt, vt Ecclesias Christo adducerent, & in eius fide & seruitio conseruarent. Paulus certe fatetur, ipsis potestatem datam ad aedificationem, non ad destructionem. Hos imitari debebant hodie pontifices, qui cum illorum successione glorientur, pro sua tamen libidine omnia agunt, Ecclesiam nouis legibus grauant, terminos antiquos transferunt, in sectas diuidunt, vt plures fere inueniantur, qui ab hominibus denominari velint, quam qui vno Christo contenti sint. Quod si qui ipsis contradicat, eum excommunicationis fulmine a societate Ecclesiae eiiciunt, & (vt Propheta ait) bellum contra eum sanctificant. Sunt ergo illi coloni similes, de quorum perfidia & ingratitudine paulo post dicet Dominus: In praesenti autem omnes Dei amorem & studium agnoscant, quo in nobis excolendis vtitur, & memores nos illius vineam esse, fructus feramus nostra professione dignos, vt in nobis ille glorificetur, & nos aeternum seruemur in CHRISTO IESV, Domino & Seruatore nostro vnico: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: Num. 18; Matt. 18; 1 Cor. 9. In the first place, however, it must be considered in this passage in what manner God governs and administers his Church. The whole work is indeed his, and therefore Paul wrote to the Corinthians: "You are God's field, God's building." Yet he nonetheless uses the work and ministry of men, because our weakness does not allow him to speak to us immediately; a clear example of this exists in the Israelites, who could not hear God speaking to them at Mount Sinai. As Moses then used interpreters, so afterwards he committed these functions to the priests, so that the people might seek the law and the knowledge of his will from their mouths. And when these were negligent in their office, he raised up prophets in an extraordinary way, who preached to people of every place and rank. In the New Testament he set the apostles in their place, and in them he established the ministry of the Church, which he wills to be kept for ever; and therefore he bestows from heaven the gifts of his Spirit, so that the Church may not lack faithful workers through whom she is cultivated and built up. Great is their dignity, in that God entrusts to them his Church, which (as we said at the beginning) has nothing more precious, and which he loves not only as a vineyard but as a bride. This indeed reminds them of their duty, namely that first they themselves should hold her dear and burn with a holy zeal for her, such as we read Paul once had. Meanwhile let them remember that they are not lords of the vineyard but farmers appointed by the Son of God, to whom all the fruit ought to return. A farmer has no right to uproot the vines carelessly at his own pleasure, much less to sell the vineyard, pledge it to others, or move its boundaries. Thus neither were such things formerly permitted to the priests, nor afterwards to the apostles, who attempted none of these things, but were wholly devoted to bringing Churches to Christ and keeping them in his faith and service. Paul certainly confesses that power was given to them for building up, not for destruction. Today the pontiffs ought to imitate these men, who boast of their succession from them, yet act entirely as their own lust directs: they burden the Church with new laws, move the ancient boundaries, divide it into sects, so that there are almost more who wish to be named after men than who are content with the one Christ alone. And if anyone contradicts them, they cast him out of the fellowship of the Church with the thunderbolt of excommunication, and (as the Prophet says) they sanctify war against him. Those farmers, therefore, are like those of whose treachery and ingratitude the Lord will speak shortly after. For the present, let us all acknowledge the love and care of God with which he works to cultivate us, and, mindful that we are his vineyard, let us bear fruit worthy of our profession, so that he may be glorified in us and we may be kept for ever in Christ Jesus, our one Lord and Saviour, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCL.
units.tr: HOMILY CCL.

units.la: Cum autem tempus fructuum appropinquasset, misit seruos suos ad agricolas, vt eius fructus acciperent. Agricolae autem captis eius seruis, alium quidem ceciderunt, alium vero trucidarunt, alium autem lapidarunt. Rursum misit alios seruos plures prioribus; & fecerunt eis itidem.
units.tr: When the time of the fruits drew near, he sent his servants to the husbandmen, that they might receive his fruit. But the husbandmen seized his servants: one they beat, another they killed, and another they stoned. Again he sent other servants, more in number than the first; and they treated them in the same way.

units.la: ETsi Dominus noster IESVS CHRISTVS parabolam hanc contra Iudaeorum Sacerdotes & Scribas adduxerit, vt horum ingratitudinem & improbitatem arguat, & ijsdem pasnas dignas denuntiet, illa ipsa tamen vniuersalem doctrinam comprehendit, qua offenditur quae sit Ecclesiae in terris conditio, quid dq; facere deceat eos, qui eius membra germana esse volunt, in primis autem quid cauere debeant ij, quibus illius curam & administrationem Deus credidit. Primum in his occurrit, quod vineam Deus plantauit: quo docetur, Ecclesiam non temere nasci, sed a Deo plantari, qui eandem donis quoq; necessarijs instruit. Nam si nos sperites, peccatores & filij irae sumus, nec digni, qui Dei peculium aut vinea dicamur. Nisi ergo hic nos eligat, & eo honore dignetur, nunquam eo perueniemus proprijs viribus. Administratur autem Ecclesia per seruos Dei, qui colonis conferuntur, eo quod hanc Verbi praedicatione excolere debent, & eafacere, quae ad eius aedificationem & conseruationem maxime sunt necessaria. Itaque seruos, non Dominos Ecclesiae se esse semper meminerint, ne aliquid temere agant, sed magni illius
units.tr: Although our Lord Jesus Christ brought forward this parable against the priests and scribes of the Jews, to expose their ingratitude and wickedness and to threaten them with the punishment they deserved, nevertheless it embraces a universal teaching: it shows what the condition of the Church on earth is, what those ought to do who wish to be its true members, and above all what those ought to beware of to whom God has entrusted its care and administration. The first thing that meets us here is that God planted the vineyard. By this it is taught that the Church is not born by chance but is planted by God, who also equips it with the gifts it needs. For if we are by nature sinners and children of wrath, we are not worthy to be called God's own people or his vineyard. Unless, therefore, he chooses us and deigns to honour us with this, we shall never attain it by our own strength. The Church, however, is administered through the servants of God, who are set over the tenants, because they ought to cultivate it by the preaching of the Word and to do those things which are most necessary for its building up and preservation. Therefore let them always remember that they are servants, not the masters, of the Church, so that they do nothing rashly, but observe the will of that great householder, to whom they will one day have to render an account. The purpose of this cultivation is that the Lord may receive the desired fruit from those who are said to be his vineyard or Church. For just as the vines and the dry and useless branches are cut out of a vineyard, so God does not tolerate in the Church those who bear no fruit worthy of the Christian profession. Of these things we have spoken recently.

units.la: [illegible, ~3 letters] patrisfamilias voluntatem obseruent, cui olim rationem sunt redditur. Finis vero culturae illius est, vt fructum optatum ex ijs recipiat Dominus, qui vinea aut Ecclesia illius esse dicuntur. Vt enim ex vinea excinduntur vites & palmites aridi & inutiles: ita non fert Deus in Ecclesia iuxta eos, qui nullos fructus ferunt Christiana professione dignos. Et de his quidem nuper dictum est.
units.tr: ...to obey the will of the householder, to whom they were once to give an account. The purpose of this cultivation is that the Lord may receive the desired fruit from those who are said to be his vineyard, that is, his Church. For just as vines and dry, useless shoots are cut out of a vineyard, so God does not bear, in the Church, those who bring forth no fruit worthy of the Christian profession. And this has already been said recently.

units.la: Sequitur nunc secunda parabolae pars, qua colonorum ingratitudo & improbitas atque perfidia narratur, cuius summa est, quam modo recitauimus: Cum autem tempus fructuum appropinquauisset, misit seruos suos. Quasi diceret: Ergo etsi alio profectus peregrinari videatur Deus, non tamen vineae suae curam deposuit, sed quouis tempore fructum sibi debitum repetit. Ita vero hanc quoque partem narrat Dominus, vt demonstret, hic etiam nihil factum esse, ex quo coloni iure potuerint tam inique & turpiter agendi occasionem arripere, sed propria malitia peccauisse. Vt enim prius, cum vineam ipsius locauisset, ipse peregre abiit, neque eius vlla in re molestus fuit, quae eos in opere faciendo impediret: ita non antea misit seruos iistos, quam cum tempus fructuum appropinquauisset. Deinde non alienos & incognitos misit, sed seruos, qui eiusdem cum ipsis conditionis & ipsorum conserui erant. Etenim habet Deus non vnum modo seruorum genus, quorum ministerio pro negotiorum diuersitate vtitur. Praeterea nihil per hos exigit, quam suos fructus, qui nimirum ipsi iure debebantur. Intelligit autem Prophetas, quos ex Iudaeis excitauit (sicuti per Amos dicit: Excitaui de filijs Veltris Prophetas) si quando coloni Leuitae & Sacerdotes, officio suo defuerunt. Et in praesenti quidem secundo missi dicuntur serui illi. Cum enim coloni priores captos indignissimis modis tractauissent, & alium quidem flagris caesum dimisissent inanem, alium vero trucidassent, alium lapidauissent: rursus alios misit, quorum nihilo melior fors fuit: sed eadem iniurias ab illis passi sunt. Apud Lucam tertij quoque serui ad illos missi mentio fit, quem vulneratum eiecerunt.
units.tr: Now follows the second part of the parable, in which the ingratitude, wickedness and treachery of the tenants is related, the sum of which is what we have just recited: "And when the season of fruit drew near, he sent his servants." As if he were saying: although God may seem to have gone abroad, as if on a journey, he has not for all that laid aside the care of his vineyard, but at every season he demands the fruit owed to him. The Lord relates this part too in such a way as to show that nothing happened here from which the tenants could rightly seize an occasion to act so unjustly and shamefully; they sinned by their own malice. For just as before, when he had let out his vineyard, he went abroad himself and was in no way troublesome to them in any matter that might hinder them in their work, so he did not send those servants until the season of fruit drew near. Then he sent not strangers and unknown men, but servants who were of the same condition as they were and their fellow servants. For God does not have only one kind of servant, whom he uses for the ministry of his affairs according to their diversity. Moreover, he demands through these only his own fruit, which was rightly owed to him. But he means the prophets, whom he raised up from among the Jews (as he says through Amos: "I raised up prophets from among your sons"), whenever the tenants, the Levites and priests, failed in their duty. And in the present passage those servants are said to have been sent the second time. For when the former tenants had treated the first servants in the most outrageous ways, and had sent one back empty after beating him with whips, had killed another and stoned a third, he again sent others, whose lot was no better, for they suffered the same injuries from them. In Luke too mention is made of a third servant sent to them, whom they wounded and cast out.

units.la: Et si Iudaicae gentis historiam perlegemus, quae cum illis gesta sunt, narrationi huic probe conueniunt, & commendant ista plus quam paternam curam Dei, qui nullo vnquam tempore defuit officio, quin subinde dederit Prophetas, qui populum simul & Leuitas siue Sacerdotes moneret, hortarentur, & debita officia exigerent. Primum enim cum post obitum Iosue & patrum, qui opera Domini in Aegypto & in deserto, deniq; in occupatione terrae viderant, defecerunt ab eo post Deos alios, & (vt ex eo conijci potest) Sacerdotes in suo munere negligentiores essent, Angelum ad eos misit, qui graui oratione beneficia eius toti populo recitans, & his ipsorum ingratitudinem & turpem defectionem opponens, ad lucem publicum eos excitauit. Nec dubium est quin toto illo tempore Iudicum, quo plures dati sunt vindices, heroes nimirum fortissimi, doctores quoque & monitores habuerint plurimos, qui ipsos in officio retinere conarentur.
units.tr: If we read through the history of the Jewish nation, what happened to them agrees well with this narrative, and it sets forth God's care, more than fatherly, which never failed in its duty at any time, but again and again gave prophets who might admonish and exhort the people and the Levites or priests alike, and demand the duties owed. For first, when after the death of Joshua and of the fathers, who had seen the works of the Lord in Egypt, in the wilderness, and finally in the occupation of the land, they fell away from him to other gods, and (as may be gathered from this) the priests were more negligent in their office, he sent an angel to them, who, recounting in a weighty speech his benefits to the whole people and setting against them their ingratitude and shameful defection, roused them to repentance in public. Nor is there any doubt that throughout that whole period of the Judges, in which many deliverers were given, most valiant heroes indeed, they also had very many teachers and admonishers, who tried to keep them in their duty.

units.la: Etenim tempore Heli, summi Sacerdotis & Iudicis, cum perfidissimos & improbissimos colonos agerent eius filij Hophni & Phinees, Samuel missus est, qui Verbo Domini, cuius praedicatio rara & pretiosa aliquandiu fuerat, illos in viam reuocaret. Secundo cum post Salomonis mortem decem tribus ficta fecissent, & proprio rege creato, non solum a Dauidis domo, verum etiam a religione vera defecissent, & in regno Iuda quoque multa indigne & impie fierent, ad vtrosque innumeri Prophetae sunt missi, qui Dei nomine fructus debitos exigerent. Et in exilio Babylonico non defuerunt exactores eiusmodi: ex quorum numero Ezechiel fuit, Daniel item, Esdras & alij similes. Postquam vero ex Babylone dimissi ad sua redierunt, dati sunt Haggaeus & Zacharias, nec multo post Malachias, & instante iam aduentu IESV CHRISTI, Ioannes Bapt. qui seriam poenitentiae praedicatione non apud vulgus modo, sed in primis apud Sacerdotes & Pharisaeos, qui praecipui coloni dici & haberi volebant, instabat, vt fructus Deo redderent, quos tam diu nequicquam requisiuerat. Quod igitur in praesenti de seruis ad colonos missis dicitur, reuera olim abunde fecit Deus, qui vineam suam ipsis locauerat. At quia, vt initio monuimus, ista ad Ecclesiam totam pertinent, cuius typus hic proponitur, quaedam diligentius debent considerari.
units.tr: Indeed, in the time of Eli, the high priest and judge, when his sons Hophni and Phinehas, the most faithless and wicked husbandmen, were in charge, Samuel was sent, who by the Word of the Lord (whose preaching had been rare and precious for some time) called them back to the way. Second, when after the death of Solomon the ten tribes had made a sham, and having set up their own king had fallen away not only from the house of David but also from the true religion, and in the kingdom of Judah too many unworthy and impious things were done, countless prophets were sent to both, who in the name of God demanded the fruits owed. Nor were there lacking exactors of this kind in the Babylonian exile: of their number were Ezekiel, Daniel likewise, Ezra and others like them. But after they were released from Babylon and returned to their own land, Haggai and Zechariah were given, and not long after Malachi; and when the coming of Jesus Christ was now at hand, John the Baptist, who pressed with the preaching of a serious repentance not only the common people but especially the priests and Pharisees, who wished to be called and regarded as the chief husbandmen, so that they would render to God the fruits which he had sought in vain for so long. What is therefore said in the present passage about servants sent to the husbandmen, God in truth did long ago abundantly, he who had let out his vineyard to them. But because, as we warned at the beginning, these things pertain to the whole Church, of which this is set forth as a type, certain points must be considered more carefully.

units.la: Primum inter haec est, quod serui isti, qui Prophetarum & administrorum siue praeconum ver-bi personam sustinent, exactoribus conferuntur. Eo enim Verbi praecones de officio suo admonetur, quod est, non obiter modo docere & monere, sed instare apud omnis loci & ordinis homines, & vt huic omnes reddant quod debent. Admonet de eo Timotheum suum Paulus, non sine grauissima obtestatione, sic scribens: Obtestor ego coram Deo, & coram Domino IESV CHRISTO, qui iudicaturus est viuos & mortuos in illustri illo suo aduentu & regno suo: Praedica sermonem, insta tempestiue, intempestiue: nimirum quoad carnis prudentiam, quae nihil tempestiue & commode fieri putat, quam quod mundo probatur. At captanda quidem sunt occasiones omnes verbi administris, ut hoc cum fructu praedicent. At si nullae se offerant, & vel a praedicando prorsus abstinere oporteat, aut mundo gratificari ea dicendo quae huic arriddesprés: tunc procul relictis humanae sapientiae rationibus, id facere oportet, quod res ipsa iubet, & Deus illis mandauit. Tunc ergo cum hominum contumacia certamen suscipiant ministri, & (sicuti Isaias olim dicebat Deus) clament ex gutture, nec voci aut lateribus parcant, & instar tubae voce extollent, ut populo toti annuntient peccata sua & quae ad horum emendationem faciunt. Docet idem speculatorum typus, quibus ministri apud Ezechielem comparantur. Vt enim speculator in excubijs stans, hoste viso aut incendio exorto tuba canere debet, etsi hoc intempestinum videatur ignis, qui somnum sibi turbari indignius ferunt: ita hic fiat necesse est, licet longe alia illorum sit sententia, qui mundo placere, & carnis cupiditatibus indulgere mallent. Fecerunt hoc olim Prophetae, qui non veriti sunt clamare: Audite o domus Dauid: An parum est quod hominibus molesti estis nisi etiam Deo molestiam exhibeatis? Audite quaeso capita Iacob, & vos principes domus Israelis: Va fecerunt in Sione, & confidentibus in monte Samariae. Audite verbum Domini o principes Sodomae, & auscultate populeGomorrhae legem Dei tui, &c. Nec alio spiritu ductos fuisse Apostolos, ex primis horum sermonibus apparet, quibus Senioribus & Sacerdotibus Ierosolymitanis crimen iniustè occisi Filij Dei publicè exprobrauerunt, ut respipiscentiam feriam ab illis exigerent. Et debent horum exempla cum hoc loco diligenter conferri, ne illos nimios fuisse putemus, sed officium fecisse sciamus, cui non debent deesse, qui hodie eundem gradum in Ecclesia tenent, quem illi olim tenuerunt. Etenim hoc illud est, quod verbi ministros mundo inuisos & exosos reddit. Gratia Dei praedicationem omnes facile ferunt, & huius promissiones vna cum merito Christi sibi applicari volunt etiam prophani & impij, qui illo sibi opus esse non sentiunt. At si corruptos mores & prauafuaftudia corripi, si poenas sceleribus suis debitas denuntiari audiant, tunc iras concipiunt implacabiles, & contra Dei seruos ceu aduersus publicos hostes insurgunt etiam ij, qui prius manfuetiffimi & commodissimi hominum videbantur. Tunc ergo ministros officij memores esse decet, ne sibi ab hominibus timeant, & sibi applicet, quod olim Ieremiae dixit Deus: Ne paueas a conspectu eorum, ne pauere te faciam, &c. Ier. 1.
units.tr: First among these is that those servants, who bear the person of the prophets and of the ministers or heralds of the Word, are set over the exactors. For the heralds of the Word are reminded by this of their duty, which is not merely to teach and admonish now and then, but to press before men of every place and rank, and to see that all render to God what they owe. Paul admonishes his Timothy about this with a most serious adjuration, writing thus: "I charge you before God, and before the Lord Jesus Christ, who shall judge the living and the dead at his glorious appearing and his kingdom: Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season" [2 Tim. 4.]. That is, as far as the prudence of the flesh is concerned, which thinks nothing is done in season and fittingly except what pleases the world. But indeed all opportunities should be seized by the ministers of the Word, so that they may preach with fruit. And if no opportunities present themselves, and they should utterly abstain from preaching, or please the world by saying things that smile upon it, then, setting aside the reasons of human wisdom, they must do what the matter itself demands and what God has commanded them. Then, therefore, when the ministers take up the contest against the obstinacy of men, they must (as God once said to Isaiah) cry aloud with the throat, spare neither voice nor sides, and raise their voice like a trumpet, so as to announce to the whole people their sins and what pertains to their amendment. The same thing is taught by the type of watchmen, to whom Ezekiel compares the ministers. For just as a watchman standing on guard, when he sees the enemy or a fire breaks out, must sound the trumpet, even though this may seem untimely to those who take it more ill that their sleep is disturbed; so it must be done here, although the opinion of those is quite different who would rather please the world and indulge the desires of the flesh. The prophets did this of old, who did not fear to cry out: "Hear, O house of David: Is it a small thing for you to weary men, that you weary my God also? Hear, I pray you, heads of Jacob, and you princes of the house of Israel: woe to those who act in Zion, and to those who trust in the mountain of Samaria. Hear the word of the Lord, O princes of Sodom, and listen to the law of your God, O people of Gomorrah," and so on. Nor is it evident from the first sermons of the apostles that they were led by any other spirit, in which they publicly rebuked the elders and priests of Jerusalem for the crime of unjustly killing the Son of God, so that they might demand repentance from them. And these examples ought to be carefully compared with this passage, lest we think they went too far, but we should know that they performed their duty, which must not be lacking in those who today hold the same rank in the Church that they once held. For this is precisely what makes the ministers of the Word hateful and odious to the world. All men readily bear the preaching of grace, and even profane and wicked men wish to have its promises and the merit of Christ applied to themselves, though they do not feel any need of it. But if they hear that their corrupt morals and wicked pursuits are rebuked, and that the punishments due to their crimes are announced, then they conceive implacable anger, and even those who previously seemed the gentlest and most agreeable of men rise up against God's servants as against public enemies. Therefore the ministers should remember their office and not fear men, and should apply to themselves what God once said to Jeremiah: "Be not afraid of their faces, lest I make you afraid," etc. Jer. 1.

units.la: Secundo obseruari debet, quod exactores isti ad colonos mittuntur, ut ab his fructus hero debitos repetant. Atqui vinea fructum ferre, & ex vitibus hic colligi solet. Singulorum deinde est, qui fidem in Christum profitentur, & vel palmites in vite illa vera, aut membra Ecclesiae dici volunt, ut pro sua vocationis ratione fructus ferant sua professione dignos, & Deo seruiant in fide constantia, vitae puritate & innocentia. Caeterum ut id fiat, & Deus in omnibus glorificetur, cum primis curare debent antistites, quos ille Ecclesiae & populi sui colonos fecit. Idcirco ad hos mittuntur exactores isti. Vbi apparet vehementer falli eos, qui aliorum facta & mores nihil ad se pertinere putant, & sibi impune fore arbitrantur, si dicant: Quid ad me, quomodo quisque vitam suam instituat? aut quod vitae genus eligat? Cur ego me propter alios diffruciem? Pereant illi, quando ita lubet, ego meas res agam, & ut mihi bene sit curabo, &c. Sed eho tu quisquis es, quae Deus vel Ecclesiae ministrum, vel Reipub. praefectum esse voluit. Nonne vinea Domini exercituum est populus, quem tuae fidei credidit? Nonne te eius colonum esse fateris? Si hoc negas, indignus es, qui vel in Ecclesia vel in Rep. ciuis regni Dei censearis. Sin affirmas, qua fronte negas, illius curam ad te pertinere? Nu priuata temeritate reijcies a Deo tibi impositum onus? Atqui de tua manu non solum requiretur fructus, quae alij ferre debent, verumetiam eorum sanguis, qui vt steriles & ari di palmites peribunt, si id tua negligentia aut incuria fiat. Quod aute de administris verbi dicitur, non minus ad magistratus pertinet, qui ad Reipublicae gubernacula sedent. Nam nisi hi honestatis publicae serij custodes fuerint, peccandi licentiam & superstitiones vulgi bonis legibus coercuerint, & eafde constanter defenderint, ipsis imputabitur quicquid aduersus religionem veram su perstitiose, impie, inhonestè aut turpiter designatur: imò ipsis acceptum feretur, quicquid a Deo ira-
units.tr: Secondly, it should be observed that these tax collectors are sent to the tenants, to demand from them the fruit owed to the master. Now a vineyard is meant to bear fruit, and fruit is usually gathered from the vines here. Next, the same applies to each person who professes faith in Christ and wishes to be called either a branch in that true vine or a member of the Church: according to the nature of their calling, they should bear fruit worthy of their profession, and serve God in steadfast faith, purity of life and innocence. But so that this may happen and God may be glorified in all things, the leaders whom he has made the tenants of his Church and people must above all take care. That is why these tax collectors are sent to them. Here it becomes clear how greatly those are mistaken who think that the deeds and morals of others are no concern of theirs, and suppose they will go unpunished if they say: "What is it to me how each person orders his life, or what kind of life he chooses? Why should I ruin myself on account of others? Let them perish, if they wish; I will manage my own affairs and see to it that I fare well," and so on. But tell me, whoever you are, whom God has willed to be either a minister of the Church or a ruler of the commonwealth: is not the vineyard of the Lord of hosts the people whom he has entrusted to your faith? Do you not admit that you are its tenant? If you deny this, you are unworthy to be counted a citizen of the kingdom of God, either in the Church or in the commonwealth. But if you affirm it, with what face do you deny that its care pertains to you? Will you by your own rash presumption cast off the burden God has laid upon you? Yet the fruit that others ought to bear will be required at your hand, and also the blood of those who will perish as barren and dried-up branches, if this comes about through your negligence or carelessness. What is said about the ministers of the Word applies no less to magistrates, who sit at the helm of the commonwealth. For unless they are the faithful guardians of public honesty, and restrain with good laws the licence to sin and the superstitions of the crowd, and steadfastly defend those same laws, whatever is superstitiously, impiously, dishonourably or shamefully done against the true religion will be imputed to them. Indeed, whatever evil God sends down in punishment for public crimes will be counted against them.

units.la: S to malorum immittitur, & quo in scelera publica punire solet. Ideo Micheas cum principibū Israelis & Sacerdotum atq; Prophetarum vitia, qui ignauia & nequitia sua populo scelerum authores erant, acriter corripuisset, addit: Idcirco propter vos Zion vt ager arabitur, & Ierusalem acerrimus erit, & mons templi in excelsa saltus redigetur. Haec ad se quoq; transferant priuatim parentes & publice scholarum praefecti, quorum institutioni pueri commissi sunt. Hos enim no immerito ipsem gregis dominici, aut nouelletā Ecclesiæ, & plantulas teneras in agro Domini dixeris. Curet ergo, vt eos in vera Dei cognitione ad pietatem instituant, & verbi semen diligenter illorum cordibus commendent, vt tandem ex illo fructus enascantur, quibus Deus honoretur. Nec enim temere dictum est a Satyrico: Quo semel est imbuta recens seruabit odorem, Testa diu. Itaq; si suae disciplinae commissos vel superstitionibus imbuant, vel morum licentia corrumpi sinant, aut etiam proprio exemplo corrumpant, quos ex illis fructus olim recipere poterit Deus? aut quid illi eius exactoribus reddere poterunt, si requirantur?
units.tr: Micah, when he sharply rebuked the princes of Israel and the vices of the priests and prophets, who by their idleness and wickedness were the authors of crimes among the people, adds: "Therefore, because of you, Zion shall be ploughed like a field, and Jerusalem shall become heaps of rubble, and the mountain of the temple a wooded height" (Mic. 3.12). Let parents privately, and the heads of schools publicly, to whose instruction boys are entrusted, apply this to themselves. For these may rightly be called the shepherds of the Lord's flock, or the young plants of the Church, and tender shoots in the Lord's field. Let them therefore take care to bring them up to godliness in the true knowledge of God, and to sow the seed of the Word diligently in their hearts, so that at last fruits may spring up from it by which God is honoured. For it was not without reason that the satirist said: "The fresh jar will keep the smell of whatever it was first steeped in for a long time."
