Nequaquam, sed ut suaui illa & mellita commendatione insidias quas ipsi struebant, occultent, & ut ipse sibi cum amicis & discipulis syncerris rem esse putans, incautius aliquid effutiat, ex quo calumniandi occasionem illi possint arripere. Itaq; patrem suum diabolum imitantur, qui Euam omnium nostrum matrem olim simili astu decepit, & hodie adhuc totus in eo est, ut sub falso salutis nostrae studio mentes simplicium illectas & corruptas abducat a simplicitate, quae est in Christo. Et sane nihil vulgarius est hodie sive Rempublicam sive religionem spectes. Nam ut sub pietatis praetextu superstitiones inuehit, & seditiones excitat, qui studium salutis publicae cum lachrymis protestantur, & animas suas oppignerare audent: ita bonis legibus & pacis publicae per eos insidiatur, qui liberas gentes Regum faederibus insidiosis illaqueare, & militiae mercenariae mancipare conantur, ut ipsi ex simplicium sanguine opes atq; thesauros ingentes sibi colligant. Itaq; diligenti vigilia opus est nobis, ne facile aures praebeamus blandis istis Sirenibus, quarum cantus si admittantur, certum ac ineuitabile salutis naufragium pariunt. Interim consolationi piorum seruiat exemplum iudicij Dei, quod hic elucet. Dum enim ipsi Christo insidias struunt, & eum illaqueare studeant, seipsos fallunt, & in astutia sua capti suam authorita-
units.tr: But it is worth also seeing the manner and order of what these men pursued against the Lord in this business. First they took counsel that they might trap him in his speech. They therefore do nothing rashly or without forethought. For the sons of this age are more prudent than the sons of light in their own generation, and Daniel attributes to the Antichrist the eyes of men, that is, cunning and diligence in carrying out affairs. David too, though he says that the kings and princes of the earth rage and prepare force by which they may shake off Christ's yoke, nevertheless says that they meet together and plan how they may bring about what they want. The aim proposed to them was to ensnare him in his speech, that is, to lead him to say something too incautious, on the occasion of which they could either hand him over to the power of the governor or make him hateful and odious to the people. Next, they do not approach the Lord themselves, since they had hitherto been open enemies. Instead, to hide more securely, they send to him their disciples, and not just any of them but spies, as Luke relates, who would pretend to be righteous and lovers of truth, and with them they join the Herodians, as we have just said. And these men can wonderfully cover deceit and snares. For they not only feign zeal for righteousness and piety, but, as if they were his most devoted followers, they attribute to him all the duties of a good and faithful teacher. For they address him thus: "Teacher, we know that you are truthful, and teach the way of God in truth, and you care for no one; for you do not regard the person of men," and so on. By calling him teacher they profess that they are his disciples. What else was this than to deny Pharisaism? And it is remarkable that they could speak so well about the duty of a good teacher. First they say, "We know that you are truthful." This is the chief virtue of a teacher. For who would trust a vain and lying man? Or who would hope that he speaks true things about divine and heavenly matters, who does not hesitate to lie about things known to everyone? Then, that he teaches the way of God. Thus is described the whole plan of this life and of eternal salvation, which is delivered in the Word of God. It is called the way of God because it leads us to God, and it is not enough to hold to it, but we must walk in it. Therefore the saints pray: "Make your ways known to me, O Lord, and teach me your paths. Lead me in your truth; teach me the way of your decrees; make me walk in the path of your commandments." Let the teacher, then, show this way, and since it is found nowhere but in the Word of God, let him proclaim this alone, not his own or other men's inventions or traditions, by which God is worshipped in vain. Next, let him teach this way in truth, that is, rightly and so that it serves the edification of his hearers, lest it be said of him what Isaiah complains of the impostors of his own age: "My people, those who lead you cause you to err, and they destroy the course of your paths." They do this who promise grace and salvation to those who need correction, and (as is said of certain people in Ezekiel) sew cushions under every elbow, on which they may sleep softly, though they ought to be roused to the zeal of repentance by severe admonitions. On the contrary, they make for themselves a certain religion and sanctify war against those who do not put anything into their mouths. But that he may be able to teach in truth, the teacher must not care for anyone, nor regard the person of anyone. For those who do this and want to please men cannot be servants of God. For there will always be something to carry them off, turned aside by fear or the hope of gain. Let them therefore remember that they are servants of God, with whom there is no respect of persons. Next, that the teachers of every place and rank of men are public and common, whom the Lord has set over his whole household, and therefore none of them may be neglected or cast aside, but each must be taught, admonished, reproved and corrected, so that those things are said to all which serve their amendment and salvation. And it is agreed that Christ was such a teacher, of whom the Prophet once said, "No deceit was found in his mouth." And he himself did not hesitate to say to his most bitter enemies: "Which of you convicts me of sin?" And although it is not granted to any mortal to attain that perfection which was in him, so that he never slips in word or deed, yet as regards doctrine it becomes the ministers of the churches to strive that it be sincere for them and not adulterated by any deceit. But to return to Christ's adversaries: to what end do they say these things? Surely not to commend themselves to him? Not at all, but that by this smooth and honeyed commendation they may conceal the snares they were laying, and that he, thinking he has to do with friends and sincere disciples, may let slip something too incautious, from which they could seize an occasion for accusing him. So they imitate their father the devil, who in the same way long ago deceived Eve, the mother of us all, and to this day he is wholly intent on drawing away the minds of simple people, enticed and corrupted, from the simplicity that is in Christ, under the false pretext of concern for our salvation. And indeed nothing is more common today, whether you look at the state or at religion. For just as they introduce superstitions under the cloak of piety and stir up sedition, those who profess with tears their zeal for the public welfare and dare to pledge their own souls, so they lay snares for good laws and public peace, those who try to entangle free nations in treacherous treaties of kings and to bind them to mercenary service, so that they may gather for themselves vast riches and treasures from the blood of simple people. Therefore we need diligent watchfulness, lest we readily lend our ears to those sweet Sirens, whose song, if admitted, brings about a certain and unavoidable shipwreck of salvation. Meanwhile let the example of God's judgment, which shines forth here, serve as a consolation to the pious. For while these men lay snares for Christ himself and strive to entangle him, they deceive themselves, and, caught in their own cunning, their own authority...

units.la: Hostes Christi in sua astutia theritatem & existimationem turpiter prositentur. Etenim si præceptores suum esse fatentur, quì non videat male ipsos facere, qui alios seductores quos illius aduersarios esse, non poterant ignorare? Si viam Dei docebat, & quide in veritate, ipsi vtiq; seductores erant. Et quis dubitet publica ista confessione Apostolos & plures alios, qui hactenus Christum secuti fuerat, vehementer in fide fuisse confirmatos, quando audiebant ab ijs illum commendari, quos eius hostes acerrimos hucusq; fuisse viderant. Solet hoc frequenter accidere ijs, qui cum veritate certamen suscipiunt. Quid enim aliud faciunt qui hodie nos hæreticos & Ecclesiæ catholicæ desertores esse clamant, interim Apostolos venerantur & adorant, Diuorum item & Martyrum cultores se esse profitentur, quos eandem fidem atq; doctrinam nobiscum olim professos esse constat? Aut ergo nos diuersum ab his credere & docere demonstrent, aut nos Ecclesiæ catholicæ authoritate grauare desinant: quæ nisi nobiscum fidem in vnum Deum per vnicum Mediatorem IESVM CHRISTVM profiteatur & teneat, orthodoxa & catholica dici non poterit.
units.tr: Christ's enemies in their cunning shamefully betray their own truthfulness and reputation. For if they confess that he is their teacher, who would not see how badly they act, who call him a seducer when they could not fail to know that he was their adversary? If he taught the way of God, and indeed in truth, then they themselves were the seducers. And who can doubt that by this public confession the Apostles and many others who had hitherto followed Christ were greatly strengthened in faith, when they heard him commended by those whom they had seen to be his most bitter enemies until then? This commonly happens to those who take up a contest with the truth. For what else do those do who today cry out that we are heretics and deserters of the Catholic Church, while at the same time they venerate and adore the Apostles, and profess themselves worshippers of the saints and martyrs, who are known to have once professed the same faith and doctrine as we do? Either let them show that we believe and teach something different from these, or let them cease to burden us with the authority of the Catholic Church; which, unless it professes and holds with us faith in one God through the one Mediator Jesus Christ, cannot be called orthodox and catholic.

units.la: Porrò quæstionem ipsam videamus, quæ eiusmodi est: Dic quid tibi videtur, Q.d. Quia absq; personarum respectu hactenus de omnibus pronunciauisti, de quibus interrogatus es, procul dubio in hac quoq; causa liberè dices quod animo sentis, & quod cum veritate verbi Dei consentire nosti. Licet ne censum dare Cæsari, an non? Petitur quæstio ex præsenti, quæ tunc erat, populi Iudaici conditione. Nec enim tam stupidi erant, vt nescirent quid regibus debeatur, & de eo olim Samuel monores eorum admonuerat. Et censum ex antiquissimo instituto in Romana Republ. agi solere, non poterant ignorare, vt alibi diximus. Adhæc lex naturæ docet, æquum esse vt subditi pro facultatum suarum ratione contribuant, vt quæ ad Rempub. pertinent possint commodè administrari. Sed quod Romani ab ipsis censum exigerent, id illis iniquum & intolerabile videbatur. Primum quia populus Dei ipsi erant, Romani autem idololatræ & a Dei regno alieni. Deinde res noua erat & insolens Iudæis, qui censum nullum dederant hucusq;, nisi qui ad sarta tecta templi coseruanda per tinebat, de cuius institutione Moses in Exodo disserit. Ideo apud Lucam quærunt, Licet ne nobis, &c. Estq; quæstionis huius emphasis aut status in eo, Num Iudæis, id est, populo Dei liceat censum qui olim religionis ergo indictus fuit, dare Cæsari, principi prophano & idololatræ? De iure diuino igitur quærunt, & est quæstio hæc plena periculi, eoq; periculosior, quod in publico proponeretur, & ijs testibus, quos costabat nō dissimulaturos esse, si quid responderet, quod Cæsaris dignitati aut maiestati (vt vulgò loquuntur) posset derogare. Etenim si neget dandum esse Cæsari censum, accusabitur seditionis, quod postea Sacerdotes & Seniores fecisse scimus coram Pilato, quamuis hoc se iniuste facere scirent. Sin affirmet, populo seipsum exosum reddet, & simul gratiam bonam apud hunc inibunt Pharisæi, quibus indignum videbatur Cæsares ea exigere, quæ Deo ex antiquo iure debebantur. Sin taceat, & hanc quæstionem abs se reijciat (vt cum a quodam de hæreditate inter se & fratrem herifcunda appellaretur, eum fecisse legimus) causam miseri populi negligere, & personas respicere dicetur, sicq; sua existimationis laudem amittet. Sed quam sapienter & grauiter responderit, vt omnes hosce laqueos euaderet, in sequenti sermone Deo volente dicetur.
units.tr: Let us now look at the question itself, which is of this kind: "Tell me, what do you think, Teacher? Is it lawful to give tribute to Caesar, or not?" Since you have hitherto pronounced on everything you were asked without respect of persons, you will undoubtedly speak freely in this case too, saying what you really think, and what you know agrees with the truth of God's Word. The question arises from the condition of the Jewish people at that time. For they were not so dull as not to know what is owed to kings, and Samuel had long ago warned them about this when he admonished them. Nor could they be ignorant that a tribute has been levied in the Roman commonwealth from very ancient institution, as we have said elsewhere. Moreover, the law of nature teaches that it is fair for subjects to contribute according to the means of their property, so that the affairs of the commonwealth may be conveniently administered. But that the Romans should demand tribute from them seemed to the Jews unjust and intolerable. First, because they were the people of God, while the Romans were idolaters and aliens from the kingdom of God. Second, the thing was new and unusual for the Jews, who had hitherto paid no tax except that for the upkeep of the roof and walls of the temple, the institution of which Moses discusses in Exodus. Therefore they ask in Luke, "Is it lawful for us?" and so on. The emphasis or point of this question lies in this: is it lawful for the Jews, that is, the people of God, to give to Caesar, a profane and idolatrous prince, the tribute which was once imposed for the sake of religion? They are asking, then, about divine right, and this question was full of danger, all the more so because it was put in public, before witnesses who, it was clear, would not keep quiet if he gave any answer that could detract from the dignity or majesty (as men commonly say) of Caesar. For if he said that tribute should not be given to Caesar, he would be accused of sedition, as we know the chief priests and elders afterwards did before Pilate, although they knew they were acting unjustly. But if he affirmed it, he would make himself hateful to the people, and at the same time the Pharisees would win good favour with them, for they thought it unworthy that Caesar should exact what was owed to God by ancient right. If he kept silent and refused this question (as we read he did when someone asked him to settle an inheritance between himself and his brother), he would be said to neglect the cause of the wretched people and to respect persons, and so he would lose the praise of his good reputation. But how wisely and gravely he answered, so as to escape all these snares, will be told, God willing, in the following sermon.

units.la: In præsenti videre licet, quæ conditio sit populi, qui aliquando libertatem suam amisit, aut sponte prodidit. Fuerunt olim Iudæi liberi, vtpote Dei peculium. Sed pro tanto beneficio ingrati, reges sibi accersiuerunt, sub quibus multa pañi sunt, a quibus immunes esse poterant, si Reip. formam a Deo ipsis traditam custodiuissent. Tandem cum Sacerdotum ambitio eo vsq; progressa esset, vt ijdem quoq; regnum affectarent, & infelix gens propter Hircanum & Aristobulum in partes scinderetur, & vtrinq; auxilia extera quærerent, factum est ea occasione, vt Romani Iudæam subigerent & primò regem illi imponerent Herodem, hominem Idumæum: postea aute illa in proninciam redacta, præsides in eam mitterent. Sub quibus quàm multa duriter & iniquè passi sint, nō opus est dicere. Hi certè censum egerunt, & præsidia per vrbes disposuerunt. Ab eo tempore miseri pro restitutione libertatis multum laborarunt, & agnoscebant Dei ab ipsis alienati indicium esse, quòd censum Cæsari reddere cogerentur. Sed nequicquam multa conati sunt, cum Dei filium respuerēt, qui solus libertatis verè author est. Imò dum hunc nolunt admittere, impostoribus prædafiunt, qui dum inanibus promissis spem libertatis illis faciunt, & miseris turbarum & sedi tionum quotidie nouarum authores essent, tandem excidiū toti genti adduxerunt, quo nihil tristi-
units.tr: In the present passage one can see what the condition is of a people who once lost their liberty or surrendered it of their own accord. The Jews were once free, as being God's own possession. But ungrateful for so great a benefit, they summoned kings for themselves, under whom they suffered many things from which they could have been exempt, had they kept the form of commonwealth given to them by God. At length, when the ambition of the priests had progressed so far that they too aspired to the kingdom, and the unhappy nation was torn into factions on account of Hyrcanus and Aristobulus, and each side sought foreign help, it came about on that occasion that the Romans subdued Judea, and first set over it as king Herod, a man of Idumaean stock; afterwards, however, that land was reduced to a province and they sent governors into it. How many harsh and unjust things they suffered under these, there is no need to say. Those men certainly levied tribute and stationed garrisons throughout the cities. From that time the wretched people labored much for the restoration of liberty, and they acknowledged that it was a sign of God's having estranged himself from them that they were compelled to render tribute to Caesar. But they attempted many things in vain, since they rejected the Son of God, who alone is the true author of liberty. Indeed, while they were unwilling to admit him, they fell prey to impostors, who, while they held out to them empty promises of liberty, and were daily the authors of miserable tumults and seditions, at last brought destruction upon the whole nation, than which the world has seen nothing sadder and more cruel.

units.la: Quæstio de censu Cæsari soluendo. us & crudelius orbis terrarum vidit. Et huius generis multa alijs quoq; gentibus accidisse legimus, Lacedaemonijs nimirum, Graecis & Romanis ipsis. In horum consideratione diligenter vos versari conuenit viri Germani, ne Pontificum ambitione vos quoq; & communem patriam in partes distrahi & motibus periculosis turbari sinatis. Tuemini potius libertatem maiorum sanguine partam, & in primis Dei filium IESVM CHRISTVM ampleftimini, qui in se credentes in libertatem veram vindicat. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: The question of paying tribute to Caesar. And we read that many things of this kind happened to other peoples too, namely to the Lacedaemonians, the Greeks, and the Romans themselves. It is fitting that you, men of Germany, should diligently occupy yourselves with the consideration of these things, lest by the ambition of the Pontiffs you also allow yourselves and our common fatherland to be torn into factions and thrown into dangerous commotions. Rather defend the liberty won by the blood of your ancestors, and above all embrace Jesus Christ, the Son of God, who sets free in true liberty those who believe in him. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCLVII.
units.tr: HOMILY 257.

units.la: Cognita autem IESVS eorum malitia ait: Quid me tentatis hypocritae? Ostendite mihi numisma census. Ipsi vero obtulerunt ei denarium. Tunc dicit eis cuius est imago ista & inscriptio? Dicunt ei, Caesaris. Tunc dicit eis: Reddite ergo quae sunt Caesaris, Caesari: & quae sunt Dei, Deo. Cum igitur hoc audissent, mirati sunt: & omisso eo abierunt.
units.tr: When Jesus perceived their wickedness, he said: "Why do you test me, you hypocrites? Show me the coin of the census." And they brought him a denarius. Then he said to them: "Whose image and inscription is this?" They said to him: "Caesar's." Then he said to them: "Render therefore to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's." When they heard this, they marvelled, and leaving him, they went away.

units.la: Quamuis Dei Filius, Dominus & Seruator noster IESVS CHRISTVS diserte fatetur regnum suum non esse de hoc mundo, & suos discipulos hortetur, ut reliquis terrenis studijs in ipso caelestia & aeterna quaerant, plerique tamen terrenis intenti caelestia vel omnino negligunt, vel (quod peius est) du sub religionis praetextu immunitatem & priuata commoda quaerunt, fere tur bas dant no necessarias. Et haec multis causa est, ut cum aeternis bonis huius quoq; seculi commoda & pace amittat. Factum est hoc in Iudaeis. Habebat hi promissiones de Messia, de quo prophetae vaticinati erant, quod iugo oneris & virga exactoris confracturus, & regnum suum a mari ad mare pa-gaturus esset, sub quo ipsi laeta pace securi fruerentur. Haec cum illi secundum litera intelligeret, regnum terrenum, victorijs & opibus florens somniabant. Quae causa fuit, quod IESVM pro Messia non possent agnoscere, & insuper indignius ferrent Rom. imperij iugu, & pro libertate, qua ipsi turpiter prodiderant, subinde tumultuarentur, id quod ipsis tandem exitiu peperit. Ex hoc fonte etiam quaestio ista manauit, qua nuper Pharisaei Christum insidiose aggressi sunt, Num liceat ipsis, qui Dei peculium sint censum dare Caesari? Estq; quaestio haec plane similis quaestionibus, quas hodie multi, quos sua intemperantia ad inopiam redegit, ut praedia & agros suos oppignerarint, seditiose mouent de decimis & annuis redditibus. Qui cum nostro seculo etiam turbas dederint, & hoc nomine Euangelium multis suspectum fit, diligentius videre oportet quid hic responderit Dominus.
units.tr: Although the Son of God, our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, plainly declares that his kingdom is not of this world, and urges his disciples to seek heavenly and eternal things in him while disregarding other earthly pursuits, many nevertheless, intent on earthly things, either neglect heavenly things altogether or (what is worse) seek exemption and private advantages under the pretext of religion, and often stir up unnecessary disturbances. This is often the reason why people lose the temporal benefits and peace of this age along with the eternal goods. This happened among the Jews. They had promises about the Messiah, of whom the prophets had prophesied, that he would break the yoke of burden and the rod of the taskmaster, and would pacify his kingdom from sea to sea, under which they themselves would enjoy happy peace in security. Since they understood these things literally, they dreamed of an earthly kingdom flourishing with victories and wealth. This was the reason why they could not recognise Jesus as the Messiah, and why they bore the yoke of the Roman empire with greater indignation, and kept raising tumults for a liberty which they had shamefully betrayed themselves, a thing which in the end brought them destruction. From this same source arose the question with which the Pharisees recently approached Christ with guile: whether it was lawful for them, who are God's own people, to pay the census to Caesar. This question is plainly similar to those which many today raise seditiously concerning tithes and annual dues, people whom their own intemperance has reduced to poverty, so that they have pledged their estates and fields. Since these people have caused disturbances in our own age too, and the Gospel is for this reason suspected by many, we must look more carefully at how the Lord answered here.

units.la: Principio ab acri correptione orditur, dicens: Quid me tentatis hypocritae? Hypocritas dicit, quod religionis & gloriae Dei studium simularent, cum nihil huius ipsis cordi esset. Deinde quod ipsi tentent, id est, insidiose secum agant, accusat: Quod viros bonos nequaquam decet. Et ne temere illos corripuisse putetur, causam praemittit Mat. quod cognita ipsorum malitia, sic illos copellarit. Est autem hoc nouum diuinitatis Christi argumentum, quo eu xapδ'ioywoσvu esse apparet, qui corda & horum cogitationes scrutetur, & cognitas habeat. Quod solius Dei est, res ipsa loquitur. Quis n. nouit ea quae sunt hominis, id est, quae homo intra cor aut animum fuerit versat aut meditatur, nisi spiritus hominis, id est, mens ipsa intelligendi facultate praedita? Deinde Deus, qui hanc facultatem menti hominis solus dat? Testatur hoc ipse apud Iere. dicens: Vafrum cor hominis super omnia & inscrutabile: quis cognoscet illud? Ego Dominus & cor perscrutor & renes exploro, ut reddam cuique secundum viam suam. At Christi corda & horum cogitationes nouisse, no hoc solum exemplo constat, sed multis alijs, quae Euangelica historia nobis proponit. Quis ergo de illius diuinitate dubitet?
units.tr: First he begins with a sharp rebuke, saying: "Why do you test me, you hypocrites?" He calls them hypocrites because they pretended a zeal for religion and the glory of God, when nothing of this was in their hearts. Then he accuses them of testing him, that is, of dealing with him deceitfully, which good men should never do. And lest it be thought that he rebuked them rashly, Matthew first states the reason: that, having perceived their wickedness, he addressed them thus. This is a new argument for the divinity of Christ, by which he appears to be a knower of hearts [καρδιογνώστης], who searches the hearts and thoughts of these men and knows them. The matter itself shows that this belongs to God alone. For who knows the things of a man, that is, what a man turns over or meditates within his heart or mind, except the spirit of man, that is, the mind itself endowed with the faculty of understanding? And then, God, who alone gives this faculty to the mind of man? He himself testifies to this in Jeremiah, saying: "The heart of man is deceitful above all things and unsearchable: who can know it? I, the Lord, search the heart and test the reins, to give to each according to his way." That Christ knew the hearts and thoughts of men is established not only by this example but by many others which the Gospel history sets before us. Who, then, could doubt his divinity?

units.la: Debemus aut de eo frequenter cogitare, ut primo ex eo consolatione petamus aduersus hostium cosilia & machinationes. Sunt filij huius seculi prudentiores in generatione sua, quam filij lucis. Possunt ergo consilia & dolos atq; insidias, quas Christi feruis struunt, mirifice occultare. Et Daniel Antichristo oculos hominis, id est, perspicace astutia & calliditate in rebus agendis tribuit. Sed agat ille ut velit, et profundo licet astu crudeles hypocritae retia & laqueos suos abscondat, non potest tamen Christi oculos fallere, qui prolfraele excubat, neq; vnqua dormitat. Solet aut hic reuelare quaecunq; in Ecclesia sua permittit fruuntur, et se hoc facere velle no obscure pollicetur, cu ait: Nihil est opertu, quod no retegatur, et nihil occultu, quod no futurum fit ut cognoscatur. Nunqua ergo potestate impij astutia sua causa Christi et ecclesiae eius circuenire aut opprimere, quo minus hic cosilia illorum deprehendat et dissipet. Exempla, quibus hoc confirmetur, passim occurrunt: & nostro sa culo multa memorabilia vidimus, quæ si obseruentur, non sinent nos de Dei erga Ecclesiam cura & plus quàm paterna prouidentia dubitare.
units.tr: We ought to think often about him, so that first we may seek from him comfort against the plans and schemes of our enemies. The sons of this age are more prudent in their generation than the sons of light. They can therefore conceal wonderfully the plans, deceits and snares which they devise against the servants of Christ. And Daniel attributes to the Antichrist the eyes of a man, that is, keen cunning and craftiness in carrying out affairs. But let him act as he wills, and let the cruel hypocrites hide their nets and snares under whatever deep cunning they like; yet they cannot deceive the eyes of Christ, who keeps watch over Israel and never sleeps. He is accustomed to reveal whatever he allows to be done in his Church, and he does not obscurely promise that he wishes to do this, when he says: "Nothing is covered that will not be uncovered, and nothing hidden that will not be known." Therefore the impious can never, by their cunning, circumvent or oppress the cause of Christ and his Church, so long as he does not detect and scatter their plans here. Examples confirming this occur everywhere, and in our own age we have seen many memorable things which, if they are observed, will not allow us to doubt God's care for the Church and his more than paternal providence.

units.la: At non minus institutioni seruire debet ista consideratio. Admonet enim ne cogitationibus no stris indulgeamus, vt nonnulli solent, quos hæc fiducia dementat, quòd cogitationes liberas & im munes esse dicunt. At hi nihil homine altius de Deo sentiunt. Fabulantur Poetæ Momũ olim in humani corporis fabrica reprehendisse, quòd pectori non addita fuisset fenestra, per quam cordium arcana & cogitationes possent inspici. Atqui illa minimè opus est, cum Deo illæ pateant, qui quo ties ita opus est, & vel ipsius gloria vel suorum electorum salus id exigit, illas in lucem produce re, & omnibus manifestare potest. Imò frequenter fit, vt ipsimet impudenter effutiamus cum præ senti periculo quæ celata volumus. Meminerimus ergo semper, nos in Dei conspectu versari, qui omnia nouit, & cui de cogitationibus quoq; prauis aut obscænis nos aliquando rationem reddere o portebit. Est hoc compendium ad pietatem certissimum. Qui enim hoc sibi persuasum habent, ij multò magis linguas frænabunt, ne quid incautius loquantur, & cupiditates coercebunt, ne quan do ab eis superentur. Nobis ipsis ergo semper occinamus illud Dauidis: Quò discedam a spiritu tuo? & quò a facie tua fugiam? Domine, &c. Psal. 139.
units.tr: But this consideration ought to serve instruction no less. For it warns us not to indulge our thoughts, as some are wont to do, whom this confidence drives mad, saying that their thoughts are free and immune. But such people think nothing of God that is higher than man. The poets fable that Momus once found fault with the structure of the human body, because no window had been added to the breast through which the secrets of hearts and thoughts could be inspected. Yet such a window is by no means necessary, since these lie open to God, who, whenever it is needful, and the glory of himself or the salvation of his elect requires it, can bring them into the light and make them manifest to all. Indeed it often happens that we ourselves, to our present peril, shamelessly blurt out what we want to keep hidden. Let us therefore always remember that we live in the sight of God, who knows all things, and to whom we shall one day have to give an account even of wicked or obscene thoughts. This is a most certain summary of piety. For those who have this persuaded in themselves will far more restrain their tongues, lest they say anything too carelessly, and will curb their desires, lest at some time they be overcome by them. Let us therefore always sing to ourselves that saying of David: "Where shall I go from your spirit? And where shall I flee from your face? Lord, etc." Ps. 139.

units.la: Præterea docet exemplo suo Christus, quomodo cum hostibus veritatis ipsi quoq; agere debea mus. Nobis quidem impossibile est, vt in omnium arcana consilia penetremus, aut intelligamus quid quisq; in animo habeat. Attamen cautos & prouidos esse decet, vt sicuti Christus alibi monet, memores nobis cum hominibus rem esse, qui natura vafri & mali sunt, nobis ab illis caueamus. Deum item precemur, vt hic impiorum hostium consilia detegat, aut dissipet: nostra autem consi lia & deliberationes regat ad sui nominis gloriam. Accedat his animi fortitudo, vt cognitos do los & insidias impiorũ arguamus, & publicè testemur illos & conatus ipsorũ nobis displicere. Ni si id fiat, illi quotidie audaciores fiunt, dum aut malitiam suam adhuc occultam esse, aut se a nobis metui sibi persuadent. Exempla sunt quæ hic nos officij admonere possunt: & multum in eo peccat pij, dum alios ex seipsis æstimant, & ideo clementius aut indulgentius agunt cum ijs, qui durius tractari merebantur. Certè hic præstabat istos hypocritas dici, ne vulgus sanctitatis ipsorum fuca tæ existimatione falleretur: ita prodest omnibus laruam detrahi, qui veritati non sine publico scandalo aduersantur.
units.tr: Moreover, Christ teaches by his example how we too ought to act towards the enemies of the truth. For us it is indeed impossible to penetrate into the secret counsels of all men, or to understand what each one has in mind. Yet it is proper to be cautious and wise, so that, as Christ warns elsewhere, mindful that we have to do with men who by nature are crafty and evil, we may beware of them. Let us likewise pray God that he will detect and scatter the plans of the impious enemies, and direct our own plans and deliberations to the glory of his name. Let courage of spirit be added, so that we may expose the deceits and snares of the impious when we have recognised them, and publicly bear witness that we dislike them and their attempts. Unless this is done, they become bolder every day, persuading themselves either that their malice is still hidden, or that they are feared by us. There are examples here which can remind us of our duty, and the pious sin greatly in this, when they judge others by themselves and therefore act more mildly or indulgently towards those who deserved to be treated more harshly. Certainly here it was better that these men be called hypocrites, lest the common people be deceived by the opinion of their holiness, which was a pretence; so it benefits everyone that the mask be torn away from those who oppose the truth not without public scandal.

units.la: Cæterum vt isti dolo malo Christum tentarunt, & quæstione captiosa illum illaqueare cona ti sunt: sic Christus, vt ex ipsorum ore responsum eliciat, quo simpliciores absq; scandalo edocean tur, quid in hac causa sentire & facere debeant, hypocritæ autem isti proprio laqueo capiantur, iu bet sibi monstrari numisma census, id est, monetam eam, quæ in censu numerari solebat. Credibile enim est, Romanos præsides a Iudæis non aliam monetam accepisse, quàm quæ Romanũ in vsu erat. Et hæc causa fuit, quòd Christo denarium offerunt, quales Romanis in vsu fuisse scimus. Hoc viso quærit Dominus de imagine & inscriptione, cuius nimirum ea sit. Est enim hic vetus mos, quòd principum aut vrbium imagines & insignia monetæ imponuntur. Facit hoc ad æsti mationem monetæ, etsi hæc iusta sit & integra, authoritatem Magistratibus conciliat. Non imme ritò igitur viri boni & prudentes de nostri seculi moribus conqueruntur, quando eò vsq; progressa est quæstus cupido, vt Magistratus quosdam non pudeat ius suum, quo gloriantur, hominibus pri uatis locare, qui publicam monetam cudendo lucrum quærunt. Qui id faciunt, ij nec suæ existima tioni consulunt, nec Reip. & populi commodis prospiciunt. Sed vt in historia præsenti pergamus, respondent illi quod res est, inscriptionem hanc denarij Cæsaris esse. Ad quod Christus infert: Reddite ergo quæ sunt Cæsaris, Cæsari, & quæ sunt Dei, Deo. Quasi diceret: Cùm ipsi fateami ni vos Cæsaris moneta vti, simul testemini oportet, vos eius imperio esse subiectos. Reddite ergo Cæsari quæcunq; huic debentur. Neq; hoc cuiquam debet iniquum videri, quòd Dei populus sitis, & huius sacerdotale regnum. Nam quia Deus regna & imperia transfert, & hic vobis Cæsarem imposuit iusto iudicio, non obstat hoc, quò minus Deo quoq; reddatis, quod huic debetur.
units.tr: But just as those men tempted Christ with malicious intent and tried to ensnare him with a captious question, so Christ, in order to draw from their own mouths an answer by which the simpler folk might be taught without scandal what they ought to think and do in this matter, while those hypocrites are caught in their own snare, bids them show him the coin of the census, that is, the money which was customarily paid in the tax. For it is credible that the Roman governors had received from the Jews no other money than what was in use among the Romans. And this was the reason why they offered Christ a denarius, such as we know was in use among the Romans. Seeing this, the Lord asks whose image and inscription it bears. For it is an ancient custom that the images and emblems of princes or cities are stamped upon money. This contributes to the esteem of the currency, and even if the currency is just and sound, it lends authority to the magistrates. Therefore good and prudent men of our age have not unjustly complained about the morals of our time, when the greed for gain has advanced so far that some magistrates are not ashamed to lease out to private persons, who seek profit by minting the public coinage, the right of which they boast. Those who do this consult neither their own reputation nor provide for the advantage of the commonwealth and the people. But to proceed with the present narrative: they answer what is the case, that this inscription is of Caesar's denarius. To which Christ adds: "Render therefore to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's." As if he said: Since you yourselves admit that you use Caesar's money, you must at the same time bear witness that you are subject to his rule. Render therefore to Caesar whatever is owed to him. Nor should it seem unfair to anyone that you are God's people and that his kingdom is priestly. For since God transfers kingdoms and empires, and by his just judgment has set Caesar over you, this does not prevent you from rendering to God also what is owed to him.

units.la: In quo responso multa obseruatione dignum est, quòd inter Cæsarem & Deum distinguit Dominus, & vtriq; reddere iubet quod ei debemus. Non tollit ergo aut abolet Respublicas, aut leges politicas, vel obedientia, quae Magistratibus debetur. Olim quidem Donatistae nominus quàm Iudaeorum Pharisaei, iniquum & iniustum esse clamabant, Imperatore Rom. & huius praesides ius & imperium habere in homines Christianos, quos sanguinis sui pretio redemptos sibi consecravit Dei filius. At horum spiritu agitati Anabaptistae eosdem furores in Ecclesia inuehunt hodie. Sed sufficit his confutandis hic locus, quem generali sensu accipi debere res ipsa loquitur. De Caesare hic quaeritur, quia Iudaei tunc Caesari subiecti erant. Quod igitur de Caesare dicitur, hoc ipsum ad Magistratus omnes pertinet, qui in Repub. quaevis dominantur. Etenim non est aliqua potestas, quae non ex Deo sit. Nō poterit ergo illi obedientia negari, quin iniuria ad Deū redundet. Nō est quòd de iniquitate principū durisq; eorū imperijs quiritemur. Quod enim Petrus iubet, vt serui heris nō solis mansuetis, verùm etiā morosis ac difficilibus obediat, hoc ipsum ad Magistratus quoq; pertinet. Itaq; Apostolus dicebat: Reddite omnibus quod debetis: cui tributum debetur, tributum, &c. Rom. 13.
units.tr: In this answer it is worth noting with great care that the Lord distinguishes between Caesar and God, and bids us render to each what we owe them. He therefore does not take away or abolish commonwealths, or political laws, or the obedience that is owed to magistrates. Long ago indeed the Donatists, no less than the Pharisees of the Jews, cried out that it was wrong and unjust for the Roman emperor and his governors to have right and rule over Christian men, whom the Son of God had consecrated to himself, redeemed by the price of his blood. And the Anabaptists, stirred by the same spirit, bring these same frenzies into the Church today. But this passage is sufficient to refute them, and the matter itself shows that it must be taken in a general sense. Here the question concerns Caesar, because the Jews were then subject to Caesar. Therefore what is said of Caesar pertains to all magistrates who rule in any commonwealth. For there is no power that is not from God. Obedience therefore cannot be denied to them without the injury redounding to God. We have no cause to complain about the wickedness of princes or their harsh commands. For what Peter bids, that servants obey their masters not only when they are gentle but also when they are harsh and difficult, this same thing pertains to magistrates as well. Hence the Apostle said: "Render to all what you owe: tribute to whom tribute is owed, etc." Rom. 13.

units.la: Vt vero Magistratui, cuiuscunq; generis aut ordinis ille sit, obsequium omne debetur: ita inter subditos nemo sibi immunitatem vendicet, quasi propter vitae genus, opes, religionem, virtutes aut alia quae excogitari possunt personarum discrimina, a publicis oneribus exemptus esse debeat. Nam idem Apostolus dicit: Omnis anima potestatibus supereminentibus subiecta est. Universalis est pro positio ista, & anima nominat, quae potior ac praestantior hominis pars est, vt de animae etiam salute hic agi doceat, & ijs os obturet, qui propter spiritualia ministeria sub Ecclesiastici nominis praetextu immunes censeri volunt. Quis enim hoc priuilegio se dignum dicere poterit, qui audit Dei Filium sub censu nasci voluisse, & postea cum Messiae munus aliquandiu publice obiuisset pro ipso & Petro didrachma soluisse audit? Chrysostomus certè Pauli dictū non veritus est ita interpretari, vt monachos quoq; & sacerdotes potestatibus aut imperijs subditos esse velit. Imò sic infert: Siue Apostolus fuerit, siue Euangelista, siue Propheta, aut quisquis tandem fueris, Magistratui subiacere debes. Nec enim subiectio ista pietate euertit. At subiectionis species atq; certissimum indicium est tributorum & vectigalium, & omnium quae Reipub. nomine exiguntur & soluunturconributio. Ergo ab his nemo immunis esse poterit, nisi etiam a Repub. & communium legum atq; bonorum societate & vsu velit excludi. Poetae tradunt Herculē olim ab Argonautis relictum esse, quòd propter egregiè factorum gloriā elatus nollet communes labores in naui cum aliis subire. Cur ergo in Repub. ferantur, qui communia onera cum alijs nolunt ferre? Vide Arist. 3. polit. cap. 9.
units.tr: But just as all obedience is owed to the magistrate, of whatever kind or rank he may be, so no one among the subjects should claim immunity for himself, as if, on account of his way of life, wealth, religion, virtues, or other distinctions of persons that can be imagined, he ought to be exempt from public burdens. For the same Apostle says: "Every soul is subject to the higher powers." This proposition is universal, and it names the soul, which is the nobler and more excellent part of man, so that he teaches that the salvation of the soul is also at issue here, and it stops the mouths of those who, under the pretext of the name of the Church, wish to be deemed immune on account of spiritual ministries. For who will be able to say he is worthy of this privilege, who hears that the Son of God was willing to be born under the census, and afterwards, when he had for some time publicly performed the office of the Messiah, is heard to have paid the didrachma for himself and Peter? Chrysostom certainly did not hesitate to interpret Paul's saying in such a way as to wish that monks and priests also be subject to powers and rulers. Indeed he concludes thus: Whether you be an Apostle, or an Evangelist, or a Prophet, or whoever you may be, you ought to be subject to the magistrate. For such subjection does not overthrow piety. Now the form and most certain sign of subjection is tributes and taxes, and all the contributions that are demanded and paid in the name of the commonwealth. Therefore no one can be exempt from these, unless he also wishes to be excluded from the commonwealth and from the fellowship and use of common laws and goods. The poets tell that Hercules was once left behind by the Argonauts, because, puffed up by the glory of his outstanding deeds, he refused to undergo common labours with the others in the ship. Why then should those be tolerated in the commonwealth who are unwilling to bear common burdens with others? See Aristotle, Politics 3, chap. 9.

units.la: At quia Christus inter Caesarem & Deum distinguit, & quod vtriq; debetur, reddere iubet, non obscure nos admonet, ne officia ista confundamus. Fit hoc, si quod Deo debetur, hominibus velimus praestare & contrà. Magistratibus debemus honorē & reverentiā, cum nobis parentum loco sint. Cauendum ergo, ne qua contumelia afficiantur, adeò vt ne vitia eorum odiosè & cū contemptu notemus. Qui id faciunt, Chami similes sunt, qui patri ebrio & turpiter denudato insultabat, & ideo in maledictionem incidit. Debemus ite magistratibus dilectione, quae vt ipsis bene precemur, iubet, & ipsos apud Deū pijs votis iuuemus. Vtrūq; aut frigebit, nisi obedientia & omni obsequiorū genere testemur, nos illos ex animo reuereri ac diligere. Rursus Deo nos totos debemus quoad corpus & animā, cū vtrumq; ab illo acceperimus, & totos nos sibi ille vendicat, cū dicit: Diliges Dominum Deū tuum ex toto corde tuo. Huc pertinet fides & cordis fiducia, quae in vno Deo nobis repositā esse debet per vnum Mediatorē IESVM CHRISTVM. Fides cultū parit, qui in spiritu & veritate illi exhiberi debet secundū verbi sui praescriptū. In cultu requiritur confessio fidei, ne nos huius pudeat. Huius partes sunt Inuocatio solius Dei, & Iusiurandū, quod in illius solius nomine debet concipi. Sic enim ille de noui testamenti Ecclesia & credentibus loquitur apud Isaiā: Quisquis benedixerit sibi in terra, benedicet sibi in Deo vero: & quisquis iurauerit in terra, iurabit in Deo vero. Deniq; Deo fidei obedientia debetur, ex qua obedientia & sanctitas vitae nascitur, quae in eo consistit, vt nos ipsi sistamus viuentem hostiam, neq; nobisipsis, sed illi viuamus, qui pro nobis mortuus est & resurrexit. Haec omnia Deo ita praestari debent, vt ea in nullius hominis, ne Caesaris quidē & summi magistratus gratiā omittantur, aut aliter fiant, quàm ipse iubet. Qui enim in aliquo horum cessant, aut hominibus gratificando aliter agunt, ij Caesari reddunt, quae Dei sunt, & huic debitam fidē fallunt. Sunt ergo indigni, quibus fides habeatur. Quis enim hominibus fidelis fore speret eos, qui Deo debita officia negat? Nunquā ergo excidat, ita parendū esse magistratibus, vt tamē Deo potius obedire oporteat, qui sumus in nos ius habet. Intellexerūt hoc Apostoli qui cum in nomine Christi porro praedicare prohiberentur, responderunt: Oportet Deo potius obedire quam hominibus. Eadem mens fuit sanctorum martyrum, si quando idolis thura adolere, aut sacrificiis Deorum alienorum aliare, vel per fortunam Caesaris iurare iubebantur. Putarunt enim se Deo vero magnam iniuriam facturos, si tyrannis obedirent. Horum exempla nos imitari conuenit, neq; eos audire, qui religionis causam regibus subiiciunt, & clamant, simpliciter his obediendum esse. Nam si haec sententia admittatur, iam damnandi erunt cum Prophetis & Apostolis omnes martyres, qui fidem suam sanguine suo confirmarunt. Neq; moueant nos calumniae eorum, qui nos Magistratibus seditionis reos esse clamant. Non enim rebellis dici potest, qui quod Deo debetur, reddit: Impius autem & Dei hostis dici meretur, qui non contentus iis, quae populus ipsi debet, insuper sibi ea quoq; vendicat, quae diuini iuris sunt: Et facile est Deo ius suum vindicare aduersus iniusmodi homines, ut in suis consiliis pudefiant.
units.tr: But because Christ distinguishes between Caesar and God, and bids us render to each what is owed to it, he admonishes us not obscurely that we should not confuse these duties. This happens if we wish to render to men what is owed to God, and the reverse. We owe magistrates honour and reverence, since they stand in the place of parents. We must take care, therefore, that they be not treated with any insult, so much so that we do not note their vices in a hateful and contemptuous way. Those who do this are like Ham, who mocked his drunken father, shamefully uncovered, and for that reason fell under the curse. We owe magistrates love, which bids us pray well for them and support them with pious vows before God. Both of these will grow cold unless we bear witness, by obedience and every kind of service, that we revere and love them from the heart. Again, we owe ourselves wholly to God, both in body and soul, since we have received both from him, and he claims us wholly for himself when he says: "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart." To this pertains faith and the trust of the heart, which ought to be placed in the one God alone through the one Mediator, Jesus Christ. Faith produces worship, which must be offered to him in spirit and truth according to his own prescribed word. In worship is required the confession of faith, lest we be ashamed of it. Parts of this are the invocation of God alone, and the oath, which ought to be made in the name of him alone. For thus he speaks of the church of the New Testament and of believers in Isaiah: "Whoever blesses himself in the earth shall bless himself in the true God, and whoever swears in the earth shall swear by the true God." Finally, obedience is owed to God through faith, and from this obedience the holiness of life is born, which consists in our presenting ourselves as a living sacrifice, and living not to ourselves but to him who died and rose again for us. All these things must be rendered to God in such a way that they are omitted for the sake of no man, not even Caesar or the highest magistrate, nor done otherwise than he himself commands. For those who fall short in any of these, or who act otherwise to please men, render to Caesar what is God's and betray the faith owed to God. They are therefore unworthy to be trusted. For who would hope that a man will be faithful to men, who denies to God the duties owed him? Let it never escape us, then, that magistrates must be obeyed in such a way that nevertheless we ought rather to obey God, who has right over us. The Apostles understood this, who, when they were forbidden to preach further in the name of Christ, answered: "We ought to obey God rather than men." The same mind was in the holy martyrs, when they were commanded to burn incense to idols, to sacrifice to the gods of others, or to swear by the fortune of Caesar. For they thought they would do great injury to the true God if they obeyed tyrants. It is fitting for us to imitate their examples, and not to listen to those who make religion subject to kings and cry out that one must simply obey them. For if this opinion were admitted, then all martyrs who confirmed their faith with their blood would have to be condemned along with the Prophets and Apostles. Nor let us be moved by the slanders of those who cry out that we are guilty of sedition against the magistrates. For he who renders what is owed to God cannot be called rebellious. Rather, he deserves to be called impious and an enemy of God who, not content with what the people owe him, claims for himself also those things which belong to divine right. And it is easy for God to vindicate his right against such men, so that they are put to shame in their own counsels.

units.la: Apparet hoc in huius actionis catastrophe. Nam mirantur Christi responsum Pharisei & horum socij, nec habent quod illi opponant. Itaque omisso eo abeunt. Quis autem dubitet ex eo multum decessisse ipsorum existimationi, multos etiam eorum, qui isti colloquio interfuerunt, infidesfuisse confirmatos? Solet hoc semper fieri, ut sibi ipsis incommodent, quotquot cum Deo luctari audent. Itaq; dum hodie passim grassatur tyrannorum rabies, nos quantum in nobis est, pacem colamus cum omnibus hominibus, Magistratibus quoq; gratificemur, quantum salua fide & religione poterit fieri. At si ea petantur, quae Filij Dei sunt, qui nos redemit & sibi consecrauit, confitentes simus in eius fide & cultu, ut olim nos pro suis agnoscat, quando in gloria Patris sui cum Angelis suis sanctis veniet ad iudicandum viuos & mortuos. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: This is evident from the outcome of this affair. For the Pharisees and their companions marvel at Christ's answer and have nothing to set against it; so, leaving that aside, they go away. Who would doubt that by this their reputation greatly declined, and that many of those who were present at that conversation were confirmed in unbelief? This always happens to those who dare to wrestle with God: they bring harm upon themselves. Therefore, although today the rage of tyrants rages everywhere, let us, so far as lies in us, cultivate peace with all men, and let us also please the magistrates as far as this can be done with faith and religion preserved. But if those things are sought which belong to the Sons of God, who has redeemed us and consecrated us to himself, let us confess him in his faith and worship, so that he may one day acknowledge us as his own, when he comes in the glory of his Father with his holy angels to judge the living and the dead. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCLVIII.
units.tr: Homily 258.

units.la: In illo die adierunt eum Sadducaei, qui dicunt non esse resurrectionem, & interrogarunt eum dicentes: Magister, Moses dixit, si quis mortuus fuerit non habens filios, eius frater ducet affinitatis iure uxorem eius, & suscitabit semen fratri suo. Fuerunt autem apud nos septem fratres: & primus uxore ducta obijt: & cum non haberet semen reliquit uxorem fratri suo: similiter etiam secundus & tertius usque ad illos septem. Post omnes autem obijt & mulier. In resurrectione ergo cuius e septem erit uxor? Omnes enim habuerunt eam.
units.tr: On that day the Sadducees, who say there is no resurrection, came to him and asked him, saying: "Teacher, Moses said that if a man dies without children, his brother shall take his wife by the right of kinship and raise up seed for his brother. Now there were seven brothers among us. The first took a wife and died, and having no seed, he left his wife to his brother. Likewise the second and the third, down to the seventh. Last of all the woman also died. In the resurrection, then, whose wife will she be of the seven? For they all had her."

units.la: ET si Dominus noster IESVS CHRISTVS Pharisaeorum discipulis, qui vna cum Herodianis aliquot subornati erant, ut insidiosa quaestione de censu Caesari dando ipsum tentarent, ita responderit, ut eius sapientiam omnes admirati sint, aduersarij autem confusi discesserint, nec habuerunt quod amplius illi opponerent, non tamen quiescunt, hi, sed mox alij adsunt, qui eodem animi proposito nouam illi quaestionem mouent de resurrectione: nimirum ut coram populo illius auctoritatem eleuent, & in contemptum adducant. Est autem nobis in Christi persona consideranda electorum aut filiorum Dei fors, quae ipsis sustinenda est, quoad in terris vixerint: non melior nimirum, quam nostri praeceptoris & Domini fuit. Huic primus insidiati sunt Pharisaei hypocritae, qui sibi doctrinae & sanctitatis existimationem vendicabant. Nunc succedunt hus Sadducaei, homines prophani & Epicureorum similes, quibus lusus & iocus erat, quicquid de religione tradebatur: sicuti ex quaestione, quam in praesenti mouent, apparet. Caeterum ut primum Pharisaeorum ora obturauit, ita nunc ipsos quoq; confutat, ut omnibus ridiculi fiant, qui ipsum volebant vulgi ludibrijs exponere. Itaq; exemplo Christi excitati, nos ad certamina praeparemus, ut qualescunq; sint, qui nos aggrediuntur, ad resistendum parati simus, & fidei puritatem constanter retineamus. Quia ad tem hic de resurrectione mortuorum agitur, sine qua salus nostra & huius spes consistere non potest, non pigeat singulas huius colloquij partes penitius inspicere.
units.tr: Although our Lord Jesus Christ answered the disciples of the Pharisees, who had been put up together with some of the Herodians to test him with a tricky question about paying the tax to Caesar, in such a way that everyone marvelled at his wisdom and his opponents went away confounded, having nothing more to put to him, these men did not rest. Soon others came forward with the same intent and raised a new question to him about the resurrection, clearly so that they might lower his authority in the eyes of the people and bring him into contempt. In the person of Christ we must consider the lot that falls to the elect or the sons of God, which they must endure as long as they live on earth. It is surely no better than that of our teacher and Lord. The hypocritical Pharisees first laid snares for him; they claimed for themselves a reputation for learning and holiness. Now the Sadducees, profane men resembling the Epicureans, succeed them. For them everything that was taught about religion was a game and a joke, as is plain from the question they now raise. Yet as soon as he had silenced the mouths of the Pharisees, he now refutes these men too, so that all who wanted to expose him to the mockery of the crowd become ridiculous. Therefore, roused by the example of Christ, let us prepare ourselves for conflicts, so that whatever sort of men attack us, we may be ready to resist and keep the purity of the faith steadfast. Since the question here concerns the resurrection of the dead, without which our salvation and hope cannot stand, let us not hesitate to examine each part of this conversation more closely.

units.la: Primo aduersarij, quos Christus habuit, nominantur. Fuerunt hi Sadducaei, qui illo ipso die quo Pharisaeos & Herodianos confutarat, illum aggressi sunt. Ex quo apparet, quanta sit impiorum, qui veritatis odium animis suis semel conceperunt pertinacia, & quod nullis exemplis moueantur, etiamsi sui similibus sociis infelicius rem cessisse videant. Quin imo non pudet eos aduersus Christum illis se coniungere, a quibus alias dissentiunt. Etenim Sadducaeos & Pharisaeos inter se ita dissentire ostendimus, ut apertae inter ipsos concertationes essent. Hi enim quoad vitam & mores sanctitatis & pietatis speciem se plerisque commendabant, & insuper scripturarum interpretes volebant videri, & de vita aeterna atque regno caelorum magnifice sentiebant, & huius deside-rium atque studium publice proficebantur. Sadducaei autem etsi a iustitia sibi nomen fecisse sent, ea tamen negabant impie, quibus ad illius studium efficacissime extimulantur homines, & quae si tollas, fructum quoque praecipuum pietatis & iustitiae sustuleris. Etenim vitam homini nullam praeter hanc, quae in hoc saeculo viuitur, propositam esse dicebant, futuram vero & aeternam prorsus ignorabant. Itaque animas vna cum corporibus mori affirmabant, corporum item resurrectionem sciuriter reijciebant. Praeterea spiritus neque bonos neque malos vllos esse docebant, quod non aliud erat, quam Deum quoque negare, neque credere diabolos esse, aduersus quorum insidias nos perpetuo vigilare Scripturae docent. At quid de scripturis dicere attinet, quando has quoque maxima ex parte reijciebant, cum filius Mosis libros reciperent, reliquos omnes profabulosis aut inutilibus commentis haberent? Ne vero execrationi essent ijs, qui iustitia & honestatis natura amantes sunt, de iustitia interim honorifice loquebantur, cui studere oportet homines nullius praemij alterius causa, quam quod sine illa nec Respublica consistere posset, nec praesens haec vita commode & tuto transigi. Ideo fere magnates & opulentiores ab illis pendebant & tandem inter Seniores populi primatum tenuerunt, vt ex Actorum libro apparet, vbi contra Apostolos insurrexisse scribitur Pontifex maximus, & omnes qui cum eo erant, & hanc fuisse sectam Sadducaeorum. Vide Actorum quintum Cap.
units.tr: First, the adversaries whom Christ had are named. They were the Sadducees, who attacked him on the very day on which he had refuted the Pharisees and Herodians. From this it appears how great is the obstinacy of the impious, who have once conceived hatred of the truth in their minds, and how they are moved by no examples, even when they see that men like themselves have fared less well. Indeed, they are not ashamed to join with those from whom they otherwise differ in opposing Christ. For we have shown that the Sadducees and Pharisees disagreed with each other so openly that there were plain contentions between them. The Pharisees commended themselves to most people by a show of holiness and piety in life and morals, and moreover wished to be seen as interpreters of the Scriptures; they thought highly of eternal life and the kingdom of heaven, and publicly professed their longing and zeal for these things. The Sadducees, though they had made a name for themselves by righteousness, impiously denied those things by which men are most effectively spurred on to that zeal, and if you take these away, you also remove the chief fruit of piety and righteousness. For they said that no life is set before man except this one that is lived in this age, and they were utterly ignorant of a future and eternal life. Hence they affirmed that souls die together with bodies, and they lightly rejected the resurrection of the bodies. Moreover, they taught that there were neither good nor bad spirits, which was nothing other than to deny God too, and not to believe that there are devils, against whose snares the Scriptures teach us to watch constantly. But why speak of the Scriptures, when they largely rejected them too, accepting only the books of the son of Moses and regarding all the rest as fables or useless inventions? Yet, lest they be hated by those who love justice and the nature of honesty, they spoke with respect of justice, which men ought to pursue for no reward other than that without it neither the commonwealth can stand nor this present life be carried on decently and safely. Therefore the magnates and the wealthier men mostly leaned towards them, and at last they held the chief place among the elders of the people, as appears from the book of Acts, where it is written that the high priest and all who were with him rose up against the apostles, and that this was the sect of the Sadducees. See Acts, chapter 5.

units.la: Docent autem haec quam infelix & corrupta tunc fuerit Iudaici populi conditio, quam tetra ite religionis & Ecclesiae facies inter eos qui Dei peculium & foli gens sancta dici volebant: quando Sadducaeis locus datus est, & his publice & tuto licuit omnia religionis & pietatis fundamenta negare & conuellere, soli Christo autem & eius Apostolis veritatem docere non licuit. Accusatur postea in Caelio Dominus, quod templum destruere voluerit, & idem crimen postea Stephano protomartyri obijcitur. Interim extra omne periculum liberae suas blasphemias euomunt, & in Caelio aut Synedrio praesident, qui caelos ipsos negant, & omnem templi spiritualis, vel Ecclesiae aeconomiam destruunt. Quia vero hos Pharisaei quoque ferunt & doctrinam de resurrectione mortuorum & animarum immortalitate, quam ipsi profitebantur, in Christo palam oppugnari passi sunt, eo indicio nimis aperte se prodiderunt, quales ipsi fuerint, qui verae religionis vindices videri volucrunt, qui huius zelo toti arderent. Enimuero si serius fuisset ille zelus, & regnu Dei ex animo quaesiuissent, a Sadducaeorum cofortio no minus quam a gentibus prophanis abhorruissent, cum deteriores essent multis, qui inter gentes sapientiae titulo comendantur, ex quibus pleriq; vitam aeternam, & animas siue mentes, post emigrationem ex corporis huius ergastulo beatas viuere crediderunt & confessi sunt, vt alibi ex Cicerone demonstrauimus. At nunc cum Sadducaeos in pretio habeat, publicis honoribus dignos iudicet, & in Christo oppugnando ijsdem vt socijs vtantur, quis non videat, illos simul omnes ab omni vera pietatis & religionis sensu alienissimos & plane pphanos neq; meliores fuisse Sadducaeis, qui gentes impietate superabat? Ide dici potest de plerisq;, qui hodie Euangelij doctrina & fideles Christi seruos persequuntur. Praetexunt gloriae Dei zelu, & Ecclesiae Christi in partes scindi et Dei cultu negligi ac prophanari acerbe queruntur. Interim ijdem facile fe-runt prophanos omnis religionis illusores, blasphemos ite, quiper Diuos caelites & ipsam virginem Mariam atq; omnia sacra horribiliter deierat, vt ia nihil dica de vsurarijs impostorib. raptorib. mi-litib. sanguinarijs, impuris scortatorib. maechis & incestis, & illicitarum libidinum sectatorib. quorum amicitia colunt, quos venerantur, filios Ecclesiae dilectos vocitant, dummodo in veritate oppugnanda suam operam ipsis conferant. Vera me dicere res ipsa docet. Etenim quis audiuit haftenus in vrbe Roma aut in Italia, vbi Episcopi & Cardinales dominantur, flammis exuri homines impios Blasphemos, qui dum temerè per Mariam Virginem & Filium eius IESVM CHRISTVM deierant & execrantur, illam quidem scortum, hunc vero spurium siue nothum Dei dicunt. Horreo totus ista referens, & Deum Optimum Maximum precor, ut mihi ignoscat, quod ista referam, quae pias aures offendere possunt. At certum est, tales voces illic quotidie inter ludentes etiam audiri, & quidem impune effundi. Si quis vero, Diuam Virginem ex Spiritu Sancto concepisse, & illa sa virginitate sua Filium Dei peperisse, qui ex ipsa homo natus sit, ut pro peccatis mundi sacrificium posset fieri, ut deniq; nostra effet satisfactio, iustitia & redemptio: is dignus putatur, qui haeretica praui tatis inquisitoribus traditus exquisitissimis tormentis extrucietur. Quis ergo istos homines serio fidem Christi profiteri, & pietatis sensu aliquo affici dicat? Nisi certe intra animos suos ipsi quoq;, ut olim Sadducaei sacra omnia cum ijs, quae de caelo & inferis pie credunt, riderent: nunquam certe tam impudenter sacra venalia haberent, neq; cum Scripturis & Verbo Dei tam scurriliter luderent, neque populi simplicitate tam improbe abuterentur, & per ludibrium bonos Christianos dicerent eos, quise ab ipsis decipi & expilari sinunt sub hoc emen-tita religionis praetextu: multo minus sanguinem innoxium funderent, proditionibus omnia misc erent, & orbem Christianum bellis exteris & ciuilibus turbarent. Adde, quod ijdem in suis vrbibus Iudaeos, iuratos Christi hostes, ferunt, quos olim Constantinus Imperator non veritus est πατροκτόνας ἢ κυριοκτόνας dicere, cum quibus ceu gente inuisissima, Christiani homines nihil commune habere debeant: hos illi Synagogas habere permittunt & coetus cogere, in quibus Christum & huius seruos diris horrendis deuouent. Hos (inquam) aliqui in pretio habent, his ut medicis & consiliarijs intimis vtuntur, quibus fortunas suas & salutem omnem committunt: qui interea in germanos Christi cultores ferro & igne grassantur. Nihil ergo hodie Christiani homines a Iudaeis, qui olim fuerunt, differunt: & idcirco non mirum est quod Deum nobis iratum sentimus, qui tam atroces iniurias, quae ipsi & feruis suis fiunt, omni genere supplicium ylcifcitur.
units.tr: These things teach how wretched and corrupt the condition of the Jewish people was at that time, and how foul the face of religion and the Church was among those who wished to be called God's special people and the only holy nation: when room was given to the Sadducees, and they were allowed publicly and safely to deny and overthrow all the foundations of religion and piety, while Christ and his apostles were not allowed to teach the truth. Afterwards the Lord was accused before the council of wishing to destroy the temple, and the same charge was later brought against Stephen, the first martyr. Meanwhile, these men, safe from all danger, spew forth their free blasphemies and preside in the council or the Sanhedrin, denying the very heavens and destroying the whole economy of the spiritual temple, or the Church. But since the Pharisees also tolerated the doctrine of the resurrection of the dead and the immortality of souls, which they themselves professed, and suffered it to be openly attacked in Christ, they betrayed themselves all too plainly by this sign: what sort of men they were, who wished to appear as defenders of true religion, and who were consumed with zeal for it. Indeed, if that zeal had been sincere, and they had sought the kingdom of God from the heart, they would have shrunk from fellowship with the Sadducees no less than from profane nations; for the Sadducees were worse than many who are commended among the nations for the title of wisdom, of whom many believed and confessed that souls or minds live blessed after their departure from the prison of this body, as we have shown elsewhere from Cicero. But now, when they hold the Sadducees in esteem, judge them worthy of public honours, and use them as allies in attacking Christ, who does not see that all of them were utterly alien to every true sense of piety and religion and altogether profane, and were no better than the Sadducees, whom the nations surpassed in impiety? The same can be said of many today who persecute the doctrine of the gospel and the faithful servants of Christ. They pretend zeal for the glory of God, and bitterly complain that the Church of Christ is torn into factions and that the worship of God is neglected and profaned. Meanwhile these same men easily tolerate profane mockers of every religion and blasphemers who swear dreadfully by the heavenly saints and the Virgin Mary herself and by all sacred things; to say nothing of usurers, impostors, robbers, soldiers who thirst for blood, impure whoremongers, adulterers and incestuous men, and pursuers of unlawful lusts, whose friendship they cultivate, whom they venerate, and whom they call beloved sons of the Church, provided they lend their help to attacking the truth. The facts themselves teach that I speak the truth. For who has heard hitherto, in the city of Rome or in Italy, where bishops and cardinals hold sway, that impious blasphemers have been burned in the flames, men who rashly swear and curse by the Virgin Mary and her Son Jesus Christ, calling her a whore and him a bastard or illegitimate son of God? I shudder entirely as I recount these things, and I pray God Most Good and Most High to forgive me for recounting things that may offend pious ears. But it is certain that such words are heard there every day even among those at play, and are poured out with impunity. If anyone, however, holds that the divine Virgin conceived by the Holy Spirit, and that through her virginity she bore the Son of God, who was born of her as a man, so that he might be made a sacrifice for the sins of the world, and so that finally he might be our satisfaction, righteousness and redemption, he is thought worthy to be handed over to the inquisitors of heretical depravity and to be tortured with the most exquisite torments. Who, then, would say that these men seriously profess faith in Christ and are moved by any sense of piety? Unless surely they too, in their hearts, like the Sadducees of old, laugh at all sacred things together with what they devoutly believe about heaven and hell: they would certainly never hold sacred things for sale so shamelessly, nor play so buffoonishly with the Scriptures and the Word of God, nor abuse the simplicity of the people so wickedly, calling those good Christians by way of mockery who allow themselves to be deceived and plundered by them under this pretext of feigned religion; much less would they shed innocent blood, throw everything into confusion by betrayals, and disturb the Christian world with foreign and civil wars. Add to this that these same men allow the Jews, sworn enemies of Christ, to dwell in their cities. Constantine the Emperor once did not hesitate to call them parricides or murderers of the Lord [πατροκτόνας ἢ κυριοκτόνας], and said that Christian men ought to have nothing in common with them, as with the most hated nation. Yet these men permit them to have synagogues and to hold assemblies in which they curse Christ and his servants with dreadful imprecations. Some hold these men (I say) in high esteem; they use them as physicians and intimate counsellors, and entrust to them their fortunes and all their safety, while those same men meanwhile rage with sword and fire against the genuine worshippers of Christ. Therefore today Christian men differ in nothing from the Jews who once were; and so it is no wonder that we feel God angry with us, since he exacts punishment of every kind for such atrocious injuries as are done to himself and his servants.

units.la: Porrò videamus quaestionem Sadducaeorum, qua Dominum tentare ausi sunt. Est hoc de mortuorum resurrectione, quam a Christo tradi non poterant ignorare. Etenim in publico dixerat aliquando: Veniet hora, qua omnes qui in monumentis sunt, audient vocem Filii hominis, & prodibunt, &c. Item, Ego sum resurrectio et vita: Qui credit in me, etiamsi mortuus fuerit, viuet. Argumentum autem & occasione quaestionis ex Lege petunt, & ne impij aut temerarij putentur, a Mose initium faciunt, dicentes: Moses dixit, si quis mortuus fuerit non habens filios, eius frater ducet affinitatis iure vxorem eius, & suscitabit semen fratri suo, &c. Extat lex ista Deut. XXV. & recitatur in hunc modu: Si habitauerint fratres pariter, & mortuus fuerit vnus ex eis, & filius non fuerit ei, non nubet vxor mortui extra viro extraneo, cognatus eius ingrediatur ad eam, & accipiet eam sibi in vxorem, affinitatem contrahat cum ea. Et primogenitus, quae peperit, surget in nomen defuncti fratris sui, ne deleatur nomen eius ex Israele, &c. Membra huius legis multa et probe distincta sunt: Primo de fratribus loquitur, qui simul habitant, & ex quibus si vnus vxore ducat, alter caelebs manet. Deinde si qui vxorem duxit moriatur absque prole mascula, quae eius nomen propaga re possit, vidua eius nulli extraneo, qui no eiusdem familiae sit, nubat, sed fratri aut leuiro, vel alij pro pinquo prioris mariti. Tertio filius primus, qui ex ea nascitur, fratris defuncti nomine ceferi debet, & in eius hereditate succedere. Quarto praecipitur etiam quid fieri debeat cum eo, qui hoc officium fratri defuncto praestare dedignatur: nimirum quod vidua ei calceum detrahere & in facie eius expuere debeat: Quae ceremonia significabatur illum possessione omnium bonorum defuncti fratris cedere debere, & cu ignominia publica nomen dis calceati accipere. Et quia extra hunc casum non licebat fratris vxore attingere (ut Lex de incestis libidinibus alibi docet) iste mandati causam reddit Moses: Ne nomen defuncti deleatur ex Israele. Id est, ne familia eius pereat, et hereditas diuipetur. Et debet haec causa diligenter obseruari, ne quis hodie licitu putet fratris vxore ducere, aut aliam pro pinquiore cognationis aut affinitatis gradu in Lege prohibito coniunctam. Etenim veteri populo multa olim concessa fuerunt, quae hodie in exemplu trahi no debent, cu Respub. Israelitica cessarit, & infelices Iudaeorum reliquiae per totu orbe dispersae sint. Olim vero voluit Deus tribuum & familiarum distinctione salua esse inter illos, partim propter Messiae lineam, qui ex tribu Iuda & Dauidis familia secundum promissiones expectabatur: partim vt Rephub. illa, quae vsq; ad Mosis primum aduentum durare debuit, facilius & melius seruaretur. Et sane ad Reipub. pacem & intolli mitatem plurimum confert, vt familiae illustres & antiquae floreant. Est enim earum non vulgaris authoritas apud prudentes & cordatos, & vulgo patientius ferunt homines eorum imperia, quorum maiorum virtus & antiqua in patriam communem merita comendant: & qui tales sunt, Ieipsos fere in officio continent, ne quid praeter officium faciant, quod familiae suae aliquam ignomi nia notam inurat. E contra noui homines aut insolenter imperant, vt apud Romanos Marius fecit, aut si bene imperent, tamen inuidia multorum premuntur, quae saepius in Republica dissensionum & motuum grauissimorum causa est. Peccant ergo grauiter, nec vlla venia digni sunt, qui familias suas ipsi euertunt & dissipant: Quod fere fit per intemperantiam & petulanti luxu atque prodigalitate, quae multos ad egestatem redactos insuper vitijs teterrimis infames, & bonis omnibus exosos facit. Exempla passim in historijs occurrunt, quorum recordatio magistratus excitare debet, vt leges sumptuarias tueantur, ne turpiter pereant, qui si fortuna ipsis integra manet, Reipub. aliquando vsui & ornamento esse possunt. In primis Dei exemplum nos moueat, qui hac cosli tutione defratris defuncti vxore ducenda familias conseruare voluit. Nam per hanc occurrebatur simul fratrum odijs, ne quis propter hereditatis spem fratres sublatos vellet, & viduis orbis consulebatur, quae (vt apparet ex Ruth a historia) maritis defunctis succedebat. Admonebat praeterea, defunctorum rationem honorificam haberi debere: quod vt pietas requirit, ita alios ad imitationem eorum excitat, quos propter virtutes suas in pretio esse audiunt.
units.tr: Next let us look at the question of the Sadducees, with which they dared to test the Lord. It concerned the resurrection of the dead, about which they could not have been ignorant of what Christ taught. For he had said publicly on one occasion: "The hour is coming in which all who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of Man and will come forth," etc. Likewise: "I am the resurrection and the life: he who believes in me, even if he has died, will live." They drew their argument and the occasion of their question from the Law, and so that they might not seem impious or rash, they began with Moses, saying: "Moses said, if anyone dies without children, his brother shall take his wife by the right of kinship and raise up seed for his brother," etc. That law stands in Deuteronomy 25, and it is recited in this way: "If brothers have lived together, and one of them has died, and he has no son, the wife of the dead man shall not marry outside to a stranger; her kinsman shall go in to her and take her to himself as wife and enter into the relationship with her. And the firstborn whom she bears shall rise up in the name of his dead brother, so that his name may not be blotted out of Israel," etc. The parts of this law are many and clearly distinguished. First, it speaks of brothers who live together, of whom, if one takes a wife, the other remains unmarried. Second, if a man who has taken a wife dies without a male child who could carry on his name, his widow shall not marry any stranger who is not of the same family, but a brother or brother-in-law, or another close relative of the former husband. Third, the first son who is born of her shall be called by the name of the dead brother and shall succeed to his inheritance. Fourth, it is also prescribed what must be done with the man who refuses to perform this duty for his dead brother: namely, that the widow shall pull off his shoe and spit in his face. This ceremony signified that he must give up possession of all the goods of the dead brother, and that he would receive the name "the unshod" with public disgrace. And because outside this case it was not lawful to touch a brother's wife (as the Law teaches elsewhere concerning unlawful lusts), Moses gives the reason for this command: "so that the name of the dead man may not be blotted out of Israel," that is, so that his family may not perish and his inheritance be divided. This reason ought to be carefully observed, so that no one today thinks it lawful to take a brother's wife, or any other woman who is joined by a closer degree of kinship or affinity, which the Law forbids. For many things were once permitted to the ancient people which ought not to be drawn into example today, since the Israelite commonwealth has ceased and the unhappy remnants of the Jews are scattered through the whole world. Yet God wished that, in former times, the distinction of tribes and families should be preserved among them, partly because of the line of the Messiah, who was expected from the tribe of Judah and the family of David according to the promises, and partly so that that commonwealth, which had to last until the first coming of Moses, might be preserved more easily and better.
