And indeed, the preservation of families of distinction and antiquity contributes greatly to the peace and stability of a commonwealth. For such families have no small authority among the prudent and sensible, and people more patiently endure the commands of those whose ancestors' virtue and ancient merits toward the common country they recall. Those who are of such families largely keep themselves within their duty, lest they do anything beyond their duty that might brand their family with some mark of disgrace. On the contrary, new men either command insolently, as Marius did among the Romans, or, even if they command well, are oppressed by the envy of many, which is quite often the cause of dissensions and most grievous disturbances in a commonwealth. Those therefore sin gravely, and deserve no pardon, who themselves overturn and squander their own families. This generally happens through intemperance, wanton luxury and prodigality, which reduce many to poverty and, besides, make them infamous through most foul vices and hated by all good men. Examples occur everywhere in histories, and the memory of them ought to rouse magistrates to uphold the sumptuary laws, so that those who, if their fortune remains intact, may sometimes be of use and ornament to the commonwealth, do not perish disgracefully. Above all, the example of God should move us, who by this command concerning taking the wife of a dead brother wished to preserve families. For through this law the hatreds of brothers were at the same time checked, so that no one should wish his brothers removed in hope of the inheritance; and provision was made for widows who were left childless, who (as appears from the story of Ruth) succeeded their dead husbands. It also taught that the memory of the dead ought to be held in honour, which, as piety requires, so also stirs others to imitate those whom they hear to be held in esteem for their virtues.

units.la: Caeterum vt ad Sadducaeos reuertamur, hi neglectis iudiis, quae in hac constitutione obseruari debebant, impuris cogitationibus indulgent potius, & casum proponunt de septem fratribus, qui omnes ex hoc Mosis statuto eandem vxorem ex ordine duxerint, & quibus omnibus abfq; prole defunctis, postremo ipsa quoq; fit mortua: & quaerunt, cuius vxor illa futura sit in resurrectione? Causa quaestionis huius est, quod arbitrantur, tam multas tamq; magnas absurditates hic concurrere, vt non sit habituris quod respondeat. Etenim si illam primi aut alterius cuiusfuis ex illis vxorem fore dixerit, clamabunt reliquis iniuriam fieri, qui illam similiter duxerint nulla priuata libidine, sed ex legis praescripto, & proinde singuli illam pari iure sibi vendicare possint. Iniquum ergo esse, vt vnus alijs praeferatur, cum nullus ex illa prolem suscepserit. Sin dicat, eam in resurrectione omnibus communem fore, foeda & detestabilis haec erit libidinum incestarum confusio, quae nemini honesto probari poterit. Sperant ergo Dominum in has angustias redactum aut odio Pharisaeorum in ipsorum sententiam pedibus iturum, vt resurrectionem mortuorum absolute neget, aut aliquid absurdum pronuntiet, quod ipsum piorum omnium ludibrijs atq; odio exponat. Quo exemplo docemur, quo usq; progrediatur impietas. Impietatis indicium est, quod de vita aeterna & regno coelorum tam foedas cogitationes animo conceperunt, quales hodie in Mahumetanis merito boni omnes detestantur. Scelus vero cum sacrilegio coniunctum est, quod in re tam foeda Lege Dei abutuntur. Et licet Mosem magnifice iactarent, hoc vno argumento teguntur, quam scurriliter de illo sentiant, cum ex eius constitutionibus tam obscena & pijs auribus indigna commenta colligant. Similes horum sunt, qui hodie teterrimos errores & nefanda scelera Scripturae testimonijs violenter detorquent, aut exemplis sanctorum perperam allegatis defendunt, & excusant. Quotquot item doctrinam de nouissimo Domini aduentu & mortuorum resurrectione, quaestionibus non multum ab hac differentibus eludunt. Num aliqua eorum, quae in hoc saeculo accidunt, memoria aut recordatio futura sit? Num alij alios agnituri sint? Quibus oculis aspectura sit vxorem maritus, quae postea ipsius obitum alteri, aut etiam suo inimico nupsit? Quomodo ite posti bile sit claudos, mancos, caecos resurgere, vt viribus et sensibus integris vtatur, quibus in hac vita destituti fuerunt? Ex quibus tandem colligunt, fabulas & commenta inania esse, quaecunq; de nouissimo die & vita aeterna dicuntur, & in ea verba erumpunt, quae D. Petrus illusoribus tribuit, quos postremis temporibus dicturos scribit: Vbi est pollicitatio aduentus eius? ex quo die patres obdormierunt, omnia sic permanent ab initio creationis, & vt patres sefellit alterum & melioris vitae ipsos, qui priusquam eam attingerent, morte extincti sunt: ita nobis quoq; accidet. Quid ergo praeterea ex his concludunt isti? Hoc ipsum, quod Paulus impijs resurrectionis & vitae futurae alnega-
units.tr: But to return to the Sadducees: these men, neglecting the things that ought to have been observed in this ordinance, indulge rather in impure thoughts, and propose the case of seven brothers, who all in order, by this statute of Moses, took the same wife, and when all of them died without offspring, at last the woman herself also died; and they ask: whose wife will she be at the resurrection? The reason for this question is that they think so many and so great absurdities converge here that he will have nothing to answer. For if he should say that she will be the wife of the first or of any other of them, they will cry out that an injustice is done to the rest, who likewise took her not from any private lust but by the prescription of the Law, and therefore each could claim her with equal right. It would be unfair, then, that one be preferred to the others, since none of them had any child by her. But if he should say that she will be common to all in the resurrection, this would be a foul and detestable confusion of incestuous lusts, which could not be approved by anyone of decency. They therefore hope that the Lord, driven into these straits, either out of hatred of the Pharisees will come over to their opinion, so as to deny the resurrection of the dead outright, or will utter something absurd, which would expose him to the mockery and hatred of all the godly. From this example we are taught how far impiety may advance. It is a sign of impiety that they conceived such foul thoughts in their minds about eternal life and the kingdom of heaven, such as all good men rightly detest today in the Mahometans. Moreover, wickedness is joined with sacrilege, in that they abuse the Law of God in a matter so foul. And although they boasted magnificently of Moses, this one argument reveals how scurrilously they think of him, since from his ordinances they gather such obscene inventions, unworthy of pious ears. Like them are those who today violently twist the most foul errors and abominable crimes into the testimonies of Scripture, or defend and excuse them by wrongly alleged examples of the saints. Likewise all who mock the doctrine of the last coming of the Lord and the resurrection of the dead with questions not much different from this one. Will any memory or recollection of the things that happen in this age remain? Will people recognise one another? With what eyes will a husband look upon a wife who after his death married another, or even his enemy? How can it be possible for the lame, the maimed and the blind to rise again, so as to use their limbs and senses whole, of which they were deprived in this life? From these things at last they conclude that whatever is said about the last day and eternal life are fables and empty inventions, and they burst out into those words which St. Peter attributes to the scoffers whom he writes will come in the last times: "Where is the promise of his coming? From the day the fathers fell asleep, all things remain so from the beginning of creation," and, as the fathers were deceived about the other and better life, and those who died before they attained it were extinguished by death, so it will happen to us as well. What, then, do these men conclude besides this? Precisely what Paul attributes to the impious deniers of the resurrection and of the future life:

units.la: Ruth.4. abnegatoribus tribuit: Edamus, bibamus, cras enim morimur. Et sane audiuntur haec voces & his magis impiæ ex multis nostro sæculo. At hi omnes sibi applicent admonitionem, quam ibidem subtexit Apostolus: Ne erretis: corrumpunt mores bonos colloquia prava: Euigilate iuste, & ne peccate. Nam vt ex sequentibus patebit certo erit mundi finis, & veniet ad iudicandum viuos ac mortuos Dei Filius, IESVS CHRISTVS, vt impijs illis & pœnitere nescijs rependat prout digni sunt, electos autem suos, qui ipsi in vera fide & sanctitate seruierunt, ad se colligat, vt cum ipso viuant & regnent. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: 1 Cor. 15. The Apostle attributes to the deniers of the resurrection the words: "Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die." Indeed these words are heard, and more impious ones too, from many in our own age. But let all of them take to heart the admonition the Apostle adds in the same place: "Do not be deceived: evil company corrupts good morals." "Awake to righteousness, and do not sin." For, as will become clear from what follows, there will certainly be an end of the world, and the Son of God, Jesus Christ, will come to judge the living and the dead, to repay those impious and unrepentant people as they deserve, and to gather his elect, who served him in true faith and holiness, to himself, so that they may live and reign with him. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCLIX.
units.tr: HOMILY CCLIX.

units.la: Respondens autem IESVS dixit eis: Erratis, nescientes Scripturas, neque potestatem Dei. In resurrectione enim neque vxores ducunt, neque nuptum dantur: sed sunt vt Angeli Dei in cœlo. De resurrectione vero mortuorum non legistis quod vobis dictum est a Deo, dicente: Ego sum Deus Abrahami, & Deus Isaaci, & Deus Iacobi? Deus non est Deus mortuorum, sed viuentium. Et cum hoc audisset turba, perculsa est ob doctrinam eius.
units.tr: But Jesus answered and said to them: You are wrong, not knowing the Scriptures or the power of God. For in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but they are like the angels of God in heaven. But concerning the resurrection of the dead, have you not read what was said to you by God, who says: I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob? God is not the God of the dead, but of the living. And when the crowd heard this, they were astonished at his teaching.

units.la: Quoniam Dei Filius, Dominus noster IESVS CHRISTVS, toto eo tempore, quo inter Matth. 9. Luc. 7. Ioan. 11. vixit, inter docendum sæpe disseruit de mortuorum resurrectione, aliquos etiam miraculo suscitauit, vt communem & vniuersalem resurrectionem fore, reipsa demonstraret: nihilominus tamen non absque causa voluit paulo ante suam mortem huius articuli doctrinam atque fidem plice aduersus eius negatores acerrimos tueri: Nimirum, quod absque hoc neque fides Christiana, neque salus nostra posset consistere. Nam, Paulo teste, si mortui non excitantur, Christus quoque non est excitatus. Quod si Christus non est excitatus, inanis est fides nostra, adhuc sumus in peccatis nostris: Nempe & qui obdormierunt in Christo, perierunt. Itaque articulum hunc validissimis argumentis confirmari oportuit. Occasionem autem ad id præbuerunt Sadducæi, qui de eo quæstionem mouerunt non minus fædam & turpem quam absurdam, qua Christum intricare conantur vt aut neget resurrectionem, aut aliquid dicat, quod eius authoritati & exististimationi deroget. Sed audiamus illius responsionem, quæ tribus partibus constat. Prima erroris illos arguit, & huius causam ostendit. Secunda paralogismum, quo seipsos & alios fallebant soluit & confutat. Tertia veram de resurrectione doctrinam ex Scripturis confirmat.
units.tr: Since the Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, during the whole time he lived among men (Matt. 9; Luke 7; John 11), often spoke in his teaching about the resurrection of the dead, and even raised some by a miracle, so as to show in fact that there will be a common and universal resurrection, nevertheless he chose, not without reason, shortly before his death, to defend this doctrine and faith firmly against its most fierce deniers. Clearly, without this neither the Christian faith nor our salvation could stand. For, as Paul bears witness, if the dead are not raised, neither has Christ been raised. And if Christ has not been raised, our faith is empty, and we are still in our sins. Indeed, those also who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished. Therefore this article had to be confirmed by the strongest arguments. The occasion for this was given by the Sadducees, who raised a question about it no less foul and shameful than absurd, by which they tried to entangle Christ, so that he would either deny the resurrection or say something that would detract from his authority and reputation. But let us hear his answer, which has three parts. The first refutes those men for their error and shows its cause. The second dissolves and refutes the sophism by which they deceived themselves and others. The third confirms the true doctrine of the resurrection from the Scriptures.

units.la: Quoad primam partem, initio statim illos errare dicit, qui reliquis plus sapere videri volebant, vtpote viri politici & in rebus agendis egregie exercitati. Et mox causam erroris indicat, Ignorantiam Scripturarum & potestatis siue potentiæ Dei. Marcus illum interrogatione vsum fuisse scribit, vt animos illorum acutius feriret: Nonne propterea errastis quod nescitis Scripturas, neque potentiam Dei? Quis vero dubitet correptionem hanc tam liberam admodum displicuisse hominibus superbis & ambitiosis? At non temere exprobratur eis Scripturarum ignorantia. Nam vera enim nesciunt has, qui mentem Scriptoris non attendunt: quotquot item non tota Scripturam recipiunt, sed inter huius libros delectum habent, vt homines delicatuli & morosi in mensa solent, qui aliquos cibos probant, alios autem fastidiose reijciunt. Nam vtriusque non agnoscunt quanta sit Spiritus Sancti per Scripturas nobis loquentis maiestas. In vtroque autem Sadducæos offendisse constat. Etenim ex Scripturæ libris solos Mosis libros recipiebant, Prophetarum vero sermones & historicos pro prophanis habebant. Deinde non respiciebant mentem Mosis, qui constitutione illa, quam ipsi adduxerunt, quid in hoc sæculo inter fratres quoad rem domesticam & familiarum conseruationem fieri debeat, docere voluit, non quæ futura & cœlestis vitæ conditio sit. Itaque extra oleas currunt, quando Mosis legem ad alienum statum detorquent.
units.tr: As to the first part, he says at the very beginning that they are in error, these men who wished to seem wiser than the rest, being politicians and men thoroughly practised in worldly affairs. And soon he states the cause of their error: ignorance of the Scriptures and of the power or might of God. Mark writes that he used a question so as to pierce their minds more sharply: "Is it not for this reason that you are wrong, that you do not know the Scriptures nor the power of God?" Who could doubt that this rebuke, so frank, displeased proud and ambitious men? Yet their ignorance of the Scriptures is not charged against them without cause. For those who do not attend to the mind of the writer truly do not know them; likewise all who do not receive the whole of Scripture, but make a selection among its books, as dainty and fussy people at table do, who approve some foods and fastidiously reject others. For neither group recognises how great is the majesty of the Holy Spirit speaking to us through the Scriptures. Now it is clear that the Sadducees failed in both respects. For of the books of Scripture they accepted only the books of Moses, and they regarded the sayings of the prophets and the histories as profane. Then they did not consider the mind of Moses, who in that ordinance which they cited wished to teach what ought to be done in this age among brothers concerning domestic affairs and the preservation of families, and not what the future and heavenly condition of life would be. So they run outside the olive groves when they twist the law of Moses to an alien purpose.

units.la: Faciunt hoc multi hodie, qui ante conceptas opiniones Scripturarum testimonijs confirmare studeant, & neglecto proprio illarum sensu & scopo, omnipotentiam Dei vrgent, quam sibi adquisitis commenta probanda sufficere volunt. Sed meminerint isti, Christum non absque causa hic Scripturas potentiæ Dei præponere: ita nimirum docens, primò in Scripturis nos quid Deus velit, inquirere debere, & postea demum quando de eius voluntate nobis constat, ad illius potentiam esse recurrendum, ne dubitemus Deum quaecunq; vult posse perficere. Ordinem hunc nobis Spiritus Sanctus in Psalmis commendat, dicens: Deus noster in coelis est, omnia quae voluit fecit. Sic Abraham cum promissionem Dei haberet, ex Sara nasciturum ipsi filium, credidit Deum praestare posse quod promiserat, & contra spem sperauit: quae fides ipsi reputata est ad iustitiam. Non ergo valet argumentum ab omnipotentia Dei, nisi hunc velle conster, quod nos probatum volumus. Quis enim nescit illum non omnia facere quae potest, sed quae vult. Vult autem quae sancta, iusta & ipsi gloriosa, nobis autem salutaria sunt. Neq; facit miracula non necessaria, quibus ut magi & circulatores solent, suam potestatem & artem prodigiosis & inutilibus operibus ostentet. Nam potuisset plures mundos creare, sed unus hic sufficit, ut in eo illius sapientiam, bonitatem, omnipotentiam, & attributa reliqua consideremus & cognoscamus. Poterat item facere, ut boues volaret, piscesque in arboribus nidularentur, aliqui tibijs canerent: sed ut ista & alia huius generis fiant, neq; illius gloria, neq; nostra salutis ratio requirit. Frustra igitur nobis hodie omnipotentiam Dei obijciunt, qui carnalem corporis Christi praesentiam & manducationem asse runt, nosq; Dei omnipotentiam negare vociferantur, si dicamus corpus Christi loco certo circumscribi & contineri. Fatemur Christum, utpote verum & aeternum Dei Filium, omnipotentem esse, corpus autem eius omnipraesens esse, & in Coena realiter manibus contrectari & ore manducari negamus: quia hoc illum velle nullis Scripturis hucusq; edoctifumus. Nam nullo vnquam miraculo ille docuit, se uno eodemq; tempore in diuersis locis esse corporaliter. Capernaitas autem carnis suae manducationem somniantes ad ascensionem in coelos remisit, quo illum abijsse ficimus, cum prius non semel protestatus esset, sed porro non amplius in mundo fore, sed mundum relinquere: Quod nos non aliter quam de corpore intelligere possumus, cum de diuinitate sua veritissime dixerit: Ecce ego vobiscum sum vsq; in consummationem saeculi. In Coena vero audimus illum non corporis sui manducatione carnali, sed mortis suae, quam in corpore subijt, memoriam sanctiuis. Et Apostoli verbis credimus dicentes: Quotiescunq; editis panem hunc, & poculum hoc bibitis, mortem Domini annuntiatis, usq; quo venerit. Cum ergo ne Paulus quidem corporalem carnis Christi praesentiam crediderit, sed aduentus Christi mentionem faciat, quem nescimus alium, quam eum qui nouissimo die futurus est, religio nobis fuerit, in Coena plus quaerere quam nobis in illa Christus promisit, & Apostoli monstrant. Et merito in aduersarios nostros detorquemus illud Christi, quod Sadducaeis dixit: Erratis, nescientes Scripturas, neq; potestatem Dei.
units.tr: Many today do the same: they eagerly confirm their preconceived opinions by testimonies of Scripture, and, neglecting the proper sense and purpose of Scripture, they press the omnipotence of God, which they want to be sufficient to prove the inventions they have acquired. But let them remember that Christ did not without reason set the Scriptures before the power of God here, thereby teaching that first we must inquire in the Scriptures what God wills, and only then, when we are certain of his will, must we have recourse to his power, so that we do not doubt that God can accomplish whatever he wills. The Holy Spirit commends this order to us in the Psalms, saying: "Our God is in the heavens; he has done whatever he pleased." Thus Abraham, when he had God's promise that a son would be born to him from Sarah, believed that God was able to perform what he had promised, and hoped against hope; and this faith was reckoned to him for righteousness. Therefore the argument from the omnipotence of God is not valid unless it is shown that God wills the very thing we want proved. For who does not know that he does not do all that he can, but what he wills? He wills what is holy, just, glorious to himself, and salutary to us. Nor does he work unnecessary miracles, by which, as magicians and charlatans are wont to do, one displays one's power and skill with prodigious and useless works. For he could have created several worlds, but this one suffices, so that in it we may consider and know his wisdom, goodness, omnipotence and his other attributes. He could likewise have made oxen fly, fish nest in trees, and some men sing with flutes; but neither his glory nor the reason for our salvation requires that these or others of this kind should come about. Therefore they who assert a carnal presence of the body of Christ and a carnal eating of it, and loudly cry that we deny the omnipotence of God if we say that the body of Christ is confined and contained in a certain place, throw the omnipotence of God in our faces in vain. We confess that Christ, as the true and eternal Son of God, is omnipotent, and that his body is everywhere present; but we deny that in the Supper it is handled realistically with the hands and eaten with the mouth, because we have hitherto learned from no Scriptures that he wills this. For never by any miracle did he teach that he is bodily present in different places at one and the same time. Those Capernaites who dreamed of eating his flesh he sent back to his ascension into heaven, whither we believe he has departed, since he had previously declared more than once that he would no longer be in the world but would leave the world. We can understand this in no other way than of his body, since he most truly said of his divinity: "Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age." In the Supper, however, we hear him commend to us the memory of his death, which he underwent in the body, not the carnal eating of his body. And we believe the words of the Apostle, who says: "As often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord's death until he comes." Therefore, since not even Paul believed in a bodily presence of Christ's flesh, but speaks of the coming of Christ, whom we know to be none other than the one who will come on the last day, it would be a sin for us to seek more in the Supper than Christ promised us there and the Apostles show. And rightly do we turn against our adversaries that saying of Christ to the Sadducees: "You are wrong, not knowing the Scriptures nor the power of God."

units.la: Caeterum ad secundam refutationis Christi partem transeamus, qua Sadducaeorum foedam & absurdam de aeterna vita aut futuri saeculi conditione, siue statu opinionem confutat, & paralogismum siue fallaciam illorum arguit, dicens: In resurrectione neq; vxores ducunt, neq; nuptum dantur, sed sunt vt Angeli Dei in coelo. Error Sadducaeorum erat, quod tempore resurrectionis eundem rerum humanarum statum fore putarent, qui nunc est. Ex eo sic illi colligebant: Si mor tui ijs corporibus resurgent, in quibus nunc viuunt, sua singulis vxores restituatur oportet. Id vero διαλίαν & confusionem pariet, in qua multae absurditates concurrent, neq; euitari poterit omnis iniquitas, cum aliqui vxores plures, multae etiam mulieres pluribus viris nubant in hoc saeculo: Ergo resurrectio erit nulla. Ad argumentum hoc respondet Dominus, & illud soluit negado antecedens, quod illi statuebant. Docet enim longe alium fore statum futuri saeculi quam praesentis, in quo (ut apud Lucam annotatur) vxores ducuntur & nuptum dantur, eo quod propter mortalem conditionem, cui omnes subiecti sunt, humanum genus legitima noua soboles generatione perpetuo instaurari ac conseruari oportet, ne tandem omnino deficiat. In futuro autem saeculo, nihil huius fore ait. Quia enim filij resurrectionis erunt, id est, quia ad vitam aeternam resurgent, & mors ipsa abolebitur, ut generatione noua minime opus sit, simul etiam nullus nuptijs locus erit. Et ex positionis loco subijcit: Sunt vt Angeli Dei in coelo, adeoq; filij Dei, vt etiam in Luca dicitur.
units.tr: But let us pass on to the second part of Christ's refutation, in which he overthrows the foul and absurd opinion of the Sadducees about eternal life or the condition or state of the age to come, and exposes their sophism or fallacy, saying: "In the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but they are like the angels of God in heaven." The error of the Sadducees was that they thought that at the time of the resurrection the same state of human affairs would exist as now. From this they reasoned thus: If the dead rise in the same bodies in which they now live, each must have his wife restored to him. But this would produce confusion [διαλίαν], in which many absurdities would meet, and not all iniquity could be avoided, since in this age some men have several wives and many women marry several husbands. Therefore there will be no resurrection. The Lord answers this argument and dissolves it by denying the antecedent which they laid down. For he teaches that the state of the age to come will be quite different from the present one, in which (as Luke notes) wives are taken and men are given in marriage, because, on account of the mortal condition to which all are subject, the human race must be perpetually renewed and preserved by the lawful generation of new offspring, lest at last it fail altogether. But in the age to come, he says, nothing of this will exist. For since they will be sons of the resurrection, that is, since they will rise to eternal life, and death itself will be abolished, there will be no need of new generation, and at the same time there will be no place for marriages. And from this position he adds: "They are like the angels of God in heaven," and therefore sons of God, as is also said in Luke.

units.la: Est autem locus hic dignissimus consideratu, vt probe nobis constet, qui futuri saeculi status sit. Primo nimirum mortalitatis expers, & proinde aeternus. Nec enim mors sola (vt modo dixi mus) abolebitur, verumetiam omnes miseriae, quae vt satellites mortis cum peccato in mundum ingressae sunt: quales sunt morbi, curae, tristitia, senectus, & quacunq; vitae huius cursum possunt abrumpere. Deinde Angelis similes erunt electi: nō quidē quoad substantiam (hi enim spiritus sunt,) secunfecundum illud Psalmi: Qui nuntios suos facit spiritus, & ministros suos flammam ignis: nos autem his ipsis corporibus, quae nunc gestamus, resurgemus) sed quoad incorruptibilitatem, & animi affectiones, ut prorsus nihil in nobis sit, quod vel animo & corpori molestiam pariat, vel facium quidspiret. Tertio filij Dei erimus. Tales quidem nunc sumus, sed tales nos esse nondum apparet: tunc autem toti mundo, imo impijs etiam qui nos persequuntur, filios Dei nos esse, manifestabitur. Quod si filij sumus, etiam haeredes (ut Paulus ait) haeredes quidem Dei, coheredes autem Christi. Comprehendit hoc in se omnem beatitatem, & sunt infinitae aliae promissiones, quibus hereditatis ipsius spes confirmatur.
units.tr: It is a place most worthy of consideration, so that we may clearly understand what the state of the future age will be. First, of course, it will be free from mortality, and therefore eternal. For not only death alone (as I have just said) will be abolished, but also all the miseries which entered the world as attendants of death together with sin: such as diseases, cares, sadness, old age, and whatever else can cut short the course of this life. Next, the elect will be like the angels: not indeed in substance (for angels are spirits, according to that psalm: "who makes his messengers spirits, and his ministers a flame of fire"; but we will rise in these very bodies which we now bear), but in incorruptibility and in the affections of the soul, so that there will be nothing in us that could cause discomfort to soul or body, or breathe out anything foul. Third, we will be sons of God. We are indeed such now, but it does not yet appear that we are such; then, however, it will be made manifest to the whole world, even to the impious who persecute us, that we are sons of God. And if we are sons, then also heirs (as Paul says): heirs indeed of God, but joint heirs with Christ. This comprises all blessedness, and there are countless other promises by which the hope of that inheritance is confirmed.

units.la: Ut vero ista rarum omnium in hac vita nobis esse debet, ut primum consolationi seruiant inter huius saeculi aduersa. Sunt haec momentanea, nec diuturna esse possunt, cum vita hominis brevis sit, & in horas transeat. Dies annorum nostrorum sunt septuaginta anni (inquit Moses) aut si qui sint valentiores octoginta: quorum praecipua pars labor et dolor est: sed abripimur festinanter, & dicto citius auolamus. At quando haec vita finitur, simul omnia finiuntur, quae hanc nobis acerbam reddunt: gloria autem & beatitas, quae hanc sequetur, aeterna est. Deinde ad vitae huius institutionem seruit huius loci consideratio: ut inter praesens hoc & futurum saeculum distinguere discamus. Etenim natura, teste Solomone, singulis negotijs sua tempora destinauit: quorum momenta si ue occasiones si in terrae cultura negligantur, fructra deinceps laborauerit. At praesens saeculum peregrinationi destinatum est, quae nobis per vallem hanc lachrymarum iniuncta est a Deo ad patriam & beatas illas mansiones, quas nobis IESVS CHRISTVS in coelis parauit, quorum municipes in illo facti sumus. Non ergo addicamus nos huic saeculo, sed dum hic viuere datur, ita vitamur mundo, ut no abutamur. Quod tunc fiet, si naturae necessitati, non luxui aut libidini omnia seruiant. Abest item anxia victus & rerum temporalium solicitudo, nec dubitemus caelestem illum Patrem, qui brutis, & quidem vilissimis animantibus prospicit, nequaquam neglecturum nos, in quorum gratiam omnia sunt condita. Nec vnquam excidat, aliam vitam nos manere, in qua aeternum felices aut infelices erimus, prout in hoc saeculo bene aut male vixerimus. De his quia plerique non serio cogitant, facile in omne genus scelerum prolabuntur. Hinc leuitas & inconstantia in religione, in re domestica fraudes & impostura ac nefariae aut illicitae ditescendi artes, in motibus effrenis licentia: quibus qui absque respiscentia indulgent, sibi ipsis pericula et labores augent, & ad aeternos cruciatus damnabuntur.
units.tr: But these things ought to be, for us in this life, a rare possession, namely that they first serve for consolation amid the adversities of this age. These are momentary and cannot last long, since the life of man is short and passes in hours. The days of our years are seventy years (says Moses), or, if they are stronger, eighty; of which the chief part is labour and sorrow; but we are snatched away quickly and fly off more swiftly than a word. But when this life ends, all the things that make it bitter for us end together with it; the glory and blessedness that follow it, however, are eternal. Next, consideration of this place serves to order this life: that we may learn to distinguish between the present age and the future one. For nature, as Solomon testifies, has assigned to each undertaking its own times; if its moments or opportunities are neglected in the cultivation of the earth, one labours in vain afterwards. But the present age is destined for pilgrimage, which God has laid upon us through this vale of tears, leading to the homeland and those blessed mansions which Jesus Christ has prepared for us in heaven, and of whose citizenship we have become partakers in him. Therefore let us not devote ourselves to this age, but, while it is granted to us to live here, so use the world as not to abuse it. This will happen if all things serve the necessity of nature, not luxury or lust. Likewise anxious care for food and temporal things is absent, nor should we doubt that that heavenly Father, who provides for brute and even the lowliest animals, will by no means neglect us, for whose sake all things were created. And let it never slip from our minds that there is another life in which we will remain, eternally happy or unhappy according as we have lived well or badly in this age. Because most people do not think about these things seriously, they easily slide into every kind of wickedness. Hence come levity and inconstancy in religion, fraud and trickery in domestic affairs, and wicked or unlawful arts of getting rich, and unbridled licence in unrestrained passions. Those who indulge in these without repentance increase their own dangers and troubles, and will be condemned to eternal torments.

units.la: Sequitur tertia responsionis Christi pars, qua veram de mortuorum resurrectione doctrinam asserit, dicens: De resurrectione vero mortuorum non legistis quod vobis dictum est a Deo, dicente: Ego sum Deus Abrahami, & Deus Isaaci, & Deus Iacobi. Extant verba haec apud Mosem, cui sic locutus est Dominus, cum ei in rubo ardente apparens illum pro filijs Israelis legatum ad Pharaonem destinaret. Voluit autem praeteritis multis alijs locis, in quibus resurrectio clarius affertur, hunc allegare, quia ipsi cum Sadducaeis res erat, qui (ut alias diximus) solius Mosis libros agnoscebant pro sacris, quibus Dei verbum contineretur. Emphasim vero peculiare habet inter rogatio: Non legistis quod VOBIS dictum est a Deo? Hac enim perstringit illorum oscitantiam, qui hactenus libros Mosis negligentius legerint, neq; ad se pertinere putarint, quae in his scribuntur. Idem autem sibi dici putent omnes homines: Ut meminerint Scripturas sibi datas esse, & ipsis dici, quaecunq; in his praecipiuntur aut prohibentur: ad se item pertinere comminationes, si immorigeri sint: promissiones item, si Scripturis credant & obsequantur.
units.tr: There follows the third part of Christ's answer, in which he asserts the true doctrine of the resurrection of the dead, saying: "But concerning the resurrection of the dead, have you not read what was spoken to you by God, saying: I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob." These words are found in Moses, to whom the Lord spoke thus when, appearing to him in the burning bush, he was sending him as envoy to Pharaoh on behalf of the sons of Israel. Christ chose to cite this passage, though there are many other places in which the resurrection is declared more clearly, because he was dealing with the Sadducees, who (as we have said elsewhere) acknowledged only the books of Moses as sacred, as containing God's word. The question "Have you not read what was spoken to YOU by God?" has a peculiar emphasis. For by it he rebukes the carelessness of those who had hitherto read the books of Moses rather negligently and had not thought that what is written in them pertained to them. Let all men, however, think that the same is said to them: let them remember that the Scriptures have been given to them and are addressed to them, whatever is commanded or forbidden in them; likewise that the threats pertain to them if they are disobedient, and the promises too if they believe the Scriptures and obey them.

units.la: Sed videamus, ut hoc Dei dicto mortuorum resurrectionem demonstret Dominus. Deus (inquit) est Deus Abrahami, Isaaci & Iacobi, & se horum Deum esse professus est, cum Iacob, qui inter hos ultimus nominatur, ante annos centum decem & sex vita hac esset defunctus: At Deus non est Deus mortuorum, sed viuentium: Ergo Abraham, Isaac & Iacob viuunt. Vis argumenti est in vocabulo Dei, quod relationem habet ad eos, quorum Deus esse dicitur. Nam Deum esse alicuius, est eius vindicem, seruatorem & dominum esse. Non potest ergo Deus esse eorum qui nulli sunt, quales sane Sadducaei dicebant esse mortuos, cum neq; animas eorum viuere, neq; corpora resurrectura esse sentirent. At Christus hoc argumento utrumq; asserit. Viuere enim dicit patriarchas illos quoad animas eorum, & inde per consequens colligit, quod qui ipsorum Deum fe profitetur, corpora quoque eorum olim excitaturus sit. Est argumenti huius certitudo firmissima et irrefragabilis. Quia nisi viuant mortui & resurgant, patribus omnibus, qui obdormierunt, iniuria fiet, & promissionum omnium fides abrogabitur, simulque Dei maiestas collabetur. Debet autem hinc etiam colligi salutis nostrae certitudo. Quis enim de ea dubitabit, quando ne mors quidem nos a Deo separare potest? Quod enim de patribus hisce, qui dudum hac vita defuncti sunt, hoc de omnibus, qui crediunt in ipsum, Christus dicit, quod nimirum a morte transeant in vitam: & Lazarum Bethaniensem, qui iam quartum diem in sepulchro agebat, suum amicum vocare dignatur. Testimonia Scripturarum & argumenta, quibus mortuorum resurrectio demonstrari potest, alibi non semel adduximus.
units.tr: But let us see how the Lord demonstrates the resurrection of the dead from this word of God. God (he says) is the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob; and he professed himself to be the God of these, when Jacob, who is named last among them, had died in this life a hundred and sixteen years before. But God is not the God of the dead, but of the living: therefore Abraham, Isaac and Jacob live. The force of the argument lies in the word God, which has a relation to those of whom he is said to be God. For to be someone's God is to be his protector, preserver and lord. Therefore God cannot be the God of those who are nothing, such as the Sadducees indeed said the dead were, since they judged neither that their souls live nor that their bodies will rise. But Christ by this argument asserts both. For he says that those patriarchs live as to their souls, and from this he consequently concludes that he who professes himself their God will also one day raise up their bodies. The certainty of this argument is most firm and irrefutable. For unless the dead live and rise, injustice would be done to all the fathers who have fallen asleep, the faithfulness of all promises would be abrogated, and at the same time the majesty of God would collapse. From this, moreover, the certainty of our salvation ought also to be drawn. For who will doubt it, when not even death itself can separate us from God? For what Christ says of those fathers, who long ago departed this life, he says of all who believe in him: namely that they pass from death into life; and he deigns to call Lazarus of Bethany, who was already in the tomb for four days, his friend. We have elsewhere more than once adduced the testimonies of Scripture and the arguments by which the resurrection of the dead can be demonstrated.

units.la: Quis vero fuit disputationis euentus? Cum audisset turba, perculsa est ob doctrinam eius. Magnam ergo oportet fuisse eorum ignorantiam, qui eo dogmate percelluntur, quod omnibus no ti ssimum esse debuerat. Lucas aliquos ex Scribis Domino assensum praebuisse, & eius argumentum probauisse scribit. Quo loco nobis considerandum venit Veritatis diuinae vis, quae aduersariorum quoque corda penetrat. Maluessent Scribae & Pharisaei illum Sadducaeorum argutiis succumbuisse, ut non haberet, quod illis opponeret. Sed ipsi Veritatis luce superati coguntur fateri quod res est. Et addit Lucas, quod nemo ausus fuerit illum amplius interrogare: nimirum quod timerent ne totics repulsi vulgo ludibrio fierent, Christi vero authoritas magis confirmaretur. Huius generis exempla passim occurrunt, quae ut docent Veritatem inuictam esse: ita nostri saeculi contumaciam arguunt, quae in hoc articulo resurrectionis multi laborant. Potuit paucis istis, quae hic dixit Dominus Scribis facile facere, ut Veritati testimonium ferant. At hodie reperiuntur, qui etsi haec ipsa & plura alia ipsis dicantur, tamen omnia derident, & scurrilibus sannis eludunt ea, in quibus salutis nostrae cardo versatur. Et hi non feruntur modo, verumetiam in delitiis habentur apud eos, qui Ecclesiae capita & columnae volunt dici. Sed neminem ista offendant. Insistamus potius constanter fidei articulis, ut firmiter credamus, fore huius mundi finem, & venturum Filium Dei IESVM CHRISTVM in gloria Patris, qui & mortuos excitabit, & vnicuique in corpore suo reddet congruenter ad id quod fecerit vel bonum vel malum. Procul ergo reiectis impiis illis illusoribus & Sadducaeis impietatis instauratoribus, vigilemus & oremus bonum illum Patrem miserationum, ut digni habeamur, qui nouissimorum temporum periculosos motus fide constanti effugere, & tandem conscientia bona & syncera consistere possimus coram Filio hominis. Huic debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: What, indeed, was the outcome of the disputation? When the crowd heard it, they were struck by his teaching. It must therefore have been a great ignorance of those who are thrown into confusion by a doctrine which ought to have been most familiar to all. Luke writes that some of the scribes gave assent to the Lord and approved his argument. Here we must consider the power of divine truth, which penetrates even the hearts of adversaries. The scribes and Pharisees would rather have seen him succumb to the subtleties of the Sadducees, so that he would have nothing to oppose to them. But overcome by the light of truth, they are compelled to confess what is the case. And Luke adds that no one dared to question him any further: doubtless because they feared that, having been so often repulsed, they would become a laughing-stock to the common people, while the authority of Christ would be more firmly established. Examples of this kind occur everywhere, and as they teach that truth is invincible, so they expose the obstinacy of our age, in which many struggle over this article of the resurrection. With the few words which the Lord spoke to the scribes it would have been easy for them to bear witness to the truth. But today there are those who, even when these very things and many others are said to them, nevertheless mock everything and with buffoonish jeers scoff at those things on which the hinge of our salvation turns. And such men are not merely tolerated, but are even held in favour among those who wish to be called the heads and pillars of the Church. But let no one be offended by these things. Let us rather persist steadfastly in the articles of faith, firmly believing that there will be an end of this world, and that the Son of God, Jesus Christ, will come in the glory of the Father, who will also raise the dead and render to each one in his body, according to what he has done, whether good or evil. Let us therefore, far from those impious mockers and the Sadducees, the renewers of impiety, be watchful and pray to that good Father of mercies, that we may be deemed worthy to escape the perilous movements of the last times by constant faith, and at last be able to stand with a good and sincere conscience before the Son of man. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCLX.
units.tr: HOMILY 260.

units.la: Pharisaei vero cum audissent eum occlusisse os Sadducaeis, coacti sunt in vnum. Tunc interrogauit eum quidam ex ipsis Legis interpres, tentans eum, & dicens: Magister, quod est mandatum magnum in Lege? IESVS autem dixit ei: Diliges Dominum Deum tuum ex toto corde tuo, & ex tota anima tua, & ex tota cogitatione tua. Istud est primum & magnum mandatum.
units.tr: But when the Pharisees heard that he had silenced the Sadducees, they gathered together. Then one of them, a lawyer, tested him with a question, saying: "Teacher, which is the great commandment in the Law?" Jesus said to him: "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind. This is the first and great commandment."

units.la: Dominus & Seruator noster IESVS CHRISTVS hucusq; ad quaestiones aliquot, aduersus aduersarij sui, Scribae & Sacerdotes, ipsum insidiose tentarunt, ita respondit, ut hi qui dem turpiter confusi ex arena quasi abierint, illius autem sapientiam & acumen plane diuinum auditores omnes sint admirati. Non tamen Veritati cesserunt aduersarij, sed subinde alia via ipsum aggressi sunt, & alij alijs succenturiati successerunt, qui pugnam instaurarent. In his autem obseruari debet, primum hostium Euangelij pertinacia, qui ne vitti quidem quiescunt: huius autem nobis vsus esse debet, ne nobis otium polliceamur, sed perpetuo instatione maneamus ad repellendum conatus hostium parati. Deinde bonitas Christi consideretur, qui horum fraudes toties experiuntur, tamen amice respondet, & eos de rebus cognitu necessarijs instituit. In praesenti autem congressu suam simul potentiam & sapientiam declarat, quando aduersarium ipse capit, ut vitius Veritati setati testimonium ferat. Et quia in hoc colloquio summa pietatis vera & vita instituenda ratio continetur, vtile fuerit singulas historiæ partes excutere.
units.tr: Our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, when his adversaries, the scribes and priests, had so far tried him with insidious questions, answered in such a way that they went away from the contest shamefully confounded, while all his hearers marvelled at his wisdom and keenness, which was plainly divine. Yet the adversaries did not yield to the truth. Instead they attacked him again by another route, and one after another they came up as reinforcements to renew the battle. In this we should observe, first, the obstinacy of the enemies of the gospel, who do not rest even when beaten; we should make use of this by not promising ourselves leisure, but by remaining always on guard, ready to repel the attempts of enemies. Second, we should consider the goodness of Christ, who, though he has so often experienced their tricks, still answers them kindly and instructs them in matters that must be known. In this encounter he displays at once his power and his wisdom, when he takes the adversary himself, so that the one who was caught bears witness to the truth. And since the sum of true piety and the method of right living are contained in this conversation, it will be useful to examine its parts one by one.

units.la: Orditur autem ab occasione istius congressus Euangelista. Vident Pharisæi Dominum IESVM CHRISTVM os occlusisse Sadducæos, nec habere hos quod ipsi respondeant. Conue-niunt itaq;, & quasi hac facta iniuriam ulcisci velint, ipsi contra illum nouum certamen sus-cipiunt. Atqui de resurrectione mortuorum disputarat ille, ex quaias omnis dependet, & cuius vindices & assertores Pharifæi volebant haberi. Ergo gaudere debebant, illam argumen-tum tam validis demonstratam esse, vt vulgus quoq; in eius fide confirmaretur. Sed tanto odio Christum persecuti sunt, vt maluissent victoriam penes Sadducæos fuisse, vt illius existimatio-ni plurimum derogatum esset. Vnde apparet rursus, quod nuper diximus, illos quoq; Sadducæi non fuisse meliores, neq; religiosiores: sed eorum similes, qui hodie cum Papistis & Monachis colludere non verentur, vt puriorem & simplicem doctrinam de Cœna Domini oppugnent, & ido- lolatriam in Ecclesijs bene institutis inuehant. Gloriantur hi magnificè zelo religionis, & popu-li simplicis salutem sibi cordi esse protestantur. At cum idola defendant, & sordes Papisticas redo-cesatagant, non possumus nobis de illis plura polliceri, quàm de Pharifæis Iudæorum.
units.tr: The evangelist begins with the occasion of this encounter. The Pharisees see that the Lord Jesus Christ has silenced the Sadducees and that they have no answer to give. So they gather together, and as if they wished to avenge the injury done to their side, they take up a new contest against him. Yet he had been disputing about the resurrection of the dead, on which all religion depends, and of which the Pharisees wished to be regarded as the defenders and champions. They ought therefore to have rejoiced that this doctrine had been proved with such strong arguments that even the common people might be confirmed in their faith in it. But they persecuted Christ with such hatred that they would rather have had victory lie with the Sadducees, if only his reputation were thereby greatly diminished. From this it appears again, as we said a little while ago, that those Sadducees were no better or more religious than the others, but are like those who today do not hesitate to collude with the Papists and monks in order to attack the purer and simpler doctrine of the Lord's Supper, and to bring idolatry into well-ordered churches. These men boast loudly of their zeal for religion and protest that the salvation of the simple people lies close to their hearts. But since they defend idols and labour to restore Papist filth, we cannot promise ourselves more from them than from the Pharisees of the Jews.

units.la: Cæterum videamus, vt rem hanc instituerint. Vident (vt diximus) Sadducæos succu-buisse, vtpote homines rudes & Scripturarum ignaros, & ne in Mose quidem diligenter versatos, cuius libros solebant admittere. Sciebant præterea Pharifæorum sestam Domino suspestam esse. Itaq; non omnes simul ipsum aggrediuntur, sed vnum ex ipsorum ordine deligunt, qui in Lege probè institutus erat, & quem ingenio moderato præditum fuisse tota hac actio abundè docet. Mo-uet hic quæstionem sua professione dignam, & quæ ad religionem & salutem cognitu necessaria erat. Magister (inquit) quod est mandatum magnum in Lege, quod pra aliis pie & religiose ob-seruare debeant, qui Deo placere & salutem æternam consequi volunt. Tentandi verò causa quærit: Nimirum quod putet illum nouum quid dicturum, quod a Legis doctrina discrepet: aut si non aliud dicat, quàm quod olim Moses dixerit, non esse aliquam causam, propter quam ipse Mosi debeat præferri. In quo exemplo diligenter obseruetur, quantum noceat malorum & im-piorum hostium Christi consortium. Fuit hic doctus in Lege, vir item bonus quoad sæculum & (vt postea de illo Dominus testatus est) apud Marcum) non longè abfuit a regno Dei. Attamen quia hastenus Pharifæis conuixit, & apud hos propter eruditionem & mores honestos in pretio fuit, suum illis obsequium præstat, & ne ab illis separetur, quorum maxima erat apud plerofq; authoritas, aduersus Christum in certamen descendere non veretur. Ita multis accidere solet, qui per se non mali neq; a religione alieni omnino sunt, at alicuius commodi gratia se præsulum Papisticorum, aut principum, qui Euangelij doctrinam persequuntur, seruitio mancipant. Hi deinde multa videre & audire coguntur, quæ ipsis displicent, aut etiam ex animo dolent: at ni-si pedem illico reuocent ab horum commerciis, sit plerunq;, vt Veritatem tandem oppugnent, non verbis modò, verumetiam aperta vi & armis: quod nostro sæculo fecerunt multi, & adhuc faciunt, qui in vera religione educati, militiæ mercenariæ sese dedunt, & religionem atq; pios cul-tores Christi persequuntur. Cauti ergo sint Christiani homines, & meminerint amicitiam huius mundi esse inimicitiam cum Deo.
units.tr: Let us see, however, how they set about this business. They see (as we have said) that the Sadducees have been worsted, being unlearned men, ignorant of the Scriptures, and not even thoroughly versed in Moses, whose books they used to admit. They knew, moreover, that the sect of the Pharisees was suspect to the Lord. So they do not all attack him together, but choose one from their own order, who was well trained in the Law and who, as the whole episode amply shows, was endowed with a moderate temper. This man raises a question worthy of his profession, and one that was necessary to know for religion and salvation. "Teacher," he says, "which is the great commandment in the Law, which people who wish to please God and obtain eternal salvation ought to observe before all others with piety and devotion?" He asks in order to test him, doubtless because he thinks Jesus will say something new that departs from the teaching of the Law, or, if he says nothing other than what Moses once said, that there is no reason why he should be preferred to Moses. In this example we should carefully observe how greatly the company of wicked and impious enemies of Christ can harm. This man was learned in the Law, a good man as far as the world goes, and (as the Lord later testified of him, in Mark) he was not far from the kingdom of God. Yet because he had so far associated with the Pharisees, and among them was held in esteem for his learning and honest manners, he yields to them and, lest he be separated from those whose authority was greatest with most people, he does not hesitate to enter the contest against Christ. So it often happens to many who are not wicked in themselves and are not altogether estranged from religion, but who for some advantage hand themselves over to the service of Papist prelates or of princes who persecute the doctrine of the gospel. Then they are compelled to see and hear many things that displease them, or even grieve them inwardly; and unless they immediately withdraw their foot from such dealings, it usually happens that at last they attack the truth, not only with words but also with open force and arms. Many have done this in our own age, and still do: men brought up in the true religion who give themselves to mercenary soldiering and persecute religion and the pious worshippers of Christ. Let Christians therefore be cautious, and remember that friendship with this world is enmity with God.

units.la: Porrò CHRISTVS IESVS etsi Pharifæi responsione indigni essent, & non solum re-pulsam, sed reprehensionem & correptionem acriorem mererentur, amice tamen Legisperita re-sponder, partim quod quæstio per se pia & explicatu necessaria erat: partim quod hunc etsi Pha-risæis operam suam locaret, tamen eum lucrifieri posse sciret. Est́q; hoc nouum & consolationis plenum facilitatis eius argumentum, quo confirmatur quod apud Ioannem dicit: Eum qui venit ad me, nequaquam eiecerim foras. Etenim si istum benigni admisit & instituit, qui tentandi causa veniebat, num eos repulsam passuros putabimus, qui doctrinæ & institutionis cupidi quæstiones pias & necessarias mouent, & ipsius mandato sese accomodant, qui nos quærere iussit, & nos in-uenturos promisit, quæ ad salutem consequendam faciunt. Docet præterea exemplo suo, vt nulli occasioni desimus, qua regnum Dei promoueri, & aliqui in eius cognitione institui possunt. Quo-ties ergo de fide nostra & salutis negotio interrogamur, quibusuis ad respondendum parati simus,
units.tr: Moreover, although the Pharisees were unworthy of an answer, and deserved not merely a rebuff but a sharper rebuke and correction, Jesus nevertheless answers the lawyer kindly: partly because the question was in itself pious and necessary to explain, and partly because he knew that this man, though he had lent his services to the Pharisees, could still be won. This is a new proof of his gentleness, full of comfort, by which is confirmed what he says in John: "Whoever comes to me I will by no means cast out." For if he received kindly and instructed one who came to test him, shall we suppose that those will be repulsed who, eager for teaching and instruction, raise pious and necessary questions, and submit themselves to his command, who bade us seek and promised that we would find what leads to salvation? He teaches besides, by his own example, that we should not neglect any opportunity by which the kingdom of God may be advanced and some may be instructed in its knowledge. Therefore, whenever we are questioned about our faith and the matter of salvation, let us be ready to answer anyone whatever,

units.la: X ne Veritatis doctrinam dissimulando, eos in errore detineamus, qui veritatis studio & desiderio tenentur.
units.tr: lest by concealing the doctrine of truth we keep in error those who are held by a zeal and desire for the truth.

units.la: Ita vero respondet isti Dominus, vt non obiter modo quod nam primum & supremum manda-tum sic doceat, sed insuper summam totius Legis quoad religionem atq; vitae institutionem com-prehendat. Et ne aliquam illis calumniandi occasionem praebeat, Mosem adducit, cuius verba in Deuteronomio leguntur: Diliges Dominum Deum ex toto corde tuo, & tota anima tua, & pro omni viribus tua. Huic autem loco alium addit, qui in Leuitico habetur: Diliges proximum tuum vt teipsum. In quibus duobus mandatis Legem & Prophetas omnes consistere, postea testabitur. Priusquam vero in loci huius explicatione progrediamur, multa consideratione digna est Dei Patris bonitas, qui cum summum in nos ius habeat, & proinde leges, quas ipse vult, nobis possit praescribere, non tamen alijs praeceptis nos grauare voluit, quam quae per dilectionem possunt praestari, qua nihil iucundius, nihil vtilius, nihil magis necessarium est, & quae per omnes vitae nostrae actiones extenditur. Nam actiones vitae omnes partim ad Deum, partim ad homines alios, qui no-bis proximi sunt, referuntur. Ideo Legis summam, Decalogum nimirum, quae propria voce in monte Sinai Israelitis tradidit, in duas tabulas distribuit: quarum prima, quid Deo debeamus, docet: altera, officia, quibus proximo obstricti sumus, exponit: vtraq; autem (vt diximus) charitatis aut dilectionis officia tradit. Arguit hoc istorum ingratitudinem & amentiam, qui his non contenti, seipsos & alios grauant nouis traditionibus, quae corporalia exercitia a nobis requirunt, quorum vtilitas admodum exigua est, cum omnia ista (quod apostolus de cibis dixit) cor stabilire non possint, neq; alios ad pietatem & salutem aedificare. Etenim vt Marthae olim dicebat Dominus, vnum est necessarium: quod quoad vitae huius externa officia, proprie est dilectio, quae vt alibi Paulus ait totam Legem completitur. Porro quoad primam huius loci partem, aut supremum mandatum est, haec nobis consideranda sunt.
units.tr: The Lord answers this man in such a way that he not only teaches plainly what the first and highest commandment is, but also sums up the whole of the Law as regards religion and the ordering of life. And so that he may give them no occasion for slander, he cites Moses, whose words are read in Deuteronomy: You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength. To this passage he adds another, which is found in Leviticus: You shall love your neighbour as yourself. He will afterwards testify that all the Law and the Prophets depend on these two commandments. Before we proceed to explain this passage, the goodness of God the Father deserves much consideration: though he has the highest right over us, and so could prescribe to us whatever laws he pleases, he nevertheless did not wish to burden us with any precepts other than those which can be performed through love, than which nothing is sweeter, nothing more useful, nothing more necessary, and which extends through all the actions of our life. For all the actions of our life are referred partly to God and partly to other men who are our neighbours. Therefore he distributed the sum of the Law, namely the Decalogue, which he delivered to the Israelites in his own voice on Mount Sinai, into two tables: the first teaches what we owe to God, the second sets out the duties by which we are bound to our neighbour; and both, as we have said, hand down the duties of charity or love. This shows the ingratitude and folly of those who, not content with these, burden both themselves and others with new traditions, which demand bodily exercises from us, whose usefulness is very slight, since all these things (as the apostle said of foods) cannot establish the heart, nor build others up in piety and salvation. For, as the Lord once said to Martha, one thing is needful; and as regards the external duties of this life, that one thing is properly love, which, as Paul says elsewhere, fulfils the whole Law. Now as to the first part of this passage, or the highest commandment, these points are to be considered.

units.la: Primum, quid de Deo sentiri aut credi debeat. Nec enim illum diligere possumus, vt par est, nisi eundem recte agnoscamus: imo nisi eius cognitio praecedat, vix illum dilectione dignum esse arbitrabimur. At hic in primis obseruari debet, quod apud Marcum Dominus ex Mose praemisit, qui primum mandatum recitaturus dixit: Audi Israel, Dominus Deus noster, Dominus vnus est. Breui dicto omnia comprehendit, quae ad fidem & dilectionem Dei pertinent. Ante omnia vero Deum aut Dominum nostrum esse agnoscamus oportet. Est hoc principium & fundamentum omnis religionis: nec enim illi fidere poterimus, nisi nostrum esse intelligamus. Ideo hoc infaedere cum Abrahamo facto nobis commendat, & his verbis Legis promulgationem orditur: Ego sum Dominus Deus tuus, qui te eduxi de terra Aegypti. In nouo Testamento Christus ita orare docet, vt Deum Patris nostri nomine inuocemus. Et in Symbolo Apostolorum ideo illi fidere docemur, quod noster fit, & Filium suum Vnigenitum nobis Dominum & Seruatorem dederit. Deinde ne ab hoc principio fidei nos reuocare aut abstrahi patiamur, vnum esse credamus, non plures. Etenim summum & supremum bonum est, & proinde vnicum fit oportet. Nec enim summus esse potest, qui alios sibi pares aut aequales habet. Ideo apud Isaiam clamat: Non est alius Deus praeter me: Deus iustus & saluans nullus praeter me. Et quia in Lege graniter vetat, ne Deos alienos habeamus coram facie eius, Paulus Christianos homines eo discrimine ab alijs distinguí scribit, quod cum alij Deos plures habeant, illi vno contenti sint. Quotquot ergo alios sibi Deos fingunt, in quibus spem aliquam salutis collocant, eo ipso fe Christianos esse negant.
units.tr: First, we must consider what ought to be felt and believed about God. We cannot love him as we should unless we know him rightly; indeed, unless we know him first, we will hardly think him worthy of our love. Here above all we must notice what the Lord, quoting Moses in Mark, put first when he was about to recite the first commandment: Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is one. In a brief saying he comprehends everything that pertains to faith and to the love of God. Above all we must acknowledge that he is God, or our Lord. This is the beginning and foundation of all religion, for we cannot trust in him unless we understand that he is ours. Therefore he commends this to us in the covenant made with Abraham, and he opens the promulgation of the Law with these words: I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt. In the New Testament, Christ teaches us to pray that we invoke God by the name of our Father. And in the Apostles' Creed we are taught to trust him because he is ours, and because he has given us his only-begotten Son as Lord and Saviour. Next, so that we do not allow ourselves to be called back from or drawn away from this first principle of faith, let us believe that there is one God, not many. For the highest and supreme good is one, and therefore it must be unique. Nor can he be supreme who has others equal or like himself. So in Isaiah he cries out: There is no other God besides me; a just God and a Saviour, there is none besides me. And since the Law strictly forbids us to have other gods before his face, Paul writes that Christians are distinguished from others by this difference: while others have many gods, Christians are content with one. Whoever therefore fashions for himself other gods, in whom he places some hope of salvation, by that very fact denies that he is a Christian.

units.la: Et huc facit alterum, quod hoc loco Christus ex Mose de summo mandato docet, vt Deum vnice diligamus, & quidem super omnia. Vbi rursus nouum bonitatis Dei argumentum sese exerit. Etenim a nobis amari vult ille, quibus nihil nobiscum commune est, & qui vicissim nihil ex nobis sperare potest. Inter homines solent quidam aut generis fiducia ita superbire, aut opibus insolescere, vt dedecori sibi esse arbitrentur, si qui ipsis inferiores sunt, ipsorum studium & amorem profiteantur. Sunt item, quos beneficiorum pudet, quibus aliqui de ipsis bene merentur. At longe alius est Deus, qui nostro amore delectatur: & vt filij prodigi pater, illum tot modis in se iniuriu plus quam paterno amore complexus est: ita Deus nos solet, qui propter innatam nobis malitiam odio potius quàm amore digni fimus. Etenim si non aliud fit nostra corrupta ac vitiosa natura indi- cium, vnde hoc suffi cere poterat, quod nobis praecipi & mandari oportet, quod tot beneficijs ab il- lo prouocati sponte facere debebamus. Tanta enim horum magnitudo, vt quicunque ex hominibus sensum communem non omnino exuerunt, hunc omnis boni fontem & thesaurum esse fateantur. Qua ergo contumacia est illum non vicissim diligere?
units.tr: A second point also belongs here: in this passage Christ teaches from Moses the greatest commandment, that we love God alone, and indeed above all things. Here again a new proof of the goodness of God appears. For he wishes to be loved by those with whom he has nothing in common, and who in turn can expect nothing from us. Among men, some are so puffed up by the confidence of family, or so swollen with wealth, that they think it a disgrace to profess their zeal and love for those who are beneath them. Likewise there are those who are ashamed of the benefits which others have conferred on them. But God is quite different: he delights in our love. And like the father of the prodigal son, he has embraced us, who have wronged him in so many ways, with more than a father's love. Yet we, because of the malice innate in us, are rather worthy of hatred than of love. For if our corrupt and vicious nature offered no other evidence, this alone would be enough: that we must be commanded and bidden to do what, provoked by so many benefits from him, we ought to have done of our own accord. For the greatness of these benefits is such that all men who have not entirely cast off common sense confess him to be the fountain and treasury of all good. What stubbornness, then, is it not to love him in return?

units.la: Secundo obseruetur, qualis esse debeat dilectio. Quia vnus (vt diximus) super omnia diligi debet. Nisi enim id fiat, iniuriam ipsi fecerimus, vt mulier, quae in amoris coniugalis consortium alios praeter maritum suum admittit. Non poterit autem Deus vnus & solus a nobis diligi, nisi amor ille syncerus, & ab omni fuco alienus sit. Ad eius explicationem faciunt species illae, quae totum hominem cum suis viribus & facultatibus vniuersis comprehendunt. Inter quas primo loco cor nominatur: Diliges Dominum Deum tuum ex toto corde tuo. Cor affectuum sedes, & proinde consiliorum & actionum omnium fons est. Has igitur omnes ad eum finem dirigi oportet, vt voluntati diuinae consentiant, & gloriae Dei seruiant, ne huic per nos derogetur. Secundo anima totina mentio fit, quae in Scripturis vitam denotare solet. Hanc ergo totam Deo consecremus, vt (quod Apostolus iubet) nos sistamus hostiam viuam, sanctam & acceptam Deo: & ne configuremur fa- culo isti, aut mundo, de quo Ioannes praecipit: Ne diligite mundum, neque ea quae in mundo sunt. Peccant autem hi, qui meliorem vitae partem mundo & huius principi consecrant, tunc demum Deo seruituri, quando in aetate decrepita ad finem vitae appropinquant. Tertio ex tota cogitatione nostra Deum diligere iubemur. Graeci ςφροσυνην dicunt, quae mentis virtus est, de qua Poeta, de Pythagora dixit: Mente Deos adijt, & quod natura negabat, Visibus humanis, oculis eapestoris hausit.
units.tr: Second, let us observe what kind of love ought to be shown. Since, as we have said, God alone must be loved above all things. For unless this is done, we would do him an injury, as a wife does who admits others besides her husband into the fellowship of conjugal love. God alone, the one God, cannot be loved by us unless that love is sincere and free from all pretence. To explain this, those expressions which embrace the whole man with all his powers and faculties are relevant. Among them, the heart is named first: You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart. The heart is the seat of the affections and therefore the source of all counsels and actions. All these, then, must be directed to this end: that they agree with the divine will and serve the glory of God, so that it is not diminished through us. Second, mention is made of the whole soul, which in the Scriptures usually denotes life. Let us therefore consecrate all of it to God, so that (as the Apostle bids) we present ourselves as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God; and that we not be conformed to this age or to the world, of which John commands: Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world. But those sin who consecrate the better part of their life to the world and its prince, and only then mean to serve God when they approach the end of life in decrepit old age. Third, we are commanded to love God with the whole of our thought. The Greeks call it sophrosyne [σωφροσύνη], which is a virtue of the mind, of which the poet, speaking of Pythagoras, said: "With his mind he approached the gods, and what nature denied to human sight and eyes, he drew in."

units.la: Et Cicero mentes bonorum diuinas & caelestes atque immortales esse confessus est. In praesenti ergo omnes interiores seu animae facultates Christus intellexit cogitationis vocabulo. Apud Marcum vero totas quoque vires addit, vt alias quoque hominis facultates, siue corporis siue animae Deo vendicet, & demonstret, nihil in nobis esse, quod non totum Deo debeamus, cum ab hoc corpus & animam & vtriusque facultates omnes acceperimus.
units.tr: And Cicero confessed that the minds of good men are divine, heavenly and immortal. In the present passage, therefore, Christ understood by the word thought all the inner faculties or powers of the soul. But in Mark he adds also all the strength, so that he claims for God the other faculties of man as well, whether of body or of soul, and shows that there is nothing in us which we do not owe wholly to God, since we have received from him the body, the soul, and all the faculties of both.

units.la: Itaque dilectio Dei non in otiosa professione consistit, sed effectus parit, quae per omnem hominis vitam extenduntur. Etenim dilectionis proprium est, cum dilectio vniri velle. Ita qui Deum ex toto corde diligunt, & omnibus viribus coniunctionem cum Deo expetunt, & ab omnibus abhorrent, quae nos ab illo separare possunt: a superstitionibus nimirum & peccatis, quibus vel religio vera, vel vita innocentia polluitur. E contra, verbi Dei studium parit dilectio ista, quo hic fiepsum & voluntate suam cum vniuersis regni sui mysterijs manifestat. Sequitur ex eo obedientia & huic placendi studium. Coniuncta huic est patientia, quae omnibus aduersis superiores facit. Sic enim prophanus amor omnia vincit (vt Poeta aiunt) quis dubitet sancti illius & diuini amoris maiores vires esse, cuius subiectum omnia longè superat, quae in caelis & in terra sunt? Et quia amantes colloquijs potissimum gaudent, cum Deo autem per preces colloquimur, quo nullum colloquium iucundius, nullum sanctius & magis necessarium est: qui illius dilectione ardent, ij in precibus quoque assidui sunt, cum & inuocandi & gratias agendi occasio nunquam non sese offerat. At si ista cum nostri saeculi moribus conferas, mox patebit, quantum nobis desit: quando plerique cum mundo coniungi malunt, quàm cum Deo: Verbum eiusdem fastidiunt, nisi illud cum quaestu aliquo coniunctū videant: idem vero si ipsorum cupiditatibus reluctetur, odisse solent & perseguri: adhaec carnis contumaciam improbe vouent, periculis quibusque succumbunt, in precibus autem adeo lan- guent, vt neque periculis ad inuocationem excitari, neque beneficijs ad gratiarum actionem accendi possint. Opus ergo fuerit, vt Spiritus Sanctus dilectione Dei diffundat in cordibus nostris: quod tum fiet, si nos ad Verbi studium assuefaciamus, beneficia illius assidue meditemur, animos vero a huius saeculi gaudijs, quae fluxa & incerta sunt, ad aeterna attollamus, quae no- bis in caelis paranit Dei Filius IESVS CHRISTVS, cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: Therefore the love of God does not consist in an idle profession, but brings forth effects which extend through the whole of human life. For it is the property of love to wish to be united, since love is a desire for union. Thus those who love God with the whole heart, and with all their strength seek union with God, and shrink from everything that can separate us from him: namely superstitions and sins, by which either true religion or an innocent life is defiled. On the other hand, this love produces zeal for the Word of God, by which he makes himself and his will known together with all the mysteries of his kingdom. From this follows obedience and the desire to please him. Joined to this is patience, which makes us superior to all adversities. For if profane love, as the poets say, conquers all things, who would doubt that the power of that holy and divine love is greater, whose object far surpasses all that is in heaven and on earth? And since lovers delight above all in conversation, and we converse with God through prayers, than which no conversation is more pleasant, more holy, or more necessary, those who burn with love for him are also constant in prayer, since the occasion both to call upon him and to give thanks never ceases to present itself. But if you compare these things with the manners of our age, it will soon be plain how much we lack: for most people prefer to be joined with the world rather than with God. They despise his Word unless they see it joined with some gain; and if it opposes their desires, they are wont to hate and persecute it. Moreover, they shamelessly indulge the obstinacy of the flesh and yield to every danger, while in prayer they grow so languid that they can neither be stirred to invocation by dangers nor kindled to thanksgiving by benefits. It is necessary, then, that the Holy Spirit pour out the love of God in our hearts. This will happen if we accustom ourselves to the study of the Word, constantly meditate on his benefits, and lift up our minds from the joys of this age, which are fleeting and uncertain, to eternal things, which God's Son Jesus Christ has prepared for us in heaven, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen.

units.la: Secundum autem simile huic. Diliges proximum tuum, vt teipsum: Ab istis duobus mandatis tota Lex & Prophetæ pendent.
units.tr: And the second is like it: "You shall love your neighbour as yourself." On these two commandments hang all the Law and the Prophets.

units.la: INter actiones aduersariorum cum Filio Dei IESV CHRISTO perquàm memorabilis est hæc, in cuius tractatione nunc versamur. Nam, vt nuper audiuimus, ad illum accessit quidam Legis peritus, quem Pharisæi, vt ipsum insidiosa quæstione tentaret, subornarunt. Proponit autem quæstionem cognitu dignissimam, quod nam inter Legis præcepta obseruatu præ aliis necessarium sit. Ita vero respondet Dominus, vt duo coniungat, quibus omnia comprehendit, quæ ad veram pie & beatè viuendi rationem faciunt: simul autem in huius noui aduersarij corde sic agit, vt qui ipsum tentaturus venerat, victus veritati cedat, & præclarum testimonium ipsi ferat. Primum præceptum ex Deut. sexto Cap. adducit, quo tota religionis causa continetur: Quid nimirum de Deo sentiri debeat: quæ officiorum item, quæ illi debentur, summa sit: vt scilicet ipsum dilectione syncera complectamur, nosq; totos ei consecremus. At quia quales erga Deum simus in ijs potissimum apparet, quæ nobis cum aliis hominibus peragenda sunt, nunc alterum quoq; præceptum prima subiicit, dicens:
units.tr: Among the encounters of the adversaries with the Son of God, Jesus Christ, this one, which we are now handling, is most memorable. For, as we heard recently, a certain expert in the Law approached him, whom the Pharisees had put up to test him with a snare of a question. He puts forward a most worthy question to be known: which of the commandments of the Law ought to be observed before the others as most necessary. The Lord answers in such a way as to join two commandments, which together comprehend everything that bears on a true, pious and blessed way of living. At the same time, he so deals with the heart of this new adversary that the man, who had come to test him, is overcome, yields to the truth, and gives him a splendid testimony. He cites the first commandment from Deuteronomy chapter six, in which the whole cause of religion is contained: what we ought to think of God, and likewise what is the sum of the duties we owe him, namely that we embrace him with sincere love and consecrate ourselves wholly to him. But since what sort of people we are towards God appears above all in what we must do with other men, he now adds the second commandment, which is closely linked to the first, saying:

units.la: Secundum simile huic, Diliges proximum tuum vt teipsum, &c. Extat præceptum hoc (vt nuper quoq; diximus) in Leuitico Capite 18. & ita recitatur: Non oderis in corde tuo fratrem tuum: at plane reprehendas proximum tuum, id est, amica correptione ipsum ab errore reuocando testa ris te illum fratris loco habere: neferas propter eum peccatum, ne conniuendo ad eius vitia peccatis illius communices. Deniq; ne vlciscaris, neq; fis iniuriarum memor erga filios populi tui: sed diliges proximum tuum vt teipsum. Hoc præceptum Christus secundum dicit, respectu prioris, quod de dilectione Dei præmisit, & quia secundam Decalogi tabulam comprehendit. Adhæc priori simile esse ait: Primum, quia hic etiam, vt in priori, dilectio præcipitur: Deinde quod ex dilectione Dei dilectio proximi nascitur: Deniq; quod vt priori omnis obedientia traditur, quam Deo debemus: ita hic omne exigitur officium, quod proximo nos debere constat. Notum est enim illud Apostoli: Nemini quicquam debete, nisi hoc, vt alij alios diligatis. Quo dicto monet debitum dilectionis eiusmodi esse, vt homo Christianus semper inueniat, quod alij debeat, propter conditionem & fortem communem, cui omnes subiecti sumus. Est enim dilectio propensio animi, qua alicui bene volumus, non quidem nostrijpsius, sed aliorum causa, & id reipsa & opere testamur.
units.tr: "The second is like it: You shall love your neighbour as yourself," etc. This commandment stands in Leviticus chapter 18 (as we also said recently), and it is recited thus: "You shall not hate your brother in your heart; but you shall plainly rebuke your neighbour", that is, by a friendly correction calling him back from his error, "and you shall not bear sin on account of him", lest by conniving at his faults you share in his sins. "Finally, you shall not take vengeance, nor be mindful of injuries against the sons of your people; but you shall love your neighbour as yourself." Christ calls this commandment the second in relation to the first, which he put before it concerning the love of God, and because it comprehends the second table of the Decalogue. Moreover, he says it is like the first: first, because here too, as in the first, love is commanded; second, because love of neighbour is born from love of God; finally, because, as all obedience is handed down in the first, which we owe to God, so here every duty is required which we know we owe to our neighbour. For that saying of the Apostle is well known: "Owe nothing to anyone, except that you love one another."
