By these words he warns that the debt of love is of such a kind that a Christian man always finds something he owes to others, on account of the condition and common lot to which we are all subject. For love is an inclination of the mind by which we wish someone well, not for our own sake but for the sake of others, and we bear witness to this in deed and in work.

units.la: Est autem præceptum hoc commune, quod ex æquo omnibus hominibus datur, siue diuites, pauperes, docti indocti sint. Et vehementer errant, qui se exleges putant, & aliquam immunitatem sibi vendicant, vt feré solent inopes & egeni, qui præceptum hoc nihil ad se pertinere arbitrantur, quod non habeant quod dent, nec aliquos iuuare possint. At dilectio, quæ animi affectus est, requiritur: quam non operibus, sed cordis propensione æstimare conuenit. Inter hanc ergo & opera nos distinguere oportet. Opera ab illis exiguntur, quos facultatibus instruxit Deus, vt ea præstare possint: quæ si definint, non est quod alicuius culpæ reatum nobisipsis imponamus. Nam, vt Paulus scribit, si prius adsit promptus animus, aliquis acceptus est pro eo quod habet, non pro eo quod non habet. Verumtamen dilectio illic etiam locum habet, vbi vires nullæ sunt. Nec enim quicquam obstat, quo minus bene velis alicui, nisi iniuidia aut odijfascinum te exagitet, nec erga fratrem recte affectum esse sinat. Vt ergo diues peccat negligendo pauperem, quem iuuare poterat: ita non minus peccat pauper, qui diuiti suam fortunam meliorem inuidet. Peccat item, qui inhumaniter & rigide nimis debita exigit. At minime extra culpam est, qui paupertatis prætextu abutitur ad fallendum creditores. Neminem ergo fallant cæcæ carnis rationes, vt ab hoc debito se exemptum esse putet: sed meminerint omnes non posse aliquem mortalium quenquam abs se alienum, aut amore suo indignum censere, cum Deus iubeat inimicos quoq; diligere. Vide Matth. 5.
units.tr: This commandment is common, given equally to all men, whether they be rich or poor, learned or unlearned. And they greatly err who think themselves exempt from the law and claim some immunity for themselves, as the needy and the destitute are commonly wont to do, who judge that this commandment does not concern them, because they have nothing to give and cannot help anyone. But love, which is an affection of the heart, is required, and it is to be valued not by works but by the disposition of the heart. Between this and works, therefore, we ought to make a distinction. Works are demanded from those whom God has furnished with means so that they can perform them; if these fail, there is no reason for us to lay upon ourselves the guilt of any fault. For, as Paul writes, if a ready mind is present beforehand, a man is accepted for what he has, not for what he does not have. Yet love has its place even where there are no means. For nothing stands in the way of your wishing someone well, unless envy or the evil eye torments you and does not allow you to be rightly disposed towards your brother. So just as the rich man sins by neglecting the poor man whom he could have helped, so the poor man sins no less who envies the rich man his better fortune. Likewise he sins who demands debts inhumanly and too rigidly. But he is by no means free of guilt who uses poverty as a pretext for cheating creditors. Let not the blind reasonings of the flesh deceive anyone into thinking he is exempt from this debt; rather let all remember that no mortal can judge anyone to be a stranger to himself, or unworthy of his love, since God commands us to love even our enemies. See Matthew 5.

units.la: Itaq; propius videre oportet, quis ab vnoquoq; diligi debeat. Id vna vocula docet ex Lege Dominus, quando vt proximum diligas, iubet. Atqui ita inter homines comparatum est, vt fere omnes sibi ipsos sibi proximos esse putent. At Christum non de nobisipsis, sed alijs hominibus loqui notius est ex cir ex circumstantijs, quàm vt demonstrari oporteat. Itaq; hic legis aut praecepti diuini sensus sit mens est, vt proximo cuiq; dilectionis officium praestemus, qui illo indiget. Debet u nobis proximus censeri quisquis sit: quia eadem est omnium hominum conditio, vt quod vni accidit, quisq; sibi quoq; accidere posse cogitare debeat. Et merito probatur illud Comici: Homo sum, humani nihil a me alienum puto. Itaq; sufficiat tibi, si hominem esse videas eum, cui tuo officio aut beneficio opus est. Docetur hoc alibi per Samaritani parabolam, quae cum suo loco prolixè exposita sit, non opus est illi diutius immorari. Quid ergo non debemus iis, qui domestici fidei & fratres in Christo sunt? Vide Lucae 10.
units.tr: Therefore we must look more closely at who ought to be loved by each one of us. The Lord teaches this from the Law in a single little word, when he bids us love our neighbour. Yet it is so ordered among men that almost all think of themselves as their own neighbours. But that Christ is speaking not of ourselves but of other men is clear enough from the circumstances, without need for demonstration. So the meaning of this law or divine precept is that we should render the office of love to whoever in each case needs it. Whoever he may be ought to be counted our neighbour, since the condition of all men is the same, so that each one ought to reflect that what happens to one may happen to himself too. And rightly is that saying of the comic poet approved: "I am a man; I count nothing human foreign to me." So it will be enough for you if you see in him a man to whom your duty or your kindness is needed. This is taught elsewhere through the parable of the Samaritan, which has been set out at length in its own place, so there is no need to dwell on it longer. What then ought we not to owe to those who are members of the household of faith and brothers in Christ? See Luke 10.

units.la: At non minus diligenter modus dilectionis proximi nobis considerandus erit. Sunt enim plures, qui ignorantiam praetexunt, & propter innatam omnibus philautiam nimium esse arbitrantur, quicquid ab ipsis requiritur. Itaq; proximum quisq; vt seipsum diligere iubetur. Quis vero tam vecors est, vt quomodo seipsum diligat, ignoret? Quin ergo in seipsum descendis, & ex seipso dilectionis regulam petis? Teipsum non simulate, sed vere: non nudis aut otiosis verbis, sed reipsa & opere: non frigide, sed ardenter diligis, & in hoc incumbis, vt tibi bene sit & commodè vitas: deniq; non defatigaris teipsum diligendo, etiamsi vitijs animi aut corporis labores, quae odiù merentur, sed quo haec plura & graviora sunt, eò diligentius illa tegere & velare studes. Praeterea si tibi quid praeter voluntatem accidat, alios tibi condolere vis, & indignè admodum fers, si qui tibi insultet, aut interea suae libidini & fastui indulgeant. Ex teipso igitur documentum cape, quid factio opus sit, si in dilectione proximi Deo placere cupias. Syncera sit illa & ab hypocrisi aliena, verbis aut promissis opera respondeant, feriò item omnia facias, & in eo totus sis, vt proximo bene sit, nec te omni officio defunctum esse putato, si beneficium vnum aut alterum praestiteris, sed quoad aliquem tuae opis indigum esse videris, ad hanc illi ferendam te facilem & sedulum praebeto. Quòd si ali quis indignus videatur beneficio, tu de omnibus bene sperato, & (vt D. Petrus ex Solomonemonet) proximi vitia aut delicta operire studeas, si corrigere non potes. Vbi vero ad officia ventus fuerit, hic tibi animus sit, vt etsi omnibus alijs satisfacias, tibi ipsi non satisfeceris. Talem nobis Dominus Samaritanum describit, cuius exemplum nos imitari iubet. Is cum in terra aliena iter faceret, & hominem ignotum videret a praedonibus male multatum, quae alij illius gentis homines inhumaniter neglexerant, ipse eius commiseratione toto animo commotus est: Nec in otioso animi affectu acquiescit, sed ex itinere ad eum diuertit, & suis negotijs relictis, illius curam suscipit, & ne periculo quidem, quod ex praedonibus vereri poterat, abstterretur: quo minus faciat, quod in praesenti fieri poterat. Saucij vulnera enim abluit, oleo infuso dolorem eorum mitigat, obligat deniq; ne mora periculu graujus pariat. Inde iumento impositum ipse pedes deducit in hospitium, illic ea nocte illius curam habet, crastino autem die cum alio ipsum vocarent negotia, hospiti satisfacit, & eidem illum commendans sese pro illo sponsorem sistit: Deniq; nihil eorum praetermittit, quae quis in eiusmodi casu pro filio proprio aut fratre germano faceret. Nullis ergo limitibus certis circumscripta est charitas, sed pro viribus praestat, quantum praesens necessitas postulat, dolet autem si non tantum possit praestare, quantum necesse erat. Sibi ipsis ergo singuli applicent admonitionem aut praeceptum Christi, quod parabola isti subiicitur: Abi, & tu fac similiter.
units.tr: But the manner of love towards our neighbour must be considered no less carefully. For there are many who pretend ignorance, and, because of the self-love innate in all, think that whatever is required of them is too much. Thus each one is bidden to love his neighbour as himself. But who is so foolish that he does not know how he loves himself? Why then do you not descend into yourself and seek from yourself the rule of love? Love yourself not feignedly but truly; not with empty or idle words, but in deed and in work; not coldly but ardently, and devote yourself to this, that it may go well with you and that you may live comfortably. Finally, do not grow weary in loving yourself, even though you are burdened by faults of mind or body that deserve hatred; rather, the more numerous and grave these are, the more diligently you strive to cover and conceal them. Besides, if anything happens to you against your will, you want others to sympathise with you, and you take it very badly if anyone insults you, or meanwhile indulges his lust and pride. Therefore take from yourself the lesson of what must be done if you wish to please God in love of neighbour. Let that love be sincere and free from hypocrisy; let works answer to words and promises; likewise do everything diligently, and be wholly intent on this, that it may go well with your neighbour. Do not think yourself discharged of every duty if you have performed one or two kindnesses, but as long as you see anyone in need of your help, show yourself ready and zealous to bring it to him. But if anyone seems unworthy of a kindness, still think well of everyone, and (as St Peter admonishes from Solomon) strive to cover the faults and sins of your neighbour, if you cannot correct them. When it comes to the duties themselves, let this be your spirit: that even if you satisfy all others, you have not satisfied yourself. The Lord describes the Samaritan as such a man, and bids us imitate his example. When he was travelling in a foreign land and saw a stranger badly mauled by robbers, whom other men of that nation had inhumanly neglected, he was moved with compassion for him in his whole mind. Nor does he rest in an idle affection of the heart, but turns aside from his journey to him, and, leaving his own affairs, takes up his care, and is not even deterred by the danger which he might fear from the robbers, from doing what could be done at the moment. For he washes the wounds of the injured man, soothes their pain by pouring in oil, and finally binds them up lest delay bring a greater peril. Then, placing him on his beast, he leads him on foot to an inn, and there cares for him that night; but the next day, when his business called him elsewhere, he satisfies the innkeeper and, commending the man to him, presents himself as surety for him. In short, he omits nothing that anyone would do in such a case for his own son or his own brother. Charity, therefore, is bounded by no fixed limits, but gives as much as present necessity requires, and grieves if it cannot give as much as was needed. Let each one therefore apply to himself the admonition or precept of Christ that is added to the parable: "Go, and do likewise."

units.la: Quia vero Matthaeus breuitati studet, ex Marco peti debet huius actionis sine colloquij euentus, qui duplex fuit. Primus ad legisperitum pertinet, qui responsum hoc Domini probauit, & Vt ritati testimonium ingenuè perhibuit. Nam ait: Bene, praeceptor in veritate dixisti. Nam vnus est Deus, nec alius est praeter eum. Et diligere eum ex toto corde, & ex tota anima, & ex totis viribus, ac diligere proximum vt seipsum, plus est quàm omnia holocautomata & sacrificia. Apparet in isto homine, quàm magna veritatis vis sit, si attentè audiatur, & in animum admittatur. Venerat hic, vt Dominum dolosè tentaret, aut irretiret. At ipse captus vitiori manus dat, & publicè illi assentitur, & quidem in eo, de quo tunc inter Christum & Pharisaeos siue Sacerdotes maximè controuertebatur. Hi enim aduersus illum reuera pro aris & focis pugnabant, eo quòd metuerent, ne per eius doctrinam quaestui ipsorum derogaretur. At hic nihil veritus socios, a quibus suborna-tus erat, doctrinae Christi subscribit: quod non aliud erat, quàm Pharisaeorum superstitiones damnare. Simile quid accidit, quando Pharisaeorum serui, qui ad illum in templo capiendum emissi sunt. rant doctrinam illius magnifice commendarunt. Sunt alia quoq; huius generis exempla, in quibus cernimus tyrannos interdum Veritati cedisse, vt ex persecutoribus amici & discipuli facti fuerint. Arguitur hic infelix nostri saeculi contumacia, quando multi nec Scripturis nec signis conuincy ci & edomari possunt, vt Deum vnum esse fateantur, & vnum inter hunc & nos mediatorem IESVM CHRISTVM, a quo tamen seipsos denominant, & Christiani dici volunt. Discant omnes hunc imitari, nec pudeat Veritati cedere. Haec enim omnium pulcherrima & gloriosissima est victoria. Haec olim Dauidem & Niniuitas seruauit: & huic Scribae Dei Filius testimonium praebuit, quod non longe absit a regno Dei. Ita Veritatis confessio regni Dei ciues facit, a quo omnes excludentur, qui se illi contumaciter opponunt.
units.tr: Since Matthew aims at brevity, the outcome of this encounter, which was twofold, must be taken from Mark, without the conversation. The first part concerns the lawyer, who approved this answer of the Lord and frankly bore witness to the truth. For he said: "Well, Teacher, you have spoken truly: for there is one God, and there is no other besides him; and to love him with the whole heart, and with the whole soul, and with all the strength, and to love one's neighbour as oneself, is more than all whole burnt offerings and sacrifices." In this man one can see how great the power of truth is, if it is heard attentively and admitted into the mind. This man had come to tempt or ensnare the Lord by guile, but he himself, caught by the truth, gives up his hand to the better side, and publicly assents to him, and indeed on that very point over which Christ and the Pharisees or priests were then chiefly contending. For these men were really fighting against him for their altars and hearths, because they feared that his teaching would detract from their gain. But this man, fearing nothing from the companions by whom he had been suborned, subscribed to the teaching of Christ, which was nothing other than condemning the superstitions of the Pharisees. Something similar happened when the servants of the Pharisees, who had been sent to seize him in the temple, greatly commended his teaching. There are also other examples of this kind, in which we see tyrants sometimes yield to the truth, so that from persecutors they became friends and disciples. Here the unhappy obstinacy of our age is exposed, when many cannot be convinced and subdued either by the Scriptures or by signs, so as to confess that God is one, and that there is one mediator between him and us, Jesus Christ, from whom nevertheless they take their name and wish to be called Christians. Let all learn to imitate this man, and let them not be ashamed to yield to the truth. For this is the most beautiful and most glorious of all victories. This once preserved David and the Ninevites; and the Son of God bore witness to this scribe, that he was not far from the kingdom of God. Thus the confession of truth makes citizens of the kingdom of God, and from it all are excluded who obstinately oppose themselves to it.

units.la: Alter euentus ad Christi aduersarios refertur, de quibus scribit Marcus, quod nemo illorum amplius ausus fuerit ipsum interrogare. Conuicti licet proprii cordis testimonio tamen cedere nolunt Veritati: Attamen inuiti et reluctantes quamuis succumbunt. Est hoc proprium impiis, quod vtut fremant contumaciter, non tamen audent mutire contra veritatem, nec posunt semper, quantum posse videntur. Perrexerunt quidem ipsi de illo occidendo consultare, & vicisse vipsi sunt, quando a Iuda proditus in ipsorum manus venit, & ex Pilati sententia in crucem suffixus acerbam et ignominiosam mortem subiit. Sed moriendo vicit Christus, & resurgens de morte & inferis & tota diaboli potestate triumphauit. Non est ergo quod nobis meliorem fortem in terris polliceamur, quam illius fuit. Non mutabit enim ingenium suum mundus. Interim neq; promissis suis deerit aeternus Dei Filius. In eo igitur fortes & constantes simus, qui nos non relinquet orphanos, sed nobiscum erit vsq; ad consummationem saeculi, quando nos in regnum suum caeleste transferet. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: The other outcome is related to the adversaries of Christ, of whom Mark writes that none of them afterwards dared to question him any more. Although convicted by the testimony of their own hearts, they nevertheless refuse to yield to the truth; yet, though unwilling and struggling, they are overcome. It is characteristic of the impious that, however much they rage obstinately, they nonetheless do not dare to mutter against the truth, nor can they always do as much as they seem able. They indeed went on to plot his death, and they seemed to have won when he, betrayed by Judas, came into their hands, and by the sentence of Pilate was fastened to the cross and suffered a bitter and ignominious death. But by dying Christ conquered, and rising from death, from hell, and from the whole power of the devil, he triumphed. There is therefore no reason for us to promise ourselves on earth a better lot than his was. For the world will not change its nature. Meanwhile the eternal Son of God will not fail his promises. Let us therefore be brave and constant in him, who will not leave us orphans, but will be with us even to the end of the age, when he will transfer us into his heavenly kingdom. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCLXII.
units.tr: Homily 262.

units.la: Coactis autem Pharisaeis, interrogauit eos IESVS, dicens: Quid vobis videtur de Christo? cuius filius est? Dicunt ei, Dauidis. Dicit eis: Quomodo ergo Dauid in Spiritu vocat eum Dominum? dicens: Dixit Dominus Domino meo, Sede ad dexteram meam, vsque dum ponam inimicos tuos scabellum pedum tuorum. Si ergo Dauid vocat eum Dominum, quomodo filius eius est? Et nemo poterat ei respondere quicquam: neque ausus fuit quisquam ab illo die amplius eum interrogare.
units.tr: When the Pharisees had gathered together, Jesus asked them, saying: "What do you think of the Christ? Whose son is he?" They said to him, "David's." He said to them, "How then does David in the Spirit call him Lord, saying: 'The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet'? If David calls him Lord, how is he his son?" And no one could answer him a word, nor did anyone dare from that day on to question him any further.

units.la: Quamuis prophani homines, & etiam hypocritae superstitiosi, Veritatis lucem odio prosequuntur & extinctam velint, studium tamen illius egregie simulare norunt, dum colloquia cum pijs expetunt & quaestiones nectunt multas & varias, non quidem vt discant, sed vt simplicitas illaqueent, aut Veritatis doctrinam vulgo subpectam & exosam reddant. Quae causa est, quod fere quaestiones mouent eiusmodi, quae vel seditionem & turbas spirant vel absurdae nimis animos prophanos et impuros arguunt. Est hoc videre in IESV CHRISTI aduersarijs. Ex his enim primo Pharisaei de censu Caesari reddendo quaerunt, si forte responso inconsiderato aliquid dicat, ex quo eius calumniandi occasionem arripiant: Deinde Sadducaei de resurrectione mortuorum disputatione mouent, quae nihil absurdius, inhonestius & impudentius vel scurrilius fingi poterat. Sunt haec nobis in eum finem considerandae, vt facilius eorum dolos agnoscere, & insidias cauere dijca- mus, qui hodie similia facere non verentur. Sed opponitur hic disputatio noua, quam Christus monuit, longe alio instituto: vt nimirum publica ignorantia, quae tunc inter Iudaeos regnabat, medere- tur, & illos simul omnes instituerent in re cognitu cumprimis necessaria, & cuius vera cognitio ad pacem publicam faciebat, & simul saluti animarum aeternae seruiebat. Est nobis diligentius in hac versandum, quod non obiter & quasi aliud agens, sed in templo publice docens haec tradidit, quibus regni sui mysteria praecipua continentur. Videamus ergo primum quando & qua occasione de his coeperit agere: Deinde quaestionem ipsam, & cur eam Christus monerit: Praeterea quae fuerit disputationis iste finis fuit euentus.
units.tr: Although profane men, and even superstitious hypocrites, pursue the light of truth with hatred and would have it extinguished, they know how to feign a zeal for it splendidly, while they seek conversations with the godly and weave many and various questions. They do this not in order to learn, but to ensnare the simple, or to make the doctrine of truth suspect and hateful to the common people. This is why they mostly raise questions of such a kind as either breathe sedition and tumult, or reveal the minds of profane and impure men to be excessively absurd. This may be seen in the adversaries of Jesus Christ. For first the Pharisees asked about paying the census to Caesar, in case by chance he said something in an unguarded answer from which they could seize an occasion to slander him. Then the Sadducees raised a dispute about the resurrection of the dead, a question than which nothing more absurd, dishonourable, shameless or buffoonish could have been devised. These things are to be considered by us for this end: that we may more easily recognise the tricks of such men and learn to beware of the snares of those who today do not hesitate to do similar things. But here a new kind of disputation is set against them, which Christ urged, with a quite different purpose: namely, to remedy the public ignorance that then reigned among the Jews, and to instruct them all together in a matter especially necessary to know, whose true knowledge both made for public peace and served the eternal salvation of souls. We must dwell on this more carefully, since he delivered these teachings not casually or as if doing something else, but while teaching publicly in the temple, teachings in which the chief mysteries of his kingdom are contained. Let us see, then, first when and on what occasion he began to speak of these things; second, the question itself, and why Christ urged it; and finally, what was the outcome and end of this disputation.

units.la: Quoad primum, Pharisæi coacti aut congregati illos Dominus interrogauisse dicitur. At qui nō annotatur eos ab ipso coactos aut conuocatos fuisse, sed haud dubie quia res suas infelicius succedere, & se aliquoties iam non sine publica ignominia succubuisse viderent, & proinde nō auderent (vt nuper ex Marco annotauimus) aduersus illū denuò in certamen descendere, nisi prius diligenti deliberatione habita Christus ipsis superuenit, & ipse prior illos compellat. Nō autem ideo accusari meretur, quasi inciuilior æquo aut impudens ad concilium non vocatus accesserit. Quia enim ab illis sæpè prouocatus, sese ad respondendum hucusque facilem præbuit, licuit omnino ipsi eos interrogare, qui antistites & doctores populi volebant dici, & ex illorum oraine erant, de quibus olim dixerat Dominus: Labia Sacerdotis custodient scientiam, & legem ex ore eius requirent. Adhæc animi sibi bene conscij & ingenui indicium est, quod aduersariorum consperium non declinat, quod non vnum ex illis imperitiore cæteris insidiose obseruat, vt in eo solo sibi facta iniurias vlciscatur, & miserum toti populo deridendum propinet, sed illos simul omnes aggreditur quæstione non insidiosa, sed necessaria, & quæ diligentius cognita tam ipsis quā alijs omnibus safutem afferre poterat. Ita agere conuenit veritatis ministros, & tales esse debent disputationes piorum, vt non alius his finis aut scopus fit propositus, quam vt in veritatis & regni Dei cognitione homines instituantur, & qui prius instituti sunt magis confirmentur.
units.tr: As for the first point, it is said that the Lord questioned the Pharisees when they had been gathered or assembled. But it is not recorded that they were summoned or called together by him. Rather, doubtless because they saw their affairs turning out unhappily, and that they had several times already been worsted, not without public disgrace, they did not dare (as we noted recently from Mark) to enter the contest against him again, unless after careful deliberation. Christ came upon them first and addressed them himself. Nor does he deserve blame, as if he had come to the council uninvited, more uncivilly than was right or shamelessly. For since he had often been challenged by them and had hitherto shown himself ready to answer, it was entirely permissible for him to question those who wished to be called the leaders and teachers of the people, and who belonged to the order of those of whom the Lord once said: "The lips of the priest shall keep knowledge, and they shall seek the law at his mouth." Moreover, it is a sign of a mind that is conscious of its own integrity and generous that it does not shun the snares of its adversaries, and that it does not single out one of them, less skilled than the rest, to ambush him, in order to avenge injuries done to himself alone and to offer the wretched man up to be mocked by the whole people. Instead he attacks them all together with a question that is not insidious but necessary, and which, if it had been understood more carefully, could have brought salvation both to them and to all others. It becomes ministers of truth to act in this way, and the disputations of the godly ought to be such that no other aim or goal is set before them than that men be instructed in the knowledge of the truth and of the kingdom of God, and that those already instructed be more firmly confirmed.

units.la: Sed accedamus ad quæstionem Christi. Quid vobis videtur (inquit) de Christo? Cuius filius est? Respondent illi, Dauidis. Ex hoc Dominus aliam quæstionem infert, & vt nodum soluant petit, qui ex contradictione ipsius Dauidis nescii videbatur, qui illum suum Dominum dixit. Vbi nemo putauerit, Christū consulto argutias quæsiuisse inutiles, vt solent, qui recondita eruditionis & scientiæ existimationem affectant. Sed vt hæc quæstio ventilaretur, publica Iudæorum ignorantia, cuius initio mentione fecimus, requirebat. Nouerunt illi vulgo promissiones Dei de Messia, quem venturum prædixerat Iacob Patriarcha, quando sceptro a Iuda subl ato, Iudæi alieno imperio parerent. Eundem ex Dauidis stirpe nasciturum esse fatebantur, cui olim dixisset Dominus. Cum exaltati fuerint dies tui, dormieris cum patribus tuis, excitabo semen tuū post te, quod egredietur de vtero tuo, regnumq; eius firmabo. Item, Semel per sanctitatem meam iuraui, haudquaquam Dauidem fefellero: Semen eius in æternum erit, solium eius coram me vt Sol perstabit. Denique nihil inter Iudæos vulgarius erat, quam quod Messias promissus dicebatur Dauidis filius. At quæcunque de regno illius magnifica dicuntur, omnia de regno in terris potenti & victoriose intelligebant, nec illum homine principe aut rege maiorem agnoscebant. Et hoc errore discipulos quoque eius domesticos fascinatos fuisse, crebra horum de primatu contentiones abunde testantur: & in vulgo Iudæorum hæc perfuasio siue opinio turbarū & seditionū fere causa fuit, & quod qui rebus nouis studebant, impostoribus locum subinde dederunt, qui sub falso seu adulterino Messiæ nomine regnum affectabant. Et quia (vt alibi monuimus) hic error plerosque occupauerat, nō potuerūt pro Messia agnoscere IESVM hunc, in quo nihil apparebat, quod splendorem regium referret.
units.tr: But let us come to the question of Christ. "What do you think (he says) of the Christ? Whose son is he?" They answer: "David's." From this the Lord brings forward another question, and asks them to loosen a knot which seemed to puzzle them, arising from David's own words, in which he called him his Lord. Here no one should think that Christ sought useless subtleties in a deliberate way, as those do who aim at a reputation for hidden learning and erudition. Rather, so that this question might be aired, the public ignorance of the Jews, of which we spoke at the beginning, required it. They commonly knew the promises of God concerning the Messiah, whom the patriarch Jacob had foretold would come when the sceptre was taken from Judah and the Jews would be subject to foreign rule. They acknowledged that he would be born from the stock of David, to whom the Lord had once said: "When your days are fulfilled and you sleep with your fathers, I will raise up your seed after you, which shall come forth from your womb, and I will establish his kingdom." Likewise: "Once I have sworn by my holiness; I will not fail David. His seed shall be forever, and his throne shall endure before me like the sun." In short, nothing was more commonly held among the Jews than that the promised Messiah would be the son of David. But whatever magnificent things were said of his kingdom, they all understood of a kingdom on earth, powerful and victorious, and they did not acknowledge him as greater than a human prince or king. That his own household disciples were also bewitched by this error, their frequent contentions about primacy abundantly bear witness. And among the common people of the Jews this persuasion or opinion was mostly the cause of tumults and seditions, and those who were eager for revolution repeatedly gave place to impostors who, under the false or counterfeit name of the Messiah, aimed at a kingdom. And because (as we have elsewhere noted) this error had seized most people, they could not recognise this Jesus as the Messiah, since nothing appeared in him that bore a royal splendour.

units.la: Et est obseruanda hoc loco communis nostri hostis diaboli astutia, qua hic in fallendis hominibus vtitur. Non potuit is omnem Messiæ notitiam in hominum mentibus delere, aut spem aduentus sui eripere. Ergo huius loco talem finxit, qui principis terreni instar dominaretur: vt neglectis cœlestibus bonis homines huius sæculi commoda quærerent, & sub fidei & promissionū Dei prætextu propter illa tumultuarentur. Quod si qui non tam crasti fuerunt, hos alio errore demeta ut, vt in IESV CHRISTO Ioan. Baptistam, aut Ieremiam, aut alium aliquem ex Prophetis veteribus resurrexisse putarent. Quid quod ipsum Christum sine regni terreni solicitare ausus est, quando ipsi omniū huius sæculi regnorum splendorem & fastum ostendit? Etenim quamlibet de illo sententiam siue opinionem ferre poterat Satan, modo non pro Dei Filio & promisso humani generis redemptore agnoscatur. Hæc enim notitia atque fides regnum tenebrarum destruit, & mundi principem foras eijcit. Idcirco etiam multos planissibili Diuorum cœlitum prætextu fallit, dum hos Christo parescit, & quæ huic debetur gloriam in illos transfert. Quod Apostolorum tempore fieri cœpit, & hodie ita regnat hic error, vt Christi merito sub horum prætextu potissimum derogetur, qui dum viuerent, se totos illi impenderunt. Et hoc illud est, de quo nos Apostolus serio admonet, vt nobis a diaboli impostura cauteamus, qui seipsum transformare
units.tr: And at this point we must observe the common cunning of our enemy the devil, which he uses here in deceiving men. He could not wipe out all knowledge of the Messiah from men's minds, or snatch away the hope of his coming. So in his place he fashioned one who would rule like an earthly prince, so that, neglecting heavenly goods, men would seek the advantages of this age and stir up tumults over them under the pretext of faith and of God's promises. And if some were not so gross, he led them into another error, so that they thought that John the Baptist, or Jeremiah, or some other of the old prophets had risen again in Jesus Christ. What of the fact that he dared to tempt Christ himself with an earthly kingdom, when he showed him the splendour and pomp of all the kingdoms of this world? For Satan could pass whatever judgment or opinion he liked about him, provided that he was not acknowledged as the Son of God and the promised redeemer of the human race. For this knowledge and faith destroys the kingdom of darkness and casts the prince of the world out. Therefore he also deceives many under the plausible pretext of the saints in heaven, while he pretends to be subject to Christ, and transfers to them the glory that is due to him. This began to happen in the time of the Apostles, and today this error reigns so that Christ's merit is chiefly detracted from under the pretext of those who, while they lived, devoted themselves wholly to him. And this is that matter about which the Apostle seriously warns us, that we beware of the deceit of the devil, who knows how to transform himself

units.la: {y} Iohan. 3. norit in Angelum lucis. Itaq; non sufficit simplex Christi & nominis Christiani professio, sed dili genti scripturarum inuestigatione & examine opus est.
units.tr: Iohan. 3. into an angel of light. Therefore a simple profession of Christ and of the Christian name is not enough; diligent investigation and examination of the Scriptures is needed.

units.la: Ad hoc Iudæorum doctores in præsenti remittit, dum (vt paulo ante diximus) ex ipsius Davidis verbis quæ in Psalmis extant, quæstionem de Messia movet: Qua ratione nimirum Dauid Dominum suum dicat eum, qui post aliquot demum secula ex ipso nasci debuerit. Et ex communi sensu & recepta inter homines consuetudine argumentans sic dicere voluit. Indecens & iniquum a communi deniq; omnium gentium consuetudine alienum est, vt pater filium iam natum vocet Dominum suum, nedum vt rex aliquis filium post secula aliquot nasciturum hoc nomine dignetur: At Dauid rex potentissimus & multarum gentium domitor Messiam, quem ipso hac vita de functo multis post seculis demum ex sua posteritate nasciturum sciebat, dominum suum dixit, id que non affectu caeco aut paterna indulgentia abreptus, sed cum ex Spiritus sancti suggestione de illo vaticinaretur. Dicite ergo mihi, quae illum ratio monuerit? aut si hanc non potestis explicare, fateamini oportet, vos de mysterio hoc nunquam adhuc ea diligentia cogitasse, qua opus erat. Et vt efficacius illos percellat, verba Dauidis adducit, quae Psalmo 110. leguntur: Dixit Dominus Domino meo, sede ad dextram meam, vsq; dum ponam inimicos tuos scabellum pedum tuorum. At nisi tunc vulgo Iudæorum persuasum fuisset, psalmum illum a Dauide de promisso redemptore fuisse conscriptum, facile fuisset illis hoc testimonium vel simpliciter negare, vel aliquo cavillo eludere. At cum eos illud nequaquam posse sciret, vtiq; illos intra animos suos conuincere voluit, vt fateantur, Dauidem olim in Messia aliquid homine maius agnouisse, cuius respectu Dominum suum dixerit. Nisi enim hoc concedant, manifesta erit contradictio in iis propositionibus: Messias est Dauidis filius: Et Messias est Dauidis Dominus. Caeterum quia haec a Christo inter docendum dicta sunt, vt publicae ignorantiae mederetur, & in cognitione sua omnes rectè instituceret, proderit singulas huius loci partes diligentius excutere, vt discamus, quis sit Christus quoad suam essentiam siue personam: Quis item quoad functionem & dignitatem. Ex quibus postea patebit, quid nobis de ipsius regno sit sperandum.
units.tr: To this point the Jewish teachers are now brought back, since (as we said a little earlier) from the very words of David which stand in the Psalms he raises the question about the Messiah: by what reasoning, namely, David calls him his Lord, who ought to be born from him only after some centuries. And arguing from common sense and the custom received among men, he wished to say this: it is unbecoming and unjust, and in the end alien to the common custom of all nations, for a father to call a son, already born, his Lord; much less that some king should honour with this title a son who is to be born after many centuries. But David, a most powerful king and conqueror of many nations, called Messiah, whom he knew would be born from his own posterity many centuries after his death, his Lord; and he did so not carried away by blind affection or paternal indulgence, but while prophesying about him under the prompting of the Holy Spirit. "Tell me, then, what reason has suggested to you? Or if you cannot explain this, you must admit that you have never yet considered this mystery with the care it required." And that he may strike them more effectively, he brings forward the words of David, which are read in Psalm 110: "The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet." But unless it had been commonly persuaded among the Jews that David wrote that psalm concerning the promised Redeemer, it would have been easy for them either to deny this testimony outright or to evade it by some quibble. But since he knew they could by no means do so, he wished to convict them within their own minds, so that they would confess that David had once recognised in the Messiah something greater than a man, in respect of whom he called him his Lord. For unless they concede this, the contradiction in these two propositions will be plain: the Messiah is the son of David, and the Messiah is the Lord of David. Moreover, since these things were said by Christ in the course of teaching, to remedy public ignorance and to instruct everyone rightly in the knowledge of himself, it will profit us to examine each part of this passage more carefully, so that we may learn who Christ is as to his essence or person, and likewise as to his office and dignity. From these things it will afterwards become clear what we ought to hope for from his kingdom.

units.la: Si de persona illius dicendum sit, Iudæi hominem fore nunquam dubitarunt, imo IESVM CHRISTVM ideo aspernati sunt, quod Iosephi filium esse arbitrarentur. Et promissiones vete res diserte Messiam Iemen mulieris & Abrahami filium, Dauidis item & germen Isai dicunt. Et his aptipulantur Prophetae, qui ex virgine, & quidem Bethlehemi nasciturum esse olim tradiderunt. Itaq; sacerdotes etiā Herodi de Messia natalibus scitate consulenti potuerunt respondere: In Bethlehem Iudaeae. Sic enim scriptum est per prophetam, &c. At eunde Deum esse non credebant, quae illis erroru & incredulitatis, adeoq; impietatis omnis causa fuit. Etenim vt huic loco insistamus, si Deum & hominem esse credidissent, facilis fuisset quaestionis propositae solutio, neq; in specie contradictionis, quae reipsa nulla est, haesitassent. Dixissent enim: Messias recte dicitur Dauidis filius, quatenus homo est, ex Dauidis femine natus: Idem vero etiam vere dicitur Dauidis Dominus, quia Deus est & aeternus Dei Filius, qui prius quam ex Dauide hominem assumeret, imo priusquam Abraham esset, fuit: nec nomine modo fuit, sed reipsa, quae Dei sunt praestitit. Per ipsum enim secula condidit. Idem iam olim, Isaia tempore, regnante Achazo regnum Iuda seruauit, & domum Dauidis ex qua nasci debebat, defendit. Cur ergo non Dominum suum diceret Dauid illum, qui & Dei Filius est aeternus, & qui ipsius fuit seruator & redemptor? Sic (inquā responderent) potuissent Pharisaei, si Scripturam sacram de Messia loquentem propius & diligentius essent scrutati. Passim enim occurrunt testimonia, quae de illius diuinitate pronuntiant. Micheas etenim illius exitum ab aeterno esse testatur, qui Bethlehemi fit nasciturus. Isaias eundem Deum forte & Patrem aeternitatis vocat, & alibi dicit: Deus ipse veniet, & seruabit nos. Et rursus de eodem, Iehoua iudex noster, Iehoua legislator noster, Iehoua rex noster, ipse seruabit nos. Est ergo probe tenendum, quod Dominus noster IESVS CHRISTVS Dei Filius, in vna eademq; indi uisa persona Deus & homo est: Deus est ex substantia Patris (vt Athanasius ait) ante secula genitus, & homo ex substantia matris in seculo natus. Perfectus Deus, perfectus homo. Etenim verbum illud aeternum Dei, quod in principio erat, & per quod omnia facta sunt, factum est caro, id est, verus homo, ex anima rationali & humana carne subsistens, non quidem mutatione di nitatis minitatis in carnem, sed (vt Apostolus ad Hebraeos loquitur) feminis Abrahami assumptione in vnitatem personae, nec ab eo tempore vnquam depositus hominem, quem assumpsit, sed peracto in terris nostrae redemptionis negotio eundem in caelos euexit & ad dextram Patris collocauit, inde venturus ad iudicandum in ea forma & natura, in qua passus est. Est hoc fidei nostrae fundamentum, quod nisi constanter feruetur, illa confiffere non poterit: & multa occurrent in Christi mysteriis quae contradictoria videbuntur, & ex quibus humana ratio sese non magis explicabit, quam ex praesenti quaestione Pharisaei. Olim certe omnium haeresum causa praecipua fuit, quod naturas in Christo plenas non recte distinxerunt. Ideo Arius non potuit videre, quomodo Patri coaeternus & coessentialis esset, quem audiebat dixisse: Pater maior me est. Et hodie in Ecclesia horribiles turbas dant, qui omnipraesentiam carnis Christi & eiusdem corporalem & oralem siue Capernaiticam manducationem pertinaciter propugnant, neque conciliare possunt illius dicta: Ecce ego vobiscum sum vsque ad consummationem seculi: Et me non semper habebitis. Quisi cum orthodoxis Patribus naturarum in Christo distinctionem recte obseruarent, cum Diuo Augustino dice rent: Secundum maiestatem suam, secundum prouidentiam suam, secundum ineffabilem & inuisibilem gratiam impletur quod ab eo dictum est, Ecce ego vobiscum sum omnibus diebus vsque ad consummationem seculi: Secundum carnem vero quam verbum assumpsit, secundum id quod de Virgine natus est, secundum id quod a Iudaeis comprehensus est, quod ligno confixus, quod de cruce depositus, quod linteis inuolutus, quod in sepulchro conditus, quod in resurrectione manifestatus, Non semper habebitis me vobiscum. Quare? Quoniam conuersatus est secundum corporis praesentiam quadraginta diebus cum discipulis suis, & eis deducentibus videndo, non sequendo, ascendit in caelum, & non est hic. Ibi enim sedet ad dexteram Patris, & hic est. Non enim recessit praesentia maiestatis, etc. Sed plura de hac re alibi diximus: nunc pergamus in his quae huius loci sunt.
units.tr: If we are to speak of his person, the Jews never doubted that he would be a man; indeed they scorned Jesus Christ precisely because they supposed him to be the son of Joseph. And the promises of the old covenant expressly name the Messiah as the seed of the woman and the son of Abraham, and likewise as the offspring of David and the shoot of Jesse. The prophets, who long ago handed down that he would be born of a virgin, and indeed at Bethlehem, agree with these. Thus the priests could answer Herod, when he inquired carefully about the Messiah's birth: "In Bethlehem of Judaea; for so it is written by the prophet," and so on. But they did not believe that he was God, and this was the cause of all their errors and unbelief, and indeed of all their impiety. For, to keep to this passage, if they had believed him to be God and man, the solution of the question proposed would have been easy, and they would not have stuck fast in the appearance of a contradiction, which in reality there is none. For they would have said: the Messiah is rightly called the son of David, inasmuch as he is man, born of David's seed; but the same is truly called David's Lord, because he is God and the eternal Son of God, who existed before he assumed man from David, indeed before Abraham was, and he was not only so in name but in reality, performing what belongs to God. For through him he founded the ages. The same, in the time of Isaiah, when Ahaz reigned, preserved the kingdom of Judah and defended the house of David from which he was to be born. Why, then, should David not call Lord him who is both the eternal Son of God and the saviour and redeemer of David himself? So, I say, the Pharisees could have answered, had they more closely and diligently searched the holy Scripture speaking of the Messiah. For testimonies which declare his divinity occur everywhere. Micah indeed testifies that his going forth is from eternity, he who is to be born at Bethlehem. Isaiah calls the same one "God, the Father of eternity," and elsewhere says: "God himself will come and save us." And again, of the same: "Jehovah is our judge, Jehovah is our lawgiver, Jehovah is our king; he himself will save us." It is therefore well to hold that our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, in one undivided person is God and man: he is God from the substance of the Father (as Athanasius says) begotten before the ages, and man from the substance of the mother born in time; perfect God, perfect man. For that eternal Word of God, which was in the beginning and through which all things were made, was made flesh, that is, true man, subsisting of a rational soul and human flesh; not indeed by a change of the divinity into flesh, but (as the Apostle speaks to the Hebrews) by the assumption of the seed of Abraham into unity of person. Nor from that time did he ever lay aside the man whom he assumed, but, the work of our redemption being finished on earth, he lifted up the same into heaven and placed him at the right hand of the Father, whence he will come to judge in that form and nature in which he suffered. This is the foundation of our faith, which, unless it is steadfastly held, cannot stand; and many things will occur in the mysteries of Christ which will seem contradictory, and by which human reason will no more explain itself than the Pharisees did in the present question. Certainly in former times the chief cause of all heresies was that they did not rightly distinguish the natures in Christ. Thus Arius could not see how he could be co-eternal and co-essential with the Father, when he heard him say: "The Father is greater than I." And today in the Church those who stubbornly defend the omnipresence of Christ's flesh, and its bodily and oral or Capernaitic eating, cause dreadful disturbances, and cannot reconcile his words: "Behold, I am with you until the end of the age," and "You will not always have me." But if they observed rightly with the orthodox Fathers the distinction of the natures in Christ, they would say with the divine Augustine: "According to his majesty, according to his providence, according to his ineffable and invisible grace, what he said is fulfilled: Behold, I am with you all days, even to the end of the age. But according to the flesh which the Word assumed, according to what was born of the Virgin, according to what was seized by the Jews, what was fastened to the wood, what was taken down from the cross, what was wrapped in linen cloths, what was laid in the sepulchre, what was manifested in the resurrection: you will not always have me with you." Why? "Because he conversed in bodily presence with his disciples for forty days, and while they escorted him by sight, not by following, he ascended into heaven, and he is not here. For there he sits at the right hand of the Father, and here he is. For the presence of his majesty has not departed," and so on. But we have said more on this matter elsewhere; now let us proceed to what belongs to this passage.

units.la: Docet enim Dauid quis Christus sit quoad functionem suam & officium, & hoc omne vnico Domini vocabulo aut nomine exprimit, quo vniuersum nostrae redemptionis negotium comprehenditur. Si enim Dominus est Christus, nos serui sumus oportet, & ipsius quidem serui. Vnde vero hoc? Ex eo nimirum, quod cum peccati & diaboli mancipia essemus, ipse nos ex hac seruitute omnium miserrima redemit sanguinis sui pretio, & sibi acquisiuit, vt ipsius sumus peculium, & (vt Petrus ait) gens sancta, regale sacerdotium, domus deniq; spiritualis ad offerendum spiritualis hostias acceptas Deo per ipsum, qui ideo Christus siue Messias, id est, vnctus dicitur, quod Rex & sacerdos sit, qualem in praesenti Dauid describit. Regem enim esse docet, cum illi a Patre dictum sit: Sede ad dextram meam, vsque dum ponam inimicos tuos scabellum pedum tuorum. Et postquam fecerit potentiam suam & populi sui mores & ingenium describit, alterum quoq; illi tribuit dicens: Iurauit Dominus, neq; poenitebit eum: Tu es sacerdos in aeternum secundum ordinem Melchisedech: quem Leuitico genere & ordine praestantiorem fuisse, Apostolus ad Hebraeos proloquitur docet. Vtroq; autem officio olim functus est Iesus Christus. Nam instar regis victoriosi homines, quos hic in suam potestatem redegerat, diripuit & sibi vendicauit, & in libertatem filiorum Dei asseruit. Adhaec Sacerdotem egit, dum seipsum pro nobis in ara Crucis immolauit, Patrem caelestem placauit, iustitiam aeternam reduxit, benedictionem veram restituit. Adhuc etiam vtroque munere fungitur, dum vt rex nos tuetur aduersus hostes visibiles & inuisibiles, & vt Sacerdos pro nobis intercedit, & Mediator est vnicus apud Patrem. Restat nouissimus eius aduentus ad iudicium, quando postremus hostis noster abolebitur, Mors. Vide 1.Cor.15.
units.tr: For David teaches what Christ is as to his function and office, and expresses all this by the single title or name of Lord, in which the whole business of our redemption is comprehended. For if Christ is Lord, we must be servants, and indeed his servants. But whence is this? Clearly from this, that since we were slaves of sin and of the devil, he redeemed us from this most wretched servitude at the price of his own blood, and acquired us for himself, so that we are his own possession and (as Peter says) a holy nation, a royal priesthood, and finally a spiritual house, to offer spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through him. He is therefore called Christ or Messiah, that is, anointed, because he is King and Priest, such as David describes in the present passage. For he teaches that he is King, since it was said to him by the Father: "Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet." And after he has described his power and the manners and character of his people, he attributes to him the other office also, saying: "The Lord has sworn, and he will not repent: You are a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek," which the Apostle, in his letter to the Hebrews, teaches was more excellent than the Levitical race and order. Jesus Christ once discharged both offices. For like a victorious king he plundered the men whom he had brought under his power here, and claimed them for himself, and asserted them into the liberty of the sons of God. Besides, he acted as priest when he offered himself for us on the altar of the Cross, appeased the heavenly Father, restored eternal righteousness, and restored true blessing. Even now he also performs both offices: as king he defends us against visible and invisible enemies, and as priest he intercedes for us and is the only Mediator with the Father. There remains his last coming to judgment, when our final enemy, Death, will be abolished. See 1 Cor. 15.

units.la: Ista vero sic nobis consideranda sunt, vt simul nostri erga illum officij meminerimus: Et primo quidem illo vno Domino & Redemptore contenti, nullos nobis Dominos alios accersamus. Turpe enim fuerit, si qui tanto precio redempti fuimus, hominum serui fiamus. At peccant in eo, qui Diuos caelites inuocant, quos superstitiosi patronos suos in caelis nominare solent. Qui item ab ipsis denominari volunt, & cum in Baptismo nomen Christo dederint, nouna nomina sibi accersunt, & vt olim Corinthij fere Paulinos, Cephiltas & Apollonianos debeant: ita ipsi Francisci, Bernhardini, Dominicani dici volunt. Quod non aliud est, quam IESV CHRISTI meritum conculcare, & Dei Patris iuramentum, cuius Dauid meminit, vel le irritum facere. Præterea curandum nobis est, ne in peccati seruitutem relabamur, sed in libertate nostra constanter perstemus, neque ea vt occasione ad carnis licentiam abutamur: sed quod reliquum est vita, illi vivamus, qui pro nobis mortuus est & resurrexit. Vide 1. ad Corinthios quintum caput.
units.tr: These things, however, we must consider in such a way that we also remember our duty towards him. And first of all, let us be content with that one Lord and Redeemer and not summon any other lords for ourselves. For it would be shameful if we who have been redeemed at so high a price were to become slaves of men. Yet they sin in this who invoke the heavenly saints, whom the superstitious are accustomed to name as their patrons in heaven. Likewise, they wish to be named after them, and though they received a name at Baptism in Christ, they take to themselves new names, and, as the Corinthians once were (almost) Paulines, Cephites and Apollonians, so these want to be called Franciscans, Bernardines, Dominicans. This is nothing other than to trample underfoot the merit of Jesus Christ and to make void the oath of God the Father, which David mentions. Besides, we must take care not to relapse into the slavery of sin, but constantly persevere in our liberty, and not abuse it as an occasion for licence of the flesh; rather, for the rest of our life, let us live for him who died and rose again for us. See the fifth chapter of the First Epistle to the Corinthians.

units.la: Restat eventus disputationis huius. Primo, neminem ex toto Pharisæorum coetu fuisse scribit Matthæus, qui vel vnicum verbulum respondere potuerit. Potuerunt hactenus quæstiones insidiosas nectere Herodianis aulicis, & vulgo fucum facere: At interrogati de regni, feria, sancta, necessaria, & cuius cognitio ad ipsos maxime pertinebat, prorsus muti & infantes sunt. Deinde pudet quidem eos suæ ignorantiæ, sed ita vt qui non verita erant hucusque Dominum insidiose tentare, eos nunc pudeat interrogare de salutaribus & necessariis cognitu. Adde, quod rursus his meliores sunt multi ex rudi populo, qui Christum differente libenter audiuerunt. Docet exemplu hoc quam facile sit Deo hostibus suis os obturare, & aduersus ipsum superbientes extrema ignominia afficere, vt seipsos publice ridendos propinent. Sunt huius generis exempla passim, quorum hic nobis vsus esto, vt ex illis consolationem petamus aduersus impiorum Euangelij hostium conatus. Hac bet Antichristus oculos hominis, & videtur sæpe imperuestigabilis esse satellitum huius astutia, nec vllum nobis patere ex ipsorum tenebris effugium. Sed irritum fit plerunque quicquid conantur. Habet autem vbiq; locorum Dei Filius IESVS CHRISTVS suos, qui vocem eius audiunt, illa delectantur & indies proficiunt: quos imitari nos cenenit. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Here follows the outcome of this dispute. First, Matthew writes that no one from the whole company of the Pharisees was able to answer even a single word. Until now they had been able to weave insidious questions for the Herodian courtiers and to deceive the common people; but when questioned about the kingdom, the sabbath, the holy things, the necessary things, and matters whose knowledge pertained most of all to themselves, they are utterly mute and like infants. Then, indeed, they are ashamed of their ignorance, but in such a way that those who until now were not afraid to tempt the Lord insidiously are now ashamed to ask about things that are saving and necessary to know. Add that many of the simple people, who listened gladly to Christ teaching, are better than these. This example teaches how easily God can stop the mouths of his enemies and bring the utmost disgrace upon those who arrogate themselves against him, so that they expose themselves to public ridicule. There are examples of this kind everywhere, and let us use this one so that we may draw consolation from them against the attempts of the enemies of the gospel of the impious. The Antichrist blinds the eyes of men, and the cunning of his henchmen often seems impenetrable, and no escape from their darkness seems open to us. But whatever they attempt generally comes to nothing. Jesus Christ, the Son of God, has his own people everywhere, who hear his voice, delight in it, and make progress day by day; it is fitting that we imitate them. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPVT XXIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIII.

units.la: HOMILIA CCLXIII.
units.tr: HOMILY 263.

units.la: TVnc IESVS loquutus est turbæ & discipulis suis, dicens: In cathedra Moysis sedent Scribæ & Pharisæi; Omnia ergo quæ dixerint vobis vt seruetis, seruate & facite: sed secundum opera eorum ne facite.
units.tr: Then Jesus spoke to the crowds and to his disciples, saying: The scribes and the Pharisees sit in Moses' seat. Therefore all that they tell you, observe and do; but do not do according to their works.

units.la: PROXIMO Capite describit Matthæus aliquot IESV CHRISTI cum suis aduersariis, Scribis & Pharisæis, colloquia siue disputationes, in quibus de rebus arduis & necessariis cognitu ita disseruit, vt illi turpiter succubuerint, & tandem non auderent quicquam præterea aduersus ipsum mutire. Quia verò hi incurabili contumacia ipsum odisse & persequi pergebant, populus autem doctrina saniori delectabatur, nunc aduersus illos nouam actionem instituit, cuius prima parte hypocrisim & multiplicem illorum malitiam arguit, qua in doctrina & moribus peccabant. Deinde quales in posterum quoq; futuri sint docet, & quid discipuli porrò ex ipsis sperare debeant. Postremo illis & ingratos ac sanguinarios vrbi pœnas horribiles & triste excidium denuntiat.
units.tr: In the earlier part of this chapter Matthew records several conversations or disputes between Jesus Christ and his adversaries, the scribes and Pharisees, in which he handled matters that were difficult and necessary to know so thoroughly that they were shamefully defeated and at last dared not utter another word against him. But since these men persisted in hating and persecuting him with incurable obstinacy, while the people took delight in his sounder teaching, he now begins a new piece of action against them. In the first part of it he exposes their hypocrisy and their manifold wickedness, by which they sinned both in teaching and in conduct. Then he teaches what sort of men they will continue to be in future, and what the disciples ought to expect from them. Finally he announces dreadful punishments and grievous destruction upon the ungrateful and bloodthirsty city.

units.la: Præmittitur exordij loco breuis circumstantiarum designatio, dum sic scribit Euangelista: Tunc locutus est IESVS turbæ & discipulis suis, dicens, &c. Comprehendit his verbis tempus & occasionem huius nouæ actionis, vt eam cum ijs, quæ proximè præcesserunt, connectat. Tunc, inquit, quando Pharisæi & Scribæ toties cofuti in suis quæstionibus, & nunc quæstione, quæ Dominus de Messia ex Dauide mouit, turpis suæ ignorantiæ conuicti, non habuerunt quod porrò opponerent, populus autem non sine voluptate ipsius acumen admirareretur, vidit opportunum & necessarium esse, vt suum de Scribis & Pharisæis iudicium proderet, & toti populo indicaret, quam turpiter hucusque, ab ipsis deluti essent, & quid de eis sentire post hac debeant. Quo exemplo docemur, non satis esse, vt aduersarij conuincantur, sed præterea simplices & rudes instituti oportere, vt quid de illis sentire debeat, intelligant, & illorum dolos atq; impostauras cauere possint. Et quia hic de communi muni omnium salute agitur, publice id fiat necesse est. Fecerunt hoc olim Prophetae, quibus perpetua cum eiusmodi hominibus certamina fuerunt. Et Apostolis non satis fuit illos confutauisse, qui suo seculo fidei & doctrinae syncerioris corruptores erant, & multos seducebant, nisi de iis etiam nos admonerent, qui novissimis temporibus erant venturi, & quos hodie in Ecclesia multis impo nere videmus. Cum quibus ut hodie agi debeat, Christi exemplo docemur. Sunt equidem qui impostores eiusmodi argui & durius corripi indigne ferunt. Et mansuetudinem in Euangelij administris desiderant, qua plus profici arbitrantur, & stultum esse dicunt cum illis contendere, quos incurabiles esse, imo ferociores fieri & magis irritari noris. Vtinam vero ipsi rem diligentius perpenderent. Etenim viderent patientiae & mansuetudini nullum locum reliquum esse, vbi de gloria Dei & hominum salute agitur. Et respondeant mihi illi charitatis & modestiae nouj doctores, quis vnquam modestior & manfuetior fuit Dei Filio in carne manifestato, qui (vt olim Propheta de illo vaticinatus fuerat) non litigauit, neque clamauit, neque audiri fecit in plateis vocem suam, adhaec arundinem quassatam non confregit, neq; linum fumigans extinxit, omnes vero quos pecca torum conscientia oppressos laborare nouerat, amice ad se vocauit, & nullos durius accepit, aut de suo conspectu exclusit, quibus consolatione opus esse videbat? Vt vero idem aduersus hypocritas & populi seductores tonuit, fulminauit, dum omnis modestiae quasi oblitus, hypocritas, vulpes, fures, latrones, lupos rapaces dicit, & Vae illud horrendum infelicibus intonat, quo omnis corporis & animae calamitas & pernities continetur? Falluntur autem miserè, qui mansuetudinis spiritum vberiorem sibi pollicentur, quam in Christo fuerit, & se plus quiddam, quam ille, in lucrifaciendis hominibus profecturos esse sperant. Enimuero nullis rationibus aut artibus humanis demulceri aut vinci possunt, quos Dei verbum mitigare aut terrere non potest. Hoc enim medium illud ordinarium est, per quod fides datur, sicuti Apostolus ait: Fides ex auditu est, auditus autem per Verbum Dei. At inquis, nemo his clamoribus, minis, correptione vincitur aut placatur. Esto. Attamen populi Christiani ratio habenda est, ne si manifestos fidei hostes indulgentius tractari videant, offendantur. Et si non aliud proficiant fideles ministri, qui contra illos Verbi tubam fortius inflant, saltem suas animas liberant. Audiamus ergo Dei Filium loquentem, vt quid nobis hodie faciendum sit, discamus, quando passim reuixit spiritus ille mendax & homicida, qui olim Scribas & Pharisaeos exagitauit.
units.tr: By way of introduction the evangelist gives a brief description of the circumstances, writing: "Then Jesus spoke to the crowds and to his disciples, saying," and so on. In these words he sets out the time and occasion of this new action, so as to connect it with what immediately preceded. "Then," he says, when the Pharisees and scribes, so often refuted in their questions, and now convicted of their shameful ignorance by the question which the Lord raised about the Messiah from David, had nothing further to put forward, while the people admired his acuteness not without pleasure, he saw that it was fitting and necessary to declare his judgment of the scribes and Pharisees, and to show the whole people how shamefully they had hitherto been deceived by them, and what they ought to think of them from now on. By this example we are taught that it is not enough for adversaries to be refuted; the simple and untaught must also be instructed, so that they may understand what they ought to think of them and may be able to guard against their tricks and deceptions. And since here the common salvation of all is at stake, this must be done publicly. The prophets did this in former times, who had constant conflicts with men of this kind. Nor was it enough for the apostles to refute those who in their own age were corrupters of the faith and of sounder doctrine and were leading many astray; they also warned us about those who were to come in the last times, and whom we see today imposing on many in the Church. Christ's example teaches us how we ought to deal with them today. Indeed there are those who take it ill that such impostors should be accused and rebuked rather sharply. They want gentleness in the ministers of the gospel, by which they think more is gained, and they say it is foolish to contend with those whom they know to be incurable, or rather to become fiercer and more provoked. Would that they themselves weighed the matter more carefully! For they would see that there is no room left for patience and gentleness where the glory of God and the salvation of men are at stake. Let those teachers of charity and moderation of our day answer me: who was ever more moderate and gentle than the Son of God made manifest in the flesh, who (as the prophet once foretold of him) did not strive, nor cry out, nor make his voice heard in the streets; who did not break the bruised reed, nor quench the smoking flax; yet all whom he knew to be burdened by the pangs of a guilty conscience he called to himself kindly, and he never received harshly, or shut out of his sight, any who he saw needed consolation? But when he thundered and lightened against hypocrites and seducers of the people, forgetting, as it were, all moderation, he called them hypocrites, foxes, thieves, robbers, ravening wolves, and cried out that dreadful woe in which every calamity and ruin of body and soul is contained. Those are sadly mistaken who promise themselves a more abundant spirit of gentleness than there was in Christ, and who hope that they will achieve something more than he did in winning men. For men who cannot be softened or overcome by Christ's word, which can neither soothe nor terrify them, cannot be moved by any human reasoning or arts. This is the ordinary means through which faith is given, as the Apostle says: "Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of God." But you say that no one is overcome or appeased by these shouts, threats and rebukes. Granted. Yet regard must be had for the Christian people, lest, if they see the open enemies of the faith treated too leniently, they be offended. And if the faithful ministers, who blow the trumpet of the Word more vigorously against them, achieve nothing else, at least they save their own souls. Let us then hear the Son of God speaking, so that we may learn what must be done by us today, since that lying and murderous spirit, which once harassed the scribes and Pharisees, has revived everywhere.

units.la: Orditur a doctrina, vel potius ab ipso statu & conditione, quam suslinebant. Etenim vt hanc recte instituj oportet, ita vt de eadem recte omnes iudicent & sentiant necesse est. In cathedra Mosis (inquit) sedent Scribae & Pharisaei. Et ex eo infert: Omnia ergo quae dixerint vobis vt seruetis seruate & facite: sed secundum opera eorum ne facite. Cathedram Mosis dicit ordinarium docendi munus, quod in populo suo Deus olim instituit, quando Septuaginta Seniores sibi sibi sumpsit & ad hoc destinari voluit, vt eis de Spiritu Mosis impertiretur, & illi huic in populi gubernatione praeesse essent, & ipsum onere illo grauissimo ex parte leuarent, cui se sufficere non posse querebatur. At hic multa & diligenti obseruatione dignum est, quod in cathedra hac Mosis sedere dicit Scribas & Pharisaeos, quibus nihil tunc in orbe corruptius & sceleratius inueniri poterat: & de eis ita disserit, vt partim ipsis attendere & obedire, partim ab ijsdem omnes sibi cauere iubeat. Nam qui in praesenti ait, Omnia quae dixerint vobis vt seruetis, seruate & facite: apud Marcum & Lucam qui eandem admonitionem succinctius annotarunt, grauissime discipulis mandat: Cauete a Scribis, &c. Ex quo colligi potest, nulli loco certo Veritatis doctrinam, ne dum salutem ipsam, ita astrictam & alligatam esse, vt illi omnes ex necessitate salutis addictos esse oporteat. Frustra ergo hunc locum aduersarij nostri detorquent ad stabiliendum Romanae sedis primatum, & ex eo sic argumentantur: Si Scribis & Pharisaeis credere & obedire oportuit olim Iudaeos, eo quod in Cathedra Mosis sederent, & ex eorum numero essent, de quibus dictum erat: Labia Sacerdotis custodient scientiam, & legem ex ore eius requirent. Item si quis obedire nolit Sacerdoti, qui stat coram Domino Deo tuo, morietur, & exterminabis malum e medio tui: Quanto magis audiri debent Romani Pontifices, qui in Cathedra Petri, principis Apostolorum sedent, cui dictum est a Christo: Tibi dabo claves regni coelorum, quicquid ligaueris in terra, erit ligatum in coelis, & quic quid solueris in terra, erit solutum in coelis. Item pasce oues meas, &c. Atqui nullis Scripturis constat, eiusmodi cathedram a Deo institutam esse, cui ex successionis iure veritas & tanta potestas alligata sit: nec etiam demonstrari potest, Petro autem vllo alij Apostolorum plus a Christo quam aliis datum esse. Nam quod Petro dictum fuit propter fidei confessionem, quam omnium Apostolorum nomine ediderat, hoc ipsum postea omnibus dixit Dominus: Accipite Spiritum sanctum: Si quorum remiseritis peccata, remittuntur eis: Si quorū retinueritis retenta sunt. Hursum quae ratio est, vt Ecclesia Romana imperium & primatus tribuatur propter Petrum, cum hunc vnquam Romae venijse, nullis idoneis testibus probari possit: Romae autem illum sedisse, & cathedram habuisse tam fabulosum est, vt mirum sit, aliquem inueniri posse, qui illud asseuerare audeat. Etenim si id fecisset Petrus, praeter officium id factum esset. Ipsi enim non minus quam aliis Apostolis dictum fuit: Ite in orbem vniuersum, & docete omnes gentes. Non licuit ergo Petro in vna vrbe fixam cathedram habere, nisi Apostolicae functioni, quae illi mandata erat, ex priuato arbitrio vellet renunciare. Eiusdem farinae est, quod sedem Romanam errare posse aut hanc vilum sisma vnquam passam esse negant.
units.tr: He begins with their teaching, or rather with the very position and condition which they held. For if this is to be rightly established, all must judge and think rightly about it. "The scribes and Pharisees," he says, "sit in Moses' seat." And from this he infers: "Therefore all that they tell you, observe and do; but do not do according to their works." By "Moses' seat" he means the ordinary office of teaching, which God once instituted among his people, when he took to himself seventy elders and wished them to be set apart for this, so that the Spirit of Moses might be imparted to them, and they might preside with him in governing the people and relieve him in part of that very heavy burden for which he complained he was not equal. But here it is worth close and careful notice that he says the scribes and Pharisees sit in this seat of Moses, when nothing more corrupt and wicked could then be found in the world; and he speaks of them in such a way that he orders the people partly to attend to them and obey, and partly to beware of them all. For the Lord, when he says in the present passage, "Whatever they tell you, observe and do," in Mark and Luke, who recorded the same admonition more briefly, gives the disciples the very serious command: "Beware of the scribes," and so on. From this it may be gathered that the doctrine of truth, let alone salvation itself, is not so bound and tied to any fixed place that all men must of necessity be bound to it for their salvation. Our adversaries therefore wrongly twist this passage to establish the primacy of the Roman see, and argue from it in this way: "If the Jews were once bound to believe and obey the scribes and Pharisees, because they sat in Moses' seat and were of their number, of whom it was said: 'The lips of the priest shall keep knowledge, and they shall seek the law at his mouth'; likewise, if anyone is unwilling to obey the priest who stands before the Lord your God, he shall die, and you shall put away the evil from among you; how much more ought the Roman pontiffs to be heard, who sit in the seat of Peter, the prince of the apostles, to whom Christ said: 'I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven'; likewise: 'Feed my sheep,' and so on." Yet no Scripture shows that such a seat was instituted by God, to which truth and such great power is bound by right of succession; nor can it be demonstrated that Peter was given more by Christ than any other of the apostles. For what was said to Peter because of the confession of faith which he had made in the name of all the apostles, the Lord afterwards said to all of them: "Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them; whose sins you retain, they are retained." What reason is there, then, for the Roman Church to be granted rule and primacy on account of Peter, when it cannot be proved by any sound witnesses that he ever came to Rome; and that he sat and had a chair in Rome is so fabulous that it is a wonder anyone can be found who dares to assert it? For if Peter had done so, it would have been contrary to his office. For it was said to him no less than to the other apostles: "Go into the whole world and teach all nations." It was not lawful, then, for Peter to have a fixed chair in one city, unless he wished to renounce by his own private judgment the apostolic duty committed to him. Of the same kind is the claim that the Roman see cannot err, or that it has never suffered such a shameful schism.

units.la: Enimuero fatemur libenter, Ecclesia Romana fidem olim per totum orbem praedicatam fuisse, sed non alia fuit illa, quam quae in Diui Pauli ad Romanos epistola traditur: cum qua si conferantur quae hodie Romae siunt & inde prodeunt, ne mica quidem eius doctrinae inueniēs, quam Apostoli olim praedicarunt. Et posteris temporibus sedem hanc occupauerunt homines Simoniaci & scismatici, qui Ecclesiam in sectas diuersas sciderunt, & orbem Christianum bellis turbarunt, & maximorum scandalorum fuerunt authores. Garriunt quidem istius sedis parasiti multa de vnitate, quae ab Apostolorum tempore fuerit in Romana Ecclesia. At costat ex ipsorum historiis tempore Cornelij Romani episcopi, qui martyrij corona redimitus est, in Romana Ecclesia Nouatum fuisse, haeresis Nouatianae authorem, quae multis annis Ecclesiis passim grauissimi scismatis causa fuit, adeo vt in plerisque locis bini episcopi haberentur, vnus orthodoxus, alter vero Nouatianus. Factum hoc est sub annum nati Christi c CLI. Nec multo post alterum scismā enatum est inter Liberium & Felicem pontifices. Quid vero de eo dicemus, quod Damasus & Vrsicinus Romanam Ecclesiam turbarunt, cum in noui Pontificis electione res (vt Platina scribit) non suffragijs, sed vi & armis ageretur? Sed praestat totam historiam illam ex Ammiano Marcellino recitare, qui haec tradidit: Damasus & Vrsicinus supra humanum modum ad rapiendam episcopalem sedem ardentes scitis studijs acerrime conslistabantur, adeoque mor-tis vulnerum, discrimina adiumentis vtriusque progressus: quae nec corrigere sufficiens Vincentius (gubernator is erat imperatoris nomine) nec mollire, vi magna coactus fecerit in suburbanum: & in concertatione superauerat Damasus, parte quae ei fauebat instante. Constatq; in Basilica Sicinini, vbi ritus Christiani est conuenticulum, vno die centum triginta septem reperta cadaue ra peremptorum, efferatam diu plebem aegre postea delinitam. Idem historicus causam tanti mali in auaritia & ambitione monstraus, mox addit: Neque ego abnuo, ostentationem rerum considerans vrbanarum, huius rei cupidos ob impetrandum quod appetunt omni contentione laterum iurgari debere, cum id adepti futuri sint ita securi, vt ditentur oblationibus matronarum, procedantq; vt hiculis insidentes circumspectii vestiti, epulas curantes profusas, adeo vt eorum conuiuia regales superent mensas: qui esse poterant beati reuera, si magnitudine vrbis despecta, quam vitijs oppo-nunt, ad imitationem antistitum quorundam prouincialium viuerent: quos tenuitas edendi potan-di, parcissime, vilitas etiam indumentorum, & supercilia humum spectantia perpetuo numini vi-rusq; eius cultoribus vt puros commendant & verecundos. Hæc Marcell. Quod si illis temporibus, quando a persecutionibus nondum satis respirauerat Ecclesia, is fuerunt mores Episcoporum, & tantum apud illos potuit effrenis ambitio, num postea meliores fuisse putabimus, quando pietas & religio opibus & luxui prorsus cedere coacta Ecclesiam prorsus reliquit. Enimuero ab eo tempore vsq; ad Eugenium 4. vel Concilium Basiliense, scismata viginti duo adhuc numerari possunt, quibus propter diuersas Pontificum electiones & mutuas condemnationes orbis Christianus hor-ribiliter distractus est. Neminem ergo moueant istorum hominum prastigia, quos non pudet ea fingere, quae totius mundi testimonio falsi conuincuntur.
units.tr: Indeed, we gladly admit that the Church of Rome once had its faith preached throughout the whole world, but that faith was not other than what is set out in the Epistle of St Paul to the Romans. If what is taught in Rome today and issues from there is compared with it, not even a crumb of that doctrine which the Apostles once preached will be found. In later times this see was occupied by simoniacal and schismatic men, who tore the Church into various sects, troubled the Christian world with wars, and were the authors of the gravest scandals. The parasites of that see indeed chatter much about the unity that the Roman Church has enjoyed since the time of the Apostles. But it is clear from their own histories that in the time of Cornelius, bishop of Rome, who was crowned with the martyr's crown, Novatian, the author of the Novatianist heresy, was in the Roman Church. For many years this heresy was the cause of a most grievous schism in churches everywhere, so that in many places there were two bishops, one orthodox and the other Novatianist. This happened about the year 251 after the birth of Christ. Not long afterwards another schism arose between the popes Liberius and Felix. What shall we say of the fact that Damasus and Ursinus threw the Roman Church into turmoil, when the election of a new pontiff was (as Platina writes) carried out not by votes but by force and arms? It is better, however, to recite that whole story from Ammianus Marcellinus, who gave this account: "Damasus and Ursinus, burning beyond human measure with a fierce desire to seize the episcopal see, contended most bitterly with each other, and the progress of each side brought deaths and wounds in such numbers that Vincentius (who was the governor of the city in the emperor's name) could neither correct nor soften the matter; compelled by great force, he withdrew to the suburbs, and in the struggle Damasus prevailed, with the party that favoured him pressing on. It is established that in the Basilica of Sicininus, which is the meeting-place of the Christian rite, one hundred and thirty-seven corpses of the slain were found on a single day, and the enraged populace was only with difficulty calmed afterwards." The same historian, pointing out the cause of so great an evil in greed and ambition, adds soon after: "Nor do I deny that those who desire this office ought to strive with all their might to obtain what they seek, considering the show of the city's wealth, since once they have attained it they will be so secure that they grow rich from the offerings of matrons; they go about in carriages, dressed in fine clothes, and they provide lavish feasts, so that their banquets surpass royal tables. They could truly be blessed if, despising the greatness of the city, which they set against them as a reproach, they lived in imitation of certain provincial bishops, whose meagre food and drink, very sparing, and the plainness of their clothing, and eyes fixed perpetually on the ground, commend them as pure and modest to the eternal Deity and to its worshippers." So far Marcellinus.
