If in those times, when the Church had not yet fully recovered from persecutions, such were the morals of the bishops, and unbridled ambition held such sway among them, shall we think that things were better afterwards, when piety and religion, forced entirely to give way to wealth and luxury, utterly abandoned the Church? Indeed, from that time down to Eugenius IV or the Council of Basel, twenty-two schisms can still be counted, by which the Christian world was horribly torn apart because of the rival elections of popes and their mutual condemnations. Let no one, therefore, be moved by the tricks of these men, who are not ashamed to invent things which are proved false by the testimony of the whole world.

units.la: Videamus potius quis Domino nostro IESV CHRISTO istius consilij, quod hic discipu-lis & toti populo dedit, finis & scopus fuerit, vt ex eo huius loci verum sensum & vsum colliga-mus. Est
units.tr: Let us rather see what was the aim and purpose of this counsel which our Lord Jesus Christ gave here to his disciples and the whole people, so that from it we may gather the true sense and use of this passage. It is

units.la: Veri doctores non audiendi licet vita non respondeat doctrinae. mus. Est hic, Scribas & Pharisaos tenere ordinarium munus docendi & interpretandi Legem, & idcirco audiendos esse, etsi vita & mores illorum doctrinae non semper respondeant. Fuit autem admonitio ista plus quam necessaria, ne populus vitae illorum exemplo pessimo offensus, Legis doctrinam & Verbum Dei asperneretur. Est enim hoc commune vitium, ut plerique in vitam potius quam doctrinam antistitum respiciant. Et quia natura ad malum proclives sumus, magna exemplorum vis est ad seducendum, maxime si haec magnis authoribus commendentur, quorum authoritas non facile poterit contemni: Ut non temere Cicero scripserit, Quod exemplo fit, id etiam fieri putant homines. Fit ergo plerunque, ut malo doctoris exemplo magis moveantur, quam doctrina, etsi haec pura & ex fontibus Israelis, Scripturis nimirum sacris petita sit. Hinc voces ista vulgo audiuntur, si quando Ecclesiarum ministri quoad vita exemplum exorbitent: Cur ergo hunc audiam? cur huic credam, qui si ferio ageret, & se vera dicere sciret, quae de caelo & inferis, atque futura vitae conditione tam confidenter declamitat, aliter proculdubio vitam suam instituaret, non perpotaret, non inter pocula tam scurriliter de verbo Dei, de scripturis & fidei mysteriis loqueretur? Atqui tunc, quando Christus in terris versabatur, summa erat inter Iudaeos Sacerdotum & totius ordinis Leviticici corruptio. Regnabat inter illos inexplebilis avaritia, quae religionem omnem in quaestum turpem converterat: ambitio item cum fastu intolerabili coniunctam, rapinarum indomita licentia, hypocrisis impudens, quibus insuper multis modis corrupta & adulterata legis interpretatio accedebat. Accusabat ista Dominus publice, & hoc nomine contempti ministerij accusabatur, & non deerant, qui ipsum hostem legis & sacrorum omnium dicerent. Ne qui ergo qui ipsum in aliquo pretio habebant, ex eo occasionem arriperent excutiendi iugum Legis & disciplinae Ecclesiasticae, praemonere omnes oportuit, non propterea contemnendum esse ministerium a Deo institutum: sed qualescunque sint Sacerdotes & Scribae, nihilominus tamen legis suam authoritatem ratam manere, ut non liceat impune contemnere, quae ex hac pure & recte traduntur. Ideo dicit: Omnia quae dixerint vobis ut servetis, servate & facite: sed secundum opera eorum non facite.
units.tr: True teachers are to be heard even if their life does not match their teaching. Let us gather. Here it is: the scribes and Pharisees held the ordinary office of teaching and interpreting the Law, and therefore they are to be heard, even though their life and morals did not always match their teaching. This admonition was more than necessary, so that the people, offended by the very bad example of their lives, should not despise the teaching of the Law and the Word of God. For this is a common fault, that most people look rather to the life than to the teaching of their leaders. And since we are naturally prone to evil, examples have great power to lead us astray, especially when they are commended by great authorities whose authority cannot easily be despised. As Cicero rightly wrote: "What is done by example, men think may also be done." Thus it often happens that people are moved more by the bad example of a teacher than by the teaching, even though that teaching is pure and drawn from the fountains of Israel, that is, from the holy Scriptures. Hence these words are commonly heard whenever ministers of the Churches go astray in their life as an example: "Why then should I hear this man? Why should I believe him, who, if he were serious and knew that he spoke the truth, when he declaims so confidently about heaven and hell and the future condition of life, would surely order his life otherwise, would not drink so heavily, and would not talk so buffoonishly over his cups about the Word of God, the Scriptures and the mysteries of faith?" Yet at the time when Christ was living on earth, the corruption of the priests and of the whole Levitical order among the Jews was extreme. Among them reigned insatiable greed, which had turned all religion into shameful gain; likewise ambition joined with intolerable pride, the unbridled licence of plunder, and shameless hypocrisy, to which was added an interpretation of the Law corrupted and adulterated in many ways. The Lord openly denounced these things, and on account of this he was accused of despising the ministry, and there were not lacking those who called him the enemy of the Law and of all sacred things. Therefore, so that those who held the ministry in some esteem might not seize on this as an occasion for shaking off the yoke of the Law and of ecclesiastical discipline, it was necessary to warn everyone that the ministry instituted by God is not to be despised; whatever kind of priests and scribes they may be, the authority of the Law nevertheless remains valid, so that it is not lawful to despise with impunity what is handed down from it purely and rightly. Hence he says: "Whatever they tell you to observe, observe and do; but do not do according to their works."

units.la: Sunt igitur huius consilij & admonitionis partes duae. Docet enim distinguere inter doctrinam & vitam sine moribus Scribarum. Prima pars de doctrina est, quam audiri vult & observari, quo ad in cathedra Moysis sedeant, id est, quoad divina tradant, quae cum lege per Mosem accepta conveniunt. Nihil ergo hoc ad nostros illos, qui sedi Romanam simpliciter credendum & obediendum esse contendunt in omnibus, quae Pontifices statuunt & decernunt. Atqui nihil huius unquam Deus voluit, qui olim suos servos Prophetas iussit a suo ore pendere, & ex hoc petere Verbum, quod populo praedicent. Et graviter reprehendit apud Ieremiam eos, qui Verbi tritico inanes palcas suorum figmentorum miscebant. Et Christus, qui hic Pharisaeos audire iubet, si ex Mose docent, alibi ferio admonuit discipulos, ut ab horum fermento sibi caveant, & idem ex Isaia testatur, frustra coli Deum humanis traditionibus. Itaque ex Moysis cathedra defendebant, quam primum ex suo cerebro nova dogmata depromebant, nec digni erant, quibus fides aliqua haberetur. Ad eundem modum Petri cathedram in vanum nobis iactant, nec digni sunt qui Apostolica authoritate sese pallient, qui ab eo praecepto discedunt, quo Apostolos suos obstrinxit Dominus, cum illis diceret: Profecti docete omnes gentes, docentes eos servare omnia, quae mandavi vobis, &c. Matth. 28.
units.tr: There are therefore two parts to this counsel and admonition. For he teaches us to distinguish between the doctrine and the life of the scribes, without following their morals. The first part concerns doctrine, which he wills to be heard and observed, insofar as they sit in the seat of Moses, that is, insofar as they hand down divine things which agree with the Law received through Moses. Nothing of this, therefore, bears on those who contend that the Roman see is to be simply believed and obeyed in all things which the popes decree and ordain. Yet God never willed any such thing, he who once commanded his servants the prophets to hang upon his mouth and to seek from it the Word which they were to preach to the people. And in Jeremiah he sharply rebukes those who mixed the empty chaff of their own inventions with the wheat of the Word. And Christ, who here bids us hear the Pharisees if they teach from Moses, elsewhere warned his disciples to beware of their leaven, and Isaiah likewise testifies that God is worshipped in vain by human traditions. Thus they defended themselves from the seat of Moses, while they were producing new dogmas from their own brains, and they were not worthy to be given any credit. In the same way they boast to us of the seat of Peter in vain, and they are not worthy to cloak themselves in apostolic authority, since they depart from that command by which the Lord bound his Apostles when he said to them: "Go and teach all nations, teaching them to observe all things that I have commanded you, etc." Matt. 28.

units.la: Altera huius dicti aut consilij pars de vita & moribus Scribarum & Pharisaeorum est, & monet, non debere ex his temere peti exempla, quae in vitae regulam trahamus. Etenim vita regulam propriae Christus ipse est, qui ideo se lucem mundi dicit, & addit: Qui sequitur me, non ambulabit in tenebris, sed habebit lumen vitae. Et quod idem postea pedum ablutionem discipulis dixit: Exemplum praebui vobis, hoc ipsum ad omnes actiones eius extendi debet, quibus nobis praeivit. Huc refertur communis illa regula, quam omnibus qui eius discipuli esse volunt, praescribit, dicens: Si quis vult post me venire, abneget semetipsum, & tollat crucem suam, & sequatur me. Ideo Apostolus Paulus Corinthijs suis scribebat: Imitatores mei estote, sicut ego Christi. Est hac quoque admonitio admodum necessaria propter eos qui posteris temporibus monasticae vitae regulas condiderunt & homines sibi imitandos proposuerunt, qui a Christi regula procul recesserunt.
units.tr: The second part of this saying or counsel concerns the life and morals of the Scribes and Pharisees, and it warns that examples should not be lightly taken from them to serve as a rule for living. Christ himself is the rule of life. That is why he calls himself the light of the world and adds: "He who follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life." Likewise, when he later washed the disciples' feet, he said: "I have given you an example, so that you should do as I have done." This must be extended to all his actions, in which he has gone before us. To this belongs the general rule that he prescribes to all who want to be his disciples: "If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me." So the Apostle Paul wrote to his Corinthians: "Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ." This warning is also very necessary on account of those who in later times drew up rules of monastic life and set up men for others to imitate, men who had withdrawn far from Christ's rule.

units.la: Doctrina quae tenus credi debeat.
units.tr: How far doctrine ought to be believed.

units.la: Ezech. 3. Ierem. 1. 23. Matth. 15. 16. Isa. 29.
units.tr: Ezek. 3. Jer. 1. 23. Matt. 15. 16. Isa. 29.

units.la: Exempla non temere imitanda.
units.tr: Examples are not to be imitated lightly.

units.la: Ioan. 8. 12.
units.tr: John 8. 12.

units.la: Matth. 16. runt, & fere salutem alibi quàm in huius merito monstrarunt, quoad vitam vero non vera fan-stimonia, sed fucatæ & inanis hypocrisis hominibus incautis & superstitiosis fuerunt authores. Cæterum ne temerè de hoc admonere putetur Dominus, causas adducit, cur ab operum, quæ Scri-bæ & Pharisæi faciunt, imitatione sibi cauere debeant ipsius discipuli, de quibus proximo Ser-mone dicetur. Nunc sufficiat hoc loco didicisse, prædicationi verbi Dei hunc honorem debere de-ferri, ut huic credamus & obsequamur, a quocunque mortalium prædicetur. Ut enim subditi fi-deles principis sui edictis obediunt, licet ea ab hominibus eiusmodi promulgentur, qui neq; boni exem-pli, neq; alicuius pretij & authoritatis sunt: Ita Christianos decet Verbum Dei serio amplesti & cum hoc authoritatem suam ex seipso habeat, nō quis illud prædicet, sed quid Deus nobis illo præ-cipiat respicere, & simpliciter illis credere, quæ Dei oraculis, per Prophetas & Apostolos olim tra-dita confessiunt. Rursus quia omnes homines peccatores sunt, & in multis labimur omnes, nul-lius hominis tanta apud nos sit authoritas, ut eius exemplum deliétus, quæ aduersus Dei verbum committuntur, excusandis sufficiat. Itaq; quæcunq; ab hominibus fiunt, ad verbi Dei & Legis di-uinæ trutinam ponderentur, vita autem exemplum & regula sit æternus Dei Filius IESVS CHRISTVS, in cuius ore non inuentus est dolus, & qui solus potuit hostibus suis acerrimis in publico dicere: Quis ex vobis arguet me de peccato? Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: ...they showed that salvation is to be found anywhere rather than in his merit; as for life, they were the authors not of true testimony but of feigned and empty hypocrisy, for incautious and superstitious people. Yet lest the Lord seem to admonish rashly about this, he gives reasons why his own disciples should beware of imitating the works that the Scribes and Pharisees do, which will be discussed in the next sermon. For now it is enough to have learned in this place that this honour must be paid to the preaching of God's Word: that we believe and obey it, from whomever among mortals it is preached. For just as faithful subjects obey the edicts of their prince, even when they are issued by men who are of no good example and of no worth or authority, so Christians ought to embrace the Word of God earnestly. Since it has its authority from itself, not from who preaches it, we should look to what God commands us through it, and simply believe what the oracles of God, delivered long ago through the Prophets and Apostles, profess. Again, since all men are sinners and we all stumble in many things, no man's authority should be so great among us that his example is enough to excuse the sins committed against the Word of God. Therefore, whatever is done by men should be weighed on the scales of God's Word and divine Law. The life and rule should be the eternal Son of God, Jesus Christ, in whose mouth no deceit was found, and who alone could say in public to his fiercest enemies: "Which of you convicts me of sin?" To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCLXIIII.
units.tr: HOMILY CCLXIIII.

units.la: Dicunt enim & non faciunt. Ligant enim onera grauia difficilia-que portatu, & imponunt in humeros hominum: digito autem suo noluntea mouere.
units.tr: "For they say and do not. For they bind heavy burdens, hard to bear, and lay them on men's shoulders, but they themselves will not move them with a finger" (Matth. 23.3-4).

units.la: OVemadmodum Ecclesiæ Dei quandiu in terris agit ministrius opus est, per quos ceu pa-stores & architectos colligatur, ædificetur & feruetur: ita non minus necesse est ijs, quà Ecclesiæ membra & Filij germani esse volunt, vt quæ sit ministrorum & præsidum stiorum func-tio, & quid de illis sentiri & iudicari debeat, probe intelligant. Concurrunt enim hic duo vitia quæ vtraq; caueri oportet. Primò sunt qui antistites aut doctores impune contemni posse existi-mant, qui non ipsi omnia exacte præstant quæ docent. Itaque quàm primum illos aliquibus vitijs laborare videnf, secessionem ab illis faciunt, & in Ecclesia scisma & turbas excitant. E contra sunt alij, qui illos in tanta existimatione habent, vt quiduis recipiant quod illi tradunt, & se ex-cusatos esse arbitrantur, si doctrinæ ipsorum simpliciter credant, & exemplum eorundem in omni-bus sequantur: quæ superstitionum & errorum nocentissimorum præcipua causa est. Quapropter IESVS CHRISTVS hoc Capite de Scribis & Pharisæis Iudæorum dicturus ab admonitio-ne breui & graui orditur, cuius hæc summa est, Eos qui in Mosis cathedra sedent, id est, qui or-dinariè ad munus docendi vocati sunt, & ea docent quæ cum lege per Mosem lata consentiunt, au-diendos esse qualescunq; sint: cauendum vero, ne eosdem sequamur, si quid præter officium faciunt. At quia magna exemplorum vis est (vt nuper diximus) & hic plurimum peccatur ab ijs, qui a-lijs præsident, nunc rationes subtexere incipit, quibus postremum hoc admonitionis istius mem-brum confirmat: Et de his in præsenti dicemus.
units.tr: Just as the Church of God, for as long as it lives on earth, needs ministers, through whom, as shepherds and builders, it is gathered, built up and kept alive, so it is no less necessary for those who wish to be members of the Church and true sons to understand well what the function of ministers and presidents is, and what ought to be thought and judged of them. Two vices meet here, and both must be guarded against. First, there are those who think that teachers or leaders can be despised with impunity, because they do not themselves carry out exactly everything they teach. So, as soon as they see them labouring under some faults, they withdraw from them and stir up schism and disturbances in the Church. On the other hand, there are others who hold their teachers in such high esteem that they accept whatever those teachers hand down, and think themselves excused if they simply believe their teaching and follow their example in everything. This is the chief cause of superstitions and most harmful errors. Therefore, in this chapter, when he is about to speak of the Scribes and Pharisees of the Jews, Jesus Christ begins with a brief and weighty admonition, the sum of which is this: those who sit in Moses' seat, that is, who have been called ordinarily to the office of teaching and teach what agrees with the law given through Moses, are to be heard, whatever they are like; but we must take care not to follow them if they do anything beyond their office. But because the power of example is great (as we said recently), and because those who preside over others often sin much here, he now begins to add reasons by which he confirms this last part of that admonition. And we shall speak of these at present.

units.la: Prima est: Dicunt enim & non faciunt. Id est, prædicant Legem, præcepta eius vrgent, Mosem deniq; nunquam non in ore habent: sed eundem illis non perinde cordi esse ex eo apparet, quòd obedientiam, quæ eius præceptis debetur, securi negligunt: quæ causa est, vt ipsorum facta & actiones cum doctrina quam tradunt, non consentiant. Itaq; quia Legi contraria & vitiosa iunt, nequaquam debent in exemplum trahi. Debet hinc generalis admonitio peti, quam Doctores stu-diose obseruent: Vt nimirum ipsi sedulò & pro virili ea præstare studeant, quæ alijs præcipiunt. Nam, vt in Scholis traditur: Turpe est doctori, si culpa redarguit ipsum. Ideo Paulus Ti-motheo scribebat: Esto exemplar fidelium in sermone, in conuersatione, in charitate, in spiritu, id est
units.tr: The first is: "For they say and do not." That is, they preach the Law, they press its precepts, and indeed they always have Moses on their lips; but that he is not equally dear to their hearts is clear from the fact that they carelessly neglect the obedience owed to his precepts. This is the reason why their deeds and actions do not agree with the doctrine they hand down. Therefore, since they act contrary to the Law and viciously, they must by no means be taken as an example. From this a general admonition ought to be drawn, which teachers should diligently observe: namely, that they themselves should earnestly strive, as far as they can, to do what they command others. For, as is taught in the schools: it is shameful for a teacher if his own fault convicts him. Therefore Paul wrote to Timothy: "Be an example to the faithful in speech, in conduct, in love, in spirit,"

units.la: Ministerij status cognitu necessarius.
units.tr: The necessary knowledge of the status of the ministry.

units.la: Scribæ dicunt et non faciunt.
units.tr: The scribes say and do not.

units.la: 1.Tim.4. ˠζelo pietatis, ut donum Spiritus sanĉti tibi concessum bene vtaris, in fide item, in puritate deni-que & innocentia. Et alibi de seipso loquens ait: Corpus meum contundo & in seruitutem redi-go, ne quo modo dum aliis praedico, ipse reprobus fiam, id est, ita viuam, vt facta mea & mores testentur me non talem esse, qualem esse decet, qui aliis vitae probatae regulam praescribit. Id ve-ro quia non faciebant Scribae & Pharisaei, non abstinebant causa, ne qui ipsorum mores & studia imi-tentur, Dominus prohibet.
units.tr: (1 Tim. 4.) "in zeal for godliness, that you may make good use of the gift of the Holy Spirit given to you; likewise in faith, and finally in purity and innocence." And elsewhere, speaking of himself, he says: "I beat my body and bring it into subjection, lest by any means, while I preach to others, I myself should become a castaway" (1 Cor. 9.27). That is, he says: I so live that my deeds and manners bear witness that I am not such as I ought to be, who prescribes to others the rule of a tested life. But since the Scribes and Pharisees did not do these things, the Lord forbids us to imitate their manners and pursuits, not so that we should abstain from them for that reason.

units.la: Caeterum ne dictum hoc praeter illius mentem longius extendamus, quam par sit, diligenter ob seruari debet de quibus vitijs potissimum loquatur: Nimirum non de vulgaribus, quae ex innata carnis vitiositate & infirmitate in optimos quoque & sanctissimos Dei seruos cadunt: sed de atro-cioribus, quae manifestum legis & verbi Dei contemptum arguunt, & cum scandalo publico con-tenta sunt: qualia in illis locum habuisse infra diserte testabitur, quando dicet, Va vobis Scribae & Pharisaei hypocritae, quia mundatis exteriorem poculi patinae partem, intus autem illa plena sunt rapina & intemperantia, vel scelere, vt apud Lucam habetur. Itaque ad huius loci interpretationem non incommode aptari potest, quod Apostolus de personatis eiusmodi Legis inter-pretibus inter Iudaeos scribit: Ecce tu cognominaris Iudaeus & acquiescis in Lege, & gloriaris in Deo, & noisti eius voluntatem, & exploras quae discrepant, institutus ex lege: confidisque te ducem esse caecorum, lucem eorum qui sunt in tenebris, eruditorem insipientium, magistrum infantium, quod habeas informationem cognitionis ac veritatis in lege: Qui igitur doces alium, teipsum non doces? qui praedicas non furandum, furaris? qui dicis non moechandum, moecharis? qui abominaris idola, sacrilegium committis? qui de lege gloriaris, per legis transgressionem Deum dedecoras. Haec vtinam hodie non etiam de multis dici possent, qui Euangelii administri & praecones haberi volunt, omnia autem huic contraria faciunt, & vitam omnem sic instituunt, vt per ipsos Christus & Euangelium eius dedecoretur.
units.tr: But, lest we extend this saying beyond its meaning more than is fitting, we must carefully observe which vices he speaks of chiefly. Surely not of ordinary ones, which fall from the innate frailty and weakness of the flesh even upon the best and most holy servants of God; but of the more atrocious ones, which prove a manifest contempt of the law and the Word of God and are attended with public scandal. That such were found among them he will testify plainly below, when he says: "Woe to you, Scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you cleanse the outside of the cup and the dish, but within they are full of rapine and intemperance" (Matth. 23.25), or, as it is in Luke. So for the interpretation of this place, what the Apostle writes about such pretended interpreters of the Law among the Jews may fitly be applied: "Behold, you are called a Jew, and rest in the Law, and glory in God, and know his will, and approve the things that differ, being instructed out of the Law, and you are confident that you are a guide to the blind, a light to those who are in darkness, a teacher of the foolish, a master of infants, because you have in the Law the form of knowledge and of truth. You, then, who teach another, do you not teach yourself? You who preach that one should not steal, do you steal? You who say one should not commit adultery, do you commit adultery? You who abhor idols, do you commit sacrilege? You who glory in the Law, do you dishonour God through the transgression of the Law?" (Rom. 2.17-23). Would that these words could not also be said today of many who wish to be called ministers and heralds of the Gospel, but who do everything contrary to it and so order their whole life that through them Christ and his Gospel are dishonoured!

units.la: Hic vero etiam atque etiam caueant pij, ne propter istorum mores doctrinam reijciant, & praesenti hoc loco abutantur, vt Anabaptistae faciunt, iurati (vt sic dicam) ministrorum Ecclesiae a-deoque totius ministerij hostes: Clamant hi, neminem in Ecclesia audiri debere, quam qui per omnia irreprehensibilis & inculpatus omnia ipse praestet, quae alios docet. Et hoc fundamento iacto vt primum aliquem lapsum aut vitium in ministro accusare possunt, id doctrina fraudi esse volunt, & nephas esse clamant, vt Christiani homines eiusmodi doctoris conciones audiant, aut Sacramentis communicent in eo coetu, cui talis praeest. Quod vt simplicioribus persuadeant, ad rauim vsque vociferantur: Dicunt, & non faciunt. Quid vero hoc aliud est, quam extra oleas (quod aiunt) currere, & Christi verba contra eius mentem & expressum mandatum detorquere? Hic enim iubet Ecclesiae praefectos & ministros in omnibus, quae vt ordinarie vocati ex officio docent & mandant audire, & illis obsequi: ne autem eorundem vitia imitemur, prohibet. Cur ergo illi ex vitijs ansam arripiunt contumaciae, qua doctrinam quoque sanam aspernentur, & a Deo institutum Ecclesiae ordinem turbent? Adhaec iniqui nimis sunt, dum ministros verbi ad id contra Christi mentem astringunt, quod praestitu est impossibile. Coguntur illi vrgere Dei praeceptum, Ne concupiscas. At quis obsecro dabitur, qui ab omni concupiscentia se alienum esse possit dicere? Immo quis adeo demens est, vt idin animum velit inducere, se quoad in carne viuit, eo perfectionis peruenire posse? Attamen praedicari debent quacunque ex hoc praecepto Christus in legis interpretatione Capite quinto diserte docuit: vt auditores quae & quanta sit natura & ingenij nostri vitiositas intelligant. Paulus certe cum ex illo praecepto omnes peccati argueret, seipsum exemplo proponit, seq; carnalem & sub peccatum venundatum esse fatetur, exclamat deniq; Miserum me, quis me liberabit a corpore mortis? Num ergo indignum dicent isti homines Paulum, cuius doctrina audiatur? Quid vero de Prophetis & aliis Apostolis dicemus? Quid de Mose, cui Deus ipse lucalentum fidelitatis in domo sua testimonium perhibuit? Annon illi omnes peccato-res fuerunt? Annon omnes precati sunt, Domine, ne ingrediaris in iudicium cum seruis tuis? An non ministri Ecclesiarum omnes perinde vt reliqui homines, ex Christi mandato precari debent, Remitte nobis debita nostra, &c.
units.tr: Here, indeed, the godly should take especial care, lest on account of such men's manners they reject the doctrine, and abuse this present passage as the Anabaptists do, the sworn enemies (so to speak) of the ministers of the Church, and so of the whole ministry. These men cry out that no one should be heard in the Church except one who is blameless and irreproachable in all things and personally performs everything that he teaches to others. And once this foundation is laid, as soon as they can accuse a minister of some lapse or fault, they want that to be a reproach to his doctrine, and they cry out that it is wicked for Christian people to hear the sermons of such a teacher, or to take the sacraments in that congregation over which such a man presides. And so that they may persuade the simpler folk of this, they shout hoarsely: "They say, and do not." But what else is this than to run outside the olive grove, as they say, and to twist the words of Christ against his mind and his express command? For here he commands that the presidents and ministers of the Church, who have been called ordinarily, be heard in all the things they teach and command from their office, and be obeyed; he forbids us to imitate their faults. Why then do they seize upon faults as an occasion of obstinacy, so as to spurn even sound doctrine and disturb the order of the Church instituted by God? Moreover, they are too unjust in binding the ministers of the Word, against Christ's mind, to what is impossible. They are compelled to press God's precept, "You shall not covet." But who, I beg you, will be found who can say that he is free from all covetousness? Indeed, who is so mad as to want to persuade himself that, as long as he lives in the flesh, he can attain to such perfection? Yet whatever Christ taught in the interpretation of the Law in chapter five, from this precept, must be preached, so that the hearers may understand what and how great is the frailty of our nature and mind. Paul, certainly, when from that precept he convicted all of sin, set himself forward as an example, and confesses that he is carnal and sold under sin, and at last he cries out: "Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from the body of this death?" (Rom. 7.24). Will those men then say that Paul is unworthy to be heard? What shall we say of the Prophets and the other Apostles? What of Moses, to whom God himself bore the honourable testimony of faithfulness in his house? Were not all of these sinners? Did they not all pray: "Lord, do not enter into judgment with your servants" (Ps. 143.2)? Are not all ministers of the Churches, just like other men, bound by Christ's command to pray: "Forgive us our debts," etc.?

units.la: Nemo igitur priuatus ex hoc Christi dicto occasionem arripiat turbandi Ecclesias, vt doctri-
units.tr: Therefore let no private person seize upon this saying of Christ as an occasion for disturbing the Churches, so that doctri-

units.la: CAP. XXIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIII.

units.la: nam puram & fynceram propter minifirorum corruptos mores damnare & reijcere velit. Etenim fi quis per regiones exteras & periculosas iter faciens in aliquem incidat, qui viam rectam ipsi monstret, de diuerticulis autem & auijs fideliter admoneat, stulte fecerit, fi relicta via regia per diuerticula vagari & errare velit, eo quod monstratorem via ad illa deflectere videat: ita nimium imprudentes sunt, qui ex Dei verbo recte edocti, huius semitas deferunt, & pofi exempla doctorum deuiant, qui scientes volentes ea faciunt, quae Dei voluntati repugnant. Discant ergo priuati homines Dei bonitatem agnoscere, quando verbi fui pracones excitat, qui veritatem, quam sequi nolunt, pure docent, ab exemplis autem malis cauteant, quibus illi fibijpfis perditionis autores sunt. Magistratus autem Christiani est, tales coercere & in ordinem redigere, ne infirmi & imperiti scandalo esse pergant: Fecerunt hoc olim Janfti principes, Ezechias, Iofias, Constantinus, Theodosius, & similes, quos imitari debent, quibus hodie Ecclesiae & Reipub. Christiana gubernacula credita sunt. At quae nostri saeculi calamitas est, hodie sei in pretio sunt Doctores, qui perpotant, ludunt, scortantur, moechantur, faenerantur: & quia principes viri, qui de illis castigandis ferio cogitare debebant, tales defendunt, atq; adfacerdotia opima vel quaestuosa prouehunt, fit fere vt vitia enormia apud omnes loci & ordinis homines regnent, & (quod olim fuit fa- culi hominibus dicebat Hofeas) talis fit populus, qualis est Sacerdos. Meminerint autem Christiani homines scelera & scandala nullis vel principum vel antistitum exemplis coram Deo excusari, qui suo tempore abfq; personarum respectu omnes punit qui peccarunt. Tunc impletur, quod ijsdem prope verbis per Ifaiam ipse denuntiat. Ecce Dominus euacuat terram, denudat eam, deformat faciem eius, & incolas eius dissipat: Et erit vt populus, sic Sacerdos: vt ferunus, ita herus eius: vt ancilla, sic hera eius: vt emptor, sic venditor: vt mutuo dans, sic qui mutuo accipit: vt creditor, sic debitor. Idest, neminem sua vel dignitas vel indignitas, opulentia, vel inopia, aut quacunq; vniufcuiufq; conditio fit tuebitur, sed omnes dignas suis peccatis poenas luent. Vide huius rei exemplum in filiorum Heli historia, primo Samuelis fecundo, tertio & quarto Capitibus, &c.
units.tr: For he wishes to condemn and reject the pure and sincere doctrine on account of the corrupt morals of the ministers. Suppose someone travelling through foreign and dangerous lands meets a man who shows him the right road and faithfully warns him about side paths and byways. He would act foolishly if, having left the royal road, he wanted to wander and stray down those side paths simply because he saw that his guide had turned aside onto them. So they are very imprudent who, rightly taught from God's Word, abandon its paths and turn aside after the examples of teachers who knowingly and willingly do the things that oppose God's will. Let private persons therefore learn to recognise God's goodness when he raises up preachers of his Word, who teach the truth purely, which those people do not want to follow, and let them beware of the evil examples by which those teachers become the authors of their own destruction. It is the duty of the Christian magistrate to restrain such men and bring them into line, so that they do not continue to be a stumbling block to the weak and the unlearned. The holy princes of old did this: Hezekiah, Josiah, Constantine, Theodosius and others like them, whom the magistrates of today ought to imitate, and to whom the government of the Church and of the Christian commonwealth has been entrusted. But what a calamity of our age it is that today teachers who drink to excess, gamble, consort with prostitutes, commit adultery and practise usury are held in high esteem! And because the princes, who ought to be seriously considering how to punish such men, defend them and promote them to rich and lucrative benefices, it comes about that enormous vices reign almost everywhere, among people of every place and rank, and (as Hosea once said) the people becomes such as the priest is. Let Christians remember, however, that sins and scandals are not excused before God by the examples of any princes or bishops; he, in his own time, punishes without respect of persons all who have sinned. Then what he himself foretold, in nearly the same words, through Isaiah, is fulfilled: "Behold, the Lord empties the land, lays it bare, deforms its face and scatters its inhabitants. And it will be, as with the people, so with the priest; as with the servant, so with his master; as with the maidservant, so with her mistress; as with the buyer, so with the seller; as with the lender, so with the borrower; as with the creditor, so with the debtor." That is, neither a person's dignity nor his lack of dignity, wealth or poverty, nor the condition of any individual whatever, will protect him, but all will pay penalties worthy of their sins. See an example of this in the history of the sons of Eli, in 1 Samuel chapters 2, 3 and 4, etc.

units.la: Additur autem priori huic rationi altera quoq;, cur Scribarum & Pharifaeorum opera non debeant imitari, qui illos audiunt. Est hoc, quod ligent onera grauia ac difficilia portatu, quae humeris hominum imponant, ipsi vero eadem ne digito quidem attingant aut moueat. Peristringitur hic multiplex vitium, cuius caput praecipuum est, quod qui conscientijs afflictis & laborantibus consulere debebant, eas oneribus iniquis & non nec effarijs grauarent. Fiebat hoc primum Legis praedicatione, cuius praecepta vocat onera, eo quod per fe homini portatu non solum difficilia, verumetiam impossibilia sunt. Nam Lex (vt Paulus ait) spiritualis est & non solum externam obedientiam requirit, sed hominem totum sibi vendicat, vt nimirum nihil sapiamus, nihil cogitemus, nihil velimus aut cupiamus quod illi repugnet, aut eius praeceptis prohibetur: At quem dabis mortalium, qui proprijs viribus istud praestet? Carnales enim fumus, & venundati (vt paulo ante diximus) sub peccatum. Et quia Legi maledictio & aeterna damnationis sententia coniuncta est, qua omnes feriuntur, qui non omnibus, quae illa exigit, satisfaciunt: reuera illius onus importabile est, & eo omnes ad inferos vsq; deprimimur, nisi Dei Filius IESVS CHRISTVS nobis suppetias ferat, qui, Apostolo teste, quando aduenit plenitudo temporum, a Patre missus est, vt homo factus ex muliere, eos qui legi eramus obnoxij, redimeret. Scribae autem & Pharifaei Legem fine Christo praedicabant, imo Christum oderant, et hostiliter persequebantur. Itaque, vt postea Petrus dixit, ceruicibus discipulorum suorum iugum impone- bant, quod neq; ipsi neq; patres vnquam portare potuerunt. Etenim vt alibi loquitur Paulus, Lex litera illa occidens est, nisi Christi spiritu vuificetur.
units.tr: To this first reason is added another, why the works of the scribes and Pharisees, who taught those who heard them, ought not to be imitated. It is this: they bind heavy burdens, hard to carry, and lay them on men's shoulders, while they themselves will not so much as touch them with a finger or move them. Here is criticised a manifold fault, whose chief point is that those who ought to have cared for troubled and labouring consciences burdened them with unjust and unnecessary loads. This was done first by the preaching of the Law, whose precepts he calls burdens, because in themselves they are not only difficult but even impossible for a man to carry. For the Law (as Paul says) is spiritual, and requires not only outward obedience but claims the whole man for itself, so that we should think, will, or desire nothing that opposes it or is forbidden by its precepts. But which of mortals will achieve this by his own strength? For we are carnal, and sold under sin, as we said a little earlier. And since the Law is joined with a curse and the sentence of eternal damnation, which strikes all who do not satisfy everything it demands, its burden is truly unbearable, and by it we are all pressed down even to hell, unless the Son of God, Jesus Christ, comes to our aid. He, as the Apostle testifies, when the fullness of time came, was sent by the Father, made man of a woman, to redeem those of us who were subject to the Law. But the scribes and Pharisees preached the Law without Christ; indeed they hated Christ and persecuted him with hostility. And so, as Peter said afterwards, they laid a yoke on the necks of their disciples, which neither they nor their fathers were ever able to bear. For as Paul says elsewhere, the letter of the Law kills, unless it is made alive by the Spirit of Christ.

units.la: Deinde non legem modo simpliciter & abfq; Christo tradebant, verumetiam huic addebant suas traditiones de ieiunijs, Sabbatis, purificationibus, oblationibus fimilibufq;, qua ipsi quidem quaestuosa erant, alijs vero ad salutem prorsus inutiles, cum nihil praeciperent quam corporalia exercitia, quae parum aut nihil omnino vtilitatis afferre, idem Apostolus affirmat 1 Timoth. 4. Praeterea exemplo suo non leuiora faciebant onera ista, sed magis aggrauabant, cum (quod proprium est hypocritis) rigidi & seueri quidem essent obedientiae Legis & traditionum omnium exactores, ipsi vero nihil prorsus facerent eorum, quae ab aliis tanquam necessaria adsalutem postulabant. Sunt haec eiusmodi, ut non modo indignos fuisse doceant, ex quibus vitae exemplum peteretur, verumetiam doctrinam eorum damnant, ut cui non conueniat cum Mosis cathedra. Hic enim Christo testimonium perhibuit, & ad hunc remisit Israelitas post latam legem & institutum cultum illum, in quo posteri puppim & proram salutis confiscere putarunt. Ioannes 5. Deuteronomium 18.
units.tr: Next, they not only taught the Law simply and without Christ, but they added to it their own traditions concerning fasts, Sabbaths, purifications, offerings and the like. These were profitable to themselves, but utterly useless to others for salvation, since they prescribed only bodily exercises, which, as the same Apostle affirms, bring little or no profit at all (1 Timothy 4). Moreover, by their example they made these burdens no lighter but heavier still, since (which is the mark of hypocrites) they were strict and severe exactors of obedience to the Law and of all the traditions, while they themselves did none of those things which they demanded of others as necessary for salvation. These matters are of such a kind that they show not only that those men were unworthy to be a model of life, but that their teaching is condemned too, since it does not agree with the chair of Moses. For he bore witness to Christ, and after giving the Law and instituting that worship in which later generations thought they had the stern and the prow of salvation, he sent the Israelites back to him (John 5; Deuteronomy 18).

units.la: Caeterum in Scribis & Pharisaeis damnantur omnes, qui doctrina & exemplo similiter & conscientias & animas hominum onerat. Faciunt hoc, quotquot iustitiam & salutem in operibus nostris quaerere docent, & a Christo revocant homines, qui solus nobis a Patre factus est iustitia, satisfactio & redemptio. Qui item novos cultus & ceremonias ab hominibus excogitatas obtrudunt, quibus corpora simul & animi fatigantur, loculi item exhauriuntur, conscientiae autem laborantes recreationem nullam sentiunt. Fit hoc hodie in Papatu. Ex lege enim reducuntur in Ecclesiam, quaecunque olim veteribus gravia fuerunt, & palam audiuntur voces illae, quas Paulus cum libertate Christiana pugnare ait, & proinde inter Christianos locum habere vetat: Ne attigeris, neque gustaueris, neque contrectaris. Nihil dico nunc de votis monachorum, quibus nihil molestius, tristius & inhumanius fingi poterat. Nihil de peregrinationibus, quae non tam labores infinitos, quam curas inextricabiles & pericula vitae & famae aut exitimationis pariunt iis, qui domi relictis charis coniugibus & dulcissimis liberis, per terras & maria sequuntur vel ementitas Sanctorum reliquias, vel inanima idola, quae signis falsis & inani religionis nomine commendantur. Nihil item de Purgatorio igne, cuius terrore eo vsque adducuntur miseri, ut non seipsos modo dum viuunt, excrucient, verumetiam tam morituri testamenta condant plane inofficiosa, in quibus praeteritis legitimis haeredibus bona sua monachis & sacrificiis legant impostoribus. Taceo etiam confessionis auricularis incommoda, per quam ceu tortura quaedam in hominum arcana vsque penetrarunt, ut ea multi sacrificuli narrarint, quae nefratribus quidem germanis vnquam credi differunt etiam adhibitis quaestionibus grauissimis. Quam ista grauia fuerint etiam principibus viris, quam pernicio sa Reipub. & quoties regnorum translationes & euersiones, bella item funesta pepererint, res ipsa loquitur. Sed ne coniugii quidem, quod inter miserias vitae humanae solatium nobis esse voluit Deus, intactum reliquerunt, quin grauaminibus innumeris illud acerbum & triste fecerint: Etenim leges nouas condiderunt, quibus (ut olim Paulus praedixit) coniugij vsus alijs propter vitae genus, alijs propter affinitatis & cognationis gradus, alijs propter praesitum, alijs pietatis officium in Baptismo prohibetur: alijs autem numerata pecunia permittitur. Deniq; totus dies non sufficeret, si quis omnia conscientiarum grauamina, quae isti homines excogitarunt, exponere velit. Quid vero illi interea faciunt, qui iam seculis aliquot dominantur, & sub plausibili cathedra Dui Petri praetextu quosuis suis pedibus subijciunt? Taciti in sinu ridentes, imo publice miseris insultant, & per ludibrium bonos Christianos vocitant eos, qui ipsis per omne libidinis genus grassantibus, a coniugio legitimo abstinent: illis item toto anni tempore seipsos saginantibus esuriunt, ipsis quietis & domi securae voluptuantibus, terra mari & periclitantur. Vera medicere, norunt omnes, qui vel in claustris monachorum aliquando fuerunt, vel quid Romae inter illius sedis principes purpuratos fieri soleat, propius speculantur. Est eo infelicior istorum hominum conditio, quod doctrinam quoque adulterinam sectatoribus suis propinant. Quid ergo aliud nobis agendum restat, quam ut gratias agamus Deo Patri miserationum, qui illorum fraudibus detentos, nos in libertatem filiorum suorum transtulit. Hanc tueamur, & redemptori nostro IESV CHRISTO seruiamus, qui Veritatis doctor est irrefragabilis, & exemplo etiam suo nobis praeiuit, quod secuti vnquam erramus. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Moreover, among the scribes and Pharisees are condemned all who burden the consciences and souls of men in the same way, by their teaching and example. All do this who teach that righteousness and salvation are to be sought in our works, and who call men away from Christ, who alone was made by the Father our righteousness, satisfaction and redemption. Likewise those who thrust upon us new forms of worship and ceremonies devised by men, by which bodies and minds are alike worn out, purses too are drained, and troubled consciences feel no relief at all. This is done today in the Papacy. For from the Law are brought back into the Church all those things which were once burdensome to the ancients, and openly are heard those voices which Paul says conflict with Christian liberty, and therefore forbids to have a place among Christians: "Do not touch, do not taste, do not handle." I say nothing now of the vows of the monks, than which nothing more troublesome, sad and inhuman could be devised. Nothing of pilgrimages, which bring not so much endless labours as inextricable cares and dangers to life, reputation and good name, to those who, leaving at home their dear wives and most beloved children, travel over lands and seas to seek either counterfeit relics of the saints or lifeless idols, which are commended by false signs and the empty name of religion. Nothing either of the fire of Purgatory, by whose terror wretched men are led to such a degree that not only do they torment themselves while they live, but even when about to die they make wills utterly unjust to their lawful heirs, leaving their goods to monks and to deceivers who offer sacrifices. I pass over too the troubles of auricular confession, by which, as if by some torture, they have penetrated into the secrets of men, so that many little priests have reported things which brothers of the same blood would never be trusted with, even when the most severe questioning was applied. How grievous these things have been even to princes, how destructive to the commonwealth, and how often they have brought about the transfer and overthrow of kingdoms, as well as deadly wars, the thing itself speaks. But they have not even left untouched marriage, which God willed to be for us a comfort amid the miseries of human life; they have made it bitter and sad with countless burdens. For they have enacted new laws by which (as Paul foretold long ago) the use of marriage is forbidden to some on account of their way of life, to others on account of degrees of affinity and kinship, to others on account of a vow made, to others on account of the duty of piety in Baptism; and to others it is permitted for a sum of money. In short, a whole day would not suffice if anyone wished to set out all the burdens on consciences which these men have devised. But what are those doing meanwhile who for several centuries have held dominion, and under the plausible chair of Saint Peter as pretext subject whomever they please to their feet? Silent and laughing in their bosoms, or rather openly mocking the wretched, they call good Christians by way of derision those who, while the others indulge in every kind of lust, abstain from lawful marriage; and while those gorge themselves all year round and are hungry, these ones, who take their pleasure in quiet and safety at home, are exposed to danger by land and sea. The true reason is known to all who have ever been in the cloisters of monks, or who closely observe what usually happens at Rome among the purple-clad princes of that see. The condition of these men is the more unhappy in that they also serve up to their followers an adulterated doctrine. What, then, remains for us to do but to give thanks to God the Father of mercies, who has drawn us out of their deceits, which held us captive, and transferred us into the liberty of his sons? Let us hold fast to this, and serve our Redeemer Jesus Christ, who is the irrefutable Teacher of truth, and who has also gone before us by his own example, so that we may never go astray if we follow it. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: Omnia autem opera sua faciunt, vt spectentur ab hominibus. Dilatant enim phylacteria sua, & producunt fimbrias palliorum suorum: Amantq; primos accubitus in coenis, & primos confessus in conuentibus; & in foris salutationes, & vocari ab hominibus, Rabbi Rabbi.
units.tr: They do all their works to be seen by men. For they enlarge their phylacteries and lengthen the fringes of their garments. They love the first places at feasts and the chief seats in the synagogues, the greetings in the marketplaces, and being called by men, "Rabbi, Rabbi."

units.la: TOto hoc Capite Dominus & Seruator noster IESVS CHRISTVS aduersus Scribas & Pharisaeos, qui tunc inter Iudaeos ordinarij doctores & antistites erant, acriter disserit. Ne vero quis ex eo occasionem arriperet ipsum munus ecclesiasticum cum doctrina contemnendi, initio grauiter monet, ipsis quidem credi & obediri debere quoad in cathedra Mosis sedent & legem Dei praedicant, at diligenter cauendum esse ab ipsorum exemplo, ne qui opera et facta horum imitentur. Rationes huius admonitionis adduxit, quod bene quidem doceant, ipsi vero non praestent quae aliis mandant, imo onera grauia & intolerabilia imponant aliis, dum legis simul & traditionum suarum rigidissimi exactores sunt, quae ipsi ne digito quidem attingant. At quia illi summam iustitiae & sanctitatis existimationem jactitabant propter crebra ieiunia, eleemosynas, decimas, preces, purificationes, propter vestitum denique, ad religionis & pietatis speciem compositum, ne temere & ex affectu locutus putetur Dominus, suspicionem hanc praeoccupatione diluit, & haec omnia fucata & hypocritica esse docet, & proinde illis neminem debere moueri.
units.tr: Throughout this whole chapter our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ argues sharply against the scribes and Pharisees, who at that time were the regular teachers and leaders among the Jews. Lest anyone seize on this as a reason to despise the ecclesiastical office together with its teaching, he first warns gravely that they are indeed to be believed and obeyed insofar as they sit in Moses' seat and preach the law of God, but that one must take care not to imitate their example and works. He gives reasons for this warning: they teach well but do not practise what they command others; indeed they impose heavy and intolerable burdens on others, while being the most rigid enforcers of the law and of their own traditions, which they will not touch even with a finger. But since they boasted of the highest reputation for justice and holiness on account of frequent fasts, almsgiving, tithes, prayers, washings, and finally their clothing, arranged to show religion and piety, lest the Lord be thought to speak rashly and out of passion, he removes this suspicion by anticipating it. He teaches that all these things are feigned and hypocritical, and so no one should be moved by them.

units.la: Propositio loci praesentis est: Omnia opera sua faciunt, vt spectentur ab hominibus. Atqui alibi iubet, vt lux nostra coram hominibus luceat, vt videant nostra bona opera, glorificentq; Patrem nostrum qui in caelis est. At illic de vere bonis operibus, quae ex fide secundum Verbi Dei praescriptum fiunt, loquitur, & horum finem esse vult gloriam Dei: In praesenti vero illorum hypocrisim & fucatam sanctimoniam accusat, qua non aliud quam priuatam suam gloriam quaerebant. Itaq; sic dicere videtur: Scio quibus operibus sese ostentent, & fateor eos res suas ita insistere, vt iustissimi & sanctissimi videri possint: sed fucus & larua inanis est, quicquid faciunt. Nec enim germani Mosis discipuli sunt, qui reuerentia legis ducantur, & idcirco Deum non fyncere & ex animo diligunt & coluntur: sed priuatae gloriae studio mouentur, vt hominum iudicio magni & praeclari fiant, & ita suae existimationi simul & quaestui consulant. Cur ergo illos imitaremini, qui hoc nomine Deo exosi sunt, qui in spiritu & veritate coli vult, neq; aliud magis quam hypocrisim detestatur.
units.tr: The proposition of this place is: "They do all their works to be seen by men." Yet elsewhere he bids that our light shine before men, that they may see our good works and glorify our Father who is in heaven. But there he speaks of truly good works, which are done from faith according to the prescription of God's Word, and he wills that the end of these be the glory of God. In the present passage, however, he accuses their hypocrisy and feigned sanctimony, by which they sought nothing other than their own private glory. So he seems to say: I know by what works they display themselves, and I admit that they pursue their affairs in such a way that they can appear most just and holy; but whatever they do is a mask and an empty pretence. For they are not true disciples of Moses, who are led by reverence for the law, and therefore do not love and worship God sincerely and from the heart. They are moved by zeal for private glory, so that they may become great and distinguished in men's judgement, and thus look after their reputation and gain at once. Why then would you imitate those who on this account are hateful to God, who wills to be worshipped in spirit and truth, and detests nothing more than hypocrisy?

units.la: Debet hinc generalis doctrina peti, nunquam fore fideles Dei seruos, quibus tuto credi possit, eos qui hominibus probari cupiunt, neque gloriam Dei omnibus aliis rebus anteponunt. Notum enim est Pauli dictum, qui de seipso non veretur pronunciare: Si hominibus placerem, Christi seruus non essem. Et Dominus apud Ioan. ipsos hoc ipso argumento condemnat, dicens: Quomodo vos potestis credere, cum gloriam ab aliis captetis, & gloriam quae a solo Deo proficiscitur, non quaeratis? Graue dictum, quo non solum a fide alienos esse testatur, sed ita excaecatos & induratos esse ait, vt non possint credere. Nec aliam huius dicti rationem allegat, quam quod gloriam ab hominibus quaerant, non autem vera illius gloriae studio teneantur, qua solus Deus dat, & quam nemo hominum suis viribus aut propria industria sibi parare potest. Est hoc, vt Dei filij simus.
units.tr: From this a general doctrine should be drawn: those who desire to be approved by men, and do not put the glory of God before all other things, will never be faithful servants of God, to whom one may safely entrust oneself. For Paul's saying is well known, who does not hesitate to pronounce of himself: "If I still pleased men, I would not be a servant of Christ." And the Lord in John condemns them by this very argument, saying: "How can you believe, when you seek glory from one another, and do not seek the glory which comes from God alone?" A weighty saying, by which he testifies that they are not only alien to faith, but are so blinded and hardened that they cannot believe. Nor does he give any other reason for this than that they seek glory from men, and are not held by a true zeal for that glory which God alone gives, and which no man can obtain for himself by his own strength or industry. This is what it is to be children of God.

units.la: Hanc ex seipso nemo habet, quia omnes ex Adamo geniti sumus in corrupta illa & depravata imagine, quam hic sibi attraxit per peccatum. Hinc illa naturae vitiositas, quae sese effectis pessimis exerit, vt ab infantia vsq; figmenta cordis nostri praua sint: quod sanctissimi quiq; de seipsis confessi sunt. Itaq; filij irae sumus, quibus regeneratione opus est, quae Dei filios faciat. Huius author est solus Christus, qui deletis et expiatis peccatis nostris suae mortis et sanguinis merito, nos Patri reconciliauit: Beneficium vero istud nobis per Euangelium offert. Hoc qui audiunt, & intra animos suos cōpunctì vitiositate sua agnoscunt, ij salutem esurire & sitire incipiunt, & gloriae illius filiorum Dei desiderio accensi Christum apprehendunt, & reliquis omnibus aliis, quae in mundo eximia habentur, dignitate hanc sua sedulo tuentur, hoc vnu quaerendo, vt Deus in ipsis glorificetur. E contra qui hominibus probari volunt, ij dum illis factum faciant, nihil quaerunt amplius, sed Deum perinde ut homines ementita sanctitatis speciem falli posse sibi persuadent. Itaq; quando Euangelij lux ipsorum fraudem arguit, & simul existimationi & quaestui derogat, quem hypocrisi sua sibi pararunt, exacerbati totus animis, contra Christum furere incipiunt. Atqui tales fuisse Scribas & Pharisaeos, tota historia Euangelica testatur. Non temere ergo de illis hoc dixit Dominus, nec abs causa suos monet, ut ab illis sibi caveant. Atqui eadem causa hodie etiam multos remoratur, ut Euangelio credere non possint, neq; IESV CHRISTO locum dare, quem hostiliter oderunt. Ergo ipsi quoq; caveri, nec quisquam laruis superstitionum & inani fuco, quo sese vendicant, moveri debet, ut illis fidem habeat. Quis enim speret, eos aliorum salutis ferio consultum velle, qui suam ipsorum secuti negligunt, & humana divinis, terrena caelestibus, temporaria aeternis antepo nunt? Sed ad Christum redeamus, qui quod in genere accusavit nunc enumeratione aliquot species confirmat.
units.tr: No one has this from himself, since we are all born of Adam in that corrupt and depraved image which he drew upon himself through sin. Hence comes that vice of nature which shows itself in the worst deeds, so that from infancy the thoughts of our heart are evil, as the most holy men have all confessed of themselves. Therefore we are children of wrath, and need regeneration, which makes us children of God. Its author is Christ alone, who, having blotted out and expiated our sins by the merit of his death and blood, reconciled us to the Father; and this benefit he offers to us through the Gospel. Those who hear this, and are pricked in their hearts and acknowledge their vice, begin to hunger and thirst for salvation. Kindled with desire for that glory of the children of God, they lay hold of Christ, and they diligently esteem this dignity above all the other things which are considered outstanding in the world, seeking this one thing only, that God may be glorified in them. On the contrary, those who wish to be approved by men, while they do their deeds for display, seek nothing further, but persuade themselves that God, like men, can be deceived by a feigned appearance of holiness. And so, when the light of the Gospel exposes their fraud and at the same time detracts from the reputation and gain which they have won for themselves by their hypocrisy, they are inflamed in their minds and begin to rage against Christ. Yet the whole Gospel history testifies that the scribes and Pharisees were such people. The Lord therefore did not say this of them rashly, nor without cause does he warn his people to beware of them. But the same cause still hinders many today from believing the Gospel, or from giving room to Jesus Christ, whom they hate with hostility. So these people too must be guarded against, and no one should be moved by the masks of superstition and the empty pretence by which they present themselves, so as to put faith in them. For who would expect them to care for the salvation of others, when they neglect their own, and prefer human things to divine, earthly to heavenly, and temporal to eternal? But let us return to Christ, who, having accused them in general, now confirms it by enumerating several kinds.

units.la: Et primo quidem de hypocrisi agit, qua sibi religionis & sanctitatis singularis existimatione vestitu conciliare studebant. Nam ait: Dilatant enim phylacteria sua, & producunt fimbrias palliorum suorum. Deus in Lege mandrat populo suo, ut praecepta sua semper ob oculos haberent, & in manibus gestarent. In Exodo enim cum de epulo paschali & redemptione primogeniti eorum docuisset, ut hanc posteris suis commendare debeant, addit: Sit itaq; signum super manum tuam, & monumentum inter oculos tuos, quod Dominus eduxerit nos valida manu ex Aegypto, &c. Et rursus alibi: Sint verba ista, quae ego tibi hodie praecipio in corde tuo, & inculces eas filiis tuis, & loqueris de illis domi tuae residens, & cum in via incedis, cum cubitu vadis, & cum surgis, ligabis demq; ea in signum ad manum tuam, eruntq; monumenta inter oculos tuos, scribes quoq; ea super postes domus tuae, & in portis tuis. Item reponite verba mea in cor vestrum, & in animum vestrum, ea, ut signum ligate ad manum vestram, ut sint veluti monumentum inter oculos vestros, &c. Nominantur cor sive animus, os, oculi, manus, postes & portae, ut scirent primo in assidua & feria meditatione Legis ipsos versari debere, ne huius memoria ipsis unquam excidat: deinde eius praecepta iubentur in ore habere, ut ita constet haec ipsos in corde meditari. Nam ex abundantia cordis os loquitur, & sermo proprius animi index est: At ne ore modo appropinquarent, & labiis solis Deum colerent, in manibus quoq; illa gestare debuerunt, & reipsa obsequiu illi praestare. Deniq; ostiis & portis inscribere ea iubet Moses, ut in omni ingressu & egressu suo scirent hanc illis actionum omnium normam & regulam esse debere. Accessit his peculiare praeceptum de fimbrijs, quas in quatuor alis vestium eandem ob causam facere debebant, ut nimirum praeceptorum Dei memores essent semper, nec posti sui cordis placita ambularent. Nec temere factum puta limus, quod Deus populum suum vestitu a prophanis gentibus discerni, & in vestibus signa exta-re voluit, quae illos obedientiae, quae eius praeceptis debetur, admonerent. Etenim, ut alibi diximus, vestium origo ex peccato est, & primos parentes priusquam peccarent, nudos fuisse, nec tamen erubuisse, Moses testatur: nimirum quod nullius adhuc criminis sibi conscij, nec in animo neq; corpore aliquid vitij haberent, cuius ipsos pudere posset. At cum propter transgressionem paradiso eijcientur, vestiri eos oportuit adueꝛsus caeli iniurias & alia incommoda, quae peccatum illis & posteris peperit. Itaq; quoties nos vestibus induimus aut exuimus, de eo nos cogitare decebat, ut humiliati sub Dei manu, innocentiae studeremus, in quam nos Christus sua mortis merito restituit. Quia vero id adeo non fit, ut pleriq; vestitu superbiant, & luxurientur, eoq; gravius peccent, adhaec Legis & praeceptorum Dei memoria facile apud nos intermoriatur, peculiaribus praeceptis de vestitu nos instrui necesse fuit. Sunt ex his alia omnibus communia, qui ex populo Dei censeri volunt, qualia sunt quae modo recensuimus, & quae alibi mandant, ne vir muliebri, aut mulier virili habitu amiciatur, neue vestis ex lana & lino fiat: alia peculiaria, ut quae de Sacerdotum & Leuitarum vestibus traduntur.
units.tr: And first he deals with hypocrisy, by which they sought to win for themselves, through their clothing, a singular reputation for religion and holiness. For he says: "For they enlarge their phylacteries and lengthen the fringes of their garments." God in the Law commands his people to keep his precepts always before their eyes and to carry them in their hands. For in Exodus, when he had taught about the Passover feast and the redemption of the firstborn, and that these were to be commended to their posterity, he adds: "Let it therefore be a sign upon your hand and a memorial between your eyes, that the Lord brought us out of Egypt with a mighty hand," etc. And again elsewhere: "Let these words, which I command you today, be in your heart, and you shall teach them diligently to your sons, and shall speak of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, when you lie down and when you rise up; and you shall bind them for a sign on your hand, and they shall be as frontlets between your eyes; you shall also write them upon the posts of your house and on your gates." Likewise: "Lay up my words in your heart and in your soul, and bind them as a sign on your hand, that they may be as a memorial between your eyes," etc. Heart or soul, mouth, eyes, hand, posts and gates are named, so that they might know that they must first be occupied with constant and daily meditation on the Law, lest its memory ever slip from them; then they are commanded to have its precepts in their mouth, so that it is clear that they meditate on these in their heart. For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks, and speech is the true index of the mind. But lest they should draw near only with their mouth and worship God with their lips alone, they were also to carry these things in their hands, and actually render obedience to him. Lastly, Moses commands them to write these on the doorposts and gates, so that at every entrance and exit they would know that this must be the norm and rule of all their actions. To these was added a particular command about the fringes, which for the same reason they were to make on the four corners of their garments, so that they would always remember the precepts of God and not walk after the desires of their own heart. Nor think it was done without reason that God willed his people to be distinguished from the profane nations by their clothing, and wished signs to stand out on their garments, which would remind them of the obedience owed to his precepts. For, as we have said elsewhere, the origin of clothing lies in sin; and Moses testifies that our first parents, before they sinned, were naked and yet not ashamed: clearly because, being conscious of no crime as yet, they had no vice in soul or body of which they could be ashamed. But when they were driven out of paradise because of the transgression, they had to be clothed against the injuries of the sky and the other discomforts which sin brought upon them and their posterity. Therefore, whenever we put on or take off our clothes, we ought to think of this, so that, humbled under the hand of God, we might strive for innocence, into which Christ restores us by the merit of his death. But because this is so far from being done that most people take pride and indulge in luxury in their clothing, and so sin more grievously, and because the memory of the Law and God's precepts easily dies out among us, it was necessary that we be instructed by particular precepts about clothing. Some of these are common to all who wish to be counted among the people of God, such as those we have just recounted, and those which elsewhere command that a man not be clothed in woman's dress, nor a woman in man's, and that no garment be made of wool and linen together. Others are peculiar, such as those given concerning the garments of the priests and Levites.

units.la: Quid vero factum inter Iudaeos? Neglecto germano & mystico praeceptorum iterum sensu, Scribae & Pharisaei maiorem pietatis & religionis laudem ex vestitu venati sunt. Nam ut Divus Hieronymus scribit, Pharisaei decalogu sive decem Legis praecepta in membranis descripta fronti cum corona, adhaec dextro brachio aut manui instar armilla alligabant, ut semper ante ocu-
units.tr: But what happened among the Jews? With the genuine and mystical sense of the precepts neglected once again, the scribes and Pharisees sought greater praise for piety and religion from their clothing. For, as St Jerome writes, the Pharisees bound the Decalogue, or the ten precepts of the Law, written on parchment, to the forehead like a crown, and besides, to the right arm or hand like a bracelet, so that always before the eyes-

units.la: Hypocrisis Scribarum arguitur.
units.tr: The hypocrisy of the scribes is refuted.

units.la: los monuerentur, & ideo phylacteria vocabant, quod ad conferuandam Legis memoriam seruirent: & hac ipsa vna cum fimbriis palliorum dilatabant, & producebant, vt religiosiores viderentur mulierculis & rudi vulgo, ex quibus quaestum vberiorem captabant. Quo exemplo admonemur, quam proclivius ad hypocrisim & fucum sub religionis praetextu faciendum sit humana ratio, quae fere sibi persuadet, Deo non minus quam hominibus imponi posse. Na vt Hieronymus praeterea annotauit, suo adhuc tempore mos ille apud Indos & alios Orientales populos durauit, & fortasis hinc origine duxerunt fasciae & diademata regum, quae apud illos adhuc hodie in vsu sunt. Nec id alicui mirum videri debet, quando inter Christiani nominis profiteres superstitio ita creuit, vt plerique religionem & pietatem vestitu aut aliis rebus ludicris, quae vel manibus gestant, vel ex collo suspendunt, metiantur. Hinc initium habuit Monachorum habitus, sub cuius colore & forma illi mysteria maxima latere sibi ipsis & vulgo reliquo persuadent. Huic perfuasioni debemus globulos sacros, quibus preculas suas homines superstitiosi Deo & Diui coelitibus adnumerant. Eiusdem farinae est, quod aliqui initium Euangelij, quod est secundum Ioannem ex collo suspensum gestant, aut aliud quid, quod alicuius Diui nomine commendatur. Sunt haec & alia huius generis tam vulgaria hodie, vt non immerito cum D. Hieronymo quis exclamare possit: Va miseris nobis, ad quos Pharisaeorum vitia transierunt. Quod si haec reprehensione digna sunt, quid de illis iudicari debet, qui abstinent omni religione vestitu peregrino, lasciuo, & ad libidinem proritandam compositos fere ostentant, & fe non aliter generis sui nobilitatem testari posse exist imant, quam si vestibus sese induant, quae barbaros & Turcas potius decent, quam Christianos homines. Paulus olim nolebat, vt qui ex Corinthijs Christo nomen dederant, viri aut feminae, gentilitio habitu in coetibus Ecclesiae comparerent: & tu excusatum te putabis, si ita induaris, vt quiuis alius quam Christianus posiis dici? Isaias certe mundum muliebrem, quo aulicae mulieres & puellae suo saeculo lasciuiebant ita excutit, vt eas propter illum exitio & exilio dignas esse affirmet: Sophoni as ita minatur Deum principes viros vitare velle, qui induuntur veste peregrina. At hodie nul la vestis placet, nisi aut luxu immodico, aut nouitatis et peregrinitatis specie insolita commendatur. Hinc scandala infinita nascuntur, & iumptus inutiles fiunt, quibus familiae antiquae, & quae prius florebant, ad inopiam redactae intereunt. Viderunt hoc maiores nostri, viri non minus pij quam prudentes, qui luxum & fastum illum legibus publicis coercendum esse putarunt. Quam ergo indignum est hominibus priuatis hodie licere, vt leges bonas violent, & in eo laudem quaerant, quod reprehensionem & vituperium meretur: quod deniq; animos & mores a Christi religione alienos arguit?
units.tr: They were admonished, and so they called them phylacteries, because they served to keep the memory of the Law. They also widened and lengthened these same things, together with the tassels of their cloaks, so that they would seem more devout to silly women and the uneducated crowd, from whom they gained a richer profit. From this example we are warned how much more readily human reason inclines to hypocrisy and deceit under the pretext of religion, since it persuades itself that God can be deceived no less than men. For, as Jerome further noted, that custom lasted in his own time among the Indians and other Eastern peoples, and perhaps from this origin the sashes and diadems of kings took their beginning, which even today are still in use among them. Nor should this seem strange to anyone, since superstition has grown so much among those who profess the Christian name that most people measure religion and piety by clothing or other trifling things, which they either carry in their hands or hang from their necks. From this came the beginning of the monastic habit, under whose colour and form they persuade themselves and the rest of the common people that the greatest mysteries lie hidden. To this persuasion we owe the sacred beads by which superstitious people count their little prayers to God and the heavenly saints. Of the same kind is it that some wear the beginning of the Gospel of John hung from their necks, or something else that is commended under the name of some saint. These and other things of this kind are so common today that one may not unfairly cry out with Jerome: Woe to us wretched men, to whom the vices of the Pharisees have passed! But if these things deserve rebuke, what must be judged of those who abstain from no religious restraint in dress, and who display themselves in foreign, wanton clothing, arranged almost to stir lust, and who think they can show the nobility of their birth in no other way than by dressing in garments that suit barbarians and Turks rather than Christian men? Paul once did not want men or women who had given their names to Christ among the Corinthians to appear in the assemblies of the Church in heathen dress; and will you think yourself excused if you dress so that you could be taken for anyone rather than a Christian? Isaiah certainly so struck at the female finery with which court ladies and girls of his day indulged themselves that he declares they deserve destruction and exile on account of it. Zephaniah threatens that God will punish the princes and men who put on foreign clothing. But today no clothing pleases unless it is recommended either by immoderate luxury or by the unusual look of novelty and foreignness. Hence endless scandals arise, and useless expenses are incurred, by which old families that once flourished are reduced to poverty and perish. Our ancestors, men no less pious than prudent, saw this, and thought that such luxury and pride must be restrained by public laws. How unworthy, then, that today private individuals are allowed to violate good laws, and seek praise in what deserves reproach and blame, which in the end shows minds and manners alien to the religion of Christ!

units.la: Etsi vero Dei Filius Scribarum & Pharisaeorum hypocrisim accusat, qui vestitu superstitio sufucatum Legis studium simulabant, cuius prophani contemptores erant, minime tamen ei probantur Ecclesiarum ministri, qui ne hypocrisis argui possint, ita vestiuntur, vt a vulgo hominum nihil differant: multi etiam mercatoribus, equitibus, militibus deniq; accensferi possint. Etenim vult Deus suae Ecclesiae ministros & doctrina antistites ab alijs discerni, & proinde omnibus suis culis habitu peculiari & honestiori illi vsi sunt. In Lege prolixe describitur Aaronis vestitus, & Sacerdotum quasi proprium insigne erat Ephod, quo a reliquis dignosci poterant. Prophetas quoq; veste peculiari indutos fuisse, ex Zacharia patet, qui de pseudoprophetis coiterfis dicit, quod post hac non gestaturi sint vestem villosam, vt mentiantur. Et Ochozias Rex Israeliticus ex habitu aut vestitus descriptione intelligebat, Eliam fuisse illum, qui seruos eius a legatione ad Baalzebub reuocauerat. Et veteres Prophetas imitatus videtur Ioannes Baptista, cum illi vestis expiris camelorum contexta & zona coreacea tribuitur. In Apocalypsi vero de duobus testibus, qui ante nouissimum Christi aduentum prophetare debent, dicitur, quod saccis amicti prædicabunt. Haec propter eos annotare libuit, qui cum Euangelij praecones dici & haberi velint, asuperstitiosi quidem & hypocrito habitu monachorum & pseudospiritualium, qui in Papatu sunt abhorrent, sed e contra sagati & chlamydati militariter incedunt, serico item multo ornantur, vt de illis nequaquam dici possit, quod de Ioanne Bapt. dicebat Dominus, non fuisse eum mollibus vestibus amictum, vt solent esse, qui in domibus regum sunt: cum ipsi & aulicas frequentant, & illic non solum mollibus amiciantur, sed inter aulicos ludant quoq;, comessentur, perpotent, saltent deniq; & choreas ducant. O tempora, o mores.
units.tr: Although the Son of God indeed accuses the hypocrisy of the Scribes and Pharisees, who by their clothing pretended a zeal for the Law, cloaked in superstition, while they were in fact its profane despisers, nevertheless the ministers of the Churches are by no means approved by him if they dress so as to differ in nothing from the common crowd, so that they cannot be charged with hypocrisy; many of them could even be counted as merchants, horsemen, or, finally, soldiers. For God wants the ministers of his Church and the teachers of doctrine to be distinguished from others, and therefore in all ages they used a distinctive and more honourable dress. In the Law the clothing of Aaron is described at length, and the Ephod was, as it were, the proper badge of the priests, by which they could be told apart from the rest. That the prophets too were clothed in a distinctive garment is clear from Zechariah, who, speaking of the false prophets, says that they will no longer wear a hairy garment in order to deceive. And the Israelite king Ahaziah, from the appearance or description of the clothing, understood that it was Elijah who had called back his servants from their embassy to Baal-zebub. And John the Baptist seems to have imitated the ancient prophets, since a garment woven of camel's hair and a leather belt are attributed to him. In the Apocalypse, moreover, concerning the two witnesses who are to prophesy before the last coming of Christ, it is said that they will preach clothed in sackcloth. I have thought it worth noting these things for those who want to be called and regarded as heralds of the Gospel, who indeed shrink from the superstitious and hypocritical habit of monks and pseudo-spiritual men that is found under the Papacy, but on the contrary strut about in military cloaks and cloaks of war, and are likewise adorned with much silk; so that it cannot at all be said of them what the Lord said of John the Baptist, that he was not clothed in soft garments, as those are who are in the houses of kings. For they not only frequent the courts and are clothed in soft garments there, but they also play among the courtiers, feast, drink deeply, and finally dance and lead the dances. O the times, O the manners!

units.la: Pergamus autem in Scribarum & Pharisaeorum descriptione, quibus ambitionem quoque & auram popularis studium exprobrat Dominus: ex quo euidentissime constabat, illos quaecunque sub religionis praetextu faciebant, non aliam ob causam facere, quam ut spectarentur ab hominibus. Dicit autem de illis: Amant primos accubitus in coenis, & primos consessus in synagogis, & salutationes in foro, & vocari a hominibus Rabbi.
units.tr: Let us go on, however, with the description of the Scribes and Pharisees, whom the Lord also charges with ambition and with a zeal for popular applause; from which it was most evident that whatever they did under the pretext of religion they did for no other reason than to be seen by men. He says of them: They love the chief places at feasts, and the chief seats in the synagogues, and greetings in the marketplace, and to be called Rabbi by men.

units.la: Additur his alia adhuc species siue nota ambitionis, quod ament salutationes in foro & locis publicis, quod ab hominibus velint vocari Rabbi Rabbi. Geminatum Rabbi vocabulum gloriae studium ardens denotat, quod nimirum non obiter se doctores & magistros nominari velint, sed ita ut quales sint, publice omnibus innotescat.
units.tr: To these is added yet another mark or sign of ambition, that they love greetings in the marketplace and public places, and want to be called Rabbi, Rabbi, by men. The doubled word Rabbi denotes an ardent desire for glory, since they wanted to be named teachers and masters not in passing, but in such a way that what sort of men they were would be made publicly known to all.
