Not only did they profane the holy seed by marrying foreign wives, and burden their needy brothers with ruinous usury, and finally were more sluggish than necessary in building the temple, but they even cruelly slew, beyond all desert, the most faithful servant of God, whom God had set over them as overseer and governor of that very work, so that neither the majesty of the place, nor the memory of the time or of their recent deliverance, restrained them from so great a crime. When, a little later, the most shameful slaughter of the Son of God, in whom all the prophets and righteous men who have lived since the beginning of the world looked, befell them, he does not threaten them rashly when he says that the guilt of all the righteous blood shed will be imputed to them. Nor is he content to have said this once; he confirms it with a solemn oath, adding: Truly I say to you, all these things shall come upon this generation. By this manner of speaking he seems to signify that the men of that age were to pay such penalties for such great crimes that they ought not to promise themselves any hope of impunity from delay. For it is established from histories that the destruction of the city and temple fell in the thirty-eighth year after the death of Christ, after they had been harassed by countless calamities and continual evils. Yet this threat is far more terrible than it is thought to be. What can be said more weighty than that God himself, from heaven, addressing Cain about his brother's slaughter, demands an account of it from him, and, bringing the earth forward as a witness against him, says: The voice of your brother's blood cries to me from the ground? There was no one to act as a witness of so great a crime, or to testify to the deed. But the dumb earth performs this office for the innocent man, for it had earlier received the innocent blood as if sympathising with it, and now casts out the monstrous murderer as unworthy to be borne or nourished any longer. And what God then declared was afterwards confirmed by a perpetual law: Whoever sheds the blood of a man, by man shall his blood be shed. There is no doubt that this was said of the ordinary magistrate, whose duty it is to avenge murders with capital punishment; and this is commanded with such severity that the Lord rejects every other ransom or expiation for so great a crime. For in the book of Numbers Moses says: You shall not take a price for the life of a murderer, who is guilty, so that he must die; but he shall be put to death, lest you pollute the land in which you dwell. For blood pollutes the land, and the land cannot be cleansed of the blood shed in it, except by the blood of him who shed it. By what reasoning, then, will he be reconciled to God, whom this very man has made guilty of blood? Not without cause, therefore, did God wish that a murder whose author was unknown should be publicly expiated, with so careful and laborious a rite, by the elders and judges and all the others in whose territory the corpse was found, so that this single action alone might teach how vehemently those should abhor the shedding of blood who wish to enjoy God's favour. For this reason also, wishing to bind the prophet to the serious performance of his duty, God sends him and threatens that he will require the blood of those whom he has destroyed by his silence or idleness from his hand. But if he is guilty of blood who, by keeping silent, gives someone the cause of death, and by his words does not call back from destruction those who are perishing willingly, what will become of those who kill the unwilling against right and law, and kill for no other reason than that they are servants of God for eternal life? And what punishment will be sufficient to punish such a crime as it deserves? That these threats were neither empty nor cold, the event of the matter has taught, and the history of the destruction of Jerusalem bears ample witness.

units.la: Quare vero huius loci statum, in primis observari debet, quam periculosum sit impiorum homines & hostium Dei consortio coniungi, & patrum quoque sanguinarijs & iniquis consilijs commaniicare. Fallit multos non turpiter modo, sed infelicissime, quod sceleratorum numero exemplo & authoritate excusari putant. Et his nihil imprudentius aut inhonestius fieri posse videtur, quam a mundo separari. Atqui longe aliter Deus iudicat, qui neque personarum respectu, neque muneribus, neque ullis hominum rationibus movetur. Et qui mundo placere volunt, ij (ut Paulus de se ipso testatur) Dei servi esse non possunt: & ijdem non eam modo culpam lunt tandem, quam ipsi admiserunt, verumetiam aliorum sceleribus sese aggravant. Est enim unum & idem omnium impiorum corpus sub uno capite Satana, cui illi omnes militant, & ab eodem iniustitiae stipendium recipiunt. Cum Abelu trucidaffet Cain, egressus est a facie Domini, ex eo nimirum loco, ubi primi parentes haud dubie ex Dei iussu confederant, ubi cultus Dei purus erat, & prima promissionis doctrina exercebatur. Et civitatem propriam condidit, a filij sui nomine Hanochiam dictam, ut vel eo testaretur se in terris civitatem permanentem quaerere, nec multum curare futuram & aeternam, quam electi in coelis repositam habent. Illic etiam ex Caini posteris progeniti sunt Musices inventores & armorum fabri, ut hanc voluptatis & violentiae sedem esse constaret. Hic ergo caepit civitas hominum impiorum, ad quam ab eo tempore collecti sunt omnes reprobi, electis interim Dei praesidio tutis & securis, donec hi quoque Caini posteri se permisserunt, & aut praematura morte, aut cum illis per Diluvij aquas extincti sunt. In Abeli autem locum Seth successit, ex quo Noe progenitus est, in quo generis humani seminarium Deus Diluvij tempore servavit. Per eam igitur & stulte faciunt, qui ex mundo diuelli & separari nolunt, cum adhuc hodie Caini posteritas sive qui illum imitantur, a facie Domini quotidie abeant, & sibi civitates & arces in hoc mundo condant, in quibus salutis praesidium sibi repositum esse arbitrantur, qui Deo nolunt fide re. Ab eo tempore certe hoc unum Deus sedulo fecit, ut suos a mundo separaret. Factum hoc per Aream tempore Diluvij, & ut Abrahamo ex Chaldaea, sic Lotho ex Sodomis exeundum fuit, ne cum impijs illis & exitio devotis periret. Similiter non in Aegypto servari potuerunt filij Israel, sed & ut a prophanis, qui illic erant, non uno modo separarentur, necesse fuit. Et totius cultus Levitici hic etiam usus fuit, ut eius exercitijs & sacramentis populus ille, quem sibi Deus in peculium selegerat, a prophanis gentibus secerneretur. Sed & Dei Filius in mundum venit, & pro nobis mortuus est, ut nos e mundo selectos sibi vendicaret ab omni iniquitate, populum peculiarem, studiosum bonorum operum. Idcirco Apostoli sedulo Christianos homines hortantur, ne impari iugo copulentur cum infidelibus. Item exite (aiunt) e medio eorum, & separamini, & impurum ne tetigeritis: Ne diligite mundum, neque ea quae in mundo sunt. Ne configuremini saeculo huic. Et de spirituali Babylone clamat Angelus: Exite ex ea populemi, ne participes sitis peccatorum eius, & ex plagis eius ne accipiatis. Quid ergo absurdum fingi poterat, quam consortia cum sceleratis, adeoque ipsa sceleratis excusare, ne separationis aut secessionis a mundo authores simus. Num ergo cum Deo pugnare libet, qui ut a mundo auellamur praecipit? Vel cui grave sit a mundo discedere, qui prior a nobis discedit, & quem nisi deseramus, Deo non possumus coniungi? Pacem quidem cum omnibus hominibus, sed quantum in nobis est. At cum nemini plus quam Deo debeamus, neque in nostro iure neque potestate fuerit, propter homines qualescunque ab obsequio Dei discedere. Qui vero pios Dei cultores persequuntur, & eos crudeliter iugulant, qui uni Deo vivere cupiunt, cum Deo odia exercent, & civitatis Cainicae cives, vel potius latronum socij fiunt. Quod vicinam hodie diligentius considerarent, qui cum tyrannis persecutoribus socia arma coiunt, et foederibus exterorum principum atque regum sese obstringunt, quorum finis & scopus praeceptum est militia mercenaria, quam sibi ipsis quaestum faciunt, & ut alij ad laborem aliquem honestum conducuntur, ut alimenta sibi & suis acquirant: ita ipsi se excusatos putant, si sese ad iu-gulandos homines conduci patiantur ab iis, quibus nullum debent obsequium, nisi quod ipsi illu pro pter vilem pecuniam vendita libertate sua pollicentur: Corradunt hi vndiq; rationes, quibus in-stitutum suum defendant, & non contenti patriam communem prætexuisse, quasi publici com-modi studio ducantur, pietatis quoq; & religionis studiosi videri volunt, qui Ecclesiarum paci consulant, quando harum persecutoribus militant, qui Euangelij oppressionem palam cum Anti-christo coniurarunt. Surget contra hoc olim in magno illo die Papinianus, qui etsi nulla Christi co-gnitione imbutus, iurisconsultus autè & Romana vrbis præfectus esset sub Bassiano Caracalla, qui cum nouercam incestis nuptijs sibi copulasset, & huius filium Getam, qui suus ex eodem patre Seuero frater erat, ex matris collo pendentem crudeliter iugulasset, a Papiniano propter eximiā, qua pollebat authoritatem postulare ausus est, ut parricidium istud publicè excusaret. Sed respon-dit ille tyranno: Non tam facile est excusare parricidia quàm facere. Mori autè maluit, quàm tur-pi & iniusto obsequio se cædis iniustæ aut parricidij socium facere. Ita hodie cogitare debebant qui fidem in Christum profitentur, homicidia, rapinas, raptus matronarum & virginum, incendia & alia, quæ militiam mercenariā comitantur, non tam facile excusari ad Dei tribunal, quàm com-mittuntur. Nobis ergo istorum omnium vsus sit, ut ex mundo impio & malo separemur, & reli-gia Caini ciuitate coniungamur Ecclesiæ IESV CHRISTI, ut sub hoc capite nostro ipsi fide sanctâ & charitate non fucata seruiamus: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in sæ-cula sæculorum. Amen.
units.tr: But the nature of this passage must be noted first of all: how dangerous it is for people to join the company of the wicked and enemies of God, and to share in the bloody and unjust counsels of their fathers. Many are misled, not only shamefully but most unhappily, by thinking that they can excuse themselves by the number and authority of the wicked. To these people nothing seems more imprudent or dishonourable than to be separated from the world. Yet God judges far otherwise, for he is moved neither by respect of persons, nor by bribes, nor by any human considerations. Those who want to please the world, as Paul testifies of himself, cannot be servants of God. Such people not only bear the guilt of what they themselves commit, but also burden themselves with the crimes of others. For all the wicked form one and the same body under one head, Satan, under whom they all serve and from whom they receive the wages of injustice. When Cain had slain Abel, he went out from the presence of the Lord, that is, from the place where our first parents had doubtless dwelt by God's command, where the pure worship of God was practised and the first teaching of the promise was taught. He founded a city of his own, called Enoch after his son's name, so that by this very fact he might show that he sought a lasting city on earth and cared little for the future and eternal city which the elect have laid up in heaven. There too, from the posterity of Cain, came the inventors of music and the smiths of weapons, so that it might be plain that this was a seat of pleasure and violence. Here, then, began the city of impious men, to which from that time all the reprobate have been gathered, while the elect remained safe and secure under God's protection, until these also, the posterity of Cain, gave themselves over to sin, and were destroyed either by untimely death or together with the others by the waters of the Flood. But in Abel's place came Seth, from whom Noah was born, and in Noah God preserved the seed of the human race at the time of the Flood. Therefore those people act foolishly who are unwilling to be torn and separated from the world, since even today the posterity of Cain, or those who imitate him, daily depart from the presence of the Lord, and build for themselves cities and strongholds in this world, in which they think a refuge of safety is laid up for them, who are unwilling to trust God. From that time, certainly, God has diligently done this one thing, that he might separate his own from the world. This was done through the ark at the time of the Flood, and just as Abraham had to leave Chaldea, so Lot had to leave Sodom, lest he perish with those impious men who were doomed to destruction. Likewise the children of Israel could not be preserved in Egypt, but it was necessary that they be separated in more than one way from the profane people who lived there. And the whole Levitical worship had this purpose as well, that by its exercises and sacraments that people whom God had chosen for his own possession should be set apart from the profane nations. But also the Son of God came into the world and died for us, so that he might claim us, chosen out of the world, for himself, free from all iniquity, a people peculiar to him, zealous for good works. For this reason the Apostles earnestly exhort Christians not to be yoked unequally with unbelievers. Likewise: "Come out," they say, "from among them, and be separate, and touch no unclean thing. Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world. Do not be conformed to this age." And concerning the spiritual Babylon the angel cries: "Come out of her, my people, that you may not be partakers of her sins, and that you may not receive of her plagues." What could be more absurd to pretend, then, than to have fellowship with the wicked, and even to excuse the wicked themselves, lest we be authors of separation or withdrawal from the world? Do we then wish to fight against God, who commands us to be torn away from the world? Or is it hard for anyone to leave the world, when God first departs from us, and unless we forsake the world we cannot be joined to God? We are indeed to have peace with all men, but as far as lies in us. Yet since we owe nothing more than God, and it is neither within our right nor our power, for the sake of men of whatever kind, to depart from the obedience of God. Those who persecute the pious worshippers of God, and cruelly slaughter those who wish to live to God alone, wage war against God, and become citizens of the city of Cain, or rather companions of robbers. Those who today join arms with tyrannical persecutors, and bind themselves by treaties with foreign princes and kings, ought to consider this more carefully. The aim and purpose of such men is mercenary soldiering, which they make a source of gain for themselves; and just as others are hired for some honest labour so that they may earn their living and that of their families, so they think themselves excused if they allow themselves to be hired by those to whom they owe no obedience, to slaughter men, except that they promise this for paltry money, having sold their liberty. These men gather reasons from every side to defend their course, and not content with putting forward the common fatherland, as if they were moved by zeal for the public good, they also wish to appear devoted to piety and religion, since they look after the peace of the churches, while they serve the persecutors of the churches, who have openly conspired with Antichrist to suppress the Gospel. Against this, in that great day, Papinian will one day rise up, who, although he was unacquainted with the knowledge of Christ, was nonetheless a jurist and prefect of the city of Rome under Bassianus Caracalla. When Caracalla had joined himself in incestuous marriage to his stepmother, and cruelly strangled Geta, the son of that stepmother and his own brother by the same father Severus, hanging from their mother's neck, he dared to demand of Papinian, because of the outstanding authority he wielded, that he publicly excuse that murder of a brother. But Papinian answered the tyrant: "It is not so easy to excuse a parricide as to commit one." And he preferred to die rather than make himself, by shameful and unjust compliance, an accomplice in an unjust murder or a parricide. So today those who profess faith in Christ ought to consider that homicides, robberies, the rapes of matrons and virgins, arson, and the other things that accompany mercenary soldiering, are not so easily excused before the judgment seat of God as they are committed. Let us therefore make use of all these examples, so that we may be separated from the impious and evil world, and join the church of Jesus Christ rather than the city of Cain, so that under this our Head we may serve him in holy faith and in unfeigned love, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever and ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCLXXXIII.
units.tr: HOMILIA CCLXXXIII.

units.la: Ierusalem Ierusalem, quæ trucidas Prophetas, & lapidas eos qui ad te missi sunt, quoties volui congregare liberos tuos, quemad-modum congregat gallina pullos suos sub alas, & noluistis? Ecce re-linquitur vobis domus vestra deserta. Dico enim vobis, nequaquam me videbitis ab hoc tempore vsq; dum dicatis, Benedictus qui venit in nomine Domini.
units.tr: Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those who are sent to you! How often would I have gathered your children together, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you would not! Behold, your house is left to you desolate. For I tell you, you shall not see me from now on until you say, "Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord."

units.la: NOn poterat Dei Filius Dominus & Seruator noster IESVS CHRISTVS aliquid con-tra Scribas & Pharisæos, adeoq; contra totam Iudæorum gentem, grauius & atrocius di-cere, quàm quod nuper dixit, illos implere mensuram patrum suorum, qui Prophetas veteres tru-cidarint, & ad se missos gratia Dei præcones lapidauerint, cum ipsum persequantur, de quo illi omnes vaticinati sint: & simul minatus est, fore, ut super ipsos veniat, & ex ipsorum manibus re-quiratur omnis sanguis seruorum Dei, qui effusus est super terram a tempore Abeli vsque ad san-guinem Zachariæ Prophetæ, quem post reditum ex Babylone patres in atrio templi impie occi-derint. Nam primò quia Abeli meminit, quem frater Cainus crudeli parricidio trucidauit, huius illos socios atq; ciues esse docet, quem ex Malo illo, id est, diabolo fuisse, Ioannes postea dixit. De-inde quia vnius modò hominis cædes scelus eiusmodi est, quod non aliter quàm homicidæ sangui-ne potest expiari, quæ obsecro spes salutis esse potest ijs, quibus omnium eorum sanguinem im-putat Deus, qui ab ipsa rerum origine per annos ter mille & quadringentos pro pietate vera ab impijs iugulati sunt. Itaque non dubium est, quin Christus multis vsus sit immodestius inuehi in eos, quorum summa erat in populo Dei authoritas, tum propter Ierosolymam, quæ gentis caput erat, & in qua ipsi dominabantur: tum propter funētionem, quam vt sacrorum & doctrinæ anti-sites sustinebant. Itaque pergit, & in præsenti primum hoc illis eripit, quod tam confidentes & securos faciebat, vt omnes admonitiones & minas contemnerent: Deinde poenas minatur, quas Deo daturi sint.
units.tr: The Son of God, our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, could not have spoken more severely and bitterly against the scribes and Pharisees, and so against the whole Jewish nation, than when he recently said that they were filling up the measure of their fathers, who had killed the ancient prophets and stoned the messengers of God's grace sent to them, since they were persecuting him about whom all those prophets had prophesied. At the same time he threatened that it would come upon them, and that from their hands would be required all the blood of God's servants shed on the earth from the time of Abel to the blood of the prophet Zechariah, whom their fathers impiously slew in the court of the temple after the return from Babylon. For first, in mentioning Abel, whom his brother Cain murdered in cruel fratricide, he teaches that they are the companions and fellow citizens of that man who, as John later said, was of that Evil One, that is, the devil. Next, since the murder of even one man is a crime that cannot be expiated except by the blood of the murderer, what hope of salvation can there be for those whose charge is the blood of all those whom the wicked slaughtered for true godliness from the very beginning of the world, over three thousand four hundred years? It is therefore beyond doubt that Christ spoke too vehemently against those who held the highest authority among God's people, both because of Jerusalem, which was the head of the nation and in which they ruled, and because of the office they held as the bishops of worship and doctrine. So he goes on, and in the present passage first takes away from them what made them so confident and secure that they despised all warnings and threats; then he threatens the punishments they will suffer from God.

units.la: Quoad primum veteri dignitate superbiebat Ierosolyma. De hac enim olim Deus per Da-uidem pronunciauit: Dominus elegit Zionem, & expetiuit eam sibi sedem, dicens: Hæc mea est requies sempiterna, hic habitabo, quoniam expetiui eam. Item, Notus in Iehuda Deus, magnum nomen nomen eius in Israele. In salem est tabernaculum eius, & mansio eius in Sion. Et rursus magnus Iehoua & laudabilis valde in ciuitate Dei nostri, in monte sancto suo. Deus stabiliet eam vsq; in perpetuum: Nam hic Deus, Deus noster est in saeculum. Ipse diriget nos vsq; ad mortem. Haec & multa alia huius generis praeconia nō solis Ierosolymitanis animos faciebant, sed Iudaeos omnes fiducia magna implebant, vt in effreni scelerum licentia ipsem perpetuae impunitatis conciperent, sicuti apud Ieremiam est videre. Quapropter vix credibile videbatur, Deum haec vn- quam passurum fuisse in ea vrbe fieri, vbi ipsi Jacris praerant, quos Christus hucusq; tam duriter tractauerat. Itaq; quod in genere illis & vrbi minatus erat, nunc diligentius explicat & confirmat. Et ne inani fiducia aut potius perfuasione seipsos decipere pergant, ostendit Deum de Ierosolyma longe aliter sentire, quam ipsi sibi persuaserint. Dicit enim Ierusalem Ierusalem, quae truci- das prophetas, & lapidas eos qui ad te missi sunt, &c. Sunt autem eo diligentius haec obseruanda, quod non semel ista dixit Dominus. Eade enim simili cu grauitate antea quoq; pronuntiauit apud Lucam, cum quidam illum vt ab Herode sibi caueret, admonerent: Quibus respondet ijdem prope verbu, docens non quicquam periculi sibi a tyranno illo in Galilaea imminere, eo quod Ierosoly- ma Prophetarum caedibus & languini ita assueuerit, vt Prophetam alibi quam illic mori, vix possibile fit. Et ibidem haec etiam infert, quae in praesenti repetit, quando inter Scribas & in ipso templo verba facit, & quidem admodum pathetice, quasi diceret: Es quidem tu Ierusalem, quam Deus iam multis saeculis in deliciis habuit, vt sui cultus sedem ibi constitueret, & quam tot sancti & egregij cultores Dei expetiuerunt. Sed non respondes profession tuae. Diceris sancta, iustitiae sedes, item schola sapientiae, & idcirco Prophetarum nutrix & asylum esse debebas. Sed trucidas Prophetas & ad te missos Dei seruos lapidas, deniq; apud te crudelis carnificina & laniena exercetur, nec vspiam alibi crudelius tractantur, qui Deo religiose seruiunt. Potius ergo tibi conuenit, quod Isaias olim dixit, Quomodo facta est meretrix ciuitas fidelis? in qua iustitia habitabat, nunc autem homicida. Quod item Ieremias te speluncam latronum vocauit.
units.tr: As to the first point, Jerusalem was proud of its ancient dignity. For God once declared of it through David: "The Lord has chosen Zion and desired it for his seat, saying: This is my rest for ever; here I will dwell, because I have desired it." Likewise: "In Judah God is known; his name is great in Israel. His tabernacle is in Salem, and his dwelling in Zion." And again: "Great is the Lord and greatly to be praised in the city of our God, in his holy mountain. God will establish it for ever; for this God is our God for ever. He will guide us even unto death." These and many other praises of this kind did not only fill the minds of the Jerusalemites, but filled all the Jews with great confidence, so that in the unbridled licence of their sins they conceived a hope of perpetual impunity, as can be seen in Jeremiah. Hence it seemed scarcely credible that God would ever allow these things to happen in that city where the priests presided, whom Christ had hitherto treated so harshly. So what he had threatened in general to them and to the city, he now explains and confirms more carefully. And so that they should not keep deceiving themselves with empty confidence, or rather with a persuasion, he shows that God thinks of Jerusalem quite differently from what they had persuaded themselves. For he says: "Jerusalem, Jerusalem, who kill the prophets and stone those who are sent to you," and so on. These words must be noted all the more carefully because the Lord did not say them only once. For he had earlier spoken with similar gravity in Luke, when certain people warned him to beware of Herod. He answers them in almost the same words, teaching that no danger from that tyrant in Galilee threatened him, since Jerusalem was so accustomed to the slaughter and blood of the prophets that it is almost impossible for a prophet to die anywhere else. And there he adds also what he repeats in the present passage, when he speaks among the scribes and in the temple itself, and indeed very movingly, as if he were saying: "You indeed, Jerusalem, whom God for many ages has held dear, so that he might establish there the seat of his worship, and whom so many holy and excellent worshippers of God have desired, you do not answer to your profession. You are called holy, the seat of righteousness, and likewise the school of wisdom, and therefore you ought to be the nurse and refuge of the prophets. But you kill the prophets and stone the servants of God who are sent to you; finally, cruel slaughter and butchery are carried on among you, and nowhere else are those who serve God devoutly treated more cruelly." Rather, what Isaiah once said fits you: "How has the faithful city become a harlot? In her righteousness dwelt, but now murderers." Likewise Jeremiah called you a den of robbers.

units.la: Admonet locus hic quam parum tribui debeat locorum sanctitati & veteri dignitati, qua aliqui olim claruerunt. Etenim solet Deus saepe certos locos sibi deligere, non quod ipsi illis opus sit, sed nobis, quibus sine illis neq; cultus externus neq; doctrina aut preces publicae possunt consistere. Interim neq; Deus neq; eius gratia vlli certo loco alligata est, sicuti exemplis grauibus docemur. Tabernaculum ante Samuelis tempora in Silo fuisse scimus. Sed cum locum illum prophanarent filij Heli, non Tabernaculum modo inde transtulit Deus, sed occisis Sacerdotibus arcam foederis in Philistaeorum manus venire, & in idolaum Dagonis inferri passus est. Idcirco in Psalmis canitur: Audiuit Deus, & iratus est, & auersatus est vehementer Israelem: Et defe- ruit tabernaculum Silo, tabernaculum, quo habitabat inter homines. Imo capiendum tradidit robur suum & decus suum in manum hostis. Nec melior fuit Ierosolyma conditio, cum ijsdem morib illic viueretur. Tunc enim per Ieremiam in atrio domus Domini stantem illis dicere iusserat Dominus: Si non audieritis me, vt ambuletis in Lege mea, quam vobis proposui, vt audiatis verba seruorum meorum Prophetarum, quos ego mitto ad vos, faciam edem istam similem Silo, & vrbem hanc obiciam contumeliae omnibus gentibus terrae. Et ante illum Micheas dixerat: Propter vos Sion vt ager arabitur, & Ierusalem aceruus erit, & mons domus in excelsa sylua. Debent haec diligenter obseruari, ne ab illis nos seduci patiamur, qui hodie non minorem dignitatem Romani sedi tribuunt, quam olim Iudaei Ierosolymae & templo suo tribuerunt. Sed quia super stitiosam hanc perfuasionem non semel confutauimus, nolumus nunc huic diutius insistere. Suffi- ciat nunc monuisse cultum Dei & salutem hominum neq; loco alicui certo, neq; aliquorum successi- oni astrictam esse, locos item non monumentis seruorum Dei, sed doctrinae puritate, religione ve- ra & pietate hanc colentium commendari.
units.tr: This place shows how little the holiness of places and the ancient dignity for which some were once famous ought to be credited. For God has often been accustomed to choose certain places for himself, not because he needs them, but because we need them, since without them neither external worship, nor teaching, nor public prayers can stand. Yet neither God nor his grace is tied to any particular place, as we are taught by weighty examples. We know that the tabernacle was at Shiloh before the time of Samuel. But when the sons of Eli profaned that place, God not only removed the tabernacle from there, but allowed the ark of the covenant, after the priests were slain, to come into the hands of the Philistines and to be carried into the temple of their idol Dagon. Therefore it is sung in the Psalms: "God heard and was angry, and greatly rejected Israel; and he forsook the tabernacle of Shiloh, the tabernacle in which he dwelt among men. Indeed he gave his strength into captivity, and his glory into the enemy's hand." Nor was the condition of Jerusalem any better, since people lived there with the same morals. For then the Lord had commanded through Jeremiah, who stood in the court of the house of the Lord, to say to them: "If you will not hear me, to walk in my law, which I have set before you, to hear the words of my servants the prophets, whom I send to you, I will make this house like Shiloh, and I will make this city a curse to all the nations of the earth." And before him Micah had said: "For your sake Zion shall be ploughed as a field, and Jerusalem shall become a heap, and the mountain of the house a high wooded place." These things must be carefully noted, so that we do not allow ourselves to be led astray by those who today ascribe no less dignity to the Roman see than the Jews once ascribed to Jerusalem and its temple. But since we have already more than once refuted this superstitious persuasion, we do not wish to dwell on it longer now. It is enough now to have warned that the worship of God and the salvation of men are bound neither to any fixed place nor to the succession of certain people, and that places are commended not by the monuments of God's servants, but by the purity of doctrine, true religion, and piety of those who worship in them.

units.la: Caeterum vt magis eos conuincat, opponit ipsorum contumaciae suam bonitatem, qua cum illa nequicquam quasi lustratus sit, & ista collatione scelus illorum amplificat: Quoties volui (inquit) congregare liberos tuos, quemadmodum Gallina congregat pullos suos sub alas? & noluisti. Sen sus verborum est: Si ego in vestra salute curanda negligentior fuisse, posses o Ierusalem, aliquam excusationem afferre, & vel ignorantia vel quae hominibus fere communis est, stultitiam propriorum
units.tr: Moreover, in order to convict them more thoroughly, he sets against their obstinacy his own goodness, by which, as it were, he had cleansed himself in vain, and by this comparison he magnifies their guilt: "How often," he says, "would I have gathered your children, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings? And you would not." The sense of the words is this: if I had been negligent in caring for your salvation, you, O Jerusalem, could offer some excuse, either ignorance or that folly which is almost common to men, namely covering over the things they have chosen for themselves.

units.la: {Hac. 1} Ier. 7. placitorum prætexere. Sed cum ego nunquam defuerim officio, neque nunc demum incipiam, sed iam olim coeperim vos congregare, id est, ne instar aliarum gentium vagaremini, ad me recipere, vos autem mihi semper refiteritis, non habetis, quo vos excusetis. Ad expositionem loci huius faciunt quæ habentur apud Mosem: Mea quidem est omnis terra, sed vos eritis mihi peculium præ omnibus populis, ut sitis mihi regnum sacerdotale, et gens sancta. Et quæ in prophetis habetur: Duntaxat vos agnoni ex omnibus cognationibus terræ. Ite quæ Ezechiel prolixè commemorat de amore Dei quo sibi Iudæorum gentem, perdita plane et fœdissime corrupta ex gratuita misericordia desponsauerit. Nec teme re dicit, QVOTIES VOLVI congregare liberos tuos, &c. Nam omnis scriptura plena est testimoniorum gratia et bonitatis Dei, qua hanc gentem hic complexus est. Vt enim initio Abrahamu ex Chaldæa euocauit: deinde posteris in multiplicatis Mosem et per hunc legem et cultum externi ex ercitia dedit: ita nullum posteā fecului fuit, quo prophetæ illis defuerint, qui illos in officio cohinerent.
units.tr: {Hac. 1} Ier. 7. The hypocrites would pretend some excuse for their own ways. But since I have never failed in my duty, and am not now beginning to act, but have long since begun to gather you, that is, to receive you to myself so that you should not wander like the other nations, while you have always resisted me, you have no excuse. To the explanation of this passage belong the words in Moses: "All the earth is mine, but you shall be a peculiar treasure to me above all peoples, that you may be to me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation." Also what is said in the prophets: "You only have I known of all the families of the earth." Likewise what Ezekiel relates at length about the love of God, by which, from free mercy, he took to himself the nation of the Jews, which was utterly lost and most foully corrupted. Nor does he speak rashly when he says, "How often would I have gathered your children," and so on. For all Scripture is full of testimonies to the grace and goodness of God, by which he here embraces this nation. For as at the beginning he called Abraham out of Chaldea, and afterwards, when the descendants had multiplied, gave them Moses and through him the law and the outward exercises of worship, so there was never any age in which the prophets were lacking to them, to keep them in their duty.

units.la: Quia autem in Iudæis exemplum commune Deus proponere voluit, sua bonitatis qua genus humanum complectitur, simile hoc omnes sibi applicare debent, ut quæ omnium nostrum conditio sit, dicamus, quod item Dei in nobis tuendis et seruandis studium, quæ etiam plerorumque contumacia, quid ea mereatur, et quod eorum officium sit, qui serio salutis studio tenentur.
units.tr: Since God wished to set forth in the Jews a common example of his goodness, by which he embraces the human race, all men ought to apply this to themselves, so that we may say that this is the condition of all of us: that God is zealous in protecting and preserving us, and that many are obstinate, what such obstinacy deserves, and what the duty is of those who are seriously concerned for their salvation.

units.la: Pullus gallinarum homines conferuntur. At pullis nihil infirmius et imbellius est. Nam licet mox ex ouis exclusi discurrant, cibum aut escam quærentes, matris tamen cum ipsis quam maxime opus est, sine qua adolescere non possunt, nisi sub alis illius calescant perpetuo et foueantur. Adhæc miluos sibi infestos sentiunt, quos ex alto imminentes non facile effugere, multo minus autem eorundem viribus resistere possunt. Eadem plane est hominum conditio. Vires in nobis omnino nullæ sunt, quibus vel adolescamus, vel vitæ alimenta nobis paremus, vel nos ipsos tueamur, imo ne ad cogitandum quidem idonei sumus. Et nisi nos Deus sub umbra alarum suarum foueat, perimus, nec poterimus diaboli insidias effugere, qui rapacissimi miluij instar indesinenter nos petit, vel potius (ut Petrus Apostolus ait) ut leo rugiens oberrat, quærens quem deuoret. 1. Pet. 5.
units.tr: Human beings are compared to the chicks of hens. But nothing is weaker or more defenceless than chicks. For although, as soon as they are hatched from the eggs, they run about seeking food or feed, they still need the mother most of all with them, and without her they cannot grow, unless they are kept warm and cherished constantly under her wings. Besides, they feel the kites hostile to them, which hover from on high, and which they cannot easily escape, much less resist by their own strength. The condition of men is plainly the same. We have absolutely no powers by which we may grow up, or provide for ourselves the nourishment of life, or protect ourselves; we are not even fit to think. Unless God cherish us under the shadow of his wings, we perish, nor shall we be able to escape the snares of the devil, who like the most rapacious kite attacks us without ceasing, or rather (as the Apostle Peter says) "as a roaring lion walks about, seeking whom he may devour." 1 Pet. 5.

units.la: At non minus elucet hic Dei in nobis seruandis et educandis studium et pietas, quam gallinæ erga pullos suos. Hæc suo naturali calore pullos suos fouet, quo sola hoc illis præstat, quod nemo alius eis præstare poterat: Ita Deus sua bonitate et cura nos tuetur, et spiritu suo nobis confert, quæ nullis aliis viribus, nulla aliorum hominum industria conferri poterant. Idem nos alit verbo suo, quod nobis teneris adhuc et infirmis lactis loco, adultioribus solidus cibus, ægris vero præsens ad uersus omnes morbos medicina est. Vt item gallina pullos glocitanti voce, qua illis nihil suauius est, colligit: ita Deus nos colligit Verbo suo, quo electi in primis delectantur, et quo nihil iucundius et dulcius illis potest accidere. Et quod omnem admirationem superat, gallina cum nec ro-stro adunco, nec vnguibus rapacibus sit formidabilis, miluio tamen sese incredibili audacia opponens, pullos suos alis contra hunc et toto corpore protegit: ita Deus, quem sola propitiatio et gratia commendat et (ut Psaltes ait) facit ut timeatur, seipsum, id est, Filium suum vnigenitum pro nobis tradidit, ut huius immerenti morte peccata nostra expiaret, nosque ex diaboli tyrannide eriperet. Imo quod magis admirere, cum hic sit agnus ille, qui occisus ab origine mundi, nos ex lupi voracissimi faucibus, vel potius ex vnguibus immanissimi leonis vindicauit. Deniq; ut gallina gedum suum defraudat, ut sit quo pullos suos alat: ita Dei Filius e sinu Patris in terras descendere et in huius vitæ exilio euriem, sitim, nuditatem, infamiam, mortem deniq; subire voluit, ut nobis proficeret, non tam in præsenti quam futuro seculo.
units.tr: Yet the zeal and loving care of God in preserving and rearing us shines forth no less than that of the hen towards her chicks. The hen warms her chicks with her natural heat, which alone gives them what no one else could give them. So God, by his goodness and care, protects us, and imparts to us his Spirit, which could not be given by any other powers or by any industry of other men. He feeds us likewise with his Word, which, while we are still tender and weak, takes the place of milk; for the more mature it is solid food, and for the sick it is a ready medicine against all diseases. As the hen gathers her chicks with her clucking voice, than which nothing is sweeter to them, so God gathers us by his Word, in which the elect above all delight, and than which nothing more pleasant and sweet can happen to them. And what surpasses all wonder: the hen, though she is not fearsome with a hooked beak or with rapacious talons, nevertheless opposes herself to the kite with incredible boldness and protects her chicks with her wings and her whole body against it. So God, whom mere propitiation and grace commend, and who (as the Psalmist says) makes himself to be feared, gave up himself, that is, his only-begotten Son, for us, so that by his undeserved death he might expiate our sins and snatch us from the tyranny of the devil. Indeed, what is more wonderful, though he is that Lamb who was slain from the foundation of the world, he rescued us from the jaws of the most voracious wolf, or rather from the talons of the most savage lion. Finally, as the hen defrauds herself of food so that she may have something to feed her chicks, so the Son of God wished to descend from the bosom of the Father into the earth, and in this exile of life to undergo hunger, thirst, nakedness, infamy, and finally death, so that he might benefit us, not so much in the present age as in the future.

units.la: Sed quam contumaces et ingrati pleriq; homines sint, in Iudæis adumbratur, quorum contumacia et ingratitudo vno verbo exprimitur, cum illis dicit Christus: Et noluistis. Exprobrat eis, quod cum ipsius bonitate pugnarint, sine lusati sint, nec contenti excusasse oblatam ipsis gratiam Domini, destinata quoq; malitia eam noluerint admittere. Et quia illos noluisse dicit, no ob scure docet, causam perditionis ex ipsis esse, ut olim per Prophetam dixerat: Perditio ex te est o Israel, ex me autem salus tua. Quod si de causa quæras, quare ab ipso congregari noluerint, hanc reddi-mus, quia alia voluerunt, quæ ipsis chariora erant, de quibus in parabola de nuptijs dictum est. Alij enim pecora sua, alij prædia, alij nuptias suas vel voluptates carnis et alia studia sua regno Dei anteposuerunt. Et sane hoc reipsa declararunt, quando Filii Dei et postea huius seruos Apostolos alio
units.tr: But how stubborn and ungrateful most men are is foreshadowed in the Jews, whose obstinacy and ingratitude are expressed in one word, when Christ says to them: "and you would not." He reproaches them that, though they struggled against his goodness and were blinded by it, they were not content merely to make excuses; having also settled their malice, they would not admit the grace of the Lord offered to them. And because he says that they would not, he teaches obscurely that the cause of their destruction lies in themselves, as he had said long before through the prophet: "Destruction is from you, O Israel; your help is from me." But if you ask the reason why they would not be gathered by him, we answer that they wanted other things, which were dearer to them, of which it is said in the parable of the marriage feast. For some preferred their flocks, others their estates, others their marriages or pleasures of the flesh, and other pursuits, to the kingdom of God. And indeed they actually showed this, when they rejected the Son of God and afterwards his servants the Apostles, calling them elsewhere,

units.la: Exod. 19. Deut. 32. Amos 3. Ezech. 16.
units.tr: Exod. 19. Deut. 32. Amos 3. Ezech. 16.

units.la: Iudæi typus humani generis. alio vocantes reiecerunt, & quiduis potius quam caelestia amplexi sunt. Vnde apparet studium huius saeculi nos a caelestibus auellere, imo odium verbi parere, & ita causam praecipuam esse existij. Vt enim aegroto spem salutis nullam facere potes, qui medicum manibus repellit, & cuius stomachus crudus pharmaca omnia fastidit reijcit: nec bene sperare de filio contumaci, qui patris disciplinam admittere dedignatur: Ita fructus spem regni Dei facias ei, qui totus terrenis immersus, caelestia fastidit. Vtinam vero cum Iudaeis haec impietas sublata esset. At quid hodie vulgarius est? Plerique mundi studijs & carnis cupiditatibusediti, nihil praeterea curant: quae fere scelerum immanissimorum causa est. Dum enim (ut prophanus Poeta olim dicebat) trahit sua quenq; voluptas, & priuatis suis desiderijs omnes indulgent, fit iusto Dei iudicio, ut fides in terra rara sit, multiplicetur autem iniquitas & extinguetur charitas multorum, ut in sequenti Capite dicetur. Interim soli pro intolerabilibus habentur, qui ista arguunt ex Verbo Dei, & nisi ij essent non arbitrantur plerique aliquem fore, qui pacem & gaudia mundi interturbaret. Quae causa est, quod aliqui in illos hostiliter ferro & igne saeuiunt. Inter eos vero, qui Euangelicorum nomine & titulo gloriantur, non desunt, qui etsi doctrinam ipsam damnare non possint, ab ea tamen alieniores sunt, quod illam dissidiorum causam esse dicunt, quo vix quicquam ab illa alienum fingi poterat. Qui vero optimi habentur, ij Euangelij praecones contemnunt, ut phanaticos et non magni iudicij homines, ut hi idem dicere possint, quod olim in Apostolorum persona Paulus scribebat: Nos stulti propter Christum, vos autem prudentes in Christo, &c. At neminem ipsum offendat. Est hoc mundi infelicis ingenium: & hinc constat, negotium hoc omne ex Deo esse, non autem humanis consiliis gubernari. Beati, qui in fide IESV CHRISTI moriuntur: Non inultum autem ferent suam contumaciam impij.
units.tr: Jews, a type of the human race. and they rejected the calling and embraced anything rather than heavenly things. Whence it appears that the zeal for this age tears us away from heavenly things, and indeed breeds hatred of the Word, and so is the chief cause of unbelief. For as you cannot give any hope of health to a sick man who pushes away the physician with his hands, and whose raw stomach rejects and loathes all medicines, nor can you hope well of a stubborn son who disdains to accept his father's discipline, so you could hardly give hope of the kingdom of God to one who, wholly immersed in earthly things, loathes heavenly things. Would that this impiety had been removed from the Jews! But what is more common today? Most men, given over to worldly pursuits and the desires of the flesh, care for nothing else; and this is almost the chief cause of the most monstrous crimes. For while (as the profane poet once said) each man's pleasure draws him on, and all indulge their private desires, it comes about by the just judgment of God that faith is rare on earth, iniquity is multiplied, and the love of many grows cold, as will be said in the following chapter. Meanwhile only those are regarded as intolerable who denounce these things from the Word of God; and unless they existed, most men do not think there would be anyone to disturb peace and the joys of the world. This is the reason why some rage against them with sword and fire. Among those, however, who glory in the name and title of the Gospel, there are not lacking some who, although they cannot condemn the doctrine itself, are nevertheless more estranged from it, saying that it is the cause of dissensions, than which hardly anything more alien to it could be imagined. Those who are thought the best despise the heralds of the Gospel as fanatics and men of little judgment, so that they may say the same thing that Paul once wrote in the person of the Apostles: "We are fools for Christ's sake, but you are prudent in Christ," and so on. But let no one be offended by this. Such is the nature of the unhappy world; and hence it is clear that this whole matter is from God, and is not governed by human counsels. Blessed are those who die in the faith of Jesus Christ; the wicked, however, will not bear their obstinacy unpunished.

units.la: Sequitur enim poena, quam incurabilibus hypocritis minatur, & simul describit. Ecce, relinquitur vobis domus vestra deserta. Excidium denuntiat, quod in primis ad templum referri debet, de quo hic potissimum agi, ex sequenti Capite patebit. Emphasis autem subest vocabulis VESTRA & VOBIS: Nam perinde est, ac si dicat: Ego promiseram, me tabernaculum & domum meam inter vos constituere velle. At quia vos me non vultis admittere, age neq; ego inter vos habitabo. Itaq; domum hanc vobis relinquo desertam, ut ea ceu vestra fruamini. Itaq; doceamur hoc dicto, quid de cultibus arbitrarijs sentiri debeat, quos sine Verbo Dei ex seipsis instituunt homines. Non pro suis domibus neq; pro suo cultu agnoscit Dominus ea quae fiunt. Ideo apud Prophetas toties dicit: Quis ista requisiuit de manibus vestris? In praesenti addit: Dico vobis nequaquam me videbitis ab hoc tempore, usq; dum dicatis: Benedictus qui venit in nomine Domini. Ne gaterus omnem restitutionis spem. Quoad mundus hic durat, perpetua quoq; erit calamitas vestra, quae vos atteret. Cum vero mei illius aduentus gloriosi dies illuxerit, hunc quidem vobis laetum apparituram sperabitis, & ut hypocritae impudentes estis, tunc quoq; meo nomine gloriabimini, & in meo aduentu quasi exultabitis. At perpetuus, qui vos cruciabit calamitatum sensus, vos coget finem huius saeculi optare, ut qui meliorem conditionem vobis sit pariturus. Sed multu vos hac quoq; spes fallet. Videbitis enim me venientem in nubibus caeli, non quidem ut benedictum Domini, sed ut iudicem, quem impie & crudeliter transfixistis in cruce, & qui visus vos sceleris & impietatis conuictos ad sempiternos infernalium poenarum cruciatus damnabo. Discamus igitur ex tota Capitis huius tractatione omnem beatitatem praesentis & futuri saeculi in eo consistere, ut cum Deo vero per fidem in IESVM CRISTVM coniungamur, & in eo pullos imitemur: hi sine matre non possunt viuere, & ideo ad huius glocitantis vocem recurrunt, licet aliquando ab illa discesserint. Miluio imminente ad illius alas se recipiunt. Ita nos sine Christo sciamus salute nullam esse. Huic ergo confisi, ab eius voce pendeamus. Stulti & miseri, qui in nihilis praesidiis sperant & quaerunt. Faciebat hoc olim Achaz, cum a Syris & Israelitis bello graui peteretur. Nam spreto Dei auxilio, quod hic sponte offerebat, ad Tiglatphulazarem conuersus, Assyriorum opem implorauit, quae ipsi & posteris insidiosa fuit. Ad eundem lapidem offenderunt postea sub Ezechia Iudaei, foedere cum Aegyptijs facto, quo similiter falsi sunt. Idem factum, quando Babylonico bello imminente, Idumaeorum, Amonitarum, Moabitarum, Tyriorum & Sidoniorum societatem sibi necessariam putarunt, quae ipsis & vrbi excidium peperit. His exemplis admoniti instidiofam & exitialem sciamus esse Regum amicitia, qui hactenus in persequenda Ecclesia miluios & lupos egerunt, & ideo in uno IESV CHRISTO spe omni collocata, ad hunc unum confugiamus, & huic dicamus, Asylum meum, & arx mea tu es, sub umbra omnipotentis commorabor. Huic debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: The punishment that he threatens to the incorrigible hypocrites follows, and he describes it at the same time. "Behold, your house is left to you desolate." He announces destruction, which must be referred first of all to the temple, which is the main subject here, as will be clear from the following chapter. The emphasis lies in the words YOUR and TO YOU, for it is as if he said: "I had promised that I wished to set up my tabernacle and my house among you. But since you do not want to admit me, I will not dwell among you either. So I leave this house to you desolate, so that you may enjoy it as your own." Let us therefore learn from these words what should be thought of arbitrary forms of worship, which men devise for themselves without the Word of God. The Lord does not acknowledge as his own house or his own worship the things that men do. That is why in the Prophets he so often says: "Who has required these things at your hands?" In the present passage he adds: "I tell you, you shall by no means see me from this time until you say: Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord." Do not cut off every hope of restoration. As long as this world lasts, your calamity will also be perpetual and will wear you down. But when the day of that glorious coming of mine dawns, you will hope that it will appear joyful to you, and, shameless hypocrites that you are, you will then also boast in my name and exult, as it were, at my coming. But the lasting sense of calamity that torments you will force you to wish for the end of this age, in the hope that it will bring you a better condition. Yet this hope too will greatly deceive you. For you will see me coming in the clouds of heaven, not indeed as the blessed one of the Lord, but as judge, the one whom you impiously and cruelly pierced on the cross, and I will condemn you, convicted of crime and impiety, to the everlasting torments of the punishments of hell. Let us therefore learn from the whole treatment of this chapter that all blessedness in the present and future age consists in this, that we be joined through faith in JESUS CHRIST to the true God, and that we imitate chicks in him: they cannot live without the mother, and so they run back to the voice of this clucking hen, although they have sometimes strayed from her. When the kite threatens, they take refuge under her wings. So let us know that without Christ there is no salvation. Trusting in him, then, let us hang upon his voice. Foolish and wretched are those who hope and seek for help in nothing. Ahaz once did this, when he was hard pressed in a grievous war by the Syrians and the Israelites. For, rejecting the help of God, which here was offered freely, he turned to Tiglath-pileser and implored the aid of the Assyrians, which proved treacherous to him and to his descendants. Later, under Hezekiah, the Jews stumbled over the same stone, when they made a covenant with the Egyptians, by which they were likewise deceived. The same thing happened when, with the Babylonian war impending, they thought an alliance with the Edomites, Ammonites, Moabites, Tyrians and Sidonians was necessary for them, and this brought destruction upon them and upon the city. Warned by these examples, let us know that the friendship of kings is treacherous and deadly, since they have hitherto acted like kites and wolves in persecuting the Church, and therefore, with all hope placed in the one Jesus Christ alone, let us flee to him alone, and let us say to him, "You are my refuge," and "my fortress," I will abide under the shadow of the Almighty. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen.

units.la: CAPUT XXIIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER 24.

units.la: HOMILIA CCLXXIIII.
units.tr: HOMILY 274.

units.la: ET egressus IESUS e templo abibat: & accesserunt discipuli eius ut ostentarent ei aedificia templi. IESUS autem dixit eis: Nonne videtis haec omnia? Amen dico vobis, Non relinquetur hic lapis super lapidem. Sedente autem eo in monte olearum, adierunt eum discipuli privatim, dicentes: Dic nobis, quando haec erunt? & quod erit signum adventus tui, & consummationis seculi?
units.tr: Jesus went out from the temple and was on his way when his disciples came up to show him the buildings of the temple. But Jesus said to them: "Do you not see all these things? Truly I tell you, not one stone here will be left upon another." As he sat on the Mount of Olives, the disciples came to him privately and said: "Tell us, when will these things be? And what will be the sign of your coming and of the end of the age?"

units.la: IESUS olim Iudaeis templum & in hoc cultum externum dederat, ut per hunc in fide promissionum de Messia, id est IESV CHRISTO confirmarentur. Ideo Paulus Legem paedagogum dicit, per quem ad Christum deduci debuerint. Sed in ea elucet humani ingenii praucitas, quod quo illustrior fuit cultus ille, eo magis ipsi huic addicti Christum neglexerunt: & olim Prophetas hoc nomine hoc[?] liter persecuti sunt, quod docerent ceremonias inutiles esse, nisi omnem salutis fiduciam in Filio Dei IESV CHRISTO, promisso redemptore, haberent collocatam. Quae causa est, quod Prophetae veteres de cultus illius abrogatione & templi quoque excidio vaticinati sunt, ne ex eo sibi ipsis impunitatem pollicendo, templum in speluncam latronum converterent. Idem fecit ipse Christus, cum videret posteros patrum vestigiis insistere, adeoque horum mensuram (ut nuper audiuimus) implere. Et huc etiam referri debet totum hoc Caput, in quo primum de urbis Ierosolymae, & in primis templi excidio horribili disserit. Et hinc sumpta occasione de nouissimo suo adiudicium aduentu, & huius seculi consummatione vaticinatur. Multa autem hic audiemus, quae nostrae institutioni & consolationi seruient. Docet enim Iudaeorum exemplum, quid Christi & gratia Dei, cuius hic Mediator est, contemptores maneat. Deinde aduersus impostores, qui Christi nomen praetexunt, ad simplices seducendum, nos instruit. Praeterea consolationibus dulcissimis nos confirmat aduersus omnis generis scandala, quae tunc multos in fide labefactabunt.
units.tr: Jesus had once given the Jews the temple and its external worship, so that through them they would be confirmed in faith in the promises about the Messiah, that is, in Jesus Christ. For this reason Paul calls the Law our schoolmaster, by which they ought to have been led to Christ. But in this the wickedness of the human mind shows itself: the more splendid that worship was, the more those who were devoted to it neglected Christ. Long ago they persecuted the prophets on this very account, because the prophets taught that the ceremonies were useless unless all trust in salvation were placed in the Son of God, Jesus Christ, the promised Redeemer. This is why the ancient prophets foretold the abolition of that worship and the destruction of the temple too, lest the people, promising themselves impunity from it, turn the temple into a den of robbers. Christ himself did the same when he saw the descendants following in the footsteps of their fathers and so filling up (as we have recently heard) the measure of them. This whole chapter must also be referred to this purpose. In it he first discourses on the destruction of Jerusalem and above all the terrible destruction of the temple. Taking occasion from this, he then prophesies about his final coming to judgment and the end of this age. We shall hear many things here that serve our instruction and comfort. For the example of the Jews teaches what remains for those who despise Christ and the grace of God, of which he is the Mediator. Then he instructs us against impostors who put forward the name of Christ in order to seduce the simple. Moreover, he strengthens us with the sweetest consolations against every kind of scandal that will then cause many to fall away in faith.

units.la: Occasionem toti tractationi discipuli dederunt, qui hanc acceperunt ex iis, quae hucusque a Christo & facta & dicta sunt. Hic etenim, cum ex monte olearum urbem in conspectu haberet, & asinae pullo insidens populi acclamationibus celebraretur, illacrymauit dicens: Si vel tu noisses, vel hoc saltem tuo die, quae ad pacem tuam pertinent. Sed ea nunc occulta sunt oculis tuis. Nam veniet tempus super te, quo circumiicient tibi inimici tui vallum, & circumcingent te & constringent undique: et solo aequabunt & filios tuos intus, nec relinquent in te lapidem super lapidem: eo quod non noueris tempus illud visitationis tuae. Nuper autem cum possent vanas concertationes in apertam contentionem cum Scribis & Pharisaeis venissent, in qua hos propter errores & vitia intolerabilia exitio devouit, tandem excidium urbi & templo denuntiauit, eo quod iam saeculis aliquot Prophetas lapidauerint, & ad se missos Dei seruos crudeliter trucidarint. Ideo (inquit) relinquetur vobis domus vestra deserta. Et simul addita commina-tione, quod ipsum non amplius visuri sint, ex templo & urbe egreditur, ut qui indignabundus ab illis discedit, quibus irascitur. Obseruarunt hoc haud dubie Apostoli, & mirati sunt acrimoniam qua in Iudaeis corripiendis usus erat, & excidium quod illis denuntiarat: & doluit eis urbs & templi destructio, cum huius structura vix totus Oriens aliquid pulchrius & magnificentius haberet. In solo templo enim aedificando Herodem decem millia operariorum octo annis continuis in opere habuisse scribit Iosephus Antiquitatum libro decimoquinto, Capite 14. Quibus si addas, quae libro sexto de bello Iudaico Capite sexto leguntur, non ad ornatum modo, & magnificentiam, verum etiam ad defensionem extrui sum fuisse intelligés. Peregrinationes autem illud fiebant, non solum ex tota Iudaea, & a Iudaeis, verumetiam ex diuersissimis totius orbis locis, sicuti ex libro Actorum apparet, quo non modo ex remotissimis Aphricae regionibus, sed etiam ex Aethiopia vir princeps & summus regni Aethiopici thesaurarius, Ierosolymam ad adorandum venisse scribitur: qui etsi ipse non Iudaeus esset, nec proselytus, Ierosolymam tamen venit, ubi verum Deum, caeli & terrae creatorem, coli & adorari audierat, quod sibi patrijs superstitionibus, quibus innutritus erat, haud tenus nequaquam satis factum esse sentiret. At quia Lex prohibebat aliquem vacuum venire in conspectum Domini, quis dubitet, eos qui ex longinquo veniebant, omnis generis donaria magnifica attulisse. Ideo apud Lucam discipuli Christo non solum templi structuram, verum etiam donaria commendant, quibus ornatum erat. Itaque admirabundi monstrant Domino ista, & fortasse ipsum quoque a minis & correptionibus, quas ex illo audierant, ad laetiorem tanti aedificij contemplationem revocare volunt, ut hac vita sententiam mutet. Et haud dubie perculit animos illorum grauis illa comminatio, quod exiisse marent, nec possibile nec aequum esse, locum tam probe munitum, & a tam multis honoratum subito euerti, cultum tam magnificum aboleri, promissiones tam laetas & salutares irritas fieri: & haec quidem omnia Christo Iesu cedere, qui plerisque contemptus & inglorius putabatur, multis etiam inuisus & exosus erat.
units.tr: The disciples gave occasion for the whole discourse, having taken it from what Christ had hitherto both done and said. For here, when he saw the city from the Mount of Olives, and was being celebrated with the acclamations of the people as he rode on a colt of an ass, he wept, saying: "If you had known, even you, at least on this your day, the things that belong to your peace! But now they are hidden from your eyes. For the days will come upon you when your enemies will throw up a rampart around you, surround you and hem you in on every side, and will level you to the ground and your children within you, and they will not leave in you one stone upon another, because you did not recognize the time of your visitation." Recently, when the idle disputes had come to open contention with the scribes and Pharisees, in which he doomed them to destruction on account of their errors and intolerable vices, he at last announced the destruction of the city and the temple, because for several centuries they had stoned the prophets and cruelly slaughtered the servants of God sent to them. "Therefore," he says, "your house will be left to you desolate." At the same time, adding the threat that they would no longer see him, he went out from the temple and the city, as one who, indignant, departs from those with whom he is angry. The apostles undoubtedly observed this and marvelled at the sharpness with which he had rebuked the Jews and at the destruction he had threatened them with. The destruction of the city and the temple grieved them, since almost the whole East had nothing more beautiful and magnificent than this structure. For Josephus writes, in the fifteenth book of the Antiquities, chapter 14, that Herod kept ten thousand workmen at work for eight continuous years on the building of the temple alone. If you add to these what is read in the sixth book of the Jewish War, chapter 6, you will understand that it was built not only for ornament and magnificence but also for defence. Pilgrimages to it were made not only from all Judaea and by Jews, but also from very many places throughout the world, as appears from the book of Acts, where it is written that a prince and chief treasurer of the kingdom of Ethiopia came to Jerusalem to worship, from the most remote regions of Africa. Although he was not himself a Jew or a proselyte, he came to Jerusalem because he had heard that the true God, creator of heaven and earth, was worshipped and adored there, since he perceived that his ancestral superstitions, in which he had been brought up, did not satisfy him at all. But because the Law forbade anyone to come before the face of the Lord empty-handed, who can doubt that those who came from afar brought magnificent gifts of every kind? So in Luke the disciples commend to Christ not only the structure of the temple but also the gifts with which it was adorned. Thus, marvelling, they show these things to the Lord, and perhaps they also wish to call him back from the threats and rebukes they had heard from him to a happier contemplation of so great a building, so that he might change his mind about this life. And that grave threat undoubtedly struck their minds, that they thought it neither possible nor fair that a place so well fortified and honoured by so many should suddenly be overthrown, that so magnificent a worship should be abolished, and that such joyful and saving promises should be made void. And they thought that all of this would yield to Jesus Christ, who was regarded by most as contemptible and inglorious, and was even hated and detested by many.

units.la: Est hoc memorabile caecitatis humani ingenij exemplum, cui vel huius saeculi splendor, vel superstitio tenebras aliquas offudit. Saepius discipulis suis audientibus quaestus fuit de cultus diuini prophanatione, & adulterata Legis doctrina Christus Dominus, & nuper nefarios & horribiles abusus Scribis & Pharisaeis ita exprobrauerat, ut hos nemo negare, multo minus defendere posset. Neque nouum aut insolens videri poterat, templo excidium minari, cum idem iam olim veteres Prophetae fecissent, quidam etiam hoc nomine trucidati essent. Adhuc tamen admirantur & obstupescunt, quasi nihil huius dictum vel auditum sit vnquam: & ideo quod dicerat, impossibile & absurdum atque iniquum arbitrantur. Atqui plus admirationis & stupo- ris merebatur, verum Dei cultum & sanam Legis doctrinam ita euerti & depravari potuisse in ea gente, quam Deus sibi ex omnibus totius terrae populis in peculium delegerat, & de quo olim dixerat: Notus in Iehuda Deus, magnum nomen eius in Israele. Item, duntaxat populus sapiens & intelligens est gens haec magna. Quae enim gens huic similis est, quae habeat Deum sic sibi amicum & familiarem? Itaque satius erat templum totum cum cultu intercidere, quam religionem & Legis doctrinam perire & prophanari inter hos, quos huius quasi custodes aut depositorios Deus fecerat. Atqui non ignorabant, Solomonicum templum iam olim solo aequatum totis annis septuaginta in ruinis iacuisse. Cur ergo incredibile videatur Herodianam hanc domum interire, quae propter cades & incestus iam pridem meruerat, ut tota funditus interiret? Similis est illorum dementia, quibus indignum videtur, Papatum & ordines Monasticos cum cultu illo theatrico aboleri, cuius ne minima quidem pars ex Scripturis probari aut defendi potest: cum interim ijsdem nulla religio est Dei Verbo obloqui, quo loquente (ut Isaias ait) caeli & terra debebant obmutescere. Et cur his animarum decipulis parceretur, si sacra diminutis instituta abrogata & dissipata sunt olim, quando eis homines impij & superstitiosi turpiter abusi sint? Non possum hic non meminisse fenis cuiusdam religiosi quidem, sed quem totum superstitione a mente alienarat. Hic cum aliquando suorum operum bonorum, in primis autem peregrinationum, quas ad Diuum Iacobum Compostellanum, Mariam Aquensem, Lauretanam, Sepulchrum Domini, quod Ierosolymis vsitur, bicornem deniq; montis Sinai verticem, qui Diuae Catharinae nomine celebratur, merita enumeraret, & his ceu firmissimis & indubitatis salutis praesidijs niteretur, quidam autem eius superstitiones argumentis solidis confutaret, quibus nullo modo contradicere poterat, respondit: Videntur quidem alicuius momenti esse, quae tu affers: at si ea admittam, inutilis & superuacaneas mihi euanuerit omnis iste labor, quem in peragendis terra marique, longinquis regionibus exhausit. O stupidum hominem & nullius cerebri, qui no vidit satius esse & religiosius, ut centena millia stultorum Hierosolymam priuato cofilio excurrerint quàm vt Vnigenitus Dei Filius, qui ipsissima est Dei Patris Sapientia ex æterno Patris decrēto frustra in terris descendisse, & homo factus indignam & infamem mortem in ara crucis subijs- se dicatur, vt pro nostris delictis perlitaret? Nec multò acutius sapiunt, quibus indignum videtur, Cœnobia Monachorum, eorundem impurum cœlibatum, idolia, multo oleo & se- uo fœtentes lucernas, ex lignis & luto formatas statuas, & alia huius generis sordes e medio tolli, quàm vt hæc cogantur Filio Dei IESV CHRISTO cedere, qui nos in viua Dei tem- pla consecrauit, quiq; Dei imaginem in nobis olim collapsam fui sanguinis merito instaurauit, quiq; Lux mundi & Sol iustitiæ est, qui nisi nobis affulgeat, nobis in tenebris percundum e- rit. Imò quàm multos inuenies, qui vt fœditates istas defendant, non verebuntur homines Christianos iugulare, & in his Dei Filium spoliare, fame & siti affligere. Atqui vnius animæ iactura pretiosior est omnibus monasterijs, imaginibus & altaribus, quotquot sub cœlo sunt. Etenim non in templis manu hominum factis habitat Deus, vt Diuus Stephanus ex Ifaia an- notauit. Hæc ergo potius agamus, vt quæ simplicium animos & oculos offendunt, e medio tol- lantur, quàm vt ijs parcatur, quæ suo ornatu corporibus nocent, & animorum saluti incommo- dant.
units.tr: This is a memorable example of the blindness of the human mind, which either the splendour of this age or superstition has clouded with some shadows. Christ the Lord had often complained in the hearing of his disciples about the profanation of the divine worship and the corruption of the doctrine of the Law, and had so sharply rebuked the scribes and Pharisees for their recent nefarious and horrible abuses that no one could deny them, much less defend them. Nor could it seem new or strange to threaten the temple with destruction, since the ancient prophets had already done the same, and some had even been slain on this very account. Yet still they marvel and are astonished, as if nothing of this had ever been said or heard; and so they judge what he had said to be impossible, absurd and unjust. Yet they deserved more wonder and astonishment that the true worship of God and the sound doctrine of the Law could be so overturned and corrupted among that nation which God had chosen for himself as his own peculiar people out of all the peoples of the earth, and of which he had once said: "God is known in Judah, his name is great in Israel." Likewise: "Surely this great nation is a wise and understanding people." For what other nation is like this, that has God so friendly and familiar to itself? Therefore it would have been better for the whole temple with its worship to perish than for religion and the doctrine of the Law to be lost and profaned among those whom God had made, as it were, their guardians and keepers. Yet they were not ignorant that Solomon's temple had long before been levelled to the ground and had lain in ruins for seventy years. Why, then, should it seem incredible that this house of Herod should perish, which on account of its slaughters and incest had long since deserved to be utterly destroyed? The folly of those is similar who think it unworthy that the papacy and the monastic orders should be abolished along with that theatrical worship, not even the smallest part of which can be proved or defended from the Scriptures; while at the same time these men have no scruple about speaking against the Word of God, at whose speaking (as Isaiah says) heaven and earth ought to be struck dumb. And why should these snares for souls be spared, when the sacred institutions of God, though diminished, were once abolished and scattered, since wicked and superstitious men have shamefully abused them? I cannot help but recall a certain religious man, though one whose mind was wholly estranged from true religion by superstition. When he was once listing his good works, above all the pilgrimages he had made to Saint James of Compostela, to Mary of Aachen, to Loreto, to the Sepulchre of the Lord which is visited at Jerusalem, and finally to the two-peaked summit of Mount Sinai which is celebrated under the name of Saint Catherine, and was resting on these as the firmest and most certain safeguards of salvation, another man refuted his superstitions with solid arguments, which he could in no way contradict. He replied: "What you bring forward seems indeed to be of some importance; but if I admit it, all that labour which I have expended in undertaking journeys by land and sea to distant regions will be rendered useless and vain for me." O stupid man, of no sense, who did not see that it would be better and more devout for a hundred thousand fools to run to Jerusalem at their own private counsel, than for the Only-begotten Son of God, who is the very Wisdom of God the Father, to be said to have come down to earth in vain by the eternal decree of the Father, and, made man, to have undergone an unworthy and infamous death on the altar of the cross, so as to make atonement for our sins! Nor do those judge much more shrewdly who think it unworthy that the monastic houses of the monks, their impure celibacy, idols, lamps stinking of much oil and of smoke, statues formed of wood and clay, and other filth of this kind, should be removed from the midst, rather than that all these things should be compelled to yield to the Son of God, Jesus Christ, who has consecrated us as living temples of God, who in his own blood restored the image of God in us that had once fallen, who is the Light of the world and the Sun of righteousness, and without whose shining upon us we shall perish in darkness. Indeed, how many will you find who, to defend these foulnesses, would not hesitate to cut the throats of Christians and in them despoil the Son of God, afflicting him with hunger and thirst! Yet the loss of a single soul is more precious than all the monasteries, images and altars under heaven. For God does not dwell in temples made by human hands, as Saint Stephen noted from Isaiah. Let us therefore rather do this: let those things that offend the minds and eyes of the simple be removed from the midst, rather than spare those things which harm bodies by their ornament and hinder the salvation of souls.

units.la: At quod de ijs dicitur quæ religionis specie commendantur, ad ea quoque transferri debent, quæ sumptu & splendore externo commendantur. Etenim multos est inuenire, qui omnem lu- xum & sastum extusant eo potissimum argumento, quòd iniquum sit ea aboleri, quæ ornatu & magnificentia sua oculos spectantium pascunt. Sic superbæ palatiorum structuræ, sic nimius sup- pelleētilis apparatus, sic vestium luxus defenditur. At nulla ratio est, quæ ista in Dei conspectu absoluat aut tueatur, dileēto illo discipulo clamante: Ne diligite mundum, neque ea quæ in mun- do sunt. Nam quicquid est in mundo, cupiditas carnis, libido oculorum & sastus vitæ, non est ex Patre, sed ex mundo est. Porrò mundus præterit & cupiditas eius: Qui verò præstat volun- tatem Dei manet in æternum. Sunt ergo nimium imprudentes, quos huius mundi splendor ita ine- scat, vt animum nò possint ad cœlum attollere: vel tam confidentes reddit, vt Dei minas, quibus hic superbos terret, contemnant. Hæc potissimum præcipua omnibus cura sit, vt Deo obediant, & sub huius potenti manu humilientur.
units.tr: But what is said of those things that are commended under the appearance of religion should also be applied to those things that are commended by expense and external splendour. Many people are found who denounce all luxury and extravagance, chiefly on the argument that it is unfair to abolish things that feed the eyes of onlookers with their ornament and magnificence. In this way the proud construction of palaces, the excessive display of household furnishings and the luxury of clothing are defended. But there is no reason that can acquit or protect these things in the sight of God, since that beloved disciple cries out: "Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world. For whatever is in the world, the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes and the pride of life, is not of the Father but of the world. And the world passes away, and its lust; but he who does the will of God abides for ever" (1 John 2). They are therefore exceedingly foolish whose minds are so dazzled by the splendour of this world that they cannot raise their spirits to heaven, or who become so confident that they despise the threats of God, by which he terrifies the proud. This should above all be the chief concern of everyone: to obey God and to be humbled under his mighty hand.

units.la: Sed Dominum Christum audiamus, qui sultam & superstitiosam templi & cultus externi ad miratio̅nem grauissimè confutat. Nam ipse quoq; discipulos quasi in rem præsentem adducens, in- terrogat: Videtis ne (inquit) hæc omnia? Et mox cum graui asseueratione subiicit. Amen dico vobis, Non relinquetur vobis hic lapis super lapidem. Cœpit huius sententiæ executio intra annos a morte aut Ascensione eius trigesimo ostauo: & tam seuera fuit & feria, vt post destructos vr- bis & templi Ierosolymitani muros, nemo illos instaurare & rursus extruere potuerit. Nam ve alibi annotauimus, primo quidem sub Ælio Adriano Iudæi, duce Barcochaba patriam vrbem in staurare & terram reparare conati sunt, anno nati Christi CXXXIIII. deinde rursus sub Con- stantio anno CCCLVIII. & tandem regnante Iuliano Apostata sub annum CCCLXVII. Semper autem grauissimis cladibus repressi sunt, quæ illos ab incepto desistere coegerunt. Potissi- mum de prodigijs, quæ in postremo conatu horrenda & portentosa acciderunt, mira scribit Socra- tes Ecclesiastica historiæ libro 11. cap. XXXIII. Ex quibus discas, quàm graue sit cum Deo in certamen descendere, & aliquid tentare, quod Christi merito & regno deroget. Huius enim regnum surgere & crescere oportet, perire autem & subsidere quacunq; aduersus illum eriguntur.
units.tr: But let us hear the Lord Christ, who most gravely refutes the vain and superstitious admiration of the temple and external worship. For he too, bringing his disciples as if before the thing itself, asks: "Do you see all these things?" and straightway adds with solemn assurance: "Truly I say to you, there shall not be left here one stone upon another" (Matt. 24). The carrying out of this saying began within thirty-eight years of his death or Ascension, and it was so severe and so complete that, after the walls of the city and temple of Jerusalem were destroyed, no one could restore them and build them up again. For, as we have noted elsewhere, first under Aelius Hadrian the Jews, led by Barcochba, tried to restore their native city and repair the land, in the year 134 after the birth of Christ; then again under Constantius in the year 358; and finally under Julian the Apostate, about the year 367. Yet they were always checked by the most grievous disasters, which compelled them to abandon the undertaking. Socrates, in the eleventh book, chapter 33 of his Ecclesiastical History, writes wonderful things especially about the portents, dreadful and monstrous, that occurred in the last attempt. From these things you may learn how serious it is to enter into conflict with God and to attempt anything that detracts from the merit and kingdom of Christ. For his kingdom must rise and grow, while whatever is raised against him must perish and sink down.

units.la: Præstat autem non oscitanter considerare causas, propter quas Ierosolymam cum templo de- strui oportuit. Præcipua quidem fuit, quòd cùm tempus correctionis adesset (vt Paulus loqui- tur) & cultum Leuiticum e medio tolli necesse esset, Iudæi verò hunc pertinacius defenderent, a- deoq; Dei Filio cum Apostolis multum renitenti illum per Euangelij prædicationem demolien- ti sese hostiliter opponerent, nec rationes admitterent Apostolorum, qui vt Lex cum cultu Leui- tico honorificè quasi sepeliretur, seueritate maiori & rigore quodam vel vi opus fuit, vt Iudæi si- mul suæ impietatis pœnas darent, qua Apostolos quoq; persecuti sunt & Euangelii gentibus præ- dicare prohibuerūt. Voluit aut hoc exemplo docere Dominus, quid gratiæ suæ conteptores maneat qui huius mediatore IESVM CHRISTVM in sua veniente nolunt recipere. Est peccatū hoc nimium
units.tr: It is worth considering attentively the causes for which Jerusalem with its temple had to be destroyed.
