The chief cause was this: when the time of correction had come (as Paul speaks) and the Levitical worship had to be removed, the Jews defended it more obstinately, and they opposed hostilely the Son of God and the Apostles, who were striving to tear it down through the preaching of the gospel. They would not admit the arguments of the Apostles, who wished the Law to be honourably buried along with the Levitical worship. Therefore a greater severity and a certain rigour, even force, was needed, so that the Jews might at the same time pay the penalty for their impiety, by which they also persecuted the Apostles and forbade the preaching of the gospel to the Gentiles. The Lord wished by this example to teach what awaits those who despise his grace and who are unwilling to receive Jesus Christ, the mediator, when he comes in his own person. This sin is far too

units.tr: 1 Cor. 6. John 8. Matt. 4.

units.tr: Heb. 9.

units.la: 1.Thess.2. nimium vulgare nostro illo seculo. Etenim inuisit nos Deus per Euangelium suum, docet, monet, hortatur, corripit, consolationibus denique dulcissimis demulcet superstitionum laqueis irretitas & fatigatas multorum conscientias. At pauci sunt, qui tantum Dei beneficium agnoscant: sed plerique (quod olim Apostolus prædixit) sanam doctrinam auersantur, & huic manifestos erro- res præferendo, ab omni reformatione, non minus quàm a toxico abhorrent, & vt ab hac sese tu-tos præstent, pios Christi cultores ferro & igne persequuntur. Alij qui nondum ad tantam trucu-lentiam progressi sunt, disciplinam oderunt, & ne arguantur ipsorum errores & vitia, lucem re-ijciunt. Hic ergo nunc mundi infelicis mos regnat, quòd impune quidem peccare licet, scelera au-tem arguere aut corripere, tuto & impune non liceat. Plerique ergo qui Euangelium profiten-tur, ita viuunt, vt propter ipsos Euangelium & huius professio male audiat. Quid ergo aliud nos maneat, quàm quod istis euenit, qui postquam neq; ipsi scelera punire, neq; Verbi ministros illa cor-ripientes ferre voluerunt, lapides aduersus ipsos conitonari ceperunt, vt Christus Luca decimo nono eis minatur.
units.tr: 1 Thess. 2. common in our own age. For God has visited us through his gospel: he teaches, admonishes, exhorts, rebukes, and at last soothes with most sweet consolations the consciences of many who are entangled and wearied by the snares of superstition. Yet few acknowledge so great a benefit of God; but most (as the Apostle foretold long ago) turn away from sound doctrine, prefer manifest errors to it, and shrink from all reformation no less than from poison; and to keep themselves safe from it they persecute the pious worshippers of Christ with sword and fire. Others, who have not yet advanced to such savagery, hate discipline, and, lest their errors and vices be exposed, they reject the light. Thus now the custom of this unhappy world reigns: it is allowed to sin with impunity, but to denounce or rebuke wickedness is not allowed safely and with impunity. Therefore many who profess the gospel live in such a way that the gospel itself and its profession are ill spoken of on their account. What else then awaits us but what befell those who, since they were unwilling either to punish their own crimes or to bear the ministers of the Word who rebuked them, began to hurl stones at them, as Christ threatens them in Luke 19?

units.la: Quid vero his auditis discipuli? Vt prius, ita nunc quoque tam minaci sententia Christi graviter perculsi sunt. Ideo illo sedente in monte Olearum, quidam ex illorum numero prima-tim aut secretò illum amplius interrogarunt, quos Marcus fuisse scribit, Petrum & Ioannem, Iacobum & Andream, quos in aliis etiam actionibus Christo reliquis familiariores fuisse con-stat. Secreto autem siue priuatim illos ipsum accessisse dicitur, quod prudentiæ fuit. Nam, vt alibi diximus, tanta erat templi authoritas, vt minimè tutum esset aliquid aduersus illud dice-re, quod in ejus contemptum posset trahi, sicut in passionis dominicæ historia, aut in actione aduer-sus Stephanum ministituta apparet. Coniungunt autem quæstiones tres. Primam, Quando ista fieri oporteat, quæ dixerat, vt nimirum vrbs cum templo intereat? Alteram, quibus signis hora aduentus sui postremi cognosci aut deprehendi possit? Duabus hisce postremam addunt de consummatione seculi: quia impossibile videatur templum cadere, nisi sua ruina totum orbem con-cuteret.
units.tr: But what did the disciples do when they heard these things? As before, so now too they were gravely struck by this threatening saying of Christ. Therefore, as he sat on the Mount of Olives, some of them, first and privately, asked him further. Mark writes that they were Peter, John, James and Andrew, who are known to have been closer to Christ than the rest also in other events. It is said that they came to him in secret, or privately, which was a matter of prudence. For, as we have said elsewhere, the authority of the temple was so great that it was by no means safe to say anything against it that could be taken as contempt of it, as appears in the history of the Lord's passion, or in the proceedings against Stephen. They then join three questions. The first: when must these things happen that he had said, namely that the city with the temple would perish? The second: by what signs may the hour of his final coming be known or recognised? To these two they add a third, concerning the consummation of the age, since it seemed impossible for the temple to fall without the whole world being shaken by its ruin.

units.la: Est hoc quoque curiositatis humanæ exemplum, quæ plerunque nihil ad se pertinentia quærit: quæ causa est, quòd ex fidis admonitionibus occasiones arripit de inutilibus interro-gandi. Quæ obsecro ad discipulos vtilitas redire poterat, si momentum quoque, quo tem-plum destrui, aut mundus hic conflagrare & in nihilum resolui debet, cognouissent? Et quid ista cognitio nos hodie iuuare poterat? Sunt certè hæc ex eorum numero, quæ (vt alibi dicitur) Pa- ter in sua ipsius potestate posuit. Prodest potius scire, quid nos quoad in hisce terris vivimus, facere, & vt Deo seruire debeamus? quæ item consilia illa sint, quæ tuto sequi possimus, vt periculo-sas nouissimorum temporum vices, de quibus Dominus præmonuit, declinemus? Sed ad hunc lapidem hodie etiam multi offendunt, dum neglectis cognitu necessarijs circa inutilia occupantur. Multos autem curiositas ista, quæ infelici mundo quasi fatalis & quasi ex primis parentibus in-nata est, eò usque abripit, vt ad illicitas fatidicorum artes conuertantur, quibus nemo pius mul-tum tribuit. Nos in iis, quæ Deus nobis reuelare dignatur, illius bonitatem agnoscamus, & nos gratia, quam nobis offert, accom nodemus, vt quotidie in melius proficiamus in IESV CHRI-STO Domino & redemptore nostro, cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: This is also an example of human curiosity, which for the most part seeks things that have nothing to do with it; this is why it seizes on the occasions offered by faithful warnings to ask about useless matters. What profit, I beg you, could have come to the disciples if they had known the moment at which the temple was to be destroyed, or at which this world was to be set on fire and dissolved into nothing? And what could that knowledge help us today? Surely these things belong to those which (as is said elsewhere) the Father has placed in his own power. It is rather profitable to know what we ought to do while we live in this earth, and how we ought to serve God; and likewise which counsels are those that we may follow safely, so that we may avoid the perilous changes of the last times, of which the Lord gave warning. But many today still stumble over this stone, while, neglecting what must be known, they busy themselves with useless things. Moreover, that curiosity, which is in a sense fated for this unhappy world and innate from our first parents, drags many so far that they turn to the unlawful arts of fortune-tellers, on which no pious person places much value. Let us, in the things that God deigns to reveal to us, acknowledge his goodness, and let us make use of the grace that he offers us, so that we may advance daily towards the better in Jesus Christ our Lord and Redeemer, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCLXXV.
units.tr: Homily 275.

units.la: Et respondens IESVS dixit eis: Videte ne quis vos seducat. Multi enim venient in nomine meo, dicentes, Ego sum Christus: multosq; seducent. Futurum est autem, vt audiatis bella & rumores bellorum: Videte ne turbemini: Oportet enim omnia hæc fieri: sed nondum est finis. Insurget enim gens in gentem, & regnum in regnum: & erunt fames & pestilentiæ & terræmotus singulis locis. Hæc autem omnia principium sunt dolorum.
units.tr: And Jesus answering said to them: See that no one leads you astray. For many will come in my name, saying, I am the Christ, and they will lead many astray. But it will come to pass that you will hear of wars and rumours of wars; see that you are not troubled, for these things must happen, but the end is not yet. For nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom, and there will be famines and pestilences and earthquakes in various places. But all these things are the beginning of sorrows.

units.la: CAP. XXIIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER 24.

units.la: QVAMVIS discipuli reprehensionem grauem merentur propter quaestiones, quas de rebus futuris & nihil ad ipsos pertinentibus mouerunt, attamen IESVS CHRISTVS infirmitatis ipsorum rationem habet, & omissis iis, quae durius aduersus illos dici poterat, de illis agit quae illos scire & facere necesse erat. Est hoc magnum diuinae benitatis argumentum, quod nostrae curiositati indulgendo nos in Labyrinthos quaestionum inducat, eas quoque, quas nos temere mouemus, abrumpit, ut intra mediocritatis limites nos contineamus & circa ea sola occupemur, quae nos scire refert, & quorum scientia nos ad salutem aedificat. Exempla, quibus hoc demonstretur multa in Scripturis occurrunt, inter quae cumprimis memorabile est, quod in huius Cap. tractatione proponitur. Quaesierunt discipuli quando templum Ierosolymitanum destrui oporteat, & quae signa eius destructionem & totius mundi consummationem, quam simul cum illo concurrere putabant, praecessura sint. At Christus de signis quidem ea dicit, quae illos proderat scire, & de periculis quae cauere debeant admonet, inutilia autem & non necessaria cognitu, quae curiositatem humani ingenii augere & accendere poterant, confulto praeterit.
units.tr: Although the disciples deserve a severe rebuke for the questions they raised about future matters that have nothing to do with them, yet Jesus Christ takes account of their weakness. Leaving aside what could have been said more harshly against them, he deals with those things they needed to know and to do. This is a great proof of divine goodness: though he indulges our curiosity, he does not lead us into the labyrinths of questions, but cuts off even those questions we raise rashly, so that we keep ourselves within the limits of moderation and occupy ourselves only with those things it is useful for us to know, and by whose knowledge we are built up unto salvation. Many examples of this occur in Scripture, among which the one set out in the treatment of this chapter is especially memorable. The disciples asked when the temple at Jerusalem was to be destroyed, and what signs would precede its destruction and the consummation of the whole world, which they thought would coincide with it. But Christ speaks of those signs which it was useful for them to know, and warns them of the dangers they ought to guard against; but those things which were useless and unnecessary to know, and which could only increase and inflame the curiosity of the human mind, he deliberately passes over.

units.la: Propositio totius loci est: Videte ne quis vos seducat. Sensus est: Vos de templo quaeritis & quibus signis cognoscere debeatis, quando illius destructio fiue ruina inflet. At sunt alia maioris momenti, de quibus vos quaerere conueniebat. Quia enim templi admiratione fascinati in illo haeretis, periculum est, ne qui inde occasione arrepta vos seducant. Et ne temere de eo admonere videatur, periculum multiplex ceu digito monstrat, & ea occasione simul docet, quibus signis templi & vrbis excidium imminens agnoscere debeant. Primo multi venient (inquit) in nomine meo, dicentes: Ego sum Christus, multos seducent. Loquitur autem de impostoribus, qui sub religionis praetextu simpliciores decepturi sint. Et hos multos venturos ait, qui eo plus daturi sint, quod multos sint inventuri seductores, qui ipsos audiant, & promissum Messiam in ipsis exhiberi arbitrentur. At multos fuisse, qui id fecerint, historia testantur. Nam huc pertinet quod Gamaliel in Actis refert de Theuda, non quidem illo, cuius mentionem facit Iosephus libro 20. Antiq. cap. 2. (ut falso putauit Eusebius) sed alio qui post mortem Herodis Magni exortus est. Fuerunt autem multi alij, qui similia audacia idem tentarunt, inter quos ab eodem Gamaliele Iudas Galilaeus nominatur, & quibus merito accenseri debet Aegyptius ille, quem in rebus gestis Pauli Apostoli Tribunus cohortis dicit quatuor millia sicariorum in desertum eduxisse. Et quo propius instabat tempus illud fatale, quo de Iudaeorum gente propter immane scelus in Filium Dei commissum poena fumi debuit, eo plures exorti sunt, quos fere magicis praestigiis quoque simplici populo imposuisse, Iosephus scribit. Fuerunt autem sceleratissimi nebulones. Nam per hos factum est, ut Iudaei sub ementito Messiae nomine toties ludificati, tandem nomen quoque Messiae odisse coeperint, & Apostolorum praedicationem suspectam habuerint, quod hunc esse dicerent IESVM Mariae Virginis Filium. Denique illidum quotidianos motus in populo seditionis excitarunt, Romanis causas graues praebuerunt belli contra Iudaeos gerendi, quos exiguum tarunt satius esse simul excindi & dissipari, quam perpetuis bellis aduersus illos fatigari. Ita vero impletum fuit, quod Christus illis minatus fuerat. Ego veni nomine Patris mei, nec recipitis me: si venerit alius nomine suo, illum recipietis. Ioan. 5.
units.tr: The theme of the whole passage is: "Take heed that no one deceive you." The sense is this: you ask about the temple, and by what signs you may know when its destruction or ruin is about to come. But there are other matters of greater importance, about which you ought to have been asking. For since you are dazzled by admiration of the temple and fixed upon it, there is a danger that others, seizing the occasion from this, may deceive you. And lest he seem to give warning rashly about it, he points out the manifold danger as if with his finger, and at the same time teaches by what signs they ought to recognise the impending destruction of the temple and city. First, he says, many will come in my name, saying, "I am Christ," and they will deceive many. He speaks of impostors who, under the pretext of religion, would deceive the simpler folk. He says that many such will come, and they will be the more successful because they will find many deceivers to hear them and to think that the promised Messiah is present in them. That many did so is attested by history. For to this belongs what Gamaliel reports in the Acts concerning Theudas, not indeed that Theudas whom Josephus mentions in book 20 of the Antiquities, chapter 2 (as Eusebius wrongly thought), but another who arose after the death of Herod the Great. There were also many others who attempted the same audacious thing, among whom Gamaliel names Judas the Galilean, and to whom rightly belongs that Egyptian whom the tribune of the cohort in the acts of the Apostle Paul says led four thousand assassins into the desert. And the closer that fatal time drew near, when the nation of the Jews was to be punished for the monstrous crime committed against the Son of God, the more of them arose, whom, as Josephus writes, they deceived with almost magical tricks as well as with the common people. They were most wicked scoundrels. For through them it came about that the Jews, so often mocked under the false name of the Messiah, at last began to hate even the name of the Messiah, and regarded the preaching of the Apostles with suspicion, because they said that this Jesus was the son of the Virgin Mary. Finally, these men stirred up daily seditions among the people and gave the Romans serious grounds for waging war against the Jews, whom they judged it better to destroy and scatter together rather than to wear down with perpetual wars. And so was fulfilled what Christ had threatened them with: "I have come in my Father's name, and you do not receive me; if another comes in his own name, you will receive him." John 5.

units.la: Docet autem hoc exemplo Spiritus sanctus, quid contemptores IESV CHRISTI manebit: Nimirum, quod ab impostoribus excaecati, ipsis praeda fiunt, qui eos partim falsis & blandis promissis, partim minis ad terrorem confictis in exitium trahunt. Et hoc postremis temporibus euenturum esse, Apostoli praedixerunt. Paulus certe Timotheum praedicando instare & faniorem Euangelij doctrinam ferio vrgere iubet, eo quod quidam hanc non toleraturi sint, sed prurientes auribus ipsi sibi coaceruaturi doctores secundum cupiditates suas, ut aures a veritate auertant ad fabulas, quibus seducantur. Hanc item causam fore ait, propter quam efficacem deceptionem multis missurus sit Deus, ut Antichristo se propinent denorandos, qui dilectionem veritatis nolunt admittere. Id quomodo in Oriente impletum sit, historia testantur. Postquam enim simplex Euangelij doctrina hominibus acutis & ingeniosis, qui (ut Paulus de Graecis loquitur) hanc stultitiam putarunt, sordere coepit, in eius locum philosophiae studium succeßit, ex quo haereses enatae sunt, quae Mahumeti viam straverunt, qui tandem totum Orientem occupauit, & illic Turcae tantum ne tam negotij fecerunt: Imperatoribus, vt Occidente Gothis & aliis barbaris gentibus diripien dum permiserint. Itaq; Romam Pontifices sibi vendicarunt, & ibi constituto regno, hoc palam facere coeperunt, de quo in praesenti Dominus admonet. Se enim dixerunt esse IESV CHRI-STI vicarios: quod non aliud est, quàm ipsius Christi nomen & munus sibi vendicare. Etenim Christi munus circa sacerdotium & regnum versatur, & quia ipse Sacerdos & Rex aeternus est, vicarium nullum habet, neq; gloriam suam dat alteri. At sacerdotium nouum instituerunt Pontifices, in quo Dei Filius (vt ipsi garriunt) pro peccatis viuentium & mortuorum quotidie immoletur, & huius mystis, quos ipsi rasura & vnctione sua ad illud consecrant potestatem tribuunt re mittendi peccata, ipsi vero Leges quoq; mutant & tempora, dum coniugia prohibent, vel eorum libertatem nouis edictis astringunt, adhaec cibos a Deo creatos prohibent. Et ne infirma sit & ridicula Sacerdotij huius authoritas, hanc potestate quoq; regia armant, dum sibi tribuunt vtrunque gladium, spirituale m & temporalem, & sibi datam gloriantur omnem potestatem in coelo, & in terra, & in purgatorio, quod ipsi quoq; ceu tertiam partem mundi innenerunt, ex qua plus opum collegerunt, quàm Hispani vnquam ex Indijs suis nuper inuentis acquisierint. Deniq; adse pertinere dicunt totius mundi regna, vt ipsi reges costituere, & ex folijs suis pro libito detrahere, & regnis suis eijcere possint. Vt magis moueant & terreant incautos, qui ipsis aures praebent, coronam triplicem capiti suo imposuerunt, stemmatis autem loco inter insignia sua claues duas ostentant, quibus coelum se aperire & claudere posse dicunt quibuscunq; velint. Quis ergo dubitet, de illis intelligi debere, quod Dominus ait, venturos esse, qui se Christos esse dicant? Quid vero faciendum pijs, quos propria salutis cura solicitos habet, quando tales in Ecclesia si-bi omne imperium vendicare, & pastim in vrbibus prasidia sua, monachorum videlicet cohortes disponere, & per emissarios suos, legatos minimum a latere, orbem totum turbare videnr? Fallun tur hic multi, dum se extra culpam fore putant, si ipsi pia & sancti animi intentione simpliciter credant ijs, qui in Ecclesia prasident, & quorum authoritas regum & principum edictis confirmatur. Sed aliter Christus iubet. In prasenti enim clamat: Videte ne quis vos seducat. Et alibi monet: Si caecus caecos prasierit, ambo cadent in foueam. Oribus aut sunt, id est, electis hoc proprium esse ait, quòd suam modò vpsem audiant, alienam autem non sequantur. Quibus consentiunt, quae Apostoli monuerunt, vt ne cuius spiritui credamus, sed probemus spiritus, num ex Deo sint. Quae vt ro probationis regula esse debeat, alibi diximus, vt eadem hic repetere non sit opus. Itaq; nunc ad alia, quae Dominus pergit discipulos monere, transeamus.
units.tr: By this example the Holy Spirit teaches what awaits the despisers of Jesus Christ: namely, that, blinded by impostors, they become the prey of those who draw them to destruction, partly by false and flattering promises, partly by threats fabricated to terrify them. And the Apostles foretold that this would happen in the last times. Paul certainly bids Timothy to be instant in preaching and to press the sound doctrine of the Gospel, because some will not endure it, but, having itching ears, will heap up for themselves teachers according to their own lusts, so that they turn their ears away from the truth to fables by which they are led astray. He says also that this is the cause for which God will send upon many a powerful delusion, so that they are handed over to Antichrist to be devoured, because they are unwilling to admit the love of the truth. How this was fulfilled in the East, history attests. For after the simple doctrine of the Gospel began to be despised by clever and ingenious men, who (as Paul says of the Greeks) thought it foolishness, the study of philosophy took its place, and from this heresies sprang up which paved the way for Mahomet, who at last occupied the whole East, and there the Turks made so little trouble of it, while the emperors allowed the West to be plundered by the Goths and other barbarian peoples. And so the Pontiffs claimed Rome for themselves, and having established a kingdom there, began to do openly that of which the Lord now warns. For they said that they were the vicars of Jesus Christ; which is nothing other than claiming for themselves the very name and office of Christ himself. For the office of Christ is concerned with priesthood and kingdom, and since he is an eternal Priest and King, he has no vicar, nor does he give his glory to another. But the Pontiffs instituted a new priesthood, in which the Son of God (as they babble) is daily sacrificed for the sins of the living and the dead, and to the mystics whom they consecrate to it by their tonsure and anointing they grant the power of remitting sins; they themselves also change laws and times, while they forbid marriages or bind their freedom by new edicts, and moreover forbid foods created by God. And lest the authority of this priesthood be weak and ridiculous, they arm it also with royal power, while they claim for themselves both swords, the spiritual and the temporal, and boast that all power in heaven, on earth and in purgatory has been given to them; purgatory, which they have also discovered as a third part of the world, from which they have gathered more wealth than the Spaniards ever acquired from their recently discovered Indies. Finally they say that the kingdoms of the whole world pertain to them, so that they may set up kings themselves, and remove them from their thrones at will and cast them out of their kingdoms. In order to move and terrify the incautious who lend them their ears more, they have placed a triple crown upon their head, and in place of a coat of arms they display among their insignia two keys, by which they say they can open and shut heaven to whomsoever they wish. Who then would doubt that what the Lord says, that there will come those who say they are Christs, should be understood of them? But what should the pious do, whom anxiety for their own salvation troubles, when they see such men claiming for themselves all power in the Church, setting up their strongholds in the cities, namely cohorts of monks, and through their emissaries, legates a latere, throwing the whole world into turmoil? Many here are deceived, while they think they are free of blame if, with a pious and holy intention of mind, they simply believe those who preside in the Church, and whose authority is confirmed by the edicts of kings and princes. But Christ commands otherwise. For in the present passage he cries out: "Take heed that no one deceive you." And elsewhere he warns: "If the blind lead the blind, both will fall into the pit." He says it is the peculiar mark of the sheep, that is, the elect, that they hear only their own shepherd and do not follow another's. With this agree the things the Apostles warned, that we should not believe every spirit, but test the spirits, whether they are of God. What should be the rule of this testing, we have said elsewhere, so there is no need to repeat it here. So now let us pass on to the other things the Lord goes on to warn the disciples about.

units.la: Etenim ne qui putarent de religione modò contentiones fore ex sententiarum diuersitate ena scentes, quae facile & sine periculo componi possint, turbulentam & periculorum plenam totius mun di faciem siue conditionem, quae hinc sit secutura, praedicit. Et initio bellorum meminit, quibus ni-hil in hoc saeculo calamitosius & infeliciūs potest accidere. Futurum est (inquit) vt audiatis bella & rumores bellorum. Et paulo post horum causas indicat, addens: Insurget enim gens in gentem, & regnum in regnum: vt ostendat, non paucos modò fore, qui bellorum aleam subituri sint, sed hoc per totum orbe grassatura esse, & ita quidem, vt vix pacatis turbis aliquibus, nouae exoriantur alibi, aut false rumoribus nouis exterreantur, quispe meliorem pacis futura caperant animo concipere. At vbi bella feruent continua, ibi fames ex agrorum vastatione, & incolarum depraedatio nesequatur oportet. Huius comes ferè est pestilentia vel lues. Hae certè (vt alia omittamus) sub M. Ant. Philosopho ita seuijt, vt toti ferè exercitus Rom. peste periront. Quis vero terramo tus illic esse neget, vbi arma regnant? Caeterum hic sub terraemotibus prodigia omnia comprae-hendit, quae tunc futuras calamitates portenderunt. Haec vero vt fasta sint primum inter Iudaeos, donec bellum illud fatale exarsit, quo Ierofolyma cum templo euersa est, deinde in toto orbe, quan do post Neronis mortem Romani duces de Imperio inter se contenderunt, in Marco & Luca ne stro prolixè demonstrauimus.
units.tr: For fear that anyone might think that religious controversies would arise only from differences of opinion, which could easily and safely be settled, he foretells a turbulent world, full of dangers, and the condition of things that would follow from this. He mentions first the wars, than which nothing in this age can be more calamitous and unhappy. "You will hear," he says, "of wars and rumours of wars." And a little later he gives the causes of them, adding: "For nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom." He does this to show that there will not be only a few who must face the hazard of war, but that it will rage through the whole world, so that scarcely have some disturbances been calmed before new ones break out elsewhere, or men are frightened by false rumours, so that they cannot allow their minds to conceive better hopes of future peace. Where wars rage continually, famine must follow from the devastation of the fields and the plundering of the inhabitants. Pestilence or plague is almost always its companion. Certainly these (to pass over other things) raged under the philosopher Marcus Antoninus so fiercely that almost the whole Roman army perished of plague. Who would deny that there is earthquake where arms hold sway? Moreover, here he includes under earthquakes all the portents which foretold the calamities then to come. That these things came to pass, first among the Jews, until that fatal war broke out in which Jerusalem was overthrown with the temple, and then throughout the whole world, when after the death of Nero the Roman commanders contended with one another for the empire, we have demonstrated at length in our commentary on Mark and Luke.

units.la: Nunc autem obseruari debet, Christum de ijs, quae ante templi destructionem fieri debuerunt, ita disserere, vt eadem ad nouissima tempora etiam referri possint, quae huius saeculi consummatio nem praecedent, de quâ etiam interrogarunt discipuli. Nam etsi dies & hora, quando illa futura est, non possit cognosci, & hanc Deus nostro bono occultam esse velit, signa tamen prodest scire
units.tr: But now it must be observed that Christ, in speaking of the things which were to happen before the destruction of the temple, so speaks that the same things can also be referred to the last times, which will precede the consummation of this age, about which the disciples also asked. For although the day and hour when that will be cannot be known, and God wishes this to be hidden from us for our good, yet it is profitable to know the signs,

units.la: {y} Psal. 110. & Isa. 4. Matth. 15. Ioan. 10. & Luc. 4. Iero‑solymitanis nouissimis quo‑que temporibus seruiunt.
units.tr: Ps. 110; Isa. 4; Matt. 15; John 10; Luke 4. These also serve for the last times of Jerusalem.

units.la: CAP. XXIII.
units.tr: CHAP. XXIII.

units.la: & obseruare, quæ hanc præ foribus esse portendunt. Non temere autem fieri putabimus, quòd im- postoribus Antichristianis, hæc subtexit, quæ hic de bellis & bellorum rumoribus dicuntur. Ut enim belli Iudaici authores præcipui illi fuerunt (vt nuper diximus) ita perpetuum hoc esse, quòd vsq; ad finem seculi dissidia parient, quotquot Christi honorem vel sibi ipsis vendicando, vel in alios transferendo, Ecclesiam in sectas scindunt. Et alibi diximus, quid iam seculis aliquot Romani Pontifices fecerint, qui fere bellis inter Christianos Monarchas excitatis regnum suum stabiliuerunt. Nostri certè Annales testantur, Episcopos & legatos Roma aduentantes Heluetiæ nostræ semper inauspicatos fuisse. Idcirco hodie non absq; causa suspectæ habent Pontificum & præsulum consilia viri cordati & prudentes, quibus pax publica cordi est.
units.tr: and to observe those things which portend that it is at the doors. Nor shall we think it rashly done that he appends to these things what is said here about wars and rumours of wars, for the impostors of Antichrist. For just as the chief authors of the Jewish war were those men (as we said just now), so it is a perpetual thing that until the end of the age those who, either by claiming Christ's honour for themselves or by transferring it to others, split the Church into sects will produce dissensions. And we have said elsewhere what the Roman Pontiffs have done for some centuries past, who, by stirring up wars among Christian monarchs, have established their own kingdom. Our own annals certainly bear witness that bishops and legates coming from Rome have always been ill-omened to our Helvetia. Therefore, today, wise and prudent men, to whom public peace is dear, not without cause regard the counsels of the Pontiffs and prelates with suspicion.

units.la: Rursus autem Deus bonitatem suam hoc quoque argumento commendat, quòd vt bella & dissidia consummationis totius mundi præludia sunt, ita hæc quoq; prodigijs in cælo & aliis mundi partibus prænuntiat. Ierosolymæ certè & in Iudæa innumera acciderunt, quæ templi & legalis cultus abrogationem & totius gentis dissipationem imminere indicarunt. Et aliarum quoq; gentium historiæ testantur, verissimum esse quod Amos dicit, non oriri malum aliquod siue calamitatem, de qua Deus nos non præmoneat, vel per seruos suos Prophetas, vel signis, quæ præter naturæ ordinem fiunt. Vidit hoc Poeta gentilis, qui pastores de labefactato Reipub. Romanæ statu & ex hoc enatis calamitatibus colloquentes introducens, illos fateri scribit,
units.tr: Again, God commends his goodness by this argument also: just as wars and dissensions are the preludes to the consummation of the whole world, so he foretells these things too by portents in heaven and in other parts of the world. Certainly countless things happened in Jerusalem and in Judaea which indicated that the abrogation of the temple and the legal worship and the dispersion of the whole nation were impending. And the histories of other nations also testify that what Amos says is most true: no evil or calamity arises of which God does not forewarn us, either through his servants the prophets or by signs which occur beyond the order of nature. The pagan poet saw this, who, introducing shepherds conversing about the shaken state of the Roman commonwealth and the calamities arising from it, writes that they confess:

units.la: Sæpè malum hoc nobis, si mens non læua fuisset,
units.tr: Often this evil would have come upon us, had our mind not been perverse,

units.la: De cælo tactas nemini prædicere quercus.
units.tr: Oaks struck from heaven would have foretold it to no one.

units.la: Nec immeritò de mentis leuitate aut peruerso iudicio queruntur. Nam vt signa iftaDei nos ad monentis fidem & bonitatem paternam commendant: ita humani ingenij contumaciam arguunt, quæ vix vllis admonitionibus emollitur, vt Deo sese obsequentes præbeant.
units.tr: Nor do they complain without reason of the levity of their minds or of a perverse judgment. For just as those signs of God commend to us the faithfulness and paternal goodness of the one who warns, so they also prove the obstinacy of the human mind, which is hardly softened by any admonitions, so that men may show themselves obedient to God.

units.la: At non solùm de futuris admonet Dominus, sed & consilio quoque instruit discipulos, quod vt breue est, ita consolationem dulcem & efficacem completitur. Dicit enim, Videte ne turbemini. At quis non turbetur, si gentes passim in mutuum exitium insurgere, regna omnia tumultuari & orbem terrarum bellis ardere videat? Ab humanitatis sensu alienus, imo ferreus fuerit oportet, si quem ista non moueant. Sed & ipse Dominus, qui toto animo turbatus est, cum de mortis sua appropinquantis acerbitate cogitaret, ad vrbis conspersum fleuit, cum quid illi euenturum esset, animo versaretur.
units.tr: But the Lord does not warn only about future things; he also furnishes the disciples with counsel, which, though brief, completes a sweet and effective consolation. For he says: "See that you are not troubled." But who would not be troubled, if he saw the nations rising everywhere for mutual destruction, all kingdoms in tumult, and the earth burning with wars? He must be alien to human feeling, indeed iron, who is not moved by such things. But the Lord himself, who was troubled in his whole soul when he was pondering the bitterness of his approaching death, also wept over the city, when he was turning over in his mind what would happen to it.

units.la: Et quomodo horum consideratione conuertemur ferio ad Deum, si nos illis non moueamur? Sed ad Apostolos hoc dictum restringi debet, qui his non ita debuerunt turbari, vt mandatum ipsis prædicandi munus negligerent, aut præ metu in officio cessarent. Accidit hoc sæpe sanctis Dei seruis, qui interdum carnis infirmitate superantur, vt Mosis, Eliæ, Ieremiæ, Ionæ & aliorum exemplis docemur. Quia enim nobis bene esse volumus, non possumus non moueri, si quid acerbius nobis præter expectationem accidat. Sed ne tunc ex statione nostra deijciamur, animos obfirmare conuenit, vt abeneo muri stemus aduersus omnes fortunæ aut mundi insultus, & liceat fractus illabatur orbis, impauidos feriant ruinæ. Et sane consilij huius egregiè recordati fuerunt Apostoli, quando Sacerdotes & Seniores hominum idiotarum & illiteratorum inuictam constantiam admirati sunt. Similis fuit, viri Tigurini, maiorum nostrorum fortitudo, quando Euangelij prædicatione illustrati Pontificum & Monachorum impositas agnoscere cæperunt, & Deum illos monuit, vt oblatum libertatis animorum beneficium ampletarentur. Admiratus est tunc quæ mundus insuperabile illud animi robur, quo blanditiis, promissiones, minas & omnes aduersariorum conatus eluserunt. Nec defuit illis spiritus Domini, qui consilia eorum gubernauit, & reuera aureum & beatum dici potuit seculum illud, quo heroes illi in Ecclesia & Repub. floruerunt. Hos imitemur, nec pigeat sanctis virorum fortissimorum vestigijs insistere. Agricolæ, qui nubeculas omnes obseruant, & his visis tempestates sibijpsis præsagiunt, nunquam arant aut seminem faciunt, adeoq; seipsos sementę & messe spoliant. Ita qui ad omnes mundi huius motus tumbantur, ij semper inuenient, quod ipsos ab officio reuocet, & ita pulcherrimas promouendi regni Dei occasiones negligent, aut ex manibus elabi patientur, quas posthæa nequicquam cum lachrymis requirent.
units.tr: And how shall we be turned seriously to God by considering these things, if we are not moved by them? But this saying must be restricted to the apostles, who ought not to be so troubled by these things as to neglect the commission of preaching which they had been given, or to cease from their duty through fear. This happens often to the holy servants of God, who are sometimes overcome by the weakness of the flesh, as we are taught by the examples of Moses, Elijah, Jeremiah, Jonah and others. For since we wish well to ourselves, we cannot but be moved if anything more bitter than we expected happens to us. But that we may not then be cast down from our post, it is fitting to strengthen our minds, so that we may stand like a wall of bronze against all the assaults of fortune or of the world, and, though the broken world should fall, the ruins may strike us without fear. And indeed the apostles well remembered this counsel, when the priests and elders marvelled at the unconquered constancy of uneducated and unlettered men. Such, men of Zurich, was the fortitude of our forefathers, when, enlightened by the preaching of the gospel, they began to recognise the impositions of the Pontiffs and monks, and God warned them to lay hold of the offered benefit of liberty of soul. Then the world marvelled at that invincible strength of mind by which they mocked the flatteries, promises, threats and all the attempts of their adversaries. Nor did the Spirit of the Lord fail them, who guided their counsels, and indeed that age in which those heroes flourished in the Church and commonwealth may rightly be called golden and blessed. Let us imitate them, and let us not be ashamed to tread in the holy footsteps of the bravest men. Farmers who watch all the little clouds, and foretell storms for themselves from what they see, never plough or sow, and so they deprive themselves of sowing and harvest. So those who are tossed about by every movement of this world will always find something to call them back from their duty, and so they will neglect the most beautiful opportunities of advancing the kingdom of God, or allow them to slip from their hands, and afterwards they will seek them in vain with tears.

units.la: Caterùm quia carni durum est inter perpetua certamina non succumbere, aut saltem defatigari, tigari, vt animum despondeat, rationibus quoq; confirmat consilium quod dedit, atq; illis simul nos amplius consolatur. Primam a prouidentia Dei decreto petit, dicens: Oportet enim omnia haec fieri: quia ita Deus vult & statuit, quo aliquid decernente (vt Propheta ait) nemo illud impedire aut irritum facere poterit. At communis sensus docet, fortiter ferri debere, quod mutari aut euitari non potest. Et sane omnium certissima & efficacissima est consolatio, quae ex prouidentia Dei aranus aut sanctuario petitur. Nam nihil fortuito fieri, omnes Scripturae docent. Et quae stultitia effet putare, homini aliquid temere accidere, cum pilos capitis nostri numeratos esse, & nepaffer- culum quidem abfq; voluntate Patris nostri caelestis in terram cadere, Dominus tefletur? At sci mus illum iustum, & omnia eius iudicia iustitiam & veritatem esse. Et quia idem fidelis est, & homines vult saluos fieri, nemini iniuriam faciet, neq; nos supra vires tentari patietur. Haec qui recte considerant, hi fortes & animosi fiunt: cum e contra qui suis consiliis ducuntur, perpetuo fluent, nec possint quiescere, sed cum Dauid quiritentur: Quid deiecta es o anima mea, & intra me tumultuaris, &c? Pfal. 41. & 43.
units.tr: But because it is hard for the flesh not to give way amid perpetual conflicts, or at least to grow weary, so that the spirit is cast down, he also confirms by reasons the counsel he has given, and at the same time consoles us more. He seeks the first reason from the decree of God's providence, saying: "For these things must come to pass," because God so wills and decrees; and when he has decreed something (as the prophet says), no one can hinder it or make it void. Common sense teaches that what cannot be changed or avoided must be borne bravely. And indeed the most certain and effective of all consolations is that which is drawn from the providence of God, the safest refuge and sanctuary. For all the Scriptures teach that nothing happens by chance. And what folly it would be to think that anything happens to a man at random, when the Lord bears witness that the hairs of our head are numbered, and that not even a sparrow falls to the earth without the will of our heavenly Father? But we know that he is just, and that all his judgments are justice and truth. And since he is also faithful, and wishes men to be saved, he will do no one wrong, nor will he suffer us to be tempted beyond our strength. Those who consider these things rightly become brave and courageous; whereas those who are led by their own counsels are tossed about perpetually, and cannot be at rest, but with David complain: "Why are you cast down, O my soul, and why do you make tumult within me?" Ps. 41 and 43.

units.la: At ne putarent certamen breue fore, & propterea perpetuitate aut diuturnitate afflictionum offenderentur, addit: Sed nondum erit finis. Quasi diceret: Ne putetis vos labore omni defunctos esse, si vnam & alteram luctam fortiter sustinueritis. Etenim tota hominis Christiani vita, miliatia est super terram, nec in hominis arbitrio est, sibi ipsi ferias indicere. Et vt hoc magis confirmet, addit postremo: Haec autem omnia principiu sunt dolorum. Sensus est, adeo non debetis vobis otium & ferias polliceri, vt potius vos primum coepisse putetis, si ista omnia euenant, quae modo commemorauì. Verè autem hoc dixit quoad Iudaeos: quia enim incurabilis fuit eorum contumacia, & percusti quoq; non agnouerunt manum Domini, vt ad ipsum conuerterentur, mansit manus eius extensa perpetuo (sicut olim per Isaiam minatus erat) donec funditus excinderentur. Meminerimus autem hoc ipsum nobis quoque conuenire. Fiunt quidem quae nouissimis temporibus euentura esse, Dominus praedixit. Sauitur bello passim, & rumoribus bellorum omnia turbantur. Insurgit gens contra gentem, & simul intestinis motibus pleriq; periclitantur. Fames & fatalis egestas non vulgus modo hominum, sed viros principes & Reges premit. Quem enim dabis, qui ex ordinariis suis reddititbus statum suum tueri possit, si ab exactionibus extraordinariis sibi temperet? Recurrit subinde lues & pestilentia. Prodigiis diris & horrendis terremur. Verunta- men inter ista crescit impietas, fides deficit, charitas frigescit, & scelerum licentia indies longius progreditur. Inter eos vero qui meliores dici poterant, securitas regnat cum insatiabili illicitarum voluptatum studio, de quo infra fusius dicetur. Et dum ista vulgo fiunt, iniquius nobiscum agi putamus, si Deus diutius nos castiget. Et plerunque impatientius contra Deum murmurant homines, quibus verissime dici poterat: Nondum ad sanguinem vsque resistitis aduersus peccatum decertando, &c. Respiciamus ergo in IESVM CHRISTVM Dominum nostrum, vt ad hunc conuersi, ipsum imitemur, vt tandem omnibus malis superiores facti cum illo in caelis viuamus & regnemus, cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: But lest they think the struggle will be brief, and so be offended at the lasting or prolonged affliction, he adds: "But the end is not yet." As if he were saying: do not suppose that you are finished with all toil if you have bravely endured one or another wrestling bout. For the whole life of a Christian is a warfare upon the earth, nor is it in a man's power to declare a holiday for himself. And to confirm this all the more, he adds at last: "But all these things are the beginning of sorrows." The sense is that you must not promise yourselves leisure and rest; rather, you should think that you have only just begun, if all those things which I have just mentioned come to pass. He spoke truly in this regard concerning the Jews: since their obstinacy was incurable, and they, though struck, did not recognise the hand of the Lord so as to turn to him, his hand remained stretched out continually (as he had once threatened through Isaiah) until they were utterly rooted out. Let us remember, however, that this same thing applies to us as well. Indeed those things come to pass which the Lord foretold would happen in the last times. War rages everywhere, and all things are thrown into turmoil by rumours of wars. Nation rises against nation, and at the same time many are endangered by internal upheavals. Famine and deadly want oppress not only the common people but also princes and kings. For who will you find who could maintain his station from his ordinary revenues, if he refrains from extraordinary exactions? Plague and pestilence return from time to time. We are terrified by dreadful and horrible portents. Yet amid these things impiety grows, faith fails, charity grows cold, and the licence of crimes advances further day by day. Among those who could be called the better sort, security reigns together with an insatiable zeal for forbidden pleasures, about which more will be said at length below. And while these things happen commonly, we think we are being treated too unjustly if God chastises us for longer. And men often murmur against God more impatiently, to whom it could most truly be said: "You have not yet resisted unto blood, striving against sin," etc. Let us therefore look to Jesus Christ our Lord, so that, turning to him, we may imitate him, and at last, having become superior to all evils, live and reign with him in the heavens, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCLXXVI.
units.tr: HOMILY 276.

units.la: Tunc tradent vos afflictioni, & trucidabunt vos: & odio eritis omnibus gentibus propter nomen meum. Et tunc offendentur multi; & alius alium prodet, & odio habebit alius alium.
units.tr: "Then they will deliver you up to affliction, and will kill you, and you will be hated by all nations for my name's sake. And then many will be offended, and one will betray another, and one will hate another."

units.la: Interfigna, quae olim templi Ierofolymitani destructionem praecedere debuerunt, & hoc nouissimo seculo mundi finem praecessura sunt, de quibus discipuli Christum interrogarunt, primo loco recensuit impostores, qui falso Messiae titulo sese vendicaturi & multos seducturi sint. Deinde de seditionibus admonuit, ex quibus perpetua bella & bellorum rumores exorituri sint. Coniunxit his famem, pestilentiam & prodigia omnis generis, quibus Deus plerunq; homines securos & paenitere nescios praemonere & excitare vel terrere solet. Nunc ad ea accedit, quae potissimum ad ipsos discipulos pertinebant. Quia enim in Christo subinde regnum somniabant, ne se omnis periculis immunes fore & otio felici abundaturos putarent, necesse erat illos admoneri, quid sibi polliceri deberent: ut ad certamina crucis se praepararent, & consolationibus firmis atque solidis confirmarentur, nec inter turbas & pericula de Euangelij prospero successu dubitarent.
units.tr: The signs that were to precede the destruction of the Jerusalem temple, and that are to herald the end of this final age of the world, about which the disciples asked Christ, were recounted by him first of all: impostors who will claim for themselves the title of Messiah and will lead many astray. Next he warned of seditions, from which will arise continual wars and rumours of wars. To these he joined famine, pestilence and portents of every kind, by which God is accustomed to forewarn, rouse or terrify people who are generally secure and do not know how to repent. Now he comes to those things which pertained especially to the disciples themselves. For since they kept dreaming of a kingdom in Christ, and thought they would be free of all dangers and would abound in happy leisure, it was necessary that they be warned what they ought to expect, so that they might prepare themselves for the struggles of the cross, be strengthened with firm and solid consolations, and not doubt the prosperous success of the gospel amid tumults and dangers.

units.la: Et quia quae praevisa sunt, minus terrent aut laedunt, quid ipsis eventurum sit, diserte docet. Tunc tradent vos afflictioni. Apud Lucam ait: Ante haec omnia injicient vobis manus, & vos persequentur, &c. Quae ipsis, quae praecesserunt, ita cohaerent: Ne arbitremini vos inter laetos rerum successus & delicias otiosos spectatores fore calamitatum, quas alij sustinebunt. Tam enim hoc ab ipsis, ut potius a vobis initium fiat malorum, quibus mundum affligi oportebit. Tunc enim, quando ista debent fieri, vobis manus injicient, & erunt qui vos persequentur, & quidem ad mortem vsque. Nam trucidabunt vos. Et licet id non semper fiat, tamen inimici erunt omnibus gentibus: idque propter nomen meum. Et ne putent odium hoc leve & momentaneum fore, describit hoc ab effectis. Nam apud Lucam ait, Tradent vos in conventus, Ecclesiasticos nimirum, ut pote dignos in quorum religionem & doctrinam diligentius inquiratur. Deinde carceribus includent, & poenis quoque graviori bus multemini. Tertio, adducent ad regum & principum tribunalia.
units.tr: And because things foreseen frighten or harm less, he plainly teaches what will happen to them. "Then they will deliver you up to affliction." In Luke he says: "Before all these things they will lay hands on you and persecute you," and so on. What precedes and what follows coheres in this way: do not suppose that you will be idle spectators of the calamities that others will suffer, amid the joyful successes and delights of this world. For it is so that the evils with which the world must be afflicted begin with you rather than with others. For when these things are to happen, they will lay hands on you, and there will be those who persecute you, even to death. For they will kill you. And although this does not always happen, they will nevertheless be hostile to you, in all nations, and that on account of my name. And so that they may not think this hatred will be slight and momentary, he describes it from its effects. For in Luke he says: they will deliver you up to assemblies, namely ecclesiastical ones, as those who are worthy of being examined more closely concerning their religion and doctrine. Then they will shut you up in prisons and punish you with more severe penalties. Third, they will bring you before the tribunals of kings and princes.

units.la: Et hoc quidem Apostolis accidisse constat. Ut enim Christus, sicut Simeon ille senex beatus praedixerat, contradictionem sensit: ita Apostoli quoque quam primum praedicare coeperunt. Etenim illusores prophani auditi sunt, qui plerisque propter miraculum linguarum obstupescentibus, illos musto plenos dixerunt, & fraudulento ebrietatis vitio tribuerunt quod evidens & proprium erat Spiritus sancti opus. Mox Petrus & Ioannes, cum claudum ab utero matris miraculose in nomine IESV CHRISTI sanavissent, & populo huius miraculi novitate excitato Christum praedicarent, in carcerem abducti, & postea graviorem actionem publice contra illos institutam, non sine atrocibus minis dimissi sunt, ne posthac in nomine Christi praedicarent. Paulo post crescente numero credentium insurgit Pontifex maximus cum universa Sadducaeorum secta, quae tunc Hierosolymae dominabatur, & Apostolos simul omnes in eis manibus custodia publica mandant, & licet Angeli ministerio illos Deus liberet, & in templo docere iubeat, tamen iterum comprehensos, Concilio sistunt, & post longam & acrem disceptationem flagellatos graviter interdicunt, ne porro in nomine IESV loquantur. Dum vero ipsi, ut fidos Dei servos decet, in officio constanter pergunt, & inter alios Stephani fides sese exerit, quendam concitata plebe correptum ad Seniores abripiunt, & falsis testibus aduersus eum productis, per tumultum crudeliter lapidant. Quo facto mox publica & universalis persecutio exoritur, in qua maxime saevit Saulus, qui effrenatis foribus credentes utriusque sexus in vincula conjiciebat, & multos (ut ipse postea confessus est) indignis modis tractatos fidem abnegare & blasphemare coegit, aliquos autem occidit. Nec contentus ijs, quae crudeliter & impie fecit Hierosolymae, cum fidem Christianam in Syria florere, & Damasci plures esse audiret, qui Christo nomen dedissent, a Pontifice acceptis literis, cum satellitio armato illuc profectus est, ut quoscunque illic huius sectae sive viros sive mulieres invenisset, vinctos Hierosolymam adduceret, et, seueriori inquisitioni & iudicio subijciendos. Tandem Herodes Agrippa Ecclesiam aggreditur, & Iacobum fratrem Ioannis indicta causa gladio violenter occidit, & ut Iudaeis gratificetur, Petrum quoque carceri traditum necare voluit. Deniq; quo magis crevit Ecclesia, eo magis saevit persecutio, nec cum Apostoli desijssent, cum hi omnes sublati essent, sed posteris quoque temporibus per annos fere trecentos continuos duravit. Etenim in historijs persecutiones decem ex ordine recensentur, quas ipsi Imperatores Romani moverunt, penes quos tunc erat orbis terrarum imperium. Prima author fuit Nero, qui ut sese invidia & odio, quod sibi ipsi apud populum urbis Romae incendio conciliaverat, liberaret, & rumores, qui de ipso spargebantur, abolere, urbem a Christianis incensam fuisse dixit, & aliquibus correptis, coegit miseros diris tormentis fateri, quae causa fuit, ut ingens hominum infinitum multitudo crudelissime interficeretur. Nam teste Cornelio Tacito, iniquissimo alias nominis Christiani hoste, pereuntibus haec ludibria addita sunt, ut ferarum pellibus contecti laniatu canum interirent, aut crucibus affixi aut flammandi, atque ubi defecisset dies, in usum nocturni luminis vrerentur: adeo ut qui sontes & extrema supplicia meritos credebant, tamen eorum miserationi tangerentur, ut qui non publica utilitas
units.tr: And it is certain that this happened to the apostles. For just as Christ, as that blessed old man Simeon had foretold, experienced contradiction, so the apostles too did as soon as they began to preach. Indeed, profane scoffers were heard who, when most were amazed at the miracle of tongues, said they were full of new wine and attributed to fraudulent drunkenness what was a plain and proper work of the Holy Spirit. Soon afterwards, when Peter and John had miraculously healed a man lame from his mother's womb in the name of Jesus Christ, and the people, stirred by the novelty of this miracle, were preaching Christ, they were led off to prison and afterwards, when a more serious public action was brought against them, were released, not without fierce threats, so that they should no longer preach in the name of Christ. A little later, as the number of believers grew, the high priest rose up with the whole sect of the Sadducees, which then held power at Jerusalem, and committed all the apostles together to public custody. Although God freed them by the ministry of an angel and ordered them to teach in the temple, they were nevertheless seized again and brought before the council, and after a long and bitter dispute, they were severely flogged and forbidden to speak any more in the name of Jesus. But while they, as faithful servants of God ought, persevered steadfastly in their duty, and among others the faith of Stephen showed itself, they seized a man whom the stirred-up crowd had laid hold of, dragged him before the elders, and, with false witnesses produced against him, stoned him cruelly in a tumult. Once this was done, a public and general persecution immediately arose, in which Saul raged most of all. With unbridled fury he cast believers of both sexes into chains, and he compelled many (as he later confessed himself) to be treated in shameful ways, to deny the faith and blaspheme, and he killed some. Nor was he content with what he had done cruelly and impiously at Jerusalem. Hearing that the Christian faith was flourishing in Syria, and that there were many at Damascus who had given their names to Christ, he set out there with letters from the high priest and an armed escort, so that whatever men or women of this sect he found there he might bring back bound to Jerusalem, to be subjected to a stricter inquiry and judgment. At last Herod Agrippa attacked the Church, and without a hearing violently killed James, the brother of John, with the sword, and, wishing to please the Jews, he also wanted to put Peter, who had been handed over to prison, to death. Finally, the more the Church grew, the more the persecution raged, and it did not cease when the apostles had ceased, and once all of them had been taken away, but lasted continuously through the following times for nearly three hundred years. For in the histories ten persecutions are listed in order, which the Roman emperors themselves stirred up, in whose hands then was the rule of the world. The first was instigated by Nero, who, in order to free himself from the envy and hatred which he had brought upon himself among the people of the city of Rome by the fire, and to abolish the rumours that were spread about him, said that the city had been set on fire by Christians. After seizing some of them, he forced the wretched men by dreadful tortures to confess, and this was the cause why an immense, countless multitude of men was most cruelly put to death. For, according to Cornelius Tacitus, otherwise a most unfair enemy of the Christian name, these mockeries were added to their deaths: they were covered with the skins of wild beasts and torn to pieces by dogs, or fixed to crosses, or burned, and, when daylight failed, were set on fire to serve as nocturnal lamps. So that those who believed them guilty and deserving of extreme punishment were nevertheless moved to pity, since they were consumed not for the public good

units.la: tatis. tate, sed in seruitiam vnius absumerentur. In qua persecutione, Petrum quoq; & Paulum Apostolos martyrij coronam accepisse, Ecclesiastici scriptores tradiderunt. Secundam Domitianus excitauit anno nati in carne Filij Dei XCV i. in qua Ioannes Apostolus, postquam (vt Tertullianus de praescript. haeret. testatur) in oleum feruens demersus nihil mali accepit, in Patmo relegatus est. Tertia Traiano tribuunt, in qua Ignatius anno Christi CX. ex Asia Romam ductus, & a bestijs discerptus est. Quarta Antoninus Philosophus monit, in qua martyres facti sunt, Polycarpus, Iustinus & plures alij circiter annum Domini CLXX. in qua Ecclesiam Christus liberauit miraculose, quando exercitu Romano contra barbaros militante, & propter aquarum ipsam & sitim in extremas angustias adductio, ad preces Christianorum militum pluuia largissima milites refecit. Quintus Ecclesiae persecutor fuit Sept. Seuerus, qui inter alios Leonidem, patrem Originis sustulit, anno post Christum natum CCIII. Sextus Maximinus fuit, qui primus ex militibus sine Senatus authoritate ad Imperij fastigium ascendit. Septimus numeratur Decius, sub quo Diuus Laurentius prunis ignitis tostus gloriosomartyrio vitam hanc mortalem finiuit, citer annum Christi CCLII. Octaua persecutio authorem habuit Licinium Valerianum, quae martyres illustriores dedit Cornelium & Cyprianum. Nonam Aurelianus mouit. Decimam Diocletianus & Maximianus, qui Nicomediae conuenientes de delendis Christianis consultarunt hoc praetextu, quod differsio in religione, magnas discordias in familijs & in imperio parceret. Occasionem vero tam crudelis consilij arripuerunt ex dissidijs, quibus ipsi Christiani scindebantur, sicuti Eusebius in prologo libri octaui Ecclesiasticae historiae testatur. Nam diuulsos facilius oppri mi posse sperabant. Et erant ex Christianis multi transfugae & sycophantae, qui calumnijs suis communes hostes magis incendebant, quales nostro saeculo, pro dolor nimis multi sunt, qui fere ex dissensione Sacramentaria enascuntur. Edicta igitur propositae sunt atrocia, & innumerabiles <bl>ybiq;</bl> gentium omni suppliciorum genere occisi sunt, adeo vt annotatum sit, vno mense in diuersis septemdecim millia hominum interfecta fuisse. Duravit haec saevities annis tredecim. Inter alios autem tunc a Decio, qui apud maiores nostros in hisce regionibus nomine Augustorum cum Imperio erat, nostrae gentis Apostoli, Felix & Regula, in castro Thuricensi martyrium passi sunt, anno Christi CCCVIII. qui ex Thebaea legione elapsi in Heluetiam venerunt, & hominibus Alpinis fidem in Christo praedicarunt, quae origo fuit Ecclesiae Tigurinae, sicuti vetera instrumenta testantur. Tandem anno Diocletiani decimo nono, quo maxime arsit persecutionis feruor, pax reddita est Ecclesiae per Constantinum, sed non durabilis aut perpetua fuit. Nam post annos 47. anno nimirum Christiano CCCLXVI. Iulianus Apostata, qui abnegata religione Christi, ad gentilium idololatriam defecerat, persecutionem nouam excitauit. Et post hunc rursus alij quoq; ex Imperatoribus, & cum his barbarae gentes, quae Imperio Romano passim turbas dederunt: quales fuerunt Gothi, Vandali, Saraceni, & non multo post Turcae, qui adhuc hodie nominis Christiani hostes haereditarij dicuntur. Accesserunt his omnibus Pontifices, qui in templo Dei (vt Paulus praedixit) idest, in Ecclesia sede sua constituta, sese opponunt & efferunt aduersus omne quod dicitur Deus aut numen, & iam seculis aliquot germanos fidei Christianae profestores crudelissime per se quuntur, & fere passim omnium persecutionum authores sunt hodie.
units.tr: but for the cruelty of one man. Ecclesiastical writers have handed down that in this persecution the apostles Peter and Paul also received the crown of martyrdom. Domitian stirred up the second in the year 95 after the incarnation of the Son of God, in which the apostle John, after he had been plunged (as Tertullian testifies in De praescriptione haereticorum) into boiling oil and suffered no harm, was relegated to Patmos. The third they attribute to Trajan, in which Ignatius, led from Asia to Rome in the year of Christ 110, was torn apart by beasts. The fourth was incited by the philosopher Antoninus, in which Polycarp, Justin and many others became martyrs around the year of the Lord 170. In this persecution Christ miraculously freed the Church, when the Roman army was campaigning against the barbarians and, reduced to the extremity of distress by lack of water and thirst, was restored by a very heavy rain at the prayers of the Christian soldiers. The fifth persecutor of the Church was Septimius Severus, who, among others, destroyed Leonides, the father of Origen, in the year 203 after Christ's birth. The sixth was Maximinus, who was the first of the soldiers to rise to the height of imperial power without the authority of the Senate. The seventh is counted as Decius, under whom St Laurence, roasted on glowing coals, ended this mortal life by a glorious martyrdom, around the year of Christ 252. The eighth persecution had as its author Licinius Valerian, and it produced the more famous martyrs Cornelius and Cyprian. Aurelian stirred up the ninth. The tenth was Diocletian and Maximian, who, meeting at Nicomedia, deliberated on destroying the Christians under the pretext that difference in religion caused great discords in families and in the empire. They seized the occasion for so cruel a plan from the dissensions by which the Christians themselves were torn apart, as Eusebius testifies in the preface to the eighth book of his Ecclesiastical History. For they hoped that the divided could more easily be crushed. And there were among the Christians many deserters and informers, who, by their calumnies, inflamed the common enemies all the more, such as, alas, there are too many in our own age, who arise almost from the sacramentarian dissension. Therefore, cruel edicts were issued, and countless people of every nation were killed with every kind of torture, so that it is recorded that in one month seventeen thousand men were slain in various places. This savagery lasted thirteen years. Among others then, under Decius, who among our forefathers in these regions was with the Empire under the name of Augustus, the apostles of our nation, Felix and Regula, suffered martyrdom at the castle of Zurich in the year of Christ 308. Having escaped from the Theban legion, they came into Helvetia and preached faith in Christ to the Alpine people, which was the origin of the Church of Zurich, as the old records attest. Finally, in the nineteenth year of Diocletian, when the fervour of persecution burned most fiercely, peace was restored to the Church through Constantine, but it was not lasting or perpetual. For after 47 years, namely in the Christian year 366, Julian the Apostate, who, having renounced the religion of Christ, had returned to the idolatry of the Gentiles, stirred up a new persecution. After him other emperors too, and with them barbarian peoples, who everywhere caused disturbances in the Roman Empire: such as the Goths, the Vandals, the Saracens, and, not long after, the Turks, who even today are called the hereditary enemies of the Christian name. To all these have been added the Popes, who, as Paul predicted, in the temple of God, that is, in the Church, having set up their seat there, set themselves against and exalt themselves above everything that is called God or divinity, and for some centuries now have most cruelly hunted down the brothers who profess the Christian faith, and today are almost everywhere the authors of all persecutions.

units.la: At hoc loco multa obseruatione dignum est, cur homines Christiani tam inuisi sint mundo, vt (quod alibi dicitur) qui aliquos illorum trucidarit, sese putet Deo cultum praestare? Docet hoc vno verbo Dominus, dicens, PROPTER NOMEN MEVM. Id est, quod mihi fiditis, quod mei estis discipuli, quod me solum vestrum agnoscitis seruatorem & redemptorem, & mihi fidele praestatis obsequium. Etenim mundus ex seipso vult sapere, & Deum ex suo ingenio metitur: quae causa est, vt cultus etiam ex suo arbitrio instituat. Hos autem quia damnat & reijcit Dei Filius, & illud Isaiae superstitiosis intonat, Frustra me colunt docentes doctrinas hominum: tumultuantur fere omnes, & intolerabile illis videtur abs se institutos & a maioribus obseruatos culture damnari, & alios quidem ignorantia propria seducit, qua delectantur dum neque peccata sua & naturae suae vitiositatem, neque gratiam sibi in Christo factam agnoscunt, alijs amissi lucri, quod ex superstitione perceperunt, iactura & dolor bilem mouet, vt iniuriam sibi factam vlciscei conentur. Exemplum eius rei in Actis exhibet Demetrius Ephesius, qui totam ciuitatem, & in primis omnes argentarios, qui ex delubris Dianæ, quæ faciebant, vitium sibi parabant, contra Paulum seditiose commouit, quod cum Dianæ cultu quæstum quoq; omnem ipsis periturum diceret. Et vtinam non hodie etiā Demetrij tales apud omnis loci & ordinis homines inuenirentur. Sed & alia causa ex Deo accedit. Hic enim per Euangelium iustitiam veram requirit, quæ nos totos ipsi vendicat, fucum autem, quo mundus, qui totus in malo iacet, sese ostentat, arguit. Id vero non potest hic ferre, qui iniustus haberi non vult, & ideo lucem odit teste Christo, ne opera eius prava arguantur. Quod si fe fortius opponant viri Apostolici, & hypocritis lucem Verbi in oculos ingerant, mox hi indomitum furunt, & nihil non sibi aduersus Christi seruos licere arbitrantur. Eo autem quàm maxime arguitur peruersum & sceleratum mundi ingenium. Etenim Christus lux & vita est, atq; nobis seruandis in mundum venit, vt nobis a Deo sapientia, iustitia, & sanctificatio & redemptio fieret. Et ista nobis illeper Euangelium liberaliter offert. Quae ergo impietas est huius administros odisse & persequi, quos nobis natura, & tanti beneficij debitum commendat? Atqui faciunt hoc nonfolij, qui Christum diserte negant, vt olim gentes idolatrae, & hodie Turcae atq; Iudæi, verumetiam multi, qui illius quidem nomen profitentur, sed eius merito non contenti, gloriam eius partim sibi ipsis vendicant, partim in alios transferunt, quos sibi ipsis Seruatores & Mediatores apud Deum Patrem fingunt. Hi certe omnes persequi solent eos, qui ab vno Christo pendent, neq; in eius consortium quenquam volunt admittere. Est hodie frequens admodum hoc hominum genus. Etenim qui in Pontificum verba iurarunt, & Romana sedis aut Ecclesiae germani filij esse & haberi volunt, ijs nihil laude dignum fecisse videberis, vt magnifice & egregie de IESV CHRISTO sentias, & in illo agnoscas quaecunq; de illo olim Prophetae & Apostoli praedicarunt, eademque sanguine proprio tefari atque obsignare paratus sis: nisi huic coniungas Diuos caelites, tuorum operum merita, indulgentias Romanas, & plumbo graues bullas, purgatorium ignem, & fexcenta alia, quæ Christi meritum prorsus inutile reddunt, sicut de Circumcisione Iudaica Paulus olim ad Galatas scribebat. Et res ipsa loquitur, hanc hodie praecipuam persecutionum & suppliciorum causam esse, quod qui Christum vere amplexi sunt, Diuos inuocare nolunt, neque extra hunc alias pro peccatis satisfactiones aut victimas admittere, aut cultum exhibere imaginibus mutis, quibus Deo nihil magis inuisum est, & quibus religionem omnem aboleri veteres Christiani testati sunt. La-Eantius certe olim non dubitauit affirmare, religionem nullam esse, vbicunque fimulachrum sit. Et huius dicti grauissimas rationes reddit: Primùm, quod religio non nisi diuinis rebus constet, quæ in solis caelestibus inueniantur, & proinde in fimulachris esse nequeant, quae sive materiam sive formam species, terrena sunt. Alteram, quod religio in veritate consistat: At quicquid simulatur, id falsum sit, necesse est, neque potest veri nomen accipere, quod veritatem fuco & imitatione mentitur. At quis hoc per simulachra fieri neget, quando haec a simulando ita dicuntur. Haec cum olim sanctissimi homines sèrint, & confessi sint, qui Christianae fidei & religionis doctrinam sanguine suo obsignatam confirmarunt, hodie tamen multos superstitio ita fascinauit, vt ipsis iudicibus tutius sit hominem Christianum iugulare, aut vstulandum flammis exponere, quàm ex puteri idolo ignem aut hypocaustum incendere, vt viuas Christi imagines a frigore feruerent & tueatur. Facit ad amplificandum scelus hoc temporis notatio. Vt enim olim cum plus fatis turbarum effet in mundo, tamen a Christi seruis & fidelibus excruciandis non potuerunt renocari tyranni: Ita hodie neque bella neque alia calamitates (quae tamen infinitae sunt) tyrannos moueant, vt Ecclesiae pacem concedant. Quin saepe cum Turcis inducia fiunt, vt Ecclesia persecutionem possint continuare.
units.tr: But at this point it is worth asking closely why Christians are so hated by the world that, as is said elsewhere, whoever kills one of them thinks he is offering worship to God. The Lord explains this in a single phrase: FOR MY NAME'S SAKE. That is, it is because you trust in me, because you are my disciples, because you acknowledge me alone as your Saviour and Redeemer, and render me faithful obedience. For the world wants to be wise by its own lights and measures God by its own intellect, and so it also devises worship by its own judgment. But because the Son of God condemns and rejects these inventions, and because Isaiah's words thunder against the superstitious, "In vain do they worship me, teaching the doctrines of men," nearly all of them make an uproar. It seems intolerable to them that the worship they have established and their forefathers have observed should be condemned. Some are led astray by their own ignorance, in which they delight, since they acknowledge neither their sins, nor the corruption of their nature, nor the grace given them in Christ. Others are moved to bile by the loss and injury of the gain they have derived from superstition, and try to avenge the wrong done to them. The Acts supply an example of this in Demetrius of Ephesus, who stirred up the whole city, and especially all the silversmiths who made their living from the shrines of Diana, against Paul in a seditious way, saying that all their profit would perish along with the worship of Diana. And would that such Demetriuses were not found today among men of every place and rank! But there is another cause, which comes from God. For he who requires true righteousness through the Gospel claims us wholly for himself, and exposes the pretence by which the world, which lies entirely in evil, presents itself. This the world cannot bear, since it does not wish to be thought unrighteous, and so, as Christ bears witness, it hates the light, lest its evil works be exposed. But if the apostolic men oppose it more boldly and thrust the light of the Word into the eyes of hypocrites, these men at once rage uncontrollably and think they may do anything at all against the servants of Christ. In this, above all, the perverse and wicked nature of the world is shown. For Christ is light and life, and he came into the world to save us, so that he might become for us wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption from God. And these things he freely offers us through the Gospel. What impiety, then, is it to hate and persecute the ministers of such a gift, whom nature and the debt owed for so great a benefit commend to us? Yet not only do those do this who openly deny Christ, as the idolatrous nations once did and the Turks and Jews do today, but also many who indeed profess his name, yet not content with his merit, partly claim his glory for themselves and partly transfer it to others, whom they imagine as their own saviours and mediators with God the Father. All these are accustomed to persecute those who depend on Christ alone, and they wish to admit no one into his fellowship. This kind of men is very common today. For those who have sworn allegiance to the words of the Pontiffs, and wish to be and be considered genuine sons of the Roman see or the Church, you will seem to have done nothing worthy of praise unless you think magnificently and splendidly of Jesus Christ, and recognise in him all that the prophets and apostles once preached about him, and are ready to attest and seal the same with your own blood, unless you join to this the heavenly saints, the merits of your own works, the Roman indulgences, the bulls heavy with lead, purgatorial fire, and six hundred other things which render Christ's merit entirely useless, just as Paul once wrote to the Galatians about Jewish circumcision. And the thing itself speaks: that the chief cause of persecutions and punishments today is that those who have truly embraced Christ are unwilling to invoke the saints, nor to admit any other satisfactions or sacrifices for sins apart from him, nor to render worship to dumb images, than which nothing is more hateful to God, and by which the old Christians testified that all religion is abolished. Lactantius indeed did not hesitate long ago to affirm that there is no religion wherever there is an image. And he gives very weighty reasons for this saying. First, because religion consists only of divine things, which are found in heavenly things alone, and therefore cannot be in images, which, whether they represent matter or form, are earthly. Second, because religion consists in truth; but whatever is feigned must necessarily be false, and cannot receive the name of truth, since it counterfeits truth by disguise and imitation. But who would deny that this happens through images, since they are so called from simulating? Although the most holy men of old perceived and confessed these things, who confirmed the doctrine of the Christian faith and religion, sealing it with their blood, yet today superstition has so bewitched many that it is safer for judges themselves to cut the throat of a Christian or to expose him to be burned in the flames, than to light a fire or a furnace beside a well-idol in order to warm and protect the living images of Christ from the cold. The notoriety of this age adds to the enormity of this crime. For just as in former times, though there was already more than enough disturbance in the world, the tyrants could not be called back from tormenting the servants and faithful of Christ, so today neither wars nor other calamities (which are nonetheless innumerable) move the tyrants to grant peace to the Church. Indeed, often truces are made with the Turks so that they may continue their persecution of the Church.

units.la: Sed quaerat aliquis, Cur haec fieri sinat Deus, cui facile erat suos tueri, & impiorum tyrannorum rabiem cohibere? Sed facilis est ad hanc quaestionem respondere. Nam Petro teste, quia Deus iustus est, fere a domo sua iudicium incipit, & suos inflar auri igne afflictionum probet, & a sordibus vitiorum excoquat. Habent enim pij quoq; sua vitia, quae ipsis ex innata vitiositate inhaerent, qualia sunt securitas, ambitio, aemulatio, cotentiones, disciplinae impatientia. Accedunt his sordes, quas mundus incautis aspergit, & quae (vt alibi diximus) quotidianam pedum, id est, vitae & conuersationis nostrae ablutione requirunt. Idcirco necesse est, vt qui otio abutuntur, crucis & persecutionum
units.tr: But someone may ask: why does God allow these things to happen, when it was easy for him to protect his own and to restrain the rage of impious tyrants? But it is easy to answer this question. For, as Peter testifies, because God is just, judgment begins almost at his own house, and he tests his people as gold is tested by the fire of afflictions, and purges them of the dross of vices. For the godly too have their own faults, which cling to them from their innate corruption, such as complacency, ambition, rivalry, quarrels, and impatience with discipline. To these are added the filth which the world sprinkles on the unwary, and which (as we said elsewhere) requires the daily washing of our feet, that is, of our life and conduct. Therefore it is necessary that those who abuse their leisure be chastened and amended by the scourges of the cross and of persecutions, and brought to a better harvest.

units.la: 1. Ioan. 5. Ioan. 3. Mundi impietas arguitur. 1 Cor. 1. Gal. 5. Lib. 2 Inst. Cap. 19. Hec fieri. Cap. 4. cutionum flagellis castigati emendentur, & ad frugem meliorem adducantur. Quæ causa est, quòd ut frumentum non modo flagellis ex paleis excutitur, verum etiam molæ subijcitur, ut per hanc attritum farina fiat, & esui aptum: itapij ab impijs separati purus panis Domini fiant, sicut olim D. Ignatius deseipso scribebat, cum ex Asia Romam ducebatur bestiarum dentibus commolendus. Id vero primùm fit pijs in testimonium, sicut apud Lucam annotatur. Dum enim propter doctrinam Euangelij & fidei in IESVM CHRISTVM confessionem sanguinem suum fundere non grauantur, neq; dira mortis supplicia exhorrescunt, satis apparet, ipsos de fide Christi seriò persuasos esse, nec temerè conceptam opinionem esse, quod prædicant. Quo nomine etiam veteribus Martyres testes dicti sunt. Deinde idem hoc gentibus & tyrannis persecutoribus in testimonium cedit, ne quem habeant ignorantiæ prætextum, quo sese excusent. Hisce enim sanctorum martyrijs conuincuntur, ipsos oblatam salutis doctrinam reiecisse, & proinde dignos esse, qui contumaciæ suæ pœnas dent: de quo supra cap. 10. prolixius dictum est.
