For although a harsh winter seems to have destroyed them and taken away all natural vigour, so that nothing can be hoped from them, yet no one is so foolish or senseless that, when in new spring the face of the earth returns renewed, and the trees full of sap bring forth and push out buds, he does not understand that these are certain signs that summer is now near, and begin to rejoice at them." For all acknowledge God's irrevocable decree, which is (as Moses and Jeremiah write) that as long as this machinery of the world endures, there shall be summer and winter in their time, and likewise the seasons of sowing and harvest and the parts of the year shall alternate with one another in their turns. Yet for the whole world too God has appointed its spring and summer, which will follow one another by fixed laws. So no one will be able to hinder the face of the world from being renewed, when hardly anything of it can be hoped for. Moreover, the state of the present and future age is shadowed forth elegantly by this parable, which contains a manifold teaching and a most sweet consolation. For if you consider the sons of God, who, born again through the Word of God by the power of the Holy Spirit, live to God, winter may be reckoned both as a whole that period which is spent for them in this world. For just as winter is harsh with cold, frost, hoarfrost and storms, and strips the earth of grass, flowers and plants, and the trees of the adornment of their leaves and finally of fruit, and the animals of the warmth by which they are quickened and moved, so for pious people new storms rise up every day. For this unhappy world hates them on account of the light of the Word. Hence arise contempt, reproaches and slanders, injuries of every kind and persecutions, which at times make life itself bitter for them; and for this to happen it is necessary that weariness of this world should arise in us, lest, immersed in its pleasures and pursuits, we neglect heavenly things. But just as a joyful and fruitful summer certainly follows winter, and spring goes before it, by which (as we said a little earlier) the whole face of the world is renewed, so the most sorrowful state of things that now wearies us will give way, in its time, to the last day, on which the Son of God will appear in the clouds of heaven and will bring us a redemption that is joyful and complete in every respect. And just as the spring season comes between winter and summer, and is usually disturbed by various storms, so the times that immediately precede the consummation of the world will be full of afflictions. In these times we ought to remember that the afflictions of the pious and the rages of the impious are the buds and flowers of the plants, by which the Lord bears witness that that fatal time is at hand which will put an end to all miseries; and because he is faithful and does not allow his own to be tempted beyond their strength, he will shorten those days (as he promised above) so as to hasten his coming. Meanwhile let each one apply these things to himself privately, and be firmly persuaded that consolation will never be lacking to the pious, to soften the cross and adversities by which God is accustomed to exercise them in this world.

units.la: {d} 4 solet exercere. Et notum est illud Apostoli: Sicut abundant perpessiones Christi in nobis, ita per Christum abundat etiam consolatio nostra. Quo item magis feruet impiorum furor, eo citius ipsorum mensura implebitur, quæ illis exitium afferet, electorum vero redemptionem maturabit.
units.tr: {d} 4 And that saying of the Apostle is well known: "As the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so through Christ our consolation also abounds." Likewise, the more the fury of the impious glows, the sooner their measure will be filled up, which will bring destruction upon them, and it will hasten the redemption of the elect.

units.la: Cæterum quia diuturnior mora in aduersis fidem vehementer labefactat, iureiurando confirmat argumentum, quod ex rerum natura desumpsit. Et primò quidem, ne quis propter dilationem dubitet, ait: Amen amen dico vobis, nequaquam præterierit ætas hæc, donec omnia facta fiant. Debet hæc particula ad priorem huius capitis partem de templi & vrbis excidio referri, quod intra vnius ætatis spacium, nempe intra annos quinquaginta factum esse constat. Et necesse fuit hoc diserte exprimi. Scimus enim vulgare nimium hoc esse, quod multi ex mora impunitatis sibi cõ cipiunt, & minas quantumuis graues rident, si non illico vident ea fieri quæ dicuntur. Sed non autem fertur quod differtur, neque veritati promissionum aut comminationum Dei tempus quicquam derogat. Quia vero discipuli & qui tunc Ierosolymæ viuebant credentes, Ecclesiam totam, adeoque gentium humanum vniuersum, repræsentabant, ad hoc quoque dictum hoc referri debet.
units.tr: But since a longer delay in adversity greatly shakes faith, he confirms by an oath the argument that he has drawn from the nature of things. And first, lest anyone doubt because of the delay, he says: "Truly, I say to you, this generation will by no means pass away until all these things have come to pass." This particle should be referred to the earlier part of this chapter, concerning the destruction of the temple and the city, which is known to have happened within the span of one generation, namely within fifty years. And it was necessary that this be expressed clearly. For we know it is all too common that many, from the delay of impunity, conceive that they are safe, and laugh at threats however grave, if they do not at once see the things that are said coming to pass. But what is deferred is not therefore lost, and time takes nothing away from the truth of God's promises or threats. And since the disciples and those who then lived at Jerusalem as believers represented the whole Church, and so the whole human race of the Gentiles, this saying ought to be referred to them as well.

units.la: Constat enim, Ecclesiam duraturam esse vsque ad finem mundi, cum Dominus alibi dicat: Ecce ego vobiscum sum vsque ad consummationem seculi. Sed & genus humanum non deficiet inter turbas & pericula noxissimi temporis. Nam, vt Paulus testatur, non omnes obdormiemus, sed omnes immutabimur momento & ictu oculi, ad vltimam tubam. Itaque multi illo die superstites erunt, qui vna cum ijs, qui resurgent, rapientur in nubes in occursum Domini per aërem, vt semper cum illo sint. Et diligenter obseruari debet Dei fides & potentia, qui Ecclesiam suam inter perpetua certamina feruat, nec illam interire finit. Sanciuit ipse certamen hoc in Paradiso inter serpentem diabolum & semen mulieris. Cœpit hoc in Abele, qui a fratre suo Caino crudeliter & impie occisus est. Sed idem in Setho reuixit, in quo filiorum Dei soboles noua quasi suscitata est. Et cum propter iniquitatem humani generis hoc per Diluuium aboleri meruisset, Ecclesiam tamen arca beneficio (quæ Ecclesiæ typus fuit) in Noa mirifice Deus seruauit, & postea Patriarchæ etiam similiter inter Chananæos seruati sunt.
units.tr: For it is certain that the Church will endure until the end of the world, since the Lord says elsewhere: "Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age." But also the human race will not fail amid the troubles and dangers of that most grievous time. For, as Paul testifies, we shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet. So many will be left alive on that day, who, together with those who shall rise, will be caught up in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, so that they will always be with him. And the faithfulness and power of God, who preserves his Church amid perpetual conflicts and does not allow it to perish, ought to be carefully observed. He himself decreed this conflict in Paradise, between the serpent, the devil, and the seed of the woman. It began with Abel, who was cruelly and impiously slain by his brother Cain. But it revived in Seth, in whom a new offspring of the sons of God was, as it were, raised up. And although on account of the wickedness of the human race this had deserved to be wiped out by the Flood, God wonderfully preserved the Church in Noah, by the benefit of the ark, which was a type of the Church; and afterwards the patriarchs too were likewise preserved among the Canaanites.

units.la: In primis autem in Monarchijs, quæ alia aliis successerunt, Dei fides erga Ecclesiam eluxit, quando propter hanc hæ omnes vel collapsæ vel instauratæ sunt, vt alibi prolixè demonstrauimus. Id vt in hunc vsque diem factum est, ita in posterum quoque fiet vsque ad finem mundi. Nos vero hinc consolationem petamus, ne vel mundi delitijs insecati, vel periculis aut metu superati, nos infelici mundo configuremus, sed ceu viui lapides per fidem super petram IESVM CHRISTVM ædificati, siamus domus spiritualis & sacerdotium sanctum, gens deniq; sancta & populus Dei peculiaris, vt illius virtutes prædicemus, qui nos vocauit ex tenebris in admirabilem lucem suam. 1. Pet. 2. cap.
units.tr: Above all, in the monarchies that succeeded one another, God's faithfulness toward the Church shone forth, since all of them either fell or were restored for the Church's sake, as we have demonstrated at length elsewhere. This has happened down to the present day, and in the same way it will happen in the future until the end of the world. Let us therefore take comfort from this, so that we do not, pursued by the world's delights or overcome by dangers or fear, bind ourselves to this unhappy world. Instead, like living stones built upon the rock Jesus Christ through faith, let us be a spiritual house and a holy priesthood, a holy nation and a people belonging to God, so that we may proclaim the virtues of him who called us out of darkness into his marvellous light. 1 Pet. 2.

units.la: Quod autem iureiurando asseuerauit Christus, comparatione amplius confirmat, dicens: Cœlum & terra prætereunt, sermones autem mei nequaquam prætereunt. Nominat duas mundi partes firmissimas, cœlum & terram, in quibus Dei potentia inuista potissimum elucet. Sunt hæ opus manuum Dei, in quod nemo præter illum ius habet. Attamen interibunt, & vt vestis vetusta te corrumpentur: at Deus idem est perpetuo, & anni eius non deficiunt, & quod de præsentis vaticinij veritate inconcussa dicitur, de Verbo Dei in genere debet intelligi. Nam quod Isaias dicit, Verbum Domini manet in æternum, & tunc maxime patebit eius Veritas, quando in fine seculi huic cedet vniuersa huius mundi machina, implebuntur autem quæcunq; a Deo prædicta sunt, vt (quod alibi dicitur) ex ijs neque apex quidem aut iota vnum cadat.
units.tr: Christ confirms by comparison what he had affirmed with an oath, saying: "Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will by no means pass away." He names the two most firm parts of the world, heaven and earth, in which the unconquered power of God shines most clearly. These are the work of God's hands, over which no one but him has any right. Yet they will perish and be worn out like an old garment, whereas God is the same forever, and his years do not fail. What is said of the unshaken truth of this prophecy must be understood of the word of God in general. For what Isaiah says, "The word of the Lord abides forever," will be most fully made plain when, at the end of the age, the whole machinery of this world gives way. Everything that God has foretold will be fulfilled, so that (as is said elsewhere) not even one stroke of a letter or a single iota of it will fall.

units.la: Applicemus hoc ad omnes promissiones Ecclesiæ datas, & quoties cœlorum influentias instabiles aut tempestatum vices & mutationes incertas cernimus, in mentem nobis veniat hoc Domini dictum, nec dubitemus firmum & ratum fore quod ille de Ecclesia sua statuit. Si enim leges, quibus hæc peritura mundi machina gubernatur, stabiles sunt, num Ecclesiam, quæ ipsissimum regnum cœlorum dicitur, incertis motibus iactari putamus.
units.tr: Let us apply this to all the promises given to the Church. Whenever we see the unstable influences of the heavens, or the changing seasons of the weather and uncertain alterations, let this saying of the Lord come to mind, and let us not doubt that what he has decreed concerning his Church will be firm and sure. For if the laws by which this doomed machinery of the world is governed are stable, do we suppose that the Church, which is called the very kingdom of heaven, is tossed about by uncertain movements?

units.la: Sed & in stitutioni nostræ hoc seruiat, ne quid ex nostro arbitrio mutemus in Dei decretis. De his enim proprie dictum est, Ne transgrediaris terminos antiquos. Et si Moses reste sanciuit, ne Israelitæ transferrent terminos, quos olim Chananæi possuerant in terra sua, quanto minus loco moueri aut mutari debent quæ Deus ipse instituit? Hodie istud crimen nobis intentant aduersarij, & rij, & nos veteres ritus & constitutiones mutare clamant, & ideo haereticos esse dicunt. At hic tenendum est, non esse vetera quaecunq; vetustatis nomine comendantur: & hodie talia dicuntur, imagines in templis, Missa, sacra pro defunctis, vota monastica, Purgatorius ignis, Indulgentiae, & innumera alia, quae vetustas erudita prorsus ignorauit. Caelibatus item & teiuniorum superstitiosa obseruatio vetusta putatur. At Paulus nouissimis demum temporibus exoriturus dixit fedu flores, qui a diabolo inspirati ciborum discrimina inuehant, & coniugij vsum prohibeant. Vetus item dicitur transubstantiationis commentum. Sed Daniel hunc dicit Antichristi Deum esse, quem patres ignorarint. In Concilio Lateranensi sub Innocentio III. circa annum Domini M.CC. decretum fuit, ut Monachorum ordines augerentur. At quam multi Ordines novi ab eo tempore exorti sunt? quos rectissime locustas dixerus, de quibus in Apocalypsi nos Spiritus sanctus admonuit. Et qua ratione excusabuntur Iesuitae, qui intra annos paucos enati hodie terras & urbes omnes repleuerunt? Quid item in toto Papatu remanebit, si auferantur, quae a paucis saeculis instituta sunt? & quorum origo admodum recens demonstrari potest? In religione vetustate nullam nos agnoscere possumus, quam quae Scripturarum testimonijs nititur, Christianis autem hominibus merito suspectum est, quicquid illis contradicit. Poterat hoc prolixe demonstrari, & latissimus campus esset excurrendi in errores aduersariorum, sed sufficiat ansam praebuisse pijs & cordatis, qui colla sua ex laqueis superstitionum extricare cupiunt.
units.tr: This also serves our instruction, so that we change nothing by our own judgment in God's decrees. For it was said of these things properly, "You shall not remove the ancient landmarks." And if Moses sanctioned by law that the Israelites should not move the boundary stones which the Canaanites had once set up in their land, how much less ought we to shift or alter what God himself has instituted? Our adversaries bring this charge against us today; they cry out that we change the old rites and constitutions, and for this reason they say we are heretics. But here we must hold that not everything is old which is commended under the name of antiquity. Today such things are called old: images in churches, the Mass, sacrifices for the dead, monastic vows, purgatorial fire, indulgences, and countless other things which true antiquity utterly did not know. Likewise, celibacy and the superstitious observance of fasts are thought to be ancient. Yet Paul said that in the last times there would arise deceivers, inspired by the devil, who would introduce distinctions of foods and forbid the use of marriage. Likewise the fiction of transubstantiation is called ancient. But Daniel says that this is the god of Antichrist, whom the Fathers did not know. At the Lateran Council under Innocent III, around the year of the Lord 1200, it was decreed that the orders of monks should be increased. But how many new orders have arisen since that time? These the Holy Spirit warned us about in the Apocalypse, and most rightly we have called them locusts. And by what reasoning will the Jesuits be excused, who, born within a few years, have today filled every land and city? What, moreover, will remain of the whole Papacy if those things are removed which were instituted within the last few centuries, and whose origin can be shown to be quite recent? In religion we can acknowledge no antiquity except that which rests on the testimonies of the Scriptures, and rightly whatever contradicts these is suspect to Christian people. This could be demonstrated at length, and it would be a very wide field for running through the errors of our adversaries; but let it suffice to have offered a clue to the godly and wise who desire to free their necks from the snares of superstition.

units.la: At quando desaturis quaestio est periculum est a curiositate, qua inescati de rebus non multum necessarij cognitu quaerimus, negligimus autem quae nobis ante pedes sunt, & quae in primis & diligentissime inuestigari debebant. Fuit haec omnibus saeculis multorum & grauissimorum errorum causa, & hodie multos inescat, vt vel ex astris, vel alijs illicitis artibus ea addiscere conentur, quae Deus nos celata voluit. Ideo hoc semper prohibuit Deus, & in Lege ne spiritus fati dicos consulamus vetuit. Ne inueniatur in te (inquit) qui traducat filium suum aut filiam suam per ignem, nec diuinus, qui diuinando futura praedicat, nec mathematicus, nec veneficus, nec maleficus, nec incantator, nec qui pythones consulat, nec magus, nec qui a mortuis scisciletur. Abominatur enim Dominus omnes, qui ista faciunt, & propter istas abominationes excindet gentes istas ante te. Et Isaiae verba sunt: Quod si dixerint vobis, scisciscitamini a pythonicis & a diuinis, qui mussitant & susurrant: Annon vnaquaeq; gens suos Deos consulit? Num pro viuis ad mortuos recurras? Quin ad legem & testimonium eatur. Et qui non dixerint secundum verbum hoc, ijs non erit lux matutina. Non vult ergo nos futura aut arcana Deus discere aliunde, quam ex illis medijs, quae ipse nobis dedit, ne quam nos seducendi occasione praebeamus satanae, qui hoc vnum quaerit, vt nos a Deo abducat, quem vnum debebamus magistrum & doctorem sequi. At quia hic de re maximi momenti agebatur, in qua discipulos facile falli posse, & multos etiam posteris temporibus graviter offensuros esse sciebat (vt nostro saeculo non minus ridiculè & turpiter quam perni tiose factum esse & quotidie fieri, conflat) vt humani ingenij audaciam coerceat Christus, ipsem omnem aliquid adsequendi hic nobis negat, dicens: De die autem illo & hora nemo scit, ne Angeli quidem coelorum, sed Pater meus solus. Apud Marcum seipsum quoq; excipit, vt apertius confiteatur hanc notitiam soli Deo Patri conuenire. Eludunt quidem hoc dictum nonnulli, quasi Maiestati diuinitatis Christi multum derogemus, nisi illum & omniprasentem & omnisciens esse fateamur. At teneamus oportet, Christum, cuius persona duabus naturis integris, & inter se distinctis, diuina & humana, constat, pro assumpti hominis ratione loqui. Vt ergo qui secundum id quod Deus est, omnia creauit, omnia pascit, alit & feruat, nec quicquam ignorat: idem secundum id quod homo est, legitimo tempore pariendi ex virgine natus est, & cum aetate creuit, & profecit sapientia & gratia apud Deum & homines. Itaq; vt quoad hominem in statu humilitatis suae sicuit, efurruit, sitiit, turbatus est (spiritu, denique mortuus etiam est), idem nonnulla quoq; ignorauit: neq; aliquis (si hoc dicamus) nos in Christi maiestatem blasphemos esse, aut ipsius omnipotentiam negare dicat. Quid enim aliud dicemus, quam quod ipse de se liberè confessus est? Et quae nam meritas fuerit, vt illum alium fingamus, quam ipsi fieri voluerit? Aut ea in illo negemus, sine qui bus ipsius gloria & nostra salus non potest consistere? Haec autem in eo consistunt, quòd qui Deus aeternus & verus est, verum quoq; hominem assumere, nobis quoad infirmitates, quibus obnoxij fimus, similiter, & ita noster redemptor fieri, & per crucem in regni gloriam ingredi voluit. Horum vero nobis vsus sit, ne ipsi aliquid eorum, quae nobis accidant, indignius feramus, aut pluriues velimus scire, quam Angeli, quos ille suos internuntios fecit. Credamus autem ijs, quae Dei Filius IESVS CHRISTVS de mundi consummatione & aduentu suo gloriose nobis praedixit, ad hunc vero nos praeparemus vera & constanti fide, vt tandem dies ille nobis laetus illucescat, & cum illo ingrediamur in regnum suum caeleste. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: But when a question is asked about things which are hidden, there is danger from curiosity, by which we, enticed into seeking knowledge of things not very necessary to know, neglect what lies before our feet and what should first and most diligently be investigated. This has been the cause of many grave errors in every age, and today it entices many to attempt to learn from the stars, or by other unlawful arts, those things which God has willed to keep hidden from us. Therefore God has always forbidden this, and in the Law he forbade us to consult spirits of divination. "Let there not be found among you," he says, "anyone who makes his son or daughter pass through the fire, nor a diviner who foretells the future by divination, nor a soothsayer, nor a sorcerer, nor an enchanter, nor one who consults pythons, nor a magician, nor one who seeks the dead. For the Lord abhors all who do these things, and because of these abominations he will drive out those nations before you." And these are the words of Isaiah: "If they say to you, 'Seek out those who have familiar spirits and the wizards who whisper and mutter,' should not a people consult its gods? Should one turn to the dead on behalf of the living? Rather, let them go to the law and the testimony. And those who do not speak according to this word will have no morning light." God therefore does not wish us to learn the future or hidden things from any other source than those means which he himself has given us, lest we offer Satan an occasion for seducing us, for Satan seeks this one thing: to draw us away from God, whom alone we ought to follow as teacher and master. But since this concerns a matter of the greatest importance, in which he knew that disciples could easily be deceived, and that many would also be gravely harmed in later times (as it is clear that in our own age it has been done and is done daily, no less ridiculously and shamefully than perniciously), Christ, to restrain the audacity of the human mind, denies us any such knowledge here, saying: "But of that day and hour no one knows, not even the angels of heaven, but my Father alone." In Mark he even excepts himself, so that he may more plainly confess that this knowledge belongs to God the Father alone. Some indeed twist this saying, as if we were greatly detracting from the majesty of Christ's divinity unless we confess that he is both omnipresent and omniscient. But we ought to hold that Christ, whose person consists of two whole natures, divine and human, distinct from each other, speaks according to the nature of the man he assumed. Thus, although according to what he is as God he created all things, feeds, nourishes and sustains all things, and is ignorant of nothing, yet according to what he is as man he was born of the virgin at the appointed time of bearing, grew with age, and advanced in wisdom and grace before God and men. Therefore, just as in the state of his humiliation he, as man, hungered, thirsted, grew weary, was troubled in spirit, and finally even died, so too he was ignorant of some things. Nor should anyone say (if we speak this way) that we are blaspheming against the majesty of Christ or denying his omnipotence. For what else shall we say than what he himself freely confessed about himself? And why should we feign that he was other than he willed to be? Or should we deny in him those things without which his glory and our salvation cannot stand? These things consist in this: that he, who is the eternal and true God, willed also to assume a true man, so that in respect of the infirmities to which we are subject he might likewise become our redeemer, and enter into the glory of his kingdom through the cross. Let us therefore be content with this use of these things, so that we do not bear with impatience any of the things that befall us, nor wish to know more than the angels, whom he made his messengers. Let us believe what the Son of God, Jesus Christ, gloriously foretold to us about the consummation of the world and his coming, and let us prepare ourselves for it with a true and steadfast faith, so that at last that joyful day may dawn upon us and we may enter with him into his heavenly kingdom. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power forever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCLXXXII.
units.tr: Homily 282.

units.la: Sicut autem erant dies Noe, ita erit & aduentus Filij hominis. Sicut enim in diebus, qui praecesserunt diluuiū, edebant & bibebant, vxores ducebant & nuptum dabant ad eum vsque diem, quo ingressus est Noe in arcam: nec cognouerunt diluuiū, vsquedum veniret et sustulisset omnes: ita erit & aduentus Filij hominis. Tunc duo erunt in agro, vnus assumetur, & alter relinquetur. Duae molentes in pistrino: vna assumetur, & altera relinquetur. Vigilate ergo: nescitis enim qua hora Dominus vester venturus est. Illud autem scitote, si sciret paterfamilias qua vigilia fur venturus sit, vigilaret, nec sineret perfodi domum suam. Propterea & vos estote parati: quia qua hora non putatis Filius hominis venturus est.
units.tr: "As the days of Noah were, so also will the coming of the Son of man be. For as in the days before the flood, they were eating and drinking, marrying wives and giving in marriage, until the day that Noah entered the ark. They did not know of the flood until it came and swept them all away; so also will the coming of the Son of man be. Then two men will be in the field: one will be taken, and the other left. Two women will be grinding at the mill: one will be taken, and the other left. Watch therefore, for you do not know at what hour your Lord is coming. But understand this: if the householder knew at what watch the thief would come, he would keep watch and not allow his house to be broken into. Therefore you also must be ready, for the Son of man will come at an hour you do not expect."

units.la: Quemadmodum si de futuris agitur multi curiositate nimia peccant, & dum huic indulgent, quae caelestis Pater in sua potestate reposuit, audacius & saepe etiam per artes illicitas & media prohibita scrutantur: ita securi interea negligunt, quae necessaria cognitu & obseruatu diligentius inquirere debebant. Idcirco Dominus noster IESVS CHRISTVS de nouissimo suo aduentu & huius mundi fine, ad cuius mentionem carnis sensus vulgo exhorrescunt, differens, hoc agit, vt omissis multis de ijs signis admoneat, quae cognitu & obseruatu necessaria sunt & adiutorem aeternam conducunt. Et quia plerosque in sua socordia perituros esse sciebat, & fatalem quandam ostentationem apud omnis loci & ordinis homines tunc regnaturam esse sciebat, multa adducit, quibus nos ad vigilantiam & attentionem excitat: & ne quod dicebat, nouum & proinde incredibile putaretur, nunc exemplis aut similibus veterum iudiciorum Dei rem illustrat.
units.tr: When people inquire into the future, many sin through excessive curiosity. While they indulge in this, they search more boldly, and often even by illicit arts and forbidden means, into things which the heavenly Father has kept in his own power. Meanwhile, secure in themselves, they neglect what they ought to have inquired into more diligently, because it is necessary to know and to observe. Therefore our Lord Jesus Christ, while deferring discussion of his final coming and the end of this world (at the mention of which the senses of the flesh commonly shudder), does this: he sets aside many things about those signs and warns us about what must be known and observed and what leads to eternal help. And because he knew that most would perish through their own sloth, and knew that a kind of fatal display would then reign among men of every place and rank, he brings forward many things by which he rouses us to watchfulness and attention. And lest what he said should be thought new and therefore incredible, he now illustrates the matter with examples and with similar judgments of God from earlier times.

units.la: Primum de noui mundi hominibus petit, qui ante diluuium vixerunt, & admonitionem gratiam in genere comprehensam proponit, dicens: Sicut erant dies Noe, ita erit & aduentus Filij hominis. Quapropter quod hic de aduentu suo dicit, non ad eum modo die reflectendi debet, quo in nubibus caeli venturus est, aut paucos aliquos, qui nouissimum illum diem praecedent, sed de toto illo tempore debet intelligi, quod ab eo die, quo in carne natus est aeternus Dei Filius, ad finem mundi usque decurret. Potest enim totum mundi tempus non inepte in tres aetates diuidi. Prima est tempus patrum prisco rum, qui ante Mosem & Legem fuerunt, & vulgo patriarchae dicuntur, eo quod genus humanum ex illis in diuersas gentes aut nationes propagatum est. Altera Mosi & Legi tribuitur, & Prophetas quoque habet, de qua intelligi debet, quod Christus Legem & Prophetas ad Ioannem Baptistam vsque extendi dixit. Tertiam vocat dies Filij hominis, & sibi tribuit, qui in postrema demum aetate venire debuit, vt in ipso implerentur quae prius promissa & typis adumbrata aut praedicta erant. Ideo ipsein cruce animam Deo Patri commendaturus, prius dicebat, Consummatum est, vt testaretur, sic iam impleta esse quaecunque ad humani generis redemptionem faciunt, vt posthac nulla mundi mutatio insignior existat, pedari debeat, quae res in melius instauretur: qualem olim Chiliastae promittebant, aureum quoddam saeculum somniando, dum quae Isaias & Micheas de pace sub Christo & de armis militaribus in rustica instrumenta conuertendis, deque ferit cum pecoribus simul conuersaturis vaticinantur, secundum literam expositurus. Et hodie similis error eos fallit, qui Christi dictum, Et erit
units.tr: First he asks about the people of the old world, who lived before the flood, and he sets forth a general warning, saying: "As the days of Noah were, so will the coming of the Son of man be." Therefore what he says here about his coming ought not to be referred only to that day on which he will come on the clouds of heaven, or to the few days that will precede that last day. It must be understood of the whole period that runs from the day on which the eternal Son of God was born in the flesh until the end of the world. For the whole time of the world can not inappropriately be divided into three ages. The first is the time of the early fathers, who lived before Moses and the Law, and are commonly called patriarchs, because the human race spread from them into various peoples and nations. The second is attributed to Moses and the Law, and also includes the Prophets; this is the period of which it must be understood that Christ said the Law and the Prophets extended until John the Baptist. The third he calls the days of the Son of man, and attributes to himself, since he was to come in the final age, so that in him might be fulfilled what had been promised before and foreshadowed by types or foretold. Therefore, about to commend his soul to God the Father on the cross, he first said, "It is finished," to bear witness that all things pertaining to the redemption of the human race were now fulfilled, so that afterwards no more remarkable change of the world should be expected, by which things would be restored for the better. The Chiliasts once promised such a change, dreaming of a certain golden age, while they set out to expound literally what Isaiah and Micah prophesied about peace under Christ, about beating swords into plowshares, and about wild beasts living together with the flocks. And today a similar error deceives those who take Christ's words, "And there will be..."

units.la: Exemplum diluuij confertur cum nouissimo die. omile ynum & grex ynus de omnium gentium & sectarum generali in religione consensu expo- nunt, & in omnium sectarum erroribus atq; portentis fouendis sibi delicias faciunt. Sed tam ab- est, vt Christus nobis tale quid polliceatur, & ita securos faciat, vt potius doceat nouissimi fecu- li dies, quos sibi vendicat, corruptissimos & proinde periculosissimos fore testetur, & ita nos ad vi- gilandum expergefaciat. Et diebus Noæ suum illud seculum confert, quibus osso animæ solæ in arca seruatæ sunt: ita admonens, ne quem credentium paucitas & effrenis aut publica totius mun- di in suum exitium ruentis licentia offendat, vt eius exemplo fe quoq; abripi patiatur.
units.tr: The example of the flood is compared with the last day. Some interpret it as one flock and one fold, a general agreement in religion among all nations and sects, and they take pleasure in fostering the errors and monstrosities of every sect. But Christ is so far from promising us anything of the kind, or from making us so secure, that he rather teaches that the days of the last age, which he claims for himself, will be attested as most corrupt and therefore most dangerous, and so he rouses us to watch. He compares that age to the days of Noah, in which only eight souls were saved in the ark. Thereby he warns that no believer should be offended by the small number of believers, or by the unbridled, public license of a whole world rushing to its own destruction, so that he would allow himself to be carried away by their example.

units.la: Præstat ergo diligentius videre, qui nam & quales dies Noæ fuerint, & cum his nostri seculi mores conferre, quibus hodie viuitur, vt ad ardentius salutis æternæ & ferium pietatis ftudiu ex- citemur, quo opus est ijs, qui in aduentu Christi nouissimo coram ipso consistere cupiunt. De Noæ seculo in genere dicit Moses, Corrupta erat terra coram Deo & plena violentia. Item omnis caro corruperat viam suam. Et incurabilem fuisse malitiam illam vel ex eo patet, quod Deus pœnitere fe dicit, quod creauit hominem. Erat quidem tunc præco iustitiæ inter homines Noe, qui scelera ac cusabat, & imminente Diluuij pœna minitabatur, adhæc ne quid de illa dubitaretur, arca publice in omnium conspectu ædificabat. Sed & ipsum Noa & admonitiones eius contemnebant, nec ex- emplo monebantur, quod merito debuissent magnificare, cum homo grandæuus, spectata virtutis & authoritatis plenus, tantis impensis & labore atq; industria in extruenda arca fe fatigaret, vt imminens periculum posset effugere. Sed ita illos excæcauerat carnis studium, vt (quod hic Domi- nus dicit) facerent. Edebant, inquit, bibebant, vxores ducebant, & nuptum dabant. Horum me- minit, non quod per fe nefas fit edere, bibere, vxorem ducere aut nuptum dare (vt enim ista fiant, necessitas iubet, & Deus testatur, non esse bonum vt homo solus fit, & vt quisque vitandæ scorta- tionis causa propriam vxorem, & vnaquæq; suum maritum habeat, iubet Apostolus atq; dæmo- niorum doctrinam esse ait, fi quis ista vetet) Sed partim securitatem hominum nouissimi seculi per stringit, qui reliquis ferijs & grauioribus studijs, fe totos ventri & gulæ, Veneri deniq; & libidini dediturí sint, vt diuina & cœlestia non curent: partim luxum & intemperantiam accusat, pertina- ciam item incurabilem, quæ ipsos non sinat caput & animum ad altiorem cœlestium cogitationem attollere. Atqui in his peccaniffe primi mundi homines tempore Noæ, Scriptura diserte docet. Fuit tunc haud dubie magna terræ fertilitas, quæ causa fuit carni addictus, vt ventrem audirent, qui ipse (vt Cato dicebat) auribus caret, & alijs quoq; donis Dei abuterentur. In coniugijs ve- rò non quid Deus vellet, sed quid cæca libido distaret, spectabant, & ideo imparibus nuptijs impli- citi sunt, ex quibus Nephilim progeniti terram impleuerunt, violentia & iniurijs. Comitata sunt has omnis generis scelera. Quod ipsum de nostris temporibus dici potest. Et quando de his agitur, omnia hæc coniungi debere, alijs locis docemur. Securiores enim æquo fore postremi temporis homi- nes, Paulus non obscure affirmat, dicens: Cum dixerint, Pax & tuta omnia, tunc repentinus ipsis imminebit interitus: Et in sequenti Cap. multa aut media nocte oriturus dicetur clamor iste de ad uentu sponsi, quis nos a somno excitet. Quia vero securitas illa & improbitas ad aduentum vsque Christi durabit, turpissime falluntur, qui refpifcentiam publicam mundi in melius sperant. Hæc enim nunquam sequetur, & vt ad perpetua certamina præparemur, necesse est. Sunt quidem paf- sim publici iustitiæ præcones, qui vbicunq; sermo de nostri seculi moribus incidit, ingenue faten- tur, hanc mundi faciem non posse consistere, quo minus intereat, & mutatione in melius omnino opus esse. Sed qui emendationem vrgeant pauci sunt, imo pauci & rari sunt, qui ista a ministris attingi velint. Quod fi Magistratus aliquid conetur, nō desunt in vulgo, qui sese opponunt. Regnat igitur Ebrietas, & per hanc in securitatem profundam delabuntur homines, quæ ipsis tandem in- teritus causam afferet. Quod fi de nuptijs dicere libeat, lene effet de his consilia subinde inire, ince- stas nuptias hodie reges & principes quærunt, nec aliter familias suas in sua dignitate consistere putant, nisi inter fe coniungantur, quos non solum Lex Dei, verumetiam honestas publica coniun- giprohibet. Et hoc est, quod Daniel prædixit, Babylonia illius statuta (quæ Monarchias qua- tuor adumbrauit) pedes & digitos pedum, qui finem quartæ, id est, Romana Monarchia repræsen- tant, humano femine conferruminari oporzere. Quod hodie ita in quibusdam illustribus familijs impletur, vt in meridiana luce cæcutire videri possit, qui de his re vel leuiter dubitare velit. Multis vero adeo non religio est imparibus coniugijs sese intricare, & ingu trahere cum infidelibus, vt patrijs quoq; sedibus, vbi libera habent puriori doctrina & religionis exercitia relictis adidolo-latras concedant, in quorum ciuitates non admittuntur, nisi primum introitum cum Christi & Veritatis abnegatione redimant. Crescit ergo & augetur hominum peruersorum numerus, & fere omnes a sua vocationis via declinant, & in solum quæstum intenti non aliud quærunt, quam vt in mundo hoc commode viuant. Reges & principes viri, qui pacem publicam tueri debebant, bella mouent non necessaria, quibus orbis terrarum turbatur. Pontifices clasticum canunt, & frigidam suffundunt. Priuati homines vili mercede conducti mercenariam militiam sectantur, & vt lanij ad iugulanda pecora, ita ipsi ad mactandos homines conducuntur. Qui sacris præsunt inter Papistas, Monachi & Sacrifici, castra sequuntur, & militaria cofilia tractant, qui vero Euangelij præcones & ministri videri volunt, perpotant, ludunt, & adeo illos ministerij sui pudet, vt ne Ecclesiæ ministri videantur, moribus, vestitu, dictis, vita deniq; vniuersa scurras aut milites vel etiam gallonis referunt. Quia causa est, quod Deus iram suam non leuibus pœnis & exemplis erga homines incurabiles & pœnitere nescios declarat.
units.tr: It is therefore better to look more carefully at who and what kind of people the men of Noah's days were, and to compare with them the morals of our own age in which we live, so that we may be stirred to a more ardent pursuit of eternal salvation and a more serious pursuit of piety. This is needed by those who wish to stand before Christ at his final coming. Moses speaks in general of Noah's age: "The earth was corrupt before God and full of violence. Likewise all flesh had corrupted its way." And that this wickedness was incurable is clear from the fact that God says he repented that he had made man. Noah indeed was then a herald of righteousness among men, who accused their crimes and threatened the impending punishment of the flood; moreover, lest anyone doubt it, he built the ark publicly in the sight of all. But they despised Noah himself and his admonitions, and were not warned by his example, which they should rightly have esteemed, since this aged man, full of proven virtue and authority, wearied himself with such great expense, labour and industry in building the ark so that he might escape the impending danger. But the pursuit of the flesh had so blinded them that (as the Lord says here) they "ate, drank, married wives, and gave in marriage." He mentions these things not because eating, drinking, marrying or giving in marriage is wrong in itself. For necessity requires that these things be done, God testifies that it is not good for man to be alone, the Apostle bids each man to have his own wife and each woman her own husband to avoid fornication, and he calls the doctrine forbidding such things a teaching of demons. Rather, he partly touches on the security of men of the last age, who, neglecting their other duties and more serious studies, give themselves wholly to belly and gullet, and finally to Venus and lust, so that they care nothing for divine and heavenly things. Partly he accuses luxury and intemperance, and likewise an incurable obstinacy, which does not allow them to lift head and mind to higher thoughts of heavenly things. Yet Scripture plainly teaches that the men of the first world sinned in these things in Noah's time. There was then without doubt great fertility of the earth, which was the cause that men gave themselves over to the flesh, so that they obeyed the belly (which, as Cato said, has no ears), and abused the other gifts of God too. In marriages, however, they looked not at what God wished but at what blind lust desired, and therefore they were entangled in unequal marriages, from which the Nephilim were born and filled the earth with violence and injuries. All kinds of crimes accompanied these things, and the same can be said of our own times. When these things are discussed, we are taught in other places that all of them must be joined together. For Paul plainly affirms that men of the last time will be too secure, saying: "When they say, 'Peace and all is safe,' then sudden destruction will overtake them." And in the following chapter that cry is said to arise at midnight, or in the middle of the night, concerning the coming of the bridegroom: "who will awaken us from sleep." But because that security and wickedness will last until Christ's coming, those are most shamefully deceived who hope for a public repentance of the world, a change for the better. For this will never follow, and it is necessary that we be prepared for perpetual struggles. Everywhere there are indeed public heralds of justice who, whenever talk of the morals of our age arises, frankly confess that this face of the world cannot endure without perishing, and that change for the better is altogether necessary. But those who urge amendment are few; indeed, few and rare are those who wish these matters to be taken up by ministers. If the magistrate attempts something, there are not lacking among the common people those who oppose him. Drunkenness therefore reigns, and through it men slip into deep security, which will in the end bring them destruction. If one may speak of marriages, it would be pleasant to take counsel about them from time to time. Today kings and princes seek incestuous marriages, nor do they think their families can keep their dignity unless they are joined among themselves, though not only the Law of God but also public decency forbids such unions. This is what Daniel predicted: that the feet and toes of that statue of Babylon (which foreshadowed four monarchies), representing the end of the fourth, that is, the Roman monarchy, would have to be cemented together with human seed. Today this is fulfilled in certain illustrious families in such a way that a man could seem blind in the midday light if he doubted it even slightly. But for many it is no scruple to entangle themselves in unequal marriages and to yoke themselves with unbelievers, so that, leaving their ancestral homes, where they have free and purer doctrine and the exercise of religion, they yield to idolaters, and into whose cities they are not admitted unless they first buy their entry by denying Christ and the Truth. The number of perverse men therefore grows and increases, and almost all turn aside from the way of their calling. Intent only on gain, they seek nothing but to live comfortably in this world. Kings and princes, who ought to guard the public peace, stir up unnecessary wars by which the whole world is disturbed. Pontiffs sound the trumpet and pour cold water on things. Private men, hired for a cheap wage, pursue mercenary soldiering, and like butchers hired to slaughter cattle, they are hired to slaughter men. Those who preside over sacred things among the Papists, the monks and priests, follow the camps and handle military counsels; and those who wish to seem heralds and ministers of the Gospel drink, gamble, and are so ashamed of their ministry that they do not look like ministers of the Church at all. In morals, dress, speech and their whole life they resemble buffoons, soldiers or even gallants. This is why God declares his wrath against men who are incurable and do not know how to repent, by no light punishments and examples.

units.la: At quia hæc multos offendunt, multi autem communi exemplo abstractis impunitatis spe concipiunt, & indulgentia sua seu longanimitate Dei ad licentiam abutuntur, pœna subtexit, quæ olim primi mundi socordiam castigauit Deus, vt ex ea colligamus, quid nobis sperandum sit, si illo rursus similes simus. Cum pergerent edendo, bibendo, nuptias item faciendo vsq; ad eum diem, quo Noe in arcam ingressus est, non cognouerunt Diluuium, id est, non voluerunt agnoscere vindictam quæ præsoribus erat, quæ ex improuiso venit, & omnes simul fuistulit. Ita fiet (inquit) in aduentu Filij hominis. Voluntaria enim & crassa ignorantia seipsos indurabunt homines, & omnium admonitionum contemptu seipsos excæcabunt, vt quæ videant & sentiunt, tamen scire & videre non lint. Itaq; repente peribunt, & improuisum atq; ineuitabile exitium simul omnes obruet. Itaq; etsi illos diluuiu non cognouisse dicat, non tamen illos excusat ignorantia, cuius fons & origo fuit incredulitas, quæ animos ipsorum excæcauit, vt ignorantes esse mallent, quam Deo tredere, & fieri uari. Vt enim per fidem Noe ea cognouit, quæ nondum apparebant, & a Deo admonitus apparauit arcam, qua seipsum & domum suam seruauit, & iustitia, quæ ex fide est, hæres est factus: Ita reliqui omnes sibypsis exitialem ignorantiam accersiuerunt, qui ipsius concionibus & exemplo ad moniti, in sua nequitia perrexerunt, etiamsi virum sanctissimum, & multa authoritate graue viderent sese ad Diluuium vniuersale præparare. Ide ergo fiet nonissimis diebus, vt voluntaria illa cæcitas & stupor belluinus, qui tunc vulgo regnabit, omnes, qui Verbo Dei credere detrectant, tenebris incredulitatis exitialibus immersos perdat. Facit autem ad pœna amplificationem, quod Diluuium omnes sustulisse dicitur. Quam enim horribilis rerum facies, & triste spectaculum fuerit, cum pauculi illi, qui in arca seruati erant, hanc egressi, sefolos ex omnibus populis, qui in terris versantur, superstites esse, pastim vero hominum & pecudum, ferarum ite cadauera, quæ aquis suffocata erant, insepulta iacere viderent, quiuis astimare poterit. Potuit certe Poeta prophanus id concipere, qui gentium fabulas secutus, Deucalionem & Pyrrham solos euasisse finxit, & de Ioue canit deficiente inter alia dicit: Qui superesse virum de tot modo millibus vnum Et superesse videns de tot modo millibus vnam Ac desolatas agere alta silentia terras, &c.
units.tr: But because these things offend many, and many, following the common example and with the hope of impunity cut off, turn God's indulgence or patience into licence, the punishment is added, by which God once punished the sloth of the first world, so that from it we may infer what we are to expect if we become like them again. "They were eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage, until the day that Noah entered the ark, and they did not know the Flood," that is, they did not want to acknowledge the vengeance that was foretold, which came unexpectedly and carried them all off at once. "So it will be," he says, "at the coming of the Son of Man." For men will harden themselves by a deliberate and gross ignorance, and by despising all warnings will blind themselves, so that they neither know nor see things that they do in fact perceive and feel. Therefore they will suddenly perish, and an unforeseen and inescapable destruction will overwhelm them all together. So although he says they did not know the Flood, he does not excuse them by this ignorance, whose source and origin was unbelief, which blinded their minds so that they preferred to be ignorant rather than trust God and become wise. For as through faith Noah knew those things that were not yet visible, and, warned by God, prepared the ark by which he saved himself and his household, and became an heir of the righteousness which is by faith, so all the others brought deadly ignorance upon themselves, for although they were warned by his preaching and example, they persisted in their wickedness, even though they saw that this holy man, grave in great authority, was preparing for a universal Flood. So the same will happen in the last days: that deliberate blindness and bestial stupor, which will then reign among the common people, will destroy all who refuse to believe the Word of God, plunged in the deadly darkness of unbelief. Moreover, it adds to the severity of the punishment that the Flood is said to have swept everyone away. How dreadful the sight of things and how sad the spectacle must have been, when those few who had been saved in the ark, having come out, saw that they alone were left alive out of all the peoples who dwell on the earth, while the corpses of men and beasts and wild animals, suffocated by the waters, lay unburied, anyone can judge. Certainly the profane poet could conceive this, who, following the fables of the Gentiles, imagined that only Deucalion and Pyrrha had escaped, and sings of Jupiter lamenting, among other things, saying: "One man, of so many thousands, scarcely survives, and one woman, seen to survive of so many thousands, and the deserted lands carry on in deep silence," and so on.

units.la: At in nouissimo die triftior multo erit rerum facies. Nam etsi solitudo nulla erit, quæ alto silentio mentes expauefaciat, neq; limo in ædibus & arboribus relictio omnia squalleant, vno tamen incendio prius omnia liquescent, ædificia cuncta cum vniuersa totius mundi suppellectile conflagrabunt, & terribili planctu & eiulatu lamentabunt omnes, quos scelerum admissorum conscientia ex cruciabit, qui omnes post infandas querelas horribile illam sententiam audiet, quæ illos ad ignem illum inextinguibilem damnabit, qui paratus est diabolo & angelis suis. Eo graviora erunt hæc omnia, quod inexpectata veniet, & ex improuiso incidet securis & sibi omnia læta pollicetibus.
units.tr: But on the last day the sight of things will be far sadder. For although there will be no solitude to terrify minds with deep silence, and though everything will not be left squalid with mud on the houses and trees, yet first everything will melt in one fire: all buildings, together with the entire household goods of the whole world, will be burned, and all whom the consciousness of their committed crimes torments will lament with terrible wailing and howling. After their unspeakable complaints all of them will hear that dreadful sentence which will condemn them to that unquenchable fire which is prepared for the devil and his angels. All this will be the more severe because it will come unexpectedly, and the axe will fall suddenly upon men who promise themselves everything pleasant.

units.la: At quia nouerat Dominus socordiam nostram, quæ nobis dum aliqua spes pacis est, aut aliquæ meliores conditionis aut laetioris fortunæ speciem affulget, vix vllis minus, nedum admonitionibus ex nibus excuti potest, aliud exemplum huic simile apud Lucam addit, de Sodomæis, quos similis se- curitas perdidit. De quibus hæc dicit: Similiter etiam vt accidit in diebus Loth: edebant, bibe- bant, emebant, vendebant, plantabant, ædificabant. Quo autem die Loth exijt Sodomis, pluit igne & sulphure è cælo, & omnes perdidit. Facit hoc primum ad comminationum istarum confirmatio- nem. Quia enim duo adducit exempla, quæ improuisi interitus & excidij, quod toti orbi in nouis- simo Christi aduentu paratum est, typus fuerunt, non nouum aut insolens erit, quod tunc fiet, & i- deo stulti nimis sunt, qui id vocant in dubium. Et huc videtur Petrus respexisse, qui prophanos illos illuforec confutans & mendacij arguens, qui cum gentium philosophis mundum æternum sin- gebant, qui neq; cæpisset vnquam, neq; vnquam finem esset habiturus, & scurriliter dicebant: Vbi est pollicitatio aduentus eius? Nam ex quo patres obdormierunt, omnia ita permanent vt ab i- nitio creationis: Ita respondet, vt vtrumq; exemplum coniungens, dicat: Illud enim sponte ipsos latet, cœlos iam olim extitisse per Dei sermonem, & terram ex aqua & in aqua consistentem. Quia Ecclesiæ Christianorum scribit, de ijs autem loquitur, qui aliquando Christum professi, tunc ad Pharifæorum commenta defecerunt, non temere illos sponte latere dicit quæ de mundi creatione Scripturis traduntur, cùm Moses in primo limine statim diserte doceat, hunc in principio per Dei Verbum esse creatu, & terram quidem, quæ aquis quasi immersa latebat, his ad iussum Dei in v- num locum colletus emersisse, vt continens appareret & habitabilis fieret. Quæ causa est, quòd terra, si littora & ripas spectes, supra aquas eminere, & his fulciri & inniti videatur, cùm constet huius elementum grauitate sua pressum infra alia subsedisse, & ideo Dauid de illa dixit: Super ma- ria fundauit eam, & super flumina firmauit eam. Ex eo autem colligit Petrus, non temere fa- stum, vt quæ aquis, ceu basi & fundamento nitebatur, his tota demersa & obruta fit, cum inhabi- tantium sceleribus & peccatis, sub quorum pondere terram contremiscere, & Deum ipsum instar plaustri manipulis onusti stridere, Propheta quoq; dixit. Vt verò philosophorum de mundi æter- nitate commentum per creationem confutat Apostolus, & hunc cœpisse demonstrat: ita eundem a- liquando desiturum esse ostendit, vbi ad finem suum decurrerit. Et Diluuio opponit conflagratio nem omnium elementorum, quæ Domini IESV CHRISTI nouissimum aduentum præcedet, di- cens. Quamobrem is qui tunc erat mundus, aqua inundatus perijt (vtpote indignus, qui ab hac amplius sustentaretur.) Qui verò nunc sunt cœli ac terra, eodem sermone repositi seruantur igni in diem damnationis & exitij impiorum hominum. Tam certa verò & euidens siue perspicua est huius demonstrationis veritas, vt qui ex gentium philosophis & poetis mentis suæ oculos diligen- tius in hanc considerationem intenderunt, ista poterint perspicere. Ouidius certè Iouem de Dilu- uij pœna deliberantem describens, inter alia de illo dicit: Esse quoq; in fatis reminiscitur, assore tempus, Quo mare, quo tellus, correptaq; regia cœli Ardeat, & mundi moles operosa laboret.
units.tr: But because the Lord knew our sloth, which, as long as there is some hope of peace, or some appearance of better condition or happier fortune shines upon us, can hardly be shaken out of us by any warnings, least of all by any threats, he adds in Luke another example like this one, about the Sodomites, whom a similar security destroyed. Of them he says: "Likewise also as it was in the days of Lot: they were eating, drinking, buying, selling, planting, building. But on the day that Lot went out from Sodom, it rained fire and brimstone from heaven and destroyed them all." This serves first to confirm those threats. For since he adduces two examples, which were types of the sudden destruction and overthrow that is prepared for the whole world at the last coming of Christ, what will then happen will not be new or unusual, and therefore those who call it into doubt are exceedingly foolish. And Peter seems to have had this in view, when he refuted those profane scoffers and convicted them of lying, who, with the philosophers of the Gentiles, asserted that the world was eternal, that it had never begun and would never have an end, and mockingly said: "Where is the promise of his coming? For since the fathers fell asleep, all things continue as they were from the beginning of creation." So he answers, joining both examples together, and says: "For this they willingly forget, that the heavens existed long ago by the word of God, and the earth standing out of the water and in the water." Since he writes to the Christian Churches, and speaks of those who once professed Christ but then deserted to the fabrications of the Pharisees, he says that they wilfully forget what the Scriptures hand down about the creation of the world, when Moses in the very first lines plainly teaches that this world was created in the beginning by the Word of God, and that the earth, which lay hidden as if submerged by the waters, emerged at God's command, gathered into one place, so that dry land would appear and become habitable. This is why, if you look at the shores and banks, the earth seems to rise above the waters and to be supported and to rest upon them, although it is certain that this element, pressed by its own weight, has settled below the others; and so David said of it: "He founded it upon the seas, and established it upon the floods." From this Peter infers that it was not without reason that the land, which rested on the waters as on a base and foundation, should be wholly submerged and overwhelmed by them, since the prophet also said that the earth trembles under the weight of the sins and crimes of its inhabitants, and that God himself creaks like a cart loaded with sheaves. But as the Apostle refutes the philosophers' fiction of the eternity of the world by creation, and shows that the world had a beginning, so he also shows that it will one day cease, when it has run its course to its end. And he sets against the Flood the conflagration of all the elements, which will precede the last coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, saying: "Wherefore the world that then was, being overflowed with water, perished; but the heavens and the earth which are now, by the same word are kept in store, reserved unto fire against the day of judgment and perdition of ungodly men." The truth of this demonstration is so certain and evident that those among the philosophers and poets of the Gentiles who turned the eyes of their mind more diligently to this consideration could perceive these things. Certainly Ovid, describing Jupiter deliberating on the punishment of the Flood, says among other things about him: "He recalls that it is also in the fates that a time will come when the sea, the earth, and the royal vault of heaven will burn, and the laborious mass of the world will be in distress."

units.la: Et hæc quidem adduco, viri Christiani, non quòd fidei nostræ mysteria poetarum aut philosopho- rum prophanorum testimonijs confirmari posse putem: sed vt doceam portenti instar esse, quòd in- ter homines, qui Christi nomen profitentur, inueniuntur qui Epicureis opinionibus fascinati, ea ne gare audent, quæ gentibus non omnino incognita fuerunt, & sibi stabilem & perpetuam rerum sua- rum conditionem pollicentur in mundo hoc, quem suo tempore periturum esse, ethnici confessi sunt: vtq; horum memores ad cœlestia & æterna aspiremus.
units.tr: I bring these things forward, Christian men, not because I think the mysteries of our faith can be confirmed by the testimonies of poets or profane philosophers, but so that I may teach that it is a kind of monstrous thing that among men who profess the name of Christ there are found some who, bewitched by Epicurean opinions, dare to deny things that were not altogether unknown to the Gentiles, and promise themselves a stable and perpetual condition of their affairs in this world, which the heathen themselves confessed would perish in its time; and so, mindful of these things, let us aspire to heavenly and eternal things.

units.la: Sed vt ad Christi verba redeamus, in vtroq; exemplo Noæ & Lothi probè obseruari debet, quòd his subduētis demùm, de incurabilibus pœnas sumpsit Dominus, & quidem absq; vlla cunctà- tione has maturauit. Nam quo die Noe in arcam ingressus est, venit Diluuium, & omnes sustu- lit. Quo item die Loth ex Sodomis exiuit, Dominus pluit igni & sulphure e cælo, ac omnes perdi- dit. Secundum hæc (inquit apud Lucam Dominus) erit dies, quo detegetur Filius hominis. Edu- cet enim Dominus suos & ad se colliget. Potest enim Deus (vt Petrus ait) suos ex tentatione e- ripere. Quod vbi factum fuerit, sient illico quæ de nouissimo die prædicta sunt. Nam non tardat il- le, qui vt suis salutem certam promisit, nec quenquam illorum perire vult, sed omnes ad resipiscen- dam tendere: ita non impunè ferent suam contumaciam, qui in sceleribus incurabiles pergunt, &
units.tr: But to return to Christ's words: in both examples, Noah and Lot, it must be carefully noted that the Lord inflicted punishment on the incurable only after these had been removed, and He hastened it without any delay. For on the day Noah entered the ark, the Flood came and swept them all away. Likewise, on the day Lot went out of Sodom, the Lord rained fire and brimstone from heaven and destroyed them all. "In the same way," the Lord says in Luke, "will the day be on which the Son of Man is revealed." For the Lord will lead out His own and gather them to Himself, since God (as Peter says) is able to rescue His people from temptation. When this has happened, what has been foretold of the last day will follow at once. For He who promised certain salvation to His own is not slow, nor does He wish any of them to perish, but all to come to repentance. Yet those who persist incurably in their sins will not go unpunished for their obstinacy;

units.la: {¢} nihil tale expectantibus adueniet iustus ille iudex, ad cuius tribunal omnes omnes sistentur, qui bus tunc ludus & iocus sunt, quae de huius aduentu dicimus. Nos ergo horum consideratio diligens excitet, ut quia mundus hic totus conflagrabit, & elementa aestuantia liquescent, caelos autem nouos & terram nouam secundum promissum expectamus, in quibus iustitia inhabitat, studeamus, ut immaculati & incontaminati ab eo reperiamur cum pace. Praeterea, ut homines pios & fyn- ceros Dei cultores in honore & pretio habeamus. Vt enim sceleratis sua contumacia publicorum malorum authores sunt, nisi aliorum seueritate coerceantur, & propter vnum Achan Israelitarum castra tota olim turbauit Deus: ita propter paucos pios seruatur interdum tota ciuitates & gentes, quae alioqui peritura effent, nisi illi pro aliis intercederent. Nam, teste Mose, si in Sodoma decem Lothi similes inuenti fuissent, non periisset illa ciuitas. Et Ecclesiastica historia, dum ve- teres persecutiones describunt, fere has communum calamitatum causas fuisse testantur tyrannis persecutoribus, quod Christi seruos occidendo sibi ipsos spoliarunt illorum intercessione, quae prius fer uati fuerant, cum Ecclesia tutum hospitium praberent. Caeterum ut fere securitate nimia peccamus, quando de aduentu Christi agitur: sic tunc alia quoque vitia concurrunt, quae nos in salutis aeternae causa remorantur. Alij enim vocationis suae immemores circa res nihil ad se pertinentes & inutiles occupantur. Alij mundo addicti sunt, & cum huius finis eos excitare deberet, ipsi ad hoc saeculum, & quae in hoc grata atque iucunda habent, reprehendant. Alios praesentis vitae cupiditas fascinat, ut huic potius quam aeternae consultum velint. Multos coniunctio & consuetudo aliorum diutina & vetus detinet, quos relinquere ipsis durum & inhumanum, adeo iniquum videtur. Et horum errorum fere omnium fons est falsa illa persuasio, qua multi sibi ipsis imponunt, dum dicunt, Deum esse misericordem, qui vult omnes homines saluos fieri, nec velle, ut aeternum pereamus, aut ut nobis male sit in hoc saeculo (nam ex eo ipsi nihil eius vel gloriae vel felicitati accedere.) Ex quibus colligunt, omnes tandem salutem consecuturos esse, ut nemo in sempiternum damnetur. Quae opinio olim Originem eo vsque seduxit, ut daemonibus quoque ipsem salutis adhuc superesse diceret. Et hodie his persuasionibus, hoc unum quaerunt homines prophani & carnales, quam ut interea secure delitiantur, neque alia triftior cogitatio ipsis obrepat, quae huius vitae gaudia, quae ipsis omnibus aliis rebus chariora sunt, inturbet. Pergit ergo Dominus in describenda hominum nouissimi saeculi conditione, & quid singulis euenturum sit, quos dies ille, quo ipse venturus est, deprehendet. Nam falsis istis atque erroneis opinionibus (quas recitauimus) locutiones aut sententias aliquot parabolicas siue aenigmaticas opponit, quibus miseri isti sibi ipsos fallunt, qui has sibi delitias faciunt. Sententijs his con- iungere oportet nonnullas, quarum mentionem fecit apud Lucam, quas breuitatis causa Matthaeus praeterijt.
units.tr: {¢} that just Judge will come upon those who expect nothing of the kind, before whose tribunal all will be brought, and for whom the things we say about His coming are then a joke and a jest. Let careful consideration of these things therefore stir us up, so that, since this whole world will be burned up and the burning elements will melt, while we await new heavens and a new earth according to His promise, in which righteousness dwells, we may strive to be found by Him without spot or blemish, in peace. Furthermore, we should hold godly and sincere worshippers of God in honour and esteem. For just as the wicked are the authors of public evils unless they are restrained by the severity of others, and because of the one man Achan God once troubled the whole camp of the Israelites, so for the sake of a few godly people whole cities and nations are sometimes spared, which otherwise would have perished, unless those few interceded for the rest. For, as Moses testifies, if ten men like Lot had been found in Sodom, that city would not have perished. And ecclesiastical history, while describing the early persecutions, testifies that the causes of these common calamities were mostly these: the persecuting tyrants, by killing Christ's servants, deprived themselves of the intercession of those whom they had previously spared, since those servants had provided a safe refuge for the Church. But just as we commonly sin through excessive security when the coming of Christ is discussed, so other vices also arise at that time which hold us back from the cause of eternal salvation. Some, forgetful of their calling, busy themselves with matters that have nothing to do with them and are useless. Others are devoted to the world, and whereas its end ought to rouse them, they cling to this age and to whatever is pleasant and agreeable to them in it. Others are bewitched by the desire for present life, so that they prefer to look to this rather than to eternal life. Many are held by long-standing and old companionship and custom, which it seems so hard and inhuman, and so unjust, to abandon. And the source of nearly all these errors is that false persuasion by which many deceive themselves, saying that God is merciful, who wishes all men to be saved, and that He does not wish us to perish eternally, or to be unhappy in this age (for from that God gains nothing of His glory or happiness). From these things they conclude that all will at last attain salvation, so that no one will be condemned forever. This opinion once led Origen so far that he said salvation was still open even to the demons. And today, by such persuasions, profane and carnal people seek only this: that meanwhile they may live in security and delight, and that no gloomier thought may creep upon them to disturb the joys of this life, which are dearer to them than all other things. The Lord therefore goes on describing the condition of men in the last age, and what will happen to each one on that day when He Himself comes. For against those false and erroneous opinions (which we have recited) He sets certain parabolic or enigmatic sayings, by which those wretched men deceive themselves, who make these pleasures for themselves. To these sayings we must join some which He mentioned in Luke, and which Matthew passed over for the sake of brevity.

units.la: Praecipua est, quae summam eorum, quae agenda sunt comprehendit. In illo die, qui fuerit supra domum, & vasa eius in ipsa domo, ne descendat ad ea sumenda, & qui in agro, similiter ne reuertatur retro. Supra domum in ipsum tectum euasisse dicuntur, vasa autem sua in ipsa domo habere, qui altius supra mundum, quae communis omnium domus est, mentes in caelum sustulisse videntur, & (ut Poeta ait) pariter vitijs, iocis, reliquis altius humanis exeruisse caput: quos item conditio ipsa, quam in hoc saeculo suffinent, ad altiora vocat, nec finit humi repere, sed caelestibus intentos esse iubet. His cauendum est, ut quamuis vasa sua in domo, id est hoc mundo habeant, id est, etsi in hoc saeculo viuant, & quoad praesentis vitae vsum multis adhuc interra indigeat, propter ea tamen non descendant, id est, conditionem suam non deserant, sed pergant ad caelestia aspirare, & contemptis mundi studijs ad diuina aspirent. Confutat ergo illorum rationes, qui dicunt: Quid faciam? In mundo sumus, & terrenis huius saeculi praesidijs opus est. Miserum est egere & pauperiem perpeti. Cur qua habeo abs te vllius iniuria, relinquam, atque omnium indigus, in alios respiciam, qui fortasse infelicem negligunt, & mihi sultitiam hanc exprobrabunt, qua meipsum praeter necessariam causam in angustias coniecerim? Hic autem meminisse oportet, fortunae bona esse, & proinde incerta, fluxa & caduca esse quaecunque in mundo possidemus: non debere ergo nos, qui ad altiora iam penetrauimus aut vocamur, relictis vocationem nostra, circa res huius saeculi occupari. Ha enim non necessariae sunt ad huius vita conseruationem, cum etiam sine illis ( si ita placeat Deo ) possimus viuere. Nam non solo pane viuit homo, sed quouis Verbo, quod exit ab ore Dei. Idcirco apud Lucam recordari iubemur uxoris Lothi, quae quod animum suum rursus in Sodomam conuertisset, postquam portas egressa, coeperat viam ab Angelis monstratam ingredi, in statuam salis conuersa est. Quo exemplo Spiritus sanctus docere voluit, eos in regno Dei nunquam fructum facturos, qui ad terrena respiciunt, et ex hoc suo praepostero huius seculi studio perpetuam infamiam reportatu-ros esse.
units.tr: The chief of these is the one which sums up what must be done. "On that day, let him who is on the housetop, with his goods in the house, not come down to take them; and let him who is in the field likewise not return backward." Those are said to have climbed onto the roof itself, who have their goods in the house, that is, who seem to have raised their minds to heaven, higher above the world, which is the common house of all, and (as the Poet says) have lifted their heads above vices, jests and the rest of human things. The very condition in which they live in this age likewise calls them to higher things, and does not allow them to creep on the ground, but bids them be intent on heavenly things. Against this we must take care: though they have their goods in the house, that is, in this world, that is, though they live in this age, and though for the use of present life many still need earthly things, nevertheless they should not come down on account of these, that is, they should not abandon their calling, but continue to aspire to heavenly things, and, despising the pursuits of the world, aspire to divine things. He therefore refutes the reasoning of those who say: "What shall I do? We are in the world, and we need the earthly protections of this age. It is wretched to be in want and to suffer poverty. Why should I leave what I have without any wrong from you, and, lacking everything, look to others, who perhaps neglect the unhappy and will reproach me for this folly, by which I have brought myself into straits without necessary cause?" Here, however, we ought to remember that the goods of fortune are such, and therefore uncertain, fleeting and perishable, whatever we possess in the world; and that we who have already been called, or are being called, to higher things ought not, having abandoned our calling, to be occupied with the things of this age. For these are not necessary for the preservation of this life, since even without them (if it so pleases God) we can live. For man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God. Therefore in Luke we are bidden to remember Lot's wife, who, because she turned her mind back to Sodom after she had gone out of the gates and had begun to walk the way shown by the angels, was turned into a pillar of salt. By this example the Holy Spirit wished to teach that those who look back to earthly things will never bear fruit in the kingdom of God, and that through this perverse devotion to the things of this age they will bring back everlasting infamy.

units.la: At quia interdum ipsa vita nobis periclitari videtur, cuinos consulere oporteat, huius quoq; eandem rationem esse docet Dominus, dicens: Quicunq; studuerit animam suam seruare, perdet eam: et quicunq; eam perdiderit, viuificabit eam. Id est, dum propter me moritur, anima sua vitam aeternam parabit. Ratio huius promissionis ex fidei Christianae fundamentis petitur, quae docent, vitam hanc mortalem, adeo; ipsam mortem esse, eos autem, qui in Christo moriuntur, ex morte transfire in vitam, et ita demum vere beatos fieri. Sed pleniorem huius dicti explicationem supra Capite 16. audiuimus: quamobrem nunc plura addere non est opus. Vide Homiliam CCX.
units.tr: But because sometimes life itself seems to be in danger, about which we ought to take counsel, the Lord teaches that the same reasoning applies here too, saying: "Whoever seeks to save his life will lose it; and whoever loses it will preserve it alive." That is, whoever dies for my sake will prepare eternal life for his soul. The reason for this promise is drawn from the foundations of the Christian faith, which teach that this mortal life, indeed death itself, is nothing, and that those who die in Christ pass from death into life, and so at last truly become blessed. But we have heard a fuller explanation of this saying above, in chapter 16; therefore there is no need to add more now. See Homily CCX.

units.la: Quoad vero commercia, quae nobis cum amicis et aequalibus intercedunt, multis adeo durum et inhumanum videtur ab ijs separari, ut multi non vereantur dicere, se cum his aut illis, quibus diu confuestuerunt, aut cum maiori hominum parte damnari, quam cum alijs, quos oderunt, aut numero pauciores sunt, seruari velle. Sunt hi similes Ratholdi Frisia Orientalis principis, qui cum a Christiana religione alienus, vix multis Episcoporum precibus et laboriosa institutione eo adductus esse putaretur, ut Baptismum admissurus, et ad societatem Ecclesiae accessurus videretur, et alterum pedem in baptisterio posuisset, quasi ex Episcopo, coeli ne aut infernus plures homines continerent? Et cum hic ex Christi verbis respondisset, plures esse damnatorum, eo quod lata sit porta et spatiosa via, quae abducit in exitium, et multos esse qui per eam ingrediuntur: retraxit ille pedem ex baptisterio, et se cum maiori hominum turba manere velle dixit. At qui ita sentiunt, animum omnino prophanum praediti sunt, et fidem aut omnino nullam, aut (quod idem fere est) illam cum respectu personarum habent: quod ne fiat, Apostolus prohibet. Multi etiam nimium curiosi scire cupiunt, quae in illo die sors eorum futura sit, quibus nunc familiariter conuersantur, et dum de alijs solliciti sunt, propriam salutem negligunt. His omnibus medetur Dominus, et docet, ex omni hominum loco et ordine aliquos assumendos fore in beatorum numerum, qui (ut Paulus exponit) cum alijs electis, tam resuscitatis quam ijs, quos dies ille superstites deprehendit, ipsi obuiam per aerem in eius occursum rapiantur, aliquos vero relinquendos, sempiterno exitio nimirum, ut cum diabolo et eius angelis, cum bestia item et Pseudopropheta siue Antichristo in stagnum ignis et sulphuris conijciantur. Tunc duo (inquit) erunt in agro, simul iterfacientes, aut ijsdem operibus intenti, unus assumetur, et alter relinquetur. Duae item molentes in pistrino (per quas Christus vniuersos seruilis conditionis homines et vilissima quaeque mancipia intelligit) una assumetur, et altera relinquetur. Apud Lucam tertium adhuc par hominum additur, coniugium nempe: Illa nocte erunt duo in uno lecto: unus assumetur, et alter relinquetur. Sub his autem tribus partibus hominum omnes quotquot in mundo sunt, coniuges aut caelibes, seruos aut liberos, rusticos aut vrbanos, diuites aut pauperes, aut cuiuscunq; tandem loci sint, compleditur, et de singulis eorum idem dicit, Vnus assumetur, et alter relinquetur. Vbi primo obseruabimus, omnes sistendos fore ad tribunal Christi, nec quenquam se tunc posse huius iudicio subducere. Deinde est hoc bonitatis Dei paterna euidens testimonium, quod ex quouis genere hominum electos suos deligit, quos ad regni sui caelestis haereditatem assumat, nec quenquam propter sexum aut conditionem excludit, aut salutem ad aliquod singulare vitae genus astringit. Itaq; confutantur hic, qui vel caelibatum, vel monasticam vota, vel alia huius generis obtrudere conantur, quasi in illis solis seruari possimus. Et minimum audaces sunt, qui aliquos ordines simpliciter damnant, ut coniugium, Magistratus et similes. Atqui omnium eadem est ratio, quod in ijs aliqui seruabuntur, alij damnabuntur. Nihil erit proderit, natio, genus, sexus, aetas, conditio. Quid ergo? Sola fides per charitatem agens, et
units.tr: As for the dealings we have with friends and equals, many find it so hard and inhuman to be parted from them that they do not hesitate to say they would rather be damned with those they have long been familiar with, or with the greater part of mankind, than be saved with others whom they hate, or with a smaller number. They are like Ratbod, prince of East Frisia, who, being a stranger to the Christian religion, was barely thought to have been brought, by many prayers of bishops and laborious instruction, to the point of being about to receive baptism and join the fellowship of the Church. He had already placed one foot in the baptistery when he asked the bishop whether heaven or hell held more people. When the bishop replied from Christ's words that the damned are more numerous, because the gate is wide and the way broad that leads to destruction, and that many enter by it, Ratbod drew his foot back out of the baptistery and said he wanted to remain with the greater crowd. Those who think this way have a wholly profane mind, and either have no faith at all or (which comes to much the same) have a faith that respects persons; the Apostle forbids this. Many, too, are overly curious and wish to know what fate awaits on that day those with whom they now live in familiar company, and while they are anxious about others, they neglect their own salvation. The Lord remedies all of this and teaches that from every rank and station of men some will be taken into the number of the blessed, who (as Paul explains) together with the other elect, both those raised from the dead and those whom that day finds still alive, will be caught up in the air to meet him; and that others will be left behind, namely to everlasting destruction, to be cast with the devil and his angels, and likewise with the beast and the false prophet or Antichrist, into the lake of fire and brimstone. "Then," he says, "two will be in the field, working together; one will be taken and the other left." "Two women grinding at the mill" (by which Christ means all men of servile condition and the lowest kind of slaves) likewise: "one will be taken and the other left."
