In Luke a third pair of men is added, namely married couples: "In that night there will be two in one bed; one will be taken and the other left." Under these three pairs all who are in the world are included, whether married or single, slaves or free, country folk or townsfolk, rich or poor, or of whatever place they may be; and of each of them he says the same: "One will be taken and the other left." Here we first observe that all will be brought before the tribunal of Christ, and that no one will be able to escape his judgement. Next, this is a clear testimony of God's fatherly goodness, that he chooses his elect from every kind of men to take them to the inheritance of his heavenly kingdom, and excludes no one on account of sex or condition, nor binds salvation to any single way of life. Thus those are refuted who try to impose celibacy, monastic vows, or things of this kind, as if we could be saved only in them. And they are very bold who simply condemn certain estates, such as marriage, the magistracy and the like. Yet the reasoning for all is the same: some in them will be saved, others damned. Nation, kind, sex, age and condition will avail nothing. What then? Faith alone, working through love, and a new creature.

units.la: ɘ 2 noua creatura. Discant ergo singulí in sua vocatione pietati studere, coniuges sanctè viuant, liberos suos in timore Dei instituant, pauperes in sua egestate patientes sint, neminem defraudent, diuites bonis operibus abundent, & beneficijnt in quosuis, meminerint denique omnes terroris illius Domini, quem nemo effugiet, & quòd omnes coram tribunali Christi sisti oportebit, vt vnusquisque reportet quæ in corpore suo fecit, congruenter ad id, quæ fecerit, vel bonum vel malum.
units.tr: Let each therefore learn in his own calling to apply himself to godliness: let married people live holily, bring up their children in the fear of God, let the poor be patient in their want, defraud no one, let the rich abound in good works and be generous to all, and finally let all remember the terror of that Lord whom no one will escape, and that all must stand before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive what he has done in the body, according to whatever he has done, good or evil.

units.la: Porrò quia hora aduentus Christi incerta est, eò magis studio & vigilantia opus est, ne ex improuiso opprimamur, sed vt tales inueniat Dominus, quales inueniri debent serui industrij, qui heris suis probari cupiunt. Infert ergo in præsenti: Vigilate ergo. Non loquitur de corporis vigilia, aut matutinis Monachorum. Nam alibi, vt omni tempore vigilemus, iubet. Id verò vires nostras superat, & vt cibo ac potu nobis opus est, itafomno tarere non possumus, quo vires omnium defessas aut exhaustas instaurari oportet. Et quod olim per Zachariam Iudæus dicebat: Quando ieunastis & planxistis in quinto & septimo mense, num mihi ieunastis? & cum comeditis & bibitis, annon vobis comeditis & bibitis? Hoc ipsum similiter de papisticis vigilijs ac matutinis potest dici: Quando dormitis, annon vobis ipsis, non mihi, dormitis? Quando vigilatis, annon vobis vigilatis? Verum certè fiat, Deo illic neq; seritur neque metitur, nisi aliud accedat, propter quod probari aut improbari mereatur, quod facimus. Et vt somnus donum Dei est, ita exercitatio corporis non multum prodest ad salutem, quæ hoc potius requirit, vt a peccatis quiescamus, & Domino feriemur, quod ad Sabbatum est præstitu necessarium. Itaque ad animum hoc omne, quod de vigilia dicitur, transferri debet, qui perpetuis meditationibus de aduentu Christi & præceptis Dei excitari debet, vt ad hunc perpetuò vigilent & parati sint ad illum excipiendum. Additur autem præcepto causa, argumentum firmissimum continens. Nescitis enim, qua hora Dominus vester venturus est. Enimuerò qui frugi serui sunt, quò incertior est hora, qua herus veniet, eò diligentius vigilant, ne ille ex improuiso ipsos imparatos obruat: Ita vos facere oportet, quando bonus Dei seruus non potest censeri, nisi quem herus adueniens in officio sedulum & industrium inuenerit. Addit his aliud a vulgari more desumptum, dicens: Illud autem sciote, si sciret paterfamilias, qua vigilia fur venturus sit, vigilaret, nec sineret perfodi domum suam. Ad quod simile Petrus respexisse videtur, quando diem illum Domini sicut furem no stu venturum ait. Ita verò execrabilis hominum securitas arguitur in ijs, vbi maximè solicitos esse oportebat. In custodiendis pecunijs & ijs omnibus, quæ ad rem domesticam & victum faciunt nullius laboris aut molestiæ nos piget, imò totas noctes insomnes ducere iuuat. At quando animarum salus periclitatur, omnium immemores altum dormimus. Oberrat hinc inde communis hostis Satan instar Leonis rugientis, & quærit quem deuoret. Sed facile contemni possunt huius insidiæ a veris Christi cultoribus, qui hostem illum ab hoc deuistum & caput eius conculcatum seneorunt. Interim autem cogitandum nobis erat, ignauis & securis ab ipso Christo periculum esse, ne ex improuiso ille nobis superueniat. Et sanè tanta est in eo multorum ignauia, vt illis meritò exprobres, quod olim cuidam Satyricus: Vt iugulent homines, surgunt de nocte latrones: Tu vt teipsum serues, non expergisceris?
units.tr: Moreover, because the hour of Christ's coming is uncertain, all the more zeal and vigilance are needed, lest we be overtaken unawares, but that the Lord may find us such as faithful and diligent servants ought to be found, who wish to be approved by their masters. He therefore adds in the present passage: "Watch therefore." He is not speaking of bodily wakefulness or the matins of monks, for elsewhere he bids us watch at all times. But that surpasses our powers; just as we need food and drink, so we cannot do without sleep, by which the strength of all who are weary or exhausted must be restored. And what the Jews once said through Zechariah applies here: "When you fasted and mourned in the fifth and seventh month, did you fast for me? And when you eat and drink, do you not eat and drink for yourselves?" The same can similarly be said of the Papists' vigils and matins: when you sleep, do you not sleep for yourselves and not for me? When you keep vigil, do you not keep it for yourselves? Indeed, whatever is done, God neither sows nor reaps there, unless something else is added on account of which what we do may deserve approval or disapproval. And just as sleep is a gift of God, so bodily exercise does little for salvation, which requires rather that we rest from sins and be at leisure for the Lord, which is what the Sabbath requires. Therefore all that is said about vigilance ought to be transferred to the mind, which ought to be stirred by constant meditation on Christ's coming and God's precepts, so that it may keep vigil for him continually and be ready to receive him. A reason is added to the precept, containing a most firm argument: "You do not know at what hour your Lord will come." Indeed, faithful servants, the less certain the hour at which the master will come, the more diligently they keep watch, lest he overtake them unprepared. So you ought to do, since a good servant of God cannot be counted as such unless the master, on arriving, finds him attentive and diligent at his duty. He adds to this something taken from common custom, saying: "But know this: if the householder knew at what watch the thief would come, he would keep watch and not let his house be broken into." Peter seems to have had this similar idea in mind when he says that the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night. Thus the detestable security of men is shown up precisely where they ought to be most anxious. In guarding money and all that pertains to household affairs and livelihood we shrink from no labour or trouble; indeed we delight to pass whole nights without sleep. But when the salvation of souls is in danger, we forget everything and sleep soundly. The common enemy Satan prowls about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour. Yet his snares can easily be despised by true worshippers of Christ, who have overcome that enemy and trampled his head. Meanwhile we must consider that there is danger for the idle and the careless from Christ himself, that he may come upon us unawares. And indeed there is so much idleness in many that one may fittingly reproach them with what the satirist once said to someone: "That robbers may cut men's throats, they rise in the night; that you may save yourself, will you not wake up?"

units.la: Sed excitent nos tristia, quæ passim incidunt exempla, neque vnquam animis nostris excidat huius loci conclusio, qua Dominus noster IESVS CHRISTVS sfrugi patrisfamilias exemplum discipulis suis omnibus applicans, dicit: Propterea & vos estote parati: quia qua hora non putatis Filius hominis venturus est. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: But let the sad examples that fall under our eyes everywhere rouse us, and let the conclusion of this passage never slip from our minds, in which our Lord Jesus Christ, applying the example of the good householder to all his disciples, says: "Therefore you also be ready, for the Son of Man will come at an hour you do not expect." To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCLXXXIII.
units.tr: Homily CCLXXXIII.

units.la: Quis nam est fidelis seruus & prudens, quem constituit Dominus super famulitiū suum, vt det illis alimentum in tempore? Beatus ser-uus ille, uus ille quem cum venerit dominus eius, inuenerit sic facientem: Amen dico vobis, omnibus bonis suis praeficiet eum. Quod si dixerit seruus ille malus in corde suo: Tardat dominus meus aduentum: coepit percutere conseruos, quin etiam edere & bibere cum ebrijs: Veniet dominus serui illius die quo non expectat, & hora qua non nouit: & separabit eum, ac partem eius asignabit cum hypocritis: illic erit fletus & stridor dentium.
units.tr: "Who then is the faithful and wise servant, whom his lord has set over his household, to give them food in due season? Blessed is that servant whom his lord, when he comes, will find so doing. Truly I say to you, he will set him over all his goods. But if that evil servant says in his heart, 'My lord delays his coming,' and begins to beat his fellow servants, and also to eat and drink with drunkards, the lord of that servant will come on a day when he does not expect him, and at an hour he does not know, and will cut him in pieces and assign him his portion with the hypocrites: there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth." (Matt. 24.)

units.la: EXposuit hucusq; Dei Filius IESVS CHRISTVS spericulosum nouissimi seculi statum, monuit in genere, vt omnes homines seipsos in suum aduentum praeparare debeant. Quia verò pleriq; in iis, quae ad futura & caelestia spectant negligentiores sunt, & idcirco publicis monitoribus & excubitoribus opus est, qui illos ad officium excitent, & in singulas horas quasi ad officium faciendum vrgeant, ne hi ipsi, qui aliorum oeconomiam esse debent, vel ignaui dormitent, vel aliquid dolo malo peccent, vel etiam potestate sibi data improbe abutantur, in praesenti hoc quoq; in suo munere instituit. Estq; locus hic consideratione dignissimus. Nam & ministros Verbi & Ecclesiarum omnes, quid ipsos facere conueniat, docet, & reliquos omnes priuatim & publice instituit, vt de illis & eorum munere iudicare debeant. Vt verò magis perspicuafit tractatio, parabola eam vestit, cuius summa est: Vt paterfamilias nobilis & dues peregre abitu-rus, alicui ex feruis, quorum fidem & prudentiam probe perspectam habet, familiam commendat, vt & rem domesticam fideliter & sapienter administret, & domesticos omnes pro virili in officio contineat, vt domum reuerso possit rationem reddere: Ita ego ex mundo abiturus ad Patrem vos Apostolos & vestri similes successores constituo, qui Ecclesiae meae curam gerere, & quae cunq; ad hanc spectant, rectè administrare & omnes in ordine retinere possitis. Comprehendit parabola haec quaecunq; de Ecclesia & eius administratione, & simul de vniuerso, quod hinc dependet, saluitis nostrae mysterio dici possunt. De quibus perspicuitatis ergo hoc ordine disseremus. Primo de ministerij huius authore dicetur. Deinde quales ministri sint, quos Dominus Ecclesiae praeficit. Tertio quibus illos praefecerit. Quarto in quibus horum officium siue munus consistat. Tandem, quo praemio fideles & industrios seruos remuneretur Deus, quibus item poenis improbos multet.
units.tr: Hitherto the Son of God, Jesus Christ, has set out the perilous state of the last age and has admonished all people in general that they ought to prepare themselves for his coming. But since most people are rather careless about things that concern the future and the heavenly, there is need of public monitors and watchmen who rouse them to their duty and urge them, hour by hour, as it were, to perform it, lest these very men, who ought to be the stewards of others, either sleep idly, or sin by deceit, or even abuse with wickedness the power given to them. Therefore, in this present passage he also instructs them concerning their office. And this place is most worthy of consideration. For he both teaches all the ministers of the Word and of the Churches what it befits them to do, and instructs all the rest, privately and publicly, so that they may be able to judge concerning those men and their office. So that the treatment may be clearer, a parable clothes it, whose sum is this: a noble and wealthy householder, about to go abroad, commends his household to one of his servants whose faithfulness and prudence he has well proven, so that he may manage the domestic affairs faithfully and wisely, and keep all the household in their duty as far as he can, so that he can render an account when he returns home. So I, about to depart from the world to the Father, appoint you apostles and those like you as successors, so that you may be able to take care of my Church, administer rightly whatever pertains to it, and keep everyone in order. This parable comprises whatever can be said about the Church and its administration, and at the same time about everything that depends on it and pertains to the mystery of our salvation. Concerning these things we shall speak in the following order, for clarity. First, the author of this ministry will be spoken of. Second, what sort of ministers they are whom the Lord sets over the Church. Third, to whom he has set them over. Fourth, in what their office or function consists. Finally, with what reward God remunerates faithful and diligent servants, and with what punishments he likewise punishes the wicked.

units.la: Quoad primum, seipsum ministerij huius aut muneris authorem profitetur, cum dicit: Quis nam est fidelis seruus & prudens, quem constituit Dominus? Idcirco & in veteri & nouo Testamento ipse Deus aliquos immediate vocauit, olim quidem plerosque Prophetas, postea verò Apostolos, quos Dei Filius in hunc ordinem adoptauit: Vt nimirum testaretur, se illius authore esse. Nec obstat, quod hodie non omnes eodem modo vocantur. Eadem enim ministerij ratio est, quae aliarum functionum, quas Deus instituit. Primam mulierem ex Adami costa formatam viro coniunxit Deus, & ipse horum coniugio benedixit: vt ex eo constaret, coniugium a Deo institutum esse, & ideo de omnibus, qui legitimè coniunguntur, rectè dicitur, Quod Deus coniunxit, homo nesepa-ret. Ita cum nulla potestas sit, quàm quae a Deo est, Magistratuum quoq; omnium dignitas & authoritas, diuina merito censetur. Quotquot ergo Ecclesiae ministerio praeficiuntur, similiter a Deo electi, vel missi dici debent, qui vt ita fiat instituit & canones quoq; certos praescripsit, qui in elestionibus eiusmodi obseruari debeant. Ideo Paulus ad Ephesios scribebat, Christum esse, qui Spiritus sui dona dispensat inter homines, & alios quidem dat Apostolos, alios autem Pastores ac doctores, alios autem Prophetas & Euangelistas ad coaugmentationem sanctorum, ad opus ministerij, ad aedificationem corporis Christi. Et idem Asia ministris siue doctoribus Mileti in Syno coastis, dicebat: Attendite vobisipsos & totum gregem, in quo vos Spiritus sanctus constituit Episcopos adpascendam Ecclesiam. Ideo antiquitus per manuum impositionem Ecclesiae ministerium legitimè designatis committebatur, vt constaret publicè omnibus, eos Domino consecratos esse. Et hodie adhuc huius Ceremoniae vsus nobis esse debet, vt nemo ministros Ecclesiae a vulgo hominum nihil differre putet, aut propter vilem personam inter homines aspectum eos contemnat. Nam si hoc faciat, in ipsum Deum contemptus redundat, a quo illi missi sunt. Testatus est
units.tr: As to the first, he declares himself the author of this ministry or office, when he says: "Who then is the faithful and wise servant whom the Lord has set over his household?" Therefore, both in the Old and the New Testament, God himself called some immediately: formerly indeed many prophets, and afterwards the apostles, whom the Son of God adopted into this order, so that he might testify that he is its author. Nor does it stand in the way that today not all are called in the same way. For the principle of the ministry is the same as that of the other functions which God instituted. God joined the first woman, formed from Adam's rib, to the man, and himself blessed their union, so that it might be established that marriage was instituted by God; and so it is rightly said of all who are lawfully joined, "What God has joined together, let not man put asunder." Thus, since there is no power except that which is from God, the dignity and authority of all magistrates is also rightly regarded as divine. Therefore all who are set over the ministry of the Church should likewise be said to be chosen or sent by God; and that this may happen, he has instituted and also prescribed certain rules to be observed in such elections. Hence Paul wrote to the Ephesians that Christ is the one who distributes the gifts of his Spirit among men, and gives some as apostles, others as pastors and teachers, and others as prophets and evangelists, for the equipping of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the building up of the body of Christ. And to the ministers or teachers of Asia gathered at Miletus, he said the same: "Take heed to yourselves and to the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has made you bishops to feed the Church." Therefore, in antiquity, the ministry of the Church was committed by the laying on of hands to those legitimately designated, so that it might be publicly known to all that they were consecrated to the Lord. And even today the use of this ceremony ought to be retained among us, so that no one thinks ministers of the Church differ in no way from the common crowd, or despises them among men on account of their humble person. For if he does so, the contempt falls back upon God himself, by whom they were sent. He testified to this

units.la: 3 hoc olim Dominus, cum Samueli de Israelitis ipsum aspernantibus diceret: Non te reprobant, sed me reprobarunt. Et huic consentit Christus Apostolis dicens: Qui vos audit, me audit: qui vos spernit, me spernit, &c. Et Paulus idcirco monebat: Deus erat in Christo mundum sibi reconcilians, non imputando illis peccata ipsorum, posuitque in nobis sermonem hunc reconciliationis. Itaque nomine Christi legatione fungimur, veluti Deo vos precante per nos, &c. Est haec magna ministrorum dignitas, qua alios homines longe superant: cuius consideratio auditores terrere debet, ne docentes contemnant aut scurriliter aspernentur. Si enim secundum ius gentium quoduis supplicium merentur, imo digni sunt, qui bello excindantur funditus, qui Regis legatos pacem offerentes violant, quanto magis suam iram in eos stringit Deus, qui pacem eam reiciunt, quam nobis Dei Filius sanguine suo pretioso acquisivit? Interim hoc ipsum Verbi praecones officii sui admoneat, ne quid praeter dignitatem suam faciant, & hanc morum turpitudine prosti- tuant. Regiae maiestatis & Senatoriae gravitatis splendor in legatis relucere debet. Nam si in verbis dicacitas scurrilis audiatur, in moribus levitas appareat, una cum ipsis Magistratuum authoritas concidit. In Verbi & Ecclesiae ministris autem hoc peccatum eo gravius est, quo major est ministerii dignitas, quam sustinent, cui non solum modo publica, verum etiam gloria Dei coniuncta est.
units.tr: 3 Long ago the Lord did so, when he said to Samuel about the Israelites who despised him: "They have not rejected you, but they have rejected me." Christ agrees with this, saying to the apostles: "He who hears you hears me; he who rejects you rejects me," etc. And Paul therefore warned: "God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, not imputing their sins to them, and has placed in us the word of this reconciliation. So we serve as ambassadors in the name of Christ, as though God were pleading with you through us," etc. This is the great dignity of ministers, by which they far surpass other men. Its consideration ought to terrify the hearers, lest they despise the teachers or mock them with scurrilous contempt. For if, according to the law of nations, they deserve any punishment whatever, indeed if they are worthy to be utterly destroyed in war, those who violate the envoys of a king who offer peace, how much more does God direct his anger against those who reject that peace which the Son of God has won for us by his precious blood? Meanwhile, this same thing should admonish the heralds of the Word of their duty, that they do nothing unworthy of their dignity, and do not prostitute it by moral baseness. The splendour of royal majesty and senatorial gravity ought to shine forth in ambassadors. For if scurrilous wit is heard in their words, and levity appears in their conduct, the authority of the magistrates themselves falls together with them. In the ministers of the Word and the Church, moreover, this sin is the more grave, the greater the dignity of the ministry they bear, to which is joined not only public esteem but also the glory of God.

units.la: Secundo quales sint hi, de quibus hic agitur, videamus, & quo nomine sive titulo eos appellare Christus dignetur. Quis est (inquit) ferus? Non heram aut dominum, non satrapam, non regem, multo minus tyrannum dicit, sed Seruum. Et quia servorum non unum genus est, illud de quo hic sermo est, a ceteris distinguens, ait: Quis est servus fidelis & prudens, quem constituit Dominus super familiam suum, ut det illis alimentum in tempore? De servo igitur domus administratore loquitur, quem nos Oeconomum vel Dispensatorem solemus dicere. Itaque Ecclesiae ministrum, qui hodie vulgo Episcopi aut Antistites & Praesules dici gaudent, ita definire possumus, ut dicamus esse Seruum IESV CHRISTI & Ecclesiae, dispensatorem eius cibi, quo fidelium animae aluntur ad vitam aeternam. Et ita hunc locum Paulus intellexit, cum Corinthijs non recte de hoc ministerio iudicantibus scriberet: Sic de nobis reputet homo, ut de ministris Christi & dispensatoribus mysteriorum Dei. At quia hic Apostolus, & in horum persona omnibus horum successoribus, qui Ecclesiarum ministri sunt, loquitur Dominus, non tam in eo nobis laborandum est, quales nos aestimare debeant alij, quam ut nos nomini nobis a Christo impositio respondeamus. Nec enim temere servi vocabulo usum esse putabimus eum, qui aeterna est Patris Sapientia. Quia enim hunc superbiae fomitem ex primis parentibus, quo accensi altum sapimus, & reliquis praestare cupimus, ne is in hoc tam sancto & necessario munere se proferendi occasionem facile inveniret, nominis nota cavere voluit. Potuit eum de hoc admonere (siquidem ipsi admonitione opus esset, qui omnia novit) quam in Apostolis toties iam deprehenderat supra alios eminendi cupiditas. Ut ergo servos vocat Verbi sui praecones Dominus, ita quicunque hoc munus sibi creditum vident, quoties ex communi & recepto more se honoris causa dominos appellari audiunt, non ex eo superbiendi occasione arripiant, sed hunc honorem Verbo & Deo debere, se autem servos esse meminerint. De Augusto, potentissimo Romanorum Imperatore scribitur, quod immodicas & indecoras theatri adulationes publico edicto represserit, quo se dominum post hac appellari vetuit: quod ex Spiritu Christi, qui tunc temporis in carne natus erat, factum fuisse, quis dubitet? Quanto magis ergo IESV CHRISTI praecones hac humilitas decet, ne arroganti dominorum titulo superbiant. Multum quidem in Apostolis coercendis olim laborauit Christus, quos interdum graviter correptos repressit, ut de seipsis humilius sentirent, & alij alijs mutua praestarent officia. At quam parum apud personatos illorum successores profecerit, res ipsa loquitur. Pontifices nimirum, qui quasi cum Christo ludant, Servi servorum quidem appellari volunt, & simul humeris aliorum sublimes gestantur, triplici corona redimiti imperium in coelo, terris & inferno sibi vendicant, regna mundi universa suae ditioni subiiciunt, reges denique & Imperatores ad pedum suorum osculA inuitant, & reuera cornu illud paruum sunt apud Danielem, cui datum est os loquens grandia. Non invenisse ergo quidam de illis cecinit:
units.tr: Second, let us see what sort those are of whom we are speaking here, and by what name or title Christ deigns to call them. "Who is the servant?" he says. He does not call him mistress, master, satrap, king, much less tyrant, but servant. And since there is not just one kind of servant, he distinguishes the one of whom he speaks from the others, saying: "Who is the faithful and wise servant whom the Lord has set over his household, to give them food in due season?" He speaks, therefore, of a servant who administers a house, whom we are accustomed to call steward or dispenser. Thus we may define the minister of the Church, whom today commonly rejoice to be called bishops, prelates or overseers, as the servant of Jesus Christ and of the Church, the dispenser of that food by which the souls of believers are nourished to eternal life. And Paul understood this place in this way, when he wrote to the Corinthians who were judging this ministry wrongly: "Let a man so regard us, as ministers of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God." But since here the Apostle, and in their person the Lord, speaks to all their successors who are ministers of the Churches, we ought to be concerned less with what others may think we ought to be than with answering to the name imposed on us by Christ. For we shall not suppose that he who is the eternal Wisdom of the Father used the word servant rashly. For since he wished to guard against this spark of pride, inherited from our first parents, by which we are kindled to think highly of ourselves and to desire to excel the rest, lest it easily find in this so holy and necessary office an occasion to show itself, he wished to guard against it by the mark of the name. He could have warned them about this (if indeed they needed a warning, he who knows all things), since the desire to stand out above others had already so often been detected in the apostles. Therefore, just as the Lord calls the heralds of his Word servants, so whoever sees this office entrusted to him, whenever he hears himself called lord out of common and accepted custom as a mark of honour, should not seize on it as an occasion for pride, but remember that this honour is owed to the Word and to God, and that he himself is a servant. It is written of Augustus, the most powerful emperor of the Romans, that by public edict he suppressed the immoderate and shameful flatteries of the theatre, and forbade himself to be called lord from then on. Who would doubt that this was done by the Spirit of Christ, who had been born in the flesh at that time? How much more, then, should this humility befit the heralds of Jesus Christ, that they not be puffed up by the arrogant title of lords. Christ indeed long laboured much to restrain the apostles, whom he sometimes rebuked sharply and checked, so that they might think of themselves more humbly and render mutual services to one another. But how little he has achieved among their masked successors, the thing itself speaks. Pontiffs, to be sure, who as it were play with Christ, wish to be called "servants of servants," and at the same time are carried aloft on the shoulders of others; crowned with a triple crown, they claim for themselves rule in heaven, on earth and in hell, subject all the kingdoms of the world to their power, and finally invite kings and emperors to kiss their feet. And truly they are that little horn in Daniel, to which was given a mouth speaking great things. Hence someone wrote of them:

units.la: Roma tibi serui fuerant domini dominorum, Seruorum serui nunc tibi sunt domini.
units.tr: Rome, once the slaves were masters of masters for you; now the slaves of slaves are masters for you.

units.la: Et quidem detestabilis fastus ille Sybariticus, quo isti homines iam saeculis aliquot superbiunt, et pro quo tuendo bella quoque gerunt, quibus orbem terrarum vbiq; turbant: at grauior multo et intolerabilior est tyrannis, quae sub religionis praetextu in conscientias dominantur, et nouos fidei articulos condunt: libertatem deniq; Christianam ita circumscribunt, vt per illos gratis neq; nasci neq; mori liceat: deniq; patrimonium Petri pauperis et annulum piscatoris pleno ore iactantes, regna et opes totius mundi devorant, et (quod olim de illis Petrus vaticinatus est) per avaritiam fictis sermonibus animis simplicium, quos in nassam suam alliciunt, negotiantur.
units.tr: That detestable Sybaritic pride, in which these men have been puffing themselves up for some centuries now, and for defending which they wage wars that throw the whole world into turmoil, is indeed hateful. Much graver and more intolerable, however, is the tyranny that, under the pretext of religion, lords it over consciences and frames new articles of faith. Finally, they so restrict Christian liberty that, under their rules, one may be neither born nor die freely. Then, boasting loudly of the patrimony of poor Peter and the fisherman's ring, they devour the kingdoms and wealth of the whole world, and (as Peter once prophesied of them) by covetousness, with feigned words, they make merchandise of simple souls, whom they lure into their net.

units.la: Atqui deiecta est ia npridem spiritu oris Dominici magna ex parte tyrannis illa, vt iam ridiculi et exsufflint plerique isti Penelopes spuli, quorum potestas nuper caelo aequata esse videbatur: nec potuit eos diutius ferre Rex gloriae IESVS CHRISTVS, vt sui ministerij praetextu tam arroganter imperium in memoriam sua exercerent. Ergo neq; eos idem ille feret, qui hodie gigantes illos Verbi fulmine profligatos rursum in pedes erigere, et regnum illis restituere conantur.
units.tr: Yet that tyranny has for the most part been cast down by the breath of the Lord's mouth, so that many of those men, whose power only lately seemed raised to heaven, are now ridiculed and blown away. Christ, the King of glory, could not bear them any longer, nor suffer them to exercise their dominion so arrogantly in the name of his ministry. Therefore the same Christ will not bear them either, and those who today try to set on their feet again those giants struck down by the thunderbolt of the Word, and to restore their kingdom to them, will not be spared.

units.la: Ne alium de nouae tyrannidis surgat, nobis cauendum est fratres. Non desunt enim infelices medici, qui vulnus illud lethale, quod Christus libera ac syncera Euangelij praedicatione bestiae huic inflixit, obligare, et hanc nouis viribus instaurare satagunt: dum doctrinae libertatem nouis legibus circumscribunt, errores abolitos reuocant, ceremoniarum chaos in Ecclesiam reducunt, sacramentis, quod solius Christi est, tribuere docent, idololatriae nouas fenestras aperiunt, potestatem nouis vendicant quidam in Ecclesia statuendi et interdum propter non graues neq; iustas causas ordinarios et legitimos pastores, qui gregi suo bene et fideliter praefuerunt, expellunt.
units.tr: Brethren, we must take care lest another such new tyranny arise. For there are no lack of unhappy physicians who strive to bind up that deadly wound which Christ inflicted on this beast by the free and pure preaching of the Gospel, and to restore it with new strength. They restrict the freedom of doctrine with new laws, recall errors that had been abolished, lead back into the Church the chaos of ceremonies, teach that what belongs to Christ alone is to be attributed to the sacrament, open new windows for idolatry, and some claim for themselves in the Church a new power of making decrees, and sometimes, for causes neither grave nor just, expel the ordinary and lawful ministers who have governed their flock well and faithfully.

units.la: Nec temere hoc moneo. Annon enim huius generis exempla vidit non itapridem Germania, quando propter omnis praesentiae corporis Christi fig mentum, orthodoxae et eruditae vetustati prorsus inauditum et incognitum, sub plausibili Concordiae praetextu omnes Ecclesiae perturbatae, vbique locorum differentiam sanctorum penitus, et ministri innumerabiles, eruditione, pietate et aetate graues sedibus suis pulsi, et in exilium atque egestatem cum vxoribus et dulcibus liberis eiecti sunt? Deplorant ergo solitudinem suam Ecclesiae, Scholae primis florentes barbariem metuunt, doctores meliora meriti incertis sedibus oberrant, viduae et orphani multorum lachrymis et singultibus loca omnia sacra et prophana complent.
units.tr: I do not give this warning rashly. Has not Germany itself recently seen examples of this kind? When, under the plausible pretext of concord, all the churches were thrown into confusion, the fiction of the presence of Christ's body everywhere (a thing utterly unheard of and unknown to sound and learned antiquity) was introduced, and innumerable ministers, weighty in learning, piety and age, were driven from their seats and cast into exile and poverty, with their wives and sweet children. Therefore the churches lament their desolation; schools that once flourished fear barbarism; teachers who deserved better wander about in uncertain dwellings; widows and orphans fill every sacred and profane place with the tears and sobs of many.

units.la: At haec non modo siccis oculis spectant Vbiquitatis Apostoli, qui passim obrepunt, et harum calamitatum authores sunt: sed insuper sub Cruce gementibus acetum cum felle miscent, Arianos et Turcas atque ipso Mahumete deteriores esse clamant eos, qui IESVM CHRISTVM verum et aeternum Dei Filium esse toto corde et ore rotundo fatentur, et eundem cum vetustissimis Symbolis ex matre Virgine carnem veram assumpsisse, in qua indignam mortem passus pro peccatis mundi perlitauit, resurrectione autem gloriosa mortem vicit, et τὴν ἀνάστασιν (vt Dinii Irenaei verbis vtar) εἰς τοὺς οὐρανοὺς ἀνάληψιν, id est, per in carne factam in caelos assumptionem beatae immortalitatis fores, quas Adami culpa nobis clauserat, retulit, vere et ingenue credunt atque docent.
units.tr: Yet the apostles of ubiquity do not look upon these calamities with dry eyes; they creep in everywhere and are the authors of these troubles. Moreover, they mix vinegar with gall for those who groan under the cross, and cry out that those who confess with their whole heart and open mouth that Jesus Christ is the true and eternal Son of God, and that he, as the most ancient creeds teach, assumed true flesh from the Virgin Mother, in which he suffered an unworthy death for the sins of the world and atoned for them, and by his glorious resurrection conquered death, and who truly and sincerely believe and teach that the resurrection (to use the words of Irenaeus) was the ascension into heaven [ἀνάστασιν εἰς τοὺς οὐρανοὺς ἀνάληψιν], that is, that the assumption into heaven in the flesh opened again the gates of blessed immortality which Adam's fault had closed to us, are worse than Arians and Turks, and even worse than Mohammed himself.

units.la: Interim infinu gaudent, si dum his iniuriis immerentes grauant, ipsi securi belluantur, opum thesauros colligunt, equis phaleratis et curribus altis sublimes vehuntur. Videt hos procul dubio IESVS CHRISTVS ex alto, et veniet olim dies, quo poenas ab illis, quas meruerunt, exiget, de quibus paulo post dicetur. Non offendat ergo nunc illorum fastus et tyrannidem miseros et innocentes, qui ab illis opprimuntur: omnes vero, qui Ecclesijs seruiunt, sibi loqui putent Petrum Apostolum, cum scribit: Presbyteros, qui inter vos sunt, precor ego vna presbyter ac testis passionum Christi, atque idem gloriae patefaciendae consors: Pascite gregem, qui in vobis est, illius conspectioni vacantes non coacte, sed libenter, non turpiter affectantes lucrum, sed prompto animo: neque vt dominantes clero, sed vt qui sitis exemplaria gregis. 1.Pet.5.
units.tr: Meanwhile they rejoice secretly if, while they burden these innocent men with injuries, they themselves live carelessly in luxury, gather up treasures of wealth, and ride proudly in harnessed horses and high chariots. Jesus Christ surely sees them from on high, and a day will come when he will exact from them the punishments they have deserved, of which we will speak shortly. Let not the pride and tyranny of those men offend the wretched and innocent who are oppressed by them. But all who serve the churches should think that the Apostle Peter speaks to them when he writes: "The elders who are among you I exhort, I who am a fellow elder and a witness of the sufferings of Christ, and a partaker of the glory to be revealed: feed the flock of God that is among you, exercising oversight not under compulsion but willingly, not for shameful gain but eagerly, not domineering over those in your charge but being examples to the flock." 1 Pet. 5.

units.la: Tertio, quibus domui suae Ecclesiae suae ministros Christus praefecerit, videamus, et quam late pateat ipsorum prouincia. Docet hoc vno verbo, dum dicit se de illo loqui, quem confituerit Dominus super famulitium suum. Dicitur sic vniuersa famulorum multitudo ad vnam fa-miliam aut herum pertinens, adeoq; omnes quotquot vna familia comprehenduntur. Atqui fami-lia sive domus Domini est Ecclesia. Qui enim in templis manufactis non habitat, in medio fide-lium suorum se habitare velle pollicetur, & quem cæli cælorum non capiunt, is in humili & con-trito hominis pij & fidelis corde locum & sedem sibi deligit. Vt autem omnes quotquot Ecclesiæ membra sunt, Christus fratres suos sibi fecit & coharedes, ita ijdem ipsius serui & famuli sunt, & ad eiusdem Patris cælestis familiam pertinent. Sub illius ergo famulitio censentur, docti indocti, divites pauperes, nobiles obscuri, omnium gentium Dynastæ, Reges, Imperatores, Dictatores, Co-sules, Iudices, principes & regnorum præfecti. Nam hi omnes illius fauore & gratia ad tale fastigium euecti sunt. Eidem parent artium & linguarum professores, opifices, milites, urbani, rustici, nautæ, aurigæ, heri, serui, parentes, liberi, coniugati, cælibes: omnes deniq; cuiuscunq; sint conditionis, sexus, ætatis, loci & ordinis, qui tunc demum suum gradum & ordinem tuebuntur, & felices aut beati in eo dici poterunt, si se Christi regis regum & Domini dominantium famulos esse memi-nerint. Ex his ergo omnibus nobile illud & sanctum famulitium conflat, ex quo familia Dei Patris cælestis constituitur, in qua omnes famuli sunt & filij hæriles, serui & liberi, Reges deniq; & Sacerdotes altissimi. Huic famulitio seruum hunc, de quo nobis sermo est, præfecit Dominus, illius curam hunc vult gerere, & vt eundem omnes, qui in ipsius familia sunt, obseruent, requirit. Nemo igitur se vel liberum prorsus, vel immunem esse, gloriari poterit, nisi qui ab hac tam sancta familia, extra quam salus nulla est, velit esse alienus. Idem alibi quoq; docet Dominus. Etenim apud Ezechielem de eodem ministerio loquens: Fili hominis (inquit) speculatorem constitui te domui Israelis. At qui domum nominat, omnes, qui in domo sunt, comprehendit. Itaq; illic quoq; vni-cæ domus appellatione omnes hominum ordines ministro verbi sui subijcit. Apud Ieremiam vero apertius loquitur: Ecce ego posui verba mea in os tuum: Ecce ego constitui te hodie super gentes & super regna, vt euellas & extirpes, vt ædifices & plantes. Non ergo aliquam gentem vel vetustas vel victoria & triumphi, vel obscuritas & clades huius ministerij curæ subtrahent. Non item doctos & eruditos sua eruditio, non sua maiestas reges, non alios magistratus sua autho-ritas, non diuites sua opulentia, non pauperes sua egestas, non seruos seruitus, non ingenuos li-bertas, non cives sua astutia, non rusticos vel sua versutia vel simplicitas, non parentes liberorum educatio, non liberos sua in parentes pietas, non cælibes diu custoditus virginitatis flos, non coniuges mutuus amor & fides coniugalis, liberabit, quo minus huc Dei seruum obseruare, & ijs, quæ ex Domini ore ille profert, obedire debeant.
units.tr: Thirdly, let us see over whose house, that is, his Church, Christ has set his ministers, and how widely their province extends. He teaches this in one word when he says that he is speaking of the one whom the Lord has set over his household [famulitium]. In this way the whole multitude of servants is said to belong to one family or master, and so all who are included in one family. But the family, or house, of the Lord is the Church. For he who does not dwell in temples made by hands promises to dwell in the midst of his faithful, and he whom the heavens of heavens cannot contain chooses for himself a place and dwelling in the humble and contrite heart of a pious and faithful man. And just as Christ has made all who are members of the Church his brothers and co-heirs, so they are his servants and attendants, and belong to the family of the same heavenly Father. Under his service, therefore, are counted the learned and unlearned, the rich and poor, the obscure nobles, the lords of all nations, kings, emperors, dictators, consuls, judges, princes and governors of kingdoms. For all these have been raised to such eminence by his favour and grace. To him also obey teachers of the arts and languages, craftsmen, soldiers, townsmen, country folk, sailors, charioteers, masters, servants, parents, children, married and unmarried: in short, all of whatever condition, sex, age, place or rank, who then at last will keep their proper station and order, and can be called happy or blessed in it, if they remember that they are the servants of Christ, the King of kings and Lord of lords. From all these, therefore, that noble and holy household is formed, out of which the family of God the heavenly Father is constituted, in which all are servants and heirs as sons, slaves and free, and finally kings and most high priests. Over this household the Lord has set this servant of whom we are speaking; he wills him to take care of it, and requires that all who are in his household obey him. Therefore no one can boast that he is wholly free or exempt, unless he wishes to be a stranger to this so holy household, outside of which there is no salvation. The Lord teaches the same elsewhere too. For speaking of this same ministry in Ezekiel, he says: "Son of man, I have made you a watchman to the house of Israel." Now when he names the house, he includes all who are in the house. So there too, by the single name of house, he subjects all orders of men to the minister of his Word. In Jeremiah he speaks more plainly: "Behold, I have put my words in your mouth. Behold, I have set you this day over nations and over kingdoms, to pluck up and to pull down, to build and to plant." Therefore neither antiquity nor victory and triumphs, nor obscurity and defeat, will withdraw any nation from the care of this ministry. Nor will their learning free the learned and erudite, nor their majesty kings, nor their authority other magistrates, nor their wealth the rich, nor their poverty the poor, nor their servitude the servants, nor their liberty the free, nor their cunning the citizens, nor their craftiness or simplicity the country folk, nor the upbringing of children parents, nor filial piety children, nor the long-preserved flower of virginity the unmarried, nor mutual love and marital fidelity spouses, from being bound to observe this servant of God here, and to obey those things which he brings from the mouth of the Lord.

units.la: At simul ea quoq; vicissim obseruent ministri Ecclesiarum, quæ ad ipsos pertinent. Sunt hæc duo potissimum, quorum alterum consolationis plenum est, alterum ea gravitate nobis sui minis-terij curam commendat, vt maiori non possit. Quoniam enim in sua domo sive familia dispensatores vult esse Dominus, boni autem dispensatoris est, domini sui res & familiam augere, & no-uos subinde domesticos ipsi adducere, hoc ipsum verbi quoq; præcones faciant oportet. Id vero non poterunt præstare, nisi labores & pericula subeant grauissima. Quia enim mundus natura malus, & opera eius mala sunt, quæ argui & corripi non vult, mox si id facias, quasi profocis ac aris dimicaturus omnes suas vires contra veritatis doctrinam studijs suis inimica profert. Ideo Domi-nus IESVS CHRISTVS de eo discipulos olim admonuit, dicens: Ecce emitto vos veluti oues in medio luporum. Item eritis inuisi omnibus propter nomen meum. Et rursus: Alienos a synagogis facient vos, & veniet tempus, vt quisquis interficiat vos, videatur cultu præstare Deo. Neq; hoc nouum aut insolens esse, si quando id fiat, ex eo apparet, quod hanc veterum quoq; Prophetarum fortem fuisse scimus. Ieremias certe olim querebatur: Væ mihi mater mea, quod me peperisti virum litigatorem, & viru controuersiæ vniuersæ terræ, &c. Poterat hoc exemplis infinitis probari, quæ in Ecclesiastica historia extant: sed hıs minime opus est, cum illorum copiam nostra tem-pora suppeditent. Nec meliora nobis pollicentur Regum conuentus & Pontificum concilia, vulgi deniq; furores & fremitus Impiorum, qui passim audiuntur, & vno quasi ore, quicquid infortunij aut calamitatis incidit, solis verbi ministris acceptum ferunt. At hic nos consoletur illos, quod hanc prouinciam æternus Dei Filius IESVS CHRISTVS, ipsis demandauit. Itaq; non homi-minum, sed Dei serui sunt, qui illos certantes spectat & tuetur, vires deniq; nouas subinde suffi-cit, quibus armati certaminibus tantis sufficiunt. Vt enim fidelis imperator suis militibus non deesse vnquam, ita multo minus Christus suis seruis deerit, quibus dixit: Bono animo sitis, ego vici mundum: Ecce, ego vobiscum sum vsq; ad consummationem seculi. Matthæi vigesimo octa-uo Capite.
units.tr: Yet at the same time the ministers of the Churches should also observe in turn the things that pertain to them. Two of these are especially important. One of them is full of comfort, and the other commends the care of our ministry to us with such weight that nothing could be greater. Since the Lord wishes to have stewards in his own house or household, and it is the mark of a good steward to increase his master's property and to bring in new members of the household from time to time, the preachers of the Word ought to do the same. They cannot achieve this unless they undergo very grave labours and dangers. For the world is evil by nature, and its works are evil, and it does not want to be reproved or rebuked. As soon as you do this, it rises up with all its strength against the teaching of truth, as if about to fight for its altars and its very existence, and it opposes with all its efforts whatever is hostile to its pursuits. So the Lord Jesus Christ once warned his disciples about this, saying: "Behold, I send you forth as sheep in the midst of wolves." Again: "You will be hated by all men for my name's sake." And again: "They will put you out of the synagogues, and the time will come when whoever kills you will think he offers service to God." That this is not new or unusual when it happens is clear from the fact that we know it was also the lot of the ancient Prophets. Jeremiah once complained: "Woe is me, my mother, that you bore me a man of strife and a man of contention to all the earth," and so on. This could be proved from countless examples that appear in ecclesiastical history, but there is no need for these, since our own times supply plenty of them. Nor do the assemblies of kings and the councils of the Pontiffs promise us anything better, nor the fury and roaring of the common people and of the ungodly, which are heard everywhere, and which with one voice lay the blame for every misfortune and calamity on the ministers of the Word alone. But let this console us: the eternal Son of God, Jesus Christ, has entrusted this charge to them himself. So those who fight and are watched over by him are servants not of men but of God. Finally, he supplies new strength from time to time, by which they are equal to such great struggles when armed. For just as a faithful commander never fails his soldiers, much less will Christ fail his servants, to whom he said: "Be of good cheer, I have overcome the world. Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age." Matthew, chapter 28.

units.la: Cæterum officij quoq; hæc particula nos admonet: Vt nimirum memores cuius seruitimus, & quam late prouincia nostra pateat, sedulo saluti omnium inuigilemus, quos ille nobis credidit, & pro nobis Dei Filius mortuus est, vt suum domesticum faceret: Similiter, vt neminem vereamur, neq; personas respiciamus. Omnibus enim dicitur, quod Ieremiæ olim dicebat Dominus: Ne timeas a conspectu eorum, ne timere te faciam. Ecce enim ego te faciam ciuitatem munitam, columnam ferream & murum aneum contra omnem terram, contra Reges Iuda, contra principes eius, contra Sacerdotes, & contra vniuersum populum terræ. Itaq; cum primis huc pertinet, quod Paulus monet, vt Episcopus recte secet Verbum Domini, id est, ita omnibus accommodet, vt singulorum institutioni, ædificationi, emendationi & consolationi seruiat. Sed plura de hac re sequentur.
units.tr: Moreover, this part of the duty also reminds us that we should remember whom we serve and how wide our province extends, and that we should diligently watch over the salvation of all those whom he has entrusted to us, and for whom the Son of God also died, so that he might make them his own household. Likewise, we should fear no one and have no regard for persons. For what the Lord once said to Jeremiah is said to all: "Do not be afraid of their faces, lest I make you afraid of them. For behold, I make you a fortified city, an iron pillar and a bronze wall against the whole land, against the kings of Judah, against its princes, against its priests, and against all the people of the land." Therefore, the first thing that applies here is what Paul advises, that the bishop should rightly divide the Word of the Lord, that is, that he should so adapt it to all that it serves the instruction, edification, correction and consolation of each individual. But more on this matter will follow.

units.la: Sed & auditores hic officij admonentur, vt meminerint omnes se debitores esse, vt Verbum audiant. Quia enim homo animalis non percipit ea quæ sunt Spiritus Dei, omnibus doctrina & institutione opus est: & qui hoc negant, hi sipsos non recte norunt, eoque deterior & periculosior ipsorum fors est. Offendunt ad hunc lapidem fere magnates & principes viri, qui authoritati ipsorum aliquid decedere existimant, si a Verbi ministris vel officij sui admoneantur, vel liberius propter delicta sua corripiantur. Atqui vt Diuus Iacobus ait, in multis labimur omnes, & quod gentium Poetæ obseruarunt, interdum dormitat Homerus. Est ergo nimia hæc & periculosa confidentia, qua sibi ipsis tantum aliqui tribuunt, vt se extra omnem culpam esse dicant, neq; a quoquam volunt argui. Est quidem summa & sancta magistratuum authoritas, & grauissime peccant, qui Dijs populi sui maledicunt. At nullum hominum ordinem Deus supra se extulit, sed vt Sacerdotes, Prophetas, Apostolos, omnes deniq; Ecclesiæ & verbi sui antistites, sibi subiectos esse voluit, & ex suo ore sumere ea, quæ populo prædicent: ita magistratus suorum iudicium præsides fecit, & sua potestate armauit, qua tunc demum feliciter vtentur, si ipsius voluntatem obseruarint. Qui vero sine Deo regnare volunt, & dum suo honori consulunt, Dei gloriam profitentur, ijs seruit, quod Deus per prophetam dicit: Honore prosequar eos, qui me honore prosequuntur: & qui me contemnunt, ignominia afficientur. Ideo librum Legis Regibus tunc in primis commendatum esse volebat olim Deus, cum in throno maiestatis sue sederent, ne forte potestate sua superbe abutentur, & ijsdem Sacerdotes & prophetas addidit, qui illos suis consilijs ex Lege & Verbo Dei pectus regerent, & exorbitante interdum correptione grauiori in viam reducerent. Exempla sunt in Dauide, Iosaphato, Ezechia, quibus hoc felicissime cessit: sunt item alia tristissima in Saule, Achabo, Achazo, Sedechia & alijs, quibus hæc exitus & interitus causa fuit, quod Dei Verbo parere noluerunt.
units.tr: But here the hearers too are reminded of their duty, that all should remember that they are bound to hear the Word. For since the natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God, all need teaching and instruction, and those who deny this do not know themselves rightly, and their lot is therefore worse and more dangerous. Men of high rank and princes commonly stumble at this stone, because they think their authority is diminished if they are admonished by the ministers of the Word concerning their office, or are rebuked more freely for their sins. Yet, as the divine James says, "we all stumble in many things," and, as the poets of the nations have observed, "sometimes even Homer nods." So that confidence is excessive and dangerous, by which some attribute so much to themselves that they claim to be free of all fault and will not allow themselves to be reproved by anyone. The authority of magistrates is indeed high and holy, and those who curse the gods of their people sin most gravely. But God has raised no order of men above himself. Rather, just as he willed that the priests, the prophets, the apostles, and in short all the overseers of the Church and of his Word should be subject to him and take from his own mouth what they are to proclaim to the people, so he has made magistrates the judges of his people and armed them with his power. They will use that power happily only if they observe his will. But those who want to reign without God, and while they look after their own honour, profess the glory of God, are answered by what God says through the prophet: "I will honour those who honour me, and those who despise me will be brought to shame." For this reason God once wished the book of the Law to be commended especially to kings when they sat on the throne of his majesty, lest perhaps they should abuse their power arrogantly. He also added priests and prophets for the same people, who would guide their hearts with counsel from the Law and the Word of God, and bring them back to the right way with sometimes stronger rebuke. There are examples in David, Jehoshaphat and Hezekiah, for whom this turned out most happily. There are also other most sorrowful examples in Saul, Ahab, Ahaziah, Zedekiah and others, for whom this was the cause of their end and ruin, because they were unwilling to obey the Word of God.

units.la: Sed vt ad Seruum Ecclesiasticum redeamus, Dominum de eius officio apertius loquentem audire præstat. Definit hoc, Vt det famulitio Dei alimentum in tempore. At quia totum hoc munus spirituale est, & ad animam spectat, de animæ etiam cibo siue alimento loquitur, cui non minus quam corpori suo nutrimento opus est. At necesse est, vt alimentum cum eo, quod alid-ebet, aliquam similitudinem aut communionem habeat, vt in id conuerti & transfire possit. Sic ignem hunc materialem ligni & alijs rebus, quæ constitutionis ficcioris & leuioris sunt, ali & conseruari cernimus: fluminibus autem assidui & perennes humores ex aerio vapore & terræ frigoribus exorti suum quasi alimentum præbent. Et quod omnium oculis cernitur, corpora tam hominum quam aliorum animaliū cum ex terra constent, terrenis quoq; cibis nutriuntur. Idipsum ergo in anima quoq;, quæ præstantior hominis pars est, obseruabimus. Est hæc spiritus, & effen-tiam suam ex Deo habet, qui cum primo parenti corpus ex luto terræ formasset, inspirauit ei animam viuentem. A Deo igitur inspirata homini anima, diuino quoq; & cælesti cibo sustentetur oportet. Vt enim corpora nostra non aere aut vento, nec alio crassiore spiritu inslar Chameleontis pascun‑tur: sic nec animam, quæ spiritus cœlestis & diuinus est, aliquid terrenum aut corporeum nutrire aut alere potest. Quam ergo dicemus ambrosiam illam cœlestem & diuinum neclar, quo ad æter‑nam vitam homines aluntur? Vtiq; non aliud quàm Verbum Dei æternum & salutiferum, quod initio omnia creata sunt, & seruantur: quod item omnibus iis, quibus Deus ad nos alendos & ser‑uandos vti vult, vim nutritiuam & vegetatiuam suggerit, vt nobis seruandis sufficiat. Ideo Moses olim Israelitis dicebat: Non solo pane viuit homo, sed quouis verbo quod exit ab ore Dei. De hoc etiam alimento Dauid dicebat: Eloquia Domini dulciora melle. Et Isaias ad hunc cibum inuitans clamabat: Venite ad aquas, o vos omnes qui sititis, & vos quibus non est pecunia, adeste: comparate cibum & comedite, parate cibum sine argento & sine pretio. Vtiq; constaret satis, de quo cibo loqueretur, addit: Audcultate diligenter mihi, vt comedatis bonum, & in pinguedine oblectetur anima vestra. Inclinate aurem vestram, & ad me venite: audite, & viuet anima vestra. Vt ergo ministri cibum hunc prædicantes apponunt & rectè secant: ita ad eum percipiendum auditu siue attentione opus est, cui sides accedat oportet, qua sola salutariter apprehenduntur, quæ Verbo nobis Deus offert & pollicetur. Et meminisse oportet, Verbum hoc modo aquis, modo fauus melle stillantibus, modo lacte, interdum solido cibo conferri: nimirum pro hominum & ingeniorum diuersitate, cui illud ministri, qui eius dispensatores sunt, applicare, & (vt super diximus) rite se care debent. Vbi cumptimus temporis rationem habere oportet. Nam vt Solomon ait, omnibus tempus præsinitum est: & est tempus nascendi & tempus moriendi, tempus plantandi & euellendi, tempus occidendi & medendi, tempus demoliendi & ædificandi, tempus lachrymandi et tempus ridendi, &c. Ita in Ecclesiæ ministerio est tempus docendi & tempus monendi: tempus hortandi & tempus corripiendi: tempus consolandi & confirmandi: singulis vero momentis sese accommodent ministri, ne omissis ijs quæ dictu necessaria sunt, Ecclesiam non necessarijs onerent, quibus multi plus lædantur aut offendantur quàm ædificentur, &c. Et vehementer falluntur, qui simpliciter & absq; omni discrimine docere volunt homines, & nihil dici, quod aliquem offendere possit: quod perinde est, ac si quis in voɼoδoχείω aliquo, in quo innumeri diuersis morbis decum‑bunt, omnibus vnum remedium propinet. Ideo Dominus cibum singulis & καιρῷ, id est, tempore legitimo & opportuno depromere iubet, vt singulorum emendationi seruiat.
units.tr: But to return to the ecclesiastical servant, it is better to hear the Lord speaking more plainly about his office. He defines it thus: "to give food to the household of God in due season." But because this whole office is spiritual and concerns the soul, he is also speaking of the food or nourishment of the soul, which needs nourishment no less than the body does. But it is necessary that the food should have some likeness or affinity with that which it is to nourish, so that it can be converted into it and pass into it. Thus we see that this material fire is fed and sustained by wood and other things that are of a drier and lighter constitution. And the rivers have their constant and perennial waters, arising from the vapour of the air and the cold of the earth, which give them, as it were, their nourishment. And what is seen by everyone's eyes: the bodies of men as well as of other animals, since they consist of earth, are also nourished by earthly foods. We should observe the same thing in the soul too, which is the more excellent part of man. It is spirit, and has its essence from God, who, when he had formed the body of the first parent from the mud of the earth, breathed into him a living soul. The soul breathed into man by God must therefore also be sustained by divine and heavenly food. For just as our bodies are not fed on air or wind, nor on any other thicker spirit like the chameleon, so the soul, which is a heavenly and divine spirit, cannot be nourished or sustained by anything earthly or corporeal. What, then, shall we call that heavenly ambrosia and divine nectar by which men are fed to eternal life? Surely nothing other than the eternal and saving Word of God, through which all things were created at the beginning and are preserved. It also supplies the nourishing and vivifying power to all those means by which God wills to feed and preserve us, so that it is sufficient for our preservation. Therefore Moses once said to the Israelites: "Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God." David also spoke of this food: "The words of the Lord are sweeter than honey." And Isaiah, inviting to this food, cried out: "Come to the waters, all you who thirst, and you who have no money, come! Buy food and eat; buy food without silver and without price." It would be quite clear what food he meant, and he adds: "Listen carefully to me, that you may eat what is good, and let your soul delight in fatness. Incline your ear and come to me; hear, and your soul shall live." Therefore, just as the ministers set out and rightly divide this food when they preach it, so its reception requires hearing or attention, to which faith must be added, since by faith alone are those things apprehended savingly which God offers and promises to us in the Word. We should remember that the Word is conveyed in this way: sometimes as waters, sometimes as honeycomb dripping with honey, sometimes as milk, and sometimes as solid food, namely according to the diversity of men and their abilities. The ministers, who are its stewards, must apply it to each and, as we said above, must cut it rightly. Here they must take careful account of the right time. For, as Solomon says, a time is appointed for all things: there is a time to be born and a time to die, a time to plant and a time to pluck up, a time to kill and a time to heal, a time to break down and a time to build, a time to weep and a time to laugh, and so on. So too in the ministry of the Church there is a time for teaching and a time for admonishing, a time for exhorting and a time for rebuking, a time for consoling and a time for confirming. The ministers should adapt themselves to each moment, so that, by omitting what must be said, they do not burden the Church with unnecessary things, by which many are hurt or offended more than they are built up, and so on. Those who wish to teach men simply and without any distinction, and to say nothing that could offend anyone, are greatly mistaken. It is as if someone in some infirmary [νοσοκομείῳ], where countless people lie sick with various diseases, were to offer one remedy to all. Therefore the Lord bids food be brought out to each one at the right and fitting time [καιρῷ], that is, at the due and opportune time, so that it may serve the correction of each.

units.la: Cæterum quia in hoc fere officij aut muneris Ecclesiastici summa versatur, ne vel zelo vehementi & pio, sed non secundum scientiam abrepti ministri multos offendant, vel dum omnibus placere volunt, omnium moribus & ingenijs sese accommodando ex Verbo sale infatuatum reddant, & illius libertate turpiter prodant, de duabus virtutibus seruos suos admonet Dominus dicens: Quis est seruus fidelis & prudens, &c.? Interrogatio ista admirationis speciem habet, quæ commendationem boni seruï Ecclesiæ continet: Quasi diceret: Quantus est seruus fidelis & prudens, quanta item laude & commendatione dignus? Vt autem commendari mereatur, duo requirit: Fidem primò, quæ præcipua in dispensatore virtus est, Paulo teste, dum dicit: Sic de nobis reputet homo, vt de ministris Christi, ac dispensatoribus mysteriorum Dei. Quod superest autem, illud requiritur in dispensatoribus, vt fidus quiq; inueniatur. Fidelis autem erit, qui omnia dirigit ad gloriam Dei & populi & totius Ecclesiæ salutem: Infidus verò, qui vt suo quæstui & honori consulat, ferre potest ea quæ gloriæ Dei & hominum saluti officiunt. Debent ergo ministri (vt nuper ex Ieremia monuimus) extirpare & plantare, & ædificationi Ecclesiæ pro viribus consulere. At rursus ne zelo suo fallatur, alterum quoq; requirit, prudentiam nimirum. Opus hic Verbi studio. Vt enim labia sacerdotis scientiam custodire debent: ita hæc non potest aliunde peti, quàm ex Scripturis, quæ Verbum Dei nobis tradunt, & in hunc finem a Deo inspirata, vt utiles sint ad doctrinam, ad redargutionem, ad correctionem, ad institutionem, quæ est in iustitia. Patet hic latissimus campus, in quo sese ministri Ecclesiarum exerceant. Nam quocunq; oculos vertant, infiniti ipsis occurrent omnis ordinis, sexus & ætatis homines, qui cum vera Dei cognitione destituantur, per nos institui debent, siquidè Deo fideles esse volumus. Et quàm multi sunt, quos vel caci affectus in errores abducunt, vt ignari rerum peccent, vel scientes exorbitent? Nonne ergo propter tales argumenta & exempla obseruare & colligere oportet, quibus nos in viam renocemus, vel si illi redi‑ re nolunt, nos officium faciendo animas uostras liberemus? Nihil dico nunc de ijs, qui veteres errores & hæreses postliminio ab inferis reuocant. Sunt qui Ariana impietate imbuti, Christi æternam Deitatem vellicant. Sunt qui Eutychianis chimeris eiusdem carnem & humanitatem exinaniunt. Sunt item, qui dum maiestatis Christi & omnipotentiæ vindices & assertores videri volunt, totum abnegant. Inter eos autem qui a religione alieniores non tanti faciunt mysteria ista, vt de his serio & diligentius cogitent, Epicurus reuixit, vt nesciā, si suo seculo olim, an hodie plures discipulos habeat, cum ij quoq; quos minime putares, hominis beatitudinem carnis voluptatibus metiantur, & de futura vita, animarum immortalitate & corporum resurrectione, non falsa modò, verumetiam horrenda sentire videas. Resurgunt item quotidie Antichristiani spiritus in multorum animis, qui sub veritatis fuco veteres & dudum abolitas superstitiones restituunt. De niq; dies me deficeret, si omnia recensere velim, quæ hoc nostro seculo contra religionis & honestatis leges fiunt. Quapropter nullum studium nimium, nulla diligentia superflua erit in ministris, qui suo officio probè defungi volunt.
units.tr: But since the greatest part of this office or ministry of the Church lies in this, that ministers, either carried away by a vehement and pious zeal that is not according to knowledge, offend many, or, wishing to please everyone, adapt themselves to everyone's morals and talents and so become salt that has lost its savour from the Word, and shamefully betray its freedom, the Lord admonishes his servants about two virtues, saying: "Who is the faithful and wise servant, etc.?" This question has the air of wonder and contains a commendation of the good servant of the Church, as if he said: How great is the faithful and wise servant, and how worthy of praise and commendation? To deserve to be commended, he requires two things. First, faith, which is the chief virtue in a steward, as Paul witnesses when he says: "Let a man so account of us, as of the ministers of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God." What remains is required of stewards, that each be found faithful. The faithful steward is he who directs everything to the glory of God and the salvation of the people and of the whole Church; the unfaithful one, who looks to his own gain and honour, can tolerate those things which hinder the glory of God and the salvation of men. Ministers therefore ought (as we lately admonished from Jeremiah) to root out and to plant, and to labour for the building up of the Church as far as their strength allows. But again, lest they be deceived by their zeal, he requires a second thing, namely prudence. This comes from diligent study of the Word. For just as the lips of the priest ought to keep knowledge, so this cannot be sought from anywhere but the Scriptures, which deliver the Word of God to us and were inspired by God to this end, that they be profitable for doctrine, for refutation, for correction, for instruction, which is in righteousness. Here opens a very wide field in which the ministers of the Churches may exercise themselves. For wherever they turn their eyes, they will meet countless people of every rank, sex and age who, lacking the true knowledge of God, must be instructed by us, if we wish to be faithful to God. And how many are there whom blind affections lead into errors, so that they sin through ignorance or go astray knowingly? Must we not, then, observe and gather arguments and examples for such people, by which we may call them back to the way, or, if they refuse to return, free our own souls by doing our duty? I say nothing now of those who call back old errors and heresies from the dead, as if by right of return. There are those who, imbued with Arian impiety, pluck at the eternal Deity of Christ. There are those who, with Eutychian fancies, empty his flesh and humanity. There are also those who, while they wish to appear the defenders and champions of Christ's majesty and omnipotence, deny the whole. Among those who are more alien to religion, who do not esteem these mysteries so highly as to think about them seriously and carefully, Epicurus has revived. I do not know whether he has more disciples today than he once had in his own age, since even those whom you would least expect measure human happiness by the pleasures of the flesh, and you see them holding opinions about the future life, the immortality of souls and the resurrection of bodies that are not merely false but even horrible. Antichristian spirits also rise again daily in the minds of many, who under the mask of truth restore old superstitions long since abolished. In short, the day would fail me if I wished to recount everything that is done in this age against the laws of religion and decency. Therefore no zeal will be too great and no diligence superfluous for ministers who wish to discharge their office well.

units.la: Quæ causa est, quòd Dominus amplißima præmij promissione ministros suos excitat, & rursus grauissima pœnæ denuntiatione terret, ne in officio suo aliquid negligentius aut improbius designent. Beatus (inquit) seruus ille, quem cum venerit dominus eius, inuenerit sic facientem: Amen dico vobis omnibus bonis suis præficiet eum. Opponit hoc carnis & mundi iudicio, quo Verbi & Ecclesiæ ministri hominum miserrimi putantur, quod Paulus obseruans dicebat: Deus, puto, nos vltimos Apostolos spectandos proposuit tanquam morti addictos: Nam spectaculū factī sumus mundo, & Angelis & hominibus. Fit enim fere quod seruis œconomis, qui dum heris suis fideles sunt, scapulas perdunt, vt Comicus dicebat, id est, conferuis simul & exteris inuisi fiunt, & maximè quidem ijs, quorum saluti & honori in primis confultum cupiunt. Sed beati sunt, quia Christo seruiunt, quo nullus est remunerator fidelior & liberalior. Hic super omnia bona sua eos constituet. Dicitur hoc ἀνθρωποπαθῶς, ne quis a Deo neglectos putet eos, quos mundus hic ferè negligit. Potest enim Deus non solum tueri, verumetiam omni præmiorum genere accumulare eos, qui ipsi fideles sunt, vt ut de illis mundus iniquissimè iudicet. Et sanè super omnia tales constituuntur, cum omnium domini sint, & initiati aut instrūcti sint ad omnia quæ Deus ipsis immittit. Nam cum Paulo Apostolo norunt in quibus sunt, ijs ipsis contenti esse: norunt deprimi, norunt etiam abundare: norunt saturi esse & seurire, abundare & egere, deniq; siue viuant siue moriantur, Domini sunt. Quia enim ad hoc Christus & mortuus est & resurrexit & reuixit, vt & mortuis & viuentibus dominetur, ipsi quoq; siue viuant siue moriantur, Domini sunt. Superat tamen omnem huius seculi fortunam cœlestis vita, qua olim in beata immortalitate fruentur, quando (vt sequenti Capite audiemus) in gaudium Domini sui ingredientur.
units.tr: This is why the Lord stirs up his ministers with the promise of the greatest reward, and again terrifies them with the most grievous threat of punishment, lest they be negligent or wicked in their office. "Blessed is that servant," he says, "whom his lord, when he comes, shall find so doing. Verily I say unto you, he shall make him ruler over all his goods." This is set against the judgment of the flesh and of the world, by which the ministers of the Word and of the Church are thought to be the most wretched of men. Paul, observing this, said: "God, I think, has set forth us the last apostles as men condemned to death; for we are made a spectacle to the world, to angels and to men." For it often happens with servants who are stewards, that while they are faithful to their masters, they lose their shoulders (as the comic poet said), that is, they become hated both by their fellow servants and by outsiders, and especially by those whose safety and honour they most desire to promote. But they are blessed, because they serve Christ, than whom there is no more faithful and generous rewarder. He will set them over all his goods. This is said in human fashion, lest anyone think that those whom the world largely neglects are neglected by God. For God can not only protect but also heap every kind of reward upon those who are themselves faithful, though the world judges them most unjustly. And indeed such men are set over all things, since they are lords of all and have been initiated into, or instructed in, all that God sends them. For with the Apostle Paul they know in what state they are, and are content with it: they know how to be brought low, they know how to abound; they know to be full and to be hungry, to abound and to be in want; finally, whether they live or die, they are the Lord's. For Christ died, rose and revived for this purpose, that he might be Lord of both the dead and the living; so they too, whether they live or die, are the Lord's. Yet the heavenly life, in which they will one day enjoy blessed immortality, surpasses every fortune of this age, when (as we shall hear in the following chapter) they enter into the joy of their Lord.

units.la: Sed videamus infidelis quoq; serui mores & conditionem siue pœnam, quam illi minatur Dei Filius IESVS CHRISTVS. Quòd si dixerit seruus ille malus in corde suo, Tardat dominus meus aduentū, cœperitq; verberare conseruos, quinetiā edere & bibere cum ebrijs: Veniet dominus serui illius die, quo non expectat, & hora qua non nouit & separabit eū, ac partē ei assignabit cum hypocritis: illic erit sletus & stridor dentium. Vanas cordis cogitationes initiò argnit, quibus seipsum seruus malus decipit. Arbitratur herū suæ domus immemore reditū differre. Est hic proximus gradus ad impietatē. Nam qui ita incipiunt, mox longius progressi, persuadent sibi, Deū vel omnino nullum esse, vel prorsus non curare, quæ in terris inter homines geruntur. Sequitur ex hac persuasione quiduis agendi audacia, vt a nullo scelere abstineant, quod cæca libido dictat. Ergo edunt & bibunt cū ebrijs, id est, ventri gulæq; dediti dies noctesq; comessantur. Deus enim eorū est venter (quod Paulus quoq; annotauit) qui vt auribus caret (vt Cato dicebat) ita ratione quoq; & sanis sensibus destituitur. Et non sicitanter negligi debet, quod passim in scripturis perfidis & ini quis domus suæ administris intemperantiæ & ebrietatis notam inurit. Huius accusantur mali sacerdotes apud Isaiam dicentem. Etiam illi in vino perplexi sunt, & in sicera aberrarunt, sacerdos & propheta perplexi sunt ob siceram, obruti sunt a vino, errant in visione, vacillant in iudicio. Omnes mensæ oppletæ sunt vomitu & sordibus, vt locus non sit. At eiusmodi Sacerdotum nullum vsum esse, docet, cum infert: Quem docebit scientia, & quæ facit intelligere auscultationem?
units.tr: But let us look at the character and condition, or the punishment, of the unfaithful servant, which the Son of God, Jesus Christ, threatens him with. "But if that evil servant shall say in his heart, My lord delays his coming, and begins to beat his fellow servants, and even to eat and drink with drunkards, the lord of that servant will come on a day when he does not expect him, and at an hour when he does not know it, and will cut him asunder and appoint him his portion with the hypocrites; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth." First, he rebukes the vain thoughts of the heart by which the evil servant deceives himself. He thinks that his lord of the house delays his return, forgetful of him. This is the next step towards impiety. For those who begin in this way, once they have advanced further, persuade themselves that God either does not exist at all or does not care in the least what goes on among men on earth. From this persuasion comes a boldness to do anything at all, so that they abstain from no crime that blind lust dictates. Therefore they eat and drink with drunkards, that is, given over to belly and gullet, they revel day and night. For their god is their belly (as Paul also noted), and such a man, as Cato said, lacks ears and is likewise deprived of reason and sound senses. Nor should it be passed over lightly that, throughout the Scriptures, the unfaithful and wicked stewards of a household are branded with the mark of intemperance and drunkenness. The evil priests are accused of this in Isaiah, who says: "Even these have erred through wine, and through strong drink have gone astray; the priest and the prophet have erred through strong drink, they are swallowed up of wine, they stagger with strong drink; they err in vision, they stumble in judgment. All tables are full of vomit and filth, so that there is no place." But that such priests are of no use he shows when he adds: "Whom will he teach knowledge, and whom will he make to understand doctrine?"

units.la: Premium fidelis ministri. Num ablactatos & ab uberibus depulsos, &c. Et eodem faciunt, quae apud eundem prophetam de prophetis habentur, qui in munere suo negligentes, & insuper mali exempli authores erant. Speculatores eius omnes caeci sunt, omnes sunt ignari, canes muti, latrare non possunt, torpent, iacent, follmnum amant. Canes isti sunt robusti animi, satiari non possunt. Et mox: Venite (aiunt) vinum adferam, ut perpotemus ad ebrietatem usque, atque adeo sicut hodie ita & cras abundantia multo maior. Quam parvulam ideo addit, ut incurabiles esse ostendat. Qui enim ebrietati adiicuerunt, fere [al. infatuatus] fiunt, qui ad nihil valent porro, quam ut eiiciantur foras, & conculcentur ab hominibus. Non temere ergo Dominus hoc etiam loco feruis nequam ebrietatem tribuit, & eodem accusat, quod conseruos suos percutiant: Quod non tam de vi aperta, quae violentis manibus fit, dicitur, quae de calumniis & conuitiis, quibus fidos ministros proscindunt, ut eis odium & inuidiam conciliant. Nec enim facis est malitiosis aut infidis Ecclesiarum ministris, si ipsi officiu negligant, nisi aliorum famam laedant: quia quantum bonis & industrijs accedere uident, tantum si-bi putant decedere. Et huius meminisse debent, quibus cu eiusmodi hominibus res est, nec dubitent, Deum fore ipsorum uindicem, qui feruorum suorum innocentiam & existimationem solet tueri.
units.tr: The reward of the faithful minister. Are they weaned and taken from the breasts? And so on. The same applies to what is said in the same prophet about the prophets, who were negligent in their office and, besides, were authors of bad example. All its watchmen are blind, all are ignorant, they are dumb dogs that cannot bark, they lie stupefied and love sleep. These dogs have greedy spirits and can never be satisfied.
