And soon after: "Come," they say, "I will fetch wine, that we may drink ourselves into drunkenness, and tomorrow will be just like today, with even greater abundance." He adds "so small" to show that they are incurable. For those who have given themselves to drunkenness are almost made fools, and are good for nothing more than being thrown out and trampled by men. It is not without reason, therefore, that the Lord here also ascribes drunkenness to the wicked servants and accuses them of beating their fellow servants. This is said not so much of open violence done with violent hands as of the slanders and insults by which they tear down faithful ministers, in order to win hatred and envy for them. For malicious or faithless ministers of the Churches are not concerned if they neglect their duty, provided they harm the reputation of others; for they think that they lose as much as the good and diligent gain. Those who have to deal with such men ought to remember this and not doubt that God will be the avenger of his servants, since he is wont to guard the innocence and good name of his servants.

units.la: Et huc etiam referri debet, quod de poena seruii infidelis subiicitur: Veniet Dominus seruii illius die, quo non expectat, & hora, qua non nouit, id est, repente & ex improuiso. At quae inexpectata incidunt incommoda, grauiora sunt & magis laedunt. In praesenti vero improuisum suppliciun minatur, ut ne quis offendatur eiusmodi hominum successibus, & eos impunitate perpetua gaudiurosos putet. Non enim eximet eos a communi aliorum hominum forte, qui omnes ad Christi tribunal sistentur, dignitas & quam sibi vendicant sanctitatis opinio. Deinde separabit eum Dominus. Est quidem ἀχολουθία idem quod dissecare, unde non inepte quidam poenas, quae prodito-rib. debentur, intellexerunt: Sed quia Deus tales non pro suis agnoscit, sed ut alienos a sua familia eijcit, separatio etiam intelligi potest. Nam haec demum est diffecatio omnium atrocissima, quae homines a corpore Christi separat, ab Ecclesia nimirum, extra quam nulla salutis spes reliqua est. Ideo addit: Et partem ei assignabit cum hypocritis: illic erit fletus & stridor dentium, quae alibi de sempiternis infernalium tormentorum cruciatibus dicuntur. Infelicissimi ergo sunt, qui momenta ueae felicitatis, quae in hoc seculo eis affulget, ipse illecti, vitae & gaudij coelestis iacturam faciunt. Quia vero omnes serui Christi dicimur, singuli ista ad se transferre debent, & ante alios, qui magistratum gerunt. Horum in primis est cauere, ne quid tyrannice aut insolenter agant, sed memineriunt, populum, cui praesunt, Dei peculium aut gregem esse, qui ipsum olim de ipsorum manibus requiret. Ne item aliquibus malo exemplo sint quoad vitia, maxime quoad intemperantiam aut ebrietatem: Vbi enim haec regnant, ibi vincula & fundamenta Reip. euertuntur. Ideo Solomon olim dicebat: Vae tibi terra, cuius rex puer est, & principes tui mane comessantur. Non etiam colludant cum impijs, quibus coercendis ipsos Deus praefecit. Ad se ergo in primis pertinere putent, quod Dauid de vere pio dicit: Vilis est in oculis eius homo, nihili, sed timentes Deum honorat. Omnes deniq; , cuiusque loci & ordinis, meminerint venturum Filium Dei IESVM CHRISTVM, ad cuius tribunal omnes sistemur. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: This passage should also be referred to what is added about the punishment of the unfaithful servant: "The Lord of that servant will come on a day when he does not expect him, and at an hour he does not know," that is, suddenly and unexpectedly. Misfortunes that come unexpectedly are heavier and hurt more. Here, however, he threatens an unforeseen punishment, so that no one should be offended by the successes of such men or think that they will rejoice in perpetual impunity. For the dignity which they claim for themselves and the reputation for holiness will not exempt them from the common lot of other men, since all will be brought before the tribunal of Christ. "Then the Lord will cut him asunder." The Greek word [ἀχολουθία] means the same as to cut in pieces, whence some not unskilfully have understood the punishments due to traitors; but since God does not acknowledge such men as his own, but casts them out as strangers from his household, the separation may also be understood in this sense. For this is indeed the most atrocious of all cutting off, which separates men from the body of Christ, namely from the Church, outside of which there is no remaining hope of salvation. Therefore he adds: "And he will assign him a portion with the hypocrites; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth," which are described elsewhere as the everlasting torments of the infernal punishments. Most unhappy, therefore, are those who, enticed by the moments of wretched happiness that shine on them in this age, suffer the loss of life and heavenly joy. But since we are all called servants of Christ, each one ought to apply these things to himself, and above all those who bear the magistracy. Their first duty is to take care not to act tyrannically or insolently, but to remember that the people over whom they preside is God's own possession or flock, who will one day require it from their hands. Nor should they be a bad example to anyone in their vices, especially in intemperance or drunkenness; for where these reign, the bonds and foundations of the commonwealth are overturned. Therefore Solomon once said: "Woe to you, land whose king is a child, and whose princes feast in the morning." Nor should they collude with the ungodly, whom God has set them over to restrain. Let them therefore consider first of all that what David says of the truly pious applies to them: "A vile man is in his eyes, worthless, but he honours those who fear God." Finally, everyone, of whatever place and rank, should remember that the Son of God, JESUS CHRIST, is coming, before whose tribunal we all shall stand. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: OMINIS vita in terris perpetua militia est, & ideo excubijs quoq; & vigilijs perpetuis opus est, ne vel mundi illecebris, vel principis eius, qui idem princeps tenebrarum est, dolis & artibus circumveniamur. Haec causa est, quod Dei Filius IESVS CHRISTVS de nouissimorum temporum periculosó statu differens, de eo potissimum agit, vt ad vigilantiam & excubias illas nos excitet. Et ne quae discipulis Apostolis dixit, qui ad altiora vocati erant, ad hos solos pertinere putentur, apud Marcum vniuersali Epiphonemate locu istum concludit, dicens: Quae vobis dico omnibus dico. Vigilate. Quia ergo eadem salutis ratio omnibus hominibus proposita est, quae in fidei constantia consistit, ne ab hac nos dimoueri patiamur, sine qua nemo ieruari potest, vt ad hanc recte instruamur, necesse est. Neq; hic aliqua cura potest nisi mia esse, cum diabolus mille artifex, in angelum lucis quoq; se transformare possit, & insatiabilinos perdendi cupiditate accensus instar rugientis leonis oberret, & quaerat quos deuoret. Idcirco Christus ijs quae hucusq; dixit, hanc quoq; parabolam subtexit, qua vniuersam Ecclesiae suae condicionem adumbrat, & simul docet vt singuli sese ad caelestes nuptias, quae aeternae & beatae immortalitatis typus sunt, praeparare debeant.
units.tr: The whole of life on earth is a perpetual warfare, and therefore there is need of constant watchfulness and vigils, lest we be overcome by the allurements of the world or by the deceits and arts of its prince, who is also the prince of darkness. This is the reason why Jesus Christ, the Son of God, when speaking of the dangerous state of the last times, deals chiefly with this, in order to rouse us to that vigilance and watchfulness. And lest what he said to the disciples, the apostles, who were called to higher things, be thought to pertain to them alone, he concludes this passage in Mark with a general exclamation, saying: "What I say to you, I say to all: Watch." Since, therefore, the same way of salvation is set before all men, which consists in constancy of faith, it is necessary that we be rightly instructed in it, and that we not allow ourselves to be moved from it, without which no one can be saved. Nor can there be any lack of care here, since the devil, a thousand-fold craftsman, can also transform himself into an angel of light, and, burning with an insatiable desire to destroy, wanders like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour. Therefore, after what he has said so far, Christ adds this parable, in which he sketches the whole condition of his Church, and at the same time teaches that each one ought to prepare himself for the heavenly marriage, which is the type of eternal and blessed immortality.

units.la: Ad nouissimum vero tempus parabolam restringens ait: Tunc, id est, quando ego expectior, vt vniuersam mundi machinam a corruptione & turbis quae omnia periculorum plena reddunt, redimam, regnum caelorum simile erit decem virginibus, quae sumptis lampadibus suis exierunt in occursum sponsi. Vniuersum redemptionis negotium, quod Ecclesiae proprium est, regnum caelorum dici alias quoq; annotauimus, eo quod huius finis sit, vt ex peccati seruitio, ex diaboli tyranni de redempti in terris vitam caelestem viuamus, & tandem ad Christum colleEti regnemus in caelis. Recte autem nuptijs conferetur, quia in eo consistit vniuersa salus, vt cum Filio Dei coniuncti, qui solus Ecclesiae sponsus est, teste etiam Ioanne Baptista, per hunc Deo Patri conciliemur, vt bonorum caelestium confortes & participes reddamur. Et hic partim incomparabilis Dei bonitas elucet, qui Filio suo vnigenito Regi gloriae immortali, cui omnis potestas data est in caelo & in terra, nos desponsare dignatus est: partim salutem nostram certam, perfectam & perpetuam esse adumbratur. De Eua sua, quae ex dormientis costa formata erat, dicebat olim Adamus: Hoc nunc os ex ossibus meis, & caro ex carne mea. Ita ex coniugij iure Apostolus de Ecclesia, quae ex Filij Dei IESV CHRISTI morte enata est, & per fidem in hunc colligitur, argumentatur, illam esse carnem ex carne eius, os ex ossibus eius, & de singulis fidelibus siue credentibus dicit eos esse membra corporis Christi. De vinculo autem coniugij primus Adam simul & fecundus pronuntiarunt: Quod Deus coniunxit, homo ne separet. Vt eum Dei opus est, quod in coniugio, qui primus duo erant, vna caro fiunt: ita Deus nos Filij sui carnem fecit. Non ergo periculum est, ne quis nos ab eo diuellat. Nemo vnquam suam ipsius carnem odio habuit, inquit Apostolus: Num ergo Christus suam carnem odisset, qui est ipsa charitas? Hoc obseruasse videtur Paulus, cum ad Romanos scriberet: Quis nos separabit a charitate Christi? Rom.8.Cap.
units.tr: Narrowing the parable to the last time, he says: "Then," that is, when I shall come to redeem the whole frame of the world from corruption and from the disturbances which fill everything with dangers, "the kingdom of heaven will be like ten virgins, who took their lamps and went out to meet the bridegroom." We have noted elsewhere that the whole business of redemption, which belongs to the Church, is called the kingdom of heaven, because its purpose is that we, freed from the servitude of sin and from the tyranny of the devil, may live a heavenly life on earth and at last, gathered to Christ, reign in the heavens. And it is rightly compared to a wedding, because the whole of salvation consists in this: that we, joined to the Son of God, who alone is the bridegroom of the Church (as John the Baptist also bears witness), are through him reconciled to God the Father, and are made partakers and sharers in heavenly goods. Here, in part, the incomparable goodness of God shines forth, who has deigned to betroth us to his only-begotten Son, the immortal King of glory, to whom all power is given in heaven and on earth; and in part it is shown that our salvation is sure, perfect and everlasting. Of his Eve, who had been formed from the side of the sleeping man, Adam once said: "This is now bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh." So too, from the right of marriage, the Apostle argues concerning the Church, which was born from the death of the Son of God, Jesus Christ, and is gathered into him through faith, that she is flesh of his flesh and bone of his bones, and he says of each of the faithful, or believers, that they are members of the body of Christ. Concerning the bond of marriage the first Adam and the second alike pronounced: "What God has joined together, let not man separate." Just as in marriage the two who were first become one flesh, a work of God, so God has made us the flesh of his Son. There is therefore no danger that anyone should tear us away from him. "No one has ever hated his own flesh," says the Apostle. Would Christ then hate his own flesh, he who is love itself? Paul seems to have observed this when he wrote to the Romans: "Who shall separate us from the love of Christ?" Rom. 8.

units.la: Est autem argumentum parabolae huius Comicum plane, si sic loqui licet, & ideo suis quoq; partibus constat, quae vniuersum Ecclesiae & redemptionis nostrae mysterium explicant. Prima pars Protasim habet, qua apparatus & pompa nuptialis: qui item ad nuptias illas inuitati sunt, & quales ad eas venire debeant, depingitur, & quid fere illis soleat accidere. Altera Epitasin, quae turbas adumbrat, periculosas admodum omnibus, qui vel hypocrisi vel prophanis studijs abrepti salutem suam neglexerint. Tertia Catastrophen, laetam prorsus & fere Comicam pijs, impijs vero & hypocritis Tragicam & funestam. Nunc de singulis, quod Dominus dederit dicemus.
units.tr: The argument of this parable is clearly comic, if I may put it so, and for that reason it also has its own parts, which together set out the whole mystery of the Church and of our redemption. The first part contains the protasis, in which the preparations and pomp of the wedding are described, along with who was invited to those nuptials, what sort of people ought to come to them, and what usually happens to them. The second contains the epitasis, which sketches the disturbances, very dangerous to all who, carried away by either hypocrisy or worldly pursuits, neglect their salvation. The third is the catastrophe, altogether joyful and nearly comic for the godly, but tragic and deadly for the impious and hypocrites. Now we shall speak of each part, as the Lord shall grant.

units.la: Primae partis argumentum fiue summa est: Tunc simile erit regnum caelorum decem virgini- bus, quae sumptis lampadibus suis exierunt in occursum sponsi. Decem virgines typum Ecclesiae & omnium ad hanc pertinentium sustinent. Itaq; intelligi debet omnes, qui professione Christiani sunt. Hi omnes virgines dicuntur quoad professionem fidei. Sic Paulus Cor. Coloss. & multos alios in quibus multa reprehendit, & qui in fide etiam non erant integri, tamen sanctos & fideles dicit, eo quod fidem, quae nos Deo adducit, proficerentur. Et Cor. scribebat, se eos aptauisse vni viro, nempe Christo, vt virginem puram. At quis eius Ecclesiae status fuerit, quam multis, quamq; absurdis erroribus & vitijs, quam item crassis abusibus laborarit, nemo ignorare potest, qui ad banc scri-
units.tr: The argument or summary of the first part is this: "Then the kingdom of heaven will be like ten virgins, who took their lamps and went out to meet the bridegroom." The ten virgins stand for the Church and all who belong to it. Hence it must be understood that all who are Christians by profession are meant. All of these are called virgins with regard to their profession of faith. So Paul, in the letters to the Corinthians, to the Colossians and to many others, though he rebukes them for many things, and though they were not yet sound in the faith, nevertheless calls them holy and faithful, because they professed the faith which brings us to God. And he wrote to the Corinthians that he had betrothed them to one husband, namely Christ, as a pure virgin. But what the state of that Church was, how many and how absurd its errors and vices, how gross its abuses, no one can fail to know who has read these letters even cursorily.

units.la: f ptas epistolas vel obiter perlegerit. Debet hoc propter eos observari, qui temere arcent & excludunt eos a societate Ecclesiae, quos Deus adhuc dignos iudicat, qui ad hanc admittantur: qui item propter aliquos malos damnant totas Ecclesias, & secessionem ab eis faciunt temerariam: quod olim Donatistae fecerunt: hodie Anabaptistae in vsu habent. Admonet quidem Sponsa & Virginis vocabulum, ut Christiani in fide & vita atq; moribus sint integri: nec veri Christiani sunt, qui, quod nomine profitentur, factis negant: veruntamen non semper apud omnes haec integritas locum habebit, sed inter eos, qui Christo & Ecclesiae eius nomen deserunt: hoc discrimen semper erit, ut alij sint prudentes, alij fatui, neq; ante sponsi adventum dignosci semper poterunt, qui nam digni sunt, ut ad nuptias cum illo ingrediantur. Fieri ergo non potest, quin vehementer errent, qui praecipites nimium censuram ante tempus adhibent.
units.tr: This must be observed on account of those who rashly shut out and exclude from the fellowship of the Church those whom God still judges worthy to be admitted to it; and likewise on account of those who condemn whole churches because of some wicked members, and make a rash separation from them. The Donatists did this of old, and the Anabaptists practise it today. The word "bride" and the word "virgin" certainly admonish Christians to be sound in faith and life and morals; and those are not true Christians who deny by their deeds what they profess in name. Yet this soundness will not always be found among all; among those who desert the name of Christ and of his Church there will always be this distinction, that some are wise and others foolish, and before the bridegroom's coming it cannot always be discerned who are worthy to enter with him to the wedding. It is therefore impossible that those who hastily and too soon apply censure before the time should not err grievously.

units.la: Conuenit autem prima parabolae pars cum ea, quae apud Luc. de servis herum a nuptiis reuertentem expectantibus habetur, quos succinctos stare, & lucernas in manibus habere iubet. Christus enim pernoctans nostrae redemptionis negotio in coelos quidem abijt, non autem depositit curam Ecclesiae suae, sed suo tempore reuertetur, ut hanc totam cum vniuersa communione sanctorum quae sponsa ipsius est, ad patriam coelestem transferat, qui beatae immortalitatis locus est, vbi nuptiae illae aeternae peragentur. Nos vero omnes seruij sumus, qui illum expectare, & semper succinctos stare, id est, ad omne officium parati esse debemus. Quia vero hic de nouissimo eius aduentu, adeo, de eius reditu ad iudicium agitur, quando redemptio nostra perficietur, ijs potissimum applicatur parabola haec, qui ipsum tunc excipient, & ad reliquos etiam, qui tunc ex mortuis resuscitati ad eius tribunal sistentur, ut vocem illam laetam audiant, de qua hoc ipso cap. dicetur. Sed & singulis primatim applicari potest, quorum hora fatalis venit, ut hinc euocati migrent ad Dominum. Meminerint hi, se ad nuptias a Christo vocari, & laeti cupiant hinc soluere. Interim vtrique, sive serui sint, qui in certa statione constituti, heri sui aduentum expectant, sive infiar virginum aut conuiuarum nuptialium hinc euocantur in sponsi occursum, ne inani nominis Christiani professione se fefellant, diligenter considerent, quod de virginibus omnibus in genere dicitur quid item de fatuis aut prudentibus. Ita intelligemus quid nos facere, quidue vitare debeamus.
units.tr: The first part of the parable agrees with that in Luke about the servants waiting for their lord to return from the wedding, whom he bids stand girded and hold lamps in their hands. For Christ, having spent the night on the work of our redemption, indeed went up into heaven, but he has not laid down his care of his Church; at his appointed time he will return, to transfer the whole of it, together with the entire communion of saints who are his bride, to the heavenly fatherland, which is the place of blessed immortality, where those eternal nuptials will be celebrated. We indeed are all servants, who ought to await him and always stand girded, that is, be ready for every duty. But because here the subject is his last coming, indeed his return to judgment, when our redemption will be completed, this parable applies chiefly to those who will receive him then, and also to the rest, who will then be raised from the dead and brought before his judgment seat, that they may hear that joyful voice of which this same chapter will speak. But it may also be applied to each person individually, whose fatal hour comes, that being called hence they may depart to the Lord. Let these remember that they are called by Christ to the wedding, and let them joyfully desire to be released from here. Meanwhile, whether they are servants stationed at their post, awaiting their master's arrival, or are called hence like the virgins or the wedding guests to meet the bridegroom, let them not deceive themselves with an empty profession of the Christian name, but carefully consider what is said of all the virgins in general, and likewise of the foolish and the wise. So we shall understand what we ought to do and what we ought to avoid.

units.la: De omnibus in genere dicitur quod exierint sumptis lampadibus suis in occursum sponsi. Est hoc commune omnium Christianorum officium, ut quoad in hoc saeculo viuunt, sui sponsi, & vocationis memores in eius occursum tendant. Nec enim habemus in terris ciuitatem permanentem, sed in coelis paratus est nobis (ut modo diximus) thalamus nuptialis, in quo olim beata immortalitate fruemur. Eo autem tendere nos oportet per vallem lachrymarum, id est, per huius saeculi vitam, vbi laborum & periculorum plena sunt omnia. Non autem satis est, si iter semel ingressi fimus, sed ut in finem vsq; indefessi perseueremus oportet, ne segnescamus, aut fastidio saperati succumbamus, & vocationem nostram deseramus: ne item in huius mundi tenebris aberremus.
units.tr: Of all in general it is said that they went out, taking their lamps, to meet the bridegroom. This is the common duty of all Christians: that, as long as they live in this world, they should, mindful of their bridegroom and their calling, press on to meet him. For we have here no lasting city, but a wedding chamber is prepared for us in heaven (as we have just said), in which one day we shall enjoy blessed immortality. Yet we must travel toward it through the valley of tears, that is, through the life of this age, where all things are full of labours and dangers. Nor is it enough to have entered the way once; we must persevere tirelessly to the end, lest we grow slack, or give way wearied by disgust and abandon our calling, or likewise wander astray in the darkness of this world.

units.la: Quod ne fiat probe obseruari debet, quod in vtraq; parabola de lampadibus & lucernis dicitur. Antiquitus vulgare hoc fuit, quod tedae aut lampades sponsis praeferebantur, quod item in sponsi occursum non sine lampadibus exirent puellae & ita facto opus erat, cum pompae illae nuptiales noctumo tempore ducerentur. Atqui vniuersum illud tempus, quod in hoc saeculo degimus multa caligine & tenebris impeditum est, & nouae subinde errorum & scandalorum occasiones nobis obiiciuntur. Caliginem nobis ipsa ratio offundit, quae lux esse debebat. Exemplum item mundi tenebras abducit. Et afflictiones atq; aduersa tenebris conferuntur in scriptura, eo quod saepe nos rerum dubios & consiliorum omnium incertos reddant. Lucernis ergo & lampadibus perpetuo ardentibus opus est. Has nobis sacrae literae in verbo Dei proponunt. Ideo Dauid de lege tefatur quod oculos illuminet, & alibi precatur, ut verbum Dei sit lucerna pedibus suis & lux semitarum suarum. Et Petrus Apostolus Christianos homines attendere iubet propheticos sermones veluti lucernae in obscuro loco splendenti, donec lucifer oriatur in cordibus nostris & tandem dies ille nobis illucescat, quo ipse apparebit, & omnia reflituet. Itaq; verbum suum nobis commendat, ut hoc luceat in cordibus nostris, & ex eo petamus regulas atq; consilia, quae tuto sequamur, quam diu inter huius mundi tenebras viuimus.
units.tr: So that this does not happen, what is said in both parables about lamps and torches must be carefully observed. In ancient times it was customary that torches or lamps were carried before brides, and that the maidens went out to meet the bridegroom not without lamps; and so it was necessary, since those nuptial processions were conducted at night. But that whole time which we spend in this age is hindered by much darkness and gloom, and new occasions of error and scandal are continually set before us. Reason itself, which ought to be light, casts a mist over us for us. Example likewise draws us into the darkness of the world. And afflictions and adversities are compared with darkness in Scripture, because they often make us doubtful of things and uncertain of all our plans. We therefore need lamps and lanterns burning perpetually. These the holy writings set before us in the Word of God. Hence David says of the law that it enlightens the eyes, and elsewhere prays that the word of God may be a lamp to his feet and a light to his paths. And the apostle Peter bids Christians to attend to the prophetic words as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day star rises in our hearts and that day dawns upon us on which he himself will appear and restore all things. Thus he commends to us his Word, that it may shine in our hearts, and that from it we may seek rules and counsels which we may safely follow, as long as we live amid the darkness of this world.

units.la: Caeterum hic se ostendit discrimen illud de quo nos Dominus per virgines fatuas & prudentes admonet. De his dicit, quod cum lampadibus oleum quoq; in vasis suis acceperint, fatuas autem non item, sed sine oleo cum lucernis vacuis sponso occurrisse. Lucerna ardens dici potest coripsius Christi cognitione illuminatu, qui proprie lux illa mundi est, quae in tenebris lucet, & has vincit atq; dissipat. Ut vero corda nostra per hanc illuminetur, oleo, id est, gratia caelesti vel Spiritus sancti opus est, quae in Psalmo oleum laetitiae dicitur, quod mentes non illuminat modo, verumetiam exhilarat in Christo, ut etiamsi nobis incedendum sit per vallem umbrae mortalis, non tamen timebimus. Prudentiae autem argumentum est, quod non modo lampades habent ista, sed hoc agunt, ut adornatas, & in sponsi aduentum, id est, in omnem aduentum instructas lampades siue lucernas habeant, id est, ut non solum fidei professione gloriantur, verumetiam studeant, ut huic satis faciant. Ut enim splendor lucernae accensae non est durabilis, nisi oleo sufficiatur, hoc aute deficiente euanescit: ita externa fidei professio non prodest, sed nisi gratia spiritus nos in fide confirmet, et hanc per charitatem efficace, & periculis omnibus superiorem faciat, euanescit mox splendor ille exter nus, quo hypocritae sese vendicant, si quis turbo persecutionum nos affiauerit. Qui ergo sine gratia caelestis spiritu instructi ad Christum accedunt, recte factis virginibus conferuntur, ut alibi qui verbum audit nec facit, similis dicitur fatuo, qui magnus impensis aedificat domum super arenam, vbi fundamento solido destituta corruit, dum neq; aquarum neq; ventorum procellis potest resistere. Christianos ergo decet, ut ad Christum accedentes lucernis & oleo simul sese instruant, id est, eidem habeant, quae ex Spiritus sancti suggestione enata, per charitatem fit efficax, & vera Christi cognitione ardeat, quae nullis aduersis succumbat.
units.tr: Moreover, here appears that distinction about which the Lord warns us through the foolish and the wise virgins. Of these it is said that the wise took oil also in their vessels with their lamps, but the foolish did not, and met the bridegroom with empty lamps and without oil. A burning lamp can be taken to mean one illumined by the knowledge of Christ himself, who is properly that light of the world which shines in darkness and overcomes and dispels it. But so that our hearts may be illumined by this, there is need of oil, that is, of heavenly grace or the work of the Holy Spirit, which in the Psalm is called "the oil of gladness", because it not only enlightens minds but also gladdens them in Christ, so that even if we must walk through the valley of the shadow of death, we shall not fear. The sign of prudence, however, is that these not only have lamps, but take care to have their lamps adorned and prepared for the bridegroom's coming, that is, for every coming, that is, that they not only glory in the profession of faith but also strive to live up to it. For just as the brightness of a lit lamp does not last unless it is supplied with oil, and vanishes when the oil fails, so an outward profession of faith profits nothing; unless the grace of the Spirit confirms us in faith and makes it effective through love and superior to all dangers, that outward brightness with which hypocrites display themselves vanishes at once, if some storm of persecution strikes us. Those therefore who approach Christ without being furnished with the grace of the heavenly Spirit are rightly compared to the foolish virgins; as elsewhere he who hears the word and does not do it is said to be like the foolish man who built his house upon the sand at great expense, where, lacking a solid foundation, it collapses, since it cannot resist the storms of waters and winds. Christians ought therefore, as they approach Christ, to equip themselves with lamps and oil together, that is, to have that faith which, sprung from the prompting of the Holy Spirit, becomes effective through love, and burns with the true knowledge of Christ, which does not yield to any adversity.

units.la: Idcirco Dominus apud Lucam graviter monet, ut qui ipsi nomen dare volunt, in seipsos descendant, & sese examinent, num si opus sit, parentes odisse, & propter ipsum omnibus, quae in terris charissima habent, renuntiare possint. Si enim turrim aedificaturus, prius sumptus aut impensas diligenter subducit, num his sufficere possit, & bellum cum hoste gesturus, huius simul & proprias vires inter se conferet, ne tandem cum clade aliqua repulsus infamiam reportet, cuius ipsum sem per paenitebit: quanto eo magis nos hic indulgentios esse convenit, quod natura omnes fatui sumus. Etenim animalis homo non percipit ea, quae sunt Spiritus Dei: nec in nobis sunt facultates, quibus instrui sufficere possimus ad occursum maiestatis Dei, quae in IESV CHRISTO refulgebit, cum veniet ad iudicandum vivos & mortuos.
units.tr: Therefore the Lord warns earnestly in Luke that those who wish to give themselves his name should go down into themselves and examine whether, if need be, they can hate their parents and give up for his sake everything they hold most dear on earth. For if someone about to build a tower first carefully calculates the costs, to see whether he has enough to finish it, and a king about to make war on an enemy first weighs his own forces against the enemy's, lest he be driven back with some defeat and bring home a disgrace that he will regret for ever, how much more ought we to be cautious here, since by nature we are all fools? For the natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God, nor do we have in ourselves the abilities by which we could be equipped to meet the majesty of God, which will shine forth in Jesus Christ when he comes to judge the living and the dead.

units.la: Excutiamus ergo serio & diligenter vasa nostra, & primo quidem (ut Paulus ait, tentemus & exploremus nosipsos, num simus in fide, & nu Christi vere apprehenderimus. Hunc enim unxit Deus oleo laetitiae, id est, Spiritus S. virtute pra consortibus suis, & dat illi spiritu non ad mensuram, sed ita ut ex eius plenitudine omnes accipiamus gratia pro gratia. Curemus ergo ne inani aut falsa fidei professione Christu offendamus, & multa superbe de nobis iactemus, ad quae ipse respondeat: Nō novi vos, discedite a me qui facitis iniquitatem. Humiliemur ite sub potenti eius manu, per obedientiam fidei, & studeamus vocatione & electione nostra firmam facere, dum fidei virtute, id est sanctos & honestos mores, quorum fons est fides, his vero scientia, id est, vera voluntatis Dei cognitione, huic autem continentia, cum hac tolerantia & pietate coniungere, ut opera nostra luceant coram hominibus, & his visis alij quoq; aedificentur. Haec si nobis adsint, non inertes aut fructuosos nos efficient in cognitione Domini nostri IESV CHRISTI. Quia vero nihil horum ex nobis habemus, precibus nos indefinetur inuigilare oportet, & quae in nobis sunt dona Dei, assidua meditatione, & frequenti usu fusc itare, ut ijs faeneremur Domino. Ita augebitur & crescet in vasis nostris, perinde ut olim in vidua Sareptana lecytho oleu illud gratia Dei: nec vnquam nos deficiet lux, quae nos deducet, ut sponso nostro laeti possimus occurrere.
units.tr: Let us therefore examine our vessels seriously and diligently. First, as Paul says, let us test and examine ourselves, whether we are in the faith, and whether we have truly laid hold of Christ. For God has anointed him with the oil of gladness, that is, with the power of the Holy Spirit, above his companions, and gives him the Spirit not by measure, so that from his fullness we all receive grace upon grace. Let us therefore take care not to offend Christ with an empty or false profession of faith, or to boast proudly of many things, to which he would answer: "I never knew you; depart from me, you who work iniquity." Let us humble ourselves under his mighty hand through the obedience of faith, and let us strive to make our calling and election firm. Let us join to faith virtue, that is, holy and honest morals, of which faith is the source; to virtue, knowledge, that is, true knowledge of God's will; and to knowledge, self-control, together with patience and godliness. Then our works will shine before men, and others, seeing them, will also be edified. If these things are present in us, they will keep us from being idle or unfruitful in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ. But since we have none of these from ourselves, we must watch constantly in prayer, and by diligent meditation and frequent use we must rekindle the gifts of God that are in us, so that we may lend them out to the Lord. Thus that oil of God's grace will be increased and will grow in our vessels, just as once the oil in the jar of the widow of Sarepta did. And the light that leads us will never fail, so that we may go joyfully to meet our bridegroom.

units.la: Quam vero necesse sit nos his sedulo studere, hic ipse locus docet. Narrat enim Christus, quid virginibus istis simul omnibus acciderit. Tardante sponso (inquit) nictarunt omnes & dormierunt. Admiratur hic fatalis scitantia & securitas, quae omnibus est insita. Cunctatur plerunque Dominus, nec subito adest, quoties venturus speratur, sed paenitentia spacium permittit cotumacibus quoq;, ut interea impleatur electorum suorum numerus. Ide fit quando suis periclitantibus non illico succurrit, cum hora mortis praeter spem differtur: Cum ite aduentus sui diem extrahit, cuius spem signa praedicta quotidie nobis faciunt. In his omnibus sopor nobis obrepit: dum impatientia vel lenitate, vel securitate aut fastidio vincimur, qui in terrenis summis indefessi: & nullius vel la
units.tr: How necessary it is for us to devote ourselves earnestly to these things, this very passage teaches. For Christ relates what befell all those virgins together: "While the bridegroom tarried, they all slumbered and slept." Here we marvel at the fatal carelessness and complacency that is implanted in everyone. The Lord often delays, and does not come at once whenever he is expected to come; but he allows space for repentance even to the stubborn, so that meanwhile the number of his elect may be filled up. The same happens when he does not immediately help his own in danger, when the hour of death is put off beyond all hope, and when he prolongs the day of his coming, the hope of which the signs foretold show us every day. In all these things sleep creeps over us, while we, who are tireless in earthly affairs, are overcome by impatience or by sloth, by security or by disgust, and by the weariness of any toil

units.la: {f} Pfal. 45. ... Luc. 14. 1. Cor. 1. boris vel mora tædio superamur: tunc (inquam) dormimus, qui divinæ bonitatis consideratione et citari debebamus, & ad pietatis studium expergefieri. Nec malis modò hoc accidit, quos infelicis mundi studium aut amor excæcauit, vt de salute vix vnquam serio cogitent, verumetiam melioribus qui pietatis & cælestium studio ardere & diuinis intenti esse videntur. Ideo omnes niĥasse & obdormiuisse dicuntur. Est hoc tam vulgare inter homines, vt inter Ethnicos vulgò iactata fuerint hæc dicta, nemo sine crimine vixit. Quando quidem bonus dormitat Homerus. Nam etsi non omnes illicitis cupiditatibus ardeant, licet non omnes atrocibus vitijs laborent, aut facinora designent, quæ prophani quoq; homines detestantur, tamen remittit sæpe in pijs pietatis ardor, refrigescit cultus diuini studium, languent item, qui prius feruebant, & securi omne virtutis studium intermittunt, qui paulo ante omnes bene agendi occasiones solicité venabantur. Et quid nobis de nostro statu dolendum est, qui se putamus Apostolos præ mærore dormitauisse ad montem oliueti, nec tristitiæ mis concionibus Christi, quas hic de sua morte & immani collega ipsorum Iudæ proditoris facinore habebat, potuisse expergefieri? Et hodie plerique dormitant inter voluptatum & fælerum licentiam, dum totus mundus periclitatur. Securi stertunt antistites, somno oppressi iacent viri principes, licet orbis terrarum bellis ardeat, seditionibus scindatur, lue ac peste infestetur, fame ringatur, nec ista curæ sunt ijs, quos Deus publicos speculatores constituit. Quanto igitur studio opus est, vt seipsos singuli ad vigilantiam excitent? quanta animi deuotione precibus incumbere debemus, vt boni ille pastor Israelis qui non dormitat, fideles pastores dei, qui ferijs admonitionibus & fidis consiliis mundum ex hac communi somnolentia & fatali securitate & interitu, qui omnibus immi-nere videtur, revocent? Et de his eò maiori cura nos cogitare decet, quod hoc nouissimo seculo mortem mundi fortem nobis polliceri non possumus. Maior semper erit fatuorum numerus & hypocritarum, qui etsi lucernas Euangelij sedulò ostentent, oleo tamen cælestis gratiæ & Spiritus Sancti lucernam destituuntur, & quam ore proficentur fidem, factis negant. Et quia hi numero vincunt, & ἐπτ᾽ ἀξιόν, id est, plures mali sunt (vt Bias dicebat) fit vt meliores quoq; communi exemplo abripiantur, neq; aliqua spes melioris conditionis appareat. Quid verò fiat illis, qui dum in excusibus stare deberent, ignaui sierunt, proximo sermone dicetur. Nunc primatim & publicè oremus Dei filium IESVM CHRISTVM, vt vbiq; gentium omnes expergefaciat, vt in suam propriam & simul in publicam salutem intenti in ipsius occursum sese parent, ne propter nostram ignauiam nomen eius male audiat, & Ecclesiæ salus periclitetur. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: or delay. Then, I say, we sleep, we who ought to be roused by consideration of divine goodness and awakened to the pursuit of godliness. This does not happen only to the wicked, whom the love or pursuit of the unhappy world has blinded so that they hardly ever think seriously about salvation; it happens even to the better sort, who seem to burn with zeal for piety and heavenly things and to be intent on divine matters. Therefore all are said to have nodded and fallen asleep. This is so common among men that even among the heathen this saying was commonly repeated: no one lives without fault; indeed, "good Homer nods." For although not all are inflamed with unlawful desires, and not all are burdened with atrocious vices or commit crimes that even profane men detest, yet the ardour of the godly often slackens, the zeal for worship of God cools, and those who once burned grow faint; and those who a little before eagerly hunted every opportunity to do good become secure and drop all zeal for virtue. And why should we grieve over our own condition, when the Apostles, overcome with sorrow, fell asleep on the Mount of Olives, and could not be roused even by the sad discourses of Christ, which he was giving there about his own death and the monstrous deed of their colleague Judas the betrayer? Even today most men sleep amid the licence of pleasures and profits, while the whole world is in peril. The bishops snore in security, the men who are princes lie oppressed by sleep, although the earth is ablaze with wars, torn by seditions, afflicted by plague and pestilence, and wasted by famine; and these things are no concern to those whom God has set up as public watchmen. How great, then, must be the zeal with which each one should rouse himself to watchfulness! With how much devotion of soul we ought to apply ourselves to prayer, that the good Shepherd of Israel, who does not sleep, may call the faithful ministers of God, who by pointed admonitions and faithful counsels should recall the world from this common drowsiness and fatal security and from the destruction that seems to threaten all! And we ought to consider these things all the more carefully because in this last age we cannot promise ourselves that the world will long endure. The number of fools and hypocrites will always be greater, who, although they diligently display the lamps of the Gospel, yet lack the oil of heavenly grace and of the Holy Spirit, and deny by their deeds the faith they profess with their mouths. And because these outnumber the others, and [ἐπτ᾽ ἀξιόν] that is, "the greater part are bad" (as Bias used to say), it comes about that even the better are carried away by the common example, and no hope of a better condition appears. What will become of those who, when they ought to have stood at their posts, were slothful, will be told in the next sermon. Now let us pray publicly and together to God's Son Jesus Christ, that he may awaken all people everywhere, so that, intent both on their own salvation and on the common good, they may prepare themselves to meet him, lest because of our sloth his name be ill spoken of and the salvation of the Church be endangered. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCLXXXV.
units.tr: Homily 285.

units.la: Media autem nocte clamor ortus est, Ecce sponsus venit, exite in occursum eius. Tunc surrexerunt omnes illæ virgines, & præparaverunt lampades suas. Fatuæ autem prudentibus dixerunt, Date nobis ex oleo vestro, quia lampades nostræ extinguuntur. Responderunt verò prudentes illæ dicentes: Nequaquam, ne non sufficiat nobis & vobis: Ite verò potius ad eos qui vendunt, & ipsi vobis emite. Cum autem irent emptum, venit sponsus: & quæ paratæ erant, introierunt cum eo ad nuptias, clausaq; est ianua. Postea verò veniunt & reliquæ virgines, dicentes: Domine Domine aperi nobis. Ipse verò respondit eis: Amen amen dico vobis, non noui vos. Vigilate itaq; quia nescitis diem neq; horam, qua filius hominis veniet.
units.tr: "But at midnight there was a cry: Behold, the bridegroom comes; go out to meet him. Then all those virgins rose and trimmed their lamps. And the foolish said to the wise, 'Give us some of your oil, for our lamps are going out.' But the wise answered, saying, 'No, lest there not be enough for us and for you. Go rather to those who sell, and buy for yourselves.' And while they went away to buy, the bridegroom came, and those who were ready went in with him to the marriage feast, and the door was shut. Afterwards the other virgins also came, saying, 'Lord, Lord, open to us.' But he answered them, 'Verily, verily, I say to you, I do not know you. Watch therefore, for you know neither the day nor the hour when the Son of man will come.'"

units.la: Magnum & incomparabile bonitatis Dei plus quam paterna argumentum est, quod Filio suo Vnigenito, IESV CHRISTO, ex mortali & calamitoso hominum genere non modò sponsam deligere dignatus est, quam illi coniungeret, & regni sui cælestis ac æterni facerer consortem, verumetiam ex hominibus eos eligit, quorum ministerio vtitur, vt tanquam pronubæ & nuptiales puellæ in sponsalibus faciendis & nuptijs parandis fiue deducendis sua opera illi conferat. At non minus e contra reprehendi meretur hominum socordia, qui ad tanta dignitate vocati de ea tuenda, nō vt par erat, cogitant, sed inter mundi illecebras & studia somnum sibi obrepere patiuntur. imo sopore interdum grauantur, vt vix vllæ admonitiones & correptiones illis expergefaciendis sufficiant. Nec vulgo solum hic peccant inferiores, verum etiam meliores, & qui reliquis præstat. Ideo nuper prudentes quoq; virgines cum fatuis dormitauisse dicuntur. Et hodie hoc ipsum nossi-ne periculo, & bonorum dolore fieri experimur.
units.tr: It is a great and incomparable proof of God's goodness, more than fatherly, that he has deigned to choose for his only-begotten Son, Jesus Christ, not only a bride from the mortal and wretched race of men, whom he might join to his Son and make a partner in his heavenly and eternal kingdom, but also that from among men he chooses those whose ministry he uses, so that, like matchmakers and bridesmaids, they may contribute their work to him in arranging the betrothal and preparing or conducting the wedding. But, on the other hand, the carelessness of men deserves no less to be rebuked, for although they are called to so great a dignity, they do not think about guarding it as they ought, but allow sleep to creep over them amid the allurements and pursuits of the world. Indeed, they are sometimes so weighed down by drowsiness that scarcely any admonitions or rebukes suffice to wake them. And it is not only the lower sort who sin here, but also the better sort, and those who excel the rest. Therefore, lately, the wise virgins too are said to have slept along with the foolish. And today we experience this same thing happening, not without danger and the grief of good people.

units.la: Sed vt Deus dormitantibus veternum illud excutiat, secunda parabolæ pars docet, quæ Epi-tafim habet: Eodem plane modo, quo discipulis ad oliueti montem. Sæpe hos monebat Christus, & soporem eis exprobrabat, & quam parum magnificis promissis respónderent, quæ in vltima Cœna iactarant. Sed cum nihil proficeret monendo, amaro Sarcasmo illos pungens, ait: Dormite quod su-perest, & requiescite. Quasi diceret: Pergite vt lubet, quando verbis amicus excitari non potestis: En adest qui verberibus vos expergefaciet. Et Iudas cum armata cohorte digito monstrat, qui & ipsum inuadit, & discipulos turpi fuga dissipat. Ita in præsenti factum. Nam media nocte clamor exortus est: Ecce sponsus venit: Exite in occursum eius. Media nox repentinu & improuisum IESV CHRISTI aduentu significat, de quo Petrus scribit: Veniet nofurum sicut fur dies ille Domini. Et Paulus: Cum dicent, Pax & læta omnia, tunc repentinu eis imminet exitiu, sicuti dolor partus mulieri vterum ferenti. At repentina pericula, & improuisa vehementius terrent, & magis anxios ac folicitos reddunt. Clamore aut iflum alibi scriptura voce Archangeli & tuba Dei aut κέλευσμα vocat, quod proprie nauticu clamore denotat, quo nautæ se mutuo ad opus adhortantur, & qui molestissimus esse solet ijs, qui ad remos destinati scutica aut flagello simul cæduntur, vt remis fortius incumbant. Et sane magnum & acutum esse oportebit clamorem, qui mortuos in sepulchris iacentes excitare poterit. Quanto aut cum terrore coniunctus erit clamor ille, quando (vt Petrus dicit) simul cœli cum stridore prætcribunt, elementa vero æstuantia soluentur, terraq; & quæ in ea sunt opera exurentur. Quis nescit, quam terribili fragore concutiantur vicina loca, si domus vna & altera a summo culmine ruat? Qualis ergo erit, quando incendio terra, mare, cœli, vrbes omnes cum alijs ædificijs & animalibus quoq; conflagrabunt, & simul vniuersa totius mundi machina corruet. Debemus de hoc frequenter cogitare, vt facilius admittamus Verbi Dei admonitiones, quibus quotidie nos edocet, vt nos ad Filij sui aduentum præparemus. Nam etsi clamor ille & conflagrantis mundi stridor siue fragor pijs quoq; propter communem omnibus infirmitatem sola cogitatione terrorem parere possit, & fere toto animo horreant, qui ista seriò meditantur, beati tamen erunt tunc, qui prius sese in his meditationibus ad pietatem exercuerunt. Vt enim classico non ita terretur miles fortis, qui illo ad iuuetus didicit hoc audito in acie descendere, & cum hoste cominus cogredi: ita mouetur quide pij animus, si quæ tunc rerum facies futura sit cogitet, quia aut hunc sciit fore diem restitutionis, quo cœli noui & terra noua creabuntur, in quibus ipsi æternu cum sponso suo Christo & ipsoa eius, vniuersa electorum Ecclesia, gaudeant, momentaneus erit terror hic, quæ fides mox in gaudium ineffabile conuertet, dum de sua redemptione certi exultabunt, vt deposito hoc luteo & mortali tabernaculo ad Christum transferentur, vt in corporibus quo quæ suis eius corpori glorioso conformes fiant, & regni cœlorum possessione adeant. Alia aut erit prophanorum fors, qui mundi voluptatib. immersi cœlestia ignorat, & propria cofcientia diffate sentiunt sibi paratu esse igne illu inextinguibile, in quo cu diabolo, cui seruierunt, æterno cruciabitur.
units.tr: But so that God may shake off that drowsiness from those who sleep, the second part of the parable teaches, which has an epitaph: in exactly the same way as with the disciples on the Mount of Olives. Christ often warned them, and rebuked their sleepiness, and how little they lived up to the great promises they had made at the Last Supper. But when warning achieved nothing, he stung them with bitter sarcasm and said, "Sleep on now, and take your rest." As if he were saying: Go on as you please, since you cannot be roused by a friend's words; behold, one is here who will wake you with blows. And Judas, with an armed cohort, points him out with his finger; he attacks him, and scatters the disciples in shameful flight. So it was done in the present case. For at midnight a cry arose: "Behold, the bridegroom comes; go out to meet him." Midnight signifies the sudden and unforeseen coming of Jesus Christ, of which Peter writes: "The day of the Lord will come as a thief." And Paul: "When they say, Peace and all is well, then sudden destruction hangs over them, as the pain of childbirth comes upon a woman with child." But sudden and unforeseen dangers terrify more violently and make men more anxious and troubled. Scripture elsewhere calls this cry the voice of the archangel and the trumpet of God, or keleusma [κέλευσμα], which properly denotes the cry of sailors, by which they urge one another on to their work, and which is usually most distressing to those who are assigned to the oars and are beaten with a whip or lash at the same time, so that they may bend more strongly to the oars. And surely the cry must be loud and piercing if it is able to rouse the dead lying in their tombs. How much more terrifying, then, will that cry be, when (as Peter says) the heavens will pass away with a roar, the elements will melt with fervent heat, and the earth and the works that are in it will be burned up. Who does not know with what a dreadful crash neighbouring places are shaken if one or two houses fall from their highest roof? What, then, will it be like when the earth, the sea, the heavens, all cities with their buildings and also the animals will be set on fire together, and the whole machinery of the world collapses at once? We ought to think about this often, so that we may more readily receive the admonitions of God's Word, by which he teaches us daily to prepare ourselves for the coming of his Son. For although that cry and the roar or crash of the burning world can, by thought alone, produce terror even in the godly, on account of the weakness common to all, and those who seriously meditate on these things will almost tremble with their whole soul, nevertheless those will be blessed who have previously trained themselves in piety through these meditations. For just as a brave soldier is not so terrified by the trumpet call, since he has learned from youth to go down into battle at its sound and to engage the enemy at close quarters, so indeed the godly mind is moved if it thinks about what the face of things will then be. For they know that this will be the day of restoration, on which new heavens and a new earth will be created, in which they themselves, together with their bridegroom Christ, and the whole Church of the elect, will rejoice forever. This terror is momentary, and faith will soon turn it into unspeakable joy, while they, certain of their redemption, exult as they are transferred to Christ when this earthly and mortal tabernacle is laid aside, so that they may be made conformed in their bodies to his glorious body, and may enter into possession of the kingdom of heaven. But the lot of the profane will be different: they, immersed in worldly pleasures, are ignorant of heavenly things, and by their own conscience they feel that the unquenchable fire is made ready for them, in which they will be tormented eternally with the devil, whom they served.

units.la: Docet hoc Dominus hoc loco, nec obscure rursus de discrimine virginum prudentum & fatuarum nos admonet. Orto enim clamore isto, nullius trepidationis aut terroris metio fit, qui pruden tes perculerit: Quia enim oleum cum lucernis ad manus habuerant, lucernas suas absq; mora parurant, quæ instructa luce illis præbuerunt, ad quam inoffenso pede obuia progredi, & sponsum adue tante, omneq; eius apparatum læta speitare & excipere potuerunt. Ideo hic quoq; illas excipit, & in suum comitatum admissas introduxit in thalamum nuptialem, qui beata immortalitatis sedes est. Ita fiet pijs omnibus, qui vel vt ferui fideles, & induslrij herum cum lucernis succinctis expe ctant, vel ad Christi aduentu lucernas suas oleo cœlestis gratiae instructas habent, id est, quorum cor da luce fidei per charitate agentis ardent. His Christus dicet (vt suo loco audiemus) Venite benedicti Patris mei, possidete regnum paratum vobis a iactu fundamentis mundi. At aliter longe fatuæ, quæ hactenus quidè ad nuptias satis instructæ viræ sunt, cum lampades & ipsæ habuerent, at nunc demum multa nocte illis incommodissimum accidit, vt suam egestatem & inopiam sentire inceperint. Nam confitentur lampades suas, quae prius ardere & lucere videbantur, extingui. Id circo prudentibus dicunt: Date nobis de oleo vestro. In eo autem stultitiam suam declarant, quod non ante de necessario sibi apparatu cogitant, quam lucernas suas extingui, & se in extrema necessitate constitutas vident. Est hic typus hypocritarum, qui plerunque sapientissimi & sanctissimi mortalium videri volunt. Nam in externo cultu instituendo mire industrij sunt, & ita hunc instituunt, ut veris Dei cultoribus longe praestare videantur. Sed coram Christi tribunali externus ille splendor consistere non poterit, & quando tuba Dei audietur, quae suo clangore corda & intimos conscientiae recessus penetrabit, non plus illos iuuabit cultus externi fiducia, quam sese venditant, quam Adamum olim perizomata ficulnea, quae sibi ipsi & Euae sua fecerat, ut nuditate suam tegeret. Ut primum enim se a Deo quaeri & quasi citari audiebat, illo dicente, Adam ubi es? In pedes se coniecit, de fuga & latebris cogitas. Ita hypocritae, qui per fatuas illas figurantur, se quidem fatuas patos esse & satis lucis habere arbitrantur, dum tardante sponso aut Iudice dormiunt. At quando clamor ille audietur, qui a mortuis excitatos ad Christi tribunal omnes citabit, tum demum se imparatis esse, et in superstitionum tenebris misere haerere & vagari seu tiet, & terra sibi debiscere vellet, ne coram Christo coparere ipsos oporteret. Deinde, ut fatuae ista ad prudentium praesidia convertuntur, et ab his petunt, quod penes se a Deo acceptum in suis vasis quaerere debebant: Ita superstitiosi qui suis superstitionibus seipsos decipiunt, dum in hoc se nullo viuunt, sub vita sua fine, quando sibi hinc migrandum esse vident, se omni salute destitutos esse sentiunt, & cum Adriano Imperatore quiritantur, Animula vagula, blandula, Quae nunc abibis in loca? Pallidula, frigida, Nudula, Nec ut soles dabis iocos. Et salutis suae incerti, hanc apud eos quaerunt, quos prius toto caelo errauisse constat. Fit hoc frequenter hodie, ut tales ad opera supererogationis confugiant, quae a sacrificiis & monachis rede merunt: vel in meritis Diuorum caelitum ipsem habeant, quibus nunquam hoc in mente venit, quod haec alicui salutem afferre debeant. Idcirco Dominus prudentes respondisse ait non sine stomacho: Nequaquam. Q.d. Nunc nos tam sordidas putatis, quae in diuinis turpe quaestu captemus, & dona Dei, quae il le ex gratuita liberalitate omnibus impertit, vel prece vel pretio velimus largiri ijs, qui salute pro pria ignaui negligunt? Et rationis loco addunt: Ne nobis sufficiat nobis & vobis. Quibus verbis no obscurae fatentur, sibi non tantum esse olei, id est, gratiae caelestis, ut alijs impertiri possint: Imo si id velint, ne sibi ipsis quidem fore, quod ad salutem propria sufficiat. Quod unum sufficit confutandis nundinatoribus illis sacrorum, qui tantum sibi ipsis & suorum operum meritis tribuunt, ut opera supererogationis iactitent, quae fatuis diuendunt, qui pro vili pretio caeli & regni caelestis thesauros venales inueniri existimant. Peccant hi omnes multifariam. Nam apud homines αἰσχροκερδής, id est turpis quaestus studiosos quaerunt, quod apud unum Deum quaeri debebat. Deinde cum Simone Mago turpiter falluntur, dum Dei dona non pluris aestimant, quam quod ea pecuniis acquiri arbitrantur. Ideo illis etiam seruit illud Petri Apostoli, qui Simone horribili execratione deuouens, dixit: Argentum tuum tecum pereat: Non est tibi pars neq; fors in hoc negotio: Nam cor tuum non est rectum in Dei conspectu. At hodie soli pro catholicis & orthodoxis habentur, qui cum vacuis suis lucernis vel sibi ipsis vel alijs hac ratione volunt consulere.
units.tr: The Lord teaches this in this place, and he reminds us, not obscurely, of the distinction between the wise and the foolish virgins. For when that cry arises, no fear or terror of any kind seizes the wise, because they had the oil with their lamps at hand; they trimmed their lamps without delay, and these, once lit, gave them light, by which they could go forward to meet the coming bridegroom without stumbling, and welcome him and all his retinue with joy. Therefore he receives them here too, and, admitting them to his company, leads them into the wedding chamber, which is the blessed abode of immortality. So it will be for all the godly, who either, like faithful and diligent servants, wait for their master with lamps girded up, or who, at the coming of Christ, have their lamps supplied with the oil of heavenly grace, that is, whose hearts burn with the light of faith working through love. To these Christ will say (as we shall hear in its place): "Come, you blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world." But the foolish virgins are quite different. Although hitherto they were indeed sufficiently equipped for the wedding, and had lamps of their own, now at last, in the dead of night, it happens to them most inconveniently that they begin to feel their poverty and want. For they see that their lamps, which seemed to burn and shine before, are going out. Therefore they say to the wise, "Give us some of your oil." In this they reveal their folly, that they do not think of the necessary provision until they see their lamps going out and themselves placed in extreme need. This is a picture of hypocrites, who for the most part wish to seem the wisest and holiest of mortals. For they are remarkably diligent in establishing outward worship, and they arrange it in such a way that they seem far superior to the true worshippers of God. But before the judgment seat of Christ that outward show will not be able to stand, and when the trumpet of God is heard, which with its clamour will penetrate the hearts and the innermost recesses of conscience, the trust they place in outward worship will help them no more than it helped Adam of old, when he covered his nakedness with the fig-leaf aprons that he had made for himself and for Eve. For as soon as he heard that God was seeking him and, as it were, summoning him, and God said, "Adam, where are you?", he took to his heels, thinking of flight and hiding places. So the hypocrites, who are represented by those foolish virgins, think that they are indeed foolish, and that they have enough light, while the bridegroom or judge delays and they sleep. But when that cry is heard, which will summon all, raised from the dead, to the judgment seat of Christ, then at last they will realise that they are unprepared, and that they have wretchedly been stuck and wandering in the darkness of superstitions, and they will wish that the earth would open for them, so that they would not have to appear before Christ. Then, just as the foolish turn to the wise for protection and ask of them what they ought to have sought from God, who gave it to them, so superstitious people, who deceive themselves by their superstitions, while they live in such a way that they have no concern for this, near the end of their life, when they see that they must depart hence, feel that they are destitute of all salvation, and lament with the Emperor Hadrian: "Little soul, wandering, charming, where are you now going? Pale, cold, naked, you will not make your jokes as you used to." And uncertain of their salvation, they seek it from those whom it is well known they had long been wandering far from. This happens frequently today, that such people take refuge in works of supererogation, which they receive from the sacristans and monks; or they place their hope in the merits of the blessed saints, who never had this in mind, that these things should bring salvation to anyone. Therefore the Lord says that the wise answered, not without irritation, "No." That is, "Do you think us so mean, that we would make a shameful profit out of divine things, and would be willing to bestow for prayer or for price the gifts of God, which he freely and graciously gives to all, on those who carelessly neglect their own salvation?" And as a reason they add: "Lest there not be enough for us and for you." By these words they plainly admit that they do not have so much oil, that is, of heavenly grace, that they could share it with others; indeed, even if they wished to, there would not be enough for themselves to suffice for their own salvation. This one fact is enough to refute those peddlers of sacred things, who attribute so much to themselves and the merits of their own works that they boast of works of supererogation, which they sell to fools, who think that the treasures of heaven and the kingdom of heaven can be found for sale at a low price. All these men sin in many ways. For they seek among men those who are greedy of base gain [αἰσχροκερδής], which ought to be sought from the one God alone. Then they are shamefully deceived along with Simon the Magician, while they value the gifts of God no more highly than that they think they can be acquired with money. Therefore the saying of the apostle Peter also applies to them, who, cursing Simon with a dreadful execration, said: "May your silver perish with you. You have no part or lot in this matter, for your heart is not right in the sight of God." Yet today only those are regarded as Catholic and orthodox who with their empty lamps wish to provide for themselves or others in this way.

units.la: Sed non solum ista respondent prudentes virgines, sed falsam quoque ironiam addunt, qua fatuas ad vendentes remittunt. Ite (inquiunt) ad eos qui vendunt, & ipsa vobis emite. Quod no ita accipi debet, quasi vel in hoc vel futuro saeculo, vel in caelo vel apud inferos sint aliqui, qui venalia habeant dona Spiritus sancti. Christus enim sua gratis offert, ut apud Isa. legitur, per quae adse inuitans omnes qui seruari cupiunt, clamat: O vos omnes qui sitis, venite ad aquas: etiam vos, qui no habe tis pecunias, venite: coparate & comedite: emite sine argento & sine pretio vinu & lac. Et ibidem omne illud ceu inutile damnat, quod pro pecunia emitur, dicens: Cur expenditis pecunia pro no pane & labore vestru pro eo quod no satiat? Sed & qua ratione & quo pretio redimatur, docet, quae animas satiat: nimirum diligenti auscultatione verbi. Audiendo audite me (inquit) & comedite bonu.
units.tr: But the wise virgins do not only answer this way; they also add a false irony, sending the foolish ones away to the sellers: "Go," they say, "to those who sell, and buy for yourselves." This must not be taken to mean that there are any people, in this age or the age to come, in heaven or in hell, who have the gifts of the Holy Spirit for sale. Christ offers his gifts freely, as is read in Isaiah, where he calls out to all who desire to be saved, inviting them: "O all you who thirst, come to the waters; and you who have no money, come, buy and eat; buy wine and milk without silver and without price." And in the same place he condemns everything that is bought with money as useless, saying: "Why do you spend money on what is not bread, and your labour on what does not satisfy?" He also teaches by what means and at what price that which satisfies souls is bought: namely, by attentive hearing of the Word. "Hear me," he says, "and eat what is good."

units.la: Et Apostolus, quos mysteriorum suorum dispensatores constituit, dicebat: Dono accepistis, dono date. Ita que in Dei verbo panis et potus ille inuenitur, qui nos recreat in Domino. In eode habetur etiam oleu Spiritus S. quod vera luce in cordibus nostris accedit, qua qui sequuntur, in tenebris no errant.
units.tr: And the Apostle, whom he appointed as dispensers of his mysteries, said: "You received freely, give freely." Thus in the Word of God is found that bread and drink which refreshes us in the Lord. In the same Word is also found the oil of the Holy Spirit, which comes into our hearts as a true light; those who follow it do not go astray in darkness.

units.la: Et hunc esse huius loci sensum, parabola huius Catastrophe siue conclusio docet. Sequitur enim: Cum autem irent emptum, venit Sponsus: & quae paratae erant, introierunt cum eo ad nuptias, claufaq; est ianua. Postea vero veniunt & reliquae virgines, dicentes: Domine, Domine, aperi nobis. Ipse vero respondens, ait: Non novi vos. Venit Sponsus dum fatuae abeunt emptu oleu. Dum enim hora illa fatalis aduenerit, qua vel toti mundo fine suum afferet, vel singulis, Christus impa ratos non expectabit diutius, neq; electorum suorum, qui ia pridem seipsos, vt par est, praeparauerunt, defideriu diutius frustrabitur: sed (vt paulo ante diximus) ad fe affumptos ad coeleste gaudium introducet. Et quia tunc finalis sententia feretur, qua prudentes omnes seruabuntur, fatui vero & hypocritae omnes damnabuntur, claudetur post hanc latam ianua, nec aliud tepus erit, quo de aliquius emendatione aut iudicij five decreti mutatione aut mitigatione agi queat. Frustra item pe tent doceri, qui tepus praedicationis, & occasiones in hoc saeculo oblatas neglexerunt. Scimus quid epuloni apud inferos aftuanti, & profratribus intercedenti, vt aliquis ex defunctorum numero dofor aut monitor ad illos mitteretur, dictum fit: Habent Mosem & Prophetas, audiat eos. Item, Si Mosem & Proph.no audiunt, neq; quide quisquam ex mortuis excitetur, assentientur. Luc.16.
units.tr: That this is the meaning of this passage, the parable's outcome or conclusion shows. For it follows: "While they went to buy, the bridegroom came, and those who were ready went in with him to the marriage, and the door was shut. Afterwards the other virgins also came, saying: Lord, Lord, open to us. But he answered and said: I do not know you." The bridegroom comes while the foolish ones are gone to buy oil. For when that fatal hour arrives, which will bring an end either to the whole world or to each single person, Christ will not wait any longer for the unbelievers, nor will he any longer frustrate the desire of his elect, who have long since prepared themselves as they ought; but (as we said a little before) he will lead them, taken to himself, into heavenly joy. And since the final sentence will then be pronounced, by which all the wise will be saved, while the foolish and the hypocrites will all be condemned, the door will be shut once the sentence is passed, and there will be no further time in which anyone's amendment, or any change or mitigation of judgment or decree, could be discussed. In vain, likewise, will those seek to be taught who have neglected the time of preaching and the opportunities offered in this age. We know what was said to the rich man burning in hell, who pleaded for his brothers, that someone from the number of the dead should be sent to them as a teacher or warner: "They have Moses and the Prophets; let them hear them." Likewise: "If they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be persuaded even if someone rises from the dead." Luke 16.

units.la: Veniunt autem clauf a ianua fatuae quoq; virgines, & intromitti cupiunt. Manet enim in ex clusis quoq; salutis desiderium, vt ex alijs etia locis potest colligi, vt cruciatus fiue dolor maior fit, quae ex damnationis suae sensu percipiet. Ideo alibi ait Christus: Illic erit fletus & stridor dentium, cum videritis Abrahamum, Ifaacum & Iacobum & omnes Prophetas in regno Dei, vos autem expelli foras. Excitent nos ista ad ferium salutis studium, ne quam occasione negligamus, qua in Verbo Dei & Christi cognitione poftimus proficere: & semper in animis nostris recens obseruetur nunquam fatis obseruata Apostoli admonitio: Excitare qui dormis, & surge a mortuis, & illuce fcet tibi Christus: Videte igitur, quomodo accurate incedatis, no vt insipientes, sed vt sapientes: Redimentes occasionem, quonia dies mali sunt. De morte peccati loquitur Paulus, a qua nos excitari oportet, dum hic viuimus, & in hoc intentos esse, ne tempus nobis aliud agendo elabi patiamur. Vt enim homines frugi temporis parciffimi sunt, & hunc summum & pretiosissimum thesaurum esse existimant, ita in aeternae salutis negotio hoc ante omnia obseruetur, ne (vt Apelles olim dicebat) aliqua dies abeat, quin linea dufta superfit. Itaq; mercatoribus nos cofert Apostolus, qui vt lucrii faciant nundinarum tempora minime negligunt, & omnes alias comoditates atq; delitias lucello quam modico postponunt. Quod cum illi propter opes fluxas huius saeculi faciant, quanto magis nos propter beatae immortalitatis gaudium, & aeternam regni coelorum gloriam faciemus? Et excitet nos, quod vita haec breuis est, & facies mundi praeterit, dies vero mali & periculorum pleni sunt, quae nos a salutis via auocant. 1. Cor. 7.
units.tr: But the foolish virgins also come to the shut door and desire to be let in. For the desire for salvation remains even in those who are shut out, as can be gathered from other places too, so that the torment or grief will be greater in proportion to the sense of their damnation that they will feel. Therefore Christ says elsewhere: "There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth, when you see Abraham, Isaac and Jacob and all the Prophets in the kingdom of God, but you yourselves cast out." Let these things rouse us to a serious pursuit of salvation, so that we neglect no opportunity by which we may make progress in the knowledge of the Word of God and of Christ; and let the Apostle's admonition, never sufficiently observed, always remain freshly in our minds: "Awake, you who sleep, and rise from the dead, and Christ will shine upon you. See then how carefully you walk, not as fools but as wise, redeeming the time, because the days are evil." Paul speaks of the death of sin, from which we must be roused while we live here, and we must be intent on this, lest we allow time to slip away by our doing something else. For just as thrifty people are very careful of time and regard it as their greatest and most precious treasure, so in the business of eternal salvation this above all must be observed: that (as Apelles once said) no day passes without a line drawn. Therefore the Apostle compares us to merchants, who, in order to make a profit, by no means neglect the times of the markets, and who set aside all other conveniences and pleasures for a small gain. If they do this for the fleeting riches of this age, how much more shall we do it for the joy of blessed immortality and the eternal glory of the kingdom of heaven? Let it also rouse us that this life is short, the form of the world passes away, and the days are evil and full of dangers, which draw us away from the way of salvation. 1 Cor. 7.

units.la: Ideo statum fuefcepu parabolae Christus subtexit, dicens: Vigilate itaq;. Quod vniuersale pra ceptum esse, & ad omnis loci & ordinis homines pertinere, principio diximus. Id aut graui ratione confirmat: Quia nescitis diem neq; horam, qua Filius hominis veniet. Ex communi rerum vsu argumentum sumit. Periculum enim improuisa magis terret & nocet. Ideo alibi addit Dominus: Hoc autem scire, fi sciret paterfamilias, qua hora fur veturus fit, vigilaret vtiq;, nec sineret perfodi domum suam. Atqui venturum esse constat Christum ad iudicandum viuos & mortuos: & quamuis certo veniet, hora tamen aduentus fui nihil incertius est. Eade est ratio horae mortis quae in omnes aetates cadit, five quis puer, five iuuenis, five senex fit. Eius horam vero ita celauit Deus, vt ne Angelos quidem voluerit scire: imo neFilius hominis quidem, qui nobis a Patre sapientia factus est. Hanc autem venturam nihil huius opinantibus hominibus nouissimi seculi, Scriptura frequenter docet. Est hoc magnū bonitatis Dei argumentum. Sed ea est hominum prauitas, vt fere differamus, quae ad salutem maxime sunt necessaria. Vt ergo necessitate nos cogeret tam mortis quam aduentus fui horam attente obseruare, vtriufq; horam incertam esse voluit, vt in omnia momenta intenti & parati effemus. Interim exeplis magnis & insolitis nos quotidie excitat, prodigijs terret, quae diei istius quasi praeludia sunt, & ipsius indicium (vt Petrus ait) non dormitare docent. Nemo igitur illum tardare putet ex oscitantia: quin potius nouissimi seculi dies abbreuiabit, & propter electos suos accelerabit aduentum suum, vt machinam mundi sub hac seruitute gementem liberet. Vigilemus ergo in horas, & precemur, vt consistere possimus coram Filio hominis, & fide viua ac per charitatem ardenti instructi ad nuptias Sponsi nostri intromittamur, cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Therefore, having set out the state of the parable, Christ adds, saying: "Watch therefore." We said at the beginning that this is a general command, pertaining to people of every place and rank. He confirms it with a weighty reason: "Because you know neither the day nor the hour when the Son of Man will come." He takes the argument from the common experience of things. For danger that comes unforeseen frightens and harms more. Therefore the Lord adds elsewhere: "But know this, that if the householder knew at what hour the thief would come, he would surely keep watch and not let his house be broken into." Yet it is certain that Christ will come to judge the living and the dead; and although he will surely come, nothing is more uncertain than the hour of his coming. The same reasoning applies to the hour of death, which falls in every age, whether one is a child, a young man, or an old man. God has so hidden this hour that he did not even wish the angels to know it; indeed, not even the Son of Man, who has been made wisdom for us by the Father. Scripture frequently teaches that this coming will be unexpected by the people of the last age, who suspect nothing of it. This is a great argument of God's goodness. But such is human perversity that we generally postpone the things that are most necessary for salvation. Therefore, in order to compel us by necessity to watch carefully the hour both of death and of his coming, he willed that the hour of each be uncertain, so that we might be alert and prepared at every moment. Meanwhile he daily rouses us with great and unusual examples and terrifies us with portents, which are as it were the preludes of that day and, as Peter says, show that the sign of it is not sleeping. Let no one therefore think that he delays out of sluggishness; rather, he will shorten the days of the last age, and for the sake of his elect he will hasten his coming, so as to free the machinery of the world groaning under this bondage. Let us therefore watch every hour and pray that we may be able to stand before the Son of Man, and, instructed by a living faith and burning with love, be admitted to the marriage of our Bridegroom, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCLXXXVI.
units.tr: HOMILY CCLXXXVI.

units.la: Ita enim est, vt cum quis peregre proficiscens vocauit seruos suos, & tradidit eis bona sua. Ethuic quidem dedit quinque talenta, alij autem duo, alij vero vnum, vnicuique secundum ipsius facultatem: & peregre profectus est statim.
units.tr: For the kingdom of heaven is as a man travelling into a far country, who called his own servants, and delivered unto them his goods. And unto one he gave five talents, to another two, and to another one; to every man according to his several ability; and straightway took his journey.

units.la: A Eternus Dei Filius, qui nobis a Patre non Seruator modo, verumetiam doctor & ipsa sapientia factus est, non temere de nulla alia re frequentius cum discipulis suis Apostolis, quos ipse doctores orbis totius ordinarat, disseruit, quam de regno Dei, cuius instaurandi ergo in mundum venerat. Fecit hoc prolixe & diligenter, cum mortis hora iam instaret, vt postrema haec eius cum illis colloquia texantur. Idem illum postea per totos dies quadraginta fecisse, Lucas initio Actorum scribit, quibus a mortuis redivivus in terris cum discipulis versatus est. Vt enim quoad nos, ex eo nostra salus dependet, vt in CHRISTO IESV regni coelorum ciues fimus: ita vt huius mysteria recte intelligamus necesse est. Caeterum hic fere vulgo offendimus, dum Christum ex nobis alium fingimus, quam debebamus. Sic olim Apostoli communi Iudaeorum errore decepti Regem terrenum somniabant, qui regnum habiturus esset, qualia sunt principum huius seculi, quae ipsis multorum errorum, ambitionis item & contentionum perpetua causa & quasi fomes fuit. Et hodie hoc ipsum multis imponit, vt aliis quoque scandalorum authores sint, dum in Christo sub Evangelij praetextu alia quaerunt quam ille velit praestare. Alij quia illum in coelos ascendisse audiunt, nec amplius in mundo velle versari, ab Ecclesia quoque sua absentem fingunt, & eum quae in terris geruntur, posthac curare in vniuersum negant. Vnde impia & scelerata securitas nascitur, qualis olim in Nabalis illis fuit, qui (vt in Psalmis habetur) dicebant: Non est Deus: Dominus non videt, Deus Iacob non intelligit. Sunt denique, qui nunquam reditypum putant, vt vel suos remuneretur, vel impijs poenas suis sceleribus dignas retribuat. Itaque necesse fuit his erroribus occurrere. Factum hoc ex parte in praecedenti parabola de decem virginibus: sed diligentius hoc fit in praesenti, qua vniuersam regni sui conditionem vna cum modo, quo illud in terris administret, comprehendit. In quibus, vt omnis securitatis & licentia occasio excludatur, haec potissimum docet. Primum fe, etsi ex mundo abierit, vt non amplius secundum seculi huius rationem in terris versetur, non negligere tamen suam Ecclesiam.
