Deinde quamvis inter suum discessum & reditum ad nos ingens interuallum sit, moram tamen hanc non obstituram, quo minus suo tempore veniat & rationes omnium, quae in Ecclesia fiunt exigat, non solum ab hostibus apertis, verumetiam ab ijs, qui se domesticos fidei & seruos profitentur, & non tam destinata malitia, quam ignauia & metu ignauo peccant. Ita vero de his omnibus disserit, vt nihil eorum omittat, quae in hac causa nos instituere aut consolari possunt.
units.tr: The eternal Son of God, who was made for us by the Father not only Saviour but also teacher, and wisdom itself, spoke with his disciples, the apostles whom he had appointed as teachers of the whole world, about nothing more often than about the kingdom of God, for the restoring of which he had come into the world. He did this at length and with care when the hour of his death was already at hand, so that these, his last conversations, might be woven together with them. Luke writes at the beginning of the Acts that he did the same afterwards, for forty days, during which he lived on earth with the disciples after rising from the dead. For our salvation depends on this, that we be citizens of the kingdom of heaven in Christ Jesus, and so we must understand the mysteries of this kingdom rightly. Yet here we commonly go astray, while we fashion Christ into someone other than he ought to be. So once the apostles, deceived by the common error of the Jews, dreamed of an earthly king who would have a kingdom like the kingdoms of the rulers of this age; and this dream was a constant cause and, as it were, a fuel of many errors, of ambition, and of quarrels. Today the same thing deceives many, so that they too become authors of scandals, while under the pretext of the gospel they seek in Christ something other than he wishes to give. Others, because they hear that he ascended into heaven and no longer wishes to dwell in the world, imagine that he is also absent from his Church, and deny that he takes any care at all of what is done on earth. From this a impious and wicked security is born, such as was once in those Nabals who (as it is said in the Psalms) said: "There is no God; the Lord does not see; the God of Jacob does not understand." Finally, there are those who think he will never return to reward his own or to repay the wicked with punishments worthy of their crimes. It was therefore necessary to meet these errors. This was done in part in the preceding parable of the ten virgins, but it is done more carefully in the present one, in which he sets out the whole condition of his kingdom together with the manner in which he governs it on earth. In these matters, so that every occasion of security and licence may be shut out, he teaches especially the following. First, that he, although he has departed from the world so that he no longer lives on earth according to the manner of this age, does not neglect his Church. Next, that although there is a vast interval between his departure and his return to us, this delay will not prevent him from coming at his appointed time and demanding an account of all that is done in the Church, not only from open enemies but also from those who profess themselves to be household members and servants of the faith, and who sin not so much from settled malice as from laziness and a slothful fear. He discusses all these matters in such a way that he omits nothing that can either instruct or console us in this cause.

units.la: Partes parabolae sunt tres. Prima Christus seipsum describit, quis sit quoad suam personam, quae item fide res suas & regnum vniuersum administret. Secunda de seruorum suorum ingenijs & moribus loquitur. Tertia indicat, quanta diligentia & seueritate rationes tam a bonis quam improbis suo tempore exacturus sit, licet ad tempus dissimulare, & ad omnia conniuere videatur. At quia in Luca nostro de his omnibus copiose dictum est, in praesenti breuius percurremus ea, quae nos in causa regni Dei erudire poterunt, in qua non pigeat eadem saepius audire, cum semper occurrat, quod prius non satis fuit obseruatum.
units.tr: The parable has three parts. In the first, Christ describes himself, who he is in his own person, and how he administers his goods and the whole kingdom by faith. The second speaks of the abilities and conduct of his servants. The third shows with what diligence and severity he will at his appointed time demand an account from both good and wicked, although for a time he may seem to overlook these things and to wink at everything. But since these matters were discussed at length in our treatment of Luke, we will now run more briefly through those points that can instruct us in the cause of the kingdom of God. In this cause it is no trouble to hear the same things again and again, since what was not sufficiently noticed before always comes up again.

units.la: Primam partem a seipso ordiatur, & suam personam paucis describit, dum regni sui conditionem perinde se habere ait, vt cum quis peregre proficiscens, vocat seruos suos, inter quos bona sine facultates suas distribuit. Apud Lucam clarius omnia, vbi sic dicit: Homo quidam nobilis profectus est in regionem longinquam, vt acciperet sibi regnum. Obseruari autem debet, eum qui haec de seipso dicit, reuera esse Filium verum, Patri coessentialem & coaeternum. Vocat autem se hominem, & quidem nobilem, non vulgarem aut plebeium. Est ergo Christus in vna indiuiduaque persona Deus & homo, Deus quidem ab aeterno ante saecula natus, cuius exitus est ab initio, vt Michael Vt Micheas olim testatus est:homo autem natus præfinito tempore in sæculo.Vere autem nobilis homo est,qui vtut nobilitatem metiaris,omnes homines superat.Nam si genus siue familiam ipse habes,ex stirpe natus est,cui nulla alia vel vetustate,vel heroum ex ea progenitorum virtute & gloria conferri potest. Ex Dauid is enim domo siue familia prodijt,qua originem ducit ex sanctissimis patriarchis,Abrahamo,Isaaco & Iacobo,a quibus Deum non puduit seipsum denominare,& cum quibus fœderis societatem ille inire dignatus est. Nati sunt ex eadem Reges & Principes gloriosissimi circiter viginti,vt de Prophetis & Sacerdotibus nihil dicamus,quorum sempiterna erit memoria in Ecclesia Dei.Superat hoc,quod cum alij homines in peccato concipiantur & nascantur,Christi conceptio & nativitas pura & sancta est.Concepit enim eum Maria Virgo ex Spiritu sancto,& eundem illæsa & incorrupta Virginitatis flore peperit,quod nulli hominum vnquam ab origine mundi contigit.Est ergo Sanctus Sanctorum,in quo virtutes omnis generis ita floruerunt,vt nullius vitij,nedum sceleris a nemine vnquam argui aut accusari potuerit. Idcirco apud Ioannē hostibus infestissimis aliquando dicebat:Quis vestrum arguet me de peccato? Sed hus quoque præstantius est,quod ex æterno Dei decreto Rex gloriæ est & Sacerdos in æternum,& tales facit suos omnes,qui in ipsum credunt,& quam ipse sibi innatam habet nobilitatem aliis confert:quod nulli ne Regum quidem huius sæculi potentissimo licuit.Idcirco de illo Ioannes scribebat:Ad suum venit,& sui eum non exceperunt:Quotquot autem eum exceperunt,dedit eis hanc dignitatem,vt filij Dei fierent,nempe ijs qui credunt in nomen eius. De illo enim cecinit Dauid: Amas iustitiam,impietatem odisti,propterea quod te Deus,Deus tuus vnxit oleo lætitiæ præ consortibus tuis.Quod Petrus exponens ait:Iesum Nazarenum vnxit Deus spiritu sancto & virtute,&c. Et Baptista:Qui e cælo venit,supra omnes est:Non enim huic dat Deus Spiritum ad mensuram:Et ex eius plenitudine omnes accepimus,gratiam pro gratia.Ex illo ergo habemus quicquid virtutis nomen meretur.Atqui hæc sola est nobilitas vera, quæ nos Deo & hominibus, imo Angelis quoque commendat.Si huius sæculi nobiles spectemus,ne potentissimi quidem, qui in hoc dominantur,sui similes generare possunt:Sed tanta est illorum infelicitas,vt plerique ex illis progeniti degenerent & mala frugis sint.Itaque iam olim prouerbio locum illi fecerunt:Heroum filij noxæ. Quotquot autem Christus ex femina verbi sui regenerat,ij demum generosi sunt. Nam in eo renatos Deus pro regibus & sacerdotibus,imo pro filijs suis agnoscit.
units.tr: He begins with himself and describes his own person in a few words, saying that the condition of his kingdom is such that a man, setting out on a journey, calls his servants and distributes among them his goods and possessions. In Luke everything is clearer, where he says: "A certain nobleman went into a far country to receive for himself a kingdom." It must be observed that he who says these things of himself is truly the Son, co-essential and co-eternal with the Father. He calls himself a man, and indeed a noble one, not a common or plebeian man. Christ, then, is in one and the same person God and man: God indeed, born from eternity before the ages, whose goings forth have been from the beginning, as Micah long ago testified; but man, born in the world at a predetermined time. And he is truly a noble man, who surpasses all men, however you measure nobility. For if you regard lineage or family, he is born from a stock to which no other can be compared, either for antiquity or for the virtue and glory of the heroes descended from it. For he came from the house or family of David, which traces its origin to the most holy patriarchs Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, by whom God was not ashamed to name himself, and with whom he deigned to enter into the fellowship of a covenant. From the same stock have sprung about twenty most glorious kings and princes, not to mention the prophets and priests, whose memory will be everlasting in the Church of God. He surpasses them in this, that while other men are conceived and born in sin, the conception and birth of Christ are pure and holy. For the Virgin Mary conceived him by the Holy Spirit, and bore him with the flower of her virginity unharmed and uncorrupted, which has happened to no other man since the beginning of the world. He is therefore the Holy of Holies, in whom virtues of every kind so flourished that no one ever could charge or accuse him of any vice, much less of any crime. Therefore, in John, he once said to his most bitter enemies: "Which of you will convict me of sin?" But his nobility is also more excellent in this, that by the eternal decree of God he is King of glory and Priest for ever, and makes all who believe in him such as himself, and confers on others the nobility that he himself has by nature, which was not granted to the most powerful of the kings of this age. Therefore John wrote of him: "He came to his own, and his own did not receive him. But as many as received him, to them he gave this dignity, that they should become sons of God, namely to those who believe in his name." For of him David sang: "You love righteousness and hate wickedness; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your fellows." Peter, expounding this, says: "Jesus of Nazareth, whom God anointed with the Holy Spirit and with power," and so on. And the Baptist: "He who comes from heaven is above all. For God does not give him the Spirit by measure. And of his fullness we have all received, grace for grace." From him, then, we have whatever deserves the name of virtue. Yet this alone is true nobility, which commends us to God and to men, indeed even to the angels. If we look at the nobles of this age, even the most powerful who rule in it cannot beget children like themselves; indeed, such is their unhappiness that most of their offspring degenerate and turn out bad. So long ago they gave a place to the proverb: "The sons of heroes are a plague." But whomever Christ regenerates from the woman by his word, these at last are truly noble. For in him God acknowledges the reborn as kings and priests, indeed as his own sons.

units.la: Quid vero de seipso dicit homo ille nobilis, IESVS CHRISTVS? Quod profectus sit in regionem longinquam,vt acciperet sibi regnum. Dicit autem longinquam regionem cælos,id est beatæ immortalitatis locum,quæ regni cælestis & æterni sedes est, cælis ipsis sublimior,& (vt Paulus exponit) longe supra omnes cælos extra hunc corruptibilem mundum constituta. Illuc Christum ascendisse,ipse diserte testatur,dum se porro non in mundo fore dicit,& inter se atque discipulos hoc discrimen facit,quod illi quidem in mundo sint,ipse vero in hoc non amplius versetur, sed ad Patrem ire velit,vt illic in domo Patris,vbi habitationes multæ sunt, locum nobis paret.Quod autem de discessu suo dicit,de assumpta hominis natura,aut corpore ex Maria Virgine nato,intelligi debet.Etenim constat persona Christi ex Deo & homine,duabus distinctis naturis, ita vnitas per vnionem sine identitatem personæ,vt vtraque suas proprietates essentiales retineat.Vt ergo Deus in mundum venit, & homo factus,forma serui assumpta se exinaniuisse dicitur ab Apostolo, non tamen desijt esse Deus,sed tunc quoque in sinu Patris mansit, vt nobis enarraret, quæ nemo hominum viderat,neque oculis humanis poterat videre: Ita paratio in assumpta hominis natura nostræ redemptionis negotio,hominem in cælum subuexit,& ita eo ascendit, vt interim non desierit homo esse. Deinde qui in infimas partes terræ descenderat,in Virginis vterum scilicet(sic enim Dauid in Psalmis matris vterum vocat,dum se in occulto & inferioribus terræ partibus formatum esse canit) idem postea assumptum hominem super omnes cælos euexit,vt impleret omnia:non quidem corpore suo immenso ac infinito (vt quidam nimis curiosi & arguti de illo philosophantur,qui supra cælos locum esse negant) sed vt impleret quæcunque adhuc restabant ad redemptionem nostram,& gloriæ Patris consors factus,regnum illud sibi acciperet,de quo hic loquitur,& omnia suis donis & beneficijs accumularet,vt postea sequetur. Etsi vero ex his fir-mis colligamus,Christum post ascensionem corpore suo in terris esse desijsse,& hoc historia Euan
units.tr: But what does that noble man, Jesus Christ, say of himself? That he went into a far country to receive for himself a kingdom. By the far country he means heaven, that is, the place of blessed immortality, which is the seat of the heavenly and eternal kingdom, higher than the heavens themselves and (as Paul explains) set far above all the heavens, outside this corruptible world. That Christ ascended thither he himself plainly testifies, when he says that he will no longer be in the world, and makes this distinction between himself and the disciples: that they are in the world, but he no longer dwells in it, and wishes to go to the Father, so that he may prepare a place for us in the Father's house, where there are many dwelling-places. But what he says of his departure must be understood of the assumed human nature, or of the body born of the Virgin Mary. For it is established that the person of Christ consists of God and man, two distinct natures, so that there is a unity by union, without any confusion of the person, and each nature retains its own essential properties. Therefore, although God came into the world and was made man, and took the form of a servant, and is said by the Apostle to have emptied himself, yet he did not cease to be God, but then too remained in the bosom of the Father, so that he might declare to us what no man had seen and no human eye could see. Thus, by the work of our redemption, the preparation in the assumed human nature lifted up the man into heaven, and he so ascended thither that meanwhile he did not cease to be man. Then he who had descended into the lowest parts of the earth, namely into the womb of the Virgin (for so David in the Psalms calls the mother's womb, when he sings that he was formed in secret and in the lower parts of the earth), afterwards raised the assumed man above all the heavens, so that he might fill all things: not indeed with his immense and infinite body (as some too curious and subtle men philosophise about him, who deny that there is any place above the heavens), but so that he might fulfil whatever still remained for our redemption, and, having become a partaker of the Father's glory, might receive that kingdom of which he speaks here, and load all with his gifts and benefits, as will follow afterwards. And although from these firm points we conclude that Christ, after his ascension, ceased to be in the earth in his body, and the evangelist Luke bears witness to this

units.la: Mich.3. Gal.4. Nobilitas Christi. Psal.45. Luc.2. Ioan.1. Ioan.3. Act.10. Ioan.3.&1. Phil.2. Ioan.1. Psal.139. Christi ascensio non tollit gelista testetur, idem inter Symboli Apostolici articulos Vetustas omnis testata sit, atque hodie Ecclesia tota catholico & orthodoxo consensu confiteatur, non tamen propterea (ut quidam de nobis scurriliter calumniantur) Christi maiestatem & omnipotentiam negamus, multo minus illam abEcclesia auferimus, neque hanc illius salutari & necessaria praesentia spoliamus. Nam illum, ut regnum acciperet, non ut hoc deponeret, abijsse scimus. Idcirco primum discipulis dicebat: Data est mihi omnis potestas in caelo & in terra: Et ecce ego vobiscum sum omnibus diebus usque ad consummationem seculi. His ergo testimoniis & promissionibus confirmati, religio nobis est praesentiam Christi in terris carnalem statuere, quam ipse toties negavit, & quae illius omnipotentiae & maiestati tantum derogat, ut si quorundam commenta audiamus, maior eius gloria & potestas olim fuerit, cum in corpore mortali in terris viveret, quam nunc in caelis sit, ubi in corpore gloriosa ad dextram Patris consistit. Etenim olim non necessaria fuit corporis praesentia, & poterat Centurionis famulo mederi, & aulici regis filium a febri liberare, et sic ad illos non propius accedere, neque negata omnipotentia sua aut laesa maiestatis accusatur Centurio, qui non opus esse dicebat, ut ipse sub tectum suum ingrederetur, cum unicum verbum famulo sanando posset sufficere. Imo hoc nomine Centurionis fides omnium Iudaeorum fidei praefertur, quod quam Christus sponte ipsi offerebat corporis praesentiam, ut superuacuaneam & non necessariam recusabat. At nostri aduersarii hodie Christum nobis fingunt, qui in longinquam regionem digressus regnum depositum reliquit, neque nos vel feruare, vel corpore suo ad vitam alere possit, nisi in persona sua vnitatem etiam assumpto pane, se manibus nostris contrectandum, dentibus atterendum & faucibus deglutiendum praebeat.
units.tr: Mich. 3. Gal. 4. The nobility of Christ. Psal. 45. Luc. 2. Ioan. 1. Ioan. 3. Act. 10. Ioan. 3. & 1. Phil. 2. Ioan. 1. Psal. 139. Christ's ascension does not take away his majesty or his presence. Although the evangelist bears witness to it, and all antiquity has attested it among the articles of the Apostles' Creed, and the whole Church today confesses it with catholic and orthodox consent, we do not on that account deny (as some of us are foolishly accused of doing) Christ's majesty and omnipotence. Much less do we take him away from the Church or rob her of his saving and necessary presence. For we know that he went away in order to receive the kingdom, not to lay it down. So he first said to his disciples: "All power is given to me in heaven and on earth," and "Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age." Confirmed by these testimonies and promises, we consider it wrong to posit a bodily presence of Christ on earth, which he himself so often denied, and which detracts so much from his omnipotence and majesty that, if we listen to the inventions of certain people, his glory and power were greater when he lived on earth in a mortal body than they are now in heaven, where in a glorified body he sits at the right hand of the Father. For at that time the presence of his body was not necessary: he could heal the centurion's servant and free the royal official's son from fever without coming closer to them. Nor is the centurion accused of denying his omnipotence or wounding his majesty when he said that there was no need for Christ to enter under his roof, since a single word would suffice to heal his servant. Indeed, for this very reason the centurion's faith is preferred to the faith of all the Jews: Christ offered him his bodily presence willingly, and the centurion refused it as superfluous and unnecessary. But our adversaries today invent for us a Christ who has gone off into a distant region, leaving his kingdom behind, and who cannot keep us or nourish us with his body unless, having taken bread into his own person, he offers himself to be handled by our hands, ground by our teeth and swallowed by our throats.

units.la: Cur ergo in longinquam regionem abisse dicitur Dei Filius? Cur illic regnum accepisse dicetur, cum huius fines per caelum & terras omnes extendantur? Primum auditoribus discipulis qui tunc praesentes erant, sermonem accommodat. Nam, ut Lucas scribit, appropinquabat Ierosolyma, quam plerique regni eius terreni sedem fore sperabant, & cum illam in consp̄ectu haberent, in hanc spem magis erigebantur, ut regnum illud iamiam inchoandum esse putarent. Ut ergo hanc spem corrigat, & a terrenis cogitationibus illos auocet, longinqua regionis meminit. Deinde nobis omnibus hoc seruit, qui etsi regnum Dei intra nos est, tamen cum perfectum spirituale & caelestem, ita longe alterius conditionis, quam sint huius mundi regna, semper nobis in mentem veniat, quod ille Pilato dicebat: Regnum meum non est ex hoc mundo. Et proinde non quaeramus in eo quae huius mundi sunt, sed in Christo supernam quaeramus, vbi ille est ad dextram Dei sedens: & cum vita nostra cum Christo abscondita sit in Deo, supernam curemus, non terrestria. Praeterea peregrinari a nobis & longe recessisse videtur Christus, quando Ecclesiam suam varie affligi, & quasi deserui se videtur. Hinc querela illa sanctorum audiuntur: Cur tam procul abstitis Domine? Cur abscondis faciem tuam? Deus meus, Deus meus, cur deseruisti me? Sed tunc vicisse cogitemus Deum, etsi longe supra caelos exaltata sit gloria sua, demittere tamen se, ut videat quae in caelo & in terra sunt: neque nos ab eo diuelli possit, ut a dilectione Filij sui IESV CHRISTI separemur, quo minus hic nos protegat & feruet. Etenim nos dum in hoc corpore viuimus, aduenas esse, & a Domino peregrinari, dicit Apostolus, qui tamen tunc quoque per fidem & Spiritus sancti arrhabonem cum illo coniunctissimi sumus. Quid absurdum ergo erit, si Christum qui verus Deus est, & per quem Patri placuit conciliare sibi tum quae in terra tum quae in caelis sunt, nobis praesentem esse credamus, quantum salutis nostrae ratio requirit, licet corpore procul a nobis in caelos digressus peregrinetur? Tam quidem arcta est nostra cum Christo coniunctio, ut ex coniugii ure (ut nuper diximus) vna cum illo caro simus, adeoque non periculum est diuortij apud illum, qui ipsa charitas & veritas est: attamen cauere nos oportet, ne alium fingamus Christum, quam in Symboli articulis eum Apostoli describunt, & (quod D. Augustinus grauiter prohibet) diuinitatem hominis ita aflruamus, ut veritatem corporis auferamus. Qui enim id faciunt, ij fere Euangelica historia veritatem in dubium vocant.
units.tr: Why, then, is the Son of God said to have gone away into a distant region? Why is it said that he received the kingdom there, when its boundaries extend through all heaven and earth? First, he adapts his speech to the disciples who were then present. For, as Luke writes, they were approaching Jerusalem, which most of them hoped would be the seat of his earthly kingdom, and when they had it in view they were raised all the more in this hope, thinking that the kingdom was about to begin at once. So, to correct this hope and call them away from earthly thoughts, he speaks of a distant region. Then it serves all of us as well: although the kingdom of God is within us, yet since it is perfect, spiritual and heavenly, and of a quite different kind from the kingdoms of this world, we should always keep in mind what he said to Pilate: "My kingdom is not of this world." Therefore let us not seek in it the things that belong to this world, but let us seek the heavenly things in Christ, where he sits at the right hand of God; and since our life is hidden with Christ in God, let us care for heavenly things, not earthly ones. Moreover, Christ seems to have gone away from us and to have withdrawn to a distance when he allows his Church to be afflicted in various ways and seems to have forsaken her. Hence those laments of the saints are heard: "Why, Lord, do you stand so far off? Why do you hide your face? My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" But let us then think that God, although his glory is exalted far above the heavens, nevertheless lowers himself to see what is in heaven and on earth, and that he cannot be torn away from us, so that we are separated from the love of his Son Jesus Christ, and so that he does not protect and sustain us here. For the Apostle says that while we live in this body we are strangers and are away from the Lord, yet even then we are most closely joined to him through faith and the pledge of the Holy Spirit. What, then, would be absurd if we believed that Christ, who is true God, and through whom it pleased the Father to reconcile to himself both the things on earth and the things in heaven, is present to us as far as the reason of our salvation requires, even though in his body he has gone away into the heavens and is absent from us? Our union with Christ is indeed so close that, by the bond of marriage (as we said recently), we are one flesh with him; and so there is no danger of divorce with him, who is love itself and truth. Yet we must take care not to invent another Christ than the one the Apostles describe in the articles of the Creed, and (as St Augustine strictly forbids) not to assert the divinity of the man in such a way that we take away the truth of his body. For those who do this almost call into doubt the truth of the evangelical history.

units.la: At ne quis propterea putet Christum ab Ecclesia sic abesse, ut omnem eius curam prorsus deserfuerit, diligenter obseruari debet, illum ita de suo discipulo loqui, ut & reditus sui meminerit, simul doceat, se regnum suum quod in terris habet, non negligere, & offendat, qua ratione, & per quos
units.tr: But lest anyone think for this reason that Christ is so absent from the Church that he has entirely abandoned all care for her, we must observe carefully that he speaks of his disciple in such a way that he both recalls his return and at the same time teaches that he does not neglect the kingdom he has on earth, and makes clear by what means, and through whom,

units.la: {y} vtCbr ftu diquos hoc administret: Nimirum per Apostolos & horum successores, quibus Verbi sui praedicationem commisit, & quos donis & facultatibus Spiritus sancti instruxit, ut iis sufficiant, quae ad Ecclesiae gubernationem sunt necessaria. Etenim cum nemo bonus paterfamilias domo discessurus hanc vacuam relinquat, sed ita res suas disponat, ne temere dissipentur, multo minus negligit Dei Filius, cum Ecclesia sua salus cum Dei gloria coniuncta sit. Itaque servus suus data potestate (ut apud Marcum habetur) suum unicuique opus commendat, & ianitori ut vigilet, ne videlicet homines improbi & nequam aliquid mali dent. Ubi ante omnia observari debet, quod in praesenti servos hos vocaui dicitur. Nam eo docetur neminem in Ecclesia sibi debere privato arbitrio aliquid officij vsurpare, sed certa vocatione opus esse iis, qui utiliter in domo Dei aliquam functionem obire velint: quae de re cum non semel alibi dictum sit, non opus erit, eadem modo repetere.
units.tr: he administers it. Namely, through the Apostles and their successors, to whom he has entrusted the preaching of his Word, and whom he has equipped with the gifts and powers of the Holy Spirit, so that they may be sufficient for the things necessary for the government of the Church. For since no good householder, about to leave home, leaves it empty but arranges his affairs so that they are not carelessly scattered, much less does the Son of God neglect his Church, since her salvation is bound up with the glory of God. So his servant, given authority (as it is in Mark), commits to each one his own work, and commands the doorkeeper to keep watch, lest wicked and worthless men do anything evil. Here, above all, it must be noted that he is said to call these men his servants in the present passage. For this teaches that no one in the Church ought to assume any office for himself by private judgment, but that those who wish to perform any function usefully in the house of God need a definite calling. Since this has been said more than once elsewhere, there is no need to repeat it in the same way here.

units.la: Deinde servus isti bona sua tradidisse dicitur. Exprimitur hac particula Christi bonitas & fides, qui ne domus sua, id est, Ecclesia in periculum veniat, idoneos ministros huic praeficit: & cum ex nobisipsis ad tantam functionem nemo nostrum idoneus sit, sui Spiritus dona in miseros & indignos mortales distribuere dignatur. Et hoc est quod Dauid olim de Christo praedicauit: Cum ascendisset in sublimem, dedit dona hominibus. Quod Paulus exponens, addit: Dedit igitur ipse alios quidem Apostolos, alios vero Prophetas, alios Euangelistas, alios autem pastores & doctores. Et ne de solis illis agi putemus, quibus docendi munus creditum est, ministeria diuersa & varia esse alibi dicit, pro quorum diuersitate facultates quoque distribuantur. Nam huic quidem (ait) per Spiritum datur sermo sapientiae, alij vero fides per eundem Spiritum, alij vero dona sanationum per eundem Spiritum: alij vero facultates aedendarum virtutum, alij vero prophetia, alij discretiones spirituum, alij genera linguarum, alij interpretatio linguarum, etc. Quae enumeratio satis docet omnium horum authorem vnum esse Christum, qui ista omnia suo Spiritu in nobis agit, nos autem ex nobis ipsis nihil proprium habere. Adeo vt omnibus dici possit: Quid habes, quod non accepisti? Quod si accepisti, quid gloriaris, quasi non acceperis? Itaque modestiae studere debent ministri omnes, & qui se prae aliis ornatos vident, non efferantur: qui vero minus aliis acceperunt, non quemquam aliis invideant: sed memores, ad utilitatem publicam haec omnia data esse cum communi mandato, quo ad omnes dictum est, ut Lucas annotauit: Negotiamini donec veniam. Itaque nihil per contentionem gerant, aut per inanem gloriam, sed ex modestia alius alium se praestantiorem existimans, nemo quae sua sunt spectet, sed vnusquisque quae sunt aliorum, & abiecta inuidia & aemulatione operas suas conferant. Nec est quod aliquis quaerat, cur huic plus, alij minus datum sit. Tu enim quis es o homo, qui rationem a filio Dei exigas? Nemini hic debitor est. Potest ergo de suo constituere quod vult. Sufficiat nobis, quod vnicuique dat secundum ipsius facultatem, id est, prout vnumquemque capacem & idoneum esse nouit, & quantum communi Ecclesiae vtile est. Seruorum est de communi mandato cogitare, vt fideliter negotientur. Negotiari autem debent, non sibi ipsis priuatim, sed Domino, cuius serui sunt, & a quo fortem acceperunt, & cui, cum ille redierit, rationem reddent. Negotiationis autem huius finis aut scopus sit, vt alij quoque, quibus cum viuimus Christo lucrifiant, & in huius cognitione proficiant & seruentur.
units.tr: Next, it is said that the master handed over his goods to that servant. By this phrase Christ's goodness and faithfulness are expressed: so that his house, that is, the Church, does not come into danger, he sets suitable ministers over it. And since none of us from ourselves is fit for so great a function, he deigns to distribute the gifts of his Spirit among wretched and unworthy mortals. This is what David long ago foretold of Christ: "When he had ascended on high, he gave gifts to men." Paul, explaining this, adds: "He himself therefore gave some to be apostles, some prophets, some evangelists, and some pastors and teachers." And lest we think that only those to whom the office of teaching has been entrusted are meant, he says elsewhere that there are different and various ministries, and that the gifts are distributed according to their diversity. For, he says, to one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another faith through the same Spirit, to another gifts of healing through the same Spirit, to another the working of miracles, to another prophecy, to another the discerning of spirits, to another various kinds of tongues, to another the interpretation of tongues, and so on. This enumeration teaches sufficiently that the one author of all these things is Christ, who works all these things in us by his Spirit, while we have nothing of our own from ourselves. So it can be said to everyone: "What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as if you had not received it?" Therefore all ministers ought to strive for modesty, and those who see themselves adorned above others should not be puffed up; and those who have received less than others should not envy anyone, but, mindful that all these things have been given for the public good, with the common command that was addressed to all, as Luke noted: "Do business until I come." Therefore let them do nothing out of strife or empty glory, but in humility, each counting the other more excellent than himself; let no one look to his own things, but each to the things of others; and, putting aside envy and rivalry, let them bring their labours together. Nor is there any reason for anyone to ask why more was given to one and less to another. For who are you, O man, to call the Son of God to account? No one here is his debtor. He can therefore decide for himself what he wishes. It is enough for us that he gives to each according to his capacity, that is, as he knows each to be capable and fit, and as much as is useful to the common Church. It is for servants to think about their common command, so that they may trade faithfully. They ought to trade not privately for themselves, but for the Lord whose servants they are, from whom they received their talent, and to whom, when he returns, they will give an account. The end or aim of this trading is that others also, with whom we live, may gain for Christ and make progress and be saved in the knowledge of him.

units.la: Est haec omnium pulcherrima & quaestuosissima negotiatio, & ad omnis loci & ordinis homines pertinet. Hanc in Timoth. omnibus Ecclesiae ministris Paulus praecipit, quando illi scribit: Ne negligito donum, quod in te est, quod datum est tibi per prophetiam, id est, iubente sic per os Prophetarum Spiritu sancto cum impositione manuum presbyterij. Et seipsum nobis exemplum praebet Apostolus, in priore ad Corinthios scribens: Cum liber sim ab omnibus, omnibus meipsum seruum feci, vt plures lucrifacerem: Et factus sum Iudaeis vt Iudaeus, vt Iudaeos lucrifacerem: iis qui sub Lege sunt, vt si esse m sub Lege, vt eos qui sub Lege sunt lucrifacerem. Exlegibus vt exlex (non tamen exlex Deo, sed sublex Christo) vt lucrifacerem exleges: Factus sum infirmis vt infirmus, vt infirmos lucrifacerem. Omnibus factus sum omnia, vt omnino aliquos seruarem. Imitantur exemplum Pauli doctores, quando Verbi praedicationem omnium ingenijs ac moribus accommodant, & Verbum ita faciant, vt a quibusdam recipiatur: Deinde si vita exemplo doctrinam suam com-
units.tr: This is the most excellent and most profitable of all trades, and it concerns people of every place and rank. Paul commands it to all ministers of the Church in his letter to Timothy, when he writes: "Do not neglect the gift that is in you, which was given to you through prophecy, with the laying on of the hands of the eldership," that is, as the Holy Spirit directed through the mouths of the prophets. The Apostle also sets himself before us as an example, writing in his first letter to the Corinthians: "Though I am free from all, I have made myself a servant to all, that I might gain the more. To the Jews I became as a Jew, that I might gain the Jews; to those who are under the Law, as under the Law, though I am not myself under the Law, that I might gain those who are under the Law. To those outside the Law I became as one outside the Law (not being outside the law of God, but under the law of Christ), that I might gain those outside the Law. To the weak I became weak, that I might gain the weak. I have become all things to all people, that I might by all means save some." Teachers imitate Paul's example when they adapt the preaching of the Word to the talents and characters of all, and so present the Word that it may be received by some; then, moreover, they commend their teaching by the example of their lives.

units.la: Matth. 1. mendent. At non foli doctores hic admonentur, verumetiā ad quosfuis alios priuatim hoc pertinet, vt peccantes corrigant, & in viam reducant aberrantes. Hoc enim Deus in Lege iubet, quando praecepta dat de boue proximi aberrante, quem ad herum suum reducere, & asino inimici sub onere collapso, quem subleuare debemus. Et Iacobus idem docet, scribens: Qui auertit peccatorem ab errore viae suae, is seruat animam a morte. At quod lucrum maius? quis quaestus honestior & laudabilior est, quam quo animae Christo acquiruntur, quae sub diaboli seruitio peritura erant? Nemo autem tam vilis & obscurus, nemo tam abiectus & contemptus est, qui non aliquibus donis instructus sit, vt officium suum praestantissimum quoq; possit praestare. Possunt animas innumerabiles Deo lucrifacere, qui in Magistratu sunt, si portas suas Regi gloriae aperiant, & Euangelio locum dent, vt qui ipsorum fidei crediti sunt, in Christi cognitione instituantur: Si scholas aperiant, in quibus iuuentus recte doceatur. Negotiantur Christo Regi parentes, si illi adducunt ex se natos paruulos, vt ipsum vere colant & honorent. Ita fidelis & Christianus maritus vxorem a religione alienam, & coniunx pia atq; religiosa maritum impium & iniquum Deo lucrabitur, si viri mulieribus vt vasi infirmiori prudenter & modeste conuersentur: mulieres autem, non de ornatu sumptuoso, & ad lasciuiam composito folicitae, ita potius viuant, vt viri cum reuerentia continentiam ipsarum castam conuersationem videant. Sic Clotildis olim Clodoueum Francorum regem, & cum hoc multa millia hominum Christo lucrifecit. Sic ante Christum natum Hestera populum Dei contra Hamani insidias seruauit, & haud dubie Assuero causa fuit, vt cum multis aliis ad veri Dei cultum accederet. Hinc ergo consolatio publica petitur, ne quis se ita a Deo negligi existimet, vt se nihil in eius regno prouehendo posse arbitretur, & ideo animum despondeat. Nam etsi Christus non pari mensura facultates suas distribuit, singulis tamen dat, quantum ipsis conuenit, & quod augeri poterit, si in negotiatione fideles sint, & Domino foenerari libeat. Et tanta hic quaestus materia nobis proposita est, vt hunc diuites & pauperes adequi queant. Illi enim foenerantur Domino, & in coelis sibi thesaurum recondunt, si in pauperes benefici sint, & illos pauperiem suam patienter ferre doceant: rursum hi quoq; illis salutis occasione praebet, si eos suo exemplo ad beneficentiam studium excitent.
units.tr: (Matth. 1.) But this admonition is not for teachers alone; it also applies privately to each of us, that we correct those who sin and bring back those who go astray. For God commands this in the Law, when he gives the precept about the neighbour's ox that has gone astray, which we must bring back to its owner, and about the enemy's ass fallen under its load, which we must help to raise up. James teaches the same, writing: "Whoever turns a sinner from the error of his way saves a soul from death." And what gain could be greater? What trade is more honourable and praiseworthy than that by which souls are won for Christ, souls which were destined to perish in the service of the devil? No one is so base and obscure, no one so abject and despised, that he is not furnished with some gifts, so that he can also perform his most excellent duty. Those who hold office in the magistracy can win countless souls for God, if they open their gates to the King of glory and give room to the Gospel, so that those entrusted to their faith may be instructed in the knowledge of Christ; and if they open schools in which the young are rightly taught. Parents trade for Christ the King if they bring their own little children to him, that they may truly worship and honour him. So a faithful and Christian husband will gain for God a wife who is alien to religion, and a pious and devout wife will gain an impious and unrighteous husband to God, if husbands live prudently and considerately with their wives as with the weaker vessel; and if wives, not anxious about costly adornment and dress arranged for allurement, rather live in such a way that their husbands see in them reverence, chastity and a pure manner of life. Thus Clotilda of old won Clovis, king of the Franks, and with him many thousands of men, for Christ. Thus before Christ's birth Esther preserved the people of God against the plots of Haman, and undoubtedly was the cause why Ahasuerus, together with many others, came to the worship of the true God. Here, then, a public consolation is sought, so that no one should think himself so neglected by God that he imagines he can do nothing to advance his kingdom, and so loses heart. For although Christ does not distribute his gifts in equal measure, he nevertheless gives to each as much as suits him, and what can be increased if the faithful are diligent in this trade and are willing to lend to the Lord. And so great a subject of gain is set before us here that rich and poor alike may share in it. For the rich lend to the Lord and lay up treasure for themselves in heaven, if they are generous to the poor and teach them to bear their poverty patiently; and in turn the poor also offer the rich an occasion of salvation, if by their example they stir them up to zeal for good works.

units.la: Caeterum priusquam ex hoc loco discedamus, obseruari debet, quae Christi & regni sui fors sit inter homines. Admonet nos de hac Lucas. Etsi domo discedens suos non negligat, sed suas opes inter seruos distribuat, nec aliquem ex illis indonatum praeterreat: Ciues tamen eius oderunt illum, & post eum miserunt legatos, qui non absq; contumelia dixerunt: Nolumus hunc regnare super nos. Qua parte admonemur, idem in regno Christi inter homines, quod in regnis huius saeculi accidere. Vulgo homines conditionis praesentis piget, & ex mutatione aut rebus nouis sibi melior a pollicentur. Hinc fere in Repub. crebrae mutationes fiunt, quae plerunq; cum periculo coniunctae sunt. Nec priorum principum virtus & merita hanc mundi improbitatem, quo minus sibi indulgeat, prohibere possunt. Exempla huius generis Scripturae in Samuele, Dauide & eius posteris proponit, in quibus reuera factum est, quod in praesenti dicitur. Quoad vero Christi regnum, hic vt scandalo medeatur, quod hic maximum obiicitur, docere voluit, non eo successu regnum suum floriturum, quem tunc discipuli sibi ipsis pollicebantur, neq; ipsos extra periculum fore, si ipsi fideles esse velint. Et coepit ingratitudo haec caput exerere in ipso statim aduentu Filij Dei in carnem in ter Iudaeos, qui non cives modo, sed ab origine Ecclesiae dici poterant, cum ipsorum sint patres, & Christus ipse ex illis sit quoad carnem. De illis tamen scribit Ioannes: In suos venit, & sui eum non receperunt. Quid postea factum sit, quando captum gentibus tradiderunt, coram Pilato abnegarunt, Caesarem impium & prophanum, imo Barrabam latronem ei anteposuerunt, notius est, quam vt verbis exponere oporteat. Taceo nunc quae aduersus eius Apostolos designarunt. Nec melior Christi fors inter gentes postea fuit, quando regnum suu ex singulari gratia ad illud transfulit, quae obuijs vlnis ipsum excipere debuissent, cum iam olim a Deo adoptatae essent, qui per Dauidem dixerat: Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te: Postula a me, & dabo tibi gentes, vt sint hereditas tua, & terminos terrae, vt sint possessio tua. Sed longum esset narrare, quam indignis modis vbiq; gentium reiectus sit ille, si quando per Apostolos gratiam suam reuelare, & regnu suum inter illos constituere voluit. Nec adhuc cessauit haec mundi ingrati contumacia & rebellio, sed
units.tr: Moreover, before we leave this passage, we should observe what is the lot of Christ and of his kingdom among men. Luke reminds us of this. Although the man going away from home did not neglect his own, but distributed his goods among his servants, and passed over none of them without a gift, yet his citizens hated him and sent envoys after him, who said, not without insult: "We do not want this man to reign over us." From this we are reminded that in the kingdom of Christ among men the same happens as in the kingdoms of this age. Ordinary people are weary of their present condition and promise themselves something better from change or new things. Hence in commonwealths frequent upheavals arise, which are commonly attended with danger. Nor can the virtue and merits of earlier rulers prevent this wickedness of the world from indulging itself. Scripture sets forth examples of this kind in Samuel, David and his posterity, in which what is now said was truly done. As for the kingdom of Christ, here, in order to remedy the scandal which is most strongly brought against it, he wished to teach that his kingdom would not flourish with the success which the disciples then promised themselves, nor would they themselves be out of danger if they wished to be faithful. And this ingratitude began to raise its head immediately at the coming of the Son of God in the flesh among the Jews, who could be called not only his citizens but, from the origin of the Church, his own, since they are his fathers and Christ himself is from them according to the flesh. Yet of them John writes: "He came to his own, and his own did not receive him." What happened afterwards, when they handed him over, taken, to the Gentiles, denied him before Pilate, preferred Caesar, impious and profane, and even the robber Barabbas to him, is too well known to need to be set out in words. I now pass over what they plotted against his Apostles. Nor was Christ's lot better among the Gentiles afterwards, when out of singular grace he transferred his kingdom to them; they ought to have received him with outstretched arms, since long ago they had been adopted by God, who said through David: "You are my son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will give you the nations for your inheritance and the ends of the earth for your possession." But it would be a long matter to relate in what unworthy ways he has been rejected everywhere among the nations, whenever through the Apostles he wished to reveal his grace and establish his kingdom among them. Nor has this obstinacy and rebellion of the ungrateful world yet ceased, but today it reigns among those who wish to be and be called Christians.

units.la: hodie inter eos regnat, qui Christiani dici & haberi volunt. Reges quorum erat illum osculari, fe-re perfua dixit sibi, se non posse regnare, si Christo inter suos locum dent. Pontifices, qui illius vicarios se esse gloriantur, omnium adversus illum & Evangelium eius persecutionum, seditionum, bellorum authores sunt. Inter priuatos homines nemo tam obscurus, nemo opus & gratia Dei tam insignis, qui non audire se Christo opponere, si Evangelij praedicatione ab eo exigantur obedientiae officia, quae illi debentur. Haec causa est, quod sicut ille praedixit persecutionem patiuntur, quotquot in illo volunt pie viuere.
units.tr: today he reigns among those who wish to be and be called Christians. Kings, whose duty it was to kiss him, have almost persuaded themselves that they cannot reign if they give Christ a place among their subjects. Popes, who glory that they are his vicars, are the authors of all the persecutions, seditions and wars against him and against his Gospel. Among private men there is no one so obscure, no one whose work and grace of God is so notable, who does not hear himself set against Christ if the duties of obedience that are owed him are demanded of him through the preaching of the Gospel. This is why, as he foretold, all who wish to live godly in him suffer persecution.

units.la: Non debent autem ista nos offendere, ut vel animum despondeamus, vel fidem, quae ei debetur, abnegemus. Etenim vt ut adversus illum multa tamen ultuetur, regnum tamen suum ille non defendit modo, sed propagat indies: neq; ei armis ad hoc opus est, sed vt in Psalmo canitur, falsitem ipsi operatur brachium suum sanctum. Fremunt quidem populi, conspirant reges, consultant pontifices, concurrunt monachi & his coniuncti adsunt mercenarij Cares, quibus pulcherrimus quaestus est, qui ex sanguine fusio colligitur, & quibus ibi fas est, ubi maxima merces. Sed non proficient quicquam hominum. Ratum enim erit Dei decretum, qui olim Ecclesiae sua hostibus dixit: Societatem inite populi, at inferiores eritis: accingamini, at inferiores eritis: inite consilium, & fiet irritum. Homo enim ille nobilis, qui inter seruos suos dona sua distribuit, ut his negotientur, eisdem benedicit, ut multum foenus faciant, & veniet ut rationes exigat tam ab hostibus quam seruis. Est enim aeternus Dei Filius, Iesus Christus, cui dictum est a Patre: Sede a dextris meis, donec ponam inimicos tuos scabellum pedum tuorum. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in saecula saeculorum. Amen.
units.tr: Yet these things ought not to offend us so that we either lose heart or deny the faith that is owed him. For however much he is wronged by many, he not only defends his kingdom but spreads it daily; nor does he need arms for this work, but, as is sung in the Psalm, his holy arm works salvation for him. Indeed the peoples rage, kings conspire, the high priests take counsel, monks run together, and hired Carians join them, for whom the most splendid profit is that which is gathered from shed blood, and for whom what is forbidden is lawful where the reward is greatest. But they will accomplish nothing against men. For the decree of God will stand, who once said to the enemies of his Church: "Form a alliance, you peoples, and you shall be overcome; gird yourselves, and you shall be overcome; take counsel, and it shall come to nothing." That noble man, who distributed his gifts among his servants that they might trade with them, blesses the same servants so that they may make great gain; and he will come to demand an accounting from enemies as well as from servants. For he is the eternal Son of God, Jesus Christ, to whom the Father said: "Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet." To him belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever and ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCLXXXVII.
units.tr: HOMILY 287.

units.la: Profectus autem qui quinque talenta acceperat, negotiatus est ex iis, & fecit altera quinque talenta. Itidem & qui duo acceperat, lucratus & ipse altera duo. Qui autem unum acceperat, abiens defodit illud in terram, & abscondit pecuniam domini sui. Post multum vero temporis venit dominus seruorum illorum, & conferet rationem cum eis. Tunc accedens is, qui quinque talenta acceperat, attulit altera quinque dicens: Domine quinque talenta tradidisti mihi, ecce altera quinque lucratus sum ex eis. Dixit autem ei dominus eius: Bene habet, serue bone & fidelis: in paucis fuisti fidelis, super multa te constituam: ingredere in gaudium domini tui. Accedens autem & qui duo talenta acceperat, ait: Domine duo talenta tradidisti mihi, ecce alia duo lucratus sum super ea. Ait ei dominus eius: Bene habet, serue bone & fidelis: in paucis fuisti fidelis, super multa te constituam: ingredere in gaudium domini tui.
units.tr: But the one who had received five talents went off, traded with them, and made another five talents. In the same way the one who had received two also gained two more. But the one who had received one went away, dug a hole in the ground, and hid his master's money. After a long time the master of those servants returned and settled accounts with them. Then the one who had received five talents came forward, bringing another five, and said: "Master, you handed over five talents to me; look, I have gained another five from them." His master said to him: "Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful in a few things; I will set you over many things. Enter into your master's joy." Then the one who had received two talents also came forward and said: "Master, you handed over two talents to me; look, I have gained two more besides them." His master said to him: "Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful in a few things; I will set you over many things. Enter into your master's joy."

units.la: Quoniam sciebat Dominus noster IESVS CHRISTVS discipulos suos salsam de regno suo opinionem concepisse, & errorem hunc omnibus seculis communem fore, saepius de parabolis regno disseruit, & id tunc in primis, quando mortis suae hora instabat, per quam ex mundo erat discessurus. Inter alia autem, quae dixit facile primus tenet parabola haec, qua omnem regni sui rationem ita complectitur, ut omnibus erroribus occurrat, quos in posterum quoque omnibus seculis inter homines exoriturös esse praeuidebat. Communis inter illos est, qui vt olim Iudaeos & cum his Apostolos fascinauit, ita hodie etiam multos decipit, quod terrenum regnum, & in hoc vita gloriam, opes & felicitatem rerum omnium successus somniant. Docet ergo regnum suum non esse de hoc mundo, sed in longinqua regione, in caelis nimirum, vbi accepta omni potestate in caelo & in terra sedet ad dextram Patris. Ne vero terras, & quae in his fiunt, negligere putetur, ostendit se omni bursa seculis hibitur in seruos, qui facultatibus Spiritus sui instructi negotientur, id est, homines ipsi adducant & ad salutem lucrifaciant: & tandem reditur um nouissimo die, vt rationem ab illis
units.tr: Since our Lord Jesus Christ knew that his disciples had formed a false opinion about his kingdom, and that this error would be common in every age, he spoke often about the kingdom in parables, and especially at the time when the hour of his death was at hand, by which he was to depart from the world. Among the other things he said, this parable comes first, since in it he embraces the whole account of his kingdom in such a way as to meet all the errors that he foresaw would arise among men in ages to come. It is a common error, one that once deceived the Jews and with them the Apostles, and today still deceives many, that people dream of an earthly kingdom, and of glory, riches and happiness in this life, with success in all things. He therefore teaches that his kingdom is not of this world, but in a distant region, namely in heaven, where, having received all power in heaven and on earth, he sits at the right hand of the Father. Yet lest he be thought to neglect the earth and what happens there, he shows that he has left his goods in the hands of servants who, equipped with the gifts of his Spirit, trade, that is, bring men themselves to salvation and gain them for it; and finally he returns on the last day to demand an account from them.

units.la: Occasio huius exigat. Ita autem non obscurè mentes eos, qui ex regno Christi censeri volant, Euangelio subesse oportere, cuius praedicatione illud administratur. Ideo Paulus ad Corinthios postea scripsit: Arma militiae nostrae non carnalia sunt, sed diuinitus valida ad subuertionem munitionum, vt ratiocinationes subuertant et omnem sublimitatem, quae extollitur aduersus cognitionem Dei, et in captiuitatem redigat omnem cogitationem ad obediendum Christo. Et alibi idem Apostolus, Euangelica praedicationis finem et scopum esse dicit, obedientiam fidei. Itaque qui nec illam audire nec illius praeceptis aut legibus parere volunt, ij fere rebelles sunt, quos tandem ferreo suo sceptro comminuet. Interim quod in Apostolorum persona Ecclesiarum ministri dicitur, quibus ista proprie mandata sunt, alij quoque sibi dictum putent. Sunt enim omnes homines serui Christi, nec quisquam est, qui non aliquid doni ab illo acceperit, et olim omnes stabunt ad illius tribunal, vt rationem factorum suorum reddant, et reportent quod in corpore fecerunt, vel bonum vel malum.
units.tr: In this way he teaches, not obscurely, that those who wish to be counted in the kingdom of Christ must be subject to the Gospel, through whose preaching that kingdom is administered. Therefore Paul later wrote to the Corinthians: "The weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strongholds, casting down arguments and every high thing that exalts itself against the knowledge of God, and bringing every thought into captivity to the obedience of Christ." And elsewhere the same Apostle says that the end and aim of evangelical preaching is the obedience of faith. Therefore those who are unwilling either to hear the Gospel or to obey its precepts and laws are for the most part rebels, whom at last he will crush with his iron sceptre. Meanwhile, what is said of the Apostles, to whom these commands were properly entrusted, the ministers of the Churches should also take as addressed to themselves. For all men are servants of Christ, and there is no one who has not received some gift from him; and one day all will stand before his judgment seat to render an account of their deeds, and to receive what they have done in the body, whether good or evil.

units.la: Caeterum, quia in hoc multos fallit caro sensus, quae fere Dominum cunctari putat, et mundi illecebris capitur adeo, vt dum huic placere studet, ea quae ad Christi regnum pertinent, securè negligat: imo illum interea in caelis otiosum desidere, vel ad cardines caeli, depositá omni cura Ecclesiae, obambulare sibi persuadet, secunda parabola pars subiicitur, qua primum, quid serui illi, qui bona domum et res suas ipse commisit, fecerint, narrat: deinde de reditu suo loquitur, et, vt ipse reuersus, rationes cum illis subduxerit.
units.tr: But because the flesh deceives many in this matter, the flesh which mostly thinks the Lord is slow, and is so captivated by the allurements of the world that, while it strives to please the world, it carelessly neglects the things that pertain to Christ's kingdom; indeed, it persuades itself that in the meantime he sits idle in heaven, or walks about the corners of heaven, having laid aside all care for the Church, the second part of the parable is added. In it he first tells what those servants, to whom he had entrusted his goods and property, did; then he speaks of his return, and how, when he came back, he settled accounts with them.

units.la: Et primo quidem de seruis agit, quos impares facit, alios fideles et industrios, alios ignauos et inutiles: Et quamuis horum plerumque maior numerus sit, eo quod ex semetipso nemo hominum ad hanc functionem idoneus est, tamen vnum tantum ignaui meminit, cui primus duos opponit, quorum fidem et industriam commendat: Ex quo consolatio peti debet, ne quando defuturos putemus, qui Ecclesiae fidelem operam praestent. Qui enim olim Eliam, et cum hoc septem millia seruauit in Israele, qui ipsum syncero corde coluerunt, cum illi se solum putaret esse superstitem, hic idem hodie potest, neque domui suae vnquam deerit. Quo minus aliquos det ideo teos ministros, qui Ecclesiam suam augeant et aedificent. Quoad autem priores, qui suis talentis bene vsi sunt, inter illos quoque discrimen indicatur. Nam qui quinque talenta acceperat, negotiatus est ex ijs, et fecit altera quinque talenta. Qui vero duo tantum acceperat, similiter altera duo lucratus est. Sunt enim, testi Paulo, discrimina donorum, et ex his inter ministros gradus sunt. Etenim non pari mensura Deus dona sua distribuit, sed vnicuique admeritur pro suo arbitrio: non quidem proper personarum respectu, quia apud illum nullus est, sed quia nemini debitor est. Quis enim prior illi dedit vt reddatur ei? Singulis autem dat, quantum possunt capere, et quantum functio, quam ipsis mandauit, requirit. Nec est, vt nos propter imparem distributionem donorum quiritemur, aut illi litem moueamus.
units.tr: And first he deals with the servants, whom he makes unequal: some faithful and diligent, others lazy and useless. Although the number of the faithful is usually the greater, since no one is of himself fit for this office, he mentions only one lazy servant, and sets against him first two whose faithfulness and diligence he commends. From this we ought to draw comfort, lest we think that at some time there will be lacking those who render faithful service to the Church. For he who once preserved Elijah, and with him seven thousand in Israel who worshipped him with a sincere heart, when Elijah thought himself the only one left, can do the same today, and will never be without workers for his house. He will not, therefore, give fewer faithful ministers who may increase and build up his Church. As for the former servants, who used their talents well, a difference is also shown among them. For he who had received five talents traded with them and made another five talents; but he who had received only two likewise gained two more. There are, as Paul testifies, differences of gifts, and from these come the degrees among ministers. For God does not distribute his gifts in equal measure, but deals out to each according to his own judgment: not indeed from respect of persons, since there is none with him, but because he is indebted to no one. For who first gave to him, that it should be repaid to him? He gives to each as much as they are able to receive, and as much as the office he has entrusted to them requires. Nor should we complain about the unequal distribution of gifts, or bring a lawsuit against him.

units.la: Ipse enim nos melius nouit, quam ipsimet, qui fere philautia excaecati nobisipsis placemus, et nobis arrogamus plus quam humeri nostri ferant: quae causa est, vt saepe nobisipsis pericula non necessaria, vel etiam praesentem interitum accersamus, quemadmodum de Phaethonte et Icaro Poetae olim commenti sunt. At Deus est, qui nos ante et retro cognouit, qui corda et renes scrutatur, et proinde solus etiam nouit, quid nobis conueniat. Est autem hic obseruatio dignum, quod qui duo tantum talenta acceperat, non ideo animum deponet, nec remissior est in suo officio, quod non tantundem ab hero, quantum alter acceperat: neque priori inuidet: Ita nos cauere oportet, ne aemulatione accepti inuideamus aliis, quos nobis praestantiores esse vult Deus. Obseruari quidem debent Dei dona in fratribus et conferuntur, sed in hunc finem, vt propter haec illos pluris faciamus et veneremur: non autem, vt inde concipiamus odij et inuidia occasiones, et nos excusari posse arbitremur, si in officio faciendo simus officiantiores: Vt ergo hic etiam faeneratur iedulo, qui duo solum talenta habuit, et eo lucro, quod Dominus dat, contentus, minime murmurauit: ita nos etsi nos aliis inferiores esse, et minus etiam proficere videamus in opere Domini, non tamen segnescamus: sed soletur nos, quod idem omnium nostrum Dominus est, cui omnes faeneramur: idem Spiritus, qui in omnibus agit: quod denique Dominus tenuiorum quoque studio et industria delectatur: modo animi propensio et institutum bonum sit. Laudem merentur Euangelij praecones, qui in ciuitatibus populosis, et regnis longè lateque patentibus tibus, multos & illustres homines Christo adduxunt. E contra non pauci debent, qui in locis obscurioribus docent, & in his agentes homines rusticos & opificijs manuarijs occupatos, illi lucri faciunt.
units.tr: For he knows us better than we know ourselves, we who, blinded almost by self-love, please ourselves and claim for ourselves more than our shoulders can bear. This is why we often bring upon ourselves unnecessary dangers, or even present ruin, as the poets once invented about Phaethon and Icarus. But it is God who knows us before and behind, who searches hearts and reins, and therefore he alone also knows what is fitting for us. It is worth observing here that he who had received only two talents did not for that reason lose heart, nor was he more lax in his duty because he had not received as much from his master as the other had; nor did he envy the first. So we too must take care lest, through rivalry at what has been given to us, we envy others whom God wishes to be more outstanding than ourselves. Indeed, the gifts of God in our brothers ought to be noticed and compared, but to this end: that because of them we may value and honour them the more; not that we may take from them occasions of hatred and envy, and think ourselves excused if we are more slack in doing our duty. Therefore, just as he who had only two talents traded diligently, and, content with the gain the Lord gave him, did not murmur at all, so we, even if we see ourselves inferior to others and making less progress in the Lord's work, should not grow slack. Let us be comforted that the Lord of us all is the same, to whom we all trade; that the same Spirit works in all; and that the Lord delights in the zeal and diligence even of the humbler sort, provided the inclination of the mind and the good purpose are there. The heralds of the Gospel deserve praise who in populous cities and widely extended kingdoms have brought many illustrious men to Christ. On the other hand, not a few deserve praise who teach in more obscure places, and who gain for Christ the rustic men and those occupied with manual crafts.

units.la: Etenim in praesenti vterq; negotiatus est absq; aemulatione & inuidia, & virtunq; commendat Dominus, nec aliquid exprobrat. Idem in omni hominum ordine obseruat Deus. Et dona Dei vsu crescunt & augentur in omnibus, qui illis cum gratiarum actione recte & sedulo vtuntur. De eo igitur cogitent singuli, & quia ab illo quoq; rationem exigi audiunt, qui vnum solummodo talentum acceperat, idem de se quoq; fore non dubitent, qui inter homines contemptissimi, ab omnibus se negligunt. Vt enim Dominus, etiamsi in alto residens, ipsis caelis sublimior sit, demittit tamen se, vt quae in caelis & in terra sunt respiciat, & pauperes atq; egenos ex pulueribus extractos in regum vsq; folia euehat (quod solatio esse debet ijs, quos interdum sua tenuitas terret.) Ita hoc ipsum ad officium faciendum extimulare debet eos dem, ne propter illam se exleges esse putent, quibus in pune quiduis liceat. Peccant hic frequenter pauperes & quotquot Ecclesiae ministerium in solis terrenis & ad corporis vitu spectantibus occupari putant. Saepius enim odio se diuitibus exprobrat, quod olim Christo rationem illos reddere oporteat: At non minus ipsi quoq; ad illius tribunal sistentur, & ab illis poenas impatientia, inuidia, odij, adhaec fraudum & impostorum exiget Dominus, quibus Ecclesiae imponunt, & quae vere pauperibus debebantur, ipsi intercipiunt fuci ignavi & voraces. Sed de his alibi dicendi locus commodior.
units.tr: Indeed, both have carried on their business in the present life without rivalry or envy, and the Lord commends both and reproaches neither. God observes the same principle in every rank of people. The gifts of God grow and increase through use in all who employ them rightly and diligently, with thanksgiving. Let each person therefore reflect on this. Since they hear that the one who had received only one talent was also called to account, let them not doubt that the same will happen to them, those who regard themselves as the most despised among men and neglect themselves in the eyes of everyone. For just as the Lord, though he sits on high and is exalted above the very heavens, nevertheless humbles himself to regard what is in heaven and on earth, and lifts the poor and needy from the dust to the thrones of kings (which ought to be a comfort to those whom their lowliness sometimes frightens), so this same truth ought to spur them on to do their duty, lest they think that, because of their lowliness, they are lawless and may do whatever they like. The poor sin here often, and so do all who think the ministry of the Church is concerned only with earthly things and the needs of the body. For they often complain bitterly against the rich, that they will one day have to render an account to Christ. But these poor people will be no less summoned before his judgment seat, and the Lord will exact punishment from them for their impatience, envy, hatred, and also for the frauds and deceptions by which they impose on the Church, and which they, lazy and greedy drones, intercept from what was truly owed to the poor. But there will be a more suitable place to speak of these things elsewhere.

units.la: Nunc ad parabolam redeamus, dicitur post multum temporis redijsse herus feruorum illorum, & contulisse rationem cum eis. Id vero humani iudicij respectu dicit. Huic enim videtur tardare Dominus, & ex eo colligunt prophani homines, nunquam venturum. Hinc sermones illi scurriles illusorum quos nouissimo seculo vulgo in multorum ore futuros scribit. Vbi est pollicitatio adventus eius? Nam ex quo die patres obdormierunt, omnia ita permanent ab initio creationis. Et tandem concludunt, quod vt patres spe sua falsi, per mortem ex mundo sublati sint, illo adhuc stat te, qualis ab initio fuit: ita idem nobis quoq; euenturum esse, vt qui venturum speramus Dei Filium, qui omnia in melius restituat, similiter frustra expectemus, tandem vero viam communem omnis terrae ingrediamur, sicut omnes alij, qui ante nos mortui sunt. His vt tacite respondeat Christus, post multum temporis se rediturum dicat. Quasi dicat: Quantumuis in secula differatur aduentus meus, veniam tamen, neq; deero promissis meis. Et sane (vt alibi demonstrauimus) exigit hoc iustitia Dei, quae nisi ad exigendum rationes veniret, non posset consistere. Quia enim huius est, vnicuique reddere quod illi debetur, id vero in huius vita curriculo non fiat, & in hoc seculo fere im probi feliciter agant, & ne communibus quidem molestijs hominum obnoxij sint, pij autem continuis malis, odijs item impiorum & persecutionibus exercentur, Deum non poterimus iustum dicere, nisi aliud seculum succedat, in quo remunerator redeat. Quoties ergo diuturnior morafidem nostra labefactare incipit, recordemur admonitionis Petrinae: Vnum hoc ne vos lateat dilecti, Vnum diem apud Dominum perinde esse vt mille annos, & mille annos vt diem vnum. Et mox addit, Non tardat Dominus, qui promisit (vt nonnulli tarditatem hanc esse ducunt) sed patiens est erga nos nolens vllos perire, sed omnes ad resipiscentiam tendere, 2. Pet. 3.
units.tr: Now let us return to the parable. It says that after a long time the lord of those servants returned and settled accounts with them. But this speaks according to human judgment. For the Lord seems to delay, and from this profane people conclude that he will never come. Hence those scurrilous sayings of mockers, which he writes will be on the lips of many in the last age: "Where is the promise of his coming? For since the day the fathers fell asleep, all things continue as they were from the beginning of creation." And at last they conclude that, just as the fathers were disappointed in their hope and were taken from the world by death, while the world still stands as it was from the beginning, so the same will happen to us: we who hope for the coming of the Son of God, who will restore all things for the better, will in the same way wait in vain, and at last we shall enter the common way of all the earth, just as all others who died before us. To answer these men silently, Christ says that he will return after a long time. As if he said: however much my coming is put off into the ages, I will nevertheless come, and I will not fail in my promises. And indeed (as we have shown elsewhere) the justice of God requires this, which could not stand unless it came to exact accounts. For it belongs to justice to render to each what is owed to him, but this does not happen within the course of this life. In this age the wicked for the most part prosper and are not even subject to the common troubles of men, while the godly are continually afflicted with evils, with the hatred and persecutions of the impious. We could not call God just unless another age followed in which the rewarder returns. Therefore, whenever a longer delay begins to shake our faith, let us recall the admonition of Peter: "Let this one thing not escape you, beloved: that with the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day." And he adds shortly after: "The Lord does not delay what he has promised (as some think this to be slowness), but he is patient toward us, not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance." 2 Pet. 3.

units.la: Dum vero rationes cum seruis confert, primus ad has poscitur, qui quinq; talenta acceperat. Quo rursus admonemur, eos qui donis & facultatibus plurimis a Deo instructi sunt, propter excellentiam donorum, non aliqua immunitate frui apud Dominum: quin potius, qui multum accepit ab illo, de multis respondebit: Id vero non solum Verbi & Ecclesiarum ministri sibi dictum putent, verumetiam omnes alij, qui in eminentia constituti authoritate & potestate alios excellunt. Quid enim habent illi omnes quod non acceperint? Omnes homines nudi nascuntur, pauperes & rerum omnium indigi. Deus autem euehit quos vult, & omnis potestas ex illo est, qui diuites quoque solius facit, vt Solomon testatur, vel in egestatis luto relinquit quos vult. Ergo nullae dignitates, nulla potestas, nulla opes, nulli honores huius seculi quenquam mortalium defendent, quo minus Christo iudici olim in nouissimo die non solum de factis suis omnibus, verumetiam de quouis verbo otioso rationem reddere cogatur. Vt vero eos, qui reliquis praestant, non eximit sua excellentia, hic neq; tenuiores & inferiores sua egestas & obscuritas. Nam (vt sequetur) is quoq;, qui
units.tr: When he settles accounts with the servants, the first called to account is the one who had received five talents. By this we are again reminded that those whom God has furnished with very many gifts and resources will not, because of the excellence of their gifts, enjoy any exemption before the Lord. Rather, whoever has received much from him will answer for much. This should be taken to apply not only to the ministers of the Word and of the Churches, but also to all others who, placed in eminence, surpass others in authority and power. For what do all these have that they have not received? All men are born naked, poor and in need of everything. But God raises up whom he wills, and all power is from him, who makes some rich and, as Solomon testifies, leaves others in the mire of poverty as he pleases. Therefore no dignities, no power, no riches, no honours of this age will protect any mortal from being compelled to render an account to Christ the Judge on the last day, not only for all his deeds but also for every idle word. But just as his eminence does not exempt those who excel the rest, so likewise the lowliness and obscurity of the humbler and inferior do not exempt them. For (as will follow) the one also who [...]

units.la: Pfal. 113.

Pfal. 73. vnicum talentum aut minam acceperat, ad rationes poscitur. Nec minus placent Domino, qui in paruo fideles fuerunt, quàm ij quorum fides & industria in magnis & eximijs muneribus eluxit. Sed præstat audire, vt fidelium seruorum industriam Dominus remuneratus sit. Ijsdem verbis tam primum quàm secundum commendat, etiamsi lucrum vtriusque impar sit. Euge (inquit) serue bone. Id est, Bene habet, fecisti quod seruum bonum & fidelem decet. Sic alibi benedictos Patris sui vocat, quorum fidem in nouissimo die commendabit. At quæ maior gloria homini obtinget, quàm si in magno illo cœtu totius mundi publicè a Filio Dei commendetur, & ita quidem, vt qui illum antea persecuti fuerunt & oderunt, intra conscientias suas conuicti, eum pro seruo & amico Dei agnoscere, & seipsos condemnare cogantur? Nam vt in libro Sapientiæ scribitur, tunc iustus stabit coram oppressoribus & calumniatoribus suis cum fiducia, & hoc visò illi graui pauore percellentur, & præ inopinata salute stupescent: & pœnitentia tacti, atque præ spiritus angustia gementes, apud se dicent: Hic ne est ille, quem risui quondam habuimus? Stulti vitam eius putabamus insaniam, & exitum eius ignominiosum. Atqui vnà cum filijs Dei annumeratus est, & suam inter sanctos sortem adeptus. Aberrauimus vtiq; a via veritatis, &c. Hæc & alia multa, quæ ibi scribuntur, hoc breue ferui boni elogium continet, quo in præsenti Christus dignatur eos, qui pecunias suas fideliter ad vsuram depositerunt, & ex illis bene negotiati sunt. Itaq; vnum hoc nobis sufficere debet aduersus iniqua hominum iudicia & calumnias, quibus nomen & famam nostram proscindunt & denigrant, qui nos propter eius verbum oderunt. Nec enim hæc inania verba sunt, qualia fere sunt hominum, qui nec volunt nec possunt semper præstare, quæ polliciti sunt. Idcirco præmiū mox additur, dum ait: Ingredere in gaudium domini tui. Quod plane consentit promissionibus, quæ alibi habentur: Vbi ego sum, ibi etiam erit minister meus. Item, Ego paciscor vobis, sicut mihi pactus est Pater meus regnum: vt edatis & bibatis in mensa mea in regno meo, & sedeatis super thronos, iudicantes duodecim tribus Israel, &c. Interseritur autem hîs causa tanta retributionis: In paucis fuisti fidelis, super multa te constituam. Pauca aut parua dicit mysteria Dei, quorum dispensatio ecclesiarum ministris creditur: nö quòd vel pauca vel parua & exigua sint (cum sine his salus nostra non possit consistere) sed quòd exigua videri possunt, si cum gloria illa, quæ tunc nobis reuelabitur, & cum cœlestis regni gaudijs sempiternis conferantur, quæ captum omnem humani intellectus superant, & quæ oculus non vidit, auris non audiuit, neq; in cor hominis ascenderunt. Illic cum Ecclesia triumphante in beatæ immortalitatis loco & cœlesti paradiso collecti, Deum, qui lucem nobis nunc inaccessam habitat, videbimus facie ad faciem, neque ad eius vocem trepidi fugiemus (vt olim primi parentes nostri, cum per Paradisum ambulantis vocem audirent) sed ea iustitia velati, quam ipse nobis ex gratia contulit, æternum gaudebimus cum Filio eius vnigenito IESV CHRISTO, cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Ps. 73. had received only one talent or one mina is called to account. Nor are those who were faithful in little less pleasing to the Lord than those whose faith and diligence shone forth in great and outstanding gifts. But it is better to hear how the Lord rewarded the diligence of the faithful servants. He commends the first and the second in the same words, even though the gain of each was unequal. "Well done," he says, "good servant." That is: it is well, you have done what befits a good and faithful servant. So elsewhere he calls the blessed of his Father, whose faith he will commend on the last day. But what greater glory will fall to a man than to be publicly commended by the Son of God in that great assembly of the whole world, and in such a way that those who once persecuted and hated him, convicted within their own consciences, are compelled to acknowledge him as the servant and friend of God, and to condemn themselves? For as it is written in the Book of Wisdom: "Then the righteous will stand with great confidence before those who oppressed them and made light of their labours. When they see this, they will be shaken with dreadful fear, and they will be amazed at his unexpected salvation; and, struck with repentance and groaning in anguish of spirit, they will say among themselves: 'Is this the one whom we once held in derision? We fools thought his life was madness and his end without honour. Yet now he is numbered among the sons of God, and his lot is among the saints.
