We have indeed strayed from the way of truth,'" etc. These things, and many others that are written there, are contained in this brief eulogy of the good servant, by which Christ now deigns to honour those who faithfully deposited their money at interest and traded well with it. Therefore this one thing ought to suffice us against the unjust judgments and slanders of men, by which they tear apart and blacken our name and reputation, those who hate us on account of his word. For these are not empty words, like those of men who neither wish nor are able always to perform what they have promised. Accordingly the reward is added at once, when he says: "Enter into the joy of your lord." This plainly agrees with the promises found elsewhere: "Where I am, there also shall my servant be." Likewise: "I covenant with you, as my Father has covenanted with me a kingdom, that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom, and sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel," etc. But the cause of so great a reward is also set forth: "You have been faithful in a few things; I will set you over many things." By "few" or "small things" he means the mysteries of God, the dispensation of which is entrusted to the ministers of the Churches. Not that they are few or small or meagre (since without them our salvation could not stand), but they may seem small if they are compared with that glory which will then be revealed to us, and with the eternal joys of the heavenly kingdom, which surpass all the grasp of human understanding, and which "eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have they entered into the heart of man." There, gathered together with the triumphant Church in the place of blessed immortality and in the heavenly paradise, we shall see God, who now dwells in light inaccessible, face to face. Nor will we, trembling at his voice, flee from it (as our first parents once did when they heard the voice of God walking through Paradise), but clothed in that righteousness which he himself has bestowed on us by grace, we shall rejoice eternally with his only-begotten Son, Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCLXXXVIII.
units.tr: HOMILY 288.

units.la: Accedens autem & qui vnum talentum acceperat, ait: Domine, noueram te hominem durum esse, qui metis vbi non seminasti, & incedis vbi non sparsisti. Itaq; timens abij & occultaui talentum tuum in terra: Ecce habes quod tuum est. Respondens autem dominus eius, dixit ei: Serue male & cunctator, sciebas me metere vbi non seminaui, & inde cogere vbi non sparsi: Oportuit ergo te committere pecuniam meam mensarijs: & veniens ego recepissem meum cum fœnore. Tollite ergo ab eo talentum, & date ei qui habet decem talenta. Omni enim habenti dabitur, & augebitur: qui vero non habet, etiam quod habet, tolletur ab eo. Et inutilem seruum eijcite in tenebras extimas: illic erit fletus & stridor dentium.
units.tr: Then the one who had received one talent also came forward and said: "Lord, I knew you to be a hard man, who reap where you did not sow and gather where you did not scatter. So I was afraid, went away, and hid your talent in the ground. Behold, you have what is yours." But his lord answered and said to him: "You wicked and lazy servant, you knew that I reap where I did not sow and gather where I did not scatter. You ought therefore to have committed my money to the bankers, and when I came I would have received what was mine with interest. Take the talent from him and give it to him who has ten talents. For to everyone who has, more will be given, and he will have abundance; but from him who has not, even what he has will be taken away. And cast the unprofitable servant into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth."

units.la: QVamvis Dei Filius IESVS CHRISTVS peracto redemptionis nostrae negotio, cor- pore suo ex terris abierit, & illud in coelis ad dextram Patris sui collocarit, habet tamen in terris Ecclesiam suam, cuius ipse caput & sponsus est, & quam pupilla oculi sui chariorem diligit, cuius curam Apostolis suis & horum successoribus commendauit. Horum est, vt fidelis sint mysteriorum regni sui dispensatores, & ipsi negotientur, id est, per Euangelij praedicationem nostros quotidie discipulos ipsi adducant, qui ad salutem lucrifiant, & ipsi sanctantur tanquam virgo pura & casta, atque illi vni feruant: In eo igitur toti esse debent, quotquot Ecclesiarum & Christiministri dici & esse volunt, vt ei ad iudicium olim redeunti possint rationem reddere. Et vt salus atque beatitudo nostra omnis in hac hominum cum Deo, qui summum bonum & omnis boni fons est, coniunctione consistit: sic nulla hominis dignitas maior potest obtingere, quam si aliquorum miserio vtatur Deus, vt tanquam amici & pronubi Filij sui, sponsam suam illi adducant. Itaque de horum conditione & officio loquitur, & vniuersam ministerij Ecclesiastici rationem parabo la ista diligenter & prolixe exponit. In cuius prima & secunda parte hactenus vidimus, quid fi- dos Christi Ieruos facere conueniat, & quam laudem sine praemium abillo reportaturi sint. Reliqua vltima parabolae pars, quae ignauos seruos depingit, & quid hos maneat docet, ex qua colligi potest, quid perfidos Ecclesiarum dissipatores, quid item de apertis Christi & Euangelij hostibus iudicari debeat.
units.tr: Although the Son of God, Jesus Christ, having completed the business of our redemption, departed from the earth in his body and placed that body in heaven at the right hand of his Father, he nevertheless has his Church on earth, of which he is head and bridegroom, and which he loves more dearly than the apple of his eye. He has committed its care to his apostles and their successors. It is their task to be faithful stewards of the mysteries of his kingdom, and to trade, that is, through the preaching of the Gospel to bring daily disciples to him, winning them for salvation, and to present themselves as a pure and chaste virgin, keeping themselves for that one husband. Therefore all who wish to be and to be called ministers of the Churches of Christ ought to be wholly devoted to this, so that they may one day give an account to him when he returns for judgment. Just as all our salvation and blessedness consists in this union of humans with God, who is the highest good and the fountain of all good, so no greater dignity can fall to a human being than when God uses the ministry of some people to bring his bride to his Son, as friends and groomsmen of the Son. Thus he speaks of the condition and office of these men, and sets out the whole account of the ecclesiastical ministry carefully and at length in this parable. In its first and second parts we have so far seen what faithful servants of Christ ought to do, and what praise and reward they will receive from him. The last remaining part of the parable, which depicts the lazy servants and teaches what awaits them, shows from this what should be judged about faithless destroyers of the Churches, and likewise about the open enemies of Christ and the Gospel.

units.la: Inducitur seruus ignauus & male frugi, qui (vt ex eius propria confessione apud Lucam colligi potest) pecuniam heri sui in sudarium inuoluit, & postea in terram defodit & occultauit, nihil- mirum ne ab aliquo furtim aut violenter surriperetur. Nunc autem sponte venit in heri conspectum, cui illam reddituit cum facti sui excusatione, absurda plane & intempestiua. Nam occasionem parat priusquam accusetur, & hanc ita instituit, vt culpam suam in herum transferat, quem auaritiae & iniquitatis reum facit. Et quod magnae impudentiae argumentum est, ab eo statim ordinatur sermonem suum, quasi non aliqua insinuatione opus sit, qua animum heri mitiget. Domine (inquit) noueram te hominem durum esse. Durum dicit, quem humanum & nimis facilem expertus erat. Nam inutilem & ignauum fucum in familiam suam adoptarat, & non requisitus, neque ab aliquo coactus pecuniam suam ipsi crediderat, ex quo nullum lucrum vnquam acceperat. Quo autem argumento probat, durum & iniquum esse? Quod metat vbi non seminarit, & inde cogat, vbi non sparserit. At hoc dicendo, mendacium dicit, & iniuriam facit hero, qui cum ijs rationes confert solis, apud quos pecuniam suam cum certo mandato depositum erat: Vt nimirum ipso peregrè absente negotientur, donec domum reuertatur. Ista tamen audet dicere non sine heri contumelia: Et ex his concludit: Itaque timens abij, & occultaui talentum tuum in terra. Et quasi re bene gesta addit: Ecce habes quod tuum est. Vbi rursus mentitur os impudens. Quia enim fors cum fenore aut lucro ad herum redire debebat, non habebat quod suum erat, cum ille sine lucro ad eum rediret. Ita vero defraudatores solent, quibus non satis est, si cui fraudem faciant, nisi eundem calumniis suis pungant, & nomen eius suggillent.
units.tr: A lazy and worthless servant is introduced who (as can be gathered from his own confession in Luke) wrapped his master's money in a cloth, then buried it in the ground and hid it, no doubt lest it be stolen secretly or by force by someone. Now, however, he comes of his own accord into his master's presence and returns the money to him, with an excuse for what he has done that is plainly absurd and ill-timed. For he prepares an occasion before he is accused, and arranges it so that he shifts his fault onto his master, whom he makes guilty of greed and injustice. And, a sign of great shamelessness, he begins his speech at once, as though no insinuation were needed to soften his master's mind. "Lord," he says, "I knew you to be a hard man." He calls him hard, whom he had found human and far too easy. For he had admitted a useless and idle drone into his household, and without being asked or compelled by anyone, had entrusted his money to him, from which he had never received any gain. By what argument does he prove that his master is hard and unjust? Because he reaps where he has not sown and gathers where he has not scattered. But in saying this he lies, and does injury to his master, who settles accounts only with those to whom his money had been deposited under a definite instruction: namely, that they should trade while he was absent abroad, until he returned home. Yet he dares to say this, and not without insult to his master. And from these things he concludes: "So I was afraid, went away, and hid your talent in the ground." And as if he had done a fine job, he adds: "Behold, you have what is yours." Here again the shameless mouth lies. For since the money ought to have returned to his master with interest or profit, what he returned was not all that was his own, since he returned it without any profit. Defrauders are usually like this: it is not enough for them to cheat someone, unless they also wound him with their slanders and blacken his name.

units.la: Depinguntur autem in eius persona hypocritarum mores, qui eadem prorsus non minori im- probitate & impudentia faciunt, si quando illis cum Deo res est. Nam primum ipsi quoque in Do- mini confessum veniunt, & huius nomen profitentur, vt alij, qui fidele obsequium ei praestiterunt: Imo plura se fecisse iactant, quam ille vnquam iusserit. Huius generis sunt, quae ipse de talento in iudarium inuoluto, & in terram defossa garrit. Quis enim hoc illum facere iusserat? Et huius generis sunt, quae Isaias hypocritis tribuit, & Christus in illis accusat: quibus omnibus opponi potest, quod alibi Deus ipsis respondet: Quis haec requisiuit de manibus vestris?
units.tr: In his person are depicted the morals of hypocrites, who do exactly the same, and with no less wickedness and shamelessness, whenever they have dealings with God. For first they too come into the Lord's presence and profess his name, as do others who have rendered him faithful obedience. Indeed they boast that they have done more than he ever commanded. Of this kind are the things he prattles about the talent wrapped in a cloth and buried in the ground. For who had ordered him to do this? And of this kind are the things Isaiah ascribes to hypocrites and Christ accuses them of. Against all of these can be set what God elsewhere answers them: "Who has required these things at your hands?"

units.la: Deinde nihil agnoscit in hero praeter auaritiam, & seueritatem ac tantum non sordidam rei domesticae studium: nulla interim mentione facta bonitatis & facilitatis, quam hucusque erat ex- pertus. Sic hypocritae nihil fere in Deo praedicant, quam quod Legem dederit, & eiusdem seueritatem vindex sit: & quia illum per Mosem dixisse audiunt: Custodietis ritus meos & iudicia mea, quae si fecerit homo, viuet in eis: ex eo colligunt, per opera nostra nos iustificari & seruari oportere. Nihil autem de vitiosa hominis natura, & innata nobis prauitate, quae tanta est, vt nos Legis praecepta facere, & huic obsequi non sinat: nihil item de Christo, in quo omnes sua gratia thesauros reclusit, & qui idem nobis ab illo sapientia, iustitia, sanctificatio & redemptio factus est Neq; illud Christi ipsius in mentem venit: Sic Deus dilexit mundum, ut Filium suum Vnigenitum pro illo tradiderit, ut omnis qui credit in illum non pereat, sed habeat vitam aeternam. Multo minus illud Apostoli, Non sumus idonei ex nobis ipsis ad cogitandum. Item, In hoc est charitas, non quod nos Deum dilexerimus, sed quod ipse dilexerit nos, & misit Filium suum, ut esset propitiatio pro peccatis nostris. Vel, Nos diligimus eum, quoniam ipse prior dilexit nos. Horum (inquam) omnium immemores, opera sola in ore habent, quae sic iactant, ut Deum sibi debitorem faciant non verentur.
units.tr: Next, he recognises nothing in his master but greed, severity, and an almost squalid concern for household affairs, making no mention at all of the kindness and generosity he had experienced until then. So hypocrites proclaim almost nothing about God except that he gave the law and is the avenger of its severity. And because they hear that he said through Moses, "You shall keep my statutes and my judgments, which if a man does, he shall live in them," they conclude from this that we must be justified and saved by our works. But they say nothing about the corrupt nature of man and the wickedness innate in us, which is so great that it does not allow us to do the precepts of the law and obey it. Nor do they say anything about Christ, in whom God has opened all the treasures of his grace, and who has been made for us wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption. Nor does that saying of Christ himself come to mind: "God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son for it, so that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life." Much less does that of the Apostle: "We are not sufficient of ourselves to think anything." Likewise: "Herein is love: not that we loved God, but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins." Or: "We love him, because he first loved us." Forgetful, I say, of all these things, they have works alone on their lips, and boast of them in such a way that they do not hesitate to make God their debtor.

units.la: Praeterea contempto & abiecto mandato heri, qui negotiari iusserat, novum consilium init, & pecuniam heri linteo involutam in terram defodit, quasi ex hac fructus enascantur, qui nobis vitam aeternam pariunt. Eodem prorsus modo hypocritae relicta vocatione sua, quam ex Deo habent, novum vitae genus sibi eligunt, in quo sibi ipsis mirifice placent. Vult omnes homines negotiari Deus, & ne nobis solis vivamus, subet, sed ut aliorum saluti studeamus, quam Verbi & Ecclesiae ministri docendo, Magistratus legibus bonis & sancta Reipub. administratione, coniugesque pietate & legitima liberorum procreatione ac educatione, privati quoq; vitae ac morum sanctitate adiuvare & ita Dei gloriam propagare debent. At hypocritae his neglectis ad vitam monasticam se obstringunt, & ceu fuci ignavi in coenobiorum aluearijs delitescunt, in quibus sibi priuatim vivunt, neq; Deo neq; proximo utiles. Nam sive ieiunent, sive vigilent, sive peregrinationibus religionis ergo fatigentur, sibi, non Deo, ieiunant, sibi vigilant, sibi ipsis difficile currunt & defatigantur. Et qui inter hos optimi sunt, hoc potissimum argumento se excusare solent, quod etsi non multos lucrifaciant, neq; multum prosint, nemini tamen noceant, neq; alicui obstent, quo minus Deum recte colat & feruetur. At si non alia re nocerent, exemplo suo aliis superstitionum & scandalorum auctores sunt.
units.tr: Moreover, having spurned and cast aside the master's command to trade, he adopts a new plan and buries his master's money, wrapped in cloth, in the ground, as if fruits would spring from it that bring us eternal life. In exactly the same way, hypocrites, abandoning the calling they have from God, choose for themselves a new way of life, in which they wonderfully please themselves. God wishes all people to trade, and not to live for themselves alone, but to labour for the salvation of others. The ministers of the Word and of the Church should help toward this by teaching; the magistrate, by good laws and the holy administration of the commonwealth; spouses, by piety and the lawful procreation and upbringing of children; and private persons too, by the holiness of their life and morals. Thus they ought to spread God's glory. But hypocrites, neglecting these things, bind themselves to monastic life, and like idle drones hide in the hives of the monasteries, where they live for themselves alone, useful neither to God nor to their neighbour. For whether they fast, or keep vigil, or wear themselves out with pilgrimages undertaken for religion's sake, they fast for themselves, keep vigil for themselves, and run and tire themselves out for themselves. And the best among them are accustomed to excuse themselves chiefly on this ground: that although they win few and profit little, they harm no one, nor stand in the way of anyone worshipping God rightly and being saved. But even if they did no other harm, they are by their example the authors of superstitions and scandals for others.

units.la: Deni, ut ignavus iste ac mala frugis seruus hero dicere audet, Ecce habes quod tuum est, quasi officio omni erga hunc egregie defunctus sit: ita hypocritae se omnia quae Deo debentur, praestitisse putant, ut nihil ab ipsis possit praeterea exigi. At quo ore potest illud dicere, qui externis & frigidis caeremoniis & exercitijs corporalibus occupatus, meliorem sui partem, animam Deo negat, qui vult ut ipsum diligamus ex toto corde & tota anima, & vniuersis viribus nostris, nosque ipsos illi sistamus viuam hostiam, quae sola Deo placet, & rationalis ille cultus est, quem sci ptura passim commendat. Rom. 12.
units.tr: Finally, that lazy and worthless servant dares to say to his master, "Look, you have what is yours," as if he had fully discharged every duty towards him. So hypocrites think they have rendered everything owed to God, so that nothing more can be demanded of them. But with what face can someone say this, when he is occupied with external, cold ceremonies and bodily exercises, and denies God the better part of himself, the soul? God wants us to love him with all our heart, all our soul and all our strength, and to present ourselves to him as a living sacrifice, the only kind that pleases God, which is the "reasonable service" that Scripture commends everywhere. Rom. 12.

units.la: Sed audiamus sententiam Domini, quam hic contra seruum iustum pronuntiat, qui hypocritarum ignavorum personam sustinet. Primo seruum malum & cunctatorem dicit. Ergo non ij modo ferui mali sunt in Ecclesia, qui falsa doctrina aut alia ratione iniusta & iniqua nocent, sed etiam ij qui non promouent regnum Christi pro virili, & qui cunctando extrahunt negotia Ecclesiae, quae quam ocissime expedire oportebat. Quis enim in re rustica bonum seruum dixerit, qui opera, quae verno tempore fieri debebant, in multam aestatem vsq; aut etiam autumnum vel hyemem differt? Num vero mercator fidelem seruum putabit, qui tempora nundinarum non observans, has inutiliter praeterlabi finit? Solent quidem cunctatores eiusmodi multa praetexere incommoda, quae non sinant in praesenti eos officium facere. Sed fere in illis locum habet, quod olim Poeta dixit: Qui non est hodie, cras minus aptus erit. Quales ergo iudicari debent, qui insuper ordinem Ecclesiae turbant, & bene constituta turbant & male dissipant, quae ipsorum industria conseruari, aut aliorum negligentia collapsa in integrum restitui debebant?
units.tr: But let us hear the Lord's sentence, which he pronounces here against the unjust servant, who plays the part of the lazy hypocrite. First he calls him a wicked and dilatory servant. So those are not the only wicked servants in the Church who harm it by false doctrine or by some other unjust and iniquitous means, but also those who do not advance the kingdom of Christ to the best of their strength, and who by delay drag out the affairs of the Church, which ought to be dispatched as quickly as possible. For who would call a servant good in farm work if he postponed to the long summer, or even autumn or winter, tasks that ought to have been done in spring? Would a merchant think a servant faithful who, not heeding the market days, lets them slip by uselessly? Such procrastinators usually put forward many inconveniences that prevent them from doing their duty at present. But for most of them what the poet once said applies: "He who is not ready today will be less ready tomorrow." What, then, should be thought of those who moreover disturb the order of the Church, and who throw into confusion what was well established and scatter what, by their diligence, ought to have been preserved, or, when it has fallen through others' negligence, restored to its former state?

units.la: At ne quis aliquem excusationis praetextum inueniri posse arbitretur, qui coram Dei tribunali sufficiat, apud Lucam addit: Ex ore tuo iudicabo te serue male. Est conscientia mille testium loco, & si cor nostrum condemnet vos (scribit Apostolus) potentior est Deus corde nostro, & omnia. Quid ergo fiet, si culpae nostrae tanta sit enormitas, ut nosipsos sicuti foricos proprio indicio prodamus, quando nos excusare volumus, aut defendere? Id vero accidit hypocritis, quando de Dei seueritate, Legis rigore & iudicij diuini grauitate multa dicunt, ut quam necessaria sit operarum nostrorum iustitia, demonstrent. Nam quo plura dicunt, & illa amplificant, eo euidentius docent nobis Christo opus esse, qui nobis a Patre Mediator & intercessor datus est, & in quo vnohis. Vno hic sibi satisfactum testatur. Idem fere fit, quando Diuorum cultores videri volunt & horum exemplis sese defendunt. Quod si vero tanti faciunt Diuos, cur non credunt Paulo, qui Christum nec mori nec offerri amplius posse scribit, sed vnica oblatione consecrauisse in perpetuum eos, qui sanctificantur? Cur hodie his palam contradicunt, & Missae sacrificium ad salutem necessarium esse clamant, in qua Christi corpus & sanguis pro peccatis viuentium & mortuorum immoletur? Cur ijdem contra Ioannem Apostolum Diuos pro aduocatis & intercessoribus inuocant, & illum honorem maximum ex parte a Christo in Mariam virginem transferunt? Cur non insistunt illius verbis qui dixit? Ego sum Via, Veritas & Vita: Nemo venit ad Patrem nisi per me. Num a Ioanne, cui matrem virginem Dei Filius iam moriturus commendauit, vt eam matris loco habeant, negleetam suspicantur, aut se huius cultores magis fidos esse dicent, quam ille fuerit, qui dilecti discipuli nomen inter Apostolos habuit? Possent similia obiici ijs etiam qui Diuos & sanctos colitis nunquam non in ore habent, ita autem viuunt, vt non ex proprio ore solum, verumetiam ex factis proprijs & moribus damnentur. Si enim tanti faciunt reuera virtutes eas, quibus olim sancti illi, cum in viuis essent, claruerunt, cur non illis ipsi quoque studeant? Cur non imitantur? cur religionis Christianae professionem turpi & effreni scelerum licentia prophanant?
units.tr: But lest anyone think that some pretext of excuse can be found which will suffice before the tribunal of God, Luke adds: "I will judge you out of your own mouth, you wicked servant." Conscience takes the place of a thousand witnesses, and, as the Apostle writes, "if our heart condemns us, God is greater than our heart, and knows all things." What then will happen if our guilt is so great that, when we want to excuse or defend ourselves, we betray ourselves, like informers, by our own confession? This happens to hypocrites when they say much about God's severity, the rigour of the Law and the weight of divine judgement, in order to show how necessary the righteousness of our works is. For the more they say and enlarge upon these things, the more clearly they teach us that we need Christ, who was given to us by the Father as Mediator and intercessor, and in whom alone satisfaction is declared to have been made for us. The same almost happens when they wish to be seen as worshippers of the saints and defend themselves by their examples. But if they esteem the saints so highly, why do they not believe Paul, who writes that Christ neither dies nor can be offered again, but by one offering has consecrated for ever those who are sanctified? Why do they now openly contradict this and cry out that the sacrifice of the Mass is necessary for salvation, in which the body and blood of Christ are offered for the sins of the living and the dead? Why do the same people call upon the saints as advocates and intercessors against the Apostle John, and transfer to the Virgin Mary, in great part, that highest honour that belongs to Christ? Why do they not adhere to the words of him who said: "I am the Way, the Truth and the Life; no one comes to the Father except through me"? Do they suspect that the Virgin Mother, whom the Son of God commended to John as he was about to die, that he should have her in place of a mother, was neglected by him, or will they say that they are more faithful worshippers of her than he was, who had the name of the beloved disciple among the Apostles? The same things could be objected to those too who always have the saints on their lips, yet live in such a way that they are condemned not only by their own mouth but by their own deeds and morals. For if they truly value those virtues by which those saints shone when they were alive, why do they not strive for them too? Why do they not imitate them? Why do they profane the profession of the Christian religion by a shameful and unbridled licence in sin?

units.la: Sed vt ad noslrum hunc mala frugis seruum reuertamur, quem in praesenti Christus inducit, horum illi praeterea dixisse fingit: Si sciebas me adeo rigidum exactorem esse, oportuit te committere pecuniam meam mensarijs, & veniens ego recepissem meum cum faenore. Ex quo loco appareret quidem olim quoque in vsu fuisse, vt pecunia ad trapezitas siue mensarios ad faenus siue vsuram deponerentur. Quod autem hinc colligunt faeneratores iniqui & monopola vsurarij, qui hodie vsu rapaces exercent, quas homines Ethnici olim improbarunt, & homicidia dixerunt. Scriptura autem venenatis aspidum morsibus confert, id minime illis concedi debet. Saepe enim Spiritus sanctus parabolas petit a rebus iniquis & illicitis: quas nemo propterea licere cuiquam putabit. Apud Ezech. Deum synagogam Iudaeorum puellae fornicanti, quae seipsam turpiter omnibus publice pro stituerit, confert, & quam ipse sibi desponsarit: qui tamen in lege vetuit, ne fit scortum in Israele, neue sumnunt sacerdos meretricem ducat, & eius filiam fiscortetur lapidare iussit. Et Christus de legitimo vsu diuitiarum in Euangelio loquens dispensatores iniqui & impostoris exemplo docet ex iniquo Mammone amicos facere, qui nos post hanc vitam in aeterna tabernacula recipiant. At hinc nemo sanus colliget, dispensatores non peccare, si herorum bona perfide dissipent: Sed Apostoli dictum ratum esto, qui hoc requiri dicit, vt dispensatores fidi sint. Et huius generis multa in scripturis extant. Itaque non extra Christi institutum trahi debet, quod ille de vsura illa sanctissima dixit qua nulla potest salutarior & vtilior excogitari, ad eam quae hodie contra leges fidei & charitatis Christianae in vsu est, & fortunas fere publicas & priuatas depascitur, & fere omnibus seculis seditionum & bellorum ciuilium causa fuit. Testatur hoc non obscure Lucanus, qui inter belli ciuilis, quod Caesar & Pompeius cum patriae aut Reipub. ruina inter se gesserunt, causas, hanc quoque numerat: Hinc vsura vorax auidumque in tempore faenus. Et sub initia statim crescentis Rom. im perij, vsurariorum artes siue fraudes saepius causam fuisse constat, vt populus contra Patres siue Senatum tumultuaretur, & vel nouas tabulas, vel lege Agrariam ferri peteret. Non debet ergo inter Christianos probari, quod olim prophani & a veri Dei cognitione prorsus alieni, sola lege naturae illuminati, iniquum esse iudicarunt, & cuius iniquitas tot turbas dedit, & adhuc hodie dat vt vel ad nomen vsurae mens Christiana exhorrescere debeat. Nihil dico de eo, quod in rebus.b. ne constitutus fit, vbi sanctis & aequis legibus non modo frenum iniicitur infaciabili faeneratorum auaritiae, verumetiam eorum licentia reflringitur, qui dum turpiter omnia prodigunt, iniquis suis postulationibus molesti sunt omnibus, & ab hominibus frugi & pijs impudenter exigunt, quae hi labore suo & cura diligenti atque piafibi pararunt abstq; omni fraude & dolo, vt secundum Apostoli praeceptum suis prospiciant, neque hos inhumaniter negligendo se fidem abnegasse, & ethnicis peius esse ostendant. Minime ergo probari debent impudentes illi errones & inordinati homines, qui omni cura rei domesticae abiecta semper in ore habet illa Christi: Cuius petenti abs te dato: Mutuum date, nihil inde sperantes. Interim illi non mutuo, sed dono dari volunt, quae a quibusdam obuijs peruenient de reddendo nunquam cogitent, neque aliqua cura fratrum, quos improbe defraudant.
units.tr: But to return to this worthless servant whom Christ introduces in the present passage, he further pretends to have said to his master: "If you knew me to be such a harsh exactor, you ought to have committed my money to the bankers, and on my return I would have received mine back with interest." From this passage it appears that even in ancient times it was the custom to deposit money with bankers, or money-changers, for interest or usury. But what unjust moneylenders and monopolising usurers, who today practise rapacious usury, gather from this, the heathen once condemned, and called murders; and Scripture compares it to the poisonous bites of asps, which must by no means be granted to them. For the Holy Spirit often takes parables from wicked and unlawful things, and yet no one will think that they are therefore lawful for anyone. In Ezekiel, God compares the synagogue of the Jews to a girl who prostitutes herself shamefully and publicly to everyone, and whom he himself had betrothed; yet in the Law he forbade that there be a whore in Israel, or that a priest take a prostitute to wife, and he commanded that her daughter, if she played the harlot, be stoned. And Christ, speaking of the lawful use of riches in the Gospel, teaches by the example of the unjust and dishonest steward to make friends by means of the unrighteous Mammon, who may receive us into the everlasting tabernacles after this life. Yet no sane person will conclude from this that stewards do not sin if they faithlessly squander their masters' goods; rather, the saying of the Apostle stands firm, who says that what is required is that stewards be faithful. And many passages of this kind are found in the Scriptures. Therefore what he said about that most holy usury, than which none more wholesome and useful can be devised, must not be dragged outside the institution of Christ and applied to that usury which today is practised against the laws of faith and Christian charity, and which devours the fortunes of nearly all, public and private, and has been almost in every age the cause of seditions and civil wars. Lucan bears witness to this clearly, who, among the causes of the civil war that Caesar and Pompey waged between themselves, to the ruin of the fatherland or the commonwealth, also counts this: "Hence voracious usury and greedy interest at the due time." And at the very beginning of the growing Roman Empire it is well known that the tricks or frauds of the usurers were often the cause of the people rioting against the Fathers, that is, the Senate, and demanding either new account-books or an agrarian law. Therefore what the profane, who were entirely alien to the knowledge of the true God and enlightened by the law of nature alone, judged to be unjust should not be approved among Christians; its injustice has given, and even today gives, so much trouble that a Christian mind ought to shudder even at the name of usury. I say nothing of the case where, in a well-ordered commonwealth, wholesome and fair laws not only put a bridle on the insatiable avarice of moneylenders but also restrain the licence of those who, while shamefully squandering everything, are a burden to all by their unjust demands, and shamelessly exact from frugal and pious men what these have procured for themselves by their labour, diligent care and piety, without any fraud or deceit, so that, following the Apostle's precept, they may provide for their own, and not by inhumanely neglecting them show that they have denied the faith and are worse than the heathen. Therefore those shameless vagabonds and disorderly men ought by no means to be approved, who, having cast off all care of their household affairs, always have on their lips those words of Christ: "Give to him who asks of you," and "Lend, expecting nothing in return." Meanwhile they want what is handed to them by certain people who meet them to be given as a gift, not lent, and never think of repaying it, nor have any concern for the brothers whom they wickedly defraud.

units.la: Hebr.9.10. Digressio contra trafenneratores. Deut.23. Ezech.16. Deut.23. Leuit.21. Luc.16. 1.Cor.4. Luc.16. & quibus saepe egestatis authores sunt tangantur. Alteros autem illos moneo, ne dum horum impudentiam & improbitatem damnant, interim quaestui priuato nimis dediti, fraternae charitatis obliuiscantur, & Christum in suis membris furientem, nudum & algentem inhumaniter negligant. Sed quia haec alterius loci sunt, haec obiter attigisse sufficiat propter indefessam & inexplebilem faeneratorum malitiam, quos non pudet etiam ex Dei verbis, qui ipsa est charitas argumenta petere, quibus excusent ea, quae ipsi contra omnem charitatem designant in pauperes, quos nobis Dei Filius vnice commendatos voluit.
units.tr: Heb. 9.10. Digression against the usurers. Deut. 23. Ezek. 16. Deut. 23. Lev. 21. Luke 16. 1 Cor. 4. Luke 16. And by whom they are often made the authors of want are touched. But I warn those others, lest while they condemn the shamelessness and wickedness of these men, they, too devoted to private gain, forget brotherly love and carelessly neglect Christ, who in his members is hungry, naked and cold. But since these matters belong to another place, it is enough to have touched on them in passing, on account of the tireless and insatiable malice of the moneylenders. They are not ashamed to seek arguments from the words of God, who is love itself, to excuse the things they themselves commit against all charity toward the poor, whom the Son of God wished to be commended to us above all.

units.la: Sed poenam quoque videamus quam improbo huic & ignauo seruo denuntiat Dominus. Est haec duplex: Primum, Tollite (inquit) ab eo talentum, & date ei qui habet decem talenta. Et huius sententiae rationem reddit: Omni enim habenti dabitur, & augebitur, siue ditior fiet: qui vero non habet, etiam quod habet, tolletur ab eo. Habere dicitur, qui quod habet, se ex Deo habere agnoscit, & eo bene vtitur. Non habet ergo qui Dei donum non agnoscit, & ideo vel vt nimis vile & inutile contemnit & negligit, vel etiam eo abutitur. Est hoc frequens hodie, & (vt supra dixi-mus) multi se fatis excusatos putant, si possint dicere: Quid faciam ego quem Deus in gradu infe-riori constituit, neque alijs parem esse voluit? Cur ipse me negotijs, quae alteri illi rectius expedient, immisceam? At quia tales Deum ipsum cum suis donis contemnunt, iusto illius iudicio fit, vt donis quae acceperunt, spoliati ex gradu quoque suo deijciantur, & contemptissimi mortalium fiant, secundum illud Dei decretum quod olim contra Heli pronuntiauit, & quod in Saule etiam ratum fuit: Honorantes me honorabo, qui autem me contumelia afficiunt, contumelia afficientur. Et quoad ministros Verbi & Ecclesiarum, quos Christus Apostolorum suorum successores esse voluit, conuenit cum praesenti loco, quod alibi illis dicitur: Vos estis sal terrae: Quod si sal infatuatus fuerit, quo salietur? At nihil valet amplius nisi vt eiciatur foras & conculcetur ab hominibus. Exempla passim in scripturis & alijs historijs occurrunt, quibus hoc confirmatur, & vtinam non quotidie fierent, quae huic comminationi fidem faciunt, dum quotidie videmus inutiles & contemptibiles fieri ministros Ecclesiarum, qui donis a Deo datis non vtuntur, vel etiam abutuntur, & insuper authoritatem, quam ex ministerio suo habent, licentia vitae ac morum prostituunt. Admonet igitur inter alia locus hic, quae optima ratio sit qua existimationem nostram tueri & dona Dei in nobis augere possumus: Si nimirum Deo qui dedit, fideles simus, & tam doctrina quam vitae exemplo multos illi quotidie adducimus, qui illum vere agnoscant, & vt par est venerentur.
units.tr: But let us also look at the punishment which the Lord threatens against this wicked and idle servant. It is twofold. First, "Take the talent from him," he says, "and give it to him who has ten talents." And he gives the reason for this sentence: "For to everyone who has, more will be given, and he will have abundance; but from him who does not have, even what he has will be taken away." He is said to have who acknowledges that what he has he has from God, and uses it well. He therefore does not have who does not acknowledge God's gift, and either despises and neglects it as too cheap and useless, or even abuses it. This is common today, and (as I said above) many think they are well excused if they can say: "What am I to do, whom God has placed in a lower rank and did not wish to be equal to others? Why should I involve myself in affairs which others would handle more properly?" But since such people despise God himself along with his gifts, it comes by his just judgment that they, stripped of the gifts they have received, are also cast down from their rank and become the most contemptible of mortals, according to that decree of God which he once pronounced against Eli, and which was also confirmed in Saul: "Those who honour me I will honour, but those who despise me will be held in contempt." And as to the ministers of the Word and of the Churches, whom Christ willed to be the successors of his apostles, what is said here agrees with what is said elsewhere to them: "You are the salt of the earth. But if the salt has lost its savour, with what will it be salted? It is then good for nothing but to be cast out and trampled underfoot by men." Examples occur everywhere in the Scriptures and other histories which confirm this, and would that the things which give credence to this threat did not happen every day, while we daily see ministers of the Churches become useless and contemptible, who do not use the gifts given them by God, or even abuse them, and moreover prostitute the authority they have from their ministry to a licence of life and morals. This passage therefore teaches, among other things, what the best way is by which we can guard our reputation and increase the gifts of God in us: namely, if we are faithful to God who gave them, and bring many to him every day, both by doctrine and by the example of our life, who truly acknowledge him and venerate him as is fitting.

units.la: Sed non modo aufertur ab isto talentum, quod ignauus sudario inuolutum in terram defodé-rat, sed iubetur etiam ipse eici in tenebras exteriores, extra communionem nimirum beatorum spi-rituum, qui in loco beatae immortalitatis aeterno gaudio fruuntur, in locum, qui impiorum supplicijs destinatus est, qui cum assiduo fletu & horribili dentium stridore aeternum cruciantur: vbi (vt alibi Christus ait) vermis illorum non moritur, & ignis non extinguitur. Horum nos semper meminisse oportebat. Si enim seruus ignauus ita multari meruit, qui nullius perfidiae aut iniustitiae notoria accusari potuit quoad humanas rationes, cum hero fortem acceptam pecuniam integram restituerit, quid de illis fiet qui a Domino acceptis donis non in terram defodiunt, sed adobruunt terrenis sceleribus, ebrietate, libidine, fornicatione, auaritia, adeoque aperta apostasia facta in satanae castra transeunt, dum ne ipsi quidem volunt subesse legibus, quas Christiani magistratus ferunt, vt mini strorum Ecclesiae petulantia & corruptos mores corrigant? Vinam vero non multi, proh dolor, inuenirentur hodie, qui ista nimis impudenter faciunt. Etenim quia nostro saeculo apud omnes loci & ordinis homines regnat ebrietas, multi ex eo laudem captant, si mundi moribus se accommodent & ita sibi amicos parent. Sed magno illis constabit haec amicitia, quae (vt Iacobus scribit) est inimicitia cum Deo. Nunc horum omnium hic nobis vsus esse debet, vt singuli suae stationis memores diligenter videant, quid a Deo in mandatis acceperint, & quibus donis ab illo instructi sint, in vocatione autem sua constantes, illum bona fide sequantur, & quam plurimos Deo adducant, vt olim cum CHRISTO IESV Domino & seruatore nostro in illius gaudium ingrediantur, & cum illo viuant & regnent, cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum.
units.tr: But not only is the talent taken from that man, which the idle servant had wrapped in a cloth and buried in the earth, but he himself is also commanded to be cast out into the outer darkness, that is, outside the fellowship of the blessed spirits who enjoy eternal joy in the place of blessed immortality, into the place which is appointed for the punishments of the wicked, where they are tormented eternally with constant weeping and dreadful gnashing of teeth: where (as Christ says elsewhere) "their worm does not die, and the fire is not quenched." We ought always to remember these things. For if the idle servant deserved to be punished in this way, who could be accused of no notorious treachery or injustice by human reckoning, since he returned to his master the sum of money entrusted to him intact, what will become of those who, having received gifts from the Lord, do not bury them in the earth but smother them with earthly wickedness: drunkenness, lust, fornication, avarice; and so, having openly apostatised, pass over into the camp of Satan, while they will not even submit to the laws which Christian magistrates enact to correct the insolence and corrupt morals of the ministers of the Church? Would that, alas, many were not found today who do these things so shamelessly! For since in our age drunkenness reigns among people of every place and rank, many seek praise from it, if they adapt themselves to the manners of the world and so make friends for themselves. But this friendship will cost them dearly, for it is (as James writes) enmity with God. Now this whole matter ought to be of use to us here, so that each, mindful of his own station, may carefully see what he has received from God in commands, and with what gifts he has been equipped by him; and, steadfast in his calling, may follow him in good faith, and lead as many as possible to God, so that, as once with CHRIST JESUS our Lord and Saviour, we may enter into his joy, and live and reign with him, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever.

units.la: Amen.
units.tr: Amen.

units.la: Cùm autem venerit Filius hominis cum gloria sua, & omnes san-ƈti angeli cum eo, tunc sedebit super thronum gloriæ suæ. Et cogen-tur coram eo omnes gentes.
units.tr: When the Son of Man comes in his glory, and all the holy angels with him, then he will sit on the throne of his glory. And all nations will be gathered before him.

units.la: INter articulos Symboli Apostolici præ aliis multa & assidua consideratione dignus est, quo omnes qui Christiani dici & haberi volunt, vulgò confitentur Dominum & Seruatorem no-strum IESVM CHRISTVM sub finem huius seculi venturum ad iudicandum viuos & mortuos. Cæterum non omnes vera fide prædictos esse, vt ex animo & serio credant, quæ ore fa-tentur, ex multorum dictis & factis conjiat. Qui enim vere & ex corde credunt fore aliquando fi-nem huius mundi & venturum Filium Dei in maiestate sua, ad cuius tribunal omnes homines sti & rationem reddere oporteat non defactis modo suis, sed etiam de quouis verbo otiosò, nec illi hac meditatione excitati vitam suam & omnes huius actiones ita instituent, vt ipsos Deum se-rio timere syncera & intrepida fidei confessione, serio puriorîs religionis studio, morum sanctitate & insuperabili in cruce atque aduersis patientia testentur, neque vnquam posse carnis cupiditates & mundi illecebras a pietatis semita deflectent. Atqui videmus fieri, & eam esse mundi faciem hoc seculo, vt ijs moribus viuatur, quos nouissimus temporibus Christus et Apostoli tribuerunt. De his ille dixit: Quoniam multiplicata erit iniquitas, refrigescet charitas multorum: Filius homi-nis autem cum venerit num reperturus est fidem in terra? Passim denique fiunt inter omnis loci & ordinis homines, quæ nimis aperte testantur, plerosque homines esse sui potius quàm Dei aut proximi amantes, auaros, fastuosos, superbos, maledicos, parentibus immorigeros, ingratos, pro-phanos, charitatis expertes, implacabiles, calumniatores, immites, intemperantes, bonorum inimi-cos, proditores, præcipites, inflatos, voluptatum potius quàm Dei studiosos, qui formam quidem pietatis habeant, sed vim eius abnegarint. Talium (inquam) plenus est orbis terrarum, & id o-mnium querela docent, quæ passim audiuntur. Quis vero ipsos de fine mundi aut Christi iudicis ad uentu, ad cuius tribunal sistendi sint, vnquam cogitare putet? Quis neget illorum cordibus potius obuersari impias illas cogitationes, quas Nabalim & impijs illusoribus Dauid tribuit, non est Deus? Psal.14. & 94.
units.tr: Among the articles of the Apostles' Creed, none deserves more frequent and careful consideration than the one by which all who wish to be and be called Christians commonly confess that our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ will come at the end of this age to judge the living and the dead. Yet that not everyone who professes these things with his mouth believes them truly and sincerely from the heart may be gathered from the words and deeds of many. For those who truly and from the heart believe that the end of this world will someday come, and that the Son of God will come in his majesty, before whose judgment seat all men must stand and give an account, not only of their deeds but of every idle word, would be stirred by this thought to order their lives and all their actions so that they bear witness to their fear of God: by a sincere and fearless confession of faith, by a serious zeal for purer religion, by holiness of life, and by unconquered patience in the cross and in adversity. Such people would never allow the desires of the flesh and the allurements of the world to turn them from the path of godliness. Yet we see that it happens, and that the face of the world in this age is such, that men live by those morals which Christ and the Apostles foretold for the latest times. Of these he said: "Because iniquity shall abound, the love of many shall wax cold. But when the Son of man comes, will he find faith on the earth?" Finally, among men of every place and rank there occur things that testify all too plainly that most men love themselves rather than God or their neighbour: they are greedy, haughty, proud, slanderous, disobedient to parents, ungrateful, profane, without charity, implacable, calumnious, savage, intemperate, enemies of good men, traitors, rash, puffed up, lovers of pleasures rather than of God, who have a form of godliness but deny its power. The world is full of such people, I say, and the complaints heard everywhere teach us this. Yet who would think that such men ever consider the end of the world or the coming of Christ the judge, before whose tribunal they must stand? Who would deny that the impious thoughts which David attributed to the fool and the impious mockers, "There is no God," rather haunt their hearts? Ps. 14 and 94.

units.la: Quapropter Dominus noster IESVS CHRISTVS, cum mortis suæ hora iam appropin-quaret, prolixum sermonem de nouissimo seculo & postremo suo ad iudicium aduentu, deq; signis hunc præcessuris, instituit, & hunc totum ex ordine descripsit Matthæus, quemadmodum & prio-rem illum, quem supra sub initium suæ prædicationis in monte quodam Galilææ habuit, & in ipso vaticinium de consummatione seculi cum excidio Ierosolymæ & templi coniungit, quod viuenti-bus adhuc aliquot Apostolis debebat subsequi: vt cum hoc viderent certò fieri, quod tunc prorsus impossibile videbatur, de fine & consummatione mundi minus dubitarent. Noluit autem Domi-nus & redemptor noster illorum curiositati satisfacere, qui quæstiones de hac re inutiles & ridicu-las, imò etiam impias mouent, non vt ad pietatem & huius studium erudiantur, sed vt nouas quo-tidiè occasiones ea deridendi & negandi inuteniant, quæ de vita æterna, mortuorum resurrectione & nouissimo illius ad iudicium aduentu dicuntur. Sed ad eum scopum concionem totam dirigit Dominus, vt fatalem illam securitatem, quæ hominum animis insidet, & nouissimo tempore quasi regnabat, nobis excutiat, & omnes homines ad vigilantiam excitet, ne quis sibi ppsis omnia tuta pollicentur, interea salutis æternæ iacturam faciant. Quod multis euenturum esse Paulus prædi-xit, scribens: Cum dicent, Pax & tuta omnia, tunc repentinum eis imminet exitium, sicuti dolor partus mulieri vterum ferenti, &c. 1. Thess. 5.
units.tr: For this reason our Lord Jesus Christ, when the hour of his death was now at hand, gave a long discourse about the last age and his final coming to judgment, and about the signs that would precede it. Matthew described all of this in order, just as he also joined to that earlier discourse, which Christ gave on a mountain in Galilee at the beginning of his preaching, the prophecy of the consummation of the age together with the destruction of Jerusalem and the temple. This was to follow while some of the Apostles were still alive, so that when they saw with certainty what then seemed utterly impossible come to pass, they would doubt less about the end and consummation of the world. Our Lord and Redeemer, however, was unwilling to satisfy the curiosity of those who raise useless and ridiculous, even impious, questions about these matters, not so that they might be instructed in godliness and its practice, but so that they might find new daily opportunities to mock and deny what is said about eternal life, the resurrection of the dead, and his final coming to judgment. Rather, the Lord directs his whole discourse to this aim: to shake us out of that fatal security which sits in men's minds and which, in the last time, was as it were reigning, and to rouse all men to watchfulness, lest anyone promise himself that all is safe while in the meantime they suffer the loss of eternal salvation. Paul foretold that this would happen to many, writing: "When they shall say, Peace and safety, then sudden destruction comes upon them, as travail upon a woman with child, etc." 1 Thess. 5.

units.la: Cæterum aduentus Domini hora ne angelis quidem nota est, & quæ signa hunc præcessura dicuntur, pleraq; eiusmodi sunt, vt iam olim quoque multa eius generis acciderint. Itaq; homines præsentibus fere intenti, de futuris non cogitant, neq; his diligentius attendunt. Manent ergo in multorum cordibus dubitationes illæ, quas caro suggerit, quin piorum quoque animis obrepunt multa, quæ eos ab illa meditatione auocant, quæ illis præcipua & assidua esse debebat. Quare vt quasi in rem praesentem nos inducat Dominus Ϫπολύτωσιν sive descriptionem euidentem extre-mi sui aduentus & iudicij subijcit, quae omnes huius circumstantias ceu in tabula depictas oculis exponit, quibus etiam omnia comprehendit, quae de hac re dici possunt. Primum enim iudicem nominat, ut quis ille sit, & quomodo ad iudicium venturus sit, intelligamus. Deinde qui nam ad eius tribunal citari, & iudicio sisti debeant, docet. Tertio iudicij formam, & totum processum eius (ut vocant) describit, cum sententia finali, quae tunc tam de piis quam de impiis pronunciabitur. Postremo quid hac audita vtriq; dicturi & facturi sint. Vtus omnium hic nobis esse debet, ut qui hactenus huic saeculo addicti, & ideo securiores fuerunt, quam par est, ad ferium salutis aeternae studium excitati conuertantur, opiniones falsas abijciant, neq; indulgeant cogitationibus vanis, quibus prophani homines seipsos decipiunt, multo minus admittant curras illusores, qui dum fa-ceti esse volunt iocandi materiam hinc petunt, quod in dubium vocant, quaecunq; de nouissimo die aut mortuorum resurrectione aut iudicio extremo dicuntur, & quales in postremis temporibus multos fore, nuper ex Petri epistola posteriori demonstrauimus. Discamus praeterea ex hoc loco, quid Deo placeat, quidue displiceat, quid nos facere aut fugere oporteat, si seruari volumus: confirmemur item in doctrina verbi Dei, quae tradit esse caelos & inferos: vita deniq; alteram & aeternam, in qua pijs sua praemia, impijs merita scelerum poena retribuentur. Deus Pater luminum, det nobis, ut de tantis mysteriis ea dicamus, quae multorum mentes erudiant, & ut sancto vitae futurae desiderio omnes accendamur.
units.tr: But the hour of the Lord's coming is not known even to the angels, and the signs said to precede it are mostly of such a kind that many things of that sort have already happened long ago. Therefore men, intent for the most part on present things, do not think about the future and do not attend to it more diligently. Those doubts which the flesh suggests therefore remain in the hearts of many, and even into the minds of the godly there creep many things that draw them away from that meditation which ought to have been especially theirs and constant. Therefore, that the Lord may bring us as if into the presence of the thing itself [ὑποτύπωσιν], he sets before us a vivid description, or a clear portrayal, of his last coming and judgment. It sets all its circumstances before our eyes as if painted on a tablet, and in it he comprehends everything that can be said about this matter. For first he names the judge, so that we may understand who he is and how he is to come to judgment. Next he teaches who are to be summoned to his tribunal and brought to judgment. Third, he describes the form of the judgment and its whole process, as they say, together with the final sentence that will then be pronounced on the godly and the impious alike. Lastly, he describes what both groups will say and do when they hear it. The use of all this for us is that those who have hitherto been devoted to this age, and therefore have been more secure than is fitting, may be roused to a serious pursuit of eternal salvation and may turn, casting aside false opinions and not indulging in vain thoughts by which profane men deceive themselves. Still less should we admit those scoffers who, wishing to be witty, take material for jests from this, calling into doubt whatever is said about the last day, the resurrection of the dead, or the final judgment, and about the kind of men who will be many in the last times, as we recently demonstrated from the second epistle of Peter. Moreover, let us learn from this passage what pleases God and what displeases him, and what we must do or avoid if we wish to be saved. Let us also be confirmed in the doctrine of God's Word, which teaches that there are heavens and hells, and finally another and eternal life, in which rewards are repaid to the godly and punishment for their crimes to the impious. May God the Father of lights grant us to speak of such great mysteries in a way that instructs the minds of many, and to be all kindled with a holy desire for the life to come.

units.la: Et primo quidem, ut de iudice, quis nam hic futurus sit videamus, sic dicit: Cum autem venerit Filius hominis cum gloria sua, &c. Sunt haec verba IESV CHRISTI Filij Dei, qui Patri coaeternalis, & eiusdem cum illo maiestatis, & proinde Deus verus est, & praefinito tempore homo factus ex Virgine, non conuersione Deitatis in carnem, sed assumptione feminae Abrahami nunc in vna eademq; persona induita verus Deus & homo est. In praesenti vero Filium hominis se vocat, & hunc venturum dicit, ut iudicet: nimirum ad illud quod prius apud Ioannem dixerat, respiciens: Pater non iudicat quenquam, sed omne iudicium dedit Filio. Et huius diuini ratio nem reddens, postea addit: Et authoritatem etiam ei dedit iudicium exercendi, quatenus Filius hominis est. Itaq; solius Filij hominis hic meminit, non vt se Filium Dei esse neget, aut vt diuinitatem a iudicandi potestate excludat, vel tunc ceteraturum doceat, sed vt se in ea natura venturum demonstret, & quidem in eadem carnis forma atq; substantia, cui (vt D. Augustinus scripsit) profecto immortalitatem dedit naturam non abstulit. Ideo alibi idem pater haec Christi verba, quae modo adduximus per Ascensionis historiam exponit, sic scribens: Pater nō iudicat quenquam, quia hominibus in iudicio non apparebit, nisi Filius. Et mox: Euidentius nobis ostendit scriptura, quia ipse (Filius hominis nimirum) apparebit. Quadragesimo die post resurrectionem suam ascendit in caelum videntibus discipulis suis, & vox angelica: Viri (inquit) Galilaei quid statis aspicientes in caelum? Ille qui assumptus est a vobis in caelum, sic veniet quemadmodum vidistis eum euntem in caelum. Quomodo eum videbant ire? In carne quam tetigerunt, quam palpauerunt, cuius etiam cicatrices tangendo sibi probauerunt: in illo corpore, in quo cum eis intrauit & exiuit per quadraginta dies, manifestans se eis in veritate, non in aliqua falsitate, nō phantasmate, non vmbra, non spiritu, sed quemadmodum ipse dixit non fallens: Palpate & videte, quia spiritus carnem & ossa non habet, sicut me videtis habere. Est quidem illud iam corpus dignum caelesti habitatione, non subiacens morti, non mutabile per aetates. Non enim sicut ad illam aetatem ab infantia creuerat. Sic ab aetate quae iuuentus erat, vergit in senectutem: manet sicut ascendit, venturus ad eos, quibus antequam veniat, verbum suum voluit praedicare. Sic enim veniet in forma humana. Hanc videbunt & impij, videbunt & ad dextram positi, videbunt ad sinistram separati, sicut scriptum est: Videbunt in quem pupugerunt, &c. Haec Augustus. Quae ideo recitare libuit, quia aperte testantur, hunc verum & orthodoxum Symboli Apostolici, quo Christum ad iudicium venturum confitemur, senssum esse, quem olim tota Ecclesia tenuit & approbauit, & qui hodie etiam retineri debeat ab omnibus, qui orthodoxi & catholici esse volunt. Etenim huius doctrinae de mul tis nos admonet necessarijs cognitu.
units.tr: And first, so that we may see who this judge is to be, he says: "When the Son of man comes in his glory, etc." These are the words of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, who is coeternal with the Father and of the same majesty with him, and therefore is true God, and who at the appointed time was made man of the Virgin, not by the conversion of his deity into flesh, but by the assumption of the nature of Abraham's seed. Now, clothed in one and the same person, he is true God and man. In the present passage he calls himself the Son of man and says that he will come to judge, looking back, of course, to what he had said earlier in John: "The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son." And giving the reason for this divine arrangement, he adds afterwards: "And he has also given him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of man." Therefore he mentions only the Son of man here, not to deny that he is the Son of God, nor to exclude his deity from the power of judging, nor to teach that he would then cease to be God, but to show that he will come in that nature, indeed in the same form and substance of flesh, to which (as Augustine wrote) God certainly gave immortality without taking away its nature. For this reason the same Father elsewhere explains these words of Christ, which we have just cited, through the history of the Ascension, writing thus: "The Father judges no one, because he will not appear to men in judgment except the Son." And soon after: "Scripture shows us more clearly that he himself (the Son of man, of course) will appear. On the fortieth day after his resurrection he ascended into heaven while his disciples watched, and an angelic voice said: 'Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? He who was taken up from you into heaven will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven.'" How did they see him go? In the flesh which they touched, which they handled, whose scars too they proved by touch: in that body in which he went in and out among them for forty days, showing himself to them in truth, not in any falsehood, not as a phantom, not as a shadow, not as a spirit, but as he himself said, not deceiving: "Handle me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me have." That body is indeed worthy of heavenly dwelling, not subject to death, not changing through the ages. For it did not grow from infancy to that age which was youth, and then pass into old age; it remains as it ascended, and it will come to those to whom, before he comes, he wished his word to be preached. For he will come in human form. The impious will see him too, those placed at his right hand will see him, those set apart on his left will see him, as it is written: "They will look on him whom they pierced, etc." So Augustine. I was pleased to recite these words because they plainly testify that this is the true and orthodox sense of the Apostles' Creed, in which we confess that Christ will come to judgment: the sense which the whole Church once held and approved, and which today ought to be retained by all who wish to be orthodox and catholic. Indeed, this doctrine warns us of many things necessary to know.

units.la: Primum consolationis plenum est, quod in ea natura & substantia Christus venit ad iuditandum, in qua ipse iudicatus & pæna est. Crux ergo & infame atque dirum mortis supplicium nihil eius diminutati derogauit, nec etiam ipsum offendit, ut ideo homines odisse, aut quam ex ipsis assumpserat, naturam deponere aut prorsus abijcere voluerit. Quod ut nos confirmare debet, ne crucis, quam in culpa ipse ignominia offendamur: ita nec ea cruce aut aduersis offendi aut illis suc- cumbere debemus, quæ nobis propter eius nomen ferenda sunt. Vt enim per suam illam crucem in cælestem gloriam ascendit Christus: ita nos quoque per nostras perpessiones ad se euehet. Eius enim promissio est, Volo Pater, ubi ego sum, ibi sint etiam quos dedisti mihi. Vt enim Christus ad no- uam vitam resurrexit, & corpus eius, etsi formam & veritatem corporis retinuerit, immortale tamen & vere gloriosum factum est: ita nos quoque ad vitam meliorem resurgemus, & corpora nostra illius corpori gloriosa conformia fient. Quoties ergo sub cruce eo vsque deprimimur, ut nihil aliud quam filij hominum, id est, hominum miserrimi & abiectissimi, imo ut de semetipso Dauid dicebat) vermis & non homines esse videamur, semper in mentem veniat, eandem Christi Capi- tis nostri fortem in terris fuisse, qui tamen nunc in cælis triumphat, & olim nos ad se recipiet, ut ipsi quoque omnes moleshia & ignominia liberati, gloriae eius conformes efficiamur. Qui enim ideo ho- mo factus est, ut nos Deo Patri reconciliaret, & nos fratres suos faceret, & assumptam huma- nitatem ne in cælesti quidem gloria deponere voluit, multo minus amarem nostri, qui eum, ut ho mo fieret monuit, vnquam exuet.
units.tr: First, the consolation is full: Christ comes to judge in the same nature and substance in which he himself was judged and punished. The cross, and the infamous and dreadful penalty of death, took nothing from his dignity, and they did not so offend him that he hated men or wished to lay aside or utterly cast off the nature he had taken from them. This ought to confirm us, so that we are not offended by the shame of the cross, which Christ himself bore, and so that we neither take offence at adversity nor give way to the sufferings we must bear for his name. Just as Christ ascended to heavenly glory by his cross, so he will also raise us to himself through our sufferings. For his promise is: "Father, I desire that where I am, there also may be those whom you have given me." Christ rose to a new life, and although his body kept the form and reality of a body, it became immortal and truly glorious. So we too will rise to a better life, and our bodies will be made like his glorious body. Therefore, whenever we are so pressed down under the cross that we seem to be nothing but sons of men, that is, the most wretched and abject of men, or indeed (as David said of himself) worms and not men, let it always come to mind that the same lot fell to Christ our Head on earth, and that he who now triumphs in heaven will one day receive us to himself, so that we too, freed from all trouble and shame, may be made conformed to his glory. For he who became man so that he might reconcile us to God the Father and make us his brothers, and who would not lay aside the humanity he had assumed even in heavenly glory, will much less ever strip off our humanity, which he commanded to become human.

units.la: Deinde Filium hominis venturum, & in nouissimo die iudicem fefurum testatur Christus, ut nos contra tyrannos persecutores confirmet, qui illam in nobis, qui ipsius membra sumus, quoties die crudelissime crucifigunt, nihil minus tamen, quam illius aut Ecclesiae eius, aut vera fidei hostes videri volunt. Habent praeterea patronos pontifices, qui illos in suo instituto laudant, dilectos fi- lios, Christianissimos, catholicos, fidei defensores dicunt: adhuc hunc gratissimum Deo cultum esse aiunt, si vt omnes mactationi destinatae iugulentur, qui vt Christi honorem tueantur, illis contradi cunt. Et quia sub fucato Ecclesiae nomine & Apostolicae authoritatis praetextu omnia faciunt, vt bil tam iniustum, tam iniquum, tam crudele est, quod non excusari aut defendi posse existimant. Sed videbunt olim quem transfixerunt, quando Dei filius in nubibus caeli veniet, vt illorum iu- dex sit, qui simul causa suorum actor erit, & non solum propriae conscientiae testimonio, verumetiam conspectu suo eos arguet & conuincet. Nam cum hoc simul oculis illorum & cordibus ingerentur omnes sancti Christi martyres, quos illi iniuste & crudeliter perfequuti sunt, & aduersus illos cla mabit omnium sanguis, quos illi propter confessionem nominis Christi interfecerunt. Si enim pul- sus, qui ministrorum Christi pedibus aut vestibus inhaeret contra Verbi contemptores sufficit illis conuincendis & damnandis, quanto acrius pungentur in cordibus suis, quando ipsum Christum vi debunt, & huius conspectu sibi exprobrari sentient ingratitudinem & contumaciam suam, qua illum cum regno suo ad ipsos accedentem reiecerunt, & quacunque alia contra illum & e- ius seruos designarunt. Hac commination certe Caiaphan quoque & vniuersum Sacerdo- tum & seniorum confessum, qui ad ipsum damnandum conuenerant, terret Dominus, quan- do illis dicit: Ab hoc tempore videbitis Filium hominis sedentem ad dextram potentiae Dei, & venientem in nubibus caeli. Haec nobis applicemus fratres, neque dubium nobis fit, fore vt ad Christi tribunal sistantur olim nostri hostes, qui nunc nos damnant, & tunc nos cum illo in glo- ria videbunt, & in animis cruciatum atque terrorem sentient, qui nullis rationibus humanis mi- tigari poterit.
units.tr: Next, Christ testifies that the Son of man will come and will be judge on the last day, so that he may strengthen us against tyrants and persecutors. These men, who every day most cruelly crucify in us, who are his members, nevertheless want to appear to be enemies of neither him, nor his Church, nor the true faith. Moreover, they have popes as patrons, who praise them for their institute, call them beloved sons, most Christian, catholic, and defenders of the faith, and say that this is the most pleasing worship to God: that all those who stand against them in defence of Christ's honour should be slaughtered like sheep destined for slaughter. And because they do everything under the false name of the Church and the pretext of apostolic authority, they think nothing is so unjust, so iniquitous, or so cruel that it cannot be excused or defended. But one day they will see him whom they pierced, when the Son of God comes in the clouds of heaven to be judge of those who are at the same time the advocate of his own people. He will convict and confute them not only by the testimony of their own conscience but also by his very sight. For at the same time all the holy martyrs of Christ, whom they unjustly and cruelly persecuted, will be placed before their eyes and hearts, and the blood of all those whom they killed for confessing the name of Christ will cry out against them. For if the dust that clings to the feet or garments of Christ's ministers is enough to convict and condemn the despisers of the Word, how much more sharply will they be pierced in their hearts when they see Christ himself, and feel in his sight the ingratitude and obstinacy by which they rejected him, with his kingdom, when he came to them, and whatever else they devised against him and his servants! Certainly the Lord terrifies Caiaphas too with this threat, and the whole council of priests and elders who had gathered to condemn him, when he says to them: "From now on you will see the Son of man sitting at the right hand of the power of God, and coming in the clouds of heaven." Let us apply these things to ourselves, brothers. There is no doubt that our enemies, who now condemn us, will one day be brought before Christ's judgment seat. Then they will see us with him in glory, and they will feel in their souls a torment and terror that no human reasoning can soothe.

units.la: Sed & contra haereticorum omnium commenta & blasphemias nobis sufficere potest quod Christus in assumpta hominis persona & forma venturum affirmat. Constat illa Deo & homi- ne, quem in vnitatem personae assumpsit diuina natura. Talis vero etiam nunc est, & talis erit, quando in nouissimo die ad iudicandum veniet. Ergo impium & mendax est Nestorij commen- tum, qui personae vnitatem diffraxit, & duos Christos finxit, hominem sicut, qui Deum sibi asi- stentem habeat. Nam filius hominis veniet iudex, qui simul Dei filius est Patri coessentialis, & aeternus. Nec minus iugulantur Eutychiani veteres & noui, qui dum maiestate Christi hominis extollunt, & vbiquitico suo figmento carne eius, quae in utero virginis assumpsit omnipraesentem faciunt, humanam eius naturam diuinae exaequando negant, & quantum in ipsis est abolent. At-qui in hac se oculis nostris manifestabit Christus in illo magno die, vt supra ex Augustino docui-mus. Num vero hoc ideo faciet, vt nos illum humanae naturae proprietates essentiales eximiffe, & totum quantus est, in Deum abiisse credamus? Poterant haec fusius tractari, sed ista modo sufficiant.
units.tr: But against all the inventions and blasphemies of the heretics, it is enough for us that Christ affirms he will come in the person and form he assumed as man. That person consists of God and man, whose human nature the divine nature assumed into the unity of the person. Such he is even now, and such he will be when he comes to judge on the last day. Therefore the teaching of Nestorius is impious and false: he split the unity of the person and invented two Christs, one a man who has God standing beside him. For the Son of man will come as judge, who is at the same time the Son of God, co-essential with the Father, and eternal. The ancient and modern Eutychians are no less refuted, who, while they exalt the majesty of Christ's man, and by their ubiquitarian fiction make his flesh, which he took in the Virgin's womb, omnipresent, deny that his human nature is made equal to the divine, and abolish it as far as in them lies. Yet in that great day Christ will manifest himself to our eyes in this same humanity, as I showed above from Augustine. But will he do this so that we may believe he has laid aside the essential properties of human nature and passed wholly, in his whole greatness, into God? These matters could be treated at greater length, but for now let these suffice.

units.la: Ne quis vero nos maiestatem Christi negare aut extenuare dicat (quod hodie nimis impuden-ter faciunt aduersarij nostri, qui corporis omnipraesentiam statuendo duplicem in illo diuinitatem non verentur statuere: Primam quae ab aeterno Patri consubstantialis fit: alteram quae ex carne caeperit, postquam haec in gloriam caelestem euecta diuina natura fit exaequata. At quid aliud Ar-rius olim garriebat, quando in Christo Deum confitebatur, qui aliquando non fuisset?) videamus etiam, quomodo aut qualis iudex ille venturus sit. Cum venerit (inquit) Filius hominis cum glo-ria sua. Cum sua gloria quae ipsi propria est, non aliena, veniet. At quae haec alia est, quam diuina quam apud Patrem (vt alibi testatur) habuit, priusquam hic mundus existeret? Et si ergo haec tunc ab hominibus non conspicietur, non tamen ita latebit, quin se efficaciter & potenter exerat, & (vt modo diximus) eius sensu impij terreantur. Opponitur hoc primo eius aduentui in carnem, qui humilis fuit & infirmus. Nam licet tunc quoq; aliqua apparuerunt indicia, quibus probaba-tur, illum homine maiorem esse, tamen pauper peregrinatus est, in praesepio iacuit, mortalis item fuit eius caro, & omnibus affectionibus obnoxia, quae nos in hac vita mortali exercent & fati-gant. At olim cum gloria veniet, omnibus ijs instructus, quae superbos terrere & deijcere pos-sunt, qualem esse oportet, qui Iudex totius orbis terrarum esse volet. Ideo additur: Et omnes sancti angeli cum eo. Et horum in simili argumento apud Marcum quoq; meminit. At quanta angelorum vires sint, quanta ad defendendum pios & puniendum impios illorum potentia, exemplis infinitis docent sacrae literae. Vnus angelus omnes in tota Aegypto primogenitos intra vnius noctis spacium occidit, & Pharaonem tyrannum immanissimum filios Israelis dimittere coegit. Similiter vnius angeli ministerio in Assyriorum castris, Ezechia regnante centum & octoginta millia caduntur, & obsidione liberatur vrbs, quam hostes ipsa iam deuorarant. Helisaeus item Propheta, cum in medios hostes incidisset, angelorum praesidio seruatus est, qui cum curribus & equis, igni terribili corrusantibus, campos & montes vicinos circumquaq; occupabant: & quamuis non ab omnibus viderentur, hostium tamen oculos & manus continuerunt, ne quid contra Dei seruum facerent. Quid ergo fiet, quando in nouissimo die IESVS CHRISTVS non cum paucis, sed cum innumerabilibus legionibus & myriadibus angelorum (vt Daniel olim praedixit) ad iudicandum veniet? Quis illi resistere poterit? Quis ad eius conspectum non terrebitur & concidet?
units.tr: Lest anyone say that we deny or diminish the majesty of Christ (which our opponents today do far too shamelessly, for by positing the omnipresence of his body they do not hesitate to posit a twofold divinity in him: the first consubstantial with the eternal Father, the second beginning from the flesh, which, after being raised to heavenly glory, was made equal to the divine nature), let us also see how and in what manner that judge will come. "When the Son of man comes," he says, "in his glory." He will come in his own glory, which belongs to him, not to another. And what other glory is this than the divine glory which he had with the Father (as he testifies elsewhere) before this world existed? And even if this glory will not be seen by men then, it will not be so hidden that it does not show itself effectively and powerfully, and (as we have just said) the impious will be terrified by its sense. This glory is set first against his coming in the flesh, which was humble and weak. For although then also some signs appeared by which it was proved that he was greater than man, yet he wandered as a poor man, lay in a manger, and his flesh was mortal and subject to all the affections that exercise and weary us in this mortal life. But at last he will come in glory, equipped with all those things that can terrify and cast down the proud, as one must be who wishes to be judge of the whole world. Therefore it is added: "And all the holy angels with him." He mentions this in a similar context in Mark too. And how great the powers of the angels are, and how great their might to defend the godly and punish the wicked, the sacred letters teach by countless examples. One angel struck down all the firstborn throughout Egypt within the space of a single night, and forced Pharaoh, that most savage tyrant, to let the sons of Israel go. Likewise, by the ministry of one angel, in the camp of the Assyrians, in the reign of Hezekiah, a hundred and eighty thousand were slain, and the city, which the enemies had already devoured, was delivered from siege. Also the prophet Elisha, when he had fallen among his enemies, was saved by the protection of angels, who with chariots and horses of blazing fire occupied the fields and mountains round about; and although they were not seen by all, they restrained the eyes and hands of the enemies, so that they could do nothing against the servant of God. What then will happen on the last day, when JESUS CHRIST comes to judge, not with a few, but with innumerable legions and myriads of angels, as Daniel once foretold? Who will be able to resist him? Who will not be terrified and fall at his sight?

units.la: Sed aliud etiam addit, quo maiestatem & potentiam suam amplius declarat dicens: Tunc sedebit super thronum gloriae suae. Thronum huic scriptura passim inter nubes monstrat, in quibus ille veniet. Qualis vero futurus sit, non nostrum est curiosius inquirere. Sufficiant nobis quae in sacris literis traduntur: nec dubitemus, Dominum, qui Solomonis thronum toti orbi & regibus cun-ctis admirabilem fecit, multo gloriosiorem thronum habiturum, qui iustitia & virtute firmatus & clementia, admiratione & solatio erit electis, impijs vero omnibus terrorem incutiet, quem nunquam effugere aut superare poterunt. Enimuero, quacunq; nobis superne ex nubibus imminent, cum ter-rore singulari coniuncta sunt: vt fulgur, tonitrua, fulmina, chasmata & quaecunq; alia sunt huius generis. Quanto terribilior ergo erit Christi supra nos in nubibus diuino splendore refulgentis ma-iestas omnibus ijs, qui a fide alieni propriae conscientiae testimonio accusantur? Discipuli illi tres, Petrus, Ioannes & Iacobus, prae formidine conciderunt in facies suas, & tantum non exanimati sunt, cum guslum aliquē eius maiestatis praeberet Dominus, in qua olim veniet in regno suo. Quid ergo futurum putabimus, quando virtutes caelorum commouebuntur, caeli cum stridore praeteribunt elementa denique aestuantia liquescent: signum vero Filii hominis in caelo apparebit? Tunc certè plangent omnes tribus terrae. Quibus adde quae D. Paulus scribit: Patefiet Dominus IESVS de caelo cum angelis potentia sua, cum flammeo incendio, infligens vltionem ijs, qui Deum non nouerunt neq; auscultarunt Euangelio Domini nostri IESV CHRISTI: qui poenam pendent aeterni exitij praesente Domino & potente ipsius gloria, cum venerit vt glorificetur in sanctis suis, & admirandus fiat infidelibus omnibus, &c. Et haec quidem de persona iudicis, & eius ad iudicium aduentu dicta sufficiant.
