Faxit Deus Pater miserationum, ut horum semper memores, ita viuamus ut cum venerit, cum gaudio exultemus, neq; vlulemus & plangamus cum impijs, qui optabant pręde dolore, ut terra ipsis debiscat.
units.tr: But he adds something else as well, by which he declares his majesty and power more fully, saying: "Then he will sit on the throne of his glory." Scripture everywhere shows this throne among the clouds, in which he will come. It is not for us to inquire too curiously what it will be like. Let what the sacred letters hand down suffice for us, and let us not doubt that the Lord, who made Solomon's throne admired by the whole world and by all kings, will have a much more glorious throne. Strengthened by righteousness, virtue and clemency, it will be a wonder and a comfort to the elect, but it will strike terror into all the wicked, who will never be able to escape or overcome it. Indeed, whatever hangs over us from above out of the clouds is joined with a peculiar terror, such as lightning, thunder, thunderbolts, chasms, and whatever else is of this kind. How much more terrible, then, will the majesty of Christ be, shining above us in the clouds with divine splendour, to all those who are estranged from faith and accused by the testimony of their own conscience? Those three disciples, Peter, John and James, fell on their faces in fear and were almost lifeless, when the Lord gave them a taste of that majesty in which he will one day come in his kingdom. What then shall we think will happen when the powers of heaven are shaken, the heavens pass away with a roar, and the elements at last melt with heat, and the sign of the Son of man appears in heaven? Then indeed all the tribes of the earth will mourn. To these add what the apostle Paul writes: "The Lord Jesus will be revealed from heaven with his mighty angels, in flaming fire, taking vengeance on those who do not know God and do not obey the gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ. They shall pay the penalty of eternal destruction, in the presence of the Lord and the glory of his power, when he comes to be glorified in his saints and to be wondered at by all who believed not," and so on. Let these things suffice concerning the person of the judge and his coming to judgment. May God the Father of mercies grant that, always mindful of them, we so live that when he comes we may rejoice with gladness, and not howl and lament with the wicked, who in their grief over lost plunder wished that the earth would open and swallow them.

units.la: Porro videamus etiam, qui nam ad tribunal Christi citari & coram hoc iudice sisti debeant? Et cogentur coram eo (inquit) omnes gentes. Id fiet (vt supra docuit) angelorum ministerio, cum quibus se venturum dixit. Ait enim: Tunc emittet angelos suos cum tuba voce magna & suos electos coget a quatuor ventis ab extremo terrę vsque ad extremum cœli. Electorum meminit, non quod hi soli iudicandi sint (nam impios quoque citari debere, postea demonstrabitur) sed quia hęc in electorum consolationem dicebat, qui interdum persequutionibus dispersantur, ut impossibile videatur illos posse rursus in vnum cogi, hoc potentię suę & gloriae iudicium fore docet, quod etsi per totum mundum, imo vt quisquilię per aerem dispersi fuerint, facile tamen ipsi fore, vt suę tubę clangore per angelos ad ipsum colligantur. In praesenti vero omnes gentes nominat, sub quibus omnium seculorum & locorum homines comprehendit. Et cum eo consentit articulus Symboli Apostolici, in quo confitemur, IESVM CHRISTVM venturum ad iudicandum vivos & mortuos. Nam vivi hic dicuntur, quotquot sub Christi aduentum superstites erunt, mortui vero sunt omnes, qui ab exordio mundi vsque ad illum diem hac vita defuncti, rursus a mortuis excitabuntur, & hi simul omnes immutati & incorruptione donati, Christo obuiam rapientur, vt eius sistantur iudicio. Itaque omnes homines, quotquot sunt, fuerunt, & futuri sunt, ad Christi tribunal cogentur, vt non temere apud Germanos vulgari proverbio dicatur, neminem emansurum, qui non in nouissimo iudicio compareat. Quae ergo haec vacordia est, o homines Christiani, quae mentes nostras fascinat, vt quasi in terris istis permanentem ciuitatem habeamus, sortis nostrae futurae oblii, terrenis studijs nos totos addicamus?
units.tr: Let us see further who must be summoned to the tribunal of Christ and made to stand before this judge. "All nations," he says, "will be gathered before him." This will happen, as he taught above, through the ministry of angels, with whom he said he would come. For he says: "Then he will send out his angels with a loud trumpet, and they will gather his elect from the four winds, from one end of the earth to the other end of heaven." He mentions the elect, not because only they are to be judged (for that the wicked too must be summoned will be shown afterwards), but because he was saying this for the comfort of the elect, who are sometimes scattered by persecutions, so that it seems impossible for them to be gathered together again. He teaches that this will be a judgment of his power and glory: even if they have been scattered through the whole world, indeed like chaff through the air, it will nevertheless be easy for him to gather them to himself through the angels, at the sound of his trumpet. But here he names all nations, by which he embraces the men of every age and place. The article of the Apostles' Creed agrees with this, in which we confess that Jesus Christ will come to judge the living and the dead. For those are called living who will remain alive at Christ's coming; and all are dead who have departed this life from the beginning of the world until that day. They will be raised again from the dead, and all of them together, changed and endowed with incorruption, will be caught up to meet Christ, so that they may stand before his judgment. Thus all men, however many there are, have been, and will be, will be gathered to Christ's tribunal. So the common German proverb is not said without reason: that no one will be left who does not appear at the last judgment. What, then, is this heedlessness, O Christian people, which bewitches our minds, so that, as if we had a lasting city in this earthly life, forgetful of our future lot, we devote ourselves wholly to earthly pursuits?

units.la: Excitet autem nos communis consensus electorum & ferorum Dei, qui iam inde ab exordio mundi omnes testati sunt, venturum iudicem IESVM CHRISTVM, cui rationem omnium iniustę factorum & dictorum omnes homines reddituri sint. Nam vt Apostolus Iudas, Iacobi minoris frater, cognomento Thaddaeus scribit, de falsis fratribus & impijs fidei & Ecclesię prophanatoribus differens, inter alia dicit: Prophetauit autem etiam de istis septimus ab Adam Enoch. Ecce venit Dominus cum sanctis millibus suis, vt ferat iudicium aduersus omnes, & redarguat quicunque ex ipsis sunt impij, de factis omnibus quae impie patrarunt, deque omnibus duris quae loquuti fuerint aduersus ipsum peccatores impij. Quae prophetia tanto plus fidei & auctoritatis meretur, quod & vetustissima est, & quod eam Deus ipsius Enochi translatione confirmauit, & eo exemplo docuit, esse vitam aliam, in qua pijs sua praemia repositu sint, impios autem sua poena maneant, quas suis scelerib meruerunt. Et eandem fidem Iobi fuisse, qui & ipse non procul a Patriarcharum seculo abfuit, ex illius verbis patet, quibus seipsum inter infandos dolores & cruciatus atque animi tentationes grauissimas consolatus est, dicens: Noui quod vindex meus viuit, & nouissimo tempore adhibebit vim suam pulueri. Postquam vero circumdabor hac mea cute, spectabo Deum e carne mea: quem ego mihi contemplabor, & oculi mei videbunt, & non alius: quod vnicum est meum desiderium. Haec vero illum non solum propter se dixisse, sed etiam vicissim collocutores suos terreret, qui intempestiuis disputationibus ipsi moleistissimi erant, ex iis apparet quae subtexit: Tunc dicetis, Cur eum persequebamur, in quo fundamenta negotij salutis deprehendebantur? Timete igitur gladium vobis imminentem: quia ira iniquitates, iniquitas vltionem parit: quoniam intelligetis seu experiemini esse iudicem. Possent his addi innumera ex Prophetis, quibus doctrina haec tam confessa & indubitata fuit, vt hoc argumento populum in Babylone consolati sint, Deum, qui ex mortuis excitaturus est homines, ipsos velle & posse abductos in exilium reducere. Et Christus saepe alias huius doctrinae meminit, in primis autem memorabile est, quod apud Ioannem grauiter pronuntiat: Amen amen dico vobis, veniet hora, qua omnes qui in monumentis sunt, id est mortui, quorum corpora iam computruerunt, audient vocem Filii hominis, & qui audierint viuent: & prodibunt, qui bona fecerint in resurrectionem vitae: qui vero mala egerint in resurrectionem iudicij. Quo Paulus respiciens non veritus est dicere: Omnes sistemur ad tribunal Christi. Item alibi clarius: Omnes comparere oportet coram tribunali Christi, ut unusquisque reportet quae in corpore fecerit, vel bonum vel malum. Possent his testimonijs multa addi, quae nunc breuitatis causa omittimus. Nos autem his admoniti hoc quoque obseruemus, Deum omnium cordibus hanc notitiam ita inscripsisse, ut nulla gens tam barbara, nulla tam superstitiosa et abfurdissimis erroribus dementata fuerit, in qua non aliquis gustus futurae resurrectionis et nouissimi iudicij ex aliquibus indicijs deprehendi possit. Detestanda ergo et abominabilis est illusorum illorum impietas, qui hoc nouissimo seculo, quando quotidie fiunt, quae diem hunc praeforibus adesse testantur, illum tamen scurriliter negare et in dubium vocare audent. Nobis horum omnium vsus sit, ut nunquam non adnentus Dominici memores humiliemur sub eius potenti manu, et vigilemus omni tempore precantes, ut digni habeamur, qui effugiamus quae impijs parata sunt supplicia, et intrepida mente consistamus coram Filio hominis, Domino et redemptore nostro IESV CHRISTO, cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria et potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Let the common agreement of the elect and faithful servants of God rouse us, for from the beginning of the world they have all testified that the judge who is to come is Jesus Christ, to whom all men will render an account of all the unjust things they have done and said. For the apostle Jude, brother of James the Less, surnamed Thaddaeus, writes, speaking of false brothers and impious profaners of the faith and Church, and among other things he says: "Enoch, the seventh from Adam, prophesied of these also: Behold, the Lord comes with his holy thousands, to execute judgment against all, and to convict all the ungodly of all their ungodly deeds which they have committed in ungodliness, and of all the harsh words which ungodly sinners have spoken against him." This prophecy deserves all the more faith and authority because it is most ancient, and because God confirmed it by the translation of Enoch himself, and by that example taught that there is another life, in which the rewards of the godly are laid up, while the wicked remain under the punishment they have earned by their crimes. That Job held the same faith, and he too was not far removed from the age of the patriarchs, is clear from his words, by which he comforted himself amid unspeakable pains, torments and the most grievous trials of mind: "I know that my Redeemer lives, and at the last he will bring his power to the dust. And after my skin has been thus destroyed, I shall see God in my flesh; I shall behold him for myself, and my eyes shall see him, and not another. This is my one desire." That he said these things not only for his own sake, but also to terrify in turn his interlocutors, who were very troublesome to him with their unseasonable disputes, appears from what he adds: "Then you will say, Why did we persecute him, in whom the foundations of the matter of salvation were found? Therefore fear the sword hanging over you, for wrath brings iniquities, and iniquity brings vengeance; for you will know, or experience, that there is a judge." Countless testimonies from the Prophets could be added, in which this doctrine was so acknowledged and undoubted that they comforted the people in Babylon with this argument: that God, who is about to raise men from the dead, wills and is able to bring back those who have been carried into exile. And Christ often mentions this doctrine elsewhere, but especially memorable is what he solemnly pronounces in John: "Verily, verily, I say to you, the hour is coming when all who are in the tombs, that is, the dead whose bodies have already decayed, will hear the voice of the Son of man, and those who hear will live; and those who have done good will come forth to the resurrection of life, but those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment." Looking to this, Paul did not hesitate to say: "We must all be presented before the tribunal of Christ." Likewise elsewhere, more plainly: "All must appear before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive what he has done in the body, whether good or evil." Many more testimonies could be added to these, which for the sake of brevity we now omit. But, admonished by these, let us also observe this: God has so inscribed this knowledge on the hearts of all that no nation is so barbarous, and none so superstitious and maddened by the most absurd errors, in which some trace of the future resurrection and the last judgment cannot be discerned from certain signs. Detestable, therefore, and abominable is the impiety of those mockers who, in this last age, when things are happening every day which testify that this day is at the door, nevertheless dare to scoff at it, deny it, and call it into doubt. Let us use all these things so that we may never fail to remember the Lord's coming, and may be humbled under his mighty hand, and keep watch at all times, praying that we may be counted worthy to escape the punishments prepared for the wicked, and may stand with fearless mind before the Son of man, our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCXC.
units.tr: HOMILY 290.

units.la: Et seperabit iudex gentes, alteros ab alteris, vt pastor separat oues ab hoedis. Et statuet oues quidem ad dexteram suam, hoedos autem ad sinistram. Tunc dicet Rex iis qui ad dexteram ipsius erunt: Venite benedicti Patris mei, possidete regnum paratum vobis ab initio mundi. Esurivi enim et dedistis mihi vt vescerer: sitiui et dedistis mihi potum: hospes eram, et collegistis me: nudus, et amicuistis me: aegrotaui et visitastis me: in carcere eram, et venistis ad me. Tunc respondebunt ei iusti dicentes: Domine, quando te vidimus esurientem, et aluimus? aut sitientem et dedimus tibi potum? Quando autem te vidimus hospitem, et collegimus te? aut nudum et amiciuimus? Aut quando te vidimus aegrotum, aut in carcere, et venimus ad te? Et respondens rex dicet eis: Amen dico vobis, quatenus id fecistis vni ex istis fratribus meis minimis, mihi fecistis.
units.tr: "And he shall separate them one from another, as a shepherd divideth his sheep from the goats: And he shall set the sheep on his right hand, but the goats on the left. Then shall the King say unto them on his right hand, Come, ye blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world: For I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat: I was thirsty, and ye gave me drink: I was a stranger, and ye took me in: Naked, and ye clothed me: I was sick, and ye visited me: I was in prison, and ye came unto me. Then shall the righteous answer him, saying, Lord, when saw we thee an hungred, and fed thee? or thirsty, and gave thee drink? When saw we thee a stranger, and took thee in? or naked, and clothed thee? Or when saw we thee sick, or in prison, and came unto thee? And the King shall answer and say unto them, Verily I say unto you, Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me."

units.la: Sapientissimus ille regum Solomon gnauiter monet melius esse adire domum luctus funebris, quam domum conuiuij. Nam illic (ait) cernitur finis omnium hominum, et viuens id reponit in corde suo. Et rursum: Sapientium cor in domo luctus versatur, et cor stultorum in domo laetitiae. Quibus consentit alter ille sapiens Sirachi filius, dicens: In omnibus factis tuis memento extremorum, et in aeternum non peccabis. Qui enim ferio et assidue cogitat, mortem esse viam omnis terrae, per quam omnibus necessario ex hoc mundo exeundum est, procul dubio animum a terrenis studijs ad caelestium bonorum et vitae aeternae consideratione reuocabit, nec locum facile dabit vitiorum illecebris, quibus alij vulgo inseccantur. At si tantum potest apud homines cordatos assidua mortis recordatio, quanto plus efficaciae habebit nouissimi aduentus Christi memoria, qui olim sub finem seculi in nubibus caeli apparebit iudex vniuersi mundi, vt singulis prout in corpore vixerunt, retribuat. Enimuero fieri non potest, vt huius seculi studijs se irretiri sinat qui totam mundi machinam olim cum elementis omnibus vno incendio conflagraturam esse meminit, et tunc coram Dei Filio nihil esse, quod nos vel excusat, vel tueatur quam fides vera et animus quoad vitam piè peractam bene sibi conscius. Quapropter Dominus noster IESVS CHRISTVS, postquam discipulos suos multis ad vigilantiam et ardens salutis studium adhortatus est, de nouissimo etiam suo aduentu disserit, et vt ad hunc se praeparare debeant omnes homines docet. Et vt efficacius moueantur omnium mentes, postremi illius et vniuersalis iudicij typum nobis, seu in eeu in tabula proponit: In quo nuper vidimus, quis tunc iudex ille vniuersalis futurus, & quanta cum gloria & potentia venturus sit: quod item omnes homines, quotquot vnquam fuerunt, & su-perstites adhuc illo die erunt, ad eius tribunal sisti oporteat. Sequitur in praesenti huius iudicij forma atq; processus, cuius prima parte de electis siue germanis Dei cultoribus agitur, quos Dominus ad vitae aeternae consortium & haereditatem suscipiet: altera de reprobis, qui ad aeternos in ferorum cruciatus damnabuntur.
units.tr: That most wise king Solomon earnestly warns that it is better to go to the house of mourning than to the house of feasting: "for there," he says, "is the end of all men, and the living will lay it to his heart." And again: "The heart of the wise is in the house of mourning, but the heart of fools is in the house of mirth." The other wise man, the son of Sirach, agrees with him, saying: "In all your works remember the last things, and you will never sin." Surely whoever thinks often and diligently that death is the way of all the earth, by which everyone must necessarily leave this world, will without doubt turn his mind from earthly pursuits to the contemplation of heavenly goods and eternal life, and will not readily give place to the allurements of vices, by which others are commonly carried away. But if the frequent remembrance of death has so much power among sensible men, how much more effect will the memory of the last coming of Christ have, who at the end of the age will appear in the clouds of heaven as judge of the whole world, to render to each one according to what he did in the body. Indeed, it is impossible that he who remembers that the whole machinery of the world, with all its elements, will one day be consumed in a single fire, should allow himself to be entangled in the pursuits of this age; and that before the Son of God nothing will excuse or protect us except true faith and a conscience that is well aware of a life piously lived. Therefore our Lord Jesus Christ, having exhorted his disciples to watchfulness and to an ardent zeal for salvation, speaks also of his last coming, and teaches that all men ought to prepare themselves for it. And so that the minds of all may be moved more effectively, he sets before us, as it were in a picture, the image of that final and universal judgment: in it we have recently seen what kind of judge that universal judge will be, and with how great glory and power he will come, and that all men, as many as have ever lived and who are still alive on that day, must be brought before his tribunal. There follows in the present passage the form and course of this judgment, the first part of which concerns the elect, that is, the true worshippers of God, whom the Lord will receive into the fellowship and inheritance of eternal life; the second concerns the reprobate, who will be condemned to eternal torments.

units.la: Et principio quidem, cum nuper dixisset, omnes gentes siue homines per angelos sanctos, a qua tuor ventis, & extremis cardinibus mundi cogi oportere, ut ab ipso iudicentur, nunc quid hic co actus in vnum, ipse primum fasturus sit, docet. Et seperabit (inquit) omnes gentes alteros ab altes, ut pastor seperat oves ab haedis. Id vero opponitur confusioni, quae in hoc mundo est, & perpetuo durabit vsq; ad finem seculi. Religiones quidem diuersae sunt (ut iam de aliis vitae generibus & studijs nihil dicatur) & infectas innumeras fere mundus totus distractus est. Sunt Euangelici hypocritae, qui vno quidem Christo gloriantur, & se eius merito persidem iustificatos esse pleno ore iactant: sed quam ore profitentur fidem, factis negant. Sunt Papistae siue Pontificij Romanenses, qui in sectas sacrificorum & monachorum complures scissi sunt, nec adhuc illorum finis est, quin novae indies veteribus accedant. Sunt Canonici regulares & irregulares: Sunt Franciscani & inter hos Minores, Lignipedes, Obseruantes item, quos aliqui per αιλοφασιν sic dictos putant, quod absque omni obseruatione regularum & legum, quas Christus & Apostoli tradiderunt, viuant. Sunt Dominicani, Iacobitae, Augustiniani, Carmelitae, Carthusiani, Bernhardini, Fratres Mariae, Iesuitae, Cappucini, & alij quibus omnibus enumerandis vix dies sufficerit. Et hi omnes etsi regulis & legibus, ritibus item, statutis & vestitu quoq; differant, omnes tamen in eo conueniunt, quod fere operum suorum meritis confidunt, & singuli suum ordinem siue sectam aliis omnibus praestare, seq; Deo cultum magis gratum & acceptum exhibere, sibi persuaserunt. Sunt praeterea a nominis Christiani prorsus alieni, Turcae & Iudaei, qui se Christianos omnibus meliores esse gloriantur. Est item infinitus impiorum numerus, quos Atheistas non immerito quidam dicunt, qui cum neq; Deum neq; coelos aut inferos esse credant, tamen pro damnatis haberi nolunt. In tanta ergo confusione hominum & opinionum alij incerti rerum, quo se vertant nesciunt, & vel omnem religionem negant, vel ut omnibus se amicos & aequos praebeant, vnumquemq; in quauis religione seruari posse sentiunt, modo animi intentio bona sit.
units.tr: And first, since he had just said that all nations or men must be gathered by the holy angels from the four winds and the farthest corners of the world, so that they may be judged by him, now he teaches what he himself will first do when they have been gathered together. "And he will separate," he says, "all nations one from another, as a shepherd separates sheep from goats." This is set against the confusion that exists in this world and will last continually until the end of the age. There are indeed diverse religions (not to mention other ways of life and pursuits) and the whole world is torn apart by countless factions. There are evangelical hypocrites, who boast of Christ alone and loudly proclaim that they are justified by his merit through faith; but what they profess with their mouths, they deny by their deeds. There are the Papists, or Roman Pontifical men, who are split into many sects of priests and monks, nor is there any end to this, but new ones daily join the old. There are regular and irregular canons; there are Franciscans, and among them the Minorites, the Barefoot Friars, likewise the Observants, whom some think are called by a Greek-derived name meaning they live without any observance of the rules and laws that Christ and the apostles handed down. There are Dominicans, Jacobites, Augustinians, Carmelites, Carthusians, Bernardines, Brothers of Mary, Jesuits, Capuchins, and others, so many that there would hardly be enough days to list them all. And although all these differ in their rules and laws, and likewise in rites, statutes and dress, yet they all agree in this: they largely trust in the merits of their works, and each one has persuaded himself that his own order or sect surpasses all the others and offers a worship more pleasing and acceptable to God. Moreover, there are the Turks and Jews, who are completely alien to the Christian name, and who boast that they are better than all Christians. There is also an endless number of the impious, whom some not without reason call Atheists, who, although they believe that there is neither God nor heaven nor hell, nevertheless do not want to be regarded as condemned. In such great confusion of men and opinions, others, uncertain about things, do not know where to turn; and either they deny all religion, or, so that they may show themselves friendly and fair to everyone, they feel that each man can be kept safe in any religion, provided only that his intention of mind is good.

units.la: Sed in illo die confusio ista tolletur, & seperatio fiet, cuius author erit ipse Christus, Dei Filius & iudex vniuersalis, qui cum renes & corda scrutetur, nullo ceremoniarum splendore, nullo professionis externae fuco fallitur. Separabit autem hos omnes alios ab alijs, ut pastor oues ab haedis seperare solet. Recte autem se pastori confert, quia quantisper tempus gratiae, & huius praesentis vitae curriculum durat, pastor ille Israelis est, de quo olim Prophetae vaticinati sunt. Et talem seipsum describit in Euangelio, simulq; docet, quid ouibus suis conferat, & quibus non-nisi illae ab haedis dignoscantur. Ego (inquit) sum pastor ille bonus, qui agnosco oues meas, & agnoscor a meis: & animam meam depono pro ouibus. Ego item sum ostium: per me si quis introierit, seruabitur: & ingredietur & egredietur, & pascua inueniet. Et ego vitam aeternam do ouibus. Qui non ingreditur per ostium, fur est & latro. Oues item suas esse ait, qui vocem suam audiant & sequantur, alieni vero vocem non agnoscant. Ex quibus colligi potest, haedos & hircos esse, qui ouium quidem similes videri volunt, fidelibus caetibus sese adiciunt, & fideles Christi cultores Dei amantes se esse profitentur, interim vero inter pascua Ecclesiae non manent, sed vagi, petulantes & lasciui IESVM CHRISTVM non pro vnico Pastore agnoscunt, neq; per ostium illud vnicum ingrediuntur, sed per alias vias atq; media irrepere studeant: adhaec non sequuntur Christum, non ipsi soli adhaerent, neq; ei obediunt, sed sui cerebri placita, & proprij animi desideria illius praeceptis praeferunt. Hi omnes siue Christiani dicantur, siue Euangelici, siue Romanenses catholici, siue Iudaei siue Turcae, siue rasi & vnkti, siue cucullati, siue mitrates bicornes sint, haedi atq; hirci sint, neq; ex Christi grege censeri debent. Possunt quidem inuitis ouibus sese insinuare: & tanta est illorum sape potentia, ut absq; periculo ne reprehendi quidem vel vnico verbulo argui, nedum a caula Ecclesiæ arceri possint. Sed quando pastor ille fortis veniet, illos omnes non arguet modo, verumetiam separabit, vt toti mundo constet, qui nam oues, qui hirci aut hædi sint. Oues enim, id est, veros fideles & Christianos ad dexteram, hædos ad sinistram statuet. Per dexteram enim locus beatæ immortalitatis, per sinistram locus suppli-cij denotatur, quo colligentur omnes hypocritæ cum ijs qui posuerunt terrorem suum in terra viuentium.
units.tr: But on that day this confusion will be removed, and a separation will be made, whose author will be Christ himself, the Son of God and universal judge, who, since he searches the reins and hearts, is not deceived by any splendour of ceremonies or by any outward disguise of profession. He will separate all these people one from another, as a shepherd is accustomed to separate sheep from goats. And the comparison with a shepherd is apt, because as long as the time of grace and the course of this present life lasts, he is that shepherd of Israel of whom the prophets once prophesied. And he describes himself thus in the Gospel, and at the same time teaches what he gives to his sheep, and by which alone they are distinguished from the goats. "I," he says, "am that good shepherd, who knows my sheep, and am known by mine, and I lay down my life for the sheep. I am also the door: if anyone enters through me, he will be saved, and will go in and out, and will find pasture. And I give eternal life to the sheep. He who does not enter by the door is a thief and a robber." He also says that those are his sheep who hear his voice and follow it, while strangers do not recognise his voice. From these words it can be gathered that there are goats and he-goats, who wish to seem like sheep, join themselves to the faithful flocks, and profess that they are faithful worshippers of Christ and lovers of God; yet meanwhile they do not remain within the pastures of the Church, but wander about, wanton and lascivious, and do not acknowledge Jesus Christ as the only Shepherd, nor enter through that single door, but strive to creep in by other ways and means; moreover, they do not follow Christ, do not cling to him alone, nor obey him, but prefer the fancies of their own brain and the desires of their own mind to his precepts. All these, whether they are called Christians, or evangelicals, or Roman Catholics, whether Jews or Turks, whether shaven and anointed, or hooded, or wearing two-horned mitres, are goats and he-goats, and ought not to be counted in the flock of Christ. Indeed they can insinuate themselves into the sheepfold against the wishes of the sheep, and their power is often so great that they can not only be unreproved, not even be argued against by a single word without danger, but still less be kept away from the fold of the Church. But when that strong shepherd comes, he will not only rebuke all of them but will also separate them, so that it may be plain to the whole world who are the sheep and who the goats or kids. For he will set the sheep, that is, the true faithful and Christians, on the right hand, and the kids on the left. For the right hand denotes the place of blessed immortality, and the left the place of punishment, to which all hypocrites will be gathered together with those who have set their terror in the land of the living.

units.la: Idcirco turpis & exitialis est error eorum omnium, qui vnumquemque in sua religione, vel potius superstitione seruari sentiunt. Etenim vt vnica sola est veritas: ita fides quoque vera & religio est vnica. Vidit hoc olim Lactantius, qui religionem a vinculo pietatis sic dictam testatur, quod per hanc nos Deus sibi religauerit & obstrinxerit. Atqui vnus Christus est, per quem ad Patrem vemitur, & in quo placuit Patri omnem plenitudinem inhabitare, & per eum sibi reconciliare omnia tum quæ in cœlis tum quæ in terra sunt. Non alia ergo religio vera est, quam quæ fide in Christum constat: falsæ sunt autem & superstitiones noxiæ sunt, quæ extra Christum alibi salutem quærere docent. Separatione ergo opus est ex mundo, si religiosi & veri Dei cultores esse velimus. Hanc olim Deus instituerat, quando exeunte a facie sua Caino, Sethum huic substituit, ex quo filiorum Dei linea & genus deduceretur. Sed cum postea filij Dei caeco amore & illecebris mundi fascinati, cum filiabus hominum & Caini posteris rursus commiscerentur, Nephilim prodierunt, propter quos genus humanum horrendo Diluuij supplicio deletum est: & rursus Abrahamum e Chaldaea euocatum sibi delegit Deus, ex quo nouis filiorum suorum soboles nasceretur, & a quo veri omnium seculorum credentes dicerentur Abrahami filij, quibus vbiq; præcipitur, vt ex Babylone, id est, ex mundo exeant, & separentur a generatione prava filiorum huius seculi, neq; cum eorum studijs & operibus communicent. At ea est natura humanæ peruersitas, vt multi dignitatis suæ immemores ad infelix mundi consortium redeant, & cum illo polluantur. Ideo quotidiana pœnitentia opus est, & vt subinde pedes abluamus, Dominus iubet. Quod cum non omnes faciant, multi vero in vitijs communibus pergant, Iudex ille vniuersæ terræ, quem illi dum tempus gratiæ illius fulsit, non laeruit pastorem suum agnoscere & sequi, in magno illo die separationem faciet, in qua hædos ilos petulcos statuet ad sinistram, vt postea ad exitium sempiternum damnentur. Et de hac separatione tunc facta frequenter admonemur in Euangelio, nepij & simplices exemplo mundi & tenebris illa confusione, quæ passim cernitur inter homines, offendantur. Huc pertinent parabolæ de zizaniis, quæ cum bono femine in agro Domini succrescunt, tempore messis autem colliguntur & exuruntur. Item de sagena illa quæ cum bonis piscibus putres quoq; trahit, qui postquam sagena in litus subtracta fuerit, separantur a bonis & abiiciuntur. Eodem facit parabola de nuptijs, ad quas quidam abiq; veste nuptiali accessit, & cum alijs accubuit: sed ab hero deprehensus, ignominiose eiectus est in tenebras externas, vbi est ploratus & stridor dentium. Horum ergo diligenter meminerint, qui exemplo mundi teterrima vitia & scelera excusant, & sibi necessario publicis moribus viuendum esse putant. Sed ratum erit semper quod hic dicitur. Quicunq; nolunt relictis mundi studijs separari ab hircis fœtidis & contumacibus, olim velint nolint separabuntur, & cum diabolo cui seruierunt, relegabuntur in ignem illum inextinguibilem.
units.tr: Therefore the error of all those who think that each man is kept safe in his own religion, or rather superstition, is shameful and deadly. For just as there is only one truth, so true faith and religion are also one. Lactantius saw this long ago. He testifies that religion is so called from the bond of piety, because through it God has bound and obliged us to himself. Yet there is one Christ, through whom we come to the Father, and in whom it pleased the Father that all fullness should dwell, and through whom he has reconciled all things to himself, both those in heaven and those on earth. Therefore no religion is true except that which rests on faith in Christ. False superstitions are harmful, since they teach that salvation is to be sought elsewhere, apart from Christ. Separation from the world is therefore necessary if we wish to be religious and true worshippers of God. God instituted this long ago, when, after Cain had gone out from his face, he set Seth in his place, from whom the line and race of the sons of God would be derived. But when afterwards the sons of God, bewitched by blind love and the allurements of the world, again mingled with the daughters of men and the posterity of Cain, the Nephilim were produced, on account of whom the human race was destroyed by the dreadful punishment of the Flood. And again God chose for himself Abraham, called out of Chaldea, from whom a new offspring of his sons would be born, and from whom all true believers of every age would be called the sons of Abraham. To them it is everywhere commanded that they go out of Babylon, that is, out of the world, and separate themselves from the perverse generation of the sons of this age, and not share in their pursuits and works. But such is the perversity of human nature that many, forgetful of their dignity, return to the unhappy fellowship of the world and are polluted by it. Therefore daily repentance is necessary, and the Lord bids us wash our feet from time to time. Since not everyone does this, and many persist in common vices, that Judge of the whole earth, whom they did not blush to acknowledge and follow while the time of his grace shone, will make a separation on that great day. In it he will set those wanton goats on the left, so that afterwards they may be condemned to everlasting destruction. We are often reminded of this separation, which will then be made, in the Gospel, lest the simple and unlearned be offended by the example of the world and by that confusion of darkness which is seen everywhere among men. To this belong the parables of the tares, which grow up with the good seed in the Lord's field but are gathered and burned at harvest time. Likewise the parable of the net, which drew in rotten fish along with good ones; after the net has been dragged to the shore, these are separated from the good and thrown away. The parable of the wedding makes the same point, where a certain man came without a wedding garment and reclined with the others; but he was caught by the host, ignominiously cast out into outer darkness, where there is weeping and gnashing of teeth. Let those therefore diligently remember this who excuse the foulest vices and crimes by the example of the world, and think they must necessarily live by public customs. But what is said here will always stand. Those who, having left the pursuits of the world, do not wish to be separated from the stinking and obstinate goats, will, whether they will or not, be separated at last. Together with the devil whom they served, they will be consigned to that unquenchable fire.

units.la: At quærat hic aliquis, Quo iure secundum Euangelij sui doctrinam eos quoq; damnaturus sit Christus, quibus illud nunquam est prædicatum? Sed his Apostolus ad Romanos scribens respondet: Cum gentes, quæ legem non habent, natura quæ legis sunt faciant, isti legem non habentes sibi ipsis sunt lex: Vt qui ostendant opus legis scriptum in cordibus suis, vna testimonium reddente ipsorum conscientia, & cogitationibus sese mutuo accusantibus, aut etiam excusantibus, in die quo iudicabit Dominus de occultis hominum ex Euangelio meo per IESVM CHRISTVM. Fatetur Paulus, gentibus quidem non datam legem scriptam, vt Iudæis: at simul probat, illos praeterea no exleges esse prorsus, cum naturales notitias cordibus inscriptas habeant, quæ honesta iubent, turpia prohibent: quibus notitijs corda sic illustrantur, vt intra conscientias suas conuincantur, si quid inhonestum patrarunt: & tam efficax esse conscientiæ testimonium, vt in eum vsq; diem vigeat, & in nouissimo iudicio illis condemnandis sufficiat. Eadem autem ratio est Euangelij, cuius doctrina de naturalibus illis notitijs conuenit. Ergo etsi non omnibus illud prædicetur, habent tamen
units.tr: But someone may ask here: by what right will Christ also condemn those to whom that doctrine of his gospel was never preached? The Apostle, writing to the Romans, answers this: "When the Gentiles, who have no law, do by nature the things of the law, these, having no law, are a law to themselves; they show the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience bearing witness, and their thoughts accusing or else excusing one another, in the day when the Lord will judge the hidden things of men according to my gospel through Jesus Christ." Paul confesses that the written law was not given to the Gentiles as it was to the Jews. But at the same time he proves that they are by no means altogether lawless, since they have natural notions inscribed on their hearts, which command what is honourable and forbid what is shameful. By these notions their hearts are so enlightened that they are convicted within their consciences if they have committed anything dishonourable. And the testimony of conscience is so effective that it remains in force until that day and suffices to condemn them in the final judgment. The reasoning of the gospel is the same, and its doctrine agrees with those natural notions. Therefore, even if it is not preached to all, they nevertheless have

units.la: {y} Lib.4.cap.8. Ioan.14. Col.1. tamen hi quoq; qui non audiuerunt, quo intra corda sua continentur, neq; erit aliquid quod illos in die iudicij excuset. Vt ergo hunc locum concludamus, necesse est, fide vera conuertantur ad Christum, qui solus vestis illa nuptialis est, & hunc induant, qui in vltimo illo iudicij die seruare volunt.
units.tr: {y} Lib.4.cap.8. Ioan.14. Col.1. these notions within their hearts, even those who have not heard, and there will be nothing which can excuse them on the day of judgment. Therefore, to conclude this point, it is necessary that they be converted by true faith to Christ, who alone is that wedding garment, and that those who wish to be preserved on that last day of judgment put him on.

units.la: Sequitur sententia finalis, quaidem docetur & ostenditur simul euidenter, qui sint vere credentes, quos pro suis Dominus agnoscet & saluos pronunciabit. Priusquam vero illam audiamus, obseruatu dignum est discrimen, quo iudicium illud differt a quotidianis aut humanis, quae in hoc seculo exercentur. In his sententiam praecedit accusatio, sistuntur item testes, quorum testimonijs capita accusationis confirmentur: adhaec reis attribuuntur aduocati siue patroni, qui eos excusent vel defendant. At in praesenti nihil horum auditur. Etenim (vt modo diximus) propria conscientia accusabit & excusabit omnes. Neque opus erit testibus apud iudicem Christum, quem nihil latet, & qui sua praesentia tam electos confirmabit, quam improbos suae impietatis conuictos damnabit. Etenim ex eius conspectu consolationem percipient illi, quando videbunt illum cuius cicatrices & vibices salutis certos facient omnes, qui ipsi crediderunt: exitio autem dignos esse docebunt eos, qui ipsum non receperunt, in quo vno salus est. His praemissis, audiamus nunc quid suis dicturus sit.
units.tr: The final sentence follows, which is taught and at the same time clearly shown: who are the true believers, whom the Lord will acknowledge as his own and pronounce saved. Before we hear it, it is worth noting the difference by which that judgment differs from the ordinary human judgments which are carried out in this age. In those, the sentence is preceded by an accusation; witnesses are likewise brought forward, by whose testimony the heads of the accusation are confirmed; moreover, advocates or patrons are assigned to the accused, to excuse or defend them. But in the present case none of these is heard. For (as we have just said) each one's own conscience will accuse and excuse all. Nor will there be any need of witnesses before the judge Christ, from whom nothing is hidden, and who by his presence will confirm the elect just as he will condemn the wicked, convicted of their impiety. For the elect will receive consolation from his sight, when they see him whose scars and wounds will assure all who believed in him of salvation. But he will show that those who did not receive him, in whom alone is salvation, are worthy of destruction. With these things premised, let us now hear what he is about to say to his own.

units.la: Tunc dicet Rex ijs, qui ad dexteram ipsius steterunt, &c. Regem se vocat nunc, qui prius se Filium hominis dixerat, vt doceat incarnationem & exinanitionem, quae in assumpta carne fa- & fuit, diuinitati & maiestati suae nihil derogaturam, quo minus tunc quoq; , quando in hominis forma & vt verus homo veniet, fit Rex ille gloriae & iudex vniuersae terrae. Quid vero dicet suis? Venite benedicti Patris mei, & possidete regnum vobis paratum a iactis fundamentis mundi. Est haec irreuocabilis & plena consolationis sententia Filij Dei, cuius singula verba probe considerari debent.
units.tr: Then the King will say to those who stood at his right hand, etc. He now calls himself King, who had earlier called himself the Son of Man, to teach that the incarnation and emptying, which took place in the assumed flesh, will detract nothing from his divinity and majesty; so that, when he comes in the form of a man and as true man, he will then also be that King of glory and judge of the whole earth. What then will he say to his own? Come, blessed of my Father, and possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. This is an irrevocable sentence of the Son of God, full of consolation, and each of its words ought to be carefully considered.

units.la: Primum, Venite inquit: & sic dicendo vocat eos ex mundo & corruptibili conditione, cui prius obnoxij fuerunt, & simul absoluit eos ab omni peccato, a morte, inferis & diabolo. Nam ad se venire iubet secundum promissionem, quae saepius in Euangelio repetitur: Volo vbi ego sum, illic sit etiam minister meus: Vado vobis paraturus locum: & cum profectus fuero & paraueri vobis locum, rursus veniam & assumam vos ad meipsum, vt vbi ego sum, & vos sitis. Vbi simul confutantur fanatici, qui vt omnipraesentiam hominis Christi, quoad corpus assumptum asserant, & confirment, in altero seculo locum aliquem fore negant: & nos accusant, si cum Christo idem sentiamus & loquamur. At ipsi quando corpus Christi in certo loco esse negant, corporis veritatem negant & abolent. Tolle loca corporibus (inquit Augustinus) non erit vbi sint, & proinde non sunt.
units.tr: First, he says, Come; and in saying this he calls them out of the world and their corruptible condition, to which they were previously subject, and at the same time absolves them from all sin, death, hell and the devil. For he bids them come to him, according to the promise which is repeated often in the Gospel: "Where I am, there my minister will be also"; "I go to prepare a place for you; and when I have gone and prepared a place for you, I will come again and take you to myself, that where I am, you may be also." Here the fanatics are at the same time refuted. In order to assert and confirm the omnipresence of the man Christ as regards his assumed body, they deny that there will be any place in the other age, and they accuse us if we think and speak the same as Christ. But when they deny that the body of Christ is in a certain place, they deny and abolish the truth of the body. "Take away places from bodies," says Augustine, "and there will be no place where they are, and therefore they are not."

units.la: Deinde quos vocet, diserte exprimit, & quasi definit: Nimirum benedictos Patris. Ita vero propriam salutis & beatitudinis nostrae causam ceu digito ostendit. In Adamo enim omnes male dicti sumus & morti obnoxij, quae per peccatum cum satellitio suo, id est, agmine malorum omnium in mundum ingressa, miseros & calamitosos fecit. Itaq; benedictione noua nobis opus est: quae non aliunde quam ex Deo sperari poterat, cum propter hominem tota creatura maledictioni & corruptioni esset subiecta. Quod enim de terra dixit Deus, primo parenti, Maledicta est terra propter te & c. idipsum de alijs quoq; elementis intelligi debere ex eo patet, quod quae in vsum hominis creata erant, nunc nobis exitio & iudiciorum Dei instrumenta sunt, si hic nos punire velit. Benedicit autem hic nobis in Filio suo IESV CHRISTO. Hic enim est promissum illud semen mulieris quod caput serpentis, qui maledictionis author fuerat, contriuit: Idem semen illud Abrahami est, de quo dictum: In semine tuo benedicentur omnes gentes terrae. De eodem Paulus scripsit: Benedictus Deus & pater Domini nostri IESV CHRISTI, qui benedixit nobis omni benedictione spiritali in caelis, in Christo. Itaq; benedictio nobis obtigit non per legem aut opera legis, quae potius ma ledictione, quam ex Adamo haustimus aggrauat, cum nemo illi possit satisfacere. Quod si lex Mosis non potest benedictionem parere, multo minus lex Mahumetis aut Papae, qui differte a Christo nos reuocant ad nostra opera, quae cum optima sint, imperfecta & mutila sunt. At CHRISTI IESV participes sumus per solam fidem, quam eum apprehendimus, & eidem inferimur. Idei Baptista graviter ait: Qui credit in Filium habet vitam aeternam: Qui autem non obtemperat Filio, non videbit vitam: sed ira Dei manet super eum. Hic ergo fundatur articulus praecipuus Christianae religionis, quem Apostoli tanto opere inculcarunt: In sola redemptione, quae per Christum fit, et nos iustificari & servari ex sola fide, absque operibus legis, ex mera gratia.
units.tr: Next, he clearly states, and as it were defines, whom he means: namely, the blessed of the Father. In this way he points, as if with a finger, to the proper cause of our salvation and blessedness. For in Adam we were all cursed and made liable to death, which entered the world through sin together with its attendant band, that is, a host of every evil, and made us wretched and miserable. We therefore need a new blessing, which could be hoped for from no source but God, since the whole creation was subjected to curse and corruption on account of man. That what God said of the earth to the first parent, "Cursed is the earth because of you," etc., must also be understood of the other elements, is clear from the fact that the things created for man's use are now instruments of our ruin and of God's judgments, if he wishes to punish us here. But he blesses us here in his Son, Jesus Christ. For this is that promised seed of the woman who crushed the head of the serpent, the author of the curse. It is the same seed of Abraham of whom it was said: "In your seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed." Paul wrote of the same: "Blessed be God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places, in Christ." The blessing therefore came to us not through the law or the works of the law, which rather weigh us down with the curse we drew from Adam, since no one can satisfy it. If the law of Moses cannot bring forth blessing, much less can the law of Mahomet or of the Pope, which call us away from Christ to our own works; and these, however excellent they may be, are imperfect and incomplete. But we become partakers of Jesus Christ through faith alone, by which we lay hold of him and are engrafted into him. John the Baptist likewise says gravely: "He who believes in the Son has eternal life; but he who does not obey the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him." Here is founded the chief article of the Christian religion, which the apostles so earnestly inculcated: that we are justified and saved through the redemption which is accomplished by Christ, by faith alone, without the works of the law, by mere grace.

units.la: Id vero Dominus in praesenti quoque evidenter declarat & confirmat, quando ad quid aut in quem finem benedicti Patris vocentur. Dicit enim, Possidete regnum paratum vobis a iactis fundamentis mundi. In Graeco ponitur verbum κληρονομήσατε, quod non simpliciter possidere, sed hereditario iure aliquid obtinere significat. Hereditatis vox meritum omne excludit. Etenim ut infans heres nascitur, priusquam aliquid meritus est: ita nos Dei heredes sumus, eo quod nos pro talibus elegit Deus, priusquam aliquid boni aut mali fecimus, ut Paulus Iacobi & Esau exemplo docet. Deinde regnum paratum illis dicit a iactis fundamentis mundi. Unde sequitur paratum fuisse priusquam essemus, nec opus esse, ut ipsi hoc paremus aut acquiramus nostris operibus sive meritis. Adde, quod Deus qui praeuidit, nos propria culpa indignos fore regno illo, qui omnis beatitudinis colophon est, ab aeterno quoque Filium suum (Petro teste) praedestinavit, qui nos Patri reconciliaret & regno Dei dignos atque idoneos faceret. Ergo rursus cadit omne operum nostrorum meritum & dignitas.
units.tr: The Lord also clearly declares and confirms this at present, when he states for what purpose, or to what end, the blessed of the Father are called. For he says: "Inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world" [κληρονομήσατε]. In the Greek the verb is κληρονομήσατε, which signifies not simply to possess, but to obtain something by hereditary right. The word "inheritance" excludes all merit. For just as an infant is born an heir before it has done anything meritorious, so we are heirs of God because God has chosen us for such a state before we have done anything good or bad, as Paul teaches by the example of Jacob and Esau. Then he says the kingdom was prepared for them from the foundation of the world. It follows that it was prepared before we existed, and that there is no need for us to prepare or acquire it by our works or merits. Add that God, who foresaw that we would be unworthy of that kingdom through our own fault, which is the crown of all blessedness, also predestined from eternity his Son (as Peter testifies) to reconcile us to the Father and to make us worthy and fit for the kingdom of God. Therefore again all merit and worth of our works falls away.

units.la: Quia autem fides interna animi in IESVM CHRISTVM fiducia est, quae tota spiritu constat, neque oculis cernitur, aut ullo sensu corporeo apprehenditur: utpote spiritus sancti donum, adhaec multi fide gloriantur, qui huius virtutem & efficaciam nunquam senserunt, sed quod ore profitentur factis negant. Sententia huius causam Dominus ad externa opera refert, quae ut prioris fidei fructus in suis credentibus commendat, dicens: Esuriui enim, & dedisti mihi ut vescerer: sitivi & dedisti mihi potum, etc. Quasi diceret: Ideo vos benedictos Patris mei dico, & electos regni mei heredes, quod fidem veram efficaciter operibus & germanis fidei fructibus declarauistis. Non ergo haec eo sensu dicuntur, ut opera haec efficientes causas salutis et vitae aeternae esse testentur, sed fructus & testimonia, ex quibus fides vera agnoscitur. Nam ut modo annotavimus efficiens causa salutis indicatur, quando benedictos Patris, & regnum illis ab aeterno paratum dixit: operibus autem declararunt illi fidem, quae priusquam hanc habeat homo, nulla sunt, quae vel bona sint, vel Deo placere, nedum salutem & regnum illud beatum mereri possint. Exemplo sunt Cain & Abel, quorum uterque sacrificavit Domino, nec in sacrificii materia aliquid est, quod alter alteri praeferri debet: sed quia hic fide praeditus fuit, eius victima Deo placuit: illius vero displiecuit, quia sine fide sacrificabat. Eadem est omnium operum ratio. Quia enim Christus mediator ille est qui solus nos Deo gratos & acceptos reddit, hic autem sola fide apprehenditur, certo colligi potest sine fide neminem Deo placere, & quod non ex fide fit, peccatum esse. Atqui fides haec non inanis perfuasio, multo minus temere concepta opinio est, quae ex ipsis percipiunt homines, sed fiducia certa per charitatem efficax, quae cum sit legis completio (ut Paulus docet) opera gignit, quae Deo placent propter Christum, & cum eius voluntate consentiunt. Ita Christus ipse in Euangelio salutis nostrae summam in fide monstrat, subinde inculcans illud, Qui credit in me, habet vitam aeternam. Interim vero alibi ad opera remittit, ut ostendat, fidem non mortuam aut otiosam esse, sed per opera bona se declarare & cognosci, ut arbor ex fructibus. Iustitia autem & vita aeterna (si proprie loquendum sit) non operibus sed fidei tribui debent, quae nos iustificare dicitur, quia nos Christo inserit, qui solus nobis a Deo iustitia & redemptio factus est, 1.Cor.1. & 2.Cor.5.
units.tr: But since the inward faith of the mind is a trust in Jesus Christ, which consists wholly in the Spirit and is not seen with the eyes or apprehended by any bodily sense, being a gift of the Holy Spirit, many also boast of their faith who have never felt its power and efficacy, but deny by their deeds what they profess with their mouth. The Lord refers the sentence of this matter to external works, which he commends as the fruits of the former faith in those who believe, saying: "For I was hungry, and you gave me food to eat; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink," etc. As if he said: "Therefore I call you blessed of my Father and heirs of my kingdom, because you have effectively declared the true faith by works and by the genuine fruits of faith. These things, then, are not said in the sense that these works are efficient causes of salvation and eternal life, but as fruits and testimonies by which true faith is recognized. For, as we have just noted, the efficient cause of salvation is indicated when he calls them the blessed of the Father and says the kingdom was prepared for them from eternity; but by their works they declared that faith which, before a man has it, there are no works that are good or pleasing to God, much less can merit salvation and that blessed kingdom." Cain and Abel are examples: both offered sacrifice to the Lord, nor is there anything in the matter of the sacrifice by which one ought to be preferred to the other; but because the one was endowed with faith, his victim pleased God, while the other's displeased him, because he sacrificed without faith. The same reasoning holds for all works. For since Christ is that mediator who alone makes us pleasing and acceptable to God, and he is apprehended by faith alone, it can be surely concluded that no one pleases God without faith, and that whatever is not done of faith is sin. Yet this faith is not an empty persuasion, much less a rashly conceived opinion, which men derive from their own perceptions, but a certain trust, effective through love, which, since it is the fulfilling of the law (as Paul teaches), produces works that please God for Christ's sake and agree with his will. Thus Christ himself in the Gospel sets forth the sum of our salvation in faith, repeatedly inculcating this: "He who believes in me has eternal life." Yet at other times he refers us to works, to show that faith is not dead or idle, but is declared and known through good works, as a tree is known by its fruits. Righteousness and eternal life, however (to speak properly), must be ascribed not to works but to faith, which is said to justify us, because it engrafts us into Christ, who alone has been made by God our righteousness and redemption: 1 Cor. 1 and 2 Cor. 5.

units.la: Ut vero de operibus quoque bonis aliquid dicatur, sunt haec non quaevis, quae in specie talia esse videntur, & ex nostri animi intentione fiunt: ideo nulla hic fit mentio votorum monasticorum, & operum charitatis, quae sunt, esurienti cibum, sitienti potum, extorri & exulanti hospitium, nudo vestimentum praebere, aegrotum item invisere, captivum & vinctum iuvare & consolari, &c. Sub quibus omnia alia comprehenduntur, quae sunt huius generis. Etenim qui his vere & ex animo studient, pro cuidubio nemini nocebunt, nulli hominum quod suum est eripient, neminem defraudabunt, neque negligeno proximo, quem Deus commendavit, in muta idola aut immoderatum corporis sui cultum conferent facultates suas, quibus proximum indigere vident. Multo minus virgines aut filias proximi
units.tr: But so that something may also be said of good works, these are not just any works which seem to be such in appearance and are done from a good intention of mind. Therefore no mention is made here of monastic vows, but of works of charity: giving food to the hungry, drink to the thirsty, hospitality to the stranger and exile, clothing to the naked, likewise visiting the sick, helping and comforting the captive and the bound, etc. Under these are included all other things of this kind. For those who truly and sincerely devote themselves to these will, beyond doubt, harm no one, will snatch from no man what is his, will defraud no one, and, neglecting a neighbour whom God has commended to them, will not spend the means by which they see their neighbour in need on dumb idols or on an immoderate cultivation of their own body. Still less will they defile the virgins or daughters of their neighbour with fornication, a wife with adultery, or widows with wanton lusts. Therefore there is no need for much inquiry into which works are good and pleasing to God. These are commonly known to all: and he who commands them does not demand them for himself, but because he himself needs no such services, he orders us to render them to our needy neighbour; and whatever is done to the neighbour he will count as done to himself, as will be shown shortly.

units.la: Matth.15. proximi stupru, vxorem adulterio, viduas vagis libidinibus polluent. Itaq; non multa quæstione opus est, quæ sint bona opera, quæ Deo placeant. Sunt hæc vulgò nota omnibus: neq; ista sibi fieri postulat ille, sed quia ipse nullis eiusmodi officijs indiget, vt proximo egenti illa præstemus, iubet: & quæ huic fiunt, sibi facta putabit, vt paulò post demonstrabitur.
units.tr: Matth. 15. adultery of a neighbour's wife, or fornication with a neighbour's daughter, or the defiling of widows... Therefore there is no need for lengthy questioning as to which works are good and pleasing to God. These are commonly known to all, and he does not ask for them for himself; but because he needs no such duties himself, he commands us to perform them for a needy neighbour; and what is done to these he will regard as done to himself, as will be shown a little later.

units.la: Nunc quid pij & electi, audita hac Christi sententia, fasturi sint, videamus. Nihil horũ in seipsis agnoscunt: Domine, quando (aiunt) te vidimus esurientem, & aluimus? aut sitientē, & de dimus tibi potum? &c. Quasi diceret: Nos equidem non meminimus quicquam huius fecisse. Ita vero non idcirco dicunt, quòd Iudicem & Seruatorem suum falsi arguere animus sit, sed suæ infirmitatis & delictorum sibi conscij toto corde humilientur, cum intelligunt, se nihil fecisse, quàm quod debuerunt, & multa neglexisse, quæ debuerunt facere. Et ita de se sentiunt fideles serui Christi, dum adhuc in corrupta carne viuunt. Iob certè dicit: Timui omnes labores meos, id est, ea quoq; opera mihi suspecta sunt, quæ summo cum labore & studio illi inseruiendi Deo peregi. Dauid item fatetur: Ratio iniquitatum nostrarum superat nos. Et rursus: Si deliCta obseruaris Domine, quis sustinebit? Ne intres in iudicium cum seruo tuo. Et Christus quotidie nos precari vult: Remitte nobis debita nostra. Nam si serui inutiles sumus, etiamsi omnia fecerimus, quæ debemus facere, quales nunc dici meremur, cum tam multa omiserimus, tam multa item sint, quæ non possumus præstare, cum lex peccati, quæ est in membris nostris (vt de semetipso Paulus fatetur) nos peccato captiuos facit, vt faciamus non quod volumus, sed quod nolumus? Horum ergo adhuc memores electi in magno illo die, simul abripientur admiratione plus quàm paterna bonitatis Dei, quam hic ipsis indignis contulit, non possunt extenuare sua opera, quæ Christus tantopere de illis prædicabit. Apparet autem hoc loco quid iudicari debeat de iustitiarijs hypocritis, qui Pharifaico spiritu agitati opera sua coram Deo iactant, & illorum meritis gloriantur, & quasi ipsorum debitor sit Deus rationes acceptorum & datorum ab illo exigunt. Est hæc Lucifériana superbia, & qui hac turgent, magno suo malo sentiet, se in his rationibus deliCtorum suorum superari, cum iustitia quoq; ipsorum sit instar sordidorum centonū, neq; in iudicio Dei possit consistere.
units.tr: Now let us see what the godly and the elect will do when they hear this sentence of Christ. They acknowledge none of these things in themselves: "Lord, when did we see you hungry and feed you? Or thirsty and give you a drink?" and so on. It is as if they said: "We indeed do not remember having done any of this." They do not say this because they intend to accuse their Judge and Saviour falsely, but because, aware of their own weakness and sins, they humble themselves with their whole heart, realising that they have done nothing more than they ought, and have neglected many things they ought to have done. So the faithful servants of Christ feel about themselves while they still live in corrupt flesh. Job certainly says: "I feared all my labours" (that is, even those works that I performed with great toil and zeal in serving God are suspect to me). David likewise confesses: "The reckoning of our iniquities overwhelms us." And again: "If you mark iniquities, Lord, who shall stand? Do not enter into judgement with your servant." And Christ wills that we pray every day: "Forgive us our debts." For if we are unprofitable servants, and even if we have done all that we ought to do, what do we deserve to be called now, since we have omitted so much, and since there is so much we cannot perform, while the law of sin that is in our members (as Paul confesses of himself) makes us captives to sin, so that we do not do what we want but what we do not want? Therefore the elect, still mindful of these things, on that great day will be swept away together in wonder at the goodness of God, which is more than fatherly, which he has bestowed on them here though they are unworthy; they will not be able to diminish their works, which Christ will so highly proclaim concerning them. It appears from this passage what ought to be judged concerning the self-righteous hypocrites, who, driven by a Pharisaic spirit, boast of their works before God, glory in their own merits, and demand an account of what they have given and received, as if God were their debtor. This is Luciferian pride, and those who swell with it will feel to their great harm that in that reckoning they are overcome by their sins, since their righteousness too is like filthy rags, and cannot stand in the judgement of God.

units.la: Conciliantur hic Scripturæ loci, qui nonnullis differentire videntur, quando alicubi Deus remunerator iustus esse docetur, qui vnicuiq; rependat pro merito suo, & mercedem nobis pollicetur: alibi verò opera nostra sic deprimit, vt quæcunq; accipimus ad gratuitam Dei misericordiam referat. Sed vtrumq; electi pie & sanctè credunt. Fatentur Deum, qui iustus est, remuneratorem esse eorum, quæ bene & rectè facimus, & eundem non impunita dimittere peccata eorum, qui in illis perguntur pœnitere nescij: seipsos autem in peccato conceptos & natos, atq; peccatores esse agnoscunt. Itaq; si quid aduersum ipsis accidit, agnoscunt hoc iusto Dei iudicio fieri, & se hoc meruisse, atq; dignos esse, quos Deus humiliet, & ad emendationem cæstiget. E contra autem quia Je ipsos probè norunt, quoties beneficijs suis ipsos dignatur Deus, illa ex gratia sibi conferri sentiunt, & cum Dauide dicunt: Quid est homo, quòd memor eius es? aut filius hominis, quòd tantam eius rationem habes? Psal.8.
units.tr: Here the passages of Scripture are reconciled, which seem to some to differ: sometimes God is taught to be a just rewarder who repays each person according to his merit and promises us a reward; but elsewhere he so lowers our works that he refers whatever we receive to God's free mercy. Yet the elect believe both devoutly and holily. They confess that God, being just, is the rewarder of what we do well and rightly, and that he does not let pass unpunished the sins of those who persist in them without knowing how to repent; but they acknowledge that they themselves were conceived and born in sin, and are sinners. So if anything adverse happens to them, they recognise that it comes about by the just judgement of God, and that they have deserved it and are worthy that God should humble them and chastise them for their amendment. On the other hand, since they know themselves well, whenever God deigns to bestow his benefits upon them, they feel that these are conferred on them from grace, and they say with David: "What is man, that you are mindful of him? Or the son of man, that you take such account of him?" Ps. 8.

units.la: Ad eundem modum conciliantur Paulus & Iacobus Apostoli, quorum ille Abrahamum ex fide sine operibus, hic verò per opera, & non ex fide iustificatum fuisse scribit. Paulus enim de fide viua & efficaci loquitur, quæ per charitatem & huius opera sese exerit, vt supra de ouibus aut electis Christi diximus, & quam Abrahamus quoq; operibus bonis publicè declarauit. Opera verò excludit, ne iustificationis causam, quæ proprie fidei debetur, illis tribuat: eadem tamen non dam nat, sed passim ad ea Christianos homines hortatur (vt in eius epistolis est videre) & vt nos totos Deo sistamus viuentè hostiā. Iacobus verò de fide mortua, vel potius otiosa & inani fidei professione disserit, vt eos confutet, qui sub hac licenter peccant, & nomen Christianum prophanant: interim non negat, nos ex gratuita Dei misericordia per fidem in Christum iustificari. Et eandem fuisse illius in tota hac causa sententiam, quæ Petri & Pauli fuit historia Synodi Ierosolymitanæ docet, quæ a Luca prolixè describitur. Act.15.
units.tr: In the same way Paul and James, the Apostles, are reconciled, of whom the former writes that Abraham was justified by faith without works, and the latter that he was justified by works and not by faith. For Paul speaks of a living and effective faith, which shows itself through love and its works, as we said above concerning the sheep or elect of Christ, and which Abraham also openly declared by good works. But he excludes works so that they may not be credited with the cause of justification, which is properly owed to faith; yet he does not condemn them, and everywhere he exhorts Christian people to them (as may be seen in his epistles), and to present ourselves wholly to God as a living sacrifice. James, however, discusses dead faith, or rather idle and empty profession of faith, so that he may refute those who sin freely under this name and profane the Christian name; meanwhile he does not deny that we are justified through faith in Christ from God's free mercy. And that his view in this whole matter was the same as that of Peter and Paul, the history of the Synod of Jerusalem teaches, which Luke describes at length. Acts 15.

units.la: Cæterum vt ad præsentis loci tractationem redeamus, Dominus, vt fideles suos tam humiliter de seipsis & officijs suis sentientes confirmet & erigat, non sine iureiurando illis respondet: [illegible, ~10 letters] Amen dico vobis, quatenus id fecistis vni ex fratribus istis meis minimis, mihi fecistis. Fundatur huius sententia ratio in eo, quod Christus alibi pauperes sibi substituit. Cum enim propter vnguentum pretiosum, quod super caput eius effuderat Maria, quidam murmurarent, & Iudas pau-peres praetexeret, quibus ex illius pretio, si venditum fuisset, potuissset subuenire, respondet Domi-nus, ita nunc oportuisse fieri, vt corpus suum ad sepulturam vngeretur, eo quod ipse moriturus quidem, sed ex morte resurrecturus sit, vt officium eiusmodi ipsi pro more praestare non posset: Quoad pauperes vero (inquit) hos semper vobiscum habetis, & quandocunq; volueritis, poteritis eis bene-facere: me vero non semper habebitis. Et hoc dicendo, non obscure innuit, suam ex terris in cae-lum ascensionem non obstituram, quo minus ipsi inseruire & debita officia praestare possimus: In suas enim rationes se ascribere velle, quacunq; in suo nomine ipsius feruis aut membris fecerimus. Illud vero tunc dicere libuit propter nos, qui adhuc in hoc saeculo viuimus, vt efficacius ad commiserationem & charitatis opera erga nostra opis indigos promoueamur. Itaq; verborum Christi nos semper memores esse decet. Fratres enim suos hoc loco dicit, qui vulgo contemptissimi hominum sunt, pauperes nimirum, qui famelici, nudi, exterres oberrant, & vel morbis fedis excruciantur, aut captiui in carceribus delitescunt. Quoties ergo aliquis ex horum numero tibi occurrit, & tuam opem implorat, Christum ipsum tibi occurrere & abs te flagitare, panem, potum, vestem & qualecunq; vitae subsidium petere cogitabis. Quod enim illi indigo facis, Dei Filio IESV CHRISTO fit, qui olim in magno illo die remunerator erit fidelis & liberalis. Assidua item meditatione in animo verseemus, quod dilectus ille discipulus & Apostolus scribit: Qui habuerit mundanas facultates, & viderit fratrem suum egentem, & clauserit viscera sua coram eo, quomodo charitas Dei manet in illo? Elucet in his magna hominum peruersitas, quae fere ex mundi & huius saeculi studio enascitur. Pollicentur quidem omnes magnifice, se nihil non factu-ros propter Christum, si hic, vt olim, carne humana & mortali indutus in terris hisce viueret. Interim in pauperibus suis occurrentem nobis, & prae fame morientem no negligimus modo, sed ipsi spoliamus, defraudamus, imo occidimus quoq; & terras longe late patentes bellis ininstitu, praedationibus, incendijs deniq; vastamus & depopulamur, vt nobis bene sit. Sed quid de illis futurum sit, qui talia faciunt, sequenti sermone dicetur. Deus Pater miserationum corda nostra luce illuminet, & misericordiae atq; charitatis igne accendat, vt pro suis in illo die nos agnoscat Iudex illæ vniuersalis IESVS CHRISTVS, cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: But, to return to the treatment of the present passage: the Lord, so that he may confirm and raise up his faithful, who think so humbly of themselves and their duties, answers them, not without an oath: "[illegible] Amen, I say to you, inasmuch as you did it to one of these my least brethren, you did it to me." The reason for this sentence rests on the fact that Christ elsewhere sets the poor in his own place. For when some murmured about the costly ointment that Mary had poured over his head, and Judas made a pretence of the poor, to whom he could have given help had it been sold for its price, the Lord replied that it was right for things to happen so now, that his body should be anointed for burial, since he, though about to die, would rise again from death, and so could not perform such a duty in the usual way. "As for the poor," he said, "you always have them with you, and whenever you wish you can do them good; but me you will not always have." And in saying this he clearly intimates that his ascension from earth into heaven would not stand in the way of our being able to serve him and perform our due duties; for he wishes to reckon to himself whatever we do in his name to his servants or members. He said this then for our sake, who still live in this age, so that we might be more effectively moved to compassion and to works of love towards those who need our help. Therefore it is fitting that we always remember the words of Christ. For he means by "his brethren" in this place those who are commonly the most despised of men, namely the poor, who wander hungry, naked and as strangers, and are tormented by foul diseases, or lie hidden in prisons as captives. Whenever, then, one of this number meets you and implores your help, think that Christ himself meets you and asks of you bread, drink, clothing and whatever support of life he seeks. For what you do for him who is in need is done to JESUS CHRIST, the Son of God, who on that great day will be a faithful and generous rewarder. Let us also turn over in our minds, in constant meditation, what the beloved disciple and Apostle writes: "Whoever has worldly goods, and sees his brother in need, and closes his heart against him, how does the love of God remain in him?" In these things is revealed the great perversity of men, which arises almost from devotion to the world and this age. All of them promise grandly that they would undertake anything for Christ's sake, if he were living on earth here, clothed in human and mortal flesh, as once he did. Meanwhile, when he meets us in his poor, dying of hunger, we not only neglect him but despoil and defraud him, indeed even kill him, and we lay waste and depopulate lands spreading far and wide with wars, plunderings and finally fires, so that it may go well with us. But what will become of those who do such things will be told in the following sermon. May God the Father illuminate our hearts with the light of compassion and kindle them with the fire of mercy and love, so that the universal Judge, JESUS CHRIST, may acknowledge us as his own on that day, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCXCI.
units.tr: HOMILY CCXCI.

units.la: Tunc dicet (Rex) etiam ijs, qui ad sinistram erunt, Maledicti abite a me in ignem aeternum, qui paratus est diabolo & angelis eius. Esuriui enim, & non dedistis mihi quo vescerer: sitiui, & non dedistis potum: Hospes eram, & non collegistis me: nudus, & non amiciuistis: aegrotus & in carcere eram, & non inuisistis me. Tunc ipsi quoque respondebunt ei, dicentes: Domine, quando te vidimus esurientem, aut sitientem, aut hospitem, aut nudum, aut aegrotum, aut in carcere, & non ministrauimus tibi? Tunc respondebit eis, dicens: Amen dico vobis, quatenus id non fecistis vni ex istis minimis, nec mihi fecistis. Et abibunt illi in supplicium aeternum, iusti vero in vitam aeternam.
units.tr: Then the King will also say to those on his left: "Depart from me, you cursed, into eternal fire, which is prepared for the devil and his angels. For I was hungry, and you gave me nothing to eat; I was thirsty, and you gave me no drink; I was a stranger, and you did not take me in; naked, and you did not clothe me; sick and in prison, and you did not visit me." Then they too will answer him, saying: "Lord, when did we see you hungry, or thirsty, or a stranger, or naked, or sick, or in prison, and did not minister to you?" Then he will answer them: "Truly I say to you, inasmuch as you did not do it to one of these least, you did not do it to me." And those will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life.

units.la: Deus remunerator est. Hebr. 11.
units.tr: God is a rewarder. Heb. 11.

units.la: Grave & memorabile est dictum Apostoli ad Hebraeos: Qui accedit ad Deum, hunc credere oportet esse Deum, & remuneratorem esse ijs, qui ipsum requirunt. Etenim nisi quis dum haec firmiter teneat, & sibi probe persuasa habeat, quod revera Deus sit, qui omnia creavit, omnia gubernet & feruet: & quod idem verax & omnipotens sit, iustius deniq; qui seruis & cultoribus suis fidis promissa praemia retribuat, impijs vero & contumacibus poenas sceleribus suis debitas rependat: is nunquam vere credet Deo, neque eum metuet aut amabit: multo minus vitam suam secundum illius voluntatem instituet. Quapropter Scriptura veteris & noui Testamenti passim ista diligenter commendat. In primis autem articulus hic illustratur & aduersus omnes carnis dubiae cogitationes confirmatur in hac nouissimi iudicij descriptione. Cum enim in hoc seculo promiscue inter se viuunt homines boni & mali, & saepe rerum facies atque tanta confusio, ut pij quoque de Deo & eius prouidentia atque iustitia dubitent, quasi illi frustra seruiatur: impij vero ex impunitate sua ferociores fiunt: Docet primo Christus, fore olim discrimen & se cum iudex venerit, ante omnia separaturum oues suas ab haedis, & tunc manifestum fore vniuerso mundo, ipsum fidelem & iustum in pastorem esse. Deinde quid de veritate statuere velit, narrat: Et nuper quidem de pijs siue electis suis dixit, qui tunc ad dextera n sistentur, qui beatitudinis locum & hos benedictos Patris sui vocabit, ut ad se receptos, regni sui ab aeterno illis destinati, haeredes faciat.
units.tr: The saying of the Apostle to the Hebrews is weighty and memorable: "Whoever comes to God must believe that he exists and that he is a rewarder of those who seek him." For unless a person holds firmly to this, and is thoroughly persuaded that there truly is a God who created all things, governs them and sustains them, who is also true and almighty, and who at last justly repays with the promised rewards those who are faithful servants and worshippers, but pays the wicked and stubborn the punishments their wickedness deserves, that person will never truly believe God, nor fear or love him, much less order his life according to God's will. Therefore the Scripture of the Old and New Testament everywhere commends this diligently. Yet this article is especially illustrated, and confirmed against all doubtful thoughts of the flesh, in this description of the last judgment. For although in this world good and bad people live together indiscriminately, and the state of affairs and such great confusion often make even the godly doubt God, his providence and his justice, as if he were served in vain, while the wicked become more savage because of their impunity, Christ first teaches that there will be a distinction in time, and that when he comes as judge he will before all else separate his sheep from the goats, and that then it will be made plain to the whole world that he is a faithful and just shepherd. Next he tells what he wishes to establish concerning the truth.
