Having just spoken of the godly, that is, his elect, he said that they will stand at the right hand, and that he will call these blessed of his Father to the place of blessedness, so that, received into his presence, he may make them heirs of the kingdom prepared for them from eternity.

units.la: Sequitur altera huius narrationis pars, qua contra reprobos, qui ad sinistram in loco dam iatio nis stabunt, pronuntiabit, & ut maledictos ablegabit in ignem aeternum. Et sicuti nuper electorum suorum bona opera, quae ex fide & charitate fecerunt, magnifice commendauit: ita nunc iustis exprobrabit animos a fide & charitate alienos, ex quibus toti humano generi constare possit, ipsos reprobos & damnatione dignos esse. Sed singula huius loci ordine videamus, cui haec potissimum insunt: Primum recitatur sententia finalis contra reprobos. Secundo eius ratio redditur, quod charitatis officia, quae ipsi Christo debentur, prorsus neglexerint. Tertio opponitur his, illorum excusatio siue defensio: vbi reproborum hypocritarum ingenium & mores graphice exprimuntur. Quare to Dominus sententiam pronuntiatam ratione, quam nuper quoque allegauit, confirmat. Post quam sequitur executio veritatis, sententiae, quoad electos & reprobos.
units.tr: There follows the second part of this narrative, in which he will pronounce against the reprobate, who will stand on the left in a place of condemnation, and will send them away as accursed into eternal fire. And just as he has lately commended the good works of his elect, which they did from faith and love, so now he will rebuke the righteous for minds alien to faith and love, from which it could be established for the whole human race that the reprobate themselves are deserving of condemnation. But let us look at the parts of this passage in order, in which these matters are chiefly contained. First the final sentence against the reprobate is recited. Second, its reason is given, namely that they have utterly neglected the duties of love that are owed to Christ himself. Third, an excuse or defence of theirs is set against these charges, in which the nature and manners of the reprobate hypocrites are vividly portrayed. Then the Lord confirms the pronounced sentence by the reasoning he also cited just before. After this follows the execution of the truth of the sentence, as regards the elect and the reprobate.

units.la: Sententia Christi Iudicis finalis contra reprobos est haec: Maledicti abite a me in ignem aeternum, quod paratus est diabolo & angelis eius. Vt electos suos benedictos Patris dixit, eo quod in ipsum credunt, qui nos Patri reconciliauit, & quia in ipso nobis Pater benedixit, omni benedictione spirituali: Ita nunc impios, qui fide destituuntur & ab ipso alieni sunt, maledictos dicit: quia (vt ex Ioanne nuper annotauimus) qui non credit in Christum, is adhuc in peccato est, & adhuc manet super illum ira Dei, quae peccati paenam siue stipendium, mortem videlicet, nobis affert. Idcirco sicut pios & credentes ad se vocauit, vt regnum ipsis ab aeterno paratum possideant: ita hos abire, & procul a se facessere iubet, vt offendat, nihil cum ipso illis vnquam commune fore. Abire autem iubet in ignem aeternum, qui diabolo & eius angelis separatus. Etenim iustum & aequum est, vt qui nolunt cum Christo communicare in hoc seculo, multo minus cum illo in regno caelorum communi gaudio & felicitate fruantur: sed cum angelis malis, quibus seruierunt, procul a facie Christi reiiciantur: quae maxima est hominis calamitas: si nimirum a Deo, qui sum nunc bonum & omnis boni vnicus fons est, reiecti & exclusi mereantur. Facit autem ad amplificationem paenae: quod eiusdem supplicij consortes fore dicit cum diabolo & huius satellitibus. Quid obsecro hominem ingenuum & liberaliter educato atque virtutibus assueto, molestius aut tristius potest accidere, quam si cum capitalibus parentis sui & totius familiae suae inimicis in locum aliquem obscurum, tetrum & horribili squalore rigentem, concluderetur: quorum querelas, & conuicia absque interm issione omni audire cogeretur? nec aliquam videret rationem, qua seipsum vel alios possit ab eximere? Atqui quanto tristior & infelicior erit illorum conditio, qui in illo die relegabuntur in ignem illum inextinguibilem, qui alibi stagnum ardens igne & sulphure dicitur: vbi nullo alio solatio stipabuntur impij, quam malorum daemonum, qui neque lucem ferre, neque aliquid in Dei honorem & gloriam audire possunt, & non solum inenarrabilibus tormentis inferorum excruciati, Dei iustitiam calumniantur, & aduersus eiusdem bonitatem cum horribili fremitu grunniunt, verumetiam quam ipsi impietate sua aniserunt beatitudinem, omnibus inuidant, quibus aliquam adhuc micam diuini fauoris superesse videntur? De Lotho scribit Petrus Apostolus, quod in Sodoma vitam agens animam iustam indies iniustis illorum factis & videndo & audiendo excruciarit. Atqui qui noverat hic illum remuneratorem esse, & aliquando finem iustum habituram omnia ea, quae ipsum tunc torquebant. Quid ergo de illis fiet, qui in aeternos tartarorum carceres detrusi cum diabolis versabuntur, & eorundem cum illis supplicιorum socij fient, quorum confpeEtus vel praesentia homini intolerabilis est? Enimuero vt communio cum Deo in regno illo caelesti gaudium parit, quod nullis linguis pro dignitate explicari, nullo sensu aut captu humani ingenij comprehendi potest: ita omnes quoq; sensus superat cruciatus ille, quem reprobi apud inferos cum immundis illis spiritibus communem sentiunt. Horum enim ignis (vt apud Marcum dicit Dominus) non extinguetur, neq; vermis vnquam morietur. Et tantas tamq; diras poenas in praesenti omnibus denuntiat, qui spreta benedictione, quam Filius Dei nobis meruit, cum principe huius saeculi maledictionem aeternam subire maluerunt.
units.tr: The final sentence of Christ the Judge against the reprobate is this: "Depart from me, accursed, into eternal fire, which is prepared for the devil and his angels." As he called his elect the blessed of the Father, because they believe in him who reconciled us to the Father, and because in him the Father has blessed us with every spiritual blessing, so now he calls the ungodly, who lack faith and are alien to him, accursed. For (as we noted lately from John) whoever does not believe in Christ is still in sin, and the wrath of God remains upon him, which brings us the penalty or wages of sin, namely death. Therefore, just as he called the godly and believing to himself, so that they may possess the kingdom prepared for them from eternity, so he bids these depart and go far from him, so that he may show that they will have nothing ever in common with him. He bids them depart into eternal fire, which is separated from the devil and his angels. For it is just and fitting that those who were unwilling to share with Christ in this world should much less enjoy with him in the kingdom of heaven the common joy and happiness, but should be cast far from the face of Christ with the evil angels whom they served. This is the greatest of human calamities, if indeed they deserve to be rejected and shut out from God, who is now the good and the sole fountain of all good. Moreover, it adds to the enlargement of the punishment that he says they will be companions in the same torment with the devil and his attendants. What, I ask, can happen to a free-born man, liberally brought up and accustomed to virtue, that is more troublesome or sadder than to be shut up with the chief enemies of his parent and of his whole family in some dark place, foul and stiff with horrible squalor, forced to hear without interruption their complaints and abuse, and to see no way by which he could free himself or others? Yet how much sadder and more wretched will be the condition of those who on that day will be consigned to that unquenchable fire, which elsewhere is called a lake burning with fire and brimstone, where the ungodly will have no other comfort than the company of evil demons, who can bear neither light nor hear anything to God's honour and glory; tormented not only by the unspeakable torments of the underworld, they blaspheme God's justice and growl against his goodness with dreadful snarling, and moreover they envy all those in whom some small crumb of divine favour still seems to remain, all of whom have lost the blessedness they forfeited by their impiety. Peter the Apostle writes of Lot that, living in Sodom, he tormented his righteous soul day by day, both seeing and hearing their unjust deeds. Yet he who knew that God is a rewarder, and that all those things which then tormented him would at some time have a just end. What then will become of those who are thrust into the eternal prisons of the underworld and will dwell with devils, and become sharers with them in their punishments, whose sight or presence is intolerable to a man? Indeed, just as communion with God in that heavenly kingdom brings a joy that cannot be explained by any tongue as it deserves, nor grasped by any sense or capacity of the human mind, so that torment, which the reprobate feel in common with those unclean spirits in hell, surpasses all senses too. For the fire of these (as the Lord says in Mark) will not be quenched, and the worm will never die. He threatens such great and dreadful punishments in the present to all who, having scorned the blessing that the Son of God merited for us, have preferred to undergo eternal curse with the prince of this world.

units.la: Heic vero elucebit iustitia Dei aduersus eorum errorem, qui nisi statim puniat scelera, illum nos & omnia quae in terris geruntur negligere, aut etiam ignorare putant: & inde colligunt, felices eos esse, qui audaciter Dei mandata transgrediuntur, miseros autem & calamitosos, qui nihil audent, & actiones omnes ad Verbi aut Legis Dei regulam metiuntur: Necesse ergo esse, vt foro & tempori nos accommodemus, & praesentibus commodis fruamur. Sed contra eiusmodi sermones non minus impios quam falsos, Asaph nos instruit in Psalmis, & multi extant alij Scripturae loci admodum vtiles consideratu, inter quos memorabilis est, qui apud Malachiam habetur, vbi sic ait Propheta: Fatigauistis Dominum sermonibus vestris: Dicitis autem, Quanam re fatigauimus eum? In hoc nempe, cum dicitis: Quicunq; malum facit, bonus est in oculis Domini, & in his complacet ei: aut, Vbi est Deus iudicij? Item, Inualuerunt contra me verba vestra, dicit Dominus: & dicitis, Quid nam contra te fumus locuti? Dixistis, Frustra seruitur Deo. Nam quae vilitas, quod custodiam eius custodiuimus, & quod humiliati coram Domino exercituum incedimus? Nunc certe beatos dicimus superbos, cum qui impie agunt, aedificentur: & qui Deum tentant, ij seruantur & durant. Tales erant Israelitarum sermones tempore exilij Babylonici, & cum ex eo reuersi a vicinis gentibus infestarentur, haec autem rebus integris florebant. At quid illis respondet Propheta? Tunc qui Dominum timent, quisq; proximo suo dixit: Dominus attendit & audiuit, & scriptus est commentarius coram eo, timentibus Dominum scilicet, & qui fuppu-tant nomen eius. Et erunt mihi (dicit Dominus exercituum) eo die, quem ego facio, peculium, ipsa parcam, vt quis filio parcit sibi seruienti. Reuertimini & videbitis inter iustum & impium, eum, qui Deo seruit, & ei non seruit. Itaq; pollicetur Deus, fore diem iudicij, quando inter pios & impios discernere velit. At doctrinam hanc non magni faciunt prophani huius saeculi filij: & vt malae fidei debitores, quidius hac conditione in se recipiunt & designant, vt in illo demum die poenas dent. Sed vere pij ea quoq; audiunt, quae in Propheta proxime sequuntur. Reuertimini & vt debitis inter iustum & impium, &c. Et haec de nouissimo iudicio pronuntiat, quando a mortis resurgent homines, & proprijs oculis videbunt, Deum suos cultores remunerari, vt eos corpore & anima feruet: impios autem prout fecerunt vlcisci. Nam haec quoq; addit ijs, quae praecesserunt, Malachias: Quoniam ecce dies venit, ardens vt clibanus: & erunt omnes superbi, & omnes qui impietatem designant stipula, & inflammabit eos dies ventura, dicit Dominus exercituum, qui non relinquet eis neq; radicem neq; ramum. Quod non ita accipi debet, quasi corpora quoq; & animae quoad essentiam suam in nihilum redigantur. Etenim animae ne in morte quidem intereunt: corpora vero immutantur, vt quae prius corruptibilia erant, omni corruptione exuta vitam aeternam capacia fiant, in qua pij quidem aeternum gaudebunt, impij vero cruciabuntur, & durabunt perpetuo, vt sempiternis poenis sufficiant, pereuntibus interim & in nihilum redactis omnibus, quibus infelices confisi sunt. Nam, vt alibi dictum est, caelum & terra & vniuersa mundi machina dissoluetur, & simul omnia conflagrabunt. Quid ergo miseris reliquum erit, quo nituntur, aut ex quo aliquid praesidij sperare possint? Fallentur ergo, qui in hoc saeculo iftaridentes & in dubium vocant, quae de altera vita & inferis dicuntur, olim autem ea experiri & sentire cogentur, quae nunc nolunt credere.
units.tr: Here the justice of God shows itself against the error of those who think that God does not notice, or even does not know, what is done on earth unless he punishes wicked deeds at once. From this they conclude that those are happy who boldly break God's commands, but wretched and unfortunate are those who dare nothing and measure all their actions by the rule of God's Word or Law. Therefore, they say, we must adapt ourselves to the times and the circumstances and enjoy present advantages. Against such talk, which is no less impious than false, Asaph instructs us in the Psalms, and there are many other passages of Scripture well worth considering, among which is the memorable one in Malachi, where the prophet speaks thus: "You have wearied the Lord with your words. But you say, 'How have we wearied him?' In this, that you say, 'Everyone who does evil is good in the sight of the Lord, and he delights in them'; or, 'Where is the God of judgment?'" Again: "Your words have grown strong against me, says the Lord; yet you say, 'What have we spoken against you?' You have said, 'It is vain to serve God. What profit is it that we have kept his charge, and that we have walked humbly before the Lord of hosts? Now we call the proud blessed; those who work wickedness are built up, and those who tempt God are kept safe and endure.'" Such were the words of the Israelites in the time of the Babylonian exile, and when they returned from there and were harassed by the neighbouring nations, while these nations flourished with their wealth intact. But what does the prophet answer them? "Then those who fear the Lord spoke, each one to his neighbour: the Lord attended and heard, and a book of remembrance was written before him for those who fear the Lord and who think upon his name. And they shall be mine, says the Lord of hosts, on the day that I make, a special treasure; and I will spare them, as a man spares his son who serves him. Return and you shall see the difference between the righteous and the wicked, between one who serves God and one who does not serve him." So God promises that there will be a day of judgment, when he will separate the godly from the ungodly. But the sons of this profane world do not think much of this teaching, and, like debtors in bad faith, they take on and sign for themselves the condition that they will pay their penalties only on that day. But truly godly people also hear what the prophet says immediately after: "Return, and you shall see the difference between the righteous and the wicked," and so on. This he declares of the last judgment, when men shall rise from the dead and with their own eyes will see God rewarding his worshippers, refreshing them in body and soul, and punishing the ungodly according to their deeds. For Malachi adds this also to what has gone before: "For behold, the day comes, burning like an oven; and all the proud and all who work wickedness shall be stubble, and the coming day shall set them on fire, says the Lord of hosts, a day that will leave them neither root nor branch." This should not be taken to mean that bodies and souls are reduced to nothing as to their very being. For souls do not perish even in death; but bodies are changed, so that what was formerly corruptible, stripped of all corruption, becomes capable of eternal life, in which the godly will rejoice forever, while the ungodly will be tormented and will endure perpetually, so as to suffice for everlasting punishments, while all those things in which the wretched trusted pass away and are reduced to nothing. For, as has been said elsewhere, heaven and earth and the whole machinery of the world will be dissolved, and all things will burn together. What then will remain for the wretched, on which they may rest, or from which they might hope for any help? Therefore those will be deceived who in this age scoff at and call into doubt what is said of the other life and of hell, but who will one day be compelled to experience and feel what they now refuse to believe.

units.la: Caeterum rationem audiamus, cur Iudex Christus tam horribili sententia ignem aeternum damnet? Esuriui enim (inquit) & non dedisti mihi quo vescerer: sitiui, & non dedisti mihi potum: hospes eram, & non collegisti me: nudus, & non amiciuisti: aegrotus & in carcere eram, & non inuisisti me. Vt nuper opera piorum, ex fide & charitate manantia commendauit: ita his oppobu opponit reproborum opera, quae non possunt non certò sequi, ubi fide extincta, charitas quoq; in termoritur. Sub his autem quae hic commemorantur, reliqua omnia, quae huius generis sunt, complectitur. Nam his quasi indiciis illi abundè testantur, je fide in Christum deserti, & proinde merito ab ipso reijci & damnari. Etenim olim ille dixit: Qui non crediderit, damnabitur. Increduli tas ergo omnium operum prauorum origo est. Quia enim sola fide iustificamur, certè qui non crediderit, ne iustificatus quidem erit. Quomodo autem opera iustitiae faciet, qui non iustus est? Cùm enim fides per charitatem efficax fit & agat, neq; fidei opera erunt, neq; Deo placere poterunt, quae sine charitate fiunt. Deniq; ut uno verbo dicatur quod res est, opera mala & inhumanitatis plena, in quibus reprobi incurabili contumacia pergunt, certissima indicia sunt, quae illos fide in uniuersum carere testantur. Proderit autem hoc loco ex ordine videre, qui nam haec sententia damnentur, ut ita dijcamus, quid nos vitare, quidue facere oporteat, si damnationis aeternae poenas vel limus effugere.
units.tr: But let us hear the reason why Christ the Judge condemns to eternal fire with so terrible a sentence. "For I was hungry," he says, "and you gave me no food to eat; I was thirsty, and you gave me no drink; I was a stranger, and you did not take me in; naked, and you did not clothe me; sick and in prison, and you did not visit me." As he has just commended the works of the godly, which flow from faith and love, so here he sets against them the works of the reprobate, which cannot fail to follow surely where faith is extinguished and love too dies. Under these deeds which are mentioned here, he embraces all the others of this kind. For these, as it were, clear signs bear abundant witness that such people have been abandoned by faith in Christ, and therefore are rightly rejected and condemned by him. For he once said: "He who does not believe will be condemned." Unbelief therefore is the source of all evil works. For since we are justified by faith alone, certainly he who does not believe will not be justified either. And how will he do works of righteousness who is not righteous? For since faith is effective and works through love, neither will there be works of faith, nor can those things please God which are done without love. Finally, to say in one word what is the case, evil works full of inhumanity, in which the reprobate persist with incurable obstinacy, are most certain signs which testify that they altogether lack faith. It will be useful here to see in order who are condemned by this sentence, so that, as it were, we may learn what we ought to avoid and what we ought to do, if we would escape the punishments of eternal damnation, even a little.

units.la: Primùm damnantur hic opulenti & diuites, qui opibus huius saeculi abundant, sed immites & duri viscera sua immisericorditer claudunt erga fratres egentes, ut neq; ipsorum neq; tenerorum liberorum, quos esurire, algere & affligi vident, moueantur. Hi enim plurus faciunt caduca & friuola huius saeculi bona quàm homines, qui ad Dei imaginem conditi, Christi personam referunt, qui in ipsis slipem petit, esurit, algèt & hospitium quaerit. Et quum fratrem, quem vident, nō diligant, num Deum diligere poterunt, quem non vident, & qui ipsorum ope non indiget? Atqui charitatis lex est, proximum ut teipsum diligere: proximum autem putare debemus obuium quenq;, qui nostram opem implorat, aut quem huius egentem videmus, etsi nullus petat. Vide Samaritani parabolam. Luc.10. Nec est quod obijcias: etsi habeam quod mihi sufficit, non habeo tamen quod alijs largiar, & mihi sunt liberi, quibus ut prospiciam necesse est, ne quando ipsi ab alijs stipem petere cogantur. Etenim ut tuis vtaris, prout necesse est, Deus non prohibet: neq; charitatis lex obstat, quo minus tuis prospicias. Et notum est illud Pauli: Non hoc exigit Deus, ut alijs relaxatio fit, nobis autem oppressio, sed ut pari conditione nostra abundantia suppleat aliorum defectum. Itaq; qui plura possident, plura largiantur: qui minus faciant quod possunt: & qui quod dent nō habent, amént saltem omnes homines, fauEant egentibus, bene precentur, benevoli sint, consilio iuuent, consolationibus pijs recreent. Inprimis autem caue, ne dum tibi necessaria quaeris, necessitatem auaritia metiaris, cuius cupiditas est inexplebilis. Nam Apostolo teste, nihil intulimus in mundum, nec quicquà efferre poterimus: sed habentes alimenta & quibus tegamur, his contenti simus. Atqui natura sic conditi sumus, ut non immensis opibus sit opus: & qui mediocres, vel etiam paruas possident, fere quietius & commodius viuunt, quàm qui circa multas & immodicas fatigantur. Semper cordibus nostris obuersetur, quod filio suo Tobias dicebat: De facultatibus tuis exerce beneficentiam, nec maligne se gerat oculus tuus in prae standa benignitate: Ne auertas faciem tuam ab vllo paupere, ut nec Deus faciem suam abs te auertat. Pro ratione facultatum tuarum sis beneficus: Si multum tibi fuerit, large tribuas: sin parum, ne verearis ex pauco praestare benignitatem: Thesaurum enim bonum tibi recondes in diem necessitatis, &c. Et his consentiunt literae Prophetica & Apostolica: quae simul docent, licere pijs, ut facultatibus suis ipsi vtantur, nec exigia Deo, ut sua omnia alijs distribuant. Faciunt huc exempla Patriarcharum, Abrahami, Isaaci, Iacobi & Iosephi, & c. In nouo testamento Nicodemi, Iosephi Arimathaei, Lazari Bethanien sis & fororum: & Apostolus multa in epistolis tradit, quae rem domesticam pie & sanctè administrare docent: quorum vsus nobis esse debet, ut nostris honestè prospiciamus, & pauperes nobis habeamus commendatos. Vide 1. Thess.4. Eph.4.1. Tim.5. &c.
units.tr: First, here are condemned the wealthy and rich, who abound in the riches of this world, but are harsh and hard, who shut up their bowels without mercy against needy brothers, so that they are not moved by the sight of their own children, or of the tender young ones of others, whom they see hungry, cold and afflicted. For such people value the fleeting and frivolous goods of this world more than human beings, who were created in the image of God and represent the person of Christ, who in them seeks alms, hungers, is cold and asks for lodging. And since they do not love the brother whom they see, how will they be able to love God, whom they do not see, and who does not need their help? Yet the law of charity is that we should love our neighbour as ourselves; and we ought to regard as our neighbour anyone who meets us and implores our help, or whom we see in need, even if no one asks. See the parable of the Good Samaritan, Luke 10. Nor may you object: "Even if I have what suffices for me, I have nothing to give to others, and I have children, for whom I must provide, lest at some time they themselves be forced to beg alms from others." For God does not forbid you to use what is yours as necessity requires, nor does the law of charity stand in the way of your providing for your own. And the saying of Paul is well known: "God does not require that others should be relieved while you are burdened, but that by equality your abundance should supply their lack." Therefore those who possess more should give more; those who do less than they can should do what they can; and those who have nothing to give should at least favour all men, speak well of the needy, be kindly, help with counsel, and refresh them with godly consolations. Above all, take care that, while you seek what you need, you do not measure necessity by avarice, whose desire is insatiable. For, as the Apostle bears witness, we brought nothing into the world, and certainly we can carry nothing out; but having food and clothing, let us be content with these. Indeed we are so made by nature that we do not need immense wealth; and those who possess moderate or even small means generally live more quietly and comfortably than those who are worn out with many and excessive possessions. Let what Tobit said to his son always be before our hearts: "Use your means for almsgiving, and do not let your eye be grudging in giving kindness. Do not turn your face away from any poor man, so that God will not turn his face away from you. According to your means be generous: if you have much, give abundantly; if you have little, do not fear to give kindness even from a little. For you will store up a good treasure for yourself against the day of need," and so on. The prophetic and apostolic writings agree with these, and at the same time they teach that it is lawful for the godly to use their own means, and God does not demand that they distribute all they have to others. The examples of the patriarchs support this: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and Joseph, and so on. In the New Testament, Nicodemus, Joseph of Arimathea, Lazarus of Bethany and his sisters. And the Apostle in his epistles hands down many things which teach us to manage domestic affairs piously and holily; we ought to use these so that we may honourably provide for our own and keep the poor commended to us. See 1 Thess. 4; Eph. 4; 1 Tim. 5, and so on.

units.la: Secundò damnantur Christi sententia omnes, qui non licito & legitimo labore, aut honesta aliqua ratione se suo fq alunt, sed vsurarijs artibus, fraude doloq;: monopolijs item ditescere studeant, & fruges terrae ex Dei benedictione datas intercipiunt, ut postea mꝭ oris vendant: adhaec fallunt publicè quosuis mensura, pondere, moneta deniq;, quod hodie nimis vulgare est, quando pecunia ipsa quaestus maximus est, & inexplicabiles sunt artes, quibus non mercatores modo & fa nematores alij alios deglubunt, verumetiam infelix vulgus & mercenarij spoliantur, quibus sua merces vel detinetur, vel arroditur, ut non tota ad ipsos perueniat. Sed ad illos pertinet, quod Apostolus scribit: Agite nunc diuites, flete vlulantes super miseriis vestris superuenturis. Diuitiae vestrae putrefactae sunt, vestimenta vestra a tineis sunt vorata: aurum & argentum vestrum aerugine vitiatum est, & aerugo vestra testabitur contra vos, & exedet carnes vestras velut ignis: thesaurum congessistis in nouissimis diebus. Ecce merces operariorum, qui messuerunt regiones vestras, a vobis interceptea, clamat, & clamores eorum, qui messuerunt, in aures Domini Sabaoth introierunt, &c. Consentit his quod apud Micheam dicitur: Annon adhuc ignis, thesaurus iniquus scilicet in domo impij? & Epha perexiguum, & ira plenum? Num iustificabo bilancem iniquam, & sacculum in quo sunt lapides fraudulenti? &c. Etenim si peccant, qui officia charitatis negligunt, quanto grauior eorum culpa est, qui insuper malefaciunt, & dolis suis aliorum inopiam augent?
units.tr: Second, condemned by Christ's sentence are all who do not support themselves by lawful and legitimate labour or some honest means, but seek to grow rich by usurious arts, fraud and deceit, and likewise by monopolies, withholding the fruits of the earth that God's blessing gave, in order to sell them later at a higher price. They also cheat everyone publicly in measure, weight and finally coinage, which today is all too common, since money itself is the greatest source of gain. There are countless arts by which merchants and moneylenders fleece one another, and the poor crowd and hired workers are plundered too, their wages either withheld or whittled down so that not all of it reaches them. But what the Apostle writes applies to such people: "Come now, you rich, weep and howl over the miseries that are coming upon you. Your riches have rotted, your garments have been eaten by moths, your gold and silver is corroded, and their rust will testify against you and eat your flesh like fire. You have stored up treasure in the last days. Behold, the wages of the workers who mowed your fields, kept back by you, cry out, and the cries of those who reaped have entered the ears of the Lord of Sabaoth," etc. What is said in Micah agrees with this: "Is there still fire in the house of the wicked, the unjust treasure, and the scant measure that is full of wrath? Shall I justify the wicked balance and the bag of deceitful weights?" etc. For if those who neglect the duties of charity sin, how much graver is the guilt of those who, in addition, do wrong and by their frauds increase the want of others?

units.la: Tertio damnantur etiam hoc loco prodigi, qui opes, quas Dominus dedit, turpiter & inutiliter profundunt & dilapidant, adeo vt per illas neque Deus colatur, neque proximus emendetur, aut eius subleuetur inopia. In eo numero sunt, qui insanis aedificijs impensas faciunt immodicas, & abs que necessitate diruunt, aedificant (vt Poeta verbis vtar) mutant quadrata rotundis. Illis accenseri debent, qui supellectile sumptuosa superbiunt, vestitu luxurioso diffluunt, poculis immodicis & temulentia indulgent, dies noctesque perpotant: nec solum gratiarum actionis obliuiscuntur, quae Deo pro acceptis frugibus debentur: sed erga pauperes & egenos Christi tenacissimi & sordidi plane sunt, quos interim esurire, sitire, algere, extorres oberrare sinunt. Talium ingens est numerus hodie, qui iudicium Domini nunquam effugient. Etenim passim occurrunt famelici, qui vix duro manuum labore vitam sustentant, imo ne inueniunt quidem operandi occasionem, qua se honeste alant? Quam multa vix partu leuata decumbunt, nec habent cibos salutares, aut potum, qui puerperis salubriter seruiat? Quam multi victum necessarium mendicando quaerunt, nec quantum illis sufficit inueniunt? Qui omnes paruo & vili cibo, & potu modico contenti essent, seipsos Deo & tibi gratos praeberent, si illa abs te impetrarent. Sed plerunque fit, vt quos non piget fruges immodico luxu consumere, vino turpiter effuso menses, sedilia, caenacula ipsa perluere, socios plus satis potos, vt amplius bibant cogere, ij immites & duri sint erga pauperes, erga puerperas, egenos, adeo, vt ex pumice aquam facilius, quam ab illis poculum vini aut frustulum panis extorqueas. Hi sunt, de quibus Amos scribit: Vae securis in Sion, & confidenti in monte Samariae, qui in longinquum reiciris diem malum, qui dormiunt in lectis eburneis, se diffendentes in grabatis suis: qui agnos ex grege comedunt, & vitulos pingues ex corte, qui ad nablum concinunt, qui minimi paterit potant vnguentis deliburi, neque illis dolet quod Ioseph afflicitur. Similia his apud Isaiam quoque leguntur: & ad sententiam huius praesentis Christi confirmationem facit exemplum diuitis epulonis in Euangelio, vnà cum graui admonitione, qua omnes homines, eos in primis qui sub eius aduentum viuent, Dominus instruet, dicens: Cauete vobis, ne quando grauentur corda vestra crapula & ebrietate, ac curis huius vitae, & repente vobis superueniat dies ille, &c. Nam vt hoc quoque addam, quanta fierent ad eleemosynas tam publicas quam priuatas accessio, si omnes homines in pauperes Christi conferrent, quae vulgo intemperantia, luxu, prodigalitate turpiter dissipantur. Annon ergo qui id faciunt, digni sunt, vt ad ignem aeternum cum diabolo & angelis eius ablegentur?
units.tr: Third, condemned here too are the prodigals, who foolishly and uselessly squander and waste the wealth the Lord has given, so that through it God is neither worshipped nor the neighbour improved or relieved in his need. Among them are those who spend immoderately on mad buildings, pulling down and building without necessity; to use the poet's words, they change square into round. Those should be counted who take pride in sumptuous furnishings, indulge in luxurious clothing, excessive cups and drunkenness, and drink through day and night. They not only forget the thanks owed to God for the fruits received, but are utterly tight-fisted and squalid towards Christ's poor and needy, whom they allow to hunger, thirst, freeze and wander as exiles. The number of such people today is huge, and they will never escape the Lord's judgement. For everywhere we meet famished people who scarcely sustain life by hard manual labour, and who cannot even find an opportunity to work by which they might honestly feed themselves. How many women, barely relieved from childbirth, lie down without wholesome food or drink that would serve new mothers well? How many beg for necessary food and do not find enough for their needs? All of these, content with little and cheap food and modest drink, would make themselves pleasing to God and to you if they obtained such things from you. But it often happens that those who do not mind consuming the fruits in immoderate luxury, shamefully spilling wine so that the months, seats and dining rooms themselves are drenched, forcing companions who have already drunk enough to drink more, are harsh and hard towards the poor, towards women in childbirth and the needy. You could more easily wring water from pumice than get a cup of wine or a crumb of bread from them. These are the people of whom Amos writes: "Woe to the secure in Zion and to those who trust in the mountain of Samaria, who put far off the evil day, who lie on ivory beds, stretched out on their couches; who eat lambs from the flock and fat calves from the stall, who sing to the harp, who drink wine from bowls and anoint themselves with the finest ointments, and are not grieved over the affliction of Joseph." Similar things are read in Isaiah too. The example of the rich glutton in the Gospel confirms Christ's teaching here, together with the grave warning by which the Lord instructs all people, especially those who live at his coming: "Take heed to yourselves, lest your hearts be weighed down with carousing and drunkenness and the cares of this life, and that day come upon you suddenly," etc. And, to add this as well, how great an addition would be made to alms, both public and private, if all people gave to Christ's poor what is now shamefully squandered on intemperance, luxury and prodigality. Are not those who do this worthy to be sent away to eternal fire with the devil and his angels?

units.la: Quarto damnantur eadem sententia, qui donationes ab alijs pie factas, vt ex his Ecclesiae, Scholae, Xenodochia siue hospitalia, Eleemosynae publica aut priuata instituantur & conferuntur, intercipiunt, vt vel fibijpsis vendicent, vel in vsus alios conuertant. Vt enim olim ad tabernaculi extructionem donaria conferebant principes tribuum, alij item viri honesti & multi etiam ex plebe, ita olim in primitiua Ecclesia, crescente numero pauperum quoque, pecunias suas liberaliter contribuerunt pij, vt ceu publico aerario facto, ex eo illi alerentur, & Ecclesia necessarijs subsidijs non deficiteretur: Ita posteris temporibus idem factum esse constat, & de multorum principum & illustrium hominum liberalitate adhuc hodie testantur Ecclesiae multa Cathedrales, Collegia, Coenobia, quae olim Scholis & iuuentutis institutioni seruierunt, & hodie in multis locis, pristino aut veteri vsui restituta sunt. Non possumus autem dubitare, quin in suas rationes adscripserit Christus omnes eiusmodi donationes, neque aliam rationem excogitari posse, qua nobis facilius &
units.tr: Fourth, condemned by the same sentence are those who intercept gifts piously made by others, which were meant to establish and support churches, schools, hospices (xenodochia), and public or private almsgiving, and who claim them for themselves or turn them to other uses. Just as the princes of the tribes once brought offerings for the building of the tabernacle, and other honourable men and many also from the common people did likewise, so in the early Church, as the number of the poor grew, the pious contributed their money generously, so that a kind of public treasury was formed from which the poor would be fed and the Church would not lack necessary support. It is clear that the same happened in later times, and the many cathedrals, colleges and monasteries which once served schools and the instruction of youth, and which in many places have today been restored to their earlier or original use, still bear witness to the generosity of many princes and illustrious men. We cannot doubt that Christ counts all such gifts to his own account, and that no other way can be devised by which we may more easily and more surely make friends from the mammon of unrighteousness, who will receive us into everlasting dwellings when we fail. For the Church consists of the living members of Christ's body, and the schools are its seedbeds, in which children are educated and trained, to succeed the elders when they have departed this life, lest the Church ever be left orphaned or widowed, or become like scattered sheep, as the Israelites once were when God complained of them: "My sheep were scattered from their shepherd and became food for every beast of the field. My flock wandered over all the mountains and every high hill; my flock was scattered over all the face of the earth, and there is no one who seeks them," etc. As for the poor who are supported from public or private bequests in hospices, colleges or leper houses, does not the Son of God testify, clearer than light, both elsewhere and in the present discourse, that whatever is done to them is done to himself?

units.la: Mich. 6. Prodigi abligurItores, fastuosi, &c. lius & compendiosius ex Mammone iniquitatis possimus amicos parare, qui nos olim cum defecerimus recipiant in tabernacula aeterna. Ecclesia enim ex viuis corporis Christi membris constant, illarum seminaria sunt Scholae, in quibus a pueris educantur & instituuntur, qui aliquando senioribus hac vita defunctis in ministerio succedant, ne aliquando Ecclesia orphana aut viduae sint, aut sint instar ouium dispersarum, vt olim Israelitae erant, cum de illis quereretur Deus: Et rarunt oues meae ab sua pastore, fuerunt, et cibus omni bestia agri. Errauit grex meus in omnibus montibus, & in omni colle excelso, & in omni superficie terra dispersus est grex meus, nec est qui quaerat, &c. Quoad pauperes vero, qui vel in Xenodochijs, vel in Collegijs, vel Leprosarijs ex electionis publicis aut priuatis aluntur, annon Dei Filius tum alibi, tum in praesenti tractatione luce clarius testatur, sibi fieri quicquid illis fit?
units.tr: Mic. 6. Prodigal spendthrifts, proud men, etc. More easily and more cheaply we can make friends for ourselves from the mammon of unrighteousness, who will receive us into everlasting dwellings when we fail. For the Church is made up of the living members of Christ's body, and the seminaries of these members are the schools, in which boys are brought up and trained, so that in time they may succeed the elders who have departed this life in the ministry. This keeps the Church from becoming orphaned or widowed, or like sheep scattered abroad, as the Israelites once were, when God complained of them: "My sheep were scattered because there was no shepherd, and they became food for every beast of the field. My flock wandered through all the mountains and every high hill; my flock was scattered over the whole face of the earth, and there was no one to seek them out," and so on. As for the poor, who are supported in almshouses, colleges or leper hospitals from public or private endowments, does not the Son of God testify, as clearly as light, both elsewhere and in the present passage, that whatever is done for them is done to himself?

units.la: Quocunque ergo Ecclesiarum opes, Collegiorum & coenobiorum redditus a maioribus & pijs principibus aut bonestis viris legatos intercipiunt, & authores sunt sua auaritia & rapacitate, vt scho le & in his studiorum bonorum cursus & morum disciplina sancta impediatur, pauperes & egeni ad famem redigantur, de hiis graues poenas sumet Dominus in illo die. Grauior tamen illorum culpa est, qui stipendia ministrorum Verbi debita rapiunt & sibi vendicant, quae causa est, quod doctri-na & praedicatione Verbi sublata, fames illa in Ecclesijs oboritur, quam apud Amos minatur Ifaudiendi verbi Dei, quae fames cum tristi & horribili conscientiarum carnificina coniuncta est, quam Deus ne in hoc quidem seculo inultam abire sinit. Huius ergo sedulo meminerint Praesules, qui imperium in Ecclesias sibi vendicaunt, qui fidos & doctos Verbi praecones eijciunt, qui facrile-gia audacia ex Xenodochijs dicescunt, & rationibus iniquis & fraudulentis magistratibus impo-nunt, & ab his destinata bona in alienos vsus transferunt. Vt enim haec facinora Deus aestimetexempla Giezi, Ananiae & Saphyrae docent, in primis auste Iudae proditoris, qui cum pecunia im-pie & male quaesita, vitam quoque infelice turpiter amisit. Qui ergo horum vestigijs insistunt, nun-quam effugient vindices Dei oculos & manus in illo die, quando manifestabuntur occulta cordium. Etenim omnium est de suo largiri, vt verus Dei cultus conseruetur, Scholae aperiantur, pauperi-bus prospiciatur. Qua ergo ratio eos excusabit, qui ab alijs donata auferunt?
units.tr: Therefore, wherever those who divert the wealth of churches and the revenues of colleges and monasteries, bequeathed by our ancestors, pious princes or upright men, become the agents of their own greed and rapacity, so that schools, the course of good studies and the holy discipline of morals are hindered, and the poor and needy are reduced to hunger, the Lord will exact severe punishment from them on that day. Yet the guilt of those is greater who seize and claim for themselves the stipends owed to the ministers of the Word. The result is that, once teaching and preaching of the Word are removed, that famine of hearing the word of God arises in the churches which Amos threatens, a famine joined with the sad and horrible torture of consciences, which God does not allow to go unpunished even in this age. Let the prelates who claim dominion over the churches, who cast out faithful and learned heralds of the Word, who boldly tear sacred property from almshouses, and who impose unjust and fraudulent accounts on the magistrates and divert the goods designated for these purposes to other uses, take careful note of this. For the examples of Gehazi, Ananias and Sapphira show how God judges such crimes, and above all the example of Judas the traitor, who, having lost his life wickedly along with money impiously and wrongly gained, also perished in an unhappy and shameful way. Therefore those who tread in their footsteps will never escape the eyes and hands of God's avengers on that day, when the secrets of hearts will be revealed. For it is the duty of everyone to give from what is his own, so that true worship of God may be preserved, schools may be opened, and the poor may be provided for. By what reasoning, then, will those excuse themselves who take away what others have given?

units.la: Quinto damnantur a Christo mercenarij Cares & iniqui milites, qui belli non necessarijsmultos ad egestatem redigunt, dum exteris principibus operam suam locant, & contra Dei prace-ptum accipiunt pecuniam, vt percutiant innocentem sanguinem. Innocens quidem coram Dei tri-bunali nemo mortalium est: & iusto iudicio Deus bellis affligit eos, qui pace laeta abutuntur. In-nocens autem militum mercenariorum respectu dicitur, in quem illis nullum ius est, & qui vel ca-co odio & iniusta vindicta cupiditate, vel stipendij & praeda ipse illecti, eos bello petunt, qui nulla iniuria ipsos affecerunt. Quam vero aliam causam praetexere volent, qui exterorum regum & principum castra secuti ijs seruiunt, qui ipsis nullum mandandi ius habherent, nisi hoc ipsi illis face-rent. Hodie quidem hic quaestus honestissimus habetur, si vt lanij ad mactandas pecudes, ita isti ad iugulandos homines se conducifinant. At qui Christo nomen dedit, non sui iuris est, vt operam suam cuius ad quiduis locare possit. Pretio empti estis (scribit Paulus Corinthijs) ne estote serui hominum. At qui operam suam locant ad iniustas cedes, rapinas, incendia, stupra, agrorum popu-lationes, vrbium excidia, nonne hi diaboli serui sunt, qui omnium horum author est? Sed vnum quaero, quae fronte coram hoc iudice consistent, qui vt ipsum in membris suis diligamus, & dilectio nem hanc omni officiorum genere testemur, requirit: ipsum nimirum alendo, potando, amicienda, consolando, qui ipsi, dum bella non necessaria sequuntur, hiis omnia contraria faciunt? Enimueroin bellis segetes conculcantur, fruges vastantur, vineae excinduntur, pecudes abiguntur & ma-nentur, vrbes & pagi incenduntur, diruuntur, solo aequantur: corpora deniq; hominum non modo caeduntur & occiduntur, verumetiam contumeliose violantur, loca sacra & prophana diruuntur, & ne te nplus quidem parcitur, spoliantur ca nobia, hospitalia publica, nosodochia & reliqua huius fi-m lis charitati consecrata loca dissipantur: neq; vlla lingua exponere potest, quaecunq; in bellis eiusmodi solent fieri: & fatebuntur milites ipsi nunquam de illis tantum dici posse, quin plura dicen-da supersint. Scio non deesse multa quod respondeant, & quo se excusent. Sed dicant illi quod vtlint, veruntamen Iudex Christus sententiam, quam in carne hac mortali adhuc viuens recitauit, nunquam mutabit: Et qui sibi triumphos gloriosos & opes immensas pollicentur, in ignem aeternum abibunt, vt ibi colligantur cum omnibus, qui posuerunt terrorem suum in terra viuentium,
units.tr: Fifthly, Christ condemns the mercenary soldiers, the Carians, and the wicked soldiers who, without any necessity of war, reduce many people to poverty while they hire out their services to foreign princes and, contrary to God's command, take money to shed innocent blood. Indeed, no mortal is innocent before the judgment seat of God, and by a just judgment God afflicts with wars those who abuse a happy peace. But the innocent are spoken of in relation to mercenary soldiers, meaning those against whom they have no right, and whom they attack in war, either out of blind hatred and a desire for unjust revenge, or lured themselves by pay and plunder, though those people have done them no injury. What other cause will those men be able to plead who follow the camps of foreign kings and princes and serve those who have no right to command them, unless they themselves were to do so? Today this trade is considered most honourable, if these men hire themselves out to slaughter human beings just as butchers do to slaughter cattle. But he who has given his name to Christ is not free to hire out his services to anyone at all. "You were bought with a price," Paul writes to the Corinthians; "do not become slaves of men" (1 Cor. 7). Yet those who hire out their services for unjust slaughters, plunderings, arson, rapes, the laying waste of fields, and the destruction of cities, are they not servants of the devil, who is the author of all these things? But I ask one thing: with what face will they stand before this Judge, who requires that we love him in his members, and that we bear witness to this love by every kind of duty, namely by feeding him, giving him drink, clothing him and comforting him, when they, by following unnecessary wars, do the opposite of all these things? Indeed, in wars the crops are trampled, the fruits laid waste, the vineyards uprooted, the cattle driven off and seized, the cities and villages set on fire, pulled down and levelled with the ground. Finally, the bodies of human beings are not only cut down and killed, but also shamefully violated; sacred and profane places are destroyed, and not even temples are spared; monasteries are plundered, public hospitals, hospices for the sick and other places dedicated to this kind of charity are scattered. No tongue can describe all that is usually done in wars of this kind, and the soldiers themselves will confess that one could never say so much about these things that more would not remain to be said. I know that they have many things to answer and many excuses by which to defend themselves. But let them say what they like: nevertheless Christ the Judge will never change the sentence that he pronounced while still living in this mortal flesh. Those who promise themselves glorious triumphs and immense wealth will go into eternal fire, to be gathered there with all who have set their terror in the land of the living.

units.la: Ezech.22.cap.
units.tr: Ezech.22.cap.

units.la: Sexto, cum suijpsius captiui quoq; meminerit Christus, damnantur hoc etiam loco, quotquot captiuos non consolantur, vel aegrotos & infirmos non amice inuisunt, sed in squallore suo priore sinunt. Eos quide qui in magistratu constituti leges & iura publica administrant, vocatio sua non finit semper misericordiae aut charitatis rationem habere, qualem fontes habeti velint: sed vt secundum leges a Deo datas malum e medio auferant, necesse est: nec idcirco vereri debent, ne alicuius sanguinis reatu polluant. Notum est enim quod in Lege aliquoties repetitur, vbi capitales poenae hominibus maleficis & facinorosis denuntiantur: Sanguis eorum sit super eos. Cui illud Salomonis Prou.17. & 24. consentit, qui Deo aeque exosum dicit eum, qui absoluit sceleratum, quam eum, qui condemnat innocentem. Interim non exuatur communis humanitatis sensus, & quoties ducuntur miseri, qui quoduis supplicium meruerunt, cogitemus, quanta sit humanae naturae infirmitas, quando quod ille nunc accidit, in quosuis potest cadere, quos Deus non peculiari gratia pro sequitur. Magistratus ita captiuis praesent diligenter humanitatis officia, ne crudeles fiant, dum seueri aut iusti haberi volunt: quod fere hypocritis accidit. Et vt animae illorum seruentur, cura sit, tunc quoq; quando poenas sceleribus suis debitas exoluunt. Docet hoc proprio exemplo Christus Dominus, quando latronem in cruce ad se conuersum in gratiam recepit, & eundem Paradisi mu-nicipem fecit. Quae vero infirmis & morbo confectis debeantur officia, ex Samaritani parabola petant pij, in qua prolixe haec explicantur.
units.tr: Sixthly, since Christ also remembered those who are captive in their own persons, all who do not comfort prisoners, or who do not kindly visit the sick and the weak, but leave them in their former squalor, are condemned in this passage as well. As for those who are placed in the magistracy and administer the laws and public rights, their calling does not always allow them to take account of mercy or charity in the way the Papists would have them do. Rather, they must remove evil from the midst according to the laws given by God, and they need not fear to be polluted by the guilt of any blood. For it is well known that it is repeated several times in the Law, where capital punishments are announced against wicked and criminal men: "Let their blood be upon them." To this agrees the saying of Solomon in Prov. 17 and 24, who says that the one who acquits the guilty is as much an abomination to God as the one who condemns the innocent. Meanwhile, let the sense of common humanity not be stripped away, and whenever wretched men are led away who have deserved any punishment, let us reflect how great the weakness of human nature is, since what has now befallen him can fall upon anyone whom God does not follow with his special grace. Magistrates should diligently show the offices of humanity to prisoners, lest they become cruel while they wish to be thought stern or just, which commonly happens to hypocrites. And so that their souls may be saved, let there be care for them even when they are paying the penalties owed to their crimes. The Lord Christ himself teaches this by his own example, when he received into grace the thief who turned to him on the cross and made him a fellow citizen of Paradise. As for the duties owed to the weak and the sick worn down by disease, let the godly seek them from the parable of the Good Samaritan, in which these things are explained at length.

units.la: Scio inueniri delicatiores aliquos Christianos, & fortasse Theologos quoq; nonnullos, qui in morbis contagiosis, pestilentia in primis, fugam hominibus Christianis ita permissam esse contendunt, vt eos, qui hominem ex peste vel alio morbo contagioso decumbentem inuisunt, Deum tentare, & sibi ipsis propriae necis authores esse dicant. De contagio philosophice non libet disputare, sed illud ad medicorum scholas remitto: mihi cum Christianis hominibus res est, qui omnia per Dei prouidentiam gubernari & vnicuiq; mortalium finem dierum suorum a Deo praefinitum esse norunt: qui item firmiter credunt eum, qui ignis vim continere potuit, ne Danielis socijs in fornace ardentem conijcis, noceret, & Danielem inter leones feruare, non minus contagia morborum, quam alia regere posse, neque aliquid esse in rerum natura, quod temere grassetur. Scimus praeterea a Deo immitti pestilentias, & Dei sagittas & tela esse, quae & noctu & interdiu, nunquam autem incerto impetu volant. Itaque in abdito Excelsi sedemus, sub vmbra alarum Omnipotentis. Et quia hic iubet aegrotantes inuisere ac consolari, & beatos pronunciat omnes, qui id faciunt, non solum temerarios & praecipites nimium, verumetiam impios dicimus eos, qui morbo (vt ipsi aiunt) contagioso affectus est. Deum tentari dicunt, si quis ad eos accedit, qui morbo (vt ipsi aiunt) contagioso affectus est. Obiiciunt illi ceu Aiacis clypeum, Legem Dei de leprosis, qui segregari debuerunt. At hanc typicam partim, partim politicam fuisse constat. Deinde ea nihil derogat charitatis officijs. Nam segregare iubebat lepra infectos, non autem negligere. Ideo Christus ipse illos tangere dignatus est, & fere pra aliis suo fauore completi. Nemo igitur sibi ipsi delitias faciat, dum timori ignauo indulget, sed singuli quid proximo laboranti debeatur, considerent. Rata enim erit Domini IESV CHRISTI ad vltimum iudicium venientis sententia: Abite maledicti in ignem aeternum, qui paratus est diabolo & angelis eius: quia aegrotus eram, & non venistis ad me, &c.
units.tr: I know that some more fastidious Christians, and perhaps some theologians too, are to be found who contend that in contagious diseases, above all in plague, flight is so permitted to Christian people that they say those who visit a man lying ill with the plague or another contagious disease tempt God and become the authors of their own death. I do not wish to dispute about contagion in a philosophical way; I refer that matter to the schools of the physicians. My concern is with Christian people, who know that all things are governed by God's providence, and that the end of each mortal's days has been determined in advance by God; who likewise firmly believe that he who was able to restrain the power of fire, so that it did not harm Daniel's companions thrown into the burning furnace, and who preserved Daniel among the lions, can govern the contagions of diseases no less than other things, and that there is nothing in nature which rages at random. Moreover, we know that pestilences are sent by God, and that they are God's arrows and weapons, which fly both by night and by day, yet never with an uncertain stroke. Therefore we sit "in the secret place of the Most High, under the shadow of the Almighty." And since Christ here commands us to visit and comfort the sick, and pronounces blessed all who do so, we say that those who shun the man who is infected (as they call it) with a contagious disease are not only rash and excessively headlong, but even impious. They say that God is tempted if anyone approaches one who is affected (as they call it) by a contagious disease. They throw at them, as if it were Ajax's shield, the law of God concerning lepers, who were to be segregated. But it is clear that this law was partly typical and partly political. Moreover, it takes nothing away from the duties of charity, for it commanded that those infected with leprosy be separated, not that they be neglected. For this reason Christ himself deigned to touch them, and was almost more than others filled with favour towards them. Let no one therefore indulge himself in pleasures while he yields to cowardly fear, but let each consider what is owed to a suffering neighbour. For the sentence of the Lord Jesus Christ, who is to come to the last judgment, will stand: "Depart, you cursed, into eternal fire, prepared for the devil and his angels; for I was sick, and you did not come to me," etc.

units.la: Possent his multi alij connumerari, qui in misericordiae & dilectionis leges peccant: sed ex ijs quae dicta sunt, de reliquis facile iudicabunt pij. Omnium vero hic nobis vsus est: vt qui vel in Repub. vel Ecclesia rebus praesident, pro virili curent, vt charitas regnet inter eos, quos ipsorum fidei Deus credidit, e contra homines iniustos, auaros, raptores, impuros arceant & Verbi Dei sacra praedicatione atque bonarum legum disciplina in ordinem cogant, ne quiduis pro sua libidine faciant. Nec enim ij soli peccant, qui iniurias faciunt, verumetiam qui eas non prohibent cum possunt. Deinde in hoc speculo sese contemplentur singuli, atque vitam moresque suos examinent: vt nent: ut si quid hactenus peccarunt, sedulo emendent & apud Deum culpam deprecentur, dum tempus gratiæ est. Qui vero hactenus aliorum iniurijs expositi fuerunt, & adhuc se a plerisq; negligi vident, cogitent hanc in ipsis IESV CHRIS T I fortem esse, & in ferenda cruce patientes sint: quando audiunt Filio Dei fieri quod ipsis fit. Dabit is vires, ut sint ferendo, neq; supra vires tentari sinet. Omnium vero iudex & remunerator apparebit iustus & fidelis.
units.tr: Many others could be counted among those who sin against the laws of mercy and love, but from what has been said the godly will easily judge about the rest. Here the use of all this for us is this: that those who preside over affairs either in the commonwealth or in the Church should, as far as they can, take care that charity reigns among those whom God has entrusted to their faith; on the other hand, they should keep out unjust, greedy, rapacious and impure men, and bring them into order by the sacred preaching of God's Word and by the discipline of good laws, so that they do nothing at their own whim. For those sin not only who commit injuries, but also those who do not forbid them when they are able to. Then let each one look at himself in this mirror and examine his life and morals, so that if he has sinned up to now, he may diligently amend it and beg pardon for his fault before God, while there is still time of grace. But those who until now have been exposed to the injuries of others, and who see that they are still neglected by most people, let them think that this is their lot in Jesus Christ, and let them be patient in bearing the cross, since they hear that what is done to them is done to the Son of God. He will give them strength to endure, and will not allow them to be tempted beyond their strength. But the judge and rewarder of all will appear just and faithful.

units.la: Quid vero hac Filij Dei sententia, quouis fulmine terribiliori audita respondebunt hypocritæ, qui ad sinistram stabunt? Domine (inquient) quando te vidimus esurientem aut sitientem, aut hospitem, aut nudum, aut ægrotum, aut in carcere, & non ministrauimus tibi? Non agnoscunt culpam. Etenim ut pij & electi non sidunt suis operibus, nec tam humiliter de IESV CHRISTO sentiunt, ut de eo se aliquid mereri posse existiment: ita hypocritarum fiducia omnis in propriis ipsorum operibus sita est: opera vero bona externi cultus & ceremoniarum splendore metiuntur. In his ergo quia toti occupantur, tanti etiam ea faciunt, ut je plus fecisse putent quam vnquam fecerint. Itaq; verba hæc non videntur abs; stomacho proferri. Quasi diceret: Accusas me negleéti officij, quasi te esurientem, sitientem, algentem, captiuum, ægrotum neglexerimus. Quia vero non recordamur, nos te vnquam in eiusmodi necessitate vidisse, iniuriam nobis facis. Enimuero si talem vidissemus potius genium nostrum defraudare & oculi pupillam offendere voluissemus, quam nostro deesse officio. Ita solent hypocritæ fibijpsis nihil non polliceri de sua pietate. Sed non mouetur eiusmodi verborum fuco Deus. Et in præsenti respondebit Christus: Amen dico vobis, quatenus non fecistis vni ex istis minimis, nec mihi fecistis. Ergo semper verum & ratum est in pauperibus ipsum Christum negligi. Non intelligunt hoc hypocritæ impij, quia non agnoscunt, in quam sublimem dignitatem inopes Deus euexerit, quos Filio suo æquales fecit. Calua est ergo & inutilis excusatio omnis quam prætexunt, qui illis negletis circa alia occupantur, quæ Deus nusquam mandauit.
units.tr: But what will the hypocrites answer to this sentence of the Son of God, heard with a thunderclap more terrible than any other, those who will stand on the left? "Lord," they will say, "when did we see you hungry or thirsty, or a stranger, or naked, or sick, or in prison, and did not minister to you?" They do not acknowledge their fault. For just as the godly and the elect do not rely on their own works, nor think so humbly of Jesus Christ that they suppose they can merit anything from him, so the whole confidence of the hypocrites rests on their own works; and they measure good works by the splendour of outward worship and ceremonies. Because they are wholly taken up with these, they think so highly of them that they believe they have done more than they ever did. So these words do not seem to be spoken in anger. It is as if he said: "You accuse me of neglecting duty, as if we had neglected you when you were hungry, thirsty, cold, captive, or sick. But since we do not remember ever seeing you in such need, you do us an injustice. Indeed, if we had seen you in such a state, we would rather have defrauded our own genius and offended the pupil of our eye than have failed in our duty." This is how hypocrites are wont to promise themselves everything concerning their own piety. But God is not moved by the gloss of such words. And now Christ will answer: "Truly I say to you, inasmuch as you did not do it to one of these least, you did not do it to me." Therefore it is always true and settled that Christ himself is neglected in the poor. The wicked hypocrites do not understand this, because they do not recognise to what lofty dignity God has raised the needy, whom he has made equal to his Son. So every excuse they put forward is empty and worthless, those who, while neglecting these, are occupied with other things that God has nowhere commanded.

units.la: Sequitur huius loci conclusio, quæ simul finem & postremum actum huius seculi continet. Nam dicit Dominus: Et abibunt illi in supplicium æternum, iusti vero in vitam æternam. Asseritur hic postremus symboli Apostolici articulus, quo vitam æternam confitemur, quæ huius mortalis vita curriculum secutura sit. Negant illam, imo scurriliter ridet homines Epicurei, & quæstiones mouent non minus impias quam vanas, quibus in dubiu vocent, quæcunq; de æterna vita pie dicuntur & creduntur. Quærunt enim quomodo anima abseq; interitu perpetuis cruciatibus dolent. Quomodo corpora in sempiternis supplicijs durare possint. Et alia eius generis, quorum D. Augustinus in libro de Ciuitate Dei meminit contra gentes & infideles disputans. Atqui in rerum natura extant exempla, quæ his possunt fidem facere. Et idem Pater Salamandram producit in medijs ignibus viuentem, & pauonis carnem cœstam siue assam in aliquot menses incorruptam a putredine conseruari scribit. Cur ergo de ijs dubitemus, quæ de vita æterna a prophetis & apostolis, imo ab ipso Dei Filio tam grauiter & constanter in vtroq; Testamento asseuerantur: & fine quibus Dei iustitia non posset consistere, ut alibi prolixe demonstrauimus. Credamus ergo firmiter esse vitam æternam, ad quam omnes prodibunt, qui bona fecerunt, ad resurrectionem vitæ: qui vero mala egerint, ad resurrectionem condemnationis. Initio quidem mox a resurrectione separabit in dex omnes homines, sicut pastor separat agnos ab hædis (vt nuper diximus) & hos quidem ad sinistram, illos vero ad dexteram statuet. Deinde sententiam finalem pronunciabit, quam hactenus audiuimus. Sequetur mox biuiu, in quo boni a malis, pij ab impijs, electi a reprobis ita separabuntur, ut nulla posthac conuentio aut permixtio sperari possit. Et vt nulla lingua neq; vox ineffabilem illam beatitatem electorum eloqui poterit, quam oculus non vidit, neq; auris audiuit: ita omnem sensum & intellectum excedet dolor & cruciatus ille, quo reprobi apud inferos quoad corpus & animam æternum cruciabuntur. Loci scripturæ sacræ passim occurrunt, qui beatorum gaudia & damnatorum supplicia abunde describunt. Nobis vnus hic locus sufficiat, ut fide vera & sancto charitatis studio accensi ita viuamus, ut huius vitæ curriculum emensi, olim quoq; in lata electorum resurrectione in consp ectu Filij Dei IESV CHRIS T I ad eius dextram statuamur, & cum illo ingrediamur ad regni sui æterni possessionem, quod ille præparauit, vere diligentibus se: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Now follows the conclusion of this passage, which contains both the end and the final act of this age. For the Lord says: "And they will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life." Here is asserted the last article of the Apostles' Creed, in which we confess the eternal life that is to follow the course of this mortal life. The Epicureans deny it, or rather mock it with buffoonery, and raise questions no less impious than vain, by which they call into doubt whatever is piously said and believed about eternal life. For they ask how the soul can suffer perpetual torments without perishing, and how bodies can endure in everlasting punishments; and other questions of this kind, which Augustine recalls in his book on the City of God, disputing against the pagans and unbelievers. Yet there are examples in nature that can give credit to these things. The same Father also reports the salamander living in the midst of fires, and writes that the flesh of a peacock, whether cooked or roasted, has been preserved uncorrupted from putrefaction for some months. Why then should we doubt those things about eternal life which the prophets and apostles, indeed the Son of God himself, so gravely and constantly affirm in both Testaments, and without which God's justice could not stand, as we have shown at length elsewhere? Let us therefore firmly believe that there is eternal life, to which all shall come forth who have done good, to the resurrection of life, but those who have done evil, to the resurrection of condemnation. At first, immediately after the resurrection, the Judge will separate all men as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats (as we said recently), and will set the one on the left, the others on the right. Then he will pronounce the final sentence, which we have heard hitherto. Next will follow an eternal life, in which the good will be separated from the evil, the godly from the ungodly, the elect from the reprobate, so that no later association or mixing can be hoped for. And just as no tongue or voice will be able to express that ineffable blessedness of the elect, which eye has not seen nor ear heard, so that pain and torment, by which the reprobate will be tormented eternally in body and soul in hell, will exceed all sense and understanding. Passages of Holy Scripture occur everywhere that describe abundantly the joys of the blessed and the punishments of the damned. For us this one passage is enough, so that, kindled with true faith and holy zeal for love, we may so live that, having finished the course of this life, we may also one day, at the broad resurrection of the elect, in the sight of the Son of God Jesus Christ, be set at his right hand, and enter with him into the possession of his eternal kingdom, which he has prepared for those who truly love him; to whom be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: AMICO LECTORI RODOLPHUS GVALTHERUS S.
units.tr: TO THE FRIENDLY READER, RUDOLPH GWALTHER, GREETING

units.la: Quoniam in passionis & mortis Dominicae historiam in tribus Evangeliis, quæ annis superioribus expositimus, Homilias dedimus prolixiores, neque quam opus erit eadem nunc repetere, Itaque in Matthaeo breuitati studebimus, prima solummodo rerum Capita perstrinxisse, & homiliarum syluulas dedisse contenti. Nos ingenua & bona fide damus amice Lector, quod dedit Dominus. Tu his pro tuo candore fruitor, & si copiosiora cupis, aliunde petito. Vale.
units.tr: Since in the three Gospels that we expounded in previous years I gave fairly lengthy homilies on the history of the Lord's passion and death, and since it is not necessary to repeat the same material now, I have decided in Matthew to aim for brevity: I have been content to touch only on the main headings of the events and to offer short sketches of the homilies. We give you, friendly reader, in honest and good faith, what the Lord has given us. Enjoy these things with your usual candour, and if you want fuller treatment, seek it elsewhere. Farewell.

units.la: CAPVT XXVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVI.

units.la: HOMILIA CCXCII.
units.tr: HOMILY CCXCII.

units.la: ET factum est cum finisseт Iesus omnes istos sermones, dixit discipulis suis: Scitis intra duos dies Pascha fore, & Filium hominis tradendum vt crucifigatur. Tunc coacti sunt principes sacerdotum & Scribæ & seniores populi in aulam pontificis maximi, qui dicebatur Caiapha. Et simul consultarunt, vt Iesum dolo præhenderent, & occiderent. Dicebant autem non in festo, ne tumultus fiat in populo.
units.tr: And it came to pass, when Jesus had finished all these sayings, that he said to his disciples: You know that after two days the Passover is coming, and the Son of man is to be handed over to be crucified. Then the chief priests and the scribes and the elders of the people were gathered together into the palace of the high priest, who was called Caiaphas. And they took counsel together how they might seize Jesus by craft and kill him. But they said, "Not during the feast, lest there be a tumult among the people."

units.la: ON temere Christiana Ecclesia hunc morem recepit, vt quamuis Euangelium IESV CHRISTI assidue prædicetur, summatim tamen quotannis exponatur vniuersa passionis & mortis Dominicae historia. Nec pigere debet homines Christianos huic aliquot horas impendere: quandoquidem nulla alia historia cognitu vtilior & magis necessaria est. Comprehendit enim quæcunque ad veram & salutarem Dei cognitionem pertinent: neque inter huius operis vllum aliud est, in quo eius attributa, qualia sunt, Iustitia, Bonitas, Veritas, Sapientia, Omnipotentia, & quæ his connexa sunt, euidentius perspici possint. Accedunt his duo alia, ad quæ singulas partes historiæ, seu ad scopum propositum, debent dirigi.
units.tr: It is not without good reason that the Christian Church has adopted the custom of setting out, once a year in summary form, the whole history of the Lord's passion and death, even though the Gospel of Jesus Christ is preached constantly. Christian people should not begrudge spending a few hours on it, since no other history is more useful or more necessary to know. For it contains everything that pertains to the true and saving knowledge of God, and there is no other part of this work in which his attributes, such as justice, goodness, truth, wisdom and omnipotence, and whatever is connected with them, can be seen more clearly. To these two further things must be added, to which the individual parts of the history, or the purpose proposed, ought to be directed.

units.la: Primum est humani generis redemptio, quæ aliter non poterat perfici, & cuius ergo Dei Filius in mundum venerat. Etenim sumus omnes peccatores: & quia peccatum noxa capitalis est, sine sanguine non expiatur. Non proderat autem sanguis pecudum, quia nullum habent nobiscum naturæ communionem. Neque etiam profuisset si pauculi aliquot vel plures pro omnibus aliis piacula fuissent. Itaque æterno consilio prædinatus fuit æternus Dei Filius, qui homo & frater noster factus, peccata totius mundi in se transferret, & suo sanguine expiaret. Id vero in hunc finem obseruari debet, vt sciamus historiam hanc ad nos pertinere: & cum hæc propter nos facta sint, nos eorundem esse authores & reos. Ne ergo quasi nos extra omnem culpam simus, circa Iudam, Caiaphan, Pilatum, Herodem, milites & alios, qui hic præ aliis peccarunt, occupemur: sed singuli causas mortis Christi in seipsis quærant: & his cognitis conterantur: credant item se meritò Filij Dei redemptos esse, & in posterum studeant sanctitati & innocentiæ.
units.tr: The first is the redemption of the human race, which could not otherwise be accomplished, and for the sake of which the Son of God had come into the world. For we are all sinners, and because sin is a capital offence, it is not expiated without blood. Yet the blood of beasts did not help, because they have no natural fellowship with us. Nor would it have profited if a few or even many sacrifices had been made for all others. Therefore the eternal Son of God was foreordained by an eternal counsel, so that he, made man and our brother, might take upon himself the sins of the whole world and expiate them with his own blood. This must be observed to this end: that we know this history pertains to us, and that since these things were done on our account, we are their authors and guilty parties. Therefore, lest we think ourselves free of all blame, let us not occupy ourselves with Judas, Caiaphas, Pilate, Herod, the soldiers and others who sinned here more than the rest; rather, let each one seek the causes of Christ's death within himself, and, having recognised them, be broken in heart. Let each also believe that he has rightly been redeemed by the Son of God, and in future strive for holiness and innocence.

units.la: Alterum est exemplum, quo nobis Christus præiuit. Hic enim passus est pro nobis (inquit Petrus) relinquens nobis exemplar, vt insequeremini vestigia ipsius. In hoc obseruanda, quæ piorum fors semper futura sit in mundo. Adhæc ad Christi imitationem præparemur. Requiritur hoc ab omnibus Christianis, quibus omnibus dicitur a Paulo: Imitatores mei estote, quemadmodum ego Christi sum. Obseruetur hic obedientia, quam Christus Patri præstitit, cui obediit vsque ad mortem, mortem autem crucis. Deinde patientia, qua aduersa quæuis superauit, & vt agnus non aperuit os suum. Constantia item, qua in finem vsque perseuerauit. Et inter hæc exemplum charitatis qua he-
units.tr: The second is the example which Christ has set before us. For he suffered for us, says Peter, leaving us an example that we should follow in his steps. Here we must observe what the lot of the pious will always be in the world. Moreover, let us be prepared to imitate Christ. This is required of all Christians, to whom Paul says: Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ. Let us observe the obedience which Christ rendered to the Father, to whom he was obedient even unto death, indeed the death of the cross. Then his patience, by which he overcame all adversities, and like a lamb did not open his mouth. Likewise his steadfastness, by which he persevered to the end. And among these, an example of love, by which he
1 Pet. 2.

units.la: 1. Cor. 11. qua hostes quoq; prosequuntur. Hæc nos imitari conuenit. Inter omnia autem nos consoletur, quod per crucem triumphauit & resurrexit ad vitam nouam. Per fidem enim & nos vincemus, modo resurgamus indies ad vitæ nouitatem. Roman. 6. &c. Hu præmissis ad historiam passionis Dominicæ accedemus, cuius causæ primo loco consideranda venient.
units.tr: 1 Cor. 11. by which he embraces even his enemies. It is fitting that we imitate these things. Above all, let us be comforted by the fact that through the cross he triumphed and rose again to a new life. For through faith we too shall conquer, provided we rise daily to newness of life. Rom. 6, etc. Having premised these things, we shall now come to the history of the Lord's passion, the causes of which must first be considered.

units.la: Prima & propria causa mortis IESV CHRISTI est bonitas siue amor Dei, quo (vt ipse apud Ioannem air) ita dilexit nos, vt Filium suum vnigenitum pro nobis traderet, vt omnis qui credit in eum, non pereat, sed habeat vitam æternam. Ea autem argumento constat, salutem nobis absq; omni nostro merito obtigisse. Nam si nos inspicias, odio, non amore digni eramus: cum natu ex peccatores simus & morte æterna digni. Debet hoc nos in fide confirmare. Cur enim de eius gratia dubitemus, qui ne Filio quidem vnigenito parcere voluit? Interim discamus Deum, qui ita dilexit nos, vicissim diligere, & huic nos & omnia nostra impendere.
units.tr: The first and proper cause of the death of Jesus Christ is the goodness, or love, of God, by which (as he himself says in John) he so loved us that he gave his only-begotten Son for us, so that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life. This is established by the argument that salvation has come to us entirely without any merit of our own. For if you look at us, we were deserving of hatred, not of love, since we are by nature sinners and worthy of eternal death. This ought to confirm us in faith. For why should we doubt his grace, who did not wish to spare even his only-begotten Son? Meanwhile let us learn to love in return the God who has so loved us, and to devote ourselves and all that is ours to him.

units.la: Cæterum causæ huic principali mortis Christi alia accedunt mediæ ex hominibus, qui non Dei decretum respexerunt, sed prauis affectibus ducti illum occidi curarunt. Et de his quidem diligenter scribitur, vt discamus, quid nobis cauendum sit, si in ipsum Dei Filium nolumus similiter peccare, & æternæ salutis iacturam facere. Appareat item, vt impij interdum non alia faciant, quàm quæ Deus fieri decreuit, nec tamen illius decretis excusentur.
units.tr: Besides this principal cause, there are also middle causes arising from men, who did not regard the decree of God but, driven by wicked desires, took care that he should be killed. These things are written about in detail so that we may learn what we must guard against, if we do not wish to sin likewise against the very Son of God and suffer the loss of eternal salvation. It also appears that the wicked sometimes do nothing other than what God decreed should be done, and yet are not excused by his decrees.

units.la: Ex his autem, qui humanis consiliis moti Christum occiderunt, primi prodeunt Sacerdotes cum Scribis & Senioribus populi, qui de illo occidendo consultarunt. Id vero mirum & stupendum videri poterat, cum illorum officij esset, populum Christo adducere. Nam legis & diuini cultus antistites erant. At legis sinis atq; scopus est Christus: cultus vero omnis sacrificijs & externis ritibus constabat, qui omnes ad Christum deducebant. Quid ergo absurdius dici poterat, quàm Christi hostes fieri eos, quorum neq; religio neq; vita sine illo constabat? Sed religio iam pridem extincta erat, & sacerdotum ordo suam stationem reliquerat.
