Distributio communionis cum Christo symbolum est. Manducatio fide opus esse docet, qua sola ille percipitur. Cauillantur haec multi, & rusticos, imo barbaros dicunt. Sed rustici fimus, modo Christi imitatores fimus. Nobis non sordet fabri Filius. Aduersarij nostri videant, ne ipsis idem quod Corinthijs obijci possit, quos Apostolus negauit Cenam Dominicam edere, cum a Christo traditum ritum mutauissent.
units.tr: But the rite handed down by Christ must be observed steadfastly, since it is without doubt the best and full of mysteries. For the Apostles delivered it to the churches as they received it from Christ (as appears from Paul). Let the celebration therefore be a public assembly, and let nothing be regarded as private, which the private Mass, that source of profit, entirely abolishes. Next, the Supper should not be celebrated without a holy sermon. For sacraments do not stand without the Word of God, since (as Augustine says) when the word is added to the element, a sacrament comes into being. And if you take away the word, it is just as if someone removed the seal from a written document. What then would be sealed by it? Indeed, if the Supper is celebrated without a preceding holy sermon, Christ himself is removed from his own Supper, and the faithful soul will have nothing of which to partake. Next, "Do this," says Christ, "in remembrance of me," that is, just as I have done for you as an example. But it seems a rustic thing if some common person handles the holy symbols with his hands, puts them to his mouth, and passes them to the neighbour sitting beside him. Yet under this rustic appearance lie profound mysteries. For, as we said recently, when the symbols are taken into our hands by the Lord's own command, he testifies that he wishes us to be his. The breaking of the bread and the pouring of the wine into the cup signify the confession of sins, namely that we are of the number of those who nailed the Son of God to the cross and poured out his blood. The distribution of the communion is a symbol of fellowship with Christ. The eating teaches that faith is needed, by which alone he is received. Many cavil at these things and call them rustic, even barbarous. But let us be rustic, provided we are imitators of Christ. The son of a craftsman is no shame to us. Let our opponents see that the same charge cannot be brought against them that could be brought against the Corinthians, whom the Apostle rebuked for not eating the Lord's Supper, since they had changed the rite handed down by Christ.

units.la: Praecipua vero cura nobis fit, vt quod Dominus tota hac actione nobis mandat, sedulo praestemus: Vt nimirum omnia fiant in suam memoriam, & mortem suam annuntiemus. Sub morte Resurrectio quoq; & Ascensio comprehenduntur, quibus nostra redemptio perficitur. Ideo ex veteri Ecclesia more Symboli Apostolici articuli recitantur, dum Cena peragitur. Recordatio autem eiusmodi sancitur, quae cum gratiarum actione coniuncta fit: nec verbis solis constat, sed animum, imo totum hominem requirit, vt illi vni viuamus, qui pro nobis mortuus est & resurrexit. Tam enim excellens est hoc beneficium Christi, vt huic celebrando nulla verba suffi-ciant, & propter carnis tarditatem perpetuis stimulis opus est. Quod propter eos obseruari debet, qui verbum internum & inspirationes nescio quas occultas fingunt, praedicationem autem externam & exercitia fidei externa vt superuacanea negligunt. Atqui Cena vsurpari debet donec venerit. Et recte olim Theodoretus monuit: Tunc demum non opus erit corporis signis, quando corpus ipsum apparebit. Huius memores faciamus officium, & ad hoc sedulo praeparemur. Soletur autem nos, quod eius memoriam celebramus, qui nos videt, nobis item suo Spiritu & virtute adest: Caeterum vt a benedictione & gratiarum actione Cenam mysticam exorsus est Dominus, ita eandem cum hymno finiuit, quem vna cum illo cecinerunt discipuli. Quo exemplo toti Ecclesiae gratiarum actio commendatur: qua inter omnia sacra, in primis autem hic opus est, cum tota haec actio in eum finem potissimum instituta, & olim Eucharistia vulgo dicta fit, quam sacrificium Deo gratissimum esse, Scriptura omnis docet. At hymno dicto exit Christus in montem olivarum, & preces illas ardentes fundit, quae ab Ioanne describuntur: quibus fipfum & omnes in fe credentes Deo patri commendat, adeoq; testamentum condit, cuius summa est, vt secum sint in caelis perpetuo omnes, qui fecundum Apostolorum doctrinam in ipsum credunt. Haec ergo fidei regula est, quam qui sequuntur, a salute excidere non possunt. Suo autem exemplo docet Christus, quo animo ipsi quoq; crucem & quaeuis aduersa adire debeamus. Oremus ergo Deum patrem, vt propter Filium suum IESVM CHRISTVM nos inter huius vitae palaestram feruet, & in regnum suum caeleste transferat. Amen.
units.tr: Our chief concern, however, is to carry out faithfully what the Lord commands us in this whole action: namely, that everything be done in his memory, and that we proclaim his death. Under the death are included also the resurrection and ascension, by which our redemption is completed. Therefore, following the ancient custom of the Church, the articles of the Apostles' Creed are recited while the Supper is performed. Moreover, the remembrance that is enjoined is one joined with thanksgiving; it does not consist in words alone, but requires the soul, indeed the whole man, that we may live to him alone who died for us and rose again. For this benefit of Christ is so excellent that no words suffice to celebrate it, and on account of the weakness of the flesh we have constant need of goads. This must be observed on account of those who invent an inward word and I know not what hidden inspirations, and neglect external preaching and the external exercises of faith as superfluous. Yet the Supper ought to be used until he comes. And Theodoret rightly warned long ago: "Then at last there will be no need of the signs of the body, when the body itself appears." Let us be mindful of this duty, and prepare ourselves for it diligently. We are comforted, however, by the fact that we celebrate the memory of him who sees us, and who is also present to us by his Spirit and power. Furthermore, just as the Lord began the mystical Supper with blessing and thanksgiving, so he finished it with a hymn, which the disciples sang together with him. By this example thanksgiving is commended to the whole Church, which is especially needed among all the sacred acts here, since this whole action was instituted chiefly for that end, and was once commonly called the Eucharist, which all Scripture teaches is a sacrifice most pleasing to God. Then, the hymn having been sung, Christ goes out to the Mount of Olives and pours out those fervent prayers that John describes, by which he commends himself and all who believe in him to God the Father, and thus makes a testament whose sum is that all who believe in him according to the teaching of the Apostles should be with him in heaven for ever. This, therefore, is the rule of faith, and those who follow it cannot fall from salvation. By his own example Christ also teaches with what spirit we too ought to approach the cross and whatever adversities. Let us pray therefore to God the Father, that for the sake of his Son JESUS CHRIST he may strengthen us in the wrestling-ground of this life and transfer us into his heavenly kingdom. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCXCVI.
units.tr: HOMILY CCXCVI.

units.la: Tunc dicit eis IESVS: Omnes vos ista nocte offendemini in me. Scriptum est enim: Percutiam pastorem, & dispergentur oues gregis. Postquam autem surrexero, praeibo vobis in Galilaeam. Respondens vero Petrus, dixit ei: Etiamsi omnes offendantur in te, ego nunquam offendar. Dixit ei Iesus: Amen dico tibi, ista nocte antequam gallus vocem mittat, ter me abnegabis. Dicit ei Petrus: Etiamsi oportuerit me mori tecum, non te abnegabo. Similiter & omnes discipuli dixerunt.
units.tr: Then Jesus said to them: "You will all be offended in me this night. For it is written: 'I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered.' But after I am raised up, I will go before you into Galilee." Peter answered and said to him: "Even if all are offended in you, I will never be offended." Jesus said to him: "Truly I tell you, this very night, before the cock crows, you will deny me three times." Peter said to him: "Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you." All the disciples said the same.

units.la: Postquam Filius Dei IESVS CHRISTVS peracta cum discipulis postrema Cena & hymno dicto exiuit, vrbem egressus trans torrentem Cedron in hortum abiit, in quo fepius solitus fuerat cum suis conuenire, & in quo fe captum irifcibat, vt fe voluntarium mori testaretur, & sua
units.tr: After the Son of God, Jesus Christ, had finished the last supper with his disciples and had gone out after singing a hymn, he left the city, crossed the brook Kidron and went into a garden, where he had often been accustomed to meet with his own, and where he knew he would be seized, so that he might bear witness that he was going to die willingly, and his

units.la: Christus discipulos de periculis quae instant admonet. sua obedientia, quam Patri vsque ad mortem praestitit, nostra peccata expiaret. Vt autem pro no-bis mortuus est, eo quod dilexit nos, ita etiam cum ia mortis hora immineret, de discipulis suis po-tius quam de seipso solicitus, de iis illos admonuit, quae ipsis cognitu necessaria erant. Nouerat e-nim quanta esset illorum infirmitas, & quam graue scandalum ex sua morte infami, & vinculi quae iam subituru erat, ipsis immineret. Praedicit ergo quid euenturum sit, vt & minus offendan-tur praemisis, & facilius a lapsu resurgant, & seipsos infide confirment.
units.tr: Christ warns the disciples about the dangers that are at hand. obedience, which he rendered to the Father even unto death, might expiate our sins. And just as he died for us because he loved us, so also, when the hour of death was upon him, he was concerned for his disciples rather than for himself, and admonished them about those things which it was necessary for them to know. For he knew how great their weakness was, and how grave a scandal, arising from his shameful death and from the bonds which he was about to undergo, hung over them. He therefore foretells what is going to happen, so that they may be less offended by what was foretold, may more easily rise again from their fall, and may strengthen themselves in faith.

units.la: Propositio admonitionis est: Omnes vos ista noste offendemini in me. De omnibus loquitur, vt commune periculum esse doceat, ne aliquis aliquam haberet maioris confidentiae occasionem. Et hac ipsa nocte, inquit, ne sibi longum otium polliceantur. Vtq; minus securi sint, scriptura testimo-nio confirmat, dicens: Scriptum est enim: Percutiam pastorem, & dispergentur oues gregis. Appa-ret hic quae sit credentium conditio in terris. Videntur interdum omnia in tuto, & quod dicitur, extra teli tactum esse, quando promissiones Dei audiuntur, nec vlla hostium insidiae cernuntur, ex quibus aliquid periculi sit timendum. Sed tunc maxime nos in excubiis stare & vigilare oportet. Non dormit enim Satan, nec quiescit mundus, in quo plures mali sunt & impij, quibus nunquam pax est (vt Propheta ait) cum est nemo ipsis molestiam exhibeat, ipsi inter suarum cupiditatum ardores aestuent, & sibi ipsis laborum subinde authores sunt, dum omnia suis viribus perfici oportet reputant. Piis autem periculum maximum ex propria carne enascitur, quae vel secura nimium dormitat, vel confidens non cogitat, quam in lubrico consistat, aut quid ipsi possit accidere. Quod si er go praeter opinionem aliquid accidit cruci & aduersis succubit. Itaq; fiet, vt qui sibi videntur sta-re, turpissime labantur: & tunc auditur vulgò, quod gentium quoq; philosophi dixerunt, a sapiente viro alienissimum esse debere, vt nimirum dicat: Non putaram. Meminerimus ergo semper, ho-minis vitam militiam esse, & arma lucis induamus. Quod si alij quid humanitus patiantur, non illico eos temere damnemus, neq; de nostra salute desperemus, si nosipsos sentiamus imbecilliores esse quam decebat. Job 7. Rom. 13.
units.tr: The subject of the warning is this: "You will all be offended in me this night." He speaks of all of them, to show that the danger is common, so that none of them should have any occasion for greater confidence. And he says this very night, so that they should not promise themselves a long respite. And so that they may be less secure, he confirms it by the testimony of Scripture, saying: "For it is written: 'I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered.'" Here appears what the condition of believers is on earth. Sometimes all things seem safe, and, as the saying goes, they seem to be beyond the reach of any missile, when the promises of God are heard and no snares of enemies are visible from which any danger is to be feared. But then especially we ought to stand on guard and keep watch. For Satan does not sleep, nor does the world rest, in which there are many evil and impious men, for whom there is never peace (as the Prophet says), unless someone causes them trouble; they burn with the heat of their own desires, and are constantly the authors of their own labours, while they think that everything must be accomplished by their own strength. But the greatest danger for the godly arises from their own flesh, which either sleeps too securely, or, being confident, does not consider how slippery its footing is, or what may befall it. If therefore something happens beyond expectation, it succumbs to the cross and to adversity. And so it will come about that those who seem to themselves to stand most firmly fall most disgracefully; and then is heard the common saying, which the philosophers of the Gentiles also expressed, that it ought to be most foreign to a wise man to say: "I did not think so." Let us therefore always remember that human life is a warfare, and let us put on the armour of light. But if others suffer something as humans do, let us not rashly condemn them at once, nor despair of their salvation, if we perceive ourselves to be weaker than we ought to be. Job 7. Rom. 13.

units.la: Obseruaa autem, non temere Christum locum de percusso pastore & ouium vel gregis dispersio-ne ex ea secuta allegare, vt admonitione hanc discipulis confirmet. Docemur hoc exemplo, quam prosit, imo necesse sit pastores Ecclesia, id est, doctores & verbi administros habere bonos & fidos, qui oues, id est, animas sibi creditas in laeta & salubria pascua verbi deducant, fideliter pascant, & aduersus lupum illum ferocem diabolum tueantur, & huius satellites tyrannos atq; seductores & stabulu & septis Ecclesia arceant. Nisi hoc sedulo fiat, in mille sectas scinduntur, qui in CHRI-STO IES V vnum esse & idem sentire debebant. Elucet autem in eo Dei bonitas, qui pa-storem nobis dedit Filium suum, qui ita nos dilexit, vt animam suam pro nobis dederit, & qui eiusdem cum Patre essentia & potestatis, non sinit sibi aliquos ex manibus suis eripi, quos semel in gregem suum recepit. Est hic ἀρχιποιμὴν, cuius administri et serui sunt alij doctores: qui dum officiu faciunt, salua manet Ecclesia. Quod si segnefcunt, aut laboribus siue periculis succubunt, quid aliud quam horribilis dispersio sequatur. Exempla omnium saculorum id testantur: & haec causa est, quod qui ipsum Christu aggredi & tentari ausus est satan, & post hunc Apostolos quoq; experiuit, vt eos ex statione deijceret, omnibus saculis doctorum ordini insidiatus est, vt vel ignauos obtruderet, vel bonos & fidos e medio tolleret. Et persecutiones fere a ministris olim e-xorsus est: quos qui odio & supplicio dignos putant, quando officium faciunt, perinde faciunt, ac si quis canes ab ouibus remouendas esse suadeat, ne latratu suo luporum rabiem accendant, vt bis sublatis ouibus tuta omnia polliceatur.
units.tr: Observe, moreover, that Christ does not without reason cite the example of the struck shepherd and the scattering of the sheep of the flock that followed from it, in order to confirm this warning for the disciples. We are taught by this example how useful, indeed how necessary, it is for the Church to have good and faithful shepherds, that is, teachers and ministers of the Word, who lead the sheep, that is, the souls entrusted to them, into the joyful and wholesome pastures of the Word, feed them faithfully, and protect them against that fierce wolf, the devil, and keep his henchmen, tyrants and seducers, away from the fold and the enclosures of the Church. Unless this is done diligently, the members who ought to be one and to think alike in CHRIST JESUS are torn into a thousand sects. But the goodness of God shines forth in this, that he gave us his Son as shepherd, who loved us so much that he gave his soul for us, and who, being of the same essence and power as the Father, does not allow any whom he has once received into his flock to be snatched from his hands. He is the chief Shepherd [ἀρχιποιμὴν], whose ministers and servants are the other teachers; while they perform their office, the Church remains safe. But if they grow slack, or succumb to labours or dangers, what else follows but a dreadful dispersion? The examples of all ages bear witness to this. And this is the reason why Satan, who dared to attack and tempt Christ himself, and afterwards also tested the Apostles, to cast them down from their post, has in every age laid snares for the order of teachers, so that he may either thrust in idle men or remove the good and faithful from the midst. And he has almost always stirred up persecutions against the ministers. Those who think they deserve hatred and punishment because they perform their office do just what someone would do who advised that dogs be removed from the sheep, so that they would not stir up the rage of the wolves by their barking, and who promised that all would be safe once the sheep were taken away.

units.la: Sed non solum de periculo praemonet discipulos, verumetiam dulcem consolationem adhibet. Nam Simoni Petro apud Lucam dicit: Ego rogaui pro te, ne deficiat fides tua. In prasenti vero addit: Postquam surrexero, praibo vobis in Galilaeã. Sunt ergo fortissima aduersus crucis & reliqua scandala argumenta consolationis, resurrectio Christi & eiusdem intercessionis. Cur enim eius morte offendatur, qui illum mortem vicific credit? Cur non in illo exulteat, qui hunc suu apud Patrem intercessorem & aduocatum esse audit? Et enim hodie adhuc pro nobis intercedit, & du-rat intercessionis huius vis. Est enim dilestus ille Filius, in quo Pater placatus est. Nobis autem inter aliahuius loci vsus esse debet, vt Ecclesiarū dispersionibus, si qua fiunt, nō offendamur. Sed lidum enim flat fundamentum Dei, habens sigillum hoc, Nouit Dominus qui sint sui, & Discedat ab iniquitate omnis qui nominat nomen Christi. Hic enim rursus colligit, quos certo iudicio disper gi finis, & quoad haec mundi machina durabit, non deerit illi locus, vbi Ecclesia sua sedem inue- nient. Tandem vero quando huius saeculi dies propter electos abbreuiabuntur, & mundus hic seip- sum indignum esse demonstrabit, qui Ecclesiae Filij Dei sedem aut hospitium praebeat: in domum Petri sui illam colliget, vbi adsuam mensam aeterno immortalitatis neBare fruatur. Luc.22.
units.tr: But he does not only warn the disciples about the danger; he also applies a sweet consolation. For he says to Simon Peter in Luke: "I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail." In the present passage he adds: "After I am raised up, I will go before you into Galilee." There are therefore very strong arguments of consolation against the cross and the other scandals: the resurrection of Christ and his intercession. For why should someone be offended by his death who believes that he has conquered death? Why should someone not rejoice in him who hears that he is an intercessor and advocate with the Father? For he intercedes for us even today, and the force of this intercession endures. For he is that beloved Son in whom the Father is appeased. Moreover, we ought to use this passage, among other things, so that we are not offended by the dispersions of the Churches, if any occur. For "the firm foundation of God stands, having this seal: 'The Lord knows those who are his; and let everyone who names the name of Christ depart from iniquity.'" For here again he gathers together those whom, by his certain judgment, he allows to be scattered, and as long as this machine of the world endures, there will not be lacking a place where his Church may find its seat. Finally, when the days of this age are shortened for the sake of the elect, and this world will show itself unworthy to offer a seat or lodging to the Church of the Sons of God, he will gather it into the house of his Peter, where it may enjoy, at his table, the eternal nectar of immortality. Luke 22.

units.la: Caeterum quia carnis nostrae infirmitas magna est, quam nisi in seipsis singuli diligenter ag- noscant, vix effugient, quin periculose offendant et labantur, de hac nouam actione instituit Chri- stus. Occasionem huic praebuit Petrus, qui eum ipsum nominatim perstrinxisset Dominus (vt pau- lo ante ex Luca annotauimus) necesse putauit, vt sui nominis dignitate afferet. Idcirco respon- dit illi, & dixit: Etiamsi omnes offendantur in te, ego nunquam offendar. Nec dubium est, Petrum quod dixit, pio & fauto zelo dixisse: sed in breui dicto multa concurrunt, quae reprehensionem non leuem merentur. Primum temeritas est confidenter de seipso pronuntiare in re incerta, cuius e- uentus adhuc ignorabatur. Deinde auget culpam, quod comparatione facta se fratribus omnibus praefert, adeoque hos prae se contemnit. Grauissimum vero quod Christo contradicit, cuius dictis sim- pliciter credere & perterrefieri debuisset. Adhaec non in praesens modo, sed etiam in futurum, quid facere velit, pollicetur. Ego (inquit) non offendar. An vero nesciebat se hominem esse, & nihil hu- manum abs se esse alienum? An excideratillius animo quid passus esset, cum simili confidentia supra aquas ambulare, & per medios flatus ad Christum progredi statuisset? Itaq; dignus erat, qui prae alijs laberetur, & de se modestius sentire disceret. Ideo dicit illi Dominus: Amen dico tibi, ista no- e antequam gallus vocem mittat, ter me abnegabis. Remedium illi adhibet, qui propter contu- maciam corripi & obiurgari merebatur. Quam turpis enim huius praesumptionis euentus futurus sit, docet. Dixerat ille nunquam offendar. At hac ipsa nocte (ait Christus) promisit tam magnifice oblitus, me abnegabis. Et quia nos lapsos esse non facile animaduertimus, imo nobis ipsis delicias facimus, dum in luto peccatorum volutamur, gallicinij meminit, & terna abnegationis, vt illo audito & obseruato, occasionem habeat Petrus, de sceleri cogitandi & a lapsu resurgendi. Et di- gnus erat confidens illesuarum virium iactator, vt victoriarum suarum tam ridiculum praeconem haberet, gallum gallinaceum. Ita solet Deus ad bruta animalia remittere eos, qui in sua schola noluntinstitui, & ipsi contradicere non verentur. Suspectum ergo sit nobis ingenium carnis, & di- scamus hoc exemplo, quo nos abripiat innata nobis praesumptio. Vbi fide & aliquot donis spiri- tualibus praeditam sentit caro, nihil non sibi tribuit. At quando fides reipsa in periculis declarari debet, fere labascimus. Ideo nos varie exercet Deus. At qui in ipso vno sperant, ij demum in sua infirmitate potentiam & virtutem Dei perficiunt, & eo magis confirmantur, quo minus vi- rium in seipsis sentiunt. Oremus ergo Dominum, vt suo spiritu nos armet, vt constantes & inui- cti in finem vsque perseueremus. Amen.
units.tr: Moreover, because the weakness of our flesh is great, and unless each person diligently recognises it in himself, he will scarcely escape stumbling and falling into danger, Christ introduces a new action concerning this. The occasion was given by Peter, who, since the Lord had named him specifically (as we noted a little earlier from Luke), thought he had to speak up for the dignity of his own name. Therefore he answered him and said: "Even if all are offended in you, I will never be offended." There is no doubt that Peter said this out of a pious and warm zeal; yet in this brief saying many things come together that deserve no slight rebuke. First, it is rashness to pronounce confidently about oneself in a matter that is uncertain, the outcome of which was still unknown. Next, he increases his fault, because by making a comparison he sets himself above all the brethren, and so in comparison despises them. But most serious is that he contradicts Christ, whose words he ought to have believed simply and been terrified by. Besides, he promises not only what he will do at present, but also what he will do in the future: "I," he says, "will not be offended." But did he not know that he was a man, and that nothing human was foreign to him? Had he forgotten what he had suffered when, with similar confidence, he had decided to walk upon the waters and advance to Christ through the midst of the winds? He was therefore worthy to fall before the others and to learn to think more modestly of himself. Therefore the Lord says to him: "Truly I tell you, this very night, before the cock crows, you will deny me three times." He applies a remedy to him who deserved to be corrected and rebuked on account of his stubbornness. He shows how shameful the outcome of this presumption will be. Peter had said: "I will never be offended." But Christ says: "This very night," having so magnificently promised, you will deny me. And because we do not readily notice that we have fallen, indeed we indulge ourselves while we wallow in the mire of sins, he mentions the crowing of the cock and the threefold denial, so that, having heard and noted this, Peter may have occasion to reflect on his crime and to rise again from his fall. And the boaster of his own powers deserved to have, as the herald of his victories, so ridiculous a crier: a barnyard cock. Thus God is wont to send back to the brute animals those who are unwilling to be taught in his school, and who do not hesitate to contradict him. Let us therefore be suspicious of the nature of the flesh, and let us learn from this example how far the presumption innate in us carries us away. When the flesh feels itself endowed with faith and some spiritual gifts, it attributes nothing to itself that it does not claim. But when faith must actually be shown in dangers, we almost always waver. Therefore God exercises us in various ways. But those who hope in him alone at last accomplish the power and virtue of God in their own weakness, and are strengthened all the more, the less they feel strength in themselves. Let us therefore pray the Lord that he may arm us with his Spirit, so that we may persevere constant and unconquered to the end. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCXCVII.
units.tr: HOMILY CCXCVII.

units.la: Tunc venit IESVS cum eis in locum, qui dicitur Gethsemane, & dicit discipulis: Sedete hic vsque quo abiens precatus fuero illic. Et assumpto Petro & duobus filijs Zebedaei, coepit contristari & grauissime angi. Tunc dicit eis IESVS: Vndiquaque tristis est anima mea vsque ad mortem: manete hic & vigilate mecum. Et progressus paululum, procidit in faciem suam, precans & dicens: Pater mi, si possibile est, abeat a me poculum istud, veruntamen non sicut ego volo, sed vt tu. Tunc venit ad discipulos, & reperit eos dormi- entes: & dicit Petro: Itane non potuistis vnam horam vigilare me- cum? Vigilate & orate, ne introeatis in tentationem: Spiritus qui- dem promptus, sed caro infirma est. Rursum secundo abijt, & pre- catus est, dicens: Pater mi, si non potest hoc poculum abire a me, quin bibam ipsum, fiat voluntas tua. Et cum venisset, reperit eos rursum dormientes: erant enim oculi eorum grauati. Et relictis eis, rursum abiit, & precatus est tertio, eundem sermonem dicens. Tunc venit ad discipulos suos, & dicit eis: Dormite quod superest & requiescite: ecce, appropinquat hora, & Filius hominis traditur in manus peccatorum. Surgite, eamus: ecce, appropinquat qui me prodit.
units.tr: Then Jesus came with them to a place called Gethsemane, and said to the disciples, "Sit here while I go over there and pray." And taking with him Peter and the two sons of Zebedee, he began to be sorrowful and very heavy. Then Jesus said to them, "My soul is exceeding sorrowful, even unto death: stay here and watch with me." And going a little further, he fell on his face, praying and saying, "O my Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will." Then he came to the disciples and found them asleep, and said to Peter, "So you could not watch with me one hour? Watch and pray, that you do not enter into temptation: the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak." Again, a second time, he went away and prayed, saying, "O my Father, if this cup cannot pass from me unless I drink it, your will be done." And when he came, he found them asleep again, for their eyes were heavy. And leaving them, he went away again and prayed a third time, saying the same words. Then he came to his disciples and said to them, "Sleep on now and rest: behold, the hour is at hand, and the Son of man is betrayed into the hands of sinners. Rise, let us go: behold, he who betrays me is at hand."

units.la: IN passione Dominica historia non postremum locum debetur actioni, qua Filius Dei IESVS CHRISTVS ad montem oliveti in horto, priusquam caperetur, habuit. Illic enim luctam fuit certamen grauissimum sustinuit cum assumpta carnis infirmitate, quam discipulis satis aperte manifestauit. Et in lucta illa mortis horrores ita vicit, ut haec nobis non amplius formidabilis fit. Nec suam modo infirmitatem discipulis ostendit, verumetiam in his, quanta sit omnium hominum imbecillitas docet, nisi Dei Spiritu confirmemur. Prodest aut singula quae hic dicuntur, ex ordine videre, ut nosipsos rectius agnoscere, & simul quibus praesidiis nostrae infirmitati succurri possit, discamus.
units.tr: In the history of the Lord's Passion, the action that the Son of God, Jesus Christ, undertook on the Mount of Olives in the garden, before he was seized, deserves no small place. For there he endured a most severe struggle with the weakness of the flesh he had assumed, which he showed quite plainly to the disciples. And in that struggle he so overcame the horrors of death that it is no longer dreadful to us. Nor does he show only his own weakness to the disciples; in them he also teaches how great the frailty of all men is, unless we are strengthened by the Spirit of God. It is useful to look at the individual things said here in order, so that we may know ourselves more accurately, and at the same time learn by what safeguards our weakness can be helped.

units.la: Orditur autem a loci notatione Matthaeus, & Christum ait venisse cum discipulis in locum, Gethsemane dictum, quem a foli fertilitate sic dictum fuisse apparet, quasi vallem pinguium dicas. Et nomini huic respondet, quod illic hortus fuisse dicitur: non is solus quem Christus frequentare solitus fuit, verumetiam Iosephi Arimathaei, qui similiter illic sibi hortum paravit, in quo sibi ipsi sepulchrum excindere voluit. At nuper monuimus, non temere factum esse, quod a Coena statim morti obuiam progreditur Dominus. Et hoc obedientiae euidens argumentum, quam Patri Deo praestitit, quem ita velle sciebat. Praecepto autem discipulos simul omnes instruit, dicens: Sedete hic, dum quo abiens precatus fuero illic. Sedere iubet, ut animis compositis esse doceat, ne ue intra se affectibus turbulentis tumultuentur. Et dum se precandi causa aliquo progredi velle dicit, ipsos quoque exemplo monet, quid faciant: ut nimirum precentur, & ita se totos Dei curae committant.
units.tr: Matthew begins with the naming of the place, and says that Christ came with the disciples into a place called Gethsemane, which seems to have been so called from the fertility of the soil, as if you were to say "valley of fat things." The name corresponds to the fact that there was a garden there: not only the one Christ was accustomed to frequent, but also that of Joseph of Arimathea, who likewise prepared a garden there, in which he wished to hew out a tomb for himself. But we noted recently that it was not without reason that the Lord, straight from the Supper, goes forward to meet death. This is clear evidence of the obedience he rendered to God the Father, whose will he knew. He instructs all the disciples together in a command, saying: "Sit here while I go over there and pray." He bids them sit, to teach them to be composed in mind, lest they be stirred within by turbulent emotions. And while he says he wishes to go somewhere to pray, he also admonishes them by his example about what they should do: namely, that they too should pray, and so commit themselves wholly to God's care.

units.la: Quia autem ipse tunc contristari & angi incipiebat, & sua angustia testes facere voluit aliquos ex discipulis, in eo horum rationem habuit, & ut infirmitati illorum consulat, aliis in tutiori loco relictis, tres tantum assumit, quos in locum certaminis proditioni & vinculis suis destinatum producit. Sunt autem hi Petrus & duo Zebedaei filij Iacobus & Ioannes, quos idcirco sibi nunc delegit, eo quod gloriae suae & maiestatis spectatores saepius fuerant: & proinde nunc ipsius infirmitate, de qua querelam acerbam auditurus erant, minus poterant offendi. His nunc ingentem animi dolorem, quo afficiebatur, fatetur, dicens: Vndiquaque tristis est anima mea vsque ad mortem. Animam suam περίλυπον dicit, ut vndique maerore obsessam & circumuallatam esse testetur. Quod ipsum quoque vocabulo ἀδημονεῖν docere voluit. Hoc enim prae maerore animo concidere, & consilij inopem esse significat. Continetur autem his verum & certum humanitatis a Christo assumptae testimonium, ne dubitemus vere hominem, & per omnia fratribus similem factu esse. Ita enim ne esse fuit, ut fidelis pontifex esset in iis, quae apud Deum agenda sunt ad expiandum peccata populi. In eo igitur versatur etiam nostrae salutis cardo. Nam eo quod perpessus fuit cum tentatus est potest etiam iis, qui tentantur succurrere. Vide ad Heb. 2. cap.
units.tr: But since he himself then began to be sorrowful and troubled, and wished to make some of the disciples witnesses of his anguish, he took their weakness into account. To look after their frailty, he left the others in a safer place and took only three, whom he brought into the place appointed for his struggle, his betrayal and his bonds. These are Peter and the two sons of Zebedee, James and John. He chose them now for this reason: because they had more often been spectators of his glory and majesty, and therefore, in his present weakness, about which they were to hear a bitter complaint, they could be less offended. To these he now confesses the great anguish of mind with which he was affected, saying, "My soul is sorrowful even unto death." He calls his soul exceedingly sorrowful [περίλυπος], to testify that it is beset and encircled with grief on every side. He wished to teach the same thing by the word to be in anguish [ἀδημονεῖν]. For this signifies being cast down in mind by grief and being without counsel. Yet in these words there is a true and certain witness to the humanity Christ assumed, so that we may not doubt that he was truly a man and in all things made like his brothers. For it had to be so, that he might be a faithful high priest in those matters which must be carried out before God for the expiation of the sins of the people. In this lies the very hinge of our salvation. For because he suffered when he was tempted, he is also able to help those who are tempted. See Heb. 2.

units.la: Non tamen Filio Dei aliquid indignum affingimus, neq; illius maiestatem negamus vel extenuamus: sed eius praedicamus bonitatem, qua ita dilexit nos, ut eo vsque se demittere voluerit, ut peccatorum noxa, cuius sarcina nobis intolerabilis erat, nos exoneraret. Et ita nobis similis fit suas esse, & nostras infirmitates pertulit, ut nulla peccati labes in ipso vnquam locum haberet. Quia vero peccata nostra in se receperat, & haec in illo Pater vlcisci batur, mors illi tam formida bilis & horribilis fuit, eo quod iram Dei peccatum, cuius pondus illi erat propter nos sustinendum. Quod ita a nobis considerari debet, ut simul meminerimus, quid miseris illis & infelicibus fiet, quos a fide alienos Christus suo patrocinio non subleuabit, qui dum diros istos cruciatus animo suo perpessus est, inferorum atrium quasi subijt, ut suos inde educeret.
units.tr: Yet we do not ascribe anything unworthy to the Son of God, nor do we deny or diminish his majesty; rather we proclaim his goodness, by which he loved us so much that he was willing to humble himself so far as to free us from the harm of sins, whose burden was intolerable to us. And he became so like us that he bore our weaknesses, yet no stain of sin ever had a place in him. But because he had taken our sins upon himself, and the Father was punishing them in him, death was so frightful and horrible to him, because it was the wrath of God against sin, whose weight he had to bear for us. This must be considered by us in such a way that at the same time we remember what will become of those wretched and unhappy people whom Christ, being alien to faith, will not relieve with his patronage. For he, while he endured these dreadful torments in his mind, as it were went down into the courts of hell, so that he might lead his own out from there.

units.la: Sed praestat videre, quid in isto agone discipulis, quos prae aliis sibi delegerat, mandarit. Manete hic (inquit) & vigilate mecum. Primum ipsos manere vel subsistere iubet illic loci, ipse paulo vlterius progrediturus: nimirum ut commodius precaretur. Deinde vigilare: ne a Satana circumuentur, de cuius insidijs ipsos nuper praemonuerat dicens, illum ipsos expetiisse ut cribraret intar tritici. At quia vires in illis nullae erant, postea ipsos quoque orare iubet. At quod discipulis iustis praecipitur, singuli sibi ipsis accommodent, & non minus ad se pertinere arbitrentur. Maneant singuli in sua statione, in quam ipsos collocauit Dominus. Vigilent item, nec putent sibi aliquem socordiae locum esse, quibus cum illo hoste res est, qui ut leo rugiens oberrat & quaerit quem deuoret.
units.tr: But it is worth seeing what he charged the disciples, whom he had chosen before the others, to do in this struggle. "Stay here," he says, "and watch with me." First he bids them remain or stand in that place, while he himself is to go a little further, namely so that he might pray more conveniently. Then he bids them watch, lest they be caught unawares by Satan, of whose snares he had lately warned them, saying that Satan had asked to sift them like wheat. But because they had no strength of their own, afterwards he bids them pray too. Let each one apply to himself what is commanded to the disciples, and not think it pertains to him any less. Let each remain in his own station, in which the Lord has placed him. Likewise let them watch, and let them not think there is any room for carelessness, since they have to do with that enemy who, like a roaring lion, prowls about seeking whom he may devour.

units.la: Praeterea cum ex nobismipsis ne ad cogitandum quidem idonei simus, sed ex Deo est, quicquid in nobis laudem meretur, nos quoque in precibus assiduos & indefessos esse oportet. Nec putemus nos in precibus nimios esse aut Deo molestiam facere posse. DeleCtatur hic importunitate illa sancta, qua pij (ut olim Tertullianus scribebat) ceu vim ipsi facere conantur.
units.tr: Moreover, since we are not even fit to think anything of ourselves, but whatever in us deserves praise comes from God, we too ought to be constant and tireless in prayer. Nor let us think that we can be too persistent in prayer, or that we can cause God trouble. He delights in that holy importunity by which the godly (as Tertullian once wrote) try, as it were, to use force upon him.

units.la: Porro quod discipulis mandauit Dominus, exemplo proprio confirmat, quo illis praeit. Nam progressus paululum procidit in faciem suam precans. Lucas a discipulis auulsum dicit, ut amorem, quo eos amplexus fuit, exprimat. Solemus enim aegre & non sine acerbo animi dolore ab iis discedere, quos ex animo diligimus, & quibus sumus nostro consilio & patrocinio propter imminentia pericula plurimum opus fore. Sentiunt dolorem hunc coniuges, parentes & alij morituri, qui astantes vident tenellos liberos in lachrymas effusos fortem suam futuram deplorantes, & simul cogitant, quam multa aduersa, tristia, iniqua & iniusta orphanis & viduis accidere soleant, per quae homines iniusti, superbi, intemperantes, illorum non fortunas modo & facultates, verum etiam corpora, pudicitiam, honorem & famam cum vita in periculum adducunt. Quae cogitatio interdum hominibus honestis & pijs ipsa morte acerbior est, quam facile superarent, si suos orphanos aut viduas prius ex hoc mundo decedere, & se simul hac cura et sollicitudine liberatos esse viderent. Sed tunc praesens hoc Christi exemplum in mentem reuocent, cui non potuit non acerbissimum esse, quod dilectos discipulos inter lupos aut hostes, feris & bestijs omnibus truculentiores relicturus est, & simul animo praeuideret vincula, carceres, supplicia & tam multa tamque infanda mortis genera quae fabituri erant: ut iam nihil dicam de iis, quae ipse in suo corpore erat passurus. Sed qui primo seipsum & discipulos cum omni credentium Ecclesia Patri commendauerat, dolorem hunc fortiter vincit, & licet durum & graue esset ab iis diuelli, quos ex toto hominum genere sibi in periculum selegerat, secedit tamen ab illis, ut non tam suam quam ipsorum quoque causam apud Patrem inter precandum ardentius agat. Ita nos quoque faciamus: & qui se ab iis relinqui & deseri vident, qui ipsis parentum aut fratrum loco, aut coniuges fideles fuerunt, quorum deniq; consortio non possunt sine magno incommodo carere, cogitent se Patri Deo commendatos esse, qui eos sub vmbra alarum suarum custodit, & angelos suos in ipsis feruandis occupatos habet. Adhaec ipsi quoque ad vnum Deum in omni necessitate confugiant per preces, quae tutissimum in aduersis asylum sunt. Et sane per se consolationis plenum est, quod mala & pericula nobis licet deprecari: neq; peccant, qui id faciunt, modo Christum Dominum imitentur.
units.tr: Furthermore, what the Lord commanded the disciples he confirms by his own example, going before them. For, going a little further, he fell on his face, praying. Luke says that he was torn away from the disciples, to express the love with which he embraced them. For we are accustomed to part with great difficulty, and not without bitter grief of mind, from those whom we love from the heart, and whose counsel and protection we shall greatly need because of impending dangers. Spouses, parents and others who are about to die feel this grief; standing by, they see their tender children dissolved in tears, lamenting their coming fate, and at the same time they think how many adverse, sad, unfair and unjust things are wont to befall orphans and widows, through which unjust, proud and intemperate men endanger not only their fortunes and means but also their bodies, chastity, honour and reputation, together with their life. This thought sometimes is more bitter to honest and pious men than death itself, which they would easily overcome if they saw their orphans or widows die first out of this world, and themselves freed at the same time from this care and anxiety. But let them then call to mind this present example of Christ, for it could not but be most bitter to him that he was to leave his beloved disciples among wolves or enemies, more savage than all wild beasts. At the same time he foresaw in his mind the chains, prisons, punishments and so many and so unspeakable kinds of death they were going to suffer, not to mention what he himself was about to suffer in his own body. Yet he, who had first committed himself and the disciples, together with the whole Church of believers, to the Father, bravely overcomes this grief. Although it was hard and grievous to be torn from those whom he had chosen out of the whole human race for danger, he nevertheless withdraws from them, so that in praying he might plead more ardently, not so much his own cause as theirs, before the Father. So let us too do likewise. Those who see themselves left and deserted by those who have been to them in place of parents or brothers, or faithful spouses, whose company they cannot finally do without with great inconvenience, let them think that they are commended to God the Father, who keeps them under the shadow of his wings and has his angels occupied in preserving them. Besides, let them also flee to the one God in every need through prayers, which are the safest refuge in adversity. And indeed it is in itself full of consolation that we may pray against evils and dangers; nor do those sin who do so, provided they imitate the Lord Christ.

units.la: Hic in faciem procidens (quod extremae subiectionis indicium est) dicit: Pater mi, si possibile est, abeat a me poculum istud: veruntamen non ut ego volo, sed ut tu. Continetur hic exemplum simul & formula, in quae inter precandum respiciamus. Pathetice dicit, Pater mi, & ita eum vocat, ex cuius aeterno decreto se praedestinatum esse sciebat, ut mortis dira & infamis merito nos redimeret. Ita nos tunc quoque patrem nostrum agnoscamus Deum, quando nos ab illo durius tractari sentimus. Deinde si possibile est, abeat a me poculum istud. Non dubitauit, Deo omnia esse possibilia, sed quia omnipotentiae Dei limites sciebat voluntate & decreto Dei circumscribi, hoc autem esse ut ipse pro nobis moreretur, sic loqui voluit, ne quid illi contrarium petere videretur. Poculum vero aut calicem dicit crucis supplicium ex communi scriptura more, quae ita docet nobis afflictiones a Deo certa mensura distribui. Et ne quid temere Deo praescribere putetur, per correctionem addit:
units.tr: Falling on his face here (which is the sign of the deepest submission), he says: "My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will." Here we have both an example and a form of words to observe in prayer. He speaks with feeling, "My Father," and addresses as Father the God by whose eternal decree he knew himself predestined to redeem us by a dreadful and infamous death. So too we should acknowledge God as our Father when we feel that he deals more harshly with us. Next: "If it is possible, let this cup pass from me." He did not doubt that all things are possible with God, but since he knew that the limits of God's omnipotence are bounded by God's will and decree, and that it was God's will that he himself should die for us, he spoke in this way so as not to seem to ask for anything contrary to that will. He calls the punishment of the cross a "cup," following the common usage of Scripture, which teaches us that afflictions are distributed by God in a fixed measure. And lest he seem to prescribe anything rashly to God, he adds a correction:

units.la: [illegible, ~5 letters] addit: Veruntamen non vt ego volo, sed vt tu. Et hoc quoque ex assumpta humana natura inge-nio siue affectu loquitur, cuius petitiones non semper cum arcano Dei decreto consentiunt. Perse quidem non peccatur, quando nobis bene esse volumus, & mala deprecamur. Sed aliquid diuinae voluntati aut decreto repugnans petere, id demum peccatum est. Enimuero nisi mortis horrorem sensisset Christus, non magis laudem meruisset ipsius patientia & obedientia, quam moriendo Patri praestitit, quam truncus aut stipes, qui dum secatur aut vritur, nihil ingemiscit. In eo igitur obedientiae Christi virtus elucet, quod etsi ipsi graue esset tam indignis modis tractari, & aliter haec fieri cuperet caro, tamen simpliciter se totum voluntati Patris subijcit, dicens: Veruntamen non vt ego volo, sed vt tu. Sit haec nobis perpetua in precibus nostris petitionum omnium regula. Si enim hanc obseruauit Dei Filius, in cuius ore non est inuentus dolus, quanto magis hac sequi debemus nos, qui in peccato concepti & nati, malis & illicitis desiderijs circumferimur, & plerunque alia volumus, quam Deus velit, qui solus bonus est? Etsi ex animo Deum dicimus Patrem, lex naturae monet, vt eius voluntati non reluctemur, ne nos ille filios degeneres dicat, & cum Iudaeis adafinos & bones remittat, quorum exemplis edoceamur, quid nos facere conueniat. Accedat autem in precibus fidei & obedientiae constans perseuerantia, ne remissiores simus, si quando non illico nos exaudiat Deus. Sape enim hic differt opem. Ideo Christus tertio ad preces reuertitur, & eandem precatione repetit. Ita nos facere oportet, neque irritae erunt preces nostrae apud Deum, qui etsi non largitur quod rogamus, tamen spiritu consolationis nos confirmat, ne in fide succumbamus. Quod hic quoque factum fuisse constat. Nam etsi non solum differt opem Pater, verumetiam agonem ita crescere patitur, vt sudorem sanguineum ipsi extorqueret, venit tamen ab illo missus Angelus, qui ipsum confortat. Et ita perpetuo solet nobis adesse Deus, neque nos supra vires tentari sinit. 1. Cor. 10.
units.tr: [illegible] he adds: "Nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will." He speaks this also out of the human nature he had assumed, in its intellect or affection, whose petitions do not always agree with the hidden decree of God. In itself it is not sinful when we wish ourselves well and pray against evils. But to ask for something that opposes the divine will or decree, that is indeed sin. Indeed, unless Christ had felt the horror of death, his patience and obedience, which he showed the Father in dying, would not have deserved praise any more than a log or a stump does, which groans not at all while it is being cut or burned. The virtue of Christ's obedience therefore shines forth in this: although it was grievous to him to be treated in such unworthy ways, and his flesh would have wished things otherwise, yet he simply submitted himself wholly to the Father's will, saying: "Nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will." Let this be the constant rule of all our petitions in prayer. For if the Son of God, in whose mouth no deceit was found, observed this, how much more ought we to follow it, we who, conceived and born in sin, are carried about by evil and unlawful desires, and for the most part want other things than God wills, who alone is good? Although we call God our Father from our hearts, the law of nature warns us not to resist his will, lest he call us degenerate sons and send us away with the donkeys and dogs of the Jews. Let us be taught by their examples what we ought to do. Moreover, let constant perseverance in prayer, joined with faith and obedience, be added, so that we are not more slack if God does not hear us at once. For he often delays his help. Therefore Christ returns to prayer a third time and repeats the same words. So we also ought to do; our prayers will not be in vain before God, who, though he does not grant what we ask, nevertheless strengthens us with the spirit of consolation, so that we do not succumb in faith. It is clear that this also happened here. For although the Father not only delayed his help but allowed the struggle to grow so intense that it wrung bloody sweat from him, yet an angel was sent by him and came to strengthen him. And so God is wont always to be present with us, and does not allow us to be tempted beyond our strength. 1 Cor. 10.

units.la: Sed videamus, quid interea fecerint discipuli, qui promisis tam magnificis se ostentarunt, quando ad mensam de eo differebat, quod ipsi euenturum erat. Dicitur autem Christus postea pre-ces semel facias, venisse ad discipulos, & cum eos inueniret dormientes, dicit Petro: Itane non potuistis vnam horam vigilare mecum? Dormiunt nunc confidentes illi. Ideo Petrum compellat Dominus, qui se in mortem cum ipso abire velle promiserat, & ignauiam turpem exprobrat, quae ipsos non patiatur vel vnam horam vigilare. Et Emphasim habet singularem particula ME-CVM. Quid enim pro alijs facerent, qui pro Christo, quo Domino & Seruatore gloriantur, nihil volunt facere aut perpeti? Idcirco quod prius iusserat, repetit, dicens: Vigilate, & orate. Et simul de periculo admonet: Ne introeatis in tentationem. Et quia ne nunc quidem concidisse sciebat fe-rociam confidentis carnis, quae ipsos prius deceperat, addit: Spiritus quidem promptus, sed caro in-firma est. Deq; eo admonuisse contentus, neque pluribus cum illis altercari volens, ipse secundo abit ad precandum, iterum dicens: Pater mi, si non potest hoc poculum abire a me, quin bibam ipsum, id est, si omnino ratum esse vis, quod de mea morte acerba statuisti, age fiat voluntas tua. Reuersus aut ad discipulos, reperit eos rursus dormientes. Adeo enim non mouit eos prior admonitio cum exprobratione coniuncta, cuius ipsos merito pudere debuisset, vt ne potuerint quidem aliud quam dormire. Cuius affectionis causam allegat Euangelista, Quod oculi ipsorum grauati essent. Naturaenim fit, vt ex maerore oculi somno grauentur, quod Dei beneficium est, qui ita nobis medetur, ne tristitia toti absorbeamur. At Christus cognita discipulorum ignauia, non tamen indignatur, vt se ab his turpiter prodi aut negligi dicat, sed illis relictis ad preces redit, atque eundem sermonem tertio repetit. Estque hoc memorabile exemplum, cuius nos meminisse oportet, si quando homines promissis minus respondent, & nos abijs quoque negligi sentiamus, quorum fidem nobis perspectissimam esse putauimus. Non tamen ex illis de Dei fide iudicemus, qui nunquam fallit in se fidentes, eoque ardentius ad illum recurramus, cuius auxilium tunc maxime se profert, quando humana omnia cessant.
units.tr: But let us see what the disciples meanwhile did, who had displayed such great promises, when at table he spoke of what was about to happen to him. Afterwards, Christ, having made his prayer once more, came to the disciples, and finding them asleep, says to Peter: "So you could not watch with me for one hour? Now they sleep, those who were so confident." The Lord addresses Peter, who had promised that he was willing to go with him even to death, and reproaches him for the shameful sloth that did not allow them to watch even one hour. The particle "WITH ME" carries a special emphasis. For what would they do for others, who boast of Christ as their Lord and Saviour, yet are unwilling to do or suffer anything? Therefore he repeats what he had earlier commanded, saying: "Watch and pray." At the same time he warns them of the danger: "Lest you enter into temptation." And because he knew that even now the boldness of the confident flesh, which had earlier deceived them, had not been broken, he adds: "The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak." Content to have admonished them on this and not wishing to quarrel with them further, he himself goes away a second time to pray, again saying: "My Father, if this cup cannot pass from me unless I drink it, that is, if you really wish what you have decided about my bitter death, let your will be done." Returning to the disciples, however, he finds them asleep again. So far did the earlier admonition, joined with reproof, which should rightly have shamed them, fail to move them, that they could do nothing but sleep. The evangelist gives the cause of this state: because their eyes were heavy. For it is natural that eyes grow heavy with sleep from grief, which is a benefit of God, who thus provides for us lest we be wholly swallowed up by sadness. Yet Christ, perceiving the disciples' sloth, does not take offence, as if he were shamefully betrayed or neglected by them, but leaves them and returns to prayer, repeating the same words a third time. This is a memorable example, which we ought to remember whenever men fall short of their promises and we feel ourselves neglected by those whose fidelity we thought most certain. Yet we should not judge God's faithfulness by them, for he never fails those who trust in him, and therefore we should run all the more eagerly to him, whose help appears most fully precisely when all human help fails.

units.la: In primis autem in discipulis apparet, quod sit carnis & hominum, qui carnis zelo ducuntur, ingenium. Feruent quoad aliqua in ipsis est Christi notitia, & hic ad mensam, id est, dum res ad-huc prospere & fecunda sunt, de sua cruce disserit. Sed quando ipse in verbo & membris suis af-fligitur & angitur, dormiunt illi, quasi quae alijs accidunt, nihil ad illos pertineant. Et dummodo
units.tr: Above all, in the disciples appears the nature of the flesh and of men who are driven by carnal zeal. They are fervent so long as some knowledge of Christ is in them, and here at table, that is, while things are still prosperous and fruitful, he speaks of his cross. But when he himself is afflicted and distressed in his word and in his members, they sleep, as if what happens to others had nothing to do with them. And provided

units.la: ifa.1. ipsis bene sit, omnia securi negligunt, neque ullis rationibus quantumuis grauibus aut iniuriis excitari possunt. Id vero nos obseruare decet, non vt odio se aliquos contemnamus aut damnemus, sed vt nulli homini fidamus, sed vni Christo, bono ipsi pastori, qui non dormitat: et in hac actione sui illustrem egregium specimen praebuit. Psal. 121.
units.tr: Isa. 1. things go well for them, they neglect everything in security, and cannot be roused by any reasons, however weighty, or by any injuries. We ought indeed to observe this, not so that we despise or condemn anyone out of hatred, but so that we trust no man, but only Christ, the good Shepherd, who does not sleep; and in this action he gave a notable and outstanding example of himself. Ps. 121.

units.la: Interim non temere factum putabimus, quod Dominus veternum hunc et ofcitantiam discipulorum non dissimulat, sed quia admonendo nihil proficiebat, tandem amarulentius exprobrat quoque, imo corripit et quasi insultat, dicens: Dormite quod jupereft et requiescite. Quasi diceret: Agite, si qui locus aut tempus est fo cordia et otij, illo fruimini. Sed videbitis magno vestro incommodo, nunc aliam rem agi. Nam ecce, appropinquat hora, fatale illud tempus, quo Filius hominis prodetur in manus sceleratorum, qui aduersus Dei regnum conspiraverunt. Quin ergo surgite, ignaui, vt ex periculo iamiam imminenti vos eruetis. Et Iudam ceu digito monstrans, ait: Ecce appropinquat, qui me prodit. Quo exemplo docemur quid eos maneat, qui securi nimis neque periculis alienis neque admonitionibus publicis aut priuatis excitari possunt, vt de salute sua serio cogitent. Incidunt fere in subita aduersa, ex quibus seruari nulla ratione possunt, adeoque verberibus excitantur, qui verba contemnunt. Exempla quibus hoc confirmetur, in historijs passim occurrunt, et quotidie huius mali praeludia cernimus. Oremus igitur serio Dominum, vt ipse nobis auftres et oculos aperiat, vt quae nostra saluti seruiunt obseruemus, ne propter nos Dei gloria periclitetur, sed haec illustrata per nos propagetur et multi nobiscum in Christo vincant et triumphent.
units.tr: Meanwhile we shall not think it happened by chance that the Lord does not hide this drowsiness and sluggishness of the disciples; but since his admonition achieved nothing, at last he reproaches them more bitterly, indeed rebukes them and almost mocks them, saying: "Sleep on now and take your rest." As if he said: "Act, if there is any place or time for carelessness and leisure, enjoy it. But you will see, to your great cost, that another matter is now afoot. For behold, the hour draws near, that fatal time when the Son of man will be betrayed into the hands of wicked men, who have conspired against the kingdom of God. Why then do you not rise, you idle men, so that you may save yourselves from the danger now at hand?" And pointing at Judas as if with a finger, he says: "Behold, he who betrays me is at hand." From this example we are taught what awaits those who are so secure that they can be roused neither by the dangers of others nor by public or private admonitions to take their own salvation seriously. They almost always fall into sudden adversity from which they cannot be rescued by any means, and so those who scorn words are roused by blows. Examples confirming this occur everywhere in histories, and every day we see the first signs of this evil. Let us therefore seriously pray the Lord that he himself may open our ears and eyes, so that we may observe what serves our salvation, lest the glory of God be endangered on account of us, but that it may be spread abroad, illuminated through us, and that many may conquer and triumph with us in Christ.

units.la: HOMILIA CCXCVIII.
units.tr: HOMILY CCXCVIII.

units.la: Et adhuc eo loquente, ecce, Iudas vnus ex duodecim venit, et cum eo turba multa cum gladijs et fustibus, a principibus sacerdotum et senioribus populi. Is vero qui prodebat eum, dederat eis signum, dicens: Quemcunque osculatus fuero, is est; Praehendite eum. Itaque statim cum venisset ad Iesum, dixit: Aue Rabbi. Et deosculatus est eum. At Iesus dixit ei: Amice, quorsum ades? Tunc accesserunt, et manus iniecerunt in Iesum, et praehenderunt eum. Et ecce, vnus ex iis, qui erant cum Iesu, extensa manu exeruit gladium suum, et percussit seruum pontificis maximi, abstulit auriculam eius. Tunc ait ei Iesus: Converte gladium tuum in locum suum. Quicunque enim acceperint gladium, gladio peribunt. An putas me non posse nunc precari Patrem meum, qui huc sistat mihi plures quam duodecim legiones Angelorum? Quomodo ergo implerentur scripturae, quae dicunt sic oportere fieri?
units.tr: While he was still speaking, behold, Judas, one of the twelve, came, and with him a great crowd with swords and clubs, sent by the chief priests and the elders of the people. Now he who betrayed him had given them a sign, saying: "Whomever I kiss, he is the one; seize him." And immediately he went up to Jesus and said, "Hail, Rabbi!" and kissed him. But Jesus said to him: "Friend, why are you here?" Then they came forward, laid hands on Jesus and seized him. And behold, one of those who were with Jesus stretched out his hand, drew his sword, struck the servant of the high priest, and cut off his ear. Then Jesus said to him: "Put your sword back in its place, for all who take the sword will perish by the sword. Do you think that I cannot now pray to my Father, and he would send me more than twelve legions of angels? How then would the Scriptures be fulfilled, which say that it must happen this way?"

units.la: Indulgenter quidem fert Dominus et Seruator noster infirmitates nostras, nec temere eos abijcit, qui quando ipse in suo verbo aut Ecclesiae suae membris periclitatur, non eo animi aut fidei ardore et constantia causam suam agunt, qua opus erat, et quam Deus a seruis suis requirit. At si quos hac indulgentia et facilitate abuti, et subinde ignauiores seu negligentiores fieri videat, illos non verbis modo feueroribus corripit, verumetiam ceu seruiles excitat, dum periculu gravioribus obijcit, vt de salute propria cogantur diligentius cogitare. Vidimus id nuper in ijs, quae proxime praecesserunt: quando discipulos somno oppressos et nimium securos acriter corripuit, ne inanibus minis ipsos territare putaretur, hostes simul superuenientes digito monstrauit. Et vt hoc quoque ipsum serio fecisse constet, confirmationi seruit quod nunc huius loci initio sequitur. Scribit enim Matthaeus, adhuc loquente Iesu, Iudam, vnus ex duodecim discipulis domesticis, et cum eo magnam turbam coniuratorum cum gladijs et fustibus, qui omnes missi erant a principibus sacerdotum et senioribus populi. Ita vero frequenter fit, vt quando admonitiones nihil proficiant, verbera verbis coniungantur. Huius generis esse quando poenae fiue plaga duram, tibus adhuc signis et prodigijs, quae illas portenderunt, nos ferire incipiunt. Caeterum in praesenti loco locus hic totus hoc ordine nobis considerandus est, ut primo videamus, qui nam & quales aduersus Christum conuenerint. Deinde qualem se nunc ipse gesserit, qui hactenus videri poterat certa mini succubuisse. Postremo Petrus inducitur, qui admissam ignauiam culpam zelo carnis, qui rursum in ipso exarserat, emendaturus, in contrarium peccat, & dum fortis videri vult, magis ridicu lus fit, ut nouam reprehensionem mereatur.
units.tr: Our Lord and Saviour indeed bears patiently with our weaknesses, and he does not lightly cast off those who, when he or the members of his Church are in danger, do not defend their cause with the ardour, faith and steadfastness that it requires, and that God demands of his servants. But if he sees that some abuse this indulgence and gentleness and grow ever more sluggish or careless, he does not rebuke them with words alone but also rouses them, as one would slaves, by setting greater dangers before them, so that they are compelled to think more carefully about their own salvation. We saw this recently in what immediately preceded: when he sharply rebuked the disciples, who were weighed down by sleep and far too secure, lest anyone think he was frightening them with empty threats, he pointed with his finger at the enemies who were coming upon them at the same time. And to make it clear that he did this in earnest, what he now relates at the beginning of this passage serves as confirmation. For Matthew writes that while Jesus was still speaking, Judas, one of the twelve disciples, came, and with him a great crowd of conspirators with swords and clubs, all of whom had been sent by the chief priests and the elders of the people. This is indeed often how it goes: when warnings achieve nothing, blows are added to words. Of this kind are the signs and portents that foreshadowed the punishments and plagues, which begin to strike us even while they are still hard. But in the present passage the whole section must be considered in this order: first, we should see who and what sort of men gathered against Christ; second, how he himself now conducted himself, he who until now could seem to have yielded to a certain fear; last, Peter is introduced, who, wishing to make amends for the cowardice he had admitted, and for the zeal of the flesh that had flared up again in him, sins in the opposite way, and, wanting to appear brave, becomes more ridiculous, so that he deserves a fresh reproof.

units.la: Quoad primum, Lucas inter Christi aduersarios numerat aliquot ex primariis sacerdotibus & praefectos templo ex senioribus. Habuerunt hi secum suos seruos & aliorum sui ordinis hominum seruos. Acceperunt his omnibus milites Romani, quos a praeside acceperint oportet. Dux omnium fuit Iudas, nuper discipulus Christi & cum aliis Apostolis ad praedicandum missus. Sunt hi diuersi gente, professione & religione. Nam alij Iudaei, alij Ethnici fuerunt: alij sacerdotes, alij ex senioribus & politicis, virisalij heri, alij serui, alij viri militares. Sed quia omnes impij & mali sunt, contra Christum conuenire possunt, ex cuius nece singuli priuatum quaestum quaerunt. In primis autem obseruatu dignum est, quomodo hanc causam egerint. Primo cum vrbem Regis in ftar ingressus templum a turpi & impia sacrorum nundinatione repurgauisset, quaestionibus captio nis aggressi sunt, ut vel populo inuisum vel contemptum facerent. Sed quia vicli semper succubuerunt, nunc vim parant. Nec vero iniusti & iniqui videantur, magistratus sibi conciliare conantur, & quasi ipsis cum homine seditiosō res sit, milites a praeside accipiunt, quorum terrore populi furor & motus, si quis surgat coerceatur. Sed omnes superat Iudas apostata, qui ex discipulo proditor fa ctus, osculo illum prodidit, ne forte alium illius loco comprehendant. Hac ratione adhuc hodie ad uerfarij nostri progrediuntur, qui Christi fidem & religionem opprimere conantur. Debebat Verbo Dei & Scripturis pugnare, ut nos errorus conuincerent, suas vero superstitiones & errores defenderent. At quia se adeo nihil proficere sentiunt, ut saepe pueris quoq; & mulierculis ridiculi fiant, ideo ad vim conuertuntur: & quia huius illos pudet, Ecclesiae causam se agere simulant, & Concilia praetexunt, fingunt item controuersias ciuiles, & actiones forenses instituunt, de feudis & inuestitura ministrorum Ecclesiae, de decimis & redditibus aliis Coenobiorum, ut Principes viros & magistratus inter se committant. Tunc vero maxime nocent sequestri, qui cum pacem colere & promouere videri volunt, blandis verbis & promissis magnificis fallunt, & Iudas agunt. Exempla hodie tam multa occurrunt, quibus illud Dauidis confirmatur, quo omnem hominem mendacem esse pronuntiat, ut illis recensendis nullus dies sufficeret. Nunquam ergo obliuiscamur admonitionis Christi, qui olim per Prophetam dixit: Ne credatis amico, id est, amicitiam simulanti, & ab ea, quae iacet in sinu tuo, fores oris tui obserua. Et in Euangelio iterum: Cauete vobis ab hominibus. Inimici cuiusq; sunt domestici eius. Vide Mich. 6. Matth. 10.
units.tr: As to the first point, Luke numbers among Christ's adversaries some of the chief priests and the captains of the temple from among the elders. These had with them their own servants and the servants of other men of their rank. Roman soldiers were also taken, as they had to be obtained from the governor. Judas was the leader of them all: a recent disciple of Christ who had been sent out with the other apostles to preach. These men differ in nation, profession and religion. Some were Jews, others Gentiles; some were priests, others elders and public men, some were men of rank, some servants, others soldiers. But because all are wicked and evil, they can unite against Christ, for each of them seeks private gain from his death. Now, the first thing worth noting is how they went about this affair. First, when he had entered the city like a king and cleansed the temple of the shameful and impious trade in sacred things, they set about trapping him with questions, so that they might make him hated or despised by the people. But since they were always defeated, they now prepare violence. And lest they seem unjust and lawless, they try to win over the magistrates, and, as if they had to deal with a rebel, they take soldiers from the governor, whose terror would restrain the people's fury and any movement if anyone should rise. But Judas the apostate surpasses them all: having become a traitor from a disciple, he betrayed him with a kiss, lest they seize someone else in his place. In this same way our adversaries still advance today, trying to crush the faith and religion of Christ. They ought to fight with the Word of God and the Scriptures, so as to refute our errors and defend their own superstitions and errors. But because they feel they achieve so little that they often become a laughingstock even to boys and silly women, they turn to force; and because they are ashamed of this, they pretend to be pursuing the cause of the Church, putting forward councils, inventing civil disputes and instituting lawsuits over fiefs and the investiture of ministers of the Church, over tithes and other revenues of monasteries, so that they may set princes, men and magistrates against one another. Then the go-betweens do the greatest harm: wishing to appear to cultivate and promote peace, they deceive with smooth words and magnificent promises, and act like Judas. Today there are so many examples that confirm David's saying, by which he declares that every man is a liar, that no day would suffice to recount them. Let us never forget the warning of Christ, who long ago said through the prophet: "Do not trust a friend," that is, one who feigns friendship, and "guard the doors of your mouth from her who lies in your bosom." And again in the Gospel: "Beware of men. A man's enemies will be those of his own household." See Mic. 6. Matth. 10.

units.la: Sed qualis tunc Christus fuerit, videamus, qui paulo ante se omni abiecta, animo concidisse videbatur. Iam fortis hostibus obuiam progreditur, & quem tam solicite quaerant, interrogat. Et illis IESVM Nazarenum nominantibus respondet, Ego sum: Et simul occultas suae potentiae vires exerens, illos sternit, ut simul omnes supini cadant. Iterum vero in pedes erectos, similiter compellans, simili virtute sternit: hoc exemplo docens, quam formidabilis sit nominis sui potentia semper futura hostibus suis, qui aduersus ipsum mundo & huius principi militant. In Euangelio certe ad nomen IESV conremiscunt daemones. Prae alijs autem obseruari debet, quod Iudam amicissimum compellat, dicens: Amice, quorsum ades? Et ut Lucas annotauit: Iuda, osculo Filium hominis prodis? Quae verba cor adamantinum flectere poterant, cum simul ipsi pristinam conuersationem, quae nihil poterat dulcius fingi, in mentem renocarent. Cuius specimen ut nunc quoq; omnibus praeberet, apud Ioannem addit: Si me quaeritis, finite hos abire. Quo vno dicto discipulos aduersus hostium furorem seruat, seipsum vero his vinciendum & abducendum tradit. Ita vero docet suo exemplo, quatenus carnis infirmitati indulgere debeamus? eo vsq; nimirum, ut fortes si mus, quando necessitas nostrae vocationis & Dei gloriae sic postulat: Vt item nostrae fidei credites non negligamus. Christum certe discipulorum rationem diligentissimam habuisse, apparet, quando Patri in feria illa precatione iam in mortem abiturus, dixit, Quos dedisti mihi, ego custodini, & nemo ex ijs perijt, nisi filius ille perditionis, &c. Ioan. 17.
units.tr: But let us see what Christ was like then, he who a little before seemed to have collapsed in spirit, with all his courage cast aside. Now he boldly goes out to meet the enemies, and asks whom they so anxiously seek. When they name him Jesus of Nazareth, he answers, "I am," and at once, exerting the hidden powers of his majesty, he throws them down, so that they all fall flat on their backs. Again, when they get up on their feet, he addresses them in the same way and strikes them down with the same power, teaching by this example how formidable the power of his name will always be to his enemies, who fight against him together with the world and its prince. In the Gospel, certainly, the demons tremble at the name of Jesus. But above all it must be observed that he addresses Judas as a most dear friend, saying: "Friend, why are you here?" And as Luke noted: "Judas, do you betray the Son of Man with a kiss?" These words could bend a heart of adamant, since they recalled to his mind their former fellowship, which could not be imagined to be sweeter. To show this to them all, he adds in John: "If you seek me, let these men go." By this one word he protects the disciples against the fury of the enemies, while he himself hands himself over to be bound and led away. In this way he teaches by his own example how far we ought to indulge the weakness of the flesh: namely, only so far that we are brave when the necessity of our calling and the glory of God so demands; likewise, that we do not neglect the trust due to our faith. Certainly Christ showed the most careful concern for his disciples, as is evident when, in that prayer to the Father, now about to go to death, he said: "Those whom you gave me, I have kept, and none of them has perished, except the son of perdition," etc. John 17.

units.la: Vt autem in cohorte illa elucet incurabilis eorum contumacia, qui in huius mundi gratiam adulterfus Christum conspirauerunt: sic hodie multa huius generis in nobis ipsis experimur: quanda morbis aut aliis iudiciorum eius exemplis prostrati, ad institutum redimus: Sed sit hoc magno nostro malo. Nobis ergo dici potest, quod olim paralytico dictum fuit: Ecce sanus factus es, ne peccaueris. Simul soletur nos Christi potentia, qui hostibus immanissimis circumuentur, dicto suos discipulos seruare potuit. Quam ergo infelices sunt, qui hominum metu se deuinci sinunt, ut ab hoc tanto vindice deficiant, & propter mundum hunc prauum & aduersarium ipsum & Euan gelium eius abnegent, quod potentia Dei est ad salutem omni credenti, Rom.1. Quin ex ipsis vin culis Christi consolationem petamus. Hac enim ideo ille in se recepit, ut nos a laqueis peccati & vinculis mortis atque inferorum redimeret. Et feramus patienter, quae ille nobis iniecit vincula morborum omnis generis aduersorum, quibus carnis nostrae ferociam castigat.
units.tr: And just as the incurable obstinacy of those in that band, who conspired against Christ for the sake of the favour of this world, shines out, so today we experience many things of this kind in ourselves: sometimes, struck down by illnesses or other judgments of his, we return to our resolve; but let this be to our great harm. So to us can be said what was once said to the paralytic: "Behold, you are made well; sin no more." At the same time the power of Christ comforts us: though surrounded by most savage enemies, he was able by a single word to keep his disciples safe. How unhappy, then, are those who allow themselves to be bound by fear of men, so as to fall away from so great a defender, and, for the sake of this wicked world, which is his adversary, deny both him and his Gospel, which is "the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes," Rom. 1. Rather, let us seek consolation from the very chains of Christ. For he took them upon himself so that he might redeem us from the snares of sin and the bonds of death and of hell. And let us bear patiently whatever chains of diseases of every kind, or adversities, he lays upon us, by which he curbs the wildness of our flesh.

units.la: Sed ad Petrum veniamus, qui se cum Christo in mortem abire velle promisit. Videamus ergo quid fecerit, quando mortis periculum & occasio tanti promissi praestandi se offerebat. De eo sic scribit Matthaeus: Ecce vnus ex ijs, qui erant cum IESV, extenja manu exeruit gladium suum, & percussoferuo Pontificis maximi, abstulit auriculam eius, &c. Magnum & forte facinus animo concepit Petrus: sed si recte consideretur, non magnam laudem reportauit. Etenim quod debebat facere, & quod abjq; periculo cum laude fieri poterat: Vigilare nimirum cum Christo & precari: id non facit. Nunc iniussus audet facinus, quo seipsum & Dominum IESVM cum discipulis omnibus in praesens vita periculum adducere poterat. Deinde totus ardet, & reliquos etiam tantum non incitat, clamans, Domine, percutiemus ne gladio? Euentus vero pugnae ridiculus est. Nam auriculam solam aufert seruulo Pontificis, cuius caput petebat. Tandem atrium Pontificis ingressus ostiaria voce terretur, & feruorum quaestionibus cedit, ut Christum turpiter neget. Est hic typus omnium, qui inconsulto zelo & carnis affectu abrepti, Deo non vocante, res magnas aggrediuntur. Et vtinam hodie non multa similia fierent, quae simpliciores & pios graui ter offendunt, impios autem ferociores reddunt. Interim Pontificis seruus Malchus docet suo exemplo, quid euenire fere ijs, qui Antichristianis praesulibus se in seruitium addicunt. Est aurium obedientiae & fidei symbolum in scripturis. Sed aurem dextram amittunt tales, ut verbum Dei vel omnino non audiant, vel sinistris auribus illud audiant, & ex eo fiant deteriores.
units.tr: But let us come to Peter, who promised that he would go with Christ even to death. Let us see, then, what he did when the danger of death and the opportunity to make good on his great promise were set before him. Matthew writes of him: "Behold, one of those who were with Jesus stretched out his hand and drew his sword, and struck the servant of the high priest and cut off his ear," and so on. Peter conceived a bold and brave deed, but if it is considered rightly, he gained little praise. For what he ought to have done, and what could have been done with credit and without danger, was to keep watch and pray with Christ, and this he did not do. Instead, unbidden, he dared a deed by which he could bring himself and the Lord Jesus, with all the disciples, into danger of life.
