units.tr: The first and root of all the evil (as we noted recently) was that Peter, forgetful of Christ's very serious warnings, followed him at a distance when he was led away, entered also the courtyard of the High Priest, and sat down with the servants to see how the matter would end. Here, soon, one occasion after another arose, and by degrees he slipped into worse. For while he was still sitting outside in the courtyard, a maidservant, the doorkeeper (as John calls her), came up to him and, addressing him, said, "You also were with Jesus the Galilean." The other girl spoke of him to the bystanders no more harshly: "This man was with Jesus the Nazarene." Yet this was a trivial occasion for so grave a sin. For if you consider the character of these servant girls, it was ridiculous for an Apostle to be frightened by the voice of a woman. Moreover, the words themselves sounded in no way threatening or terrifying. For even if they said that he had been with Jesus, he had nothing to fear from that. Until then many men and women of every place and rank had been with Christ, and none of them had suffered any harm from his company. Why, then, should Peter be afraid, who a little before, fighting at the Mount of Olives, had escaped safely from the midst of his enemies? But carnal confidence is wont to degenerate into the most cowardly fear when it sees its first attempt fail; and this happens all the more if we take flesh as our counsellor, as we see Peter did here. For his first answer to the girl shows that he was seeking a way of escape. He wants to appear ignorant of the matter when he says, "I do not know what you are talking about." Surely you know now, Peter, what this Galilean Jesus is? Do you not know him to be the one of whom you yourself said earlier, "You have the words of eternal life; and we believe and know that you are the Christ, the Son of the living God"? Or is it now that you are ashamed of him whom you were not ashamed of when he was a poor and wretched fisherman? And what other reason can be given for such a doubtful stance before the authorities? But answering in this way gains him nothing. You wish to put off the girl in this manner, so that by freely confessing Christ you do not come into danger, and yet not be said to have denied him. But hear the Holy Spirit pronouncing on your deed: "But he denied it before them all, saying, 'I do not know what you are talking about.'" So he denied Christ, not before a worthless little woman or an obscure servant girl, but before all, that is, before those whose favour he thought he had to win. From this a general doctrine must be drawn: Christ is denied not only in plain words, but perhaps also by dissimulation. The mother, as it were, of this dissimulation is carnal prudence, which bids us reject the cause of faith as if it had nothing to do with us. This is so common today that many seek their praise for prudence in precisely this, when they are asked about the faith. But let those who are ashamed of the Lord's words and of his own in this adulterous and sinful generation hear the Lord's saying: "Whoever is ashamed of me and of my words in this adulterous and sinful generation, of him also will the Son of Man be ashamed, when he comes in the glory of his Father with the holy angels." For carnal reason is wont to suggest other counsels as well, when it is consulted as a counsellor; and Matthew, speaking of the other servant girl also, clearly shows this. For he writes that Peter went out into the porch, no doubt to avoid the occasions of sin which he had begun to feel. For he saw that it would not be safe for him to remain in the High Priest's house. But since he ought to have leapt out at once, as from a fire, he wishes to make a withdrawal of such a kind that it will not make him suspected, nor be the cause of some new danger. So he gradually, and as if doing something else, wishes to slip away. But here too he gains nothing, for he now openly denies Christ, whom he had begun to be ashamed of. For with an oath he says, "I do not know the man." And so he is not only a cowardly concealer of the faith, but a plain liar and a perjurer. These are the fruits of confidence and carnal prudence, by which those are commonly governed who are wont to follow the courts of the princes of this age and of the Antichristian prelates, so that they may warm themselves among their attendants, that is, make a profit.

units.la: Et hoc facit quod apud alios Evangelistas differtè narratur de Petro, qui cum nec in aula, nec in vestibulo Caiaphae fetuo versari posse videret, non tamen erupit ut par erat, sed sua prudentia & carnis rationi adhuc indulgens servus pontificum se intermiscuit, inter quos ad igne con sedit, ut se calefaceret. Illic iam gravior & periculosior abnegandi occasio offertur. Nam a servis illis tentatur, qui non simpliciter dicunt, illam aliquando cum Iesu fuisse, sed argumentis urgent, quae ex ipsius ore petunt, dicentes: Vere & tu ex ipsis es: nam & locutio tua te manifestum facit. Erat enim alia Galilaeorum dialectus quam eorum qui Iudaeam incolebant. Quo magis ergo negabat se cum Christo fuisse, eo magis patebat eum Galilaeum esse. Quae causa fuit ut deterationibus temerarijs execrationes quoque adderet, quibus seipsum devovebat. Et est observatu dignissimum, in pontificis aula tam frigidum fuisse Petrum, qui prius pro aliis in Christi amore ferue bat. Typum enim nobis exhibet eorum, qui alicuius commodi externi causa Christo renunciant, ut adversarijs & hostibus eius magis propitijs vtantur. Quid enim aliud fiat ijs, qui ab eo recedunt, qui est soliusticiae, quam ut primum tepidi fiant, & mox frigescant etiam. Nolunt quidem tales videri, & ideo prunas superstitionum, quae religionis speciem aliquam referunt, vndiq; congerunt, & cultus subinde novos instruunt, & se interdum probe calere putant. Sed non alius ille calor est, quam quem Isaias idolorum sculptoribus tribuit, qui partem aliquam ligni in imaginem formant, qui proni adorant & pro Deo colunt: ex alia parte focum incendunt, coquunt sibi cibum & ad ignem sedentes dicunt, Euge caleo. Talis omnino iam est Petrus qui dum sibi ipsi consulere vult, subinde in peius proficit, & seipsum proprij oris testimonio condemnat. Dum enim negat se nouisse Christum, nonne fatetur se indignum esse, quem hic pro suo agnoscat? Et dum in aula Pontificis sibi locum parat, ut ex regni Christi caelestis aula eiiciatur, meretur.
units.tr: This is also what the other Evangelists relate at length about Peter. Since he could not remain in the courtyard or in the porch of Caiaphas without danger, he did not break away as he should have, but still indulging his prudence and carnal reason, he mingled with the High Priest's servants, and sat down among them by the fire to warm himself. There a more serious and dangerous occasion for denying presented itself. For he is tested by those servants, who do not simply say that he was once with Jesus, but press him with arguments drawn from his own speech, saying, "Surely you also are one of them, for your speech betrays you." For the dialect of the Galileans was different from that of those who lived in Judea. Therefore the more he denied being with Christ, the more plainly he showed himself to be a Galilean. This was the reason he added curses to his rash oaths, by which he called down destruction upon himself. And it is most worthy of note that Peter, who had previously been so fervent for others in the love of Christ, was so cold in the High Priest's courtyard. For he presents to us a picture of those who renounce Christ for the sake of some external advantage, so that they may make themselves more pleasing to his adversaries and enemies. For what else happens to those who fall away from him who is the Sun of righteousness, than that at first they become lukewarm and soon grow cold altogether? Such people certainly do not want to appear so, and therefore they heap together from every side the embers of superstitions, which bear some semblance of religion, and from time to time they set up new forms of worship, and sometimes think they are glowing with a proper warmth. But that warmth is no different from the warmth which Isaiah ascribes to the makers of idols, who fashion a piece of wood into an image, bow down before it, worship it and honour it as God, while on the other side they kindle a fire, cook their food, and sitting by the fire say, "Aha, I am warm." Peter is just such a man, who, while he wants to look after himself, goes from bad to worse, and condemns himself by his own mouth. For when he says he does not know Christ, does he not confess that he is unworthy to be acknowledged here as one of his? And while he prepares for himself a place in the High Priest's hall, he deserves to be cast out of the heavenly court of Christ's kingdom.

units.la: Sed observandi debet in his singulare prouidentia Dei consilium, qui Petrum quem confidentio rem aequo esse sciebat, & qui aliquando afflictionum omnium Christi testis esse debuit, propriae infirmitatis sensu & experimento (ut sic loquar) suae incredulitatis ad constantiam maiorem exercere & armare voluit. Quis enim dubitet illum postea eo magis incaluisse in afferenda illius gloria, quem adeo turpiter aus se negatum esse cogitabat. Debemus idem de omnibus speraire quos hi mites diuini amoris, & hac causa est, ut ipsis omnia adiumento sint in bonum. Nam ut pro carnis corruptae ingenio occasiones peccandi facile arripiunt: ita eosdem Spiritus Christi accendit & excitat, ut non minus industrij sint & prompti in obseruandis occasionibus, quibus ipsos ad respipiscendum Dominus reuocat.
units.tr: But in these events we ought to notice the singular counsel of God's providence. He wished to train and arm Peter, who had been overconfident and who ought to have been a witness of all Christ's sufferings, toward greater steadfastness through the sense and experience (so to speak) of his own weakness and unbelief. Who could doubt that Peter afterwards burned all the more to proclaim Christ's glory, since he had thought himself so shamefully denied by Christ? We ought to hope the same for all whom the gentle love of God embraces, and this is why all things work together for their good. For just as the flesh of corrupt nature readily seizes on occasions for sinning, so the Spirit of Christ kindles and stirs those same people, so that they are no less diligent and ready to seize the occasions by which the Lord calls them back to repentance.

units.la: Exemplum eius rei etiam in Petro apparet, cuius paenitentiam ita Euangelistae describunt, ut
units.tr: An example of this appears also in Peter, whose repentance the Evangelists describe in such a way that

units.la: Matth. 26. formam tran- lant, quae perpetuo in Ecclesia observari debet. In illa ordinem diligenter spectare oportet, vbi duo concurrunt. Primum occasiones narrantur, quae illum moverunt, vt de salute serio cogitaret. Fuerunt hae aliae externae, aliae internae. Ad externas pertinet, quod gallus mittit vocem suam, & quidem bis, vt expresse & distincte Marcus annotavit. Fit ergo illud, de quo Dominus illum admonuerat, vt haberet quo in viam revocaretur. Quia enim pro carnis ingenio externis intenti sumus & ducimur, vt foris adhibeantur nobis media oportet, quibus excitemur. Itaque per galli cantum hic significantur omnes admonitiones quae foris adhibentur a Deo, & quae multae atque variae sunt. Huc referri debent privatae amicorum admonitiones. Obtestationes item & calumniae hostium, quae si prudenter observentur, saepe plurimum prosunt, quando de iis admonent, quae amici veri prae amore vel non observant in nobis, vel dissimulant, dum nolunt offendere. Sunt item improuisi casus, quibus peccantes excitat Deus: Tale quid erat quod Balaami asina praeter morem refragabatur, vt illius pedem ad murum leteret: vt nimirum inde colligeret, hoc non fine certo Dei consilio fieri. Idem prodigiorum vsus est, quibus similiter excitamur, vt de Dei ira se de caelo & in aliis mundi partibus nobis manifestante cogitemus. In primis pertinet huc praedicatio Verbi externa: Et hinc originem duxit mos ille vetustus, quo omnis templorum vastigijs & turribus gallorum imagines imponuntur, quibus officij admonentur antistites, vt peccantes obser- uent & de poenitentia admoneant. Sed fructu foris admonemur, nisi corda Deus moueat, vt ijs, quae fiunt & dicuntur, attendant. Ideo vt primum galli cecinit, Dominus (vt Lucas annotauit) conuersus, Petrum intuitus est: qui recordatus verborum eius, quae ipsi inter coenandum dixerat, coepit de seria ad Dominum conuersione cogitare. Et hoc quidem ordine adhuc vtitur Deus. Est enim humani generis amantissimus, & nos vult saluos fieri & in veritatis cognitionem venire.
units.tr: (Matt. 26.) they set out a pattern which ought always to be observed in the Church. In it we must carefully note the order, in which two things come together. First, the occasions are related which moved him to think seriously about his salvation. These were partly external and partly internal. Among the external ones is that the cock sounded its voice, and indeed twice, as Mark expressly and distinctly noted. So what the Lord had warned him of came to pass, that he might have a way by which he could be turned back to the right path. For since we are inclined and led outward by the nature of the flesh, outward means must be applied to us by which we are roused. Thus by the crowing of the cock are signified all the admonitions that God applies from without, and these are many and various. To this belong the private admonitions of friends; likewise the entreaties and accusations of enemies, which, if they are wisely heeded, often help greatly, since they warn us of things which true friends, out of love, either do not notice in us or pass over, because they are unwilling to offend. There are also unexpected events by which God rouses sinners. Something of this kind was the case when Balaam's donkey, contrary to its custom, resisted and pressed his foot against the wall, so that he might gather that this did not happen without a definite counsel of God. Likewise there is the use of portents, by which we are similarly roused to think of God's wrath, which he makes manifest to us from heaven and in other parts of the world. Above all, the external preaching of the Word belongs here. From this came that ancient custom by which images of cocks are placed on the summits of temples and towers, to remind the ministers that they should watch over sinners and admonish them about repentance. But we are admonished outwardly to no profit unless God moves the hearts to attend to what is done and said. Therefore, as soon as the cock crowed, the Lord (as Luke noted) turned and looked upon Peter, who, remembering the words he had spoken to him at supper, began to think seriously of turning back to the Lord. God still uses this order even now. For he is the most loving of the human race, and wills that we be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth.

units.la: At hic Petrum nos imitari oportet, ne nobis ipsis remoras salutis opponamus. Non contem- nit ille vocem galli, quia auris vilis & contempta: quia item quotidianum hoc est, vt post mediam noctem galli canant: sed cogitat quid Dominus dixerit: quid item hic de peccato isto abnegationis pronunciarit. Ex iis ergo de suo facto iudicat, & scelveris atrocitate cognita, absque mora egreditur ex pontificis domo, & flet amare: nimirum animo reputans vetera beneficia Christi, & simul cogitans unde exciderit. Ista vero non potuerunt fieri, quin locum, qui scelerus occasionem dederat, & huius authores animo suo detestatus sit. Lacrymae autem cordis contriti indicium fuerunt, & simul de confessione peccati testantur. Conuenit ergo Petri exemplum cum multis aliis, quae in scripturis proponuntur: qualia sunt Dauidis, peccatricis apud Lucam & similium. Debent autem sibi ipsis accommodare singuli quod Petrus fecit, vt quid nos facere conueniat, discamus. Peccatur passim apud omnis loci & ordinis homines: & quia (vt Dominus de nouissimis temporibus praemonuit) charitas refrixit, iniquitas vero abundat, Dei quoque ira sese manifestat vbique, neque cessat Dominus excitare gallos suos, & inter hos verbi praecones, qui non cantu solum, sed increpatione & minis ad poenitentiam totum mundum excitant. Inter haec vero non obscuris indicijs gratiam & bonitatem suam Deus nobis offert, & indignos oculis benignis respicit, intra animos nostros conuincit, vt multi etiam inuiti cogantur scelera fateri, & sibi ipsis pessima quaeque omnentur. Agnoscamus ergo haec diuinitus fieri, nec contra Deum fremamus: sed excitemur a laetifero somno qui hucusque dormuimus, & relictis infelicis mundi studijs ad germanos discipulos Ecclesiae reuertamur, quibus Petrum quoque se iterum coniunxisse ex ijs apparet, quae post resurrectionem facta sunt. Ita nobis quoque illucescat Christus, vt nos in gratiam receptos seruet ad nominis sui gloriam. Amen.
units.tr: But here we ought to imitate Peter, so that we do not place hindrances to our salvation in our own way. He did not despise the crowing of the cock, as if it were a cheap and contemptible sound, since it is an everyday thing for cocks to crow after midnight. Instead, he thought about what the Lord had said, and what he had declared here about this sin of denial. From these things he judged his own deed, and, recognising the enormity of his crime, he went out of the high priest's house without delay and wept bitterly, no doubt reflecting on Christ's past benefits and at the same time considering from what height he had fallen. Indeed, these things could not happen without his detesting in his mind the place which had given occasion to his crime, and those who were its authors. His tears were a sign of a contrite heart, and at the same time bear witness to the confession of sin. Peter's example therefore agrees with many others set forth in the Scriptures, such as those of David, of the sinful woman in Luke, and of similar cases. Each person ought to apply to himself what Peter did, so that we may learn what it becomes us to do. Sin is committed everywhere, among men of every place and rank; and since (as the Lord forewarned of the last times) love has grown cold and iniquity abounds, God's wrath also makes itself manifest everywhere. Nor does the Lord cease to rouse his cocks, and among these the heralds of the Word, who rouse the whole world to repentance not only by crowing but by rebuke and threats. Meanwhile God offers us his grace and goodness through clear signs, looks on the unworthy with kindly eyes, and convicts our hearts within, so that many, even unwilling, are compelled to confess their crimes and to be stung by their own worst deeds. Let us therefore acknowledge that these things happen by divine ordering, and not rage against God. Rather, let us be roused from the joyless sleep in which we have slept until now, and, leaving the pursuits of this unhappy world, return to the true disciples of the Church, with whom Peter too is seen to have been joined again, from what happened after the resurrection. So may Christ also rise upon us, so that he may keep us, received into grace, to the glory of his name. Amen.

units.la: CAPUT XXVII. HOMILIA CCCII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVII. HOMILY 302.

units.la: MAne autem cum esset, consilium ceperunt omnes principes sacerdotum & Seniores populi aduersus IESVM, vt eum mor te multarent. Et vinctum eum abduxerunt, ac tradiderunt Pontio Pilato praesidi. Tunc Iudas qui eum prodiderat, videns eum damnatum esse, poenitens, retulit triginta argenteos nummos ad principes sacerdotū & Seniores, dicēs, Peccavi prodito sanguine innoxio. At illi dixerunt: Quid ad nos? tu videris. Et ipse abiectis illis nūmis argenteis in templo, recessit: & abiens strangulauit se. Principes autem sacerdotum acceptis nummis illis argenteis, dixerunt: Non licet eos mittere in Corbonam, quoniam pretium sanguinis est. Consilio autem capto, emerunt ex eis agrum illum figuli ad sepulturam hospitum. Quapropter vocatus est ager ille, ager sanguinis usque in hodiernum diem. Tunc impletum est quod dictum est per Ieremiam Prophetam dicentem: Et acceperunt triginta nummos argenteos, pretium aestimati, qui aestimatus fuit a filiis Israel. Et dederunt eos ad emendum agrum figuli, sicut constituit mihi Dominus.
units.tr: When morning came, all the chief priests and the elders of the people took counsel against Jesus, so that they might put him to death. They bound him, led him away, and handed him over to Pontius Pilate the governor. Then Judas, who had betrayed him, seeing that he had been condemned, was seized with remorse and brought back the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and elders, saying, "I have sinned in betraying innocent blood." But they said, "What is that to us? See to it yourself." So he threw the silver pieces down in the temple, departed, and went and hanged himself. The chief priests took the silver pieces and said, "It is not lawful to put them into the temple treasury, since it is the price of blood." After taking counsel, they bought with them the potter's field, to bury strangers in. For this reason that field has been called the Field of Blood, even to this day. Then was fulfilled what was spoken by the prophet Jeremiah, who said: "And they took the thirty pieces of silver, the price of him who was valued, whom the children of Israel valued, and gave them for the potter's field, as the Lord appointed me."

units.la: MEMORABILE est Ioannis Apostoli & Euangelistae de Filio Dei Domino & redemptore nostro dictum, illum ad suos venisse, suos autem ipsum non recepisse. Suffragatur huic tota Euangelij historia, in primis vero ea pars, qua eius passio & mors describitur. Hac enim docet omnes hominum ordines aduersus illum conspirauisse. Inter Iudaeos enim qui Dei peculium erant, & ad quos Christus potissimum pertinebat, cum ipsis promissus, & ex ipsdem natus esset, erant primi Sacerdotes, Scribae & Seniores. At hi omnes illum oderunt, & non quieuerunt, donec in potestatem suam redactum occiderunt. Ab his pependit populus, olim in suas tribus diuisus, in quo infimum locum tenebant ferui tum publici tum privati. At nullus horum ordinum est, qui se sanguinis Christi immunem possit dicere, cum ex Apostolorum numero vnus prodat illum, alter turpiter neget, reliqui omnes turpi fuga eum deserant. At quia Iudaeus non licebat aliquem occidere, ipsi vero vellent publica auctoritate eum mori, vt mortis ignominia in doctrinam eius redundaret, & hanc in contemptum & odium adducerent: narratur nunc vt in Concilio damnatum Pilato praesidi tradiderint: quae prima huius loci pars est. Additur huic infelix Iudae proditoris exitus.
units.tr: It is a memorable saying of the apostle and evangelist John concerning the Son of God, our Lord and Redeemer, that he came to his own, and his own did not receive him. The whole history of the Gospel bears this out, especially that part which describes his passion and death. For it teaches that men of every order conspired against him. Among the Jews, who were God's peculiar people, and to whom Christ chiefly belonged, since he had been promised to them and born from among them, the chief priests, scribes and elders were the foremost. Yet all of these hated him, and did not rest until they had got him into their power and put him to death. The people depended on these leaders; the people, once divided into their tribes, among whom the public and private slaves held the lowest place. And none of these orders can say that it is free of the blood of Christ: one of the number of the apostles betrayed him, another shamefully denied him, and all the rest deserted him in shameful flight. But since it was not lawful for the Jews to put anyone to death, and they wished him to die by public authority, so that the disgrace of his death would reflect on his teaching and bring it into contempt and hatred, it is now related that they, having condemned him in council, handed him over to Pilate the governor. This is the first part of this passage. There is added to it the unhappy end of Judas the traitor.

units.la: Ad primam pertinet quod scribitur: Mane autem cum esset, consilium ceperunt omnes principes Sacerdotum & Seniores populi aduersus IESVM, vt eum morte multarent, & vinctum eum abduxerunt, ac tradiderunt Pontio Pilato praesidi. Fuit hic secundus hostium Christi consentus vel tertius. Primus enim censeri poterit, in quo postea Lazarum a mortuis excitatum decretum fuit necesse esse, vt ipse moriatur, ne creditur eius authoritate populus tumultuetur, & Romani aliquid durius cum totius populi incommodo in illos statuant. Secundus cuius initio Capitis praecedentis mentio facta est, ex quo aliqui ex sacerdotibus cum templo praefectis & feruis atque militibus ad illum capiendum emissi sunt, & in quo (vt nuper audiuimus) illum impietatis damnarunt, vt mortis reum: & feruis suis turpiter & crudeliter illudendū tradiderunt. At quia (sicut nuper diximus) ipsis non licebat illum absq; praesidis consensu occidere (quod paulo post ipsi apud Ioannem confessi sunt) necesse fuit nouo & tertio conuentu, in quo deliberaretur, quid Pilato praesidi pretendere, & quas sua condemnationis causas praetexere velint. Itaq; vesperi quidem, cum diem totum inter laboriosas curas & consultationes consumpsissent, tandem fessi se quieti & somno dederunt (quo interim Dominus Christus non potuit frui, quem illorum seruis inhumanissime tractauerunt.) At ne quid negligant in re quae ipsis tantopere cordi erat, primo diluculo surgunt, & denuo conuenientes consilium ineunt, de quibus criminibus Christum accusare velint, vt Pilato persuadeant dignum iudicari debere, qui ignominioso aliquo & diro mortis supplicio multetur. Interim (vt fieri solet) de IESV capto sparsum est in vrbe rumor, & apud Pontificis domum populus confluxit, & post deliberationem longam, in qua crimen blasphemiae, & quod se Filium Dei dixisset (vt Lucas scribit) repetitum confirmarunt, tota populi multitudine ipsos ciuitate, vinctum abduxerunt ad praetorium & Pilato Praesidi Romano tradiderunt.
units.tr: To the first part belongs what is written: "When morning came, all the chief priests and the elders of the people took counsel against Jesus, so that they might put him to death; and they bound him, led him away, and handed him over to Pontius Pilate the governor." This was the second, or indeed the third, meeting of Christ's enemies. The first may be counted as the one in which it was decided that Lazarus, raised from the dead, must die, lest the people be stirred to tumult by his authority, and the Romans, with harm to the whole people, impose something harsher on them. The second, of which mention was made at the beginning of the preceding chapter, is when some of the priests, with the temple officers, servants and soldiers, were sent out to seize him; and in it (as we heard just now) they condemned him for impiety as deserving death, and handed him over to their servants to be shamefully and cruelly mocked. But since (as we said just now) they were not permitted to put him to death without the governor's consent, which they later admitted before John, it was necessary to hold a new and third assembly, in which they would deliberate what to put forward to Pilate the governor, and what grounds of condemnation they wished to allege. So in the evening, when they had spent the whole day in laborious anxieties and consultations, they at last, weary, gave themselves over to rest and sleep (a rest which in the meantime the Lord Christ could not enjoy, whom the servants of these men treated most inhumanly). But so that they might neglect nothing in a matter that lay so close to their hearts, they rose at first dawn and, meeting again, took counsel about what crimes they should accuse Christ of, so as to persuade Pilate that he ought to be judged worthy of some shameful and dreadful death penalty. Meanwhile (as usually happens) news of Jesus' arrest spread through the city, and the people flocked to the house of the high priest. After a long deliberation, in which they repeated and confirmed the charge of blasphemy, and that he had called himself the Son of God (as Luke writes), the whole multitude of the people with them led him bound out of the city, to the praetorium, and handed him over to Pilate the Roman governor.

units.la: Omnis loci & ordinis hominum reiecerunt. Ioan. 1.
units.tr: They rejected men of every place and rank. John 1.

units.la: Praesidi Romano traditur Christus. Ioan. 11.
units.tr: Christ is handed over to the Roman governor. John 11.

units.la: CAP. XXVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVII.

units.la: Vbi primum obseruari debet, quod hic subest salutis & redemptionis nostrae mysterium. Nam ideo ad prophanos & ethnicei iudicis tribunal sistitur Dei Filius, vt nobis suo merito accessum tutum faceret ad thronum gratiae, a quo procul arceri merebamur. Hinc ergo consolationis argumenta petenda sunt in tentationibus conscientiae: simul huius nos meminisse decet, quando qui nullius scelerus nobis conscij sumus, vt facinorosi tractamur, vt omnibus suspecta fiat nostri nomini existimatio.
units.tr: Here we must first observe that the mystery of our salvation and redemption lies hidden in this passage. The Son of God is brought before the tribunal of a profane, heathen judge so that, by his merit, he might make a safe approach for us to the throne of grace, from which we deserved to be kept far away. Therefore, arguments of consolation are to be sought here in the temptations of conscience. At the same time, we should remember that when we are conscious of no crime, we are treated as criminals, so that our good name becomes suspect to everyone.

units.la: Interim proditur hic pontificum & seniorum populi Dei, qui architecti Ecclesiae videri & dici volebant, improbitas: qui controuersiam de Messia, praecipuo religionis capite, iudici prophano & gentili, atque alienorum deorum cultori subiiciunt. Quis enim hos veri Dei cultu vt quam ferio curauisse dixerit? Similes his sunt, qui hodie fratres, Christi professores apud Turcarum tribunalia accusant: qui item veteres & publicos hostes in patria viscera adducunt, vt horum armis verum Dei cultu extinguant. Euenit ijs haud dubie idem quod Iudaeis, quibus ciuiles ambitiosorum sacerdotum differentiones huius mali causa fuerunt. Vtinam alieno exemplo saperet Germania. Imo vtinam in vicina Gallia & Belgico obseruarent, quae ad suam pacem faciunt.
units.tr: Meanwhile, the wickedness of the high priests and elders of the people of God is exposed here. They wished to be seen and called the architects of the Church, yet they submit a controversy about the Messiah, the chief article of religion, to a profane and gentile judge, a worshipper of alien gods. For who would say that these men took the true worship of God seriously? Similar to them are those who today accuse fellow Christians, professors of Christ, before Turkish courts. Likewise, they bring old public enemies into the bowels of the fatherland, so that by their arms they may extinguish the true worship of God. Undoubtedly the same thing has happened to them as to the Jews, for whom the civil quarrels of ambitious priests were the cause of this evil. Would that Germany were wise from another's example! Indeed, would that they would take note of what makes for peace in neighbouring France and Belgium.

units.la: Praeterea docemur praesenti exemplo, quae vulgi inconstantia & ingratitudo fit. Alias Christum quaesiuerunt Iudaei, vt regem crearent: & ante paucos dies illum acclamationibus laetis exceperunt ac deduxerunt: adhaec vestes supersternendo se ad omne officium paratos esse cofessi sunt. Nunc indignum iudicant, qui in populo Dei censeatur, & eius caput iudicis ethnici arbitrio subiiciunt. Ne ergo vulgo quis fidat, bestia multorum capiti, neque ingratitudine simili aliquis offenda-tur. Seruabit enim ingenium suum mundus: quod est feruere, si quando priuati commodi ipsi se offert. At si haec fallat, & in primis, si religionis & veritatis causa periclitandum sit, rarus est, qui hoc sibi persuaderi sinat, vt caelestia terrenis, futura & aeterna praesentibus bonis anteponat. Beati sunt, qui Domino fidunt, & mercedem quae in caelo ipsis repositae est, respiciunt.
units.tr: Moreover, the present example teaches us how fickle and ungrateful the crowd is. Previously the Jews sought Christ to make him king, and a few days before they received and escorted him with joyful acclamations. They also confessed that they were ready for every duty by spreading their garments before him. Now they judge him unworthy to be counted among the people of God, and they subject his head to the judgment of a heathen. Therefore, let no one trust the crowd, the beast with many heads, and let no one be offended by similar ingratitude. For the world will keep its nature: it boils over whenever private advantage presents itself. But if that advantage deceives, and especially if one must face danger for the sake of religion and truth, there are few who allow themselves to be persuaded to prefer heavenly things to earthly, and future and eternal goods to present ones. Blessed are those who trust in the Lord and look to the reward laid up for them in heaven.

units.la: Caeterum priusquam narret Euangelista nosier, quid Pilatus cum Christo egerit, interseritur hoc loco infelix Iudas proditoris interitus, quem sceleris sui conscientia in desperatione abduxit, vt sibi ipsi mortem violentam accerseret. Habet autem haec historia pars locos aliquot memorabiles, & obseruatu dignos. Primus est exemplum falsae & inutilis poenitentiae, quod verae & falsae poenitentiae exemplo, quod in Petro nuper vidimus, opponitur. Alter est de Sacerdotum improbitate, qui Iudae tanti sceleris simul & interitus authores fuerunt. Tertius de IESV CHRISTI potentia, & quam facile illi fit suos hostes vlcisci. Quartus quam horrenda & abominabilis sit sanguinis innocentis effusio. Vbi exemplum horrendum iudicij diuini proponitur in eos qui Christum pretio vel vendunt vel emunt, seu sanguinis seruorum Christi reos faciunt. Quibus accedit mysterium redemptionis, quo totius mortis Christi fructus adumbratur. De quibus breuiter dicemus, quae annotare opus est.
units.tr: Before our evangelist tells what Pilate did with Christ, the unhappy death of the traitor Judas is inserted here. The consciousness of his crime drove him into despair, so that he brought a violent death upon himself. This part of the history contains several memorable points worth observing. The first is an example of false and useless repentance, which is set over against the example of true repentance that we recently saw in Peter. The second concerns the wickedness of the priests, who were both the authors of Judas's great crime and of his death. The third concerns the power of Jesus Christ, and how easily he can avenge his enemies. The fourth is how horrible and abominable the shedding of innocent blood is. Here a dreadful example of divine judgment is set forth against those who either sell or buy Christ for money, or make themselves guilty of the blood of Christ's servants. To these is added the mystery of redemption, in which the whole fruit of Christ's death is foreshadowed. Concerning these points, we will briefly say what needs to be noted.

units.la: Quoad poenitentiam Iudae, initio videntur omnia convenire cum Petro. Videt aliquem esse de Christo, nec aliquem superesse vitae eius spem, cum a Iudaeis publica concilij authoritate damnatus, & nunc Pilato praesidi ex populi consensu traditus sit. Etenim sperauit fortasse hucusque, illum non passurum, vt aduersarij aliquid durius in ipsum statuant, cum diuinitatem suam toties ante declarasse: aut populum non tam facilem fore, vt in Sacerdotum partes transfiret, & cum his aduersus Christum tam bene de plerisque meritum conspiraret. At nunc videns se omnis pe falsum, & simul priore quam cum illo habuit consuetudine in mentem reuocans, sceleris admissi poenitentia ducitur, & corde suo conteritur adeo, vt pecuniam, quae illius ipsi causa fuerat, oderit & detestetur. Nam triginta argenteos refert ad principes sacerdotum, & his fatetur sceleris sui, dicens: Peccaui prodito sanguine innoxio. Et sane non leuem esse oportuit animi dolorem, qui hanc confessionem misero extorsit. Sed quia fide destituitur, a Petri exemplo tandem declinat. Nec enim ad Christi discipulos, vt Petrus reuertitur, vt Ecclesiae se reconciliet, sed ad sacerdotum principes & seniores se confert, qui illi sceleris authores fuerat, & quos capitales Christi hostes adhuc esse nouerat. Illis sceleris fatetur, & eius conscientia absorptus suspendit se. Fuit ergo haec inutilis poenitentia, qualis in Papatu docetur. In qua peccati agnitionem, cordis contritionem, confessionem & quidem sacerdotibus factam, & his mandata satisfactione est videre. Sed quia fides ipsi deest finis horum omnium est suspendium. Ita fit omnibus qui fide in Christum destituti, aliis viis siue medijs sibi & saluti suae volunt consulere. Hos enim tentationum suarum artibus & laqueis circumuenit Satan. Fide ergo opus est, quae in Dei promissiones & misericordiam respiciat, quarum omnium complementum in uno IESV CHRISTO habetur, qui idem poenitentiae & remissionis author est, ut Ecclesia Apostolica fatetur. Act. 5.
units.tr: As to the repentance of Judas, at first everything seems to agree with Peter's. He sees that there is a plot against Christ and that no hope of his life remains, since he has been condemned by the Jews with the public authority of the council and now handed over to Pilate the governor with the consent of the people. Perhaps he had hoped until now that Christ would not suffer, that the adversaries would not decide anything harsher against him, since he had so often declared his divinity; or that the people would not be so easily turned over to the side of the priests, and would not conspire with them against Christ, who had deserved so well of most of them. But now, seeing that all his hope has failed, and at the same time recalling his former familiarity with Christ, he is led to repentance for the crime he committed. He is so crushed in heart that he hates and detests the money which had been the cause of it for him. For he brings the thirty pieces of silver back to the chief priests and confesses his sin to them, saying: "I have sinned by betraying innocent blood." Indeed, the anguish of mind that extorted this confession from the wretched man must have been no slight one. But because he lacks faith, at last he turns aside from Peter's example. For he does not return, as Peter did, to Christ's disciples, to be reconciled to the Church. Instead, he goes to the chief priests and elders, who had been the authors of his crime, and whom he knew were still Christ's mortal enemies. He confesses his sin to them, and, overwhelmed by his conscience, hangs himself. This, therefore, was the useless repentance such as is taught in Papacy. In it one sees the acknowledgment of sin, contrition of heart, confession, indeed confession made to priests, and satisfaction enjoined by them. But because faith is lacking, the end of all these is hanging. This happens to all who, lacking faith in Christ, want to look after themselves and their salvation by other ways or means. For Satan ensnares them with the wiles and snares of their temptations. Faith is therefore necessary, a faith that looks to God's promises and mercy, the fulfilment of all of which is found in the one Jesus Christ, who is also the author of repentance and forgiveness, as the Apostolic Church confesses. Acts 5.

units.la: Deinde horribilis est, quae hic elucet, sacerdotum improbitas & ingratitudo. Ipsi enim tanti sceleris ei authores fuerunt, nec extra culpam sunt, cum pretium sanguinis contra innocentem ipsi exposuerunt. At ijdem nunc miserum & desperabundum, non solum deferunt, & omni consolatione destituunt, sed responso suo, perinde ut violento impetu propellunt in desperationis barathrum. Cum enim dicunt, Tu videris, satis testantur, scelus hoc atrocius esse, quam ut ipsi ei mederi possint: & ita ad sua opera illum remittentes, suspendij illi authores sunt. Hanc mercedem recipiunt, quicunque cum impijs praesulibus & Antichristianis conspirant. Nam ablegantur ad suas satisfactiones, quae non aliud quam desperationem pariunt: cum conscientiae ipsius nihil praeter fides in me ritum Christi possit reflinguere.
units.tr: Next, the wickedness and ingratitude of the priests, which shine forth here, are appalling. They were the authors of so great a crime, and they are not free from blame, since they themselves offered the price of blood against the innocent. Yet these same men now not only hand over the wretched man and deprive him of all consolation, but with their answer they drive him, as if by violent force, into the abyss of despair. For when they say, "See to it yourself," they sufficiently testify that the crime is too atrocious for them to be able to heal it. So, sending him back to his own works, they become the authors of his hanging. Those who conspire with impious prelates and Antichristians receive this reward. For they are sent away to their satisfactions, which produce nothing but despair, since nothing except faith in the merit of Christ can wipe away the stain upon one's conscience.

units.la: Nec officiunt praeteriri debet potentia Christi diuina, qua suos hostes potentissime vlcisci-tur. Nam etsi in Concilio damnatus, nunc vinctus quoque coram iudice Ethnico stet, iamiam in crucem infamem suffigendus, ita tamen hostes suos vlciscitur, ut nullus ad ipsos ex iniuria sibi facta fructus perueniat. Iudas non modo sceleris propria confessione se infamat, sed insuper vitam sibipsi aufert, & pecuniam quae ipsi vita charior fuerat, sponte abijcit, ut ne vnius horulae spacio il-la frui possit. Sacerdotes vero primarij authores sceleris seipsos infamant, dum scelus expiare volunt. Similia exempla videmus in tyrannis persecutoribus, qui Ecclesiam, quae Christi sponsa est, infestarunt. Qui enim olim in statu humilitatis suae tantum potuit, quid non posset nunc, quando omni potestate in caelo & in terra accepta, ad dexteram Patris considet.
units.tr: Nor should the divine power of Christ be passed over, by which he most powerfully avenges his enemies. Although he has been condemned in the council and now stands bound before the heathen judge, about to be fastened to the infamous cross, he so avenges his enemies that no fruit from the wrong done to him reaches them. Judas not only defames himself by confessing his crime, but moreover takes away his own life, and willingly throws away the money which had been dearer to him than life, so that he could not enjoy it for a single hour. But the chief priests, the principal authors of the crime, defame themselves while they wish to expiate it. We see similar examples in tyrannical persecutors who have harassed the Church, which is Christ's bride. For if he could do so much once in the state of his humility, what could he not do now, when, having received all power in heaven and on earth, he sits at the right hand of the Father?

units.la: Docet item exemplum hoc, quam horrenda & abominabilis censeri debeat sanguinis innocentis effusio. Horret sceleris hoc Iudas, & pecuniam quae illius causa ipsi fuerat, ceu prunas ardentes ex sinu excussas abijcit. Eandem horrent & abominantur sacerdotes, ut eam neque in templi thesauros reponere, neque aliis sacris usibus addicere, neque quantumuis auari inter sua reponere volunt. Interim ipsi quoque scelus admissum non obscure fatentur. Et dum hoc expiare volunt, empto ex illa agro figuli in sepulturam peregrinorum qui religionis ergo Ierosolyma aduentantes, interdum moriebantur: hic quoque inde nomen accepit, ut ager sanguinis dicatur: Et simul de illo exponitur Ieremiae vel potius Zachariae locus, ut publica gentis Iudaicae ingratitudo illis exprobretur: qui Dei Filium & Messiam suum non maioris aestimauerint. Docet autem nos exemplum hoc iudicare de pretio sanguinis: quod ita abominatur Deus, ut ex illo sanguinea & cruenta in eius conspectu aestimentur, quaecunque ex eo emuntur aut fiunt. Et quod sacerdotibus istis accidit, ut per petuam sceleris sui memoriam ad posteros transmiserint, dum illud expiare volunt: hoc ipsum fit omnibus, qui ut caedes iniustas, rapinas & alia scelera expient, anathemata in templis suspendunt: digni qui cum filijs Iacobi conferantur, qui tunicam filij Iosephi laceram & cruentam illius oculis ingerebant. Sed in primis agnoscant hic iudicium Dei iustum omnes qui Christum pretio iniquo vel emunt vel vendunt.
units.tr: This example also teaches how horrible and abominable the shedding of innocent blood must be judged. Judas shudders at this crime and throws away the money that was the cause of it for him, as if casting burning coals out of his bosom. The priests shudder and abhor the same money, so that they are unwilling either to put it into the temple treasury, or to devote it to other sacred uses, or even to keep it among their own goods, however greedy they are. Meanwhile, they too do not obscurely confess the crime they committed. And while they wish to expiate it, they buy with that money the potter's field as a burial place for strangers who, coming to Jerusalem for the sake of religion, sometimes died there. The place received its name from this, so that it is called the field of blood. At the same time, the passage of Jeremiah, or rather Zechariah, is applied to it, so that the public ingratitude of the Jewish nation may be reproached to them, for they did not esteem the Son of God and their Messiah more highly. This example teaches us to judge about the price of blood: God so abhors it that whatever is bought or made from it is counted bloody and bloodstained in his sight. And what happened to these priests, that they transmitted to posterity a perpetual memory of their crime while wishing to expiate it, this same thing happens to all who, to expiate unjust murders, robberies and other crimes, hang votive offerings in temples. They deserve to be compared with the sons of Jacob, who presented their father with the torn and bloodied tunic of Joseph. But above all, let those who buy or sell Christ for unjust money recognise here the just judgment of God.

units.la: Concurrit autem cum his omnibus redemptionis & salutis nostrae mysterium, multa & dulcissima consolationis plenum. Peregrinamur omnes in hoc mundo, & hinc nobis exeundum est per mortem, quae olim peccati poena fuit. Hanc Christus sui sanguinis pretio concertit, ut nobis iam via fit ad quietem sempiternam, cuius non ante participes efficimur, quam cum hinc soluimus, & vitam hanc mortalem cum immortali commutamus. Soletur etiam, quod ut Christo nihil accidit, quam quod olim a Deo sic decretum & a Prophetis praedictum fuit: Ita nobis quoque qui in eum credimus, & per fidem eius membra facti sumus. Cogitemus ergo nos diuinae prouidentiae consilio gubernari, & dies nostros in manu Dei esse. Et inter omnia aduersa nobis applicemus, quod in hac iniquissima sanguinis sui aestimatione sibi ex Propheta applicat Dei Filius: Sic mihi constituit Dominus. Cur vero nobis iniquum aut durum videatur, quod ex Dei decreto fit, cuius iudicia sunt iustitia & veritas? Hunc oremus ex toto corde, ut nos seruet & regat ad sui nominis gloriam. Amen.
units.tr: Along with all these things comes the mystery of our redemption and salvation, full of many sweet consolations. We are all pilgrims in this world, and from here we must depart through death, which was once the penalty of sin. Christ has made this death an entrance by the price of his own blood, so that it is now a way for us to eternal rest. We do not share in that rest until we leave this place and exchange this mortal life for an immortal one. We may also take comfort in this: nothing happened to Christ except what God had decreed long ago and the Prophets had foretold. So it is with us too, who believe in him and have become members of him through faith. Let us therefore consider that we are governed by the counsel of divine providence, and that our days are in the hand of God. In all adversity let us apply to ourselves what the Son of God applies to himself from the Prophet, in this most unjust estimation of his blood: "So the Lord has appointed for me." Why should it seem unjust or hard to us that it happens by the decree of God, whose judgments are justice and truth? Let us pray to him with our whole heart that he will keep and rule us to the glory of his name. Amen.

units.la: Iesus autem stetit coram praeside, & interrogauit eum praeses, dicens: Tu nes Rex ille Iudaeorum? Dixit autem ei Iesus: Tu dicis. Et cùm ipse accusaretur a principibus sacerdotum & senioribus, nihil respondit. Tunc dicit ei Pilatus: Non audis quàm multa aduersum te testificentur: Et non respondit ei ad vllum verbum: ita vt admiraretur Praeses valde.
units.tr: Jesus stood before the governor, and the governor asked him, saying, "Are you the King of the Jews?" Jesus said to him, "You say so." And when he was accused by the chief priests and elders, he made no answer. Then Pilate said to him, "Do you not hear how many things they testify against you?" But he gave him no answer to any word, so that the governor marveled greatly.

units.la: Dominus noster IESVS CHRISTVS non solùm occidi, sed priusquam idfieret, gentibus tradi & ad Ethnici praesidis tribunal sisti debuit: partim vt nobis ad tribunal Dei accesjum securum faceret: partim vt suo exemplo nos consoletur, ne impatientiores simus, si quando nobis idem accidat, vt digni iudicemur, propter quos alienigenorum vel Turcarum tribunalia fatigentur. Vt vero in hac actione inprimis elucet sacerdotum improbitas & iniquitas, qui hominem suae gentis, & in hoc causam religionis hominis prophani, & a veri Dei cognitione alieni iudicio subiciunt: digni, qui similiter ipsi etiam postea Romanis traderentur, & cum suis superstitionibus toti orbi ludibrium fierent. Ita considerantu dignum est quales se in hac actione illi gesserint: & proinde locum hunc ex Ioannis 18. capite farcire oportet. Illic de eis dicitur, quod in praetorium non intrarint ingredi ne polluerentur, sed se puros seruarent, vt epulo paschali possent vesci. Est hoc Pharisaicae, id est, fucata sanctimoniae exemplum, quam illis supra exprobrauit Christus, quando dicit, ipsos colare culicem, deglutire autem camelum. Metuunt pollutionem legalem ex loco in litis sacro, in quo sententiae capitales pronuntiantur: non metuunt autem offensam Dei, quam sanguinis innoxij effusione merebantur. Itaque in scelere ipsofanctii & iusti videri volunt, quod hypocritis proprium est. Nunc ad Pilatum venIamus.
units.tr: Our Lord Jesus Christ had to be not only killed, but, before that happened, handed over to the Gentiles and brought before the tribunal of a heathen governor. This was partly so that he might make our access to the tribunal of God safe, and partly so that by his example he might console us and keep us from being more impatient if the same thing happens to us, that we are judged worthy to have our cases dragged before the courts of foreigners or Turks on account of whom we suffer. In this action, the wickedness and injustice of the priests stand out above all. They subject to the judgment of a foreigner a man of their own nation, a man charged with a matter of religion, a man profane and estranged from the knowledge of the true God. They deserved to be handed over in turn to the Romans, and to become a laughingstock for the whole world with their superstitions. So it is worth considering what sort of men they showed themselves to be in this affair, and therefore we ought to fill out this passage from John chapter 18. There it is said of them that they did not go into the praetorium, lest they be defiled, but kept themselves pure so that they might eat the Passover feast. This is an example of Pharisaic, that is, feigned, sanctimony, which Christ reproached them for when he said that they strain out a gnat and swallow a camel. They feared legal pollution from entering a place of judgment in which capital sentences are pronounced, but they did not fear the offense of God, which they incurred by shedding innocent blood. Thus they wish to seem holy and righteous in the very crime, which is characteristic of hypocrites. Now let us come to Pilate.

units.la: Hic cùm illi nollent ingredi praetorium, ipse ad eos exit. Occasionem iustam habebat illos vincim fastidiendi, cùm ad ipsum ingredi dedignarentur, aut illos in aliud tempus reijcere. Sed bonis iudicis officium facit, & aequaniter fert illorum contumaciam, & quia eos tam serio causam hanc vrgere videt, non vult ipse cunctari, ne mora alicui priuatim vel toti Reipublicae noceat. Interim non praecipitat sententiam, sed quaerit, de quibus IESVM accusent, dicens: Quam accusationem affertis aduersus hominem istum? Et hoc quidem abfq; odij aut inuidiae significatione: nec vllo praeiudicio occupatus: cùm pontifices praeiudicio peccarint, & in quaerendis testimonijs falsis laborarint. At Pilati aequitas illos non monet, vt curent, ne ipsi ethnico homine non sint iniquiores, sed superbè suam authoritate vrget, & petere audent a praeside, vt abfq; diligentiori inquisitio ne sententiam ferat. Nisi iste (inquiunt) esset malefactus, non tradidissemus eum tibi. Fuit haec turpis insolentia, quae eos eò vsq; inflauit, vt praeside cupiant pro carnifice abuti, qui pro ipsorum arbitrio aut libidine, causa adhuc incoperta, debeat re agere. Et hos imitantur hodie personati praesules, qui similiter haereseos damnant omnes, qui ab ipsis dissentiunt, & viros principes ad arma excitant, quibus illos extirpent, nec volunt causam propius cognosci: Et vtinam principes, qui se Christianos dicunt, omnes Pilatum imitarentur: sed multi tunc demum se Catholicos esse putant, si istorum lictores sint, & gladium vel faces & ignem pro illorum nutu exerant.
units.tr: When they were unwilling to enter the praetorium, he himself came out to them. He had a just reason to despise them, since they disdained to enter to him, and to put them off to another time. But he performs the duty of a good judge and bears their obstinacy calmly, and since he sees them pressing this case so earnestly, he does not want to delay, lest the postponement harm anyone privately or the whole commonwealth. Meanwhile he does not rush to sentence, but asks what they accuse Jesus of, saying: "What accusation do you bring against this man?" And he does this without any sign of hatred or ill will, and without being influenced by any prejudgment, whereas the high priests had sinned through prejudgment and had labored to find false witnesses. But Pilate's fairness does not warn them to take care not to be less fair than a heathen man. Instead, they proudly press their authority and dare to ask the governor to pronounce sentence without a more careful inquiry. "If this man (they say) were not a malefactor, we would not have handed him over to you." This was a shameful insolence, which swelled them up so far that they wanted to use the governor as their executioner, to act, a cause not yet examined, at their pleasure or whim. Today the masked prelates imitate them, who likewise condemn as heretics all who dissent from them, and stir up princes to arms to root them out, and do not want the cause to be examined more closely. Would that the princes who call themselves Christian all imitated Pilate! But many then think themselves Catholic only if they are the lictors of those men, and draw the sword, or torches and fire, at their nod.

units.la: Pilatus non ita, sed indignabundus respondet: Accipite eum vos, & secundum legem vestram condemnate eum. Ita vero illis exprobrat, quòd qui reliquis gentibus volebant sanctiores haberi, tam iniqua peterent. Et legis ipsorum meminit, vt simul religione perstringat, qua ipsi gloriabantur. Iam ergo illos sui pudere incipit, & accusationis capita exponunt, quae vt ex aliis licet colligere, tria praecipua fuerunt. Primum, quòd populum seducat: Alterum, quòd tributum & censum Caesari negando seditionem moliatur: Postremum, regnum affectet, dum se dicit esse Regem Iudaeorum. Atqui haec fere sunt, de quibus veritas & eius ministri siue praeconès etiam hodie accusantur. Seductores dicuntur, qui Christum praedicant, qui ipse est Via & Veritas. Quia vero principes viri religionis causam fore leuiorem putant, quàm vt de illa multi velint laborare, alia quoque crimina adduntur, quòd videlicet seditionis spiritu agitati immunitate quaerant & suae...
units.tr: Pilate does not do so, but answers in indignation: "Take him yourselves, and condemn him according to your law." Thus he reproaches them, because they, who wanted to be thought holier than the other nations, asked for such unjust things. He also mentions their law, so as to strike them with the very religion in which they boasted. Now they begin to be ashamed before him, and they set out the heads of the accusation, which, as may be gathered from the other Gospels, were three chief ones. First, that he misleads the people. Second, that by denying tribute and tax to Caesar he stirs up sedition. Last, that he aims at the kingdom, since he says he is King of the Jews. Yet these are almost the same charges on which the truth and its ministers, or heralds, are accused even today. Those who preach Christ, who himself is the Way and the Truth, are called seducers. And because the princes of this world think the cause of religion too trivial for many to labor over it, other crimes are added as well: namely, that, driven by a spirit of sedition, they seek immunity and their own ...

units.la: {y} De quibus Christus accusetur. Ioan. 14. qua iura publica euertat, adhæc authoritati magistratuum legitimorum deroget, quod item minis-tri Ecclesiarum dominium omne ad se transferre cupiant. Sed cum hæc Christus ita negarit, & excusarit, vt Pilato præsidi satis factum sit, & veteres sint ista calumniæ, nemo illis hodie offendi debet. Et cum hodie Episcopi & præsules alij, qui sub Apostolicorum titulo regnum sibi vendicant, cuius affectatores nos esse calumniantur, agnoscamus veterem diaboli sophisticam, neque clamoribus istis moueantur viri principes Christiani, vt sese aduersus Euangelij doctrinam exacerbari sinant. Ratum enim manet quod Pilato respondit Christus, Regnum meum non est de hoc mundo. Et (vt Christianus Poeta olim cecinit.) Non appetit terrestria, qui regna dat cælestia.
units.tr: {y} By what Christ was accused (John 14). They overturn public law, and moreover they detract from the authority of lawful magistrates, and likewise the ministers of the Churches desire to transfer all lordship to themselves. But since Christ denied and excused these things in such a way that Pilate the governor was satisfied, and since these calumnies are old, no one should now be offended by them. And since today bishops and other prelates, who claim a kingdom for themselves under the title of Apostolic succession, and of whose aspirations they falsely accuse us, we should recognize the old sophistry of the devil. Let Christian princes not be moved by those outcries, nor allow themselves to be provoked against the doctrine of the Gospel. For what Christ answered Pilate remains firm: "My kingdom is not of this world." And (as a Christian poet once sang) "He who gives heavenly kingdoms does not seek earthly ones."

units.la: Sed quæ modo ex Ioanne adduximus, qui ista prolixius describit, a Matthæo breuiter perstringuntur, qui hoc solum attingit, IESVM sletisse cora præside: nimirum ne quis hodie offendatur, si ministri Euangelicæ doctrinæ ad tribunalia sistentur, & læsa maiestatis accusentur. Nam hoc ipsum Christo accidit, qui idem nobis quoque euenturum esse prædixit. Hic certe Pilatus, etsi iusti & boni iudicis officio fungatur, tamen grauissimi sceleris suspicione aliqua Christum grauat. Nam interrogat illum dicens: Tune es Rex ille Iudæorum? Erat hoc vulgare & tritum inter Iudæos, quod de Messia ferebatur, qui regnum Danidis instauraturus esset, & Israeli libertatem & regnum pristinum instauraturus. Et hæc hucusque multarum seditionum & cladium grauissimarum causa fuerat. Recte ergo & ex officio facit hoc Pilatus, quod hanc quæstionem mouet. Quasi diceret: Tu ne ille es, qui restitutionis spe hactenus populum lassasti, quæ tot & tantarum turbarum & motuum periculosorum causa fuit? Et quia ex officio hoc quærebat: Christus etiam amicè respondet: & ita quidem, vt veritatem neque neget neque dissimulet, simul tamen suspicionem male conceptam diluat. Nam simpliciter respondet: Tu dixisti. Quod affirmantis formulam esse, iam non semel monuimus. Interim (vt nuper quoque diximus) docet regnum suum non esse eiusmodi, vt Romanis & Imperatori suspectum esse debeat: Idque probat reipsa, cum nullus ministris aut satellitibus stipatus sit, qui pro ipso pugnent. Et quia nulla turba hactenus propter Christum exorta erat, cuius ipse poterat author putari: Iudæi autem (vt Lucas annotauit) Galilææ mentionem faciunt, quasi hanc quoque cum Iudæa turbauisset, Pilatus, qui pro more principum huius seculi pro Christo & religione nolunt periclitari, se autem causa hac molesta & odij sine inuidiæ plena liberari cupiebat, eum ad Herodem, qui tunc Ierosolymæ erat transmisit: qui de multis interrogatum remisit cum ludibrio: cui tamen luculentum innocentiæ testimonium adiunxit.
units.tr: But what we have just brought from John, who describes these things at greater length, Matthew touches on briefly. He mentions only that Jesus stood before the governor, no doubt so that no one should now be offended if ministers of the Gospel doctrine are brought before tribunals and accused of treason. For this very thing happened to Christ, who foretold that it would happen to us too. Here indeed Pilate, although he performs the duty of a just and good judge, nevertheless burdens Christ with some suspicion of a most serious crime. For he asks him, saying: "Are you that King of the Jews?" This was a common and familiar notion among the Jews, that the Messiah would come to restore the kingdom of David and to restore freedom and the former kingdom to Israel. Up to that point this notion had been the cause of many seditions and most grievous disasters. Pilate therefore rightly and in the course of his duty raises this question, as if he were saying: "Are you not that man who until now has wearied the people with hope of restoration, which has been the cause of so many great and dangerous disturbances and uprisings?" And because he asked this as part of his office, Christ also answers him kindly, in such a way that he neither denies nor conceals the truth, yet at the same time removes the ill-formed suspicion. For he simply answers, "You have said it," which, as we have already noted more than once, is the form of affirmation. Meanwhile (as we also said recently) he teaches that his kingdom is not of such a kind that it ought to be suspect to the Romans and the Emperor. He proves this by the fact itself, since he was surrounded by no attendants or guards who would fight for him. And since no crowd had so far arisen on account of Christ, of which he could be thought the author, but the Jews (as Luke notes) mention Galilee, as if he had also thrown that region into turmoil along with Judea, Pilate, who, after the manner of the princes of this age, did not want to be endangered for Christ and religion, but wished to be freed from this troublesome business full of hatred and ill will, sent him to Herod, who was then at Jerusalem. Herod questioned him at length and sent him back with mockery, though he added a clear testimony to his innocence.

units.la: Itaque ipse sua falsus Pilatus, denuo cum Christo ipse cœpit agere, qui cum iam ante respondisset, porro tacuit, licet accusationibus aduersarij instarent, & Pilatus ei diceret: Non audis, quam multa aduersus te testificentur? Ex quo dicto apparet, non quieuisse sacerdotes, sed turbam falsorum testium secum traxisse, vt causam suam facilius obtinerent. Sed recte & merito tacuit ille. Sciebat enim se multum dicendo nihil profecturum esse apud eos, qui odio implacabili ipsum persequebantur. Deinde veritatis testimonium dederat sufficiens. Præterea quæ illi afferebant haud dubie eiusmodi erant, vt non merentur responsum, nec aliquid facerent ad causam aduersariorum confirmandam, qui actionem capitalem contra ipsum instituerant. Ita enim Deus decreuerat, vt Messias non propter aliud crimen moreretur, quam quod Dei Filius & rex Iudæorum, idque promissus ille redemptor & seruator esset. Nam ex eo apparet, illum vere propter nos mortuum esse, & simul arguitur detestabilis illorum ingratitudo & impietas, qui non modo non agnoscunt hunc suum redemptorem, sed oderunt quoque, & adhuc non minus quam Iudæorum sacerdotes in verbo & membris suis ferro & igne persequuntur.
units.tr: So Pilate, false to his own duty, began again to deal with Christ himself. Christ had already answered him once, and now he kept silent, although the accusers pressed their charges and Pilate said to him: "Do you not hear how many things they testify against you?" From this remark it appears that the chief priests had not been quiet, but had brought along a crowd of false witnesses to help them win their case more easily. Yet he kept silent rightly and deservedly. For he knew that by speaking much he would accomplish nothing with those who pursued him with implacable hatred. Moreover, he had already given sufficient testimony to the truth. Besides, what they alleged was undoubtedly of such a kind that it did not deserve an answer, nor would it help to confirm the case of the adversaries, who had brought a capital action against him. For God had so decided that the Messiah should die for no other crime than that he was the Son of God and king of the Jews, and that he was the promised redeemer and saviour. From this it is clear that he truly died for us, and at the same time the detestable ingratitude and impiety of those is exposed who not only fail to acknowledge this their redeemer, but also hate him, and who even now persecute his word and his members with sword and fire no less than the chief priests of the Jews did.

units.la: Nos autem in hoc Christi silentio discamus, quid nos facere conueniat, si quid huius nobis accidat. Primum non pudeat nos Veritatis & Euangelij IESV CHRISTI, qui vt nos seruaret testatam fecit hanc bonam professionem (vt Apostolus scribit) coram Pontio Pilato, & nostrum reatum in se suscepit, vt nobis liberum ad thronum gratiæ accessum & ad Patrem clamandi liberatem impetraret. Quod si videamus nos nihil proficere aduersus hostium rabiem & calumnias, ipsi quoque silentio innocentiam nostram testemur, & (vt Christus meminit) animas nostras possidemus in patientia nostra: quæ neque in hoc seculo quidem apud aduersarios nostros fructu suo carebunt.
units.tr: But let us learn from this silence of Christ what we ought to do if anything of the kind happens to us. First, let us not be ashamed of the truth and of the gospel of Jesus Christ, who, to save us, made this good confession (as the Apostle writes) before Pontius Pilate, and took our guilt upon himself, so that he might obtain for us free access to the throne of grace and freedom to cry out to the Father. But if we see that we accomplish nothing against the rage and slanders of our enemies, let us also bear witness to our innocence by our silence, and (as Christ reminds us) possess our souls in our patience; and this patience will not lack its fruit even in this world, in the sight of our adversaries.

units.la: Pilatus Christum de regno interrogat.
units.tr: Pilate asks Christ about the kingdom.

units.la: Quale regnum Christi.
units.tr: What sort of kingdom Christ's is.

units.la: Christus iterum tacet.
units.tr: Christ is silent again.

units.la: Quid in simili causa fieri debeat. 1. Tim. 6. Luc. 21. Pilatus miratur Christi silentium.
units.tr: What ought to be done in a similar case. 1 Tim. 6. Luke 21. Pilate marvels at Christ's silence.

units.la: CAP. XXVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER 27.

units.la: bit. De Pilato enim scribit Matt. quod Christi silentium vehementer admiratus fit: nimirum, quod huius causas & quae hic latebant mysteria ignoraret. At cur non seipsum ad attentiorem consideratione excitat, cum videret hominem innocentem inter tam multas tamque graves iniurias tam constantem esse? Sed ut Sacerdotum iniustitiam & iniquum odium silentio suo arguit & vicit Dominus; ita praesidis quoque ignaviam & impium fluporem toti mundo detexit. Similia solent hodie etiam fieri, ut saepe impijs quoque admirationi fit martyrum patientia, qua infandos cruciatus tormentorum & immanem carnificum petulantiam vincunt, & ex qua multi interdum occasionem accipiunt, ut de illis & tota causa illorum honestius sentire incipiant, & in religione vera ad salutem proficiant. Horum meditatio nos confirmet, neque dubitemus Christum, qui mundum et principem eius vicit, nobis vicisse, & proinde fidem in hunc nostrum quoque esse victoriam, quam in illo tuam quoque obtinebimus, quando hostium potentia succumbuisse videmur. Licet ergo nobis cum Apostolo exclamare: Quis nos separabit a Caritate Christi? num afflictio? num angustia? num persecutio? num fames? num nuditas? &c. Imo in omnibus plus quam victores sumus per eum, qui dilexit nos. Confirmat enim nos beata illa spes, quam habemus de illustri illo adventu magni Dei ac Seruatoris IESV CHRISTI: quem cum horribili terrore videbunt, qui illum transfixerunt, nos autem illi per aerem obviam rapti, cum eodem in aeternum viuemus. Ipsi sit gloria.
units.tr: bit. For Matthew writes of Pilate that he was greatly amazed at Christ's silence, no doubt because he did not know the causes and the mysteries that lay hidden here. But why did he not rouse himself to closer attention, when he saw that a man innocent amid so many and such grave injuries was so steadfast? But just as the Lord by his silence exposed and overcame the injustice and unjust hatred of the priests, so too he laid bare to the whole world the cowardice and impious stupor of the governor. Similar things are customarily done even today: the patience of the martyrs often becomes a matter of wonder even to the impious, since by it they overcome unspeakable torments and the savage insolence of the executioners, and from it many at times receive an occasion to begin to think more honourably about them and their whole cause, and to advance to salvation in the true religion. Let the meditation on these things strengthen us, and let us not doubt that Christ, who conquered the world and its prince, has conquered for us, and therefore that our faith is also a victory in this, which we too shall obtain in that, when we seem to have yielded to the power of enemies. Therefore we may with the Apostle cry out: "Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Shall tribulation? or anguish? or persecution? or famine? or nakedness?" etc. Nay, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us. For that blessed hope which we have of the illustrious coming of the great God and Saviour Jesus Christ confirms us: whom they who pierced him shall see with horrible terror, while we, caught up to meet him in the air, shall live with him forever. To him be glory.

units.la: HOMILIA CCCIIII.
units.tr: HOMILY CCCIIII.

units.la: Praeses autem in festo consueuerat turbae dimittere vnum vinctum, quem voluisset. Habebant vero tunc vinctum insignem, qui dicebatur Barabbas. Ipsis igitur coactis, dixit eis Pilatus: Vtrum vultis dimittam vobis, Barabbam, an Iesum qui dicitur Christus? Sciebat enim, quod per inuidiam tradidissent eum. Sedente autem eo pro tribunali, misit ad eum uxor eius, dicens: Nihil tibi sit cum iusto illo: multa enim passa sum hodie in somniis propter eum. Principes autem sacerdotum & seniores persuaserant turbae, ut peterent Barabbam, Iesum vero perderent. Respondens autem praeses, dixit eis: Vtrum e duobus illis vultis ut vobis dimittam? Ipsi vero dixerunt, Barabbam. Dixit eis Pilatus: Quid igitur faciam Iesu qui dicitur Christus? Dicunt ei omnes: Crucifigatur. Praeses autem ait: Enimuero quid mali fecit? At illi amplius clamabant, dicentes: Crucifigatur. Videns autem Pilatus, se nihil proficere, sed maiorem tumultum fieri, accepta aqua abluit manus coram turba, dicens: Innoxius ego sum a sanguine huius iusti: vos videritis. Et respondens universus populus, dixit: Sanguis eius super nos & super filios nostros. Tunc dimisit eis Barabbam; Iesum autem flagellatum tradidit ut crucifigeretur.
units.tr: Now the governor was accustomed at the feast to release to the crowd one prisoner, whomever they wished. They then had a notorious prisoner called Barabbas. So when the crowd had gathered, Pilate said to them: "Whom do you want me to release to you, Barabbas or Jesus who is called Christ?" For he knew that they had handed him over out of envy. While he was sitting on the judgment seat, his wife sent to him, saying: "Have nothing to do with that righteous man, for I have suffered much today in a dream because of him." But the chief priests and elders had persuaded the crowd to ask for Barabbas and to destroy Jesus. The governor answered and said to them: "Which of the two do you want me to release to you?" They said: "Barabbas." Pilate said to them: "What then shall I do with Jesus who is called Christ?" They all said to him: "Let him be crucified." The governor said: "But what evil has he done?" They shouted all the more, saying: "Let him be crucified." When Pilate saw that he was gaining nothing, but that a greater tumult was arising, he took water and washed his hands before the crowd, saying: "I am innocent of the blood of this righteous man; see to it yourselves." And the whole people answered and said: "His blood be on us and on our children." Then he released Barabbas to them, but having scourged Jesus he handed him over to be crucified.

units.la: Quamuis Pilatus praeses in causa Filij Dei IESV CHRISTI initio boni iudicii officium fecerit, quando noluit Iudaeis & horum Pontificibus gratificari, ut ipsum non audiutum & causa non prius cognita condemnaret, non tamen hoc profuit, eo quod non perseuerauerit in eo quod bene coeperat. Inconstantia autem huius causa fuit, quod veri Dei cognitione & timore caruit. Hic enim sapientia vera initium & caput est, adeoque franum, quo homines in officio continentur. At timore Dei deiectum & prophanum hominem fuisse, Ioannes Euangelista testatur, qui illum ad Christi piam admonitionem excanduisse scribit. Cum enim ille omne regni sui ratione ei exposuisset, ut facile videret, nihil ex illo periculi esse Romano Imperio, sed quaestione esse de religione & eius veritate, contemptim respondet: Quid est veritas? Et quamuis innocentem esse intelligat, non tamen tuetur innocentem, sed neglecto iusti iudicii officio, ad artes & humanas Pro. 1. Ioan. 18. humanæ prudentiæ consilia conterritur, quibus hoc vnum quærit, vt se inuidia & odio liberet. Et licet institutum eius sanctum & bonum sit: vt nimirum Christus Iudæorum rabiem & dirum sup-plicium euadat: quia tamen non recta via progreditur, ex vno vitio in aliud prolabitur, & subin de in peius proficit. Id euidentissime apparet in hoc loco, quo docetur, quibus rationibus Deus bo-num Pilati institutum adiuuarit, & vt in eo confirmari potuerit, si illis voluisset recte vti. Deinde annotatur quoq;, quibus obstaculis impeditus, imo vinctus fit, vt bono animi proposito religio Chri-stum ad mortem damnauerit. Hæc autem ita narrantur, vt interim multa concurrant innocen-tiæ Christi testimonia, quibus nostræ redemptionis mysterium magis confirmatur & illu-stratur.
units.tr: Although Pilate the governor, in the case of the Son of God Jesus Christ, at the start did his duty as a good judge, when he refused to gratify the Jews and their chief priests by condemning him unheard and without the case being first examined, this did him no good, because he did not persevere in what he had well begun. The cause of his inconstancy was that he lacked knowledge of and fear of the true God. For this is the beginning and the head of true wisdom, and so the bridle by which men are kept in their duty. That Pilate was a man cast down and profane, without the fear of God, the Evangelist John bears witness, who writes that he flared up at Christ's pious admonition. For when Christ had explained to him the whole nature of his kingdom, so that he could easily see that there was no danger from it to the Roman Empire, but that the question concerned religion and its truth, he answered with contempt: "What is truth?" And although he understood that he was innocent, he did not protect the innocent man; neglecting the duty of a just judgment, he was terrified by the arts and the counsels of human prudence, by which he sought this one thing, that he might free himself from envy and hatred. And although his purpose was holy and good, namely that Christ might escape the rage of the Jews and a dreadful punishment, yet because he did not proceed by the straight way, he slipped from one fault into another and kept sinking into worse. This appears most clearly in this passage, where we are taught by what reasons God would have aided Pilate's good purpose, and how he might have been confirmed in it, had he chosen to use those reasons rightly. Then it is also noted by what obstacles he was hindered, or rather bound, so that religion, which was good in his mind's purpose, condemned Christ to death. These things are narrated in such a way that meanwhile many testimonies to Christ's innocence come together, by which the mystery of our redemption is the more confirmed and made clear.

units.la: Primum occasione liberandi & dimittendi Christi ex veteri consuetudine sumit, quæ erat, vt in festo Paschatis in populi gratiam vnum ex vinctis dimitteretur. Quæ consuetudo per κλεῖαν irrepsisse videtur, qua superstitioni exemplum Dei æmulari voluerunt, qui olim eo tempore patres ex Ægypto & dura Pharaonis tyrannide liberauerat. Vbi simul meminisse debebant, eodem tempore legem datam, qua Deus homines totos sibi vendicat in obsequium, & maleficos punire & occidere iubet. Perperam ergo hoc factum fuit, quod illi in dimissione sceleratorum cultum aliquem Dei constituerunt. Sedita solet carnis ratio, quando in diuinis vult ex seipso sapere. Et videntur Romani hunc morem illis reliquisse, vt populo, qui ad seditiones proclivius erat, magis obsequente uterentur. At nunc Pilatus hinc occasionem petit, quā non male vti potuisset, si Dei timore armatus, huic potius quam hominibus studuisset placere. Cum enim inter captiuos teneretur Barrabas, insigniter malus (nam in seditione non itapridem exortā, eadem fecerat) hunc cum Iesu con-fert, & populo eligendi quem vellent optionem facit liberam: non putans tam improbos aut im-prudentes fore, vt nequissimam hominem sancto & innocenti, imo tanto benefactori præferant. At qui poterat occasione ista fortiter vti, & populum ossi.ij admonere, vel etiam pro imperio cogere, ne ex gratia ipsis concessa consuetudine ad seditiones, & ad seruandum illarum authores abuteren-tur. Vel quæ necessitas ipsum cogebat, vt ESVM quem innocentem esse sciebat, maleficiis accen-feret? Sed quia semel cæpit exorbitare, partim imprudenter a populo impetrare cupit, quod in ipsi-us propria potestate erat: partim iniquè & iniusto populi iudicio subijcit eum, quem ipse ex officio debebat defendere. Turpe nimis fuit, quod nuper oblitus maiestatis Romani imperij, Christum Herodi transmisit. At turpius nunc eundem cum latrone & seditiosò confert, cuius innocentiam Herodis testimonio commendari intellexerat. Euangelista certè, vt culpam Pilati grauiorem faciat, propriæ conscientiæ testimonio Pilatum conuictum fuisse docet. Namsciebat (inquit) quod per inuidiam eum ipsi tradidissent.
