units.tr: From the sixth hour there was darkness over all the land until the ninth hour. And about the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, saying, Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani? That is, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? Some of those who stood there, when they heard it, said, This man calleth for Elias. And straightway one of them ran and took a sponge, filled it with vinegar, put it on a reed, and gave him to drink. The others said, Let be, let us see whether Elias will come to save him. Jesus, when he had cried again with a loud voice, yielded up the ghost. And behold, the veil of the temple was rent in twain from the top to the bottom; and the earth did quake, and the rocks rent; and the graves were opened, and many bodies of the saints which slept arose, and came out of the graves after his resurrection, and went into the holy city, and appeared unto many. Now when the centurion, and they that were with him, watching Jesus, saw the earthquake, and those things that were done, they feared greatly, saying, Truly this was the Son of God.

units.la: Euangelistae non modo priores partes historiae de passione & morte Domini nostri exponunt, verumetiam quae eius mortem comitata & consecuta sunt, diligenter narrant. Nam etsi in iis quae hucusque audiuimus multa sint innocentiae Christi argumenta, potentiae item & virtutis eius diuinae, quae nos aduersus conscientiae tentationes & hostiles mundi & principis eius terrores consolantur, pleraque tamen sunt triflia & ignominiae plena. At nunc gloria ipsius ita se exerit, vt in iis quoque eam videre liceat, quae hanc omnino obliterare & sepelire videntur. In quibus omnibus hoc non postremum fuerit, quod declaratur esse dilectus Dei Filius, quem Pater semper exaudit, vt ipse prius testatus est. Quia enim CHRISTVS precatus fuit, vt passionis suæ hi- storiam ita moderetur Pater, vt simul suæ gloriæ rationem habeat, hoc in ipso mortis articulo ita factum videbimus, vt de eo nihil porro dubitari possit. Proderit ergo singula, quæ hic commemo- rantur, non oscitanter inspicere, vt in fide, ex qua omnis salus nostra dependet, magis confir- memur.
units.tr: The evangelists do not merely set out the earlier parts of the history of the passion and death of our Lord; they also carefully relate what accompanied and followed his death. For although in what we have heard so far there are many proofs of Christ's innocence, and likewise of his divine power and virtue, which comfort us against the temptations of conscience and against the hostility of the world and the terrors of its prince, nevertheless most of it is lowly and full of ignominy. But now his glory displays itself in such a way that it can be seen even in those things which seem utterly to obliterate and bury it. Among all these, this is not the least: that he is declared to be the beloved Son of God, whom the Father always hears, as he himself earlier testified. For since Christ prayed that the Father would so order the history of his passion that it also took account of his glory, we shall see this brought about at the very moment of death in such a way that nothing further can be doubted about him. It will therefore be profitable not to look at each of the things recorded here in a half-hearted way, so that we may be made the more firm in the faith, on which all our salvation depends.

units.la: Primo dicit Matthæus noster, cui duo alij, Marcus & Lucas assentiuntur, a sexta hora, quando Dominus in crucem suffixus est, tenebras factas esse super vniuersam terram, vsque ad horam nonam. Quod Solis deliquium præter naturæ cursum accidisse, interpretes fere pleriq; consentiunt, cum Luna tunc pleno orbe refulgeret, in eo autem differunt, quod non omnes vniuersales fuisse tenebras illas fatentur, sed solam Iudæam ab illis fuisse obscuratam. At quoniam totius terræ meminit Euangelista, & Christus se lucem mundi dicit, totum nimirum, non absurde nos si- suros existimo, si illius obitum tenebras vniuersales, quæ totum terrarum orbem inuoluerint, co- mitatas fuisse dicamus. Et ita veteres quoq; sensisse, ex Eusebio apparet, qui in Chronicis hæc annotauit: IESVS CHRISTVS Filius Dei salutarem cunctis prædicans viam & miracula, quæ in Euangelijs scripta sunt, fecit: discipulos suos diuinis imbuens Sacramentis, vt vniuersis gentibus conuersionem ad Deum nuntient, imperat: secundum prophetias, quæ de Deo fuerant præ- locuta, ad passionem venit anno Tiberij decimo octauo, quo tempore & in aliis Ethnicorum com- mentarijs hæc ad verbum scripta reperiuntur: Solis sasta defectio, & tenebræ super vniuersam terram: Bithynia terræmotu concussa, & in vrbe Nicena ædes plurima corruerunt. Quæ omnia his congruunt, quæ in passione Saluatoris acciderunt. Et mox idem ex Plegonte, qui Adriani Cæsaris libertus fuit, & quem egregium Olympiarum supputatorem vocat, hoc quoq; addit: Quarto autem anno CCII. Olympiadis magna & excellens inter omnes, quæ ante eam acciderant, defectio Solis est sasta: Dies hora sexta itain tenebrosam noctem versus, vt stellæ cælo visæ sint: & terræmotu in Bithynia Nicena vrbis multas ædes subuerterit. Tertullianus vero ve- tustior Eusebio scriptor, qui non diu ab Apostolorum seculis abfuit, in Apologetico suo contra gen- tes scripsit, de Christi morte differens: Eodem momento dies medium orbem signante Sole subduƈta est. Deliquium vtiq; patianerunt, qui id quoq; super Christo prædicatum non scierunt: & tamen e- um mundi casum relatum in archiuis vestris habetis. Quis vero suspicetur, grauissimus scriptorem in libro grauissimi argumenti hæc annotare voluisse, nisi eorum fides omnibus compertissima suis- set? Quid vero aliud significauit Eclipsis ista, quam Christum esse lucem mundi, & Solem iusti- tiæ (vt Malachi dicit) quem qui amittunt, in tenebris horrendis errent & perëant? Quia vero Iudæi volentes cæcutierunt, & (vt Isaias prædixerat) videntibus oculis noluerunt videre, pro- pius & vehementius hoc quoq; prodigiu illos terrere debuit. Videntur ergo hæ tenebræ opponi illis quæ olim in Ægypto acciderunt, quando totam Ægyptum occupantibus tenebris, solis Israelitis in terra Gosen clara lux fulsit. Nunc enim postquam illi Christum reiecerunt, Euangelij lux per totum orbem terrarum diffusa omnes gentes illuminauit, qui (vt Paulus ait) prius tenebræ fue- runt, horribili interim cæcitate laborantibus Iudæis, qui neq; consolationibus Euangelij, neq; mi- nis Dei, neq; pœnis & calamitatibus illis mouentur, quæ illos iam per annos plus mille quingen- tos miserrimè fatigant. Terreat ergo nos Iudaica gentis exemplum, ne vnquam obliuiscamur ad monitionis Christi, qui illis dixit: Dum lucem habetis, credite in lucem, vt filij lucis fitis, ne vos te- nebræ deprehendant. Nam qui ambulat in tenebris, nescit quo vadat. Ioan. 12. cap.
units.tr: Our Matthew, whom the other two, Mark and Luke, agree with, first says that from the sixth hour, when the Lord was fastened to the cross, darkness came over the whole earth until the ninth hour. Most interpreters agree that this eclipse of the sun happened outside the normal course of nature, since the moon was then shining in full orb. They differ, however, on whether that darkness covered everything. Some admit that it was not universal but darkened only Judea. But since the Evangelist mentions the whole earth, and Christ calls himself the light of the world, I think it is not unreasonable to say that his death was accompanied by a universal darkness that enveloped the whole orb of the earth. That the ancients also thought so appears from Eusebius, who noted in his Chronicles: "Jesus Christ, the Son of God, preaching the saving way to all and performing the miracles written in the Gospels, instructing his disciples in the divine sacraments and commanding them to announce the conversion to God to all nations, came to his passion, according to the prophecies that had been spoken about God, in the eighteenth year of Tiberius. At that same time, in other commentaries of the Gentiles, these words are found written: 'An eclipse of the sun, and darkness over the whole earth; Bithynia shaken by an earthquake, and many buildings collapsed in the city of Nicaea.' All these things agree with what happened at the Savior's passion." Soon afterwards Eusebius adds the same from Phlegon, a freedman of the emperor Hadrian, whom he calls an outstanding reckoner of the Olympiads: "In the fourth year of the 202nd Olympiad, a great and excellent eclipse of the sun, greater than all that had happened before, took place. Day turned into night so dark that the stars were seen in the sky at the sixth hour; and an earthquake in Bithynia overthrew many buildings in the city of Nicaea." Tertullian, a writer older than Eusebius, who lived not long after the age of the Apostles, wrote in his Apology against the Gentiles, discussing Christ's death: "At that same moment the day was darkened, the sun being withdrawn from the middle of the sky. Certainly they suffered an eclipse who did not know that this too had been foretold about Christ; and yet you have that event of the world recorded in your archives." Who would suspect that so grave a writer, in a book of such weighty subject, wished to record these things unless their testimony had been fully known to all? What else did that eclipse signify than that Christ is the light of the world and the Sun of righteousness (as Malachi says), whom those who lose stray and perish in dreadful darkness? But because the Jews, willing to be blind, closed their eyes and, as Isaiah had foretold, would not see with seeing eyes, this portent ought to have terrified them all the more closely and vehemently. These darkness, therefore, seems to be set over against what once happened in Egypt, when, while darkness covered all Egypt, a clear light shone only for the Israelites in the land of Goshen. For now, after they rejected Christ, the light of the Gospel, spread through the whole earth, has illumined all nations, who (as Paul says) were formerly darkness, while the Jews labour meanwhile under a dreadful blindness. They are moved neither by the consolations of the Gospel, nor by the threats of God, nor by those punishments and calamities which have now wretchedly wearied them for more than fifteen hundred years. Let the example of the Jewish nation terrify us, then, lest we ever forget the warning of Christ, who said to them: "While you have the light, believe in the light, that you may be sons of light, lest darkness overtake you. For he who walks in darkness does not know where he goes." John 12.

units.la: Sequitur: Circiter vero horam nonam exclamauit IESVS voce magna, dicens: Eli Eli la- ma sabachthani, hoc est, Deus meus Deus meus, cur deseruisti me? Est hoc dictum IESVS CHRISTI inter ea quæ in Euangelio de illo recitantur celeberrimum, & quod pra alijs mul- ta & diligenti consideratione dignum est. Nam & vera humanitatis argumentum continet, quo illum probatur fidelem esse Pontificem, qui per omnia tentatus vt nos, nobis qui tentamur posse & velit condolere & compati: & simul dilectum illum Filium esse constat, quæ Pater in extrema tentationum angustia exaudiuit, nec eum succumbere passus est. Itaq; optimus huius loci & eorum quæ prius in horto ad montem oliueti acciderunt, interpres mihi quoq; (vt quibusdam alijs doctis- simis
units.tr: It follows: "But about the ninth hour Jesus cried out with a loud voice, saying: Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani, that is, My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" [Eli Eli lama sabachthani] This saying of Jesus Christ is the most famous of all those reported about him in the Gospel, and it deserves more careful and diligent consideration than the rest. For it contains a true argument of his humanity, by which he is shown to be a faithful High Priest, who, tempted in all things as we are, both can and will sympathise with us who are tempted. At the same time it establishes that he is that beloved Son whom the Father heard in the extreme distress of temptation and did not allow to succumb. Therefore, as it seems to me also (as to some other most learned

units.la: Tenebrae trium horarum. fratribus) videtur Apostolus, qui ad Hebraeos scribit de Christo: Qui in diebus carnis suae, id est, dum in carne mortali & infirma nostra natura adhuc in terris nobiscum degeret, deprecationibus & supplicationibus oblatis cum clamore valido & lachrymis, apud eum qui poterat ipsum servare a morte, & exauditus est ex metu. Supra Matthaeus Christum dicit coepisse ἀλλὰ ἀδῆλον ... quae significant aliquem ita turbari & maerore affici, ut consilij incertus vndiquaque angatur. At hac Christo sic tribui debent, ut meminerimus, hos affectus in illo, utpote vero homine, locum habuisse, absque peccato tamen. Etsi enim illis tentaretur, qui alioqui in Deum non cadunt, neque ut alij multi in Scripturis Deo ἀθεόπνευστος tribuuntur, nihil tamen decessit obedientiae fidei, quae se totum Deo consecrauerat: & hac causa fuit, quod cum se tam graviter tentari sentiret, eo quod totius mundi reatum in se receperat, & proinde inferni terroribus cruciaretur, qui hanc vocem tristissimam illi extorserunt, non tamen desperatione absorptus est, sed ad Patrem conuersus, huic deprecationes & supplicationes cum clamore valido & lachrymis obtulit. Fidei autem euidens argumentum est, quod etsi ex infirmitate carnis, se a Deo derelictum esse queritur, nihilominus tamen eundem suum Deum vocat, & quidem vocege-minata: Deus meus, Deus meus. Neque fefellit eum fides sua. Nam exauditus est ex metu, id est, dum ex tantis angustijs, & reuera (ut Psalmus habet) ex profundo, adeo ex gurgite inferni propter totius mundi peccata clamaret, quorum reatu premebatur, Deus illum exaudiuit ita, ut hoc metu & terrore non absorptus fit aut succubuerit, sed ipse mortem & inferos deuicerit. Exauditus autem eum Pater, quia dilectus ille Filius est, quem ideo in mundum miserat, ut nos ex peccatis & horum poena, id est, morte & inferis liberaret. Interim nostrae consolationi nobis multifariam seruit hic locus. Primum ne terreamur, si tanta sint tentationum angustiae, ut propria ratio & mens, nos a Deo desertos esse testentur, neque quoad homines aliqua salutis spes nobis affulgeat. Nec enim in electis est hoc Dei irati indicium: nam si hoc esset, nunquam tale quid Filio suo vnigenito passus esset accidere. Deinde qui Filium suum exaudiuit ex metu, ne in hoc tam diro tentationum certamine vincereatur: nos quoque, propter illum exaudiet, ut in illo nos quoque vincamus. Teneamus modo hoc fidei principium, quod hic Dominus profitetur, dum Deum suum dicit, & qualem Propheta & Apostoli semper confessi sunt. Et cur non nostrer esset Deus, qui nos elegit priusquam essemus? qui creauit? Filium pro nobis tradidit, & in eo adoptauit, ut illius cohaeredes essemus? Taceo nunc promissiones & beneficia, quibus illas ita obsignauit & confirmauit, ut de ipsis nemo sine scelere dubitare possit. Imo quo abiectior & perturbationem animo & corpore Christum fuisse audimus, eo minus de nostrorum peccatorum expiatione per illum facta & eius merito parta salute dubitemus. Sic enim propter nos a Deo Patre derelinqui oportuit Christum, ut nos ex simili tentatione liberaret, dum nobis vicit mundum & mundi principem vna cum morte & inferno. Nec inefficacem fuisse hanc illius victoriam, & quae ex hac electis nascitur, consolationem, ex Martyrum beatissimorum constantia apparet, qua ipsi quoque armati, dolores & cruciatus similes vicerunt.
units.tr: Darkness of three hours. brothers), the best interpreter of this passage, and of what happened earlier in the garden at the Mount of Olives, is the Apostle who writes to the Hebrews about Christ: "Who, in the days of his flesh, that is, while he was still dwelling with us on earth in mortal flesh and our weak nature, offered up prayers and supplications with strong crying and tears to him who was able to save him from death, and was heard because of his fear." Above, Matthew says that Christ began [ἀλλὰ ἀδῆλον ...] to be distressed, words which signify that someone is so troubled and afflicted with grief that he is anxious and uncertain of his purpose on every side. Yet these affections must be ascribed to Christ in such a way that we remember they had place in him as a true man, but without sin. For although he was tempted in these ways, which do not otherwise befall God, and are not, as with many others in the Scriptures, attributed to God as "not inspired by God" [ἀθεόπνευστος], nothing was lost of the obedience of faith, which had wholly consecrated him to God. And for this reason, when he felt himself so grievously tempted, because he had taken upon himself the guilt of the whole world, and therefore was tormented by the terrors of hell, which forced from him that most sorrowful cry, he was nevertheless not swallowed up by despair, but turned to the Father and offered to him prayers and supplications with strong crying and tears. Clear evidence of faith is that, although from the weakness of the flesh he complains that he has been forsaken by God, he nonetheless calls the same God his God, and indeed doubles the word: "My God, my God." His faith did not deceive him. For he was heard because of his fear, that is, while he cried out from such straits, and truly (as the Psalm has it) out of the depths, indeed out of the abyss of hell, because of the sins of the whole world, under whose guilt he was pressed. God heard him in such a way that he was not swallowed up or overcome by this fear and terror, but himself overcame death and hell. The Father heard him because that Son is beloved, whom for this reason he had sent into the world, to deliver us from sins and from their punishment, that is, from death and hell. Meanwhile this passage serves us in many ways for our consolation. First, let us not be terrified if the straits of temptation are so great that our own reason and mind testify that we are forsaken by God, and that no hope of salvation shines on us as far as men are concerned. For this is not a sign of God's wrath against the elect; for if it were, he would never have allowed such a thing to happen to his only-begotten Son. Next, he who heard his Son out of fear, lest he be overcome in so dire a struggle of temptation, will also hear us for his sake, so that we too may conquer in him. Let us hold fast only to this principle of faith, which the Lord here professes when he calls God his own, as the Prophets and Apostles always confessed him to be. And why should he not be our God, who chose us before we were, who created us, who gave his Son for us and adopted us in him, so that we might be his co-heirs? I pass over now the promises and benefits by which he sealed and confirmed them, so that no one can doubt them without sin. Indeed, the more abject and disturbed in mind and body we hear Christ to have been, the less should we doubt the expiation of our sins made through him and the salvation won by his merit. For Christ had to be forsaken by God the Father for us in this way, so that he might deliver us from a like temptation, since for us he conquered the world and the prince of the world, together with death and hell. That this victory of his was not without effect, and that the consolation born from it for the elect is real, appears from the constancy of the most blessed Martyrs, who, armed with the same, overcame pains and torments like these.

units.la: Caeterum Euangelista non absque causa Versum Psalmi, quo Christus in sua querimonia vsus est, prater morem in Hebraeo idiomate recitant sub Christi persona, ut amarus ille Sarcasmus, cuius occasio ex ... aeque acerba & magis impia astantibus Iudaeis petita est, possit exprimi. Cum enim Eli Eli dixisset Dominus, quod significat, Deum meum, Deum meum, illi ad Eliae nomen alludunt, quasi hunc in auxilium vocarit, cum nullum huius exemplum in veteri Scriptura vspiam habeatur. Et quia quidam militum acetum propinare vellet, quod homo militaris eo sciret in vulnerati mortem accelerare, alij neidfaciat, prohibent, nimirum vt diutius cruciētur, & ipsi nouam habeant illusionis occasionem, si Elias illum liberaturus nullus veniat. Est enim insatiabilis impiorum crudelitas, si quando etiam hodie ipsis cum Christi martyribus res est: Sed hos tunc soletur exemplum Filij Dei, qui ipsos suo spiritu & virtute confortabit. Interim hodie etiam suae impietatis pudeat, qui Christo in cruce pendenti in suis membris ludibria & sannas, quouis aceto acriores propinant. Mox quidem iterum dixit se sitire: sed salutem nostram sitiuit: quam confestim illo aceto gustato, sua mortis merito nobis paravit.
units.tr: Moreover, the Evangelist did not without reason record the verse of the Psalm that Christ used in his lament, reciting it in the Hebrew idiom contrary to custom, under Christ's person, so that the bitter sarcasm could be expressed. The occasion for it was taken from the bystanders, who were no less cruel and even more impious. When the Lord said "Eli, Eli" [My God, my God], which means "my God, my God," they played on the name of Elijah, as if he had called him for help, though there is no example of this anywhere in the Old Testament. And when one of the soldiers wanted to give him vinegar, which a soldier knew would hasten the death of a wounded man, the others forbade it. Clearly they wanted him to be tormented longer, and to have a fresh occasion for mockery, if Elijah came to deliver him and no one came. The cruelty of the wicked is insatiable, and it is still so today, when the martyrs of Christ are in the same position. But the example of the Son of God comforts them, and his Spirit and power will strengthen them. Meanwhile, let those today who offer to Christ, hanging on the cross in his members, mockery and jeers more bitter than any vinegar, be ashamed of their impiety. Soon Christ said again that he thirsted. He thirsted for our salvation, and as soon as he had tasted the vinegar, he won for us by the merit of his death what he had prepared for us.

units.la: Christus impie ridetur.
units.tr: Christ is impiously mocked.

units.la: CAP. XXVII. [running head left]
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVII.

units.la: Sequitur enim: IESVS cum rursum clamasset voce magna, emisit spiritum. Quid vero clamarit, Lucas annotavit his verbis: Pater in manus tuas depono spiritum meum. Vere ergo mortuus est Dominus: sed ita ut nulla vis ipsi inuito animam eripuerit, sed ipse eam volens & propria potestate deposuerit, quod se facturum in Euangelio Ioannis promiserat. Ita vero Patri ad extremum vsq; spiritum obediens fuit, quod rursus nostrae redemptionis certitudinem confirmat. Interim clamor hic diuinae virtutis nonum argumentum est. Supra enim vires humanas est, vt morituri alta & articulata voce loquantur, nedum vt altum clament. Exemplo suo autem docet Christus, quid faciant, qui ex hac vita euocantur. Nos quidem vitam neq; deponere debemus, neq; possumus, quando autem Dominus nos vocat, voluntarij sequamur. Est enim haec via vniuersae terrae (vt Dauid dicebat) eaq; omnium iucundissima & saluberrima. Nam hanc ingressi quiescimus a laboribus nostris, & curis atq; molestijs omnibus liberamur, quae nos in hac vita exercent. Liberamur autem, si animas Deo Patri, qui illas dedit commendamus. Haec enim IESVS CHRISTI voluntas est, vt qui verba eius audit, & credit ei, qui misit illum, in iudicium non veniat, sed transeat a morte in vitam. Vt item qui in ipsum credunt, illic sint, vbi ipse est. At ipse in Dei manus suam animam deposuit: qui nostras quoq; ad se recipiet.
units.tr: For it follows: "Jesus, when he had cried again with a loud voice, yielded up the spirit." Luke recorded what he cried in these words: "Father, into your hands I commend my spirit." The Lord truly died, but no force took his soul from him against his will. He laid it down by his own power, as he had promised he would do in the Gospel of John. He was obedient to the Father even to the last breath, which again confirms the certainty of our redemption. Moreover, this cry is a ninth proof of divine power. It is beyond human strength for the dying to speak in a high and articulated voice, let alone to cry out loudly. By his example Christ teaches what those should do who are called out of this life. We ought not, and indeed cannot, lay down our life on our own. But when the Lord calls us, let us follow him willingly. For this is the way of all the earth (as David said), and the most pleasant and wholesome of all. For when we enter it we rest from our labours, and we are freed from all the cares and troubles that beset us in this life. We are freed, provided we commend our souls to God the Father, who gave them. For this is the will of Jesus Christ: that whoever hears his words and believes him who sent him does not come into judgement, but passes from death to life; and that those who believe in him may be where he is. Indeed, he committed his soul into the hands of God, and God will receive ours too.

units.la: Sed narrantur deinceps adhuc alia signa, quae mortem Christi sequuta sunt, & partim de eius innocentia, partim de diuinitate eius testantur: praeterea fructum passionis & mortis eius adumbrant, denique poenas graues Iudaeis minantur, qui vt viuum persecuti sunt, ita ne mortuo quidem crediderunt. Primum ex his est, quod aulaeum siue velum templi scissum est in duas partes a summo vsq; ad imum. Vsus illius erat, quod distinguebat Sanctum exterius a Sanctorum, quae bus caelum ipsum & beatae immortalitatis sedes figurabantur. De vtroque autem tabernaculo Apostolus ad Hebraeos scribit: His ita ordinatis, in primis quidem tabernaculum quouis tempore ingrediuntur Sacerdotes, qui ritus obeunt: In secundum vero semel quottannis solus Pontifex non sine sanguine, quem offert pro seipso & pro populi erratis: Hoc declarante Spiritu Sancto, nondum patefactam fuisse viam ad Sacrarium, priore Tabernaculo adhuc consistente: quod erat exemplar pro tempore illo praesenti, quo scilicet Tabernaculum adhuc stabat & in vsu erat, &c. Itaque cum Christus in cruce moreretur, & nouum Testamentum morte sua compleret (vt alibi diximus) & postea caelum ascendit, patefecit nobis viam in caelum, vt nihil impediat, quo minus ipsi quoque eo accessum habeamus liberum ad thronum gratiae. Interim simul adumbratur, abolitum esse iam Tabernaculum cum ceremonijs Mosaicis & vniuerso cultu Legis, qui hucusque duraverat. Quia vero hic durare debuit, quoad Iudaica Respublica staret, non obscure docebat haec Vetuli scissio, sublatam esse iam a Iudaeis protectionem omnem, nec quicquam superesse, quo imminens ipsis excidium arceri possit. Est q; hoc memorabile exemplum, quo offenditur, vt Deus hostes suos in ipsorum conatibus capiat. Etenim ideo Christum occisum voluerunt Sacerdotes, vt cultum externum, & quem ex hoc capiebant quaestum possent retinere. At mors eius causa fuit, ob quam & hunc & templum cum Sacerdotio euerti oportuit. Quis ergo stabiles putet ceremonias alias, quae in veterum locum successerunt, non alijs autem quam hominum traditionibus nituntur?
units.tr: But then other signs are related which followed the death of Christ. Some bear witness to his innocence, some to his divinity. Moreover, they foreshadow the fruit of his passion and death, and finally they threaten the Jews with grievous punishments, for they persecuted him while he lived and did not believe in him even when he was dead. The first of these is that the curtain, or veil, of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom. Its use was to separate the outer Holy Place from the Holy of Holies, which signified heaven itself and the seat of blessed immortality. The Apostle writes to the Hebrews about both tabernacles: "With these things thus ordained, the priests always go into the first tabernacle to perform the rites; but into the second only the high priest goes, once a year, not without blood, which he offers for himself and for the errors of the people." The Holy Spirit declared by this that the way into the sanctuary was not yet opened while the first tabernacle still stood, "which was a figure for the present time, in which both gifts and sacrifices were offered, while the tabernacle was still standing and in use," and so on. Therefore, when Christ died on the cross and completed the New Testament by his death (as we have said elsewhere), and afterwards ascended into heaven, he opened the way to heaven for us, so that nothing hinders us from having free access there to the throne of grace. At the same time it is shown that the tabernacle, with the Mosaic ceremonies and the whole worship of the Law, which had lasted until then, was now abolished. But since it was to last only as long as the Jewish commonwealth stood, this tearing of the veil clearly taught that all protection had now been removed from the Jews, and nothing remained by which the impending destruction could be averted. It is also a memorable example, by which we see that God catches his enemies in their own schemes. For the priests wished Christ to be killed so that they might keep the external worship and the gain they made from it. But his death was the cause for which both that place and the temple, together with the priesthood, had to be overthrown. Who, then, would think that other ceremonies, which have taken the place of the old ones, are stable, if they rest on nothing but human traditions?

units.la: Accedit Veli scissioni terraemotus, manifestum irae Dei signum, vt apud Amos est videre. Cum enim vsurariorum artes exposuisset Dominus, & quaecunq; hi contra charitatem proximi dignant, tandem inquit: Annon super his terra contremiscat, & omnis eam inhabitans lugeat? Quin vniuersa ea, vt fluuius intumescet, &c. Nec vulgaris fuit hic terraemotus, sed tantus tamq; vehemens, vt petrae ab eo scissae sint. Tanta fuit sceleris in Christum commissi indignitas: impijs autem & contumacibus sua exprobratur duritiès, quos nulla rationes mouere possunt, vt peccatorum poenitentia ducantur. At sint illi faxis duriores, vincet tamen & (si opus fit) inuitos commin uet Deus, qui simul propter electos suos orbem terrarum Euangelij praedicatione concutiet, vt ex lapideis cordibus carnea fiant, quae per fidei obedientiam Christo subijciantur. Coharet hiis quod sepulchra nonnulla aperta sunt, & multa corpora Sanctorum, qui dormiuerant surrexerunt, & post resurrectionem Christi e monumentis egressi introierunt in Sanctam ciuitatem, & multis apparuerunt. Et Sancta ciuitas dicitur Ierusalem, quia veteri cultui consecrata erat, & ritibus vacabat, quorum
units.tr: To the tearing of the veil was added an earthquake, a plain sign of God's wrath, as may be seen in Amos. For when the Lord had set out the practices of the usurers, and whatever else they dared to do against the love of their neighbour, he finally said: "Shall not the land tremble for this, and everyone who dwells in it mourn? Indeed the whole land will swell up like a river," and so on. This earthquake was not ordinary, but so great and violent that rocks were split by it. So great was the outrage of the crime committed against Christ. But the hardness of the impious and obstinate is rebuked, those whom no reasons can move to be led to repentance for their sins. Yet let them be harder than flints: God will overcome them and, if need be, will crush them even against their will. At the same time, through the preaching of the Gospel he will shake the world, so that stony hearts become fleshy, and are made subject to Christ through the obedience of faith. To this belongs the fact that some tombs were opened, and many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep were raised. After the resurrection of Christ they came out of the tombs, entered the holy city, and appeared to many. The city is called holy because it was consecrated to the old worship and devoted to its rites, the fulfilment of which was found in the one Son of God alone.

units.la: Amos 8. Sepulchra aperta sunt. suorum complementum in uno Filio Dei habebatur. Voluit autem ipsos excitari Dominus, ut doceret, verum esse, quod alias dixit, se esse resurrectionem & vitam. Itaq; mortis Christi fructus præcipuus & naturæ ordinem omnem superans hic est, quod vitam nobis restituit, & hanc quidem immortalem & æternam, quæ nullis vicibus neq; ulli corruptioni subjicitur.
units.tr: Amos 8. The tombs were opened. The Lord wished them to be raised, to teach that what he had said elsewhere is true, that he is the resurrection and the life. Therefore the chief fruit of the death of Christ, which surpasses the whole order of nature, is this: that he restores to us life, and indeed immortal and eternal life, which is subject to no changes and to no corruption.

units.la: Restat, ut qui signorum ipsorum effectus fuerint, videamus: Nulli nimirum apud Sacerdotes & Scribas, qui in scelere suo magis induruerunt. At Centurio & qui cum illo asseruabant IESUM, visis his timuerunt: nec inanis fuit timor hic, sed veri confessionem ipsis extorsit, ut dicerent: Vere Filius Dei erat iste. Fuerunt hi primitiæ gentium: & magnum est hoc misericordiæ Dei argumentum, qui ex carnificibus Filij sui confessores fecit, ne desalute propria desperarent. Discamus autem horum exemplo non negligere a Deo nobis exhibita signa: cum olim eiusmodi multa in Prophetis & ab ipso Christo prædicta sint. Quis vero dubitet, hunc fuisse fructum confessionis Christi, qui pro ijs Patrem precatus est, qui ipsum in crucem suffixerunt? Cur ergo nos de eius gratia & merito desperemus, qui iam reconciliati Deo, hæredes salutis sumus, cohæredes autem IESV CHRISTI: qui sibi fidentes nunquam deserei. Ipsi debetur honor & gloria.
units.tr: It remains to see what effects these signs had. Certainly none among the priests and scribes, who grew ever harder in their wickedness. But the centurion and those who were guarding Jesus with him, when they saw these things, were afraid. This fear was not in vain, but drew from them a confession of the truth, so that they said: "Truly this was the Son of God." These were the firstfruits of the Gentiles, and this is a great proof of the mercy of God, who made confessors of his Son's executioners, so that they would not despair of their own salvation. Let us learn from their example not to neglect the signs God shows us, since many such things were foretold long ago by the Prophets and by Christ himself. Who, then, could doubt that this was the fruit of the confession of Christ, who prayed to the Father for those who fastened him to the cross? Why, then, should we despair of his grace and merit, we who are now reconciled to God, heirs of salvation, and fellow heirs with Jesus Christ, who never forsakes those who trust in him? To him be honour and glory.

units.la: HOMILIA CCCVIII.
units.tr: HOMILY CCCVIII.

units.la: Erant autem illic mulieres multæ procul spectantes, quæ sequutæ fuerant IESVM a Galilæa, ministrantes ei. Inter quas erat Maria Magdalene & Maria Iacobi & Iosé mater, & mater filiorum Zebedæi. Cum autem serum diei esset, venit homo dives ab Arimathæa, nomine Ioseph, qui & ipse discipulus fuerat IESV. Is adijt Pilatum & petijt corpus IESV. Tunc Pilatus iussit reddi corpus. Et Ioseph cum accepisset corpus, involuit illud sindone pura, posuitq; in monumento suo novo, quod excíderat in petra: & advoluto saxo magno ad ostium monumenti, abijt. Erat autem illic Maria Magdalene & altera Maria sedentes contra sepulchrum. Postero autem die quæ sequitur Parasceues, coacti sunt principes Sacerdotum & Pharisæi ad Pilatum, dicentes: Domine, meminimus planum illum dixisse, cum adhuc viveret: Tertio post die surgam. Iube ergo muniri sepulchrum usque in diem tertium: ne quando veniant discipuli eius noctu, & furentur eum, dicantq; populo: Surrexit a mortuis: & erit vltimus error peior priore: Dixit eis Pilatus: Habetis custodiam, abite, munite sicut scitis. Ipsi autem profecti munierunt sepulchrum, obsignato lapide, cum custodia.
units.tr: Many women were also there, watching from a distance; they had followed Jesus from Galilee and served him. Among them were Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James and Joses, and the mother of the sons of Zebedee. When evening had come, a rich man from Arimathea named Joseph, who had himself also been a disciple of Jesus, went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus. Then Pilate ordered that the body be given to him. Joseph took the body, wrapped it in a clean linen cloth, and laid it in his own new tomb, which he had cut out of the rock. He rolled a great stone against the door of the tomb and went away. Mary Magdalene and the other Mary were sitting opposite the sepulchre. On the next day, which followed the Preparation, the chief priests and the Pharisees came together before Pilate and said: "Sir, we remember that deceiver saying, while he was still alive, 'After three days I will rise again.' Therefore order the tomb to be guarded until the third day, lest his disciples come by night, steal him away, and tell the people, 'He has risen from the dead.' Then the last error would be worse than the first." Pilate said to them: "You have a guard; go, make it as secure as you know how." So they went and made the sepulchre secure, sealing the stone and setting a guard.

units.la: REstat vltima pars historiæ de passione & morte Domini nostri IESV CHRISTI, cuius sepultura quoque describitur. Oportuit autem non solum mori, verum etiam sepeliri Dei Filium, qui morte sua nos debebat redimere, ut constaret, hunc vere mortuum, nos a non aliqua imagine mortis (ut olim Mahumet & alij quidam finxerunt) sed vera eius morte redemptos esse. Et prodest nos de morte Christi certiores fieri, ut nostram, quæ nobis subeunda est, minus horreamus. Qui enim hanc vincere potuit, & iam vitæ facere ex ea, quæ prius pœna peccati, & damnationis æternæ quasi præludium erat, idem nos quoque confirmare poterit, ne vel mortis dolore, vel eorum quæ mortem sequuntur, quantumvis carni terrifica sint, horrore a flatione sua deijciamur. Et huc pertinet, quod etsi hactenus omnia, quæ passus est Dominus, tristia & ignominia plena fuerint: statim tamen in ipso (ut sic dicamus) mortis articulo, Christi gloria & maiestas se exerere: ut nuper in prodigijs mortem eius comitantibus vidimus. Et quoad sepulturam, non clam aut furtim sepelitur eius corpus, non item negligenter abijcitur (sicuti olim Iehoiakimo Ieremiæ minabatur) sed cum præsidis Romani consensu, nec sine publica authoritate sepelitur Do-
units.tr: The last part of the history of the passion and death of our Lord Jesus Christ remains, and his burial is also described. It was fitting that the Son of God, who was to redeem us by his death, should not only die but also be buried, so that it might be established that he was truly dead, and that we were redeemed not by some image of death (as Muhammad and certain others once imagined) but by his true death. It also helps us to be more certain about Christ's death, so that we may dread less the death we ourselves must undergo. For he who was able to overcome death, and to make of it a passage to life, when it had formerly been the punishment of sin and a kind of prelude to eternal damnation, will also be able to strengthen us, so that we are not cast down from our standing by the pain of death, or by what follows death, however terrifying these are to the flesh. To this also pertains the fact that, although everything the Lord suffered until now was sad and full of shame, yet at the very moment (so to speak) of death, the glory and majesty of Christ immediately showed themselves, as we saw recently in the portents that accompanied his death. As for his burial, his body is not buried secretly or furtively, nor is it carelessly cast away (as was once threatened to Jehoiakim concerning Jeremiah), but with the consent of the Roman governor and under public authority the Lord is buried

units.la: Ioan. iij. / Effectus signorum in morte Christi. / Ioel 2. / Matth. 14. / Luc. 23. / Ierem. 22. / Isa. 53. minus in loco honesto, ab hominibus honestis, & modo etiā honesto, sicuti ab Isaia olim fuerat prædictum. Quia vero simul alia concurrunt, quæ observatu digna & salutaria sunt, singula diligentius debent inspici.
units.tr: Joh. 3. / The effect of the signs at Christ's death. / Joel 2. / Matt. 14. / Luke 23. / Jer. 22. / Isa. 53. in an honourable place, by honourable men, and in an honourable manner too, as Isaiah had foretold long ago. But since several other things concur here that are worth observing and are salutary, each must be examined more carefully.

units.la: Exorditur hunc locum Matthæus a mulieribus nonnullis, quæ inter mortem & sepulturam Christi media & veniunt, spectatrices fuerunt. Et multas fuisse scribit, inter quas præ cæteris insignes fuerunt Maria Magdalene, & Maria Iacobi (quem minorem dicunt) & Iosé mater, quæ apud Marcum Mariæ virginis soror, & a Ioanne Maria Cleophæ dicitur. Additur hīs mater filiorum Zebedæi. De omnibus hoc in genere dicitur, quod Christum Ierosolymam ascendentem, ut pro peccatis mundi perlitaret, secutæ, & hunc usque etiam in crucem suffixo adhæserint. Sunt ergo mulieres ista exemplum constantis fidei, quæ neque timerum difficultate, neque vinculis, neque flagris, neque diro & infami crucis supplicio, imo ne morte quidem se offendi passæ sunt, ut ab illo secessionem facerent, quæ viuente & miraculis florentem coluerunt. Efficit eo præclarior hæc mulierum constantia, quod discipulos longe superarunt, qui primū turpi fuga diserpi, deinde excepto Ioanne, omnes in latebras sese abscondērunt. Quotquot ergo veram & solidam fidei laudem ambiunt, constantiam huic addant, & saltem præsentia sua animum ijs addant, quos aliter iuuare, aut expe riculis eripere non possunt. Interim non temere annotauit Matthæus, illos procul sive a longe spe tauisse. Etsi enim in spectaculo sanctissimo occupatæ essent, non tamen decori sui immemores, me dijs viris sese inferunt impudenter. Id vero sexui muliebri in primis observandum est. Nam si ab illo pudorem auferas, aliarum virtutum omnium, quibus ornatur, condimentum sive fulcrum abstuleris. Quid enim conferat mulieri impudenti forma aliud quam annulus aureus in naribus suis? Prou. 11.
units.tr: Matthew begins this passage with some women who came and were spectators between the death and the burial of Christ. He writes that there were many, among whom the most outstanding were Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James (whom they call the younger) and of Joses, who in Mark is called the sister of the Virgin Mary and in John is called Mary of Cleophas. The mother of the sons of Zebedee is added to these. Of all of them it is said in general that they followed Christ as he went up to Jerusalem to make atonement for the sins of the world, and that they clung to him even to the cross on which he was fastened. These women are therefore an example of steadfast faith: neither the hardship of the journey, nor chains, nor scourges, nor the cruel and infamous punishment of the cross, nor even death itself, could offend them so that they withdrew from him whom they had honoured while he lived and flourished in miracles. This constancy of the women is made all the more remarkable because they far surpassed the disciples, who first fled in shameful flight and then, except for John, all hid themselves in hiding places. Whoever therefore seeks true and solid praise for faith should add this constancy to it, and at least by their presence lend courage to those whom they cannot otherwise help or rescue from danger. Meanwhile Matthew did not note without reason that they watched from afar. For although they were occupied with a most holy spectacle, they did not forget their modesty and did not shamelessly thrust themselves among men. This especially must be observed by the female sex. For if you take shame away from a woman, you have removed the seasoning and support of all the other virtues with which she is adorned. For what does an impudent woman's beauty profit her, but a gold ring in her nose? Prov. 11.

units.la: His præmissis præcipuum sepulturæ authorem inducit Matthæus, Iosephum ab Arimathæa, quem diuitem, & discipulum IESV fuisse scribit, occultum tamen hactenus (vt Ioannes scripsit) quod Iudæos plus æquo reuereretur. Alij virum bonum & iustum fuisse dicunt, & iustitiæ argumentum afferunt, quod licet Christum defendere non posset, tamen non suffragatus est illorum consilio vel facto, qui Christum occiderunt. Quod ita dicitur, ut non obscure demonstretur, illum nihil commercij habuisse cum Filij Dei carnificibus. Et quia hoc omnibus satis notum erat, publicam protestationem intercessisse oportet, quia hoc testimonium sibi apud omnes comparauit. Et est multa obseruatione dignum, quod Iosephus et dives & senator Ierosolymitanus esset, nihilominus IESV CHRIST discipulus, id est, vir Christianus, & regni Dei, quod expectabat, ciuis fuit. Ergo neque opes neque honores per se aliquem a regno Dei excludunt, modo pietati studeat, & (vt Dominus docet) ante omnia quærat regnum Dei. Vult enim inueniri Deus, neque cuiquam regni sui thesauros inuidet. Exempla, quibus hoc probatur, infinita passim occurrunt, quæ commemorare longum foret. Sed sufficiat nobis Iosephus, qui cum ferum esset dieiparasceues nimirum, nec tamen dum caperat Sabbathum, quod totum in sepulchro quieuit Dominus, accessit Pilatū, & (vt Marcus annotauit) fidenti animo vel intrepida mentis fiducia venit: cum opes fere soleant auaros meticulosos reddere, cum cogitant, se multum habere quod amittant, ille eo audacior est in eo, quod toti Senatorum & Sacerdotum collegio displicere sciebat. Imo plus audet omnibus illis, qui viuente Christo, eius aperti discipuli fuerunt. Facile etiā impetrat a Pilato quod petit. Quia enim ad gloriam Filij Dei & resurrectionis eius faciebat tota sepulturæ historia, Deus hominis prophani animum mouit, vt quod petebatur, neque vellet neque posset negare. Et vt Ioannes narrat, præter omnem expectationem, Nicodemus se illi coniungit, qui Iosepho sese & laborum & sumptuum socium præbuit. Excitet ergo exemplum hoc viros politicos, qui in aliqua authoritate constituti sunt, vt officio suo diligenter inuigilent, nec pigeat eos propter Christū aliquid aggredi, quod cum labore aut periculo coniunctum videtur. Gravibus enim & duris successum felicem potest dare Deus, qui corda non priuatorum modo hominum, verumetiam regum habet in sua manu. Dabit ergo facile laborum socios, si nos ipsi fideles erimus.
units.tr: With these things said beforehand, Matthew introduces the chief author of the burial, Joseph of Arimathea, whom he describes as rich and a disciple of Jesus, but hitherto secret (as John wrote), because he was more reverent toward the Jews than was right. Others say that he was a good and just man, and they offer as evidence of his justice that, although he could not defend Christ, he did not lend his support to the counsel or deed of those who killed Christ. This is said in such a way as to show clearly that he had no dealings with the executioners of the Son of God. And since this was well known to all, he must have made a public declaration, because by it he won this testimony for himself among everyone. It is also worthy of much notice that Joseph, though rich and a senator of Jerusalem, was nevertheless a disciple of Jesus Christ, that is, a Christian man, and a citizen of the kingdom of God for which he was waiting. Therefore neither riches nor honours in themselves exclude anyone from the kingdom of God, provided he strives for godliness and, as the Lord teaches, seeks the kingdom of God above all things. For God wishes to be found, and does not begrudge anyone the treasures of his kingdom. Examples proving this occur everywhere in endless number, and it would be long to recount them. But let Joseph suffice for us. Although it was already evening, namely the Preparation, and yet the Sabbath had not yet begun (on which the Lord rested entirely in the tomb), he approached Pilate and came, as Mark noted, with a bold spirit and a fearless confidence of mind. Since riches usually make the greedy timid, as they think they have much to lose, he was the bolder in doing what he knew would displease the whole body of senators and priests. Indeed, he dared more than all those who, while Christ was alive, were his open disciples. He also easily obtained from Pilate what he asked. For the whole history of the burial was serving the glory of the Son of God and of his resurrection, so God moved the heart of this profane man so that he neither wished nor was able to refuse what was asked. And, as John relates, beyond all expectation Nicodemus also joined him, who became a partner with Joseph both in labour and in expense. Let this example therefore stir up those public men who are placed in some authority to watch carefully over their office, and let them not shrink from undertaking anything for Christ's sake that seems to involve labour or danger. For God can give a happy outcome even to grave and difficult matters, since he holds in his hand the hearts not only of private men but also of kings. He will therefore readily give us companions in our labours, if we ourselves are faithful.

units.la: Quid vero cum corpore Christi facit Iosephus? Acceptum inuoluit sindone: at cum aromatibus, myrrha & aloe, inuolutum fuit, idque propter spem resurrectionis, quam ita fouebant & confirmabant veteres, alibi diximus. Deponit item in suo monumento, quod sibi pri noum excideret, ne vel ne vel alius quis aut Dominus alterius virtute resurrexisse putetur. At dum suum sepulchrum Christo concedit Ioseph, sibi ipsi omnia sepulchra sanctificat. Ita nobis sanctificantur omnia quae prius ipsi nos Christo consecramus, ut eius vsui cedant. Sed & ingens lapis ad ostium monumenti advolvitur: quod sive honoris ergo factum sit, sive causa custodiae sepulchri, sive ut resurrectionis veritas certior & gloria maior esset, non temere id factum est, neque peculiari mysterio caruit. Ut neque illud etiam quod de mulieribus repetitur, quae contra sepulchrum, aut ex eius regione sederunt. Fecerunt hoc, ut situm sepulchri melius spectarent, & facilius extremum unctionis officium illi impenderent: quod tamen Maria Lazari soror iam pridie praevenerat, ut suo loco diximus. Interim de illarum constantia Spiritus sanctus amplius testari voluit: quod nec sepulto quidem Domino eius cum amorem deposuerint. Et ut illarum exemplum imitentur necesse est, quotquot in Christo volunt salui fieri. De sepultura & eius ratione ac usu non opus est plura addere, cum de iis alibi dictum sit. Observetur tamen in mulierum exemplo: ut ne luctu quidem, qui funera comitari solent, nos ab officio revocari patiamur, sed si nobis eripiantur, sine quibus vix videmur commode vivere posse, non tamen segnescamus, sed eo fortius insistamus operi nobis per Dominum commissio.
units.tr: What, then, does Joseph do with the body of Christ? He wraps it in a linen shroud; and it was wrapped with aromatic spices, myrrh and aloes, and this for the sake of the hope of resurrection, which the ancients cherished and confirmed in this way, as we have said elsewhere. He also lays it in his own tomb, which he had hewn out for himself, so that no one, not even another man or the Lord himself, should be thought to have risen by another's power. And while Joseph grants his own sepulchre to Christ, he at the same time sanctifies all sepulchres for himself. So, for us, all those things are sanctified which we first consecrate to Christ, so that they may serve his use. But also a huge stone is rolled to the door of the tomb. Whether this was done out of honour, or for the sake of guarding the sepulchre, or so that the truth of the resurrection might be more certain and its glory greater, it was not done without reason and it lacks no special mystery. The same holds for what is repeated about the women, who sat opposite the sepulchre, or in its region. They did this so that they could better watch the place of the tomb and more easily render the last office of anointing to him; yet Mary, the sister of Lazarus, had already anticipated this the day before, as we said in its place. Meanwhile, the Holy Spirit wished to bear further witness to the constancy of those women, in that they did not lay aside their love even when the Lord was buried. And all who wish to be saved in Christ must of necessity imitate their example. There is no need to add more about burial and its manner and use, since this has been spoken of elsewhere. Let this be observed, however, from the example of the women: that we should not allow ourselves to be called away from duty even by the grief which usually accompanies funerals; but if those things are snatched from us without which we scarcely seem able to live well, let us nonetheless not grow slack, but press on all the more bravely with the work committed to us by the Lord.

units.la: Caeterum etsi universa mundi machina creatori suo, Filio Dei condoluerit, & de sceleris aduersus hunc destignati indignitate multis prodigiis testata sit, nondum tamen satis factum est Sacerdotibus & Pharisaeis, quorum invidia & odium adhuc est insatiabile. De prophanorum hominum odiis olim Poeta dixit: Pascitur in vivis liuor, post fata quiescit:
units.tr: Moreover, although the whole machinery of the world grieved with its Creator, the Son of God, and bore witness by many portents to the indignity of the crime committed against him, nevertheless the priests and Pharisees were still not satisfied, and their envy and hatred remain insatiable. A poet once said of the hatred of profane men: "Envy feeds on the living; after death it is quiet."

units.la: Et frequenter commiseratione mouentur erga defunctos, qui vident, quam indigne praeter meritum tractati sint. De Caesare certe scribitur, quod cum in curia vulneribus viginti tribus confossus esset, animos populi mox conuersos fuisse, ut sublatis ex rogo torribus ad percussorum domus festinarent, ut eas incenderent: multos vero quaesiuisse illos, ut captos discerperent. At sacerdotum principes & Pharisaei barbaris militibus inhumaniores adhuc oderunt, quae post innumerabilia in omnis loci & ordinis homines beneficia in cruce pendentem & foede laniatum viderant. Nam postera die, quae Parasceue sequitur, ad Pilatum coacti, nouam accusationem instituunt, dicentes: Domine, meminimus planum illum dixisse, cum adhuc viueret. Tertio post die surgam. Iube muniri sepulchrum usque in diem tertium, ne quando veniant discipuli eius nocte, & furentur eum, dicantque populo, Surrexit a mortuis, & erit ultimus error peior priore. Quo loco, num contumaciam istorum hominum aut impudentiam cum impietate coniunctam potius admirere, dubites. Plenum & impostorem vocant, cuius innocentia Pilatus praeses, Herodes, coelum, terra, Sol, petrae, milites, testimonium tulerant: & quem ipsi nullius sceleris potuerunt convincere. Deinde non vlla Sabbati religione tenentur, cuius violati toties Christum accusauerant: ipsi vero nunc proditoria consilia & cruenta in Sabbato tractant: imo sepulchrum muniunt, milites accersunt & alia faciunt, quae sine labore & molestia fieri non poterant. Vehementer ergo falluntur, qui impios aliqua ratione cicurari posse arbitrantur. Non est pax impiis, inquit Isaias, sed iustis, quod quiescere non possunt. Isa. 57.
units.tr: And people who see how unworthily, beyond their deserts, the dead have been treated are often moved to pity. Of Caesar it is certainly written that when he had been stabbed with twenty-three wounds in the senate house, the minds of the people were soon turned, so that they snatched up torches from the funeral pyre and hurried to the houses of the assassins to set them on fire; and that many of them sought those men so that they might tear them apart if they caught them. But the chief priests and Pharisees hated him more savagely even than the barbarous soldiers did: the very man who had hung on the cross and been foully torn, after countless benefits conferred on men of every place and rank, whom they had seen. For on the following day, which is the Preparation, they were compelled to go to Pilate and brought a new accusation, saying: "Sir, we remember that that deceiver said, while he was still alive: After three days I will rise. Order the sepulchre to be guarded until the third day, lest his disciples come by night and steal him and tell the people, 'He has risen from the dead,' and the last error be worse than the first." Here one may hesitate whether to marvel more at the obstinacy of these men or at their impudence joined with impiety. They call him a deceiver, whose innocence Pilate the governor, Herod, heaven, earth, the sun, the rocks and the soldiers had attested, and whom they themselves could convict of no crime. Then they are held by no scruple about the Sabbath, the violation of which they had so often charged against Christ; yet now they plot treacherous and bloody schemes on the Sabbath; indeed they guard the sepulchre, summon soldiers and do other things which could not be done without labour and trouble. They are therefore greatly mistaken who think that the impious can somehow be tamed. "There is no peace for the wicked," says Isaiah, "but the righteous, because they cannot rest." Isa. 57.

units.la: Pilatus, qui paulo ante Iosepho se facilem praebuit, in tradendo corpore Domini, nunc Sacerdotibus quoque morem gerit. Quia enim homo prophanus resurrectioni nihil tribuit, non vult prophetare huius commentum (ut ipsi videbatur) cum quoquam altercari. Dicit ergo illis: Habetis custodiam, id est, milites templi custodiae destinatos: abite, munite sicut scitis. Itaque munierunt sepulchrum, obsignato quoque lapide, nimirum a praeside: ne quis abstrahat crimine liberae maiestatis illum loco mouere, ac monumentum effringere possit. Et hoc quidem permittit fieri Deus, quia iustorum conatus gloriam resurrectionis posteaillustrarunt, Sacerdotes vero sibi pso nouam accersierunt molestiam, quando milites proprios illius testes esse audiunt, quibus contradicere non tutum erat: sed silentium, imo turpe mendacium, multa pecunia ab illis redimere coacti sunt. Neminem ergo impiorum successus laeti offendant. Non sunt hi diuturni. Tueamur autem salutem IESV CHRISTI merito partam fide forti & indefesso sanctitatis studio, per quod nos quoque in illo resurgemus, & victores erimus.
units.tr: Pilate, who shortly before had shown himself compliant to Joseph in handing over the body of the Lord, now also humours the priests. For since a profane man ascribes nothing to the resurrection, he does not wish to argue with anyone about what seemed to him a fiction of the prophets. So he says to them: "You have a guard," that is, the soldiers assigned to the watch of the temple: "go, guard it as you know how." And so they guarded the sepulchre, the stone also being sealed, no doubt by the governor's authority, so that no one could remove it or break open the tomb on a charge of treason against the majesty of the state. God indeed permits this to happen, because the efforts of the righteous later illuminated the glory of the resurrection, while the priests brought new trouble upon themselves, when they heard that the soldiers were witnesses of it, and it was not safe to contradict them; so they were compelled to buy their silence, indeed a shameful lie, from them for a large sum of money. Let no one, therefore, be offended and glad at the success of the impious. Their success is not lasting. Let us rather hold fast to the salvation of Jesus Christ, won by merit, with a strong faith and an unwearied zeal for holiness, through which we too shall rise again in him and be victors.

units.la: Sacerdotum odium implacabile contra Christum.
units.tr: The implacable hatred of the priests against Christ.

units.la: Sepulchrum munitur custodibus.
units.tr: The sepulchre is guarded by watchmen.

units.la: IN EVANGELIVM MATTHAEI CAPUT XXVIII. HOMILIA CCCIX.
units.tr: On the Gospel of Matthew, Chapter 28, Homily 309

units.la: EXtremo autem Sabbato, cùm lucesceret in primum diem hebdomadis, venit Maria Magdalene & altera Maria, vt spectarent sepulchrum: Et ecce, terræmotus factus est magnus. Angelus enim Domini cum descendisset e cœlo, & accessisset, deuoluit lapidem ab ostio, sedebatq; super eum. Erat autem visus eius vt fulgur, & vestimentum eius album sicut nix. Custodes autem concusi præ illius timore, & facti sunt sicut mortui. Respondens autem Angelus, dixit mulieribus: Vos vero ne timete. Scio enim vos IESVM crucifixum quærere: Non est hic, Surrexit enim prout dixit. Venite, videte locum, vbi iacebat Dominus. Et cito profectæ dicite discipulis eius, eum surrexisse a mortuis. Et ecce, præcit vobis in Galilæam: illic eum videbitis. Ecce, dixi vobis. Tunc egressæ cito a monumento cum timore & gaudio magno, currebat vt nuntiarent discipulis eius. Cùm aut proficisceretur, vt renuntiarent discipulis eius, ecce, IESVS occurrit eis, dicens: Aucte. Illæ autem accesserunt, & præhenderunt eius pedes, & adorauerunt eum. Tunc ait eis IESVS: Ne timete, abite, renuntiate fratribus meis, vt abeant in Galilæam; & illic me videbunt.
units.tr: Now after the Sabbath, as the first day of the week began to dawn, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary came to see the sepulchre. And behold, there was a great earthquake. For the angel of the Lord descended from heaven, came and rolled back the stone from the door, and sat upon it. His appearance was like lightning, and his clothing white as snow. The guards, shaken for fear of him, became as dead men. But the angel answered and said to the women: "Do not you fear. For I know that you seek Jesus who was crucified. He is not here, for he has risen, as he said. Come, see the place where the Lord lay. And go quickly and tell his disciples that he has risen from the dead. And behold, he goes before you into Galilee; there you will see him. Behold, I have told you." Then they went out quickly from the tomb with fear and great joy, and ran to tell his disciples. But as they went to report to his disciples, behold, Jesus met them, saying: "Hail." And they came near and took hold of his feet and worshipped him. Then Jesus said to them: "Do not be afraid. Go, tell my brothers that they should depart into Galilee, and there they will see me."

units.la: CRIPTVRA sacra vnanimi consensu testatur, æternum Dei Filium propter nos in mundum venisse & hominem factum esse, vt peccatores saluos faceret. Et hæc vera et propria consolatio est, quæ per Euangelium nobis offertur. Vt vero inter multas atq; graues tentationes certior fit, quæ ex illa percipimus salutis fiducia, sæpius nos admoneri oportet, omnia abunde præstitisse Christum, quæ ad humani generis redemptionem necessario requirebantur. Primo enim peccata omnia expiauit vno die, vt Zacharias promiserat, & his deletis, Deum Patrem nobis placauit. Et huc referri debent, quæ de illius morte hucusque sunt exposita. Deinde mortem, quæ peccati stipendium erat, resurrectione sua vicit, & eius imperium fregit, vt quæ nobis vt peccati pœna debebatur, iam in ipsum credentibus lætus fit ad vitam beatam & immortalem translitus. Quia ergo resurrectio eius nostræ redemptionis quasi complementum est, Apostoli in suis concionibus præcipue testificantur: Euangelistæ autem illius historiam non minus diligenter quam mortem eius describunt. In præsenti primo tempus annotatur, quo ex mortuis resurrexit Dominus. Secundo, quibus primum eius resurrectio innotuerit. Tertio quis & resurrectionis & annuntiationis eius modus fuerit. Quo loco Angelorum de illa concio sive testimonium asscribitur.
units.tr: Holy Scripture testifies with one consent that the eternal Son of God came into the world for our sake and was made man, so that he might save sinners. This is the true and proper comfort that is offered to us through the Gospel. But so that, amid many and grievous temptations, we may be more certain of the confidence of salvation that we derive from it, we ought often to be reminded that Christ has supplied abundantly everything that was necessarily required for the redemption of mankind. First, he expiated all sins in one day, as Zechariah had promised, and by blotting these out he reconciled God the Father to us. To this must be referred what has been set forth so far concerning his death. Next, he conquered death, which was the wages of sin, by his resurrection, and broke its power, so that what was owed to us as the punishment of sin is now, for those who believe in him, changed into a joyful passage to a blessed and immortal life. Since therefore his resurrection is, as it were, the completion of our redemption, the apostles bear witness to it especially in their sermons, and the evangelists describe its history no less carefully than his death. In the present passage, first, the time is noted at which the Lord rose from the dead; second, to whom his resurrection first became known; third, what the manner both of his resurrection and of its announcement was. In this place, the sermon or testimony of the angels concerning it is ascribed to them.

units.la: Tempus sic notauit Matthæus: ὀψὲ δὲ σαββάτων, τῇ ἐπιφωσκούσῃ εἰς μίαν σαββάτων. Quo loco plerisq; interpretibus impositum est, quod ὀψὲ pro vespera acceperunt, postremum nimirum diei parte, cum hic potius de prima, quæ alias diluculum dici solet, agatur. Patet hoc ex reliquis Euangelistis, qui omnes distinctius locuti sunt. Marcus enim sic ait: ἀνατείλαντος τοῦ ἡλίου, id est, & cum exactum esset Sabbatum, valde mane, primo die hebdomadis veniunt ad monumentum exoriente Sole. Idem prope Lucas, cuius verba sic sonant: τῇ δὲ μιᾷ τῶν σαββάτων ὀρθρου βαθέως ἦλθον ἐπὶ τὸ μνημεῖον. Id est, vna, sive prima Sabbatorum aut hebdomadis, profundo diluculo, venient ad monumentum. Ioannes vero sic: τῇ δὲ μιᾷ τῶν σαββάτων Μαρία ἡ Μαγδαληνή ἔρχεται πρωὶ σκοτίας ἔτι οὔσης εἰς τὸ μνημεῖον, id est, prima autem hebdomadis venit Maria Magdalene, cum adhuc tenebræ essent, ad monumentum: Quapropter cùm tres Euangelistæ diserte vesperam
units.tr: Matthew noted the time thus: "ὀψὲ δὲ σαββάτων, τῇ ἐπιφωσκούσῃ εἰς μίαν σαββάτων" [But late on the Sabbath, as it began to dawn toward the first day of the week]. Here most interpreters have taken the word "ὀψὲ" to mean "evening," understanding it of the last part of the day, whereas here the reference is rather to the first part, which is otherwise usually called daybreak. This is clear from the other evangelists, who all speak more distinctly. For Mark says: "ἀνατείλαντος τοῦ ἡλίου" [when the sun had risen], that is, when the Sabbath was past, very early on the first day of the week they come to the tomb as the sun rises. Luke says almost the same, and his words sound thus: "τῇ δὲ μιᾷ τῶν σαββάτων ὀρθρου βαθέως ἦλθον ἐπὶ τὸ μνημεῖον" [on the first day of the week, very early in the morning, they came to the tomb]. That is, on the first, or first of the Sabbaths or of the week, at deep dawn, they came to the tomb. John, however, says: "τῇ δὲ μιᾷ τῶν σαββάτων Μαρία ἡ Μαγδαληνή ἔρχεται πρωὶ σκοτίας ἔτι οὔσης εἰς τὸ μνημεῖον" [but on the first day of the week Mary Magdalene comes early, while it was still dark, to the tomb]. Therefore, since the three evangelists expressly

units.la: Zach.3.
units.tr: Zach.3.

units.la: Quando resurrexit Dominus. vesperam excludant, diluculi autem meminerint, quae prima pars fuit eius diei, qui nouam hebdomadem post exactum festum Pafchatis exordiebatur, superuacaneum mihi videtur, vt particulam siue Aduerbium ὀψὲ pro vespera interpretemur, quae aduerbialiter posita exponi potest per ὀψὲ. Ita enim Graeci vulgo loquuntur, ὀψὲ τῆς ἡλικίας, pro vergente ad senium aetate: post exactum atatis iustae & rebus agendis matura tempus. Deinde dum ferum Sabbathorum dicit, non septimum diem, qui magnum Sabbathum Paschale erat, nec singulos septimanae dies intelligit, sed Hebraeorum more totam septimanam, quae pluribus (vt sic dicam) Sabbathis constabat, cum dies illi omnes ad Pascha pertinerent, & propterea azymi dicerentur. Vt ergo Matthaeus cum reliquis tribus concilietur, videtur locus hic commode sic reddi posse. Post exactum tempus sabbatorum & totius hebdomadae Paschalis, cum lucesceret in primum diem hebdomadis. Ita enim exclusio vesperae vocabulo ambiguitas tollitur, quae multos mouit, vt quaestiones non necessarias mouerent; nec tamen vis aliqua fiet aduerbio ὀψὲ, quo minus in sensu proprio, & huic loco in primis conueniente accipiatur. Haec pluribus in praesenti tractare libuit, quia alibi breuius ista attigimus. Quod si vero ex praecedenti historia repetamus, Christum in die Parasceues mortuum & in huius vesperam, cum adhuc ab hora nona tres superessent, sepultum esse, secundus eius in sepulchro iacentis dies erit Sabbatum magnum Pasc̄hatis: at qui primus nouae hebdomadis dies numeratur, tertius est ab eius morte & sepultura: quo se resurgere velle toties discipulis promiserat, vt id hostibus quoque iam pridem innotuisset: qui, vt nuper audiuimus, sepulchrum muniri, & adhibitis custodibus armatis asseruari voluerunt, vt resurrectionem eius impedirent. Sed ne vnam quidem horulam id possunt: quin vix dum oriente tertij diei aurora, excusso mortis imperio e monumento prodeat. Est hoc euidens argumentum Veritatis & omnipotentiae IESV CHRISTI, quo nos in fide decretorum & promissionum eius omnium confirmemus. Huius enim generis exempla multa sunt: quorum omnium hic vsus nobis esto, ne quid de illius fide dubitemus, cui omnis potestas data est in caelo & in terra. Porro primae, quibus refuti resurrectio Christi innotuit, fuerunt mulieres, quae ex Galilaea vsque Christum secutae, ei ministrauerant, & omnium quae perpessus est, spectatrices fuerant. Nunc autem primo diluculo adsunt, vt pro more gentis extremum honorem ipsi impendant: quae ipsis occasio di minitus oblata fuit, vt primae illum resurrexisse discerent. Habent igitur luculentum suae pietatis praemium: & simul altius mysterium hic latet: quo admonemur Filium Dei muliebris quoque sexus redemptorem esse. Nam vt primae promissionis, quae Adamo in Paradiso facta fuit, verba docent, hoc Dei decretum fuit, vt ex eo sexu iustitia & salus nasceretur, qui nobis peccati & mortis causa fuerat. Multaut quidem illum Deus pluribus poenis, sed ne ideo se omni spe gratiae & salutis excidisse putaret, olim promissiones illae datae sunt, & in mulieribus saepe singularia virtutum maximarum exempla sunt edita, & nunc primus innotuit resurrectio, quae nostrae redemptionis colophonem continet. Qua autem iustarum studia, qui mores fuerint, & quibus praemiis illas remuneratus sit Deus, non opus est hic repetere, cum alibi de his abunde sit dictum. Sed quaerat aliquis cur Dei Filius sanctissimas mulieres resurrectione sua praevenerit, neque dignatus sit eo honore, vt corpus suum condirent, quod sacerdotum ferui & milites prophani tam multis tam indignis modis violauerant? Sed necesse erat doctrinam eius confirmari, qua pauperes sibi subsistuit, vt in hos conferamus, quae in ipsum, si in terris ageret, vellemus conferre officia. Etenim si hoc officium ab iis recepisset, nobis omnem de illo bene merendi occasionem ereptam putaremus, quibus non idem contingeret. Nunc vero cum in vnoquoque egeno hoc nobis offerri audimus, quod omnes fere pij sibi dari cupiunt, dulcissima haec consolatio est, qua confirmemur, ne officia nostra Christo displicere putemus. Praeterea superstitionibus medetur, quas orituras sciebat nostrae temporibus, dum alij eius meritum & gratiam, alij corpus quoque illius certis locis, temporibus, adhaec certis vitae generibus astringunt. Ridiculi homines, ne quid de illis grauius dicam, qui quam Christus ipsis peperit libertatem, nouis superstitionum vinculis constringunt. Sed de his quo que plura alibi. Sed modum resurrectionis Christi videre praestat, qui gloriosissimus fuit: vt quod ex ignominia crucis iam exortu erat scandalum, aboleretur. Nam primo terraemotu magnum factum fuisse dicitur: qualem in morte quoq; accidisse dictum est nuper. Ut vero ad indignam sui creatoris necem tellus horruit, & eius hostibus poenas graues minata, adeoq; vt indignos, quos ipsa ferat detestata est: ita nunc quasi exultans gestit eum luci victorem reddere, quem infinum suum recepe-rat. Deinde ne terræmotus hic vulgaris aut leui de causa euenisse putetur, angelus de cœlo descen-disse dicitur. Qui ergo in terra habuit hostes homines, qui eum in sepulchro retinere voluerunt, huic e cœlo aduentiunt ministri angeli, qui ipsum liberent: & vnus quidem angelus terra vniuersam con-cutit, vt testetur nihil esse quod ipsius gloriam impediat. Hic certe confidenter ad sepulchrum ac-cedens, lapidem ab officio ipsius reuellit, nihil Cæsaris sigillum veritus, cuius nomine Pilatus illum obsignauerat: & ne quid sibi metuere videatur angelus, non reuellit modo lapidem, sed ei insidet, quasi expectaturus eos, qui iniuriam Cæsari & eius sigillo factam vltifici velint. Et ne quis mire-tur, illud pauos esse milites Romanos, quorum tunc summa erat in toto fere orbe terrarum autho-ritas describitur, talem fuisse angelum, qui vel solo aspectu terrere potuerit aduersarios. Erat au-tem vultus eius (inquit Euangelista) vt fulgur, & vestimentum eius vt nix. Fulgur sola species ter-ret, & solo fragore suo animos humanos mouent, quæ illud comitantur tonitrua. Veritus vero al-bus victoriæ symbolum est. Quid vero fiat, si vtrumq; in cœlestibus spiritibus concurrat, quorum ministerio Deus in suis operibus siue iudicijs exequendis vtitur? Non temere ergo hic additur: Custodes præ illius timore concussos esse, & factos esse sicut mortuos. Examinatis ergo iacuerunt, nec quicquam in illis virium fuit, donec Deus illos pauos esset rursum ad se redire. At si tanta est vnius Angeli maiestas & potentia (quod & alia innumera exempla testantur) quis non fateatur insuperabiles esse Christi vires, cui myriades angelorum seruiunt? Nos autem consoletur hæc eius potestas. Nostra enim est Christus, nobis vicit: nobis deniq; Angelos obstrinxit, vt nobis seruiant, circa nos castramentetur: nos deniq; manibus ferant atq; defendant. Sed & ipsius promissio est: Ecce ego vobiscum sum vsq; ad consummationem sæculi. Caterum orationem angeli audia-mus, quia mulieres compellauit, quæ tribus partibus constat. Prima solatur territas, dicens: Vos vero ne timueritis. Sic interpretari libuit, vt Emphasim quæ particulæ VOS inest, exprimerem. Sic enim dicere videtur Angelus: Veni quidem perter-refaciendis Christi hostibus, qui metu examinati iacent. At veltra longe alia fors est, quas non ti-mere, non animo turbari, sed exultare decet. Et huius dicti rationem reddit: Scio enim vos IESVM crucifixum quærere. Quia autem hic quæri vult, non poterit aliquo iure irasci aut infestum se præbere ijs, qui hoc sceleratio faciunt. Et ipse Christus, vt ijs congratulemur in cœlo iubet, qui seruant tur. Cur ergo terrori effemus ipsum quærentibus, in quo vnofalus inueniri potest? Est autem memoratu dignum, eundem Angelum, qui milites terruit, mulieres Christum pie quærentes consolari. Est hoc perpetuum, & ideo Euangelij quoq; doctrina & vniuersa, quæ per hanc traditur fa-lutis ratio impijs & hypocritis terrori, electis autem solatio est, sicuti alibi exemplis & rationibus demonstrauimus. Secunda sua orationis parte, de Christi resurrectione angelus testimonium fert. Et huc pertinet quod initio dicit: Scio vos IESVM crucifixum quærere: ne mulieres ipsum de alio aliquo loquī putent. Deinde singulis verbis argumentum & pondus inest. Nam de IESV crucifixo loquens dicit: Non est hic. Id vero de corpore dici nemo sanus dubitat. Et quia proximum erat, vt quæreretur: Vbi ergo est? Præuertit quæstionem angelus: Surrexit prout dixit. Ne quid nouum dicere putetur, ad veteres promissiones eas reuocat, & simul earum obliuionem siue negligentiam corripit. Tertio quasi in rem præsentem eas introducturus: Venite (inquit) videte locum, vbi iacebat Dominus. Quorsum vero hæc omnia? Nimirum vt demonstret, illum vero suo & natura-li corpore resurrexisse, & huius quoq; proprietates naturales atq; essentiales retinuisse. Quod ipse postea apparitionibus & demonstrationibus plurimis docuit, quas nunc repetere non est opus. Nos teneamus firmiter, corpus Christi ita amortuum resurrexisse, vt natura sua visibile & palpabile sit, membris & partibus suis constet, & loco etiam suo certo contineatur. Nam postremum hoc ne gare absurdum foret, cum angelus loci, in quo illud iacuit, nunc autem non amplius iaceat, ta di-ferte meminerit. Seruiunt autem omnia ad confirmationem Symboli apostolici de resurrectione Filij Dei in carne nati, quam ut constanter credamus, plurimum refert. Primum enim confirmatur iustificationis nostrae articulus. Quia enim mortem vicit resurgendo, peccatu plane expiari oportet, quod illius aculeum fuisse Paulus docet, & idem illum traditum dicit propter offensas nostras, & excitatum propter iustificationem nostri. Deinde asseritur hic animarum nostrarum immortalitas. Nisi enim Christi anima, quae vere hominis anima, & vsq; ad mortem perturbata fuit, immortalis manisset, neq; ad corpus redire, neq; illud vitae restituere potuisset. Adhaec corporum nostrorum resurrectio stabilitur: quia nos secum esse vult Dominus. Ut ergo ipse in morte non mansit: ita neq; nos in morte manebimus. Sed regnum Christi innumerum & aeternum esse constat, cum ne mors quidem ipsi aliquid potuerit derogare: & hic fundamentum habetur eius consolationis, qua Apostolus nos sub levat, dicens, Neq; vitam neq; mortem nos separare posse a dilectione Christi: & nos Domini esse, sive vivimus, sive morimur. Rom. 8. & 14.
units.tr: When the Lord rose, let them shut out the evening, and let them remember the morning, which was the first part of that day which began the new week after the festival of the Passover was over. It seems superfluous to me to interpret the particle or adverb ὀψὲ as "evening," since when used adverbially it can be explained by ὀψὲ. For the Greeks commonly speak this way: ὀψὲ τῆς ἡλικίας [late in life], meaning an age drawing toward old age, that is, a time after a suitable age has been completed and mature for doing things. Next, when he says "after the Sabbaths," he does not mean the seventh day, which was the great Paschal Sabbath, nor does he mean the single days of the week. He means, in the manner of the Hebrews, the whole week, which consisted of several Sabbaths, so to speak, since all those days belonged to the Passover and were therefore called unleavened. So that Matthew may be reconciled with the other three, this passage seems fitly rendered thus: "After the time of the Sabbaths and of the whole Paschal week was over, as it was dawning toward the first day of the week." In this way the ambiguity of the word "evening," which has moved many to raise unnecessary questions, is removed, and yet no violence is done to the adverb ὀψὲ, which may be taken in its proper sense and is most suited to this place. I have wished to treat these matters at some length here, since elsewhere we have touched on them more briefly. But if we go back to the preceding history, Christ died on the day of Preparation and was buried in its evening, when three hours still remained from the ninth hour. Then his second day in the tomb will be the great Sabbath of the Passover, and the first day of the new week is counted as the third from his death and burial. He had promised the disciples so often that he would rise on that day that this had long since become known even to his enemies. As we heard recently, they wished the sepulchre to be fortified and guarded by armed sentries, in order to prevent his resurrection. Yet they could not manage even a single hour, for he came forth from the tomb, having shaken off the power of death, scarcely as the dawn of the third day was rising. This is a clear proof of the truth and omnipotence of Jesus Christ, by which we may be confirmed in faith in all his decrees and promises. Examples of this kind are many, and let this one serve us all, so that we do not doubt concerning the faith of him to whom all power is given in heaven and on earth.
