Moreover, the first to whom the resurrection of Christ was made known were the women, who had followed Christ from Galilee, had ministered to him, and had been witnesses of all he suffered. Now, at early dawn, they are present to pay the last honour to him, as is the custom of their people, and this opportunity was offered to them by God, so that they should be the first to learn that he had risen. They therefore have a splendid reward for their piety. At the same time, a deeper mystery lies hidden here, by which we are reminded that the Son of God is also the Redeemer of the female sex. For, as the words of the first promise made to Adam in Paradise teach, it was God's decree that righteousness and salvation should be born from that sex which had been the cause of our sin and death. God indeed punished her with many penalties, but lest she should think that she had therefore fallen from all hope of grace and salvation, those promises were given long ago, and in women there have often been remarkable examples of the greatest virtues. And now the resurrection, which contains the completion of our redemption, has first been made known. As for what the studies and manners of these righteous women were, and with what rewards God recompensed them, there is no need to repeat it here, since this has been said abundantly elsewhere. But someone may ask why the Son of God anticipated the most holy women by his resurrection, and did not deign to grant them the honour of anointing his body, which the servants of the priests and the profane soldiers had violated in so many and such unworthy ways. But it was necessary that his teaching be confirmed, by which he made the poor his substitutes, so that the services we would wish to render to him, were he living on earth, we should render to them. For if he had accepted this service from them, we would think that every opportunity of deserving well of him had been snatched from us, to whom the same would not happen. Now, however, when we hear that this is offered to us in every needy person, which almost all the godly desire to be given to themselves, this is a most sweet consolation, by which we are confirmed not to think that our services displease Christ. Besides, he remedies superstitions, which he knew would arise in our times, when some bind his merit and grace, and others bind his body also to certain places, times, and, besides, to certain kinds of life. They are ridiculous people, not to say anything more severe about them, who bind with new chains of superstition the freedom which Christ won for them. But concerning these things too, more is to be said elsewhere. It is worthwhile, however, to see the manner of the resurrection of Christ, which was most glorious, so that the scandal which had already arisen from the ignominy of the cross might be done away with. For it is said that at the first a great earthquake occurred, such as was also said recently to have happened at his death. And just as the earth shuddered at the unworthy slaying of its Creator, and threatened grave punishments to his enemies, and abhorred those unworthy men whom it was bearing, so now, as if exulting, it rejoices to restore to the light him whom it had received into its depths. Then, lest this earthquake be thought to be ordinary or to have occurred for a slight cause, it is said that an angel came down from heaven. So he who on earth had human enemies who wished to keep him in the tomb, has heavenly ministers, angels, coming to him to set him free. And one angel shakes the whole earth, to bear witness that nothing can hinder his glory. This one, approaching the sepulchre with confidence, rolls away the stone from its place, not fearing at all the seal of Caesar, in whose name Pilate had sealed it. And lest the angel seem to fear anything, he not only rolls away the stone but sits upon it, as if waiting for those who wish to avenge the injury done to Caesar and his seal. And lest anyone wonder that the Roman soldiers, whose authority at that time was supreme over almost the whole world, were terrified, we are told that the angel was of such a kind that he could terrify the adversaries by his appearance alone. "His appearance," says the Evangelist, "was like lightning, and his clothing like snow." Lightning terrifies by its appearance alone, and by its crash alone it moves human minds, and thunderclaps accompany it. But whiteness is the symbol of victory. What would happen if both of these came together in heavenly spirits, whose ministry God uses in carrying out his works or judgements? It is not for nothing, therefore, that it is added here that the guards, shaken with fear of him, became as dead men. They lay therefore stunned, and there was no strength left in them, until God saw fit to bring them back to himself. But if the majesty and power of one angel is so great (as other countless examples also testify), who would not confess that the powers of Christ are invincible, he whom myriads of angels serve? Let this his power console us. For Christ is ours; he has conquered for us; finally, he has bound the angels to himself so that they may serve us, encamp around us, and at last bear us in their hands and defend us. This is also his promise: "Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age." Let us now hear the angel's speech, since it addresses the women, and it consists of three parts. In the first part he comforts them, being afraid, saying, "But you, do not fear." I thought it right to translate it thus, so as to express the emphasis which lies in the particle "you." For the angel seems to say: "I have indeed come to terrify the enemies of Christ, who lie stunned with fear. But your lot is quite different; you ought not to fear, nor be troubled in mind, but to rejoice." And he gives the reason for this saying: "For I know that you seek Jesus, who was crucified." And because he wishes that he be sought, he will not be able by any right to be angry with or hostile to those who do this, which is not a wicked thing to do. And Christ himself orders that we be congratulated in heaven, those who are saved. Why then should we be terrified, we who seek him, in whom alone salvation can be found? It is worth recalling that the same angel who terrified the soldiers consoles the women who piously seek Christ. This is a constant pattern, and so the doctrine of the Gospel and the whole plan of salvation which is handed down through it are a terror to the impious and hypocrites, but a comfort to the elect, as we have shown elsewhere by examples and reasons. In the second part of his speech, the angel bears witness concerning the resurrection of Christ. To this pertains what he says at the beginning: "I know that you seek Jesus, who was crucified," lest the women think that he is speaking of some other person. Then in each word there is force and weight. For speaking of Jesus who was crucified, he says: "He is not here." No sane person doubts that this is said of the body. And since the next question was bound to be, "Where then is he?", the angel anticipates the question: "He has risen, as he said." Lest it seem that he is saying something new, he recalls them to the old promises, and at the same time he rebukes their forgetfulness or negligence of them. Thirdly, as if about to bring them in to see the thing present: "Come," he says, "see the place where the Lord lay." But to what end are all these things? Surely to show that he rose in his true and natural body, and retained its natural and essential properties. This he afterwards taught by very many appearances and demonstrations, which there is no need to repeat now. Let us hold firmly that the body of Christ rose from the dead in such a way that by its nature it is visible and tangible, consists of its own members and parts, and is also contained in its own definite place. For to deny this last point would be absurd, since the angel so clearly recalls the place where it lay, but where it no longer lies. Now all these things serve to confirm the article of the Apostles' Creed concerning the resurrection of the Son of God born in the flesh, and it matters greatly that we believe it steadfastly. For first, the article of our justification is confirmed. For since he conquered death by rising, sin must surely be expiated, which Paul teaches was the sting of death, and he says that the same was delivered up on account of our offences and raised again for our justification. Next, the immortality of our souls is asserted here. For unless the soul of Christ, which was truly a human soul and was troubled even unto death, had remained immortal, it could neither have returned to the body nor restored it to life. Moreover, the resurrection of our bodies is established, because the Lord wills us to be with him. As he did not remain in death, so neither shall we remain in death. And it is agreed that the kingdom of Christ is unending and eternal, since not even death could take anything away from him. And here is the foundation of that consolation by which the Apostle raises us up, saying that neither life nor death can separate us from the love of Christ, and that we are the Lord's, whether we live or die. Rom. 8. & 14.

units.la: Postremo, ut discipulus nuntient, Christum resurrexisse, angelus praecipit mulieribus. Cito, inquit, Prophetae, dicite discipulis eius, eum resurrexisse a mortuis. Marcus nominatim Petri mentionem facit, scribit: Nimirum ut qui Christum turpiter abnegarat, se in gratia receptum esse fateret. Nos vero admonemur, resurrectionem Christi ad omnes pertinere, qui eius discipuli sunt, id est, qui vocem eius audiunt, & ipsi credunt. Ita enim ille oves suos & germanos Dei Patris filios definit. Neq; est, ut quis propter inhaerentem nobis infirmitatem carnis aut fidem imperfectam desperet. Qualies enim discipuli fuerint, & quam indigni, quos tanto honore & salute dignatur Dominus, saepe iam diximus. Sed vicit omnes illorum naevos & errores immensus & incomparabilis Christi amor, qui ei, ut seipsum pro nobis miseris traderet, causa fuit. Idem nos quoq; confirmet in tentationibus, quae interdum fidem nostram labefactant. Et sane consolationem quae ex Angeli verbis potest peti, Christus mox confirmabit, quando mulieribus Angelo obsequentibus, occurrens, amice illas salutat, feq; illis contrectandum praebet: ita nunquam deest officium faciendi. Dominus, & idem certe mandatum ad discipulos repetens, illos fratres suos vocat, & simul in Galilaeam abire iubet, ubi ipsum visuri sint. At scimus hanc illis patriam fuisse, & ibi Dominum cum illis familiarissime conversatum fuisse, cum in terris vixeret. Mulieribus ergo ipsi occurrens, & idem mandatum repetens, non obscure testatur, se illarum curam nequaquam deposuisse, sed ipsas in veram patriam reducere velle, ubi aeternum cum ipso vivunt. Haec vero omnia nobis applicemus, & harum exemplo excitati quaeramus Christum tunc quoq;, quando se occultare, imo extinctus esse videtur. Et si quando tunc denno nobis affulgens mandare videtur, quod ratio dissuadet, & gaudia, quae per Evangelium offeruntur, cum periculo & timore coniunctus sunt, pergamus tamen forti & constanti animo in illius mandatis, qui difficultates omnes e medio tollere poterit, & omnes qui per fidem fratres eius facti sunt, regni quoq; sui haeredes facere. Ipsi sit honor, gloria in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: Lastly, that the disciples may be told that Christ has risen, the angel instructs the women: "Go quickly, say to his disciples that he has risen from the dead." Mark expressly mentions Peter and writes: no doubt so that he who had shamefully denied Christ might confess that he had been received back into grace. We are, however, reminded that Christ's resurrection pertains to all who are his disciples, that is, who hear his voice and believe it themselves. For thus he defines his sheep and the true sons of God the Father. Nor should anyone despair because of the weakness of the flesh that still clings to us or because of imperfect faith. We have often said already what sort of disciples they were, and how unworthy, these whom the Lord deigns to honour with such great dignity and salvation. But the immense and incomparable love of Christ, which was the cause of his giving himself up for us wretched people, overcame all their blemishes and errors. May it likewise strengthen us in temptations, which sometimes shake our faith. And indeed Christ will soon confirm the consolation that can be drawn from the angel's words: when the women, obeying the angel, are running, he meets them, greets them kindly, and offers himself to be touched by them. Thus the duty of doing good is never lacking. The Lord, repeating the same command to the disciples, calls them his brothers, and at the same time bids them go away into Galilee, where they will see him. But we know that this was their homeland, and that the Lord had lived there on very familiar terms with them while he dwelt on earth. Therefore, by meeting the women himself and repeating the same command, he clearly testifies that he has by no means abandoned their care, but wishes to lead them back to their true homeland, where they live with him forever. Let us apply all these things to ourselves, and, roused by their example, let us seek Christ even then, when he seems to hide himself or even to be extinguished. And if at such a time he shines upon us again and seems to command what reason dissuades, and the joys offered through the Gospel are bound up with danger and fear, let us nevertheless press on with a brave and steadfast mind in obedience to his commands, to him who is able to remove all difficulties from the midst and to make all who have become his brothers through faith heirs also of his kingdom. To him be honour and glory forever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCCX.
units.tr: HOMILY CCCX.

units.la: Proficiscentibus autem ipsis, ecce, quidam ex custodia venerunt in urbem, & annuntiaverunt principibus Sacerdotum omnia quae facta fuerant. Tunc coacti cum Senioribus, consilio capto, pecuniam multam dederunt militibus, dicentes: Dicite, Discipuli eius nocte venerunt, & eum furati sunt nobis dormientibus. Quod si hoc auditum fuerit apud Praesidem, nos persuadebimus ei, & securos vos praestabimus. Ipsi vero accepta pecunia, fecerunt sicut erant edocti: & divulgatus est iste sermo apud Iudaeos usq; ad hodiernum diem.
units.tr: While they were on their way, behold, some of the guard came into the city and reported to the chief priests everything that had happened. Then they gathered with the elders, took counsel, and gave a large sum of money to the soldiers, saying: "Tell people that his disciples came by night and stole him away while we slept. And if this comes to the governor's ears, we will persuade him and see that you are kept safe." So the soldiers took the money and did as they had been taught. And this story has been spread among the Jews to this very day.

units.la: Paulus Apostolus de Evangelio differens, in posteriori ad Corinthios ait, bonam fragrantiam Christi vocat, his quidem odore mortis ad mortem, illis vero odorem vitae ad vitam. Quia enim potentia Dei est, hae in eo etiam apparet, quod efficaciter praedicatione sua per omnia perrumpit, vt non solum electi, qui illa gaudent & feruantur, verum etiam impijs annuntietur, qui inuite vt non solum electis, qui illa gaudent & feruantur, verumetiam impijs annuntietur, qui inuiti & damnationis suae testimonium illud audiunt. Est hic videre admirabile prouidentiae Dei consilium, quod nostrae saluti filium, quae interdum impiorum quoq; opera & ministerio vtitur. Exemplum eius rei praefens histo-ria euidens praebet. Nam in praedicatione resurrectionis IESV CHRISTI, quae nostra salutis complementum est, vsus est hucusq; Deus mulierum sanctarum opera, quas Angelus instituit, vt illam Apostolis annuntiarent: sed & ipse Dominus illis occurrit, seq; ipsum eis videndum & vt illam Apostolis annuntiarent: sed & ipse Dominus illis occurrit, ...
units.tr: The Apostle Paul, discussing the Gospel in his second letter to the Corinthians, calls it the good fragrance of Christ: to some it is the odour of death unto death, and to others the odour of life unto life. For the power of God is in it, and it shows itself in this, that by its preaching it breaks through everything effectively, so that it is announced not only to the elect, who rejoice in it and are saved, but also to the ungodly, who hear it unwillingly as a testimony against their own condemnation. Here we can see the wonderful counsel of God's providence, which uses even the works and service of the wicked for our salvation. The present history gives a clear example of this. For in the preaching of the resurrection of Jesus Christ, which is the completion of our salvation, God has so far used the work of holy women, whom the angel commissioned to announce it to the apostles. But the Lord himself also met them and showed himself to be seen by them, ...

units.la: [Transcription of the remaining body text is incomplete: the scan is too skewed and the small italic type too degraded to read reliably letter by letter across the whole page.] consultant tam politici, quam Ecclesiastici proceres. Vbi obiter videmus, non semper bene & re- he fieri, quod cum consilio fit. Supra enim similiter publice in conuentu de Christo occidendo con- fultatum est: & nunc rursus de opprimendo, aut sal tem de neganda resurrectione Christi consul-tatur, sine qua salus nostra non potest consistere. Et de hostibus illius Dauid Psalmo secundo vaticinatur, quod Reges & principes concurrant, fremant, meditentur: sed obseruetur meditatio-nes eiusmodi fere inanes & friuolas, non modo iniustas & iniquas esse. Imo quod vulgo dicitur, Malum consilium esse consultori pessimum: hoc plerunque hostibus Christi euenit, vt nemini homi-num consilia illorum nocentiora sint, quam illis ipsis.
units.tr: ...the civil as well as the ecclesiastical leaders take counsel. Here we see in passing that what is done with counsel is not always done well. For earlier, in the same way, a public meeting deliberated about killing Christ; and now again they deliberate about suppressing him, or at least denying his resurrection, without which our salvation cannot stand. Concerning his enemies David prophesies in the second Psalm that kings and princes gather together, rage, and plot; but it is to be observed that such plots are almost empty and frivolous, and not only unjust and iniquitous. Indeed, what is commonly said, that bad counsel is most harmful to the one who takes it, usually happens to the enemies of Christ, so that no one's counsels are more harmful to men than theirs are to themselves.

units.la: Consilij summa est, Veritati mendacium opponi debere: eo enim potissimum opprimitur aut saltem obscuratur Veritas. Ne consilium vero inane fit, militibus hoc rursus suggerunt, de quo prius, cum muniri cuperent sepulchrum, Pilatum admonuerunt, periculosum esse, ne discipuli no-cte veniant, & corpus Christi suffurentur. Id nunc accidisse aiunt. At turpe & inhonestum est, ab aliquo petere, vt in tuam gratiam mendacium dicat: & qui honestatis atque pietatis vel religio-nis cura aliqua tenentur, ij nunquam obliuiscuntur eius, quod olim Sapientes inter Gentes dixe-runt: Amicos vsque ad aras coli debere, adeo, vt nemo nobis in tanto pretio sine auctoritate sit, vt propter illum testimonio falso peccemus. Et scimus veteres Romanos in militibus cum primis fi-dem requisiuisse. Idcirco Sacerdotum principes, vt hanc religionem militum animis eximant, pe-cuniam multam illis pollicentur, quae mendacij hoc ab eis volunt redimere, quo publicam populi salutem subuertant. At periculum imminebat a praeside. Scimus enim quam obseruantes discipli-na militaris fuerint Romani: & nota est Agrippa Herodis seueritas, qui milites, quibus Pe-trum Apostolum custodiendum dederat, dux & capitis supplicio plecti iussit, quia hunc ex manibus eius fuisse audiebat, neque illi de eo rationem ipsi reddere possent. Quid ergo speraret ipsi, si ipsi fa-terentur, sua ignauia accidisse, vt homo mortuus ex sepulchro obsignato, ipsis multo somno oppres-sis, eriperetur? Ne quid ergo periculi metuant milites, pollicentur, ipsos causam illorum auturos, si ad Praesidem deferatur, & huic sua auctoritate perfuasoros, vt securos faciant. At quia hic de Sacerdotij Iudaici dignitate agebatur, hanc autem illi hoc mendacio stabilire, & labascentem in-staurare volunt, quid aliud agunt, quam quod sepulchrum & sacra sua prophanis Ethnicis militibus suspectos faciunt, adeoque religionem omnem, cuius sidices & tutores videri volebant, gentium & idololatrarum ludibrijs exponunt. Consilium ergo illi Sacerdotes multa immanissima scelera, quae neque plebeios quidem homines decent, qui humanitatis amantes videri volunt, ne dum sacrorum & religionis antistites. Nam pecuniam pollicendo militibus, ipse praedae illos accendunt, a qua il-los omni studio reuocare debebant, vt olim Ioannes Baptista fecit. Deinde mentiendi formam il-lis praescribunt, cum hoc genus hominum alioqui ad calumnias proclive sit. Praeterea impunita-tis ipse illos armant, quos potius metu disciplinae in officio continere debuissent. At quia haec o-mnia acciderunt inter Christum & eius inimicos hostes, quid nobis hodie seruandum sit, obseruari debet.
units.tr: The sum of their counsel is that a lie must be set against the truth, for by this above all the truth is suppressed, or at least obscured. So that their counsel may not be empty, they now suggest this to the soldiers, as they had earlier, when they wanted the tomb secured, warned Pilate that it was dangerous lest the disciples come by night and steal the body of Christ. They now say that this has happened. But it is shameful and dishonourable to ask anyone to tell a lie for your sake; and those who are held by some care for honesty, piety, or religion never forget what the wise men among the Gentiles once said: that friends are to be honoured even to the altars. So much so that no one should be so precious to us that, for his sake, we sin by a false testimony. We know that the ancient Romans demanded fidelity above all from their soldiers. Therefore the chief priests, to remove this sense of duty from the soldiers' minds, promise them a large sum of money, which they want to buy from them by this lie, so that they may overthrow the public salvation of the people. But danger threatened from the governor. For we know how strictly the Romans observed military discipline, and the severity of Herod Agrippa is well known, who ordered the officer and the guards to whom he had entrusted the apostle Peter to be put to death, because he heard that Peter had escaped from their hands and they could not give an account of him. What then would they hope for, if they confessed that through their own negligence a dead man had been taken from a sealed tomb while they lay in deep sleep? So, that the soldiers may fear no danger, the priests promise that they will take up their cause, and if the matter is reported to the governor, they will persuade him by their authority to make them safe. But since this concerned the dignity of the Jewish priesthood, and they wish by this lie to establish it and restore what is tottering, what else are they doing than making their tomb and their sacred things suspect to the profane Gentile soldiers, and so exposing all religion, whose defenders and guardians they wished to appear, to the mockery of the nations and idolaters? Therefore those priests devised many monstrous crimes, which do not befit even common men who wish to appear lovers of humanity, much less the leaders of sacred things and of religion. For by promising money to the soldiers, they inflame them with greed, from which they ought to have called them back with all earnestness, as John the Baptist once did. Then they prescribe for them the form of the lie, although this kind of men is otherwise prone to slander. Moreover, they arm them with impunity, whom they ought rather to have kept in their duty through fear of discipline. But since all these things happened between Christ and his enemies, we must observe what we ourselves should keep today.

units.la: Primo, quod quo magis Sol lucet, eo magis caecutiunt impij, quibus illius lux dolet, quae causa est, quod in peius indies proficiunt. Deinde eos, qui contra Christum semel conspirauerunt, ex ijs quo peiores fieri, quibus emendari poterant, si communi saltem sensu vterentur. Tertio quibus praesidijs & fulcris superstitio & religio falsa nitatur: Mendacijs nimirum & pecunijs, siue opi-bus. Nec enim frustra praeditum a Daniele, Antichristum possidere thesauros terrae. Olim qui-dem census tabernaculo & templo ad sarta tecta conferebatur, vt sacra historia docet. Sed tunc Sacerdotum auaritia in alios vsus conuersi erant sacri reditus, vt pecuniae templi neque pauperes alerent, neque sacris seruirent, sed ex Iudae proditoris manibus Christus emeretur, & nunc ex pe-cunia sacra redimatur mendacium, quo Sacerdotes per impios milites omnem Christi gloriam & publicam populi salutem sepeliri conati. Et hoc olim quoque D. Hieronymi tempore factum fuisse, ex eius verbis patet, quae in hunc locum scripsit: Omnes qui stipe templi & his, quae conferuntur ad vsus Ecclesiae abutuntur in alijs rebus, quibus suam expleant voluntatem, similes sunt Scriba-rum & Sacerdotum, redimentium mendacium & Saluatoris sanguinem. Quod quam multiplici & quàm sceleratà fra sss hostis fiat, vix dies totus ad enarrandum sufficeret. Hùc pertinet luxus plus quàm Sibaritici, quos Romanæ Ecclesiæ præsules satrapas vincunt. Hùc referri debent quæ ex sacris peculijs in concubinas, scorta & hùs turpiores libidinis ministros conseruntur. Ex templorum redditibus alantur milites, scurræ, mimi, lenones, equi, canes, simiæ & omnis generis bestiæ, fiunt bombardæ, bella geruntur, quibus totus terrarum orbis turbatur, corrumpuntur regum & principum consiliarij, conducuntur sicarij & venefici, proditores, qui eos e medio tollant, qui ista accusant, & vt par est, reprehendunt. Interim ne hi quidem extra omnem culpam sunt, qui pluriore religione & doctrina gloriantur: sed inter hos etiam bonorum Ecclesiasticorum abusuta peccatur, vt non credibile sit Christum dupassurum, vt sub sanctò nominis sui prætextu religio pessimorum hominum auaritiæ & libidini serviat. Sed cùm ista olim facta sint, ne offendamur hominibus. Qui olim Iudæorum Sacerdotibus officinam iniquitatis exercuit, id ipsum hodiè etiam facit, & multos male perdet: vt alibi prolixè dictum est. Præterea habemus hoc loco leuitatis militaris exemplum. Interfuerunt milites isti rebus omnibus, viderunt prodigia in morte Domini ædita, tenebras horroris plenas, terræmotu, petras dissilientes, sepulchra aperta, surgentes multos quasi manu prostrati lacuerunt ex animis, & vix dum ad se redierant, vt ista sacerdotibus nuntiarent: attamen pecuniæ causa non verentur mentiri, nec tanti iudicis iram metuunt. Vides hic quid de talibus speres, de quibus verissimè olim Lucanus dixit: Ibi fas, vbi plurima merces. Certè proprij honoris cura illos a scelere reuocare debebat, ne seipsos tam turpiter infamarent. Dicunt discipulos Christi, homines inermes, infirmos & peregrinos ipsis armatis corpus, quod custodiæ ipsorum mandatum erat, abstulîsse. Quid viri militares de propria ignauia turpius dicere poterant? Annon videntur se vel hoc nomine supplicio dignos esse? Dicunt hoc ipsis dormientibus factum. Ast dormierunt, vnde istud notum? Si strepitu illorum excitati sunt, cur non insecuti sunt abeuntes? Certè ipsi expediti, hoc onere grauatos facile assequi poterant. Sed vt astute sua commenta palam faciant impij, fere vt sorices suo scse indicio produnt.
units.tr: First, the more the sun shines, the more the ungodly are blinded, and they are pained by its light; this is the reason why they grow worse day by day. Second, those who have once conspired against Christ become worse from those things by which they could have been corrected, if they had at least used common sense. Third, consider the supports and props on which superstition and false religion rest: namely lies and money, or wealth. For it is not without reason that Daniel foretold that Antichrist would possess the treasures of the earth. In former times, indeed, the tithes were brought to the tabernacle and the temple for the upkeep of the buildings, as sacred history teaches. But then the greed of the priests turned the sacred revenues to other uses, so that the money of the temple neither fed the poor nor served the sacred rites; Christ was bought with the hands of Judas the traitor, and now a lie is bought with sacred money, by which the priests, through wicked soldiers, have tried to bury all the glory of Christ and the public salvation of the people. That this also happened in the time of St. Jerome is clear from his words, which he wrote on this passage: "All who abuse the offering of the temple and what is contributed for the uses of the Church, to fulfil their own desires in other things, are like the scribes and priests who bought a lie and the blood of the Saviour." How manifold and how wicked the enemy's deceit is in this matter, a whole day would scarcely suffice to describe. To this belongs a luxury more than Sybaritic, which the prelates of the Roman Church surpass as satraps. To this must be referred what is spent from the sacred endowments on concubines, prostitutes, and ministers of more shameful lust. From the revenues of the temples are fed soldiers, buffoons, mimes, pimps, horses, dogs, apes, and all kinds of beasts; cannons are made, wars are waged, by which the whole world is thrown into confusion; the counsellors of kings and princes are corrupted; assassins and poisoners are hired, and traitors who remove from the way those who accuse these things and, as is right, rebuke them. Meanwhile, not even those are free from all blame who boast of greater piety and learning; but among these too, abuse of ecclesiastical goods is practised, so that it is hard to believe that Christ would allow religion, under the sacred pretext of his name, to serve the greed and lust of the worst men. But since these things were done in former times, let us not be offended at men. He who once carried on a workshop of iniquity among the priests of the Jews does the same thing today too, and he destroys many; as has been said at length elsewhere. Moreover, we have here an example of military levity. Those soldiers were present at all these things; they saw the portents displayed at the Lord's death, darkness full of horror, the earthquake, rocks splitting, tombs opened, and many dead rising; they lay as if struck down by a hand, and scarcely had they come to themselves when they went to report these things to the priests. Yet for the sake of money they are not ashamed to lie, nor do they fear the anger of so great a judge. You see here what you may hope for from such men, of whom Lucan said most truly: "There is right where the reward is greatest." Surely concern for their own honour ought to have called them back from such crime, lest they disgrace themselves so shamefully. They say that the disciples of Christ, unarmed, weak, and foreigners, carried off the body which had been committed to their guard. What could soldiers say more shamefully about their own cowardice? Do they not seem to deserve punishment for this alone? They say it happened while they were sleeping. But if they were asleep, how is that known? If they were roused by the noise, why did they not pursue those who were leaving? Surely, unencumbered themselves, they could easily have overtaken men weighed down by such a burden. But the wicked, in order to make their schemes plain, reveal themselves by their own evidence, much as mice betray themselves.

units.la: Porrò huius consilij succèssum subijcit Matthæus, dicens: Diuulgatum est hic sermo apud Iudæos vsque ad hodiernum diem. Potest hoc de toto hoc negotio intelligi: Vt primum milites de discipulis rumorem in populo sparserint de corpore Christi furto sublato: cui crediderunt, qui sacerdotum partes souebant. Nihil enim tam absurdum & ineptum est quod non fidem inueniat apud horum parasitos, qui vbi illis assentari in animum induxerunt, vel esslamma cibum peterent. Quod obseruari debet propter eos, quibus mirum vel incredibile videtur, his postremis seculis orbe Christi nunquam tam multis portentis errorum deceptum fuisse. Quasi verò mundus non semper fuit suis similis, ad errores nimirum proclius: adeò vt falli & seduci cupiat. Meretur ergo sua ingratitudine vt excæcatus errores sibi accessat, & in ijs pereat: sicuti de Antichristo scribens, Apostolus olim monuit. Deinde verò latius etiam hic locus accipi potest: quòd nimirum sermo de militum & Sacerdotum pecunia corruptis vulgatus sit, & Sacerdotum quoque commentum publicè innotuerit. Nec enim tanta potuit esse apud omnes impudentissimorum hominum authoritas, quin apud elestos fidem inueniret Euangelij prædicatio, qua discipuli Christum resurrexisse docebant: & passim erant, qui illum viderant, vt res neque celari neque negari posset. Confirmationi serviet postrema historiæ Euangelicæ pars de qua in sequenti Sermone agetur. Nostrum est CHRISTO IESV & eius resurrectioni testimonium ferre, qua mortem vicit, peccatum omne expiauit, & aeternum in cœlis regnat redemptor & Seruator noster vnicus. Ipsi sit laus & gloria. Amen.
units.tr: Matthew goes on to tell how this scheme turned out, saying: "This saying has been spread abroad among the Jews until this day." This may be understood of the whole affair: as soon as the soldiers had spread the report among the people that the disciples had stolen away the body of Christ, the rumour was believed by those who favoured the priests' cause. For nothing is so absurd and foolish that it does not find belief among these men's hangers-on, who, once they have resolved to flatter them, would sooner swallow a flame for food. This should be noted on account of those who think it strange or incredible that in these last ages the world of Christ has never been deceived by so many monstrous errors. As if the world had not always been like itself, and naturally prone to errors, so much so that it wishes to be deceived and led astray! Justly, then, on account of its ingratitude, the blinded world is given over to the errors it desires, and perishes in them, as the Apostle once warned when writing about Antichrist. Moreover, this passage can also be taken more broadly: the story, that the soldiers were bribed with money and the priests' fabrication became publicly known. For the authority of the most shameless men could not be so great among all that the preaching of the Gospel, by which the disciples taught that Christ had risen, would fail to find belief among the elect; and there were many everywhere who had seen him, so that the matter could neither be hidden nor denied. The last part of the Gospel history, which will be treated in the following sermon, will serve to confirm this. It is our duty to bear witness to CHRIST JESUS and to his resurrection, by which he conquered death, expiated every sin, and reigns eternally in heaven, our only Redeemer and Saviour. To him be praise and glory. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCCXI.
units.tr: HOMILY 311.

units.la: Vndecim autem discipuli profecti sunt in Galilæam, in montem vbi constituerat eis IESVS. Et cùm vidissent eum, adorauerunt eum: quidam autem dubitauerunt. Et accedens IESVS loquutus est eis, dicens: Data est mihi omnis potestas in cœlo & in terra.
units.tr: Then the eleven disciples went away into Galilee, to the mountain where Jesus had appointed for them. And when they saw him, they worshipped him, but some doubted. And Jesus came up and spoke to them, saying: All power is given to me in heaven and on earth.

units.la: Profecti autem docete omnes gentes, baptizantes eos in nomine Patris & Filij & Spiritus sancti: Docentes eos seruare omnia quæ mandaui vobis: & ecce, ego vobiscum sum omnibus diebus, usque ad consummationem seculi. Amen.
units.tr: Go therefore and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you. And behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age. Amen.

units.la: ANgelus Dei, qui sanctis mulieribus, quæ redemptori nostro IESV CHRISTO extremum honorem impenserant ad monumentum venerant, de eius resurrectione testificatus est inter alia promisit, quòd ipse cum discipulis omnibus illum in certo Galilææ loco visuras sint: & idem ipse Dominus paulò post ijsdem mulieribus occurrens pollicetur, & vt hoc discipulis renuntient mandat. Etenim opus erat illos priusquam durioribus certaminibus obijcerentur, ad sua redire & diligentius instrui & confirmari: Idcirco fidelissimè eis promissa præstitit Christus. Nam in Galilæam illos reduxit, aliquot diebus cum illis familiariter versatus est, deque regno Dei cum ipsis disseruit, miraculis denique nouis confirmauit, quorum aliqua ab Ioanne narrantur. Cæterum quia promissio illa de insigni aliqua actione facta fuerat, in qua cum illis de suo munere & legatione Apostolica, cui eos prædestinarat, actuirus esset, Matthæus omissis multis aliis, hanc in præsenti narrat: quæ omnino videtur ea fuisse, cuius Paulus ad Corinthios meminit, quando eum fratribus amplius quingentis apparuisse scribit. Nam etsi hic vndecim solum nominentur, quos designauit Apostolos, nihil tamen obstat, quo minus credamus, vniuersam credentium multitudinem tunc confluxisse: quia Apostolos in cætu celebri & frequenti initiari oportuit, vt maior esset illorum authoritas.
units.tr: The angel of God, who had come to the tomb to the holy women who had paid the last honour to our Redeemer Jesus Christ, bore witness to his resurrection and, among other things, promised that the disciples would see him in a certain place in Galilee. The Lord himself, meeting the same women shortly afterwards, makes the same promise and orders them to report it to the disciples. For before they were exposed to harder conflicts, they needed to return home and be more carefully instructed and strengthened. Therefore Christ faithfully fulfilled what he had promised. For he led them back into Galilee, spent some days familiarly with them, discoursed with them about the kingdom of God, and finally confirmed them with new miracles, some of which are related by John. Moreover, since that promise concerned some notable action in which he was to deal with them about their office and apostolic commission, for which he had destined them, Matthew, leaving out many other things, narrates this one here. It seems altogether to have been the same occasion to which Paul refers to the Corinthians when he writes that he appeared to more than five hundred brethren. For although only the eleven whom he had designated as apostles are named here, nothing prevents us from believing that the whole multitude of believers came together then. The apostles had to be installed in a large and well-attended assembly, so that their authority might be greater.

units.la: Commodè autem hac actione historiam Euangelij Matthæus concludit, vt ea consultationi Sacerdotum & Seniorum opponat, qui nuper cum militibus nouam aduersus Dominum coniurationem fecerunt, vt eius resurrectionem turpi mendacio & calumnia de corpore furtim sublato impiè negarent. Erat calumnia hæc periculi plena. Nam discipulis læsæ maiestatis crimen intentabatur, vt qui a præside obsignatum sepulchrum effregissent, & supplicio digni essent. Itaque rursus de regno Christi actum videbatur, cum hac calumnia grauatis, neque a præside neque sacerdotibus & senioribus aliquid tutum esset. Sed ecce suam exististimationem mirifice feruat Dominus, & non modo vndecim illos tuetur, sed simul plusquam quingentos ex diuersis locis cogit in vnum locum, inter quos publice fe regem cæli & terræ designat, & simul regni sui administratores constituit, quos mandatis instructos emittit in vniuersum orbem: eam deniq; Ecclesiæ suæ formam tradit, quæ ad finem seculi vsque permanere debeat. Fuit hæc inter solennes, quas in terris Christus habuit, actiones vltima, ad quam cum tanto numero credentes conuenerint, & hic publice sint instituta Ecclesiæ primordia, adeo vt hanc Ecclesiæ natiuitatem dicere possis. Decet omnino, vt diligenter singulæ partes considerentur.
units.tr: Matthew fittingly concludes his history of the gospel with this action, to set it against the counsel of the chief priests and elders, who lately, with the soldiers, made a new plot against the Lord, impiously to deny his resurrection by a shameful lie and calumny that the body had been stolen away. This calumny was full of danger. For the charge of treason was levelled against the disciples, as men who had broken the seal set on the tomb by the governor and so deserved punishment. Thus it seemed that the kingdom of Christ was again at an end, since, weighed down by this calumny, nothing was safe either from the governor or from the priests and elders. But behold, the Lord wonderfully preserves his own reputation: he not only protects the eleven but at the same time gathers more than five hundred from various places into one place. Among them he publicly declares himself king of heaven and earth, and at the same time appoints administrators of his kingdom, whom, once instructed with commands, he sends out into the whole world. Finally, he hands down that form of his Church which ought to endure until the end of the age. This was the last of the solemn actions which Christ performed on earth, and it was at this one that believers came together in such numbers; here the beginnings of the Church were publicly established, so that you could call this the birth of the Church. It is certainly right that each part be considered carefully.

units.la: Principio vndecim discipuli profecti in Galilæam conuenerunt in eum montem, quem illis IESVS constituerat. Paruerunt ergo eius mandato, nec aliquid praetexunt, quo se excusent. Ipse etiam non deest promissis, sed præstat fidem, & se conspiciendum præbet, indignis licet, & nunc quoque infirmioribus adhuc quàm debebat. Nam etsi illum coram videant, quidam tamen dubitauisse dicuntur. Illum quidem ex mortuis resurrexisse multis testibus & argumentis didicerant, vt de eo vix possent dubitare. Hærebant autem in multorum animis reliquiæ consternationis prætersitæ, & credibile est, quòd cum in ipso, qui ferui formam depositerat, iam nihil quàm diuinum & cælestè appareret illos attonitos hæsitauisse, num quem astantem conspicabantur, esset Christus ille, qui prius cum ipsis fuerat. Ita frequenter nobis sit, vt aliquo nobis optimè noto occurrenti dicamus: Tune es ille, an alius? &c. Nec ante cessauit illa discipulorum hæsitatio & pauor, donec ille propius accedens seipsis familiariorem præbuit. Tunc collectis rursum animi viribus, adorauerunt illum: Quod nimirum ex resurrectione ipsis constaret, esse Dei Filium, & haud dubie forma & habitus totus refusitati illos in admirationem raperet. Quid enim hic fatum putabis, cum duo discipuli, cum quibus Emmaunt iuit Dominus, postea fasti sint, cordafua intra ipsos arsisse, quando eum scripturas explicantem audiuerunt? Nunc ad primarium
units.tr: First, the eleven disciples went into Galilee and assembled on that mountain which Jesus had appointed for them. They therefore obeyed his command and offered no excuse to hide behind. He too does not fail in his promises, but keeps faith and presents himself to be seen, although they are unworthy and still weaker than they ought to be. For although they see him with their own eyes, some are nevertheless said to have doubted. They had learned from many witnesses and proofs that he had risen from the dead, so that they could scarcely doubt about him. But remnants of the recent consternation still lingered in the minds of many. It is credible that, since in him who had laid aside the form of a servant nothing now appeared but what was divine and heavenly, they were astonished and hesitated, wondering whether the one standing before them was that Christ who had previously been with them. So it often happens to us that we say to someone we know very well, who meets us in an unexpected way: "Are you that man, or someone else?" and so on. Nor did that hesitation and fear of the disciples cease until he, drawing nearer, showed himself more familiar to them. Then, gathering their strength of mind again, they worshipped him, because from the resurrection it was certain to them that he was the Son of God; and no doubt his whole form and bearing, now restored, carried them away in wonder. For what do you suppose happened when the two disciples with whom the Lord walked to Emmaus later said that their hearts had burned within them when they heard him explaining the Scriptures?

units.la: • 3 hujus loci caput accedamus, quod est de legatione Apostolica, quam undecim discipulis credidit: ubi haec observari debent. Primum de seipso disserit, ut cuius nam legati sint, intelligant, et quid de toto hoc munere iudicari debeat. Deinde munus eorum definit, et mandatis instruit. Praeterea opem et defensionem suam pollicetur.
units.tr: Now let us come to the main point of this chapter, which concerns the apostolic commission he entrusted to the eleven disciples. In this, the following points should be observed. First, he speaks about himself, so that they may understand whose envoys they are, and what ought to be judged about this whole office. Then he defines their task and instructs them with commands. Besides, he promises his help and protection.

units.la: Ad primum pertinet: Data est mihi omnis potestas in caelo et in terra, id est, ego sum caeli et terrae Dominus, cui ius est in universum mundum, quique omnibus, quae in caelo et in terra sunt, imperio. Hoc vero non ambitiose de se dicit, sed quia ut talis esset rei necessitas requirebat. Qui enim legatos aliquo amandare vult, ut in illis locis ius et imperium habeat, necesse est, nisi se prudentiorum ludibrijs velit exponere. Quia ergo Christus salutis aeternae legatos et dispensatores constituere voluit, opus erat, ut potestate terrena simul et caelesti instructus esset. Non poterat enim nobis constare salus, nisi pater nobis placaretur, et aperiretur via sanctorum in caelis. Deinde in terris defensione opus est, quia Ecclesia adhuc militans aduersus hostes omnis generis visibiles et invisibiles feruetur. Ne quid ergo dubitaretur, id praemitti oportuit. Quis enim nisi his auditis, credidisset in caelis rata fore, quae Apostoli in terra promittunt aut minantur? soluit et ligant? Confirmationi vero feruit, quod non modo plenam et perfectam potestatem sibi vendicat, sed hanc legitimam quoque et iustam se habere testatur, utique non raptam ex privato affectu, sed datam sibi a Patre: quod alibi docet: Omnia mihi tradita sunt a Patre meo.
units.tr: To the first point belongs the statement: All power is given to me in heaven and on earth. That is, I am the Lord of heaven and earth, who has the right over the whole world, and who rules everything that is in heaven and on earth. He does not say this ambitiously about himself, but because the nature of the matter required that he be such. For whoever wishes to send envoys somewhere, so that they may have right and authority in those places, must do so, unless he wishes to expose them to the mockery of the more prudent. Therefore, since Christ willed to appoint envoys and stewards of eternal salvation, it was necessary that he be furnished with both earthly and heavenly power. For our salvation could not stand unless the Father were appeased for us, and the way to the saints in heaven were opened. Then, on earth, defence is needed, because the Church, still militant, must be preserved against enemies of every kind, visible and invisible. So, lest anything be doubted, this had to be put first. For who would have believed, unless he had heard this, that what the apostles promise or threaten on earth would be ratified in heaven, that they loose and bind? He also confirms this by declaring that he possesses not only full and perfect power, but that he has it lawfully and justly, not seized from private desire but given to him by the Father. He teaches this elsewhere: All things have been delivered to me by my Father.

units.la: Nobis autem huius dicti vis esse debet, ut ex eo aestimemus Euangelij et Ecclesiae ministerium, per quod Dei Filius suum solium quasi in terris constituit, ut electos ad se in caelum eueheret, adeoque illum in ministris suis caelitus nobis loqui putemus: Si quem ergo vilis et contempta, adeoque mundi exosa ministrorum Euangelij species offendit, is ad ministerij authore oculos attollat, ad IESVM CHRISTVM scilicet, qui de omnibus legitime vocatis et missis dixit: Qui vos audit me audit, etc.
units.tr: For us, the force of this saying ought to be that from it we may judge the ministry of the gospel and of the Church, through which the Son of God establishes his throne, as it were, on earth, so as to carry the elect up to himself in heaven; and thus we should believe that he speaks to us from heaven through his ministers. If therefore the lowly and despised appearance of the ministers of the gospel, and their hatefulness to the world, offends anyone, let him lift his eyes to the author of the ministry, namely Jesus Christ, who said of all who are lawfully called and sent: He who hears you hears me, etc.

units.la: Deinde quid illis mandet, videamus: Profecti docete gentes. Graece legitur μαθητεύσατε, quod non inepte aliqui interpretantur: Discipulos facite. Constat enim Euangelij finem esse obedientiam fidei, quae nos Christi discipulos facit, quales initio communi nomine dicti fuerunt, qui Christo nomen dabant. Et cum postea Apostolatus vel muneris apostolici partes duas faciat, doctrinam nimirum (et hanc sub vocabulo διδάσκειν comprehendit) et baptismum, sub quo non male universa Sacramentorum administratio continetur, recte nos facturos puto, si quod hic dicitur, μαθητεύσατε omnes gentes de generali mandato exponamus, quod Apostolis omnibus datum fuit, ut nimirum omnes gentes, quae antehac in varias sectas dispersae fuerant, Christo adducerent, ut ab hoc uno denominarentur: quod quanto studio fecerint, Pauli exemplum docet, qui ad Corinthios de hac re tam serio et constanter disserit, ut contra fidei Christianae principia eos peccare demonstret, qui ex doctoribus suis aliud quam Christi nomen affumebant.
units.tr: Next, let us see what he commands them: Go, teach all nations. In Greek it reads μαθητεύσατε [mathēteusate], which some interpret not inaptly as "make disciples." For it is established that the end of the gospel is the obedience of faith, which makes us disciples of Christ, as those who gave their name to Christ were initially called by the common name of disciples. And since afterwards he divides the apostolate, or the apostolic office, into two parts, namely teaching (and he comprehends this under the word διδάσκειν [didaskein]) and baptism, under which the whole administration of the sacraments is not badly included, I think we shall do well if we explain what is said here, μαθητεύσατε, make disciples of all nations, as the general commission given to all the apostles: namely, that they should bring all nations, which had hitherto been scattered into various sects, to Christ, so that they might be named from this one. How eagerly they did this the example of Paul shows, who discourses to the Corinthians on this matter so seriously and steadfastly that he demonstrates that they sin against the principles of the Christian faith who took up from their teachers any name other than the name of Christ.

units.la: Itaque Apostolici munera colophon nobis est, ut Filio Dei IESV CHRISTO discipuli adducantur, et huic per obedientiam fidei subiciatur omnis sublimitas, quae extollitur aduersus cognitionem Dei, in tantum tantum redigatur omnis cogitatio ad obediendum Christo.
units.tr: Thus the chief task of the apostles is to bring disciples to the Son of God, Jesus Christ, and through the obedience of faith to subject to him every height that lifts itself up against the knowledge of God, so that every thought is brought into obedience to Christ.

units.la: Id vero per Euangelij praedicationem fieri, in praesenti ipse Dominus facis aperte testatur, ut alijs testimonijs non sit opus. Nam emissurus in orbem terrarum seruos suos, qui regnum suum passim instaurarent, et gentes omnes illi subiicerent, non viros principes aut militares mittit, qui vel huius saeculi authoritate, vel armis hominum in sua verba iurare cogant, sed Apostolos suos, non alijs quam spiritualibus armis et Dei virtute validis instructos emisit, et quid ipsis mandarit, postea diserte adhuc explicabit. Nunc aut probe obseruabis, cum Apostolorum munus universum in eo consistat, ut homines Christo adducantur, et eius discipuli fiant, non posse aliquem Apostolorum vel vicarium vel successorem dici, qui non huiusmodi studiorum finem sive fiopum praefixum sibi habet. Vide ergo quid de praesulibus larvatis iudices, qui cum Apostolici dici velint, huius saeculi dominia affectant, et principes agunt contra Christi mandatum, qui Apostolis, ne quid huius tentent, graviter interdixit.
units.tr: The Lord himself openly testifies that this is done through the preaching of the Gospel, so no other testimony is needed. When he was about to send his servants out into the world, to restore his kingdom everywhere and bring all nations under him, he sent no princes or soldiers, who would compel men to swear to his words by the authority of this age or by human arms. He sent his apostles, equipped with no weapons but spiritual ones and strong in the power of God, and he later explained plainly what he had commanded them. Now observe carefully that, since the whole office of the apostles consists in bringing men to Christ and making them his disciples, no one can be called an apostle's vicar or successor if he does not have this aim set before him in his labours. See then what you make of the masked prelates, who, though they want to be called apostolic, aspire to the lordships of this age and act as princes, against Christ's command, which sternly forbade the apostles to attempt any such thing.

units.la: Porro dum omnes gentes sibi adducere iubet Dominus, non obscure omnes homines peccati et erroris arguit, imo omnes damnat. Nam si Iudaei per Legem Mosis, gentes vero per huius saeculi seculi sapientiam seruari potuissent, vt Christi discipuli fierēt, minimè opus erat. Sed vtrifq; Euan gelium prædicari & Christo illos adduci oportuit. Ergo extra Christum totus mundus in tenebris erat, & infelix perierat. Sufficit hoc ijs confutandis, qui vt fe bellos & commodos homines omni- bus præbeant, vnumquemq; in sua religione, vel superstitione potius seruari posse garriunt. Adde hic, quod vt Christo fe adduci patiantur omnes homines, iustitiæ lex iubet. Illi enim omnes gentes a Deo Patre datæ sunt, qui olim illi dixit: Postula a me, & dabo tibi gentes, vt sint hæreditas tua, & terminos terræ, vt sint possessio tua. At Dei est gentiū fines & terminos constituere, & regna de gente in gentem transferre. Cum ergo hic Filio suo omnes gentes subiecerit, perduellionis rei sunt, quicunq; huic non obediunt. Vide Pfal.2.
units.tr: Moreover, when the Lord bids them bring all nations to him, he clearly charges all men with sin and error; indeed, he condemns them all. For if Jews could have been saved by the Law of Moses and Gentiles by the wisdom of this age, there would have been no need at all for them to become disciples of Christ. But it was necessary that the Gospel be preached to both and that they be brought to Christ. Therefore outside Christ the whole world was in darkness and had perished wretchedly. This suffices to refute those who, to show themselves agreeable and accommodating to everyone, chatter that each man can be saved in his own religion, or rather superstition. Add here that the law of justice commands all men to allow themselves to be brought to Christ. For all nations were given to him by God the Father, who once said to him: "Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance and the ends of the earth as your possession." But it is God's prerogative to fix the bounds of nations and to transfer kingdoms from one people to another. Since therefore he has subjected all nations to his Son, those who do not obey him are guilty of treason. See Psalm 2.

units.la: Vt autem huic adducantur omnes homines, duobus opus est. Iubet enim, vt baptizent disci- pulos quos fecerunt, in nomen Patris & Filij & Spiritus sancti, doceantq; eos feruare omnia, quæ ipse illis mandarit. Habent religiones omnes sacra sua, quibus initiantur, qui illis nomen dant, & tesseris suis insigniuntur fere omnes festæ. Vt ergo veteri Testamenti populū circumcisione infi gniri & ab aliis gentibus distingui voluit Deus: ita noui Testamenti credentes, qui ipsi nomen dabant, Christus Baptismo tingere iussit, cuius primus administer fuit Ioannes: & nunc Apostolis qui prius eundem nomine Christi administrauerant (vt Ioannes scribit) mandat, vt fi quos ipsi di- fcipulos faciant, eos baptizent. Iubet autem baptizare in nomen Patris & Filij ac Spiritus fan- &ti. Id vero non est simpliciter baptizare inuocato nomine Patris & Filij ac Spiritus sancti, sed Deo vni & trino consecrari. Non ergo hic primum instituitur baptismus, qui iam ante erat, nec quis baptizari aut non baptizari debeat, docetur, sed quid cum ijs, qui iam adulti Christo volunt nomen dare, agi debeat, traditur. Nam (vt alij quoq; annotarunt) periculum erat, ne Apostoli, qui ex Iudæis nati, & in Mosaicis sacris educati erant, credentes ex gentibus circumcisione & sacris a Mose acceptis initiarent. Hoc enim factum fuit a quibusdam post patefactam iam in orbe do- strinam de fidei iustificatione, & non exiguas turbas dedit in Ecclesia: sicuti in Actis est videre. Diserte ergo iubet, vt discipulos suos non Mosi, sed vero Deo, vni & trino, Patri nimirum, Filio & Spiritui sancto cofecrent: Non quod hic diuersus fit ab eo, quem Patres veteres coluerunt: sed quod iam manifestari debuit sacrosancta trinitatis mysterium, quod hucufq; absconditum fuerat. Nec temere in baptismi vsu publice pandi debuit hoc mysterium: qui baptismi fructus abfq; eius cognitione non percipitur. Nam qui seruari volunt, ij a Patris Dei gratia & misericordia, qui fa lutis omnis fons est, incipiant oportet, qui nos sibi in Filio reconciliat: Hic vero sua mortis meri- to redemptos & Spiritus Janfti virtute regeneratos innouat & Dei filios facit. De his ergo nos admoneri necesse est, quando primum in fide Christiana initiamur.
units.tr: In order that all men be brought to him, two things are needed. For he commands them to baptize the disciples they have made, in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, and to teach them to keep all that he has commanded them. All religions have their own rites, into which those who give their name are initiated, and almost all festivals are marked by their own tokens. Just as God willed the people of the Old Testament to be marked by circumcision and distinguished from the other nations, so Christ ordered that believers of the New Testament, who give their own name, be washed with baptism, whose first minister was John. And now he commands the apostles, who had earlier administered the same baptism in Christ's name (as John writes), that if they make disciples, they baptize them. He commands them to baptize in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. This is not simply to baptize with the invocation of the name of Father, Son and Holy Spirit, but to consecrate the disciple to the one triune God. Therefore baptism is not instituted here for the first time, since it already existed, nor is it taught who ought or ought not to be baptized; rather, it is handed down what must be done with those who, already adults, wish to give their name to Christ. For (as others also have noted) there was a danger that the apostles, who were born of Jews and brought up in Mosaic rites, would initiate believers from the Gentiles with circumcision and the sacred rites received from Moses. Some did indeed do this after the doctrine of justification by faith had been made known throughout the world, and it caused no small disturbance in the Church, as can be seen in Acts. He therefore plainly commands them to consecrate his disciples not to Moses but to the true God, one and triune, namely the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. This is not because the God here is different from the one the ancient Fathers worshipped, but because the most holy mystery of the Trinity, which had remained hidden until then, ought now to be made manifest. Nor should this mystery be rashly laid open in public in the use of baptism, since the fruit of baptism is not received without knowledge of it. For those who wish to be saved must begin with the grace and mercy of God the Father, the fount of all salvation, who reconciles us to himself in the Son. The Son, in turn, renews those redeemed by the merit of his death and regenerated by the power of the Holy Spirit, and makes them sons of God. Therefore we must be reminded of these things when we are first initiated into the Christian faith.

units.la: Et obseruetur non ofcitanter ordo, quem Christus tradit. Primum simpliciter vult sibi disci- pulos adduci, nec vt curiosis quæstionibus nouitij exerceantur iubet. Deinde fi qui adduẛti nomē ipsi dederint, eos baptismo tingi, & Deo Patri, Filio & Spiritui sancto initiari vult. Et hoc quā simplicissime fecerunt Apostoli, qui iam baptizandos nullis quæstionibus grauioribus fatigarunt: sicuti videre est in exemplo Eunuchi Æthiopis, Carcerarij Philippensis, primorum deniq; credentium, qui ad primam Petri concionem conuersi sunt. Sciuerunt enim (vt Paulus scribit) la- ste fouendos esse teneriores, qui solidioris cibi, id est, altiorum mysteriorum nondum capaces sunt. Nimium ergo importuni sunt, qui hodie de sacramentis quæstiones mouet inextricabiles, ad quas doctores quoq; acutissimi hæreant, quibus fi non pro ipsorum nutu respondeas, mox hæreticus dice- ris. etiamsi in nullo prorsus Symboli Apostolici articulo offendas. Hi plerunq; dum religiofiores alijs esse volunt, superstitiosi fiunt, & religionis vera sensum atq; vim ex animis hominum eximunt.
units.tr: Let the order that Christ hands down be observed carefully. First, he wills simply that disciples be brought to him, and he does not command that novices be exercised with curious questions. Then, if those who are brought have given their name, he wills that they be washed with baptism and initiated into God the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. The apostles did this as simply as possible, not wearying those to be baptized with any heavy questions; as can be seen in the example of the Ethiopian eunuch, the Philippian jailer, and the first believers who were converted by Peter's first sermon. For they knew (as Paul writes) that the weaker ones, who are not yet capable of solid food, that is, of the deeper mysteries, must be nourished with milk. Therefore those are far too troublesome who today raise inextricable questions about the sacraments, questions on which even the most acute teachers stick fast, and if you do not answer them as they wish, you will at once be called a heretic, even if you offend against no article of the Apostles' Creed. These men, for the most part, while they wish to be more religious than others, become superstitious, and they remove the true sense and force of religion from men's minds.

units.la: Ne quis tamen hæc ita accipiat, vt externam professionem & vsum fignorū sufficere putet, & tandem eo delabatur, vt quod ore profitetur, vita & moribus neget: quod hodie multi, prob do lor, faciunt: alterum quoq; mandat Apostolis: Vt quos baptismo tinxerunt, doceat feruare omnia quæ præcepit ipse. Postulat hoc baptismi ratio. Est enim initiationis sacramentū, quo nobis Deus beneficia in Christo collata obsignat, & nos vicissim sibi obstringit: & ea conditione baptizamur in nomen Patris & Filij & Spiritus sancti, vt huic Deo vni & vero viuamus. Iubet aut omnia
units.tr: Yet let no one take these things to mean that an outward profession and the use of signs is enough, so that he finally slides into denying with his life and morals what he professes with his mouth, as many today, alas, do. He also commands the apostles a second thing: that those whom they have washed with baptism they teach to keep all that he commanded. The nature of baptism requires this. For it is the sacrament of initiation, by which God seals to us the benefits conferred on us in Christ and in turn binds us to himself; and on this condition we are baptized in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, that we may live to this one true God. Moreover he commands that all things

units.la: Officia baptizatorum, qui Christo nomen dederunt. seruari,ut ita ad universam Euangelij doctrinam extendat,quod dicitur,ne quis sibi licitum putet delectum facere inter Christi praecepta,ut inter cibos homines delicatuli. Posset ergo latissime extendi: at nobis sufficiat omnia praecepta Christi duobus membris copulati: ut dicamus alia ad fidem & cultum Dei, alia ad mores & vitae institutionem pertinere. Praecepta fidei & religionis sunt, quae quid de Deo sentire & credere, & ut eundem colere debeamus, docent: quae itę superstitiones, errores, falsos cultus, & quaecunq; veritati aduersantur, prohibent. Praecepta morū & vitae fere sub charitate comprehenduntur, quam legis totius completione Paulus dicit. Et huc referri debet, quod Ioannes dilectus ille discipulus scribit: Hoc est mandatum eius, ut credamus nomini Filij eius IESV CHRISTO, & alij alios diligamus, sicut mandauit nobis. Poterit tamen perspicuitatis ergo tertius praeceptorum Christi ordo his addi, quibus innocentia & sanctitatis praecepta continentur. Ad praecepta admonitiones, hortationes, correptiones, minae pertinet: ut rursum fidei in IESVM CHRISTVM consolationes accenseri debent: quarū omnium fons est Dei Filius, qui nobis Patrem placauit, & in quo omnes promissiones sunt. Ita & Amen.
units.tr: The duties of the baptized, who have given their name to Christ, are to be kept; and so this extends to the whole doctrine of the Gospel, lest anyone think it lawful to pick and choose among Christ's precepts, like dainty people among foods. It could therefore be extended very widely, but for us it is enough to group all of Christ's precepts under two heads: some pertain to faith and the worship of God, others to morals and the ordering of life. The precepts of faith and religion are those which teach what we ought to think and believe about God and how we should worship him; they forbid superstitions, errors, false worship, and whatever is opposed to the truth. The precepts of morals and life are for the most part comprehended under love, which Paul calls the fulfilling of the whole law. To this must be referred what John, that beloved disciple, writes: "This is his commandment, that we believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ and love one another, as he commanded us." Nevertheless, for the sake of clarity, a third group of Christ's precepts may be added, in which the precepts of innocence and holiness are contained. To the precepts belong admonitions, exhortations, corrections and threats; likewise the consolations of faith in Jesus Christ ought to be counted in. The fount of all these is the Son of God, who reconciled the Father to us and in whom all the promises are. So be it.

units.la: Patet hic latissimus dicendi campus, quem si quis semel ingressus fuerit, vix exitū inueniet. Priusquam vero ab hoc loco discedamus, ministri Ecclesiarum, qui Apostolorum vices hodie obtinent, frequenter meminerint, Filium Dei certam doctrinae formam & summam discipulis suis dilectis tradidisse, dum illis mandauit, ut ea docerent quae ipse praecepit. Noluit ergo ut ipsi doctrinae genus pro suo arbitrio fingant & refingant, aut in domo sua Ecclesia, cuius dispensatores sunt, aliquid temere mutent. Ita olim Prophetae certis mandatis astricti fuerunt, ut verbum ex ore Domini peterent, quod populo praedicarent, neq; paleas suas loco tritici diuini venderent. Quod si nihil huius licuit ijs, quorum fides speciatissima, vocatio aut & missio miraculis & testimonijs tam multis tamq; gravibus confirmata fuit, ut nemo sine manifesta impietate de illis potuerit dubitare: quid de ijs dicemus, qui hodie sibi omnem in Ecclesia potestatem vendicant, cum plerique, neq; sacris neq; prophanis literis solide instituti sint, neq; morum probitate & vitae innocentia commendentur? Ut certe pastoris est non alienam vocem inferre in ouile Christi, ne fur aut latro esse deprehendatur: ita oues quoq; nullius alterius quam veri pastoris vel principis pastorum vocem audire debent, nisi illis scientibus volentibus perire libeat. Vide Ioan. 10.
units.tr: The field of discourse opens up here, and once a man has entered it he will scarcely find his way out. Before we leave this place, let the ministers of the Churches, who today hold the place of the apostles, often remember that the Son of God gave his beloved disciples a fixed form of teaching and a summary of doctrine, when he commanded them to teach what he himself had commanded. He therefore did not want them to invent and remodel the kind of teaching at their own pleasure, or to change anything rashly in the house of God, the Church, whose stewards they are. So of old the prophets were bound by fixed commands to seek the word from the mouth of the Lord and preach it to the people, and not to sell their chaff in place of the divine wheat. If those men were allowed none of this, whose faith, calling and sending were confirmed by so many and such weighty miracles and testimonies that no one could doubt them without manifest impiety, what shall we say of those who today claim for themselves all power in the Church, when most of them are not solidly grounded either in sacred or in profane letters, and are not commended by the uprightness of their morals or the innocence of their lives? Just as it is the duty of a shepherd not to bring a strange voice into the sheepfold of Christ, lest he be caught as a thief or robber, so the sheep too ought to hear the voice of no one but the true shepherd, or rather the chief of shepherds, unless they knowingly and willingly wish to perish. See John 10.

units.la: Rursus meminisse debent Christiani homines cuiusc unq; sint loci aut ordinis: idcirco Euangelium ex Filij Dei decreto & iussu praedicari, non ut sciant & intelligat quid ius velit, sed ut praecepta eius ferent. Ille enim serius, qui nouit voluntatem domini sui, nec se comparauit, nec fecit ex voluntate eius, caedetur multis plagis. Et nō omnis (inquit Dominus) qui dicit mihi, Domine, Domine, intrabit in regnum meum, sed qui fecerit voluntatem Patris mei, qui in cœlis est. Etsi vero hanc nemo hominum perfecte praestare poterit, nec quisquam coram Deo iudice subsistere posset, si hic delicta nostra respicere, & prout meremur, nos punire velit, non tamen spem salutis abijcere, sed ad Filium Dei refugere debemus, qui nos cum Patre in gratiam reduxit. Hunc enim qui non nouerat peccatū, pro nobis peccatū fecit, ut nos efficeremur iustitia Dei in eo.
units.tr: Again, Christians of whatever place or rank should remember that the gospel is preached by the decree and command of the Son of God, not so that they may know and understand what their Lord wills, but so that they may carry out his precepts. For that servant who knew his master's will, and neither prepared himself nor acted according to his will, will be beaten with many stripes. "Not everyone," says the Lord, "who says to me, Lord, Lord, will enter into my kingdom, but he who does the will of my Father who is in heaven." Although no one among men can perform this perfectly, and no one could stand before God the judge if he were to look upon our sins and punish us as we deserve, yet we must not cast away the hope of salvation, but flee to the Son of God, who reconciled us with the Father into grace. For he who knew no sin was made sin for us, so that in him we might be made the righteousness of God.

units.la: Caeterum legationis Apostolicae munus arduum & plenum periculi erat, ipsi vero (ut Paulus de seipso & alijs fatetur) thesaurum hunc gestabant in testaceis vasis, ut iam de aduersarijs vndiq; imminentibus nihil dicamus: dicerent ergo: Quid faciemus inter tot hostes? quibus armis nos defendemus? Itane nos inermes agnos lupis mpacibus, vrsis & leonibus obijcis? Sed omnibus quae in hanc sententiam dici poterant, Dominus dictum breue, & dulcissimae consolationis plenum opponit: Et ecce ego vobiscum sum omnibus diebus, vsq; ad consummationem saeculi. Connectit hoc non temere cū praecedentibus, ut illud inter pericula & labores sui muneris discerent subinde in mentem reuocare. Adhaec demonstrandi particula eos excitat, & quasi in rem praesentem adducit. Dicm cum ait: ECCE EGO: ita omnino vult dicere: Ille ego dilectus Dei Filius, in quo Pater placatus est, qui me alias lucem mundi, panem vitae, fontem aquae viuentis, pastorem fidum & fortem professus sum, & cui nunc data est potestas in cœlo & in terra, etsi in cœlos corpus subducam, neque porro in mundo versaturus sim, vos autem in mundo futuri litis, nō tamen vos deseram. Imo ego ipse vobiscum ero, non paucis annis aut saeculis, sed vsq; ad consummationem saeculi. Ne ergo timueritis. Qui enim hactenus vobis affui, ut nihil vobis defuerit: qui vos defendi, ut me capta & vinctio vincto nihil tamen patieremini, quod vitæ officeret: qui meipsum ex mortuis reduxi, qui mortis imperium fregi, portas inferorum expugnaui, veteris serpentis caput contriui, vobis in posterū quoq; adero, vt nihil vobis officiat, & dabo, vt quod olim promisit Pater, super leones & aspides ambulecis, & leunculos & dracones conculcetis: dabo deniq; (vt apud Marcum annotatur) vt qui ve stræ doctrinæ crediderint, similes gratiæ participes fiant, & serpentes tollant, & ex toxicis quoque sumtis nihil lethale sentiant. Hæc omnia hic Christus pollicetur, & quæcunq; ex his similia colligi possunt. Nec inanes fuisse has promissiones, Marcus non obscurè testatur, dum ait: Dominus prædicantibus apostolis vnà operatum fuisse, & sermonem confirmasse per signa consequentia. Consentit his etiam Ecclesiastica historia & ipse rerum euentus. Qui enim fieri potuisset, vt fides in IESVM CHRISTVM & eius prædicatio per tot obstacula perrumperet, & in hunc vsque diem sub cruce vinceret & triumpharet, nisi præsenti Filij Dei præsidio seruaretur? Quòd vero hinc aliqui corporalem eius præsentiam colligunt: aliqui item ex hoc loco demonstrare conantur, Ecclesiam errare non posse, & pro oraculis venditant quæcunq; ipsi ex suo cerebro fingunt, tam putidum est, vt confutatione nullam mereatur apud eos, qui in Christi schola rectè instituti, hunc suam sapientiam esse agnoscunt. Nos quia promissionem hanc ad consummationem seculi vsque extendit Dominus, constanter credamus nobis quoq; datam esse, & hanc opponamus temerarijs hostium conatibus. Nam hi quoq; non plus hodie efficient, quam olim Iudæorum sacerdotes & seniores, qui figmentis, armis & publica authoritate IESV CHRISTI resurrectionem impedire & supprimere conati sunt:
units.tr: The office of apostolic embassy was arduous and full of danger, and the apostles themselves (as Paul confesses of himself and others) carried this treasure in earthen vessels. Let us say nothing yet of the adversaries threatening on every side. They might have said: "What shall we do among so many enemies? With what weapons shall we defend ourselves? Do you throw us, unarmed lambs, to ravening wolves, bears and lions?" But to all that could be said to this effect the Lord sets a brief saying, full of the sweetest consolation: "And behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age." He does not join this carelessly to what goes before; he wants them to recall it again and again amid the dangers and labours of their office. The particle of showing, "behold", also rouses them and, as it were, brings him into their presence. When he says "BEHOLD, I", he certainly means this: "I am that beloved Son of God in whom the Father is well pleased, who have at other times professed myself the light of the world, the bread of life, the fountain of living water, the faithful and strong shepherd, and to whom now all power in heaven and on earth has been given. Although I withdraw my body into heaven and will no longer dwell in the world, while you will be in the world amid future strife, yet I will not forsake you. Indeed I myself will be with you, not for a few years or ages, but to the end of the age. Do not fear, then. For I who have hitherto been present with you, so that nothing has been lacking to you; who defended you when I was seized and bound, so that you suffered nothing that could hinder your life; who brought myself back from the dead, broke the power of death, stormed the gates of hell, and crushed the head of the old serpent, will be with you hereafter as well, so that nothing shall harm you. I will give what the Father long ago promised: that you shall walk upon lions and asps, and trample young lions and dragons underfoot. Finally, I will give (as Mark records) that those who believe your teaching shall become sharers of the same grace, take up serpents, and, even when they have swallowed poisons, feel nothing deadly." Christ promises all these things here, and whatever similar things may be gathered from them. Nor were these promises empty, as Mark plainly bears witness when he says that the Lord worked together with the preaching apostles and confirmed the word by the signs that followed. Ecclesiastical history and the very course of events agree with this too. For how could faith in Jesus Christ and its preaching have broken through so many obstacles, and to this day conquered and triumphed under the cross, unless it had been preserved by the present protection of the Son of God? As for those who infer from this his bodily presence, and others who try to demonstrate from this place that the Church cannot err and peddle as oracles whatever they fashion from their own brains, that is so foul that it does not deserve refutation among those who are rightly trained in Christ's school and recognise this as their wisdom. Since the Lord extends this promise to the end of the age, let us firmly believe that it was given to us too, and set it against the rash attempts of our enemies. For these too will accomplish no more today than the priests and elders of the Jews once did, who by fabrications, arms and public authority tried to hinder and suppress the resurrection of Jesus Christ.
